For example, the Euclid weak lensing survey requires the uncertainty in the mean redshift of each tomographic bin to be controlled at the level of [FORMULA] (Euclid Collaboration, 2020; Euclid Collaboration, 2021). Achieving this level of precision represents a major challenge for photometric redshift methodologies. In recent years, machine learning (ML) methods have become widely adopted for photometric redshift estimation (Salvato and others, 2019; Newman and Gruen, 2022). ML methods can learn complex nonlinear relationships between photometric observables and galaxy redshifts, often outperforming traditional template-fitting approaches in terms of prediction accuracy and computational efficiency. Various algorithms have been explored including Multi-Layer Perceptron (Collister and Lahav, 2004; Sadeh et al., 2016), Nearest Neighbor Fitting (De Vicente et al., 2016), Random Forest (Carliles et al., 2010; Zhou et al., 2021; Lu et al., 2024), (Boosted) Decision Tree (Gerdes et al., 2010; Carrasco Kind and Brunner, 2013), Sparse Gaussian Process (Almosallam et al., 2016), Convolutional Neural Network (Hoyle, 2016; D’Isanto and Polsterer, 2018; Schuldt et al., 2021; Li et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2022), and Normalizing Flow (NF) (Crenshaw et al., 2024; Sun et al., 2023; Ren et al., 2026). Traditional ML approaches often focus on predicting a single redshift point estimate. Beyond point estimates such as the mean or median redshift, it is essential to characterize the uncertainty in redshift predictions, which can be represented by the full redshift probability density function (PDF). Normalizing Flows (NFs) (Tabak and Turner, 2013; Rezende and Mohamed, 2015) provide a flexible framework for modelling complex probability distributions through a sequence of invertible transformations from a simple base distribution to a target distribution. Their ability to perform exact likelihood evaluation, efficient sampling, and expressive modelling of non-Gaussian and multimodal densities makes them well suited to photo- [FORMULA] estimation, where redshift PDFs can exhibit asymmetric shapes, extended tails, and multiple peaks due to photometric degeneracies. Accurate reconstruction and calibration of tomographic redshift distributions, [FORMULA] , are essential for reliable cosmological inference, as systematic errors in these distributions can propagate into cosmological parameter estimates. Existing approaches to redshift-distribution calibration include self-organizing maps (SOM) (Carrasco Kind and Brunner, 2014; Masters et al., 2015; Buchs et al., 2019; Wright et al., 2020) and clustering-based methods. The latter can be divided into clustering-redshift approaches using external spectroscopic reference samples (Newman, 2008; McQuinn and White, 2013; Ménard et al., 2013; Schmidt et al., 2013), self-calibration methods using photometric clustering alone (Schneider et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2017; Peng et al., 2022; Xu et al., 2023), and combinations of these approaches (Zheng et al., 2024). Clustering-redshift techniques have been widely applied in different surveys (Gatti et al., 2018; Cawthon and others, 2022; Hildebrandt et al., 2021; Rau et al., 2023; Choppin de Janvry et al., 2026). However, recovering the detailed shape of [FORMULA] can be challenging due to degeneracies with galaxy bias and other observational effects. In this context, redshift distributions reconstructed from photometric redshift PDFs can provide complementary information that may be combined with clustering-based constraints. Stacking individual photo- [FORMULA] PDFs has been widely used to reconstruct redshift distributions, particularly for weak-lensing tomography (Bordoloi et al., 2010; Bonnett, 2015; Euclid Collaboration, 2021). Building on these studies, we systematically quantify the performance of continuous NF PDFs in tomographic [FORMULA] reconstruction across photometric-redshift bins, compare their performance with QRF, and assess the impact of post-hoc PDF calibration, including at high redshifts. To investigate the potential of NFs for applications in large galaxy surveys, we construct million-scale datasets by combining spectroscopic redshifts from DESI Data Release 1 (DR1) (DESI Collaboration, 2026) with photometric measurements from the DESI Legacy Surveys (Dey and others, 2019). We evaluate the models using independent spectroscopic testing samples from non-overlapping sky regions, allowing us to assess probabilistic photo- [FORMULA] estimation and [FORMULA] reconstruction within a controlled spectroscopic sample. We also compare the NF with Random Forest (RF) and Quantile Random Forest (QRF) baselines. Importantly, the NF framework is not inherently specific to DESI, but provides a flexible methodology for probabilistic photo- [FORMULA] estimation that can be adapted to different photometric surveys. The conditioning features can be adjusted according to the available photometric measurements, allowing the framework to be retrained and calibrated for different galaxy populations and observational datasets, including those from Euclid and LSST. However, the performance obtained from the DESI-selected spectroscopic samples should not be interpreted as the expected accuracy for the broader photometric populations of these surveys. Extending the methodology to such populations will require careful assessment of spectroscopic representativeness and selection effects. As shown in Section 4.3, empirical CDF calibration (Kuleshov et al., 2018; Dey et al., 2021) produces an approximately uniform PIT distribution for the validation sample, while modest deviations remain when the mapping is applied to the independent testing sample. Calibration also improves [FORMULA] in several tomographic bins. However, the validation and testing samples exhibit similar photometric features and redshift distributions (Fig. 11), leaving the effectiveness of this approach for more distinct galaxy populations uncertain. Compared with simpler approaches such as temperature scaling (Guo et al., 2017), empirical CDF recalibration with 101 interpolation knots provides greater flexibility in correcting complex PIT deviations. However, the resulting mapping is determined by the PIT distribution of the calibration sample and is therefore not necessarily universal. Even an accurately determined calibration mapping may not remain valid for a target population with different photometric properties or redshift distributions. This limitation is particularly relevant to practical photo- [FORMULA] applications, where representative spectroscopic samples are often unavailable for the target population. Therefore, the key challenge is not simply to achieve a uniform PIT distribution on the validation sample, but to develop calibration methods that remain reliable across different galaxy populations. Future work could explore alternative post-hoc calibration approaches, such as isotonic regression (Niculescu-Mizil and Caruana, 2005), and methods that account for photometric features or individual PDF properties, such as non-Gaussianity and multimodality, while evaluating their transferability using independent datasets. Importantly, achieving PIT uniformity does not necessarily guarantee accurate reconstruction of tomographic [FORMULA] , further motivating calibration methods that are both transferable across galaxy populations and reliable for distribution-level cosmological analyses (Rau et al., 2015; Euclid Collaboration, 2020; Euclid Collaboration, 2021). In our tomographic analysis, we find that the NF results generally outperform the QRF ones, whereas the advantage is less pronounced for the full sample. These findings, together with the point estimate results, are consistent with the interpretation that NF photo- [FORMULA] estimation excels when the data are noisy and sparse (Ren et al., 2026). Our analysis also highlights several practical characteristics of NF-based photo- [FORMULA] inference. First, repeated training runs show noticeable run-to-run variations even when the same training and testing samples are used (see Section 4.2). This training-induced variability introduces an additional source of uncertainty beyond the systematic effects associated with the data. Further investigation of convergence, optimization, model architecture, and initialization is therefore required to determine whether this variability can be substantially reduced. At the same time, the continuous probabilistic representation provided by NFs offers useful flexibility for PDF-based analyses. For diagnostics such as PIT, the NF provides an explicit continuous predictive distribution, while individual PDFs can be sampled at arbitrarily fine numerical resolution without retraining the model. For the smaller high-redshift sample, the reduced computational cost allows us to draw 1,000 or more Monte Carlo samples per source. Hence, the continuous formulation of the NF is convenient for probabilistic diagnostics and individual-PDF studies. Although the training and testing samples occupy non-overlapping sky regions, both are constructed from the DESI spectroscopic sample using the same photometric and quality selections from DESI Legacy DR10. As the primary goal of this study is to validate the probabilistic photo- [FORMULA] estimation and [FORMULA] reconstruction methodology, this controlled setting allows us to assess the performance of the NF model without introducing additional differences in sample selection. However, this experimental design does not fully investigate its generalisability to broader photometric populations with different distributions of colours, magnitudes, or galaxy types. In particular, the tomographic [FORMULA] accuracy achieved in this work should not be interpreted as the expected performance for Euclid weak-lensing source galaxies. Recent studies have highlighted the importance of spectroscopic incompleteness and sample representativeness for redshift calibration (Lange et al., 2026; Blanco et al., 2026). Nevertheless, the NF framework itself is not specific to DESI but offers considerable flexibility in modelling conditional redshift distributions. It can be adapted to different photometric surveys, including Euclid, LSST and CSST by incorporating their respective photometric features and retraining or recalibrating the model using suitable reference data. The method may also be particularly promising for lens galaxy samples, whose photometric properties can be more similar to those of DESI spectroscopic targets. Future applications will require careful assessment of selection effects and differences between the spectroscopic training and target photometric populations. 6 Conclusions In this work, we investigate conditional Normalizing Flows (NFs) for probabilistic photometric-redshift estimation and redshift-distribution reconstruction using DESI DR1 spectroscopic data and DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys photometry. The main analysis uses an independent test sample of 2,028,371 sources spanning around [FORMULA] , with the NF evaluated over five independent training realisations and compared with the Random Forest (RF) and Quantile Random Forest (QRF) models. For point estimation, the NF achieves lower [FORMULA] and outlier fractions compare to RF and QRF across the full redshift range, although its bias is slightly larger than that of QRF and exhibits greater run-to-run variation. At higher redshifts ( [FORMULA] ), where the performance of all three models generally deteriorates due to the limited samples’ number at high redshift (see Fig. 2), the NF demonstrates a clearer advantage in bias, scatter, and outlier fraction, consistent with Ren et al. (2026). However, point-estimation metrics alone do not fully capture the advantages of the NF, which provides continuous conditional redshift distributions that retain information about their widths, asymmetries, and extended tails. This advantage becomes more apparent in tomographic [FORMULA] reconstruction. Across the first seven tomographic bins, the NF generally recovers the spectroscopic redshift distributions more accurately than QRF in terms of distribution width, Wasserstein distance, JS divergence, and probability overlap, although QRF achieves smaller mean-redshift biases in some bins. In the highest-redshift bin ( [FORMULA] ), the NF shows a particularly substantial improvement over QRF across the reconstruction metrics, including its ability to recover the extended low-redshift tail. For the full-sample [FORMULA] , both probabilistic methods perform well, indicating that the advantages of the NF are more pronounced in tomographic reconstruction than in global distribution-level statistics. We further evaluate the probabilistic calibration of the NF PDFs using the probability integral transform (PIT) and apply a redshift-dependent empirical CDF recalibration derived from an independent validation sample. When transferred to the spatially independent test sample, the calibrated PIT distributions move closer to the uniform expectation, although residual miscalibration remains. The recalibration also leads to improvements in tomographic [FORMULA] reconstruction in several redshift bins, particularly in the mean-redshift accuracy, while largely preserving the overall distribution shapes. After calibration, the mean absolute redshift biases in the second through fifth tomographic bins at [FORMULA] fall below the Euclid accuracy benchmark of [FORMULA] . At higher redshifts, the results are less consistent, although substantial reductions in the mean-redshift bias are achieved for [FORMULA] and [FORMULA] . These findings demonstrate the flexibility of continuous NF PDFs for post-hoc calibration, while also showing that improved probabilistic consistency does not necessarily translate into better [FORMULA] reconstruction across all metrics. Collectively, our results demonstrate that the advantages of Normalizing Flows for photometric-redshift inference extend beyond point-estimation accuracy to their flexible representation of the full conditional redshift probability distribution. Retaining this probabilistic information can improve tomographic [FORMULA] reconstruction, particularly when broad or multimodal redshift distributions lead to substantial leakage across photo- [FORMULA] bin boundaries. Nevertheless, the observed run-to-run variability, the uncertain generalisation to different photometric populations, and the limitations of post-hoc PDF calibration remain important challenges. Future work should explore more transferable calibration strategies, evaluate NFs on different target populations and against a broader range of probabilistic photo- [FORMULA] methods, and incorporate the reconstructed redshift distributions into galaxy-clustering and weak-lensing likelihood analyses to quantify their impact on cosmological inference. It nevertheless took three more decades to detect (Byram et al., 1966; Gursky et al., 1971), and another to characterise (Mitchell et al., 1976; Serlemitsos et al., 1977), the hot intracluster medium (ICM), in which most of the clusters’ baryonic mass resides. Since then, measurements of the ICM’s thermodynamic properties have informed research on topics such as feedback by active galactic nuclei (AGN), low-density plasma physics, and cosmology (Sarazin, 1986; Voit, 2005; Pratt et al., 2019, for reviews, see;). These observations of the ICM, however, have largely been limited to the nearby Universe ( [FORMULA] ), mainly because the observed X-ray surface brightness suffers from cosmological dimming. This has not halted attempts to characterise the thermodynamic distribution of the ICM at early epochs ( [FORMULA] ; see, for instance, McDonald et al. 2017; Mantz et al. 2020; Tozzi et al. 2022; Mantz et al. 2026), but such observations require Chandra and/or XMM-Newton integration times approaching the megasecond regime. These long integrations are essential for obtaining spectroscopic temperature estimates of the hot electrons in the ICM by fitting a plasma model to the observed X-ray spectrum. The temperature estimates, in turn, are crucial for accurately inferring cosmological parameters (Pratt et al., 2019) and for studying astrophysical phenomenon in clusters, such as shock fronts, cooling flows, and sloshing motions (Markevitch and Vikhlinin, 2007; McNamara and Nulsen, 2012, e.g.,). A much more time-efficient approach to obtaining estimates of thermodynamic properties of the ICM is to use observations in both the millimetre (mm) and X-ray regimes (see, e.g., Birkinshaw et al. 1991, Hughes and Birkinshaw 1998, Mroczkowski et al. 2009; Mroczkowski et al. 2012, Adam et al. 2017, Siegel et al. 2018, Shitanishi et al. 2018, Castagna and Andreon 2020, Churazov et al. 2021, Ruppin et al. 2021, Okabe et al. 2021, Andreon et al. 2023, and Lepore et al. 2024). The mm-wave regime probes the hot ICM through inverse Compton scattering of cosmic microwave background (CMB) photons, a phenomenon known as the thermal Sunyaev-Zeldovich effect (tSZ effect; Sunyaev and Zeldovich 1972; for a review of the tSZ effect and its applications in astrophysical studies, see Mroczkowski et al. 2019). Because the tSZ effect probes the integrated thermal electron pressure along the line of sight, and the surface brightness of the X-ray emission is roughly proportional to the line-of-sight integral of the square of the thermal electron density, one can infer a temperature map of the ICM using the ideal gas law. Therefore, the ratio of the tSZ flux to the square root of the X-ray flux yields a pseudo, electron-density-weighted temperature distribution at a much higher angular resolution than usually achievable when deploying the X-ray-only spectroscopic method (Wicker et al., 2026, see also,). However, we do observe a dip in the electron temperature and entropy distribution to the south of the X-ray peak (cf. Figure 11). This feature is most prominent in the XMM-Newton entropy map. Given that the single-halo model is elongated along the north-east to south-west axis, the southern residual flux may trace an on-axis merger seen as a sloshing, appearing as a gradient in the azimuthally averaged residual map; similar features are found in the local Universe and likewise attributed to sloshing (Okabe et al., 2021, see, e.g.,). An X-ray AGN co-spatial with a CO J=2-1 line emitter is detected at this position and is likely to be an off-centred BCG in the merger remnant. At the same location the near-IR galaxy population is visibly disturbed, resembling the remnant core of a group colliding with the host. The presence of sloshing was previously suggested by McDonald et al. (2017), based on the bright off-centred flux seen in the surface brightness. While the low significance of the entropy dip means this interpretation remains speculative, the inclusion of ALMA data consistent with pressure equilibrium, combined with resolved measurements of the temperature and entropy distributions, strengthens the case. Similarly, a sloshing cold front has been posited in SpARCS104922.6+564032.5 at [FORMULA] (Hlavacek-Larrondo et al., 2025) which was invoked to explain the origin of a tentative mini radio halo. Resolved tSZ observations, carried out in a similar fashion to those presented in this work, could test this hypothesis. Vice versa, L-band MeerKAT data of CL J0459 do not yet reveal a radio halo (M. Pannella et al., in prep.); deeper radio measurements or more thorough analysis would therefore be valuable for further studying the co-evolution of the thermal and non-thermal ICM. Regarding the temperature profiles shown in Figure 10 and presented in Section 4.1.4, we find a large discrepancy between our Chandra+ALMA method and the results of Mantz et al. (2026). At large radii, the temperature extrapolates to zero owing to the difference in slope between the gNFW and Vikhlinin profiles, with the electron pressure distribution steepening faster than the electron density. Even for gNFW- [FORMULA] , the temperature approaches zero at [FORMULA] . We regard this feature as a direct consequence of the parametrisation rather than a physical effect. Future work performing a full joint-likelihood analysis combining X-ray and tSZ data could place priors on the temperature floor, properly accounting for this behaviour. The temperature distribution at small radii is also inconsistent with the XMM-Newton measurements of Mantz et al. (2026) as well as the overall distribution of the temperature at intermediate redshifts (McDonald et al., 2014). The steepening of the electron temperature profile originates from the steep inner slope, [FORMULA] , of the gNFW profile. Adopting the best-fitting A10 spherical model as the input for the X-ray analysis, we find a relatively cooler core, while still “hot” peaking at [FORMULA] keV. The hot core is consistent with the hot core visible in the projected temperature map (Figure 11). Through a new methodology that jointly models the 2D surface brightness distributions of mm-wave and X-ray data, we measured radial electron pressure, density, temperature, and entropy profiles as well as projected thermodynamic maps of the ICM, using a combination of ACT, ALMA, Chandra, and XMM-Newton data. We illustrated this on CL J0459.6-4946 ( [FORMULA] ). Adding new, deep ALMA Band 1 and 3 measurements to the extensive archival data revealed the following: ALMA Band 1 is uniquely well suited to study the ICM at “X-ray-like” angular resolutions in the mm-wave regime at high redshifts. With only a fraction of the observing time required in Band 3, ALMA Band 1 offers high-resolution mapping comparable to the main ALMA array in Band 3 with spatial scales as large as the one probed by Band 3 ACA but with [FORMULA] its collecting area, a larger field of view, and lower system temperatures. The improved [FORMULA] -coverage reduces our dependence on parametric profiles needed to interpolate and extrapolate the flux distribution, potentially paving the way towards less restrictive ICM parametrisations. By detecting CO line emission from cluster member galaxies with ALMA, we determined spectroscopic redshifts for our sources. We constrained the redshift of CL J0459 to [FORMULA] , based on the median velocity distribution of 11 CO [FORMULA] =2–1 emitters, two of which also have corresponding CO [FORMULA] =1–0 detections. By coupling MBProj2D with our [FORMULA] -based forward model, we modelled the 2D X-ray surface brightness distribution using the maximum likelihood radial pressure profile from the ALMA modelling. The ALMA+Chandra analysis reproduced the thermodynamic profiles obtained from the [FORMULA] deeper XMM-Newton data, even beyond [FORMULA] . The inferred profiles show a hot, high-entropy core declining radially, while the entropy follows a more self-similar behaviour out to [FORMULA] . The electron pressure and density profiles deviate from standard templates such as Arnaud et al. (2010) and McDonald et al. (2014). The hot core and flat entropy distribution, combined with a relatively small effective path length [FORMULA] and a relatively large clumpiness factor of [FORMULA] within [FORMULA] , suggest that CL J0459 has a compact, hot, dynamic core that is in the midst of thermalising its ICM. This translates also to a relatively large hydrostatic mass bias albeit with large errorbars. Deeper JWST lensing observations will provide the S/N needed to test this case and constrain the hydrostatic mass bias as a function of radius. The ICM shows evidence for a cold, low-entropy, high-density region to the south of the cluster core. The absence of any corresponding perturbation in the Compton- [FORMULA] map indicates this region is in pressure equilibrium, consistent with a sloshing cold front. Although its existence was previously posited (McDonald et al., 2017), our analysis, in combination with a large hydrostatic mass bias and the presence of an off-centred BCG at the location of the cold front, strengthens this interpretation. This is unprecedented at [FORMULA] , and demonstrates the unique capability of mm-wave instrumentation to push the study of cluster thermodynamics to high redshift. To summarize, CL J0459 has a disturbed ICM with a hot core that radially declines to lower temperatures. Although the temperature falls radially, the entropy distribution remains rather flat around [FORMULA] keV cm2 up to [FORMULA] . This nearly flat distribution with a clumpy ICM and a short effective path length suggest that CL J0459 is dynamically active, possibly in the midst of thermalising its ICM by means of on-axis minor merger that is dissipating its kinetic energy to thermal energy. With any case study though it is hard to draw general conclusions, in our case about the overall thermal evolution of the cosmic web’s most over dense regions. However, this paper provides a path forward: with current facilities, only a relatively short X-ray exposure (122 ks) is sufficient when combined with 3h-long ALMA measurements to fully characterise the ICM at high redshift. This opens a path towards studying how large-scale structure formation imprints on the thermodynamics of young and distant galaxy clusters for larger samples. (2017); Gress et al. (2017); Kuzmichev et al. (2020); Budnev et al. (2020). The complex is located in the Tunka Valley, 50 km from the Lake Baikal. Several of our previous studies have demonstrated that the TAIGA-HiSCORE array is also suitable for searching for submicrosecond optical transients (10 ns–150 ns) of astrophysical origin Panov et al. (2021); Panov et al. (2025), i.e., it can be used as a tool for optical astronomy. An essential feature of the TAIGA-HiSCORE array compared to conventional optical telescopes is the ability to search for very rare events due to the instrument’s wide field of view, which is on the scale of one steradian. Due to the astroclimatic conditions in the Tunka Valley the TAIGA astrophysical complex carryes out measurements from approximately mid-autumn, then in winter, and up to mid-spring each year. These periods are referred to as the TAIGA winter seasons. The search for astrophysical optical transients using the TAIGA-HiSCORE array has been ongoing since the 2018–2019 winter season. The results of the 2018–2019 season are published in the paper Panov et al. (2021), and the results of the three seasons 2019–2020, 2020–2021, and 2021–2022 are published in the paper Panov et al. (2025). No candidates to submicrosecond optical transient were found up to now. This new paper presents the results of optical transient searches in the new HiSCORE seasons 2022–2023 and 2023–2024. Additionally, the method was extended to include a search for gamma-ray bursts that can accompany the optical flashes of the evaporation of primordial black holes. The physical motivation for searching for astrophysical optical transients in the submicrosecond range of durations is discussed in detail in our article Panov et al. (2025), where one can also find references to the relevant literature. The three main sources of such optical transients considered in Panov et al. (2025) were: 1) flashes of light associated with the evaporation of the remnants of primordial black holes; 2) stochastic variability of the radiation of the plasma accreting onto the stellar mass black holes; 3) laser pulses from an extraterrestrial civilization. Some notes regarding primordial black hole evaporation should be done here. The final stages of a black hole evaporation cannot currently be fully understood, as they must be described within the framework of a theory of quantum gravity, that is not yet known. We emphasize that, despite the insufficient understanding of the processes accompanying the final stages of black hole evaporation, there is reason to believe that the final explosion, completing the evaporation, will be accompanied, among other signatures, by an optical flash. Such a flash may be caused, in particular, by synchrotron radiation from high-energy charged particles emitted by the black hole remnant into the interstellar magnetic field, where the primordial black hole was immersed before the explosion Rees (1977); Blandford (1977); Petkov et al. (2019). Another signature of a black hole evaporation could be groups of high-energy gamma rays (multi-TeV energies) that arrive from a single point in the sky within a short time interval. High-energy gamma ray astronomy is the primary purpose of the TAIGA-HiSCORE array. Since the array detects not only the occurrence of a gamma ray but also its direction of arrival, such narrow spatiotemporal groups of gamma rays can be easily identified by TAIGA-HiSCORE if they occur. The search for the evaporation of black holes using such groups of gamma rays has already been carried out in a number of works Alexandreas et al. (1993); Amenomori et al. (1995); Linton et al. (2006); Petkov et al. (2008); Bugaev et al. (2009b); Bugaev et al. (2009a); Abdo et al. (2015); Archambault, S. et al. (VERITAS Collaboration) (2017); Ackermann et al. (2018); Albert et al. (2018); Aharonian et al. (2023). However, as noted in Petkov et al. (2019), detecting black hole evaporation simultaneously using several different methods would be much more interesting and useful. It was proposed in Petkov et al. (2019) to use several different instruments simultaneously for this purpose, but the TAIGA-HiSCORE array allows for a multimessenger approach to be implemented within a single instrument. Using various event signatures, HiSCORE allows for the detection and discrimination of both narrow spatiotemporal groups of gamma-ray photons and optical flashs that can accompany black hole evaporation. This is a multimessenger method inplemented within a single instrument. The aim of this work is not only to search for submicrosecond optical transients of astrophysical origin, regardless of their nature, but also to implement a multimesenger approach to searching for the evaporation of primordial black holes within the framework of a single TAIGA-HiSCORE instrument. The article consists of two relatively independent parts. One examines the search for submicrosecond optical transients (Section 3), and the other examines the search for narrow spatiotemporal groups of EAS events (Section 4), which can be interpreted as groups of gamma-ray quanta accompanying the evaporation of black holes. Each Section 3 and 4 of the paper describes the corresponding methodology and results. Section 2 presents a description of the HiSCORE instrument and the 2022–2023 and 2023–2024 season data common for the entire paper, in Section 5 the main results are discussed. 2 The HiSCORE instrument and the data of 2022–2023 and 2023–2024 seasons The HiSCORE (High Sensitivity Cosmic Rays and Gamma Explorer) array consists of 120 Cherenkov optical stations, each with four photomultiplier tubes (PMTs) with a total entrance pupil area of approximately 0.5 m2. All four PMTs of the optical station have common field of view. It is difficult to determine the exact size of the field of view of optical station because it depends on the brightness of the flash of light, but it is a value of the sclale of one steradian. The stations form a grid with a step of 106 m, which covers an area slightly greater than one square kilometer. All optical stations are oriented identically, but their orientation may vary from season to season. The integration time of the optical station electronics is 10 ns, and the maximum duration of the recorded optical signal is set at 150 ns (this value is adjustable). Optical stations are sensitive to the visible range of light. The station detection threshold is approximately 3000 green light quanta per square meter within an integration time of 10 ns, which roughly corresponds to an object with a brightness of -4m (Venus at its highest brightness). The design and construction details of the HiSCORE array are presented in the papers Tluczykont et al. (2011); Gress et al. (2017). In the main operating mode of the HiSCORE instrument, the optical stations measure the amplitudes of the light signal caused by the Cherenkov light of the EAS, as well as the temporal evolution of the Cherenkov light front, reconstructed from the stations time triggers sequence. It is possible from this data to reconstruct the arrival direction of a cosmic particle (charged particle or gamma ray), the position of the shower axis, its initial energy, and several other important EAS characteristics. Fig. 1 (left panel) shows a generic EAS event from the 2023–2024 season, detected by the HiSCORE array. The figure shows the locations of HiSCORE optical stations, with colored circles indicating the optical stations that have been triggered in the event. The circle square is proportional to the logarithm of the signal amplitude, the white numbers inside the circles indicate the optical station’s signal duration in nanoseconds, and the circle color encodes the optical station’s trigger time. The black numbers represent the optical station numbers adopted by the TAIGA collaboration. The top portion of the “event portrait” contains a list of the event parameters obtained during the data processing. Among the parameters there is the direction of the shower axis, reconstructed by fitting the light front of EAS with a flat front (FTheta=11.9 FPhi=-46.4 FDecl=42.9 FRA=4.29 h in Fig. 1, left panel) and with a spherical front (STheta=11.8 SPhi=-47.7 SDecl=43.2 SRA=4.30 h), in both cases in local and equatorial coordinates. Theta means zenith angle, Phi means snadard geographical azimuth, both in degrees; Decl means declination (degrees) and RA means right accession (hours). Prefix F relates to a flat front reconstruction, prefix S relates to a spherical front reconstruction. There are some other parameters, which we will not discuss here. It can be seen that the EAS events generally have the appearance of a “spot” located somewhere within the area occupied by the array. The shower axis passes near the center of the spot and it is clearly seen that the amplitudes of the signals of optical stations near the shower axis are greater than at the periphery of the shower. The main calibration procedures of the HiSCORE instrument include amplitude calibration of optical station signals and correction of optical station trigger timing errors. The goal of amplitude calibration is to equalize the amplitude distributions of optical station signals. During each night, all optical stations should produce identical signal amplitude distributions, indicating identical gains of the optical stations. The identity of the amplidute distributions of different optical stations permits to compare correctly the strengths of the signals of different stations within each event. Correction of optical station trigger timing errors eliminates small uncertainties in the time delays of optical communication links and is performed using LED signals from drones passage the HiSCORE array. The calibration methods used in this work were identical to those described in detail in the paper Panov et al. (2025), so we will not dwell on the details of these methods here. Unlike the EAS arrays, which detect charged particles and can operate 24/7 year-round, the HiSCORE array, which relies on EAS Cherenkov light detection, can only operate on clear, moonless nights. The total HISCORE exposure during the 2022–2023 winter season was 696.7 hours, with a total of 248,752,575 events detected. During the 2023–2024 winter season, the exposure was 659.3 hours, with a total of 268,145,330 events detected. The time signal sequence of each optical station is recorded independently, and then the events records are generated off-line. The sign of an event was the fact that at least two optical stations were triggered within a 6.5 [FORMULA] s time window. The size of the time window is determined by the linear dimensions of the HiSCORE array. Thus, the minimum “multiplicity” of an event is two optical stations. The statistics presented above apply to the events with a multiplicity of at least two. However, for an event with a multiplicity of two, it is impossible to reconstruct the shower’s axis direction. The minimum multiplicity of an event for which the reconstruction of direction is possible is three. In this case, reconstruction can be performed using a plane front approximation, but it is impossible to estimate the accuracy of the approximation, since the plane is drawn precisely and uniquely by three points. The inability to determine the accuracy of the approximation creates troubles for the problems considered in this paper. Actually events with a multiplicity of at least five were used for the final analysis. For such events, either a flat-front approximation or a spherical-front approximation can be used to reconstruct the event axis direction. In both cases, the quality of the approximation can be assessed by the deviation of the actual station trigger times from the fitting surface. For the winter 2022–2023 season, 81012017 events with a multiplicity of at least five stations were detected, and for the 2023–2024 season, 87994903 such events were detected. The number of events with a multiplicity of at least five is approximately one third of the total number of detected events with a multiplicity of at least two. 3 Search for submicrosecond optical transients Two main signatures were used to select potential candidates for distant optical transients in this paper: the event area signature and the signature of the altitude [FORMULA] of the center of the event’s reconstructed spherical light front. However, searching for narrow spatiotemporal groups of events, which could be another signature of black hole evaporation, has also independent significance. This section presents the method and results of the search for narrow spatiotemporal groups of events with the TAIGA-HiSCORE Cherenkov array in the data of the 2022–2023 and 2023–2024 seasons of observation. The definition of spatial (or more precisely, angular) proximity of events for searching for narrow groups is simple. Events are expected to arrive from exactly the same point in the sky during black hole evaporation, therefore the notion of “spatial proximity” of events will be defined simply by errors in determining angular coordinates. The concept of temporal proximity of events is more complex. The energy threshold of the HiSCORE array is approximately 50 TeV for detecting of gamma-rays. This value corresponds to events involving four optical stations. Since our data processing involves events of at least five stations, we will use a slightly higher threshold of 100 TeV in our estimations. Therefore detecting a narrow temporal group of gamma-quanta for HiSCORE means detecting at least two gamma-quanta with the energies above 100 TeV within a time interval, which we will consider to be “small” in a certain sense. The question is the following. What is the time interval near the end of a black hole evaporation in which Hawking gammas with energies above 100 TeV can be emitted? This time will define the scale of “smallness” of the time interval for defining the notion of a narrow temporal group of events. It is expected that the spectrum of Hawking gamma quanta is the black-body radiation Planck spectrum, the temperature of which is defined by the mass of the black hole. The Planck distribution of the energies [FORMULA] of Hawking gamma quanta for a Hawking temperature [FORMULA] is shown in Fig. 8. The dependence of the Hawking temperature on the time [FORMULA] until the end of the BH evaporation is also shown in a small table within the Fig. 8. It is evident from Fig. 8 that Hawking gamma-rays with energies above 100 TeV can be emmited intensively starting from a time of approximately 10 ms until the end of BH evaporation, when the Hawking temperature is 36 TeV. Gamma-rays with energies of 100 TeV fall approximately at the maximum of the Planck distribution in this case. One might therefore think that short time intervals for searching for narrow groups of gamma-rays should be understood as time intervals of 10 ms and less. However, it turns out that for a time interval of 10 ms there will be a very large background of a chance EAS coincidences in the HiSCORE array (see below). We study in this work time intervals of 1000 [FORMULA] s and below, down to fractions of a microsecond. However, how can the HiSCORE array detect events with interval times between events shorter than 1000 ns while events are formed using a 6500 ns time window? We will demonstrate below how this problem can be solved, but before we begin to search for such narrow spatiotemporal event groups, we consider “long” inter-event time intervals, for which the maximum possible event duration of 6500 ns can be considered to be short. Since the time window for generating a single HiSCORE event from triggers of individual optical stations is 6.5 [FORMULA] s, particle arrivals separated by less than 6.5 [FORMULA] s time interval cannot be detected by HiSCORE as separate events. Details of the temporal structure of such multiple events will allow us to reconstruct the exact difference in the arrival times of the component events (see details below). The algorithm for searching for multiple events – candidates for narrow spatiotemporal pairs – is as follows. Among all HiSCORE events, we search for those in which the event structure at ground level resembles two (or more) disconnected spots – subevents. There are a great many such complex events in the HiSCORE data. For each subevent, the shower direction is reconstructed, and if the subevent axes point to the same point in the sky, the event is considered to have passed the primary filter and becomes a candidate for narrow spatiotemporal pairs. However, such events also turn out to be very numerous. The origin of such events is that an EAS from a single particle can be detected as two spatially disconnected spots simply for a chance reasons – due to the spatial inhomogeneity of the shower or because some optical stations failed to operate due to electronic instability. This also happens, albeit rarely. Since both subevents in such cases are part of the same EAS, the reconstructed directions of their axes naturally point to the same point in the sky. The origin of events of this type is related to the fact that the lower right corner of the HiSCORE array is “cut out”. Since statistical fluctuations in the Cherenkov light flux in EAS wings are large, discontinuities in the shower structure can often arise here naturally. First-principles calculations of far-wing absorption in He-broadened CO2 infrared spectra We report theoretical predictions and modeling of far-wing absorption of CO2 broadened by He over a wide temperature range (200–1000 K), relevant to exoplanet atmosphere studies. Accurate modeling of He-broadened CO2 absorption is essential for opacity calculations used to characterize the composition, structure, and climate of exoplanet atmospheres. In particular, the strong CO2 band at 4.3 [FORMULA] m has been clearly identified in the spectra of several exoplanets observed with the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). Requantized classical molecular dynamics simulations were first performed to predict absorption in the far wings of the 4.3 [FORMULA] m band of CO2. The resulting predictions show excellent agreement with available experimental data at room temperature. The theoretical predictions and measured data were then used to parameterize an impact energy-corrected sudden model, which allows us to accurately reproduce the far-wing absorption of He-broadened CO2 in several infrared spectral regions over the (200–1000) K temperature range. Finally, for applications to exoplanet atmosphere opacity calculations, we derived temperature-dependent [FORMULA] -factor corrections that account for the sub-Lorentzian behavior of the far wing of the major infrared bands of CO2. 1 Introduction Carbon dioxide (CO2) is a key absorber in exoplanet atmospheres, particularly in gas giants, for which the 4.3 [FORMULA] m CO2 absorption band (i.e., the [FORMULA] band) was clearly detected in spectra obtained with the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) (e.g., Rustamkulov et al. 2023; Carter et al. 2024; Balmer et al. 2025; Fu et al. 2025). Accurate knowledge of CO2 absorption, from the band center to the far wings, is essential not only for the characterization of exoplanet atmospheres but also for modeling their thermal structure and climate, which depend strongly on the opacity in the deeper atmospheric layers. One of the main limitations in interpreting observations and in climate modeling lies in the accuracy of atmospheric opacity calculations, mainly due to the limited knowledge of pressure broadening and far-wing absorption together with their temperature dependence (Niraula et al. 2022; Chaverot et al. 2023). In contrast to terrestrial atmospheric conditions, relatively few laboratory studies investigated the line shape of CO2 broadened by the dominant constituents of giant exoplanet atmospheres, namely H2 and He (Wilzewski et al. 2016; Tan et al. 2022). In addition, the temperatures relevant to exoplanet atmospheres span a very broad range, from about 100 K to 3000 K (Fortney et al. 2019), well beyond the limits accessible to most laboratory experimental setups. Recent efforts have focused on accurate measurements and calculations of the H2 and He pressure-broadening coefficients of CO2 lines at temperatures relevant to exoplanet atmospheres (see Hendaoui et al. 2025; Hendaoui et al. 2026a; Hendaoui et al. 2026b and references therein). These data are expected to significantly improve the accuracy of opacity calculations for H2- and He-rich exoplanet atmospheres. However, only a limited amount of information is available for the far line wings, restricted to narrow spectral regions and room temperature. It is now well established that absorption in the far wings is significantly weaker than predicted by a Lorentzian profile (Hartmann et al. 2021). To our knowledge, only a few studies have investigated far-wing absorption of CO2-He mixtures (Burch et al. 1969; Baranov et al. 1981; Dokuchaev et al. 1985; Thibault et al. 1994; Ozanne et al. 1995). Burch et al. (1969) measured absorption in the far-wing regions of the [FORMULA] band between 3770 and 3860 cm-1 and of the [FORMULA] band between 6990 and 7002 cm-1 at room temperature. From these measurements, they introduced a band- and wavenumber-dependent factor, [FORMULA] , smaller than unity, to describe the observed sub-Lorentzian behavior. Dokuchaev et al. (1985) measured CO2 absorption in mixtures with He, Ne, Ar, Xe, H2, D2, and N2 at 294 K in the 2390–2465 cm-1 spectral region and showed that the far-wing absorption in a CO2–He mixture is significantly weaker than that in a CO2–N2 mixture, in agreement with the findings of Burch et al. (1969). Ozanne et al. (1995) measured far-wing absorption in the [FORMULA] and [FORMULA] bands, in the 2400–2500 cm-1 and 6990–7010 cm-1 spectral regions respectively, at room temperature and high densities. Their results were consistent with those of Dokuchaev et al. (1985) in the [FORMULA] band wings. The sub-Lorentzian behavior observed in the far wings is due to collisional interference between lines (line mixing) and to the breakdown of the impact approximation. Interactions between He atoms and molecules are generally weak, with a steep repulsive wall and a small well that rapidly vanishes at larger intermolecular distances. As a result, collision durations are much shorter than the mean time between successive collisions (Tran et al. 2023; Reed et al. 2023; Tran et al. 2026), suggesting that non-impact effects should be negligible in He-broadened CO2 spectra. Ozanne et al. (1995) successfully used an impact Energy-Corrected Sudden (ECS) model to describe line-mixing effects in CO2-He absorption spectra at room temperature and high densities. This model enables the calculation of collisional line interferences from rotational state-to-state transfer rates. Good agreement with measurements was obtained from the band centers to the far wings in both the [FORMULA] and [FORMULA] bands. Similar approaches were applied to model line-mixing effects at the band centers and in the near wings for various spectral regions (Boissoles et al. 1994; Boissoles et al. 1996; Khalil et al. 1996; Rodrigues et al. 1998; Hartmann et al. 1999; Boulet et al. 1999). These studies, however, were limited to room temperature only, likely because both measured spectra and line-broadening coefficients required to constrain the models were only available under such conditions. More recently, classical molecular dynamics simulations (CMDS) were used to predict far-wing absorption for pure CO2 and CO2–H2O mixtures, with very good agreement with measurements (Hartmann et al. 2010; Hartmann et al. 2018). This method, based on the use of accurate intermolecular potentials and Newtonian equations of motion, enables the computation of spectral line profiles from the line center (Nguyen et al. 2018; Nguyen et al. 2020; Ngo and Tran 2025; Tran et al. 2025) to the far wings without the use of adjustable parameters. CMDS were also successfully applied to predict pressure-broadening parameters over wide temperature ranges for various species, including He- and H2-broadening coefficients of CO2 lines (Hendaoui et al. 2026a; Hendaoui et al. 2026b). In this work, we use CMDS to predict far-wing absorption of the [FORMULA] band of He-broadened CO2 over a wide temperature range, from 200 K to 1000 K. The predictions are compared with experimental data available at room temperature. The CMDS results are then used to parameterize the temperature dependence of the impact ECS model. Indeed, the latter is based on the use of some empirical parameters to calculate the rotational state-to-state transfer rates. These empirical parameters are obtained from fits of far-wing absorption predicted by CMDS at various temperatures. Once validated, this ECS model enables calculations of far-wing absorption for He-broadened CO2 in various infrared bands over a broad temperature range. For practical applications, the resulting far-wing absorptions are finally fitted using temperature-dependent [FORMULA] -factor corrections suitable for atmospheric radiative transfer and opacity calculations. The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 presents the CMDS calculations, while Sect. 3 describes the ECS model and the associated data used. Comparisons between modeled absorptions, CMDS predictions, and available measurements are presented in Sect. 4. In Sect. 5, we derive the [FORMULA] -factor parameterization of the far-wing absorption computed with the ECS model and illustrate its impact on opacity calculations. Conclusions are given in Sect. 6. 2 CMDS We first computed far-wing absorption spectra of CO2 broadened by He using the requantized CMDS (rCMDS) approach described in Hendaoui et al. (2026b). That study demonstrated that He-broadening coefficients of CO2 lines predicted by rCMDS are in very good agreement with experimental data over a wide temperature range, from 123 K to 760 K. The simulation methodology, based on the formalism described in chapter 3 of Allen and Tildesley (1987), was detailed in our previous studies devoted to the prediction of pressure-broadening coefficients of CO2 lines with various collision partners (Ngo and Tran 2025; Tran et al. 2025; Hendaoui et al. 2026a; Hendaoui et al. 2026b). In the present work, simulations were performed at four temperatures: 200 K, 296 K, 500 K, and 1000 K. Mixtures containing 50% CO2 and 50% He were considered, but only CO2–He interactions were included in order to reduce the computational cost. Since the contribution of three-body (and higher) interactions is negligible, this approximation is equivalent to simulating CO2 infinitely diluted in He at a total pressure equal to the He partial pressure. The He pressures considered were 10 atm at 200 K and 296 K, 20 atm at 500 K, and 60 atm at 1000 K. For each temperature and pressure condition, we simulated a large number of particles ( [FORMULA] ) initially placed in cubic boxes with periodic boundary conditions. The position of the center of mass, translational velocity directions, angular momenta, and molecular orientations (for CO2) were randomly initialized, while translational and rotational speeds were sampled from Maxwell–Boltzmann distributions. Using an accurate intermolecular potential (Korona et al. 2001; Hendaoui et al. 2026b) and Newton’s equations of motion, the time propagation of the system was computed at each time step, up to a maximum simulation time [FORMULA] . This procedure enables the calculation of the autocorrelation function (ACF) of the dipole moment (along the molecular axis for a parallel band of CO2). The Fourier–Laplace transform of the ACF directly yields the spectral density, or, equivalently, the band-normalized spectral profile. A requantization procedure was then applied to convert the classical angular momenta into quantum rotational states. To do so, we used the same approach as in Hendaoui et al. (2026b), which was shown to provide very good predictions of He-broadening coefficients over a wide temperature range. In addition, the distinction between the [FORMULA] - and [FORMULA] -branch transitions was introduced by considering the sign of the angular momentum along the [FORMULA] axis: positive values were assigned to the [FORMULA] branch, whereas negative values were assigned to the [FORMULA] branch. Finally, the requantized angular momentum values used in the ACF calculations were directly linked to the relative positions (with respect to the band center) of the strong [FORMULA] band lines at 4.3 [FORMULA] m. The resulting rCMDS spectrum therefore reproduces the structure of the CO2 [FORMULA] band and can be directly compared with measured absorption profiles. To compare the rCMDS predictions with the measurements, we scaled the spectra using the integrated [FORMULA] -band intensity obtained from line-by-line calculations based on the HITRAN molecular spectroscopic database (Gordon et al. 2022) and, for temperatures above 500 K, the HITEMP high-temperature spectroscopic database (Rothman et al. 2010). We note that a direct comparison between the rCMDS-predicted absorption for the [FORMULA] band and measurements in the 2400–2600 cm-1 spectral region is possible because the contributions from weaker bands are negligible there. Figure 1 presents the results obtained at 296 K. The rCMDS results exhibit residual oscillations originating from two main effects. First, despite the large number of simulated molecules, the computed ACF is not perfectly smooth and still contains short-time fluctuations associated with individual collision events. These fluctuations become increasingly visible in the far-wing regions, where absorption is very weak. Second, the oscillations observed in the rCMDS results are also due to the limited time extent of the calculations of the ACF. This introduces a convolution of the true absorption spectrum with a cardinal sine function, which also produces oscillatory structures in regions of weak absorption. To reduce these artifacts, an apodization procedure similar to that commonly used in Fourier-transform spectroscopy was applied. Specifically, the ACF was multiplied by a Gaussian window function that remains close to unity while the ACF is significant and smoothly decreases to zero as the maximum simulation time [FORMULA] approaches. The fluctuations are significantly reduced by apodization, although they are not completely eliminated, particularly in the very far wings (Fig. 1), where the absorption is extremely weak. As shown in Fig. 1, the rCMDS predictions are in very good agreement with experimental values of Dokuchaev et al. (1985); Ozanne et al. (1995). They clearly show large deviations from absorption calculated using simple Lorentzian profiles. It is important to emphasize that no adjustable parameters were introduced in the rCMDS calculations. These results demonstrate that these first-principles calculations are capable of accurately predicting far-wing absorption of CO2 broadened by He. For comparison, Fig. 1 also shows the results obtained with the Lorentzian line-shape model but imposing a line-wing cutoff at 25 cm-1, an assumption commonly adopted in opacity databases and retrieval codes used for exoplanet atmosphere studies, including TauREx, NEMESIS, CHIMERA (Barstow et al. 2020) and MAESTRO (Gharib-Nezhad et al. 2024). As can be seen, this simplified treatment significantly underestimates the far-wing absorption of CO2 broadened by He, highlighting the importance of properly accounting for the non-Lorentzian far-wing behavior in opacity calculations. Additional rCMDS calculations were subsequently performed at 200 K, 500 K, and 1000 K. For each temperature and pressure condition, the rCMDS-calculated spectrum of the [FORMULA] band was scaled to have the same integrated band intensity as the corresponding line-by-line spectrum. Excellent agreement is observed between the rCMDS predictions and the spectra computed using the ECS model over both the low- and high-frequency wings of the band, from the near-wing to the far-wing regions. In contrast, the Lorentzian calculations substantially overestimate both the rCMDS and ECS results. The discrepancy increases with increasing distance from the band center, reaching more than three orders of magnitude in the far wings. The 25 cm-1 line-wing cutoff calculations, on the other hand, yield far-wing absorption that rapidly decreases to zero and therefore significantly underestimate the rCMDS and ECS results. It is important to note that rCMDS calculations account for both collisional line-mixing and collision-duration (non-impact) effects. The excellent agreement between the rCMDS predictions and the impact-based ECS model demonstrates that non-impact effects have a negligible influence on the far-wing absorption of CO2 broadened by He. This finding is consistent with previous studies (Tran et al. 2023; Reed et al. 2023; Tran et al. 2026), which showed that non-impact effects of molecule–He collisions are negligible. For systems involving stronger intermolecular interactions, such as CO2–CO2, however, non-impact effects must be taken into account to accurately describe far-wing absorption (Tran et al. 2011). These results clearly demonstrate the importance of realistic far-wing line-shape corrections for modeling CO2 opacity in He-rich atmospheres. 6 Conclusions Far-wing absorption of CO2 broadened by He is predicted for the first time using first-principles calculations. These calculations, based on requantized classical molecular dynamics simulations (rCMDS), involving no empirical parameters, provide the spectral density, or equivalently the band-normalized absorption spectrum, from the band centers to the far wings. All collisional effects including the two main mechanisms responsible for the sub-Lorentzian behavior observed in the far wings, namely line-mixing and non-impact effects, were accounted for in the rCMDS. Comparisons between the predicted far-wing absorption and experimental data in the far-wing region of the CO2 [FORMULA] band showed excellent agreement. Combined with previous studies demonstrating accurate predictions of pressure-broadening coefficients over a wide temperature range, these results confirm the ability of rCMDS to accurately describe the full range of collision effects affecting molecular absorption spectra. Because non-impact effects are expected to be negligible for He-broadened CO2 spectra and because rCMDS remain computationally demanding, available experimental data together with rCMDS predictions in the far-wing region of the [FORMULA] band, for temperatures between 200 K and 1000 K, were subsequently used to constrain an impact-based spectral model that accounts for collisional line-mixing effects. The resulting model and associated parameter set provide an accurate representation of far-wing absorption in several spectral regions and can therefore be used to predict the far-wing absorption of He-broadened CO2 throughout the infrared spectrum. Using the far-wing absorption calculated with this model, we derived a set of temperature-dependent [FORMULA] -factor corrections that reproduce the sub-Lorentzian behavior of all major infrared CO2 bands. These corrections provide a physically based set of parameters for modeling of the far-wing absorption of CO2 broadened by He over a wide temperature range, in contrast to the commonly used line-wing cutoff approximations. They can be readily implemented in opacity calculations for CO2 in He-rich atmospheres, such as those encountered in exoplanetary environments.

The joint analysis of galaxy density and cool gas distribution in this work reveals distinctions that crucial for understanding how environment regulates gas accretion, star formation, and ultimately galaxy quenching. 1 Introduction A central aim of extragalactic research is to establish the relative contribution of internally versus externally driven physical processes throughout the evolution of galaxies. In the nearby universe, environmental density correlates with several galaxy properties such as their star-formation, stellar mass, and metallicity (Gómez et al., 2003; Kauffmann et al., 2004; Poggianti et al., 2006; Khoram et al., 2025, e.g.,), with these trends established as early as [FORMULA] (Muzzin et al., 2012; Darvish et al., 2016, e.g.,). At higher redshifts, however, large-scale structures are still actively assembling, shaped by continuous growth from the reionization era through Cosmic Noon (Muldrew et al., 2015, e.g.,), so the environmental indicators used in the local Universe are no longer reliable tracers of galaxy evolutionary stage. Tracing the redshift evolution of these environmental trends is therefore essential for identifying their physical origins, which likely reflect a combination of density-sensitive processes such as ram pressure stripping, starvation, and tidal interactions, and differences in halo assembly history (Roberts et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026, e.g.,). Among the most important processes governing galaxy evolution is the formation and quenching of massive galaxies. Massive quiescent galaxies detected in the early Universe seem to have experienced a swift halt in star formation, although the underlying processes driving this transformation are still widely debated (Man & Belli, 2018; Whitaker & Bezanson, 2026, e.g.,). The Cosmic Noon epoch — marked by elevated rates of star formation, galactic quiescence, and halo development — offers a valuable opportunity to examine these interconnected processes (Dekel et al., 2009; Madau & Dickinson, 2014; Behroozi et al., 2019). Although feedback from active galactic nuclei (AGN) is commonly cited as the dominant mechanism responsible for quenching star formation (Di Matteo et al., 2005; Somerville & Davé, 2015; Beckmann et al., 2017; Belli et al., 2024; Bugiani et al., 2025; Davies & Belli, 2026), alternative investigations emphasize the considerable contributions of the environment, such as strangulation, gas exhaustion, and dynamical disturbances triggered by galaxy mergers (Ellison et al., 2024; Suess et al., 2025; Khoram et al., 2026). The physical mechanisms responsible for the rapid buildup and subsequent early quenching of galaxies in various environments remain largely unclear. A key obstacle lies in the difficulty of detecting protoclusters, which at [FORMULA] are neither fully collapsed nor virialized, extending across tens of comoving megaparsecs (Chiang et al., 2013; Muldrew et al., 2015). Unlike mature clusters, these structures may not have yet developed a hot intracluster medium, rendering standard cluster-finding techniques including extended X-ray emission and the Sunyaev-Zel’dovich effect largely ineffective. Identifying protoclusters therefore hinges on the statistical detection of galaxy overdensities. Despite significant progress in the pre-JWST "era" with ground- and space-based instruments (Laigle et al., 2016; Fossati et al., 2017; Weaver et al., 2022, e.g.,), measurements of galaxy environments at high redshift remained limited by relatively large photometric-redshift uncertainties, shallow imaging depths, or high stellar-mass completeness limits. These limitations made environmental studies beyond [FORMULA] increasingly uncertain, with surveys primarily sensitive to the most massive and luminous galaxies (Baxter et al., 2025, e.g.,). Consequently, tracing the full diversity of environments and the emergence of large-scale structure during cosmic noon remained challenging. The advent of JWST has significantly improved these measurements through its unprecedented depth and near-infrared imaging and grism spectroscopy capabilities, enabling more accurate photometric redshifts and the detection of substantially fainter galaxy populations. Recent studies using JWST data have begun reconstructing the large-scale structure and environmental density field across several deep extragalactic surveys (Casey et al., 2023; Hatamnia et al., 2026, e.g.,). In particular, the COSMOS-Web survey (Casey et al., 2023) has enabled environmental measurements over a contiguous [FORMULA] field with greatly improved redshift precision and mass completeness, allowing the identification of overdense structures and the study of environment-driven galaxy evolution out to [FORMULA] . Advances in photometric redshifts and galaxy number counts have been complemented by large spectroscopic programs which have constructed three-dimensional maps of the cool gas distribution. By targeting Ly [FORMULA] absorption imprinted on the spectra of background Lyman-break galaxies (LBGs) and quasars, these maps trace the spatial distribution of neutral hydrogen (HI) with high fidelity, providing a view of the intergalactic medium (IGM) that is independent of galaxy counts (Horowitz et al., 2019; Newman et al., 2020; Ata et al., 2021, e.g.,). Crucially, the two tracers are not necessarily interchangeable: comparisons at [FORMULA] –3 reveal a relation far more complex than a one-to-one correspondence (Momose et al., 2021; Newman et al., 2022; Dong et al., 2023, e.g.,), including configurations in which galaxy-rich regions appear HI-poor and vice versa. Such mismatches have so far been mostly interpreted as a consequence of incomplete galaxy censuses, in which galaxies in these regions are missed owing to their intrinsic properties, such as low stellar mass or strong, wavelength-dependent obscuration that dims their observed luminosity. In this work, we leverage both probes of cosmic structure available in the well-studied COSMOS field: the galaxy number densities measured from COSMOS-Web (Hatamnia et al., 2026) and the neutral hydrogen maps derived by the LATIS survey (Newman et al., 2020). Within the COSMOS field, the most prominent structure at cosmic noon is the Hyperion proto-supercluster (Cucciati et al., 2018), an extended overdensity at [FORMULA] spanning tens of comoving megaparsecs and comprising several distinct density peaks. Its multi-component morphology is characteristic of a structure caught mid-assembly, with several cores expected to differ in mass, dynamical state, and gas content; constrained simulations predict that these peaks will evolve into separate clusters by the present day (Ata et al., 2022). Hyperion therefore offers a rare opportunity to examine environmental effects within a structure whose subcomponents span a range of evolutionary stages, provided that results obtained for one core are not generalized to the whole structure. Our goal is to address two of the most actively debated questions in galaxy evolution: what drives the rapid formation and quenching of massive galaxies, and what governs the persistence of quenching once it is established. In addition to the environmental measurements, we make use of recent JWST/NIRSpec data with medium spectral resolution from the Blue Jay survey (Belli et al., 2026), which we augment with a sample of public low-resolution prism spectra. We are thus able to link IGM properties to the stellar mass, AGN activity, outflow signatures, and SFH (or equivalently mass assembly history) of individual galaxies. Non-parametric SFHs now allow formation and quenching epochs to be dated for individual systems at cosmic noon (Leja et al., 2019a; Park et al., 2024, e.g.,), while JWST spectroscopy has begun to directly reveal the feedback acting during the transition itself (Davies et al., 2024; Belli et al., 2024; D’Eugenio et al., 2024, e.g.,). Combining these internal diagnostics with independent environmental measurements allows us to compare the contributions of the two quenching channels. Our aim is not only to build a more complete picture of the interplay between galaxies and their large-scale environment, but also to shed light on the development of the environment itself. This paper is organized as follows. In Sect. 2, we present our spectroscopic sample, while in Sect. 3 we introduce the independent environmental measurements used throughout this work. In Sect. 4, we investigate how galaxy formation and quenching depend on environment, followed by Sect. 5, where we explore neutral hydrogen (HI) as an independent tracer of environment. Hidden Neutrino Active Galaxy Candidates: Prospects for Catalog and Stacking Searches with IceCube, IceCube-Gen2, and KM3NeT In high-energy neutrino astrophysics, the identification of high-energy neutrino sources is a central goal, and jet-quiet active galactic nuclei (AGNs) have emerged as promising candidates. For this purpose, we present a theory-guided, intrinsic X-ray selected sample of hidden neutrino AGN candidates consisting of [FORMULA] X-ray bright AGNs (X-HiNAC), combining the Swift/BAT and BASS surveys with dedicated NuSTAR observations and spectral analyses. We compile their intrinsic X-ray fluxes, spectral properties, luminosity distances, and supermassive black hole masses, to provide a coherent sample for neutrino source searches. The sample is physically motivated but remains model independent given that the neutrino flux is proportional to the intrinsic X-ray flux. Using the magnetically powered corona model, we also demonstrate the prospects for individual-source and stacking searches with IceCube-Gen2 and KM3NeT. We identify promising individual targets and find that stacking the remaining sources, excluding NGC 1068, could yield a [FORMULA] detection within [FORMULA] years under favorable model assumptions at the current and upcoming neutrino observatories. We highlight systematic uncertainties in the adopted source parameters, particularly the black hole masses, for which different measurement techniques can yield estimates differing by up to an order of magnitude. Such uncertainties can significantly affect the predicted neutrino emission, motivating more precise black hole mass measurements and improved broadband X-ray observations. Our findings motivate improved multiwavelength characterization of nearby AGNs and provide a guide for investigating their role as high-energy neutrino sources. I Introduction Identifying the astrophysical sources of high-energy neutrinos remains one of the central goals of multimessenger astronomy. Since the discovery of the astrophysical neutrino flux by IceCube in 2013 [2, 3], significant progress has been made toward identifying its origins. This includes evidence for neutrino emission from the Galactic plane [7, 10], and identification of neutrino emission from the nearby Seyfert galaxy NGC 1068 [6, 8, 9]. More recently, IceCube has also reported evidence of neutrino emission from populations of X-ray-bright Seyfert galaxies [11, 12]. Upcoming neutrino telescopes, including KM3NeT [17], IceCube-Gen2 [4, 55], and P-ONE [18], will provide improved sensitivity for identifying individual neutrino sources and measuring their contributions to the all-sky astrophysical neutrino flux. Among the proposed neutrino source populations, active galactic nuclei (AGNs) are particularly promising, especially following the evidence for neutrino emission from NGC 1068 [6, 8, 9, 11]. Its neutrino emission, together with gamma-ray observations [20] and upper limits at very high energies [16], points to scenarios in which high-energy neutrinos originate from compact, gamma-ray obscured regions. In such environments, a large optical depth to [FORMULA] pair production ( [FORMULA] ) suppresses the escaping very-high-energy gamma-ray emission, with the absorbed energy reprocessed to lower energies, as required from all-sky neutrino and gamma-ray fluxes [83]. The vicinity of supermassive black holes (SMBHs) provides a natural environment for such neutrino production, where magnetic dissipation and turbulence may accelerate nonthermal protons that produce high-energy neutrinos through hadronuclear ( [FORMULA] ) and photohadronic ( [FORMULA] ) interactions [85, 57, 59, 82, 56, 84, 70, 46, 86, 34, 68, 102]. The emission regions are constrained to be [FORMULA] Schwarzschild radii ( [FORMULA] ), which motivate studies about compact, X-ray-emitting coronae of AGNs [82, 40, 32, 39]. The use of X-ray-selected AGN samples for neutrino searches has been explored in several previous studies. In particular, K. Murase et al. [85] investigated neutrino production in AGN coronae and discussed the prospects for identifying nearby X-ray bright sources using the BASS sample. They found more promising AGNs in the southern sky, which are good targets for upcoming neutrino detectors such as KM3NeT. Building on this approach, A. Kheirandish et al. [59] investigated the expected neutrino emission from a sample of nearby X-ray-bright Seyfert galaxies and their detection prospects with current and future neutrino telescopes. More recently, K. Murase et al. [84] and [89] showed the most promising neutrino-active galaxies, including NGC 4151. The IceCube Collaboration subsequently performed catalog-based searches for neutrino emission from Seyfert galaxies selected using Swift/BAT and BASS measurements [11, 12]. These studies have established X-ray-selected AGN samples as promising targets for individual-source and stacking searches. However, the selection of candidates and their relative rankings depend on the adopted X-ray measurements, energy bands, treatment of intrinsic nuclear emission, and the exclusion of merger and jet activities. In particular, earlier studies primarily used intrinsic [FORMULA] keV X-ray fluxes to identify promising neutrino candidates, while more recent IceCube searches have also considered selection in harder X-ray bands, such as [FORMULA] keV, which are generally less affected by photoelectric absorption. Nevertheless, even hard X-ray emission can be substantially attenuated in heavily obscured and Compton-thick AGNs, for which recovering the intrinsic nuclear continuum requires careful treatment of absorption, Compton scattering, and reflection [75, 27]. Furthermore, existing X-ray samples combine observations and spectral analyses performed under different assumptions, and updated broadband measurements can lead to significant revisions of the inferred intrinsic luminosities. Consequently, the ranking of promising neutrino candidates can depend significantly on the adopted X-ray band and spectral modeling. For example, NGC 4151 ranked fifth or sixth in the IceCube sky based on the intrinsic [FORMULA] keV fluxes in BASS, but rose to the second brightest when considering the broader [FORMULA] keV band. This highlights the importance of systematically comparing intrinsic X-ray fluxes across different energy ranges when identifying promising neutrino-source candidates. Another important consideration is the uncertainty in the physical properties of the central SMBHs. In particular, SMBH mass estimates obtained using different measurement techniques can differ substantially [50]. Since the SMBH mass enters the Eddington ratio and influences the physical conditions governing neutrino production, these uncertainties can significantly affect the predicted neutrino spectra and detection prospects. A consistently characterized sample incorporating updated intrinsic X-ray measurements, spectral properties, luminosity distances, and SMBH mass estimates is therefore valuable for systematic comparisons among candidate sources and for guiding future neutrino searches. Motivated by these considerations, we construct a sample of X-ray bright AGNs for high-energy neutrino searches with current and next-generation neutrino telescopes. We refer to this sample as X-HiNAC (intrinsic X-ray selected Hidden Neutrino Active galaxy Candidates). We combine the BASS and Swift/BAT surveys with dedicated NuSTAR observations and broadband spectral analyses, and apply a set of selection and validation criteria to obtain a final sample of [FORMULA] AGNs. For these sources, we compile their intrinsic X-ray fluxes in the [FORMULA] keV and [FORMULA] keV bands, spectral properties, luminosity distances, and SMBH masses. The two energy bands provide complementary measures of the intrinsic emission and allow us to examine how the ranking of promising neutrino candidates depends on the adopted X-ray energy range. Importantly, the sample is constructed independently of the detailed neutrino production model used for our forecasts and provides a reference sample for scenarios in which the neutrino flux approximately scales with the intrinsic X-ray flux ( [FORMULA] ). As a representative application, we adopt the magnetically powered corona model [85, 86] to calculate benchmark fluxes of the expected neutrino emission under three model assumptions. We then estimate the corresponding neutrino event rates at IceCube-Gen2 and KM3NeT, accounting for their effective areas, angular resolutions, and atmospheric neutrino backgrounds, and investigate the prospects for individual-source and stacking searches. We also evaluate the combined neutrino flux from our sample and compare it with the diffuse astrophysical neutrino flux measured by IceCube. Beyond these detection forecasts, our study highlights the observational uncertainties that currently limit reliable neutrino predictions and provides a reference sample for future neutrino searches. II High-energy neutrino production in Jet-Quiet AGNs Jet-quiet AGNs are promising sources of high-energy neutrinos, particularly if cosmic rays (CRs) are accelerated in compact regions surrounding the central SMBH. In such environments, relativistic protons can interact with the ambient gas and radiation fields through hadronuclear ( [FORMULA] ) and photohadronic ( [FORMULA] ) processes, producing high-energy neutrinos through the decay of charged pions. The dense radiation fields can also efficiently attenuate the accompanying high-energy gamma rays, making these regions potential gamma-ray obscured neutrino sources [see a review, 87, and references therein]. A representative scenario is the magnetically powered corona model [85], in which magnetic fields generated in the accretion disk emerge in the corona and dissipate through magnetic reconnections and turbulence.
