IV Concluding Remarks In this work, we have developed a framework for on-the-fly [FORMULA] -MLFF MD simulations of WDM, wherein we have employed a Yukawa reference model that captures the dominant screened-Coulomb interactions between the ions, with its parameters fit on the fly to Kohn–Sham DFT data, in conjunction with an MLFF scheme based on the kernel method and Bayesian linear regression that learns the differences in the energies, atomic forces, and stresses between the Yukawa model and Kohn–Sham DFT. We have implemented this framework in the real-space electronic structure code SPARC, extending its on-the-fly MLFF capability. Choosing warm dense carbon as a representative example, we have verified the accuracy and performance of the formalism through comparisons with Kohn–Sham DFT results in the literature. In so doing, we have demonstrated that [FORMULA] -MLFF has significantly lower errors in the energies, atomic forces, and stresses than the standard MLFF scheme at a comparable cost, and that AIMD simulations of WDM can be accelerated by up to three orders of magnitude while retaining ab initio accuracy. Furthermore, we have applied this framework to calculate the equation of state, structure, and transport properties of magnesium at densities of 5.22 to 10.44 g/cm3 and temperatures of 600 kK to 1.5 MK. We have found that the pressure, self-diffusion coefficient, and shear viscosity obey power laws in temperature and density, that the dynamic structure factor exhibits a well-defined ion-acoustic mode whose negative dispersion is characteristic of strongly coupled liquids, and that the Stokes–Einstein relation holds to within about 10% over the conditions considered. Overall, the proposed formalism promises to enable simulations of WDM with ab initio accuracy at a small fraction of the cost of AIMD. The Bayesian error estimate that triggers the DFT calculations is inherited from the standard MLFF scheme, and the results for carbon indicate that it is conservative. Calibrating this estimate against the errors observed at the DFT calls, while also accounting for the error of the Yukawa model itself, could further reduce the number of DFT calculations required. In addition, the development of specialized kernels and descriptors for the learned correction, which is smoother and of smaller magnitude than the quantities themselves, is likely to improve the accuracy and transferability of the model. Finally, extending the current implementation to enable GPU acceleration of the key computational kernels [80, 81] will further reduce the wall time for large MD simulations. These represent worthy subjects for future research. Intermolecular and Interfacial Origins of Layering in a Near-Isotropic Organic Glass Former Physical vapor deposition can produce organic glasses with enhanced stability and pronounced structural anisotropy (layering) even when the constituent molecules are nearly spherical. However, the microscopic origin of the layering in spherical molecular glass formers remains unclear. We investigated vapor-deposited films of 9-(3,5-di(naphthalen-1-yl)phenyl)anthracene (α,α-A) by grazing-incidence wide-angle X-ray scattering, atomistic molecular dynamics, and coarse-grained simulations. Experimentally, the layering signal varies nonmonotonically with deposition temperature and is strongest near 0.8 [FORMULA] . Simulated scattering calculations reproduce the principal experimental features and show that the layering peak does not originate from shifts in single molecule degrees of freedom. In fact, the simulated deposited and bulk glasses show largely the same single-molecule conformations. Interestingly, a one-site coarse-grained liquid with isotropic interactions develops a comparable interfacial layering signature. These results indicate that layering in α,α-A arises primarily from collective density correlations generated at the free surface during deposition rather than from conformational bias or orientational ordering. The findings connect structural anisotropy in vapor-deposited molecular glasses to the generic interfacial organization of simple liquids. I Introduction Organic light-emitting diodes (OLEDs) are critical components in modern phones and consumer electronics. Small organic molecules, which transfer negative and positive charges to the emissive layer, are used to create electron and hole transport layers in OLEDs.[22] This charge transport is governed not only by the single molecule electronic structure but also by the alignment of molecules relative to each other, where strong alignment can facilitate orders of magnitude increases in charge transport fluxes.[52, 19] Strong molecular alignment often manifests as anisotropy, or the dependence of the structure and performance on the direction of the material. Thus, understanding the fundamental physics driving this anisotropy could be used to more effectively engineer OLEDs. Physical vapor deposition (PVD) is a popular method to produce anisotropic glass films with enhanced electronic properties.[32, 16] In PVD, evaporated molecules are deposited onto a heated substrate (T [FORMULA] ). The presence of this substrate has also been connected to orientational order in films made of nonspherical molecules[18, 19, 33] and even phase separation.[1] The process leaves a heated free surface exposed to vacuum, where the molecules can re-organize differently than in the bulk.[5] Simulation work has shown that layers can form at the free surface[21] and that the orientation of nonspherical molecules is a feature of equilibrium supercooled liquids,[12, 7] suggesting that anisotropic order could arise from equilibrium effects that are buried during deposition. Hence understanding the general trends in how molecular shape and deposition conditions affect the resulting structure of the film has been a central goal of the field.[16, 6, 53] Still, much of this work still does not explain the formation of layered structures in near-spherical molecules, which do not exhibit the orientational preferences seen in highly-anisotropic glass formers. Here, we combine experiment and simulation to investigate the deposited structure of a model isotropic glass former, 9-(3,5-di(naphthalen-1-yl)phenyl)anthracene (α,α-A), [FORMULA] K, shown in Figure 1. This molecule possesses equal length and width, but the steric repulsion of the large aromatic groups produce frustrated intermolecular interactions. Photoluminescence experiments have shown that this molecule behaves isotropically.[31] However, in PVD films of α,α-A spherical ellipsometry[31] and grazing incident X-ray scattering experiments reveal optical anisotropy[53], showing that birefringence can be due to orientation effects or due to packing in the process of PVD. We seek to determine how the intramolecular degrees of freedom and center of mass ordering interact to create molecularly layered films. To do so, we analyze the structure of glasses deposited at different temperatures using grazing incidence wide angle X-ray scattering (GIWAXS), which provides nanometer level resolution of the experimental structure which we compare with molecular dynamics (MD) simulations at the all-atom and coarse-grained level. From these simulations, we compute how the interactions at different length scales contribute to the structure. Our results indicate that the layering of spherical molecules does not impose detectable shifts in the single molecule conformations, and that the total structure is well described by intermolecular correlations of the functional groups and liquid-like centers of mass ordering. We test this finding by comparing results against a highly-coarse-grained equilibrium model of the surface, and find surprisingly good agreement. This result extends previous understanding of the enhanced surface mobility of deposited glasses by identifying an underlying thermodynamic minimum based on a highly general liquid model. Next, we consider the contributions of the various molecular degrees of freedom to the total structure by using the structure factor of Equation (4). This equation is closely related to the X-ray scattering signal of the previous section but without the added complication of [FORMULA] -dependent atomic form factors. Using simulation data, we calculated the structure factor of various subsets of the atoms in the simulation. The resulting signal is shown in Figure 3, where we separate the simulation data into layered (a,b,c,d) and unlayered (e,f,g,h) sets. Simulations with a layering peak of at least 60% of the isotropic halo intensity are classified as layered. We calculated the total structure factor (a,e), the average single molecule structure factor (b,f), and the structure factor of the molecular centers of mass (c,g). The convolution of the single molecule and center of mass structure factors is an approximation of the total structure factor that neglects the correlations between the conformations of neighboring molecules. In other words, it represents a structure with the same center of mass positions but with noninteracting molecules. The difference between the total structure factor and the noninteracting convolution we term the “molecular interaction” structure factor, shown in Figure 3(d,h). This is the excess correlation arising from the interactions between nearby molecules. The isotropic halo of the total structure factor comes from the correlations between molecules. The observation that the halo in the single molecule structure factor in Figure 3(b,f) is at a larger length scale (0.9 Å-1) than the molecular interaction halo in Figure 3(d,h) (1.2 Å-1) indicates that the functional groups of neighboring molecules approach closer to each other than the groups on the same molecule (Figure 3(b,f)). We also observe that the halo in the total structure factor (1.2 Å-1, Figure 3(a,e)) matches that of the molecular interactions. This suggests that the molecular level structure is based on the interlocking of the molecular functional groups, rather than each α,α-A molecule taking up their own roughly spherical volume and interacting at the edges of their spheres. This implies that a key barrier for relaxation is the steric frustration of the enmeshed structure. In addition, the isotropic halo in the experimental GIWAXS signal corresponds to this length scale, especially Peak 3 (1.14 Å-1, Figure 2(b)), and would therefore appear to be a direct experimental probe into the tangled structure of the film. Comparing the layered and unlayered structure factors, the single molecule (Figure 3(b,e)) and molecular interaction structure factors (Figure 3(d,h)) are similar between them. The layering signal arises entirely from the ordering of the centers of mass (Figure 3(c,g)). It may be intuitive to suppose that layering would be accompanied by a change in single molecule conformation or orientation. Perhaps layering accesses an entirely different, more stable molecular level organization. Indeed, for nonspherical molecules, layering is strongly associated with the onset of ensemble level orientational order. [33, 50, 17, 12] For α,α-A however, we observe no such trend, which would appear as an anisotropic signal in the single molecule structure factor. The lack of orientational order also agrees with evidence from spherical ellipsometry measurements of α,α-A,[31, 53] which implies the layering mechanism is at a larger length scale. It also suggests that the molecular degrees of freedom could be accounted for in a simplified isotropic effective interaction. This interpretation is also supported by the use of machine learning molecular descriptors, see Section IV in the supplementary material. Given the significance of the equilibrium interfacial liquid identified in the literature[41, 2, 7] and the results of the all-atom structure factor analysis, we consider a simplified coarse-grained model where each molecule is represented by a single isotropic bead. This approach differs from the coarse-graining approach most commonly used in the field, where a small number of beads are used to roughly approximate a molecule’s shape.[2, 12, 50, 33, 53] We justify the complete neglect of molecular shape by appealing to the isotropy of the single molecule and molecular interaction structure factors (Figure 3(b,d,f,h)). Determining the optimal coarse-grain interactions for a given system is a complex and open problem. However, as we are interested in more general physical trends, we avoid this problem by simply choosing a pairwise Morse potential for our particles due to its softness and use in highly coarse-grained systems. [55, 28, 11] This simplified model potential is meant to probe the applicability of general liquid physics to the deposited α,α-A glass, rather than the role of specific features of the molecule. For our simplified equilibrium model, we therefore simulate a Morse liquid of 25,000 particles exposed to vacuum at the each interface (see Section V.3 in Methods). The comparison between the one dimensional structure factors for the centers of mass from the all-atom simulation and the particles in the Morse simulation, shown in Figure 4(b), shows that the Morse liquid structure factor is more strongly peaked than that of the atomistic centers of mass. The Morse potential in this case is more repulsive at short distances than the actual effective interaction. The intensity plots of Figures 4(c,d) reveal the presence of the layering peak in the all-atom and Morse liquid simulations. A discrepancy between the two simulations is the prominence of the isotropic halo in the Morse liquid. This halo represents the underlying bulk liquid ordering, which corresponds to the oscillations of the radial distribution function seen in liquids. A similar feature can be observed in the all-atom structure factor although much fainter and broader, indicating liquid-like ordering is weaker in the all-atom system. The short range repulsiveness of the Morse potential leads to the narrowness of the halo in the liquid and the presence of many particles in the bulk below the surface increases the relative signal of the bulk structure. Importantly, that we observe a strong layering peak even with a simple untuned potential is strong evidence that the center of mass ordering of a deposited glass film comes from a more general phenomenon of simple liquids. To understand this phenomenom in the simplified model, we consider the temperature dependence of the structure factor peaks from the coarse-grained equilibrium model in Figure 5. The peak corresponding to ordering in the bulk (green), which arises from the isotropic ordering of the Morse liquid far from the surface, shows no temperature dependence over the examined range. In contrast, the layering peak (blue) is strongly dependent on the temperature. This peak corresponds to the liquid structure at the surface, and moves to lower wavevector magnitudes as the temperature increases. Figure 5b shows the relative intensity of the layering signal with respect to the bulk signal decays exponentially with temperature. The shift of the layering peak to longer length scales and the decrease in intensity indicates the breakdown of the layered structure at high temperatures, with only the bulk liquid structure commonly associated with liquids remaining. This temperature dependence in the Morse model suggests that the high temperature sensitivity of vapor deposited glasses may similarly correspond to the sensitivity of the underlying equilibrium simple liquid surface. III Discussion Our results suggest that layering in PVD glass films is the result of the molecular center of masses interacting as an equilibrium liquid. We demonstrate that a simple equilibrium coarse-grained model is able to replicate key features of the all-atom simulation (Figure 4) and demonstrate a surface structure highly sensitive to temperature (Figure 5). We propose, based on structure factor analysis of the all-atom simulation data (Figure 3) and experimental GIWAXS data (Figure 2) that the molecular interactions are mediated by the flexible aromatic groups of α,α-A resulting in a simple, isotropic effective potential. Therefore we conclude that the layering in α,α-A deposited films is closely related to a general equilibrium phenomenon of simple liquids and this effect is likely general to other molecular PVD films. Our results build on previous work concerning the origin of the anisotropic structure and increased stability of PVD glasses. Enhanced mobility has long been used to explain PVD glass’s enhanced stability,[43] although it has been observed that greater surface diffusion does not necessarily lead to more stable glasses, such as in α,α-A [38] or in polymeric glasses.[10] The equilibrium surface has been empirically connected to molecular layering,[41] although the reason why this kind of center of mass ordering is the relevant thermodynamic minimum across a wide variety of molecular glasses has not been elaborated upon. Our results suggest that the liquid-like ordering at the surface is a prominent thermodynamic driving force for many small organic glass formers. We expect these results to be applicable to PVD glasses with mostly spherically shaped molecules, with deviations expected when effective interactions become directional, such as with molecular anisotropy or strong intermolecular interactions [48, 35]. Thus, while the layering effects in isotropic molecules parallel those of non-spherical molecules, the causal mechanism differs. IV Conclusion In this study, we combined grazing-incidence X-ray scattering with atomistic and coarse-grained simulations to identify the microscopic origin of the molecular-scale layering in vapor-deposited α,α-A. Our analysis separates translational layering from molecular orientation and intramolecular conformation. We find that the experimentally observed anisotropic structure factor feature is primarily associated with intermolecular center-of-mass correlations and does not require orientational or conformational ordering. Our results are consistent with previous work showing that the unique properties of the deposited glass arise from surface equilibration and subsequent burying, with the temperature sensitivity coming from the careful balance of surface mobility and thermodynamics.[45, 4, 37] The various features of molecular layering have become well understood in recent years, but the molecular organization within the film and its origin has remained unclear. Our work provides evidence that molecular conformations and interactions need not significantly change from bulk behavior to allow for layering. This work suggests that the intramolecular degrees of freedom mediate simple interactions between the molecules and that the layering of α,α-A is a result of the molecular centers of mass behaving as an equilibrium simple liquid at the surface. This finding suggests that the physical driving force of glass morphology entails a competition between surface effects (which would favor layering) and the frustration of local molecular interactions. This finding can motivate further experimental exploration of superconductivity in hydrogen intercalated TMDs through ionic-liquid gating or alkali co-intercalation. I Introduction Transition-metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) are layered materials with chemical formula MX2, where M is a transition metal (e.g., Ta, Nb, Mo) and X is a chalcogen (S, Se, or Te). Each layer consists of covalently bonded X–M–X atoms, with adjacent layers coupled by van der Waals interactions. TMDs occur in a variety of structural polytypes that differ in both the local coordination of the metal atoms and the stacking sequence of the layers. In particular, the notation 1H denotes a single layer with trigonal-prismatic coordination. In the bulk 2H polytype, these layers are stacked in an AA’ sequence, with successive layers rotated by [FORMULA] radians relative to each other. This stacking restores inversion symmetry in the bulk, which is absent in the isolated monolayer. Owing to their interplay of electronic, structural, and optical properties, TMDs have become a promising material class for studying correlated quantum phases [59, 36, 57, 13, 62]. In this work, we focus on the 2H polytypes of TaS2 and NbSe2, two prototypical TMDs in which charge-density-wave (CDW) order coexists with superconductivity [59, 36]. TaS2 and NbSe2 are known to crystallize in several polytypes, including 1T, 2H, 3R, and 6R, whose distinct electronic properties arise from differences in coordination and interlayer stacking [29, 41, 58]. These materials provide a useful platform for studying the interplay between charge-density-wave (CDW) order and superconductivity because both phases are highly sensitive to dimensionality, stacking, and external perturbations. Alternative stacking sequences can significantly modify the balance between CDW order and superconductivity, as demonstrated in 6R-TaS2 and related phase-engineered compounds [2, 61], while external stimuli such as pressure can likewise induce substantial changes in the superconducting state [28]. NbSe2 has become a model system for investigating the evolution of intertwined CDW and superconducting orders from the bulk crystal to the monolayer limit [55, 64, 14], while comparative studies across the 2H-TMD family have established that the nature of the CDW state depends strongly on dimensionality [33]. Importantly, both 2H-TaS2 and 2H-NbSe2 exhibit CDW ordering vectors along the [FORMULA] –M direction of the Brillouin zone, with [FORMULA] in 2H-TaS2 [30] and 2H-NbSe2 [35]. This related ordering vector and the broader similarities in their electronic structures provide a consistent basis for comparing calculations and assessing how external perturbations modify competing ordered phases. In bulk 2H-NbSe2, the transition temperatures are [FORMULA] K and [FORMULA] K for superconductivity, whereas bulk 2H-TaS2 has a lower superconducting transition temperature of [FORMULA] K [58]. The sensitivity of these competing phases to structural and electronic tuning is evident across different dimensional limits. In monolayer TaS2, [FORMULA] increases to [FORMULA] K [42], while in monolayer NbSe2 the CDW onset temperature rises to [FORMULA] K and [FORMULA] is reduced to [FORMULA] K [55]. Beyond dimensionality alone, the phase balance can be manipulated through carrier-density control and chemical modification. Chemical co-intercalation [63, 34], electrostatic gating [46, 60], and intercalation [32, 9, 10, 45, 53] have all been shown to alter the competition between CDW order and superconductivity, while experimental studies on related TMD systems further highlight the important roles of disorder and electron–phonon coupling in stabilizing these phases [11]. Together, these studies establish 2H-TaS2 and 2H-NbSe2 as particularly suitable model systems for investigating how intercalation-driven electronic and structural modifications reshape the CDW and superconducting ground states. Hydrogen is a particularly attractive intercalant because its small size allows access to coordination environments that are unavailable to heavier atomic species. Hydrogen insertion changes the carrier density through charge transfer to the host layer and also reshapes the local chalcogen coordination around the transition-metal site. In hydride compounds, this combination is associated with record superconducting critical temperatures, such as [FORMULA] K in H3S [16] and [FORMULA] K in LaH10 [17, 51] at pressures of [FORMULA] – [FORMULA] GPa. In this work, we propose that layered TMDs provide a complementary route for introducing hydrogen in an ambient-pressure setting, in which H occupies interstitial sites of a structured host. Among the most recent developments motivating this work are the reports that gate-driven hydrogen intercalation can strongly alter the CDW order in TMDs and induce superconductivity. In particular, protonation of 1T-TiSe2 by ionic-liquid gating was shown to induce superconductivity with [FORMULA] K, while the CDW anomaly in the resistivity is suppressed to about 1% of its pristine intensity and the CDW onset temperature remains essentially unchanged [47], with NMR pointing to an inhomogeneous, disorder-driven CDW state in the protonated samples [48]. Notably, the accompanying first-principles calculations indicate that at about one H atom per formula unit, hydrogen acts beyond rigid-band electron doping and partially fills the Ti- [FORMULA] band, mimicking the band filling of superconducting Nb-based 2H TMDs such as 2H-NbSe2 [47]. This points to the 2H polytype as a natural host for H-driven superconductivity, further motivating our choice for this material. More generally, the weak van der Waals coupling between adjacent TMD layers provides a natural environment for intercalation, enabling guest species to occupy the interlayer space while preserving much of the host lattice. Likewise, in situ molecular intercalation has very recently been found to enhance [FORMULA] in 2H-TaS2 devices [44]. Together, these advances establish hydrogen-based intercalation as a potential route to engineer the competition between CDW order, semiconducting behavior, and superconductivity in layered TMDs. What remains unresolved, however, is the microscopic structure-property relation in the 2H hosts: which interstitial sites H preferentially occupies in 2H-TaS2 and 2H-NbSe2, which concentrations are thermodynamically and dynamically viable, and how site-selective H incorporation reshapes the electronic structure and superconducting response. To address these questions, we first identify and classify the distinct interstitial environments available to hydrogen in the 2H structure, and then determine which of them remain favorable upon relaxation and at increasing H concentration. This establishes the structural and thermodynamic landscape on which the electronic reconstruction must be understood. We next examine how the stable configurations modify the pristine band filling and lattice dynamics, in particular whether hydrogen suppresses the CDW instability by simply shifting the Fermi level into the pre-existing gap or by producing a more substantial reorganization of the host states. Finally, having identified which H arrangements are semiconducting and which retain metallicity, we evaluate their superconducting properties and use carrier doping to assess whether intercalation can provide a route toward enhanced [FORMULA] in 2H-TaS2 and 2H-NbSe2. Quantum dynamics of ultrasmall magnetic skyrmions in atomic-defect landscapes Magnetic skyrmions are prime candidates for future information technology, and their fate in devices is settled by the defects they encounter. In ultrathin films, skyrmions can be as small as a couple of nanometers, carrying only a few tens of magnetic moments, while atomic defects reshape their energy landscape on the atomic scale. Here, we demonstrate that such ultrasmall skyrmions can behave quantum mechanically and that their quantum dynamics is unusual. Since the gyrotropic force dominates, the two coordinates of a ferromagnetic skyrmion are canonically conjugate and the skyrmion behaves as a particle in the lowest Landau level of an effective magnetic field, with a magnetic length of 0.6 Å. Utilizing skyrmion-defect interaction profiles of Cr and Fe adatoms and dimers in PdFe/Ir(111), obtained from atomistic spin simulations parametrized from first principles, we unveil quantized gyrotropic orbits with level spacings of 20–85 [FORMULA] eV, bound not only by pinning defects but also, counter-intuitively, by repulsive ones. Saddle points of the energy landscape act as quantum beam splitters for skyrmions, and quantum depinning reaches rates of 1–100 Hz below the critical current. Embedded impurities, in contrast, bind the skyrmion so strongly that it ceases to behave as a rigid particle, defining a strong-coupling regime. For the Gilbert damping typical of ultrathin films, the quantized levels remain well resolved. The thermal-to-quantum crossover lies between 40 and 160 mK, which is within reach of millikelvin scanning tunneling microscopy, where tip-induced escape statistics and electron spin resonance STM can reveal the quantized gyrotropic motion of skyrmions pinned at defects crafted atom by atom. I Introduction Magnetic skyrmions [1, 2] are non-collinear spin-textures with particle-like properties, which are under intense scrutiny for their potential as bits of information in future spintronic devices [3, 4]. Their nucleation, motion and stability are, however, strongly affected by material inhomogeneities, which are ineluctable in any device [5, 6, 7, 10, 8, 9]. In this context, PdFe/Ir(111) became a playground of choice, since single skyrmions of a few nanometers can be written and deleted with a scanning tunneling microscope (STM) [5]. From first principles, it was established that single [FORMULA] and [FORMULA] atoms, either embedded in the Pd overlayer by substituting a Pd atom (inatoms) or deposited on top of it (adatoms), pin or repel skyrmions, following a universal M-shaped dependence on the [FORMULA] -band filling reminiscent of the cohesive energies of transition metals [10] (see also Refs. [11, 12] for MnSi and Co/Pt(111)). Building multi-atomic defects atom by atom enriches further the energy landscape, which can host off-centred minima and even coexisting pinning and repulsive domains [13]. Upon application of a current, the skyrmion experiences a gyrotropic motion, clockwise around pinning defects and counter-clockwise around repulsive ones [14]. All of these investigations treat the skyrmion as a classical object, and so does the rich body of work on pinning, depinning and creep reviewed recently in Ref. [9]. Thermally activated hopping and creep were described utilizing stochastic Thiele equations [15, 16] and observed experimentally [17, 18]. In contrast, the quantum regime remains largely unexplored. Interestingly, the skyrmions under scrutiny are ultrasmall, with a diameter of about 2 nm and only a few tens of Fe moments, while the skyrmion-defect interaction profiles vary on the scale of a few Ångström. A natural question arises then: is the motion of such a skyrmion still classical, or does its position acquire a quantum-mechanical nature? Quantum aspects of skyrmions were mostly addressed with model potentials. For example, the quantized motion of a skyrmion in a pinning well [19, 20], its quantum depinning out of an impurity potential [21], the collapse of skyrmions [22, 23], quantum skyrmion liquids and frustrated quantum magnets [24, 25], as well as skyrmion qubits based on the helicity degree of freedom [26, 27, 28]. However, the connection to realistic defects with a well-defined chemical nature, which can be designed and manipulated atom by atom, is terra incognita. The key to the answer lies in the gyrotropic (Magnus) force entering the Thiele equation [29]. In contrast to a massive particle, the dynamics of a ferromagnetic skyrmion is dominated by this force, which acts as a Lorentz force on a charged particle in a strong magnetic field. Quantum mechanically, the skyrmion is thus a particle living in the lowest Landau level (LLL). It has no kinetic energy, and the energy landscape generated by the defect becomes its Hamiltonian. This has three remarkable consequences, which define the backbone of this work: (i) the skyrmion can be bound by repulsive defects as well as by pinning ones; (ii) at saddle points of the landscape, an incoming skyrmion is split into two outgoing paths, similarly to an electron at a quantum point contact; (iii) close to the depinning threshold, the skyrmion escapes from a pinning centre by tunneling in phase space rather than through a barrier. These three regimes are illustrated schematically in Fig. 1. Here, we develop this picture and combine it with the skyrmion-defect interaction profiles of PdFe/Ir(111) obtained from reported first-principles-based investigations [10, 14, 13]. After introducing the theory in Sec. II and the energy landscapes in Sec. III, we address the quantized gyrotropic orbits in Sec. IV, the saddle points in Sec. V and the quantum depinning in Sec. VI. Possible experimental signatures are discussed in Sec. VII before concluding. We note that Lin and Bulaevskii [19] quantized the skyrmion motion in a model pinning well, while Psaroudaki and Loss [21] predicted the quantum depinning of a skyrmion out of a model impurity potential, with a crossover temperature of about 20 mK. In contrast, we consider realistic wells, hills, ring-like wells and saddle points, anchor the energy scale to atomistic dynamics and establish the link to defects already explored theoretically and experimentally. VII Experimental signatures PdFe/Ir(111) is an ideal platform. Skyrmions can be written, deleted, pinned and moved with STM tips [5, 6], and the experiments of Ref. [6] already demonstrate the main ingredients required here. Inlayer defects pin skyrmions at well-defined off-centre positions, single Co adatoms are almost inert, in line with first-principles predictions [10], while Co clusters pin skyrmions strongly enough to drag them across the surface upon lateral manipulation of the cluster. These experiments were, however, performed at 4.2–8 K, an order of magnitude above the crossover temperatures of 40–160 mK found here, which explains why only classical pinning has been observed so far. Dilution-refrigerator STM is therefore required. We note that the quantum depinning of a related magnetic soliton, the vortex core in permalloy disks, has already been observed experimentally [43]. The Heisenberg-model landscapes were obtained at 10 T for a skyrmion of about 3 nm [13]. It is the size of the skyrmion, rather than the field itself, that determines the curvature of the landscapes, and this size corresponds to experimental skyrmions at about 1–1.5 T. Our estimates therefore apply to the lower part of the experimental field range. Treating the defect as a local perturbation of the exchange or of the anisotropy, as done in Ref. [6], our effective model shows that the curvature of the landscape increases by a factor 1.7–3.3 when the skyrmion shrinks from 3.9 to 1.6 nm, i.e. when the field is raised from 1 to 3 T. Quantum effects are therefore enhanced at the highest fields compatible with isolated skyrmions, around 3 T, where the level spacings and crossover temperatures of Table 1 could increase by up to about a factor of two, and where the magnon gap of about 1 meV freezes magnon-mediated damping. Within STM, the tip itself offers also an elegant possibility. The local exchange and stray fields of a spin-polarized tip, as well as the tip height, tilt the energy landscape in a controlled fashion, while dragging a cluster [6] displaces the pinning potential itself. The escape of the skyrmion from its pinning site, or its switching between two neighboring minima, can then be monitored as telegraph noise in the tunneling current with the tip parked at low bias; noise spectroscopy has already proven to be a sensitive probe of skyrmion motion [44]. Rates of 1–100 Hz, as found in Sec. VI, are ideal for such time-resolved measurements. Above [FORMULA] , the switching rate follows the Arrhenius law of thermal activation, as expected from stochastic Thiele equations [16] and observed for skyrmion creep [17]; below [FORMULA] , it becomes temperature independent, which is the most robust signature of quantum motion. Electron spin resonance STM (ESR-STM) [45] offers a more direct, spectroscopic route, as also proposed for the readout of skyrmion helicity states [27]. The gyrotropic level spacings of the pinned skyrmion, 5–20 GHz for the adatoms and dimers of Table 1, fall precisely within the frequency window of ESR-STM. A radio-frequency voltage applied to the junction modulates the tip-induced potential and thus exerts an oscillating force on the skyrmion, driving transitions between neighboring orbital levels. Indeed, a uniform oscillating force [FORMULA] enters as [FORMULA] , and since [FORMULA] in an isotropic well, it couples only levels with [FORMULA] , with a Rabi energy [FORMULA] . A modulation of the tip-induced potential by 0.1 meV over 5 Å yields [FORMULA] eV, comparable to the linewidth [FORMULA] , such that the transitions can be driven efficiently. The resulting change of the time-averaged position of the skyrmion is detected through the spin-polarized tunneling current, similarly to the detection of the spin resonance of single atoms. Such a measurement would provide three pieces of information. First, the resonance frequency gives directly the curvature of the energy landscape, [FORMULA] , allowing a defect-by-defect test of the ab initio landscapes. Second, the linewidth measures the damping; with [FORMULA] –50, the resonance can be resolved in frequency sweeps. Third, the temperature dependence reveals the quantum regime. We note that for a harmonic landscape the quantum and classical gyrotropic frequencies coincide, as for any harmonic oscillator. The quantum nature manifests itself through the anharmonicity of the landscape: thermal occupation of higher orbitals shifts and broadens the resonance, and below [FORMULA] this shift and broadening saturate at their zero-point values. Two challenges should be kept in mind. ESR-STM has so far been applied mostly to atoms on thin insulating layers, and the coupling between the radio-frequency field and the skyrmion position on a metallic substrate remains to be quantified. Yet, the classical gyrotropic resonance of magnetic vortices is routinely excited by microwaves, and its skyrmionic analogue at the atomic scale would by itself constitute an important milestone. A skyrmion positioned on top of a repulsive defect would, in addition, survive for several orbital periods, with a lifetime settled by the damping rather than by the shape of the hill. All these experiments require reading the skyrmion position with sub-Ångström resolution without perturbing it. The spin-mixing magnetoresistance is helpful in this respect: at the vicinity of implanted defects it varies on the ångström scale, and early [FORMULA] impurities enhance the tunneling signal by up to about 350% [46], such that the defect pinning the skyrmion can also act as its position sensor. The choice of the bias voltage is, however, critical. At [FORMULA] V, where the non-collinear magnetoresistance is large, the injected electrons are energetic enough to write and delete skyrmions [6], whereas at a bias of a few mV even currents of tens of nA leave the skyrmion intact [6]. Low-bias detection with a spin-polarized tip, exploiting the tunneling magnetoresistance, is therefore preferable, and the tip–skyrmion interaction itself has to be accounted for as part of the energy landscape. Since the tip potential can reach the meV scale, it should be kept smooth on the scale of [FORMULA] and weak compared to the defect landscape, by working at large tip–sample distances; a controlled tip potential is, in turn, precisely what enables the tilt of the landscape discussed above. VIII Discussion and conclusions Our investigations bear some limitations, which define natural next steps. The energy landscapes were extracted from published maps, interpolated from a finite grid of skyrmion positions, which limits the accuracy of the curvatures; we quantified this uncertainty, which remains moderate except for the top of the Cr hill and the Cr saddle. Dense landscapes computed directly would sharpen our predictions, while a joint quantization of the position and of the internal modes would extend the theory to the strongly interacting embedded impurities found in ab-initio calculations. Finally, a first-principles evaluation of the damping of the skyrmion-defect complex would refine our estimates of the quality factor. Our findings also bear on the interpretation of geodesic nudged elastic band (GNEB) simulations [47], which are commonly utilized to evaluate energy barriers and lifetimes of skyrmions. We note that the barriers and wells discussed here are skyrmion-defect interaction energies, not the barriers for nucleation or collapse of the skyrmion. GNEB calculations remain, however, the natural input of our approach: the barrier height and the curvatures at the minimum and at the saddle point determine both the classical escape rate and the quantum exponent [FORMULA] of Eq. (11). Below the crossover temperature [FORMULA] , rates extrapolated from harmonic transition-state theory underestimate the actual escape rate, since the skyrmion tunnels in phase space instead of being thermally activated over the saddle point. Combining GNEB with the quantum treatment, as done for skyrmion collapse [23], offers a natural route to quantitative lifetimes at millikelvin temperatures. Our findings open appealing perspectives beyond PdFe/Ir(111). Magnetic nanostructures are not passive: the Cr dimer switches its spin chirality when approached by a skyrmion, and frustrated Cr trimers modify their non-collinear state [13, 48]. Moments following the skyrmion adiabatically contribute a Berry phase, which locally renormalizes [FORMULA] and thus [FORMULA] . Where adiabaticity breaks down, at the vicinity of such switches, the skyrmion becomes coupled to a discrete quantum spin, which could pave the way toward entangling the position of a skyrmion with a localized moment. In antiferromagnetic, synthetic antiferromagnetic or altermagnetic hosts, the gyrotropic force vanishes altogether. The skyrmion becomes then a regular massive particle, able to tunnel coherently between the two minima of a dimer. In frustrated magnets, the helicity of the skyrmion offers yet another quantum degree of freedom, which was proposed as the basis of skyrmion qubits [26, 27, 28]. Interestingly, defect engineering is required there to shape the double-well potential of the helicity [26]. We envision designed defects as a natural route toward skyrmionic two-level systems. To summarize, the gyrotropic force transforms a ferromagnetic skyrmion into a particle living in the lowest Landau level, with a magnetic length of 0.6 Å, and its defect-induced energy landscape into its Hamiltonian. For PdFe/Ir(111), we predict quantized gyrotropic orbits in both pinning wells and repulsive hills, with spacings of 20–85 [FORMULA] eV, saddle points acting as quantum beam splitters and quantum depinning at rates of 1–100 Hz below the critical current. Embedded impurities, which interact much more strongly with the skyrmion, define instead a strong-coupling regime in which position and internal modes have to be treated jointly. For the damping typical of ultrathin films, the quantized levels remain well resolved. The thermal-to-quantum crossover lies between 40 and 160 mK. The defects maximizing these effects can be crafted atom by atom, and tip-induced escape statistics as well as ESR-STM, at millikelvin temperatures and fields around 3 T, offer realistic routes to reveal them. Our work promotes atomic defects from inhibitors of skyrmion motion to building blocks of quantum skyrmionics.

Evidence for topological flat band magnetism in Co3Sn2S2 Correlations and topology are central pillars in the study of emergent electronic phases. Topological flat bands near the Fermi level unite these concepts, providing a route towards correlated topological phenomena and unconventional magnetism. Despite theoretical predictions, momentum-resolved observation of a topological flat band at the Fermi level has remained elusive. Using angle resolved photoemission spectroscopy, we observe a flat band at the Fermi level within the topologically non-trivial electronic structure of the magnetic kagome Weyl semimetal Co3Sn2S2. We further uncover a strong temperature dependence in which the flat band shifts across the Fermi level, accompanied by a reconstruction of the Fermi surface. Strikingly, this evolution occurs on the same temperature scale as previously reported anomalies in the magnetic response. Together, these results provide evidence for topological flat band magnetism in Co3Sn2S2, establishing a microscopic setting in which topology, electronic correlations, and magnetism become intertwined. To realise new quantum phases with potential device applications, a key step is to bridge electronic topology with strong electron correlations. Correlated electron systems have revealed rich physics including magnetism, Mott insulators, and unconventional superconductivity [1], while topological materials have introduced geometric concepts such as the Berry phase as foundational to electronic behavior [2]. Yet, to date, electronic correlations and Berry curvature driven band topology have largely been studied in isolation, limiting our understanding of emergent phenomena at their intersection. A promising route to unify these frameworks lies in topological flat bands [3, 4]. In such systems, electronic flatness coincides with non-trivial topology, strongly enhancing the density of states and interaction effects when the flat band approaches the Fermi level. This provides a route to correlated topological phases, including fractional anomalous quantum Hall states [5], fractional topological insulators [6], topological superconductivity [7], and, in magnetic systems, topological flat band magnetism. Magnetic kagome metals have emerged as leading candidates to realise this physics [3]. The kagome lattice naturally hosts flat bands through destructive interference in nearest-neighbor hopping models [8]. When combined with strong spin-orbit coupling (SOC), Dirac and band crossings near the K and [FORMULA] points are gapped, rendering the flat bands topologically nontrivial (Fig. 1(d)). However, topological flat bands reported to date reside well below the Fermi level, excluding them from low energy physics [9, 10, 11, 12]. The kagome system Co3Sn2S2 is a magnetic Weyl semimetal that combines strong electronic correlations, topologically non-trivial bands, and unconventional magnetic behavior [13]. Angle resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) and theoretical work established its ferromagnetic Weyl semimetallic character, sparking extensive experimental and theoretical interest [14, 13, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20]. Density functional theory (DFT) predicts flat band states, while scanning tunneling microscopy and optical studies have reported an enhanced momentum integrated density of states near the Fermi level consistent with flat band signatures [15, 16, 17]. However, direct momentum-resolved observation of a flat band at the Fermi level has remained elusive [14, 13, 18, 19, 20], leaving its possible connection to the unusual magnetic response unresolved. At the same time, differing ARPES observations concerning the role of SOC have complicated the interpretation of the low energy electronic structure. Here, combining ARPES with DFT and dynamical mean field theory (DMFT), we resolve an extended flat band at the Fermi level within the topologically non-trivial electronic structure of Co3Sn2S2. Calculations including dynamical electronic correlations reveal a pronounced renormalisation of the flat band states, highlighting the importance of correlations to the low energy electronic structure. Upon increasing temperature, the flat band shifts through the Fermi level, accompanied by a substantial reconstruction of the Fermi surface. Strikingly, this evolution occurs on the same temperature scale as previously reported magnetic anomalies. Together, these observations provide evidence for topological flat band magnetism in Co3Sn2S2, establishing a microscopic setting in which topology, electronic correlations, and magnetism become intertwined. Surface terminations and spin–orbit coupling. The Co3Sn2S2 kagome lattice system is realised through Co atoms decorated with non-magnetic Sn atoms (Fig. 1(a)). This magnetic kagome layer is sandwiched between hexagonal S and Sn layers, giving rise to two surface terminations (Fig. 1(c)), as previously observed with STM [15, 16]. We confirm this finding by presenting raster scan X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) measurements at the Sn core-level binding energy (Fig. 1(e, f)). Figure 2(c, d) displays the measured Fermi surface for each termination, using a photon energy [FORMULA] eV at [FORMULA] K. Photon energy scans presented in supplementary materials (SM; Fig. S1) verify that [FORMULA] eV corresponds approximately to the bulk L point [13, 18, 19]. In this geometry, bulk state contributions project onto the 2D Brillouin zone such that the T–W and T–U bulk directions map onto the [FORMULA] - [FORMULA] and [FORMULA] - [FORMULA] directions, respectively (Fig. 1(b)). The measured Fermi surfaces (Fig. 2(c,d)) confirm strong variation in spectral features depending on the surface termination [20]. This is consistent with orbital contributions inferred from prior [21] and our own Fermi surface calculations from DFT (Fig. 2(a,b)). Consistent with prior ARPES work [14, 13, 18, 19, 20], three point-like features are observed at the Fermi level around [FORMULA] , marking the edges of elliptical nodal line pockets (black arrows and dashed lines in Fig. 2(c,d)). Yet, the role of SOC in Co3Sn2S2 has been debated [18, 19]. Cuts through these features (Fig. 2(e,f)) resolve this by revealing a clear SOC-induced gap for Sn-terminated [19] surfaces but not for S-termination. This difference, based on different terminations, explains the prior conflicting reports [18, 19]. Another termination effect is the emergence of a large spectral gap ( [FORMULA] meV) centered around [FORMULA] eV on the Sn-terminated surface (Fig. 2(e), Fig. 3(d-f), Fig. 4(a-d)). Here, we employ the term ”spectral gap” to describe a region in which no band crossings are observed experimentally, whereas the calculated density of states (DOS) is small but non-zero. This spectral gap persists throughout the 3D momentum space (SM; Fig. S2), and is reflected in the calculated DOS (Fig. 4(i)). In contrast, this spectral gap is absent for the S-terminated surface. Flat band. Theoretical DFT calculations predict a flat band along the high-symmetry a-a direction (Fig. 3(a); SM Fig. S6). In agreement with this prediction, ARPES measurements taken at [FORMULA] eV on the Sn terminated surface along this direction (Fig. 3(d)) reveal a flat band near the Fermi level (Fig. 3(a)). Similar features are also observed on the S-terminated surface (Fig. S3(a)), suggesting that the flat band is not specific to a particular surface termination and is consistent with a bulk-derived origin. The presence of these bands is further emphasised in the second derivative plots shown in Fig. S3. This observation aligns with prior optical and STM studies that suggested the presence of flat bands in this system [15, 16, 17]. The characteristics of these experimentally observed bands are highlighted through a series of cuts near the Fermi level as a function of [FORMULA] (Fig. 3(b,c)). The resulting enhancement of the DOS provides a clear spectroscopic signature of flat band formation. The flat band exhibits a bandwidth of approximately 18 meV across the Brillouin zone, indicating that electron kinetic energy is strongly quenched due to destructive interference that suppresses wavefunction delocalisation. Experimentally, the band remains flat over an extended momentum range of at least 0.6 Å-1 (Fig. 3(b,c)), corresponding to roughly 75% of the Brillouin zone in this direction, even as its spectral weight diminishes near the Fermi level. We further confirm that the flat band extends along [FORMULA] (Fig. 3(f)), while similar flat band spectral weight persists over a photon energy range, corresponding to different [FORMULA] values (SM; Fig. S2). However, the experimentally observed intensity is not uniformly distributed: the flat band spectral weight appears in separated momentum patches that collectively cover about 50% of the Brillouin zone. To better understand this behavior in Co3Sn2S2, we compute the spectral function along [FORMULA] – [FORMULA] (Fig. 3(e)), incorporating both bulk and surface-state contributions. While the calculations qualitatively capture the overall band structure, particularly at higher binding energies, they significantly underestimate the extent of the flat band near the Fermi level. This discrepancy is consistent with a recent study showing that calculations for Co3Sn2S2 generally fail to fully reproduce experimental spectral features [22]. Such differences were attributed to the strong sensitivity of the surface electronic structure to local termination and disorder, which are not captured by idealized slab calculations. Nevertheless, the computed band (Fig. 3(a,e)) exhibits a small upward dispersion – similar to the observed flat band in other kagome systems [10, 12] – suggesting that portions of the experimentally observed flat band lie above the Fermi level. This dispersion combined with matrix element effects likely leads to the observed intensity distribution. The emergence of flat bands in Co3Sn2S2 is particularly intriguing in light of its established [13, 23, 20] topological character. Theoretical analysis [24] of the Chern number reveals that [FORMULA] -planes away from the Weyl nodes exhibit enhanced topological character with large Chern numbers ( [FORMULA] and [FORMULA] ) [24]. The flat band observed in our data is located within these topologically non-trivial regions of momentum space, placing it within the strongly topological low energy electronic structure of Co3Sn2S2. This conclusion aligns with transport measurements showing pronounced anomalous Hall conductivity arising from Berry curvature near Fermi level [25, 14]. Temperature dependence. With the flat bands established at the Fermi level, we next examine their temperature evolution. In Co3Sn2S2, magnetic order strongly influences the low-energy electronic structure through the exchange splitting and spin polarisation of states predominantly derived from Co- [FORMULA] orbitals. As the temperature increases toward the Curie temperature ( [FORMULA] ), the bulk magnetisation progressively decreases (Fig. 4(h)), reducing the exchange splitting and modifying the spin polarisation of states near the Fermi level. This evolution of the magnetic order is therefore expected to substantially reorganise the low-energy electronic structure. These effects are reflected in the electronic structure of Co3Sn2S2 (Fig. 4(a-e)), as revealed by temperature dependent cuts along [FORMULA] - [FORMULA] (Fig. 4(a-e)) on the Sn terminated surface. The flat bands progressively shift in energy and cross the Fermi level above [FORMULA] K (Fig. 4(a-d)), reflecting a total shift of about [FORMULA] meV. This shift is further illustrated by comparing the high temperature Fermi surface map with the low temperature constant energy surface at [FORMULA] meV (Fig. 4(f,g)). Even though the intensity is different, the surfaces are remarkably similar. Evidence of these shifts is also apparent in the EDC curves (Fig. 4(e), Fig. S4), where peaks near the Fermi level move above it while the incoherent background decreases, consistent with a rigid band shift rather than a loss of coherent peak intensity. These results are consistent with the contrast between the calculated ferromagnetic and non-magnetic electronic structures (Fig. 4(i,j)). This temperature induced band shift has two notable consequences. First, the electronic structure exhibits a clear Fermi-surface reconstruction, as evident from the high- and low-temperature Fermi surfaces (Fig. 4(g) and Fig. 2(d)). Second, the crossings of flat bands and nodal lines around [FORMULA] K correlate closely with previously reported magnetic anomalies [23, 26, 27]. Unlike nonmagnetic flat band systems, where temperature primarily induces thermal broadening or minor energy shifts [28], the flat band observed here shifts in energy. These results link the temperature dependent band reconstruction in Co3Sn2S2 to magnetic order, providing evidence for topological flat band magnetism at low temperatures. Electronic correlations. To further examine the role of electronic correlations, we performed bulk DMFT calculations including dynamical correlations of the Co- [FORMULA] states. Compared with the corresponding DFT calculation, electronic correlations lead to a narrowing of several low energy bands and a pronounced renormalisation of flat band features (Fig. S7). Spin- and orbital-resolved calculations further show that the calculated bands at the Fermi level are strongly spin-polarised and predominantly derived from Co- [FORMULA] states (Fig. S8). This close connection to the magnetic Co- [FORMULA] electronic structure, together with the correlation-induced band renormalisation, indicates that the low energy electronic structure is sensitive to both magnetic order and dynamical electronic correlations, consistent with the pronounced temperature-dependent band evolution observed experimentally in Fig. 4. Topological flat band magnetism. Magnetic probes, including neutron diffraction, bulk magnetisation, and muon spin relaxation, have reported anomalous magnetic responses in Co3Sn2S2 around [FORMULA] K [23, 26, 27], coinciding with a significant modification in the anomalous Hall conductivity [26]. However, the microscopic origin of these anomalies has remained unclear. Recent neutron and Mössbauer measurements identify a canted, noncollinear ferromagnetic state that persists throughout the magnetically ordered regime [29], further arguing against these anomalies originating from a transition between distinct bulk magnetic phases. Instead, our ARPES measurements provide a direct momentum–energy resolved perspective, revealing that these magnetic anomalies coincide with a reconstruction of the Fermi surface. The overall band shift evolves on the same temperature scale as the temperature dependent magnetisation, linking the observed reconstruction to magnetic order. Notably, this reconstruction involves the observed flat band crossing the Fermi level. Taken together with the correlation-induced renormalisation and strong spin polarisation of the flat band states revealed by our calculations, these observations provide evidence for topological flat band magnetism in Co3Sn2S2. They establish a microscopic setting in which topology, electronic correlations, and magnetism become intertwined through the energetic position of a flat band. Establishing whether the flat band itself drives the anomalous magnetic response will require experiments that controllably tune its energetic position while directly tracking the corresponding magnetic response. We construct its reparametrization invariant form and determine corresponding equations of motion. 1 Introduction and Summary Modified theories of gravity have been studied for many years for several reasons. One important reason is their potential phenomenological applications since they provide hints on how to solve current cosmological problems, as Hubble tension or mistery of cosmological constant. Another argument for studying modified theories is purely theoretical, since we would like to see whether it is possible to construct generalized theories of gravity whose structure is beyond the standard Enstein-Hilbert action [1, 2]. A famous example of modified theories of gravity is [FORMULA] gravity where an action is general function of scalar curvature [FORMULA] [3]. Another example of an interesting modification of gravity are Dirac-Born-Infeld inspired theories of gravity [4]. Lesser-known example of an alternative theory of gravity is the so-called Rastall gravity [5], where the basic premise is the denial of the presumption of conservation of matter stress energy tensor. Remarkably, this idea became popular in recent years with number of papers that discuss its phenomonological consequences, see for example [9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16]. This fact is even more remarkable when we think deeply about theoretical arguments for an existence of this theory. In more details, it was nicely discussed in [7] that it is very difficult to implement non-conservation of stress energy tensor since matter part of the action is diffeomorphism invariant and hence thanks to the Noether theorem stress energy tensor is conserved when the matter equations of motion are satisfied. On the other hand such a non-conservation of the stress energy tensor can be implemented at the level of gravity equations of motion when the relative coefficients between Ricci tensor and scalar curvature are changed. However then it was shown in [6] that Rastall gravity equations of motion can be rewritten into the form of General relativity equations of motion by simple rearrangement of the matter content of theory. Quantum superposition of Cosmic String spacetimes Since the quantum nature of spacetime is anticipated by a theory of Quantum Gravity, the possibility of spacetime superposition would be a natural consequence. This spacetime interference phenomena could bring us some clues about what effects could be expected over quantum fields and their interaction with matter. In this article, we investigate the effect of the superposition of a Cosmic String spacetime on the Unruh-De Witt detector. This is of interest as the spacetimes possess flat geometry but non-trivial topology. We analyze the effect of the interference of a Cosmic String with different topological charge over the Unruh-De Witt detector response function to vacuum fluctuations. We obtain some quantum interference effects, due to the superposition of spacetimes, which would be absent if a classical probabilistic mixture of spacetimes would be considered. In this manner, we obtain real physical consequences that would be indications of a Quantum Gravity phenomena. I Introduction Cosmic strings are topological defects that could arise in the early stages of the primordial universe. Many grand unification theory predict cosmic strings as a natural consequence. They form as vortices of the Higgs field that could appear after some symmetry-breaking phase transition [43, 16, 50, 65]. They have significant gravitational lensing properties and could be a primary source of ultrahigh frequency gravitational waves [59, 16]. Cosmic strings also provide a window into quantum gravity via string theory insofar as they could have been produced in the early universe and stretched to macroscopic scales [70], though there is no evidence of this at present. The quest for a definitive quantum theory of gravity is still an unfinished task. Although the two dominant proposals, string theory and loop quantum gravity, have led to very interesting results and new theoretical perspectives, a conclusive experimental-based verification is still lacking [4]. Indeed, obtaining a measurable quantum property of spacetime is a key objective for any theory of quantum gravity. From this perspective, indications of quantum gravitational phenomena in table-top experiments are an interesting line of research. This bottom-up approach embraces a phenomenological study of quantum gravity. By analyzing mesoscopic quantum systems and measuring microscopic gravity effects, this line of research aims at obtaining definitive results about the interplay between quantum theory and gravitation [15, 52, 9, 29]. Within this approach, we could implement an operational method to look for the implications of quantum gravity phenomena, as spacetime quantum superposition. A generic phenomenological expectation of any quantum theory of gravity is that of placing spacetime in a state of superposition, with the accompanying interference effects between the different spacetime states. Recently a method for investigating detectable signatures of spacetimes in quantum-controlled superpositions of different configurations was proposed [24]. This approach is grounded in quantum field theoretic methods in curved spacetime, and considers the evolution of a two-level system coupled to the quantum spacetime through its interaction with an ambient quantum field. It has subsequently been explored for its possible implications for the quantum nature of spacetime [15, 22, 24, 23]. Superposed black hole spacetimes have been of particular interest; UDW detectors were employed to obtain quantum signatures of black hole mass superposition, with results commensurate with an extension of Bekenstein’s conjecture [22]. Quantum interference due to the superposition of de Sitter spaces have also been studied [24], and even superpositions of flat Minkowski spacetime with different periodically identified dimensions, have been shown to exhibit non-trivial quantum intereference [23]. This approach offers a unique perspective in understanding the phenomenology of spacetime superposition [21, 3, 1], which has been considered in the context of generalizations of quantum reference frames [18, 30, 35], decoherence [7, 19], and indefinite causal structure [71, 33] and low-energy quantum gravity [10, 15, 14, 28]. To this end, in this paper we investigate the response of a model detector placed in a superposition of cosmic string spacetimes. Cosmic string spacetimes are locally flat and are characterized by a single parameter [FORMULA] , the linear energy density of the string [66, 34, 65, 5, 26]. They have very interesting non-trivial topological properties. The spacetime around a cosmic string is characterized by a deficit angle [66, 34, 5, 47]. The effects of this axial topological structure on quantum fields can be described using the method of images [44, 25, 32, 26]. In a cosmic string background, quantum fields can develop many interesting properties due to this non-trivial topology. For example, the quantum vacuum state can exhibit Casimir-Polder zero-point energy mechanical effects [44, 25, 11, 56, 32, 26]. An Unruh–DeWitt (UDW) detector probes the field two-point function and therefore provides an operational way to distinguish the cosmic-string vacuum from Minkowski vacuum; its transition probability differs from the Minkowski case even for inertial trajectories [64, 20, 62, 17, 12, 39]. Recently it has been shown that vacuum entanglement harvesting can be enhanced in a cosmic string background [55, 54, 53, 48, 41, 40, 37, 31, 38]. The effects of a superposition of cosmic strings will, amongsst other possiblities, be manifest in a quantum vacuum. Here we seek to understand the resultant observational signatures via UDW detectors and the subsequent implications for quantum gravity. We employ units [FORMULA] . I Introduction In spontaneous scalarization, a solution with vanishing scalar field becomes unstable once the coupling between the scalar and curvature (or matter) crosses a critical value. Nonlinear terms may then halt the growth and support solutions with a nonzero scalar field, although whether such branches exist, and whether they are stable, has to be established model by model. The mechanism was discovered for neutron stars in scalar–tensor theories [1] and later extended to black holes coupled to the Gauss–Bonnet invariant [2, 3, 4]; Ref. [5] reviews the subject. The linear onset is usually located by looking for a static solution of the scalar equation in which curvature acts as an effective mass. Such a zero mode marks a candidate bifurcation point, and the existence of a nonlinear branch must then be shown separately. Wormholes are a natural, if less explored, setting for this mechanism. Under the usual assumptions, traversable wormholes require matter that violates the null energy condition [6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12]. This alone does not force the Ricci scalar to be nonzero, but for the Ellis geometry it is, whereas it vanishes for the vacuum black holes of general relativity. Scalarized wormholes have already been built in Einstein–scalar–Gauss–Bonnet gravity [13, 14, 15]. We focus on the Ellis wormhole [16, 17]: smooth, free of horizons, ultrastatic, and asymptotically flat on both sides of the throat. Two of its properties single it out for Ricci-type scalarization. Its Gauss–Bonnet invariant vanishes identically (Sec. II), so the channel that scalarizes black holes is closed. Its Ricci scalar, by contrast, is negative everywhere and is fixed on shell by the trace of the supporting matter. The coupling [FORMULA] is therefore the wormhole analog of the coupling to the trace of stellar matter that scalarizes neutron stars [1]. The linear problem is that of a massless scalar with nonminimal coupling on the fixed Ellis background. Taylor showed that, for a class of wormholes that includes Ellis, the [FORMULA] -wave becomes unstable when [FORMULA] [18]. Quasinormal modes, scalar clouds, and the self-force on Ellis–Bronnikov geometries have also been studied [19, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24]. Of particular relevance here, Ref. [21] found that a minimally coupled scalar admits no smooth, localized linear clouds on this background. With a nonminimal coupling the situation is different. Smooth static clouds exist, but only at a discrete set of couplings that we compute exactly. Each of these thresholds marks the onset of a new unstable mode in the scalar sector; whether every threshold also gives rise to a branch of fully backreacted solutions is a separate nonlinear question. Three features of the problem allow us to go well beyond a generic test-field calculation. First, [FORMULA] enters the gravitational and matter equations only quadratically, so its linear perturbations around the scalar-free Ellis solution decouple from those of the metric and of the phantom field. The test-field spectrum is then the exact [FORMULA] sector of the full linear problem (Sec. IX). Second, the substitution [FORMULA] turns the radial equation into a trigonometric Pöschl–Teller problem. This yields the whole tower of thresholds, and, once the roles of coupling and frequency are exchanged, it also yields a compact Sturm–Liouville problem for the growing modes. Third, in that compact problem the threshold eigenvalues are isolated. The birth of each unstable mode can therefore be treated by ordinary perturbation theory, even though in the original variables the threshold sits at the edge of the continuous spectrum. Finally, the time evolutions support saturation for the initial data tested but are not a proof of global attraction or nonlinear stability. The Fluctuation–Dissipation Theorem and Dynamical Love Number in Schwarzschild Black Holes We study the real-time response of a Schwarzschild black hole in the Hartle–Hawking state to an external massless scalar field. Using a complexified radial contour to represent the Schwinger–Keldysh closed time path, we describe dissipation, thermal fluctuations and conservative tidal response within a common framework. Before performing tidal matching, we derive the equilibrium fluctuation–dissipation relation directly from the radial construction for every scalar multipole at arbitrary real frequency. In the low-frequency tidal expansion, we recover the known relation between the logarithmic running of the conservative dynamical Love coefficient at order [FORMULA] and the leading dissipative response at order [FORMULA] . We explain how the same leading absorptive coefficient enters both relations at low frequency and trace the unit coefficient of the running relation to the Schwarzschild horizon slope. In the Hartle–Hawking state, this common coefficient relates the logarithmic running directly to the zero-frequency thermal noise. Kubo–Martin–Schwinger analyticity determines the thermal noise from the dissipative response, whereas the near-zone radial equation and tidal matching determine the conservative logarithmic running. 1 Introduction A compact object placed in a slowly varying external field develops an induced multipole moment. Its linear response contains a conservative part, described at low frequency by static and dynamical Love coefficients, and a dissipative part associated with absorption Flanagan and Hinderer (2008); Rodríguez et al. (2026); Chakraborty and Pani (2026). The conservative static Love numbers vanish for four-dimensional Schwarzschild and Kerr black holes Binnington and Poisson (2009); Damour and Nagar (2009); Charalambous et al. (2021); Kehagias and Riotto (2025); Combaluzier–Szteinsznaider et al. (2026); Gounis et al. (2025). For the Schwarzschild scalar problem considered here, the leading nonvanishing response is absorptive and linear in frequency, while the leading conservative dynamical response appears at order [FORMULA] and contains logarithmic scale dependence. Causality and positivity arguments provide generic bounds on the tidal Love numbers of gravitating objects Kehagias and Riotto (2026a); Apostolidis et al. (2026); Kehagias and Riotto (2026b). In the worldline effective theory of compact objects, the conservative response is encoded in local worldline operators, while dissipation is described by correlation functions of internal worldline degrees of freedom. Their coefficients are fixed by matching to the full gravitational solution Goldberger and Rothstein (2006); Goldberger et al. (2021); Goldberger and Rothstein (2020); Rodríguez et al. (2026). Recent calculations have revealed a simple relation between the leading dissipative response and the logarithmic running of the leading dynamical Love coefficient of Schwarzschild black holes Charalambous et al. (2021); Perry and Rodriguez (2023); Ivanov et al. (2024); Combaluzier–Szteinsznaider et al. (2026). In the conventions used here, where [FORMULA] is the retarded tidal response kernel, [FORMULA] is the renormalization scale, and [FORMULA] is the Schwarzschild radius; see Ref. Rodríguez et al. (2026) for a review. At the order displayed, the left-hand side is determined by the leading horizon absorption, while the right-hand side extracts the logarithmic running of the conservative response. Dimensional analysis in systems with a unique scale allows their coefficients to differ by an arbitrary dimensionless number, yet for Schwarzschild that number is unity Combaluzier–Szteinsznaider et al. (2026). Related structures have been found at higher orders in the frequency expansion, where the most transcendental terms continue to display a close connection between conservative and dissipative response, although the relations become more intricate Caron-Huot et al. (2025); Combaluzier–Szteinsznaider et al. (2026). This has motivated the interpretation of (1) as a fluctuation–dissipation type correspondence Combaluzier–Szteinsznaider et al. (2026); Rodríguez et al. (2026). As already noted in Ref. Combaluzier–Szteinsznaider et al. (2026), however, (1) involves only the causal response. The genuine fluctuation–dissipation theorem concerns a different relation. In a thermal state it connects the dissipative part of the retarded kernel to the symmetric, or noise, correlator, where [FORMULA] is the inverse temperature. Unlike (1), this relation follows from the Kubo–Martin–Schwinger (KMS) condition Kubo (1957); Martin and Schwinger (1959) and is naturally implemented in a real-time formalism that keeps track of both response and fluctuations. One purpose of this paper is to derive (2) directly for a Schwarzschild black hole and to determine precisely how it is related to, and distinguished from, the running relation (1). To do so, we use the Schwinger–Keldysh closed-time-path formalism to describe the causal response and equilibrium fluctuations within a single generating functional Schwinger (1961); Keldysh (1965); Chou et al. (1985); Kamenev (2011). In the standard gravitational realization of this formalism, the two branches of the closed time path are represented by two Lorentzian segments joined to a Euclidean segment that prepares the thermal state Son and Starinets (2002); Herzog and Son (2003). An economical reformulation was developed by Glorioso, Crossley and Liu Glorioso et al. (2018). One complexifies the radial coordinate and lets its contour encircle the horizon. The two sides of the radial contour represent the two Schwinger–Keldysh branches, while the analytic continuation around the horizon implements their thermal relation. No independent boundary condition is imposed at the horizon beyond requiring a single analytically continued bulk field on the full contour. The construction also organizes the derivative expansion while keeping track of the horizon logarithms and their monodromy. We apply this construction to a minimally coupled massless probe scalar on a fixed Schwarzschild background in the Hartle–Hawking state. We express the finite-frequency problem in terms of exact ingoing and outgoing radial solutions, for which a Mano–Suzuki–Takasugi (MST) representation Mano et al. (1996) is available, and use a separate low-frequency expansion for tidal matching. Our first result is a direct contour derivation of (2) for the finite-radius Dirichlet kernels, valid for every scalar multipole and arbitrary real frequency within the quadratic field problem. The relation itself is guaranteed by the KMS property of the Hartle–Hawking state Higuchi and Lima (2022), and fluctuation–dissipation relations for black holes go back to Ref. Candelas and Sciama (1977); here it is obtained directly from the radial construction. At leading order in the low-frequency expansion, the tidal kernels inherit the same relation. The Bose–Einstein factor is generated by the monodromy of the radial solutions together with the imaginary Schwarzschild-time shift between the two branches. The KMS relation is therefore encoded in the analytic continuation defining the Hartle–Hawking contour. Our second result concerns the running relation (1). We show directly in the low-frequency radial problem, for every scalar multipole, that absorption and logarithmic running involve the same horizon amplitude of the static solution, while their ratio is fixed by the horizon slope [FORMULA] , with [FORMULA] the surface gravity. We want to determine the expectation value, in a specified quantum state, of the multipole moment induced on a black hole by an applied external field. For definiteness, the external field will be a massless scalar. Throughout the main text we consider an eternal Schwarzschild black hole in the Hartle–Hawking thermal state Hartle and Hawking (1976), working in the probe-field approximation and neglecting the backreaction of the thermal bath. Two features of the problem make the in–in formalism particularly appropriate. The first is causality: linear response is governed by a retarded correlator, whereas the in–out formalism naturally produces time-ordered correlators. The second is that the exterior region is an open system. Tracing over the inaccessible degrees of freedom gives reduced dynamics that need not be unitary. In thermal equilibrium, these dynamics exhibit both dissipation and fluctuations, which should be described within the same real-time framework.
