I Introduction Mandelstam introduced loop variables, the matrices that describe parallel transport along a curve for a given connection, as the basic objects of a path-dependent formulation of gauge theories and gravity [1, 2]. Yang [3] and Voronov and Makeenko [4] developed the idea further. On an open curve a loop variable depends on the curve and on the frames chosen at its end points. On a closed curve it defines the holonomy, whose conjugacy class does not depend on the frame. The trace of the holonomy, the gravitational Wilson loop [5], therefore carries frame-independent information about the global structure of spacetime. Holonomies are also the basic variables of loop quantum gravity [6, 7, 8]. Gravitational holonomies are known for Kerr [9], Schwarzschild–Droste [10], Taub–NUT [11], rotating black strings [12], black cigars [13], Friedmann–Robertson–Walker cosmologies [14], and spacetimes with topological defects [15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21]. In the Schwarzschild case Rothman, Ellis, and Murugan [10] found what they called band holonomy invariance: on certain circular orbits the holonomy returns to the identity after a finite number of turns. Gödel-type spacetimes [22] are an obvious place to look next. They are homogeneous and rotating, and they contain closed timelike curves (CTCs) [23]. Rebouças and Tiomno [24] showed that the homogeneous Gödel-type metrics form a family labeled by the ratio of the vorticity [FORMULA] to a curvature scale [FORMULA] . The family contains the original Gödel universe, a causal solution that is locally [FORMULA] , and, in the limit [FORMULA] , the Som–Raychaudhuri (SR) metric [25]. These geometries have reappeared in string theory [26, 27, 28, 29, 30], and their quantum mechanics is closely tied to the Landau problem [31, 32, 33, 34, 35, 36, 37, 38, 39]. They also appear as analog geometries. Chapline and Mazur [40] argued that a superfluid with a dense vortex lattice in rigid rotation is described on large scales by a metric of SR type. Transport in Gödel-type spacetimes has been studied before. Loop variables and Wilson loops in the Gödel universe were studied in Ref. The horizon boundary condition and exterior potential determine the wave response. At low frequency, the absorption cross section of a minimally coupled massless scalar approaches the horizon area [1, 2], while at high frequency the photon sphere determines the geometric capture cross section and its leading oscillatory correction [3]. In addition, the unstable circular null orbit sets the geodesic stability scale [4]. These limits provide useful checks on numerical wave computations. It is well-known that the partial wave method relates absorption to transmission probabilities and elastic scattering to phase shifts. Early calculations were carried out for Schwarzschild black holes [5, 6, 7], and a general treatment is given in Ref. [8]. Its applications to Reissner–Nordström (RN), Bardeen, and Hayward black holes have been described in [9, 10, 11, 12]. Charged dilatonic black holes have also been studied for scalar-wave scattering [13] and for both absorption and scattering in Einstein–Maxwell–dilaton theory [14]. Comparison with Schwarzschild and RN black holes have also been used to study scalar scattering by considering tidal (negative) charge [15]. The deflection function and backward glory approximation connect these wave calculations to null geodesics computation [16, 17]. On the other hand, regular black holes formed a distinct class in absorption and scattering studies. The Bardeen and Hayward models provided nonsingular black-hole solutions [18, 19], and later works surveyed and extended this class [20, 21, 22]. By contrast, the Bakopoulos–Nakas (BN) spacetime describes asymptotically flat black holes with scalar hair in Einstein gravity with a minimally coupled scalar and a reconstructed self-interaction potential. The original work has focused on static solutions, slow rotation, and axial perturbations [23], while exact black hole solutions were found with normal and phantom scalar fields [24]. The latter is considered as an very intereting black hole solution with scalar charge [FORMULA] . In this work, we investigate absorption and scattering in these two branches, which both may reduce to Schwarzschild solution when the scalar charge vanishes. For Frolov black holes, matching the critical or glory impact parameter with RN or Hayward black hole showed similar absorption and scattering patterns at intermediate and high frequencies [25]. Whether such a matching also captures the finite-frequency BN wave response is a main concern of the present work. We therefore wish to compare backgrounds at the same ADM mass, varying [FORMULA] and determining the corresponding horizon radius. Null geodesics and scalar partial waves are then used to compare the normal and phantom branches as well as to compare normal BN and RN black holes at independently matched capture and glory scales. Unitary implementability of Darboux transformations We investigate the unitary implementability of the canonical transformations corresponding to Darboux transformations in the Hamiltonian formalism recently developed for gauge invariant perturbations of nonrotating black holes. Starting from the formalism in the black hole interior, we demonstrate that these canonical transformations are unitarily implementable under general conditions on the effective potentials appearing in the master equations of the perturbations. We also show that the privileged massless Fock representation of the perturbative variables selected by admitting (Heisenberg) unitary dynamics, employed in our quantization, is not unitarily equivalent to the simple massless representation of the master variables satisfying the effective Regge-Wheeler equation. This highlights the importance of the choice of master variables in which the quantum representation is initially defined. Furthermore, we show that not all such choices of variables possessing unitarily implementable dynamics can be reached through Darboux transformations, but rather through more general canonical transformations. These results advance our understanding of the relationship between well-established classical relations in black hole perturbation theory and their quantum representations, explaining how isospectral Darboux transformations can be extended to include all the infinitely many possible values of the angular momentum such that they are unitarily implementable in a quantum field theory context. I Introduction Black hole (BH) perturbation theory offers a privileged and natural arena for exploring a vast range of phenomena, encompassing stability analyses to understand the fate of classical singularities (see e.g. Ref. [1]), response dynamics to small disturbances like infalling matter, nearby objects, or binary mergers, and gravitational wave observations, which bring BH dynamics into direct contact with experiment [2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]. Additionally, within this set of fertile fields to explore, one finds the compelling challenge of passing from classical to quantum descriptions of gravity [8, 9]. BHs are by themselves a canonical scenario to probe strong gravity regimes, where quantum geometry phenomena are expected to be relevant. Besides, given the nonlinear character of General Relativity, the separation of the background geometry and small fluctuations around it provides a more tractable setting than the full theory for investigating how gravitational degrees of freedom can be represented and quantized. Although this obviously does not solve the problem of quantum gravity, it isolates fundamental conceptual questions that can be addressed within a well-defined framework. On the other hand, it is well-known that if we describe perturbations of the geometry by metric perturbations, some of those perturbations correspond in fact to perturbative gauge degrees of freedom. Since the background spacetime and the perturbed one are distinct manifolds, one introduces a map to identify points on both manifolds and uses its pullback to compare the physical, perturbed metric with the background one. However, there does not exist a unique or privileged identification, which yields different expressions for the metric perturbations. Hence, an infinitesimal change of the identification map characterized by a vector field will result in a Lie derivative correction term of the first-order metric perturbation, that is essentially as small as the former, i.e. of the same perturbative order. Indeed, we can circumvent this issue by choosing a particular gauge and fixing this freedom [10]. But to prevent us from losing generality and to ensure that both our observables (once we move to the quantum realm) and our results do not depend on our choice, the most satisfactory approach is to work with perturbative quantities that are gauge invariants [10, 11, 12, 13]. They can be constructed by summing background-dependent combinations of the linear perturbative terms, and imposing that they have vanishing Poisson brackets with the relevant perturbative gauge constraints (at least weakly), obtained in turn by linearization of the perturbed diffeomorphism constraints of General Relativity11 1 In fact, these perturbative gauge constraints can be Abelianized (at the considered dominant perturbative order), simplifying all considerations [15, 16]. [14, 15]. Even though gauge freedom can be controlled in this way, the true physical degrees of freedom of the perturbations can still admit different descriptions in terms of different variables. Employing expansions in spherical harmonics, these gauge invariant variables can be identified with the coefficients of the expansions, and therefore be treated as fields in [FORMULA] dimensions [16] (with the dimensions of the spherical orbits of symmetry removed). These fields are usually called master functions, or master variables, and their dynamics are governed by evolution equations, called master equations, that can be written as (bidimensional) wave equations subject to a potential. Different choices of master functions imply distinct potentials. The Regge-Wheeler and Zerilli equations, respectively governing the Cunningham-Price-Moncrief (CPM) and Zerilli-Moncrief master functions, usually adopted to describe the axial and polar gravitational perturbations of the Schwarzschild spacetime respectively, serve as an illustrative example [10, 17, 18, 19]. Remarkably, although their potentials differ, the two equations (and the respective master functions satisfying them) are related by a Darboux transformation (DT) [20]. Moreover, the existence of this transformation ultimately impacts the associated spectrum of quasinormal modes [21], namely the complex-frequency solutions to the master equations such that they satisfy exterior boundary conditions of ingoing nature at the BH horizon and outgoing nature at spatial infinity [2]. Indeed, the DT ensures that the two related master equations present the same quasinormal frequencies when one considers any fixed value of the angular momentum in the spherical harmonics decomposition [22, 23, 24, 25, 26]. This property is referred to as isospectrality. An interesting avenue of research to investigate is whether this isospectrality persists when the classical background is replaced with an effective geometry that incorporates quantum corrections. Recent studies indicate that isospectrality may be broken within certain effective loop quantum BH models [28, 27], such as the widely studied Ashtekar-Olmedo-Singh model [29, 30, 31], if the potentials of the master equations are evaluated directly on the effective background without any further effective modifications. This calls for a deeper analysis, to understand whether the results are a mere artifact of the simple prescription used to implement quantum corrections effectively, or whether the reason for isospectrality breaking can be traced to a more fundamental, intrinsic feature of the quantization of the perturbations in the modified effective background geometry. Traditionally formulated at the level of master functions in a second-order formalism (like in Lagrangian formulations), DTs for BHs constitute maps from one differential equation governing the behavior of the perturbations, in principle in the BH exterior, to another equation of the same general type. This is achieved by transforming the perturbative variables and, consequently, the potential of its associated equation of motion, while establishing a correspondence between the solutions of the original and transformed equations, which reflects a subjacent mathematical symmetry between the two apparently different descriptions [21, 32, 33]. Hence, while two differential (master) equations seem different, their solutions can encode equivalent physical dynamics. However, it is important to mention that not every pair of different potentials is related by a DT; the potentials and transformation must satisfy specific consistency conditions, including a particular Riccati equation for the function defining the transformation, as we will later specify. Conversely, DTs can also be understood within a Hamiltonian approach as a distinguished class of canonical transformations [14, 16]. As a matter of fact, for this kind of approach, it is convenient to develop the theory in the interior of the BH, where the Hamiltonian evolution will truly take place in a timelike direction, with metric functions depending only on the parameter identified as the (interior) time coordinate, therefore simplifying the description. Consequently, the (Fourier) modes of the master functions will evolve dynamically in the interior [14, 15, 16]. To relate this Hamiltonian dynamics to the exterior description, we can write the background dependence of the perturbed system solely in terms of background phase space variables and introduce a suitable symplectomorphism, i.e. a complex canonical transformation, such that it connects the interior background geometry to the exterior background geometry of the BH. As shown, e.g. in Refs. [29, 30, 31, 28], it is remarkable that physical phase space functions such as the Hamiltonian remain real by means of their functions possessing an invariant range under this transformation or by passing from the positive real axis to the negative one. Thus, once in the exterior, where the roles of the timelike and radial coordinates are interchanged, we obtain a Hamiltonian interpreted as dictating the radial evolution of the system. In principle, the respective descriptions associated with different Fock representations in the BH interior can be extended to the exterior. In the present work, we will focus our attention on the quantum field theory obtained from the gauge invariant perturbations when the quantum corrections to the background are incorporated in an effective description for it. Classical backgrounds in General Relativity may be considered as a particular case in which no quantum correction is made. For this quantum field theory, a fundamental issue is the quantum equivalence of different representations when the infinite number of modes that compose the perturbations are taken into account. This includes the infinite possible positive integer values of the angular momentum label [FORMULA] of the spherical harmonic defining the mode. Prior to examining isospectral features between different choices of master variables, it is therefore essential to determine whether the transformation relating the two sets of variables can be implemented as an operator that respects the quantum equivalence of the resulting descriptions. Does a classical DT admit a unitary implementation in the quantum representation chosen for the gauge invariant perturbations, or can the choice to perform the transformation before quantization affect the resulting quantum theory? If the answer to the first question is in the negative, should one first perform the classical canonical transformation and then quantize the resulting variables, or should one quantize the original system? The order would not affect the physics if a unitary transformation exists between the quantum descriptions of the two Darboux-related variables, establishing them to be equivalent. Let us emphasize that, while for a system with finitely many degrees of freedom, the unitary implementation of a given canonical transformation is generally much less problematic or trivial, the situation is more subtle when considering gravitational perturbations which comprise an infinite set, and in particular an infinite number of different angular momentum values. Even if the transformation is well-defined as a unitary map for each (fixed) individual value of [FORMULA] , its implementation across the infinitely many [FORMULA] -modes is not guaranteed to be unitary [34, 35]. Thinking about the classical DT as a map that changes the perturbative (master) variables (or as a Bogoliubov transformation, if preferred, between the associated creation and annihilation variables) and that, correspondingly, changes also the form of the perturbative Hamiltonian and equations of motion, it is natural to wonder about the existence of a unitary operator implementing the transformation in the quantum realm when all possible modes are taken into account. Addressing this issue is therefore a primary concern when determining whether the classical freedom to choose different master variables persists after quantization as a freedom to change to alternative equivalent representations. On the other hand, some previous works [36, 37] argue that, in the present scenario of a nonrotating BH, a privileged family of equivalent quantum representations can be selected by respecting the background symmetries and by requiring unitarily implementable dynamics. By adopting one of these representations, the quantization can be claimed to be unique up to unitary equivalence. Moreover, the imposition of unitarily implementable dynamics in the form presented in Refs. [36, 37] allows us to split the field dynamics into a part corresponding to the Heisenberg (unitary) dynamics associated with the field and another part that can be addressed as contributions arising from the evolution of the background itself22 2 In this regard, the study of particle detectors provides an example of how these ideas can be applied, and in fact be beneficial, in curved spacetimes, as explored in Ref. [38].. In light of these considerations, the aim of this work is twofold. First, we demonstrate that canonical transformations associated with the DTs are unitarily implementable, even for effective backgrounds, so that the resulting quantum description is independent of whether the DT is performed prior to quantization or implemented at the quantum level. Our proof applies to a broad class of potentials that depend on the angular momentum label and exhibit asymptotic growth proportional to [FORMULA] for large [FORMULA] . We further assume that, with respect to their local dependence, the potentials are continuous within the analyzed regions of the BH (and bounded in the boundaries of the exterior, so as not to affect the boundary conditions on quasinormal modes). We also impose a well-motivated asymptotic requirement (for large [FORMULA] ) on a constant of motion appearing in the Riccati equation that determines the DT, and therefore the difference between potentials. Beyond these conditions, the proof is general and does not rely on any specific form of the potentials. In addition, we show that the privileged massless representation corresponding to master variables with unitarily implementable dynamics, while providing a representation also for the master variables on which the DTs act, is not unitarily related to the massless representation associated with this last set of variables, which is a different representation. Finally, the second objective of this work arises from a natural question: can every representation in the unitary family selected by the criterion of unitary dynamics and symmetry invariance be reached through a canonical DT? We will show that the answer is negative. The structure of this paper is organized as follows. In Sec. VI Conclusions The description of DTs as a set of canonical transformations in the Hamiltonian framework of nonrotating BH geometric perturbations opens a new avenue for investigating how a classical symmetry affects the quantum theory, concretely its representation, serving as a particular example. In the present work, we have taken the BH interior as our starting point. Since all elements in our analysis, including the gauge invariant perturbations, are expressed in terms of phase space variables, the extension of the quantum field theory to the exterior can be accomplished by introducing a symplectomorphism. Under the transformation the roles of the coordinates in Eq. (1) interchange. Since the variable [FORMULA] is proportional to the product of the two canonical background variables of the [FORMULA] -sector, and the Hamiltonian (of the background and the gauge invariant perturbations) depends on this sector only through [FORMULA] and even powers of [FORMULA] , the reality of these functions on phase space is preserved. For all Hamiltonian considerations, the complex symplectomorphism merely changes the domain of definition of [FORMULA] from positive to negative values. On the other hand, by adopting the so-called oscillator-adapted [FORMULA] variables, we were able to select a (unique) representation on the interior of the BH (when the background is classically or effectively described). This representation belongs to a family of equivalent representations in which the dynamics can be made unitarily implementable. We have then introduced a general canonical transformation to reach the so-called CPM variables, on which the DTs act naturally. We have demonstrated that, in the above unique family of Fock representations, the canonical transformations associated with this class of DTs are unitarily implementable under very mild assumptions. More specifically, our proof applies to a general class of potentials [FORMULA] that, similarly to what happens with the Regge-Wheeler potential [FORMULA] , grow asymptotically as proportional to [FORMULA] for large [FORMULA] , and differ from [FORMULA] by terms that are of the asymptotic order of [FORMULA] or negligibly smaller. This assumption covers a large set of potentials, including of course the Regge–Wheeler potential itself, and the Zerilli potential [14, 15, 16]. Our asymptotic condition on the difference of potentials comes from the requirement that the constant of motion [FORMULA] associated with the DT be asymptotically of order [FORMULA] or of a higher power, a condition much weaker than the most important physical example, namely the Chandrasekhar transformation, where this constant scales as [FORMULA] [16]. Although at certain stages we have referred to backgrounds in General Relativity to illustrate our discussion, all the calculations are valid for effective backgrounds if one evaluates the corresponding phase space variables and their dynamical derivatives on effective trajectories. This is achieved by computing Poisson brackets with the corresponding effective Hamiltonian. Such a Hamiltonian incorporates effective corrections that encode the influence of the physical phenomena departing from the classical Einsteinian theory. One interesting example is the effective description of loop quantum cosmology for BHs, for instance, for the effective geometries put forward in Refs. [29, 30, 31] to take into account loop quantum gravity effects. In this sense, it is worth commenting that, whereas the Hamiltonian formalism in the interior may find obstructions in the essential BH singularity of classical General Relativity, requiring a careful analysis if it is not excluded from within the interval of dynamical evolution, this singularity is solved in effective descriptions such as those of loop quantum cosmology [54], allowing a well-defined Hamiltonian treatment in the whole interior region, extending beyond the classical singularity. Moreover, since the extension of the Hamiltonian treatment of the perturbations to the exterior is accomplished by a change in the domain of definition of certain functions on the [FORMULA] -sector of phase space, as far as this change does not modify any of the arguments presented in our proof of unitary implentability of the DTs, the results about such unitarity should still hold when conveniently applied to the extended quantum field theory of the gauge invariant perturbations. A careful discussion of this issue will be carried out elsewhere [55]. In a certain sense, our results about the unitarity of the DTs are stronger than the well-known results in General Relativity about the equivalence of the physics described by the master functions and master equations that these DTs relate, which hold for each fixed value of the angular momentum [FORMULA] . These last results include, in particular, the equivalence of the spectrum of quasinormal modes in the exterior geometry, i.e. their isospectrality. This stronger nature of our unitarity results does not only reflect the aforementioned applicability to effective backgrounds, but also the remarkable fact that they refer to the entire set of modes with all possible values of [FORMULA] , and not just to modes with a given value of this angular momentum label. By studying the canonical map from the oscillator-adapted [FORMULA] variables to the CPM variables, we have also demonstrated that the choice of variables in which the representation is selected is important. As our proof shows, this map is not unitarily implementable by itself. So, for instance, making a massless representation choice in one or the other set of variables does not yield equivalent representations. Therefore, if unitarily implementable dynamics is sought, or used as the physical criterion to select a privileged quantization, the representation must be selected in the oscillator-adapted [FORMULA] variables and transported via the canonical map to the CPM variables. Another goal of this article has been achieved by showing that, within our preferred family of Fock quantizations, there exist unitarily implementable transformations (respecting therefore the unitary dynamics) that cannot be generated by any canonical DT. Thus, the family of DTs does not exhaust all the freedom in the choice of representations within the family admitting unitarily implementable dynamics. Crucially, our findings provide a rigorous theoretical justification for works such as Ref. [45], where a classical DT mapping between the axial and polar sectors was employed at the classical level without explicitly verifying its potential quantum implications. By establishing the unitary implementability of these maps, our results confirm that the effective master Regge-Wheeler equation derived in that work via hybrid loop quantum cosmology [56] methods remains robust, unaffected by quantum modifications arising from the relation between the potentials. This work paves the way for several future investigations. Among them is the possibility of exploring whether and how isospectrality can be extended to effective backgrounds. Having established that DTs are unitarily implementable in the representations considered here, and that this result is valid even for effective backgrounds provided that all phase variables and their derivatives are suitably evaluated on effective trajectories, it is natural to analyze in detail how this quantum-corrected effective description modifies the correspondence between Darboux-related potentials in General Relativity, and how isospectrality may be broken if such modifications are not incorporated [27, 28]. Finally, it would be worthwhile to investigate whether the procedure to select a unique representation that we have employed here can instead be formulated in terms of local geometric and canonical data, rather than relying on asymptotic properties of its dynamics in a suitably chosen description. For example, Ref. [57] explores criteria for characterizing physically appropriate representations in curved spacetimes directly from local data. Within the present framework, it would be interesting to investigate how these proposals transform under DTs, and whether they can be used to select the appropriate representation directly in the CPM variables.

The structured pseudospectrum of Schwarzschild black hole The non-Hermitian nature of black hole quasinormal modes (QNMs) can give rise to remarkable spectrum instability. Such instability is naturally characterized by the pseudospectrum for the operator. However, conventional pseudospectrum analyses permit arbitrary operator perturbations that may not correspond to physically admissible modifications. In this work, we introduce the structured pseudospectrum into black hole perturbation theory. We construct two physically motivated perturbation spaces based on effective field theory and the Rezzolla–Zhidenko parametrization, and get their structured pseudospectra using two distinct norms. Our numerical results show that imposing physical constraints substantially reduces the accessible spectrum instability, especially for higher overtones. More importantly, at sufficiently small perturbation scales [FORMULA] , the structured pseudospectrum around isolated QNMs exhibits approximately elliptical contours with preferred directions that depend on both the mode and the perturbation space, revealing an anisotropic structure beyond the familiar circular behavior of the conventional pseudospectrum. I Introduction When a black hole is perturbed, it relaxes back toward equilibrium through the emission of gravitational waves. In the linear regime, this relaxation is characterized by quasinormal modes (QNMs), whose frequencies form a discrete spectrum of complex-valued eigenvalues. The real part of each QNM gives the oscillation frequency, while the imaginary part governs the damping rate. These modes are fixed by the black hole background and by appropriate boundary conditions, typically purely ingoing waves at the horizon and purely outgoing waves at infinity. As distinctive spectral fingerprints of black holes, QNMs provide a powerful tool for testing the Kerr hypothesis and probing gravitational dynamics in the strong-field regime. This research framework is known as black hole spectroscopy [51, 6, 52, 7, 17]. Recent advances have increasingly highlighted the non-Hermitian (NH) character of the QNM problem. Since QNMs are defined by purely ingoing boundary conditions at the horizon and purely outgoing boundary conditions at spatial infinity, the resulting spectral problem is inherently non-Hermitian [4]. NH physics is characterized by the phenomena such as avoided crossings and exceptional points (EPs). In black hole perturbation theory, studies associated with EPs have drawn growing attention in recent years. Avoided crossings (ACs) near EPs can induce resonant excitation between QNMs [60, 53, 77, 64, 48, 78]. If sufficiently many parameters are available, the AC can be tuned to collapse into an EP. It is well known that, for a Kerr black hole where perturbations are described by Teukolsky equation, when quantum numbers [FORMULA] , [FORMULA] are fixed, the only parameter that can be varied is the reduced angular momentum. Consequently, a Kerr black hole can only exhibit the AC phenomenon [60, 53]. Therefore, the mass parameter of scalar [21, 22, 23], the positive cosmological constant [63, 71, 61], and the electric charge [24, 1] are considered into the Kerr black hole, and EPs are found accordingly. There are also many studies on EPs in the case of spherically symmetric spacetime. For the case in which a small bump is added to the effective potential, the investigations of EPs are carried out in [88, 14, 43, 64, 65, 59, 66]. In addition, there exists the study of the EP for the scalar QNMs of hairy black holes [27]. Modified QNM boundary conditions can also generate the EPs [82, 54]. The existence of thin spherical shells in spacetime can also lead to EPs [84, 42]. For higher-dimensional parameter spaces, EPs can form exceptional lines (ELs), which have been explored in gravitational systems [14, 61, 24]. Such ELs exhibit an intrinsically directional spectral response [14, 84]. By introducing so-called spectral sensitivity anisotropy matrix, we can quantitatively investigate the spectral splitting anisotropy associated with the EL [84]. In the time domain, the usual expansion of the ringdown signal as a sum of independent QNMs can fail in the vicinity of an EP. For a second-order EP, a contribution proportional to [FORMULA] appears [88, 66, 27, 45]. NH physics is characterized not only by phenomena such as ACs and EPs but also by spectrum instability. In the field of black hole perturbations, the history of studying spectrum instability is even longer. Such question was first raised in [62], where the segmented approximation of effective potential is studied. One can refer to similar approaches for studying spectrum instability in [67, 31, 86, 83, 73]. A small smooth correction to the effective potential is also a widely studied model for investigating spectrum instability [5, 28, 29, 89, 18, 44, 58, 74, 43, 50]. A negative deformation of the potential may give rise to dynamical instability of spacetime [57, 56, 15]. Recently, Ref. [33] indicates that although a secondary bump in the effective potential generated by matter fields around black holes may lead to spectrum instabilities, in anisotropic-fluid models it corresponds to unphysical matter configurations. Small perturbations to the QNM boundary conditions are capable of inducing appreciable shifts in the spectra as well [63, 76, 36, 82, 87]. Known alterations to the effective potential enable us to ascertain precisely how the spectrum migrates as the parameters are varied. Nevertheless, if only the strength of the operator modification is known, then although the precise spectrum displacement cannot be ascertained, the range of spectrum migration can still be inferred by computing the pseudospectrum. The pseudospectrum is a norm-dependent diagnostic. It quantifies the smallest perturbation, within a specified perturbation class and norm, that can make a trial frequency an eigenvalue of a perturbed operator. The pseudospectrum approach to the (in)stability of black hole QNMs was first studied in [46, 47, 41]. Building on this work, a substantial body of work concerning pseudospectra has emerged [35, 12, 15, 3, 40, 2, 9, 30, 16, 72, 34, 55, 81, 26, 10, 75, 8, 32, 11, 13, 92, 91, 39, 49]. More recently, the pseudospectrum behavior near the EPs has also been studied [14, 37]. Localized deformations of the effective potential have been shown to destabilize even the fundamental QNMs [28], whereas subsequent investigations have emphasized that some configurations responsible for such instabilities may be incompatible with physically acceptable matter models [18, 33]. The central question is therefore not merely whether the QNM spectrum is sensitive to small perturbations, but which aspects of this instability persist when the perturbations are restricted to a specified physical model. More generally, the structured pseudospectrum (see Chapter [FORMULA] in [79]) provide a framework for incorporating prescribed perturbation constraints into spectrum stability analysis. The physical significance of the structured pseudospectrum is that it quantifies, within a prescribed class of physically admissible perturbations, the instability of black hole QNM spectra and the range over which they may shift. This motivates a model-dependent assessment of spectrum stability, in which both the admissible family of deformations and the norm used to quantify their magnitude are specified explicitly. In this work, taking the Schwarzschild black hole as reliable model, we apply the structured pseudospectrum to black hole perturbation theory for the first time.
