V Conclusions and discussion In this work, we investigate the structured pseudospectra of Schwarzschild black holes by restricting the effective potential deformations to physically motivated perturbation spaces. In particular, we consider two classes of perturbations inspired by effective field theory (EFT) and the Rezzolla–Zhidenko (RZ) parametrization, respectively. To characterize the pseudospectra, we have employed two different norms and established a hierarchy relating the corresponding structured spectral distances to the conventional unstructured one [refer to inequalities (36)]. Our numerical results show that the spectrum instability predicted by the conventional pseudospectrum is substantially suppressed when the perturbations are restricted to the considered physical spaces. This behavior is observed for both the fundamental mode and the first overtone, with a particularly pronounced contrast for the latter (see Fig. 3 and Fig. 4). Although the unstructured pseudospectrum suggests that extremely small operator perturbations can produce appreciable spectral displacements, considerably larger perturbations are required within the EFT- and RZ-motivated sectors. These findings indicate that much of the strong spectrum instability revealed by unrestricted perturbations may not be accessible within a given class of physical deformations. Another important finding concerns the geometry of the pseudospectrum contours. For sufficiently small [FORMULA] , the unstructured pseudospectrum approaches a circular shape around an isolated simple QNM. In contrast, the structured pseudospectra retain approximately elliptical-like contours, whose orientations and elongations depend on the particular QNM and the underlying perturbation model. For the structured spectral distance [FORMULA] , the contour is exactly the asymptotic ellipse. Mathematical proof for this can be found in Appendix D, while the numerical verification can be found in Fig. 5. The difference between the unstructured pseudospectrum and the structured pseudospectrum reveals that physically constrained perturbations introduce preferred directions of spectral migration, even in the small perturbation regime. Therefore, the structured pseudospectrum provides information not only about the magnitude of spectrum instability but also about its directional dependence, which is absent from the locally circular structure of the unstructured pseudospectrum. There are some things that can be further explored based on the present work. Here, we list some investigations that can be done in the future. Unstructured (ordinary) pseudospectrum of Kerr black hole has been obtained in [11, 91], which motivate us to study the structured pseudospectrum of Kerr black hole. Total transmission modes (TTMs) which are another important modes on black hole perturbation theory can also be considered [90, 38, 92, 85, 68, 80, 70, 25]. The structured pseudospectrum for TTMs is a very natural next step for studying.
High Energy Physics - Experiment: Celebi: Design and Realization of a Reproducible Physics Analysis Framework Reproducibility in modern physics analysis requires more than preserving source code or individual workflow descriptions. An analysis evolves continuously through changes in code, configuration, parameters, input datasets, and dependency structures, making it necessary to maintain a coherent representation of both the analysis itself and the provenance of its results. We present Celebi, a framework for organizing and preserving evolving physics analyses while keeping the analysis definition lightweight and separate from generated data products. At the system level, Celebi maintains the analysis definition and its preserved states in an Analysis Repository, while execution and generated results are handled separately through a Production Factory. The middleware layer, Yuki, connects preserved analysis states to the execution infrastructure by constructing executable Snakemake workflows and dispatching them to supported workflow runners. This separation allows the analysis representation to remain independent of a particular execution backend. This paper focuses on the main design concepts introduced in Celebi. The workflow architecture provides an explicit and modular representation of the materials constituting an analysis and their dependencies. A structured file organization gives this model a concrete and human-readable realization in the analysis repository, separating reusable algorithms, task-specific configurations, parameters, documentation, and dependencies into well-defined objects. Finally, the impression mechanism preserves immutable states of these objects together with the corresponding states of their dependencies, providing persistent identities for particular analysis configurations and allowing generated results to be associated unambiguously with the analysis state from which they originate. Together, these concepts provide a coherent representation of an evolving physics analysis and establish a foundation for reproducibility, provenance tracking, collaboration, and long-term analysis preservation. 1 Introduction Open and reproducible research has become an important objective of the scientific community and is increasingly encouraged by policymakers and funding agencies [1, 2]. Reproducibility allows scientific results to be independently verified and revisited, while openness facilitates collaboration, reuse, and the accumulation of scientific knowledge. Achieving these goals, however, requires more than making the final data products available. As emphasized in Ref. [2], the software, configurations, workflows, and explanations involved in producing a result are also part of the research process and should remain accessible and interpretable. Reproducibility therefore needs to be considered throughout the research lifecycle rather than only at the stage of final publication or preservation. This requirement is particularly relevant in high-energy physics, where scientific results are obtained through long chains of computational processing. At experiments such as those at the LHC, detector signals are first processed through centrally managed production systems before being delivered to physicists in forms suitable for further analysis. These centralized production workflows are typically standardized and maintained by the experimental collaborations. The focus of this work begins after this stage: we consider the individual analysis of prepared datasets, where researchers develop selections, derive intermediate quantities, perform statistical analyses, evaluate systematic uncertainties, and eventually produce physics results. Individual physics analyses are highly iterative: code, parameters, input datasets, analysis strategies, and dependencies may all change during development. Consequently, an analysis is better regarded as an evolving collection of computational materials and their relationships than as a single static workflow. A result produced at an earlier stage may depend on a particular combination of code, configuration, parameters, input data, and upstream processing steps, whose exact state can become difficult to reconstruct after the analysis has evolved. A central requirement is therefore provenance. For a generated result, it should remain possible to identify the analysis state from which it originated, including the relevant code, configuration, parameters, inputs, and upstream dependencies. Maintaining this connection is essential both for reproducing historical results and for understanding the evolution of an analysis. The importance of analysis preservation and reproducibility has long been recognized within the high-energy physics community. Community-wide efforts on data preservation were already discussed systematically in Ref. [3]. The CERN Analysis Preservation portal (CAP) [4] provides a centralized environment in which researchers can document and preserve information about their analyses, while REANA [5] provides infrastructure for executing reusable and containerized research workflows. Workflow-management systems such as Snakemake [6] further provide convenient mechanisms for expressing computational dependencies and automating the execution of complex analysis pipelines. These systems provide important building blocks for reproducible research, but workflow execution and analysis preservation alone address only part of the analysis-management problem considered here. During everyday development, the analysis itself continues to change, and the correspondence between its current structure, its historical states, and the results generated from those states must also be maintained. Conventional workflow descriptions are generally designed to specify how computations should be executed, whereas source-code version-control systems record states of files and repositories. Neither mechanism alone necessarily provides an explicit representation of an individual analysis object together with the exact preserved states of its dependencies and the results associated with that state. This motivates an analysis-management layer that complements both workflow execution and conventional version control. In this work, we introduce Celebi, an analysis-management framework designed to provide such a representation. Celebi separates the lightweight materials that define an analysis, including code, configuration, parameters, documentation, and dependency information, from the potentially large data products generated during execution. These materials are organized in an Analysis Repository, where their relationships and evolving states can be managed explicitly. Generated results and execution are handled separately through a Production Factory, with the Yuki middleware providing the connection between preserved analysis states and the execution infrastructure. The detailed implementation of this execution layer is outside the scope of this paper. The focus of this paper is the design of the analysis representation itself. We introduce three closely related aspects of this design. First, the workflow architecture describes the analysis in terms of the materials required to define each computation and the dependencies among them. Second, the file organization provides a concrete and human-readable realization of this representation within the Analysis Repository. Third, the impression mechanism provides immutable identities for particular states of analysis objects together with the corresponding states of their dependencies. These concepts allow an evolving working analysis to coexist with persistent, identifiable analysis states to which generated results can be associated unambiguously. The remainder of this paper first gives an overview of the Celebi system and its major components. It then presents the workflow architecture, its realization in the repository structure, and the impression mechanism used to preserve particular analysis states and their provenance. 2 Overview of the Celebi system The Celebi system separates the representation and preservation of an analysis from the execution of the corresponding computations. Its architecture consists of two main components: the Analysis Repository and the Production Factory, connected through the Yuki middleware. The Analysis Repository contains the lightweight materials required to define an analysis, including source code, configurations, parameters, documentation, and dependency information. These materials are represented as structured analysis objects and can evolve continuously during normal development. Selected states of these objects can be preserved as immutable impressions, allowing particular analysis configurations to remain identifiable after the working analysis has changed. The Production Factory is responsible for executing preserved analysis states and managing the resulting data products. This separation keeps potentially large generated datasets outside the persistent analysis representation while maintaining their association with the analysis states from which they were produced. An overview of the Celebi architecture is shown in Fig. 1. Yuki provides the interface between the Analysis Repository and the execution infrastructure. Given an impression submitted for execution, Yuki resolves its dependency structure and constructs the corresponding Snakemake workflow. The workflow is then dispatched to an available runner for execution. Celebi is not tied to a particular execution backend: different runners can be used depending on the available computing environment, while Snakemake provides a common workflow representation across them. REANA [5] is one currently supported execution platform. Yuki also monitors workflow execution and maintains the association between the resulting outputs and the impressions from which they were produced. In this way, the execution infrastructure can evolve independently of the persistent analysis representation. The following section focuses on the design of the Analysis Repository and introduces the workflow architecture, the organization of analysis objects, and the impression mechanism used to identify preserved analysis states. 3 Design and realization of the Celebi analysis model This section introduces the main design concepts used by Celebi to represent an evolving physics analysis. The discussion is organized around three closely related aspects. First, the workflow architecture defines the components of the analysis and the dependencies among them. Second, the file organization provides a concrete and human-readable realization of this model in the Analysis Repository. Finally, the impression mechanism preserves identifiable states of the otherwise editable analysis. Together, these concepts connect the logical structure of an analysis, its representation in the repository, and the provenance of the results generated from it. The conceptual design of the Production Factory, including Yuki, is relatively straightforward, whereas its implementation involves substantial engineering complexity and is therefore not discussed in detail in this paper. A physics analysis typically consists of a sequence of computational steps in which the output of one step may be required by another. The resulting dependencies naturally form a directed acyclic graph (DAG), commonly referred to as a workflow. For a small analysis, these dependencies may be encoded implicitly in scripts, whereas more complex analyses are often expressed using dedicated workflow-description systems. Making the workflow explicit provides a machine-readable representation of the analysis logic and facilitates automation, review, reuse, and reproducibility. Celebi extends this conventional view by representing not only the ordering of computations, but also the analysis materials required to define them. Source code, computational procedures, task-specific parameters, and dependency information are treated as explicit components of the analysis representation. The workflow therefore describes relationships among the materials that define the computation rather than only the temporal or logical ordering of execution steps. Celebi refers to this representation as a materialized workflow. The term materialized emphasizes that workflow entities are represented by concrete objects in the Analysis Repository, together with the code, configuration, parameters, and dependency information required to define them. The workflow is therefore not confined to a centralized abstract specification; it is realized directly through the analysis materials maintained in the repository. A central distinction in this model is made between an algorithm and a task. An algorithm describes how a computation is performed, whereas a task describes a particular application of that computation with specified parameters and upstream dependencies. Separating these two roles allows the same computational procedure to be reused in different parts of an analysis, or with different inputs and parameter values, without duplicating its implementation. It also distinguishes the definition of a computational method from the particular analysis state in which that method is used. Consider a simple analysis in which a sample following a Gaussian distribution is generated and subsequently fitted. At the level of an abstract task graph, the analysis may be represented as [FORMULA] where the edge expresses the dependency of the fitting step on the generation step. In Celebi, the computational definitions used by Gen and Fit are represented separately from the corresponding tasks. The Gen task therefore depends on its algorithm, while the Fit task depends on both its own algorithm and the upstream Gen task. The workflow consequently records dependencies among the materials required to define the analysis, rather than only the ordering of two executable steps. A second design choice concerns generated intermediate data. With the exception of externally supplied inputs, an intermediate data product is produced by a particular task and is therefore associated with that task. Celebi consequently does not require each generated dataset to appear as an independent persistent workflow node. Instead, a downstream task records a dependency on the upstream task responsible for producing the required data. For example, a data-explicit workflow could represent a dependency as [FORMULA] In Celebi, the persistent dependency is represented as [FORMULA] while the concrete output associated with task1 is resolved by the execution layer when the downstream computation is constructed. This representation keeps potentially large generated datasets outside the persistent workflow description while retaining the dependency needed to identify their origin. The persistent representation therefore records the provenance-relevant materials required to identify a computation: its algorithm, parameters, upstream dependencies, external inputs, and execution conditions. Under controlled execution conditions, this information provides the basis for reproducing the intended computation without requiring its generated outputs to be included directly in the workflow definition. External datasets form an important exception because they originate outside the workflow and have no upstream producing task; their representation is discussed in Sec. 3.2. The workflow specification is distributed among the analysis objects. Rather than requiring a single global file containing the complete DAG, each relevant object records its own direct dependencies. The complete workflow can then be reconstructed from these local relationships. This locality allows an analysis component and its dependencies to evolve without requiring unrelated parts of a monolithic workflow description to be rewritten. The resulting workflow consists primarily of lightweight and versionable analysis materials rather than generated data products. A particular state of these materials defines a provenance-relevant state of the analysis from which computations can be carried out. The next subsection describes how this abstract representation is realized concretely in the structure of a Celebi repository. The workflow model described above is realized in a Celebi repository. The repository contains the lightweight materials required to define the analysis, including source code, configurations, parameters, dependency metadata, and documentation. Workflow entities are represented as structured objects in the file system, so that the logical organization of the analysis has a direct and human-readable representation in the repository. Celebi defines four object types: project, directory, algorithm, and task. They serve two complementary roles. Project and directory objects provide the hierarchical organization of the repository, while algorithm and task objects represent the materials that participate directly in the workflow. Project: the root object of a Celebi repository, representing the analysis as a whole. Directory: an organizational object used to group related analysis components according to a human-readable hierarchy. Algorithm: a reusable definition of a computational procedure, including the code and configuration required to describe how the computation is performed. Task: a concrete workflow object describing the use of analysis inputs within a particular part of the workflow. For a computational step, a task associates an algorithm with the corresponding parameters and upstream dependencies. A task may also provide the interface through which externally produced data enter the workflow. For computational steps, the separation between algorithms and tasks distinguishes reusable computational logic from its concrete invocation. For example, the same fitting algorithm may be used by several tasks corresponding to different datasets or systematic variations. The algorithm object can remain unchanged, while each task records the particular parameters and dependencies relevant to that invocation. This separation reduces duplication and makes it explicit whether a variation originates from a change in the computational procedure or from the conditions under which it is applied. Dependencies are expressed between objects rather than through hard-coded paths to generated outputs. A task can assign local aliases to its dependencies, allowing its computational definition to refer to upstream analysis components through stable logical names. For an internally generated input, the dependency therefore refers to the upstream task responsible for producing the data rather than to the physical location of a particular output file. This realizes the task-to-task dependency model introduced in Sec. 3.1 and separates the persistent analysis structure from transient data locations. External input datasets require a slightly different treatment because they are not generated by an upstream computation within the analysis. Celebi represents such an input through a task object that records how the externally supplied data are identified and exposes them to the workflow as an available output. Such a task therefore defines the boundary at which data produced outside the Celebi workflow enter the analysis, rather than representing a computation that produces the data itself. Downstream tasks can depend on this object through the same task-to-task dependency mechanism used for internally generated data. For an internally generated input, the upstream task identifies the computation responsible for producing the required output; for an external input, the corresponding task instead identifies data that already exist outside the workflow. In this way, both internally generated and externally supplied inputs can be incorporated through a uniform dependency model without introducing persistent data objects as separate workflow nodes. Each repository object also carries local metadata and documentation describing its role and configuration. Keeping this information with the corresponding analysis component makes the repository self-describing at the level of individual objects and supports both human inspection and programmatic interpretation of the workflow. With this organization, the Analysis Repository contains the relatively small materials that define the analysis rather than its potentially much larger generated products. The repository can therefore remain lightweight as the analysis evolves, while still retaining the information required to describe its logical structure and computational configuration. The remaining problem is how to identify a particular state of this continuously editable representation. Celebi addresses this through the impression mechanism described below. Objects in the Analysis Repository represent the current working state of an analysis and are expected to change during normal development. Reproducibility, however, requires a stable way to identify a particular state even after the working analysis has evolved. Celebi introduces impressions to separate these two roles: objects remain editable, whereas selected states of those objects can be preserved immutably. An impression is an immutable representation of a Celebi object at a particular analysis state. It records the materials defining the object together with references to the impressions corresponding to its dependencies. An impression therefore identifies not only the local state of one object but also the precise preserved states of the upstream objects on which it depends. Each impression is assigned a persistent identifier that remains associated with that immutable state. For an object with dependencies, the impression metadata records the identifiers of the exact predecessor impressions on which it depends. These immutable references preserve the dependency state of the workflow at the time the impression is created. Consequently, two preserved states may differ because of a change in an upstream dependency even when the local contents of the object itself remain unchanged. Once an impression has been created, it is not modified. Changes to the corresponding code, parameters, configuration, or dependencies instead produce a new working state, which may subsequently be recorded as a new impression. The repository can therefore continue to evolve without altering previously preserved analysis states. The impression mechanism is complementary to conventional source-code version control. A version-control commit records a state of a repository as a collection of files, whereas an impression identifies the state of an individual analysis object together with the exact preserved states of the workflow dependencies relevant to that object. The two mechanisms therefore operate at different levels: version control records repository history, while impressions provide analysis-level identities that can be associated directly with generated results. Celebi uses impressions as a complement to, rather than a replacement for, conventional source-code version control. Because the persistent analysis representation consists primarily of lightweight materials, impressions can also remain compact. Code, parameters, configurations, and dependency information can be preserved directly, while potentially large generated datasets remain outside the impression itself. Instead, such datasets are associated with the task impression under which they were produced. For a task impression, the combination of its local preserved state and the impressions of its dependencies identifies the analysis configuration associated with that computation. A generated result can therefore be bound to the corresponding task impression. Following the dependency chain provides access to the code, parameters, configurations, and upstream input states associated with the production of that result. When the working representation of an object changes, it no longer corresponds to its previous impression. Results associated with that previous impression are therefore historical results rather than results of the current working state. They are not discarded, however: they remain associated with the immutable impression under which they were produced. Celebi can consequently distinguish the evolving current analysis from preserved historical states while maintaining the provenance of results from both. The three concepts introduced in this section play complementary roles. The workflow architecture defines the analysis components and their dependencies; the file organization realizes this representation as a structured and editable repository; and impressions provide persistent identities for selected states of that evolving structure. Together, they allow Celebi to maintain a direct relationship between the organization of an analysis, its evolution over time, and the provenance of the results produced from it. 4 Summary This work presents Celebi, a framework for representing and preserving evolving physics analyses. Celebi organizes analysis code, configurations, parameters, external inputs, and dependencies into a lightweight materialized workflow, where the components defining an analysis are represented directly as structured repository objects rather than only as abstract execution steps. Reproducibility and provenance are supported through immutable impressions, which preserve the state of an object together with references to the exact preserved states of its dependencies. Generated results can therefore remain associated with the analysis state from which they were produced even as the working analysis continues to evolve. Execution is separated from this persistent analysis representation. The Yuki middleware converts preserved analysis states into Snakemake workflows and dispatches them to supported workflow runners, allowing different execution backends to be used without changing the underlying analysis model. REANA is one currently supported execution platform. Together, the materialized workflow, structured repository organization, and impression mechanism provide a foundation for provenance tracking, reproducible execution, collaborative development, and long-term preservation of high-energy-physics analyses.

Celebi: Towards Reproducible and FAIR Physics Analysis Modern physics analyses evolve continuously as datasets, selections, parameters, software environments, and analysis strategies are updated. Over the lifetime of an analysis, this evolution can make it difficult to determine the conditions under which an earlier result was produced or to transfer the analysis reliably between collaborators. I designed and developed Celebi as an analysis-management framework that maintains a persistent connection between evolving analysis materials and their generated results. Celebi organizes reusable algorithms, tasks, and their dependencies into a structured workflow, preserves selected states as immutable impressions, and associates retained results with the states responsible for their production. This organization supports analysis modification, systematic variations, collaboration, and review while the working analysis continues to evolve. Celebi supports controlled rerunning of preserved analysis states. When results remain retained, they can be inspected and compared together with their corresponding states. By capturing provenance during everyday analysis development, Celebi reduces the need to reconstruct analysis history retrospectively and provides a practical foundation for more transparent and reusable physics analysis. 1 Introduction Open and reproducible research requires preserving not only scientific results but also the computational processes through which they are obtained [1, 2]. This is particularly important in high-energy physics, where analyses involve complex processing chains and evolve over long periods. While large experiments maintain centralized data-processing workflows, individual physics analyses involve changing selections, configurations, statistical procedures, and systematic studies. Managing these evolving analyses while retaining the context of their results is the focus of this work. As an analysis develops, changes to code, parameters, inputs, and dependencies can make it difficult to recover the conditions under which earlier results were produced. For example, a result presented during an internal review may no longer correspond to the current analysis after subsequent modifications. This challenge becomes more pronounced in collaborative projects, where multiple configurations and analysis variations must coexist. Reliable analysis management therefore requires a persistent connection between each generated result and the analysis state responsible for its production. Existing tools address different aspects of reproducibility and preservation. Snakemake [3] manages computational dependencies and workflow execution, while REANA [4] supports reproducible execution in containerized environments. The CERN Analysis Preservation portal (CAP) [5] provides infrastructure for documenting and preserving analyses. Maintaining the connection between an evolving working analysis and the results produced throughout its development, however, remains a distinct analysis-management challenge. Celebi addresses this challenge by organizing analysis materials into structured components and preserving selected analysis states. Generated results remain associated with the states under which they were produced, even as the working analysis continues to evolve. By separating lightweight analysis definitions from generated data products while retaining their relationships, Celebi facilitates analysis modification, algorithm reuse, systematic variations, and historical result management. This paper focuses on the practical implications of Celebi for physics analysis development, collaboration, review, and preservation. Its underlying workflow architecture, repository organization, and impression mechanism are described in a companion paper [6]. 2 Overview of the Celebi system Celebi separates potentially large data products generated during execution from the lightweight materials defining a physics analysis, including code, configurations, parameters, documentation, and dependencies. Its two main components are the Analysis Repository, which maintains the evolving analysis definition, and the Production Factory, which handles execution and generated results. The middleware layer Yuki connects the two, allowing preserved analysis states to be executed and their results to be associated with the corresponding analysis definitions. Celebi distinguishes the editable working analysis from immutable impressions. An impression identifies a preserved state of an analysis component together with the preserved states of its dependencies. Results are associated with task impressions, so their provenance remains identifiable even after the working analysis changes. Celebi supports controlled rerunning of preserved analysis states. Such rerunning depends on the continued availability of the required inputs, software environments, and execution infrastructure. 3 Celebi throughout the physics analysis lifecycle Celebi simplifies the management of evolving physics analyses by organizing analysis components and their dependencies into a structured, modular representation. Analysts can modify, reuse, and reorganize components while retaining the relationships between preserved analysis configurations and their results. Changes to inputs, algorithms, or configurations may require several downstream computations to be updated or repeated. Celebi simplifies the management of such changes by explicitly representing analysis components and their dependencies. Each component records its own dependencies, removing the need for a single, centrally maintained workflow description. Together, these relationships define the workflow and allow affected downstream tasks to be identified without manually tracing scripts or intermediate files. Individual components can thus be modified without rewriting unrelated parts of the analysis. Celebi also separates reusable algorithms from the tasks that apply them. An algorithm defines a computational procedure, while a task specifies its application with particular parameters and upstream dependencies. The same algorithm can be used by multiple tasks without duplicating its implementation, for example when fitting different datasets or studying alternative configurations. This modular organization facilitates the management of related analysis configurations. Because components are represented as structured repository objects, they can be copied, reorganized, and modified through familiar file-system-like operations while retaining their dependency relationships. Optimization studies and systematic variations can consequently share unchanged components while modifying only the parts that differ. This reduces duplication and makes differences between configurations more explicit. Celebi manages generated results in association with the analysis states responsible for their production, rather than treating them as independent output files. Results organized only by filenames or directory structures can become difficult to interpret as the analysis evolves, particularly when the original configuration is no longer the current one. In Celebi, results are associated with immutable task impressions. These impressions identify preserved code and configuration, including task parameters, together with the exact impressions of upstream dependencies. This allows the provenance of a result to be traced through the analysis. Even if a task uses the same algorithm and parameters, a change to an upstream input can produce a distinct preserved analysis state. Recording the dependency impressions makes it possible to distinguish these configurations and keep their results associated with the appropriate states. Figure 1 illustrates this relationship. For example, a mass-fit result presented during an internal review may later be superseded following changes to the event selection or fitting model. Recovering the earlier configuration would otherwise require manually matching the result to the relevant code, parameters, and inputs. When results remain retained, they can be accessed and compared together with their respective preserved analysis states, making it easier to identify differences in their configurations. This approach complements conventional source-code version control. While Git tracks repository-level changes, Celebi explicitly connects results to preserved states of individual analysis components and their dependencies, reducing the need for manually maintained provenance records. Physics analyses often involve multiple collaborators and several rounds of internal review. Effective collaboration requires a shared understanding of analysis structure, computational procedures, and the configurations used to produce results. When this information is scattered across scripts, configuration files, documentation, and personal directories, an analysis can be difficult for others to navigate and understand. Celebi organizes analysis materials, documentation, and dependencies into structured repository objects. Collaborators can inspect a selected component together with its local documentation and dependencies, without first reconstructing the complete analysis from unrelated files. This helps collaborators understand and contribute to specific parts of an analysis. Immutable impressions also give collaborators and reviewers stable references to particular analysis states. Reviewers can inspect the configuration associated with a result even after the working analysis has evolved. When changes are introduced in response to review comments, updated states and results can be retained alongside those examined in earlier review rounds, facilitating comparisons between revisions. Figure 2 shows the Celebi bookkeeping interface, through which users can browse analysis components and inspect results associated with a selected preserved state. The same organization facilitates analysis handover and long-term preservation. Structured components and accompanying documentation reduce reliance on individual conventions and personal knowledge when an analysis is transferred to new collaborators. By capturing provenance during ordinary analysis development, Celebi reduces the need to reconstruct analysis history retrospectively when results are reviewed, transferred, or preserved. These capabilities provide a basis for extending FAIR principles from research data to the computational analyses that produce scientific results. Reusing a result requires not only its output data but also sufficient information about the code, configurations, parameters, dependencies, and provenance involved in its production. By associating results with identifiable analysis states, Celebi provides a foundation for finding and reusing analysis materials and outputs. Its structured representation supports programmatic interpretation and can facilitate interoperability with other infrastructures, while the separation of analysis definitions from generated data facilitates their independent preservation. These features do not by themselves establish full FAIR compliance, but contribute to more transparent and reusable physics analyses. 4 Summary Celebi simplifies the management of physics analyses throughout their lifecycle. Its modular organization and explicit dependencies make analysis components easier to modify, reuse, and reorganize, while immutable impressions retain the link between generated results and the analysis states responsible for their production. These capabilities support historical result inspection, collaboration, and review with less reliance on manual bookkeeping. They also support systematic variations and controlled rerunning of preserved states, provided that the required inputs, software environments, and execution infrastructure remain available. Maintaining analysis states and provenance during everyday development also provides a natural starting point for long-term preservation. In this way, Celebi offers a practical foundation for extending FAIR principles beyond research data to the computational analyses used to produce scientific results.

Reinforcement Learning in High-Energy Physics: A Survey from Accelerator Control to Theory Exploration Reinforcement learning (RL) is a machine learning paradigm in which an agent learns a decision-making policy through repeated interaction with an environment, guided by a scalar reward signal rather than explicit supervision. Supervised and unsupervised learning have become indispensable tools in high-energy physics (HEP), but they learn from fixed datasets, whereas many HEP tasks are closed-loop decisions: the data an algorithm observes depend on the choices it makes, the feedback is sparse or delayed, and the objective is often measured on a real machine or through a stochastic simulation rather than computed by a differentiable model. This survey reviews the application of RL to such tasks across HEP: accelerator control and feedback, data quality monitoring, jet grooming, clustering, and representation, charged particle tracking, beyond-the-Standard-Model (BSM) and string model building, detector design, trigger control, analysis, and formal quantum field theory computation. It provides a self-contained introduction to the RL methods these applications rely on, covering model-free, model-based and planning, multi-agent, offline, inverse and imitation, and bandit approaches; it reviews each domain against its traditional methods and summarizes the available head-to-head comparisons across domains. The applications span a gradient of maturity, from policies deployed on real accelerators and evaluated on recorded collision data to exploratory studies in formal theory. RL is most advantageous for repeated tasks with a fast simulator, decisions inside fast control loops, operation under faults and corrupted measurements, physics-based rewards in place of labels, and sequential discrete constructions with a reusable policy, while Bayesian optimization, genetic algorithms, and differentiable methods remain competitive elsewhere. We conclude with the open challenges that recur across domains, including reward design, sim-to-real transfer, safety, the lack of shared benchmarks, and the statistical validity of policy-driven decisions. 1 Introduction High-energy physics (HEP) is the science of the fundamental constituents of matter and their interactions, studied by colliding particles at high energies and observing the resulting debris with large, specialized equipment, called particle detectors. At the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN, proton bunches cross at a rate of 40 MHz, at a center-of-mass energy of 13.6 TeV in Run 3 (14 TeV by design), and the collisions are recorded by detectors containing of order [FORMULA] readout channels, generating petabytes of data annually. The fundamental challenge is to extract physics signals, such as new particles or deviations from the Standard Model (SM) predictions, from events produced by known background processes that outnumber them by many orders of magnitude. Extracting a signal requires a multi-stage pipeline. Recorded data go through triggering, reconstruction, and event selection; the backgrounds are then estimated, and the data are compared against simulated samples produced with event generators such as Pythia8 [1] and detector-response models such as Geant4 [2]. A discovery is only claimed once the observed excess reaches a significance of five standard deviations relative to the background-only hypothesis. Machine learning has long been part of this pipeline, from boosted decision trees for particle identification [3] to deep learning for fast detector simulation [4, 5], anomaly detection [6, 7, 8], and signal-background classification [9, 10]. The vast majority of these applications, however, belong to two paradigms: supervised learning, which requires labeled examples, and unsupervised or self-supervised learning, which exploits the structure of unlabeled data. In both, the model learns from a dataset whose distribution is fixed in advance and does not depend on the outputs of the model itself. Reinforcement learning (RL) [11] is a third paradigm, complementary to the other two, in which an agent learns a policy, i.e., a mapping from observations to actions, by interacting with an environment and receiving scalar reward signals. The agent is not told which action is correct; it discovers how to act through trial and error, and the data it learns from depend on the actions it takes. This makes RL suited to HEP problems that can be formulated as sequential decision-making under uncertainty, in particular when the reward is sparse, i.e., most transitions carry zero or uninformative reward, or delayed, i.e., the consequences of an action appear only many steps later, so that credit must be assigned across the whole sequence of decisions. Many HEP problems have this structure. A particle accelerator must be tuned and stabilized as beam conditions change, under hard safety constraints, with an objective such as beam transmission or orbit stability that is measured on the real machine rather than computed by a differentiable model. A data quality monitoring system must decide, for each incoming histogram, whether to classify it automatically or to query a human shifter, trading accuracy against annotation effort. A trigger must adapt its thresholds during a fill to keep its output rate within the bandwidth budget as pileup and background composition change. A jet grooming algorithm must decide, node by node along the clustering tree, which soft emissions to remove. A detector layout is built one layer at a time and scored only once complete, through a stochastic full simulation. A theorist searching for consistent beyond-the-Standard-Model (BSM) models or string compactifications must navigate a discrete, combinatorially vast space of symmetry groups, charge assignments, and compactification data, where consistency can only be checked on a complete construction. In each case, the problem maps onto a Markov decision process (MDP): there are states, actions, transition dynamics, a reward, and a horizon. Sequential structure and a non-differentiable objective are not, by themselves, sufficient reasons to prefer RL. Bayesian optimization [12], evolution strategies [13], and genetic algorithms [14, 15] also optimize black-box objectives, and gradients through an accurate differentiable model of the system are more efficient than model-free exploration when such a model is available, whether used directly [16] or inside RL training [17]. What distinguishes RL from these alternatives is that it returns a policy, a map from every state to an action, rather than a single optimum, and that this policy acts in closed loop: each action changes the state that later decisions observe. The evidence reviewed in this survey identifies five conditions under which this makes RL the more suitable choice: Repeated tasks with a fast simulator. The training cost is paid once and amortized over many deployments of the same policy [18]. Decisions inside fast control loops. A trained policy can act within loop periods too short for iterative optimizers, with microsecond inference on dedicated hardware [19, 20]. Robustness to faults and corrupted measurements. Policies trained over a distribution of operating conditions degrade more gracefully than classical controllers when the system itself degrades [21]. Physics as the training signal in place of labels. The reward can encode first-principles knowledge where ground truth is unavailable, such as a scattering likelihood [22] or a matrix element [23]. Sequential discrete construction with a reusable policy. When the objective is defined only on a complete construction, a trained policy transfers across instances [24]. In the last setting, learned policies have occasionally exposed structure that experts had not articulated, as in a result on chiral families in string compactifications that was subsequently proven [25]. Conversely, Bayesian optimization remains preferable in the opposite regime; Section 10.3 returns to these conditions with the supporting evidence from the full review. These properties have led to a growing body of work applying RL across the HEP workflow, from accelerator operation and detector design to analysis and formal theoretical computation. We use the term HEP broadly: besides collider experiment and phenomenology, we include accelerator physics, the operation of detectors in non-collider experiments such as cryogenic dark matter searches [26], and formal theory, from string phenomenology to the conformal bootstrap. Existing reviews either catalog machine learning papers without a methodological synthesis or focus on a single domain. The HEP-ML Living Review [27] and its successor [28] list RL papers within a broad catalog of machine learning references for particle physics, but do not compare them. Edelen and Huang [29] review machine learning for accelerator design and control, including notable RL applications, and Ghribi [30] proposes a living review pipeline for artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) applications in accelerator physics. Ruehle [31] reviews data science methods for string theory, RL included; Giarnetti and Meloni [32] focus on RL techniques for the flavor problem; and Martín-Guerrero and Lamata [33] review the interplay of RL and physics in general, without a focus on HEP. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first survey dedicated to RL across HEP sub-fields: accelerator control, data quality monitoring, jet physics, charged particle tracking, BSM and string model building, detector design, trigger control, analysis, and theoretical computation. Its contributions are: (i) a self-contained RL background calibrated for HEP researchers; (ii) a per-domain contrast of RL with traditional methods, with the available head-to-head evidence summarized across domains in Table 3; and (iii) a discussion of open problems and future research directions at the RL--HEP interface.11 1 We use the term reinforcement learning broadly to include deep RL, tabular RL, bandit algorithms, planning methods such as Monte Carlo Tree Search that use learned policy and value functions, and the RL fine-tuning of pretrained generative models, such as with group relative policy optimization (GRPO) [34]. Section 2 covers the necessary reinforcement learning background. It introduces the RL framework from classical principles to the main deep RL algorithms, including model-based RL and planning with Monte Carlo Tree Search. It then briefly covers the RL sub-fields most relevant to the surveyed applications: multi-agent RL, offline RL, inverse RL and imitation learning, bandit algorithms, and, more briefly, meta, multi-task, continual, hierarchical, Bayesian, and multi-objective RL. It closes with a discussion of practical challenges that are especially relevant in the HEP setting: reward design, sim-to-real transfer, safety constraints, sample efficiency, real-time inference and deployment, and physics-informed RL. Sections 3 to 9 review RL applications across seven domains of HEP. Sections 3 to 8 follow the same structure: a background subsection introducing the physical problem and its traditional algorithmic solutions, a detailed review of existing RL-based work, and a closing subsection identifying open problems and promising future research directions. Section 9 collects heterogeneous applications and therefore follows this structure within each of its subsections. Section 4: Data quality monitoring, where human-in-the-loop RL and bandits are used to reduce expert annotation effort and to detect detector malfunctions online. Section 5: Jet physics, covering RL-based jet grooming, hierarchical clustering, and the ordering of particle constituents for downstream classifiers. Section 6: Charged particle tracking, where RL formulates track finding as a graph MDP with physics-informed rewards, extended to constrained multi-agent settings. Section 7: Beyond-the-Standard-Model model building, where RL explores the discrete space of consistent theories: Froggatt–Nielsen flavor and axion models, graph- and grammar-based model spaces, and string compactifications. Section 8: Detector and instrument design, where RL optimizes geometry and configuration with simulation-based rewards. Section 9: Analysis, event processing, and theoretical computation; a heterogeneous category covering trigger control, data caching for distributed analysis, background and systematics modeling, combinatorial event reconstruction, and formal quantum field theory (QFT) computation (integral reduction, symbolic simplification, and the conformal bootstrap). Section 10 summarizes the landscape, including the cross-domain comparison of Table 3, discusses the open challenges that recur across domains, and outlines the conditions under which RL is advantageous at the RL–HEP interface. 2 Reinforcement Learning Reinforcement learning (RL) is a learning paradigm at the intersection of multiple fields like computer science, psychology, neuroscience, mathematics, economics, and engineering, whose aim is to solve decision-making problems. A physical (e.g., a robot, a piece of equipment) or software RL agent discovers how to behave in an environment (i.e., a real or simulated world) by maximizing a cumulative reward signal obtained through repeated interaction [11]. Unlike supervised learning, no labeled input-output pairs are provided; unlike unsupervised learning, there is an explicit goal encoded in a reward function, either designed or provided. RL has produced landmark results in board and video games [35, 36, 37], robotics [38], and control [39], and is increasingly applied in scientific domains where the objective function is non-differentiable, or the data are generated through interaction. For a thorough treatment of classical and modern RL, we refer the reader to the textbook by Sutton and Barto [11] and the survey by Li [40]. In model-based RL (MBRL), the agent uses either a given or learned explicit model of the environment dynamics [FORMULA] to find a policy, without being forced to interact with the real environment for every gradient step [66]. A dynamics model is typically learned by supervised regression on a dataset of observed transitions [FORMULA] . Three design decisions characterize any MBRL planner. First, the starting state for planning: the most common choice is to plan from the current state, though priority-based methods start from states with the highest estimated value error. Second, the planning budget: approaches such as Dyna and AlphaGo plan for a fixed number of model steps after each real step; others, such as PILCO [70], collect a full real episode before re-planning the entire trajectory. Imitation learning (IL) covers methods that learn a policy from expert demonstrations [FORMULA] without a reward function. The simplest form is behavioral cloning (BC): supervised regression of actions on observations, treating the problem as a standard classification or regression task. BC is sample-efficient but fragile: small deviations from the training distribution compound over time because the agent experiences states never seen during training, causing the predicted trajectory to diverge quadratically in the horizon (covariate shift). Mitigation strategies include data augmentation, collecting recovery demonstrations, and dataset aggregation (DAgger) [81], which queries the expert to label states visited by the current learned policy in an active learning loop. Multi-armed bandits are a special case of RL in which each episode consists of a single decision step: the agent selects an action (“arm”) and receives a reward, with no state transitions or temporal credit assignment. The fundamental challenge is the exploration–exploitation tradeoff: exploiting the arm with the highest known expected reward may miss a better arm that has been sampled too rarely. The Upper Confidence Bound (UCB1) algorithm [85] addresses this by adding an optimism bonus to the estimated value of each arm: where [FORMULA] is the empirical mean reward of arm [FORMULA] , [FORMULA] is its pull count, [FORMULA] is the total number of rounds, and [FORMULA] controls the exploration strength. UCB achieves near-optimal regret (the gap between cumulative reward and the oracle that always plays the best arm) of [FORMULA] for [FORMULA] arms and [FORMULA] rounds. Thompson Sampling [86] maintains a posterior distribution over arm reward rates and selects the arm with the highest sampled value at each step, achieving similar regret bounds with often better empirical performance. Contextual bandits extend the above by conditioning the action choice on a context vector [FORMULA] that encodes the current situation. LinUCB [87] assumes a linear reward model [FORMULA] and maintains a ridge regression estimate of [FORMULA] for each arm, with an UCB-style confidence ellipsoid for exploration. For non-linear reward models, neural contextual bandits [88] replace the linear head with a neural network while preserving the UCB structure. Semi-bandits [89] provide richer feedback: the agent selects a composite action (e.g., a subset of arms) and observes the reward for each component individually. This additional signal enables faster learning when the action space is structured. Bandit algorithms are used in HEP data quality monitoring (DQM, Section 4), where each monitoring decision, such as which detector channels to observe, is treated as stateless and the semi-bandit structure captures the multi-channel nature of detector monitoring. The key distinction from full RL is that bandit methods assume no state transitions: successive monitoring decisions in a run are treated as independent. This is a modeling choice rather than a fundamental constraint; as DQM systems mature, incorporating run-level temporal correlations will likely motivate a transition to full sequential RL formulations. Several RL paradigms beyond the single-task setting recur in the open problems of the following sections. Meta-RL [90, 91] learns, from a distribution of related tasks, a policy or a learning procedure that adapts to a new task from a small amount of experience; model-agnostic meta-learning (MAML) [90] does so by learning an initialization from which a few gradient steps suffice. Multi-task and transfer RL [92, 93] share representations or policies across tasks, so that a policy trained on one task can be reused on another with little additional data. Continual RL [94] learns from a sequence of changing tasks without catastrophic forgetting of the earlier ones. Hierarchical RL [95, 96] decomposes a task into temporally extended sub-tasks: in the options framework, an option [FORMULA] comprises an initiation set [FORMULA] of states in which it is available, an intra-option policy [FORMULA] , and a termination condition [FORMULA] , and a high-level policy that selects options acts on a slower timescale over a semi-Markov decision process. Bayesian RL [97] maintains a posterior distribution over the environment dynamics or the reward model, rather than over returns as in distributional RL, and uses it to balance exploration and exploitation. Multi-objective RL [98, 99] optimizes a vector of rewards and returns a set of Pareto-optimal policies, or a single policy conditioned on a preference vector, instead of a single scalarized trade-off; scalarized multi-objective rewards are discussed in Section 2.8.1, together with curriculum learning. Deploying RL to real physical systems introduces a set of challenges that are largely absent from simulation benchmarks. Dulac-Arnold et al. [100] identified nine such challenges empirically: limited real-system samples, actuation and sensing delays, high-dimensional continuous spaces, hard constraints, partial observability, multi-objective rewards, real-time inference, offline log data, and policy explainability. HEP applications encounter most of these simultaneously, making the practical considerations below not just theoretical guidance but design requirements. The reward function is the most critical and most difficult design choice in any RL application. A poorly specified reward leads to reward hacking: the agent finds high-reward behaviors that satisfy the letter of the objective but violate its intent. The classic example is a boat-racing agent that achieves high reward by collecting bonus items in circles rather than finishing the race [101]; analogous failure modes arise in HEP when a beam-tuning agent optimizes a transmission proxy without respecting emittance constraints, or when a jet grooming policy removes constituents that satisfy the reward criterion but destroy infrared and collinear (IRC) safety. Reward shaping adds auxiliary reward terms to guide early learning without changing the optimal policy, provided the additional terms are potential-based: [FORMULA] [102]. Any such shaped reward preserves the set of optimal policies of the original MDP. In accelerator control, intermediate rewards based on partial beam transmission or upstream orbit deviation serve this role, providing dense feedback during a tuning sequence whose true outcome is only known at the end. Sparse rewards arise naturally in several HEP problems: the resolution of a detector design is known only after full simulation of the complete design [103], and the consistency of a BSM model or a string compactification can be fully assessed only once the construction is complete. Most reviewed works nevertheless shape these objectives into dense per-step rewards, such as step-wise improvements of beam quality or of a consistency score (Sections 3 and 7). Three complementary approaches address sparsity: reward shaping (above); curriculum learning [104], which starts the agent from easier sub-problems and progressively increases difficulty, used in RL-ABC [105] as stage learning; and hierarchical RL [95, 96] (Section 2.7.5), which decomposes the problem into a high-level policy selecting sub-goals and a low-level policy achieving them, providing denser intermediate rewards naturally. Multi-objective rewards are the norm rather than the exception in HEP. Accelerator operation must optimize transmission while satisfying emittance and safety bounds; detector design must balance resolution, cost, and material budget. Naive scalarization of multiple objectives into a weighted sum is sensitive to weight choice and can miss Pareto-optimal solutions. Distributional RL methods [55] allow direct optimization of risk-aware objectives such as the Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR), which is relevant when avoiding worst-case outcomes (e.g., beam loss events) matters as much as maximizing expected return. When a reward is genuinely difficult to specify, IRL and GAIL (Section 2.7.3) offer alternatives by inferring the reward from expert demonstrations. Many HEP RL policies, in particular for accelerator control, are trained in simulation and then deployed on real systems. The sim-to-real gap has two sources: model error (the simulator does not perfectly reproduce real physics) and distributional shift (the real system drifts over time due to temperature, radiation damage, or mechanical settling, while the simulator remains static). Both can degrade performance and, in safety-critical settings, cause dangerous behavior. Domain randomization [106] varies simulator parameters (magnet strengths, beam emittance, noise levels) over a wide range during training, forcing the policy to learn behaviors that are robust across the distribution of possible conditions rather than optimized for a single nominal model. Kaiser et al. [107] and Awal et al. [108] both apply domain randomization to achieve zero-shot or near-zero-shot transfer from simulation to real accelerators. System identification fits simulator parameters to match real observations before or during deployment, narrowing the gap at the cost of additional measurement campaigns. Domain adaptation fine-tunes the policy on a small number of real transitions after simulation training, which is particularly effective when real data collection is feasible but expensive. In HEP settings where interactions are severely limited (e.g., an operational collider where beam time is allocated in shifts), a fast simulator is typically used as the training environment, and few or no real correction steps are needed after deployment; when no reliable simulator exists, a surrogate learned from operational data can play the same role, as in model-based RL (Section 2.6). Many HEP control tasks carry hard operational safety constraints. In accelerator operation, beam loss must not exceed activation thresholds; quench limits on superconducting magnets impose instantaneous current change bounds; the bias currents of cryogenic detectors must remain within narrow windows or risk damaging the sensor. These constraints cannot be treated as soft reward penalties because a single violation may cause irreversible damage. Constrained MDPs (CMDPs) [109] formalize this by augmenting the standard MDP with auxiliary cost functions [FORMULA] and requiring the policy to satisfy [FORMULA] for each constraint [FORMULA] . Lagrangian relaxation converts this into an unconstrained saddle-point problem: the constraint multipliers [FORMULA] are adapted online to maintain feasibility. Action projection is an alternative: after computing the unconstrained policy action, it is projected onto the feasible set defined by the constraints, using a lightweight quadratic program at each step. Control barrier functions (CBFs) [110] provide formal forward-invariance guarantees: if the system state satisfies the safety condition at time [FORMULA] , the CBF filter on the policy action guarantees it will satisfy it at [FORMULA] . In HEP, safety-constrained RL has so far been handled primarily through reward penalties and conservative action clipping rather than formal CMDP methods; this gap is one of the key open problems identified in Section 3.6. RL algorithms can require millions of environment interactions to converge. In simulation, this is acceptable; on real physical systems, it is prohibitive. A full accelerator simulation may take seconds per step; a Geant4 detector simulation takes hours; and every step on a real machine consumes scarce beam time. Sample efficiency is therefore a first-order design requirement in all HEP RL applications, not merely a performance metric. The main strategies for improving it are: replay buffers (DQN, SAC, TD3), which allow each real transition to be reused for multiple gradient updates; model-based planning (Section 2.6), which substitutes real interactions with cheaper simulated ones; transfer learning, which initializes policy or value networks from pre-trained representations (e.g., from a related beamline or a lower-fidelity simulator) to reduce the number of new interactions required; and data augmentation, which synthetically expands the observed transition distribution by applying state-space transformations that preserve physical validity. Control systems in HEP operate at fixed frequencies: for example, the LHC orbit feedback runs at tens of hertz, detector front-end readout operates in nanosecond windows, and Level-1 trigger systems must decide within microseconds. For RL policies to be deployed in these loops, inference latency must match the control frequency. Standard neural network inference on CPUs achieves millisecond latency, sufficient for slow accelerator tuning tasks (seconds per correction step) but not for fast feedback loops. Deployment on field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs) via tools such as hls4ml [111, 112] compiles trained neural networks to a synthesizable hardware description, achieving nanosecond-to-microsecond latency. St. John et al. [19] demonstrated this for the Fermilab Booster, compiling a trained RL controller to an FPGA and testing it on a bench setup. As RL is adopted in faster HEP control loops, hardware-aware neural architecture design and quantization-aware training will become standard requirements. A recurring theme across all HEP RL applications is the incorporation of domain knowledge directly into the RL formulation: in many HEP settings, physics constraints define what a valid solution looks like, and embedding them into the RL problem is the only way to guarantee that learned policies respect them. Physics knowledge manifests at four levels of the RL problem, in particular: State representation. Beam optics parameters (Twiss functions, dispersion) or beam statistics can provide a compact, physics-grounded state for accelerator agents, as in the Elegant-based environments of Section 3.2, although most deployed agents act directly on beam position monitor (BPM) or screen readings. Graph-based hit structures encode the geometric relationships between detector layers for tracking agents. Particle four-momenta and energy flow representations capture the relevant degrees of freedom for jet agents. Reward function. The Coulomb scattering probability serves as a label-free physics reward for tracking (Section 6), replacing hit-to-particle truth associations with a physical consistency criterion. In jet grooming, the reward favors the removal of soft wide-angle radiation, a qualitative proxy for the IRC-safety considerations behind analytic groomers (Section 5). Consistency with observed quark mass ratios and mixing angles provides the reward signal for BSM model-building agents (Section 7). Action space. Restricting actions to physically plausible parameter ranges, such as bounded magnet current increments, reduces the effective search space, focusing exploration on regions where the physics is well-defined. Masks can also remove infeasible actions entirely: grammar masks admit only symmetry-allowed couplings in BSM model building (Section 7.3), and a safety layer [113] enforces unique hit assignments in multi-agent tracking (Section 6.3). Environment model. Fast differentiable simulators such as Cheetah [114] for linear accelerator optics provide physically accurate dynamics models for MBRL without the cost of full particle tracking codes. Learned surrogates can also be constrained to a physically interpretable form: the sparse dictionary surrogate of Colen et al. [115] recovers the linear energy-gain law of the CEBAF linacs and constrains the policy through it. The methods introduced in this section are organized as modular components of a generic RL system, as shown in Figure 2: this also serves as a common frame for the HEP applications reviewed in the following sections, since each of them fixes one choice per component. In addition, these applications provide concrete opportunities to embed physics domain knowledge in RL agents. For a comprehensive discussion of general methods to enable physics-informed RL, we suggest the reader consult the survey of Banerjee et al. [116]. 3 Accelerator Control and Beam Optimization Particle accelerators are among the most complex control systems in science. A modern synchrotron or linear accelerator contains hundreds to thousands of independently controlled elements: dipole and quadrupole magnets, radio-frequency (RF) cavities, collimators, and correction coils, all of which must be jointly tuned to steer, focus, and accelerate a particle beam to the required energy, intensity, and emittance. The control problem is further complicated by time-varying disturbances (ground motion, power supply ripple, temperature drifts, radiation damage), beam loading effects, and hard safety constraints: excessive beam loss can quench superconducting magnets, damage vacuum components, or activate surrounding material. In practice, a modular control system is built to manage this complexity. Such a system combines low-level hardware parameters with higher-level accelerator physics parameters, whose physics-to-hardware translation is stored in databases and software rules derived by human domain experts. For correction and tuning, low-level feedback loops and high-level physics algorithms adjust beam parameters based on instrumentation observables. The critical limitation of this approach is portability: a control module is designed and tuned for a specific accelerator, so each newly commissioned machine requires brand-new tools for tuning and performance optimization. This is both costly and time-consuming; even a marginal improvement in the control pipeline translates into improved scientific yield across the many domains that rely on particle accelerators: fundamental physics research, medical treatments, vaccine development, and materials science. Accelerator control has historically relied on a combination of optics models, hand-crafted feedback controllers, response matrix inversion, and extensive expert manual tuning. Model-based control using measured or simulated transfer matrices is effective when the machine is well characterized but degrades as the model becomes stale due to thermal or mechanical drift. The proportional-integral-derivative (PID) controller [117] applies a correction proportional to the instantaneous error, its integral over time, and its derivative: it is reliable and well-understood but must be re-tuned for each machine configuration and cannot handle non-linear dynamics or multi-element coupling. Numerical optimization methods are widely used to minimize an objective function over the parameter space of the accelerator without requiring an explicit model. The Nelder–Mead simplex [118] is a widely used gradient-free method in accelerator operation, applied to routine tuning of injection efficiency, orbit, and beam intensity; it is robust and simple to implement but converges to local minima and scales poorly with the number of parameters. Robust Conjugate Direction Search (RCDS) [119] improves over the simplex by exploiting approximate curvature information and is widely deployed for orbit and optics correction at synchrotron light sources. Extremum seeking (ES) [120] is a model-free, gradient-estimation technique suitable for real-time optimization of drifting systems; it has been applied to free-electron laser (FEL) pulse energy maximization, beam trajectory control, and multi-objective emittance optimization at LCLS and AWAKE. The covariance matrix adaptation evolution strategy (CMA-ES) [13] and other evolutionary strategies maintain a population of candidate solutions and update a covariance matrix to adapt the search direction, offering better global search capability than simplex methods at the cost of more function evaluations. Bayesian optimization (BO) [12] treats the accelerator as an expensive black-box function, builds a Gaussian process (GP) surrogate of the objective, and selects the next query point by maximizing an acquisition function (e.g., Expected Improvement or Upper Confidence Bound). BO is sample-efficient for low-to-moderate-dimensional problems and can incorporate safety constraints [121] and prior physics knowledge into the GP model [122]; a further extension by Boltz et al. [123] uses neural network surrogate models trained on beam dynamics simulations or historical data as informative prior mean functions, substantially accelerating convergence in high-dimensional spaces even when the surrogate only partially matches experimental conditions. The GP surrogate nevertheless scales as [FORMULA] in the number of observations, and standard kernels lose accuracy beyond a few tens of parameters, which motivates sparse or structured GP approximations. Genetic algorithms (GA) and particle swarm optimization [124] have been applied to multi-objective beam optics design [125] but require large numbers of objective evaluations and produce a static solution that does not adapt online. Most of these methods treat each tuning task as an independent optimization run and do not learn a reusable mapping from machine state to corrective action. Accelerator tuning is inherently a sequential decision problem: adjusting one magnet changes the beam state seen by downstream elements, which may then require further corrections. This state-dependent, sequential structure makes it a natural MDP. The MDP formulation for accelerator control is typically: state: a vector of beam diagnostics (beam position monitor readings, current transformer measurements, emittance estimates); action: incremental changes to magnet currents or RF phases; reward: a scalar encoding beam quality, such as the negative root-mean-square error (RMSE) between measured and reference trajectory, transmission fraction, or emittance. Once trained, an RL agent computes each corrective action from the current accelerator state in a single forward pass (Figure 3) and typically converges within a few steps, whereas numerical optimizers must query the machine iteratively for each new task. RL offers the following structural advantages over traditional approaches: It operates online and, when trained over a distribution of machine conditions, can follow moderate drifts without retraining. It optimizes directly against non-differentiable physical objectives: transmission efficiency, emittance, or luminosity. With a fast simulator or a learned surrogate, the training cost is moved offline, so that the number of real-machine interactions at deployment can be much smaller than for online optimizers such as BO [18]. It can incorporate safety constraints through reward penalties, safe action filtering, or, in principle, constrained MDPs (Section 3.6). A single trained policy can, in principle, generalize across machine configurations and tasks, unlike control modules designed for a single deployment. The accelerator control problem embeds nearly all of the real-world RL challenges discussed in Section 2.8: data efficiency, large and partially observable state and action spaces, hard safety constraints, multi-objective rewards, real-time inference, and the need for policy explainability. The earliest and most developed strand of RL for accelerator physics concerns beam steering and tuning: the problem of adjusting corrector magnets to minimize orbit distortion or maximize beam transmission along a beamline.
