The key quantitative findings are the following. In simulation, RLO reaches a median final beam deviation about an order of magnitude smaller than BO and converges in several times fewer steps. On the real machine, the gap narrows: RLO outperforms BO in a majority of the live trials, with notably smoother actuator trajectories; erratic magnet movements cause hysteresis and power supply glitches on real hardware, so smoothness is operationally significant beyond pure accuracy. RLO is also orders of magnitude faster at inference than BO, since it requires a single forward pass of the policy network rather than acquisition function optimization at each step, making it suitable for real-time control loops where the latency of BO is prohibitive. The practical trade-off is equally clear: BO requires no simulation, no training, and transfers to new lattices or working points without re-engineering; RLO requires a high-speed simulation, substantial reward-engineering effort, and a separate training phase for each new task. The authors state that BO is the right choice when a fast simulation is unavailable, the lattice is subject to frequent modification, or a quick deployment is needed; RLO is preferable when tuning quality and inference speed are paramount, and the engineering investment can be amortized over many deployment cycles. For large machines such as the High-Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC), where many correctors must be tuned, conditions evolve over fills, and real-time feedback loops are required, this analysis suggests that RLO could become an attractive option, provided the necessary simulation infrastructure is in place; a first simulation study of an LHC feedback loop is discussed in Section 3.4. The works above are tuning problems: the agent drives the machine toward a target configuration within an episode of tens of steps, after which the settings are held fixed. A distinct class of problems is feedback: the agent acts continuously at the rate of the control loop to reject disturbances, so latency constraints of micro- to milliseconds dominate the design, and the policy must be executed on dedicated hardware close to the actuators. addressed gradient magnet power supply (GMPS) regulation at the Fermilab Booster synchrotron, where the task is to track a time-varying current reference with high accuracy and low latency. Because building an accurate physics simulator of the Booster is difficult, the authors construct a surrogate model: an LSTM network trained on real accelerator operational data to emulate the dynamical response of the Booster. This surrogate serves as a safe and cost-free training environment for a double DQN agent that selects among a small set of discrete adjustments of the regulator. The agent is trained to maximize the negative absolute regulation error, [FORMULA] , where [FORMULA] is the tracking error, and improves the reward by about a factor of two over the existing PID controller on the surrogate. The key engineering contribution is the implementation of the trained network on an FPGA, with an inference latency of a few microseconds, well within the loop period of tens of milliseconds of the Booster regulation; the FPGA controller was tested on a bench setup rather than in the operational loop. A preceding study by Kafkes and Schram [144] validated the LSTM digital twin of the GMPS and showed that a DQN policy trained on it stabilizes the regulation under realistic time-varying disturbances, with a preliminary two- to fourfold improvement over the PID baseline; the authors motivate offline training on the twin by the risk of training online on the operational system. performed RL feedback control on the Karlsruhe Research Accelerator (KARA) storage ring, damping induced horizontal betatron oscillations in real time. The observation is the last eight horizontal beam position samples from a beam position monitor at the revolution frequency of about [FORMULA] , and the action is the signal sent to a stripline kicker. A compact PPO actor with a single hidden layer runs on the AI Engine array of an AMD-Xilinx Versal device, with a full inference loop of [FORMULA] . Training is split between the device and the control room: an experience accumulator on the device collects transitions, the policy update runs on a control room computer, and the updated weights are loaded back onto the hardware. The agents are trained from scratch on the real machine and are compared with the commercial bunch-by-bunch feedback installed at KARA, which is based on finite impulse response (FIR) filters: the authors summarize the performance as comparable, and every trained configuration, across reward definitions and network sizes, reaches a higher damping rate than the FIR controller. This is a direct experimental answer to the latency question raised in Section 3.6: online RL with microsecond inference is feasible on current hardware. The work builds on an earlier KARA framework by Wang et al. [145], which targeted inference latencies below [FORMULA] on a Xilinx Zynq UltraScale+ device for longitudinal beam dynamics feedback and validated it on cart-pole and pendulum control tasks. studied RL for the tune feedback of the LHC, the component of the beam-based feedback system that corrects the horizontal and vertical betatron tunes. In a dedicated Gym simulation of the feedback loop, the state is the pair of normalized tune errors and the action sets the current changes of 16 tuning quadrupoles. Five algorithms are tested (NAF, PPO, SAC, TD3, and the model-based AE-DYNA), and the best NAF and PPO agents reach the target in about 9 steps on average, compared to about 20 for the reimplemented proportional-integral (PI) controller, which inverts the tune response matrix. When one or three actuators are stuck at a random setting, both agents degrade more gracefully than the PI controller: with one stuck actuator, the PI controller fails in all test episodes, whereas the NAF agent still succeeds in one third of them, and with three, the agents end closer to the target. The study is simulation-only, but it targets an operational LHC feedback loop directly, with the same actuators and observables as the existing controller. A striking application of RL to physics instrumentation control beyond the accelerator domain is the work of the CRESST collaboration [26]. CRESST operates cryogenic phonon detectors with transition-edge sensors (TES) at millikelvin temperatures in the Gran Sasso underground laboratory, targeting direct dark matter-nucleus scattering. Optimal detector sensitivity requires careful and simultaneous tuning of the TES temperature and the bias current in its readout circuit: small deviations from the optimal operating point degrade energy resolution significantly. This tuning has historically been performed manually by a trained physicist, a process that can take up to several hours per detector and does not scale to the large detector arrays envisioned for next-generation searches. The authors automated this procedure with RL in two settings: first, training on a simulation of the CRESST detector response used as a virtual RL environment; second, training live on three physical CRESST detectors operating in the Gran Sasso underground setup. In both cases, SAC agents optimized a standard detector as fast as human experts and with comparable results. This work carries two important implications for the field. First, it shows that an RL agent can be trained and operated live inside a deep underground physics experiment, interfaced with the experiment control software, in an environment where manual intervention is costly. Second, autonomous detector tuning is a prerequisite for the large detector arrays of future experiments: the planned CRESST upgrade foresees several tens to hundreds of detector modules, and because the agents need no manual interaction, the procedure can be run in parallel for all of them. All existing deployments handle safety through reward penalties, episode resets on constraint violation, or conservative action clipping. None provides formal safety guarantees. Constrained MDPs with Lagrangian relaxation and control barrier functions (Section 2.8.3) offer principled alternatives: the former would encode beam loss, quench, and actuator limits as explicit cost constraints, while the latter would certify that the machine state remains in the safe set at every step. An additional challenge specific to model-based accelerator RL is propagating safety constraints through the learned surrogate model: an action that the surrogate predicts to be safe may still violate constraints on the real machine due to model error. Ensemble-based uncertainty estimates [130] are a first step toward addressing this, but robust constraint satisfaction under surrogate model uncertainty remains an open theoretical problem with direct operational consequences. Safe model-based RL [146] offers a more principled path: by maintaining a Lyapunov function over the state space and using a Gaussian process model of the dynamics, the agent can certify a growing safe region of the parameter space and guarantee that exploration never leaves it. The GP dynamics model provides calibrated uncertainty estimates that tighten the safe region where the surrogate is reliable and expand it only as new data confirms safety, providing exactly the uncertainty-aware constraint propagation that ensemble methods approximate heuristically. Adapting this framework to the accelerator setting requires replacing the GP with a more scalable model, such as a neural network ensemble, and incorporating the known physics of beam optics as a structured mean function; both remain open research directions. The key open question is whether the Lyapunov stability certificates can be maintained when the dynamics model is a high-dimensional neural network rather than a GP, where coverage guarantees are harder to establish formally. Current policies are trained for a specific beamline and machine configuration. Building policies that generalize across lattice configurations, facilities, or beam energies would dramatically reduce the engineering effort for new deployments. The lattice-agnostic approach of [128] is an early step, demonstrating zero-shot generalization, in simulation, to lattice sections of two different linacs through domain randomization over lattice parameters. The cross-facility generalization problem is structurally equivalent to sim-to-real transfer (Section 2.8.2): the target facility is an out-of-distribution environment relative to the source, and the gap has the same two components, namely model error in the physics simulation and distributional shift in operating conditions. The methods developed for sim-to-real transfer therefore apply directly: Domain randomization over lattice parameters, magnet misalignment, and beam emittance during training forces the policy to discover behaviors that are robust across a family of machines rather than optimal for a single nominal configuration [106]. System identification [114] can narrow the remaining gap by fitting the simulation parameters of a new facility to a small number of real measurements before deployment, reducing the effective distribution shift to a residual that the built-in robustness of the policy can tolerate. Meta-RL (Section 2.7.5) treats each facility as a distinct task within a shared latent space of accelerator configurations [91], so that the policy can specialize to a new facility from a handful of interactions. First steps exist at the AWAKE electron line: Hirlaender et al. [147] use MAML to adapt a policy within 3 to 6 interaction steps to a POMDP whose hidden parameters drift over time, and a Gaussian process model-based variant addresses few-shot training when no simulation is available [148]. Model-based RL with online planning [69] offers a complementary route to generalization. If the world model [149] is expressive enough to represent the dynamics of a family of accelerators, the agent can adapt to a new facility by updating its world model from a small number of real transitions and re-planning with the updated model, without retraining the policy network. Planning algorithms such as MCTS or model-predictive control [150] can then generate facility-specific action sequences at deployment time by rolling out the updated model, combining the data efficiency of model-based methods with the flexibility of online re-planning. Offline RL from archived operational logs of multiple facilities (Section 2.7.2) could pretrain a broad prior over accelerator dynamics without any real machine time, which a lightweight online fine-tuning step could then specialize to a new target. In principle, a truly general RL agent could optimize the full operational workflow of a particle accelerator, generalizing across equipment types (linear, circular) and tasks (magnet tuning, beam regulation, injection); recent progress in zero-shot sim-to-real transfer [107, 108] and lattice-agnostic policies [128] suggests that steps toward this goal are feasible. The Fermilab Booster [19] and KARA [20] works (Section 3.4) demonstrated hardware inference with microsecond latency for single feedback loops, the latter with online training on the real machine. Extending this to full-machine control at LHC or HL-LHC frequencies requires co-design of RL policy architectures with hardware constraints: policies must be small enough to fit on the target FPGA device, execute within the timing budget of the control system, and remain robust to the fixed-point arithmetic of hardware inference. Three complementary techniques reduce the computational footprint of a trained policy without retraining from scratch: Quantization-aware training [151] reduces the precision of network weights and activations during training to match hardware arithmetic; the work of Kresse and Lampert [152] demonstrates that continuous-control RL policies can be quantized to as few as 2–3 bits per weight with negligible performance loss on MuJoCo benchmarks [153] and deployed to an Artix-7 FPGA with microsecond inference latency and micro-joule energy consumption per action. Crucially, the same work finds that input quantization must be treated separately: the precision of the input state is generally the bottleneck, because quantization error in the first layer prevents the policy from distinguishing similar sensor states that matter for fine control, whereas deeper layers, where the information is spread over a more redundant latent space, tolerate much lower bitwidths. Pruning [154] removes redundant parameters to reduce model size, and hls4ml [112, 111] compiles trained neural networks directly to synthesizable hardware description language, enabling sub-microsecond FPGA inference for neural network classifiers in the LHC L1 trigger system. Policy distillation [155] is a complementary approach that is particularly well suited to the FPGA deployment problem: a large, expressive teacher policy is trained first without hardware constraints, and a compact student policy is then trained via supervised regression on the action distribution of the teacher rather than by direct RL. The student inherits the behavior of the teacher while being dramatically smaller and faster; the compression ratio can be adjusted freely to meet the FPGA resource budget, unlike quantization, which is constrained by the fixed-point arithmetic of the hardware. Hardware-aware RL training, where the quantization and latency constraints are incorporated as penalties during policy optimization, remains an open research direction. The recurrent networks usually employed to handle partial observability (Section 2.2) are particularly expensive in hardware: LSTM [45] and gated recurrent unit (GRU) [156] cells require sequential state updates that cannot be fully parallelized on an FPGA, motivating the development of hardware-friendly alternatives such as linear recurrent units [157] or S4-based state-space models [158] for RL policy networks: the latter requires only a fixed-size state vector multiplication step during update, with no gating operations, making it significantly cheaper on an FPGA than an LSTM of comparable capacity. Operators will hand control of a machine to a policy only if they can check that its decisions follow from the physics of the beamline, yet none of the deployments reviewed above evaluates an explanation of the learned policy. Colen et al. [115] take a first step by making the constraints that shape the policy inspectable, rather than the policy itself. In TD3 agents with learnable constraints (LC-TD3) for surrogate environments of the CEBAF linacs, calibrated on historical data and ranging from a single cryomodule to the 197 cavities of the North Linac, a learned surrogate predicts the energy gain from the state and action, and a penalty on the predicted energy enters the actor objective, so that the policy minimizes heat load and trip rate within the target energy band. When the surrogate is a sparse dictionary model in the spirit of sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics [159], it yields a closed-form expression for the energy gain, linear in the cavity gradients, whose coefficients agree with the ground-truth cavity parameters of the environment: operators can therefore verify the physics behind the constraint the agent obeys. On the North Linac, the constrained agents converge to the target energy band in 88% to 100% of the trials for every objective, whereas TD3 with the energy penalty in the reward converges in at most 50%; in the multi-objective setting, the sparse variant achieves the largest Pareto front coverage, while the neural surrogate variant fails to satisfy the energy constraint. The approach does not require a differentiable environment, but it converges more slowly and to worse configurations than DDRL [17], which starts from an accurate differentiable surrogate, and it has not yet been tested on the real machine. The explanation, however, covers the constraint and not the policy. Policy distillation, introduced above for FPGA deployment, offers a route to the latter: the student can be chosen for readability rather than size, for example a soft decision tree or a program in a domain-specific language (Section 7.5), or, for steering and orbit correction, a low-order map from BPM readings to corrector settings that operators can compare directly with the inverted orbit response matrix. A single compact student could then serve both purposes, fitting the latency budget of the control loop and remaining readable by operators. The open questions are how much fidelity to the teacher such a student retains in the nonlinear regimes where RL outperforms classical controllers, and whether its explanations remain valid after transfer to the real machine. Bent crystals are used at CERN in two settings whose setup is a sequential alignment task, and both are candidates for RL. At the SPS, a thin bent crystal placed upstream of the electrostatic septum shadows the septum blade and reduces slow extraction losses; the crystal is currently set up with numerical optimizers, and RL agents have been proposed to shorten the setup time [160], but no RL results on this task have been reported so far. At the LHC, crystal collimator alignment is currently addressed with supervised models trained on beam loss monitor signals [161]. Both problems share the same structure: the crystal angle is changed in small increments, and beam loss monitor readings provide feedback after each move, which maps onto an episodic MDP with a learned, possibly zero-shot transferred, policy in place of a scan. The open question is whether such a policy reduces setup time or improves robustness relative to the optimizers and supervised models already in operation, which requires the same kind of direct comparison that Kaiser et al. [18] carried out for beam tuning at ARES. 4 Data Quality Monitoring Large-scale particle physics experiments such as ATLAS [162], CMS [163], LHCb [164], and ALICE [165] operate detectors with of order [FORMULA] readout channels, sampled every 25 ns during LHC bunch crossings. The resulting data rates reach tens of terabytes per hour, and before any physics analysis can proceed, human operators must validate the recorded data; detector subsystems must be operating correctly, and runs or luminosity blocks affected by malfunctions like noise bursts, high-voltage trips, dead channels, or timing misalignment, must be flagged and excluded. This process is called data quality monitoring (DQM) and is of paramount importance: undetected detector malfunctions introduce biases that can invalidate entire physics analyses, while overly conservative flagging discards good data and reduces statistical power. In a typical LHC experiment, DQM is performed at two levels. The online stage occurs synchronously with data-taking, at fixed time intervals of several minutes: the time needed to accumulate enough counts for statistically meaningful histogram evaluation. When anomalies are detected, they must be corrected before data collection continues, so speed of detection takes priority over depth of analysis. The offline stage runs after data recording is complete; the absence of time constraints allows evaluation of high-level distributions requiring larger datasets and more time to reconstruct, catching anomalies that the online pass missed and flagging the corresponding data for exclusion. Both stages currently rely heavily on expert shifters who inspect hundreds of diagnostic histograms per run and issue binary good/bad certifications, amounting to thousands of expert decisions per year across the LHC experiments. Automated DQM has been pursued through threshold-based alarms and reference histogram comparison, using statistical tests such as the Kolmogorov–Smirnov (KS) test and the [FORMULA] test against reference histograms accumulated from good runs. More recently, supervised classifiers and autoencoder-based anomaly detectors have been trained on reference data from good runs, with or without labels [166, 167]. A representative recent example is the work of Asres, Omlin, Wang et al. [168], who apply a semi-supervised hybrid autoencoder, trained on healthy data and incorporating convolutional, graph, and recurrent neural networks, to spatio-temporal anomaly detection in the CMS Hadron Calorimeter (HCAL). The authors show that transfer learning from a model pre-trained on a different section of the calorimeter reduces the number of trainable parameters and the amount of training data needed for a new section, and improves robustness to anomalies contaminating the training data, addressing a key practical bottleneck in DQM automation. MEDIC [169] (Monitoring for Event Data Integrity and Consistency), a simulation-driven framework that uses a modified version of the Delphes fast detector simulation [170] to generate controlled fault scenarios, enables the study and development of DQM methodologies without requiring real experimental data: the neural network learns to both identify anomalies and localize the specific malfunctioning detector components responsible, going beyond binary good/bad classification. Supervised approaches achieve good accuracy when labeled data are abundant, but suffer in low-label regimes: expert annotation is expensive, labels for rare or novel failure modes are scarce, and the distribution of detector conditions shifts over time as the machine and detector age. Conversely, unsupervised and transfer-learning approaches mitigate the labeling burden but remain static once trained and cannot incorporate expert feedback to correct systematic mistakes. None of the existing automated approaches actively solicit human expertise in a principled way: the human shifter is either in the loop for every decision or out of it entirely. The DQM problem can be formalized as a sequential decision-making task with an adaptive human in the loop. An RL (or bandit) agent observes diagnostic histograms, decides which ones to flag for expert review, and updates its policy based on the feedback of the expert. This framing has three structural advantages over static supervised approaches. First, it naturally minimizes annotation effort by actively selecting the most informative queries: requesting human intervention only when the agent is uncertain, rather than for every histogram or for none. Second, it adapts online to concept drift: as detector conditions change, the policy updates from the new feedback without requiring a full retraining cycle. Third, in the bandit formulation, it provides theoretical regret guarantees on the number of missed anomalies over time, which static classifiers cannot offer. Bandit algorithms are particularly well suited to the stateless, high-throughput DQM setting where each certification decision is largely independent. Instead, a full RL formulation with state transitions becomes appropriate when sequential decisions within a run are correlated (e.g., when the status of one subsystem affects the expected behavior of a downstream subsystem). Figure 4 contrasts the two formulations reviewed below. Jullian Parra et al. [171] provide the first proof-of-concept for applying human-in-the-loop RL to automate the DQM process in particle physics experiments. The setting is motivated by DQM at the LHC experiments and is developed on a simplified synthetic dataset that captures the essential structure of the problem: a stream of histograms, each representing a detector observable, must be classified as good or bad with as few expert queries as possible. The system implements a multi-agent PPO architecture with two cooperating agents. The predictor observes the current histogram and emits a binary good/bad classification. The checker observes both the histogram and the decision of the predictor and decides whether to query the human shifter; if queried, the label given by the shifter is used to update the predictor. The objective of the predictor is to match the judgment of the human; the objective of the checker is to call the shifter only when the predictor is uncertain, minimizing total annotation effort while maintaining accuracy. The state space of the DQM environment comprises the current histogram, the operating mode of the detector, and the human label if the shifter has been called. To handle scarce labeled data, the authors propose data augmentation: artificially generated histograms are inserted into the training stream to accelerate learning and improve generalization to new operating conditions. Three key results emerge. First, the system learns to request human intervention selectively, primarily at the start of training or after operating conditions change, and rarely calls the shifter once the predictor is accurate. Second, random and unbiased noise in human classification can be reduced: a predictor trained on shifter labels flipped at random in 30% of the cases exceeds the 70% accuracy of those labels, and the accuracy improves further when the shifter can consult the outputs of the predictor before deciding, so that algorithm and shifter improve through mutual feedback. Third, the framework adapts online to changing detector conditions without retraining, a property that static supervised classifiers lack by construction. A preliminary test on a real offline dataset from the LHCb experiment supports the synthetic setup as a proxy: on 2 300 shifter-labeled data points, an agent trained only on augmented synthetic data reaches 91% accuracy on nominal and 75% on anomalous points, although the shifter labels may themselves be noisy and the dataset cannot be released. The main open challenge, according to the authors, is robustness against shifter bias: a mismatch between the average knowledge of the shifters and that of the detector experts introduces correlated label noise that the current system does not address; the authors suggest reference histograms built from the decisions of the shifters and periodically checked by detector experts. An alternative approach treats DQM monitoring as a bandit problem, without maintaining state across rounds: at each round, the agent selects which detector channels to observe and receives feedback only on the observed channels. Bower [172] introduces the Adversarial Thresholding Semi-Bandit (ATSB) formalism and applies it to real-time monitoring of the anode currents of the ALICE TRD [173]. The operational challenge is as follows: the TRD automatically switches off a device channel when the current exceeds a safety limit, but doing so reduces the data-collection capacity of the experiment. A monitoring agent must therefore selectively observe channels whose current exceeds or deviates from a threshold, intervening before the automatic shutdown triggers and allowing the human operator to take preventive action. Formally, the ATSB problem extends the classical non-stochastic multi-armed bandit (MAB) to a semi-bandit setting with thresholding feedback. In each round [FORMULA] , the player selects a subset of the [FORMULA] arms (detector channels) [FORMULA] . In the semi-bandit setting, the player observes individual arm rewards rather than only the total reward of the selected subset, enabling fine-grained credit assignment across a large number of detector channels. The adversarial (non-stochastic) formulation is critical: because detector conditions can change arbitrarily over time, for example due to beam instabilities, radiation damage, or environmental fluctuations, no stationary reward distribution can be assumed. In the latter setting, which is the use case of major practical interest, AliceBandit identified deviations in TRD anode current channels hours before a trip event, enabling the human operator to take preventive action before the automatic shutdown triggered. The two RL-based DQM approaches reviewed here occupy opposite ends of the decision-making spectrum: ATSB [172] treats each monitoring decision as stateless and provides formal regret guarantees, while the multi-agent PPO system [171] maintains an explicit agent state and adapts its query behavior as detector conditions change. Table 2 places both against traditional automated DQM methods in terms of feedback, label requirements, online adaptation, guarantees, and validation on real data. This contrast reflects a genuine open question: whether the sequential structure of a data-taking run is rich enough to warrant full RL, or whether the marginal gain over bandit methods justifies the added complexity. Answering it will require validation on real experiment data across multiple runs and operating conditions; so far, only a preliminary offline test on LHCb data exists for the PPO system [171]. Current systems query experts reactively, based on the uncertainty of the agent about the current histogram. Combining RL with principled uncertainty quantification, using calibrated predictive uncertainty (e.g., conformal prediction [174] or Bayesian deep learning [175]) to identify histograms where annotation is most valuable, would improve sample efficiency further. A natural extension is to model the attention budget of the expert explicitly: for example, the agent should not only ask “is this histogram anomalous?” but also “is this the right moment to ask, given that the shifter has already been queried five times in the last hour?” Two families of RL methods are particularly well-suited to this setting. The first is distributional RL (Section 2.3). The spread of its return distribution reflects the intrinsic (aleatoric) variability of the outcome of a certification decision, not the epistemic uncertainty of the agent, which requires ensembles or Bayesian methods (below). In the DQM context, a wide return distribution for a given histogram signals an ambiguous case, making it a natural trigger for an expert query; conversely, narrow distributions can be acted upon autonomously without annotation. This connects directly to the risk-sensitive behavior enabled by distributional RL: the agent can be configured to be systematically conservative (preferring to query when uncertain) by targeting a low quantile of the return distribution, rather than its mean, for decision-making. Bayesian RL (Section 2.7.5) is complementary: in the DQM setting, the posterior becomes a posterior over detector malfunction rates and anomaly distributions that is updated as expert labels arrive; information-theoretic criteria, such as the expected information gain, then guide the query decisions of the agent, selecting the histogram that would most reduce uncertainty about the current detector state. Both approaches address a key limitation of the existing systems: the queries of the discussed PPO-based DQM agent [171] are based on a point estimate of its own prediction confidence, which does not quantify how much new information each query would provide relative to the total annotation budget of the expert. The PPO-based DQM system has been validated mainly on synthetic data, with only a preliminary offline test on real LHCb data [171]. The critical next step is systematic validation on real experiment data: real detector histograms exhibit long-tailed failure distributions, correlated multi-subsystem anomalies, and label noise patterns that synthetic datasets cannot fully capture. Deployment in a shadow mode, where the RL agent runs alongside the existing DQM system without affecting decisions, would allow controlled comparison and identification of failure modes before operational adoption. Four RL sub-fields offer complementary tools for bridging this gap. Offline RL (Section 2.7.2) is the most directly applicable: years of archived DQM decisions and expert certifications constitute a large fixed dataset from which a policy can be learned without any new interaction with the real experiment. Conservative methods such as CQL are critical here, because the behavioral policy, i.e., the human shifter, covers only a subset of possible detector conditions. Inverse RL (Section 2.7.3) complements offline RL by inferring from certification histories the implicit reward that experienced shifters have been optimizing, rather than requiring an explicit reward to be hand-designed. This is valuable because expert DQM judgment encodes subtle heuristics (e.g., tolerating minor calorimeter noise during early fills but flagging it at peak luminosity) that are difficult to articulate as a scalar reward but are readily recoverable from demonstration data via maximum entropy IRL [83]. Meta-RL (Section 2.7.5) addresses the rapid adaptation problem: detector conditions shift between LHC runs, fills, and years, so a policy trained on Run 2 data may underperform on Run 3 without retraining. A meta-learned policy that treats each run period as a separate task can adapt to new conditions from a handful of expert labels, rather than requiring a full offline training campaign each time. Model-based RL (Section 2.6) is useful in the shadow-mode deployment phase: a learned model of the anomaly dynamics of the detector can generate synthetic failure scenarios from the small number of real anomalies observed in shadow operation, augmenting the scarce real data and accelerating policy improvement before full deployment. Each RL-based DQM application reviewed here targets a single detector subsystem. Building a shared RL policy across multiple subsystems, or even multiple experiments, via transfer learning or multi-task RL would reduce the engineering overhead for new deployments and exploit cross-subsystem correlations. For example, a fault in a shared clock or trigger system can appear simultaneously in several subsystems; a shared policy could detect such correlated signatures faster than independent single-subsystem agents. Multi-agent RL (Section 2.7.1) is the most natural framework for multi-subsystem DQM: each subsystem is assigned a dedicated agent that observes its local histograms and issues local certification decisions, while under centralized training with decentralized execution the critic has access to all subsystem observations simultaneously. This allows the joint policy to capture cross-subsystem correlations, such as the correlated signatures above, without requiring any single agent to process the full set of experiment histograms at inference time. Competitive dynamics between agents can further be used to model the resource allocation problem: when the total annotation budget is limited, agents must implicitly negotiate the uncertain histograms of which subsystem are most valuable to present to the shifter. Transfer learning and multi-task RL (Section 2.7.5) enable policies trained on one subsystem or experiment to be reused elsewhere with minimal additional data. A policy pre-trained on CMS tracker histograms shares structural similarities with one needed for ATLAS inner detector monitoring: both involve spatial hit occupancy maps, timing distributions, and noise rate histograms, differing mainly in granularity and geometry. Multi-task RL with a shared encoder and task-specific heads would allow a single model to serve multiple subsystems simultaneously, while transfer learning via fine-tuning on a small number of labeled histograms from the new subsystem would dramatically reduce the annotation cost of deploying DQM RL in a new experimental context. Detector conditions change on timescales of years due to radiation damage, hardware replacements, and operating condition changes. Continual RL (Section 2.7.5) is a natural fit for the long-horizon DQM problem: as the detector evolves, the agent must retain knowledge of historical failure modes while incorporating new ones, without resetting its policy from scratch at each run period. Standard replay buffers, elastic weight consolidation [176], and progressive neural network architectures [177] are candidate mechanisms for preserving past knowledge while permitting new learning. A recent perspective on deployable continual learning for particle accelerators [178] identifies the accelerator applications in which continual learning could maintain model performance under distribution drift; an analogous framework for detector DQM would need to handle the additional complexity of non-stationary anomaly distributions and evolving expert labeling criteria over multi-year run periods. 5 Jet Physics Jets are collimated sprays of hadrons produced by the fragmentation of quarks and gluons created in high-energy collisions. They are the most abundant objects in LHC events and are central to a vast range of physics analyses, from precision quantum chromodynamics (QCD) measurements to searches for new physics. Working with jets requires a series of algorithmic decisions: how to cluster detector deposits into a jet, how to remove contaminating soft radiation (grooming), and how to order or represent jets and their constituents as inputs to downstream ML tasks. Each of these is a discrete or sequential decision problem, making jet physics a natural domain for RL. Standard jet clustering algorithms such as anti- [FORMULA] [179], [FORMULA] [180], and Cambridge/Aachen (C/A) [181, 182] define a distance metric between pseudo-particles and merge the closest pair iteratively until all pairs exceed a jet radius threshold [FORMULA] . The anti- [FORMULA] algorithm is the standard jet reconstruction algorithm at the LHC: its clustering sequence produces geometrically regular, cone-like jets that are straightforward to calibrate, but its merging criterion is entirely fixed and insensitive to the internal structure or physics goal of the analysis. Grooming algorithms such as Soft Drop [183] post-process the clustered jet by recursively undoing the groupings in the C/A tree and removing the softer branch whenever the Soft Drop condition [FORMULA] is not satisfied, where [FORMULA] is the momentum fraction and [FORMULA] is the angular separation between the two branches. Soft Drop is IRC-safe by construction and widely used for jet mass measurements and boosted object tagging, but its parameters [FORMULA] and [FORMULA] are hand-tuned and constant across all jets, regardless of their kinematic configuration. Input ordering for sequence-based classifiers (LSTM, transformer [184]) that take lists of jets or jet constituents is typically chosen by [FORMULA] ordering or angular ordering, without optimization for any specific downstream task. All three problems (clustering, grooming, and ordering) share the structure of a sequential decision process in which the objective (e.g., mass resolution, tagging performance, or IRC safety) depends on the full sequence of decisions, not just any individual step. This delayed, holistic reward structure is precisely what RL is designed to optimize. RL offers two concrete advantages over hand-crafted algorithms. First, a learned policy can adapt its decisions to the specific phase-space configuration of each jet: a grooming agent can be more aggressive on jets with large soft contamination and more conservative on others, whereas Soft Drop applies the same criterion uniformly. Second, RL can optimize directly against a physics observable, such as a discriminant score, a mass resolution, or a likelihood, that has no closed-form gradient with respect to the algorithmic decisions, making standard backpropagation inapplicable. These problems are instances of a pattern that recurs across several of the applications reviewed in this survey: the agent builds or refines a partial object one edit at a time, a feasibility mask restricts the admissible edits, and an evaluator scores the result (Figure 5). The partial object can be a jet clustering tree or an input ordering (this section), a track candidate on a hit graph (Section 6), a BSM model encoded as a charge matrix, a field graph, or a token sequence (Section 7), a detector configuration (Section 8), or an assignment of reconstructed objects, a system of integral identities, or a symbolic expression (Section 9). The domains differ mainly in the evaluator, which ranges from analytic physics models to full detector simulation and learned classifiers. This paper illustrates a general and transferable principle: RL can optimize discrete preprocessing decisions that have no closed-form gradient with respect to the downstream loss, simply by using the downstream performance to select the training targets of the ordering policy. The same principle applies to any sequential representation choice in particle physics such as constituent selection, variable ordering, and feature masking, where the optimal choice depends on the downstream task. Current work optimizes grooming, clustering, and ordering independently. A unified RL policy trained jointly on all three decisions and coupled end-to-end to a downstream physics analysis could discover synergies between them that sequential optimization misses. The main challenge is defining a reward that reflects the full analysis goal (e.g., signal significance or exclusion limit) without intermediate surrogates, as the gradient of such an objective through discrete decisions is not available. This setting is naturally framed as a multi-objective RL problem (Section 2.7.5): grooming quality (mass resolution), clustering quality (parton shower log-likelihood), ordering quality (downstream classifier performance), and IRC safety are four distinct objectives that cannot in general be simultaneously maximized, and a scalarized reward would fix an arbitrary priority among them. A preference-conditioned policy [99] would instead let the physicist select the operating point at inference time, for example preferring mass resolution for a boosted [FORMULA] search and tagging performance for a top tagger, with one trained policy shared across analyses. Jet constituent lists have variable length and permutation symmetry, making them natural candidates for graph neural network (GNN) representations [195]. The implications of adopting a GNN policy backbone go beyond a better state encoder and affect the RL algorithm itself in three ways. First, a permutation-equivariant GNN policy [196] constrains the policy class to respect the physical symmetry of the jet: the action distribution is invariant to any reordering of the constituents, which tightens sample complexity and prevents the agent from exploiting arbitrary input orderings. Second, each message-passing layer propagates information across the constituent graph before emitting an action, providing a form of implicit look-ahead over the [FORMULA] -hop neighborhood that is baked into the forward pass rather than achieved by explicit tree search. Third, when actions are defined as edge additions or removals on the constituent graph, the action space changes at every step as merges are applied, requiring modifications to standard policy gradient estimators: the policy must be evaluated over the current edge set via a masked softmax or auto-regressive edge sampling scheme, and advantage estimation must account for credit flowing through both the temporal and graph-topological dimensions simultaneously. The emergence of cross-task foundation models for jet physics, such as OmniJet- [FORMULA] [197], raises the question of whether an RL policy pretrained on diverse jet samples could generalize across grooming, clustering, and ordering tasks simultaneously. A pretrained jet representation used as a shared state encoder across all three RL problems would reduce the engineering overhead of per-task policy design, but the benefits extend further than architectural convenience. First, in a transfer learning scenario, the foundation model backbone provides a rich prior over jet kinematics that the RL policy can exploit from the first training step rather than learning from scratch. Because the encoder already captures the relevant structure of the jet constituent space, the policy head only needs to learn the task-specific decision logic on top of a fixed or lightly fine-tuned representation. This translates directly into higher sample efficiency: fewer environment interactions are needed to reach a given level of performance, which is practically significant given that training RL policies on realistic jet samples from full Geant4 [2] simulation is computationally expensive. Second, foundation model backbones offer a principled path toward sim-to-real transfer for jet RL policies. A common failure mode of simulation-trained policies is that the state representation is sensitive to low-level features that differ between simulation and real detector data: calorimeter granularity, noise thresholds, or particle flow calibrations. A foundation model pretrained on both simulated and real jets, or fine-tuned with domain adaptation techniques on real data, would produce a state encoder whose representation is robust to these low-level distributional shifts. The RL policy operating on top of this encoder would then inherit that robustness, requiring only a lightweight fine-tuning step on real data rather than a full retraining cycle. This two-stage approach, pretraining a general encoder followed by RL fine-tuning of the decision head, mirrors the paradigm that has proven effective in natural language processing (pretrained language models fine-tuned with RL from human feedback (RLHF) [198]) and, with supervised rather than RL fine-tuning, in robotics (self-supervised sensorimotor pretraining followed by task-specific fine-tuning [199]), and represents a promising but as yet unexplored direction for jet physics. None of the RL jet algorithms reviewed here enforces IRC safety: the grooming policy of [185] addresses it only through the reward. A general treatment of IRC safety as a constrained RL problem, applicable to clustering, grooming, and ordering, has not yet been developed. Connecting constrained RL theory (Section 2.8.3) to the formal definitions of IRC safety [200] in perturbative QCD [201] is an open theoretical problem with direct implications for the use of learned jet algorithms in precision measurements. The safe RL literature offers two complementary tools for this problem. The first is Lyapunov-based safe model-based RL [146], which maintains a certified safe region of the state space and proves that data collection can expand this region without ever leaving it. Translated to jet grooming, the constraint cannot be a property of a single partial sequence, since IRC safety is a property of the algorithm as a whole; it would instead be expressed as conditions on the decision rule, for example that the removal decision be insensitive to the addition of soft or collinear branches, and the agent would be certified to respect them at every de-clustering step. The second is model predictive control (MPC) for safe exploration [150], which uses a learned GP model of the dynamics to construct confidence intervals over future trajectories and guarantees that the trajectory satisfies safety constraints at every step via a terminal set constraint. In the jet context, the dynamics model would predict the kinematic consequences of a grooming or clustering decision, and the MPC layer would reject actions whose predicted trajectories violate the IRC safety condition before they are applied. Both approaches also highlight a broader benefit of model-based RL for IRC-safe jet algorithms. A model-free agent with a per-step action mask can only exclude inadmissible actions at the current step; it cannot reason about whether a currently admissible action leads to a state from which no admissible completion exists. A model-based agent with look-ahead can verify, before committing to a merge or removal, that at least one admissible continuation exists from the resulting state, analogously to how MPC guarantees the existence of a feasible return trajectory at every timestep [150]. This look-ahead capability would be especially valuable in clustering, where the properties of the final tree depend on the full sequence of merges and a single early decision can preclude admissible completions. Planning with MCTS or [FORMULA] [190] already provides this look-ahead property implicitly; embedding IRC safety as an explicit constraint into the tree search is a natural and well-motivated extension. 6 Charged Particle Tracking Charged particle tracking is the reconstruction of particle trajectories from discrete position measurements (hits) left in a tracking detector. A tracker consists of multiple layers of detector cells; when a charged particle crosses a cell, it deposits charge in one or more adjacent pixels, producing a hit whose centroid estimates the true particle position. In a typical LHC detector, each bunch crossing contains tens of overlapping soft-collision vertices (pileup) on top of the hard interaction of interest, resulting in tens of thousands of hits across of order ten detector layers. Associating the correct hits to each particle trajectory is a combinatorial assignment problem whose complexity grows super-linearly with pileup multiplicity. At the HL-LHC, with up to 200 pileup interactions per bunch crossing, thousands of charged particles, and of order [FORMULA] space-points per event, tracking will be one of the dominant computational bottlenecks in offline reconstruction [202]. Tracking traditionally involves four sequential steps: seed generation, track finding, track fitting, and track selection. Seed generation constructs an initial estimate of the five helix parameters [FORMULA] by connecting hits in adjacent detector layers. Track finding extends each seed through subsequent layers, branching when more than one compatible hit is found. Track fitting uses the Kalman filter [203] to estimate the particle state from the sequence of hit measurements, propagating the state between layers and incorporating material effects via the estimated radiation length. Track selection removes fake candidates that are not associated with a real charged particle. The Kalman filter is the standard algorithm for LHC tracking and provides theoretically optimal state estimation given the assumed linear dynamics; its limitation is the combinatorial explosion of track candidates as pileup increases, with reconstruction time growing super-linearly with detector occupancy. The required computing time is projected to exceed the available CPU budget at HL-LHC conditions without significant algorithmic advances [204]. More recently, graph neural networks (GNNs) have been applied to tracking as a graph edge classification problem, with hits as nodes and edges representing candidate track segments [202]. The Exa.TrkX pipeline processes detector hits as a graph and predicts edge labels (true track segment vs. combinatorial background) using message-passing GNNs, achieving competitive efficiency with significantly reduced computational cost on GPU hardware. GNN-based trackers are differentiable and scalable, but require labeled training data: ground-truth hit-to-particle associations must be extracted from Monte Carlo simulation, potentially introducing discrepancies between simulation and reality. RL offers a qualitatively different framing of the tracking problem. Rather than learning a discriminator for pre-generated track candidates, an RL agent actively navigates the detector hit graph, deciding at each step which hit to follow next. The key advantage is that this formulation is naturally label-free: the reward can be defined in terms of physical consistency without requiring hit-to-particle truth associations. Specifically, the trajectory of a charged particle traversing a detector is governed by multiple Coulomb scattering, which determines the expected angular deflection between successive detector layers; this provides a physics-grounded reward signal that distinguishes genuine tracks from combinatorial fakes purely from the measured hit positions. Furthermore, because the reward depends on the material and geometry of the detector rather than on labels from a particular simulation, the formulation could ease the transfer to new detector configurations, where supervised GNN approaches are typically retrained; this potential has not yet been demonstrated. Kortus et al. [207] extended the single-agent tracking formulation to a constrained multi-agent setting. Multiple agents operate simultaneously on the hit graph, each responsible for reconstructing a different proton track. The agents compete for hits, since two agents cannot claim the same hit for different tracks, and cooperate toward a joint objective, the total amount of particle scattering over all reconstructed tracks in a readout frame. Training is centralized and execution decentralized: the actors use only local information, while global information shared between all agents is available to a centralized critic during training. The constrained optimization framework ensures that the learned joint policy satisfies the combinatorial constraints of the assignment problem at each step, rather than only in expectation. In practice, uniqueness of the hit assignment is enforced by a safety layer that solves a linear assignment problem for each joint action, and a cost-margin term in the gradient estimation steers the policy toward lower total assignment cost, which the authors relate to wider regions of high reconstruction performance and reduced predictive instabilities. In the terms of Figure 5, several policies edit the same hit graph, and the safety layer acts as a joint feasibility mask over their actions. On simulated data from the proton imaging detector, the constrained policies outperform a conventional sequential track follower as well as single- and multi-agent RL baselines, with the advantage of the constraints most visible at high particle densities. The formulation is relevant to the high-pileup regime of the HL-LHC, where many tracks compete for the same hits, but its computational scaling and any speed-up from parallel agents have not yet been evaluated. Existing RL tracking work uses the Bergen pCT DTC geometry with modest hit multiplicities. Scaling to the [FORMULA] hits per event of a real LHC silicon strip or pixel tracker at HL-LHC pileup, while maintaining reconstruction efficiency and fake rate comparable to the Kalman filter, remains the central open challenge. A flat single-agent policy faces two compounding difficulties at LHC scale: the action space at each step grows with the number of hits in the next layer, and the episode length grows with the number of detector layers, making the credit assignment problem progressively harder as the detector size increases. Hierarchical RL (Section 2.7.5) addresses both difficulties. A high-level manager policy selects subgoals, such as a track seed, a region of the detector to search, or an intermediate waypoint hit, and a low-level worker policy executes primitive hit-association actions to reach each subgoal, receiving dense intrinsic rewards in addition to the per-step scattering reward. This decomposition is particularly natural for tracking: seeding (identifying promising hit triplets) and track extension (growing the seed hit by hit) are already treated as separate algorithmic stages in the Kalman filter pipeline, so the hierarchical decomposition aligns with existing domain structure rather than imposing it artificially. Current RL tracking policies are trained exclusively in simulation. Because the scattering reward is label-free, it can in principle be evaluated directly on recorded hits: the hit graph of each recorded event is itself a valid environment, and interacting with it requires no ground truth. Training on recorded data would let the policy adapt to detector conditions that simulators model imperfectly: dead channels, non-uniform efficiency, and radiation damage. The main obstacles are the absence of truth for validating the reconstructed tracks and the cost of training on large volumes of recorded events. Logged outputs of the standard reconstruction could additionally serve as demonstrations for imitation learning or as a fixed dataset for offline RL (Section 2.7.2), where conservative methods such as CQL [79] and IQL [80] limit extrapolation to hit associations absent from the log. A hybrid approach using RL for the combinatorial hit association step and the Kalman filter for subsequent track fitting and smoothing could combine the flexibility of RL with the theoretical optimality of the Kalman filter for state estimation given a fixed hit assignment. This two-stage pipeline aligns with how modern tracking is already structured and would allow RL to be introduced incrementally into existing reconstruction software frameworks such as ACTS [208], without replacing the entire pipeline. 7 Beyond the Standard Model: Model Building and Theory Exploration The Standard Model (SM) of particle physics [206], despite its extraordinary predictive success, leaves fundamental questions unanswered: the origin of the fermion mass hierarchy [209], the strong charge-parity (CP) problem [210], the nature of dark matter [211], and the matter-antimatter asymmetry [212]. Physicists address these by constructing theories beyond the Standard Model (BSM) [213]: extensions of the SM gauge group, matter content, or symmetry structure that predict new particles or interactions while remaining consistent with all existing measurements. The space of phenomenologically viable BSM models is vast, discrete, and largely unexplored. A theorist searching for models consistent with observed quark masses, lepton mixing angles, and collider constraints must navigate a combinatorial space of symmetry groups, field representations, and charge assignments. The number of candidate models scales as [FORMULA] where [FORMULA] is of order ten (e.g., of order [FORMULA] charge assignments for the quark sector of a single- [FORMULA] Froggatt–Nielsen model with charges between [FORMULA] and [FORMULA] [214]), making systematic enumeration infeasible even for the simplest symmetry extensions. This search is typically performed by hand, guided by theoretical prejudice and experience, or by exhaustive enumeration with automated consistency checks. Both approaches scale poorly as the number of free parameters grows. Manual model building relies on theoretical insight to restrict attention to well-motivated corners of BSM space, such as minimal extensions or natural solutions to the hierarchy problem. Automated scans use random sampling or grid search over discrete parameter spaces, combined with fast spectrum calculators (e.g., SPheno [215, 216], FlexibleSUSY [217]) and comparison to experimental constraints via tools such as CheckMATE [218] and data from the HEPData repository [219]. Markov Chain Monte Carlo and nested sampling, in particular the MultiNest algorithm [220], have been used extensively for continuous BSM parameter estimation, from early global fits of the constrained minimal supersymmetric Standard Model (CMSSM) [221] to the modular GAMBIT framework [222]; however, these techniques presuppose a fixed particle content and symmetry structure chosen in advance and only sample couplings and masses within that fixed topology, rather than searching over the discrete model-building choices themselves. Bayesian optimization has been applied to continuous BSM parameter spaces [223] but struggles with the discrete structure of symmetry assignments; its Gaussian process surrogate is not well-suited to categorical spaces. Genetic algorithms have been used for string landscape exploration [14] but are not sample-efficient when the fitness function requires an expensive spectrum calculation, and they do not learn a generalizable policy; direct comparisons on string flux vacua and on heterotic monad-bundle models found GA and RL complementary rather than one dominating the other (Section 7.4). BSM model building is a sequential decision process: a model is constructed step by step by assigning charges, representations, or symmetry factors to fields. The consistency of a model with observations can be fully evaluated only once the model is specified; in practice, the reviewed works shape this objective into per-step rewards based on improvements of a consistency score. This combinatorial structure, together with the need for strategic exploration rather than local search, maps naturally onto the RL framework. In the terms of Figure 5, the partial object is the model under construction, the feasibility mask encodes the grammar or consistency conditions on fields and couplings, and the evaluator is a spectrum calculation or a likelihood; terminal states are collected as an ensemble of viable models. This formulation places BSM model building directly within the domain of RL for combinatorial optimization (CO) [224, 225], a field that has produced learned solvers for routing, graph problems, and discrete assignment tasks by training policies to construct solutions element by element. The key insight shared between combinatorial optimization and BSM model building is that hand-crafted heuristics, which encode domain knowledge about which partial solutions are worth extending, can be replaced by a learned policy that generalizes across problem instances. In the CO literature, pointer networks [205] and graph attention networks [226, 227] have proven effective as policy backbones for discrete construction problems; the GNN-based policy of Wojcik et al. [228] follows the same architectural paradigm, with the BSM model grammar playing the role of the problem-instance graph and the charge or coupling assignments playing the role of the solution being constructed. Three specific advantages of RL over the classical alternatives follow from this framing. Unlike genetic algorithms [14], RL learns a policy that generalizes across related model-building tasks and can be guided by intermediate physics-motivated reward shaping, rather than restarting the search for each new task; in heterotic model building, agents trained on one Calabi–Yau manifold remain more efficient than random walkers on new ones [24]. Unlike Bayesian optimization [223], RL scales naturally to discrete combinatorial spaces; GP surrogates are not well suited to categorical variables without special kernels, and their [FORMULA] cost in the number [FORMULA] of evaluated models [229] limits them to a number of evaluations that is a negligible fraction of model spaces with [FORMULA] or more configurations. Connecting RL model builders to automated spectrum calculators has been demonstrated for a single observable [240]; scaling this to full collider constraint databases (e.g., HEPData, CheckMATE) remains a necessary engineering step. The key challenge is that spectrum calculations can take seconds to minutes per model, while RL requires millions of environment interactions for convergence (about 1.6 million sampled models in Section 7.3). Two complementary strategies target this bottleneck: Model-based RL with a learned surrogate for the spectrum calculator [68] replaces the expensive simulator with a fast neural network approximation, enabling millions of imagined model evaluations between real spectrum calls; the approach mirrors what Hirlaender and Bruchon [130] did for the FEL with a neural network ensemble as the environment model. Example-based reward learning. Classical inverse RL (Section 2.7.3) infers a reward from expert demonstrations, but the BSM literature records finished models rather than the sequences of decisions that produced them. Published models can instead serve as examples of successful outcomes, from which a reward or value function is learned without demonstrations [246, 247]. Because such a learned reward is cheap to evaluate, it can pre-filter candidates before expensive spectrum calls, and a policy trained against it would explore the BSM space in a way that is consistent with human theoretical intuition without being limited to it. Two caveats apply: the literature provides positive examples only, and it is a biased sample shaped by analytic tractability and by which model classes were popular, so the learned reward inherits these biases unless they are corrected. As the number of simultaneous physical requirements grows, reward shaping becomes more challenging: naive scalarization of constraints into a single reward can lead the agent to sacrifice one constraint to optimize another, and the optimal weight vector is unknown a priori. Multiple techniques can avoid this, such as: Constrained MDPs (Section 2.8.3) encode each physical requirement as a separate cost signal with its own budget, and primal-dual methods such as reward constrained policy optimization [248] keep the policy feasible. The formulation fits requirements with a binary character, such as whether a model reproduces the observed CKM matrix to within experimental uncertainty, encoded as an indicator cost. Because the constraint holds in expectation, individual models produced by the policy can still violate it and must be filtered at evaluation time. Multi-objective RL (Section 2.7.5) avoids fixing the weight vector in advance: a preference-conditioned policy [99], conditioned on a preference vector [FORMULA] , can be varied at inference time to trace trade-offs between, for example, quark mass accuracy and lepton mixing consistency, without retraining. With linear preferences, such methods recover the convex coverage set, that is, the convex part of the Pareto front; trade-offs in concave regions of the front are not recovered. Within this limit, the recovered front is physically informative: its shape indicates which pairs of constraints are in tension and which can be jointly satisfied without compromise. Curriculum learning (Section 2.8.1; [249]) addresses the sparse joint reward problem by introducing constraints progressively during training. The natural curriculum in BSM model building is ordered by computational cost. In the FN setting, fermion masses and the CKM and PMNS mixing follow from the same diagonalization of the Yukawa textures, and axion properties such as the domain wall number and the axion-photon coupling are analytic functions of the charges [232], so these checks are cheap. Fitting the [FORMULA] coefficients and the flavon VEV requires a numerical optimization per model, and observables such as the dark matter relic density require external spectrum and relic-density codes. Training the agent first against the cheap constraints and progressively introducing the expensive ones prevents the agent from being overwhelmed by a sparse joint reward and reduces the total number of expensive evaluations. Reward decomposition [250] learns separate value functions for each physical constraint and combines them at decision time via a linear sum, allowing the agent to disentangle which actions satisfy which constraints. The sampling distribution of a trained BSM model-building policy can be read as an implicit prior over the space of viable models, although Section 7.3 shows that this distribution is also shaped by the reward design and by factors unrelated to the physics. Extracting interpretable physics from the policy, for example, identifying which symmetry patterns it prefers and why, is an open problem at the intersection of explainable RL (XRL) [251] and theoretical physics. The string landscape studies of Section 7.4 show that this is possible in practice: learned strategies have exposed correlations in flux vacua [244] and suggested a structural result on chiral families that was then proven [25]. In attention-based GNN policies, such as graph attention networks [226], the attention weights over graph edges provide a natural first layer of attribution: they indicate how strongly each coupling relation contributes to the decision of the policy at each step, and can be inspected post hoc to identify recurring structural motifs in discovered models. Such attention-based attribution has not yet been reported for the BSM policies of Section 7.3. Attention weights are also not reliable explanations on their own: they often disagree with gradient-based importance measures, and markedly different attention distributions can yield the same prediction [252]. Causal RL [253, 254] offers a stronger notion of interpretability by incorporating a structural causal model (SCM) of the state variables into the learning process, so that the agent reasons about interventions rather than correlations across sampled trajectories. In BSM environments the reward is a known, deterministic function of the model parameters, so reward-level interventions, such as changing a charge [FORMULA] and re-evaluating consistency, are directly computable without causal machinery. The value of causal methods lies instead in explaining the policy: identifying which features of the current partial model causally drive its decisions, as opposed to features that merely correlate with them in the training distribution. Policy distillation into soft decision trees [255, 256] compresses the neural policy into a binary tree of soft decisions: each inner node applies a learned sigmoid filter to the whole input, and each leaf holds a fixed action distribution. An explanation is the sequence of filters along the most probable path, which is more transparent than a deep network but does not yield if-then rules over individual features, since the splits are oblique rather than axis-aligned. For FN models, where the state is a fixed-length charge vector, the learned filters can be read as weighted combinations of charges that steer the construction; variable-size graph states, as in Section 7.3, would first require a fixed-length encoding. Programmatic policy distillation [257] offers a complementary path: a trained neural policy guides a search over programs in a domain-specific language, yielding a policy that is directly readable and could, in principle, be reused in automated theory-building pipelines. 8 Detector and Instrument Design The design of a particle physics detector is one of the most complex and high-stakes engineering optimization problems in science. A modern collider detector such as ATLAS [162] or CMS [163] incorporates of order [FORMULA] channels across multiple subsystems: tracking detectors, calorimeters, and muon systems, each with hundreds of free geometric and material parameters. Design decisions are strongly coupled; the longitudinal segmentation of a calorimeter affects the energy-flow algorithm, which in turn affects jet reconstruction and therefore all analyses using jets. A single full simulation of a design candidate using Geant4 [2] typically takes hours to days of CPU time, making exhaustive optimization infeasible. A detector configuration can be formally represented as an ordered collection of components [FORMULA] , where each [FORMULA] corresponds to a sub-detector or functional module [258]. Each component is parameterized by a vector [FORMULA] encoding physical layout, material choices, and engineering properties. Detector design has historically been driven by engineering judgment and parametric studies: a small number of design parameters are varied manually while the rest are fixed, and simulation is run at a grid of points. More systematic optimization uses Bayesian optimization (BO) with a Gaussian process surrogate over the simulation output [259], which is sample-efficient but limited to low-to-moderate-dimensional continuous parameter spaces; the GP surrogate becomes inaccurate and computationally expensive as dimensionality grows. The differentiable programming approach, pioneered by the MODE Collaboration [16, 260], represents the detector geometry in a differentiable framework and back-propagates gradients from physics observables to design parameters. This is powerful for continuous parameters but requires the full simulation pipeline to be differentiable, which excludes discrete design choices (e.g., the number of detector layers) and stochastic simulation steps. Differentiable approximations using hybrid Monte Carlo gradient estimators [260] have been developed within MODE to partially address this, but surrogate-based gradients remain tied to reduced models and inherit their limitations. A recent complementary approach uses diffusion model surrogates as fully differentiable emulators of the simulation-reconstruction chain [261], enabling gradient-based design exploration in both continuous and discrete parameter spaces; discrete choices such as materials are handled by optimizing a probability assigned to each category rather than the category itself. RL complements both BO and differentiable programming by naturally handling the discrete and sequential nature of detector design: the number of layers, the choice of material at each position, and the placement of sub-detectors are all discrete decisions that can be made sequentially, building the configuration one component at a time. The reward is the score [FORMULA] evaluated by a full or fast simulation, with no differentiability required. Detector design therefore follows the construction pattern of Figure 5, with the partially built detector as the object, layer placement as the edit, and a full or fast simulation as the evaluator; unlike the previous cases, the agent observes only part of the design and receives the score only at the end of the episode (Section 8.2). A recent review by Figalli, Qasim, Owen, and Serra [258] provides a comparative perspective on all three methodologies and concludes that RL is particularly well suited to combinatorial and mixed-discrete-continuous design spaces, while BO excels for low-dimensional continuous problems and differentiable programming is most powerful when large portions of the pipeline can be made differentiable. Qasim, Owen, and Serra [103] presented the first systematic application of RL to physics instrument design. They formulate detector design as a sequential MDP in which the agent places or configures detector elements one at a time until the design is complete or the resource budget is exhausted. At each step, the agent predicts a continuous action to determine the position of the next layer and a discrete action to select the physical properties of that layer (e.g., sensor type and granularity). The environment is partially observable: the observation sent to the agent contains only the current longitudinal location and the remaining resource budget (or the number of layers already placed), not the full geometry. The reward [FORMULA] is the design score of the instrument quantifying its resolution, awarded only at the final interaction step; the agent may also receive a penalty for design violations (e.g., two layers placed too close together) at intermediate steps. Two empirical studies are presented: Calorimeter longitudinal segmentation: the agent sequentially places active sensor layers along the calorimeter depth, choosing the position and the sensor type (thickness) of each layer. The reward is derived from the energy resolution for electromagnetic and hadronic showers, evaluated with Geant4 simulations whose stored output is reused across designs, which reduces the cost of one design evaluation to a fraction of a second on a GPU. The PPO agent finds designs that improve the hadronic resolution substantially with respect to a hand-designed reference segmentation, while the electromagnetic resolution agrees with the reference within statistical uncertainty. Current RL detector design work optimizes geometry with a fixed reconstruction algorithm. A joint optimization, where the detector geometry and the reconstruction algorithm (e.g., clustering parameters, track seeding strategy) are co-optimized by a single RL policy, could discover configurations that are suboptimal for any fixed reconstruction approach but excel when the algorithm is adapted to the geometry. [258] identify this as one of the primary open challenges for AI-assisted detector design, noting that multiple sub-detector co-optimization requires maintaining a consistent simulation of the full detector so that cross-subsystem correlations relevant to global performance are preserved. Real detector design involves multiple competing objectives: physics performance, cost, power consumption, radiation tolerance, and maintainability. Multi-objective RL (Section 2.7.5) could provide a family of design options spanning the performance-cost tradeoff, giving engineers principled choices rather than a single optimized point. Distributional RL (Section 2.3) is a natural complement: by optimizing tail-sensitive criteria such as CVaR over the return distribution, the agent can explicitly target designs that perform well in the worst-case physics or calibration scenarios rather than only on average. A multi-agent formulation in which each agent is responsible for optimizing a specific sub-detector (tracker, calorimeter, muon system) under a shared material budget and geometric acceptance constraint would allow the joint design to be decomposed into manageable sub-problems while preserving the global coupling between subsystems through the shared constraint and a centralized critic. Competitive dynamics between agents (each sub-detector competing for a share of the material budget) and cooperative dynamics (the global physics score rewards all agents jointly) reproduce the structure of real detector design review processes, where subsystem groups negotiate resource allocation under experiment-wide performance targets.
