Refining the proposals of the LLM with a trust-region optimizer over the continuous layer positions narrows the gap without closing it, which the authors attribute to the discrete design choices, such as sensor types, that the refinement cannot change. This finding suggests a hybrid approach, which the authors propose as future work, in which an LLM proposes an initial design, possibly guided by human knowledge, which RL then refines in both its continuous and discrete choices. This hybrid paradigm, in which LLMs reduce the human effort required to structure and supervise optimization while RL performs the reward-driven search, offers a concrete path toward closed-loop, end-to-end detector design at the scale of complexity required for next-generation facilities. 9 Analysis, Event Processing, and Theoretical Computation This section covers a heterogeneous set of RL applications that do not fit neatly into the preceding sections but share a common structural property: they formulate combinatorial or sequential decision problems in HEP, spanning real-time triggering, data management, data analysis, event reconstruction, and formal QFT computation, where the feedback is complex, expensive, or delayed. Because the sub-topics differ substantially in domain and methodology, traditional methods and open problems are discussed locally for each sub-section rather than in a unified background and a closing section. The applications in this section span four distinct levels of the HEP workflow. At the real-time data-taking level (Section 9.2), RL controls the trigger system that decides which collision events to record. At the data management level (Section 9.3), RL decides which files the distributed computing infrastructure caches for analysis. At the analysis level (Sections 9.4–9.5), RL addresses problems in extracting physics signals from recorded data: background and systematics modeling, and combinatorial event reconstruction. At the theoretical computation level (Section 9.6), RL optimizes the algorithmic procedures of formal QFT computation, both perturbative (integral reduction and polylogarithm simplification) and non-perturbative (the conformal bootstrap). The unifying thread is that all of these problems involve discrete or sequential choices with a reward that depends on the full decision sequence, precisely the setting for which RL is designed. Combinatorial event reconstruction, integration-by-parts (IBP) reduction, and polylogarithm simplification follow the construction pattern of Figure 5, in which the agent edits an assignment, a system of identities, or an expression; trigger control and data caching instead follow the control loop of Figure 3. Together, they illustrate that the reach of RL in HEP extends well beyond the operational and instrumentation domains covered in earlier sections. Particle collisions at the LHC occur at a rate of 40 MHz, producing a raw data volume of approximately 40 TB/s that cannot be stored in full. An event-selection system, the trigger, must therefore decide in real time which collisions to record and which to discard, reducing the rate by about four orders of magnitude before writing to permanent storage. The trigger must be simultaneously sensitive to a wide range of physics processes at varying rates of occurrence; it must reject nearly all background while preserving events that may contain new physics signatures. Modern LHC triggers operate in two stages. The Level-1 (L1) trigger is implemented in custom FPGAs and application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) and must process each crossing within [FORMULA] , reducing the rate from 40 MHz to roughly 100 kHz using simple object-based selections (e.g., transverse energy [FORMULA] threshold, isolated muon or electron [FORMULA] cuts). The High-Level Trigger (HLT) then runs a software-based reconstruction on the accepted events, reducing the rate further to [FORMULA] (kHz) for permanent storage. In practice, trigger menus, i.e., the complete sets of physics selection criteria and their associated rate thresholds, are largely static: thresholds are set during commissioning and updated only infrequently, requiring expert optimization against simulated event samples. As pileup increases and background compositions shift over a fill, static menus become miscalibrated, reducing signal efficiency or causing rate violations that induce detector dead-time. We identify three structural reasons why RL is well suited to trigger control. First, decisions must be fast, and compact policies with few parameters can be trained to fit within the latency budget. Second, the objective is indirect: the trigger should maximize the yield of physics analyses, a goal that is difficult to encode as a differentiable loss; policy-gradient methods estimate the gradient of the expected reward from sampled actions and therefore do not need a differentiable objective. Third, operating conditions shift across runs; policies trained over a range of conditions can remain robust to moderate shifts, and model-based RL can plan for anticipated changes. The indirect objective also makes reward design the central challenge. Because analysis yield is not observable online, existing controllers optimize proxies: tracking a target background rate within a tolerance band and maximizing the efficiency on a few benchmark signal processes, with weights tuned by grid search [263]. A second proxy rewards events that are unlikely under a model of known background processes, as anomaly-detection triggers already do with autoencoder scores [264]. A third route learns from logged operations: the threshold and prescale changes made by trigger experts during data taking are demonstrations for inverse RL (Section 2.7.3), and logged trigger decisions can pretrain a policy with offline RL (Section 2.7.2). Logged data contain only events accepted by the deployed trigger, so both routes must correct for this selection when evaluating thresholds looser than those actually used. Ding et al. [263] cast online trigger threshold tuning as a streaming MDP and train a policy to adapt trigger thresholds in real time. The work develops and evaluates three policy families: a baseline DQN [36], a critic-free Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) [34] adapted to the streaming setting, and an adaptation of Group Filtered Policy Optimization (GFPO) [265], originally proposed to shorten LLM reasoning, which here enforces background-rate feasibility before advantage normalization by filtering the group of candidate actions according to whether their implied rate lies within the tolerance band [FORMULA] . Two filtering rules are introduced: GFPO-F keeps the candidates with the smallest absolute rate error, regardless of feasibility, while GFPO-FR keeps feasible candidates first, ranked by signal efficiency, and pads the group with the out-of-band candidates closest to feasibility when too few are feasible. GRPO without filtering fails under distribution shift because the sampled group of candidate actions frequently contains zero feasible actions; group-relative normalization then reinforces out-of-band actions. GFPO resolves this by filtering the normalization group toward rate-feasible candidates, yielding consistent gains in the InBand fraction, the fraction of time steps in which the background rate lies within the tolerance band, and, on Monte Carlo streams, gains of up to 2% in signal efficiency during in-tolerance intervals. The approach is evaluated on Monte Carlo streams and, crucially, on real CMS collision data (Run 283408), to which the policies trained on Monte Carlo are transferred without any fine-tuning. On real data, GFPO-F and GFPO-FR raise the InBand fraction of the [FORMULA] trigger from 0.43 for the PID baseline to 0.99 and 0.95, respectively, and that of the anomaly-detection trigger from 0.41 to 0.69 and 0.61. The gain in rate stability comes with a trade-off in signal efficiency: on the [FORMULA] trigger, the overall [FORMULA] efficiency increases by 0.2 to 0.35 percentage points, whereas the [FORMULA] efficiency within the tolerance band decreases by about 2 percentage points, and a similar decrease is observed for GFPO-F on the anomaly-detection trigger. The authors describe this, to their knowledge, as the first demonstration of RL-based trigger control on real LHC collision data, and as such it represents a significant milestone for RL in HEP beyond simulation. A closely related precursor by Emami, Tosciri, Salvi et al. [264] introduced the self-driving trigger concept on CMS Open Data, combining an [FORMULA] selection with autoencoder-based anomaly detection and adapting the thresholds in real time with a proportional-derivative controller, whose gains are tuned by grid search; the integral term of a full PID loop was found to have no significant effect. For menus with several trigger paths, the authors define cost functions that trade off background rate, signal efficiency, and bandwidth, and evaluate them with an idealized controller that knows the upcoming data. The work does not train an RL agent, but it defines the control problem, the classical baselines against which RL controllers can be compared, and cost functions that could serve as their training objective. Ding et al. regulate a single scalar threshold per trigger and train an independent policy for each, while real LHC trigger menus contain hundreds of items whose rates share a global bandwidth budget, so a change to one threshold affects the total accept rate. The authors identify multi-trigger coordination, with the feasibility filter applied over a joint threshold vector under a shared budget, as the next step; it requires a policy that acts on all thresholds simultaneously, and the emulated-collider benchmark of [263] provides a natural testbed. Transfer to other experiments such as ATLAS and LHCb has not yet been tested, and deployment within the latency budget of hardware triggers faces the constraints discussed for accelerator control in Section 3.6. LHC analysis data are distributed across a worldwide computing infrastructure, and regional caches close to the users reduce access latency and network load. A cache must decide which requested files to store and which stored files to evict, under a fixed storage budget and a request pattern that drifts as analyses evolve. Classic replacement policies such as least recently used (LRU), least frequently used (LFU), or size-based eviction are fixed heuristics: they write every requested file and differ only in what they evict, so they cannot trade cache throughput against the cost of writing and deleting data. Tedeschi et al. [266] introduced QCACHE, in which two Q-learning agents manage a CMS cache: an admission agent decides whether to store a requested file, and an eviction agent decides which cached files to keep. The reward is defined by cache hits and misses over a time window, and the agents are trained on historical CMS request data for the Italian region. A follow-up [267] develops this into three policies for a data lake model of distributed analysis. SCDL uses a single admission agent with LRU eviction triggered by occupancy watermarks, which the authors describe as closer to a contextual bandit than to full RL. SCDL2 adds a tabular eviction agent whose actions range from keeping all files of a category to deleting all of them. The DQN variant replaces both tables with deep Q-networks over a state of file size, request frequency, time since the last request, data type, cache occupancy, and hit rate. The policies are evaluated on 2018 CMS analysis-job monitoring data for the Italian region with simulated caches of 100 to 1000 TiB. Because hit rate alone ignores the cost of writing data, the figure of merit is a score defined as throughput, i.e., data read on hits normalized to an infinite cache, divided by cost, i.e., data written plus deleted. The RL policies rank first on this score at every cache size, for example 0.34 for the DQN variant against 0.19 for LRU at 100 TiB, while LRU retains the highest raw throughput; the simulator represents the bandwidth limit only through a daily threshold on requests, and access latency is not part of the figure of merit. Both studies evaluate a single regional cache in a simplified simulation that does not model access latency. Open steps are latency-aware simulation, validation in a production cache, and coordinated admission across the sites of a data lake, where the decisions of one cache change the request patterns seen by others and the problem becomes multi-agent. Because request patterns drift as analyses evolve, the policies also face the non-stationarity discussed for data quality monitoring in Section 4.4. In searches for rare decay modes or new physics, the dominant challenge is accurate determination of the background: the contributions from known SM processes that mimic the signal. Traditional background estimation relies on data-driven techniques [206]: control regions (signal-depleted phase-space regions where the background model is normalized to data), sideband fits (interpolating the background shape from mass sidebands into the signal window), and the ABCD method (extrapolating background rates from three control regions defined by inverting two uncorrelated selection criteria). Before any of these techniques is applied, the analyst must decide which background processes to model. In beauty hadron decay analyses, for example at LHCb [164], many decay channels can mimic a given signal through similar final states, misidentified particles, or kinematic overlaps; because simulating each candidate background is expensive, only those judged most relevant are simulated, and the choice relies on the intuition and expertise of the physicist rather than on a systematic method. A missed background biases the measurement and complicates its interpretation. Systematic uncertainties are traditionally handled through nuisance parameters and validated on control channels, but an effect missing from the uncertainty budget is, by construction, not covered by either. Hijano Mendizabal et al. [268] introduced a hybrid RL and genetic algorithm (GA) framework that, given a signal decay, determines the set of relevant background decays. A transformer-based agent, trained with a single-player variant of AlphaZero [75], builds each candidate background as a sequence of tokens representing the decay chain. Because the reward is available only once a complete decay has been built and the trajectory space is large, pure RL struggles to find any rewarded trajectory; the GA therefore searches the trajectory space first, and the successful trajectories it finds serve as demonstrations for the agent, which combines a policy-gradient objective with an imitation term. In a toy scenario with 40 particles and [FORMULA] -meson signal decays, the GA finds most of the relevant backgrounds of the training signals, and the fine-tuned agents find all 94 of them and essentially all 42 relevant backgrounds of signals not seen during training, which a GA would have to search again from scratch. Golutvin et al. [269] use RL to stress-test a measurement against systematic effects absent from its uncertainty budget. They invert the usual logic: assuming the SM, they ask what hidden mismodeling would be needed to reproduce an observed deviation. For a branching-fraction measurement they use gradient-based optimization; for the angular observable [FORMULA] of [FORMULA] , measured by LHCb as [FORMULA] in the [FORMULA] bin, they train a DQN agent. The hypothesized mismodeling is a per-event efficiency weight [FORMULA] , in which each factor is linear in the transverse momentum of one muon, separated by the muon charge relative to the kaon, and floored at 0.1 to remain physical. The state is the parameter vector [FORMULA] of this weight, each action increases or decreases one parameter by a step that shrinks from 0.1 to 0.01 as the fit improves, and episodes last at most 200 steps. The reward is piecewise in [FORMULA] against the measurements: negative and proportional to it above 3, increasing as it falls between 0.1 and 3, and a large terminal bonus below 0.1. The study uses a RapidSim [270] fast simulation of [FORMULA] decays rather than a full detector simulation. Fitting the signal channel alone, the agent finds a mismodeling that shifts [FORMULA] by about 0.24, comparable to the observed tension and to the 0.28 shift found by direct [FORMULA] minimization, but this mismodeling shifts the [FORMULA] control channel far beyond its uncertainty. Adding the control channel to the reward caps the achievable shift at about 0.01, so an efficiency mismodeling of this form cannot explain the [FORMULA] anomaly. The authors note that RL is more flexible than the optimization-based approach for non-differentiable simulators but computationally more expensive, and that a definitive statement requires a full detector simulation. The stress test of Golutvin et al. searches a two-parameter efficiency model, linear in muon [FORMULA] , on a fast simulation. Extending it to high-dimensional families of mismodeling, spanning several detector effects at once, and to full detector simulation would make each evaluation far more expensive, so sample efficiency becomes the limiting factor and learned surrogates of the simulation (Section 2.6) a natural remedy. One formulation is a two-player game, in which the analyst chooses control channels and the advocate searches for the mismodeling that best survives them; turning such a search into a routine robustness check for measurements that deviate from the SM is an open goal. At hadron colliders, the assignment of final-state reconstructed objects (jets, leptons, photons) to the hypothesized decay products of a hard scatter is a combinatorial problem. For a top-quark pair event with fully hadronic decay, there are [FORMULA] possible assignments of jets to quarks. Traditional solutions rely on [FORMULA] minimization over kinematic constraints (e.g., [FORMULA] boson and top quark mass windows) or on learned discriminants trained on simulation with known truth assignments. Dillon and Spannowsky [23] formulate final-state particle assignment as an MDP solved by a DQN with a permutation-invariant transformer backbone. The state is a complete one-to-one mapping between final-state four-momenta and the partons of the matrix element; each action either swaps two particle-parton assignments or does nothing, swaps already used in the episode are masked, and an episode lasts at most [FORMULA] steps for [FORMULA] partons, the maximum number of swaps needed to reorder the final state. The reward is the logarithmic change in the magnitude of the tree-level matrix element produced by the action, evaluated without any per-event truth labels: where [FORMULA] is the magnitude of the matrix element for the mapping [FORMULA] , so that swaps that increase the matrix element are rewarded and the return of an episode equals the total logarithmic gain. On parton-level [FORMULA] , [FORMULA] , and [FORMULA] events with fully hadronic decays, where the number of possible mappings grows from [FORMULA] to [FORMULA] , the agent finds mappings whose matrix elements closely match those of the true assignments; reconstruction efficiencies decrease with multiplicity, from most [FORMULA] events being fully reconstructed to about a third of the [FORMULA] events. Momentum smearing, used as a proxy for detector effects, degrades the performance only moderately. The paper reports no comparison with [FORMULA] minimization or supervised assignment methods, and a separate network is trained for each process. This work demonstrates that physics knowledge can be encoded in the reward function via matrix element evaluation, replacing the need for supervised truth labels with a first-principles theoretical calculation. Full event reconstruction (assigning all final-state objects, inferring invisible particles, and estimating the primary vertex) is a much harder combinatorial problem than the assignments considered in [23]. The continuous part of this problem is already addressed by generative models: conditional normalizing flows [271] reconstruct neutrino kinematics in semileptonic [FORMULA] events [272] and in dileptonic final states with two neutrinos [273]. Combining RL for the discrete assignment decisions with such flows for the continuous kinematic completion is a promising direction for holistic event-level inference, and the [FORMULA] , [FORMULA] , and [FORMULA] samples of [23] offer a starting benchmark. Multi-loop perturbative calculations in QFT require the reduction of large numbers of Feynman integrals to a smaller basis of master integrals via IBP identities [274]. The Laporta algorithm [275] performs this reduction by constructing and solving a system of linear equations among the integrals. The efficiency of the algorithm depends critically on the ordering in which integrals are generated and eliminated: a good ordering can reduce the number of arithmetic operations by orders of magnitude compared to a naive one. Finding good orderings has historically required expert heuristics and is a bottleneck for state-of-the-art multi-loop calculations. Zeng [276] proposes two methods for optimizing IBP reduction ordering, demonstrated on one-loop massive bubble integrals as a tractable benchmark. The problem is formulated as a combinatorial optimization over the ordering of IBP equation generation (from pairs of seed integrals and IBP operators) and of integral elimination, with the objective of minimizing the total number of arithmetic operations. In the RL formulation, the state encodes the status of a fixed board of candidate seed integrals, the actions alternate between selecting a seed–operator pair and selecting an integral to eliminate, and the reward is the negative cost of each step: where [FORMULA] counts the arithmetic operations performed at step [FORMULA] , so that the return equals minus the total cost of the reduction. The first method uses RL: a neural network policy interacts with the IBP reduction environment and learns the ordering by trial and error. The second uses metaheuristics: simulated annealing [277] minimizes the computational cost as a black-box function of priority values that control the ordering, with a small neural network compressing the parameter space for large-scale problems. The resulting schemes are competitive with the most efficient human-designed algorithms: the RL agent reaches this level on the smallest benchmark, while the larger cases are handled by the metaheuristic approach. The discovered schemes are interpretable and resemble existing human-designed seeding strategies. Together with earlier work on symbolic simplification, discussed next, this establishes formal QFT computation as an application domain orthogonal to the experimental and phenomenological applications in other sections. Feynman integrals often evaluate to polylogarithms, whose analytic expressions are simplified by applying functional identities in a well-chosen order. Dersy, Schwartz, and Zhang [278] cast the simplification of dilogarithm expressions as a game in which each move applies an inversion, reflection, or duplication identity, and train an RL agent to reduce the expression; comparing it with a transformer-based approach, they find both effective, but the latter more powerful and more promising for practical symbolic manipulation. Beyond perturbation theory, Kántor, Niarchos, and Papageorgakis [279, 280] applied SAC to the conformal bootstrap, searching for approximate solutions of the truncated crossing equations of two-dimensional conformal field theories (CFTs) and recovering known theories such as the 2D Ising model and the compactified free boson. With Richmond [281], they extended the method to the six-dimensional [FORMULA] superconformal bootstrap, using SAC as a stochastic optimizer for four-point functions of scalar superconformal primaries in the energy-momentum multiplet. Starting from the supergravity limit and varying the central charge adiabatically, the searches produce two curves built from 80 CFT data points (70 for unprotected long multiplets and 10 for protected short multiplets), which the authors conjecture to describe the A- and D-series [FORMULA] theories. The results are competitive with standard numerical bootstrap bounds and with data from the operator product expansion (OPE) inversion formula [282], and the implementation is released as the BootSTOP code. Natural extensions of the IBP work include RL for sector decomposition ordering in numerical integration and for the selection of integral basis elements in the differential equations method. For analytic simplification, the dilogarithm result above suggests that RL is more likely to help as a search component combined with learned proposals than as a standalone simplifier. Learned heuristics for IBP reduction are also being pursued without RL: concurrently with Zeng, von Hippel and Wilhelm [283] and Song et al. [284] used FunSearch [285], a program search guided by large language models [286], together with genetic programming to discover interpretable priority functions, and evaluated them on multi-loop integrals, whereas RL has so far been demonstrated on the one-loop bubble. A head-to-head comparison of RL and program search on shared multi-loop benchmarks, and hybrids in which an RL policy proposes reductions that program search then distills into explicit heuristics, remain open. 10 Conclusions and Outlook This survey has reviewed the application of reinforcement learning across seven domains of HEP, in the broad sense defined in Section 1.1. The picture that emerges is one of a field that has moved from isolated proof-of-concept demonstrations to a growing body of methodologically diverse and physically grounded work, tested on real machines and, in a few cases, on real collision data. In accelerator control (Section 3), RL agents have been trained or tested on real machines at CERN, DESY, Elettra, KIT, Brookhaven, Forschungszentrum Jülich, and the Institute of Modern Physics in Lanzhou, and trained policies have been implemented on FPGA hardware at Fermilab. At KARA, an agent trained online on the machine controls a feedback loop with microsecond inference on dedicated hardware. The same paradigm tunes the operating point of cryogenic dark matter detectors in the Gran Sasso underground laboratory. This is the most mature application domain, with the largest number of studies. In data quality monitoring (Section 4), two complementary approaches have been proposed: a human-in-the-loop multi-agent PPO system that queries the shifter only when needed, developed on synthetic data with a preliminary test on real LHCb data, and an adversarial semi-bandit that monitors ALICE TRD anode currents on real data and flags deviations hours before a trip. Systematic validation across runs and operating conditions remains the main open step. In jet physics (Section 5), RL has produced learned algorithms for grooming, clustering, and input ordering that match or improve on hand-crafted baselines, with the grooming policy adapting its decisions to the kinematic configuration of each jet rather than applying a fixed rule; the clustering results are obtained on a simplified parton shower model. In charged particle tracking (Section 6), RL has established a label-free track-finding formulation that uses the Coulomb scattering likelihood as reward, competitive with supervised and heuristic baselines on a proton imaging detector and robust across imaging conditions. Constrained multi-agent extensions enforce unique hit assignments, a prerequisite for dense environments, although scaling to HL-LHC occupancies has yet to be shown. In BSM model building (Section 7), RL has emerged as a principled tool for navigating the discrete, combinatorially vast space of consistent theories. Applications span Froggatt–Nielsen flavor models, axion model building, graph-based exploration of extended matter sectors with GNN policies, grammar-constrained generation of Lagrangians fitted to experimental data, and string compactifications, where RL was applied first. The connection to RL for combinatorial optimization explains why RL suits this setting, but direct comparisons remain scarce: the two available comparisons with genetic algorithms, on flux vacua and on heterotic monad-bundle models, found the methods complementary rather than one dominating the other. In detector and instrument design (Section 8), the first systematic RL-based optimization studies have been published, improving on a hand-designed reference segmentation for calorimeters and extending the formulation to spectrometer tracker placement; head-to-head comparisons with Bayesian optimization and differentiable approaches are still missing. Distributionally robust RL with Wasserstein ambiguity sets has been proposed to handle simulator misspecification, and hybrid pipelines in which LLMs propose designs and RL refines them are a promising direction to further reduce human engineering effort. In analysis, event processing, and theoretical computation (Section 9), RL has been applied to trigger threshold control, evaluated on recorded CMS Open Data without fine-tuning; file caching for distributed CMS analysis; background determination in beauty hadron decays; the stress-testing of a measurement against systematic effects missing from its uncertainty budget; combinatorial event reconstruction rewarded by matrix element evaluation; and formal QFT computation, namely the ordering of IBP integral reduction, the simplification of polylogarithm expressions, and the search for solutions of the conformal bootstrap. Across domains, the reviewed works follow three recurring formulations. In the first, the agent controls a physical system or a data stream over time, as in accelerator tuning and feedback, trigger control, and data caching (Figure 3). In the second, the agent monitors a detector data stream and decides when to involve a human expert, who either labels the queried data or acts on the raised alarms (Figure 4). In the third, which emerges across Sections 5 to 9, the agent constructs an object edit by edit under feasibility constraints, enforced by a mask or by reward penalties, and an evaluator scores the result (Figure 5): the object can be a jet clustering tree, a track candidate, a BSM model, a detector configuration, an assignment of reconstructed objects, or an integral reduction ordering. The formulation largely determines the bottleneck: machine time and safety in control, expert attention in monitoring, and the cost of the evaluator in construction. Table 3 collects the RL works reviewed in Sections 3 to 9 that report empirical results, together with the baseline each is compared against and the outcome of that comparison. Of its 50 entries, 24 compare RL quantitatively with a traditional method, such as an optimizer, a controller, a heuristic, or a non-RL learned model: 16 find RL better on the primary metric, in some cases with a trade-off on a secondary one [263, 267] or only in part of the studied settings [17, 141], 6 comparable or complementary, one worse, and one reports mixed results. Works with several baselines are classified by the comparison against the traditional ones, ignoring human, sampling, and RL baselines, and counted as mixed when RL outperforms some traditional baselines but not others [188]. Eleven further works compare only against human operators or their labels (five), random or Markov chain sampling (four), or other RL agents (two); two validate against a reference configuration or a known solution; and 13 report no comparison. Evaluation on a real machine or on recorded data appears in 15 works: 12 in accelerator and detector operation, and the remaining three in data quality monitoring and trigger control. Head-to-head evidence against strong traditional baselines is therefore concentrated in accelerator control, jet physics, and analysis, and is largely absent from BSM model building, where most studies report no baseline or compare only against random sampling. Despite significant progress across seven domains, a set of fundamental challenges recurs throughout the HEP RL literature; addressing them is necessary for RL to be adopted widely in the field. The reward function is often the most critical and difficult design choice in RL applications. Rewards that capture both the underlying physics and the constraints of the system or equipment can be difficult to design or prohibitively expensive to evaluate, so surrogate objectives that are easier to define and compute are commonly used instead. Such rewards are computed from measured or simulated proxies of the physical objective, and an optimizer will exploit any divergence between the proxy and the objective. The reviewed works offer concrete examples. At ARES, the beam parameters measured on a diagnostic screen are false once the beam leaves the screen: a Bayesian optimizer required an explicit penalty for this case and still took many steps to recover the beam, and aggressive optimizer settings overfit to falsely positive noisy samples of the objective [18]. In the LHC tune feedback, the reward depends only on the tune error, which is consistent with the observation that a trained agent terminates episodes with non-zero corrections where the PI controller settles near zero [21]. In graph-based BSM exploration, the distribution of sampled models reflects the reward design as well as the physics [228]. Inverse RL (Section 2.7.3) can recover a reward from expert behavior, and multi-objective RL (Section 2.7.5) defers the choice of weights between competing objectives to deployment time rather than fixing it during training. In HEP, machine and deep learning models are commonly trained on simulated data, which can be generated in large amounts and for precisely controlled scenarios, whereas real data are scarce and expensive. RL agents are likewise trained in simulation and then deployed on real systems, and the resulting distribution shift can degrade their performance. The reviewed works show that this gap can be bridged: agents trained only in simulation have been deployed without retraining at AWAKE [126], domain randomization over unobserved machine parameters enables zero-shot transfer at ARES and COSY [107, 108], trigger policies trained on Monte Carlo streams transfer to recorded CMS data without fine-tuning [263], and refitting a learned dynamics model to the current machine state adapts the agent to the real system [140]. Pretrained physics foundation models [197, 287, 288] are natural candidates for policy encoders that could be fine-tuned with RL, but none has yet been used as an RL backbone; the closest evidence is the pretrain-then-RL recipe used in theory generation [240] and early work on RL fine-tuning of language models for accelerator tasks [289]. Every domain has a scarce resource that limits how many interactions an agent can afford. In accelerator control it is machine time: the ARES agents are trained for millions of steps, which is feasible only with a fast simulator [107]. In DQM it is expert attention, since every query to the shifter has a cost [171]. In detector design it is full simulation, which becomes affordable only by reusing stored Geant4 output across designs [103]. In BSM model building it is the evaluation of each candidate model, with about 1.6 million models sampled in a single graph-based scan [228]. In tracking and trigger control, Monte Carlo is cheap, and policies are so far trained in simulation only [22, 263]: for tracking, the label-free scattering reward could in principle be evaluated on recorded hits, whereas recorded trigger data contain only the events accepted by the deployed trigger. Model-based RL, offline RL from archived logs, and pretrained representations are the main remedies; none has yet been demonstrated at the scale of a full LHC experiment. Physics equipment changes over time, and policies must follow it. Accelerators drift: agents trained on the AWAKE electron line need more steps, or fail, weeks or months after training [141], which motivates online model learning at NSLS-II [140], meta-RL adaptation to drifting hidden parameters at AWAKE [147], and continual learning for deployed accelerator systems [178]. In DQM, the human-in-the-loop agent queries the shifter mainly after operating conditions change [171], and the bandit formulation is adversarial precisely because detector currents are not stationary [172]. In trigger control, pileup and background composition change within a fill, and group-relative policy optimization fails under this shift unless candidate actions are filtered for rate feasibility [263]. Detector designs must remain valid across alternative physics tunes and calibrations over multi-year operation, which motivates distributionally robust RL [258]. In model building, the reward is defined by current measurements, so updated experimental inputs change the target and require retraining or adaptation of the policy. The RL applications reviewed here present safety constraints of different nature. In particular, we distinguish among: Operational safety. In accelerator control and detector design, violations are physical and potentially irreversible: unsafe actions on a machine may cause equipment downtime, radiation damage, or destroyed equipment, whereas material budget violations or mechanical interference discovered late in the design process may be irreversible given the multi-year lead times of custom detector components. Informational safety. In trigger control and DQM, violations are informational and cumulative: rate violations cause detector dead-time that permanently discards physics data, and over-certifying bad data corrupts downstream physics analyses in ways that may not be immediately detectable. Theoretical safety. In jet physics and BSM model building, violations are theoretical: an IRC-unsafe policy produces results that are formally meaningless in perturbation theory, regardless of their empirical performance on simulation, and a BSM model violating exclusion limits is physically inconsistent and must be discarded. The reviewed works already contain the first dedicated mechanisms: a safety layer that guarantees unique hit assignments in multi-agent tracking [207], rate-feasibility filtering and bounded threshold updates in trigger control [263], and grammars that exclude inconsistent theories from the action space of model-building agents [228, 240]. Except for those in trigger control, these mechanisms act as the feasibility mask of the construction pattern (Figure 5), and they enforce their constraints exactly because the constraints are known analytically: grammar validity and hit uniqueness can be checked before an edit is applied; no reviewed jet algorithm yet enforces IRC safety in this way. In control problems, the constraints depend on the response of the machine, which is known only approximately. Action clipping and reward penalties alone are practical mitigations that provide no formal safety guarantee; constrained MDPs [109] and safe model-based RL (Section 2.8.3) offer principled solutions to this challenge. Several of the reviewed results lack a classical baseline: the graph-based and grammar-based BSM scans are not compared against random or Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling [228, 240], and RL-based detector design has not been compared head-to-head with Bayesian optimization [103]. Comparisons at equal budget, measured in machine interactions or simulator calls and repeated over several random seeds, are needed to establish where RL helps. For construction problems, the shared structure of Figure 5 suggests a common environment interface, in which the state, the edits, the feasibility mask, and the evaluator are specified per domain, so that the same baselines, such as random sampling, Markov chain Monte Carlo, beam search, and genetic algorithms, can be run on every task. Open resources on which such comparisons can be built already exist: the Cheetah beam dynamics code [114], the RL-ABC beamline environments [105], the Ginkgo jet model [192] and libGroomRL [187], the MEDIC fault-injection framework for DQM [169], CMS Open Data together with the public trigger-control code of [263], and the ACTS Open Data Detector with the ColliderML high-luminosity dataset [208, 290]. When an RL policy makes decisions on which data are recorded or certified, physics analyses inherit them. An adaptive trigger changes the event selection over time [263], and automated DQM decides which data enter an analysis [171]: the resulting selection efficiencies must remain measurable, and their systematic uncertainties controlled, for cross-section measurements to remain valid. This requires, for example, logging the policy state alongside the data and monitoring the selection with independent reference samples. Adversarial stress tests of measurements against hidden systematic effects [269] indicate the kind of validation that policy-driven selections will need. The applications reviewed in this survey span a gradient of maturity. Accelerator and trigger control have produced results on real machines and on real collision data; data quality monitoring, tracking, and detector design have validated prototypes on simulated or recorded data; BSM model building and formal computation remain exploratory, although RL-based string model building has already produced new candidate models and structural results. Across this gradient, the common first obstacle is formalizing a physics task as a Markov decision process, which requires a shift in how HEP problems are approached: 1) the task must be framed as a decision process in which the agent interacts with the problem, rather than as a static learning problem; 2) instead of collecting labeled data, as in supervised learning, a reward function must be defined that guides the agent toward the desired solution; and 3) since particle physics problems are not standard RL tasks, the lack of off-the-shelf simulators and learning environments requires researchers to build their own before addressing the target problem. The evidence reviewed in this survey does not support RL as a universal replacement for established methods; rather, it identifies the conditions under which RL is the more suitable choice, anticipated in Section 1.1 and supported here by the reviewed results: Repeated tasks with a fast simulator. When a task recurs on a stable system, the training cost is amortized over many deployments: at ARES, RL-trained optimizers reach a lower final beam error than Bayesian optimization in most real-machine trials, at an inference cost orders of magnitude lower [18]. Decisions inside fast control loops. Where iterative optimizers cannot run within the loop period, a trained policy can, as in the microsecond-latency feedback at KARA [20] and the FPGA implementation of a regulation policy for the Fermilab Booster, tested on a bench setup [19]. Robustness to faults and corrupted measurements. Policies trained over a distribution of conditions degrade gracefully when the system does: with stuck actuators, the LHC tune feedback agents stay closer to the target than the PI controller, which fails [21], and RL-trained optimizers recover a beam lost from the diagnostic screen within a few steps [18]. Physics as the training signal in place of labels. The reward can encode first-principles knowledge where ground truth is unavailable, from the Coulomb scattering likelihood in track finding [22] to tree-level matrix elements in event reconstruction [23]. Sequential discrete construction with a reusable policy. When the objective is defined only through a sequence of discrete choices (Figure 5), a trained policy can be reused across instances: in string model building, agents remain efficient on manifolds they were not trained on [24]. Conversely, Bayesian optimization remains preferable for new setups, rarely repeated tasks, and systems without a fast simulator [18]; optimization through a differentiable surrogate, used directly or inside RL training, is more efficient than model-free RL when the objective is smooth and high-dimensional [17]; genetic algorithms perform comparably when a set of solutions rather than a policy is needed [15, 14, 17]; and transformers proved more powerful than RL for symbolic simplification [278]. Because the construction problems of Sections 5 to 9 share the structure of Figure 5, techniques developed in one domain apply to the others, although the corresponding communities rarely cite each other. Tree search, through MCTS guided by a learned policy or [FORMULA] with an analytic heuristic, has so far been used only in jet clustering [188, 190], and could equally guide BSM model building or detector design, where each evaluation is expensive. Detector design penalizes infeasible layer placements in the reward [103], whereas BSM model building excludes infeasible edits through grammar masks [228, 240], and multi-agent tracking through a safety layer [207], so that the agent does not need to learn the constraint. Pretraining the policy before RL fine-tuning, used in theory generation [240] and in jet ordering [193], has not yet been tried in tracking or detector design. As the field moves toward the HL-LHC and future colliders such as FCC-ee, RL systems will be judged on metrics that reflect operational and physics requirements rather than on the return of a benchmark environment. In accelerator control, the relevant quantities are the time and number of machine interactions to convergence, the final beam quality, the smoothness of actuator trajectories [18], the inference latency relative to the loop period [20], the performance retained under drift without retraining [140], and the number of constraint violations. In trigger control, they are the fraction of time within the target rate band, the signal efficiency on benchmark processes, the smoothness of threshold updates [263], and the stability and measurability of the trigger efficiency over time. In DQM, they are the number of expert queries per run, the rates of missed bad data and of good data wrongly flagged, and the detection lead time [172]. In tracking, they are efficiency, fake rate, and time per event at high pileup, compared with the combinatorial Kalman filter. In detector design, they are the physics figure of merit against cost and material budget, the number of full-simulation calls, and the robustness of the design across physics tunes and calibrations [258]. In model building and formal computation, they are the number of viable models per expensive evaluation, the coverage of the model space relative to random or Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling, the rediscovery of known models, and the computational cost relative to standard heuristics [276]. Across domains, the compute spent on training must be weighed against the operational savings it enables. A methodological convergence with large-scale machine learning is also emerging. Group-relative policy optimization, developed for language models [34], now appears in trigger control [263] and in theory generation, where it fine-tunes a pretrained transformer [240], mirroring the pretrain-then-RL recipe of language model alignment [198]. Combined with the physics foundation models discussed above, this suggests a path toward policies that start from broad pretrained knowledge and are specialized to a facility or task with RL. Throughout the survey, RL has often found decision rules that match or improve on those designed by domain experts. This does not mean that traditional approaches, which are deeply grounded in physics knowledge, should be abandoned; rather, they should be complemented by RL where the conditions above apply. Conversely, traditional methods and domain knowledge are a source of inspiration, and their combination with RL, through physics-informed rewards, constrained action spaces, and differentiable or learned models of the system, may mitigate or even resolve many of the theoretical and practical challenges discussed here and in the previous sections. Beyond reviewing which high-energy and particle physics problems can be addressed with RL, this survey aims to enable physics researchers to become familiar with the RL formalism quickly, so as to foster future research on both existing and new particle physics problems; to this end, we reviewed not only the basics of deep reinforcement learning but also its sub-fields, such as offline, inverse, and model-based RL, that are most relevant to the surveyed applications. A Note On Lattice Definition of Gauge Theories With Chiral Fermions Because of the fermion doubling problem, it has been a longstanding challenge to describe a lattice algorithm for studying four-dimensional gauge theories coupled to chiral fermions. Recently, an algorithm to do so has been described by Craig, extending partial results in the previous literature. Here we describe a variant of this algorithm, based on interpolating a lattice gauge field over the continuum (as in Craig’s work) and coupling the interpolated gauge field to continuum chiral fermions. The same variant was also proposed recently by Hsu. In any dimension and for any anomaly-free representation, this approach can be implemented on a computer in principle, but not in practice by Monte Carlo methods because the chiral fermion path integral is not positive. 1 Introduction Lattice gauge theory [1] provides a very satisfactory regularization of four-dimensional Yang-Mills theory, and has offered an effective starting point for nonperturbative numerical exploration of this theory, as pioneered in [2]. The same framework is applicable – with considerably more difficulty – for gauge theories like QCD with fermions in vector-like representations. However, because of the fermion doubling problem, which is well characterized by the Nielsen-Ninomiya theorem [3], it has been notoriously difficult to describe in this framework gauge theories with chiral fermions, such as the Standard Model of particle physics. Ginsparg and Wilson proposed a strategy to circumvent the fermion doubling problem [4]. Building on the domain wall fermions of Kaplan [5], Narayanan and Neuberger [6, 7] interpreted the chiral fermion determinant as an overlap. Neuberger [8] and Hasenfratz [9] then derived lattice Dirac operators that satisfy the Ginsparg-Wilson relation, and Lüscher [10] showed that this implies an exact chiral symmetry of the classical lattice action. But this framework does not provide any immediate way to define a suitable measure for integration over these fermions, so quantization is not obvious. However, Lüscher was able to define such a measure for chiral gauge theories with abelian gauge group [11], thus achieving a lattice regularization for such theories. One important ingredient in this construction was a restriction to “admissible” gauge fields – gauge fields whose plaquette curvatures are small. The extension of Lüscher’s construction to nonabelian gauge theory was not straightforward. Lüscher himself showed that a nonabelian version of his construction works to all orders of perturbation theory around the trivial connection [12], and there were several other partial results [13, 14, 15]. Very recently, Craig overcame the difficulties and, with the aid of several new ideas, finally constructed a lattice regularization of chiral gauge theories in enough generality to encompass the Standard Model [16]. In this article, we will revisit this subject, and explain a slightly different route to the objective using two key facts. The second of these facts was also used by Craig, and the first is closely related to facts that he used. Actually, following the appearance of Craig’s paper and while the present one was being written, another paper appeared by Hsu [17] also describing a lattice regularization of chiral fermions and using the same key facts that the present article is based on. We will say more about Hsu’s paper and the background to it in section 1.2. Our analysis gives several generalizations of previous results (very likely the arguments in [16, 17] can be modestly extended to yield these generalizations). First, we use no special properties of the gauge group or fermion representation, so in four dimensions our analysis applies for any gauge group and anomaly-free fermion representation. Second (provided one follows the general analysis in section 2.4 of [18] or in the appendix of [19] rather than the simpler explanation we give in section 2.1), our discussion generalizes to any anomaly-free fermion system in any dimension, such as chiral fermions in two dimensions or more exotic cases such as nonperturbative anomalies of three-dimensional fermions in theories with time-reversal symmetry. Finally, our discussion applies on an arbitrary compact Euclidean spin manifold, not necessarily a torus. One might question the importance of this generalization, as lattice gauge theory is usually formulated on a torus. However, since gravity does exist in the real world, part of the consistency of anomaly-free chiral gauge theories such as the Standard Model is that they can be consistently coupled to gravity. And part of the consistency of that coupling is that these models can be defined in Euclidean signature on any spin manifold. We now summarize the two key facts that we will use. This summary is detailed enough to explain the main ideas of the paper. The first key fact is that in continuum Yang-Mills theory with any gauge group [FORMULA] , the path integral for fermions in any anomaly-free representation, chiral or not, coupled to any classical background field [FORMULA] (and any background spacetime metric), is always well-defined. The representation has to be free of both perturbative and nonperturbative (global) anomalies. This statement may sound like a tautology; if the fermion path integral in some representation is not well-defined, we declare that this representation is anomalous. What gives the statement its force is the following: (1) In learning how to define the fermion path integral for anomaly-free theories, one also learns to determine all possible nonperturbative anomalies – that is, anomalies beyond the standard perturbative anomalies. One of the most interesting properties of the TFIM is the models ability to demonstrate a quantum phase transition (QPT). Unlike classical phase transitions, which one can observe in a multitude of different physical systems, a QPT will occur at, or very close to, absolute zero. Due to the absence of thermal energy, we conclude that all observed phenomena are driven by quantum effects. Before we discuss QPTs with application to the TFIM we shall first give a brief overview of phase transitions. We typically put phase transitions into two different classes, first-order and continuous. First-order transitions are most likely what we have in our mind when we picture a phase transition. These are transitions for which two phases can exist simultaneously at the point of transition, e.g. water turning into ice. Unlike first-order, continuous transitions are those for which the two phases cannot co-exist at the critical point. An important example of continuous phase transitions is the ferromagnetic transition of iron at [FORMULA] [vojtaQuantumPhaseTransitions2003], above which the material no longer exhibits strong magnetism, which is characteristic of ferromagnetism. In the context of the TFIM we will be concerned with continuous phase transitions. When considering such continuous phase transition it will be useful to consider a so called order parameter. An order parameter is a mathematical quantity that takes a finite value when the system exists in the ordered phase, and vanishes in the disordered phase. When we say ordered vs disordered we are referring to the difference between the system being arranged in some regular/repeating pattern versus the contrary. In the context of the TFIM the ordered phase is the (anti-)ferromagnetic phase (the type of ferromagnetism depends on the sign of the coupling constant [FORMULA] however for simplicity we shall omit the ‘anti’ for the rest of this discussion). It is clear that this is the ordered phase, as ferromagnetism is the result of parallel alignment of spins [chikazumiPhysicsFerromagnetism1997], which causes strong magnetic effects, such as those one would observe when placing a material such as iron near a permanent magnet. It has been known for some time that classical computers have a hard time simulating quantum physics beyond trivial systems. This is a consequence of the postulates of quantum mechanics, which require that physical quantities be represented as operators on a Hilbert space [FORMULA] , the dimension of which scales exponentially with the number of particles. This problem led Richard Feynman, in a 1982 conference [feynmanSimulatingPhysicsComputers1982], to propose using a quantum computer to simulate quantum systems, which classical computers cannot efficiently simulate. Over time, the original ideas of Feynman and others have evolved into the modern day pursuit of developing a universal quantum computer, a technological challenge requiring advances across physics, engineering and computer science. In its most general form, quantum computation exploits key features of quantum mechanics, most notably superposition and entanglement. These phenomena underpin the potential advantages of quantum devices over their classical counterparts, as will be explored throughout this chapter. Exact chiral symmetry, non-Hermiticity, and the axial anomaly on the lattice: A symmetry-class criterion for disorder-induced undoubling A lattice Dirac operator built to keep chiral symmetry exact by weighting the derivative with a quenched random field, the chiral disordered fermions (CDF) of [L. Jacobs, Phys. Rev. Lett. 51, 172 (1983)], is reexamined with tools unavailable when it was first formulated. We show that the disorder-averaged operator satisfies [FORMULA] exactly, to all orders in the disorder strength: the disorder lifts the doubler degeneracy, pushing the doublers off the real axis into a complex (imaginary) mass while the physical mode stays exactly protected, yet it does so through non-Hermiticity rather than a Ginsparg–Wilson relation. As a consequence its axial index vanishes through every available channel: the Hermitian trace [FORMULA] (Karsten–Smit; Tiburzi), the bi-orthogonal index for non-Hermitian operators (Guo, Ma, and Zhang), and, closing the last loophole, the algebraic (Riesz-projector) index even when the operator is defective at an exceptional point; the last step extends Zenkin’s theorem, that a chirally symmetric normal lattice Dirac operator has zero index, to non-normal and defective operators, which the CDF operator requires. The CDF operator therefore cannot reproduce the axial anomaly, not by a tunable near-miss but by an identity forced by the very chiral symmetry it preserves. We organize this and the neighboring constructions by the Dirac channel that carries the lattice structure: disorder in the [FORMULA] (chirality-preserving) channel realizes an Altland–Zirnbauer chiral class and can never carry an index, while disorder in the scalar channel, the coefficient of [FORMULA] , breaks chiral symmetry and reproduces Callan–Harvey / domain-wall physics. A one-parameter family interpolates between the two, with the index a step function of the engaged channel: the 1983 operator and Kaplan’s domain wall emerge as the two poles of a single disordered family, distinguished not by the disorder but by the channel that carries it. The picture unifies the lattice-QCD undoubling lineage with the tenfold-way classification of disordered Dirac fermions, and settles the fate of the disorder route to chiral lattice fermions. I Introduction Species doubling is the central obstruction to putting chiral fermions on a lattice. Karsten and Smit tied it to the triangle anomaly [1], and Nielsen and Ninomiya elevated it to a no-go theorem [2, 3, 4]: a lattice Dirac operator that is simultaneously local, translation invariant, Hermitian, and exactly chirally symmetric must double. The known escapes each relax one hypothesis—Wilson fermions give up chiral symmetry [5], Ginsparg–Wilson/overlap fermions realize it in a modified ( [FORMULA] ) form [6, 7, 8, 9], and domain-wall fermions realize a single chiral mode as an edge state in an extra dimension [10, 11]. A less-travelled route relaxes Hermiticity instead, keeping chiral symmetry exact. One of the earliest such proposals [12]—which we call chiral disordered fermions (CDF)—weighted the lattice derivative with a quenched, ultralocal random field, with the hope that the anomaly would re-emerge from the disorder average as a measure effect, in the spirit of Fujikawa [13]. That program, and the cluster of non-Hermitian/disordered constructions around it [14, 15, 16, 17, 18], was set aside in the late 1980s—refuted in instances but never explained. Gross, Lepage, and Rakow found the Weingarten–Velikson model still doubled [17]; Pelissetto found ghost states and a vanishing anomaly [18]. The closest relative of the CDF construction is the random-block lattice of Chiu [19, 20, 21, 22], in which the sites are the Cartesian product of random coordinates in each direction and the random spacings enter the lattice derivative as link weights. The randomness therefore sits in the [FORMULA] channel, exactly where the CDF field sits, and the action is chirally and gauge invariant; unlike the CDF operator it is anti-Hermitian, so that the determinant is positive and single-flavor dynamical simulations were possible. In two-dimensional QED on the random-block lattice, ensemble-averaged observables that do not depend on exact zero modes agree with the Schwinger-model solution on the torus [22], while in topologically nontrivial backgrounds the construction produces neither exact zero modes nor the correct index [23]. In the language of Sec. V the random-block lattice is the normal member of the chiral class whose non-normal member is the CDF operator; the two share the index obstruction and differ in the fate of their doublers (Sec. VIII). The verdicts of the 1980s were verdicts on individual models, delivered before the Ginsparg–Wilson/overlap understanding existed. For the normal member of the class the failure was shown to be forced by Zenkin’s theorem [24], applied to the random-block lattice by Chiu and Zenkin [23]; for the non-normal CDF operator it required the bi-orthogonal machinery of non-Hermitian topology [25] and the defective extension of Sec. IV. Here we supply the explanation. We prove that the disorder average of the CDF operator [12] keeps [FORMULA] exactly to all orders (Sec. II), that it lifts the doublers off the real axis without becoming Ginsparg–Wilson (Sec. III), and that its axial index vanishes in every sense—including, closing a loophole left open by the assumption of diagonalizability, at exceptional points (Sec. IV). We then show (Sec. V) that the decisive variable is the Dirac channel carrying the disorder, i.e. the Altland–Zirnbauer symmetry class [26], and that a single family interpolates between the CDF operator and domain-wall fermions with the index as a step function of the channel. We stress at the outset that the general statement—exact chiral symmetry forbids the lattice anomaly—is not ours: Zenkin proved it for normal operators in 1998 [24], and Guo, Ma, and Zhang for the bi-orthogonal index of diagonalizable ones [27]; our contribution is the disorder-averaged realization, the extension to non-normal and defective operators (which the CDF operator requires, being non-normal), and the symmetry-class synthesis. Finally we ask whether any gauge-sector observable can stand in for the index and find that none can (Sec. VI): the topological susceptibility, the static quark potential, and the induced photon mass are all screened in the chiral channel as in the mass channel, because they couple to charge while the anomaly resides in chirality; they count charged modes, not their chirality. This leads us to two conjectures (Sec. VIII)—that the index is the unique discriminator, and that the CDF operator, made dynamical, would break the confining string by anomaly-free screening. VI Gauge-sector observables and the shadow of the anomaly The index of Sec. IV is a chirality-resolved quantity. IV is, in this sense, the only probe of the index itself—a point we sharpen into a conjecture below. VII Discussion It is worth stating the relation to prior work plainly. That exact chiral symmetry at finite lattice spacing precludes the axial anomaly is, in the Hermitian setting, long understood: implicit in the doubler cancellation of Karsten and Smit [1] and made explicit for minimally-doubled actions by Tiburzi [28]. That any chirally symmetric normal operator, local or not, on a regular or random lattice, has zero index is Zenkin’s extension of the Nielsen–Ninomiya theorem [24]; its form for the bi-orthogonal index of a diagonalizable non-Hermitian operator is due to Guo, Ma, and Zhang [27], whose general argument and two-dimensional check we reproduce. Our own additions are deliberately narrow: the disorder-averaged CDF operator [12] satisfies [FORMULA] exactly and nonperturbatively; the no-go survives the loss of diagonalizability, so that non-Hermitian degeneracy cannot evade it (Sec. IV); and the whole family—chiral and mass channels alike—is organized by its Altland–Zirnbauer symmetry class. The physical conclusion is clarifying rather than merely negative. The disorder route does lift the doublers—pushing them off the real axis into a complex mass—but it cannot regulate the anomaly, and the reason is the exact chiral symmetry it was built to preserve. Undoubling and anomaly reproduction are distinct requirements: the first is met by any lifting mechanism, the second only by one that breaks chiral symmetry in the [FORMULA] -Hermitian channel. A chirality-preserving lifting, however ingenious, carries no index. Read this way the result is a unification. The lattice-QCD undoubling lineage—Karsten–Smit [1], Nielsen–Ninomiya [2], Wilson [5], Ginsparg–Wilson and overlap [6, 7, 9], Kaplan’s domain wall [10] and Callan–Harvey inflow [11]—and the condensed-matter classification of disordered Dirac fermions—the Altland–Zirnbauer classes [26], random-mass Dirac with its Jackiw–Rebbi modes and Dyson singularity [37, 38]—are two views of one criterion: which Dirac channel carries the structure fixes the symmetry class, and the class fixes whether an index, and hence the anomaly, can appear. There is also a circle closing here. The construction of Ref. [12] and Kaplan’s domain wall [10] enter this family as its two poles: the same quenched random field, placed in the [FORMULA] channel, gives the exactly chiral, anomaly-free CDF operator; placed in the scalar (mass) channel, it seeds domain walls at its zero crossings and gives the anomaly-carrying construction that succeeded. The two are not rival tricks but the two exact limits of one disordered operator—the two ways of splitting the Nielsen–Ninomiya hypotheses, non-Hermiticity against soft chiral breaking—distinguished by nothing except the Dirac channel that carries the field. What was proposed in 1983 as a route to chiral lattice fermions returns, four decades on, as the chiral-class pole of the family whose mass-channel pole is the route that worked. VIII Conjectures and outlook Two statements reach beyond what we have proved. We set them out as conjectures, each with its supporting evidence and the calculation that would settle it. Conjecture 1 (gauge-sector blindness). No gauge-invariant, chirality-blind observable distinguishes two lattice fermions with the same long-range charged spectral content, whatever their indices; in particular, none detects the vanishing of the index of a chiral-class operator. The statement must be read with care. The photon mass does separate the CDF operator from the overlap operator by its value, a result close to the naive one against [FORMULA] (Sec. VI), but it separates the naive operator in the same way and for the same reason: [FORMULA] counts the long-range charged modes with the same sign for every species, whereas the anomaly counts them with their chirality, and the CDF doublers are long-range. The three probes of Sec. VI are evidence for the conjecture in this form, and the heuristic is sharp: any such observable factors through the charged spectral density, which the index leaves invariant. A proof would make that factorization precise. The cleanest test is the Ginsparg–Wilson operator of Ref. [35], which shares the local anomaly of the overlap operator and differs from it only in the absence of topological zero modes: the conjecture predicts the same [FORMULA] for the two, with the index as the only quantity that tells them apart. Conjecture 2 (anomaly-free deconfinement). Made dynamical, the CDF operator breaks the confining string of the two-dimensional gauge theory—it screens the static charge and gives the photon a mass—without an axial anomaly. This would be a confining theory deconfined by anomaly-free charged matter, with no counterpart among Wilson, overlap, or real-mass fermions, for which confinement-breaking and the anomaly are welded together. The naive operator is not a counterexample: it, too, deconfines with zero net anomaly (Fig. 4), but only by being four massless anomalous fermions in disguise, their anomalies canceling pairwise [1]. The CDF theory is undoubled—a single protected massless pole—and yet the screening persists, carried by modes that are neither massless nor decoupled: screening without either masslessness or an anomaly. That is its distinguishing ingredient, the imaginary-mass doubler spectrum: neither massless nor conventionally massive, long-range enough to screen (Fig. 4) yet chirally trivial. The long-range two-point function and the robust positivity of [FORMULA] support it. The random-block lattice supplies the control. There the doubled modes acquire masses of order [FORMULA] because their chiral symmetry is spontaneously broken, and the associated Goldstone boson decouples with them [19]; this is not in conflict with Sec. III, where [FORMULA] forbids a scalar self-energy in the averaged operator, and it names the real difference between the two members of the class: spontaneous breaking in the normal ensemble against an imaginary mass in the non-normal one. The ensemble-averaged propagator in the free-field limit and the vacuum polarization tensor in weak-coupling perturbation theory agree with their continuum values beyond about three average lattice spacings [19, 20]; and with dynamical fermions on [FORMULA] random-block lattices of size [FORMULA] , the chiral correlation function agrees with the exact Schwinger-model solution on the torus [22]. The two constructions share the symmetry class and the index obstruction but not the fate of their doublers, so Conjecture 2 is a statement about the CDF realization and its long-range IMF sector, not about the chiral class as a whole. Since both lattices also carry a protected massless physical mode, which in two dimensions screens by itself, a side-by-side comparison must isolate the doubler contribution, for instance the [FORMULA] component of Fig. 4. Two caveats frame Conjecture 2, and both are old acquaintances. The first is reflection positivity. The imaginary-mass doublers are precisely the modes Pelissetto identified as ghosts [18], and Alonso and Cortés already observed that the simplest chirally invariant undoubled actions violate Osterwalder–Schrader positivity at the ultralocal level [16]. A dynamical theory whose screening is carried by complex-mass poles must therefore either restore positivity in its physical sector or accept that the “deconfinement” diagnoses the non-standard reality of the IMF sector rather than a new physical phase; the conjecture asserts the behavior of the observables, and we deliberately leave its interpretation open. The second is the measure. With U(1) links, [FORMULA] is complex in general—the [FORMULA] pairing does not by itself enforce reality—so the dynamical theory carries a phase problem, on top of the quenched-versus-annealed choice for the disorder average of the determinant. (Ma and Zhang obtain a positive partition function for paired flavors of their one-sided non-Hermitian fermions [25]; whether an analogous pairing tames the CDF measure is open.) It is a virtue of the calculation proposed below that it requires neither: the disorder-connected correlator is evaluated on quenched ensembles and sidesteps the dynamical measure entirely. Both conjectures turn on a single object: the disorder-averaged, disorder-connected current–current correlator [FORMULA] , evaluated with the conserved lattice current and with an analytic handle on the imaginary-mass fermion loop, extrapolated in momentum and quark mass. Its zero-momentum transverse part is [FORMULA] ; whether the [FORMULA] -oscillating doubler contribution survives that sum decides at once whether the string breaks (Conjecture 2) and whether any gauge observable can (Conjecture 1). We regard this as the natural next calculation—and as the point at which the imaginary-mass structure of the CDF operator does something that neither a naive nor a Ginsparg–Wilson operator can. It should be computed side by side on the CDF and random-block lattices: identical screening would place the effect in the chiral class, different screening in the imaginary-mass structure. The calculation was performed in general [FORMULA] -gauge and analysed within the BRST formalism. The regularisation-induced breaking of gauge and BRST invariance was determined via the regularised quantum action principle, where the breaking is rewritten in terms of a local operator insertion. We have provided the full 1-loop counterterm action, including both singular and finite symmetry-restoring counterterms, which render the theory UV finite and re-establish the Slavnov-Taylor identity for Green functions with arbitrary off-shell momenta. To our knowledge, this constitutes the first complete 1-loop renormalisation of the full Standard Model in [FORMULA] -gauge within the self-consistent BMHV scheme that includes both types of counterterms, providing a finite theory and the explicit restoration of the spuriously broken symmetry. All results were obtained employing automated computational frameworks. The [FORMULA] -operator inserted Green functions, which are technically more challenging than ordinary ones, were computed twice using two independently developed computational setups, one built around FORM and the other based on Mathematica, and agree across both.
