Heavy quarkonium dynamics beyond the binding energy over temperature expansion We revisit the pNRQCD open-quantum-system description of bottomonium in a quark–gluon plasma, writing the full master equation in a spherical basis and establishing a framework for its numerical treatment. The equation does not rely on an expansion in the ratio of the binding energy over the temperature, while retaining the Born, Markov, and dilute approximations. It depends on suitable convolutions of Coulombic Green’s functions with real-time chromoelectric correlators, rather than a finite set of transport coefficients. It contains jump-operator contributions that enter with both positive and negative signs, so it is not of a Lindblad type. We utilize optimal operator rotations to minimize the negative sector and define a positive-sector approximation that retains only the optimized positive terms, obtaining in this way a Lindblad equation that can be simulated efficiently with the open-source code QTraj for arbitrary chromoelectric spectral functions. We treat the discarded sector as a systematic uncertainty associated with positivity-breaking effects of the pseudo-Lindblad generator. Positivity breaking effects can be attributed to the approximations made in the derivation of the quarkonium master equation, such as the Born–Markov approximations. Using a spectral model constrained by known infrared and ultraviolet limits, we compute the in-medium width and Bjorken-evolved survival probabilities of the [FORMULA] . The computations show the convergence of the binding-energy-over-temperature expansion at high temperatures and provide the first large-scale quantum-trajectory simulation results for bottomonium in the low temperature regime. We can thus follow the bottomonium evolution over the full temperature range relevant in heavy-ion collisions. I Introduction Quantum chromodynamics (QCD) becomes deconfined at high temperatures and high energy densities, where quarks and gluons form the quark-gluon plasma (QGP) — a strongly coupled state of hot QCD matter. The QGP is the central object of study in heavy-ion physics. A key signature to access the QGP in heavy-ion collision experiments is quarkonium suppression. The phenomenon of quarkonium suppression was proposed by Matsui and Satz [46], who predicted that a thermal screening of the quark-antiquark potential would lead to a sequential melting of charmonium states with increasing temperature. Since then, a large body of research has investigated the suppression of quarkonium states due to the effects of a hot QGP [7]. In particular, in recent years, an emerging approach, combining non-relativistic effective field theories [31] with the open quantum system framework [33], gained traction [5, 58]. Exploiting the hierarchy of scales characterizing heavy quarkonium, it is possible to derive a quantum master equation for the real-time evolution of the quark-antiquark pair [20, 21, 15, 52, 57, 47, 4]. This approach differs from the static picture introduced by Matsui and Satz, as it describes the full non-equilibrium evolution of the quarkonium in the medium. Moreover, in contrast to semiclassical evolution equations, the open quantum system approach preserves the quantum nature of quarkonium states. In this work, we focus on bottomonium suppression, where the large bottom-quark mass leads to a separation of scales that makes the application of non-relativistic effective field theories particularly well-suited. Bottomonium suppression has been previously studied in the open quantum system framework using potential non-relativistic QCD (pNRQCD). In Refs. [20, 21], the authors derive a quantum master equation for the non-equilibrium evolution of bottomonium in the QGP. Initially, the derived master equation is a Redfield equation, which generally is not of the Lindblad type. The authors of Refs. [20, 21] then use an expansion in the binding energy of the quarkonium over the temperature of the QGP, to which we refer as the [FORMULA] expansion, to simplify the master equation. At leading order (LO) in the [FORMULA] expansion, which corresponds to the strict Brownian limit, they show that the master equation becomes of the Lindblad type. In this case, the evolution depends on few transport coefficients, which are defined in terms of chromoelectric correlators and capture the non-perturbative, strongly-coupled behavior of the medium. In Ref. [23], this approach is extended to next-to-leading order (NLO) in [FORMULA] . Beyond NLO it is not possible to reconstruct a Lindblad equation. The simulation code QTraj [49], based on the Monte Carlo wave function algorithm [37], enables large-scale simulations of the LO and NLO Lindblad equations and thereby provides phenomenological predictions of quarkonium suppression observables, measured by CMS [53, 56], ATLAS [1], ALICE [3], and STAR [2]. While the [FORMULA] expansion enables simulations at high temperatures, we need to go beyond that expansion to describe the bottomonium evolution in the medium at lower temperatures. This is relevant since, as the QGP gradually cools down, the bottomonium spends a considerable amount of time at low temperatures. In Ref. [8], the non-Markovian evolution was studied by solving the unexpanded Redfield equation. However, that work neglects quantum jumps and uses simulations on small lattices. Very recently, the authors of Ref. [42] obtained a universal Lindblad equation that likewise avoids imposing a hierarchy between the temperature and quarkonium energy gaps within the Born–Markov approximation. There, a complete numerical solution of the coupled color singlet-color octet quark-antiquark pair evolution was left for future work. In this work, we go beyond those treatments by (i) including quantum-jump terms, (ii) using for the chromoelectric correlator a model consistent with known constraints, (iii) carrying out simulations on larger lattices, and (iv) studying excited states. Motivated by the need of an accurate low-temperature description for phenomenological applications, in this work, we study the pNRQCD quantum master equation without expanding in the binding energy over temperature. We start from the pNRQCD master equation, which is a Redfield equation, and develop a QTraj-compatible large-scale quantum-trajectory treatment within an optimized positive-sector approximation. This means that, based on work from the open quantum system community [12, 11], we exploit the freedom to choose a jump operator basis that minimizes the norm of the negative contributions in the master equation. We then showcase large-scale simulations of the underlying dynamics and compare them to the LO and NLO in [FORMULA] master equations. Our approach relaxes the assumption [FORMULA] , while retaining the Born and Markov approximations. By removing the [FORMULA] requirement, our work thus provides the first large-scale quantum-trajectory simulation of bottomonium dynamics below [FORMULA] MeV within the pNRQCD master-equation framework. Using the Born–Markov approximation and after projecting the master equation onto spherical harmonics, the time evolution equation for the density matrix [FORMULA] of the heavy quark-antiquark pairs in the medium gets the general form where [FORMULA] and the jump-operators [FORMULA] are operators acting on the heavy quark-antiquark Hilbert space, and the coefficient matrix [FORMULA] , which couples the jump-operators, is commonly referred to as the Kossakowski matrix [41]. Diagonalizing [FORMULA] yields independent jump-operator contributions weighted by its eigenvalues. If some of these eigenvalues are negative, the resulting evolution is not guaranteed to be positive, and the master equation is thus not of the Lindblad form. Following Refs. [13, 12], we refer to the diagonal representation containing both positive- and negative-weight jump terms as pseudo-Lindblad form. Although this master equation is not guaranteed to preserve the positivity of the density matrix throughout the evolution, contributions generating unphysical negative eigenvalues should turn out to be suppressed as long as the Born–Markov approximation remains valid. We treat the impact of the negative terms as a systematic uncertainty and study their size in Sec. III.2 and Sec. III.3. Simulating the full non-Lindblad master equation, including the negative terms, is challenging, as the stochastic unraveling implemented in the QTraj code is not directly applicable. While specialized unraveling schemes that solve non-Lindblad master equations have been developed [43, 32, 34, 40, 12], computationally, these unraveling algorithms are significantly more demanding than the unraveling algorithms applied to solve Lindblad equations. To enable large-scale simulations, we instead apply optimal rotations of the jump operators that minimize the negative terms in the pseudo-Lindblad equation. We then define a positive-sector approximation by retaining the optimized positive terms and discarding the residual negative sector. The approximation yields a Lindblad equation that can be simulated efficiently with QTraj. This approach for treating negative contributions in a master equation was first introduced in Ref. [13] and realized on an extended Hubbard chain. Here, we apply it to the non-equilibrium evolution of bottomonium and demonstrate that the approach is computationally feasible for large-scale simulations. The optimize-and-truncate approach is similar in spirit to the approach taken for the NLO in [FORMULA] equation. The difference is that here the hierarchy between the positive and negative sectors is not obtained from the [FORMULA] power counting, but from an explicit numerical minimization of the negative sector. The optimize-and-truncate approach allows us to investigate the dynamics of bottomonium at lower temperatures and compare the results with the expanded LO and NLO master equations. Without the [FORMULA] expansion, the medium effects cannot be absorbed into transport coefficients, but instead depend on suitable convolutions of Coulombic Green’s functions with real-time chromoelectric correlators. At leading order in the gauge coupling, the chromoelectric correlators are equal to the correlator of two chromoelectric fields connected by an adjoint Wilson line that we call, for short, adjoint correlator [48, 29]. The different correlators were also identified with the adjoint correlator in the LO and NLO formulation. In the general formulation developed here, we keep the chromoelectric correlators distinct and thus derive the All-Orders master equation without this approximation. For the numerical study, however, we adopt the equal correlator approximation to enable a direct comparison with previous work. Perturbatively, the adjoint correlator has been computed in real time [14, 51], and imaginary time [29]. While first lattice computations of the Euclidean chromoelectric correlator have been performed [38, 19], the extraction of the corresponding real-time correlator is hindered by the inverse problem. A complementary strategy is to compute the correlator(s) directly in real time, avoiding analytic continuation altogether: lattice simulations have been used in this way to extract gauge-field spectral functions [16], albeit within the classical-statistical approximation and predominantly in highly-occupied, far-from-equilibrium settings, so that a full non-perturbative real-time determination of the thermal adjoint correlator remains an open problem. In this work, we model the spectral function imposing infrared and ultraviolet constraints, and use the resulting real-time correlator as input to the master equation. In this way, we provide a practical numerical recipe for implementing arbitrary spectral functions in the QTraj simulation by precomputing the necessary operators and using optimal operator rotations. IV Conclusion and outlook The central result of this work is a framework that couples the real-time evolution of bottomonium in the quark-gluon plasma directly to suitable convolutions of Coulombic Green’s functions with chromoelectric correlators, removing the restriction that the medium dependence be encoded only in few transport coefficients. By avoiding to expand in the binding energy over temperature, while enabling a quantum-trajectory-based simulation, we extend the open-quantum-system description of bottomonium suppression across the entire temperature range relevant to heavy-ion collisions, including the low-temperature regime below [FORMULA] MeV that was previously inaccessible. We project the original master equation onto spherical harmonics, obtaining the All-Orders master equation, consisting of 12 jump operators. Six of them enter the master equation with a negative sign, breaking positivity and thus leading to a master equation that is not of the Lindblad type. The resulting master equation can, in principle, be simulated with a stochastic unraveling scheme. However, while simulations with [FORMULA] that neglect quantum jumps can be performed efficiently, a full simulation requires substantially more computational resources than in the Lindblad case, making large-scale simulations impractical. To enable simulations that include quantum jumps, we take a different route. Assuming that the approximations made in the derivation of the master equation are justified, we expect the negative contributions to be small. Under this assumption, we utilize the concept of optimal operator rotations to select a basis for the jump operators that minimizes the norm of the negative jump operators. We then retain only the positive sector of the optimized representation, obtaining a Lindblad equation, which can be efficiently unraveled using a standard Monte Carlo wave function approach. To perform the simulations in practice, we build a model for the spectral function of the chromo-electric correlator that smoothly interpolates between the known IR and UV limits. Using the obtained correlator, we compute the in-medium widths of the 1S bottomonium with and without the negative terms. At low temperatures, the resulting width decreases rapidly, while the width at the next-to-leading-order in [FORMULA] remains notably larger. This behavior may be phenomenologically important, since the reduction of the All-Orders width acts in the opposite direction to the expected increase of [FORMULA] toward lower temperatures and may therefore partially compensate the associated enhancement of the suppression. Different choices of the norm in the operator optimization do not have a significant impact. Simulating the evolution of the bottomonium in a Bjorken medium, we find that the [FORMULA] survival probability is described well by [FORMULA] simulations, while the excited states require full simulations including quantum jumps. Comparing the All-Orders and NLO simulations, we find that the [FORMULA] survival probability shows slightly more suppression in the AO [FORMULA] case, as expected from the in-medium width calculation. Since quantum jumps have a negligible effect on the [FORMULA] survival probability, future phenomenological studies can estimate the systematic uncertainty associated with discarding the negative sector by comparing the computationally inexpensive [FORMULA] evolutions corresponding to the AO [FORMULA] and full AO master equations, without requiring a full stochastic unraveling of the latter. In the [FORMULA] simulations, the [FORMULA] and [FORMULA] survival probabilities show only very small corrections between the AO [FORMULA] and AO master equations, suggesting that the positive sector approximation is well behaved for the excited states. Comparing the full simulations of the AO [FORMULA] master equation, including quantum jumps, with the NLO master equation, the excited states agree well at high temperatures, while at low temperatures, the All-Orders master equation leads to less suppression. The presented results enable the extension of open-quantum-system-based simulations of bottomonium suppression to temperatures below [FORMULA] MeV, thereby allowing the treatment of the entire temperature range relevant to heavy-ion collisions. A natural next step will be to study the phenomenology of bottomonium suppression, including hydrodynamics and feeddown, using this framework. The key input to this program is the real-time chromoelectric correlator, which fully characterizes the color medium beyond a finite set of transport coefficients. Standard lattice-QCD calculations determine correlators in Euclidean time, and extracting the corresponding real-time correlator requires solving an ill-posed analytic-continuation problem, commonly referred to as the lattice inverse problem. One possible avenue for constraining the correlator is to combine lattice data with theoretical information, for example, within a Bayesian analysis. Complementary real-time approaches, including classical-statistical lattice simulations [16], complex-Langevin simulations [17], Hamiltonian and tensor-network techniques [9], and quantum simulations of lattice gauge theories [45, 10], may provide additional information. Supplying real-time correlators as input to the All-Orders master equation derived here would connect non-perturbative real-time QCD directly to quarkonium-suppression phenomenology. Finally, this work paves the way for further refinements of the open quantum system formulation. A first step beyond the Markov approximation would be to compute the operators in Eq. (11) over a finite upper integration time, yielding time-dependent operators. In the future, a full phenomenological study should also consider higher-order perturbative corrections to the Coulomb potential [27] in the All-Orders master equation, which are expected to affect excited states. Tests of an EP-Preserving Wake Force A universal quadratic coupling of ultralight scalar dark matter to ordinary matter preserves the weak equivalence principle for unscreened point particles. A finite test body is nevertheless not a passive probe: it distorts the scalar field that accelerates it. We show that this field distortion produces a differential acceleration between concentric test masses, even when their microscopic coupling is universal. We calculate this signal including how each test mass distorts the field acting on the other, deriving the weak-screening limit and extending the calculation to stronger screening using concentric spherical layers. Applying the model to MICROSCOPE, we find differential signals in both its equivalence-principle sensor SUEP, whose test masses have different compositions, and its reference sensor SUREF, whose test masses have the same composition. We combine both sensors with the dark matter wake near Earth to recast the published MICROSCOPE measurements. Within this model, existing measurements probe scalar masses up to approximately [FORMULA] eV and couplings below the supernova bound. An analysis using the additional frequency components of the scalar signal could extend the mass reach and probe couplings below the BBN bound. I Introduction A universally coupled force with an inverse-square dependence is difficult to distinguish from gravity [1, 2, 3]. A standard search strategy is to exploit its finite range, looking for departures from the inverse-square law [4, 5, 6]. Light dilatons provide a well-studied example of scalar-mediated forces with both composition-independent and composition-dependent contributions [4, 2, 7]. Forces generated by scalar dark matter with universal quadratic couplings to matter face a similar challenge. Earth distorts the ambient dark matter field, producing a wake force whose spatial dependence can differ from gravity [8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14]. Quadratic couplings also allow matter to screen the field [15, 8, 16, 12]. For positive couplings, this screening can suppress the force near Earth’s surface, motivating experiments in space. However, even there the satellite housing can suppress the signal reaching the apparatus [17]. Screening also offers a way to distinguish a universal dark matter force from gravity. Bodies with different internal structures can distort the field differently and therefore acquire different accelerations, even when their microscopic coupling is identical. Previous work proposed exploiting this effect by comparing the motion of two satellites with different internal structures [17]. Here we show that separate satellites are not required. Concentric test masses can also develop a differential signal. Each mass modifies the field acting on both, so their accelerations must be calculated within a common field solution. This makes experiments such as MICROSCOPE [18, 19] sensitive to a wake force, even for a universally coupled scalar. MICROSCOPE was designed to search for violations of the weak equivalence principle by comparing the accelerations of concentric test masses. It carried two pairs, SUEP with masses of different compositions and SUREF with masses of the same composition [20]. If the masses were passive probes of the same field, a universal coupling would produce no differential acceleration in either pair. Even weak scattering changes this expectation. The outer mass modifies the field gradient experienced by the inner mass, allowing their accelerations to differ. This effect depends on the dimensions and densities of the masses, without requiring composition-dependent microscopic couplings. Both SUEP and SUREF can therefore be sensitive to a wake force from universal couplings. Interference between dark matter waves scattered by MICROSCOPE’s nested test masses has also been studied for momentum transfer forces at much higher dark matter masses [21]. Related studies in chameleon theories have examined how nested test masses and surrounding material shape the scalar field [22, 23]. MICROSCOPE calibration measurements have also been used to constrain the resulting displacement-dependent force [24]. In the regime considered here, the dark matter wavelength is much larger than the apparatus, and the differential acceleration arises from the combined distortion of the dark matter field by the Earth and the nested test masses. In this letter, we derive the differential acceleration of concentric test masses, including their mutual screening. Within a spherical-shell approximation, we obtain the leading weak-screening contribution and extend the calculation to arbitrary screening strength. We use this description to assess the joint sensitivity of SUEP and SUREF to the Earth-induced wake force, and revisit the complementary sensitivity from LAGEOS II orbital precession [25]. At leading order in the local long-wavelength expansion, the contribution generated from the spatially uniform incident field is fixed relative to the satellite. Its variation follows the incident field intensity along the orbit, without the spin modulation of the Earth-induced gradient. It therefore contributes at orbital harmonics rather than the EP band used in our recast. The spherical model is intended to approximate the screening of the external gradient. These results show how experiments designed to test the equivalence principle can also probe universally coupled scalar dark matter through the mutual screening of their test masses. For concentric bodies, the differential signal depends on their dimensions and densities even when their microscopic couplings are identical. The effect is strong enough that even the existing analysis, which uses only part of the signal, provides constraints competitive with other experimental probes. Quantum Simulation of Hadronization: From String Breaking to Event Generation High-energy collisions produce large numbers of quarks and gluons that are bound into hadrons by the confining interactions of quantum chromodynamics (QCD). This hadronization process is intrinsically real-time and non-perturbative. Event generators describe hadronization using phenomenological models with parameters fitted to data rather than calculated from QCD. Uncertainties in these models limit the precision of certain measurements at the Large Hadron Collider. Quantum computers could enable first-principles simulations of these dynamics. Existing quantum simulations of gauge theories have demonstrated string-breaking dynamics. This white paper summarizes the conclusions of the InQubator for Quantum Simulation workshop From String Dynamics to Event Generation with Quantum Simulation. We develop a roadmap for extending these simulations to inform phenomenological models of hadronization. A sequence of toy models is proposed for connecting current quantum simulations to QCD. The observables that should be extracted are listed, and the challenges that separate present simulations from quantitative predictions are identified. We propose a staged program in which quantum simulations first provide qualitative modifications to event generators and later provide quantitative input. I Introduction High-energy physics is directly probed at particle colliders where large numbers of quarks and gluons are produced. As these particles propagate, the confining interactions of QCD bind them together into hadrons. This hadronization process is intrinsically real-time and non-perturbative. In event generators, it is described by phenomenological models such as the Lund string model and the cluster model, whose parameters are fit to data [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]. Direct simulations of these dynamics on classical computers suffer from a sign problem and require exponentially scaling resources [7, 8]. Quantum computers offer the potential to directly probe these dynamics, and simulations of string breaking in low-dimensional gauge theories have recently been performed on quantum hardware [9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17]. The uncertainties of the phenomenological models are now a limiting systematic at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). The default Pythia tune depends on [FORMULA] fitted non-perturbative parameters and under-predicts LHC baryon yields [18]. Charm fragmentation is not universal across collision systems. The [FORMULA] ratio measured in [FORMULA] collisions is several times the value expected from [FORMULA] tuning, and it is under-predicted by the generator tunes available at the time of the measurement [19]. The ratio is described once string-junction fragmentation is added, but charm-strange baryon ratios remain under-predicted [20]. The spread between models is commonly used as an estimate of the hadronization uncertainty, although it does not provide a systematically improvable error bound. In a recent comparison of three generator tunes, none described the identified-particle transverse-momentum spectra measured in [FORMULA] proton-proton collisions at the LHC, and the predictions of the different hadronization models differed by up to [FORMULA] [21]. Retuning the flavor parameters improved one spectrum at the expense of another, which suggests that improvements to the underlying models are required [21]. Non-perturbative modeling is one of the dominant systematic uncertainties on the top quark mass, and hadronization limits the extraction of [FORMULA] from event shapes [21]. Current hadronization models rely on relatively simplistic classical models. In the Lund string model, the color field between separating charges is treated as a one-dimensional flux tube of constant tension [FORMULA] GeV/fm. The tube breaks through the production of [FORMULA] pairs with a Schwinger-like probability proportional to [FORMULA] [22, 23]. Here [FORMULA] is the squared transverse mass of a quark with mass [FORMULA] and transverse momentum [FORMULA] . Successive breaks are assumed to be causally disconnected, so that they can be ordered arbitrarily. Longitudinal momenta are drawn from a simple fragmentation function [FORMULA] , with [FORMULA] being the light-cone momentum fraction carried by the hadron. Transverse momenta are drawn from a Gaussian and compensated locally between neighboring hadrons [1, 24, 2, 4]. Each break is assigned a definite energy, momentum, and production vertex, so the description is classical even though it is motivated by quantum mechanics. The cluster model replaces the string with preconfined color-singlet clusters that decay according to phase space [3, 5, 6]. Over time, cluster models have acquired string-like properties and string models have acquired cluster-like properties. The Pythia manual records further limitations. Strangeness suppression is a fitted number, the transverse momentum width exceeds the Schwinger value, hadron spin enters only through fitted suppression factors, and glueballs are absent [4]. The Hagedorn temperature is the temperature at which the exponentially growing density of hadronic states makes the partition function of a hadron gas diverge. Thermodynamical fragmentation near this temperature describes identified spectra better in several respects [25]. A time-dependent tension [FORMULA] has been proposed as an extension of the Lund model, but is constrained by the lattice value only in the static, late-time limit [26]. The rope and shoving models introduced for overlapping flux tubes at LHC densities contain new ingredients that cannot currently be calculated from first principles [27]. None of these dynamical assumptions has been tested directly against QCD itself. Testing the models against data rather than against QCD has three structural limitations. A color string cannot be prepared experimentally, so hadronization is never separated from the short-distance process and the parton shower that precede it. Detectors observe only the asymptotic final state, so the dynamics of hadron formation is not directly visible. No rigorous systematic uncertainty can be assigned to a phenomenological model, and the spread between models is the usual substitute. Therefore, additional data alone cannot establish whether the assumptions listed above hold, and it will be necessary to compare directly against QCD. Performing this comparison requires a first-principles calculation of real-time confining dynamics. Euclidean lattice QCD determines static quantities to high precision, and static string breaking has been observed as a flattening of the static potential in QCD with two and with three dynamical flavors [28, 29]. Some dynamical quantities are also accessible from Euclidean correlators. The finite-volume formalism of Lüscher gives two-particle scattering amplitudes below inelastic thresholds [30], and large-momentum effective theory (LaMET) gives parton distributions from equal-time matrix elements in boosted hadrons [31, 32]. However, the inclusive real-time evolution of a breaking string is not something that can be achieved with Euclidean lattice QCD. Its extraction requires an analytic continuation that is exponentially ill-conditioned [33, 34, 7, 35]. Additionally, Euclidean methods do not give the matrix elements of the soft functions defined in soft-collinear effective theory (SCET), which contain several light-like directions and need an inclusive sum over final states [36, 37, 38, 39, 40, 35]. Classical simulation of the real-time quantum state requires resources that scale exponentially with the volume, and tensor-network methods are limited by the growth of entanglement. Jordan, Lee, and Preskill showed that quantum computers can simulate the dynamics of a quantum field theory with resources polynomial in the number of lattice sites [41, 42], and finite density carries no sign problem in a Hamiltonian simulation. Community planning documents identify hadronization and final-state dynamics as targets for quantum simulation [43, 44, 45]. However, a direct simulation of a collider event is not practical. The lattice spacing must resolve the largest energy scale in the event and the lattice extent must contain the smallest, so the number of sites scales as [FORMULA] . This gives [FORMULA] for the Large Electron-Positron Collider (LEP) and [FORMULA] for the LHC at [FORMULA] – [FORMULA] qubits per site, and most of those sites would describe physics far above [FORMULA] that perturbation theory already handles [46, 35]. Therefore, the relevant question is which non-perturbative object a quantum computer should compute. The organizing principle adopted in this white paper is to identify the smallest quantum object that is inaccessible to classical methods, and compute it directly rather than produce it in a simulated collision. This white paper summarizes the conclusions of the InQubator for Quantum Simulation workshop From String Dynamics to Event Generation with Quantum Simulation. Section II reviews the hadronization models used in event generators and the uncertainties of their parameters. Section III describes the toy models that connect present simulations to QCD and the physics that each of them can provide. Section IV lists the observables that should be extracted. Section V identifies the challenges that separate present simulations from quantitative predictions. Section VI summarizes the state of hardware and describes a staged program. The individual contributions on which these conclusions are based are reproduced in the appendices. II Hadronization models in event generators The role of hadronization. Monte Carlo event generators such as Pythia [47], Herwig [48], and Sherpa [49] simulate the full chain of physics in a high-energy collision: the hard scattering cross section, initial- and final-state parton showers, multiple parton interactions, and finally the non-perturbative hadronization of the resulting colored parton ensemble into observable hadrons. Hadronization is the last and least theoretically controlled step. However, it is unavoidable, and every observable quantity at a hadron collider is sensitive to it. Improving hadronization models is therefore not only scientifically important but computationally urgent. Hadronization should be treated as interesting science in its own right, not merely a nuisance absorbed into tuned parameters. The Lund string model. The dominant hadronization model in Pythia is the Lund string model [1]. Its physical basis is color confinement: at large quark-antiquark separations, the chromoelectric field is compressed into a flux tube approximated as a one-dimensional string with tension [FORMULA] , giving a linear potential [FORMULA] . String breaking in the Lund model and in a quantum simulation of a lattice gauge theory is shown schematically in Fig. 1, together with the Lund parameters that such simulations are expected to inform. When the string stretches sufficiently, it breaks via the Schwinger mechanism [22]: a quark-antiquark pair tunnels through the color-electric field with probability where [FORMULA] is the mass of the produced quark, [FORMULA] is its transverse momentum, and [FORMULA] . This formula simultaneously explains the approximately Gaussian transverse momentum spectrum of produced hadrons and the suppression of heavy flavors: [FORMULA] . The longitudinal momentum distribution is governed by the Lund symmetric fragmentation function where [FORMULA] is the light-cone momentum fraction carried by the hadron, [FORMULA] and [FORMULA] are free parameters, and the functional form is motivated by the Wilson area law [FORMULA] for the string worldsheet. Critically, the Schwinger formula (1) assumes a spatially and temporally uniform color-electric field. The actual breaking tube is short, inhomogeneous, and dynamically evolving. Moreover, recent quantum simulation studies [50] demonstrate that the string state carries nonlocal quantum correlations along its full length that are absent from this semiclassical picture. Corrections from non-uniform fields and from the quantum entanglement structure of the breaking state could modify the pair production rate by order-one factors. String-breaking parameters and their uncertainties. Several parameters of the Pythia string-breaking tune [18] are poorly constrained and correlated with each other and with the parton shower infrared cutoff. The strangeness suppression parameter cannot explain the [FORMULA] enhancement observed by ALICE as a function of charged multiplicity [51]. The diquark rate leads to a factor of [FORMULA] underprediction of the [FORMULA] ratio at low [FORMULA] [52]. The vector-to-pseudoscalar meson ratio is predicted as [FORMULA] from spin counting but is tuned to [FORMULA] – [FORMULA] , a discrepancy with no theoretical explanation. Extensions of the string model. Several extensions address multi-string effects in dense hadronic environments. Rope hadronization [27] models overlapping color strings in high-multiplicity events as coherent ropes with enhanced effective tension, producing enhanced strangeness and collective flow-like behavior. String shoving [53] introduces repulsive interactions between strings, generating azimuthal anisotropy without hydrodynamics. The thermal string model adds a Boltzmann factor to the tunneling probability. All of these extensions introduce additional free parameters based on semiclassical estimates with no first-principles derivation from quantum field theory. Quantum simulation of multi-string systems would contribute genuinely new information that is not accessible otherwise. The discovery that strings carry nonlocal quantum correlations [50] suggests that these semiclassical models may be missing qualitatively important physics. The cluster model. Herwig and Sherpa use the cluster model [3], in which color-singlet clusters of adjacent partons form at the shower scale [FORMULA] through preconfinement and decay to hadrons through phase-space-weighted two-body processes. The preconfinement mechanism has never been tested non-perturbatively. A quantum simulation of the full showering-plus-hadronization process could determine whether this assumption accurately captures QCD confinement dynamics. III Toy models A full quantum simulation of QCD with dynamical quarks in [FORMULA] dimensions will be challenging to perform. This goal can be reached by developing techniques in simulations of simplified theories, each of which retains some features of real hadronization physics and discards others [8, 54, 43, 55, 56, 57, 58, 59, 60, 61]. The value of a given model is set by which assumption of the phenomenological models it can test, which degree of freedom of QCD it adds, and how clearly its artifacts can be identified. This section describes the models in that order, from the theory with the fewest degrees of freedom to the theories closest to QCD, and states for each what physics it provides. Fig. 2 shows the proposed hierarchy of toy models for studying hadronization physics. [FORMULA] lattice gauge theories: A [FORMULA] gauge theory with matter is the simplest confining lattice theory. The string-breaking dynamics in these theories is set by resonance conditions. This limits the distances at which the string is allowed to break. These conditions can be determined analytically, which enables them to be used as a benchmark for hardware performance [62, 63]. Simulations on a trapped-ion platform have demonstrated that string breaking begins at the ends of the string rather than through pair creation in its bulk [9]. The Lund model assumes that successive breaks are independent, and that they occur throughout the string with equal probability. The edge effects in this model are the first observed violation of this assumption in a quantum simulation. In one spatial dimension, [FORMULA] lattice gauge theories can be mapped onto Ising models, which enables their efficient implementation on quantum computers [64, 65, 66, 67, 68]. [FORMULA] lattice gauge theories are also amenable to near-term simulation in two spatial dimensions [69, 70]. In multiple spatial dimensions, the gauge fields become dynamical, enabling string oscillations in addition to breaking, both of which have been observed in recent quantum simulations [14, 71, 13, 72, 73]. However, the continuum limit of these models is not a gauge theory. This restricts the connection to hadronization to purely qualitative comparisons of lattice dynamics. Despite this restriction, qualitative features found in [FORMULA] gauge theories can be used to guide simulations of toy models that share more similarities with QCD. Furthermore, qualitative insights could guide modifications to hadronization models that are then fit to experimental data. 1+1D U(1) gauge theory with bosonic matter: The compact Abelian Higgs model is scalar quantum electrodynamics (QED) with compact matter fields. The theory can be truncated down to a single spin-1 degree of freedom per link without breaking the symmetries of the model [74, 75, 76, 77, 78]. The truncated theory can be realized in analog neutral atom simulations, making it amenable to near-term quantum simulation [79, 80, 81]. Furthermore, this model is amenable to tensor network simulations [79, 82]. The Abelian Higgs model is the simplest confining lattice gauge theory with a continuum limit, which will enable probing qualitative features observed in [FORMULA] theories in the continuum. 1+1D U(1) gauge theory with fermionic matter: The Schwinger model, QED in [FORMULA] dimensions, replaces the bosonic matter in the Abelian Higgs model with fermionic matter. It shares several qualitative features with QCD such as confinement, chiral symmetry breaking, and a [FORMULA] vacuum [83, 84, 85]. This theory is the simplest one where the Schwinger-mechanism picture on which the Lund string is built can be tested [86, 87, 88, 50, 89, 90, 91]. Tensor network simulations with dynamical sources have demonstrated that the hadrons produced by string breaking follow a Boltzmann distribution [92, 93, 94, 95, 96]. Therefore, this model allows a first-principles answer to whether fragmentation is thermal or tunneling-like, at least in one dimension. Heavy external charges can be used to probe in-medium energy loss [97, 98, 99]. More sophisticated aspects of hadronization can be probed by including multiple flavors. A four-flavor deformed Schwinger model with an [FORMULA] flavor structure can encode light and strange flavors plus an effective spin. Numerical simulations demonstrate that the multi-flavor model generates hyperon spin correlations through multiparton exchange that are absent from the default Lund model [100]. The Schwinger model is the simplest field theory containing gauge fields and fermionic matter [101, 102, 10]. This allows qualitative features of hadronization to be probed; however, this model is restricted to only producing mesons. 1+1D Non-Abelian gauge theory with fermionic matter: The next step towards QCD is to simulate theories in [FORMULA] with fermionic matter and non-Abelian gauge groups. [FORMULA] with staggered fermions in [FORMULA] dimensions is the simplest non-Abelian theory. Preliminary simulations have been performed of this theory and resource estimates have been made for what is necessary to scale up the simulations [103, 12, 104, 105, 106, 107, 108, 109, 110]. An [FORMULA] gauge theory with dynamical quarks in [FORMULA] shares the same gauge group as QCD and has been simulated on existing quantum computers [111, 112, 113, 114, 115, 116]. This theory contains both baryons and mesons, which will allow probes of the differences between how hadronization produces these types of particles [117, 118, 119]. The simulations performed in these theories can give insight into which qualitative features observed in the simpler models are artifacts of an Abelian gauge group, and which may persist in full QCD [120]. 2+1D gauge theories: Theories in one spatial dimension do not contain dynamical gauge fields. A plaquette chain is the simplest lattice geometry in which there are dynamical gluons, and is a good first step towards seeing qualitative changes from a purely [FORMULA] calculation [121, 122, 123, 124, 125, 126]. In a full [FORMULA] simulation, the flux string becomes dynamical, and it is possible for emitted hadrons to carry transverse momentum. Performing simulations in [FORMULA] requires the implementation of a plaquette term, which introduces new computational difficulties [127]. Despite this, exploratory calculations have been performed for lattice gauge theories in [FORMULA] [128, 129, 130, 17, 131, 132, 133, 134, 135, 136, 137, 138, 139, 140, 141, 16, 142]. The inclusion of dynamical gauge fields also introduces glueballs into the spectrum of the theory [143, 15, 129, 136, 125, 126]. Glueball production is not present in existing hadronization models, and simulations in [FORMULA] are the simplest place where this assumption can be tested. In addition, the second spatial dimension will allow for the emission of soft transverse radiation, which will allow for probing qualitative features of hadronization that do not exist in a single spatial dimension. IV Observables In principle, any observable can be measured in a quantum simulation. In practice, each observable has a cost in state preparation, circuit depth, and shots. This section lists the observables that should be extracted and what extracting them requires. Conventional observables. The quantities that event generators currently fit are the natural first targets. The Lund kernel is fixed by the string tension [FORMULA] , the fragmentation function [FORMULA] , the tunneling factor, and the breakup proper times, all tuned against [FORMULA] event shapes and already in tension with LHC data [4, 144, 19]. Simulations can supply these quantities rather than fit them. The assumptions listed in Section I can also be tested one at a time. The models contain phenomenological spacetime information, while a Hamiltonian simulation gives the local energy and charge densities along the string, the timescale of hadron formation, and the transition from partonic to hadronic degrees of freedom. This will allow first-principles probing of the assumptions that go into the phenomenological hadronization models currently being used. The form of [FORMULA] , the Schwinger-like generation of transverse momentum, the dependence of both on the quark mass, and the assumed independence of successive breaks are each directly testable. Microscopic breaking mechanisms, including pair nucleation inside the flux tube, screening of endpoint charges, and string revivals, can also be directly probed in quantum simulation. Dynamical string tension. Static string tensions can be directly probed with traditional lattice techniques. The energy of a string grows linearly with its length and then saturates, and piecewise-linear fits give the static tension [FORMULA] and the breaking length [FORMULA] . The dynamical tension, denoted [FORMULA] as in the Lund model, is a different quantity from [FORMULA] . It is a fitted parameter in Pythia and differs from the static tension obtained from Euclidean lattice QCD. Rope and close-packing models make the effective tension density-dependent by construction rather than by derivation, and the constant-tension assumption for expanding strings rests on static lattice evidence alone [27, 25]. No agreed definition or extraction protocol currently connects simulated string dynamics to the effective [FORMULA] a generator would consume. Such a definition must be developed before simulated dynamics can be matched to event generators. Physics the generators omit. Hadronization models are based on a few insights into the hadronization mechanism, such as the linearity of the QCD potential. Many other aspects of string breaking are simplifying assumptions. For example, neither string nor cluster models produce glueballs, and in both models, hadron spin enters only through the relative production rates of spin multiplets. Neither default model contains spin dynamics or spin correlations for light hadrons [4, 5]. String breaking models produce baryons through diquark breaking of the string, popcorn configurations, and string junctions. Direct simulations of string breaking are likely to provide new insights into basic principles in hadronization that can be used to improve the classical modeling. The temperature and chemical potential dependence of hadronization physics will also be accessible from quantum simulation. Entanglement and magic. Entanglement entropy has been identified as a physical diagnostic of string breaking [145, 62, 50, 104, 136]. However, stabilizer states can be maximally entangled while being classically simulable. Magic provides a measure of how far a state is from a stabilizer state. The presence of substantial magic and entanglement in a quantum state is necessary for that state to be hard to simulate classically [146, 147]. Magic behaves differently from entanglement in lattice gauge theories where both have been computed [148, 149, 150]. In Schwinger-model simulations of static string breaking, all complexity measures peak at the breaking point, with non-local magic located on the string and absent from the screened charges [50, 91, 90]. Whether analogous correlations develop in real-time string breaking and survive into the hadronic final state can be answered by simulation. If they produce measurable correlations between hadrons that existing models do not reproduce, the models will need new parameterizations, and the universality of any such parameterization can then be tested across observables. Long-distance matrix elements in effective field theories. Effective field theories (EFTs) separate long- from short-distance physics, and identify long-distance matrix elements as important targets for quantum simulations. SCET separates hard, collinear, and soft physics [36, 37, 38, 39, 40, 151]. For an event shape [FORMULA] measured in [FORMULA] collisions, the cross section factorizes as [FORMULA] , where the soft function [FORMULA] [152, 153, 154, 155, 156, 157] encodes universal non-perturbative information. It is described by matrix elements of soft Wilson lines [FORMULA] and [FORMULA] along the light-like directions of the two jets. Two properties make it a quantum-computable target [35]. With a lattice regulator, the soft function is a sum of squared amplitudes, so it is positive. It is also normalized, since the vacuum is normalized, the Wilson-line operator is unitary, and the sum runs over a complete set of states. Therefore, it can be sampled by preparing the interacting vacuum, applying the unitary that creates the Wilson lines, and measuring the event shape of the final state as the experiment does. Additionally, it describes only physics below the soft scale [FORMULA] , so the lattice spacing is set by [FORMULA] rather than by the collision energy. Defining the soft function fully differentially in the energy flow [FORMULA] [158, 159, 160, 157] allows a single simulation to be post-processed into the soft functions of all event shapes computed from the measured energy flow, without an assumption of universality [35]. However, a single simulation fixes the directions and color representations of the Wilson lines. Therefore, soft functions for hadron collisions, multijet final states, and gluon jets each require a separate simulation. The energy flow also does not determine hadron species or baryon number. A three-dimensional soft function of this kind is likely more than a decade away. Additionally, the shower infrared cutoff [FORMULA] must be treated as a factorization scale [161]. The measurement problem for hadrons. Extracting information about hadronization requires performing measurements that can identify hadrons in the final state. For scalar field theories, Jordan, Lee, and Preskill proposed performing both state preparation and measurement through adiabatic switching between the free and interacting theories [42, 41]. In this construction, the adiabatic switch defines the observables of the simulation, since it maps the interacting final state onto free particles that can be counted and binned in momentum. For confining gauge theories the free limit is the wrong starting point, since in a free theory of strongly interacting particles the degrees of freedom are quarks and gluons while the asymptotic states are hadrons. The strong-coupling limit provides a replacement. In this limit, the vacuum is a product state with no electric flux excited, hadrons are localized excitations, and hadron numbers and positions follow from local measurements. Switching back to strong coupling before readout maps the final state into a basis where these observables are simple to evaluate, but the required circuit depths are large as described in Section V. The circuit depth can be reduced by replacing adiabatic switching with a unitary that is variationally optimized to prepare the vacuum and single hadron states [12]. Alternatively, one can variationally construct creation and annihilation operators for hadrons and perform measurements of these operators [11, 162]. V Challenges Several distinct problems separate present demonstrations from input that an event generator could use. They are listed here together with the current state of each. Continuum extrapolation. Every simulation is performed at finite lattice spacing, and a continuum limit must be taken before comparison with QCD. Present real-time quantum simulations mostly sit deep in the strong-coupling regime, far from where lattice dynamics can be matched to physical dynamics [136]. Probing the continuum limit is also expensive for the classical methods currently used to validate quantum simulations. As the lattice spacing is reduced, the correlation length in lattice units grows, the entanglement across any cut grows with it, and the bond dimension needed for a fixed accuracy grows at every lattice spacing along the continuum extrapolation [8, 104]. Real-time dynamics can also suffer from lattice artifacts without a static analog. For example, in the Schwinger model, the sub-luminal maximum lattice velocity produces spurious fragmentation of fast hadrons [97]. The errors due to a finite lattice spacing can be reduced through the use of improved Hamiltonians that systematically improve the scaling of errors with lattice spacing [174, 175, 176]. Formulation and truncation dependence. Many lattice Hamiltonian formulations exist, and each one has its trade-offs. Electric-basis formulations give a mostly local Hamiltonian with discrete basis states that can be mapped onto a quantum computer. The electric basis works best at large values of the bare coupling, but the continuum limit is reached by reducing the bare coupling. The error introduced by an electric basis cutoff falls off as a factorial of the field cutoff, which may enable the use of relatively low truncations in physical simulations [177]. Note that a cutoff that is too small produces real-time dynamics that differ qualitatively from the untruncated theory even where static quantities extrapolate cleanly [104]. Loop-string-hadron and dressed-site formulations work with gauge-invariant electric basis states, at the cost of more complicated circuits and a larger local dimension [178, 179, 180, 181]. Mixed or gauge-fixed bases allow one to work at small values of the coupling and with a fully gauge-invariant basis at the cost of locality [182, 183, 184, 185, 186, 187]. Alternatively, one could use discrete subgroups of the gauge group. Quantum simulations with discrete gauge groups can be implemented in a scalable manner, but extrapolation to the continuum requires more care as they do not live in the same universality class as the continuum theory [188, 189, 190, 191, 167, 192, 168, 193, 170, 194]. Quantum link models provide yet another option for formulating lattice gauge theory Hamiltonians and approaching the continuum limit [195, 196]. Each of these formulations has different systematic errors and computational costs. This is a strength of the program, as the same physics can be simulated in different formulations to determine which features of string breaking are universal and which are formulation artifacts. Resource estimation. Before running a simulation, one should know how large a computer is necessary, and how many gates need to be implemented to perform the simulation. Resource estimates in quantum computing are commonly performed using triangle inequality bounds to rigorously upper bound the error induced in the approximation to the time evolution operator. These estimates have been developed for various compilation strategies for lattice gauge theory dynamics [197, 198, 103, 183, 199, 166, 165, 200, 163, 201, 173]. However, the formalism behind these estimates does not capture the deviation of simulated dynamics from the quantum field theory being simulated. The Trotter error bounds they rely on are obtained from triangle inequalities applied to nested commutators. These bounds are loose, often by orders of magnitude. Furthermore, they bound the deviation from a particular lattice-regularized time evolution rather than the deviation from continuum physics. Alternatively, the finite time step used in quantum simulation can be understood as a temporal lattice spacing. One can then approach the continuum by taking the spatial and temporal lattice spacings to zero simultaneously [202, 203, 204]. This will likely require far fewer resources than requiring that the Trotter error vanishes at each fixed lattice spacing. Table 1 provides resource estimates from the literature for the toy models that have been proposed in Section III. State preparation. Extracting continuum physics from lattice field theories requires preparing low-energy states where the description of the lattice physics by an effective continuum theory is valid. In the present quantum simulations of string breaking dynamics, the initial state is a flux tube prepared on top of some approximation of the vacuum state. In the strong coupling regime, the vacuum is close to a product state in the electric basis, and a string can be prepared by exciting the links along a path. As the coupling is reduced toward the continuum, the vacuum becomes an interacting gauge-invariant state with magnetic fluctuations whose correlation length in lattice units grows, and a string placed on the strong-coupling vacuum is no longer a low-energy state of the theory. Two approaches have been developed to reach the vacuum of lattice gauge theories outside of the strong coupling limit. The first is to perform adiabatic switching from a solvable limit of the theory [205, 42, 41]. The circuit depth to implement this procedure grows as the minimal gap along the switching path decreases. Alternatively, one can use a variational state preparation procedure [131, 106, 206, 207, 111, 208, 209, 10, 11, 210, 211, 135, 12, 212, 213]. Hamiltonian VQE ansätze that alternate electric, magnetic, and matter layers can produce gauge-invariant ground states without penalty terms [214, 215]. Alternative ansätze that are chosen to match the symmetries of the vacuum state have also been used. Variational circuits optimized on small systems can be used to inform state preparation on larger systems through the scalable circuit formalism. This approach exploits the fact that, once the lattice exceeds a few correlation lengths, the optimal parameters converge exponentially with system size, so parameters determined on small lattices can be extrapolated to lattices that cannot be simulated classically [208, 12]. This procedure has been verified for the vacuum and for single-hadron states, but its depth still grows with the correlation length. Extracting observables. Factorization identifies soft and shape functions as the natural quantum targets, with lattice resolution set by the soft scale rather than the collision energy [35]. However, no published prescription matches a quantum-simulated string-breaking amplitude to a shower at a defined [FORMULA] [161], and no procedure maps a lattice calculation onto Lund parameters with controlled errors. A further separation is unsolved. The quarks at the ends of a string move apart with high energy and inject a perturbative collinear short-distance scale. This implies that a naive string simulation mixes hadronization with perturbative collinear physics. The two must be separated, presumably through a factorization theorem using SCET [36, 37, 38, 39], before a simulation can constrain the models quantitatively. These gaps remain open. Device noise. Quantum computers do not operate perfectly, and each operation on them suffers from some degree of noise or error. This device noise is the primary source of limitations of existing quantum computers. In lattice gauge theory simulations, a fixed physical evolution time requires a number of Trotter steps that grows as the lattice spacing is reduced, and the circuit depth per step grows with the truncation of the gauge group. Therefore, the accumulated error per circuit grows along the continuum extrapolation and along the approach to QCD. In present simulations, the effects of device noise are often addressed with error mitigation techniques such as dynamical decoupling [216, 217], readout mitigation [218, 219], Pauli twirling [220, 221], zero noise extrapolation [222, 223], and operator decoherence renormalization (ODR) [224, 114, 68, 208, 10, 225]. These techniques have enabled successful simulation of hadron dynamics in the Schwinger model with [FORMULA] qubits at a CNOT depth of [FORMULA] [10]. These mitigation techniques are limited by the circuit depth, as they must amplify a signal that decays exponentially with the depth of the circuit [226, 227, 228]. As quantum computers improve, the noise can be systematically removed with the use of quantum error correction. Gauge theories offer a unique opportunity as their Hilbert space contains redundancies that can be combined with application-specific error-correcting codes. In the near term, these redundancies can be used for post-selection to remove errors that take the system outside of the physical Hilbert space [11, 14, 17]. VI Hardware and program Over the past several years, quantum simulations of gauge theories have progressed from few-qubit demonstrations to simulations of confining dynamics on more than [FORMULA] qubits in both one and two spatial dimensions [101, 10, 229, 13, 142, 230, 162, 17, 15, 16, 130, 150]. The consistent lesson of these simulations is that state preparation is classically inexpensive while time evolution is not. The computational cost of classical simulation grows rapidly with evolution time [10, 15]. However, no demonstrated quantum advantage for gauge dynamics exists. Every hardware result to date has been validated against a classical baseline. Going beyond the limits of classical simulation requires advancement in available quantum hardware. The hardware available over the next several years is set by published development plans. IBM’s quantum development plan schedules the Kookaburra module with a quantum low-density parity-check memory for release in 2026, entanglement between modules with Cockatoo in 2027, and the fault-tolerant Starling system in 2029, specified as [FORMULA] logical qubits executing [FORMULA] gates [231, 232]. In June 2026, the U.S. Department of Energy announced the Quantum Genesis initiative, whose goal is the deployment of a fault-tolerant quantum computer with logical qubits numbering in the low hundreds by 2028, with high energy physics among the named applications [233]. Note that these plans specify logical qubit counts of order [FORMULA] and gate counts of order [FORMULA] . Against the resource estimates above, such a machine would run the [FORMULA] -dimensional and small [FORMULA] -dimensional simulations described in this white paper with error correction, but it would not run a [FORMULA] -dimensional simulation of QCD with matter, whose costs exceed these numbers by many orders of magnitude [55, 163]. Therefore, the proposed near-term program is written for mitigated devices of a few hundred physical qubits, and the medium-term program plans for the first error-corrected devices. In the near term, the deliverable is qualitative modification of event generators rather than full event simulation. Since the dynamics of hadronization have never been accessible, there is no reason to expect that the current models contain all of their relevant features. The most valuable results of a simulation may be qualitative features that no model anticipates, and observables and analysis techniques must be developed to find such features rather than only to test the assumptions listed in Section I. Note that no quantum-simulated quantity has yet been inserted into a production generator, and which object should be handed over, whether a soft function, a fragmentation kernel, or a multiplicity distribution, remains to be settled. Qualitative features of hadronization can be probed through simulations of the ladder of toy models proposed in Section III. The Schwinger model comes first, because analytic results allow the systematic errors of a simulation to be validated [234]. Non-Abelian theories in [FORMULA] dimensions add color, plaquette chains add dynamical gluons and a magnetic term without being two-dimensional, and [FORMULA] -dimensional [FORMULA] adds transverse string dynamics and glueballs [229, 164]. Each stage of this ladder gets closer to full QCD, and qualitative features present in all of them may be worth incorporating into event generators. Every stage requires the same four ingredients, which are preparation of the vacuum, insertion of a colored source, real-time evolution, and measurement of observables. They must also be performed with controlled truncation error and continuum extrapolations. These simulations should be performed for hadronization both in the vacuum and at finite temperature and density. This is directly relevant to heavy-ion collisions, where the decadal priorities of the hot-QCD community explicitly welcome such work [235, 97, 93]. Table 2 lists proposed milestones for this program and which models need to be simulated to reach the milestone. In the long term, extension to [FORMULA] -dimensional QCD with matter depends on fault-tolerant resources [55, 163]. Realizing any of this at scale will require quantum devices to be integrated as accelerators within existing high-performance computing workflows, together with the classical benchmarking and verification on which every claim will rest [43, 45]. VII Conclusions In this white paper, the case for applying quantum simulation to hadronization has been set out. Hadronization has been identified as a limiting systematic at the LHC. The limitations of classical methods have been stated. Euclidean lattice QCD reaches elastic scattering through finite-volume methods and parton distributions through LaMET, but it does not reach the real-time evolution of a breaking string or the matrix elements of operators with several light-like directions. Tensor-network methods are limited by the growth of entanglement. Quantum computing provides a way around these limitations. Factorization has been used to identify the non-perturbative objects a quantum computer should compute. The toy models used in present simulations have been described together with the physics each provides. The observables to be extracted have been listed. They include the momentum, flavor, and multiplicity quantities that generators currently fit. They also include the entanglement and magic measures that have no counterpart in any generator, but may provide a new viewpoint on the dynamics of hadronization. The qualitative features of string breaking and hadron production are already accessible on current devices, and qualitative modifications to event generators are a realistic near-term deliverable. Quantitative accuracy will likely require further hardware and algorithmic development. It will also be necessary to develop a prescription that separates perturbative collinear physics from hadronization in a string simulation. The fault-tolerant machines scheduled for 2028 and 2029 are specified at a few hundred logical qubits, which is sufficient for the low-dimensional stages of this program. These low-dimensional simulations will provide useful insights for future simulations of QCD in [FORMULA] dimensions.

Nevertheless, its particle nature remains unknown. Among the most extensively studied candidates are weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs), whose abundance may be generated through thermal freeze-out in the early Universe. The apparent connection between a weak-scale annihilation cross section and the observed DM abundance—the so-called WIMP miracle—has traditionally motivated models in which a single particle accounts for the entire DM density. The absence of convincing non-gravitational signals, together with increasingly stringent limits from collider, direct-detection, and indirect-detection searches, has significantly restricted the simplest realizations of this paradigm Abercrombie and others (2020); Abdallah and others (2015); Arcadi et al. (2018); Arcadi et al. (2025). An equally plausible possibility is that the dark sector contains more than one stable particle. In multi-component DM scenarios, the observed density is shared among two or more species, each contributing only a fraction of the total abundance Tucker-Smith and Weiner (2001); Zurek (2009); Esch et al. (2014); Yaguna and Zapata (2020); Bélanger et al. (2020); Bélanger et al. (2023); Costa et al. (2022). More importantly, the thermal histories of the different components need not be independent Belanger and Park (2012). Interactions among the dark particles can induce conversion, semi-annihilation, and semi-conversion processes, thereby coupling their Boltzmann equations and qualitatively modifying the freeze-out dynamics Díaz Sáez et al. (2021); Yaguna and Zapata (2022); Escalona et al. (2026). These processes can weaken the usual connection between the relic abundance and the couplings probed by direct-detection experiments, opening viable regions that would not be available in the corresponding single-component models. A central model-building question in such scenarios is the origin of the stability of the different DM particles. In many constructions, stability is imposed through additional discrete symmetries, such as [FORMULA] or products thereof Yaguna and Zapata (2020); Yaguna and Zapata (2022); Qi and Sun (2025); Frank et al. (2025). Although perfectly consistent at the phenomenological level, these symmetries are often introduced specifically for this purpose. It is therefore worthwhile to investigate frameworks in which the stability of multiple dark particles follows instead from an underlying gauge symmetry. Such a framework becomes especially attractive when the same gauge extension also addresses another open problem of the Standard Model (SM), such as the origin of neutrino masses.
