Nuclear Theory: [FORMULA] -decay widths from two-potential approaches and WKB prefactors The accurate calculation of [FORMULA] -decay widths can be obtained with several equivalent descriptions of the Gurvitz-Kalbermann two-potential approach (TPA) or a semiclassical WKB description having both correct barrier penetrability and consistent inner-state normalization prefactor. This prefactor, which is related to the assault frequency, is implemented in several ways in the literature, producing systematically different results that can be mistaken for [FORMULA] preformation effects. We benchmark single-particle [FORMULA] -decay widths across 161 even-even nuclei ( [FORMULA] – [FORMULA] ) using several TPA descriptions and WKB calculations with four common prefactors, employing a Woods-Saxon potential fixed by the quantization-constrained parameter method. The TPA formulas agree to within a few parts in [FORMULA] , highlighting their robustness. Among semiclassical prefactors, only the widely used round-trip (RT) approximation closely reproduces the TPA widths to within a few percent. An Airy-function analysis reveals this [FORMULA] averaged WKB prefactor is the correct leading-order semiclassical normalization of the exact quasibound state, clarifying the counterintuitive empirical observations associated with the WKB prefactors. Our benchmark identifies the WKB prefactor appropriate for [FORMULA] -decay tunneling analysis and provides a clean reference for isolating preformation and structure effects in future studies. 1 Introduction Alpha decay is a fundamental quantum tunneling process in nuclear physics and plays a central role in the study of heavy and superheavy nuclei Gamow [1928], Gurney and Condon [1929], Smits et al. [2024], Qi et al. [2019], Belli et al. [2019], Delion and Dumitrescu [2023], Wei et al. [2024]. Measured lifetimes and branching ratios constrain cluster formation, shell effects, and nuclear structure at the limits of stability. Microscopic quartetting and pocket-potential studies confirm that [FORMULA] clustering is predominantly a surface phenomenon governed by shell structure, Pauli blocking, and medium effects Röpke et al. [2014], Xu et al. [2016], Yang et al. [2021], Zheng et al. [2024]. This connection is particularly important for current superheavy-element (SHE) programs at JINR, RIKEN, GSI, and related facilities, where new isotopes are routinely established through correlated [FORMULA] -decay chains Smits et al. [2024], Roberto et al. [2023], Belli et al. [2019]. The experimentally measured half-life inherently includes contributions from both the [FORMULA] preformation within the parent nucleus and its subsequent tunneling probability through the Coulomb barrier. Because the preformation factor is strongly model dependent Qi et al. [2019], Delion and Dumitrescu [2023], Lovas et al. [1998], deviations from experiment can be attributed to preformation or structure effects only after the tunneling width itself has been computed under controlled theoretical assumptions and approximations. Establishing such a controlled theoretical baseline is the primary purpose of this work. The semiclassical Wentzel-Kramers-Brillouin (WKB) approximation has been a primary tool for systematic [FORMULA] -decay studies for decades due to its broad applicability and low computational cost Buck et al. [1992], Mohr [2006], Pei et al. [2007], Ismail et al. [2010], Kelkar and Castañeda [2007], Chien and Phuc [2022]. However, while the action integral robustly determines the exponential penetrability, the absolute width also requires an assault frequency (or a normalization prefactor) that encodes the motion of the quasibound state in the inner pocket. On this point, there is a lack of consensus among the prefactor descriptions used in [FORMULA] -decay studies. Kelkar and Castañeda emphasized that WKB decay widths are meaningful only when the quantization condition, the penetrability, and the prefactor are implemented consistently within a single semiclassical framework Kelkar and Castañeda [2007]. In practice, round-trip-period, harmonic-oscillator, and classical-frequency prescriptions all remain in active use Chien and Phuc [2022], Sharma and Sharma [2022], Bao et al. [2014], Deng and Zhang [2021], Kelkar and Castañeda [2007], while the semiclassical reduction of the two-potential approach by Gurvitz and Kalbermann supplies a more foundational normalization, built from the form factor of the WKB wave in the pocket Gurvitz and Kalbermann [1987]. Because all of these descriptions share the same penetrability, the choice of prefactor uniformly shifts every width in a calculation by a common factor. The practical question is therefore not whether WKB is an accurate tool for systematic [FORMULA] -decay analysis, but which prefactor correctly reproduces the absolute width of a fully quantum calculation and why it does so. Fully quantum-mechanical approaches for tunneling decay resolve the prefactor ambiguity by construction, because the normalization of the decaying state is consistently determined from the wave function rather than prescribed. The two-potential approach (TPA) of Gurvitz and Kalbermann separates the interaction into an inner quasibound problem and an outer scattering problem, yielding the decay width in a compact analytical form Gurvitz and Kalbermann [1987], Gurvitz [1988]. The four Gurvitz-Kalbermann (GK) formulas used below are the volume, surface, and boundary representations of this single construction. Gurvitz and collaborators later proposed the modified two-potential approach (MTPA), which replaces the sharp potential split with a controlled matching scheme in the barrier region Gurvitz et al. [2004]. The reliability of these quantum formulations has been tested in several important comparisons. Åberg et al. demonstrated that TPA widths are practically identical to distorted-wave (DW) method Kadmensky and Kalechits [1971] widths for spherical proton emitters, and their erratum recorded the perplexing empirical fact that the simple averaged (round-trip) WKB normalization, rather than the more elaborate one from GK matching, gives the closest agreement with DW results Åberg et al. [1997], Åberg et al. [1998]. More recently, Alavi et al. Alavi et al. [2024] carried out the analogous comparison for uranium [FORMULA] decay with a microscopic double-folding interaction, finding very good agreement among TPA, direct, and DW widths and showing that the TPA result is insensitive to the choice of separation radius. More recently, Bo shows that the WKB can reproduce the [FORMULA] -decay half-lives data with comparable accuracy with the DW method while being less sensitive to the potential parameters Bo [2026]. The present work extends this line of investigation by broadening the quantum TPA methods comparison from a single isotopic chain to the even-even [FORMULA] -decay landscape and by confronting the resulting TPA reference with the commonly used semiclassical prefactor families in the WKB method. A spherical baseline of this kind is also timely. Recent studies have pushed the tunneling problem well beyond the spherical TPA picture. Li and Xu formulated a three-dimensional TPA (3D-TPA) for deformed [FORMULA] emitters Li and Xu [2023], Zheng et al. connected pocket formation and [FORMULA] clustering to nuclear-medium effects and applied a deformed pocket-type dynamical double-folding potential with deformed TPA widths Zheng et al. [2024], Zheng et al. [2025], You et al. surveyed even-even nuclei with a deformed TPA You et al. [2025], while Cheng and Xu combined 3D-TPA with physics-informed neural networks Cheng and Xu [2026]. Before deformation, channel coupling, or microscopic preformation factors are layered onto the calculation, however, the method dependence of the single-particle width for a fixed spherical input should be pinned down, since otherwise effects at the level of tens of percent can be mistaken for structure properties. This work accordingly pursues three aims. The first is to verify that the four Gurvitz TPA formulas and the MTPA matching expression define the same single-particle [FORMULA] width for a fixed Woods-Saxon (WS) input, thereby establishing a stable quantum reference over a broad even-even dataset. The second is to identify which WKB prefactor preserves that quantum width closely enough for practical surveys. The third is to explain the observed discrepancies between these descriptions. An Airy-function analysis of the quasibound-state norm shows that the familiar [FORMULA] averaging is not a crude shortcut but the correct leading-order semiclassical normalization of the exact state, whereas the literal Gurvitz-Kalbermann prescription retains a spurious turning-point contribution evaluated precisely where the WKB amplitude breaks down. The long-noticed and surprising empirical agreement of the averaged round-trip prefactor with the TPA in Ref. Åberg et al. [1998] is revisited and explained in light of Airy-function analysis. All calculations use a WS interaction fixed by the quantization-constrained parameter method (QCPM) introduced in Ref. Nga et al. [2026]. The QCPM-derived WS potential serves as a fixed common input throughout, so that the comparison isolates the part of the single-particle width scale generated by the tunneling, matching, normalization, and radial quantization conventions themselves rather than by any width or preformation fitting. The global comparison covers 161 even-even emitters with parent mass numbers [FORMULA] –252, supplemented by a separate 10-nucleus run spanning [FORMULA] –294 as an illustrative benchmark over a wider region of the nuclear chart. Global and crustal properties of neutron stars We investigate how the treatment of the neutron star crust affects both the global properties of the star and the properties of the crust itself. Three approaches are compared: a direct connection between a fixed crust and the core equation of state (EOS), a smooth crossover between them, and a unified EOS in which the crust is computed within a compressible liquid-drop model with the same nuclear empirical parameters of the relativistic mean-field model used for the core. For each approach, we consider four values of the symmetry energy slope, [FORMULA] MeV. For a [FORMULA] star, some global properties are weakly to moderately affected: the radius and the moment of inertia agree within 1% among the three approaches. On the other hand, the tidal deformability obtained with the direct connection is up to 21% lower than the unified one for [FORMULA] MeV. A much larger contrast comes from the crustal properties. Relative to the unified EOS, the direct connection yields a crust that is 15–36% thinner, 6–12 times less massive, and that carries a fraction of the total moment of inertia 5–8 times smaller (0.3–1.1% instead of 2.8–6.2%). The differences between crust treatments are thus comparable to or larger than those arising from variations in [FORMULA] for crustal properties, while they remain subleading for global ones. I Introduction Neutron stars (NS) are the densest stars in the Universe, which makes them the perfect laboratory for connecting nuclear physics and astrophysics. The NS structure can be divided into layers, and many nuclear-physics inputs are essential. The surface is believed to be covered with 56Fe and neighboring elements. The solid outer crust is composed of highly exotic nuclei (embedded in a free electron gas) that progressively become more neutron-rich with increasing depth until unbound neutrons appear. This marks the transition to the inner crust, where neutron-rich nuclei coexist with a neutron (super)fluid. Therefore, understanding the properties of nuclear matter and finite nuclei is essential for the crust of NS. In the core, nucleons can no longer form clusterized matter, and neutrons, protons, and leptons form a homogeneous liquid in beta equilibrium [31]. The crust is thus the region of the NS where the connection between terrestrial nuclear physics and astrophysics is most direct. Matter is still organized into nuclei, and the outermost layers are made of isotopes that can be produced and studied in the laboratory, so that their composition and EOS are determined almost model independently by measured atomic masses [15, 31, 7]. Mass measurements of exotic neutron-rich nuclei have progressively extended this experimental knowledge deeper into the outer crust [66]. Beyond the neutron drip, the neutron fluid stabilizes clusters that are much heavier and more neutron-rich than any nucleus produced in terrestrial laboratories, and the description must rely on nuclear models [15, 7]. Describing this sequence consistently therefore requires a model that is anchored to experimental nuclear masses at low density and that can be extrapolated, together with the properties of homogeneous matter, toward the core. A comprehensive review of the physics of NS crusts can be found in Ref. [15]. Over the last years, considerable effort has been devoted to quantifying how uncertainties in the nuclear physics input propagate into crustal properties. Compressible liquid-drop models informed by nuclear-matter empirical parameters and experimental masses have been used to correlate the crust composition, the neutron-drip and crust-core transition points, and the crust thickness with the properties of nuclear matter [30, 29], to perform Bayesian analyses of the crust-core transition [10], and to establish general predictions for the crustal moment of inertia [11]. Bayesian frameworks have also been employed to construct prior distributions of crust models, including the nuclear pasta phases [4], and inner-crust EOSs consistent with chiral effective field theory, with quantified theoretical uncertainties, have recently become available [28]. In parallel, it has been shown that non-unified EOSs, in which a standard crust is attached to an independently derived core EOS, introduce spurious uncertainties in the stellar radius [25], that the results depend on the matching procedure itself [23], and that the treatment of the crust can even affect the empirical relations used to interpret observations [22]. Matching procedures nevertheless remain common in practice, particularly with relativistic mean-field models of the core. It is therefore worth assessing, within a single nuclear model, how the choice of crust treatment compares with the uncertainty stemming from the density dependence of the symmetry energy, both for the crust itself and for the star as a whole. These uncertainties will soon become observationally relevant. Next-generation gravitational-wave observatories, such as the Einstein Telescope [1] and Cosmic Explorer [58], will considerably improve these measurements. For a single binary NS event, the radius of a NS is expected to be measured with uncertainties of about 200, 100, and 50 m for networks with one, two, and three such detectors, respectively [35]. This precision is comparable to the radius differences between unified and non-unified EOSs [25, 23], which also affect the tidal deformability [55]. In the electromagnetic domain, the enhanced X-ray Timing and Polarimetry mission (eXTP), planned for launch in 2030, will extend the pulse-profile modelling pioneered by NICER [26, 59, 17], to a larger and more diverse population of NSs [38]. The consequences of the crust treatment, however, go beyond the stellar radius. Several observed phenomena are governed by the crust itself rather than by the global structure of the star. Pulsar glitches are commonly attributed to angular momentum stored in the superfluid neutrons of the inner crust, which requires the crust to carry a minimum fraction of the total moment of inertia [39], a requirement that becomes considerably more demanding once the entrainment of free neutrons by the crustal lattice is taken into account [3, 14]. The quasi-periodic oscillations detected in magnetar giant flares have been interpreted as torsional modes of the crust [36, 62, 61], and the thermal relaxation of accreting NS after an outburst probes the thickness and composition of the crust [8]. All of these depend on the crustal mass, thickness, and moment of inertia, which are set mainly by the density and pressure at the crust-core transition. These quantities may therefore be far more sensitive to how the crust is modelled than global observables such as the radius or the total moment of inertia, and it is natural to ask whether the simplifications adopted in non-unified EOSs, harmless for the latter, remain acceptable for the former. We find that the crust treatment is a subleading source of uncertainty for the global properties of the star, but a dominant one for its crustal properties, to the point of determining how the latter depend on [FORMULA] . Introduction.—Spin polarization has emerged as a powerful probe of the rotational dynamics of matter created in heavy-ion collisions. In non-central collisions, a large orbital angular momentum is generated perpendicular to the reaction plane, creating a vortical structure of the produced matter [18]. Such vorticity can be transferred to the spin degrees of freedom of produced particles through spin–vorticity coupling [7, 9], leading to a global polarization of hadrons along the angular momentum (see, e.g., Refs. [11, 13, 10, 21] for reviews). The first statistically significant observation of global [FORMULA] and [FORMULA] polarization by the STAR Collaboration established spin polarization as a new observable for exploring the dynamical properties of strongly interacting matter [5]. Of particular interest is the intermediate-energy region of a few GeV. Measurements by the STAR Collaboration in fixed-target Au+Au collisions at [FORMULA] GeV revealed a sizable global [FORMULA] polarization [1]. At even lower energies, the HADES Collaboration measured large [FORMULA] polarization in Au+Au and Ag+Ag collisions at [FORMULA] and [FORMULA] GeV, respectively [4]. These observations extend the increasing trend of global polarization toward lower collision energies and indicate that the few-GeV region provides a particularly interesting environment for studying spin dynamics in strongly interacting matter. Recent theoretical calculations also suggest that the global [FORMULA] polarization may exhibit a broad maximum around [FORMULA] – [FORMULA] GeV [15, 16]. The High Intensity heavy-ion Accelerator Facility (HIAF) [26], which has recently entered trial operation in China, will provide us with new opportunities to explore heavy-ion collisions in this intermediate-energy and high-baryon-density regime. The proposed Hyperon-Nucleon Spectrometer (H-NS) at HIAF aims to perform systematic measurements of hyperon polarization in [FORMULA] , [FORMULA] , and [FORMULA] collisions, opening prospects for dedicated studies of spin phenomena in this energy range [6]. A particularly intriguing opportunity at HIAF is provided by collisions between strongly deformed nuclei such as 238U. The intrinsic shape of the colliding nuclei has recently attracted considerable attention at higher collision energies. At the RHIC energies, the nuclear crossing time, of the order of [FORMULA] fm/ [FORMULA] , is much shorter than the characteristic timescale of rotational quantum fluctuations of a deformed 238U nucleus, [FORMULA] – [FORMULA] fm/ [FORMULA] [2]. Consequently, the nuclear orientation is effectively frozen during the collision, allowing each collision event to capture a “snapshot” of the intrinsic nuclear shape. This idea has enabled the nuclear-shape imaging using high-energy U+U collisions at RHIC [2, 17, 14]. The situation at intermediate collision energies is qualitatively different. The nuclear crossing time increases to several fm/ [FORMULA] which remains orders of magnitude shorter than the rotational timescale of 238U. The orientation of the deformed nucleus can therefore still be regarded as essentially frozen throughout the collision. However, unlike at ultrarelativistic energies, where the nuclear geometry is rapidly encoded into the initial condition of the produced medium, the finite crossing time at intermediate energies allows nuclear deformation to influence the collision dynamics throughout the overlap stage. Consequently, the intrinsic nuclear shape can affect compression, baryon stopping, and rescattering, thereby modifying the subsequent vortical evolution of the system. This raises a fundamental question: Can the intrinsic shape of colliding nuclei leave a characteristic imprint on the spin polarization of produced hadrons through the dynamical generation of vorticity? Different orientations of the prolate 238U nuclei modify not only the collision geometry but also the distribution of orbital angular momentum and the resulting vortical structure of the system. Through spin–vorticity coupling, these orientation-dependent vortical structures are expected to leave characteristic imprints on the global polarization of produced hadrons. Therefore, spin polarization in the intermediate collision energies is not only of interest by its own but also may serve as a novel probe of nuclear deformation. Our aim is to determine how nuclear-shape information is reflected in global [FORMULA] polarization and to provide predictions for future measurements at HIAF. I Introduction The origin of nucleon mass remains one of the most challenging frontiers in quantum chromodynamics (QCD)—the fundamental theory to describe strong interactions—and nuclear physics. A nucleon weighs around 1 GeV but three quarks that make this nucleon only weigh around 10 MeV. In the QCD vacuum, the [FORMULA] chiral symmetry spontaneously breaks down to [FORMULA] by the quark-antiquark condensate, which generates nucleon mass. However, Lattice QCD simulations [3, 1, 2] and QCD sum rule studies [20, 21, 24] suggest that spontaneous chiral symmetry breaking does not account for the entire nucleon mass. In particular, a nonzero component of the nucleon mass may persist even after chiral symmetry is restored. This idea is adopted by the parity doublet model (PDM) [10, 19], in which the nucleon mass is divided into a chiral variant contribution generated by spontaneous chiral symmetry breaking and a chiral invariant contribution that remains even in the chiral symmetric phase. To explore chiral invariant mass, strongly interacting matter under extreme conditions, such as high temperature or high density, provides a particularly useful setting. For instance, in high density regime, chiral symmetry is partially restored and chiral condensate is reduced, while the chiral invariant mass remains. In the past few years, there are many studies aiming on how to constrain chiral invariant mass based on neutron star observational data [40, 30, 29, 15, 23, 27, 16, 14]. In particular, Refs. [30, 29, 15, 23, 27, 16, 14] use a PDM-NJL crossover model, in which neutron star equation of state is constructed by combining low density hadronic matter made from the parity doublet model and high density quark matter from Nambu-Jona-Lassino type quark model. Comparing the resultant mass-radius relation with neutron star observational data, it is found that the chiral invariant mass is more than half of nucleon mass. However, for simplicity, pion condensation has not been included in previous studies based on PDMs. Pion is a meson with a relatively small mass [FORMULA] , and carries isospin number. Its chemical potential [FORMULA] is equal to the isospin chemical potential [FORMULA] , [FORMULA] . Introduction: Three nucleon short range correlations (3N-SRCs) represent a unique configurations in the ground state wave function of the nucleus and nuclear matter. In momentum space, nucleons in 3N-SRCs emerge with momenta well above the characteristic Fermi momentum of the system. The possibility of an inelastic transition in the intermediate state of the 3N system such as [FORMULA] where [FORMULA] is a baryonic resonance creates the possibility of irreducible 3N-nuclear force in the pairwise NN interactions. Such forces are used to obtain the correct magnitude of binding energies of tritium and other light nuclei. However, they contain a substantial repulsive part which for high density nuclear matter produces a stiff equation of state. One such application to pure neutron matter[1] in the 2000’s resulted in a prediction of neutron stars with masses above two-solar masses. Convergence of many-body truncations in the in-medium similarity renormalization group The in-medium similarity renormalization group (IMSRG) is a leading ab initio method for describing atomic nuclei. Most applications truncate the flowing operators at the normal-ordered two-body level, neglecting induced higher-body terms. Convergence with increasing operator rank remains poorly understood, particularly in strongly correlated systems. We systematically assess the many-body truncation hierarchy in the single-reference and multi-reference IMSRG, retaining normal-ordered operators through the four-body and three-body levels, respectively. Using an exactly solvable pairing-plus-particle-hole model, we quantify successive higher-body corrections over a broad range of interaction strengths, spanning weakly to strongly correlated regimes. The multi-reference formulation exhibits faster and more robust convergence than its single-reference counterpart, with the advantage becoming most pronounced at strong coupling. In this regime, higher-rank irreducible density matrices play an essential role in achieving convergence of the many-body expansion. 1 Introduction Solving the quantum many-body problem for a given Hamiltonian, particularly in the presence of strong correlations, is a central challenge in modern physics. In nuclear physics, the development of high-precision interactions within chiral effective field theory, which incorporates the symmetries of quantum chromodynamics, has increased the need for accurate ab initio methods that quantitatively connect these interactions to nuclear observables. Substantial progress over the past decade has enabled such methods to solve the many-body Schrödinger equation in a systematically improvable manner across an increasingly broad range of nuclear masses Hergert [2020], Scalesi et al. [2026]. Among these approaches, the in-medium similarity renormalization group (IMSRG) Tsukiyama et al. [2011], Hergert et al. [2016] has emerged as a particularly versatile framework, with applications spanning light to heavy nuclei Stroberg et al. [2021], Hu et al. [2022], Kuske et al. [2026]. The IMSRG addresses the quantum many-body problem through a continuous sequence of unitary transformations that progressively decouple a chosen reference state from other states. While its time and memory requirements scale polynomially with the size of the single-particle basis and depend only indirectly on the particle number, IMSRG transformations generate operators of increasingly high rank, making it computationally demanding to retain them all. In most applications, the flowing operators are therefore truncated at the normal-ordered two-body (NO2B) level, defining the IMSRG(2) approximation Hergert et al. [2016]. Comparisons with other methods using the same Hamiltonian suggest that the omitted three- and higher-body operators have relatively small effects (about [FORMULA] ) in the ground-state energies of near-closed-shell nuclei Hergert [2020]. Their effects may be more substantial in strongly correlated systems, particularly in open-shell deformed nuclei. Because retaining higher-rank operators is computationally demanding, systematic studies of convergence behaviors beyond the IMSRG(2) truncation remain scarce. Such studies are essential to quantify many-body truncation errors in IMSRG calculations. In recent years, the single-reference IMSRG (SR-IMSRG) has been extended to include all or selected contributions from normal-ordered three-body (NO3B) operators Heinz et al. [2021], Stroberg et al. [2024], He and Stroberg [2024]. Calculations for closed-shell nuclei using chiral nuclear Hamiltonians in small model spaces have demonstrated subpercent errors in the ground-state energies. More recently, SR-IMSRG(4) was implemented for the Richardson pairing model Hu et al. [2026], revealing that contributions from operators beyond the NO3B level grow significantly with the pairing strength [FORMULA] and reach a few percent of the total correlation energy when [FORMULA] becomes comparable to the single-particle level spacing. An alternative to employing a high-order SR-IMSRG( [FORMULA] ) truncation is to use a correlated reference state, leading to the multi-reference (MR) framework. Through generalized normal ordering with respect to such a reference state, the MR-IMSRG can incorporate pairing correlations Hergert et al. [2013], deformation Yao et al. [2020], and other static correlations Gebrerufael et al. [2017] in open-shell nuclei more efficiently. This capability introduces additional terms involving higher-rank irreducible density matrices (also known as cumulants), but does not change the computational and memory scaling with the single-particle basis size [FORMULA] . Previous studies have shown that MR-IMSRG(2) can describe low-lying states of strongly deformed nuclei Gebrerufael et al. [2017], Yao et al. [2020], Belley et al. [2024], Zhou et al. [2025], Zhou et al. [2026], which are challenging for the single-reference formulation. Nevertheless, the size of the correlations omitted at the MR-IMSRG(2) level remains unclear. Quantifying corrections from explicit NO3B and higher-body terms in MR-IMSRG and comparing the convergence of the multi-reference and single-reference formulations as the many-body truncation order increases are therefore important steps toward establishing a controlled truncation hierarchy for (MR-)IMSRG calculations. In this work, we present the first numerical implementation of the MR-IMSRG framework to explicitly retain all terms through the NO3B level, yielding the MR-IMSRG(3) approximation, and systematically benchmark the convergence of many-body truncations in both the SR-IMSRG and MR-IMSRG formulations. Using an exactly solvable pairing-plus-particle-hole (P3H) model over a broad range of interaction strengths Davison [2023], Chen et al. [2026a], we quantify the corrections to the ground-state energy obtained by retaining operators of successively higher body rank. All other qualitative conclusions remain unchanged. 4 Summary We have implemented the MR-IMSRG(3) framework for the pairing-plus-particle-hole model and systematically investigated the convergence of many-body truncations in the single-reference (SR) and multi-reference (MR) IMSRG formulations, retaining normal-ordered operators through the four-body (NO4B) and three-body (NO3B) levels, respectively. Benchmarks against exact solutions over a range of pairing strengths quantify the energy corrections obtained by successively increasing the retained operator body rank. The results show that the MR formulation generally exhibits faster and more robust convergence than its SR counterpart, particularly in the strong-pairing regime. These findings offer important guidance for assessing many-body truncation errors in IMSRG calculations of open-shell nuclei with modern chiral interactions. They also illustrate the merit of incorporating collective correlations, e.g., from the spontaneous breaking of gauge or rotational symmetries, into the reference state while letting the MR-IMSRG evolution capture dynamical few-particle correlations. I Introduction Neutron stars provide a unique laboratory for studying strongly interacting matter under extreme conditions, where the baryonic matter is highly isospin asymmetric and can reach densities several times nuclear saturation density [1, 2, 3]. Their macroscopic properties are governed by the equation of state (EoS) of dense nuclear matter, making neutron-star observations an important probe of the high-density EoS [4, 1]. In particular, pulsar timing measurements based on the relativistic Shapiro delay have provided precise masses for several massive neutron stars, including PSR J1614-2230 [5], PSR J0348+0432 [6], and PSR J0740+6620 [7], establishing a robust lower bound approximately 2 [FORMULA] on the maximum mass supported by the EoS. Complementary constraints on the mass-radius relation have been obtained from X-ray pulse-profile modeling by the Neutron Star Interior Composition Explorer (NICER), including observations of PSR J0030+0451 [8, 9, 10], PSR J0740+6620 [11, 7, 12], PSR J0437-4715 [13], PSR J1231-1411 [14] and PSR J0614-3329 [15, 16]. Moreover, the binary neutron-star merger GW170817 has provided constraints on the tidal deformability and, consequently, on the radius of neutron stars [17, 18, 19]. Numerous theoretical studies have investigated the connection between the nuclear EoS and neutron-star properties using different nuclear many-body approaches and nucleon-nucleon interactions, including effects associated with nuclear symmetry energy [20, 21, 22, 23, 24, 25, 26]. Symmetry energy effect on hot nuclear matter and proto-neutron stars We examine the effects of symmetry energy on proto-neutron stars (PNSs) by employing equation of state (EOS) described by the relativistic mean-field (RMF) model. The thermal properties of dense matter and the bulk properties of PNSs are investigated under the assumptions of isothermy, isentropy, and fixed lepton fractions. The polytropic index is calculated at finite temperature, revealing a negative correlation with the PNS maximum mass that the EOS can support. The properties of PNSs during the heating and cooling stages along their evolution line are explored under different combinations of lepton fraction and entropy. We investigate the correlation between the symmetry energy slope [FORMULA] and the properties of PNSs. As [FORMULA] increases, the PNS radius also increases; however, this effect diminishes with a growing lepton fraction for the isentropic case. I Introduction The equation of state (EOS) relating pressure to energy density (or mass density) plays a key role in determining the global structure of cold neutron stars (NSs) older than a few minutes, which have temperatures below 1 MeV [1, 2]. IV Summary In this work, we calculate effect of symmetry energy on the EOS of hot nuclear matter and the bulk properties of PNSs. We employ the RMF framework and introduced two parameter sets, TM1e and TM1, which preserve the same saturation properties except differing only in symmetry energy and its slope. To investigate the thermal effect, we consider conditions of isothermy, isentropy, and neutrino trapping with fixed lepton fractions. In the isothermal case, thermal effects directly contribute to the pressure but reduce both isospin asymmetry and symmetry energy. We find that the influence of thermal effects diminishes at high densities, where nuclear interactions become more significant. In the isentropic case, neutrinos contribute less to the thermodynamic quantities compared to electrons and muons. Additionally, a larger lepton fraction [FORMULA] indicates a more symmetric nuclear matter environment, resulting in lower corresponding energy and pressure compared to neutrino free nuclear matter. Under the isentropic condition, a rapid temperature decrease is observed near the crust of PNS. Lower [FORMULA] (TM1e) leads to higher inner temperatures with neutrino free. We calculate the bulk properties of PNSs at finite temperature and different snapshot stages along the evolution line. Our findings indicate that the central density decreases with increasing temperature or entropy. Additionally, we observe that the polytropic index curve of EOS exhibits a negative correlation with the maximum mass of the PNS within the same model, regardless of whether the case is isothermy, isentropy, neutrino free or neutrino trapping. Overall, our results indicate that symmetry energy effect significantly influence the EOS, the isospin asymmetry, the polytropic index as well as the properties of PNSs at finite temperatures and evolution stages. Especially during the heating stage, the mass-radius relations differ considerably from those of cold NSs due to the symmetry energy effect. Introduction.— The determination of the composition of neutron stars (NS) from their properties is presently an active field of research. It is expected that these objects can provide information on the high density and low temperature region of the QCD phase diagram [1], a region that is presently not accessible in the laboratory. However, it has been shown that recovering the proton fraction from the [FORMULA] -equilibrium equation of state (EOS) is challenging due to the degeneracy introduced through the isoscalar and isovector nuclear force channels [2, 3, 4]. This could indicate that identifying non-nucleonic degrees of freedom inside NS may be even more complex, as different composition scenarios may produce similar behaviors of the EOS or the mass-radius NS curve. The inclusion of information that raises the degeneracy will be necessary to distinguish different degrees of freedom. Several agnostic descriptions have been used to identify the region in the pressure-energy density phase space that is populated by the current astrophysical and theoretical constraints and to determine the speed of sound behavior with density [5, 6, 7, 8, 9]. Even though these approaches are important for providing insight into the EOS covering the unknown density range between the low density region constrained by chiral effective field theory [10, 11] and the high density constrained by perturbative QCD [12, 13, 14], they do not allow a clear determination of the NS composition and relevant degrees of freedom. It has been shown that the mass-radius or mass-tidal deformability curves determined from a given EOS model may convey some information about the composition of the NS [15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20]. The signatures proposed in these works rely on the knowledge of the slope and curvature of the mass-radius or mass-tidal deformability curves. One expects that with the upcoming NS observatories, such as the enhanced X-ray Timing and Polarimetry mission—eXTP [21], Square Kilometer Array [1], Einstein Telescope [22], Cosmic Explorer [23], NewAthena [24], the uncertainties associated with the determination of the radius, mass, and tidal deformability will be much smaller. In this letter, we show that the behavior of the mass-radius curve may provide a clear indication of the NS composition, in particular, of the presence of quarks. It has been shown previously that a mass-radius curve with a negative slope for all masses above one solar mass indicates that the underlying EOS contains, with a very large probability, only nucleonic degrees of freedom. If the mass-radius curve presents a range of masses with a positive slope, then there should be a radius maximum defined by [FORMULA] . I Introduction HICs are used to create quark–gluon plasma (QGP) matter at extremely high temperatures and energy densities. Owing to its extremely short lifetime of about [FORMULA] – [FORMULA] , the QGP cannot be observed directly, and its properties are instead inferred by comparing experimental measurements with dynamical model calculations [1, 2]. Over the past two decades, observables such as transverse-momentum spectra and anisotropic flow [FORMULA] have been extensively used to constrain the transport properties of the QGP[3, 4, 5, 6], in particular its shear and bulk viscosities [7, 8, 9, 10]. More recently, with the increasing precision of both experimental measurements and event-by-event simulations, the same data–model comparison strategy has also been used to extract nuclear-structure parameters [11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18]. For example, the STAR Collaboration measured [FORMULA] , [FORMULA] , and [FORMULA] in U+U and Au+Au collisions, and compared their cross-system ratios with event-by-event hydrodynamic calculations. By varying the deformation parameters in the simulations, these observables can be used to constrain the quadrupole deformation and triaxiality of [FORMULA] [18]. A relativistic heavy-ion collision evolves through several stages, including the initial collision and energy deposition, pre-equilibrium evolution, hydrodynamic expansion of the QGP, hadronization, and the subsequent hadronic stage [19, 20]. During the evolution, pressure gradients generated by the initial geometry drive the collective expansion and convert spatial anisotropy into momentum-space anisotropy of the final-state particles. Consequently, information about the initial geometry is retained in final-state observables such as anisotropic flow and multiparticle correlations [21, 22, 23, 24, 25, 26, 27, 28, 29]. Therefore, a reliable description of the initial state is essential for interpreting final-state observables and extracting the underlying physics of the collision [30]. Traditional MC models are commonly used to generate nuclear configurations for heavy-ion collision simulations by treating a deformed nucleus as a classical rotor: in each event, a definite intrinsic orientation is randomly assigned, and the nucleon positions are sampled from the corresponding deformed one-body density [31, 32, 33, 34]. For even–even nuclei, however, the physical ground state has [FORMULA] and is rotationally invariant. The classical configurations generated by conventional MC models carry definite orientations, which is inconsistent with the rotational invariance of an even–even [FORMULA] ground state [33]. Motivated by the importance of rotational-symmetry restoration, we recently proposed a quantum-mechanical description of nuclear configurations by extending the conventional MC sampling procedure [35]. In this approach, the [FORMULA] nucleus is treated as a quantum rotor, with its ground state represented as a coherent superposition of intrinsic states with different orientations, thereby approximately restoring the rotational symmetry of the nuclear ground state. Recent studies have also explored the impact of rotational-symmetry restoration on the interpretation of nuclear deformation in ultrarelativistic heavy-ion collisions using different theoretical approaches [36, 37]. Replacing the classical rotors with the approximately symmetry-restored quantum rotors changes the spatial distribution of participant nucleons and thus the collision initial geometry. Since information about the initial geometry is propagated to the final state through the subsequent dynamical evolution, an important question is how the quantum-rotor treatment affects experimentally accessible final-state observables after the full collision evolution. In this work, we systematically investigate this question in symmetric collisions of the representative even–even nuclei [FORMULA] , [FORMULA] , [FORMULA] , and [FORMULA] , covering both light and heavy nuclear systems and prolate and oblate deformations. For each system, we employ both the classical-rotor and quantum-rotor treatments within the same extended MC Glauber framework, while keeping all settings of the subsequent dynamical evolution identical. This allows us to isolate the effects arising from the different treatments of the nuclear configuration. We focus on final-state observables closely related to nuclear deformation, including anisotropic flow [38], normalized symmetric cumulants [39, 40, 41], the Pearson correlation coefficient between [FORMULA] and the event-averaged transverse momentum [FORMULA] [42, 43], and the corresponding cross-system covariance ratio. IV Summary and conclusions In this work, we employ an extended MC Glauber model to describe both classical (fixed-orientation) and quantum (orientation-superposed) rotors, with the rotational symmetry of even-even nuclei restored in our approximate quantum treatment. By comparing the classical and quantum results, we systematically investigate the effects of quantum superposition on initial-state geometric anisotropies and final-state collective observables in high-energy nuclear collisions. Experimental data are also included in our figures as a reference. However, our primary focus is not on reproducing the experimental observables, but rather on assessing the magnitude of the corrections arising from the quantum-rotor treatment. A complete description of the experimental data would require a global fit involving adjustments of many model parameters. In the initial state, we find the quantum correction to the mean-squared eccentricity exhibits a nonmonotonic dependence on nuclear mass number, remaining sizable for light nuclei and non-negligible even for heavy nuclei. After approximately subtracting the fluctuation contribution, the magnitude of the geometry-driven quantum correction decreases largely monotonically with increasing mass number. Furthermore, we find that quantum superposition suppresses the geometric eccentricity more strongly for prolate nuclei ( [FORMULA] ) than for oblate nuclei ( [FORMULA] ). Physics: NEONATAL EEG SEIZURE PREDICTION WITH QUANTUM-INSPIRED CONTINUOUS-VARIABLE (BOSONIC) RESERVOIR COMPUTING We study short-horizon neonatal seizure prediction on Helsinki-style (HUH) preprocessed EEG feature tables using quantum-inspired reservoir computing. Under strict subject-wise cross-validation on imbalanced preictal–interictal windows, we test whether reservoir constructions shaped after (i) gate-based qubit dynamics and (ii) continuous-variable (bosonic/photonic) dynamics provide a practical sequence encoder relative to strong classical baselines. Both reservoirs are executed here purely in classical simulation on a single GPU; accordingly, we do not claim quantum advantage, but rather evaluate whether quantum-shaped dynamics act as useful, low-footprint random feature maps with a trained linear readout. We compare against Random Forests and RBF–SVMs, and report AUROC, AUPRC, per-subject AUPRC, expected calibration error, and stratified bootstrap confidence intervals. Across our experiments, the CV/bosonic reservoir is consistently competitive and can improve AUPRC over the baselines, while the gate-style reservoir is more sensitive to hyperparameters. These results suggest that quantum-inspired, photonics-motivated reservoirs can be practical sequence encoders for neonatal EEG feature tables under conservative subject-wise evaluation. 1 Introduction Neonatal seizures are early markers of brain injury but are often clinically silent, so continuous multichannel EEG is used in the NICU. Because expert review is scarce, automated pipelines based on hand-crafted spectral, amplitude, asymmetry, and connectivity features followed by SVM-like classifiers have been widely studied [16, 17]. Later, CNN and CNN–RNN models on EEG-derived time–frequency images improved sensitivity and reduced false positives [11, 12], but these models are heavier, need more data, and can struggle with the missingness and per-subject heterogeneity typical of clinical EEG tables. More recent neonatal work explores prediction and large-scale detection with deep learning on quantitative or raw EEG [8, 6]; in contrast, we focus on the clinically common feature-table setting and ask whether quantum-shaped reservoirs provide a lightweight sequence embedding under strict subject-wise splits. In parallel, quantum machine learning (QML) proposed to use quantum evolutions as fixed, high-dimensional feature maps with only a classical readout [14]. Quantum reservoir computing (QRC) is a convenient instance: a randomly parametrized quantum system is driven by an input sequence and only a simple output layer is learned [3, 4]. Continuous-variable and photonic variants show how classical signals can be injected as small displacements, mixed by random interferometers, and weakly nonlinearized [7, 9]. We take a realistic, Helsinki-style (HUH) neonatal EEG feature table (subjects, absolute time indices, seizure/preictal flags, numeric descriptors), build per-subject fixed-length sequences (18 steps, [FORMULA] 6 minutes), and test whether such quantum-shaped reservoirs provide measurable gains over strong classical baselines under subject-wise cross-validation on imbalanced preictal–interictal labels. The pipeline standardizes on train folds only, imputes clinical NaNs, and reports AUROC, AUPRC, bootstrap uncertainty, calibration, and per-subject AUPRC. We use two encoders: (i) a gate-style, stateful reservoir that unrolls the whole sequence in one circuit-like evolution and reads out single- and two-body observables, and (ii) a continuous-variable (bosonic) reservoir that projects features to multiple modes, applies randomized linear mixing with weak nonlinearity, and time-multiplexes to expand dimensionality. Both run fully quantum-inspired on GPU. In this setup, the CV reservoir is the most stable and often matches or slightly exceeds tree and kernel baselines, while the gate-style reservoir is competitive but more hyperparameter-sensitive. 2 Related Work Classical feature-based neonatal EEG seizure detection has been shown to work in clinical conditions and to tolerate strong class imbalance [18]. Deep learning models operating on raw EEG or time–frequency representations (CNNs and variants) have improved neonatal seizure detection when large annotated corpora are available [11, 12, 6]. For short-horizon prediction, recent work demonstrated that minute-scale neonatal seizure risk estimation is feasible with deep learning on quantitative EEG [8], though external validation and careful split protocols remain important. Independently, quantum reservoir computing (QRC) showed that driving a fixed, randomly parametrized quantum dynamical system and training only a linear readout can yield powerful sequence processors [3, 4]. Martínez-Peña et al. analyzed the information-processing capacity of reservoirs and emphasized the “large linear memory with weak nonlinearity” regime [9]. On the continuous-variable side, photonic primitives—displacements, interferometers, and weak nonlinearities—provide a natural recipe for CV reservoirs and CV quantum neural networks [7]. Importantly, the broader reservoir-computing community has also demonstrated fast, hardware-friendly photonic reservoirs that motivate CV-style designs [1], and recent proposals outline feasible photonic quantum reservoirs using photon-number-resolving measurements [10]. Our work connects these strands by keeping the clinically realistic feature-table setting and strict subject-wise evaluation, while swapping the sequence encoder for (i) a gate-style and (ii) a bosonic/CV-style quantum-inspired reservoir that runs fully in software. It supports two quantum-inspired sequence encoders: a gate-style variant that follows the inject–entangle–readout pattern of discrete qubit reservoirs, and a continuous-variable (bosonic) variant based on displacements, interferometric mixing, weak nonlinearity, and time multiplexing. On Helsinki-style (HUH) data the CV/bosonic reservoir was the strongest performer, suggesting that quantum-shaped dynamics can extract clinically relevant structure from short preictal windows. Because the pipeline also reports per-subject AUPRC, calibration curves, and bootstrap confidence intervals, it provides a complete and defensible sequence-encoding evaluation, and its modular design allows the same reservoirs to be rerun on higher-fidelity backends in the future. The Skin Detector System of the LZ Dark Matter Experiment This paper presents the design, calibration, and performance of the Skin Detector component of the LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) dark matter experiment. The Skin Detector consists of approximately 2 tonnes of liquid xenon instrumented with 131 photomultiplier tubes, surrounding the central time-projection chamber and functions as an active veto system for background rejection. Energy calibration with monoenergetic gamma sources established a position-dependent energy scale and determined prompt and delayed veto thresholds. Radon decays in the Skin can be identified with less than 15 mm spatial resolution, revealing stable convective flow patterns with measured velocities ranging from 2-4 mm/s that persisted throughout extended data-taking periods. The achieved Skin veto threshold meets or exceeds the design goal of 100 keV throughout the Skin volume. The prompt veto efficiency for gamma rays emitted following electron capture in 127Xe is found to be ( [FORMULA] )%, consistent with the simulated value of ( [FORMULA] )%. M-shell EC decays are used to validate the LZ detector sensitivity for low-mass dark matter during the first science run. 1 Introduction In this article, we describe the design and performance of the LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) Skin Detector. The LZ experiment [1] is a dark matter direct detection experiment designed to achieve unprecedented sensitivity to weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs), one of the leading candidates for dark matter. Located at the 4850-foot level of the Sanford Underground Research Facility (SURF) in Lead, South Dakota, USA, LZ utilizes a dual-phase xenon time projection chamber (TPC) to detect nuclear recoils from WIMP interactions. To date, LZ has published results from three science runs, referred to as WS2022 [2], WS2024 [3], and WS2025 [4], with world-leading constraints on spin-independent and spin-dependent WIMP-nucleon cross sections. Figure 1 shows the layout of the LZ experiment. Ionizing interactions in the TPC produce two distinct signals: a prompt scintillation pulse (S1) and a delayed electroluminescence pulse (S2) from ionization electrons extracted into the gas phase. Voltages applied to three wire-mesh grid electrodes (cathode, gate, and anode) create the electric field configuration necessary for electron drift, extraction and electroluminescence. The S1 and S2 signals are detected by two arrays of photomultiplier tubes (PMTs) located above and below the LXe TPC volume. The timing and spatial distribution of S1 and S2 allow for three-dimensional event reconstruction, and their relative sizes allow discrimination between nuclear and electronic recoils. However, given the extreme rarity of potential WIMP interactions, additional background suppression is essential. To this end, LZ employs both passive shielding and two active veto systems, the xenon Skin Detector and the Outer Detector (OD). The Skin Detector, regions 1 and 2 in Fig. 2, refers to the instrumented LXe volume outside the TPC field cage but within the inner cryostat vessel (ICV). The TPC electrodes and the grounded ICV create a horizontal electric field in the Skin volume, approximately within the range 3–6 kV/cm in WS2022 and from 1.5–2 kV/cm in WS2024 and WS2025. With no electroluminescence region, the Skin Detector produces only S1-like signals. The Skin Detector serves a dual purpose: electrically, it provides the necessary standoff between the biased TPC components and the grounded ICV; functionally, it acts as an active veto for background events. A gamma-ray that Compton scatters in the TPC and then deposits additional energy in the Skin will produce a coincident signal that is inconsistent with the expected single-scatter topology of a WIMP interaction. Similarly, neutrons that scatter in the TPC and are subsequently captured in the Skin or OD can be identified through delayed coincidences. By rejecting such events, the Skin significantly enhances the background rejection capability of the experiment, especially for events near the edge of the detector volume where external backgrounds are more likely to penetrate. In addition to its veto function, the Skin Detector serves as a diagnostic tool for characterizing the background environment of the experiment. With sufficient light collection and timing resolution, the Skin enables energy and position reconstruction of interactions within its volume. This allows for the identification of radioactive contaminants, such as gamma rays from detector materials, neutron captures, and alpha decays from radon progeny. Notably, the Skin has demonstrated sensitivity to decay chains from 222Rn and 220Rn, enabling spatial mapping of the liquid flow by tracking the decay pairs. The Skin has also been used to tag electron capture decays of xenon isotopes such as 127Xe, which produce low energy Auger electrons and X-rays with associated gamma-ray emission [5]. This paper presents a study of the LZ Skin Detector, including its hardware configuration, energy calibration, position resolution, and veto performance. Section 2 describes the detector geometry, PMT configuration, and readout system. Section 3 details the methods used to calibrate the Skin position and energy scales using external and internal gamma-ray sources. Section 4 presents the reconstruction of internal alpha emitters, position reconstruction performance, and mapping of the liquid flow. Section 5 evaluates the Skin’s veto capabilities for prompt and delayed signals, comparing measured performance with design requirements. 2 Detector Description The Skin Detector is a single-phase LXe scintillator volume that envelops the TPC [1], providing an active veto for any interactions producing energy deposits in the Skin volume (Fig. 2). It is optically and electrically separated from the TPC and is divided into two regions: a cylindrical "Barrel" surrounding the vertical walls of the TPC and a "Dome" located beneath the bottom PMT array. Together, these regions contain approximately 2 tonnes of LXe and form a contiguous volume between the TPC field cage and the ICV. The Skin’s Barrel has an azimuthally symmetric geometry, with its radial thickness varying from 4 cm near the liquid surface to 8 cm at the bottom, due to the tapered shape of the ICV [6]. The vertical extent of approximately 160 cm covers the liquid volume from just below the liquid surface to the bottom TPC PMT array. The Skin’s Dome, with an outer radius of 82 cm matching the lower parts of the Barrel, occupies the space below the bottom TPC PMT array above the bottom of the inner cryostat. The Dome varies in depth from a few cm to a maximum depth of about 12 cm. Calibration Source Deployment (CSD) tubes [7] located between the inner and outer cryostat vessels allow source deployment near the Skin and Outer Detector at azimuthal angles of [FORMULA] = 0∘, 120∘, and 240∘, reaching down to the cathode. Both Skin regions are lined with high-reflectivity polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) to enhance light collection efficiency for vacuum ultraviolet (VUV) scintillation light. The PTFE used is Technetics 8764, made from Daikin M17 powder, which was selected after an R&D campaign for its combination of high VUV reflectivity of [FORMULA] 97% [8, 9] and low intrinsic radioactivity. PTFE tiles of 1 mm thickness line the inner surface of the ICV. The tiles are held in place by PTFE washers and screws mated to low-profile, threaded titanium buttons glued to the ICV wall using cryogenic-grade MasterBond EP29LPSP epoxy. The tiles cover the full inner surface except the high-voltage (HV) feedthrough region. The outer surface of the TPC field cage is also made of PTFE, serving as an additional reflective boundary. The Skin Detector is instrumented with a total of 131 PMTs as shown in Fig. 3, distributed across the Barrel and Dome regions to provide high-efficiency detection of scintillation light from interactions in the surrounding LXe. The PMTs were selected to balance light collection performance, mechanical constraints, and radiopurity requirements. Two models of Hamamatsu PMTs are used: 93 of the compact 1-inch-square R8520-406s, and 38 of the larger 2-inch-diameter R8778s, with the latter reused from the LUX experiment [10]. The upper Barrel region is equipped with R8520-406 PMTs, arranged in a single layer just below the liquid xenon surface and mounted facing downward. These PMTs are attached to the outer surface of the TPC field cage. At the top of the detector, they are supported by the weir structure that sets the liquid level in the TPC. The compact form factor of the R8520-406 allows dense packing within the limited radial space available in the upper Skin, with three gaps present to allow for drainage tubes for the weir (visible in the upper right part of Fig. 2). These PMTs are optimized for xenon scintillation light collection, as they feature a quartz window and a bialkali photocathode with a quantum efficiency of 30% at 175 nm and a collection efficiency for electrons at the first dynode of 70% [11]. The lower Barrel region is instrumented with 20 R8778 PMTs, positioned radially around the base of the TPC and oriented upward. Eighteen of these PMTs provide uniform coverage of the lower Barrel region, and two are specifically directed toward the HV feedthrough region, where it was not possible to attach the PTFE liner. These PMTs also feature similar characteristics with a quantum efficiency of 33% at 175 nm and a collection efficiency of 90% [10]. The Dome is instrumented with an additional 18 R8778 PMTs, mounted horizontally beneath the bottom PMT array. These are arranged in two concentric rings: 12 PMTs facing radially outward and 6 facing radially inward. This configuration is designed to optimize light collection efficiency in the Dome, which has a complex geometry due to the curvature of the cryostat and the presence of structural supports and cables. All R8778 PMTs as well as the bottom TPC PMT array (consisting of 241 R11410 PMTs [12]) are sleeved in PTFE to enhance reflectivity and reduce photon absorption on metal surfaces. The Skin includes a dedicated LED calibration system with 30 LEDs (470 nm) distributed across the detector: 12 above the upper Barrel PMTs, 12 below the lower Barrel PMTs, and 6 in the Dome region. The LEDs are housed in PTFE structures to diffuse light and provide uniform illumination. This system operates at low intensities to measure single photoelectron response for per-PMT gain calibration, and at higher intensities to characterize afterpulsing ratios as a diagnostic of PMT vacuum quality. The Skin PMTs are read out using the signal processing and data acquisition (DAQ) infrastructure developed for the LZ experiment [13]. PMT signals are transmitted through vacuum feedthroughs located on the top and bottom cryostat flanges and then routed to analog front-end electronics housed in mini-crates attached directly to feedthroughs. Amplifier cards provide an amplification of a factor of 40 with a shaping time of 60 ns full width at one tenth maximum [13]. The amplified signals are digitized per channel, with sampling rates of 100 MHz and 14-bit resolution. The DAQ system employs a pulse-only-digitization scheme to reduce data volume, storing only waveform segments surrounding detected pulses. A series of trigger sources determine when data are recorded in LZ [13], and Skin waveforms are recorded for all trigger types. In WS2022, the Skin itself could not trigger the detector; subsequently, a dedicated Skin trigger was implemented to enable efficient recording of radon-chain alpha decays, which are a key calibration source for the Skin Detector. The Skin trigger achieves a high efficiency of 99.5% for these decays while maintaining a low trigger rate of approximately 0.5 Hz, ensuring compatibility with the overall LZ trigger budget of [FORMULA] 20 Hz. 3 Detector Calibration The ability to reconstruct the location and energy depositions of events in the Skin is essential for optimizing the veto performance and for characterizing background populations. To quantitatively determine the Skin’s position resolution, we exploit the coincidence between 220Rn and 216Po alpha decays, as these decays can be assumed to occur at the same physical location given the 146 ms half-life of 216Po. Inhalation–exhalation asymmetry in pressure-driven airflow through a population-derived median unilateral human nasal cavity ABSTRACT This study investigates inhalation–exhalation asymmetry in population-derived median unilateral human nasal cavity under pressure-driven breathing using time-resolved computational fluid dynamics (CFD). A standardized geometry reconstructed from averaged CT data of 30 adults was subjected to a sinusoidal nasopharyngeal pressure waveform over a complete breathing cycle. Low, intermediate, and high pressure amplitudes were considered to quantify breathing-phase-dependent changes in flow rate, Reynolds number, wall shear stress, nasal resistance, and olfactory-region airflow. For identical imposed pressure magnitudes, inhalation produced a consistently larger flow rate and lower aerodynamic resistance than exhalation, demonstrating a direction-dependent pressure–flow response. Increasing breathing intensity increased Reynolds number and nasal resistance while largely preserving the spatial pattern of the flow. During inhalation, stronger airflow penetrated further into the superior nasal cavity and produced higher and more localized wall shear stress, whereas exhalation exhibited smoother airflow redistribution. The breathing-phase asymmetry also affected regional ventilation: the fraction of total airflow reaching the olfactory region increased with inspiratory intensity and reached approximately 6% under the high-pressure condition, while the expiratory fraction remained comparatively insensitive to breathing intensity. These results demonstrate that pressure-driven transient simulations naturally capture geometry-dependent inhalation–exhalation differences that are suppressed when identical flow rates are prescribed for the two breathing phases, with consequences for both global nasal resistance and regional airflow delivery. I Introduction Nasal breathing warms and humidifies inspired air, filters inhaled particulates, and transports odorants to the olfactory epithelium before air enters the lower airways [26, 5]. These functions arise from the complex three-dimensional anatomy of the nasal cavity, particularly the nasal valve, turbinates, and olfactory cleft, which produce highly non-uniform velocity, pressure, and wall shear stress distributions [3, 31]. The intricate geometry, together with the cyclic nature of respiration, makes experimental characterization of nasal airflow challenging, and computational fluid dynamics (CFD) has therefore become an important tool for investigating nasal aerodynamics in both healthy and diseased airways. CFD studies have provided detailed insight into airflow organization, pressure loss, nasal resistance, particle transport, and olfactory ventilation using anatomically realistic nasal geometries reconstructed from medical imaging [26, 13]. Subsequent investigations extended these analyses to patient-specific anatomies, statistical shape models, and pathological conditions, demonstrating the strong influence of geometry on airflow distribution and regional ventilation [12, 2, 1]. Although steady-state simulations remain widely used, transient CFD has shown that cyclic breathing produces breathing-phase-dependent variations in airflow, pressure distribution, and wall shear stress that cannot be fully captured under steady assumptions [14, 8, 17, 23]. Most numerical studies consider bilateral nasal cavities, in which airflow is partitioned between two parallel passages. In healthy adults, the nasal cycle produces alternating congestion and decongestion that modifies the resistance of each side while maintaining relatively stable overall nasal resistance [5, 31]. However, airflow may predominantly pass through a single nasal cavity during the nasal cycle or in pathological conditions such as septal deviation, partial obstruction, and nasal polyps [20, 7]. Under these conditions, the loss of the parallel flow pathway increases unilateral resistance and alters regional airflow organization. Unilateral models therefore provide a useful framework for isolating side-specific aerodynamic behaviour and systematically investigating local resistance and airflow distribution. Most CFD studies prescribe the inlet flow rate, whereas physiological breathing is driven by pressure differences generated by the respiratory system. Pressure-driven formulations allow the flow rate to develop naturally from the interaction between the imposed pressure difference and the nasal geometry, providing a more physiological representation of breathing [6, 8, 23]. Despite extensive CFD investigations, systematic transient studies of representative unilateral nasal geometries under pressure-driven breathing remain limited. Many computational investigations employ subject-specific anatomies, for which the predicted airflow characteristics may be strongly influenced by individual anatomical features. Population-derived standardized geometries provide a complementary framework by representing central anatomical tendencies across multiple subjects, allowing fundamental aerodynamic mechanisms to be examined without attributing the results to the anatomy of a particular patient. Such models are particularly useful for investigating directional effects arising from the intrinsic geometry of the nasal passage. The present study therefore employs the population-derived standardized median nasal model of Liu et al. [16], constructed from CT measurements of 30 adults with normal nasal anatomy, to investigate pressure-driven airflow through a representative unilateral nasal passage over a complete respiratory cycle. Three pressure amplitudes representing low, intermediate, and high breathing effort are considered. By prescribing pressure rather than flow rate, the inhalation and exhalation flow rates are allowed to emerge from the interaction between the imposed pressure difference and nasal geometry. The analysis focuses on whether this formulation produces an inherent directional asymmetry in flow rate and resistance and examines its consequences for Reynolds number, wall shear stress, pressure loss, and airflow delivery to the olfactory region. The outline of the paper is as follows. Section II describes the flow geometry, computational mesh, and the numerical methods employed in our simulations. In Sec. III, we analyse the simulation results, focusing on the breathing dynamics, nasal resistance, and airflow in the olfactory region. We discuss the implications of our results in Sec.
