Measurement-angle control of a continuously monitored quantum oscillator: purification limits and optimal protocols We study the dynamic purification of a continuously monitored quantum harmonic oscillator coupled to a thermal bath, where the control is the quadrature measurement angle of up to two detectors with prescribed strengths and efficiencies. Within the Gaussian regime, the conditional state covariance obeys a deterministic Riccati equation, and we ask what purity can be reached and sustained by manipulating the angle in time, in analogy with rapid-purification protocols for qubits. We propose, analyze, and compare constant-rate, greedy, vibrational, and variational monitoring strategies on the basis of sustained purity starting from the thermal bath state, and quantify to what extent they are able to maintain higher purity levels compared to lab-fixed or phase-locked detectors. We highlight structural features, operational limits, and optimal protocols from each strategy and study how model parameters shape control performance. We observe that in the absence of measurement-frame anisotropy, the time-dependent strategies achieve higher but similar performance. Once this symmetry is broken, their performances diverge, either improving or worsening depending on the relative timescales of oscillator dynamics, thermalization, and measurement. I Introduction The ability to purify quantum states lies at the heart of modern quantum science, as a means to overcome the inherent fragility of quantum systems as they interact with noisy environments. It is a prerequisite for high-fidelity computation, communication, and sensing, and has recently emerged as a salient thermodynamic resource in the context of continuously monitored quantum batteries [1, 2, 3, 4]. In essence, purification under continuous monitoring happens because the obtained measurement record carries information about the system, which in turn may be utilized to update or “localize” the state via Bayesian inference [5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10]. The effectiveness of this process, which is determined in large part by the available detector specifications, can be further enhanced based on the choice of observables being monitored at different points in time. For instance, adaptively changing the measured spin component of a continuously monitored qubit can enhance its average purification rate [11]. Related enhancements have since been identified in higher-dimensional systems and for the simultaneous monitoring of complementary spin observables [12, 13, 14]. In general, whether one particular strategy outperforms another could also depend on the chosen figure of merit [15, 16], as is common in quantum feedback control [17]. In continuous-variable systems, the interplay between information gain and noise becomes particularly transparent in the Gaussian regime. In this case, the conditional quantum state evolves under diffusive monitoring according to a quantum analogue of the classical Kalman–Bucy filter [18, Chapter 8.1.3], in which the covariance matrix obeys a deterministic Riccati equation and only the first moments inherit the stochasticity of the measurement record [19, 20, 21]. Because the purity of a Gaussian state is fixed entirely by its covariance matrix [22], measurement-induced purification then reduces to a deterministic control problem. As a consequence, protocols that adapt the measurement to the evolving covariance can be designed in advance, without reference to any particular measurement record. Earlier studies on measurement-based control in continuous-variable systems for quantum thermal machines and cooling applications have focused on either optimizing static measurement specifications, or designing feedback-actuated system Hamiltonians [23, 24, 25, 26, 27, 28, 3, 29, 30, 31, 32, 33, 34, 35]. Herein, we address a complementary situation in which the detectors are specified in advance and only the orientation of the measured quadratures in phase space are accessible for control, as is the case in adaptive homodyne detection and backaction-evading measurements of mechanical motion [36, 37, 38, 39, 40, 41, 42, 43]. In this setting, we quantify the purity that can be reached and sustained in a thermally damped oscillator, and explain the dependence of purification performance on the system parameters. Conclusions. We have studied how the orientation of continuously monitored quadratures can be used as a control resource for purifying a thermally damped harmonic oscillator when the underlying detector strengths or efficiencies are fixed. The Gaussian setting makes this a deterministic covariance-control problem and isolates the competition among information gain, measurement backaction, Hamiltonian rotation, and thermalization. Four increasingly general control classes were considered, both in the isotropic setting [FORMULA] , and the anisotropic one [FORMULA] . For the isotropic case [FORMULA] , rotational symmetry strongly constrains the problem, and the different time-dependent control strategies considered herein approach essentially the same rotationally averaged behavior. This suggests that simply implementable protocols such as constant-rate or vibrational are near-optimal, and more complex optimizations are not necessary. Once [FORMULA] , however, this symmetry is broken and the strategies separate. The anisotropy can either reduce or enhance purification, depending on how the measurement-induced covariance deformation competes with rotation and thermal relaxation. A natural next step is to incorporate physical control constraints directly into the optimization, including finite modulation bandwidth and latency. Because the covariance evolution is deterministic, the measurement-angle protocols considered here can in principle be precomputed and do not require real-time processing of the measurement record. Moreover, one may consider more general sources of measurement anisotropy, such as relative squeezing between detectors, nonorthogonal measurement axes, or direction-dependent environmental noise, and investigate the overall role of symmetries in control performance. Finally, multimode Gaussian systems provide another natural setting in which several covariance directions and measurement geometries may compete simultaneously. Beyond the Gaussian regime, the conditional uncertainty itself can become stochastic, so genuine feedback on the measurement record may offer further advantages. The same ideas may also be useful in monitored quantum thermodynamics and quantum-battery settings, where purification and information acquisition can act as operational resources [1, 2, 3, 4]. More general optimal-control formulations for continuously monitored systems, including Pontryagin-based approaches [51], provide a natural route for extending measurement-basis control to these settings. *

Missed jumps along routes available without the link can produce similar records, obscuring its presence. Introduction.—Quantum sensing uses detected events to infer weak interactions [1, 2, 3]. Continuous monitoring provides their times and types, from which count rates and temporal correlations can be determined [4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9]. A weak coherent link opens a shortcut between distant sites. An early arrival, however, does not by itself establish that the link is present. A particle following a route available without the link can leave a similar record if its intervening jumps go undetected. The link can change arrival times while leaving stationary count rates unchanged. Can detector placement reduce the required efficiency and time resolution to distinguish these processes, without increasing the stationary collected flux? A weak signal can become easier to distinguish when it produces outcomes that the background almost never produces [10, 11, 12, 13, 14]. Detector crosstalk can remove this advantage [15], while recording events at finite resolution can reduce the information in correlated records [16]. Quantum-trajectory and waiting-time methods already account for missed jumps, multiple detection channels, and event correlations [1, 18, 19, 20, 21]. The remaining question is how the location of losses sets the efficiency and time resolution needed to detect a weak transport link. An excess of early arrivals alone cannot settle this question. Other events and correlations may carry information, and collecting further events takes time. Any bound on the observation time must therefore include the complete record and all elapsed time. We compare two detector arrangements, C and S, on a fixed eight-site ring. In S, the easiest background route to hide crosses one more well-monitored bond than in C, while the leading direct-link signal is unchanged. The weaker background leaves longer waits informative and permits coarser timing. At a common observation-time scaling, the tolerated missed fraction and bin width change from square-root order in C to fourth-root order in S as the link weakens. We bound the time required by every decision using the binned counting record. A rule using three event counts per bin attains the same powers. At common settings, the dynamics, stationary collected flux, and entire selected return-time distribution are identical. The advantage thus comes from revealing background routes, rather than producing sensing opportunities more rapidly. Mathematics:
HideOut - User Protection Against Localization with Throughput Guarantees in Mobile Networks Channel state information (CSI) in cellular networks is primarily used to maintain quality of service (QoS), yet it leaks privacy-sensitive information, in particular the user equipment’s (UE) location. CSI is reported in plaintext on a publicly available schedule; thus, capturing it on the air and using a well trained AI model to localize the UE is straightforward. This simplicity in the attack execution makes it a serious privacy vulnerability. Using conventional privacy enhancing techniques, such as additive perturbation from differential privacy, to protect location data can potentially degrade the downlink communication quality. 1. Introduction Cellular networks are becoming sensing systems as well as communication systems. In 5G-Advanced and emerging 6G deployments, the same radio measurements that support beamforming and link adaptation can also be used to infer a User Equipment’s (UE’s) location. The 3GPP architecture already includes a Location Management Function (LMF) that collects positioning-related measurements from UEs (3rd Generation Partnership Project (3GPP), 2024). Recent learning-based positioning systems further strengthen this capability. Neural networks can map channel state information (CSI) directly to UE coordinates, exploiting multipath, blockage, and other propagation effects that are highly location-dependent (Colpaert et al., 2023; Vuckovic et al., 2024; Pan et al., 2025). Thus, CSI is no longer only a communication primitive, but also a high-resolution location signal. This dual use creates a privacy risk. A UE must report CSI to receive efficient downlink service, but that same report may allow a network-side localization service to infer the UE’s precise position. Such location information can reveal sensitive attributes such as home and workplace, mobility routines, social relationships, and visits to sensitive places (Wang et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2025). Protecting only the location record after LMF is therefore insufficient: if the localization service can infer location directly from CSI, then privacy must be enforced before or during CSI reporting. Existing location privacy mechanisms do not address this leakage channel. Coordinate-level defenses such as [FORMULA] -anonymity, geo-indistinguishability, and local differential privacy perturb or generalize a location after it has already been estimated (Andrés et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2022). Signal-level defenses are closer to our setting, but most prior work targets WiFi or other short-range sensing systems, where preserving communication often means only that packets remain decodable (Cominelli et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2019; Xiao et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024). However, this assumption does not carry over to cellular downlink transmission, as the base station (BS) uses the reported CSI to compute the precoder, making the achievable rate depend continuously on CSI fidelity. This leads to the central challenge of this paper (Fig. 1): a UE cannot simply randomize or suppress its CSI to hide its location. Perturbing CSI may mislead a learning-based localization model, but it can also misalign the downlink beamformer and reduce the UE’s own rate. The privacy mechanism must therefore satisfy two requirements simultaneously: it should increase the localization error of the network-side model, while guaranteeing that the protected CSI remains useful for downlink precoding. This privacy–service coupling is specific to cellular CSI feedback and is not captured by generic adversarial attacks or by prior WiFi-oriented signal-level privacy mechanisms. We propose HideOut, a communication-aware CSI perturbation mechanism for protecting UE location against ML-based cellular localization. As depicted in Fig. 2, the UE reports a perturbed CSI matrix instead of its original measurement. The perturbation is optimized to increase the localization loss of a neural positioning model, but each update is projected onto a wireless-feasible set that guarantees a user-selected bound on downlink SE loss. Mathematically, we show that under Maximum Ratio Transmission (MRT) precoding, a bound on SE degradation can be converted into an angular constraint on the reported channel direction. This yields a projection-based mechanism whose rate feasibility is enforced by construction, rather than by tuning a soft penalty term. HideOut supports both white-box and black-box localization services. In the white-box setting, the UE computes perturbations using gradients of the deployed localization model. In the more realistic black-box setting, the localization model is proprietary. The UE trains a local surrogate from its own CSI-location pairs and relies on transferability of adversarial perturbations (Papernot et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2017). Unlike standard black-box adversarial attacks, however, HideOut must satisfy a physical layer constraint in which every protected CSI report must remain sufficiently aligned for downlink precoding. In summary, our paper’s contributions are: [FORMULA] CSI feedback as a privacy attack surface. We formulate location privacy in mobile networks as a client-side defense problem over CSI feedback. The formulation captures a distinctive privacy–service coupling. The same CSI report is used by the localization service to infer position and by the base station to compute the downlink precoder. [FORMULA] Rate-constrained adversarial CSI perturbations. We derive an angular feasibility condition that converts a SE budget into a constraint on the reported channel direction under MRT precoding. HideOut uses this condition to project gradient-based perturbations onto a rate-feasible set. [FORMULA] Black-Box protection via surrogate transfer. Limitations and Deployment Considerations Our evaluation considers localization models trained on clean CSI and tested on protected CSI. A network-side adversary could attempt to harden the localizer through adversarial training, detect distribution shifts in CSI reports, or fuse CSI with independent positioning or classical sources. HideOut should therefore be viewed as a client-side protection mechanism against CSI-only localization, not as a complete defense against all forms of cellular tracking. Extending the defense to adaptive and multi-modal localization services is an important direction for future work. Computing HideOut in the real world requires the UE to locally store and execute a trained surrogate localization model. Offline training is not a major bottleneck, as necessary training data can be collected prior to deployment or synthesized using channel simulators, and then the model can be fine-tuned using on-device measurements. Non-volatile memory cost is also not a major limiting factor when executing HideOut in real-world deployments. For instance, in the surrogate pool we used for evaluation, models ranged from 2,418 to 17,069,538 parameters. Under a standard 32-bit single-precision floating-point (fp32) representation, this corresponds to a local memory footprint ranging from approximately [FORMULA] to [FORMULA] , which modern commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) smartphones can easily accommodate. Real-time execution under network timing constraints, however, poses the primary challenge for real-world deployments. Computing HideOut, in fact, requires the execution of an initial forward pass followed by alternating gradient updates and cone projections. These operations must be executed within the typical reporting intervals of the CSI feedback loop for each new location. However, CSI reporting, which can be configured as periodic, semi-persistent, or aperiodic (3rd Generation Partnership Project (3GPP), 2022b), uses configurable reporting periodicities ranging from 4 to 320 slots, corresponding to time intervals from approximately 0.5 ms to 320 ms depending on the configured numerology. As HideOut execution time scales with the dimensions of [FORMULA] , the surrogate model parameter count, and the number of iterations [FORMULA] , for highly mobile scenarios or with deep architectures, HideOut can introduce a non-negligible hardware strain. Related Work ML-based localization from CSI. Recent work has shown that CSI contains sufficient location-dependent information for accurate positioning. CNN-based systems can directly estimate UE coordinates from massive-MIMO CSI measurements (Colpaert et al., 2023; Vuckovic et al., 2024), while integrated feedback-positioning architectures jointly optimize CSI reconstruction and localization (Guo et al., 2024). These systems demonstrate that location information is embedded in CSI and can be extracted by machine-learning models. We instead ask how a UE can suppress such information before reporting CSI, while preserving the report’s utility for downlink precoding. Location privacy above the physical layer. Most location-privacy mechanisms protect coordinates after localization has already occurred. Geo-indistinguishability adds calibrated noise to reported locations so that nearby positions are difficult to distinguish (Andrés et al., 2013). L-SRR uses local differential privacy for location-based services (Wang et al., 2022). At the cellular-network level, Pretty Good Phone Privacy reduces location tracking by decoupling long-term subscriber identifiers from network access (Schmitt and Raghavan, 2021). These mechanisms protect released locations or identifiers, but they do not prevent a network-side localization service from inferring a UE’s position directly from raw CSI used by the communication system. Signal-level privacy in wireless systems. A smaller body of work acts directly on wireless signals or measurements. For geometry-based cellular localization, Checa and Tomasin design a privacy-preserving beamformer that hides angle-of-departure information at the cost of achievable rate (Checa and Tomasin, 2020), while Khan et al. reshape angular power so that a false direction appears dominant (Khan et al., 2025). These works expose the coupling between localization and communication when both depend on explicit geometric channel features. Most signal-level privacy work, however, targets WiFi or short-range sensing. Cominelli et al. randomize transmitted WiFi I/Q samples to disrupt CSI-based device-free localization while preserving communication (Cominelli et al., 2020). Zhou et al. learn adversarial transformations that remove selected behavioral information from WiFi CSI while retaining information needed by another classifier (Zhou et al., 2019). FooLoc modifies WiFi training symbols so that an access point obtains misleading CSI fingerprints (Xiao et al., 2023), and Li et al. perturb WiFi packet preambles to manipulate learning-based sensing without interrupting communication (Li et al., 2024). These systems demonstrate that wireless signals can be manipulated for privacy or attack, but they do not address the cellular feedback loop in which the same CSI report is consumed by both a localization service and a downlink precoder. Adversarial perturbations and black-box transfer. HideOut is related to adversarial machine learning, where perturbations are optimized to increase a model’s loss while satisfying a constraint on the modified input (Kurakin et al., 2017). Black-box attacks often rely on surrogate models and transferability of adversarial examples (Papernot et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2017). However, standard adversarial attacks constrain perturbations with generic norms such as [FORMULA] , which do not capture the physical effect of CSI perturbations on beamforming. HideOut differs by replacing the generic norm constraint with a wireless feasibility constraint derived from the downlink SE budget. Positioning of HideOut. Prior work establishes that CSI can support accurate localization and that wireless measurements can be transformed to reduce sensing leakage. However, we did not find prior work that lets a UE protect its own location by perturbing its cellular CSI feedback while enforcing a selected downlink-rate budget. HideOut addresses this setting directly: the UE protects its location before CSI disclosure, the localization service processes the protected report, and the base station still uses the same report for downlink precoding. 8. Conclusions We presented HideOut, a client-side defense against CSI-based localization in mobile networks. HideOut perturbs CSI feedback to increase the error of neural localization models while enforcing a downlink SE budget derived from the wireless link. By converting the rate-loss constraint into a feasibility set under MRT precoding, HideOut replaces generic adversarial norm constraints with a communication-aware projection step. Our evaluation shows that HideOut substantially degrades CSI-based localization across multiple neural architectures and under black-box transfer while keeping rate loss within user-selected budgets. These results suggest that mandatory CSI feedback can be protected before disclosure, but they also highlight a broader lesson: privacy defenses for AI-enabled wireless systems must account for the physical layer utility of the data they perturb.

Energy-Efficient UAV Covert Communications via Metaheuristic Optimization Wireless communication systems increasingly require not only confidentiality but also transmission undetectability, motivating covert communications. This paper studies an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) enabled covert communication system where a UAV serves a legitimate receiver in the presence of multiple active and colluding wardens with imperfect location information. We maximize covert energy efficiency (CEE) by jointly optimizing the UAV’s 3D trajectory and transmit power while accounting for energy. To address the resulting non-convex problem with robust covertness constraints, we develop Genetic Algorithm (GA) and Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO)-based metaheuristic algorithms and compare them with a Block Coordinate Descent with Successive Convex Approximation (BCD-SCA) benchmark. Numerical results show that the proposed methods improve CEE while satisfying covertness constraints. I Introduction Unmanned aerial vehicles have emerged as a promising platform for future wireless communication networks due to their high mobility, flexible deployment, and reliable line-of-sight (LoS) links with ground terminals [1]. Compared with terrestrial infrastructure, UAV-assisted systems can be rapidly deployed in areas where fixed base stations are unavailable, damaged, or costly to install. Therefore, UAVs have been widely studied for emergency communications, coverage enhancement, data collection, relaying, and Internet-of-Things (IoT) connectivity [2]. Despite these advantages, UAV-enabled communication faces important security and privacy challenges. Due to the broadcast nature of wireless channels and the high altitude of UAV platforms, legitimate transmissions may be overheard or detected by unintended ground nodes. In critical scenarios such as military operations, disaster response, surveillance, or confidential sensing, protecting only the message content is insufficient [3]. It is also necessary to hide the existence of the transmission itself, which motivates covert communication, also known as low-probability-of-detection communication [4]. A key challenge in UAV-enabled covert communication is the limited onboard energy. Unlike ground nodes, a UAV consumes energy for both wireless transmission and propulsion, including hovering and maneuvering. Since propulsion energy often dominates communication energy, trajectory design plays a crucial role in the overall system performance [5, 6]. The problem becomes even more challenging in adversarial environments with active and colluding wardens. Active wardens may transmit jamming signals to degrade the legitimate link, while colluding wardens can jointly process their observations to improve detection capability. Moreover, imperfect warden location information caused by sensing errors, outdated estimates, or adversarial mobility may lead trajectory and power control strategies to violate worst-case covertness constraints [7]. Existing studies on UAV covert communication have mainly focused on covert throughput maximization through joint trajectory and transmit power optimization [8]. Other works have considered energy-efficient UAV communication, but often without explicitly accounting for adversarial detection constraints or active colluding wardens [9]. Consequently, the joint optimization of UAV trajectory and transmit power for covert energy efficiency under active colluding wardens and uncertain warden locations remains insufficiently explored. This motivates the need for a robust optimization framework that can simultaneously handle mobility constraints, propulsion energy consumption, transmit power allocation, and worst-case covertness requirements. To address this gap, this paper investigates robust covert energy efficiency maximization for a UAV-enabled covert communication system. The main contributions include: (i) We formulate a robust covert energy efficiency maximization problem for UAV-enabled covert communication in the presence of active and colluding wardens with uncertain locations. (ii) We derive a deterministic reformulation of the worst-case covertness constraint based on the aggregate received power at the wardens, enabling tractable feasibility checking during optimization. (iii) We develop GA and PSO optimization algorithms for jointly optimizing the UAV trajectory and transmit power under mobility, energy, and covertness constraints. (iv) We compare the proposed metaheuristic approaches with a BCD-SCA benchmark and provide numerical results showing their effectiveness in improving covert energy efficiency while maintaining robust covertness. The signal-processing origins of quantization include Bennett’s analysis of quantization noise in pulse-code modulation [5] and Lloyd’s least-squares design conditions, developed in 1957 and published in 1982 [27]. In high-resolution theory, Zador separated the source-dependent contribution to asymptotic distortion from a constant depending on dimension and the distortion measure [39]. The defining optimization ranges over all quantizers. Gray and Neuhoff [15] give a detailed account of these developments and of the distinction between finite-rate design and high-resolution analysis. Ajjanagadde’s proposed facet bound extends the planar method by replacing the triangles over polygon edges with pyramids over Voronoi facets [2, §4.3.4]. Section 3 gives the required pyramid comparison and the precise relation to his conjectures. His improvement of the sphere bound for unrestricted quantizers in sufficiently large dimensions instead uses truncated balls and variation in cell volumes [2, Theorem 10]. Computing systems use quantization to reduce storage, arithmetic cost, and communication for model weights, activations, gradients, and learned data representations. For randomized gradient quantization, QSGD analyzes the tradeoff between communication and the variance introduced by quantization [3]. For images, Zhang and Wu learn lattice generating matrices adapted to the latent distribution [43]; Lei, Hassani, and Saeedi Bidokhti study lattice transform coding, including block and nested-lattice constructions [23]. For neural-network inference, Deep Compression combines pruning, learned weight sharing, and entropy coding [18], while Jacob et al. develop training procedures for integer-only inference with quantized weights and activations [19]. For large language models, LLM.int8() treats activation outliers in higher precision [9], while SmoothQuant reduces them by rescaling weights and activations [38]. GPTQ, published as OPTQ, uses approximate second-order information to quantize weights [13]; AWQ uses activation statistics to choose weight-scaling factors [25]. Quantization also reduces the memory occupied by attention keys and values. KIVI uses different quantization groupings for the key and value caches [26]. TurboQuant combines random rotations with scalar quantization and, for inner-product estimation, a correction of the residual error; its applications include attention caches and nearest-neighbor search [41]. Training raises additional questions about numerical range and the propagation of rounding errors. Stochastic rounding has been used in fixed-point training [17] and in training with eight-bit floating-point numbers [36]. The FP8 formats studied by Micikevicius et al. allocate exponent and mantissa bits to accommodate different numerical ranges [28]. Wang et al. reduce the cost of generating random numbers in integer training by sharing stochastic-rounding thresholds and correcting the resulting structured rounding error [37]. For model adaptation, QLoRA keeps a four-bit base model fixed and trains low-rank adapters [10]. In retrieval, product quantization partitions an embedding into blocks and represents each block by a codeword [20]. Anisotropic vector quantization adapts the distortion criterion to inner-product search [16]. Recommendation models use quantized embeddings to allocate storage across categorical features [21], and TIGER uses residual vector quantization to construct item identifiers for generative retrieval [29]. These applications involve source distributions, finite codebooks, clipping, and task-dependent losses. Letter to a Young Black Mathematician: History, Storytelling, and Belonging in Mathematics What does it mean to tell the story of a mathematician? Written as a letter to a young Black mathematician, this article reflects on how stories shape our understanding of mathematics and our sense of belonging within the mathematical community. Through the lens of Hidden Figures Revealed, a project documenting Black mathematicians at The Ohio State University, I discuss humanity, mathematics, and context as three guiding principles for mathematical storytelling. In particular, I reflect on how this framework emerged through archival research, shaped historical narratives, and informed mathematical learning experiences. Dear Young Black Mathematician, “You’re the first Black woman I’ve seen work in the department in the last twenty years.” I was in the break room. At this point I don’t remember why anymore. I could have been warming up lunch or picking up a stack of papers from the printer; I just remember her voice. It was gentle, but husky. She sat among the other Black custodial workers. They were trying to think if they could recall another Black woman during their years cleaning the building on Ohio State’s campus that housed the math faculty and postdocs. They couldn’t. I remember them nodding in approval as if my being there was something noteworthy to witness. I remember the warmth in her words and in their presence, and how the energy of that moment was captured over the several years in smiles across rooms, nods in elevators, and casual chatter during the times I crossed paths with them throughout the department. I remember feeling that they saw me, and during those moments when I saw them, I was not alone. My first postdoc brought feelings of isolation I hadn’t experienced coming from a graduate program where I had never been the ‘only’ across a variety of axes of diversity. And yet I found myself entering a department where I was the only Black woman among nearly two hundred faculty, staff, postdocs, and graduate students. I wonder if you know this feeling. A haunting awareness that your aptitude for this subject facilitates your belonging, but that parts of who you are could also keep you apart from its community. The strange experience of loving mathematics, yet sensing you are standing on the outside while being inside: a kind of mathematical double consciousness:11 1 The Souls of Black Folk Du Bois (1903) is a seminal text by W. E. B. Du Bois that develops the notion of double consciousness which he notes as the experience of Black Americans seeing themselves simultaneously through one’s own eyes and through the eyes of a society that understands Blackness as other.” I use the phrase “mathematical double consciousness” here to describe the experience of seeing oneself simultaneously as a Black person and as a mathematician. Note that I speak of my own experiences here, and do not presume that every Black mathematician feels tension between these dual perspectives. “one ever feels his twoness” Du Bois (1903). I wish I could say that I took those feelings of isolation and paid them no mind as I navigated the research and teaching milestones that came at the beginning of my postdoc. I am certain that from the outside I looked well adjusted: I was doing “all the things.” But there were times I was stifled and could not get out of my head. The seminar I sat in silently for an entire semester, too afraid to speak. What if I was wrong? What if my question made no sense? The moments I couldn’t immediately answer a student’s question in lecture, the insecurity welling up deep in my stomach was enough to make me dry heave after class. I was representing something bigger than myself here. I was the only Black woman. I could not mess up. There were other moments. The dinner with the speaker where I talked about my Hidden Figures course, sharing that we taught the women at NASA were working to get to the moon, while in Virginia, in the same era, there was a generation of Black children denied education, prompting a tangent from my postdoc mentor at the time about misunderstood historical governors.22 2 Context: At our seminar dinner we discussed teaching assignments and I was describing the Hidden Figures course I co-designed. I shared it was remarkable how much progress was made within NASA by the Black and white women computers, in contrast with the segregated conditions within Virginia, prompting a brief discussion about how the actions of some historical governors were misunderstood. In September 1958, Governor J. Lindsay Almond Jr. ordered public schools in Charlottesville, Front Royal, and Norfolk closed rather than allow desegregation. In Prince Edward County, officials closed public schools in 1959 rather than comply with a federal desegregation order. Although the county’s public schools were closed, many white families were able to establish and attend segregated private schools, while most Black children were left without meaningful access to schooling. The public schools remained closed until 1964 Bonastia (2009). While he talked about how George Wallace was frequently misjudged, I texted under the table to my father who grew up in Birmingham, Alabama in the 1960s, ‘was George Wallace the one that said segregation segregation segregation?’ The phone buzzed with an incoming message with a slight correction, ‘segregation now, segregation tomorrow, segregation foreverWallace (1963).’ I tried to write off this discussion as an intellectual exercise, but then there was the research meeting with the same mentor that started casually with the remark, ‘you know, when people see you, they see diversity.’ I responded I could not help how people saw me, which seemed to satisfy him, but I was too frazzled to focus afterwards. Still, I kept moving. Producing. Stuffing down the feelings of isolation and otherness as neatly and meticulously as I could. In the summer of 2020, when the #ShutDownSTEM initiative called on STEM researchers to pause their usual activities for a day of reflection and action around antiBlack racism in academia and STEM, those feelings came rushing back. I hope you haven’t felt the need to charge on like this, to avoid the discomfort. I wish I had admitted to myself sooner it was not sustainable. I was two years into my postdoc then. I found myself reflecting on what Phyllis had said. I remembered her voice and the sentiment, you’re the first Black woman here in 20 years. Was it possible that I was the only Black woman to ever work for the department? I had to know. While the world was ‘shutdown,’ I began poring over the history of the department where I worked, desperate to see if what I believed was true, that there were other Black mathematicians who preceded me, that I was not alone. This inclination is what led me to her. In 1974 Rada Higgins earned a PhD in mathematics from Ohio State. She was later identified as the 20th Black woman in the United States with this degree. She was my existence proof. I found an old black and white photo of her in the archives for the 1965 Ross Mathematics Program at The Ohio State University. There she was, studying elementary number theory under Arnold Ross, sharp in polka dots in the front row of her peers, arms tucked slightly behind her back (Figure 1). I wonder if she spoke up in groups. I wonder if she doubted herself when she was asked questions. I wonder if she felt like she belonged. She applied to Ohio State for graduate school and began her doctoral studies in 1969. Over 50 years later I was starting in the same department. I had a named postdoc as a Ross Assistant Professor, in honor of the mentor who supported her. I had gone looking for proof that someone like me had existed in the department before me, and I found her. It was like I was an undergraduate again at my first math conference, running into the first Black woman mathematician I had ever seen, Jana Talley. I asked her for a hug, asked if she really had a PhD. Something in me changed after meeting her, her very existence shifted a PhD from something that felt overwhelming to something I could possibly do. Like she noted, I just needed to find support. I did not interact with Rada. We did not embrace. But knowing that I was not the first changed me. It lifted the burden I felt from being the “only.” I wanted to know more. I wanted to know about her research, her family, and her career. I wanted to know what it was like for her, what it meant to become a Black mathematician in Columbus in the 1960s and 1970s. I wanted to make her existence known, and to learn more about other Black mathematicians from the department. This became a personal fixation. It felt important that whoever came after me would not be faced with some version of you’re one of a handful of Black people to matriculate through here in the last two decades. I reached out to departmental personnel for historical records and scoured the internet for evidence, mining sites like the Mathematicians of the African Diaspora (MAD) Williams (1997) and Mathematicians of the African Diaspora Database’s Ensemble of Researchers (MADDER) National Association of Mathematicians (2020); Walker et al. (2019) to find as many Black people from Ohio State as I could who had earned an undergraduate, master’s, or doctoral degree in mathematics.33 3 The Mathematicians of the African Diaspora (MAD) is an online repository documenting Black mathematicians and their contributions Williams (1997). It was created and maintained by Scott Williams until his retirement. The Mathematicians of the African Diaspora Database’s Ensemble of Researchers (MADDER) is ongoing and expanded Williams’ work into a modern searchable database of Black mathematicians National Association of Mathematicians (2020); Walker et al. (2019). In time, I learned that nearly 200 mathematicians who identified as Black had earned degrees from The Ohio State University.44 4 This number was confirmed through the Hidden Figures Revealed project described in Clark (2025). They went on to careers spanning academia, industry, and education: university presidents, authors, lawyers, and mathematicians. And yet to many, their stories remained hidden. That search ultimately became the project “Hidden Figures Revealed: Dynamic Narratives and History of Black Mathematicians from The Ohio State University.” With the support of collaborators and grant funding, what began as a solitary archival effort grew into the first comprehensive historical study of Black mathematicians at a single institution Clark (2025). But here I want to be honest with you: this project started with a need to affirm, first for myself, then for you, that we are not alone. As I learned more, I began to ask other questions: What does it mean to tell the story of a mathematician? What gets preserved and what disappears? What happens when we refuse to choose between the person and the mathematics? What if a mathematical story could attend to the person, the mathematics, and the world in which that mathematics took place? There are many ways to respond to stories and history. There are many ways to work toward a mathematical community in which more people can see themselves belonging. I am writing to you now from the beginning of my journey as a research professor, wondering what I can do to make my own way while clearing a path for you. One day, you too may begin to think about if, when, or how you want to do something concrete to make mathematics more inclusive for yourself or for others. As for me, I choose history. I choose storytelling. “I’m interested in the way in which the past affects the present and I think that if we understand a good deal more about history, we automatically understand a great deal about contemporary life.” – Toni Morrison Morrison (2008) – As you learn mathematics, you will encounter many names. Some will come from theorems, some from techniques, some from conjectures, and some from entire areas of mathematics. If your experience has been anything like mine, there may not always be a story attached to the mathematics you encounter. I learned about math without mathematicians. Even some of my favorite subjects in school were presented in ways that were stuffy, formulaic, or abstract, with very little attention to the people who developed the mathematics or to the political and social contexts in which they lived. The more historical work I have done, the more I have come to see how much the past can tell us about the present. This is certainly true in mathematics. Knowing where an idea came from, who developed it, what problem they were trying to solve, and what was happening around them has often made the mathematics feel more alive to me. I want to encourage you to look for mathematical stories. I will share one of my favorites. When I was younger, I learned the quadratic formula through a song set to the tune of “Pop Goes the Weasel.” It served as a mnemonic to memorize: where “ALL over 2 - A” was analogous with the “POP goes the weasel” in the original song. Years later as an undergraduate, I read William Dunham’s Journey to Genius, and learned there were formulas for roots of cubic and quartic polynomials! I learned about the secrecy, the oaths, and the rivalries surrounding the discovery and publication of solutions to the cubic among Cardano, del Ferro, Tartaglia, and Lodovico Ferrari Dunham (1990). I also learned that there was no such formula for quintic polynomials. I was wildly entertained by the tragic tale of Évariste Galois and his work on whether there was a formula for solving quintic polynomials. The answer was no, and he was able to prove it using the symmetries of the roots of polynomials Stewart (2003). He sadly died in a duel, infamously spending the night before writing up notes on his mathematical ideas Rothman (1982). It took 14 years for his manuscripts to be published, and another century before the theory was formalized in the way that we learn it today in abstract algebra Galois (1846); Artin (1998). The immortalization of his work often tidies up the struggles he faced in life. He tried to send his work to Cauchy and Poisson. Rejected Rothman (1982). He enrolled in what is now École Normale Supérieure to study mathematics. Expelled Toti Rigatelli (1998). He frequently pushed back against the French monarchy. Jailed Toti Rigatelli (1998). I don’t know where all of this went when I was introduced to group theory. By then, Galois was a name attached to theory. His history had been separated from the mathematics. I understand why this happens. Especially now as a professor, I understand the constraints and pressure to progress through the curricula. But the ultimate consequence of my training is that, aside from isolated instances, I learned to think about mathematics independently from mathematicians. Is it any wonder that I was 22 years old when I realized other Black women mathematicians existed, or that I had no idea Ohio State had a rich history in cultivating Black mathematical talent? In graduate school I got the book Hidden Figures: The American Dream and the Untold Story of the Black Women Who Helped Win the Space Race by Margot Shetterly Shetterly (2016) as a gift after passing my comprehensive exam to advance to candidacy. I could not get enough of the story. I cried when I saw the movie. I imagine you are familiar with the story. I relished the attention it received, but there were times I felt uneasy about the framing of these women as ‘sentimental firsts’ 55 5 In Between the World in Me, Coates laments history books that “spoke of black people only as sentimental ‘firsts’—first black five-star general, first black congressman, first black mayor—always presented in the bemused manner of a category of Trivial Pursuit.” Here he encourages a treatment of Black history that is just as serious as other Western histories and not reduced to heroism, struggle, or novelty Coates (2015). I was worried that many were treating the women from the Hidden Figures story this way. Coates (2015). I was excited they were being celebrated, but I wanted to know, what mathematics did they actually do? What problems were they solving? How were their opportunities shaped by the historical and political circumstances surrounding the Space Race? I developed a Hidden Figures course based on their story with John Johnson to try and answer these questions by exploring the mathematics of the Space Race through the eyes of its human computers The Ohio State University College of Arts and Sciences (2019); Edmonds and Johnson (2021). We purchased slide rules from the International Slide Rule Museum to lend authenticity to the daily tools they might have used in their work. (I developed an affinity for the Post 1460 Versalog.) We also examined the historical context influencing their opportunities in mathematics in the mid-20th century, as well as their communities, personal lives, and backgrounds. As I worked on the course, I realized this was no different from how I felt about the stories of Cardano, Tartaglia, Ferrari, and Galois. I didn’t want to choose between the person and the mathematics. The story made me crave the math. When I worked on Hidden Figures Revealed, I knew I wanted to take a similar approach. I did not want to reduce people we learned about to their mathematical contributions, and I did not want their mathematics to disappear beneath their biographies. I wanted to know about the person, their mathematics, and the world in which they were doing that mathematics. That became the framework I kept returning to. I came to think of these as three principles for mathematical storytelling: humanity, mathematics, and context (Figure 2). I don’t think there is a hard and fast rule about the weight each should carry in a particular story. Some stories may lean heavily toward the mathematics. Others may require more historical or biographical context. But I don’t think any of the three should disappear entirely. These principles guard against three different kinds of incomplete stories. Humanity without mathematics can turn a mathematician into an inspirational symbol whose actual intellectual work disappears. Mathematics without humanity can make that work feel disembodied, as though ideas emerge independently of the people who develop them. And both can become misleading without context. A career can begin to look inevitable, or like the product of individual talent alone, when it was also shaped by institutions, communities, historical events, and opportunities. Context without mathematical content creates a different problem. It may tell us something important about a person’s life without telling us much about their life as a mathematician. For me, the point is not to give these three dimensions equal weight, but to resist allowing any one of them to erase the others. There are, of course, longstanding traditions for how to do this that don’t explicitly invoke these three principles. I am not trying to invent a new method of storytelling. Scientific biographies have long connected people’s lives to the development of scientific ideas Söderqvist (2007), and historians of science have reminded us that scientific work does not happen in isolation from the intellectual and social worlds around it Shapin (1994). Literary journalism offers another tradition of paying close attention to people, events, and context Kramer (1995). You may remember learning that a good story should answer the questions ‘who, what, where, when, why, and how.’ These questions help us establish what happened. But when we tell the story of a mathematician’s life, there are other questions worth asking, too. What do we choose to include? What do we leave out? What do we make visible about a person’s life, and what disappears from view? People who study mathematics education have asked some of these questions by using mathematical stories and autobiographies to understand how people experience mathematics and how those experiences become part of how they see themselves as mathematicians, teachers, or learners Drake (2006); McCulloch et al. (2013). This matters to me because I believe the stories we encounter can shape what we think a mathematician looks like, what a mathematical life can look like, and whether we can imagine ourselves in one. So how do you tell a multifaceted mathematical story? When you tell stories about mathematicians, incorporate humanity by asking the question: Who was this person? There are the classics. Where someone went to school, what degree they earned, or where they worked. But you should dig beyond pedigree whenever possible. Where do they come from, what did they care about, what did they do outside of mathematics, what communities were they a part of, and what experiences shaped their pathway into and within mathematics? The stories we tell should also answer the question: What mathematics did they do? This one seems obvious, but I think it is worth saying. If we are telling stories about mathematicians, I don’t want the mathematics to become incidental. There should mathematics in a story about a mathematician. This presents many challenges due to vastness of our subject and the myriad of specialties. But it also presents a neat opportunity to dive into the ideas that lit somebody else up, to immerse yourself in familiar or completely new research areas. I want people to encounter the ideas that these mathematicians worked on, even if that means finding creative ways to make those ideas accessible for themselves or others. That could mean narrowing to one aspect of a person’s research program, like a dissertation or a single paper. It could mean developing an activity that allows a student to encounter their mathematical ideas without having to understand the mathematics at the level at which it was originally developed. Pick one place to start. One idea to digest. From there you can decide the level of breadth and depth of the mathematical story you want to share. We should also consider the question: What was happening around them? Mathematical lives don’t happen in a vacuum. They navigate shifts in colloquial knowledge as well as competing frameworks for moving central ideas in their fields forward. They live through political movements and social changes. They encounter barriers, opportunities, institutions, and communities. Mathematical stories should include not just who someone was or the mathematics they did, but what was happening around them that helped shape the path they took. How can we paint the political, social, and historical backdrop that colored their experiences within the mathematical community? There is a responsibility that comes with all of this. Historical records are incomplete. We may sometimes know what someone did but not why they did it, or what happened in time but not how someone experienced it. We can’t project our imaginings. We can’t make things tidy because it is convenient. Not every person has to become a hero, a symbol, or a cautionary tale. We have to lead with honesty and be sincere about what we know, what we infer, and what we can’t corroborate. Even if you are not called to tell the stories of other mathematicians, I encourage you to think about these principles to process your own mathematical journey. The part that usually takes the most time when I process my own story is context. I was not always used to thinking about my research as influenced by external events. Here’s an example. In 2020, there were widespread racial justice protests across the world after the murder of George Floyd. The #ShutDownSTEM initiative was a reaction to this. Locally, Ohio State established a seed fund for racial justice, and I earned one of the inaugural awards to lead a team to study the Black math history of the department. Meanwhile, insecure about my relationship with my research mentor and more broadly disillusioned with my doctoral research, I started to work with a group in the department under a Research Training Group66 6 The National Science Foundation’s funds Research Training Groups that foster collaborative research environments that enhance training for graduate students and postdocs. The group at Ohio State was supported by NSF #DMS-1547357 RTG: Algebraic Topology and Its Applications. that studied Applied Algebraic Topology. At the same time, during the 2021 redistricting, Moon Duchin’s lab was collaborating with organizations in Columbus as well as Ohio State to do community mapping to push for fairer maps from the state’s new legislative redistricting commission Chambers et al. (2022); Metric Geometry and Gerrymandering Group (2021). She reached out to one of my mentors in the department for help. He thought it would be a good opportunity and recommended me. Then there was another piece of context I did not fully appreciate at the time. On his first day in office, President Joe Biden signed an executive order to advance support for racial minorities in the federal government Biden (2021). Federal agencies developed strategic plans in response National Science Foundation (2021a). Part of the NSF’s plan included a new postdoctoral fellowship program designed to broaden participation in the sciences National Science Foundation (2021b). I wrote a proposal for this new award on how to think about applications of metric geometry and applied algebraic topology to electoral redistricting. I emphasized my Hidden Figures work in my broader impacts. I was an inaugural recipient of that award. It changed my life and my research program. There is a version of this story where I simply say I changed research directions and received a fellowship. It’s technically true, but it’s too tidy. The actual story is full of people, institutions, politics, funding opportunities, and some serendipity. My mathematical trajectory did not happen in isolation from the world around me. Neither did the trajectories of the mathematicians I had been studying. This framework helped me take a list of names of Black mathematicians from Ohio State and begin to see the people, mathematics, and worlds behind those names. I came to see that the three principles aren’t independent. The person influences the mathematics, the mathematics interacts with the world around them, and the world around them shapes what mathematical opportunities are available to a person. This way of learning and telling stories has helped me feel deeply connected to mathematics, even when I don’t always see myself in the broader mathematical community. If this is something you have ever struggled with, maybe it can help you too. In any category of “firsts,” there is always an underlying question of how “the first” decided that it was within his or her power to become that which no one like him or her had become before. The answers Elbert Frank Cox and Euphemia Lofton Haynes (the first Black male and female Americans to earn doctoral degrees in mathematics) might have given to this question, unfortunately, are unknown. What began as my attempt to find the Black mathematicians who came before me had become a research project with a grant, a team, and plans to hire student fellows. I was now responsible for leading people through a project that I was still learning how to do myself. I wish I could tell you that you will always feel ready for the things you are asked to do. You won’t. For me, this was one of the first indications that historical research of living mathematicians involved forms of responsibility that were quite different from those I had encountered in mathematical research. This was completely different than mathematical research, and even that research was new to me as I moved into a new field. Everything was new. I was overwhelmed. I felt the familiar insecurity welling up deep in my stomach. I could not mess up. I wanted to lead well. I wanted to tell their stories right. But how? Erica Walker was one of few people I knew who had done something similar. I read Beyond Banneker: Black Mathematicians and the Paths to Excellence Walker (2014) in 2020. I can’t remember if it was before or after #ShutDownSTEM, but I knew that when we started the Hidden Figures Revealed project I wanted to use it as a guide. Our meeting and her book gave me a model for how interviews, historical context, and individual stories could be woven together without reducing the mathematicians to their identities or their achievements. She had interviewed thirty five mathematicians and organized their stories into three time periods, each marked by common historical experiences, including legal and de facto segregation. We adopted a similar approach for Ohio State, using the degrees earned by Black mathematicians in the department to help identify three research periods. The seven Black mathematicians who earned PhDs in mathematics from Ohio State all received their degrees between 1963 and 1984. We called them the Pioneers and this became Research Period 1. This was the period we studied the most. Have you ever considered how intimately the Civil Rights Movement and other fights for racial equity in the United States are connected to mathematics? I had not before this project. In 1979, five years after Rada Higgins finished her PhD, Columbus was still dealing with the consequences of the 1954 Brown v. Board of Education Supreme Court ruling. Over twenty years later, the 1977 case Penick v. Columbus Board of Education from the U.S. District Court ruled the city still had de facto segregation in its public school system and needed to desegregate. The city fought this ruling up to the Supreme Court and lost. In 1979 they began desegregation via busing. There was a dramatic decline in Columbus public school enrollment in the decades that followed. I cannot say from the evidence we found how these changes affected the Ross Program’s local recruitment, but they formed part of the environment in which the program operated. “White flight” to the suburbs, along with other families and educators abandoning city schools, led to the closure of several schools. East High School, where Rada Higgins went to school, remains open today. Another school, Central High School, was forced to close its doors due to low enrollment. Part of it has been historically preserved as part of the Center of Science and Industry (COSI). This area was part of my jogging route when I was working on this project. The juxtaposition is striking. Carolyn Mahoney’s first year of her PhD was in 1979. She was the last Black woman to earn a PhD in mathematics from Ohio State, earning her degree in 1984. She and Rada Higgins were both able to pursue graduate studies at Ohio State with support from the National Science Foundation. They pursued PhDs during a period of increased federal investment in science and mathematics education associated with the Space Race and the National Defense Education Act of 1958. This expansion of federal support helped create new opportunities for mathematical research, education, and enrichment, including programs like the Ross Mathematics Program and fellowship opportunities for faculty at Historically Black Colleges and Universities (HBCUs). Guy Hogan and Thyrsa Frazier Svager were able to take advantage of a special NSF program that provided fellowships to faculty at Historically Black Colleges and Universities (HBCUs) that were teaching but did not yet have a doctoral degree Clark (2025). Everything we learned provided more context. We could not provide a vivid picture of the lives of every single Black math PhD from Ohio State during this time period. We could, however, take care to understand key historical, institutional, social, and political factors that formed the environment in which mathematicians at Ohio State studied and worked during each Research Period. At the time there was an exhibition Queens of the Heartland featuring illustrated portraits with panel text for thirty women who were leaders of social change with deep connections to Ohio. Most archival work constructs simple narratives, when they arrived at Ohio State, what degrees they earned, where they worked, and sometimes what they had accomplished. But it does not always answer the question Erica Walker had asked about the “firsts”: how does someone come to believe that it is within their power to become something that no one like them had become before? We could not know from the archive whether McWorter’s family history shaped his mathematical imagination. But he came from a family of firsts, inventors, and pioneers. What does it mean to grow up surrounded by evidence that the boundaries of what is possible can be crossed? This archive piqued my interest in McWorter. I wanted to find more, and we did. A black and white photo in the university newspaper in 1982 shows a picture of him smiling with a structure he had built, created with 30 sticks that never touch (Figure 4). A textbook for an honors linear algebra course, describing a unique pedagogical approach to the common task of computing the characteristic polynomial of a square matrix with real coefficients. Research records showing a breadth of work in fractal theory. We had focused on context in terms of the social and political circumstances of a time period, but I also wanted to understand the mathematical context. Along my journey as a research mathematician, I’ve found without this context my understanding of certain concepts, fields, and even individual results feels fragmented, incomplete. And yet, many of the mathematicians I look up to seem to have an innate ability to connect theories, fields, and histories of results into a larger mathematical picture. Maybe stories can help us make those connections. This project was an opportunity for me to use storytelling not just to learn about mathematicians, but to learn mathematics. McWorter, in particular, gave me a clear place to begin. What is a fractal? Why did he care about them? What was happening in the mathematics of fractal geometry while he was working in the field? And what might his work tell us about the mathematical community he was part of?  Fractals are geometric objects whose structure can persist across different scales. Some fractals exhibit self similarity, when you zoom you see patterns that resemble the larger object. Fractal like objects were being studied long before the word “fractal” was introduced. In the nineteenth century, Karl Weierstrass produced an example of a continuous function that is nowhere differentiable, challenging the familiar picture of a curve as something smooth. In 1904, Helge von Koch gave a geometric construction of what is now called the Koch curve. It begins with a line segment, and each segment is iteratively replaced by four smaller segments, each of which is 1/3 the length of the original segment. Applying this construction to all three sides of an equilateral triangle produces the Koch snowflake (Figure 5). Repeating this process produces increasingly intricate boundary, while retaining the same basic pattern at every scale. The Koch curve was the first time I saw that dimension does not always have to be an integer. I am accustomed to thinking of a line as one dimensional and a region of the plane as two dimensional. These ideas developed across several areas of mathematics before there was a field called fractal geometry. Work in analysis, set theory, topology, and complex dynamics produced many of the objects and ideas that would later be brought together under the language of fractals by Benoît Mandelbrot. While working at IBM’s Thomas J. Watson Research Center, he used computers to investigate and visualize irregular and self similar structures, connecting mathematical ideas to phenomena such as coastlines and other naturally occurring forms of roughness. He introduced the term fractal in 1975 and helped establish fractal geometry as a mathematical research area. This history changed the way I understood McWorter’s work. By the 1980s, mathematicians were studying self-similarity, dimension, iteration, and irregular geometric structure with the aid of computers. It also gave me an appreciation for what productivity could look like when working in a growing research area, with like minded colleagues and graduate students down the hall.1010 10 Several students in the 1990s had theses dealing explicitly with fractal theory. McWorter’s story was beginning to take shape across all three dimensions of our framework: his family and career, his mathematics, and the mathematical and historical context around him. This introduced another challenge for our project. How could we help someone else encounter that mathematics?  We wanted to introduce others to the stories of Black mathematicians from Ohio State. How do you introduce someone to a mathematician they have never heard of, whose mathematics they’ve never encountered? How do you help students see research mathematics as something people actually do? We decided to introduce their math through play. We designed workshops for middle school students featuring three parts: focusing on humanity, mathematics, and context. Carolyn Mahoney worked in matroid theory. I learned with my students that a matroid is a mathematical structure that abstracts the idea of independence from linear algebra.
