We made a modified version of “Dots and Boxes” inspired by this idea (Figure 7).1111 11 In the game, students took turns drawing lines on a grid to enclose boxes and claim the enclosed area. They lost a point if they created a cycle. Mathematically, creating a cycle meant the corresponding set of edges was no longer independent. Of course, we did not lead with this language while they were playing! Guy Hogan studied group theory, so we designed a puzzle hanging activity that introduced the idea of operations through a physical sequence of moves (Figure 8). A plus meant moving a weight on a string to the right over two thumb tacks, a minus meant moving the string to the left. What did plus plus minus plus do? Was there a way to create a sequence that would create the weighted string to fall with the removal of just one pin? It seemed impossible. We started with humanity and spent about 30 minutes with the students before introducing the mathematics. We asked them what they thought mathematicians did, what they knew about research. Had they ever heard of the Republic of Panama? That’s where Guy Hogan grew up. He went to an HBCU, Talladega College, in Alabama, had they ever heard of HBCUs? Did they know anyone who left the state to go to college? For Mahoney, we talked about her work developing mathematics curricula in schools and asked what, if anything, students would change about mathematics education in their own schools. Hogan eventually left mathematics for a legal career, so we asked whether their favorite subjects had ever changed. Why do people care about operations? In the puzzle game we composed moves that behaved like operations, but there were no numbers involved. Mathematicians like Guy Hogan study operations abstractly in subjects like group theory. We talked about the movement of robots and how rotations can be viewed as operations that can be composed. We talked about video games and how they use mathematics to help the characters move across the screen. For the matroid activity, we returned to graphs. We had students write their favorite musical artists as nodes on a board, then they decided to put edges between them if they were the same type of artist. We discussed how this could be a helpful way to organize connections. We talked about social media. Our archival work gradually developed into a framework for storytelling that shaped the narratives we created about Black math alumni. The principles of humanity, mathematics, and context guided our research and ultimately became a way to facilitate mathematical discovery, both for middle school students and for ourselves. The workshops made the framework operational. The goal was not simply to tell students that Black mathematicians had done interesting work. We want to show them new mathematical ideas, learn about the people whose ideas inspired the activity, and understand something about the worlds in which they lived. This gave a proof of concept that our framework could do more than shape a story, it could also shape how someone encounters mathematics. I hope you reflect on these principles of mathematical storytelling, mathematics, humanity, and context, and think about how they could work in practice. From now on, listen closely to the mathematical stories around you and how they are told. How often do they detail history? How often do they make the mathematics itself visible? How often do they allow you to encounter the person who did the mathematics? If one of these pieces is missing, ask what becomes harder to see. We can, and should, do more. We can open up our mathematical community to ourselves and to the public. “I am what time, circumstance, history, have made of me, certainly, but I am also, much more than that. So are we all.” – James A. Baldwin Baldwin (1984) – If you haven’t heard it already, there’s a pervasive toolbox metaphor in mathematics. The idea is that we all have a box that we fill over time with different techniques and methods. Each class you take, each research experience, each conversation with another mathematician is an opportunity to add something new. I hope you find ways to travel, to attend conferences and lectures and seminars, to build your understanding of theory, to learn about applications that interest you, and to spend time thinking deeply about problems that linger in your head for weeks and months. Each of these experiences connects you to more mathematicians, to more ideas, and gives you more to add to your box. Even when it feels like you don’t know enough, stop and peek. There are so many pieces waiting to be connected. Have conversations. Bridge the gaps. You have the capacity for this. Let yourself grow. The archival research I did through Hidden Figures Revealed has inspired my present work to do a Census of Black mathematicians who earned PhDs in the mathematical sciences across the United States. The NSF Ascending Postdoc helped me add tools related to data science to my mathematical toolbox. Now I view information from these historical studies as data. I can consider degrees earned and work experiences, patterns of matriculation, institutional pathways, and research networks from quantitative instead of qualitative perspectives and use applied mathematical tools to study the mathematical community. I could not have imagined this when I began my postdoc years ago. It did not occur to me that I could write my own mathematical story and build a research program that centers equity related questions concerning shape, structure, and society, part of the emerging field of quantitative justice. Your mathematical life will probably not look the way you imagine it now. You will find questions you did not know you wanted to ask. You will learn mathematics you did not know existed. You will meet people who change the way you think. You will discover parts of yourself that you had not yet figured out how to bring with you into mathematics. I hope that you learn stories that connect you to mathematics, and pull you in and keep you here. I hope that if you want to keep going, you find pathways into the mathematical professions of your dreams. To do this you will have to keep adding tools as you go. The mathematical world you are entering is changing fast.1212 12 I am writing this as things like anti intellectualism, the demographic cliff in higher education, and the rapid incorporation of AI into research pipelines create seismic shifts in what it means to do mathematics. You will have to grow in ways that are unique to your generation. You will encounter new problems and new opportunities that I cannot anticipate. You may struggle to reconcile your love for mathematics amid cultural tension, societal unrest, and an endless list of things to learn. You may face the pang of disappointment that follows when you realize the toolboxes of many, when it comes to centering inclusion and diversity, are empty. You may have peers or colleagues who are increasingly frustrated at hearing sentiments like this expressed, who are tired of conversations about inclusion, who believe enough talent will supersede it all, that the math that draws you together exists independent from the politics of our society. Who don’t want stories with context, and don’t want stories with humanity. They believe the stories worth telling center mathematics and mathematics alone. They also do not want this romantic notion challenged, preferring the fairytale, a merit based utopia where the cream of the crop rise no matter what. You will have to decide how to navigate this. I hope you do not mistake their discomfort for evidence that the mathematical community is not for you. I hope you remember that your job is not to convince someone that you belong. Storytelling is a tool. I want it to be featured in more mathematical toolboxes. I want you to consider adding it to yours. I don’t mean that every mathematician needs to become a historian. I don’t mean that every mathematics course needs to become a history course. And I certainly don’t mean that storytelling is a solution to the complicated structural reasons that people enter, leave, or remain in mathematics. But I think there is a practice here that can be learned, adapted, and used when it makes sense. I think we can learn to tell stories that introduce people, not just math majors or graduate students or members of the professoriate or industry, but the general public, to mathematics rather than simply decorating mathematics with biographies. I think we can recover histories that help people see themselves as part of a mathematical community. I think we can ask who someone was, what mathematics they did, and what was happening around them, and let all three answers matter. Short, clean stories can dilute the complexity of history. Brown v. Board of Education outlawed ‘separate but equal’ in public education in 1954, but Columbus, Ohio, continued to confront school segregation for decades, including through court ordered desegregation and busing beginning in 1979. Fractal geometry was not simply invented by Mandelbrot in 1975. There was a longer history of work on irregular and self similar objects before this theory was formalized. There were other classes of fractals being generated by computers during the time period that the Mandelbrot set was gaining popularity, including those attributed to William McWorter, Jr. The history of Black mathematicians at Ohio State cannot be reduced to a story of isolated “firsts.” In 2021, I was the only Black woman mathematician in the Department of Mathematics at The Ohio State University, yet between 1963 and 2020 there were 7 PhDs, 20 master’s degrees, and 141 bachelor’s degrees awarded to Black mathematicians. You may enter many rooms and realize you are the only person who looks like you. I experience this, so did the Black mathematicians from Ohio State. If you find yourself standing at the edge of these rooms wondering whether there is a place for you inside, literally or figuratively, I hope you remember that there are more stories than the ones you have been told. That is perhaps the thing I most want you to take from this letter. Stories can make visible what has been hidden. Stories can transform a name into a person, a theorem into a history, and a career into something shaped not only by individual choices but by relationships, institutions, opportunities, and circumstances. As wonderful as they can be, stories can also flatten. Please resist this. Use them as a tool to push against prevailing, but reductive, narratives, especially the ones that hand wave why entire demographics are less represented in our community. That is what I did in some sense. I challenged a narrative that there had been no one like me in the math department at Ohio State before. I found Rada Higgins, then I found hundreds of other names. The names led to archives, the archives led to mathematics, and the mathematics led to questions about mathematicians and the worlds in which they worked. I started looking for evidence that I was not alone, and in seeking to tell their stories, I developed a framework centering humanity, context, and mathematics as a way to tell stories about mathematicians in general. Your mathematical story is still being written. Lean in as you encounter stories around you. Think deeply about your own. Ask the right questions. Who are you? Where are you from? What mathematics do you do? What narratives have you told yourself about what is possible for your future? What assumptions have you made about your place in the mathematical community, and what have you been told? What becomes possible to imagine when you consider the communities and context in which you learn and do your work? What needs to stay the same? What needs to change? I hope Hidden Figures Revealed gives you something concrete to hold onto, a model of earnest efforts to more fully understand the history that shaped the mathematical community you are entering. So you might learn from those who came before you, understand the stories of Black mathematicians, and begin to have a more nuanced understanding of why there is a dearth of Black mathematicians. This project was also for anyone who loves mathematics, especially those whose stories are rarely centered. It is for anyone who has ever felt alone in mathematics, who has pushed past the fear that the weight of an entire community hinges on their success. This project was as much for me as it was for all of you. It was my way to reconcile my love of math with the rest of it. I hope you find your own way. Mathematically yours, A fellow mathematician

Hopf Algebra of Graphs for Operator Splitting Methods Motivated by combinatorial identities arising in the study of Operator Splitting methods and their description in terms of bipartite rooted trees, we establish a connection between Operator Splitting methods and the theory of combinatorial Hopf algebras. We show that the inclusion–exclusion expansion of the elementary weight of a rooted tree over its rooted subforests can be interpreted as the antipode of Schmitt’s Hopf algebra of graphs. This interpretation recovers known identities for operator splitting and partitioned Runge–Kutta methods from general properties of the antipode. We further show that adjoint operator splitting methods can be described algebraically through the antipode and the canonical involution of the original method. The resulting framework also yields new combinatorial identities and connects the analysis of geometric numerical integrators with the theory of incidence Hopf algebras. 1 Introduction Graph theory has played a fundamental role in the development of modern numerical time integration methods by providing a combinatorial framework for analyzing the order conditions of high-order integrators. A fundamental contribution in this direction was the pioneering work of Butcher, who observed that the elementary differentials and elementary weights associated with Runge-Kutta (RK) methods can be naturally indexed by rooted trees [9, 11]. This correspondence transformed the derivation of order conditions into a combinatorial problem, allowing the structure of rooted trees to be exploited in the systematic construction and analysis of numerical integrators. Since then, rooted trees have become an indispensable tool in geometric numerical integration, giving rise to the theory of B-series and revealing deep algebraic structures underlying RK and related methods [20, 19, 12]. The combinatorial structure of B-series through rooted trees led to the discovery of an algebraic structure underlying numerical integration methods. In particular, the set of rooted trees can be endowed with the structure of a Hopf algebra [13, 8], providing a powerful framework for studying the composition, substitution, and inversion of B-series. Remarkably, this Hopf algebra was independently discovered in the context of perturbative quantum field theory by Connes and Kreimer [14], in the context of renormalization. Operator splitting (OS) methods, on the other hand, constitute an important class of numerical integrators for initial value problems whose vector field can be decomposed into a sum of simpler components [19]. These methods construct an approximation by composing the exact or approximate flows associated with the individual subproblems. As with RK methods, the design and analysis of high-order splitting schemes rely on understanding intricate algebraic and combinatorial order conditions, motivating the search for mathematical structures that organize these conditions in a systematic way. Traditionally, these order conditions are derived through repeated applications of the Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff (BCH) formula [5, 4], which expresses the composition of exponentials of non-commuting operators as the exponential of an infinite series of nested commutators. By recursively applying the BCH formula to the composition defining a splitting method and comparing the resulting Lie series with the exact flow, one obtains the algebraic constraints on the coefficients required to achieve a prescribed order of accuracy. The present work is motivated by the study of fractional step Runge–Kutta (FSRK) methods through the combinatorial properties of the elementary weights associated to bipartite rooted trees [16, 15]. In that setting, elementary weights can be expressed in terms of the operator-splitting coefficients and expanded over subforests obtained by deleting edges from the original tree. These expansions lead to identities involving the tree factorial and reveal a systematic pattern of alternating signs. The recurrence of such identities naturally suggested the existence of an underlying algebraic framework governing these combinatorial phenomena. In this paper we develop this connection using Schmitt’s Hopf algebra of graphs for the case of trees, where the expansions over subforests and the associated inversion formulas become manifestations of the coproduct and antipode. This viewpoint not only explains and unifies the identities obtained for FSRK methods but also extends them to a broader class of OS schemes. We first formulate the subforest expansions and the associated identities for elementary weights, including their interpretation through the edge-deletion poset and Möbius inversion. We then show how the expansion operator is related to the antipode, providing an algebraic explanation for identities that arise in the analysis of FSRK and operator-splitting methods. Finally, we apply this framework to operator splitting—including adjoint and palindromic methods—and to partitioned Runge–Kutta methods. In addition to recovering known identities, these applications yield new combinatorial relations and clarify the role of incidence-algebra structures in geometric numerical integration. Rather than treating the complete system as a whole, one may exploit this decomposition to construct numerical methods that separately approximate the evolution generated by each component. OS methods are based precisely on this principle. They approximate the solution of (1) by composing the solution operators associated with the individual subproblems, thereby replacing the original evolution by a sequence of simpler ones. This strategy often leads to computationally efficient schemes and, in many situations, inherits desirable geometric or physical properties from the constituent flows. Among the most widely used examples are the Lie–Trotter and Strang splittings, which provide first and second-order approximations, respectively [6]. FSRK methods build upon this idea by replacing the exact evolution of each subproblem with a suitable RK discretization [19]. Then, the overall method combines the flexibility of RK schemes with the structure of OS methods, making it possible to construct high-order integrators while preserving the advantages associated with the decomposition of the original problem. Theorem 4 provides the principal algebraic interpretation of the present work. Although the operator [FORMULA] was originally introduced in the study of FSRK methods to describe the dependence of elementary weights on subforests, the theorem shows that it is, in fact, a fundamental object in the Hopf algebraic structure of graphs. Consequently, many of the combinatorial identities satisfied by [FORMULA] are no longer isolated phenomena, but rather manifestations of general properties of the antipode. This identification establishes a direct connection between the combinatorics of OS methods and the theory of incidence Hopf algebras. The edge-deletion poset provides a complementary perspective. Its incidence algebra and Möbius function encode the same alternating-sign structure, linking the subforest expansions to Möbius inversion. Our motivation stems from the study of bipartite rooted trees, whose coloring properties naturally relate them to the chromatic theory of graphs [2]. Indeed, a graph is bipartite if and only if it admits a proper [FORMULA] -coloring, while the chromatic polynomial is classically expressed as a Möbius inversion over the Boolean lattice of edge subsets. In the present context, it provides a systematic way for interpreting the identities associated with the operator [FORMULA] . Beyond providing a unified framework for previously known identities in OS and PRK methods, such as Theorems 1 and 2 and the identity (14), this approach has enabled us to derive new combinatorial identities, including Propositions 3 and 2. In particular, adjoint operator splitting methods admit an algebraic interpretation involving Möbius inversion and the canonical involution of the original method. Furthermore, just as Runge–Kutta methods can be understood through the structure of the Connes–Kreimer–Butcher Hopf algebra, OS methods can be naturally described within the framework of Schmitt’s Hopf algebra of graphs. This connection opens a route to studying further algebraic and combinatorial properties of geometric numerical integrators.

Inference in an interactive multi-type branching network with partial information We study statistical inference for a high-dimensional stochastic interaction model observed only through low-dimensional aggregate data. The model describes pairwise communication between [FORMULA] individuals as a collection of mutually interacting branching processes with immigration, where activity on one directed pair may trigger subsequent activity in the reverse direction. The latent interaction counts are not observed. Instead, for each individual, only the total number of messages sent and received in each time slot is available. This aggregation gives rise to an inverse problem in which the parameters governing the latent pairwise dynamics must be recovered from substantially compressed observations. 1. Introduction Interactions between individuals in digital communication systems — such as email exchanges, messaging platforms, and online discussion threads — generate complex dependence structures that evolve over time. Activity between two individuals may trigger subsequent activity in the opposite direction, while interaction intensities may differ across pairs. Statistical inference becomes particularly challenging when the individual pairwise interactions are not directly observed. A natural question is whether the parameters governing such latent interactions can be recovered from aggregate activity. This problem arises in communication networks, but also in network traffic monitoring, partially logged communication systems, and other interacting count processes in which observations are available only after aggregation. The central statistical difficulty is that aggregation substantially reduces the dimension of the available data while retaining dependence generated by the unobserved interaction mechanisms. Model & objectives — In this paper, we study a stochastic model for pairwise interactions among [FORMULA] individuals. For each ordered pair [FORMULA] with [FORMULA] , the latent process records the number of interactions from [FORMULA] to [FORMULA] at each time point. Thus, the latent system contains [FORMULA] pairwise processes. We assume, however, that these processes are not observed individually. Instead, for each individual we observe only the total outgoing and incoming activity. The observation dimension is therefore [FORMULA] , compared with the latent dimension [FORMULA] . The two dimensions coincide when [FORMULA] , while for [FORMULA] the observation scheme strictly reduces the dimension of the available data. The main question of the paper is whether the parameters governing the latent pairwise dynamics can nevertheless be identified and estimated from these aggregate observations. Our approach is based on stationary moment relations. In particular, while marginal moments generally contain only aggregate information, lagged covariances retain information about the direction and strength of the interaction mechanism. We exploit these temporal relations to construct an explicit identification map and a corresponding method-of-moments estimator. We focus on a parametric specification in which the immigration and offspring distributions are each indexed by a single parameter. The main example is Poisson immigration combined with Bernoulli offspring. Under the corresponding stability conditions, we show that a finite collection of observable moments identifies all latent parameters. The estimator is obtained directly from empirical moments of the aggregate observations and therefore does not require reconstruction of the latent pairwise processes or maximization of a high-dimensional latent-data likelihood. The resulting procedure has two main advantages. First, it uses only the aggregate observations that are available in the proposed observation scheme. Second, the parameter recovery is explicit, so that the estimator can be implemented by evaluating empirical moments and applying the inverse moment map. We establish consistency and asymptotic normality under the Poisson–Bernoulli specification. Literature & contribution — The model considered in this paper belongs to the broad class of branching processes with immigration. Classical foundations for branching processes with immigration can be found in [1, 13], while multitype branching processes and their long-term behavior are treated in detail in [2, 7]. Related interaction structures have been studied in coupled branching systems and multitype population models [3, 9, 14]. A second relevant strand of literature concerns statistical inference under partial or indirect observation. In many stochastic systems, individual-level processes are latent while only aggregated measurements are available. Such problems arise, for example, in ecological models, epidemiology, queueing networks, and other partially observed stochastic systems [5, 6, 15, 16]. Related aggregation problems also arise in dynamic network models; see, for example, [11]. The present setting differs in that the aggregation is applied to a high-dimensional interacting branching system, while the objective is to recover parameters governing the underlying pairwise dynamics. From a statistical perspective, inference for branching systems has been studied using likelihood-based methods, estimating equations, and moment-based procedures. Moment methods are particularly natural when the latent process is high-dimensional or only indirectly observed. An example of inference for partially observed multitype branching systems is given in [10]. Our contribution is to study parameter identification and estimation for a fully coupled [FORMULA] -dimensional interaction system when only [FORMULA] aggregate processes are observed. We derive observable moment relations that retain information about the latent pairwise interactions, establish identification under the Poisson–Bernoulli specification, and construct an explicit method-of-moments estimator. We further establish consistency and asymptotic normality of the resulting estimator. The identification argument also illustrates a broader point: aggregation does not necessarily eliminate information about latent interaction mechanisms. In the present model, temporal dependence generated by the alternating interaction between the two directions of each pair remains visible in the aggregate observations and can be used for parameter recovery. Concluding Remarks In this paper, we studied parameter estimation for a stochastic interaction model when only aggregate observations are available and the underlying pairwise interaction processes are unobserved. By exploiting the stationary moment structure of the model, we showed that the latent parameters can be identified and estimated directly from aggregate data, without reconstructing the latent processes or maximizing a high-dimensional likelihood. Under the Poisson–Bernoulli specification, we obtained an explicit pairwise inverse map from observable moments to the model parameters and established consistency and asymptotic normality of the resulting estimator. Numerical experiments illustrated the finite-sample performance of the procedure and its expected [FORMULA] scaling. The identification analysis also clarifies the role of zero-valued parameters. In particular, a zero immigration parameter does not necessarily prevent identification, whereas configurations involving zero response parameters or vanishing observable moments may require additional restrictions. Thus, identification depends not only on the number of available moment equations, but also on the structure and independence of the selected moments. Although communication networks provide the motivating example, the framework applies more broadly to partially observed interacting count processes in which latent pairwise interactions generate observable aggregate quantities. For example, aggregate activity may be observable in online social networks even when detailed interaction data are unavailable because of privacy, data-storage, or data-collection constraints. Several directions for further research are natural. Sparse networks. The analysis in Section 5.2 shows that zero-valued parameters can create additional identification problems. An important direction is therefore to develop estimation methods that explicitly exploit sparsity while accounting for these identification issues. More general interaction structures. The present model is based on pairwise interactions and specific immigration and offspring mechanisms. It would be natural to allow for interactions involving more than two individuals, time-varying parameters, or more general observation and censoring mechanisms. Alternative estimating systems. The explicit inverse map used here provides an exactly identified estimating system. One could instead combine first moments with additional lagged moments to obtain overidentified estimating systems, which could be useful for specification testing or for improving statistical efficiency. Growing networks. Our asymptotic results treat the number of individuals as fixed. Extending the theory to settings in which the network size grows with the number of observations would be important for applications involving large networks.

Beyond Typical Strings: Sampling the Complexity Landscape Uniform random sampling of strings is overwhelmingly dominated by high-complexity strings, leaving the much smaller set of low- and intermediate-complexity strings largely unexplored. Here, we adapt the nested neutral set estimator (NNSE), a Monte Carlo rare-event sampling method, to estimate the distribution P(K) of complexity values for binary strings of fixed length. NNSE allows us to explore the full complexity landscape, including exponentially rare low-complexity regions that are inaccessible to direct sampling, for string lengths up to several hundred. We apply the method to several widely used complexity measures: Lempel–Ziv 76 (LZ76), Lempel–Ziv 78 (LZ78), context tree weighting (CTW), the block decomposition method (BDM), and block entropy. We further introduce uniform complexity weighting (UCW), which gives equal weight to different complexity levels rather than to individual strings. Using NNSE to perform UCW sampling allows us to compare complexity measures across their full range in a dataset-independent way. This reveals differences in their behavior for low- and intermediate-complexity strings that are practically inaccessible to conventional uniform sampling. II Complexity Measures We consider the following complexity measures: LZ76 [12], LZ78 [1], CTW [13, 14], block entropy [16], and BDM [15]. We briefly summarize each below; see Appendix A for details. LZ76 is a classical parsing-based measure of finite-sequence complexity [17], while LZ78 is a related dictionary-based universal coding scheme whose codelength provides a natural compression-based complexity measure. In contrast, context tree weighting (CTW) predicts each successive bit using a Bayesian mixture over context-tree models. We define the CTW complexity of a sequence as the cumulative log-loss incurred by these predictions. CTW has demonstrated strong predictive performance on real-world datasets [18] and is supported by a rigorous Bayesian framework for combining variable-order Markov models. Block entropy is particularly simple to understand. It calculates the complexity of a string using the Shannon entropy of fixed-length substrings (blocks). We use a sliding window with overlapping blocks to obtain a finer-grained estimate. Finally, we consider BDM, which approximates Kolmogorov complexity using precomputed algorithmic complexities of [FORMULA] strings on 5-state Turing machines, which are then combined into blocks for a complexity measure. We have a separate subsection for BDM as both its uncorrelated (default) and correlated (slower but finer-grained) variants exhibit some unusual properties. Many other complexity measures exist. We chose the measures above because they are well established and span a range of approaches to practical string complexity. But NNSE can be applied directly to these and other measures. V Discussion The principal contribution of this work is methodological. We show that the NNSE provides practical access to exponentially rare regions of complexity space that are effectively inaccessible under uniform random sampling. This makes it possible to estimate the distribution [FORMULA] over many orders of magnitude and to study complexity measures across their full range of values rather than only in the neighborhood of typical high-complexity strings. For binary strings, this extends the practical range of exhaustive analysis from lengths of roughly [FORMULA] to several hundred or more, while remaining independent of any particular dataset. While the NNSE can access the expected near exponential scaling of [FORMULA] at low [FORMULA] , it also reveals unexpected results, such as reproducible fine-scale structure in CTW and previously unreported oscillations in the default implementation of BDM, and a sharp transition at low complexity in the correlated variant. A second more general contribution is the introduction of uniform complexity weighting (UCW). Many calculations in information theory use uniform string weighting (USW), where every string is equally likely. Although this is a natural choice, USW is overwhelmingly dominated by strings of near-maximal complexity. Consequently, it can obscure precisely the region of complexity space that is often of greatest practical interest. UCW instead gives equal weight to each complexity level, allowing low- and intermediate-complexity strings to be studied without introducing biases associated with particular datasets. This change in viewpoint can lead to qualitatively different conclusions. For example, the average single-bit sensitivity of every complexity measure increases under UCW, with the largest changes occurring for LZ78 and BDM. These differences between measures are not apparent under USW because low-complexity strings form an exponentially small fraction of sequence space. UCW also provides a natural framework for comparing complexity measures directly, revealing patterns that would be much harder to observe using conventional sampling approaches. Rather than asking whether two complexity measures perform similarly on a particular corpus, this approach asks whether they assign similar notions of complexity across the entire space of binary strings. For example, the cross-correlations suggest that LZ76 and CTW produce remarkably similar complexity orderings despite arising from rather different principles. The present work also has several limitations. Although NNSE reproduces exact complexity distributions whenever exhaustive enumeration is feasible, we do not yet have rigorous theoretical bounds on its convergence rate or sampling error. The behavior of LZ78 illustrates this limitation: its comparatively high single-bit sensitivity makes low-complexity regions more difficult to explore and leads to significantly slower convergence than for LZ76 or CTW. Likewise, several empirical observations reported here—including the spike structure of CTW and the oscillatory behavior of uncorrelated BDM—remain theoretically unexplained. These should therefore be regarded as observations generated by systematic computation rather than as fully understood mathematical phenomena. Our framework is readily extensible. Since the NNSE depends only on the ability to evaluate a local measure, it can be applied to essentially any computable description-length estimator, including modern neural compression methods [27], probabilistic sequence models [28], and future approximations to Kolmogorov complexity. Beyond complexity measures, the same rare-event methodology may prove useful whenever one wishes to characterize exponentially small subsets of very large combinatorial spaces. While this paper is primarily empirical and methodological, perhaps the most interesting longer-term implication concerns theory itself. Many existing theoretical results concern asymptotic behavior under USW, whereas practical applications often depend on the comparatively small subset of low- and intermediate-complexity strings. It would be valuable to develop analytical results directly for UCW, just as many existing results have been developed for USW.

IV Conclusion The VPM composes the gradients of two unrelated potentials and is therefore variationally inconsistent, i.e., it has no potential of its own. Its tangent is unsymmetric, and [FORMULA] loses monotonicity in a band near the pinning circle that small time steps reach. In composite models, [FORMULA] can change sign. There, damped Newton stalls, which explains the failures of the local inversion, and where [FORMULA] , [FORMULA] is not injective, the inversion has three solutions, and damped Newton often converges to a wrong solution. For Newton-type solvers in the scalar potential formulation, we therefore recommend the exact unsymmetric tangent, or Broyden’s update, which needs no derivative of the material law but has no descent guarantee. Under rotational flux, the tangent should not be symmetrized, neither directly nor by symmetric quasi-Newton updates such as BFGS, and smaller time steps do not help. Unlike for the EBM, mesh-independent convergence is not guaranteed, and under rotational flux, convergence deteriorates under mesh refinement. Additional considerations, such as the thermodynamic consistency of the VPM, i.e., whether its dissipation rate is non-negative and maximal and whether it fits the variational framework of rate-independent systems [13], are left for future work. Coinduction in Grounded Arithmetic A grounded arithmetic counts a sentence as true only when a terminating process establishes it; a sentence no such process settles has no value. Such a logic can state that an event happens, but not that it never happens under unbounded choice. This paper extends such a logic so that it can. The base is Reflective Grounded Arithmetic (RGA) with Inductive Grounded Arithmetic (IGA)’s least-fixed-point reading and ground induction. It adds a separate greatest-fixed-point former [FORMULA] with Park’s coinduction rule, proves that one former cannot carry both ground induction and coinduction, and adds a dichotomy rule: the classical disjunction between a least-fixed-point atom and the greatest-fixed-point atom of its dual, under a derivable premise that the body’s leaves are decided. The systems are sound for an explicit model reading every [FORMULA] -body at its greatest fixed point, hence consistent; they agree with the least model wherever it has a value and prove sentences it leaves without one. The dichotomy replaces the underivable hypothesis that an order is well-founded by the derivable one that its steps are decided; the change of model pays for the move. With ground induction the dichotomy derives the omniscience rule of the sibling arithmetic OGA, so the system has no semantics whose certificates for universals are its own proofs. The systems prove, as single sentences, that every decided tree is well-founded or has an infinite branch given by a term, total in the new model; that random assignment terminates while its divergent twin runs forever; that a fair loop terminates and the alternating-bit protocol delivers every message; that open games are determined; that the termination gap in Nakata and Uustalu’s trace semantics closes; and that Cinderella wins the bucket game at capacity three. Isabelle/HOL checks every result. 1 Introduction Five buckets of capacity three stand in a circle. Every round the Stepmother pours one unit of water, divided among the buckets as she likes; then Cinderella empties two adjacent buckets. The Stepmother wins if a bucket ever overflows. Does Cinderella have a strategy that keeps the water in the buckets forever? At capacity three she does, and a single round-robin invariant certifies it; smaller capacities are not attempted here. The game is a standard benchmark for infinite-state safety games [9, 5]. Look at what the two players claim. The Stepmother claims that an overflow happens: a terminating event, witnessed by a finite play. Cinderella claims that it never happens, whatever the Stepmother pours, and a unit can be divided in infinitely many ways, so the plays branch without bound at every round. A logic that counts as true only what a terminating process establishes can state the Stepmother’s claim. It can also state that one given play never overflows, a universal over the play’s rounds. It cannot state Cinderella’s claim, a “never” over unboundedly branching plays, except as the negation of a claim that nobody has shown false. This paper is about such logics, and about the step that lets them say what Cinderella says. A grounded arithmetic is one in which a sentence is true only when a terminating computation, or a well-founded tree of them, makes it so; a sentence that no such process settles is not false but has no value. Picture a logician leafing through a book of computations and coloring some of them true. The grounded tradition colors only terminating ones. What if the logician also colored certain computations that never terminate? Not all of them: the Liar never terminates, and coloring the Liar true is the inconsistency that grounded logic exists to avoid. The question is which non-terminating computations deserve the color. The answer this paper gives is the coinductive one. A computation deserves the color when it is an instance of a recursive definition declared for the greatest fixed point and lies in that fixed point, so that the definition’s own unfolding never refutes it. The paper’s thesis is that a grounded arithmetic supports that reading exactly, with its rule, its model and its limits stated as theorems. The setting is Reflective Grounded Arithmetic (RGA) [22], a paracomplete arithmetic, one in which a sentence may be neither true nor false, where every term is a computation and self-reference is native: a fixed-point former turns any body into a term that unfolds to itself. Its extension IGA, Inductive Grounded Arithmetic [24], adds the elimination rule for every positive self-referential term, called ground induction, and with it the grounded meaning of a positive recursive definition is its least fixed point: accessibility, well-foundedness, the winning positions of a game, and RGA’s own truth predicate are single terms with induction principles. Kripke’s least fixed point leaves the truth-teller ungrounded while other fixed points settle it, and Kripke singled out the intrinsic fixed points, whose verdicts no fixed point contradicts, and the maximal intrinsic one [37]. [FORMULA] is neither minimal nor intrinsic (Remark 4.3): it commits to the greatest fixed point for truth at every declared [FORMULA] -body, a choice made by the polarity of the declaration, body by body. Visser’s survey treats the structure of the fixed points of the truth jump [60], and Burgess’s analysis of their complexity [12] is the classical reference for what calibrating [FORMULA] would involve. The axiomatic theories of Kripkean truth take the other route: the Kripke–Feferman theory KF [19], whose standard models are the fixed points of the jump, and the partial-logic theory PKF of Halbach and Horsten [29], sound for the fixed points as partial models, are sound for a whole class of fixed points, where INGA commits to one non-minimal fixed point and proves what holds there. Field’s paracomplete theory [20] builds on Kripke’s least fixed point with a conditional of its own; the grounded conditional of §2 is instead a premise sequent at an undecided hypothesis. Fitting’s Kripke–Kleene semantics for logic programs [21] and the well-founded semantics [59] work with the same split of a three-valued operator into a truth and a falsity part that §3 uses. Baelde’s [FORMULA] MALL [4], linear logic with least and greatest fixed points, has [FORMULA] equal to [FORMULA] of the dual by construction, which is the duality the dichotomy restores at bodies with decided leaves; Tiu and Momigliano’s Linc- [57] has both Park rules on defined atoms and proves cut elimination. Both are proof-search frameworks rather than arithmetics, and both have the duality that a grounded system lacks. The theories of iterated inductive definitions [11] are the inductive side of the same picture. The paper claims no calibration of DINGA or [FORMULA] against these theories. Cyclic proof systems [10], and cyclic arithmetic, which Das calibrates by quantifier complexity [17], obtain induction and coinduction from a global condition on a finite cyclic proof; whether that condition can be stated and checked in a grounded setting is an open question the paper does not touch. The coinduction rule here is Park’s rule, stated in Isabelle as weak_coinduct, which Paulson developed definitionally from Knaster–Tarski greatest fixed points [48]; the codatatype package of Isabelle/HOL [58, 7] and Lochbihler’s library of lazy lists and streams, of the kind used for Nakata–Uustalu-style traces [40], supply coinductive types, which the paper does without (§6). Capretta’s delay monad and the treatments of termination against non-divergence built on it are the type-theoretic analog of the search example, and of non-termination stated positively as a run [14]. The grounded reading of implication at an undecided hypothesis, and why it is forced, is the subject of the IGA paper; both rules here are shaped by it. 11 Limits, Open Questions, and the Artifact Two rules separate DINGA from IGA. The coinduction rule reads a body of the [FORMULA] class at its greatest fixed point, and the systems that have it are sound for an explicit model, consistent, semantically conservative over the least model, and unsound for the least model by design: they derive never-refuted instances that the least model leaves without a value. The dichotomy rule supplies the classical disjunction between a least-fixed-point atom and the greatest-fixed-point atom of its co-body, under a derivable premise; it trades the hypothesis that an order is well-founded for the derivable one that its steps are decided, and the change of model pays for the trade (§5.3). A second cost, inherited from ATI (Theorem 5.3), is the loss of every certificate-grounded semantics: RGA and IGA are proof-grounded, while OINGA and DINGA, like OIGA, have no certificate-grounded semantics; unlike OIGA they are unsound for the least model by design, and their warrant is [FORMULA] . With the two rules, streams, runs, branches, the regions of a game, and the termination or divergence of a search are single sentences, and the map of §9 says what each costs. Genuine alternation is not supported, and the paper does not propose it. Of the two classical routes around opposite-polarity dependence, random assignment for fairness is carried out, up to the alternating-bit protocol’s eventual delivery (Theorem 7.6), and progress measures for Büchi and parity conditions are the natural next example. Streams enter bodies as parameters, not as points. Stream bisimilarity for systems with infinite branching, and up-to context techniques, would need codes read by an evaluator (a prediction, §4). Player I’s strategy in an open game is not extracted. Whether INGA proves termination from non-divergence without ATI is open, and so is whether INGA is proof-grounded. Whether OINGA derives every instance of the dichotomy is open; [FORMULA] cannot separate the two systems. The calculus of ground induction with the dichotomy but without [FORMULA] is already unsound for the least model, so it pays the dichotomy’s price without [FORMULA] , and every rule of OIGA holds in it, ATI as a derived rule; what model and strength that calculus has is open. The strength of [FORMULA] in reverse-mathematical terms, and the complexity of the [FORMULA] -truth sets of the controller’s region, are not established beyond a lower bound: [FORMULA] ’s truth set is not hyperarithmetic (§7, classical, by an argument). The bucket game’s threshold capacity is not settled here; the certificate is for capacity three and above, and that bound is attained against the strategy it certifies (Theorem F.5). Which non-terminating computations deserve to be colored true? The paper’s answer, at the level of declared bodies (Remark 4.3): the instances of a body of the [FORMULA] class, written with [FORMULA] ’s tag, that lie in the greatest fixed point of its truth operator, relative to the least fixed point of the oracle map. They are never refuted; nothing the least model values changes; and reading at the greatest fixed point is not the same as coloring the never-refuted true, since the two coincide only for bodies that satisfy Theorem 3.2. Isabelle/HOL (Isabelle2025-2) checks every theorem in this paper; the remarks are arguments and are not mechanized. No session in the chain enables quick_and_dirty, the build-time checks fail on any oracle, and an axiom check confirms that every axiom beyond those of Isabelle/HOL’s Main is a recorded definition, a type definition or a type arity; the sessions of the coinduction chain proper (OIGA, OIGA_Coind, IGA_PGSem, IGA_Closing, Coind_Dinga) add none of the last two kinds, and the build fails if one appears. The sessions, over the RGA development (RGA, with the model interface, and RGA_Kit), are GCalc_Core (the base abstract calculus), AGA, OGA (the replay, Kőnig’s lemma and the Kleene tree: OGA_Coind_Kit, OGA_Koenig_FB, OGA_Kleene_Tree), IGA (the former, the model and the dichotomy rule: theories IGA_Nu, IGA_Nu_Sound, IGA_Nu_Rule, IGA_Dich, IGA_Coind and companions), OIGA (the abstract calculi with the rules and the systems: GNu, GDich, GShell and their companions), OIGA_Coind (streams, games, fairness and the other examples), IGA_PGSem (the theorems on certificate-grounded semantics), IGA_Closing (ATI from the dichotomy, the closed-off oracle, DINGA with a primitive-recursive step decider and its recursively enumerable derivability through the equality with OINGA with the dichotomy, whose proof checker is there), and Coind_Dinga, the junction over OIGA_Coind and IGA_Closing (the examples restated at DINGA, the axiom check, and OINGA’s recursively enumerable derivability). The whole chain builds with isabelle build -d hol Coind_Dinga; a clean build of the chain takes about seven minutes with ten threads on an Apple-silicon workstation. Ad-conditions for higher-order recurrences: Dunkl and matrix-valued settings The ad-conditions of Duistermaat and Grünbaum characterize bispectrality for a pair of differential operators. M. Reach observed that a sequence of functions which is simultaneously an eigenfunction of a second-order differential operator and satisfies a recurrence relation of arbitrary order must satisfy a different kind of ad-conditions. We prove that the Reach ad-conditions are also sufficient, by an argument which is purely algebraic. This motivated us to explore ad-conditions in two new directions: to Dunkl differential-difference operators, where the coefficients of the ad-condition become elements of the Dunkl algebra and the reflection enters as a coefficient, and to matrix-valued orthogonal polynomials, where we exhibit ad-conditions for several families of exceptional matrix-valued polynomials satisfying five- and seven-term recurrence relations. 1. This was the first appearance of the so-called ad-conditions as a necessary and sufficient condition for bispectrality, involving a pair of differential operators, one of order two and the other one of arbitrary order. In [11, 12] one sees how the use of these conditions leads to the “classical orthogonal polynomials”, whose study goes back at least to S. A Preconditioned Semismooth Newton Method for Box-Constrained Elliptic Optimal Control Problems with Random Coefficients We consider the optimal control problem of an elliptic PDE with random diffusion under pointwise box constraints on the control. The constraints make the optimality conditions nonsmooth, with an active set that is not known in advance, and the random diffusion couples the state and the adjoint across all stochastic modes. To design a solution algorithm for this problem, we rely on the Fenchel duality viewpoint. Fenchel duality absorbs the box constraint into the objective and yields an exact reduced problem in the elliptic adjoint variable alone. After a stochastic Galerkin–finite element discretization, eliminating the state leaves a strongly monotone, piecewise smooth equation, which we solve directly by a matrix-free semismooth Newton method with the box projection retained exactly and with no outer iteration, penalty or smoothing parameter. Next, we introduce and analyze a current-set preconditioner, which adds the active-set correction of the current Newton step to a mean-diffusion reference operator and is inverted exactly by a rank-1 update. For implementation, we use a cheaper preconditioner that keeps only a fraction of free control values. Numerical experiments show second-order convergence of the state, and Newton and PCG counts that stay bounded under mesh refinement and growth of the stochastic dimension. 1 Introduction Optimal control problems governed by partial differential equations (PDEs) are ubiquitous in computational science and engineering, and both a mature theory and a large body of numerical methods are available in the deterministic case [35, 14]. Pointwise control bounds [FORMULA] change the picture. The first-order conditions are no longer a system of equations but a variational inequality, or equivalently a nonsmooth equation built from the metric projection onto the admissible box [20, 15]. Three consequences follow. First, although the reduced objective is strongly convex, the resulting Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) system is nondifferentiable, so classical Newton methods do not apply. Second, the set of indices at which the bounds are attained—the active set—is not known in advance and must be discovered as part of the solution process. Third, the standard remedies—penalization, interior-point regularization, smoothing—replace the exact constraint by an approximation governed by an additional parameter, and recover it only in the limit. In the deterministic problem, the primal–dual active set (PDAS) strategy of Bergounioux, Ito and Kunisch [9] treats the bounds exactly by alternating between a prediction of the active set and the solution of an equality-constrained subproblem. Hintermüller, Ito and Kunisch [18] subsequently showed that PDAS is precisely a semismooth Newton (SSN) method for the projection-based reformulation, which explains its local superlinear and mesh-independent convergence [11, 28, 30, 36, 19]. In most applications the PDE coefficients are uncertain and are modelled by random fields and lead to optimal control problems under uncertainty [27]. The random variable may be discretized by sampling, by stochastic collocation [10, 22, 21, 34], or by stochastic Galerkin (SG) projection onto a global orthogonal polynomial basis [16, 40, 23, 26, 4, 24, 32]. We use SG, which yields a single coupled system: the discrete state operator is a sum of Kronecker products, and state and adjoint interact across all stochastic modes. Combining pointwise constraints with random coefficients is harder than treating either feature alone. For control constraints, the projection onto the box is available in closed form and need not be regularized, yet stochastic Galerkin discretizations of such problems have been studied mainly from the approximation side: Shen et al. [33] derive a priori error estimates for obstacle-type control constraints, and Winkler and Yücel [38] combine error estimates for a Dirichlet boundary control problem with a primal–dual active set solver and block-diagonal preconditioning. There, the control is deterministic and acts on [FORMULA] , so the active set stays decoupled from the stochastic tensor structure. Solvers for stochastic control problems are developed in [8, 7, 2, 25, 1, 3, 6]. None of them treats control constraints. An alternative is the Fenchel duality viewpoint, where the dual absorbs the constraint into the objective. Clason and Kunisch [12] found the duals of certain unconstrained elliptic control problems structurally more favourable than the primal problems, and Wang et al. [37] derived the Fenchel dual of a linear parabolic problem with box constraints on the control, in which the constraints are embedded in an unconstrained, differentiable dual objective, and solved it by conjugate gradients and by semismooth Newton. They also identified the obstacle that reappears here: semismooth Newton applied to the primal problem treats the box and the PDE constraint simultaneously, so the varying active set changes the structure of the Newton equation and the preconditioner has to be adjusted at every step. In the stochastic setting, this obstacle is sharper: control values are indexed by pairs of a spatial node and a quadrature point, so the active-set term of the Jacobian matrix has no Kronecker structure. A preconditioner containing it exactly must be rebuilt at every step, whereas a mean-based Kronecker preconditioner is cheap but blind to the location of the free set. In this paper, we develop a dual-based SSN framework for optimal control problems governed by elliptic PDEs with random coefficients and pointwise box constraints on the control. We derive the Fenchel dual in Bochner spaces over the parameter domain, which absorbs the control constraints into an unconstrained dual objective in the adjoint variable, and establish the corresponding optimality system and primal–dual recovery relations. After stochastic Galerkin–finite element discretization, we derive the exact finite-dimensional dual and solve the resulting reduced equation directly by a matrix-free semismooth Newton–PCG method, in which the box projection is retained exactly, and no outer iteration, penalty, or smoothing parameter is required. In both the function space and the discrete setting via stochastic Galerkin–finite element methods, the dual formulation yields an unconstrained problem in the adjoint variable and reduces to a single semismooth equation without a duality gap. In this work, we show how such MEP formulations can be leveraged to obtain refined information about the solution set of the polynomial system. We demonstrate, in the setting of single-input single-output [FORMULA] -norm model order reduction, how the Thom–Porteous formula can be used to derive an exact count of the complex solutions of the critical equations derived from Walsh’s theorem. We prove, under suitable genericity assumptions, that their set of complex solutions is finite and that all solutions occur without multiplicity. Moreover, we derive an explicit formula for the total number of complex solutions as a function of the model orders. Throughout, we provide a self-contained and application-oriented exposition of the algebro-geometric tools required for our analysis, with the aim of making them accessible to the broader engineering community. 1 Introduction Systems of polynomial equations arise frequently in engineering applications; still, solving them comprehensively—numerically or symbolically—is computationally challenging. For such systems, one typically has access to unconditional but only coarse upper bounds on the number of affine solutions, such as those provided by Bézout’s theorem. Nevertheless, having a precise a priori count of the solutions is valuable both for the design and use of computational methods. It provides a concrete proxy for the expected computational cost and can be used to validate computations by confirming that the full solution set has been recovered. A multiparameter eigenvalue problem (MEP) generalizes the standard eigenvalue problem [FORMULA] by allowing multiple spectral parameters and by dropping the restriction of linearity in the parameters [4, 46, 11]. For rectangular MEPs [44, 25], one looks for all [FORMULA] and nonzero [FORMULA] such that where [FORMULA] is a tall, [FORMULA] matrix whose entries are polynomials in [FORMULA] . The solutions [FORMULA] are called eigentuples [11] and [FORMULA] the corresponding eigenvector. For [FORMULA] and [FORMULA] linear in [FORMULA] , we recover the (generalized) eigenvalue problem. Several systems of polynomial equations arising in applications from systems and control have been shown to exhibit a partially linear structure, such that they can be reformulated as a rectangular MEP, see for example [7, 45, 14, 1, 31]. In these cases, instead of solving the system directly using general-purpose polynomial system solvers (e.g., [9]), one can alternatively obtain the solutions by computing the eigentuples of the corresponding MEP using specialized solvers (e.g., [44, 25, 43]). In this paper, we argue that the reformulation of the system of polynomial equations as an MEP can also yield more theoretical structural insights into the problem at hand. In particular, two central results in algebraic geometry, when applied in the context of these MEP reformulations, can be used to obtain finer information about the solution set of the polynomial system. When a polynomial system is expected to have finitely many solutions, the fiber dimension theorem is a useful tool to verify this. Consequently, where finiteness of the solutions can be established, the Thom–Porteous formula, applied to the determinantal variety associated with the MEP reformulation, can often be used to derive an exact count of the affine complex solutions. To ground our discussion, we illustrate the use of these tools in the context of a problem from systems and control: the [FORMULA] -norm model reduction problem for single-input single-output (SISO) linear time-invariant (LTI) models, in which a given model is approximated by one of lower order. It corresponds to a non-convex optimization problem and may therefore admit multiple local optima, which can be characterized as (a subset of the) real-valued common roots of a system of polynomial equations [13, 38, 21, 30]. These equations, commonly referred to as the critical equations, follow from Walsh’s Theorem [47], which, together with the Thom–Porteous formula, motivates the title of this paper. We study the complex solution set of the critical equations as a whole and refer to its elements as the critical points. When the given higher-order model is sufficiently generic, the set of critical points is known to be finite [6, Theorem 3]; in fact, simple poles suffice for this to hold [22, Theorem 3.2]. This observation has motivated several approaches that use algebraic and numerical linear algebra methods to enumerate all such critical points; see, e.g., [21, 36, 3, 1, 30]. When complete, such enumerations allow one to certify global optimality. However, they are computationally feasible only for relatively small problems and are therefore best regarded as theoretical tools, mostly used for benchmarking purposes. Practical solution approaches, such as the iterative rational Krylov algorithm (IRKA), scale to large problems by iteratively enforcing the first-order optimality conditions, but converge at best to a single local optimum, without any guarantee of global optimality; see, e.g., [20] and references therein. Despite the extensive literature on [FORMULA] -norm model reduction, an exact count of the critical points for arbitrary problem sizes is, to the best of our knowledge, not available. For the co-order one case, i.e., when the order is reduced by one, [21] provides an upper bound. Recent work showed that the critical equations allow for an MEP reformulation [30]. Moreover, we show for generic higher-order models that the solutions of the critical equations occur without multiplicity, a property favorable for numerical computation (Section 3.2). Assuming the higher-order model has only simple poles, we derive an explicit formula for the number of critical points, that is, the total number of complex solutions to the critical equations, as a function of the full and reduced orders (Theorem 3.6). For higher-order models with one or more multiple poles, we illustrate how the aforementioned count can be used to derive an upper bound on the number of critical points (Section 4.1). Although we consider the continuous-time case throughout, our analysis easily extends to a discrete-time setting (Section 4.2). We provide a self-contained, application-oriented exposition of the key algebro-geometric tools, making them accessible to a broader engineering audience (Section 3 and Appendix A). In the specific context of the [FORMULA] -norm model order reduction problem, we applied the fiber dimension theorem and the Thom–Porteous formula to obtain an exact a priori count of the complex solutions to the critical equations. This result is substantially sharper than the coarse bounds available from, for instance, Bézout’s theorem. Our formula shows that the number of critical points grows rapidly with the problem size, reflecting the computational complexity observed in engineering practice. The most demanding part of the analysis was proving that the incidence variety [FORMULA] defined by the critical equations is irreducible, reduced and of the same dimension as the space of input variables. By contrast, the analysis of the bad locus—corresponding to extraneous solutions introduced by the MEP formulation—was favorable, as we were able to show that the bad locus is most often empty. The methodology presented here is not restricted to the model reduction problem under consideration, but can be applied more broadly to other polynomial systems and multiparameter eigenvalue problems arising in related applications. For instance, in our related work [27] we employed a similar strategy in the context of a system identification problem. In Examples 5.3 and 5.4, we illustrated that for specific problem instances, in particular when the higher-order model has multiple roots, the bad locus [FORMULA] can be non-empty and contain points of higher multiplicity. Moreover, Example 5.6 touches on how the critical equations change when the poles of the reduced model follow a prescribed multiplicity structure. A detailed understanding of these special cases is an interesting direction for future work. In the case of a higher order model of full McMillan degree [FORMULA] and simple poles, we have reproven the main result of [22] on finiteness of critical points (cf. Section 3.3). It remains an open question whether the critical points can ever form an infinite set, for any higher order model (of degree [FORMULA] ). We conjecture that the critical points always form a finite set, and have verified this in the case of a finite bad locus. Example 5.6 also illustrated that stationary points of a lower-order problem can reappear in a (possibly restricted) higher-order problem as degenerate stationary points, that is, as models with pole-zero cancellations and thus McMillan degree strictly smaller than [FORMULA] . For the (unrestricted) problem in discrete time, such points were characterized in [5, Proposition 2.7]. By formulating the model order reduction problem (2) over [FORMULA] , we have excluded these degenerate points from the search space. However, even though they are never local minimizers [38, Theorem 5.3], they can appear as saddle points or local maxima in the optimization landscape and may therefore still be of practical interest. A systematic understanding of how many such degenerate stationary points arise, and how they influence the optimization landscape, is another interesting research direction. In our related work [27], lower-order solutions similarly appear as separate components of the critical equations. Another natural extension is to investigate how the presented analysis generalizes to frequency weighted [FORMULA] -norm model order reduction (see, e.g., [26]), where a nontrivial weight function is incorporated in the approximation criterion. A foundational method in TDA is persistent homology (PH) which constructs a sequence of shapes from a data set, and measures how the homology classes evolve as we vary some parameter. The input is the data set and the output is a persistence barcode or diagram. The persistence barcode is computable and stable[16, 40]. PH has been successfully applied to various other domains including biological data [8, 10, 28, 39], audio data [20, 35, 34], and the social sciences [19]. For more applications, see the database on non-theoretical uses of topology (DONUT) [23]. However, there are many reasons that one might wish to analyze data along multiple parameters; for example, 1-d persistence can be quite sensitive to outliers. More generally, many data sets require analysis on more than one parameter, making the use of multiparameter persistence ([13, 22]) particularly helpful. Unfortunately, the generalization of a persistence barcode for modules over more than 1-dimension is not straightforward; although such barcodes can be defined, they fail to be complete invariants (see, for example, Section 4.1 of [11]). Thus, this leads us to look elsewhere for other partial invariants of multiparameter persistence modules. One such partial invariant is the fibered barcode, defined for bipersistence modules in [29, 30]. To obtain the fibered barcode of a bipersistence module [FORMULA] , the parameter space [FORMULA] is fibered by lines [FORMULA] with positive slope. Each of these lines represents a restricted module [FORMULA] which has a 1-d persistence barcode. The fibered barcode for a module [FORMULA] is defined as a map the set of all such lines to the space of persistence barcodes who’s image contains the collection of all possible restrictions of [FORMULA] obtained on any line with positive slope. The fibered barcode is useful in that it is computable and provides a visual interpretation of data that varies along 2 parameters. It also determines the matching distance between two multiparameter persistence modules, which can be computed from the fibered barcode for bipersistence modules [4, 27]. In this paper, we look to generalize the fibered barcode for bipersistence modules by viewing the parameter space as a directed space, and looking at filtrations obtained along non-decreasing paths, i.e. dipaths. Doing this allows for a larger class of possible obtained 1-d modules than can be obtained by restricting to lines with postive slope- it may be the case that there exists a restricted modules obtained along a dipath that is not obtainable on any line with positive slope. Additionally, we look to leverage tools of directed topology, like directed homotopy of dipaths, to identify broad classes of barcodes included in the image of the fibered barcode. We look to distinguish equivalence classes within the extended fibered barcode via two types of equivalence: combinatorial equivalence of persistence barcodes and simplicial equivalence of filtrations. There are several related ways that other mathematicians have investigated the fibered barcode or looked to understand multiparameter persistence modules by restriction to subposets. By viewing multiparameter persistence modules as sheafs, projected barcodes ([9, 21]) can be obtained by considering derived pushforwards of these modules along [FORMULA] . Other restriction based invariants include [17], which develops a method for computing the generalized rank invariant of a bipersistence module by restricting the module to zigzag paths along the boundaries of intervals in the parameter space; this is generalized in [18] to certain nice [FORMULA] -parameter persistence modules for [FORMULA] . Invariants arising from general order-preserving embeddings of representation-finite posets are studied in [2]. Bipath persistent homology, studying persistence modules generated by two filtrations with common endpoints, is introduced in [3]; [1] provides a framework in which bipath persistence can be understood using zigzag persistence. Finally, in [37], authors generalize the matching distance to monotone piecewise-linear paths in parameter space. Our paper focuses on understanding the underlying filtrations and persistence modules obtained by restricting to any monotone path. The outline of the paper is as follows. Section 4 introduces the two types of equivalence between restricted modules that we investigate: combinatorial equivalence of diagrams and simplicial equivalence of filtrations. Modeling and Analysis of Cooling-Induced Isotropic–Nematic Transitions in Pharmaceutical Liquid Crystals This paper studies the phase transition from an isotropic to a nematic liquid crystal driven by controlled cooling, motivated by the manufacturing of next-generation pharmaceutical drugs. Using the non-isothermal Ericksen model for liquid crystals with a variable degree of orientation, we formulate the problem as a stiff, quasilinear system of parabolic partial differential equations. We establish a consistent thermodynamic framework, prove the well-posedness of the system, and conduct a rigorous asymptotic and numerical scaling analysis of the moving phase boundary in a cylindrical cell subjected to bottom-wall convective cooling. Our analysis identifies a critical sample thickness that separates two distinct physical regimes. Below this threshold, the transition follows the cooling dynamics and the material remains quasi-isothermal. Above the thickness threshold, bulk thermal diffusion governs the dynamics, imposing a dominant thermal delay characterized by a concave quadratic propagation front. These results demonstrate that scaling from laboratory characterization to industrial production fundamentally alters the spatial thermal history of the material, providing a predictive mathematical framework to optimize cooling protocols for kinetic arrest. A Introduction. In this article, we study the isotropic–nematic phase transition in a thermotropic liquid crystal subjected to a prescribed cooling process. Our work is motivated by the processing of liquid-crystalline pharmaceutical compounds, for which the temperature history can influence the phases formed and, ultimately, the properties of the resulting material. We formulate a non-isothermal extension of Ericksen’s theory of liquid crystals with variable degree of orientation, neglecting macroscopic flow. The resulting evolution couples orientational relaxation and heat conduction. F Conclusions We have investigated the cooling-induced isotropic–nematic phase transition in thermotropic liquid crystals, motivated by the processing of liquid-crystalline pharmaceutical materials and, in particular, itraconazole. Within a non-isothermal extension of Ericksen’s theory of liquid crystals with variable degree of orientation, we have developed a thermodynamically consistent description of the coupling between orientational relaxation and heat conduction. The resulting nonlinear parabolic system accounts for the evolution of the scalar order parameter and temperature, including the effects of anisotropic thermal conductivity and heat exchange with an externally controlled cooling bath. We highlight two aspects of the mathematical formulation. First, along with the classical polynomial Landau–de Gennes bulk potential, we have considered the singular Ball–Majumdar potential, which incorporates the physical restrictions on the eigenvalues of the orientational order tensor. To overcome the implicit character of this potential, we have constructed an explicit approximation that retains its endpoint singularities and the coexistence conditions associated with the isotropic–nematic transition. We have established convergence of this approximation and of the corresponding coexistence parameters. Second, we have investigated the well-posedness of the coupled non-isothermal problem, establishing local existence, uniqueness, and regularity of solutions, together with separation from the physical bounds of the order parameter and a continuation criterion. The nondimensional and asymptotic analysis reveals the importance of the widely separated time scales governing orientational relaxation, thermal diffusion, and externally imposed cooling. In particular, comparison of the thermal diffusion time with the cooling time identifies a characteristic sample thickness separating two regimes of thermal evolution. For sufficiently thin samples, the temperature remains nearly uniform across the material, whereas for thicker samples the finite rate of thermal diffusion produces significant spatial delays. The reduced thermal equations yield approximate descriptions of the propagation of the isotropic–nematic transition-temperature isotherm, with a concave quadratic dependence of its time of evolution on the vertical coordinate. These results illustrate how changes in sample dimensions may substantially modify the thermal history during cooling. The transition-temperature isotherm should, however, be distinguished from the actual isotropic–nematic interface, whose evolution also depends on the kinetics of orientational ordering and possible metastability. Several extensions of the present work are of interest. An extension of the model to include the subsequent nematic–smectic A transition is currently under way. This requires introducing additional order parameters to describe the development of smectic layering and their coupling to nematic orientation and temperature. Such an extension is particularly relevant to itraconazole, for which the sequence of isotropic, nematic, and smectic phases plays an important role in determining the material state attained during cooling. Other directions include a more detailed investigation of the dynamics of the phase interface, the influence of temperature-dependent material coefficients and nucleation mechanisms. These developments would provide a basis for studying the competition between phase ordering, thermal transport, and kinetic arrest in the preparation of liquid-crystalline pharmaceutical materials.
