We prove that every spectral finite union of pairwise disjoint bounded intervals whose lengths satisfy at most four linearly independent rational relations tiles the real line, and that each of its spectra has at most five cosets modulo its least period. This includes every spectral union of at most five bounded intervals. The proof combines specialization preserving subset-sum equalities with rigidity of exchanges between finite spectral fibers. We also obtain common tiling complements for all spectra of primitive sets of at most seven elements in finite cyclic groups, and establish the sharp eleven-point range in which consecutive pairs force periodicity of the dual set. 1. On potential density of rational points on hyperkahler varieties In this paper, we prove that the rational points on hyperkähler varieties in each of the four known deformation families admitting a rational Lagrangian fibration are potentially dense. Furthermore, we give several applications and construct examples of hyperkähler varieties beyond these families satisfying the potential density property. Our approach is first to prove that rational points on hyperkähler varieties admitting two rational Lagrangian fibrations with distinct associated isotropic rays are potentially dense. We then construct a projective Shafarevich–Tate twist admitting two such fibrations, together with a dominant rational map from the twist to the original variety. 1. Introduction The study of the distribution of rational points has a long history. Two notable classical results are the Mordell–Weil theorem [41] on the structure of rational points on abelian varieties and Faltings’ theorem [13] on the finiteness of rational points on curves of genus at least two. By Faltings’ theorem, such curves provide examples of varieties whose rational points are not Zariski dense over any finite extension of a number field. However, abelian varieties, including elliptic curves, behave differently. By [15, Proposition 3.1], every abelian variety over a number field admits a nondegenerate algebraic point, whose cyclic subgroup is Zariski dense. After a finite extension making this point rational, we obtain a Zariski dense set of rational points. Let [FORMULA] be a variety over a number field [FORMULA] . Therefore, a natural question is: under what conditions are the rational points on varieties potentially dense? One of the initial conjectures in this direction is the Bombieri–Lang conjecture [9], which generalizes Faltings’ theorem and predicts that rational points on varieties of general type are not Zariski dense. In the opposite direction, Campana [11] conjectured that rational points on special varieties are potentially dense. Several works have studied this problem and related questions. Hassett and Tschinkel [16] constructed examples of K3 surfaces of geometric Picard rank one with Zariski dense rational points over complex function fields, while van Luijk [40] constructed K3 surfaces of geometric Picard rank one over number fields with infinitely many rational points. More recently, Martínez-Marín [29] established a uniform bound on the degree of a field extension needed to obtain infinitely many rational points on K3 surfaces of degree two. Isomorphism classes and geometric classification of three-dimensional Jordan algebras and the length function We investigate the algebraic classification of Jordan algebras of dimensions at most three over arbitrary fields with more than two elements. Our approach combines the theory of nilalgebras and radicals with Peirce, Wedderburn decompositions and the length function. In characteristic two, we adapt the Peirce decomposition to organize the classification, including the field-dependent isomorphism conditions among parametrized families. We also study the varieties of Jordan algebra structures up to dimension three over an algebraically closed field of characteristic two. Besides explicit degenerations and standard arguments, we introduce the alicyclic and characteristic conditions as geometric obstructions to degeneration. We determine the rigid algebras and irreducible components in both dimensions. In dimension three, one component is the nine-dimensional affine space of square-zero products; unlike the other three components, it contains no open orbit. 1. Introduction Jordan algebras originated in 1932 in the study of the mathematical foundations of quantum mechanics, when Pascual Jordan introduced a class of commutative nonassociative algebras [25] in an attempt to formalize aspects of quantum mechanics. This approach was further developed by Jordan, von Neumann and Wigner in 1934, classifying finite-dimensional formally real Jordan algebras [26]. Expanding these works, Albert obtained fundamental results on their structure, including Peirce decompositions, the study of radicals and a version of the Wedderburn principal theorem [27, 28, 29]. These investigations were followed by the classification and representation of semisimple Jordan algebras by F. Jacobson and N. Jacobson [30]. Later, in 1983, Zelmanov worked on prime Jordan algebras providing a substantial advance in the structural classification of Jordan algebras beyond the finite-dimensional semisimple condition [34]. The algebraic classification of low-dimensional Jordan algebras has been historically developed in parallel to the classification of other classes of nonassociative algebras. In 1975, Gerstenhaber and Myung classified four-dimensional commutative power-associative nilalgebras over fields of characteristic different from two [35]. Another significant advance was made by Petersson in 2000, who classified all two-dimensional nonassociative algebras over arbitrary fields [36]. Nevertheless, extending classifications to higher dimensions introduces additional difficulties, particularly concerning field-dependent restrictions such as the existence of roots for quadratic and cubic polynomials. Kashuba and Shestakov investigated three-dimensional Jordan algebras over algebraically closed fields placing restrictions on the characteristic of the field [20] and the arithmetic reasoning posed an obstacle to extend the presented method to arbitrary fields of positive characteristic. In 2016, Hegazi and Abdelwahab classified nilpotent Jordan algebras of dimension at most three over arbitrary fields [9]; however, this did not cover nonnilpotent Jordan algebras completely, as it could not include nilalgebras that need not be nilpotent in characteristic two. More recently, Cedilnik and Jerman classified three-dimensional zeropotent algebras over arbitrary fields [17], covering an important subclass of Jordan algebras in characteristic two, but leaving algebras with nonzero squares beyond its scope. Recently, Diniz, Gonçalves, da Silva and Souza obtained a classification of two-dimensional Jordan algebras over arbitrary fields of characteristic different from two [4]. These developments reveal the remaining difficulties in obtaining a unified low-dimensional classification over general fields, especially in characteristic two, where the usual linearization of polynomial identities may not provide a complete linearization, classical structural decompositions require reconsideration, and isomorphism classes can depend essentially on the arithmetic of the ground field which need not be algebraically closed. The theory of deformations of algebras was initiated by Gerstenhaber in 1964, who developed a framework for studying deformations and rigidity of associative algebras [37]. In his work, Flanigan consolidated the geometric aspects of the theory, investigating varieties of algebra structures and orbit closures [38]. In 2005, Alberca Bjerregaard, Loos and Martín González investigated derivations and automorphisms of Jordan algebras in characteristic two [39], although the degeneration relations and irreducible components of the low-dimensional varieties remained outside their investigation their work pioneered the investigation of the geometric aspects of the variety of Jordan algebras in characteristic two. Subsequently, Kashuba studied the varieties of unital Jordan algebras of dimension four and five in 2006, determining their irreducible components [21], but without encompassing nonunital algebras or characteristic two. In 2007, Kashuba and Shestakov investigated the geometric classification of three-dimensional Jordan algebras [20], leaving characteristic two out of the scope of their work. In 2018, Kashuba and Martin classified the variety of five-dimensional nilpotent Jordan algebras, showing that one of its five irreducible components contains no dense orbit and is instead determined by an infinite family of nonisomorphic algebras [23]. However, their investigation was restricted to nilpotent algebras over fields of characteristic different from two and three. The geometric analysis of the present work therefore develops additional tools instead of relying only on previously established degeneration arguments. For instance, an algebra of dimension [FORMULA] is called alicyclic when, for every element [FORMULA] , the vectors [FORMULA] are linearly dependent. We show that this is a Zariski-closed, isomorphism-invariant condition and hence is preserved under degeneration. In dimension three we also consider polynomial relations between coefficients of the characteristic polynomial of the multiplication operator [FORMULA] , the resulting characteristic conditions are likewise preserved under degeneration. Together with polynomial identities, annihilator and automorphism dimensions, and explicit one-parameter changes of basis, these conditions supply obstructions to nonexistent degenerations. The paper is organized as follows. In Section 3 we classify commutative associative algebras of dimensions one, two and three. The treatment separates nilalgebras from algebras admitting idempotents, this is essentially the same reasoning that Goodaire and Zhou [24] have used for the study of alternative rings, uses Peirce decomposition and the Wedderburn-Artin theory where appropriate, and gives isomorphism conditions for the parametrized families. Section 4 studies Jordan algebras, isolating the cases that are not associative and treating characteristic two separately, including the contribution of zeropotent structures in dimension three. In Section 5 we use Peirce decompositions to complete the analysis of three-dimensional unital and nonunital Jordan algebras. The length and the introduced polynomial degree provide complementary ways of sorting associative cases, the resulting classification is again followed by criteria for identifying isomorphic parametrized algebras. Finally, Section 6 concerns the geometric classification over algebraically closed fields of characteristic two. We establish the degeneration criteria described above and determine the orbit closures in dimension two. In dimension three, we determine the irreducible components and the rigid algebras. The resulting picture highlights both the effectiveness of geometric obstructions to degeneration and the ways in which Jordan algebra varieties in characteristic two differ from the more familiar settings. 2. Painlevé VI superintegrability and Heun–Racah algebras We study the two fourth-order quantum superintegrable systems in the Euclidean plane that separate in polar coordinates and whose angular potentials are determined by the general four-parameter sixth Painlevé transcendent. One system has an oscillator radial term and the other an extended-Coulomb radial term. For both systems we give the fourth-order quantum integral explicitly, derive the cubic symmetry algebra and its Casimir, and construct a deformed-oscillator realization. At fixed energy the two algebras are specializations of the Heun–Racah algebra. Their structure functions contain the same quartic angular factor, determined by the Painlevé VI parameters, while different radial factors distinguish oscillator and Coulomb dynamics. The Coulomb integral is obtained by transforming the Cartesian Hermitian symmetry at the operator level. The lower-order terms generated by the polar coordinate change are essential for commutation with the Hamiltonian. The two quantum systems are also related by the Levi-Civita transformation and coupling-constant metamorphosis, which gives a direct correspondence between their Painlevé parameters, algebras, Casimirs and representations. Earlier exceptional-Jacobi models arise at special rational parameter values, whereas the results here apply to the full four-parameter Painlevé VI family. We also compare the quantum results with the corresponding classical Poisson algebras. 1 Introduction A two-dimensional quantum Hamiltonian [FORMULA] is superintegrable when it admits two additional symmetry operators [FORMULA] and [FORMULA] such that [FORMULA] are algebraically independent. Their commutators often generate a polynomial algebra, and the Casimir and finite-dimensional representations of that algebra can provide spectral information without solving the Schrödinger equation directly [1, 2, 3, 4]. Painlevé transcendents entered this subject through the third-order systems separating in Cartesian coordinates [5, 6], whose polynomial algebras and representations were worked out in [7, 8]; see [9] for the general framework of [FORMULA] th-order integrals and [10] for a review of the Painlevé cases. The fourth-order systems that separate in polar coordinates contain an especially rich family of exotic potentials [11, 12], as do their Cartesian counterparts [13]. With the compatibility conditions reduce the angular problem to the Cosgrove–Scoufis SD-I.a equation [14], whose general solution is expressed through the four-parameter sixth Painlevé transcendent. Two radial choices are relevant here: the oscillator term [FORMULA] and the extended-Coulomb term [FORMULA] . Each system has a second-order separation integral and an independent fourth-order integral, but the radial dynamics and leading fourth-order tensors are different. Painlevé VI had already appeared in third-order polar superintegrability [15]. Related fourth-order standard potentials and the general [FORMULA] th-order polar setting are discussed in [16, 17]. In earlier work we studied rational members of the oscillator family using exceptional Jacobi polynomials [18, 19, 20, 21]. Those special cases have a cubic quantum algebra and a deformed-oscillator realization, with structure constants expressed through the SD-I.a parameters. Here we show that the same algebraic structure extends to a general Painlevé VI angular potential: the oscillator algebra, Casimir and representation formulas hold for arbitrary values of the four Painlevé parameters. We also carry out the corresponding calculation for the Coulomb branch, for which no four-parameter quantum polynomial algebra had previously been displayed. For both systems we begin with the differential symmetry: we write the fourth-order integral in polar coordinates, establish its commutation with the Hamiltonian using the Painlevé determining equation, and only then derive the polynomial algebra. The order matters in the Coulomb case, where the integral is classified in Cartesian form and its transformation to polar coordinates produces lower-order terms that have no counterpart in the principal symbol. Once these terms are included, the oscillator and Coulomb calculations run in parallel. At fixed energy the resulting cubic algebras are central specializations of the Heun–Racah algebra [22, 23]. Their deformed-oscillator structure functions share the same quartic angular factor, which is expressed through the monodromy parameters of [FORMULA] , while the remaining factor carries the radial dynamics. We also determine the finite-dimensional algebraic modules and compare their energy formulas with direct radial separation. Which algebraic module is realized physically still depends on the chosen real angular solution and its boundary conditions. The two quantum systems are related by the Levi-Civita transformation together with coupling-constant metamorphosis [26, 27, 28]. We derive the two branches independently and then use this correspondence as a cross-check, relating their Painlevé parameters, structure constants, Casimirs and representations. The classical Poisson algebras are discussed at the end. As the classical limit is singular, they serve for comparison and not as a source for the quantum coefficients. The recognition problem for 4-manifolds and the unknotting problem for 2-spheres in 4-manifolds We show that there is no algorithm to decide whether or not a given 4-manifold is PL homeomorphic to the connected sum of 7 copies of [FORMULA] . We also show that the TOP and PL unknotting problems for all surfaces in the connected sum of 7 copies of [FORMULA] are unsolvable. 1. Introduction In this paper we address two algorithmic questions in 4-dimensional topology: the homeomorphism problem for 4-manifolds and the unknotting problem for 2-spheres in 4-manifolds. To ensure that the objects under consideration can clearly be described by a finite amount of data we assume that our manifolds and knots are PL. Thus the homeomorphism problem asks whether or not two given closed, connected PL manifolds are homeomorphic. There are two versions: we can ask if they are PL homeomorphic or merely homeomorphic (TOP homeomorphic). (We will use CAT to denote either TOP or PL.) In [M] Markov showed that both these problems are algorithmically unsolvable. The proof is based on the existence, proved by Novikov [N] and Boone [B], of a finitely presented group with unsolvable word problem. Given such a group, Adjan [A] and Rabin [R] showed how to construct, for some [FORMULA] , a [FORMULA] -relator Adjan-Rabin set, i.e. a recursively enumerable set [FORMULA] of finite [FORMULA] -relator group presentations such that there is no algorithm to decide whether or not the group presented by a given [FORMULA] is trivial. Markov showed that if there exists such a set then the CAT recognition problem for [FORMULA] is unsolvable: there is no algorithm to decide whether or not a given PL 4-manifold is CAT homeomorphic to [FORMULA] . Borisov constructed a 12-relator presentation of a group with unsolvable word problem [Bo], and the author showed that from a finite [FORMULA] -relator presentation of a group with unsolvable word problem one could construct an [FORMULA] -relator Adjan-Rabin set [G1]. It follows that the CAT recognition problem for [FORMULA] is unsolvable; see [St1],[St2],[CL]. In [G2] the author made minor improvements to both the algebraic and topological parts of the argument and showed that the CAT recognition problem for [FORMULA] is unsolvable. A new approach was taken by Tancer in [T]. Defining the deficiency of a group presentation with [FORMULA] generators and [FORMULA] relators to be [FORMULA] , he showed, using Freedman’s topological classification of simply-connected 4-manifolds [F], that if there exists an Adjan-Rabin set of deficiency [FORMULA] (i.e. each presentation has deficiency [FORMULA] ), then the TOP recognition problem for [FORMULA] is unsolvable. Moreover, Tancer constructed an Adjan-Rabin set of deficiency 9, thereby showing that the TOP recognition problem for [FORMULA] is unsolvable. In an earlier version of this work we proved the unsolvability of the CAT recognition problem for [FORMULA] . To do this we modified Borisov’s argument by proving a more general version of the embedding theorem in [Bo, Section 3], which enabled us to construct an Adjan-Rabin set of deficiency 8. Recently Kegel, Li and Ren made a major improvement to Borisov’s construction to get a 3-generator 9-relator presentation of a group with unsolvable word problem [KLR]. Using this they produced an Adjan-Rabin set of deficiency 7, proving the unsolvability of the TOP recognition problem for [FORMULA] , and a 9-relator Adjan-Rabin set, proving the unsolvability of the PL recognition problem for [FORMULA] . We use their group in this paper. Similarly, for Theorem 1.7 we use the 13-relator universal group given by Ren [Re], which improves on the 21-relator example of Valiev [V]. Beyond the reduced Landau–Lifshitz–Bloch equation: Singular potential, global well-posedness, and micromagnetic limits We study the full nonlinear mean-field Landau–Lifshitz–Bloch equation in micromagnetics arising from Garanin’s spin-polarisation model prior to the usual near-equilibrium reduction. The equation combines a singular inverse-Langevin potential with a mobility whose longitudinal component degenerates at saturation, together with exchange, anisotropy, and the nonlocal whole-space stray field. The natural state space is the closed unit ball [FORMULA] . For any [FORMULA] initial data satisfying [FORMULA] , including saturated data of infinite free energy, we construct global weak solutions and derive instantaneous separation from saturation [FORMULA] . This restores uniform parabolicity and yields the thermodynamic formulation and exact energy identity for positive times. We further establish a quantitative low-temperature limit to the Landau–Lifshitz–Gilbert equation and prove convergence of global trajectories to a single equilibrium. A spectral Curie-type threshold characterises the stability of the paramagnetic state and yields exponential relaxation above the threshold. Finally, for uniformly separated data we prove strong well-posedness, including global strong solutions in one- and two-dimensional domains, and exponential stability of non-degenerate equilibria, with a small-data global theory in three dimensions. 1. Introduction Classical micromagnetics describes the magnetisation by a vector field of unit length, leading to the Landau–Lifshitz–Gilbert (LLG) equation. This description is appropriate at sufficiently low temperatures, where longitudinal variations of the magnetisation are negligible, but it becomes inadequate near and above the Curie temperature. In that regime, the magnetisation represents a local thermal average of microscopic spins and its magnitude is no longer fixed. The Landau–Lifshitz–Bloch (LLB) equation introduced by Garanin in [14, 15] removes this constraint and allows the magnetisation to take values in the closed unit ball. It has since been extensively studied in the physics literature [8, 16, 20, 21] to model ultrafast heat-assisted magnetisation dynamics relevant in magnetic memory at high temperatures. On the properties of the potential and the spherical harmonic expansions for general planets The convergence of spherical harmonic expansions (SHEs) of gravitational potentials below the Brillouin sphere has been a long-standing problem in potential theory and geodesy. In previous work, some of the present authors gave a necessary and sufficient condition for convergence along a fixed ray, formulated in terms of analyticity of a longitudinal average of the balayage density. Metastability of the Meissner state in the three-dimensional Ginzburg–Landau model with pinningThanks: Funding information: ANID FONDECYT 1231593. We study the persistence of the Meissner state in the three-dimensional magnetic Ginzburg–Landau model with a spatially dependent pinning term. Factoring out the equilibrium profile associated with the pinning term reduces the problem to the analysis of a weighted Ginzburg–Landau functional. In the extreme type-II regime, we construct locally minimizing vortexless configurations for applied fields extending far beyond the first critical field. We obtain quantitative estimates showing that these configurations remain close, up to gauge transformations, to a Meissner-type state determined by a weighted London problem. We also prove the uniqueness, up to gauge transformations, of the locally minimizing Meissner-type branch within a quantitatively controlled class of local minimizers. A central difficulty is to derive elliptic estimates that remain uniform in the Ginzburg–Landau parameter in the presence of the resulting spatially dependent weight. Under a small-BMO assumption on this weight, we obtain the required regularity and extend to the three-dimensional pinned setting the metastability picture previously established for the homogeneous model. 1. Introduction The magnetic Ginzburg–Landau model [17] provides a phenomenological description of superconducting materials under applied magnetic fields. Its configurations depend on a complex-valued order parameter, which describes the local superconducting state, and on a magnetic vector potential for the induced magnetic field. A fundamental parameter of the model is the Ginzburg–Landau parameter [FORMULA] , which distinguishes between type-I and type-II superconductors. Throughout this work, we write [FORMULA] and consider the regime [FORMULA] , corresponding to extreme type-II superconductors. At low applied fields, a superconducting sample is expected to be in the Meissner state, characterized by the expulsion of the magnetic field from the interior of the material. As the intensity [FORMULA] of the applied field increases, this state eventually ceases to be globally minimizing and configurations containing vortices become energetically favorable. Vortices are defects in the superconducting state that carry quantized magnetic flux; in three dimensions, they concentrate along curves and are therefore referred to as vortex lines or filaments. The threshold at which they first become energetically favorable is known as the first critical field and is denoted by [FORMULA] . In the extreme type-II regime, its leading order is proportional to [FORMULA] . The first critical field is, however, an energetic threshold and does not necessarily coincide with the loss of stability of the Meissner state. Although vortex configurations have lower energy above [FORMULA] , a locally minimizing vortexless solution may persist for substantially larger applied fields. The field at which this branch loses stability is known as the superheating field, denoted by [FORMULA] . This distinction was made rigorous in the three-dimensional homogeneous setting in [29]. More precisely, it was proved that below the first critical field the Meissner solution is, up to gauge transformations, the unique global minimizer of the Ginzburg–Landau energy. Beyond this threshold, a Meissner-type solution persists as a local minimizer at least for [FORMULA] , and is unique, up to gauge transformations, at least for [FORMULA] . Thus, when the applied field is gradually increased, vortex nucleation is expected to be delayed beyond [FORMULA] and to occur only when the vortexless branch becomes unstable. This loss of stability is associated with the superheating field, which is expected to be of order [FORMULA] ; see, for instance, [10]. The purpose of the present work is to investigate to what extent this picture remains valid for the three-dimensional Ginzburg–Landau functional in the presence of material inhomogeneities described by a spatially dependent pinning term. The performance of type-II superconductors is strongly affected by the motion of vortices, which produces dissipation and limits the current that the material can carry while remaining superconducting. Material inhomogeneities may restrict this motion by acting as pinning sites for vortices. This provides one of the main motivations for introducing spatially dependent coefficients into the Ginzburg–Landau model. Such an approach goes back to Likharev [23], who proposed to account for spatial variations of the superconducting properties by allowing the coefficients in the energy functional to depend on the position. Vortex pinning has been the subject of considerable interest in the physics of superconductivity. The review [21], for instance, discusses how different types of defects and inclusions give rise to complex pinning landscapes, which influence vortex configurations and play an important role in enhancing the critical current, namely the maximal current that can be carried without losing the superconducting behavior. In a more microscopic direction, experimental work on FeSe-based superconductors has provided direct evidence that local defects can act as pinning centers for vortices [11]. These works provide physical motivation for considering spatially dependent pinning terms in the Ginzburg–Landau functional rather than restricting the analysis to the classical homogeneous model. For a more detailed discussion of the physics underlying vortex pinning and its implications, see, for instance, [23, 35, 9] and the references therein. Introduction More than half a century ago, Bacry and Lévy-Leblond [1] started what could be termed the kinematical Erlanger programme, in effect adding “time” to Klein’s famous programme of studying geometries via their symmetry groups. In their original paper they classified kinematical Lie algebras for a class of four-dimensional spacetimes. The corresponding kinematical Lie groups act on the spacetimes as a composition of rotations, boosts and spatial and temporal translations. Their classification was subject to the assumptions of spatial isotropy and the existence of time-reversal and parity automorphisms. These latter “by no means compelling” [1] assumptions were lifted in work of Bacry and Nuyts [2], who still worked in four spacetime dimensions and still subject to spatial isotropy. More recently, this classification was extended to arbitrary dimension via deformation theory: [3] (recovering the classification of Bacry and Nuyts), [4] (in higher spacetime dimension) and [5] (in three spacetime dimensions), but always under the assumption of spatial isotropy. Based on these results, the simply-connected spatially isotropic homogeneous spacetimes (i.e., the kinematical Klein geometries) were classified in [6], resulting in a small class of geometries, including lorentzian, galilean and carrollian, which were further studied in [7]. A natural continuation of this programme is to lift the assumption of spatial isotropy and the natural first step is to consider the case of coisotropy-one: where the rotational subalgebra acts on the tangent sphere (i.e., the space of directions) with codimension-one orbits. This is a much richer class of spacetime geometries and their classification, which is substantially harder, is the goal of a series of papers commencing with this one. Universality of Large-Scale Geometry For Critical Random-Cluster Models The understanding of the behaviour of critical lattice models in two dimensions has made immense progress in the past couple of decades, with conformal invariance as its conjectured end goal. We consider here the critical random-cluster model (or FK-percolation) on a large class of graphs — namely bi-periodic isoradial graphs — with cluster-weight [FORMULA] . Following up on the establishment of rotational invariance at criticality in [9], we prove that the large scale behaviour of these models is asymptotically the same on all such graphs. These include the critical homogeneous models on the square, triangular and hexagonal lattices. 1 Introduction The successful import of the renormalisation group formalism from quantum field theory was a landmark achievement in statistical mechanics11 1 We refer to [15] for a historical exposition. that, while remaining elusive from a rigorous point of view, yielded two concrete predictions: Critical statistical mechanics models should be universal in the sense that their scaling limits should not depend on the choice of underlying lattice. The scaling limits should enjoy conformal symmetries. In particular, since the planar conformal group is infinite dimensional, scaling limits of 2D statistical mechanics models should enjoy incredibly rich symmetries. With Schramm’s introduction of the SLE in [30], this conjectural picture took on a much more tangible form, and the subsequent twenty years have seen a staggering amount of progress, establishing the conjecture of conformal invariance in a number of different models (see [1, 2, 4, 5, 16, 17, 23, 28, 29, 31] for a non-exhaustive list). However, with the exception of [2, 16, 17], these approaches are characterised by exploiting very particular features of discrete holomorphicity in the models and as such, do not offer robust methods for treating other models. Another approach is to focus on universality. That is, rather than taking a single model and trying to compute its scaling limit directly, take a class of related models and show that all of their possible scaling limits must agree. Such an approach has also seen some development in the last fifteen years, starting with bond percolation in [19], extending to more general random-cluster models in [10] and lately, being used to establish not only universality across a class of square lattices, but rotational invariance of any possible scaling limit in [9]. In this paper, we combine the results of [9] with some of the conceptual techniques from [19] in order to extend the universality result of [9] to a larger class of graphs. As a special case, we establish large scale rotational invariance of the critical random-cluster model on any bi-periodic isoradial lattice. Our approach does not require smallness of the potential. As part of the analysis, we also establish endpoint versions of the bilinear Christ-Kiselev lemma. 1. Bilinear refinements have been developed in several directions. They are closely connected with bilinear Fourier restriction estimates for the paraboloid; Tao [56] proved an essentially sharp bilinear restriction theorem for transverse frequency supports, leading to a broader range of bilinear Schrödinger estimates. Change-of-variables methods for bilinear estimates appear in related dispersive problems studied by Kenig, Ponce, and Vega [34, 35], and in the Schrödinger setting in the work of Colliander, Delort, Kenig, and Staffilani [11]. Shao [50] obtained sharper restriction estimates under cylindrical symmetry, while mixed-norm bilinear estimates have also been useful in critical NLS analysis [17]. Although many classical proofs rely on the spacetime Fourier transform, there are also proofs emphasizing physical-space mechanisms. Tao [55] obtained a physical-space proof of the classical bilinear Strichartz and local smoothing estimates, while Hernandez [24] used a decomposition of Schrödinger solutions into localized tubes. Such methods are particularly relevant to settings in which the exact Fourier representation of the free propagator is unavailable. The bilinear theory extends beyond Euclidean space. On compact surfaces, Burq, Gérard, and Tzvetkov [5] proved bilinear eigenfunction estimates, and Hani [23] obtained bilinear refinements of Strichartz estimates on closed manifolds. On tori, bilinear and multilinear bounds have been obtained using lattice-point counting and function spaces adapted to the linear evolution [30, 28]; on irrational tori, Fan, Staffilani, Wang, and Wilson [19] employed a decoupling argument. Related bilinear estimates are available for balls and disks [1, 54] and for waveguides [14, 16, 15]. These results show that bilinear frequency interactions depend sensitively on the geometry and spectral structure of the underlying space. Such bilinear estimates are particularly effective in nonlinear dispersive problems. In Bourgain’s high–low method [3], they are used to show that the Duhamel term enjoys additional regularity (compared to the initial data) and smallness in the energy space (a smoothing effect), a key step in establishing global well-posedness below the energy space. Bilinear estimates also play an important role in the [FORMULA] -method, where they help control the increment of the modified energy [40, 54, 10, 9, 12, 23, 48]. In critical problems, such as the mass-critical global well-posedness theory, bilinear estimates are important ingredients for the inverse Strichartz estimate, identifying the frequency and spatial scales at which concentration occurs in the profile decomposition. The presence of Galilean invariance in the mass-critical setting makes such bilinear control particularly important. On compact manifolds such as the torus, where dispersion is weaker than in Euclidean space, bilinear (and sometimes trilinear) estimates are also essential in the energy-critical theory [27, 28, 30, 29, 63, 62, 54, 53, 39, 25, 26, 46, 52]. A direct motivation for the present work comes from [60], where a mass-critical NLS global well-posedness problem on the three-dimensional hyperbolic space was studied. Due to the mass-critical nature of the problem, a bilinear Strichartz estimate is needed in the profile decomposition argument. The authors were able to use a change-of-variables trick to translate the bilinear Strichartz estimate on [FORMULA] to a bilinear estimate on [FORMULA] with a cost of introducing a negligible potential (which can be gauged away) into the linear Schrödinger operator. Such a simplification, however, is specific to the structure of the problem and is not available for general Schrödinger operators. Recent work of Gavrus, [20], establishes direct bilinear estimates on hyperbolic space without using the change-of-variables trick. This naturally raises the question of whether bilinear Strichartz estimates remain valid when the free Schrödinger operator is perturbed by a potential. More generally, one would like to understand to what extent the frequency-separation gains in the free estimates persist under such perturbations. This is the main question addressed in the present work. Bilateral Christoffel–Geronimus–Uvarov formulas for mixed-type orthogonality on algebraic supports Christoffel-type determinant formulas construct both normalized polynomial families and their reproducing kernel for mixed-type orthogonality in several variables after independent rational matrix transformations on the two arguments. The pairing may have a rectangular matrix of functionals, with separate degree bounds on each component, and may be supported on an algebraic variety. The reduced matrices are calculated from the original biorthogonal polynomials, rational moments, polynomial division and the masses left free by division; their nonvanishing determinants characterize existence and uniqueness. For measure pairings the rational data are expressed by Cauchy and multivariate Fantappiè transforms. Exact dimension counts incorporate the four matrix factors and the relations of the support. For normal degree-ordered original families and fixed factors, when the component degrees on each side differ by a bounded amount and the normalization dimension grows at most like one degree layer, the resulting orders are bounded on curves and grow at most linearly on surfaces. For pairings allowing scalar factors to move between arguments, called balanced pairings, an exact obstruction determines whether a bilateral mass decomposes into unilateral masses when the denominators act injectively. Residue duality provides coordinates for division and mass quotients on integral curves, including singular points, and on the finite surface quotients specified here. Explicit singular-curve families retain nondegenerate residue pairings as denominator zeros coalesce. Positive congruences admit a further reduction by orthogonal projection, while balanced pairings give simultaneous intertwining identities for all coordinate multiplication matrices. 1. Introduction The objective is to calculate orthogonal polynomials after independent rational matrix transformations on the two arguments of a pairing. The calculation must preserve the prescribed degrees of each polynomial component and the equations defining its algebraic support. The results give the transformed polynomials, their reproducing kernel, the complete freedom of added masses, and the sizes of the determinants required to compute them. In mixed-type multiple orthogonality, a polynomial row is required to be orthogonal to prescribed polynomial columns. Conclusions The bilateral functional equation leads to a determinant construction for mixed-type orthogonality on algebraic supports. Starting from the original biorthogonal data, the ordered matrix factors, the rational moments required by division and a chosen homogeneous mass, the construction expresses the transformed orthogonality conditions as a finite linear system. Its image conditions preserve the relations of the support and the prescribed component bounds. Consequently, the determinant of the reduced system characterizes normality, while its bordered determinants give the normalized polynomials and their reproducing kernel. The functional equation also determines the full freedom in the transformed pairing. For balanced masses with regular denominator determinants, its exact sequence distinguishes the obstruction to unilateral decomposition from the ambiguity of the summands. Common components of the denominator zero sets can support mass directions that require the joint bilateral equation. The size of these determinants reflects both the transformation and the polynomial spaces on which it acts. In the degree construction, the Hilbert function counts the independent polynomial classes on the support, and the finite mass rank accounts for the contribution of the chosen mass. Polynomial rank computations then remove redundant directions and give the size of the smaller system. These counts explain why fixed perturbations, under compatible growth of the component degrees, have bounded determinant orders on curves and at most linear orders on surfaces. The formulas based on consecutive scalar degrees, matrix division and reduced linear systems eliminate different polynomial spaces; their respective counts specify the sizes of those representations under the stated hypotheses. To form these systems explicitly, the quotient conditions must themselves be expressed in computable coordinates. On integral curves, dualizing differentials and the geometric Cauchy kernel supply dual coordinates for matrix remainders, including at singular points. On surfaces, an additional scalar equation selects a finite quotient, and ordered matrix divided differences reconstruct each quotient class as a finite sum of its residue pairings. Applied to the respective quotients, these coordinates describe the masses and the divisibility tests required by the polynomial formulas. The explicit curve family also shows how this description behaves when the mass support reaches a singular point. The residue quotients remain nondegenerately paired and an explicit minor proves that the matrix mass keeps its rank. Normality of the finite Gram matrices, proved for the stated component bounds, then gives regular limits of the normalized polynomials and kernels. For positive symmetric congruences, the intersection of the original space with its rationally transformed counterpart permits a further reduction. The resulting two positive matrices determine both the normalized polynomials and the kernel; the coprimality count and the nodal matrix family identify situations in which positive masses, including bivariate derivative masses, leave the reduced order unchanged. This reduction applies to both balanced forms and the nonbalanced Sobolev forms exhibited at the node, because the orthogonal decomposition uses the positive forms on the specified finite spaces. With equal component bounds on the line, this construction assembles the polynomial rows into monic matrix orthogonal polynomials and yields their matrix norms and Christoffel–Darboux kernel. In particular, the triangular Hermite weights of Durán and Grünbaum illustrate how the common space determines the small orders of the corresponding formulas. The one-variable and Laurent reductions connect the general formulas with their standard specializations, while the description of positive masses identifies the admissible additions in the symmetric setting. When both the original and transformed pairings are balanced, their polynomial bases also give four-factor intertwining identities for coordinate multiplication. These bilateral Darboux identities use the same connection matrices for every coordinate and preserve the defining relations of the support. The explicit positive elliptic matrix measure supplies a square realization in which both coordinate matrices are symmetric. Thus, under the balance and normality hypotheses of the recurrence construction, the polynomial and kernel formulas determine the transformed recurrence matrices with the original order of the four matrix factors. Mutual Information Estimation via Triangular Transport Maps: Finite Sample Guarantees and Sample Allocation We study finite sample guarantees for transport based mutual information estimation. Mutual information can be estimated by first learning the conditional and marginal densities and then evaluating their log-density ratio by Monte Carlo. Given training samples, we use triangular transport maps to learn these densities and then compute the mutual information estimate on an independent batch of evaluation samples. For conditional density estimation using triangular transport maps, we establish non-asymptotic guarantees over realizable Hölder classes by viewing the conditional density as an ordinary density with respect to the product of the law of the conditioning variable and Lebesgue measure. This allows standard density estimation techniques to be applied directly to the conditional density estimation. These results yield finite sample guarantees for the resulting mutual information estimator and characterize how a fixed sample budget should be allocated between training and evaluation in order to minimize the mean squared error. Numerical experiments support the predicted training and evaluation error rates and illustrate the resulting sample allocation tradeoff. 1 Introduction Mutual information (MI) measures statistical dependence and quantifies how much observing one random variable reduces uncertainty about another. It plays an important role across science and engineering, including material science (Baptista et al., 2024), remote sensing (Chen et al., 2003), clinical trials (Ogungbenro et al., 2009), and optimal experimental design (Lindley, 1956; Chaloner and Verdinelli, 1995; Huan et al., 2024). Although the definition is simple, estimating MI can be difficult when the relevant densities or expectations are analytically intractable (Huan et al., 2024; Li et al., 2026). A variety of MI estimators have been proposed. Nested Monte Carlo methods require likelihood evaluations and can converge slowly at finite sample sizes (Rainforth et al., 2018; Huan et al., 2024). When only samples are available, commonly used alternatives include [FORMULA] -nearest-neighbor estimators (Kraskov et al., 2004) and variational methods such as MINE (Belghazi et al., 2018), NWJ (Nguyen et al., 2010), and related bounds (Poole et al., 2019). Another class of approaches estimates the densities appearing in the MI density ratio and then evaluates the resulting plug-in estimator (Foster et al., 2019). Flexible implementations include conditional normalizing flows (Orozco et al., 2023; Dong et al., 2024) and Knothe–Rosenblatt (KR) rearrangements (Koval et al., 2024; Cui et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026). Transport maps are particularly attractive for this purpose because they represent complicated target distributions through invertible transformations to simple reference measures (Marzouk et al., 2016; Spantini et al., 2018). With a triangular KR structure, conditional distributions are naturally encoded in blocks of the map, making the construction well suited to MI estimation, which requires both conditional and marginal densities. A Note on the NP-Hardness on Quadratic Optimization over Doubly Stochastic Matrices and the Gromov-Wasserstein Problem The Gromov-Wasserstein problem is an extension of the regular optimal transport problem that is adapted for pairs of distributions residing in incomparable spaces. Broadly speaking, given a pair of metric measure spaces, the Gromov-Wasserstein problem seeks couplings between these spaces that minimize the distortion between the metric evaluations. In this note we record the fact that the Gromov-Wasserstein distance between finite metric spaces is NP-Hard to compute. Our argument relies on a reduction from the Hamiltonian Cycle Problem, and it builds on ideas in Vayer [36] and Ryner et. al. [27] that draw connections between the 2-Gromov-Wasserstein and the Quadratic Assignment Problem. During the preparation of this manuscript we learned of the appearance of [2], whose result essentially supersedes ours. We hope this note serves as a useful companion whose proof is, hopefully, more elementary and easier to understand. 1 Introduction The optimal transport (OT) problem concerns moving mass from one location to another in a manner that minimizes the total cost associated with transportation. The OT task was originally developed in the context of logistics and economics. In recent years, the OT task has been applied in a range of scientific and engineering applications including statistics, signal processing, and computer vision tasks among others; today, it forms the backbone of a number of machine learning techniques. These include a Conditional Gradient / Frank-Wolfe based method [37], one based on entropic regularization [25], one based on low-rank assumptions on the cost [29] (among many others). These methods are currently deployed on Python toolboxes [8, 11]. Unfortunately, these methods are only able to compute local or approximate solutions, and are generally unable to provide convergence guarantees to a global solution. There is a different line of work based on semidefinite relaxations – these have the advantage in that they do solve (5) to global optimality frequently [5, 32, 33] while providing a certificate of global optimality; however, these methods require the solution of a semidefinite programming instance, which is considerably more expensive compared to local methods. On this note, a closely related approach is one based on the moment–SOS hierarchy [23, 33] – these are capable of computing the optimal value to the GW problem in a fashion that is independent of how the metric space is discretized; the drawback is that it is often challenging to extract the corresponding transport map. Last, we mention analytical approaches – these include computing exact values for specific families of distributions [1, 28] and lower bounds as in [21], as well as adaptations for networks [6] and ultrametric spaces [19]. Finally, we investigate the long-time average behavior of solutions to the time-dependent system with no discount, finding that solutions converge to the solution to the second-order ergodic problem as [FORMULA] . 1 Introduction The theory of mean field games of controls is closely related to the theory of mean field games, which was introduced independently by Lasry and Lions in [44] and by Caines, Huang, and Malhamé in [37]. Mean field games (MFGs) and mean field games of controls (MFGCs) are both differential games in which players seek to minimize costs that depend on the collective behavior of all the players, and it is well-known that Nash equilibria can be characterized by solutions to coupled systems of PDE. The difference is that in a mean field game, this cost depends only on the distribution [FORMULA] of players’ states, whereas in a mean field game of controls, this cost depends on the joint distribution [FORMULA] of players’ states and controls. Thus, while the system of PDE characterizing a Nash equilibrium for a MFG consists only of a Hamilton-Jacobi equation satisfied by the optimized value function [FORMULA] and a Fokker-Planck equation satisfied by the distribution of player states [FORMULA] , in the system corresponding to a MFGC, there is an additional fixed-point relation satisfied by the joint distribution [FORMULA] of states and controls. This variant of a mean field game was initially called an extended mean field game (see [25, 26]), but the terminology “mean field game of controls” is now standard, cf. [14]. Many papers have examined the asymptotic behavior of solutions to MFGs. For example, in [3, Section 3], the authors give some conditions under which MFG models can approach agent based models (ABMs) as the discount factor [FORMULA] becomes very large. This inspired the authors of [1] to examine the asymptotic behavior of a rescaled MFG system as [FORMULA] and [FORMULA] , and a recent paper (see [20]) obtained quantitative convergence rates in the case that [FORMULA] is fixed. See also [22] for related work. In [19, 49], the authors not only prove convergence as [FORMULA] but also analyze the precise rates of convergence. The papers [12, 13, 21] studied the long-time average of solutions to second-order MFG systems as the time horizon [FORMULA] for both local and nonlocal couplings, the long-time average of solutions to first-order MFG systems as [FORMULA] was studied in [2, 9, 16, 11], and the long-time average behavior of solutions to the master equation was studied in [15]. Finally, in the stationary setting, the papers [24, 38, 50] have investigated vanishing discount problems in first-order stationary MFG systems. Compared to traditional MFGs, MFGCs have received far less attention in the literature, but they have gained attention in recent years, with most of the results focusing on well-posedness. In 2022, Kobeissi proved the well-posedness of second-order MFGCs in the periodic setting and the whole space under both monotone and non-monotone couplings (see [40, 41]). More recent papers have investigated the well-posedness of MFGCs under various boundary conditions, invariance and state constraints, and even with fractional diffusion replacing standard diffusion (see [4, 6, 29, 31, 33, 34]). The associated master equation was also recently studied in [39, 45, 47]. Other noteworthy papers on special cases of MFGCs include [8, 17, 18, 28, 30, 32, 35, 36]. A block-encoding approach to the Segawa-Suzuki spectral mapping theorem We revisit the Segawa–Suzuki spectral mapping theorem for abstract Szegedy-type quantum walks from a block-encoding viewpoint. Retaining both eigenspaces of the involution underlying the chiral symmetry yields a natural two-by-two block representation in which the usual discriminant operator and its counterpart form the diagonal blocks. The non-endpoint spectral mapping theorem then follows from an elementary Schur decomposition, substantially simplifying the original proof by avoiding its invariant-subspace decomposition and approximate-eigenvector arguments. The same framework establishes the result for the spectrum, point spectrum, and Fredholm essential spectrum and gives a direct block-theoretic description of the endpoint inherited and birth eigenspaces. We illustrate the construction with a one-dimensional split-step quantum walk. 1. The Continuum Limit of the Deep Linear Network The Deep Linear Network (DLN) is a simple version of a Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) in which the activation function is the identity and the bias vector is the zero vector. We examine the behavior of the model when the number of weight matrices, which is finite in the original model, goes to infinity. We show that a plausible continuum limit is a dimensionally reduced version of the Yang-Mills equation on the torus, revealing an unexpected geometric interpretation of infinite-depth DLNs. While we do not prove this rigorously, it is a very pretty calculation. It also gives some insight into several features of the construction. We note that the choices of boundary conditions on the ends of the discrete series survive better in the continuum limit. Also, the regularizing functional which uses the moment map survives nicely in the continuum limit, whereas the regularizing functional using the size of approximating terms has no sensible limit. This surely is useful information for the choices we make in the finite-dimensional theory, and might also be useful in the more complicated MLP setting. 1. Unconstrained support points can leave a convex support Support points provide a practical and effective way to approximate a probability distribution by a small set of equally weighted representatives through energy-distance minimization. In many applications, the variables satisfy convex constraints that the representatives should also respect. We investigate whether unconstrained support points automatically satisfy such constraints and show that this is not guaranteed. We construct counterexamples using three planar observations, a density with full triangular support, and positive-definite matrix data admitting an indefinite optimal representative under the Frobenius norm. We also identify cases in which containment holds, establish stability under distributional perturbations, and quantify the objective cost of imposing a convex-hull constraint. For a fixed number of representatives and a positive population constraint gap, empirical configurations with vanishing global objective error eventually leave the sample convex hull almost surely. 1 Introduction and setup Support points provide a practical way to represent a probability distribution by a small set of equally weighted points chosen through energy-distance minimization (Mak and Joseph, 2018). Other representative-point methods include principal points, which minimize the expected squared distance to the nearest representative (Flury, 1990), and kernel herding (Chen et al., 2010). The energy distance used by support points is proportional to squared maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) for a suitable kernel (Sejdinovic et al., 2013; Muandet et al., 2017), connecting support points to kernel-based methods. Projected support points address high-dimensional data reduction (Mak and Joseph, 2017), while SPlit, Data Twinning, MMD quantisation over observed candidates and kernel thinning construct representative subsets of the observations (Joseph and Vakayil, 2022; Vakayil and Joseph, 2022; Teymur et al., 2021; Dwivedi and Mackey, 2024). Many sampling problems involve convex constraints, including sampling from convex bodies (Lovász and Vempala, 2006) and simulating normal distributions under linear restrictions (Botev, 2017). When support points are used to represent such distributions, it is natural to require that they respect the same constraints. Constraint Qualifications and Regularity Conditions for Nonlinear Constraint Systems Constraint qualifications (CQs) and regularity conditions (RCs) play a fundamental role in establishing global iteration and oracle complexity results for first-order methods on solving functional constrained optimization problems. Various conditions have been proposed and employed in the literature, with their validity established for different classes of applications. However, the use of different conditions across existing studies makes it difficult to directly compare their theoretical results and underlying assumptions. In this report, we systematically review several widely used CQs and RCs and investigate their relationships. In particular, we establish implications among these conditions and identify cases in which the implications are strict, thereby clarifying their relative strengths. This work aims to study the stochastic optimal control problems of controlled stochastic differential systems driven by both Brownian motions and fractional Brownian motions via dynamic programming principle. The stochastic Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation is obtained. Different from the classical case, the obtained stochastic Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation is a backward stochastic partial differential equation driven by both fractional Brownian motions and standard Brownian motions, whose solution is a pair of random fields. It is well known that Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman dynamic programming principle and Pontryagin’s maximum principle are the two most important methods to solve stochastic optimal control problems when the system is driven by Brownian motion (e.g. [FORMULA] in (1)). This work is to fill this gap to obtain a DPP in solving the optimal control problem [FORMULA] subject to the system (1). DPP was introduced by Bellman in the 1950s for deterministic optimal control problem. Combining with probability theory and It [FORMULA] ’s formula, DDP for stochastic optimal control problem and related Hamiltonian-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB, in short) equation have been extensively investigated. There are many research papers and books on this topic, among them we refer to [24, 5] and the references therein. To describe the long-range phenomenon in real-world, stochastic differential equations (SDEs, in short) driven by fractional Brownian motion and related control problems have recently been extensively studied. Some related works about SDEs driven by fractional Brownian motion are referred to [17, 2, 18, 12, 13, 6, 11]. For the control problem, Hu and Zhou[15] and Duncan and Pasik-Duncan [4] obtained the Markovian control for linear quadratic (LQ, in short) case. Hu and Peng [14] investigated backward stochastic differential equations (BSDEs in short) driven by fractional Brownian motions. For nonlinear control problems driven by fractional Brownian motion, the maximum principle has been largely studied. Han et al. [7] studied the maximum principle for general control system driven by fractional Brownian motion. The adjoint equation is a linear BSDEs driven by both fractional Brownian motion and the underlying standard Brownian motion. Buckdahn and Jing [1] investigated the control problem with mean-field. Sun [19] studied the control problem of nonconvex control. Zheng and Hu [25] studied partially observed stochastic control problem. Han and Li [8] studied the control problems driven by fractional noises in discrete-time version. But to the best of our knowledge, until now there is no any work concerning DPP for stochastic optimal control problems driven by fractional Brownian motions. Despite the long-standing success of the DPP in the classical Brownian (Markovian) setting, its extension to fractional noise has remained largely open due to the loss of the Markov property. By exploiting the structure of fractional Brownian motion and its underlying Brownian representation, we establish a rigorous dynamic programming framework and derive a stochastic HJB equation in the form of a backward stochastic partial differential equation driven jointly by fractional Brownian motion and standard Brownian motion. A verification theorem is further obtained, providing a precise characterization of optimal controls and clarifying the relationship between the dynamic programming approach and the stochastic maximum principle. As an application, we study an LQ optimal control problem of controlled systems driven by both Brownian motions and fractional Brownian motions. The value function is shown to admit a quadratic representation, and the optimal control is characterized explicitly through a backward stochastic Riccati equation. In contrast to the classical Markovian case, the resulting optimal control is adapted but generally non-Markovian, reflecting the intrinsic memory effect of fractional noise. The existence and uniqueness of solutions to the associated backward stochastic Riccati equation are also established, thereby completing the dynamic programming analysis for the linear–quadratic framework. Notice that throughout this paper the diffusion coefficient [FORMULA] is assumed to be independent of the control. On the other hand, from the viewpoint of the stochastic maximum principle, Han et al. derived necessary optimality conditions for controlled systems driven by fractional Brownian motion (see Theorem 5.7 of [7]). Yet their conditions include the constraint [FORMULA] , which essentially excludes any nontrivial control dependence in [FORMULA] . Therefore, both the DPP approach and the maximum principle face intrinsic difficulties in this setting. Consequently, the optimal control problem for fractional Brownian motion–driven systems with control-dependent diffusion coefficients is still an open problem. Here we present a simple example to show there may not exist an optimal control in the control dependent diffusion case, which suggests that we may need to impose significantly more conditions or more restricted admissible control space. A Parallel Adaptive Proximal ADMM for Linearly Constrained Separable Composite Optimization Problems We propose and analyze an adaptive proximal alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM), based on Jacobi-type updates, for linearly constrained separable nonconvex composite optimization problems. The objective consists of two block-separable functions, one continuously differentiable and weakly convex, and the other convex and Lipschitz continuous. The proposed method is adaptive to all problem parameters and allows inexact solutions of the block proximal subproblems. At each iteration, we solve all block subproblems in parallel, then apply a novel test to decide whether to update the Lagrange multiplier and/or the penalty parameter. Without any rank assumptions on the constraint matrices, we establish an [FORMULA] iteration-complexity bound for obtaining an approximate first-order stationary point. This matches the best-known complexity for cyclic proximal ADMM methods and improves the existing complexity of Jacobi-type schemes in this general nonconvex setting. Numerical experiments on a nonconvex quadratic program illustrate the proposed method’s computational benefits. 1 Introduction In this article, we provide the iteration-complexity analysis for the Parallel Adaptive Proximal Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers, referred to as P-Adapt-ADMM, when solving the linearly constrained, composite optimization problem where [FORMULA] is a proper closed convex function which is Lipschitz continuous on its compact domain, [FORMULA] is a continuously differentiable, weakly convex function on the domain of [FORMULA] , [FORMULA] is a linear operator, and [FORMULA] is a vector in the image of [FORMULA] . ADMM is an efficient block-decomposable first-order method for solving (1)–(1) (see e.g., the survey [1]). Two common strategies for updating the primal blocks are the Gauss–Seidel and Jacobi schemes, often referred to as cyclic and parallel updates, respectively. In the Gauss–Seidel scheme, the blocks are updated sequentially, each update using the latest values of the preceding blocks. In the Jacobi scheme, all blocks are updated from the information available at the start of the iteration, so the block subproblems can be solved simultaneously, and the new primal point is formed after all of them are completed. Their applications include image restoration, semidefinite programming, robust principal component analysis, phase retrieval, and matrix completion for the former (see, e.g., [11, 39, 34, 40, 41]), and exchange and consensus problems, graphical model selection, and multi-period optimal power flow for the latter (see, e.g., [5, 2, 14, 32]). For [FORMULA] , under the coefficient growth condition [FORMULA] , we prove that approximation at the order [FORMULA] is equivalent to membership in the parity-compatible Besov space [FORMULA] . Mere convergence under the same coefficient budget does not imply this regularity. For unconstrained approximation along a nested parameter sequence, a single ridge function gives a counterexample when [FORMULA] , whereas for [FORMULA] the endpoint Besov inverse conclusion follows from a Bernstein inequality under antipodal quasi-uniformity. The inverse conclusion is also recovered when the prescribed rate holds for two quasi-uniform parameter sequences whose union is antipodally separated. 1 Introduction The approximation theory of shallow neural networks seeks to quantify how the approximation error depends on the network width, the activation function, the regularity of the target, and the size of the representing coefficients. For Barron and variation-type spaces, dimension-independent rates are commonly obtained through probabilistic or greedy discretization arguments Jones (1992); Barron (1993); Barron (1994); DeVore and Temlyakov (1996); Bach (2017); Klusowski and Barron (2018); Siegel and Xu (2022a); Siegel and Xu (2022c); Siegel and Xu (2022b); Mhaskar and Mao (2023). For Sobolev classes, the rate instead reflects both smoothness and dimension Mhaskar (1993); Petrushev (1998); Pinkus (1999). These direct estimates give sufficient conditions for attaining a prescribed rate. The converse question—what regularity is forced by that rate—is subtler and is closely related to Bernstein inequalities, inverse approximation theorems, and the structure of neural-network approximation classes Siegel and Xu (2022c); Siegel and Xu (2023); Guo and Zhou (2020); E and Yu (2019); Bernstein et al. (2020); Huang et al. (2023). Spatial Token Interleaving and Two-Pass BP Decoding for Semantic Image TransmissionThanks: The code is available at https://github.com/Yifan-Usyd/STI-SemCom. Semantic error control coding (SECC) can correct the residual errors of a standard channel code with a foundation model that supplies a prior on the source content, but existing SECC schemes are designed for text. In this paper, we develop SECC for image transmission with spatial token interleaving and a two-pass belief propagation (BP) schedule. At the transmitter, a vector-quantized (VQ) tokenizer converts an image into tokens, which are transmitted in multiple low-density parity-check (LDPC) code blocks of fifth-generation New Radio (5G NR). In raster order, a block that BP fails to decode corrupts consecutive token rows, so the interleaver reorders the tokens such that adjacent tokens are carried by different blocks, without additional transmitted bits. At the receiver, after the first BP pass, token recovery fuses the token probabilities given by BP with the predictions of the autoregressive model Emu3-Gen, and the second BP pass decodes each block again with the fused distributions as priors on the information bits. On Kodak24 at 0.5 channel uses per pixel and a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of 0.15 dB, the second pass removes 92% of the token errors left by token recovery, and interleaving reduces the final token error rate by 88%. At medium to high SNR, the proposed receiver exceeds deep joint source–channel coding baselines with the same channel uses by at least 1.2 dB in peak signal-to-noise ratio. I Introduction Token communications [1] represent an image by discrete tokens and transmit them over a wireless link [2]. A vector-quantized (VQ) tokenizer [3] divides the image into a grid of patches and represents each patch by the index of the nearest entry of a learned codebook. Unlike deep joint source–channel coding (JSCC) [4, 5], which maps an image directly to channel symbols, token communications can protect the tokens with the channel codes of existing standards [6]. The data channels of fifth-generation New Radio (5G NR) use low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes and segment a transport block longer than 8448 bits into code blocks, which are encoded and decoded separately [7]. An image usually needs more bits than one code block. With the Emu3 tokenizer [8], which represents each [FORMULA] patch by one index, any image larger than about [FORMULA] pixels needs more than 8448 bits. Belief propagation (BP) decodes the code blocks separately, and near the BP threshold, it leaves residual errors in some blocks while decoding the others correctly. Semantic error control coding (SECC) [9] can correct such errors with a foundation model that supplies a prior on the source content, i.e., the probability of each source symbol given its context, while the channel code keeps its algebraic structure. Hao et al. [10] showed for text that multiple short codes with semantic correction outperform a single long code, because a decoding failure is confined to one block and the other blocks provide the context for its correction. For images, DiffCom [11] guides diffusion posterior sampling with the received signal, and text-guided token prediction reconstructs images whose tokens are protected by 5G NR polar codes [6]. Autoregressive (AR) models such as Emu3 [8] provide the prior for image tokens as the probability of each codebook index given the preceding tokens. The SECC schemes in [12, 13, 14, 10] are designed for text. For images, two problems remain, which concern the context of an erroneous token and the decoding of the model output. An image prior corrects an erroneous token from the tokens around it on the grid. In raster order, i.e., row by row, a code block carries consecutive token rows, e.g., about nine for a [FORMULA] image with the Emu3 tokenizer. A failed block then corrupts a band of the image, and the correctly decoded blocks provide context only for the token rows at the two edges of the band. Bit-interleaved coded modulation [15] permutes coded bits rather than tokens, and character interleaving for text [14] separates neighbors along one dimension only. Moreover, the model output is not decoded again in [12, 13, 6], where the model selects among the candidate paths of a list Viterbi decoder [12] or corrects the decoded symbols [13, 6], so the parity constraints of the code cannot correct the errors that the model leaves. In this paper, we propose spatial token interleaving and a two-pass BP schedule for semantic image transmission. At the transmitter, the Emu3 tokenizer converts an image into tokens. The interleaver reorders the tokens by a fixed permutation known to the receiver, without additional transmitted bits, such that adjacent tokens are carried by different blocks and thus have independent errors. The interleaved tokens are then transmitted in multiple 5G NR LDPC code blocks. At the receiver, after the first pass of BP decoding, token recovery fuses the token probabilities given by BP with the predictions of the Emu3-Gen model [8]. The second BP pass decodes each block again with the fused distributions as prior log-likelihood ratios (LLRs) of the information bits, so that the parity constraints correct the errors left by token recovery. On Kodak24 at 0.5 channel uses per pixel (CPP) and a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of 0.15 dB, the second pass removes 92% of these errors, and interleaving reduces the final token error rate (TER) by 88%. At medium to high SNR, the peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) of the proposed receiver exceeds those of SwinJSCC [5] and FAJSCC [16] by at least 1.2 dB at the same CPP. Related works. The Parisi formula for the Sherrington–Kirkpatrick model was established through the interpolation bound in [10] and the matching bound in [21]. Variational formulas were subsequently obtained for multi-species Sherrington–Kirkpatrick models in [16], the Potts spin glass in [18], and models with vector spins in [17]. For scalar spherical spins, the free-energy formula was proved for even [FORMULA] -spin interactions in [20] and extended to include odd [FORMULA] in [9]. The Parisi formula for multi-species spherical models was obtained in [2] under a convexity assumption on the covariance function. In these multi-species models, the covariance depends on one scalar overlap for each species. The covariance in (1.3) may instead depend on every entry of [FORMULA] . The closest earlier results involving full matrix overlaps concern several spherical systems coupled by a constraint on their mutual overlaps. A Guerra interpolation bound for these constrained systems was derived in [19]. The matching bound was proved in [13] for copies of spherical models with even [FORMULA] -spin interactions, and the corresponding Crisanti–Sommers formula was obtained in [12]. For these copies, the covariance is a sum of even powers of individual overlap entries. The tensor expansion (1.2) also allows products of different entries and need not be convex. Moreover, the free energies in those works retain the mass of a neighborhood of the prescribed self-overlap. Our normalized constraint measure separates this contribution from the constrained free energy, and the term [FORMULA] restores it in Theorem 1.1. The Hamilton–Jacobi approach provides a way to study such non-convex covariance functions. A bound by the solution of an infinite-dimensional Hamilton–Jacobi equation was proved in [14]. A critical-point representation of the limit was obtained in [6] under the assumption that the enriched free energy converges. Convexity of the initial condition turns this representation into a Hopf formula in the centered Ising setting of [5] and in the multi-species spherical setting of [7]. In the latter case, this convexity holds for every deterministic external field. Our proof follows this strategy at each fixed self-overlap, with convexity on the cone of matrix-valued paths supplied by Proposition 2.15. The variable self-overlap then requires the additional optimization over [FORMULA] . For compactly supported vector spins with a product reference measure, convergence without assuming convexity of the covariance was proved in [11]. The limit was subsequently identified in [4] by minimizing, over the empirical spin distribution, the sum of a relative entropy and a constrained Hamilton–Jacobi solution. These results apply directly to the product block models used in Section 3. Passing from these blocks to [FORMULA] requires the comparison in Lemma 3.2, since [FORMULA] is not a product over the columns. Non-convex multi-species Ising models with arbitrary deterministic external fields were treated in [3] by first fixing the magnetization of each species. The resulting initial condition is convex in the path, and optimizing over the magnetizations gives a variational formula over Brownian martingales. This shares with [4] and the present paper the strategy of identifying constrained free energies before optimizing over the constraint. The constraints are different: magnetization in [3], empirical spin distribution in [4], and the full self-overlap [FORMULA] here. In our setting, disintegration of the product surface measure gives the explicit cost [FORMULA] , while the constrained limit is the Hopf formula (1.12) with the explicit initial condition (1.9). The constrained free-energy formulas also have applications to ground states and the structure of their variational minimizers. For the coupled spherical models considered above, [1] derives a variational formula for the ground-state energy by taking the zero-temperature limit of the Crisanti–Sommers formula.
