Naturalization of Vinti’s intermediary orbit—or how to get rid of small divisors in Brouwer’s satellite solution A naturalization, in the sense of Deprit, of Vinti’s dynamical system makes the construction of a first order analytical satellite perturbation solution without critical divisors possible. The process gives hints on how to recast Brouwer’s classical solution in a form that is free from small divisors too. The functionality of classical perturbation solutions is in this way extended to the close vicinity of the critical inclination. The new analytical solution bears terms that may grow unbounded, but their negative effects do not disclose in time intervals in which this kind of solution may be useful in practice. 1 Introduction Simple analytical solutions to the artificial satellite problem dating back to the beginning of the space era (Sterne, 1958; Garfinkel, 1958; Vinti, 1959; Aksnes, 1965; Cid and Lahulla, 1969), still find application these days in spacecraft trajectory design or onboard orbit propagation (Gurfil and Lara, 2014; Duffy, 2016; Wright, 2016; Senecal, 2023). Beyond the practicable Keplerian orbits they take Earth’s oblateness effects into account, and are gathered under the general denomination of main problem intermediaries. Research on intermediary orbits continues today, either in the search for more significant models (Deprit, 1981; Hautesserres and Lara, 2017; Biria and Russell, 2018; Lara, 2019; Biria and Russell, 2020) or with the aim of refining computational algorithms for the efficient evaluation of existing intermediaries (Vinti, 1998; Wiesel, 2015; Biria, 2023; Shepperd, 2024). Effective intermediary orbits replicate the general features of the mean, perturbed dynamics (Aksnes, 1965). In particular, they succeed in detecting two different regions of orbits with direct and retrograde motion of the perigee, respectively. The limit case in which the rotation of the perigee vanishes establishes a boundary of “frozen orbits” separating these two regions. However, it is well known that minor effects of the main problem dynamics, or comparable small perturbations produced by the higher order harmonics of the gravitational potential, split the solution space into different regions of orbits with rotating and oscillating periapses (Petty and Breakwell, 1960; Struble, 1961; Kozai, 1961; Hagihara, 1961; Izsak, 1962). Since these little effects are ignored by main problem intermediaries, the approximations provided by intermediary orbits do not capture the behavior of orbits with oscillating periapses—a flaw that is commonly attributed to their integrable character (Deprit and Miller, 1988; Coffey et al., 1994; Lara, 2026). Simple analytical solutions exist too that model the Earth’s shape more accurately than main problem intermediaries can do, and hence better approach the actual dynamics (Garfinkel, 1959; Kozai, 1959; Brouwer, 1959). But because these perturbation solutions are based on the complete reduction of the perturbation Hamiltonian to its secular terms, they neither cover the full range of solutions. Therefore, their application is constrained to the case of orbits with rotating line of apsides, which is the only instance in which the use of averaging operations is justified for the argument of the periapsis (Tisserand, 1868). Since both kinds of orbits—with oscillating an rotating perigees—exist about the Earth, separate analytical solutions are needed to tackle each distinct orbital regime (Hori, 1960; Izsak, 1962; Garfinkel, 1966; Jupp, 1987). On the other hand, the small value of the Earth’s oblateness makes that the stripes separating the regions with direct and retrograde rotation of the perigee, where the orbits with oscillating perigees may exist, are certainly narrow. As a consequence, the main efforts in the development of operational tools have been devoted to the analytical modeling of orbits with rotating perigees (Hoots and Roehrich, 1980; Coffey and Deprit, 1982; Coffey and Alfriend, 1984; Solomon, 1991; Vallado et al., 2006; Fraysse et al., 2012; Lara et al., 2018). Remark that this fact in no way denies the interest of satellite missions based on orbits with oscillating perigees (Shapiro, 1996; Ulybyshev, 2009). An additional trouble regarding analytical perturbation solutions obtained by total Hamiltonian reduction, which is not shared by intermediary orbits, is the appearance in the formal solution of divisors that vanish at the so-called critical inclinations [FORMULA] . They ensue from the elimination of the long-period terms related to the perigee dynamics. Still, the singularity should not be much of worry because the region about the critical inclination is mostly filled with orbits with oscillating perigees, a case that, as it was already asserted, is not covered by these kinds of analytical solutions. But the appearance of critical divisors has undesired effects on orbits with rotating perigees too. To wit, the series representing the perturbation solution loose accuracy when approaching the critical inclination, even to the extent of turning their predictions into illusory (Brouwer, 1959). Protective limits for avoiding this sort of degradation in the convergence of the series are then stablished in practice. They roughly encompass inclinations in the interval ranging from 61 to 66 degree, or a corresponding interval of retrograde orbits (Coffey et al., 1996). The existence of elliptic orbits with oscillating perigees about the critical inclination is determined by the physical nature of the Earth’s potential. Accordingly, it has been claimed that the problematic divisors “cannot be removed by any method” (Hori, 1960). The general acceptance of this premise turned the concerns on the evaluation of analytical perturbation solutions just into an issue of computational nature (Solomon, 1991; Hoots et al., 2004). However, to our knowledge, Hori’s (1960) categorical statement lacks supporting mathematical evidence. Thus, the question of whether the inability to remove the critical divisors from rotating-perigee perturbation solutions is intrinsic to the problem, as claimed, or, on the contrary, is instead related to the widely accepted philosophy of the perturbation methods used at the time remains open. Developing additional efforts to further elucidate this point seems, therefore, sufficiently justified. In this regard, it is worth noting that intermediary solutions are free from offending divisors. Then, finding a transformation that, up to some truncation order, turns the original Hamiltonian into the Hamiltonian of a main problem intermediary would prevent the trouble of the small divisors. More generally, without constraining to the case of intermediary orbits, the transformation would operate a preparatory simplification on the original Hamiltonian (Deprit, 1981; Deprit and Ferrer, 1989; Deprit and Miller, 1989). In this way the simplified Hamiltonian would act as a surrogate for the artificial satellite problem that could be approached by perturbations without the trouble of the critical divisors. Finding this kind of proxy might notably improve the accuracy of classical perturbation models in predicting the behavior of rotating-perigee orbits in the vicinity of the critical inclination. The desired transformation certainly exists. The inspiration for finding it lays on a recent demonstration regarding Vinti’s dynamical system (Vinti, 1959; Izsak, 1960). Namely, that the models obtained from increasing truncations of Vinti’s expanded Hamiltonian in spherical harmonics give rise to corresponding, successive, radical reductions of the size of the region of elliptic orbits with oscillating perigees (Lara, 2026). Beyond usual applications of Vinti’s analytical solution as a common intermediary of the artificial satellite problem, such transformation would assign to Vinti’s dynamical system the role of a natural intermediary in the sense of Deprit (1981). In this naturalization process, an infinitesimal contact transformation is computed that turns a simplified gravitational model comprising only the perturbations due to the Earth’s second and fourth zonal harmonics into the first significative truncation of Vinti’s dynamical system. This kind of simplification does not affect formally the model, but simply removes one of the parameters by slightly tuning the value of the zonal harmonic coefficient of degree four. The answer is positive, but with some precisions regarding the way of achieving it. More precisely, a naturalization based on a higher-order truncation of Vinti’s dynamical system can certainly be applied. It would remove the critical divisors associated to the higher-order contribution of the even zonal harmonics, which appear both in the higher-order corrections and the higher-order secular terms. Needless to say, however, Vinti’s dynamical system does not consider the odd zonal harmonics of the Geopotential. The fact that the third zonal harmonic is free from small divisors in Brouwer’s first-order theory was crucial to applying the proposed naturalization. But this is not at all the case of higher-order theories, where the third zonal harmonic is affected of small divisors in the long-period corrections of the second order as well as in the third-order secular terms, cf. (Coffey et al., 1996). Additionally, the contribution of the fifth zonal harmonic, where critical divisors are concomitant to the long-period corrections as soon as at the first order, was ignored for the smallness of the Earth’s [FORMULA] coefficient. In these cases, it is remarked, the small divisors cannot be removed by a naturalization based on Vinti’s dynamical system. The fact that elimination of divisors related to the critical inclination cannot be generally extended with the naturalization process presented here does not mean that the removal cannot be achieved. However, it would require the nontrivial task of identifying all the undesired terms of the zonal potential that give rise to the small divisor issue. A possible way of doing that would be approaching by Lie transforms the removal of only the “nonessential” long-period terms, cf. (Lara, 2021). Then, the remaining, essential long-period terms—which would introduce the small divisors in the classical approach—would be directly removed by a contact transformation. The latter, of course, should spring unbounded corrections. On the other hand, because the composition of Lie transformations is canonical (Henrard, 1970), splitting (Deprit, 1981), composing (Lara, 2021; Lara et al., 2024), or altering the order in which the different Lie transformations are applied (Alfriend and Coffey, 1984; Cid et al., 1986; Abad et al., 2001) is mostly a matter the user’s choice. Therefore, once the harming terms have been identified, the perturbation theory could be approached after a preliminary simplification that introduces the opposite of the undesired terms. In this way, the undesired inclination-resonant terms would cancel out in the following construction of the perturbation theory by Lie transforms or by any other perturbation approach. Finally, it is worth mentioning that carrying out a preliminary simplification of the original Hamiltonian model based on the original “elimination of the parallax” (Deprit, 1981), or analogous simplifications inspired by it (Coppola and Palacián, 1994; Lara, 2019), could provide supplementary advantages regarding the implementation or evaluation of an operational code. In summary, the design of a general method for dealing properly with all the critical divisors that may appear either in a higher-order perturbation theory, or when dealing with higher-fidelity models including the effects of additional zonal harmonics, as well as its possible effectivity for accurately propagating orbits with circulating periapsis close to the critical inclination, is a nontrivial problem that requires a careful study of the mentioned possible lines of attack. While it falls out of the scope of the current investigation, the topic is of undeniable interest, and could be approached as future research. 6 Conclusions That the naturalization of Vinti’s dynamical system can be used to remove annoying divisors related to the critical inclination of [FORMULA] from classical, first-order, analytical perturbation solutions, has been demonstrated. The technique is inspired by Deprit’s original naturalization of common intermediaries of the main problem of the artificial satellite, and shares analogous merits and drawbacks. In particular, the proposed infinitesimal transformation bears secular, as well as mixed secular-periodic terms. Undeniably, this is a weak point of such naturalization. However, that the unbounded terms are confined to the second order of the Earth’s oblateness coefficient is certainly good news, as it is also the fact that these kinds of terms do not corrupt the transformation of the semimajor axis. Moreover, beyond Vinti’s dynamical system, the naturalization has been polished so that it only begets mixed secular-periodic terms, thus further delaying the appearance of harmful effects. In this sense, the new approach acts as a typical medical remedy. Namely, while the medicine is intended to fix a major health issue (small divisors), it may also cause adverse reactions (mixed terms) as a minor side effect of the healing. That existing analytical perturbation solutions based on total Hamiltonian reduction do not cover the case of orbits with oscillating perigees is well known. It is also the case of the new approach. However, because the new solution smooths the mean phase space close to the boundary separating the regions of rotating- and librating-perigee orbits, it avoids the usual lack of convergence of the series representing the long-period oscillations close to the critical inclination. Hence it better approaches the actual dynamics in that region. Needless to say, this is true only in the times in which the effects of the mixed terms remain buried by the errors stemming from the unavoidable truncation of perturbation solutions. That the proposed approach is constrained to the particular theories discussed (first order, and dealing only with the more significant harmonics of the Earth’s gravitational potential) stems from the physical nature of Vinti’s dynamical system. Possible avenues for extending the method to the case of zonal models of higher fidelity, or to progress to higher orders of the perturbation approach, have been outlined. However, devising a general procedure for identifying the inclination resonant terms of an arbitrary truncation of the zonal potential does not seem a trivial task. If considered of practical application, it would deserve further separate efforts. Introduction An additively idempotent semiring is an algebra whose addition is a semilattice operation and whose multiplication is associative and distributes over addition on both sides. Such algebras are also called semilattice-ordered semigroups. Examples include tropical semirings, semirings of relations, and endomorphism semirings of semilattices; see [10, 14]. Throughout the paper we use the signature [FORMULA] without constants. Thus an identity or zero element of an algebra, when present, is not named in the signature. The finite basis problem and the structure of subvariety lattices are two basic questions in the study of semiring varieties. For semigroups, these questions have a long history; see the survey of Volkov [22]. In the semiring setting, the interaction between the two operations leads to further difficulties. Dolinka constructed a nonfinitely based finite semiring [5], developed criteria for inherent nonfinite basability [7], and studied related examples and endomorphism semirings [8, 9]. Jackson, Ren and Zhao [11] subsequently showed that nonfinite basability can occur even when the multiplicative semigroup has a finite identity basis. Several classes of semiring varieties admit explicit structural descriptions. Polin [15] studied minimal semiring varieties. Subvariety lattices or term normal forms have been described for ordered bands and commutative multiplicatively idempotent semirings [13, 4]. Other classifications concern varieties generated by two-element ai-semirings [21] and commutative ai-semiring varieties satisfying power identities [19]. The finite basis problem has also been studied systematically for three-element semirings [25], for several classes of four-element semirings [17, 24, 18], and for extensions of small nonfinitely based examples [23]. Subvariety lattices can also be large: Dolinka [6] constructed an interval of semiring varieties of cardinality continuum. A limit variety is a nonfinitely based variety all of whose proper subvarieties are finitely based. Ren, Jackson, Zhao and Lei [16] constructed limit varieties of ai-semirings using flat extensions of groups and a combinatorial example. They also proved existence results for further limit varieties. Pure Spinor Factorization of Belinski–Zakharov Solitons and Regular Gravitational InstantonsThanks: Email: steffen.aksteiner@gmail.com. We show that the Belinski–Zakharov soliton construction factorizes into signed Pfaffian tau-functions, revealing a pure-spinor description of the metric and its regularity conditions. We derive analytic restrictions on the integral rod data, prove uniqueness for the asymptotically flat balance problem at fixed rod structure and periods, and give a conditional criterion for global existence. Combining these results with exhaustive enumeration of the admissible data and rigorous existence certificates, we construct a catalogue of regular asymptotically flat solutions representing 356 rod-word classes through twelve turning points, and 52 isolated regular asymptotically locally flat solutions through eight turning points. Analytic positivity and smooth-completion results establish regularity beyond the finite numerical solve. Based on this catalogue, we investigate two organizations of the solution space: generalized rank-two root systems and compositions of simpler endpoint geometries. The endpoint composition rules reproduce exactly all retained asymptotically flat words through twelve turning points. 1. Introduction A gravitational instanton is a complete oriented Ricci-flat Riemannian four-manifold with finite curvature energy. For an effective isometric two-torus action, the boundary intervals of the orbit space record the circles that collapse. These intervals are called rods; their endpoints are turning points, or nuts. A primitive integral vector specifies each collapsing circle. The ordered vectors encode topology, whereas their normalization determines the cone angles. The central question is which rod configurations admit smooth Ricci-flat realizations and how the resulting families of gravitational instantons are organized. The discovery of the Chen–Teo instanton [8] showed that the regular asymptotically flat (AF) solutions extend beyond the Euclidean Kerr family, including its Schwarzschild limit. It disproved the proposed Riemannian analogue of black-hole uniqueness and opened the problem of describing a larger moduli space. Li and Sun subsequently proved the existence of an infinite sequence of AF toric instantons with arbitrarily many turning points [20]; beyond the Kerr and Chen–Teo members, these metrics are non-Hermitian. Teo gave an explicit construction of the four-turning-point member, reducing the remaining balance condition to a quintic equation [26]. The present work seeks the structure beyond this sequence. We derive restrictions on the possible rod data, construct a certified catalogue of regular solutions, and use it to test two descriptions of the moduli space: one through root arrangements and polygon walks, the other through compositions of endpoint geometries. The Belinski–Zakharov (BZ) method constructs metrics from finitely many spectral poles and charge parameters [5, 6]. Twistor theory describes the same field equations through a rational matrix on the symmetry axis, called the patching matrix [27, 13]. Harmonic-map methods instead start from prescribed rods and give a canonical metric, generally with conical singularities [19, 20]. Two recent representation results make the finite algebraic approach particularly significant. Dunajski, Mason and Tod give a complete twistor representation of toric gravitational instantons with asymptotically locally flat or asymptotically locally Euclidean ends. They construct the rational patching matrices recursively and recover the associated metrics by linear algebra [12]. Andersson, Dahl and Nilsson prove that simply connected toric instantons with AF or asymptotically locally flat (ALF) ends and a finite positive number of turning points admit a flat-seed BZ representation [4]. An ALF end has a circle of bounded length at infinity; precise conventions are given below. These results reduce geometric classification to finite data, but the cone-balance conditions still have to be solved.
