Software Engineering (cs.SE): “We Used It Anyway”: Low Trust and High Adoption of Large Language Models in Requirements Engineering Education Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) are reshaping how students approach Software Engineering activities, particularly those centered on textual artifacts. This paper reports on the experience of integrating a non-restrictive LLM use within a first-year Master’s course in Software Engineering, in which students completed a semester-long Software Engineering project divided in a Requirements Engineering (RE) phase and a software testing phase. Following the completion of the RE phase of the project, we administered a 12-question survey to 43 students to investigate which LLM tools they used, for which activities, how they evaluated AI-generated outputs, and how they envisioned the role of LLMs in future Software Engineering curricula. Our findings show that LLM use was nearly universal among respondents and concentrated primarily on text-intensive activities such as use-case narratives, consistency checking, brainstorming, and refinement of existing artifacts. Despite this widespread adoption, most students perceived AI-generated outputs as inferior to their own work, frequently reporting issues related to incorrect or incomplete content, mismatches with course-specific conventions, over-engineering, and limitations in diagram generation. Nevertheless, students continued to rely extensively on LLM as a reviewer, critic, and productivity aid rather than as a fully autonomous artifact generator. We also observe that students’ choice of models was strongly influenced by access to premium subscriptions available for free for student accounts, highlighting the role of economic accessibility in shaping educational AI ecosystems. The results suggest that the most significant challenge in the adoption of LLMs within Requirements Engineering education is not whether students use these tools, but whether they possess the skills required to critically evaluate, contextualize, and correct its outputs. 1 Introduction Recent years have witnessed the emergence and diffusion of freely accessible Large Language Models (LLMs), impacting significantly how students work in higher education. These systems can, in fact, produce extended and plausible textual artifacts on most topics and for most of the assignments that are administered to the students. In Software Engineering courses, many Requirements Engineering (RE) assignments are fundamentally textual and require the production of largely natural language-based documents (e.g., requirements documents, use case narratives, glossaries). They involve the translation of domain knowledge and stakeholder intent into structured textual and graphical artifacts. making them very plausible targets for LLM assistance [17] [18]. However, empirical studies have also shown that LLMs can be an effective support tool for text-intensive tasks such as brainstorming or drafting, while at the same time presenting relevant issues such as lack of domain understanding, inconsistencies, and a tendency to hallucinate when asked to generate graphical, context-dependent artifacts [17]. RE activities are highly context-dependent, and a requirements document (for both real and simulated systems) must reflect stakeholder perspectives, constraints, and conventions that might be unknown to a general-purpose LLM. At the same time, LLMs remain a tool that future Software Engineers must properly understand, being aware of the risks coming from a superficial utilization; it is of paramount importance to integrate traditional SE courses with guidance on how to use LLMs to assist SE tasks. Despite the rapid growth of empirical research on LLMs in computer science and engineering education in general [13] [14], few works have examined how students use them within a structured, multi-deliverable software engineering project. This paper presents an experience report gathered within a master’s course in Software Engineering, through the administration of a survey to 43 students who had completed the requirements engineering phase of a semester-long group project. The survey aimed at collecting data on tool choice, task coverage, supported activities, output quality, model comparison strategies, and proposal for future AI integration in the course. The goal of this study is not to mandate a policy on LLM utilization or adoption in Software Engineering courses, but rather to interpret the natural utilization of LLMs that emerged spontaneously among students when tasked with traditional requirements engineering tasks. The final objective of the analysis is to gather and report actionable recommendation for curriculum and project design for SE courses. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work on LLM adoption in engineering education and on LLMs in requirements engineering. Section 3 describes the course, the project structure, and the survey design. Section 4 presents the results, which we discuss in Section 5. The lessons learned from the study are presented in Section 6, and Section 7 analyzes the threats to the study’s validity. Lastly, Section 8 draws conclusions and outlines the next steps we plan to undertake following the survey. 2 Background and Related Work Prior work has extensively explored students’ perceptions of LLMs across generic higher education contexts, highlighting a combination of strong perceived utility and persistent concerns regarding ethics, trust, and educational impact. Noroozi et al. investigated students’ perceptions of LLMs in the context of peer feedback activities [7], finding that while only 44% of students actively used LLMs, most participants still perceived the technology as moderately or very helpful for low-level writing tasks; concerns were however expressed regarding inaccurate information, unreliable citations, and potential reduction of learning opportunities. Similarly, Maxwell et al. examined demographic differences in student perceptions of LLMs across a large-scale survey involving 482 higher education students [6], revealing widespread adoption and high levels of comfort with LLMs for both general and academic purposes, with reported improvements in productivity, support to academic success, albeit with similar concerns to those raised by the work by Noroozi et al., while also highlighting demographic differences impacting LLM perception. Another relevant contribution is provided by Chan and Zhou, who developed an Expectancy-Value Theory (EVT)-based instrument to investigate how students’ perceptions influence their intention to use LLMs in higher education [5], finding a strong positive correlation between perceived LLM value and willingness to use such a tool for academic purposes, together with perceived drawbacks such as ethical concerns and potential negative consequences negatively impacting intention to use LLMs. Daher et al. explored higher education students’ perceptions of LLM tools across cognitive, social, affective, and behavioral dimensions [8], and found that students described LLM systems as helpful, motivating, and capable of increasing their confidence. Narrowing the focus to Software and Requirements Engineering (RE), using Large Language Models in education introduces both promising opportunities and important challenges. Students and educators are increasingly exploring how tools like ChatGPT can support the teaching and learning of core RE competencies, and these tools have demonstrated particular value in enhancing brainstorming activities and helping students understand complex problems from multiple perspectives, thereby providing more realistic views of underlying complexities in real-world requirements engineering tasks [11]. However, the adoption of LLMs in RE education requires careful pedagogical design to maintain learning integrity and skill development. Research shows that while students appreciate AI’s efficiency in generating requirements and its ability to accelerate development processes, they simultaneously recognize the critical need for human oversight to ensure accuracy and quality [10]. A hybrid approach that combines AI-generated and manually crafted requirements has proven most effective, balancing artificial intelligence’s advantages with essential human insights and domain expertise. Additionally, educators must address practical challenges such as students’ difficulties in creating effective prompts and the time-consuming process of refining AI-generated outputs to meet curriculum standards. To maximize educational value, institutions implementing generative AI in RE courses should establish clear frameworks for responsible tool use, emphasizing how LLMs can serve as a pedagogical partner that enhances rather than replaces the critical thinking and analytical skills that define professional requirements engineering practice [9]. Extensive research has been performed regarding requirements engineering tasks that can be automated with LLMs. Hemmat et al. reviewed the application of Large Language Models in Software Requirements Engineering [4], showing that LLMs are increasingly employed in requirements elicitation, specification, modeling, validation, and quality assurance tasks such as generating UML diagrams, refining requirements, supporting traceability, and automating consistency checking. The paper also analyses optimization strategies such as prompt engineering, fine-tuning, and LoRA adaptation, while highlighting challenges related to hallucinations, poor domain understanding, and structural inconsistencies in generated artifacts. Arora et al. analyzed the role of LLMs across the complete requirements engineering lifecycle [2], discussing how they can support elicitation, specification, and analysis; additional focus is also given to validation activities, while also warning that current LLMs remain limited by contextual understanding, explainability issues, hallucinated outputs, and difficulties in handling complex project-specific constraints. Khan et al. identified elicitation, modeling, prioritization, specification, validation, and traceability as the most common application domains for LLMs in Requirements Engineering[3] and reported that GPT-based systems dominate the current literature because of their effectiveness in processing natural language artifacts and generating structured documentation, while also discussing common prompting strategies, evaluation methodologies, and limitations such prompt sensitivity, lack of standardized benchmarks, and difficulties in evaluating the semantic correctness of generated requirements artifacts. A specific research thread focused on LLMs for RE activities (LLM4RE) concerns the automated generation of graphical modeling artifacts starting from natural language descriptions. Cámara et al. [17] performed one of the earliest studies on this trend, exploring the capabilities of ChatGPT when applied to Unified Modeling Language (UML) tasks, finding that the tool struggled on multiple sides, with syntactic deficiencies, inconsistencies in the response format, and scalability limitations when producing structural models. Ferrari et al. [21] also investigated ChatGPT’s ability to generate diagrams, focusing on UML sequence diagrams, and identified key challenges such as needing iterative, RE-focused prompting strategies and requiring a way to express tacit domain knowledge when communicating with agents. Similar conclusions were reached by Wang et al. [18], who found that LLMs can be effective assistants, while at the same time presenting limitations that require careful human intervention. Our prior work also explored this research area, exploring the ability of LLM agents to generate UML class diagrams in RE-oriented modeling exercises, proving that LLM agents have a good understanding of modeling rules and conventions, while at the same time presenting significantly worse ability to represent domain constraints [19]; a subsequent study compared multiple LLM agents and observed that certain LLMs are more suited for different quality aspects, and that detailed prompting strategies can improve diagram quality [20]. 3 Methodology In this section we document the structure of the course and the course-long project, and the survey that was administered to the students. The study was conducted in the context of a Software Engineering course offered in the first year of a Master’s degree programme in Computer Engineering at the Polytechnic University of Turin. The course is mandatory for students in the Computer Engineering orientation and is taken in the second semester of the programme. The background of the students is typically a bachelor’s degree in Computer Engineering or closely related fields, but with limited experience in professional software development projects. The course is organized around lectures on SE principles and is paired with a non-mandatory course-long project, which is evaluated for 10 points out of the total grade’s 33. The number of enrolled students in the course ranges between 300 and 400 yearly, divided into two separate editions of the course, taught respectively in Italian and English. The course’s topics aim to provide a general overview of the software engineering pipeline, starting from requirements engineering activities in its first half before moving to testing techniques in the latter part; both halves see a combination of theory and practice introduced through the creation of an example platform for music sharing: in the first half of the course, when a new topic is introduced during theory lectures, the corresponding part of the requirement document is produced in practical sessions. In the second half, the teachers provide an implementation of the platform that is then used to conduct live examples of how to apply different testing techniques. The course project consisted of the design and specification of Participium, a citizen-participation web platform for supporting the reporting and management of urban issues (geo-localized reports, map/table views, lifecycle management, notifications, and administrative dashboards). The system was conceived as an open-source platform potentially reusable by other municipalities, requiring students to reason about both citizen-facing interaction workflows and internal operational processes of public administrations. The course project is divided into two sequential phases. The first phase, covering roughly the first 6 weeks of the course, covers the activities related to the Requirements Engineering lifecycle, which are referred to as tasks: I) Task 1: Project Management: Product Breakdown Structure (PBS), Work Breakdown Structure (WBS), Gantt chart, and risk register; II) Task 2: Requirements Engineering: Stakeholder analysis, context diagram, user personas, user stories, and functional/non-functional requirements; III) Task 3: Use Cases: Use-case diagram, narrative descriptions for each use case, and a traceability table linking use cases to functional requirements; IV) Task 4: Architecture and Design: Class diagram and deployment diagram. The description of the Participium platform given to the students at the beginning of Phase 1 as the context for the project is available online, together with the reference solution for the first phase, provided to the students after the deadline for the submission of their deliverables111https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.32287281. The second phase is instead split into six assignments that introduce testing concepts by asking students to define test suites on a demo platform developed by course instructors, with a new assignment each week and a platform update, to simulate a real-world scenario where students act as testers for an application developed by other developers. Groups of 4–5 students work on a common software project specification throughout all phases of the project. The groups are constructed algorithmically in order to maximize intra-group and inter-group diversity, by adopting the algorithm described by Torchiano et al. [1]. Each group of students is assigned a private repository hosted on the versioning system used in the course (namely, GitLab). All task submissions are done by pushing to the main branch of the repository, which is forked by a master repository curated by the instructors, where the instructions for each task are pushed weekly. Task submissions are then reviewed by the instructors and returned along with formative feedback (in the form of textual comments on the deliverables) before the next task begins. The survey comprised 12 questions, a mix of closed-ended (single-choice and multiple-choice) and open-ended items, grouped into thematic blocks related to the following Research Questions (RQs): RQ1: Which models are used the most by students? RQ2: In which tasks are LLMs used the most? RQ3: What is the perceived quality of the LLM agents’ output? RQ4: How do students envision the integration of LLMs in SE curricula? The full questionnaire is reported in Table 1. The survey was hosted on the Google Form platform and administered in English to both editions of the course. Open-ended responses were analyzed using open coding, a qualitative method rooted in grounded theory in which codes are assigned inductively from the data, grouped into themes, and then revised through a second pass to improve consistency [15] [16]. The open-coding procedure was performed by one of the authors of the manuscript, with a second pass involving all authors for checking the assignment of codes. Each open-ended question was coded independently, using a per-question theme set; a response could be assigned only one theme per question. Closed-ended responses were summarized by frequency counts. 4 Results and Discussion In this section, we report the results of the questionnaire administered to the course students. The survey received 43 respondents (28 male, 14 female, 1 non-binary/prefer not to say), with ages ranging from 21 to 32 (median 23). LLM use during Phase 1 was essentially universal: all 43 respondents reported using at least one tool. In Figure. 1(a) we report the adoption of different tools. Gemini (Google) was by far the most widely used tool (33 respondents, 77%), followed by ChatGPT/OpenAI (19, 44%) and Claude by Anthropic (13, 30%). Smaller numbers reported using Copilot (3), Mistral/Le Chat (2), Perplexity (1), and Deepseek (1). These counts allow for multiple tools per respondent. Figure 1(b) shows the frequencies of the codes applied to the answers of question 1.2. 7 of 22 respondents who used multiple tools mentioned that the decisive factor was the availability of a Pro subscription plan offered free to student accounts, with several explicitly noting that they would have preferred Claude or another tool had access been equivalent. This finding aligns with prior observations that students’ tool choices in naturalistic settings are strongly conditioned by economic constraints [13]. Only 10 of the 22 respondents cited quality of reasoning or output as their primary reason for preferring one tool over another. Notably, Claude was cited most frequently when quality was the stated criterion: respondents who preferred it described it as less dispersive, more critical, and less prone to simply agreeing with whatever the user proposed. Two respondents valued different tools for different sub-tasks, using one for ideation and another for final consistency checks, adopting a pattern of tool orchestration that suggests a more sophisticated appropriation of LLM capabilities. Answer to RQ1: The most widely adopted LLM tool by students was Gemini by Google (77% of the respondents). Tool selection is mostly conditioned by perceived quality of the LLM outputs and economic reasons (i.e., availability of free student licenses). Table 2 reports the distribution of AI use across the four project tasks. LLM use was not uniform: it was largely used in Task 3 (Use Cases) (36/43, 84%), which was also identified as the task with the highest LLM use (22/40, 55%). In Task 2 (Requirements Engineering), LLM agents were used by 32 out of 43 students (74%), followed by Task 1 (25/43, 58%) and Task 4 (18/43, 42%). The open coding of question 2.3 reveals the predominance of LLM use in Task 3, which required students to define multiple use cases and write a structured description covering involved actors and related stakeholders, goals, preconditions, primary scenario and exceptional flows, and post-conditions. The large amount of text, the structured format, and the importance of consistency between the graphical representation and the narrative all influenced AI use in this task. The most common motivation (11 respondents) was consistency and completeness checking, for goals such as verifying omissions or ensuring consistency with earlier deliverables. The second most common theme (10 respondents), the high volume of text to produce, also points out to the fact that students prefer using LLMs to automate tedious and wordy activities. Other, less common, motivations such as brainstorming and idea generation (6) and lack of domain or contextual knowledge (5) indicate that students interact with LLMs to enumerate details that they may have missed, to compensate for the unfamiliarity with real-world software development practices that the project implicitly required, or to provide contextual information connected with the municipality-related aspects of the project. This use of LLMs as a proxy for professional experience reflects a legitimate pedagogical gap in courses that ask students to reason about industrial software systems without giving them adequate domain understanding. At the same time, it poses the risk of students trying to acquire domain knowledge that could not be present in the training set of general-purpose LLMs, leading in the worst case to hallucinated responses. Question 2.4 allowed multiple selections from a predefined list of alternatives. The results (Figure 2(b)) reveal a strong concentration on Checking/critiquing own work (32 mentions, 74%), indicating that students preferred embedding LLMs in their work pipelines to check the outcome of their autonomous work instead of using them to generate deliverables from scratch. This trend is confirmed by the high number of mentions for Brainstorming/initial ideas (29, 47%), Searching examples/inspiration (17, 40%), and Understanding the task (15, 35%). The emerging picture shows workflows that are better aligned with educational goals than pure delegation by preserving cognitive engagement with the tasks. Answer to RQ2: The answers to the survey reveal that LLM tools were mostly used in tasks requiring text-intensive and repetitive activities. The most mentioned reasons for using LLMs were checking the students’ own work and brainstorming initial ideas, suggesting the use of such tools as reviewers rather than deliverable generators. Question 3.1 was defined to understand whether the students perceived LLM output as worse than their own work. 34 of 43 (79%) reported that AI-generated output was worse than what they would have produced themselves, while only 4 (9%) reported the opposite. This finding is non-trivial: despite a widespread perception that AI output was inferior, the students still made extensive use of the LLM tools. This finding pairs well with the utilization of LLMs as checkers and generators of first ideas to be later refined. Perceived inferiority of the LLM output, in fact, does not necessarily translate to deliverable inferiority if the students invest their time in correction after a first draft generation. The open coding of question 3.2 reveals five distinct failure modes, summarized in Figure 5. The most frequent, incorrect or incomplete content (9 mentions out of 27 valid responses), covers cases in which AI output was factually wrong, hallucinated, or missing key project-specific elements. Several respondents described AI suggesting actor-to-use-case connections that violated the conventions taught in the course, or generating user stories for features that were not part of the defined project scope. The second most frequent failure mode, style and formatting mismatch (7 mentions), is analytically distinct from content incorrectness: in this case, the LLM output was not semantically wrong but did not conform to the specific format, naming conventions, or structural templates that the course prescribed. This mismatch can only be addressed with extensive prompt engineering (e.g., few-shot prompting by providing examples, providing detailed descriptions) that introduces the course-specific conventions; in fact, multiple students reported that the AI tools were able to follow instructions correctly when supplied with explicit requests and format specifications. Excessive detail or over-engineering (4 mentions) and diagram generation limitations (4 mentions), the following failure modes, reflect the tendency of LLMs to produce artifacts that are more complex than required, requesting selective reduction of the generated outputs, as well as the fundamental limitation of current LLMs in producing correct, immediately usable diagram representations: even structured formats such as PlantUML or JSON often required significant manual correction. This is consistent with the finding in the broader LLM4RE literature that diagram generation remains one of the weakest capabilities of current agents [23]. Slightly more than half of respondents (22/43, 51%) compared the output of two or more models for at least some tasks; Figure 6 shows the frequencies of codes for the answer to question 3.4. Personal judgment based on course knowledge was by far the dominant selection strategy (11/20 respondents who provided a substantive answer), showing that most students did not accept AI output passively but applied their own understanding to evaluate it; it also implies that the quality of AI-model selection is bounded by the student’s own conceptual understanding. The secondary strategies, quality comparison between models (5 respondents) and manual merging of outputs (3 respondents), suggest that some students adopted more sophisticated multi-model workflows: using one model’s output to critique or correct another’s (a practice similar to the paradigm defined in literature as llm-as-a-judge [22]), or selectively combining the best elements of each. Answer to RQ3: The majority of students perceived that the quality of the output generated by LLMs was inferior to their own efforts. The most frequent motivations for subpar output by LLMs were incorrect or incomplete content and errors in style and formatting. Slightly more than half of the respondents performed comparisons between the outputs of different models, both based on personal judgment and using other LLMs as judges. A large majority of respondents (33/43, 77%) believed that LLMs could be usefully integrated into the course, with only 6 (14%) disagreeing and 4 (9%) unsure. The open coding of question 4.2 produced seven themes, whose frequencies are shown in Figure 4. The most frequent theme in the answers is the requirement to teach prompt engineering and critical evaluation of AI output (7 respondents). This answer can be considered as a direct consequence of the failure modes mentioned previously. Students recognize that obtaining useful AI output in a course-specific context requires skills that they currently lack and that the course does not teach. This answer entails important consequences for the management of curricula at higher education institutions, since prompt engineering is a topic of advanced courses in the second year of the master’s programme, but it might be beneficial to cover the topic before any Software Engineering course. This is also a valuable insight in the usual debate about the use of LLMs in education: rather than arguing about whether AI should be permitted or not, students are requesting that the curriculum help them use it more effectively and more critically. The second theme is using AI to accelerate repetitive or verbose tasks (6 respondents), in line with the dominant motivation pattern identified in the answer to RQ2. Students view the text-generation capability of AI as a legitimate tool for managing the workload of documentation-intensive tasks, provided the output is carefully reviewed. The theme of AI to support understanding of unfamiliar contexts (4 respondents) sees students describing using AI as a substitute for the domain expertise they lacked and points to a possible integration strategy in which AI is positioned explicitly as a contextualization tool rather than a generation tool. Finally, two respondents proposed an empirical comparison approach: having students produce artifacts with and without AI assistance, then comparing and discussing the results in class, to expose the gap between AI capability and course-standard quality and serving both as an AI literacy activity and as an empirical experimentation about requirements engineering in practice. Answer to RQ4: A large majority of the respondents expressed the desire for a better integration of LLMs in the course, principally in the form of classes about efficient prompt engineering techniques, or as a companion tool to support repetitive and verbose tasks in student projects. 5 Discussion Our findings are largely consistent with prior work on LLM adoption in higher education and RE education, while also revealing several RE-specific characteristics emerging from project-based workflows. Similar to previous studies, our respondents perceived LLMs as highly useful for productivity, brainstorming, and supporting writing-intensive activities, despite simultaneously expressing concerns regarding reliability, correctness, and excessive dependence on AI-generated outputs. In the specific context of RE education, our findings further reinforce the importance of human oversight and critical evaluation in AI-assisted RE tasks, while also finding that students naturally integrated LLMs into complex projects, primarily using them as reviewers, consistency checkers, and contextualization tools rather than as autonomous artifact generators. Several of the failure modes directly reflect the technical limitations highlighted in recent LLM4RE literature reviews. The strong influence of free premium subscriptions on tool adoption and the widespread use of multi-model comparison workflows emerged as distinctive aspects of our study that are currently underexplored in existing Requirements Engineering education literature. 6 Lessons Learned In this section, we discuss the main lessons learned from our experience, to provide actionable guidelines for course instructors and researchers in the field: LLMs are a baseline tool within student projects: All the respondents used at least one LLM during their project activities without any prohibition or encouragement. Course designs that assume no LLM use is done are misaligned with actual student practice and do not guarantee better alignment with the intended learning outcomes. Acknowledging and guiding the use of LLMs is more productive than ignoring or prohibiting it. The highest-valued AI activities in RE are review and brainstorming: The most satisfactory use of LLMs involved independent artifact production, preliminary brainstorming, or validation, correction and completion of drafts, preserving student cognitive engagement while leveraging LLM agents’ capacity for consistency checking. Instructors could formalize the LLM-assisted workflow by designing tasks involving an AI-assisted review phase. Course-specific context is a barrier to useful AI output: Students are aware that LLMs are not capable of understanding what the course requires, even by using examples and providing additional material. Instructors can address this by publishing course-specific AI prompt templates, or by making the prompt engineering phase an explicit and assessable part of the project. Prompt engineering and critical evaluation should be explicitly taught: The most common student proposal for LLM integration was to teach them how to write effective prompts and how to evaluate AI output critically. A short dedicated module covering prompt design, output evaluation criteria and hallucination detection strategies, organized early in computer engineering curricula, would provide a skill directly transferable to professional settings. Access inequality distorts tool choice and potentially learning outcomes: The dominance of Gemini as the preferred tool was driven primarily by free Pro subscriptions for student accounts, not by perceived quality, while students who had access to paid subscriptions had better-quality AI assistance. This differential is an equity concern that educators and institutions should address through, for example multi-model institutional licences. 7 Threats to Validity We report the threats to the validity according to the classification of Feldt and Magazinius [12]. Internal validity. The open coding was performed by a single researcher; a second pass was conducted to improve consistency, but does not substitute formal inter-rater agreement procedures. The survey was administered after all four tasks were performed, introducing recall bias for earlier tasks. Construct validity. Self-reported data on AI use intensity and output quality are subject to social desirability bias: students may have underreported use, or framed it more critically to avoid negative instructor judgment, despite LLM use not being discouraged. We did not collect data on the actual content of prompts or AI outputs, limiting the depth of possible analysis of AI-human interaction. External validity. The study is based on a single class at a single institution, in a specific national and institutional context. Gemini’s prevalence reflects a free student subscription programme that may not exist elsewhere. The findings should be treated as exploratory and hypothesis-generating rather than as generalizable claims. 8 Conclusion In this paper, we reported the results of a preliminary experience integrating LLMs into the RE phase of a master’s Software Engineering course project. We found that students used LLMs extensively, due to the verbose and time-consuming tasks, but also perceived the produced output as inferior to their own work in most cases. Several failure modes were also reported by students, such as style and format mismatches, hallucinated content, over-engineering, and diagram generation limitations; we argue that the reason behind these issues is the gap between the general-purpose capabilities of current LLMs and the course-specific, context-dependent nature of requirements engineering artifacts. The most consistent request from students was support from instructors in the form of guidance on prompt engineering skills, domain knowledge, and critical evaluation capacity; we argue that the most important curricular response to the LLM era in RE education is not the definition of policies but a pedagogical need to provide the aforementioned guidance. This is a form of AI literacy that is both educationally valuable and relevant to professional practice, due to future software engineers being expected to work alongside AI tools. In our future work, we plan to replicate the survey in the second half of the course project to observe the LLMs’ impact on testing tasks; furthermore, we plan to adjust our course syllabus to empirically evaluate the impact on the quality of the generated artifacts when students receive AI guidance up-front before working on project activities.

Code-Grounded Agentic Explanations for Static Analysis Vulnerability Findings Static application security testing (SAST) tools surface vulnerabilities early and their verdicts are rule-based and auditable. Yet developers routinely dismiss findings they cannot interpret. Large language models can supply the missing explanation, but designs that also hand the model the detection give up the auditability that makes static analysis defensible. We keep detection with the analyser and give the model only the explaining. A preliminary user study with 20 participants and a workshop with 19 practitioners yielded five requirements. Guided by these we redesigned SAFE, an open-source IntelliJ IDEA plugin that explains findings from any analyser reporting in the Static Analysis Results Interchange Format. It tiers explanations by demand, ties them to the reported data flow, and replaces the single-prompt backend with an agent that must consult the repository and the rule that fired before answering. A within-subjects crossover experiment with 24 participants compared the redesign against its predecessor. Perceived usability rose from 77.3 to 85.0 on the System Usability Scale. Actionability gained most among the explanation-quality items, the aspect both earlier studies flagged as weakest, and the odds of a correct remediation were 2.6 times higher. Triage accuracy and time per finding were indistinguishable, which we read as uninformative rather than as equivalence. Trust was the one measure that did not move, and the closing interviews indicate that grounding made findings easier to understand rather than easier to believe. Participants also drew a boundary no requirement anticipated, wanting the tool to find and explain while they judge and apply. Static application security testing (SAST) tools detect potential security vulnerabilities early in the development process, and their verdicts are rule-based, reproducible, and auditable. Yet SAST tools remain underused in practice Wadhams et al. (2024), and a major reason is the poor usability and quality of the explanations they provide. A large-scale study of the usability criteria addressed by static analysis tools Nachtigall et al. (2022); Nachtigall et al. (2019) found that many tools’ terse rule identifiers and generic messages fail to meet basic usability criteria. Some of the usability criteria include warning messages that expose the tool’s internal reasoning, explanations about the consequence of an issue, or the identification of the underlying weakness. Developers who cannot tell why a warning was raised, whether it is real, or how to fix it tend to dismiss it. Large language models (LLMs) are capable of closing this explanation gap. However, most existing approaches rely on the LLM for both detecting and explaining vulnerabilities Mao et al. (2024); Yang et al. (2025). This gives up the auditability that makes SAST suitable for security-critical processes, and systematic comparisons report that models and analysers fail in different ways rather than one superseding the other Gnieciak and Szandala (2025). The concern is not only that detection becomes unauditable. A model’s stated reasoning is itself weak evidence of how it reached an answer, because chain-of-thought explanations can be steered by features of the input that the model never mentions while remaining fluent and plausible, with accuracy dropping by as much as 36 % under such manipulations Turpin et al. (2023). An explanation is therefore most trustworthy when the reader can check it against something outside the model. Commercial offerings already pair a language model with an analyser, though they aim at repair rather than explanation. GitHub’s Copilot Autofix generates suggested patches for CodeQL alerts GitHub (2026), and Snyk’s DeepCode AI Fix does the same for Snyk Code, using program analysis to narrow what the model attends to Berabi et al. (2024). Both are tied to their vendor’s own detection engine, so neither travels to an analyser a team already runs, and in both the explanation is a by-product of proposing a fix rather than the artefact being produced. Our concern is the reverse. A developer must first decide whether a finding is real, which is a judgement a patch does not help with, and that judgement needs an account of the analyser’s reasoning rather than a suggested diff. We instead pursue a hybrid approach in which the SAST tool detects the vulnerability and the LLM explains it. Prior work has similarly applied models to analyser output, most closely by inspecting the warnings a SAST tool has already produced in order to filter false positives and describe them in natural language Wen, Cheng et al. (2024). A second line of work changes what a model has access to rather than what it is asked. Agentic systems give the model a set of tools and let it decide which to call and in what order, so that it gathers evidence over several steps instead of answering from a single fixed prompt Yao et al. (2023). In software engineering this has been applied to writing and repairing code, where an agent navigates a repository, runs commands and edits files until a task is complete Yang et al. (2024); Wang et al. (2024); Gauthier (2024). The same mechanism is useful for a different purpose. An explanation that has to refer to a developer’s own code cannot be assembled from a snippet chosen in advance, because what is relevant depends on where the untrusted value came from and what the flagged rule checks, and neither is known until the model has looked. Retrieval decided by the model is therefore a better fit than a prompt fixed before it starts. In previous work, we introduced the first version of the Static Analysis Findings Explainer (SAFE), an IntelliJ IDEA plugin that uses LLMs to explain the vulnerabilities detected by SAST tools, and evaluated the completeness of the generated explanations with software security trainers Johnson et al. (2025). Two limitations remained. The trainers judged whether an explanation read the way an expert would write one, which is not the same question as whether it helps a developer act, and they judged it in a demonstration rather than while triaging findings in their own project, so the study could not observe what a developer decided, how long it took, or whether the fix they proposed was right. The explanations were also assembled from the analyser’s output and a snippet extracted around the finding. The model never saw the definition of the rule that fired and could not follow a data flow across files, which left it paraphrasing textbook knowledge of the weakness class. In this paper we extend that work from evidence to redesign. A preliminary user study with 20 participants compared an initial prototype against a baseline SAST tool, establishing that developers clearly prefer LLM-generated explanations while exposing the limitations above. A structured workshop with practitioners from industry and research then supplied what such a tool must do in practice, and we consolidate both studies into five takeaways and five requirements. The redesign follows from those requirements. Explanations are tiered so that the essentials are visible at a glance, each one links to the data flow the analyser reported, and an agentic backend grounds it in the developer’s own codebase by reading and searching the project before answering. Unlike a general-purpose coding agent, it is constrained to explain the analyser’s existing verdict and is forbidden from detecting or patching anything itself. We evaluate the result against its predecessor in a within-subjects crossover experiment with 24 participants. The two builds differ in several respects at once, so the comparison establishes that the redesign performs differently rather than isolating which of its parts is responsible. Perceived usability improves, the widest perception gain is actionability, which both formative studies had identified as the weakest part of the earlier explanations, and participants propose better fixes. Triage accuracy is indistinguishable between the tools, and we read that null as uninformative rather than as evidence of equivalence. One measure stays flat, and it is the one the design was expected to move. Participants rate the evidence trail as no more worthy of trust than the text it replaced, even though it is the part of the redesign that can be checked. The closing interviews locate the reason. Participants anchor their trust to their own reading of the code, and they value the trace for taking them to it quickly. Those interviews also surface a boundary no requirement anticipated, since participants want the tool to find and explain while they judge and apply. In summary, this paper makes the following contributions: two formative studies of LLM-generated vulnerability explanations, a user study with 20 participants and a workshop with 19 practitioners, consolidated into five takeaways and five requirements; a requirements-driven redesign of SAFE whose architecturally novel component is an agentic backend constrained to explain a SAST tool’s existing verdict; the open-source SAFE IntelliJ IDEA plugin Fraunhofer IEM (2025), which delivers these explanations directly in the Integrated Development Environment (IDE) for any SARIF-producing SAST tool; a within-subjects crossover experiment with 24 participants comparing the redesigned system against its predecessor on the same findings. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reports the preliminary study at the foundation of our work and the industry workshop we conducted to obtain additional feedback. Section 3 describes the redesigned plugin and the agentic explanation approach. Section 4 reports the evaluation of the approach, and Section 5 discusses the results. Section 6 surveys related work, and Section 7 concludes the paper. Before redesigning the plugin, we drew on two formative studies. A preliminary user study in Section 2.1 established how developers read LLM-generated explanations of SAST warnings, and an industry feedback workshop in Section 2.2 showed how such explanations have to behave in a professional setting. Section 2.3 consolidates both into five takeaways, from which Section 2.4 derives the requirements for the redesign. Our work builds on a preliminary user study of an initial plugin prototype. The IntelliJ IDEA plugin listed the vulnerabilities reported by a SAST tool, and on request a controller assembled a prompt from the warning message, the affected code snippet, and surrounding project context, sent it in a single request to GPT-4, and rendered the explanation next to the finding. The study asked how large language models can be used to comprehensibly explain warnings generated by static analysis tools. We conducted a within-subjects study Charness et al. (2012) with counterbalanced tool order Lewis and Sauro (2021), comparing the prototype against Qodana JetBrains (), the JetBrains SAST plugin for IntelliJ IDEA, so that both conditions shared the same IDE surface. We chose a user study over automatic text-similarity metrics such as BLEU or ROUGE because those do not assess explanations from the perspective of the users they are meant to serve Wardatzky et al. (2024), and over an automated judge, whose agreement with human raters is itself contested Chiang and Lee (2023). We hypothesized that its explanations help developers identify vulnerabilities more effectively (H1) and more efficiently (H2) than the baseline, and that developers rate them higher (H3). As material we scanned the OWASP Benchmark Foundataion () with Semgrep [30] and randomly selected two findings for each of five injection vulnerability types, four of which appear in MITRE’s CWE Top 25 Corporation (2025). In an online survey, 20 students and professionals judged from screenshots whether a reported vulnerability was real, once per tool for each type, and rated both tools on a 6-point scale. Because the ratings are ordinal and the sample is small, we report Wilcoxon signed-rank tests throughout. Effectiveness and efficiency remained inconclusive. Measured as the proportion of correctly classified warnings, the ten participants who started with the prototype reached a mean of 0.52 with it and 0.56 with Qodana, while the ten who started with Qodana reached only 0.30 with the prototype and 0.24 with Qodana. Within each group the difference between the two tools was not significant, with [FORMULA] for the group that started with the prototype and [FORMULA] for the group that started with Qodana. Effectiveness was therefore dominated by the order in which participants saw the tools rather than by the tools themselves, which left H1 unresolved. The survey setting, in which reading long explanations dominates task time, left H2 unsupported. Satisfaction clearly favored the prototype and supports H3. Participants rated it higher on every feedback item, with a per-participant mean of 4.24 across all explanation-quality items versus 3.45 for Qodana and 13 of the 20 participants preferring it. On the matched clarity item, the prototype reached 4.45 versus 3.45 ( [FORMULA] , pooled across both order groups). It scored highest on the clarity of the explanation, on referring to the actual vulnerable code, and on improving understanding over the SAST tool (each [FORMULA] ), and lowest on the level of detail of the mitigation steps ( [FORMULA] ). The study also exposed limitations of the prototype. Participants found the explanations too long and asked for output that states the presence of a vulnerability directly and reveals cause and mitigation only on demand. The fixed explanation structure sometimes pushed the model to explain false positives as if they were real vulnerabilities, and individual respondents noted explanations that contradicted the SAST tool’s verdict. Mitigation detail was the lowest-rated aspect, with participants asking for corrected code examples. The prompt was assembled from the warning message and code snippet, so the model was not left to reason about the finding entirely on its own. It never saw the definition of the rule that had fired, however, and it could not read beyond the extracted code snippet, so its account of why the analyser objected rested on the rule’s message rather than on the conditions the rule actually checks, and vulnerabilities spanning several files could not be adequately explained. Finally, the screenshot-based survey could not capture how developers interact with explanations in a live IDE. The insights of Section 2.1 guided the first version of the SAFE plugin, which we evaluated with software security trainers in a workshop paper Johnson et al. (2025). Both evaluations were indirect, since the preliminary study showed screenshots in an online survey and the trainer evaluation targeted an educational rather than an industrial setting. We therefore conducted a structured feedback session during the consortium meeting of a research project, the first setting in which the plugin was used by its actual target group, in order to understand the concerns of practitioners who work with security findings and to derive requirements for the second version. The session followed a World Café format that combined moderated discussion, hands-on interaction, and a short survey. An opening discussion covered the pain points participants face when acting on vulnerabilities, the support they expect from an explanation tool, and the factors that would make such a tool unusable. Participants then used the plugin on real findings and assessed the generated explanations in context, so that feedback rested on actual interaction rather than on abstract expectations, and a closing discussion collected improvement ideas and conditions for practical use. The consortium meeting included 19 participants from industry and research, among them security experts (1), product team members (3), developers (5), and researchers (9). Six of them completed a two-part survey with Likert items and open text fields, four in the role of developer, one as security expert, and one as researcher. Five rated their experience with secure programming as medium and one as rather extensive, and three found it rather difficult to understand the technical background and impact of vulnerabilities. On a 5-point scale, four respondents rated the plugin as rather useful, one as medium, and one as rather not useful ( [FORMULA] ), while two items on the trustworthiness of the explanations reached means of [FORMULA] and [FORMULA] with no rating below the midpoint. The single low usefulness rating came from the most experienced respondent and did not concern explanation quality. That participant noted that the motivation to start reviewing a thousand findings is often missing, and still gave the highest trust rating of all respondents because one trusts the underlying expert system. This matched the dominant theme of the discussions, namely the difficulty of dealing with findings at scale. Participants described the number of findings as overwhelming without support for grouping or prioritization, reported difficulty in assessing relevance, risk, and impact, and lacked a clear entry point once a scan produces hundreds of results. Participants valued being able to trace the path of unsafe data through the code, described the step by step data flow view as the best aspect of the plugin, found the explanations far more understandable than the SAST output, and considered the IDE integration valuable because it places support in their working context. At the same time they reported that explanations still contain too much text and do not make the relevant information immediately visible, asking for colored highlighting, markers that indicate which part of the text answers which question, and a very short summary. Generic examples were seen as insufficient, since mapping such an example onto the concrete finding is exactly the work one would have to do without a tool. Participants therefore asked for quick fixes, mitigation strategies, and example code derived from their own project, together with estimates of how critical a finding is and how much effort a fix takes. On usability they asked for affected files to be marked in the file tree, for short explanations at the affected code, for a clearer link between an explanation and the underlying data flow, and for explicit source attribution. The preliminary study told us how a single explanation should read. The workshop told us how explanations must behave once a developer meets hundreds of them inside a real project. We consolidate both into five takeaways that drive the requirements in Section 2.4. Conciseness is a matter of structure, not only of length. The preliminary study identified verbosity as the main weakness, and although the second version already shortened the explanations, workshop participants still reported too much text. They asked for a visible hierarchy, a short summary at the top, and markers that reveal which part of the text answers which question, so conciseness has to come from progressive disclosure rather than from compression alone. Actionability has to reach the user’s own code. Both studies rated mitigation guidance as the weakest part of the explanation, and the workshop sharpened the earlier request for corrected code examples into a criterion, since a generic example shifts the translation work back to the developer. Actionable support means fixes and examples derived from the analyzed project, complemented by an indication of severity and remediation effort. The unit of work is the finding set, not the single finding. This takeaway has no counterpart in the preliminary study, whose participants assessed one isolated warning at a time, whereas in practice the volume of findings dominates. The most experienced respondent framed missing prioritization as the reason a vulnerability explainer may still go unused, so explaining findings well while leaving their ordering to the user solves only part of the problem. Explanations must be visibly anchored in the analysis and in the code. The preliminary study observed explanations that framed false positives as real vulnerabilities and occasionally contradicted the SAST tool, which we attributed to reasoning over an isolated snippet, and the workshop confirmed the same gap from the opposite direction, as participants valued the data flow view yet could not always see how the explanation related to it. Explanations must therefore be traceable to the reasoning and evidence of the underlying analysis, which means to the rule whose conditions the analyser checked as well as to the data flow it reported, with explicit sources and affected locations marked in the editor and the file tree. Trust and adoption depend on the surrounding workflow. Trustworthiness was rated favorably, but the free text responses show that this trust was largely inherited from the established tools behind the plugin rather than earned by the explanation itself, and participants named fast results, low resource consumption, and integration into the environments and pipelines they already use as conditions for adoption. The preliminary study reached a related conclusion methodologically, since its screenshot-based setting could not capture live IDE interaction, so the explanation has to live where the work happens and be evaluated there as well. Takeaways T1, T2, and T4 concern the explanation itself, while T3 and T5 concern the workflow into which it is embedded. The plugin should therefore not be understood as a text generation layer on top of static analysis results, since its usefulness depends on the broader socio-technical context in which developers, security experts, and product teams work with security findings. Based on the takeaways T1 to T5 of Section 2.3, we derive five key requirements for the second version of the SAFE plugin: Conciseness and comprehensibility (T1). The plugin should provide concise, comprehensible explanations accessible to users with different security expertise levels, communicating essential information without overwhelming detail. Code and data-flow linkage (T4). Explanations should be clearly linked to the underlying warning, the affected code location, and the relevant data flow. Prioritization and actionability (T2, T3). The plugin should support prioritization and actionability by helping users assess relevance, identify remediation starting points, and make informed decisions. IDE-workflow integration (T5). The plugin should integrate smoothly into existing workflows through contextual IDE visibility, code annotations, and file-tree markers. Transparency and trust (T4, T5). Explanations should be transparent and trustworthy through traceability, links to evidence, and appropriate communication of uncertainty. These requirements complement the general usability criteria for static analysis tools identified in prior work Nachtigall et al. (2022); Nachtigall et al. (2019), such as internal reasoning, clickable traces, explaining consequences, explanation by example, and connecting warnings to code. While those criteria address the warning message itself, R1–R5 additionally capture the workflow-level concerns raised by the workshop participants: managing and prioritizing large numbers of findings, acting on them within the IDE, and trusting the generated explanations. Section 3 describes how the redesigned plugin addresses these requirements. Guided by the requirements derived in Section 2.4, we redesigned the SAFE plugin and its explanation generation. SAFE deliberately does not detect vulnerabilities itself but instead makes the analyser’s verdict intelligible to the developer who has to act on it. Detection remains with an established SAST tool that applies its own ruleset to the code, and whose results are auditable and reproducible. Figure 1 shows the architecture, consisting of the SAFE plugin and The SAFE Agent. The SAFE plugin extracts and enriches the findings inside IntelliJ IDEA, turns a selected finding into a prompt, and renders the returned explanation across the explanation and data-flow panes and the editor. The SAFE Agent is a separate service in which an orchestrator drives a language model that must consult the user’s codebase through a set of tools before it answers, so that the explanation is grounded in the project’s source code rather than in generic textbook knowledge of the underlying weakness class. In the next sections, we describe the SAFE’s architecture, the plugin’s user interface, agentic grounding, and the structured explanations. Findings enter the plugin through two routes. First, SAFE integrates with Qodana JetBrains (), the JetBrains SAST plugin for IntelliJ IDEs, and extracts the findings displayed in its tool window. Second, SAFE parses files in the Static Analysis Results Interchange Format (SARIF) 2.1.0 Corporation (), so that the findings of any SAST tool that exports SARIF can be explained. Each finding is normalized to the rule identifier, severity, warning message, source location, the affected code snippet, and, when available, the source-to-sink data-flow trace. That trace and the rule behind it are the analyser’s own reasoning, and they are the starting point rather than something the model reconstructs. The agent is required to look up the rule that fired and to read the endpoints of that trace before it writes anything. An explanation is therefore an account of why this rule objected to this code path, anchored to the evidence the analyser produced, rather than an independent opinion about whether a vulnerability exists. This is what separates the approach from LLM-only detection, and it is why the plugin keeps the analyser’s verbatim message beside the generated text instead of replacing it. Each finding is enriched with deterministic metadata. SAFE resolves the inspection identifier to a Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) entry Corporation (2023) using a curated mapping together with a bundled copy of the MITRE CWE catalogue. This yields a ground-truth weakness name and description that both the prompt and the user interface reference. Resolving the CWE outside the LLM avoids misattributed weaknesses that would undermine the faithfulness of the explanation and the trust of its users (R5). In addition, the steps of the data-flow trace are classified into the roles source, propagator, call, sanitizer, and sink, which later makes individual steps interpretable in isolation. Enriched findings are listed in the findings pane, and the finding the developer selects is handed to a prompt generator that assembles the request from the normalized fields, the resolved CWE, and the classified data-flow steps. The request is then passed to the active explanation provider. Alongside the SAFE Agent of Section 3.5, which Figure 1 depicts, the plugin also supports direct single-request providers, so that a deployment without the agent service still produces an explanation. The agent is the design we propose, and it is the backend used in the redesigned build we evaluate. The agent runs as a separate service in Python and FastAPI, built on LangChain and LangGraph LangChain, Inc. (); LangChain, Inc. (), and streams partial results to the plugin over server-sent events so that a developer sees the explanation form rather than waiting on a complete response. Whether the SAFE agent or a single-request LLM provider is used is configured in the plugin settings and the credentials are stored in the IDE’s password safe. Every backend returns an explanation conforming to the schema of Section 3.4, and generated explanations are cached persistently. Reopening a project therefore issues no new model calls, and the same finding can carry parallel explanations from different backends. The workshop feedback (Section 2.2) and the preliminary study (Section 2.1) directly shaped a redesign of the plugin’s user interface. Figure 2 shows the result on a SQL-injection finding reported by a SAST tool in a Java web application. The tool window is organised into three panes: findings, explanation and data-flow. Findings shows which static analysis findings exist and which of them have already been explained. Explanation gives information about the meaning of a selected finding. Data-flow indicates how the untrusted data reaches the vulnerable operation. The numbered regions of the explanation pane are referenced individually below. A single action populates the tool window either from the results the Qodana plugin is currently displaying or from a SARIF file chosen through a file picker. The Not explained branch in Figure 2 holds findings that are already present, navigable, and marked in the editor. A dropdown in the action bar switches the active provider, marks the current one, and refreshes the tree so that it shows which findings already carry an explanation from that provider. The same control is what let a single finding hold parallel explanations from different backends during the evaluation in Section 4. The findings pane groups the findings of an analyser run by explanation status, CWE, directory, and file, with severity icons and a CWE badge whose tooltip shows the catalogue description, and a filter narrows the tree by file, rule, or CWE. The figure shows three findings already explained and two not yet examined. This gives an overview of what kinds of weaknesses the analyser reported and which of them have already been examined. It supports prioritization across large numbers of findings, which was one of the dominant pain points named in the workshop (R3). The first version tiered explanations by audience, using a selector that regenerated the entire explanation at a user-chosen depth of beginner, intermediate, or advanced. Participants nevertheless found the explanations too long and asked for key information to be visible at a glance. The redesigned interface therefore tiers by demand. Every finding opens with a title and its CWE badge (1) and a one-sentence TL;DR (2), followed by the what (4), why (5), where (6) and fix (7) core sections, while the in-depth material sits behind the opt-in deep-dive disclosure (8). The analyser’s own rule identifier and message are preserved verbatim behind a further disclosure (3), shown expanded in the figure, so the rewriting by the LLM never hides the verdict it is rewriting (R1, R5). An inline glossary annotates security terms such as taint and deserialization with hover definitions, which keeps the default text concise without losing precision (R1). When the finding carries a taint trace, the data-flow pane renders it as a stepped list in which each hop is labelled with its role and links to its file and line. Every step also carries an explanation of its own. Selecting a step opens it below the list, as Figure 2 shows for the sink at the end of the trace. These per-step explanations are requested as part of the same structured response as the rest of the explanation (Section 3.4), so opening one costs no further LLM call and the trace stays consistent with the prose that describes it. Each one says what that particular hop does to the untrusted value at that file and line, which is the question the raw trace leaves open. The analyser’s own message for the step is kept above it verbatim behind the same kind of disclosure used for the finding message (3), so a developer can always compare the generated wording against what the tool reported (R5). Because a step is only interpretable once its role is known, this reuses the deterministic classification into source, propagator, call, sanitizer, and sink rather than asking the LLM to infer it. Opening a step explanation and jumping to the corresponding editor location remain separate actions, so the same progressive disclosure that governs the explanation text also governs the trace (R1). The where section (6) links back to the same source and sink locations, so the prose and the trace refer to each other instead of sitting side by side. Workshop participants valued the flow view most but could not always see how it related to the explanation text, and these links close that gap (R2). The tool window is only one of the two interfaces the plugin uses. The other is the editor, which is where developers spend their time and where workshop participants wanted findings to arrive instead of in a separate dashboard (R4). Every imported finding receives a gutter icon and a highlight on the flagged line at import time, so an analyser run is visible in the code before any explanation has been requested. Hovering a gutter icon shows the explanation for that line in a tooltip, which makes a quick check possible without opening the tool window at all. When a finding carries a taint trace, the individual steps are highlighted as well, each in the colour of its role, so a developer can follow the untrusted value through the code in the same terms the data-flow pane uses. Navigation runs in both directions. Selecting a finding or one of its steps moves the caret to the corresponding location, and the gutter icon opens the matching explanation in the tool window. Because explanations are cached persistently, reopening a project restores both the tree and the highlights without issuing new LLM calls. An editor listener reapplies the highlights whenever a file with stored explanations is opened again. An explanation therefore stays attached to the code it describes instead of living in a report that the developer has to keep in a second window. Every explanation backend must return its answer in a fixed schema. Its sections decompose the explanation along the questions developers ask when diagnosing potential vulnerabilities with static analysis tools Smith et al. (2015). We adopt in particular the what, where, why, and how decomposition of SECGen Mamede et al. (2025), which restructures raw SAST output into a developer-friendly report and thereby also admits automated validation of the generated text. Answering these four questions for every finding is what makes the explanation comprehensible to users with different levels of security expertise (R1). Table 1 lists the resulting sections and what each of them must contain. Fixing the structure serves three purposes. The plugin can parse and render each section independently in its tiered layout, and it can check automatically that a backend returned every required section before the explanation reaches the user. The developer encounters every explanation under the same headings, which builds a stable mental template and reduces orientation effort over time (R1). Finally, explanations produced by different backends remain structurally comparable. A direct LLM call is fast, but it can only describe the weakness class in general terms, because the model sees the warning message and a code snippet rather than the project the finding lives in. The industry workshop surfaced the consequences. Participants found the resulting explanations verbose, hard to connect to their own code, and prone to arguing that a false positive is a real vulnerability. The SAFE Agent addresses this by grounding the explanation in the user’s actual codebase. The same finding, explained by the agent, references the developer’s real variables, methods, and call sites, and reflects what the triggered rule actually checks. The plugin treats the agent as just another explanation provider, sending the same prompt and receiving the same explanation schema, so users switch between agentic and direct explanations from the same control. Inside the agent, an orchestrator relays the prompt to the language model, executes the tool calls the model issues against the project, and feeds their results back, repeating this until the model returns the final explanation. The model must therefore consult the repository before answering. Table 2 lists the six tools available to it. Two of them establish what the analyser checked and where, two retrieve code, and two navigate the project tree. The system prompt mandates that the agent first looks up the rule that fired and reads the flagged code span together with the endpoints of the data-flow trace. It explicitly forbids generic textbook responses that do not reference the inspected code. The rule lookup matters because SAST rules are only noisy proxies for the CWE they are tagged with. The same CWE can be reported by structurally different rules, and a rule frequently encodes assumptions that a CWE-level description would miss. Grounding the explanation in what the rule actually checks aligns it with the analyser’s verdict rather than with a generic description of the weakness class (R2). This is a narrower remit than a general-purpose coding agent carries Yang et al. (2024); Wang et al. (2024); Gauthier (2024). The agent produces an account a developer reads rather than a patch, stays bound to a rule’s existing verdict rather than forming one, and navigates only the artefacts that substantiate the reported trace. It can neither modify code nor issue a verdict, which is why the tool set in Table 2 is deliberately small. Tool use also changes what the developer can observe. The stream carries an event for every tool invocation, so the sequence of consulted files and rules constitutes an evidence trail, so each explanation is traceable to the concrete artifacts the agent read (R5). Finally, on-demand file access scales to repositories of arbitrary size, since the agent retrieves only the artifacts it decides to consult instead of filling the context window of the model with the codebase. To assess whether the redesign of the SAFE plugin improves triage support in practice, we conducted a controlled within-subjects user study that follows the ACM SIGSOFT Empirical Standard for experiments with human participants Ralph (2021). The study evaluates the first version of the SAFE plugin against the redesigned plugin. Throughout the study, the plugins are identified using deliberately neutral names, and we retain them here. SAFE-Blue is the first version of the plugin which explains a vulnerability with a single direct LLM request and tiers the result by audience through a beginner, intermediate, and advanced depth selector. SAFE-Red is the second version plugin, which replaces that selector with the fixed tiered presentation of Section 3.3 and generates its explanations with the agent of Section 3.5. The colours carry no meaning beyond identifying the two builds to participants. We ask three research questions about SAFE’s redesign as a whole, because that is what participants used and what the study can speak to. SAFE-Red bundles the tiered presentation of Section 3.3 (R1), the code-grounded agentic explanations of Section 3.5 (R2, R3), and the workflow integration of Section 3.3 (R4, R5). These are not separable in the artefact and are not separated by the design, so the questions name the system. The study establishes whether a redesign built to satisfy R1 to R5 performs differently from the design it replaces. Does the requirements-driven redesign of SAFE, comprising structured tiered presentation, code-grounded agentic explanations, and IDE-workflow integration, change participants’ decision quality relative to the prior single-prompt design, both for detection and for remediation? Does the redesigned plugin change time-to-decision relative to the prior design? Do participants rate the redesigned plugin differently from the prior design on explanation quality, IDE-workflow integration, usability, and trust? RQ1 is split into H1a on triage correctness and H1b on fix-family correctness, because R2 and R3 attach to remediation independently of detection. RQ2 covers H2 on time per finding. RQ3 registers one hypothesis per perception construct named by a requirement rather than a single aggregate, namely H3a on perceived explanation quality with its clarity, actionability, and confidence-support sub-constructs (R1, R3, R5), H3b on usability, H3c on IDE-workflow integration (R4), and H3d on trust (R5). Every hypothesis is stated in null and alternative form and every alternative is two-sided. We decline a directional commitment because no member of the family has unambiguous prior evidence. The default SAFE-Red explanation is shorter and more structured than the SAFE-Blue one, which could equally help by removing noise or hurt by placing essential detail behind an opt-in tier. Its optional deep-dive layer resembles the SAFE-Blue explanation and could equally help through deeper grounding or hurt by inducing over-reliance among the participants who open it.
