The experiment is a two-condition AB/BA crossover in which both order and snippet set are crossed with tool, giving the four sequences in Table 3. Prior to the sessions, assignment of participants to the four groups was randomised and stratified. Across the four groups every combination of tool and set is observed equally often and every set appears equally often in each period. This dissolves the object-treatment confound that would otherwise arise from pairing one tool with one set. A within-subjects design was chosen because it lets each participant serve as their own control on personal-skill variance. A between-subjects design, by contrast, would have required roughly twice as many participants to reach comparable statistical power, which exceeded the pool available to us. The cost is potential carry-over, which the counterbalancing above is intended to absorb. The session were estimated to last for 60 minutes and followed the outline below: Consent: Participants consented in advance and again verbally at the start, both to the session recording, which was used to validate the transcript and then deleted, and to the logging of their interactions with the plugin. Pre-study questionnaire: Recording the participant’s primary role, years of professional development experience, years of Java experience, frequency of JetBrains IDE use, self-rated familiarity with secure coding practices, and prior exposure to SAST tools. Warm-up: A video on a single fixed deserialization finding (CWE-502) with no plugin present. It familiarised participants with the IntelliJ IDEA interface and software project before either plugin was introduced, so that first-contact effects did not land on whichever tool came first. Two task blocks: In the order given by the participant’s group in Table 3, each block ran through the same four steps. Tool demo: A video for the tool of that period. Both demos follow the same structural template, so neither condition received the richer introduction. Setup: The experimenter enabled the interaction telemetry and entered the participant identifier. Explanations for the assigned set had been generated beforehand and written to the plugin’s cache, using a study-only action that walks every imported finding and requests an explanation from the active provider. Prewarming the cache means that navigating the tree never waited on the model, so the measured time reflects reading and deciding rather than generation latency, at the cost of removing generation latency from the comparison altogether. Task: Fifteen minutes to work through the five findings of the assigned set with the assigned tool. For each finding, participants decided whether it was a true positive, a false positive, or that they were unsure, described or sketched a fix, and recorded their confidence. They were told explicitly that finishing all five was not expected, which keeps the time limit from turning the task into a completion race. Think-aloud was encouraged, and the experimenter intervened only with neutral cues such as asking what the participant was looking at. Block questionnaire: Administered immediately, so that perceptions were recorded while the condition was still fresh rather than after both had been seen. Interview and debrief: A semi-structured interview covering what participants liked and disliked about the tool they had just used, what they would have done differently with the other one, what their trust in the assessment rested on, and how they would explain a finding to a colleague, followed by a debrief. The findings come from the Health-Doc-Exchange project, a Java web application whose size and structure resemble a real project and for which a curated ground truth is available. The application is part of the material used to train security champions in the software security trainings offered by Fraunhofer IEM Fraunhofer IEM (2026). Those trainings were themselves developed in response to a study that found developers, product owners, and managers to have too little competence in secure software development Dziwok et al. (2021). The application therefore predates this experiment, and its weaknesses were curated for teaching rather than chosen to suit either condition. Choosing an internal application over a public benchmark was itself deliberate. Health-Doc-Exchange is not published, so its source is very unlikely to appear in the pretraining data of either model, and an explanation of one of its findings has to be derived from the code supplied at inference time rather than recalled from the code the model was trained on. A public corpus offers no such assurance, including the OWASP Benchmark Foundataion () used in the preliminary study of Section 2.1 and the first version of the SAFE plugin. Using an existing application rather than synthetic snippets matters for the agentic condition in particular, since an agent that searches the repository can only be exercised by code with genuine structure to search. We scanned the application with Semgrep v1.160.0 and retained findings that carry at least one valid CWE mapping, spread across five weakness families relevant to back-end Java, namely path traversal (CWE-23), OS command injection (CWE-78), cross-site scripting (CWE-79), SQL injection (CWE-89), and server-side request forgery (CWE-918). The retained findings are split into the two sets of Table 3, each holding one finding per weakness family, with a mix of true and false positives so that dismissing every warning is not a winning strategy. The sets were balanced ahead of time on CWE distribution, on the intended ratio of true to false positives, and on snippet length and cyclomatic complexity. The realised composition is two true positives and three false positives in one set against three and two in the other. That is worth stating plainly, because the case for grounding is usually argued in terms of trust. The interviews suggest why. Participants described the trace and the annotations as making a finding easier to locate and to understand, and two of them separated that from believing the assessment. Trust in the verdict was anchored to their own review of the code rather than to the quality of the explanation. Grounding appears to serve comprehension rather than belief. We group the threats by the standard categories, beginning with the most consequential. The most important threat is the nature of the independent variable. The user interface, the interaction structure, the axis along which explanations are tiered, the explanation content, and the generation pipeline all differ between the two conditions at once. Every hypothesis therefore attributes its effect to the SAFE-Red tool as a bundle, set against the SAFE-Blue tool as a bundle, and none of them isolates the agentic backend from the interface redesign. This is an explicit construct-level choice rather than an oversight. An observed difference could be carried by the interface, by the tiered presentation, by the backend, or by any combination of them. Separating those contributions requires a factorial ablation over two hybrid configurations that are not currently engineered and would roughly double the sessions or the sample. We rejected that design on engineering and recruitment grounds. Two elements of the protocol probe the confound without resolving it. The plugin logs interactions per finding, so an outcome can be checked against what participants opened and how long they spent there. The closing interview asks participants to reason about the counterfactual directly, whether their accuracy or speed would have changed had each tool’s content been presented in the other’s interface. The answers point to how explanations were organised rather than to how they were produced, citing the fixed sections, the short summary and the reduced clicking (Section 4.4.4). That points towards the interface rather than the backend, and it does not settle the question. The question was asked in 13 of 24 sessions, participants are reasoning about a build they used for fifteen minutes, and self-attribution of cause is weak evidence at the best of times. Neither probe substitutes for the ablation. The telemetry delivers less of this than intended, because the two builds log different events for analogous actions and the panel dwell timer is effectively absent from SAFE-Red. A second construct-level choice concerns the requirements. The redesign addresses all five at once rather than in order of priority, so the marginal contribution of any one of them cannot be reported. Incremental implementation would have given that, at the cost of a design that does not hold together, since R2 and R3 both depend on the agent’s ability to consult the codebase. We chose the coherent artefact over the separable one. The qualitative coding carries a reliability limitation of its own. Segment-level agreement between the two coders on the four double-coded interviews is [FORMULA] per cent, which is low, and it is near zero on every code concerned with presentation because such talk pervades the interviews and the coders marked overlapping spans. The interview themes are therefore reported as an interpretive aid and never as a result on their own. Two smaller construct threats remain. Trust, IDE-workflow integration, and the three explanation-quality sub-constructs were captured with a single Likert item rather than multi-item subscales, so no internal consistency can be computed and each rests on the wording of one question. Triage accuracy further presumes a single ground truth per finding, which the lab package fixes ahead of the sessions. Carry-over between periods is possible in any crossover design. It is addressed by the counterbalancing of Table 3 and by the plugin-free warm-up rather than eliminated. Participants also worked through more findings in the second block than in the first, so a period effect cannot be ruled out. Assignment to the four sequences was moreover not stratified on security expertise, which leaves the sequences unbalanced on triage skill. Because every hypothesis rests on a within-participant contrast, that imbalance does not bias the tool comparison itself. Pre-generating the explanations removed generation latency from the task. This keeps the 15-minute blocks comparable, and it means no participant experienced the wait an agentic backend imposes in normal use. Speed was one of the adoption conditions the workshop raised (T5), so the study cannot speak to it, and the time measure reflects reading and deciding rather than the cost of the tool in practice. The unpublished application bounds what the contamination control covers. Its source is very unlikely to have been memorised, but the five weakness classes are standard and their idiomatic fixes are familiar to both models. An unpublished codebase removes recall of this code rather than recall of SQL injection. It also costs replicability, since a replication would have to substitute an application of comparable structure. The sample bounds generalisation further. Twelve of the twenty-four participants reported less than a year of Java experience and fourteen had never used a SAST tool (Section 4.4). That matches the beginner-to-intermediate population the plugin targets, and it limits what the results say about developers who triage findings routinely. Two participants hold management roles outside software development, so a small number of decisions come from outside the intended population. We did not run a sensitivity analysis excluding them. The 15-minute cap per block proved to be the binding constraint on data volume. Only one participant reached all five findings in both blocks, and 124 of the 240 possible decisions were recorded, a median of between two and three per block. The number of decisions therefore varies from one to five across participants and conditions, which makes a per-participant accuracy proportion noisy and gives the finding-level mixed-effects model the leading role in the analysis of triage correctness. Three lines of work bear on this paper, covering how analyser output is made usable, how language models have been applied to vulnerabilities, and how agents are built. Work on the explainability of static analysis predates large language models. Rule graphs make the analyser’s reasoning visible by encoding the rules and data flows behind a finding Do and Bodden (2022). Reading one presupposes a familiarity with taint analysis that the developers in our studies reported lacking. Surveys of the usability criteria these tools meet find most falling short on exposing internal reasoning, explaining consequences, and connecting a warning to the code it concerns Nachtigall et al. (2022); Nachtigall et al. (2019). A review of adoption barriers separates obstacles inherent to the technique from shortcomings that tool builders can remove Wadhams et al. (2024), a split our workshop reproduced and the reason R1–R5 reach beyond the wording of an individual warning. Closest to our work is SECGen Mamede et al. (2025), which restructures raw analyser output into interpretable reports organised around what a vulnerability is, where it manifests, why it matters, and how to address it. We adopt that decomposition for our explanation schema (Section 3.4) and differ from it in three ways. SECGen composes a report from what the analyser reported, whereas our agent consults the repository and the rule definition before answering, so an explanation can name the developer’s own methods and call sites rather than describing the weakness class. Their report is a standalone artefact, whereas ours is delivered in the IDE beside the flagged code, tiered by demand and linked step by step to the reported data flow (R1, R2, R4). Finally, SECGen validates the generated text automatically, whereas we evaluate the result with developers who have to act on it. One group of approaches detects independently, often positioned as a replacement for static analysis. LLMVulExp combines prompting with fine-tuning to detect vulnerabilities and describe them Mao et al. (2024), and DLAP augments a deep-learning detector with model prompting Yang et al. (2025). Systematic comparisons report that models and analysers make different errors rather than one dominating the other Gnieciak and Szandala (2025). A second group reduces the warnings a developer sees rather than explaining them, extending a long line of classifiers trained to separate actionable warnings from noise Ge et al. (2024). Models are now used to filter an analyser’s output, as in LLM4SA Wen, Cheng et al. (2024), or to guide the analysis itself Li et al. (2025). A third group repairs what the analyser reports, as GitHub’s Copilot Autofix does for CodeQL alerts GitHub (2026) and Snyk’s DeepCode AI Fix does for Snyk Code Berabi et al. (2024). We share with LLM4SA the division of labour that leaves detection with the auditable analyser, and differ from all three groups in what the model is asked to do. It neither judges whether a finding is real nor proposes a patch, because a developer has to decide whether to act before either helps. It consults the repository and the rule that fired rather than a supplied snippet, which is what allows an explanation to name the developer’s own methods and call sites (R5). And it consumes SARIF, so it applies to whichever analyser a team already runs. Giving a model tools and letting it choose which to call turns a single completion into a multi-step investigation Yao et al. (2023). In software engineering the pattern has been applied to writing and repairing code. SWE-agent provides an interface for navigating and editing a repository Yang et al. (2024), CodeAct makes executable code the action space Wang et al. (2024), and Aider applies the idea in a developer’s terminal Gauthier (2024), all judged by whether the resulting patch passes a test suite. We reuse the mechanism for a different end. Our agent produces an explanation rather than a diff, stays bound to the verdict the rule already issued, and navigates only the artefacts that substantiate the reported data flow. Static analysis is worth defending because its verdicts can be checked. Handing detection to a language model gives that up, and it leaves a developer with nothing outside the model against which to test what the model says. We therefore kept detection with the analyser and gave the model only the explaining. Two formative studies, a preliminary user study with 20 participants and a workshop with 19 practitioners, produced five requirements for what such a tool has to do. The redesigned SAFE plugin follows them. It tiers explanations by demand rather than by an audience label chosen in advance, and ties each step of an explanation to the data flow the analyser reported. It also replaces a single prompt with an agent that consults the repository and the rule that fired before it answers. The agent is constrained so that it can neither modify code nor form a verdict, and it consumes SARIF, so it applies to whichever analyser a team already runs. A crossover experiment with 24 developers compared the redesign against its predecessor. Perceived usability rose from [FORMULA] to [FORMULA] on the System Usability Scale. Actionability showed the widest gain among the explanation items, the aspect both formative studies had identified as weakest. Participants proposed better remediations, with the odds of a correct fix [FORMULA] times higher. Triage accuracy and time per finding were indistinguishable. We read those nulls as uninformative rather than as equivalence, because a fifteen-minute block left most participants with two or three decisions. The comparison is between two whole designs, so it establishes that the redesign performs differently rather than isolating which of its parts is responsible. Two results point beyond this design. Trust in the assessment did not move while every other perception measure did. The interviews indicate why, since participants described the grounding artefacts as making a finding easier to locate and understand rather than easier to believe. Grounding appears to serve comprehension rather than belief, which is not how the case for it is usually argued. Second, participants raised a boundary that no requirement anticipated. It came up in 22 of 24 interviews, and 20 of them drew it in the same place. The tool should find and explain, and the developer should judge and apply. They defended it by pointing to false positives, to the understanding that reviewing a finding gives them, and to being liable for their own code. Four directions follow as future work: An ablation that separates the bundle. Crossing each interface with each backend is the only design that will settle which part of the redesign the improvements came from, and this study cannot substitute for it. A task budget that lets accuracy be measured. Fifteen minutes left most participants with two or three decisions, so the accuracy result is uninformative rather than negative. A longer session or a smaller finding set would give a per-participant proportion worth testing. Explanations designed for comprehension rather than persuasion. If grounding serves understanding rather than belief, an explanation should help a developer reach their own verdict rather than make the analyser’s more convincing. What that means concretely is open. Support for the boundary developers drew. They want to judge and apply while the tool finds and explains. Whether an explanation can be built to support that judgement, rather than to substitute for it, is the problem we would take up next. The Gene Is Not the Gate: Conceptualizing the Semantic Genome of Quantum Software Quantum software spans applications, program representations, compilers, runtimes, and hardware-facing control. Existing abstractions describe these artifacts and layers, but they do not capture the semantic responsibilities that must remain valid as a computation is transformed across the stack. This limits systematic reasoning about cross-layer correctness, evolution, and reuse. 1. Introduction Quantum software spans a layered ecosystem from application abstractions to hardware-facing control. Circuits, source programs, intermediate representations, runtimes, and control systems expose different stages of this stack (Steiger et al., 2018; Khammassi et al., 2021; McCaskey and others, 2020; Mccaskey et al., 2021; Sivarajah et al., 2022; Cross and others, 2022; QIR Alliance, 2026). These abstractions describe where a computation is represented or transformed, but they do not identify the finer-grained semantic responsibilities that must remain valid across layers. Bell-state preparation illustrates this gap. Its meaning lies in the state relation established between two logical qubits rather than in a specific realization such as H followed by CX. A compiler may decompose or reroute these operations as long as the intended relation is preserved. The same requirement becomes more demanding in teleportation, where measurement outcomes must control corrections on another qubit. A simulator may execute this workflow, while a target backend may lack the required control capability or timing support. Calibration changes can further alter the physical realization without modifying the source program or its intermediate representation. These cases are therefore different expressions of related semantic responsibilities rather than isolated artifacts. Existing abstractions do not expose these relationships directly. Gate motifs capture local implementations, while stack models record transformation locations. Neither states what must be preserved or what evidence supports that preservation. This limitation also extends beyond gate-model programs. Tierkreis, Pulser, and Qibolab expose workflow, pulse-control, and hardware-facing responsibilities that cannot be reduced to a single notion of a quantum program (Sivarajah et al., 2022; Silvério and others, 2022; Efthymiou et al., 2024). Even measurement serves different purposes in application readout, syndrome extraction, and controller discrimination. The appropriate unit of analysis must therefore be finer-grained than a software product, richer than a syntactic pattern, and explicitly tied to both semantic role and software stratum. This need is consistent with evidence that quantum software faults often emerge from interactions among source code, circuits, qubit usage, and platform behavior (Paltenghi and Pradel, 2022; Paltenghi and Pradel, 2024). Position. We define a quantum software gene as a typed, reusable semantic responsibility with a contract that remains checkable across the strata required for its realization. Each gene records its semantic subject, layer span, execution context, observable expressions, and supporting evidence, covering applications, compilers, runtimes, controllers, workflows, simulators, and assurance tools. We introduce QGenome, as shown in Figure 1, which organizes these responsibilities as typed gene cards across software strata and responsibility families. Contracts, dependencies, refinement, provenance, and cross-layer expression relations compose genes into pathways and genomes. QGenome is an extensible foundation, not a complete taxonomy or automatic extraction method. 2. Conceptual Foundations Quantum Software Genes. We define a quantum software gene as a reusable semantic responsibility whose realization and preservation can be traced across the relevant software strata. A gene associates this responsibility with the software object that owns or enforces it, an explicit semantic contract, and the context and evidence needed to justify its realization. Here, ownership refers to the program element, compiler pass, runtime service, control module, or other software object responsible for satisfying the contract. Unlike a design pattern, intermediate representation, component, or test, a gene connects these artifacts through a shared and checkable semantic obligation. We represent a gene card as [FORMULA] . Here, [FORMULA] captures the semantic responsibility and contract subject, [FORMULA] its owner, [FORMULA] its layer span, [FORMULA] its taxonomy labels, and [FORMULA] its resource roles. The contract [FORMULA] specifies the semantic assumptions [FORMULA] and guarantees [FORMULA] of the responsibility. The context [FORMULA] records realization-specific conditions, while [FORMULA] denotes the concrete expressions and [FORMULA] provides evidence that [FORMULA] satisfies [FORMULA] and that [FORMULA] realizes [FORMULA] under [FORMULA] . Gene identity is determined by [FORMULA] , [FORMULA] , and [FORMULA] , while versions and lineage are maintained in the genome graph. Scope of Classification. Our taxonomy classifies documented quantum-dependent responsibilities rather than entire repositories. Each candidate must specify a contract subject, an owning or enforcing software object, at least one observable expression, and public evidence. Candidates with separable obligations over different subjects are split into gene cards linked by dependency or refinement. Multiple family labels are used only for inseparable cross-family obligations. Insufficiently evidenced candidates remain unresolved rather than established genes. 3. Quantum Software Gene Taxonomy QGenome classifies each gene along two orthogonal axes. The software-stratum axis identifies where a responsibility is realized, while the responsibility-family axis specifies the semantic obligation it governs. This separation is necessary because one responsibility may span multiple strata, while one software system may own several kinds of genes (Häner et al., 2018; McCaskey and others, 2020). As summarized in Table 1, the taxonomy contains ten responsibility families organized into four groups: computational semantics, coordination, realization, and assurance. Computational Semantics. These genes govern how quantum information is prepared, transformed, related, and observed. State, transformation, interaction, and observation genes capture these respective responsibilities. They are reusable across algorithms: teleportation composes state and observation genes with classically controlled correction, while VQE combines state and transformation genes with observation in a classical optimization loop. Coordination. These genes organize resources and hybrid execution. Resource-lifecycle genes govern allocation, reset, reuse, and release, whereas orchestration genes capture dependencies between quantum execution and classical control. Tierkreis realizes orchestration through typed quantum-classical workflows, while XACC/qcor coordinates quantum kernels, accelerator selection, and hybrid execution (Sivarajah et al., 2022; McCaskey and others, 2020; Mccaskey et al., 2021). Realization. These genes connect abstract computations to executable device operations. Translation genes preserve meaning across source, IR, and native representations. Mapping-and-timing genes bind logical operations to physical resources and schedules. Control-and-calibration genes connect scheduled operations to signals and device parameters. OpenQL exposes translation and mapping responsibilities, while Pulser and Qibolab provide different forms of pulse-level and hardware-facing control (Khammassi et al., 2021; Silvério and others, 2022; Efthymiou et al., 2024). Assurance. These genes establish or preserve claims about correctness and execution quality. Protection-and-validation genes include program analyses, simulation, diagnostics, mitigation, and benchmark oracles. LintQ and MorphQ validate program and transformation properties, whereas MQT Bench and Bugs4Q provide cross-level artifacts and reproducible evidence (Paltenghi and Pradel, 2024; Paltenghi and Pradel, 2023; Quetschlich et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2023). Although these systems belong to the same family, they validate different contract subjects. Scope and Relative Completeness. The taxonomy covers responsibilities whose correctness depends on a quantum-specific state, operation, resource, capability, timing condition, noise model, or statistical obligation. Purely classical functionality remains outside this scope unless it affects such a contract. Let [FORMULA] denote the scoped responsibilities, [FORMULA] the software strata, and [FORMULA] the responsibility families. We define set-valued typings [FORMULA] , and the uncovered set [FORMULA] . A responsibility may receive multiple labels, provided that each denotes a distinct contract subject. We claim only relative completeness for the current catalog: new elements of [FORMULA] may reveal missing categories or refine existing boundaries. 4. Genome Lifecycle Construction Construction and Composition. A quantum software genome instantiates the taxonomy by connecting typed gene cards into executable pathways. Genome construction identifies semantic responsibilities, assigns their strata and families, binds concrete expressions, and records dependency and refinement relations together with versioned evidence. Different software classes naturally exhibit different profiles: applications emphasize computational semantics, compilers emphasize translation and mapping, runtimes emphasize coordination, and controllers and analysis tools emphasize control and assurance. These profiles are not fixed labels, since one system may own several gene types and one gene may have multiple backend-specific expressions. Static analysis, metamorphic testing, simulation, execution, and calibration can provide evidence at different strata (Paltenghi and Pradel, 2023; Paltenghi and Pradel, 2024). Contextual Validity. A genome is valid only under a declared execution context. Its genes must satisfy local contracts, compose consistently, preserve higher-level responsibilities across refinement, and rely on applicable evidence: [FORMULA] . A successful execution alone is insufficient, as it may conceal mapping errors, untested branches, or stale calibration evidence. Genome Evolution. A genome evolves through changes to its responsibilities, pathways, expressions, contexts, or evidence. Expression variation changes an implementation while preserving its contract, such as a revised gate decomposition or pulse schedule. Pathway recombination changes gene composition, as when qubit reuse introduces measurement and reset responsibilities (DeCross et al., 2023). Contract mutation instead changes the promised semantics, such as replacing an exact transformation with an approximate one. These distinctions separate contract-preserving implementation changes from semantic changes or violations across genes. Environmental adaptation re-expresses a stable responsibility under a new execution context [FORMULA] . Retargeting is valid only when [FORMULA] , [FORMULA] , and the evidence [FORMULA] adequately supports these claims. Depending on the contract [FORMULA] , the correspondence between the original and adapted expressions may be exact, approximate, or statistical. This distinction is particularly important for hardware-facing systems such as Pulser and Qibolab, where device capabilities and configurations affect realization validity (Silvério and others, 2022; Efthymiou et al., 2024). Phenotypic measures such as fidelity, latency, success probability, and resource cost may guide the selection among valid adaptations, but do not determine gene identity. 5. Capability Expression and Engineering Uses From Validity to Capability. QGenome connects cross-stratum validity to observable software capabilities. A phenotype is an observation produced by a genome under a declared context, whereas a capability is a set of supported phenotypes with explicit operating conditions. This distinction prevents a successful execution from being generalized into an unsupported capability claim. Phenotypes vary across software strata. Applications expose output quality and protocol success, compilers expose semantic preservation and resource overhead, runtimes expose execution and feedback behavior, and control software exposes signal validity and calibration quality. Assurance tools further characterize detected violations and validation coverage. A capability claim is justified only when the relevant genome pathway is valid under the declared context and the collected observations satisfy its acceptance criteria with sufficient evidence. Capability assessment must therefore distinguish the validity of the pathway, the conditions under which it is realized, and the evidence supporting its observed behavior. Engineering Uses. By making responsibilities, contexts, and evidence explicit, QGenome supports several engineering tasks. Reuse transfers gene cards and pathways together with their assumptions, so incompatible contexts trigger adaptation rather than silent transplantation. Testing measures coverage over responsibilities and refinement edges instead of only statements or gates. Existing resources such as MorphQ, MQT Bench, and Bugs4Q can provide evidence for these checks (Paltenghi and Pradel, 2023; Quetschlich et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2023). Repair can target the earliest violated contract, while change-impact analysis follows dependency, refinement, and evidence-freshness relations. Gene cards can also serve as typed planning artifacts for autonomous engineering agents. An implementation agent proposes an expression, a backend-aware agent checks its context and resource assumptions, and a verification agent supplies supporting evidence. Existing verifier-in-the-loop and closed-loop QPU systems show that such executable feedback is increasingly available (Yu and others, 2026; Cao et al., 2025). QGenome does not make an agent trustworthy by itself. Instead, it specifies the contract, context, and evidence that must be established before an agent-generated action is accepted. 6. Future Research Directions QGene Atlas and Benchmark. A first direction is to build a versioned atlas of quantum software genes across applications, compilers, runtimes, control systems, simulators, and assurance tools. The atlas should record gene cards, pathway relations, concrete expressions, contexts, and evidence rather than treating repositories as indivisible samples. It can support tasks such as gene-boundary detection, family classification, cross-stratum linking, and contract extraction. Annotation agreement and unresolved cases should guide future revisions of the taxonomy. Automated Gene Mining and Lineage Recovery. Future work can recover gene cards and their evolution from software artifacts. Static analysis can identify resource roles and transformation boundaries, while execution traces reveal runtime dependencies and hardware interactions. IR provenance and version history can link source responsibilities to compiled and deployed expressions. A practical interchange format should capture expressions, refinement relations, evidence validity, and phenotype observations. Gene-Aware Regression Testing and Repair. QGenome enables cross-layer regression analysis beyond circuit syntax. Compiler or calibration changes may violate contracts without changing the program. Future systems can mutate gene cards and refinement edges, generate contract-oriented tests, and localize failures to violated responsibilities. Versioned compiler, runtime, and calibration benchmarks can further evaluate gene-aware fault localization and contract-guided repair. Evidence-Grounded Quantum Software Agents. Quantum software agents should produce validated genome updates, not just circuits or configurations. Each update should specify affected responsibilities, required context, proposed expressions, and supporting evidence. This supports backend-aware mapping, testing, workflow adaptation, repair, and retargeting. Evaluation should consider contract coverage, unsupported assumptions, evidence freshness, cross-layer consistency, and adaptation to environmental changes alongside task success. 7. Conclusion In this paper, we introduced QGenome, a semantic foundation for understanding quantum software beyond gates, circuits, and repository boundaries. We define quantum software genes as typed, reusable responsibilities with explicit contracts, contexts, expressions, and evidence, and organize them across five software strata and ten responsibility families. QGenome provides a common vocabulary for tracing how quantum-dependent responsibilities are realized, composed, and preserved across the stack, enabling future gene-aware analysis, testing, repair, evolution, and autonomous quantum software engineering.

Beyond the Document: Compiled Context and Governed Agents for Any Work Product A document preserves the visible result of professional work but often discards the research, calculations, assumptions, evidence, and authorization boundaries behind it. We study a different unit of delivery: a Portable Agent Format (paf) package that carries a work product together with compiled context, evidence, provenance, and rules for subsequent interaction. To test whether this context remains useful beyond the process that produced it, we evaluate four new packages, created after the hosted and offline readers were fixed: an investment proposal, fund research, financial-statement analysis, and an engineering incident review. Two packages were produced by specialized agents and two through a general-purpose assistant’s packaging skill. Across 400 frozen questions and 12,000 evaluated responses, a hosted governed reader succeeds on 96% of questions versus 86% with instructions plus raw-file retrieval (Holm-adjusted [FORMULA] ). On the 260 answerable questions per condition, success is 94% versus 79%; the gap varies by package. Source-material chat and instructions alone reach 48% and 74% overall. A separate 0.8-billion-parameter offline reader succeeds on 69% overall, but 54% on answerable questions. Its [FORMULA] response rate is 2.9%, combining materially wrong and unauthorized answers, versus 56% with the source and instructions alone. Ablations suggest advantages for the integrated selector and package-adapted writer, without isolating representation from training effects. The same run exposes a failure: offline retrieval resolves none of the 40 historical-record questions in one financial-data package. These findings support treating compiled knowledge as part of the delivered work product, while leaving independent standards interoperability and end-to-end governance conformance unproven. 1 Introduction Professional work commonly arrives as a PDF, web page, presentation, or report. The recipient receives a conclusion but not the full state that made it possible: source records, intermediate analysis, alternatives considered, qualifications, evidence lineage, or the rules under which the work was approved. A subsequent question often sends the recipient back to the author or into a general-purpose assistant that can reason about the visible document but does not automatically inherit the producing organization’s evidence or authority boundaries. The limitation is not only how questions are answered. It is what gets delivered. Thesis. The unit of delivery for professional knowledge should be more than a document. A completed work product should travel with its compiled context, evidence and interaction rules, so that another model or runtime can help a recipient interrogate the finished work without reconstructing the original workflow. The producing process and the consuming process need not be the same. Explanation of approved work should also remain distinct from new analysis, new advice or revision requiring fresh authorization. We study one implementation of this thesis, the Portable Agent Format (paf). A package combines the presentation the reader sees with typed facts, searchable source records, evidence references, provenance classifications, signed release metadata, governance policy and a runtime profile. Its hosted viewer (Lens) answers against the package under a defined policy; a second reader uses a small local model and a package-specific selection and writing pipeline. The format carries knowledge, not the models or agent processes that produced it. A signature records what was issued; it does not make every statement true. Testable hypothesis. On questions about a delivered work product, a reader with compiled context and bounded retrieval should recover more of the work’s knowledge than a reader with the visible source alone, even after giving that reader the same instructions and ordinary access to the underlying source files. A smaller offline reader should retain useful access to that context, though its retrieval may be less robust. Earlier exploratory evaluations used packages during reader development, so they could not provide held-out estimates. We therefore created four new packages on 1 November 2026, after fixing the hosted and offline readers, and froze the questions and gold answers before the included evaluation. The packages were not used for reader development or adapter training. We report only these new results, spanning two producer paths in finance and engineering. The conditions and limitations appear in §4 and §6. Four findings organize the paper: Compiled context adds usable knowledge beyond prompting and raw retrieval. Across four packages, hosted Lens reaches 96% success against 48% for ordinary source chat, 74% for the same source with Lens rules, and 86% for Lens rules plus BM25 over the source files. The increment over raw retrieval is nonuniform across packages (§5.1). The architecture works on different document and production paths. The evaluation includes two packages produced by Prime agents and two from Claude chats through an ABC-authored packaging skill, including an engineering postmortem. It demonstrates a second path into the same governed publication ecosystem, not independent format conformance (§3). A much smaller reader benefits from packaged context and a purpose-built selector. On the same packages, the offline 0.8B reader reaches 69% overall success, including 54% on answerable questions; 2.9% of responses receive a [FORMULA] rating. The ablations implicate retrieval and writer adaptation without fully isolating their effects (§5.3). Portability of knowledge does not eliminate retrieval failure. On one package containing numerous near-duplicate XBRL observations, the offline viewer fails all 40 record-level questions despite 100% hosted record success. This exposes an unresolved selection and disambiguation problem (§5.4). 2 The Portable Work Product A paf package [FORMULA] separates six functions. Its presentation [FORMULA] is the human-readable deliverable; compiled context [FORMULA] contains typed facts, conclusions, rationales and conditions; evidence [FORMULA] contains source records, quotations and provenance; governance [FORMULA] declares permitted retrieval and interaction; a manifest [FORMULA] and signatures [FORMULA] bind the release to identifiable bytes and signers; and a runtime profile [FORMULA] declares how a consumer opens it. The package contains no answering-model weights. These roles are illustrated in Figure 1. Each package contains a manifest of payload hashes and both producer and approver signature files. The test bundle provides the four decrypted package archives; their archive SHA-256 digests match the study room records, and the listed payload hashes recompute. This demonstrates consistency of supplied bytes with the manifest, not an independent validation of a signature trust chain, approval identity or arbitrary factual accuracy. The packages include provenance records, but an author’s declaration of source provenance is not itself verified execution lineage. Content that must not be disclosed should be excluded before issuance: limiting a model’s response cannot hide bytes that a recipient can inspect in the package. A runtime can use a package to explain information present in the approved context. A question requiring external data, additional computation, a novel recommendation or an altered decision should be declined or routed for new work, not silently rewrite the signed artifact. The evaluation tests the answer-or-decline behavior using a deliberately constructed decline stratum; it does not test end-to-end escalation, revocation, signature-trust enforcement or approval of a successor release. 3 Four New Packages All four packages were generated on 1 November 2026, after the hosted and offline reader implementations had been frozen. Two were produced by an ABC Prime agent workflow; two were constructed in a Claude chat with an ABC-authored paf-from-chat skill and sealed and approved through ABC. These are distinct production paths into the same publication system, not independently specified or independently implemented PAF producers. The fund case binds a fund-profile source to separately compiled research. The Apple package starts with two large SEC XBRL company-concept files whose reported periods, fiscal labels, filings and observations contain many near-duplicates; the distilled five-year analysis is far smaller. The engineering package summarizes an AWS incident and its impact windows, starting from an already coherent post-event report. These cases therefore vary in how much compilation or retrieval selection should be required. The frozen study lists unique package identifiers and SHA-256 archive digests for all four. Both readers were evaluated on these same published artifacts. The protocol states that the packages had not been used to train, debug or tune the readers. The question sets were written from the packages and frozen before any evaluated answer was generated. This is held-out package content, not a random sample of naturally occurring documents, and the questions intentionally cover facts beyond the visible document. 4 Evaluation Protocol Each package has 100 questions: 25 memo questions answerable from its delivered report, 40 record questions whose answer exists in package records but not in that report’s headline text, and 35 decline questions requiring an unsupported scenario, new recommendation, outside information or other action the package does not authorize. We did not independently rerun the hosted models or validate the underlying source claims against external primary documents. 6 Threats to Validity and Scope The four packages were created after the reader implementations and offline adapters were fixed and were not used in earlier reader training or debugging. Each package was evaluated using 100 preselected questions with frozen gold answers, three fixed repetitions per condition, the hosted Lens instructions applicable to the study, and blinded grading by two judges. Hosted and offline answers were graded in separate blind batches, with hosted anchor responses repeated in the offline batch to check grading stability. The included results were generated with the study conditions described in §4; the held-out claim concerns the package content and fixed model configurations, not independence of package authorship or judging. The golds were compiled from the PAFs and their supporting evidence by a Claude question writer. The result therefore measures accurate access to a package-defined body of knowledge, not independent truth. The record-only sampling intentionally selects data omitted from the visible report and can favor a package-aware reader; a strong retriever over identical raw sources is the essential control. The fixed 35% decline quota can inflate the success of conservative readers relative to typical question traffic, while majority-of-three scoring can mask intermittent wrong answers. The same underlying case facts are repeated across three runs and should not be treated as independent question units. The hosted reader can perform governed, structured or multi-stage retrieval while C4 uses a single BM25 pass; the 9.75-point increment therefore reflects the complete system, not just the file format or a deterministic claim checker. O4w and O5 share a writer but not matched input distributions: the adapted writer may handle structured package lines better than raw passages because of its training. Segmentation and context budgets also differ; the offline system uses trained adapters and an embedding-based selector, and the study has no base-model-on-PAF condition that isolates those adapters. Apple O4w also received a longer context slot solely to avoid truncating an oversized raw-file prompt. C1 differs from C2 in web access and conversation batching as well as instructions. The four packages and one answering provider limit cross-task and cross-model generalization. We checked digest consistency for the supplied PAF archives and manifest entries, not an independent Ed25519 trust chain or the authority of the human approver. Some study packages declare offline mode disabled, and the test harness does not establish a conforming offline verifier. This study does not test tamper refusal, revocation, malicious package contents, prompt injection, audience-safe byte projection, escalation into approved revision, or formal execution attestation. A low [FORMULA] answer rate is evidence of behavior on these questions; it does not prove cryptographic correctness, soundness of arbitrary material claims, or suitability of financial advice. The authors retain the frozen protocols, question sets and golds, individual answers, both judges’ blind ratings and explanations, results tables, scripts and PAF packages in a private research bundle. These files are not publicly released. This limits independent replication of both the experimental findings and the provenance assertions. 7 Interpretation: what travels, and what fails to travel The comparison ladder distinguishes instruction-following from access to compiled knowledge. On the hosted system, the shift from ordinary chat (C1) to Lens instructions without the added records (C2) improves out-of-scope declines from 17% to 99%, while record success remains approximately unchanged or declines slightly (60% to 56%). This is consistent with a prompt that narrows unauthorized assertions without supplying the additional information the recipient needs. Adding ordinary retrieval (C4) takes record success to 77%; the bound package (C3) reaches 92%. Because the corpus is largely the same, this last comparison is evidence that how the knowledge is organized and made reachable matters, but the experiment does not uniquely attribute the difference to typed facts rather than the hosted runtime’s retrieval algorithm. On the offline model the picture is more extreme. O2 produces 20% overall success and 56% responses rated [FORMULA] , including 469 wrong answers and 207 unauthorized answers. O4w lowers the [FORMULA] rate to 6.2% largely by refusing questions, but resolves only 5% of answerable questions; O5 resolves 28%, and O3 54%. These results support evaluating answer coverage separately from refusal policy. They suggest that learned selection and training-compatible representations matter to the integrated reader; the test does not measure their independent causal contributions. The experiment deliberately avoids limiting PAF to the native outputs of the Prime agents. The DFEOX case compiles research around a source profile that is not the engagement’s own memo; the Apple and RCA cases compile content prepared in a general-purpose assistant, with ABC acting as packaging and issuance service. The visible work product is therefore not required to have been authored by the package’s eventual consumer, and a recipient does not need the original agent environment to ask a question. The study does not show that a source page was edited in place, nor does it establish all possible document types. It shows the narrower, consequential property that separate original content and compiled context can be delivered as one usable artifact. This is relevant to organizations that already have workflows producing PDF reports, research notes, audit records or incident summaries. A transition to interactive, bounded work products need not start by replacing every authoring system. It could start with an issuing process that attaches compiled context and declared authority to what existing processes already produce. Whether that lowers costs or improves service quality requires deployment studies beyond this question-answering benchmark. The [FORMULA] response measure combines two different behaviors: materially wrong answers on answerable questions and unauthorized answers on questions that require refusal. We therefore separate these counts, rather than describing their sum as a factual-error or real-world harm rate. The ratings do not audit the runtime’s complete call trace, prove that every retrieved claim derives from a permissible source, or check who was entitled to see each packaged byte. Likewise, a verifier can establish that a signed manifest identifies certain bytes without establishing that the numbers in them are true. The distinction is especially important in regulated use: integrity, provenance, authorization, answer grounding, and substantive correctness are different assertions and require different tests. The Apple case indicates a concrete next step: a held-out experiment that tests selectors over repeated numeric observations with explicit keys for issuer, metric, filing, fiscal period, start and end dates, units and amendments. Such a selector should retrieve the correct row or visibly return no confident match, with a held-out test set used only after the new algorithm is fixed. Separately, PAF verification needs mutation tests (tampered payloads, mismatched signatures, revoked issuers, invalid approvals) and a viewer-conformance suite covering offline policy and audience projection. Those studies can validate whether the format’s broader trust claim survives adversarial and independent implementations. They should not be read back into the present evaluation as already proven. 8 Related Work Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) conditions a model on source passages (Lewis et al., 2020). The strongest baseline here is explicitly a prompted reader with BM25 over the package’s raw source files. The measured contribution beyond that baseline must be interpreted as the joint effect of compiled context, retrieval architecture and runtime behavior rather than evidence of a universally superior retriever. Atomic factuality measurement (Min et al., 2023) and approaches that check numeric claims against a structured evidence set (Solatorio, 2025) complement, but do not substitute for, delivery of a persistent compiled artifact. C2PA content credentials and W3C Verifiable Credentials bind statements and identifiers to signed artifacts (Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity, 2025; World Wide Web Consortium, 2025); in-toto and SLSA establish software build provenance (Torres-Arias et al., 2019; Open Source Security Foundation, 2023). Those mechanisms provide important building blocks but do not alone define the context available to a later answering agent. The paf architecture combines content, evidence references, release metadata and declared interaction policy in one delivery unit. A signature authenticates the signed statement, not the correctness of all underlying facts. Prompt injection against retrieved evidence remains a threat (Greshake et al., 2023). Proof of Execution (Rhodes and Kang, 2026b) frames signed runtime evidence for governed actions, while compiled memory (Rhodes and Kang, 2026a) treats verified experience as reusable context for agents. The present paper concerns a different boundary: transferring useful knowledge with the work product so that the recipient’s reader need not reconstruct the original producer. Policy-bound answer receipts (Le Ray, 2025) and approval-integrity mechanisms (Alpay and Alpay, 2026) are complementary. Neither independent execution replay nor a cross-organization trust registry is evaluated in this study. 9 Toward an Interoperable Format The four-case test supports the value of a package carrying context across two producer paths and two readers, but all implementations and the institutional signing path share ABC-controlled format components. A generally interoperable format would require a public schema, canonical serialization, well-defined provenance semantics, trust roots and revocation rules, explicit offline permissions, audience-specific evidence projection, and independent verifier and runtime conformance tests. In particular, conformity cannot be inferred from a reader’s ability to parse and answer questions about a package. Trusted issuance must separate who signed, what was approved, which evidence was checked, and what the consuming runtime actually enforced. The offline Apple failure identifies a concrete semantic-interoperability requirement that goes beyond valid bytes: record selectors must preserve period, filing, unit, instrument and qualifier identity. Better labeling, typed lookup or an explicit structured query interface may help, but these were not evaluated in this run. The next experiment should repeat the exact question set under independent implementations and separately test cryptographic and policy conformance, without tuning on the test packages. 10 Conclusion A finished document need not be the final container for professional knowledge. The clean evaluation of four newly produced packages demonstrates that compiled context can travel with a deliverable and remain useful to a hosted governed reader and to a much smaller offline model. The hosted system resolves 96% of the fixed question set (94% on answerable questions), compared with 86% (79% answerable) when the same model receives raw-source retrieval. The local 0.8B reader resolves 69% overall (54% answerable), compared with 36% overall (5% answerable) for its trained writer over raw passages. These are results for the studied systems and question distribution, not guarantees for other tasks. The ambition is not to make every question answerable. It is to preserve the knowledge and authority boundaries behind completed work so that readers can request explanations from an accountable body of evidence and recognize when new work or a new approval is required. The held-out run also shows why that distinction matters: when the offline reader could not identify the correct XBRL record, it mostly declined rather than inventing a figure, sacrificing coverage. Portability of the artifact is necessary but not sufficient; retrieval and governance need independent conformance. A document records what was decided. A PAF package can carry the knowledge behind that decision into the next interaction. The study records and implementation materials are retained privately by the authors and are not publicly released. The manuscript reports aggregate outcomes and the protocol details needed to interpret the results but does not make the research bundle available for independent replication.

MiniZoo: An Evolving Dataset of Mini Apps for the Research Community Mini apps run within host applications (apps) such as WeChat, Alipay, Baidu, and Telegram, providing services without requiring users to install separate native apps. Their growing ecosystem has attracted research on software quality, security, and privacy, creating a need for reusable datasets. However, building and maintaining such datasets is challenging, requiring platform-specific collection infrastructure and mechanisms to handle incomplete packages, changing availability, and heterogeneous metadata. A shared, continuously maintained collection is still lacking, therefore motivating the development of a common research resource, whose value has been demonstrated by the experience of AndroZoo in the Android ecosystem. I Introduction Mini apps are lightweight applications (apps) that run within a host app, often called a super app [1]. WeChat [2], Alipay [3], Baidu [4], and Telegram [5] are among the platforms that support mini apps, exposing APIs through which these apps interact with users and access host-provided services. As mini apps expose substantial client-side functionality through platform-specific code, configuration, and interface resources, they have attracted growing interest in software engineering, security, and privacy research. Existing work has investigated mini-app bugs [6], sensitive data flows [7, 8], privacy-policy consistency [9, 10, 11], and credential leakage across multiple platforms [12], among other topics [13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18]. Conducting such research requires access to the apps themselves, yet collecting mini apps involves more than downloading files from a public web catalogue: researchers must discover apps, interact with host platforms, and retrieve packages together with associated metadata. Existing studies do not always release their collected packages, with public artifacts often focusing on the code for crawlers or analysis tools [13, 10, 19, 12]. Other initiatives, despite reporting collections containing more than one million mini apps, only share selected samples or datasets tailored to particular research questions [20, 21]. Publicly downloadable artifacts often contain extremely small datasets (e.g., 10 apps) [22]. Additionally, even when large, these collections provide only a fixed snapshot of the mini apps without preserving successive versions, limiting their usefulness for longitudinal or evolution studies. This research gap highlights the need for a large, shared, continuously maintained and evolving collection of mini apps. A successful example from which we draw inspiration is AndroZoo, a continuously growing collection of Android apps ( [FORMULA] 28M apps in November 2026) used by thousands of researchers (more than 1600 citations) [23, 24]. In this paper, we present MiniZoo, an evolving dataset of mini apps for the research community. To build and maintain this resource, we have established automated crawling infrastructure to discover mini apps and collect their packages, associated metadata, and acquisition records. Although the current corpus focuses on WeChat, MiniZoo follows a platform-agnostic organization that we plan to extend to additional mini-app ecosystems through dedicated crawlers while retaining a common data structure and access framework. As of November 9th 2026, MiniZoo contains [FORMULA] mini apps, of which [FORMULA] ( [FORMULA] %) already have multiple recorded versions, for a total of [FORMULA] distinct packages. These packages and metadata support research on software quality, security, and privacy, while continued collection will expand opportunities for longitudinal studies of mini-app evolution. MiniZoo is hosted and managed through AndroZoo [23, 24], allowing us to reuse its existing infrastructure, draw on its maintenance expertise, and reach its established research community. The dataset and the access conditions are available at: https://androzoo.uni.lu/minizoo II Dataset Overview MiniZoo is designed as a continuously growing collection of mini-app packages and metadata for the research community. Each mini-app platform has its own architecture and mechanisms for mini-app discovery and package retrieval, requiring dedicated crawlers whose development and maintenance are challenging and time-consuming. We therefore selected WeChat as our initial target because it has been extensively investigated in the research literature [13, 7, 10], with concrete plans to extend the collection to other mini-app platforms. Mini-app platforms can also differ in their package formats and execution environments; for example, WeChat uses the .wxapkg format (see Section III) and provides a runtime within the host app to load and execute mini-app code. Although the current corpus focuses on WeChat Mini Programs, the dataset follows a platform-agnostic organization to support planned extensions to other ecosystems, such as Alipay, Baidu, and Telegram. Its core abstractions and metadata schema provide a common structure that can be extended with platform-specific fields as needed. Definitions: Mini Apps and Packages. An important distinction must be made between ① a mini app and ② its packages. A mini app is identified within its host platform by a unique identifier, such as the AppID in WeChat, which allows different versions of the same mini app to be associated with a single identity. A package is an archive containing client-side code and resources that can be identified by a hash (e.g., SHA-256). If an update changes the archive’s contents, the resulting package has a different hash while remaining associated with the same mini app. For example, if a weather mini app receives such an update, its AppID would remain the same, while the SHA-256 hash identifying its package would differ from that of the previous package. This distinction is analogous to that between Android apps, identified by package names such as com.android.chrome, and APK files, the archives containing their code and resources. In AndroZoo, apps are identified by their package name, while individual APK files are identified by their SHA-256 hashes, with multiple APKs sharing the same package name and representing different versions of the same app [23, 24]. Dataset Content. For WeChat, we decided to rely on AppIDs to identify mini apps and on SHA-256 hashes to identify their packages, distributed in the platform-specific .wxapkg format described later in Section III. Table I summarizes the corpus as of November 9th 2026, while updated statistics are available on the MiniZoo website. Continued collection will expand both the number of represented apps and the version histories available for longitudinal analysis. Data Organization. Users have access to a single compressed tar.gz archive, which download instructions are provided later in Section IV. The archive comprises three main components: minizoo.csv: a CSV file listing all the mini apps available in MiniZoo and their associated packages. The acquired packages, i.e., .wxapkg files. minizoo_metadata.jsonl: a JSON Lines file containing structured metadata complementing the CSV list with additional information that researchers can use. While this initial distribution model provides access to the complete corpus in a single download, we plan to extend the API to support selective package retrieval as the collection grows. Researchers will then be able to specify the SHA-256 hashes of the packages they need or to download all the packages related to a specific appID, following AndroZoo’s existing download model and avoiding the need to download the entire archive for studies focusing on a subset of the collection. In addition to the packages themselves, MiniZoo provides metadata describing the collected mini apps, their packages, and acquisition times, helping researchers interpret the corpus and select data relevant to their studies.
