Agentic approaches prioritize planning capabilities and task autonomy at higher computational cost. Agentless approaches offer lower-cost alternatives that, as demonstrated by Xia et al. [40], achieve competitive effectiveness. Several agentic approaches have been developed for bug reproduction test generation. SWE-Agent [41] introduced a software-engineering-specific agentic system with an enriched user interface. OpenHands [8] ranks among the most effective agentic systems on SWT-Bench, extending SWE-Agent through multi-capability agent deployment to provide a more generalized framework. AEGIS [42] represents the first domain-specific agent for bug reproduction, incorporating a text generation module followed by an FSM-based feedback module. BRT Agent [43] augments the established, LIBRO [13] framework by integrating a reasoning module into its reproduction pipeline. LIBRO [13] represents an early agentless framework that combines few-shot prompting with post-generation ranking. Otter [44] employs LLM-driven planning instead of ranking, sequentially localizing files, generating a resolution plan, revising it, and executing. e-Otter++ [45]mu extends this approach by generating multiple candidate tests using Otter and critiquing and repairing them via LLM feedback. Issue2Test [46] advances SWT-Bench performance over SWE-Agent, and LIBRO by incorporating an error categorization step to refine failing tests. AssertFlip [7] adopts a similar refinement strategy through assertion inversion by generating a passing test from an LLM-produced test plan, flipping the assertion, and validating through LLM-based criticism. IV Study Design This study focuses on investigating the common pitfalls of automatic reproduction test generation and how our findings can help practitioners utilize state-of-the-art LLM-based generation tools. This study was conducted with a selection of two top open-source generation frameworks on the SWT-Bench Verified leaderboard [9]. We focus the study on the SWT-Bench Verified benchmark, as, unlike GitBugJava or CrashJs, it provides a containerized execution environment [24][25]. Developing this environment from scratch for these benchmarks would be a significant undertaking in and of itself. The environment, like the one SWT-Bench provides, ensures all evaluation attempts are consistent, thus reducing a potential source of error within a paper’s evaluations. We also perform our study on two general-purpose and lightweight LLMs, GPT-4o-mini and GPT-5-mini, which represent typical usage in the real world. Furthermore, selecting the GPT family of models allows this study to closely align with the results of OpenHands and AssertFlip on the SWT-Bench Verified leaderboard [9]. Finally, based on the existing taxonomy [39], we expand and label the invalidity of generated reproduction tests. The SWT Bench evaluation harness is used as a uniform evaluation method for each tool-model pair. There may be issues in each pair that cannot be assessed, as they do not generate a test for the harness to evaluate. For instance, AssertFlip with GPT-5-mini may have more labelled failures than AssertFlip on GPT-4o-mini, as the latter was not able to generate the same quantity of inferences for the SWT Bench harness to evaluate. Finally, to test the practicality of our findings, we apply some concrete insights from our taxonomy to improve the test generation from the practitioner’s point of view and observe significant improvement with simple issue description augmentation. Several reproduction test generation frameworks are reported on the SWT-Bench leaderboard; however, we focus on open-source frameworks to aid with taxonomy construction and reasoning about failure modes, as closed-source frameworks would hinder our ability to closely investigate the root causes of generation failures. AssertFlip and OpenHands represent the top two open-source frameworks on the SWT-Bench Verified leaderboard. Even if AssertFlip and OpenHands reflect the leading open-source frameworks at the time of this study rather than absolute state-of-the-art performance overall, this does not limit our findings. Our primary focus is identifying recurring modes of failure and actionable avenues for improvement from a practitioner’s perspective. In this study, GPT-4o-mini and GPT-5-mini are chosen for their lightweight reasoning capability. The dichotomy between these two models enables the taxonomy results to be analyzed on the basis of model as well as the generation frameworks. This further analysis will provide insights on the model’s influence in terms of generated reproduction test failure. In general, taxonomization aids in categorizing failing tests by using a standard language. Individual test failure taxonomies were decided upon after reviewing the available existing taxonomies in the background and related work. As existing taxonomy categories do not provide specific categories necessary for classifying bug reproduction test failures, we decided to develop our own. This synthesis enables a detailed analysis of test generation failures and provides more concrete insights so that practitioners can improve the generated test with targeted issue description augmentation. The thematic construction of this taxonomy required three of the authors to participate in the labelling process. Two authors began the process by agreeing on an initial set of categories and independently labelling all failing instances from our selected frameworks and LLMs. In the event of a labelling disagreement, or an ambiguous case, a third author acted as a tie-breaker to ensure every label received a majority consensus. Our initial set included Output Format Inconsistency, Wrong API Call, Incorrect Input/Mock, Logical Failure, Misunderstanding Edge Case Logic, and Misunderstanding Function Logic From Natural Language. Instances that did not adhere to this initial set were skipped. Once the initial labelling step was complete, the authors agreed on new labels to independently label the remaining instances. Once the entire labelling process was complete, the authors grouped the labels into overarching themes, creating the class-subclass dynamic presented in this paper. This process can be exemplified through the issues django-13807 and astropy-14309 on AssertFlip GPT-5-mini as well as django-15629 on Openhands GPT-5-mini (as listed in table I). django-13807 was classified as Wrong API Call due to the attempt to create a table not including a command to generate a table. This failure pattern is confirmed from the test’s execution trace, which crashes due to the table not existing. Therefore, it fit the original definition of Wrong API Call as a result of improperly generating an SQL table. Conversely, astropy-14309 failed due to the generated test’s assertion being formatted to only search for empty lists. This pattern did not fit the original labels, as, except for the final assertion, the test adhered to the correct implementation and issue logic. This failure mode was confirmed by reviewing the assertion error generated within the execution trace and by reviewing the issue text. As such, in the second round of labelling, it was assigned Incorrect Assertion. While the generated test for django-15629 was formatted correctly, it failed as a result of a misinterpretation of the original prompt. Specifically, the generated test ignored the requirement of using the migrations library in Django, thus resulting in an invalid test environment. Since the test failed to follow a clear requirement within the problem prompt, it was classified as Misunderstanding Function Logic From Natural Language. To validate the reliability of our manual annotation process, we calculated the inter-annotator agreement using Cohen’s Kappa coefficient ( [FORMULA] ). This metric is particularly suited for our study as it accounts for the agreement occurring by chance. The coefficient is defined as: where [FORMULA] represents the relative observed agreement among raters, and [FORMULA] is the hypothetical probability of chance agreement. In our evaluation, the annotators achieved a [FORMULA] of 0.953. Following the widely accepted scale by Landis and Koch [47], this value indicates “almost perfect“ agreement, confirming the high degree of consistency and reliability in our dataset labeling. Table I shows our full taxonomy with subcategories along with their definitions and examples. We present the Misimplementations, Mechanical Failure, and Requirement Misunderstanding classes to respectively represent instances of improper test state, external failure, and an incapability to understand the requirements of an issue. Misimplementations contains the Logical Failure, Incorrect Assertion, and Incorrect Input / Mock subclasses to distinguish the specific manner by which a test fails to generate a reflective bug reproduction test. Additionally, Mechanical Failure is expanded upon by including the Wrong API Call, Output Format Inconsistency, Environment Error, Not Implemented, and Incorrect File Reference subclasses to represent instances of incorrect library interaction, failed environment setup, and invalid test generation. Lastly, Requirement Misunderstanding includes the Misunderstanding Edge Case Logic and Misunderstanding Function Logic From Natural Language subclasses to articulate the source of a tool’s inability to internalize a problem’s requirements. Returning to the example issues, astropy- 14309, django- 13807, and django-15629, the former’s error pattern was grouped with Misimplementations as the generation resulted in an improper test state. Conversely, the failure pattern in django- 13807 was consistent with the Mechanical Failure grouping as an instance of external failure. The latter issue’s failure pattern, being due to a misunderstanding of the issue’s requirements, was thematically grouped within Requirement Misunderstandings. These categories, being based on software engineering phenomena, ensure the taxonomy’s generalizability outside of SWT-Bench as a tool, but must still resolve these same challenges of reproducing a bug from an issue. V Experiment Setup The test generation frameworks are executed on a 2019 MacBookPro with 32 GB of memory running macOS 15.6.1. Following the replication instructions on the respective GitHub repositories for AssertFlip [7] and OpenHands [8], Docker with Anaconda is configured. To minimize resource wastage, the experiment on OpenHands with GPT-5-mini was reused from prior work [9]. The hyperparameters, such as the number of generation iterations, for both AssertFlip and OpenHands are kept at the default values to ensure consistent results. The SWT-Bench evaluation harness [9] was used to assess the generated tests from each tool-model pair. The failing tests, along with their associated error traces (the trace of a test’s execution) from the evaluation harness, were then extracted to label and construct the taxonomy. VI Results In this section, we provide the investigation and answer for each research question. Specifically, we present the overall distribution of failure classes and discuss the common failure patterns to answer RQ1. Next, we analyze the differences between frameworks and LLMs and discuss the specific failure modes when different frameworks and LLMs are used. And finally, we present some concrete experiments showing how the finding from our taxonomy can help practitioners make concrete arguments to test generation frameworks and improve their performance. To answer this research question, three authors manually reviewed the generated reproduction test failures and labeled each instance with one of the categories from our taxonomy presented in table I. This taxonomy was constructed concurrently with labeling to ensure consistency and completeness. Figure 1.a shows the distributions of the reproduction test failures across all three framework-LLM combinations. Each bar represents a failure class with texturing to represent failure subclasses. When reading the graph from left to right, the bars respectively represent Mechanical Failure, Misimplementations and Requirement Misunderstanding. The distribution is presented as the percentage of the particular class with respect to the total number of generated test cases. This will show the relative distribution between different tool-model combinations. However, since each configuration would have a different number of generated test cases, table II also shows the raw number of failed tests in each failure class, as well as the number of valid tests and the total number of generated tests. Note that unless otherwise specified, all percentages are reported as relative to total generated tests for a specific tool-model pairing. Overall, the most prevalent failure classes across the 435 test failures are Mechanical Failure and Misimplementations. These two classes were observed in 30.0% of all generated tests. The three most prevalent subclasses of Mechanical Failure include Environment Error (12.1%), Wrong API Call (10.2%) and Output Format Inconsistency (2.6%). The first subclass presents an interesting mode of failure by which a test cannot be executed due to an error in establishing its runtime environment. Furthermore, the prevalence of Wrong API Call highlights the detriment of a lack of library-specific context. For instance, sympy-15875 failed as the model did not assume that the method under test could return None. Therefore, a relatively superficial assumption in the library’s contract led to a failed bug reproduction test. The three subclasses in Misimplementation, including Logical Failure (6.5%), Incorrect Assertion (5.8%), and Incorrect Input/Mock (3.5%), represent the main challenges of test generation: how to generate (1) a valid test oracle with (2) appropriate input, with (3) the correct testing logic. For instance, in the issue astropy-14309, the model assumed that resolving the given IndexError implied asserting an empty file registry despite there being other file types within the issue, thus resulting in an Incorrect Assertion. This demonstrates that when the tool fails to generate an effective test, it typically does so for superficial contextual or logical reasons. The subclasses of Requirement Misunderstanding were observed at a significantly lower rate than their peers. Misunderstanding Edge Case Logic and Misunderstanding Function Logic From Natural Language were respectively observed at a rate of 1.3% and 0.6%. These failures, unlike the most common subclasses, typically include added logical complexity within their class-specific domain. For instance, a non-Latin character translation failure demonstrates the added complexity of Misunderstanding Function Logic From Natural Language as it requires domain knowledge on non-Latin alphabets and Domain Name Service (DNS) translation. Overall, the majority of overall failing issues tend to fail as a result of poor test implementation or a lack of library context. Conversely, the least observed failure classes tend to suffer from a higher logical complexity. This finding suggests that most issues fail as a result of a lack of logical or contextual clarity rather than a high logical complexity, and further clarification in the issue text would help the model generate more correct test cases. We will explore applying this finding in Section VII. In this RQ, we seek to determine the influence of a tool’s test generation strategy on the distribution of observed failure classes. To do so, we investigate the differences in frequency and proportion of observed failures between AssertFlip’s 263 generated tests (figure 1.c) and OpenHands’ 464 generated tests (figure 1.e) on the same LLM (GPT-5-mini). The same analysis is done on GPT-4o-mini (figures 1.b and 1.d). The overall per-tool distributions differ significantly in their top two observed classes. For instance, Misimplementations (8.0% vs. 15.1%) and Mechanical Failure (7.6% vs. 21.8%) go from being relatively equal on AssertFlip GPT-5-mini to significantly imbalanced on OpenHands GPT-5-mini, with Requirement Misunderstanding remaining relatively marginal. This trend is primarily driven by the lower relative quantity of Environment Error on AssertFlip-GPT-5-mini relative to OpenHands (1.9% vs. 7.3%). For instance, although pytest-5262 fails on both tool-model pairs, AssertFlip produces an Incorrect Input/Mock whereas OpenHands produces an Environment Error. This failure class imbalance is also observed on both tools when using GPT-4o-mini. The higher proportion of Mechanical Failure (14.1% vs. 64.8%) compared to Misimplementations (25.4% v 25.0%) on Openhands is driven by the significantly higher proportion of Environment Error (0.0% vs. 41.3%). Due to its agentic approach, OpenHands might misconfigure the test, leading to missing files and incorrect environmental setup errors. Intriguingly, the relative proportion in Misimplementations remains stable across both tools on GPT-5-mini. For instance, Incorrect Assertion (3.0%) on AssertFlip GPT-5-mini and OpenHands GPT-5-mini (5.4%) comprise approximately a third of their respective Misimplementations class. While the subclass proportion changes on GPT-4o-mini, the same pattern of relative Misimplementation stability across both tools remains. This proportion suggests a failure parity; despite different operational paradigms, AssertFlip’s specialized inversion versus OpenHands’ agentic interaction, both tools reach a similar bottleneck where implementation failure presents itself at nearly identical rates. While both tools reach similar bottlenecks, OpenHands produces more tests while AssertFlip has a higher precision in test generation. On one hand, AssertFlip, with its verify and flip approach, already pre-verifies many test implementation details prior to reproduction test generation. This method means that AssertFlip is less likely to generate tests that have Mechanical Failure or Misimplementations leading to an overall more precise set of generated tests at the cost of reduced generation volume. On the other hand, OpenHands, with its agentic approach, generates the tests directly using LLM without implementation details verification which led to a higher rate of Mechanical Failure due largely to incorrect environmental setup. Overall, different approaches can have different effects on how precisely the tests are generated. Specifically, AssertFlip’s implementation details verification reduce the amount of generated tests but improve precision, whereas OpenHands’s agentic approach favors coverage with more tests generated at the cost of lower precision. Given that both tools heavily rely on LLMs to generate test cases, we seek to investigate the effect of model selection on the distribution of failure classes. To this end, RQ3 will compare the frequency and proportion of observed failures between GPT-4o-mini (figure 1.b and figure 1.d) and GPT-5-mini (figure 1.c and figure 1.e) on AssertFlip and OpenHands, respectively. Overall, the distribution changes significantly between GPT-4o-mini and GPT-5-mini. Using AssertFlip, with GPT-4o-mini incurs a larger portion of Mechanical Failures (14.1% vs. 7.6%) and Misimplementations (25.4% vs. 8.0%). This pattern is also observable on OpenHands with GPT-4o-mini having more Mechanical Failure (64.8% vs. 21.8%) and Misimplementations (25.0% vs. 15.1%). This difference might indicate that GPT-4o-mini makes more mistakes due to its smaller knowledge base [48] and weaker reasoning ability [49]. GPT-5-mini can generate more precise tests without Mechanical Failure and Misimplementations. Notably, on AssertFlip, Wrong API Call and Incorrect Assertion are the most prevalent failure modes in GPT-4o-mini generated tests. For example, in the case of django-15499, GPT-4o-mini generates a test that fails due to a misunderstanding that optimization logic in Django’s reduce method is a multi-step sequence. But the tool attempted to verify it using a single comparison call while asserting that the result should contain the cumulative changes of two separate operations. Since the API only handles one peer-to-peer merger at a time, the second set of changes was never actually processed. GPT-5-mini rectifies this test by utilizing the MigrationOptimizer class, which provides the correct high-level abstraction. By passing the entire list of operations into the optimizer, the test allows Django to handle the iterative reduction logic internally, accurately reflecting the desired outcome where multiple operations collapse into a single, updated CreateModel. Therefore, GPT-5-mini, unlike GPT-4o-mini, leverages its stronger knowledge base to interact with the correct API method to generate an accurate bug reproduction test. While failures generally decrease from GPT-4o-mini to GPT-5-mini, the rate of Requirement Misunderstanding increases both on AssertFlip (0.0% vs. 1.5%) and OpenHands ( 2.0% vs. 2.4%). This slight increase may account for a subset of issues which, despite overcoming Misimplementation and Mechanical Failure, fail to satisfy a problem’s requirements. For example, the issue django-15629, previously discussed in section IV, failed on OpenHands GPT-5-Mini due to a Requirement Misunderstanding. On OpenHands GPT-4-Mini, it could not even proceed to execution as a result of an Environment Error due to a Module Not Found error. Therefore, while GPT-5-mini decreases failures overall, Requirement Misunderstandings increase due to the conversion of Mechanical Failure and Misimplementations Furthermore, GPT-5-mini was able to generate significantly more tests compared to GPT-4o-mini; 263 vs. 71 on AssertFlip and 464 vs. 196 on OpenHands. This difference indicates that GPT-5-mini is much more capable at creating syntactically correct tests, which leads to both better precision and coverage. VII Discussion: Taxonomy provides insight to improve test generation with context enrichment To determine if our taxonomy can give concrete insights to practitioners, we conduct a small experiment where the insights from our findings can guide augmentations that are applied directly to an issue’s natural language description. This method can help improve the outcome of the generated test. Table III presents our attempts with specific issues (Col Issue), in different subclasses (Col Failure Subclass). The Issue Summary column describes an issue’s problem statement, and finally, we provide our concrete addition to the issue description that can help improve the generated test quality. Specifically, for each failure mode, we craft an augmentation template that focuses the LLMs on avoiding the mistake in the first place. For this experiment, we utilize AssertFlip and GPT-5-mini. Wrong API Call: For failures of this type, we focus the LLMs with the following template: Ensure to fully understand and properly use the X libraries to the fullest extent necessary to correctly replicate the bug, where X is the specific API(s) that the LLM needs to pay attention to. Table III shows the issues to which we apply this augmentation strategy. Of the six issues, two generate correct test cases after the augmentation. Specifically django-15382, django-13195, sympy-19495 and sympy-15976 fail to produce valid bug reproduction tests. Unlike the following failure categories, these samples rely upon a considerable understanding of the library they will be using to effectively replicate a bug. In each failing test, the mode of failure remained the same. This concentration of failures demonstrates how library understanding requires a significant amount of context which the tool may not be able to accommodate. For example, in django-13195, the failure persists due to the model’s inability to comprehend the complexities of the web-framework along with the necessary configuration for a web cookie. This failure can be contrasted by the success of django-13807. Whereas django-13195 failed due to insufficient API context, the subject matter of django-13807, generating a simple database table, was of reasonable complexity for the model to properly replicate. Therefore, failures within the Wrong API Call type occur due to a need for a deeper contextual understanding of the libraries. Incorrect Input/Mock: To focus the LLMs on making sure the input are generated or mocked correctly, we use the following template: Ensure to fully, to the extent needed, understand and emulate the behaviour, input requirements and state of X, where X is the specific input object or class that needs to be correctly initialized or mocked. We apply this augmentation strategy to pytest-5262 and xarray-6721, which are presented in Table III. Of the two issues, both generate correct test cases after the augmentation. By providing a simple command to sufficiently mimic the behavior of their target mock, the tools replicated their respective issue’s bug. This success demonstrates that, when given a minimal amount of context, the tool can create an effective mock, thus replicating the bug. Incorrect Assertion: To ensure the tool generates accurate assertions, we use the following template: Review your target output and the expected behaviour, make sure your assertions fully reflect the X, where X is specific target which the assertion should focus on. We apply this augmentation strategy to astropy-14309, django-13212 and sphinx-10466 which are presented in Table III. Of the three issues, all generate correct test cases after the augmentation. Therefore, the augmentation to review each issue’s expected behaviour and target output successfully resolved the failing instances. For instance, astropy-14309 resolves its index error by either checking for an empty list or a list of valid file formats. This is in contrast to the failing test which only asserted an empty list. Ultimately, this augmentation encourages the LLM to undertake a deeper review of the issue’s requirements and methods of assessment. Overall, our quick experiment shows a general success of context enrichment guided by our failure taxonomy with 7 out of 11 augmentations successfully improving the generated tests. This result shows that our taxonomy can be a concrete guide to users in improving reproduction test generation using LLMs, and future research can utilize such a taxonomy to develop techniques that automatically improve the overall performance of LLM-generated reproduction tests. VIII Threats to Validity Scope: This study analyzes OpenHands and AssertFlip using the Python language. Both tools capture the diversity of methodologies seen in LLM-driven bug reproduction tools (agentic loop and rule-based hybrid frameworks). Despite this capture, hyper-specific, tool-based failure modes from novel methodologies may be excluded from this taxonomy. Furthermore, language-specific failure modes are therefore not captured within the presented taxonomy Data Leakage: The risk of data leakage increases as models continually undergo training, since it is possible for the models to be trained on the issues within the SWT-Bench datasets. This form of leakage could introduce false positive results, as passing bug reproduction tests would be achieved via memorization rather than learning. LLM Stochasticity: Given the probabilistic nature of LLMs, the exact results, even when using the same input parameters, may differ. Naturally, this threat may diminish the independent ability to verify this taxonomy through direct replication. Despite this threat, the taxonomy can be independently assessed via extension to other tools and models. Human Subjectivity: While the labelling process followed a majority consensus model, the potential for Researcher Bias remains a threat. Individual experience with the Python ecosystem or specific libraries may have influenced the classification of failure modes. The extension of an existing taxonomy, blind labelling, and consensus methodology mitigate this threat by limiting interpretation and encouraging evidence-based justification, especially in the event of disagreement. IX Conclusion Given the importance of automated bug reproduction frameworks in improving program repair, understanding the failures of these tools is integral. This study addresses the existing literature gap by generating a taxonomy of automated bug reproduction test failures of state-of-the-art open-source frameworks using two modern GPT models. Our findings indicate that different framework approaches can lead to different precision and coverage tradeoff and more powerful LLMs are more likely to increase the quality and quantity of generated tests. We also demonstrate that our taxonomy can be used as guidance to targeted augmentation which can lead to improvement of generated reproduction tests.

The AI Era’s Lines of Code? A Case Study on What an Engineer’s Token Spend Measures Organizations use engineers’ token spend to monitor AI adoption, set budgets, and measure productivity, but the metric’s relationship with engineering output is unclear. We link five weeks of token usage in coding agents to the commits of 404 engineers at JetBrains, and analyze a company survey of 412 employees. We find that token spend varied mostly between engineers, and which engineers spent the most stayed largely the same over the five weeks. Among weeks with similar commit counts, the 90th percentile of spend was 39 to 240 times the 10th. Within an engineer, doubling spend was associated with about 10% more commits. Available work metrics explained 38% of the variation in spend between engineers and 13% of the week-to-week variation within an engineer. In the survey, respondents in technical roles reported in nearly nine of ten agent evaluations using agents for tasks beyond coding, such as analysis, research, and planning. Token spend therefore measures how much engineers use agents across many kinds of work and not the outcome and value of that work. We recommend using token spend at most for resource accounting, and evaluating agent-assisted work with evidence about tasks and outcomes. I Introduction Many engineers now write software by instructing a coding agent, reviewing what it did, and asking for changes or further work [1, 2, 3]. Whatever code these interactions produce is still recorded, as before, in commits and pull requests. Every exchange with the agent is also recorded in the agent’s usage log, or agent telemetry. For each exchange, the model provider logs and bills the tokens sent and received, along with the tool and model used. Summed per engineer and per week, these counts are the engineer’s token spend. Spend counts every exchange, including those that never lead to a commit, but it does not record what an exchange was about. Providers do not share session content by default, and few companies record it themselves, so the organization that pays usually sees only the token count, as in our data (Section III-A). Some organizations already use token spend to evaluate engineers. At Meta, an employee built a dashboard on which colleagues competed to be the company’s top token user; it was taken down after the press reported on it [4, 5]. Executives at Nvidia and Meta have said that a good engineer should use tokens worth a large share of their salary [6], and Salesforce has set minimum monthly spending targets [7]. Analytics vendors divide token cost by merged pull requests and report the ratio as return on investment [8, 9]. Each of these uses assumes that an engineer who spends more produces more. Practitioners have begun to doubt that assumption. Uber spent its 2026 budget for AI coding tools in four months; its COO said that the link between token spend and shipped features “is not there yet” [10]. One critic called token spend “the lines-of-code metric of the AI era: easy to measure, easy to game, and disconnected from actual productivity” [5]. Prior studies of whether more tokens mean more output give mixed answers. On benchmarks, agents that run longer do not reliably solve more tasks [11, 12, 13]. In deployed use, output rises far less than spend: a press summary of vendor data reports that developers who spend ten times more merge about twice as many pull requests [14], and one enterprise doubled its throughput but raised its spend at least twenty-fold [2]. Outside benchmarks, these comparisons are between engineers, or between organizations. Engineers differ in role, team, and work practices, so a difference in spend between two of them may reflect those differences as much as any difference in what they produced. No study has followed both spend and output for the same engineers over time, so whether an engineer’s spend varies with their output from week to week is not known. Telemetry from one agent shows how widely usage varies across users but does not have output data to compare it with [1], and recent panel studies measure agent use by days [3], interactions [15], or lines the agent wrote [2], and report spend only in aggregate, if at all. In this paper, we ask what an engineer’s token spend measures and what it can be used for. We study 404 engineers at a software development company whose internal gateway meters the tokens of every coding-agent call. From the gateway counts and the company’s repositories, we follow each engineer’s token spend and commits week by week for five weeks, and we analyze an anonymous survey of the company’s employees about their AI use. We ask two questions. RQ1: How closely is an engineer’s token spend related to their output? We compare an engineer’s weeks with one another, which holds the engineer fixed, and we compare engineers with each other. RQ2: Where does the token spend that is not tied to repository output go? That spend may be work that never becomes a commit, which studies of repository output would miss, or overhead. The telemetry shows when each call happened and how many tokens it used, but not what it was for, so it cannot distinguish the two. We use the telemetry to estimate the share of spend not tied to output, and the survey to learn what engineers use agents for and how many hours they report saving. We find that spend depends more on the engineer than on the week’s output (RQ1). A week with twice an engineer’s usual spend has only about 10% more commits, weeks with similar commit counts differ in spend by a factor of 39 to 240 (Figure 1), and the engineers who spend the most are largely the same over the five weeks. Up to about two fifths of spend does not vary with the week’s output, and in 89% of technical respondents’ evaluations of a coding agent, they had used it that week for something other than writing code (RQ2). Engineers choose how much to use agents, so these are associations. Our contribution is an empirical study that links engineers’ metered token spend to their repository output and to their own accounts of agent use. It shows that token spend measures how much an engineer works through agents, not what they produce, so it should not be used as a measure of productivity. II Related work Organizations started adopting token spend as a management metric before peer-reviewed research could examine it, so we follow multivocal review guidance [16] and include grey literature (vendor reports, practitioner accounts, and technical press) alongside academic work. Lines of code became a productivity measure because they were cheap to count, and they have long been criticized for penalizing expressive languages and inviting padding [17, 18, 19, 20]. Still, they stayed in use because program size is associated with effort closely enough to support cost models [19]. That history suggests that an indicator that is convenient to collect is not automatically a valid proxy for the attribute of interest [20], and that a measure that becomes a target ceases to be a good measure [21]. SPACE [22] and DORA [23], which replace single numbers with several, measure outputs, outcomes, and processes, but not the resources used, a reasonable omission while the main input was human time. For DX Core 4, which builds on both, AI makes the metrics noisier, because “the same number can now be produced by very different combinations of human and AI behavior” [24]. Empirical studies of AI-assisted development mostly observe work through commits, pull requests, and reviews [25, 26, 2, 3]. Agent telemetry adds a record of the resources used, metered per person, including the interactions that don’t produce any artifact. Most academic work on token consumption studies agent trajectories on benchmarks such as SWE-bench [27]. Accumulated context and cache reads, not generated output, account for most tokens and most cost [11, 28, 29, 1]. Spending more does not reliably increase success: accuracy peaks at intermediate cost, failed attempts cost more than successful ones, and the extra tokens go to repeated file views, retry loops, and generation after a passing solution [11, 12, 13, 1]. Much of the variance is unrelated to the task: consumption depends on model, scaffold, and language, and only weakly on expert-rated difficulty [11, 12, 13]. Token counts are also an unstable proxy for cost. Since cost became an evaluation dimension [30], many methods reduce tokens [31, 32, 33, 34, 35, 36], but fewer tokens do not always mean lower cost. Removing 38.4% of tool-output tokens increased billed cost by 6.8%, because the agent spent extra turns diagnosing and re-reading the removed context [29]. With feature, review gate, and model held constant, cost per merged feature varies about 2.5-fold across harnesses [37]. If token counts are an unreliable measure of cost at the task level, they are unlikely to be a reliable measure of value at the organizational level. We did not find any peer-reviewed study of how token spend relates to engineering outcomes across developers or organizations. Telemetry studies show that spend varies 50-fold or more between users but do not report outcomes [1, 38], and a single-developer case study links higher token use to a lower fix-commit ratio but changed model and harness at the same time [39]. Adoption studies find more commits or merged pull requests after adoption, with the gains shrinking before release [25, 26, 3, 40, 41], but they compare use with non-use and do not measure tokens. Two panel studies closest to ours measure how intensively engineers use AI tools, though also not in tokens. He et al. count AI-written lines and find that a mandate to double merged pull requests raised throughput 2.09-fold while spend increased at least 20-fold [2]; Heilman et al. count Copilot interactions and find 40.5% more completed pull requests in an engineer’s weeks of heaviest use than in weeks without use [15]. Self-reported speedups can diverge from measured time: in a randomized trial, developers took 19% longer with AI tools but thought they were faster [42]. Only analytics vendors have joined token telemetry to delivery data across organizations, and they report that throughput rises far less than spend. From the lowest to the highest usage decile, weekly pull requests nearly tripled while cost per merged pull request rose about 300-fold [8], and merged output per dollar fell by about 70% during 2026 [9]. Alongside the throughput gains, other reports find more bugs and churn, and lower acceptance once later revisions are counted [43, 14]. None of these reports is peer reviewed, and their methods are only partly disclosed. Practitioners also disagree on what token spend is. Some treat it as a measure of engagement, equating good engineering with heavy use [6] or setting a daily token threshold for adoption [44, 45]. Others treat it as a cost to cap [46] or to divide by output, or as a proxy for output itself, a practice called tokenmaxxing [5]; one practitioner observes that lines of code now correlate highly with token spend [47]. Reports of employees inflating their usage [4, 5, 48, 49] fit Goodhart-style gaming [21] but remain anecdotal. Prior work has not answered two questions about the engineers behind the telemetry. The first is what an individual’s spend reflects. Studies that join spend to output compare deciles of users or follow organizations [8, 9, 2], so they cannot separate how much an engineer habitually works through agents from how their use changes with the work at hand. The second is how much agent-assisted work ends up in the repository. Half of production agent turns are exploration or reasoning, not editing [1], yet adoption studies measure outcomes through repository artifacts [25, 2] and look for lost gains only after the first commit [41]; no study has estimated how much consumption never leads to a commit. Token counts depend on model, harness, and caching regime [11, 29, 39], so our person-week panel addresses both questions within a single tooling environment, where the counts are comparable. III Methods We combine gateway telemetry of agent use at JetBrains with repository records of the same engineers’ output. We also draw on an anonymous internal survey on AI tools that the company ran during the study period; survey responses cannot be linked to individual engineers’ telemetry or repository data. Because engineers choose how much to use the agents, all our estimates are associations, not causal effects. JetBrains builds software development tools and had about 2,600 employees at the time of the study.11 1 About JetBrains https://www.jetbrains.com/company/ We study coding-agent use as recorded by the company’s internal gateway, which logs every agent call in a consistent format. We extracted pseudonymized data from internal systems on the 584 engineers who committed to one of the company’s main IDE products in our study window, 2026-05-10 to 2026-08-08. The commit data spans the window, but our access to the gateway’s token data spans only its last weeks; we analyze the five complete weeks in that period, 2026-06-29 to 2026-08-02 (the analysis weeks). We exclude the final six days (2026-08-03 to 2026-08-08), because commits during that period may have been merged after the extract date. The seven weeks before the analysis weeks (the pre-period) have commit data but no token data. Engineers had access to AI tools in the pre-period too, so it is not a period without AI. We use the pre-period data to describe each engineer’s prior work mix (Section III-B). From the company directory we extract each engineer’s team, job title, and manager flag. We assign each engineer a role (developer, QA engineer, team lead or manager, intern, other) from keywords in the job title. QA and developer keywords take precedence over lead and manager, so a lead QA engineer is a QA engineer. The agent telemetry contains 3.1 million agent calls by 406 of the 584 engineers from 2026-06-29 to 2026-08-08. Each call records a timestamp, the agent (two agents account for nearly all tokens: Agent A for 69% and Agent B for 31%), the model, the number of tokens, and the credits charged. Most tokens are context re-sent on every turn: the median call sends about 400 times as many tokens as it receives. We measure spend in tokens; credits, the company’s cost unit, rank engineers almost identically (Spearman [FORMULA] ) and serve as a sensitivity check. Tokens measure only the inference part of the input; the engineers’ own time, the larger cost, is not in our data. Spend varies widely between engineers (Figure 2): over the five analysis weeks, the engineer at the 90th percentile used 71 times as many tokens as the engineer at the 10th. For output we measure the number of commits. We date each commit by its author date, when the change was written and the agent was used, not by the commit date, which rebases and squash merges change to be the merge time. For each commit we also know its size (lines added and deleted and files changed, recorded in bins; we use bin midpoints), whether it changes the shared IDE platform or a surrounding project, and the issues referenced in its message, with the issue’s type (bug, task, feature) from the issue tracker. In the analysis weeks, 71% of commits change the platform and 35% reference an issue. Commit counts miss code quality and work that does not change the code, such as review and design. We also considered pull requests, as some prior work did [2, 8], but lacked the data. Our unit of analysis is the person-week (Monday to Sunday): we relate an engineer’s total token spend in a week to their total commits in that week. Weeks 0 to 4 (2026-06-29 to 2026-08-02) form the panel, and weeks [FORMULA] to [FORMULA] serve only as a pre-period. A person-week is in the panel if it has any metered tokens or commits; of the 2,030 person-weeks of the 406 metered engineers, we treat the 203 with neither as weeks the person was away and leave them out. The panel has 404 engineers (the other two used the agents only after week 4; 397 with metered use in these weeks) and 1,827 person-weeks, 88% with metered use, of which 12.9% have no commit. The median active week has 8 commits. The 178 engineers with no metered use are not in the panel; in the pre-period they committed slightly more than metered users (median 65 vs. 52 commits, Mann–Whitney [FORMULA] ) and differ from them by at most 0.24 standard deviations on any pre-period covariate. The gateway does not meter chatbots or other assistants, so engineers outside the panel may use AI. We answer each RQ between engineers and from week to week within an engineer, since the two can disagree: heavy users may also ship a lot, yet a busier week need not cost an engineer more than a slower one. We model weekly token counts with Poisson regression estimated by quasi-maximum likelihood [50], which keeps zero-token weeks and estimates the mean consistently however dispersed spend is [51]. Within-person models include person and week fixed effects [52], i.e., they compare each engineer’s weeks with one another after removing the engineer’s level and anything common to all engineers in a week, such as a model release. A new frontier model arrived in week 3 and accounted for 45% of all spend within two weeks; week effects absorb such a change only on average. For engineer [FORMULA] in week [FORMULA] , the within-person model is where [FORMULA] is the engineer’s own level, [FORMULA] the week, and the elasticity [FORMULA] is the percentage change in tokens per percentage change in commits. Between-person slopes are least-squares fits on engineers’ log averages over the five weeks. Where we compare the two levels, we fit them jointly in the within–between (Mundlak) form [53, 54], so that their difference has a confidence interval. Confidence intervals are 95% percentile intervals from a cluster bootstrap over engineers [55]. The replication package (Section VII) gives the full specifications. We answer RQ1 in two steps, which Section IV-A follows: how closely a week’s spend varies with that week’s output, and what else in our data explains the rest. If spend rises in proportion to work, a week with twice the commits should cost about twice as much, as cost-per-output metrics assume. We test this with the elasticity [FORMULA] in the Poisson model of Equation 1: [FORMULA] means spend doubles when commits double, and [FORMULA] means it does not vary with them. The log of commits is undefined at zero, so we fit this model to the 1,347 engineer-weeks with both tokens and commits, from the 344 engineers who have at least two such weeks to compare. We also estimate the reverse slope, of commits on tokens; when spend and output are closely correlated, the two slopes are near reciprocals. Two things could make [FORMULA] look smaller than it is. Commit counts only approximate a week’s work, which biases slopes toward zero [56]. We therefore re-estimate [FORMULA] by instrumental variables with lines changed as the instrument [52], which ignores squashing or splitting commits because they change the count but not the lines. And output may arrive later than the spend behind it; we check this with day-level cross-correlations of spend and commits at leads and lags of up to ten working days. We repeat the estimate with lines changed and days with a commit as the output, at time units from one day to four weeks, with commit-count categories in place of log commits, and with spend split into agent calls and tokens per call, and test whether heavier-spend weeks’ commits differ in size, platform share, or issue linkage. If spend does not co-vary with commits, it may reflect other parts of the work. We first measure how much spend varies among weeks with similar output, as the ratio of the 90th to the 10th percentile of weekly spend within each quintile of weeks ranked by commits. We then ask how much of weekly tokens the metrics in our data predict: commits, lines changed, bug-linked commits, and days with a commit; then add issue-tracker activity, role, manager status, team (grouped into divisions and product ecosystems), and each engineer’s prior work mix (commit rate, commit size, and share of commits whose message references a bug). For each set we compute the share of deviance it explains relative to an intercept-only model, the Poisson counterpart of [FORMULA] [57], computed by cross-validation [58] on held-out engineers (ten folds) for differences between engineers and on held-out weeks (five folds) for changes within an engineer. Finally, we correlate each engineer’s spend with their teammates’ average spend, excluding their own (a leave-one-out mean), and repeat the within- and between-person estimates on team-weeks. We answer RQ2 in two parts, which Section IV-B follows: from the telemetry, how much spend is not tied to output and what the weeks with such spend look like; and from the survey (Section III-C), what engineers use the agents for and how many hours they report saving. We cannot identify the spend not tied to output directly, because the telemetry does not link agent calls to repository artifacts (Section III-A): in a week with no output, none of that week’s spend led to output; in a week with output, we cannot tell which part did. We therefore estimate a lower and an upper bound on the share, assuming that the spend and the commits made with it happen in the same week. We test this assumption with the lead–lag analysis of RQ1 and by repeating both bounds at time units from one day to four weeks. For the lower bound, the floor, we count only the unambiguous case, the share of all tokens spent in person-weeks with no commits, restricted to weeks with above-median spend (other cutoffs in Supplementary Material (SM) A). It misses spend not tied to output in weeks with commits. For the upper bound, the curve estimate, we predict an engineer’s spend in a week with no output from how their spend varies with output. It extends the Poisson model of Equation 1, replacing [FORMULA] with [FORMULA] : where [FORMULA] transforms output to set the shape of the curve: raw counts, square root, [FORMULA] , or a linear spline in [FORMULA] , each with [FORMULA] . We sum the prediction for a week with no output, [FORMULA] , over person-weeks and divide by total spend to obtain the share of tokens that does not vary with output. This share includes the fixed cost of using an agent at all and the spend behind hand-written output, so it overestimates. Because the share depends on the shape, we fit all four shapes and compare them on calibration in weeks with no output, out-of-sample deviance under five-fold cross-validation [58], and agreement with negative-binomial and gamma models [50], which match the Poisson mean only if the shape is right [51]. We repeat the estimate with commit size, issue type, and tool mix as predictors, and within groups. We also test whether spend precedes later output, by comparing an engineer’s commits, relative to their own mean, after a heavy-spend period with no output with those after other periods. To relate a week’s spend beyond what its output predicts to how the agent was used, we correlate each week’s residual with the engineer’s agent use that week (calls, days of use, context per call, share of generated text, tool mix, and session length) and with the next week’s bug-linked commits. A session is a run of calls separated by at most 30 minutes. The company ran an anonymous internal survey on the AI tools that employees use. Respondents indicated which company-paid AI tools they had used in the past work week and were assigned one of them to evaluate (the tool with the fewest evaluations at that point); those who had used more than one could evaluate a second tool of their choice. For each tool, respondents reported what they had used it for in the past work week, what value it had provided, and whether it had enabled work in the past month they would otherwise not have done. They also reported whether it had saved or cost them time that week and how many hours, how many colleagues the work would otherwise have involved, and its effect on six aspects of their work on a five-point scale (productivity, quality of output, efficiency on routine and on complex tasks, cognitive load, and finding information). A final question asked whether they had handled colleagues’ material they suspected was AI-generated and how much time it cost them. Free-text questions asked for the main value, the work enabled, and what saved and what cost time. The survey had 412 respondents (15.8% of employees; 525 evaluations in total): 400 evaluated at least one AI tool, 125 evaluated a second; 12 did not use any company-paid AI tool. Most respondents (72%) held technical roles, and 16% were team leads. The company invited employees without incentives through an internal post that also asked colleagues skeptical of AI to take part; 3% of respondents indicated they did not use any company-paid AI tool, a share consistent with the rest of the company. For RQ2, we analyze the 197 evaluations of the two coding agents (99.8% of metered tokens) by 184 respondents in technical roles. We report answers to the multiple-choice questions as percentages of the evaluations that answered each question; a respondent who evaluated both agents counts twice. Hours saved is the number respondents gave, negative when the tool cost time; it is a self-report about the past week. We report medians and interquartile ranges. The 289 answers to the four free-text questions were coded thematically [59] with an AI tool, and one author reviewed every code manually; the codebook is inductive, per question, with multiple codes per answer (1.6 on average). We report themes as shares of substantive answers, with quotations. To see which kinds of use go with larger reported time savings, we regress hours saved on the other answers at once, because the answers overlap: respondents who use the agent for more kinds of work also more often report enabled work and name more colleagues that the work would otherwise have needed. The predictors are coding use, the number of non-coding activity types, enabled work, and the number of colleagues the work would otherwise have needed; the controls are the tool, the division, and whether the week’s only reported value was experiments and learning. We model hours on an inverse hyperbolic sine scale, which keeps zeros and losses, standardize the coefficients, and compute bootstrap intervals over respondents (SM B). We also compare the coded free text with the closed survey items. This study examines workplace records and survey responses from employees of JetBrains, where some of the authors work. Only one author had access to the raw workplace records, and they pseudonymized them before sharing them. The Carnegie Mellon authors had access to the pseudonymized data, in which JetBrains employees are not individually identifiable, and used them only for secondary analysis. The survey was anonymous and could not be linked to individual telemetry records or to specific employees. The data analyzed in this study are not used to evaluate individual employee performance, and we report only aggregate results. We do not release individual-level records or survey responses to protect employee privacy. The study followed applicable ethical standards and the ICC/ESOMAR International Code [60]. IV Results A week with twice an engineer’s usual commits costs about 20% more tokens. The elasticity of tokens on commits, [FORMULA] in Eq. 1, is 0.26 [0.19, 0.32] (0.28 by least squares in Figure 3B). In the other direction, the slope of commits on tokens is 0.13 [0.03, 0.32], so a week with twice the usual tokens has about 10% more commits. If spend increased in proportion to output, both slopes would be near one; their product is 0.03, and proportionality ( [FORMULA] ) is rejected at every time unit ( [FORMULA] ). Output itself varies widely across weeks: an engineer’s weekly commits typically differ from their own average by a factor of about two, i.e., half or double. Two things could make [FORMULA] look smaller than it is, but neither explains the gap. First, commit counts are a noisy measure of work. Instrumenting commits with lines changed raises the within-person slope [FORMULA] to 0.48, still well short of proportional. Second, output may arrive after the spend: the day-level cross-correlation between spend and commits peaks on the same day (0.33) and is gone after about four working days (Figure 11 in SM A), so a week contains most of the lag between spend and the commits made with it. Nor does the result depend on how output and time are measured: the slope is similar for days (0.30) and two-week periods (0.21), and with lines changed (0.19) or days with a commit (0.40) as the output. With commit-count categories and no shape imposed, spend rises along the same constant-elasticity line at every output level (SM A). Nor are the commits of heavier-spend weeks different commits: no measure of their size, platform share, or issue linkage changes at [FORMULA] . A busier week brings more agent calls (0.25), each with about the same number of tokens ( [FORMULA] , [FORMULA] ). The within-person correlation is weakest among light users, 0.01 for engineers who spend under a third of the median week compared with 0.37 for those who spend over three times it, and every role, tool, and usage group stays below proportional (SM A). Between engineers, the association is somewhat stronger (Figure 3A). On person means, the slope is 0.38 with each engineer counted once and 0.44 with engineers weighted by their number of weeks with metered use, compared with 0.26 within a person. In the other direction, engineers who spend twice as much have about 8% more commits (slope 0.11). Fitted jointly, the between-minus-within difference is 0.15 [ [FORMULA] , 0.36], so engineers who commit more may be heavier users beyond what their weekly output explains, but five weeks per person is too short to be sure (Poisson fits give larger slopes, driven by five engineers). Output alone explains little of the spread in spend. Within every quintile of weekly commit counts, the engineer-week at the 90th percentile of spend uses 39 to 240 times the tokens of the one at the 10th (Figure 1). The four activity metrics (commits, lines changed, bug-linked commits, commit-days) explain 38% of the between-person variation in weekly tokens on held-out people and 13% of the within-person variation on held-out weeks (Figure 4). Commits and lines changed alone do just as well (38% between); bug-linked commits and commit-days add nothing ( [FORMULA] points), nor does issue-tracker activity, and how engineers worked in the pre-period (their commit rate, commit size, and share of bug-linked commits) adds 3 points. Given all four, the 90th-percentile person-week still uses 58 times the 10th. The engineer’s role and team explain even less. Role, the manager flag, and team together predict held-out people worse than each week’s average spend does ( [FORMULA] ), possibly because spend varies widely among engineers on the same team: an engineer’s spend correlates at 0.24 with the leave-one-out mean of their division or ecosystem and at 0.13 with that of their team. Summed to teams, spend is no more closely related to output than for individuals: the within-team slope is 0.31 for team paths and 0.27 for product ecosystems, compared with 0.25 for the same engineers (SM A). The person does account for the spread, explaining 79% of the deviance in our sample. Which engineers spend the most is stable over the five weeks; who has the highest cost per commit is not (SM A). Weeks with no commit account for 4% of all tokens, but by the curve estimate the share that does not vary with the week’s output is about two fifths. Most of the spend not tied to output falls inside weeks that did produce commits. Throughout this section, “output” means commits. Time spent on code review, design, or repositories outside our sample therefore counts as not directly tied to output, as does time spent on exploration, learning, and abandoned attempts. The lower bound is small. Of the 1,599 engineer-weeks with any metered use, 207 have no commit, mostly light-use weeks. The 49 with above-median spend account for 3.0% [1.8%, 4.5%] of all tokens; all 207 together account for 4%. By construction, the floor depends on the time unit; it is 25% for single days and 1% for two-week periods. We use the week because spend and its commits usually fall within four working days (Section IV-A). The upper bound is an order of magnitude larger. A week with no commit still costs 77% of the engineer’s average week (Figure 5), and the share of all tokens this implies depends on the shape of the curve. Raw counts attribute 89% [79%, 97%] of all tokens to zero output, the square root 63%, [FORMULA] 42% [33%, 51%], and the spline 39% [31%, 46%]. We trust the last two. Spend rises steeply over the first few commits of a week and then flattens, a shape an exponential-in-counts curve cannot take, and all three diagnostics from Section III rank counts last (SM A). Adding commit size and tool mix to the model, or fitting it to the first four weeks alone, changes the estimate by at most a few points (SM A). Even so, 39% remains an upper bound, since it includes the fixed cost of using an agent at all and the spend behind commits written by hand (Section III). We split the share by role and division, and by how much engineers use the agents (Figure 6). Across the groups that spend most of the tokens, the share barely varies: developers, team leads and managers (a role inferred from job titles), and each of the two large divisions range from 37% to 42%. It is higher only where the job is expected to produce fewer commits or the agent is used less: 50% for QA engineers, 59% for interns, and 51% and 52% for the middle and lightest thirds of users, relative to 36% for the heaviest third, who spend 79% of all tokens. The share varies far more between individual engineers than between any of these groups: per engineer the median is 46%, the middle 80% of engineers range from 31% to 68%, and the 10th and 90th percentiles of each engineer’s level of such spend differ 59-fold. Team, role, the manager flag, and prior work mix together explain only 11% of this variation on held-out people, as they explained little of spend overall (Section IV-A). A week’s spend beyond what its commit output predicts could reflect a costlier model or agent, or the same tools used differently. Our data point to both. In such weeks engineers used more of the newly released model: within person, the residual correlates with the week’s share of tokens on that model at 0.15 ( [FORMULA] ), though not with the share from either agent or from frontier models as a group, which includes older frontier models. They also worked in longer sessions: 31% of calls fall in sessions longer than two hours, compared to 18% in the person’s other weeks. Generated text is under 1% of tokens in either kind of week (0.6% vs. 0.9%), so the excess is context sent to the agent rather than code returned. The excess also does not predict bug fixes in the following week: the residual correlates with that week’s bug-linked commits at 0.03. Of the 197 evaluations of the two coding agents by technical respondents, 167 answered the questions about past-week use. In 91% of these, respondents reported that the tool had saved them time that week (median 10 hours, interquartile range 5–20), and in 88%, they reported a positive effect on overall productivity. Respondents reported using these agents for coding in 63% of evaluations and for at least one non-coding activity in 89% overall (83% among the 100 evaluations of assigned tools): processing and analyzing data (52%), brainstorming (49%), research on a topic (44%), planning work (39%), learning (28%), and writing (23%) (Figure 7). Median hours saved rise from 3 for respondents who used the agent only for coding to 10 for those who reported two or more non-coding activities (Figure 8A). In the model of Section III-C, which relates hours saved to all of these answers at once (Figure 8B), the count of non-coding activity types is associated with hours saved (0.24 [0.06, 0.43]), as is the number of colleagues otherwise needed (0.43 [0.23, 0.61]), but coding is not (0.08 [ [FORMULA] , 0.27]). Enabled work has a similar estimate whose interval includes zero (0.19 [ [FORMULA] , 0.39]). Respondents who report enabled work also chose more activities and name more colleagues, so with 134 answers we cannot separate the three (SM A). In their own words, respondents describe much of the coding-agent use as work outside their usual tasks: in unfamiliar code, domains, or technologies, on tasks they would otherwise have deferred, and in exploration. Asked for the agent’s main value, they split between speed on their usual tasks (31% of 74 substantive answers) and work in unfamiliar code, domains, or technologies (30%); 24% described exploration and a wider set of tasks worth attempting (“I can try things that I was scared to try”; Figure 13B in SM B). The 44 substantive descriptions of work done in the past month only because the agent existed show the same pattern. Of these, 36% describe work in an unfamiliar codebase, language, stack, or area (“fixed a bug in [system] despite having no prior knowledge of that codebase”). Another 25% describe tasks that would otherwise have been deferred or handed to someone else (a type-inference problem “that would otherwise take weeks so we would never have picked it up”). Prototypes and experiments account for 23%, internal tools 20%, and documents and reports 11% (Figure 9B). Only one of the 44 says the work would have happened anyway, just slower. Much of this work produces understanding before it produces a commit, or no commit at all in our data. Asked what kind of value the week’s tasks created, 59% named “experiments and learning that have not yet brought tangible value”. Respondents see part of agent use as not producing valuable output. Of the 67 substantive answers on what cost time, 49% describe wrong, plausible-but-wrong, or low-quality output (“a plausibly-looking but ultimately [useless] symptom fix”). Another 24% describe tooling friction unrelated to the model (setup, credentials, outages, quota limits), 21% the cost of prompting, context management, and steering, and 18% the cost of verifying output, which sometimes exceeds the time saved (“there is a point where time spent on prompting and reviewing exceeds the time savings”; Figure 9A). Naming a cost is not associated with a lower overall productivity rating. Respondents whose answer was coded as non-valuable output rate productivity at 4.2 compared with 4.3 and report the same median hours saved (9). The survey’s hours question asks only how much time the respondent’s own tool saved or cost them, so two costs that other questions measure are not part of that figure: the cognitive load of working with agents, and the time spent on colleagues’ AI-generated material. Among technical agent users, 31% report higher cognitive load because of AI agents and 51% lower (Figure 10). The cognitive-load rating is nearly uncorrelated with reported hours saved ( [FORMULA] , compared with 0.57 for overall productivity); respondents describe the trade (“I do more, but my brain gets much more tired”). Colleagues bear part of the cost: 55% [49%, 60%] of the 299 who answered report handling colleagues’ material they suspected was AI-generated, costing a mean 1.6 hours a week [1.2, 2.1]. Team leads handle it more often (73% vs. 50%; odds ratio 2.7, [FORMULA] ), with no more reported benefit. V Discussion We discuss what token spend measures, what that implies for its three uses (measuring productivity, monitoring adoption, and setting budgets), and what to measure instead. What token spend measures. Token spend records how much an engineer uses agents, scaled by the context included in each call and by the model in use, and in our data it varied far more between engineers than with the week’s output. Who the engineer was accounted for 79% of the variation in weekly tokens in our sample; on held-out data, output metrics predicted under two fifths of the differences between engineers and 13% of the variation within them, and role and team alone predicted held-out engineers worse than the weekly average. Within an engineer, a week with twice the usual commits had only about a fifth more tokens (Section IV-A). Token spend has been called “the lines-of-code metric of the AI era” [5], and our data support the comparison: both are easy to count and loosely related to what engineers accomplish. The two differ in what they count. Lines of code count output, and stayed in use because program size sufficiently reflected the effort behind it (Section II-A); tokens count an input, recorded whether or not anything is produced, and in our data they reflect output only weakly. Organizations should therefore treat spend as a record of agent use and not as a measure of output. Prior estimates and ours agree that output rises far less than spend. Ten times the spend corresponds to about 40% more output across Jellyfish’s usage deciles [8], to twice the output in a press summary of vendor data [14], and to at most 76% more under the mandate He et al. study [2] (our calculations, assuming constant elasticity). In our data (the slope of commits on tokens) it corresponds to about 30% more output between engineers and 35% within [7%, 109%]. The prior figures compare different engineers, grouped by spend, or follow an organization over time, during which other things changed. Our within-engineer estimate holds the engineer fixed and is similar, so the weak association is not only an artifact of comparing different engineers. Engineers chose their weekly spend, so this estimate is still not the effect that an imposed budget or target would have. By our best-fitting curves, up to about two fifths of spend does not vary with the week’s commits. This upper bound includes the fixed cost of using an agent at all and the spend behind commits written by hand (Section IV-B1); the rest may be work the repository does not record, or waste. In the survey, respondents reported uses that need not end in a commit (analysis, research, planning) and named wrong or low-quality output as the most common cost (49% of answers; Section IV-B2), so agent use in general includes both. A token spent on a prototype that informs a design counts the same as one spent on output that is discarded, so the count alone cannot separate the two. The setting may limit how far our estimates transfer. JetBrains builds AI coding tools, so some metered use may be testing of its own agents; its engineers work on established codebases, the type where He et al. report smaller AI gains [2]; and use was voluntary, with no target or mandate, so differences in spend reflect, in part, engineers’ own choices. Measuring productivity. Leaderboards [4], spending expected in proportion to salary [6], and minimum spending targets [7] all reward higher spend, and the salary comparison equates it with better engineering. Some companies have since dropped such measures after reports that engineers inflated their usage to rank higher: Meta told engineers that token counts will not be used to evaluate their impact [48], and Amazon shut down a usage leaderboard and called token usage a “deeply flawed” measure of teams’ AI use [49]. Gaming is the familiar fate of a measure that becomes a target [21], but our data suggest that spend is a weak measure of output even without a target: in our setting, where the company did not set a spending target, the 90th percentile of weekly spend within each commit quintile was 39 to 240 times the 10th. If the within-engineer association were causal, doubling an engineer’s spend through a target would raise their commits by about 10% (2% to 25%). Removing a leaderboard addresses the gaming but not these weaknesses, so companies should not evaluate engineers’ output or impact by their spend, even where no one games it, and should not expect spending targets to raise output much. Dividing spend by output, as analytics vendors do when they report token cost per merged pull request as a return on investment [8, 9], does not show the return on the spend, or how efficiently engineers use the agent. First, the ratio falls, on average, as commits rise: a week with twice an engineer’s usual commits has about 1.2 times the tokens, so its tokens per commit are [FORMULA] times the usual, i.e., 40% lower. An engineer thus tends to look more efficient in a week with more commits. Second, the ratio ranks engineers consistently overall (projected reliability 0.80) but not at the top: only 17 of the 34 engineers in the top decile by tokens per commit in odd weeks remain there in even weeks (SM A). Third, a company that divides tokens by commits treats every token as going to a commit and every commit as coming from tokens, so agent work that ends without a commit counts as cost without return, and a commit written by hand as return without cost. Fourth, the ratio changes with the model: in our data, weeks on the newer model had about 45% more tokens at the same commit count (SM A), so a company’s ratio can rise with a model release without any change in commits. Companies that want to judge whether engineers use agents efficiently should compare their spend on comparable tasks, which requires the task records described below. Monitoring adoption. A token-based count of adopters depends on the token threshold chosen to define an adopter. When Steve Yegge called AI adoption at Google shallow, Google answered with 40,000 weekly agent users and Yegge with a threshold of four million tokens a day [44, 45, 61]. Both numbers can be right, because they count the two ends of one skewed distribution. In our data, the heaviest third of users accounted for 79% of all tokens, so a headcount of weekly users can be high while few engineers cross a high threshold. Because weeks on the newer model had more tokens at the same commit count, the share above a fixed threshold would also likely rise with a model release. A token threshold is arbitrary, and the share above it changes with model releases, so organizations that monitor adoption could report the weekly headcount alongside a count that does not scale with context size, such as the share of engineers who use agents on most working days. Setting budgets. To decide how much to spend, companies need to know what the spend returns. One vendor reports merged output per dollar as a “return on token spend” and finds that it fell by about 70% during 2026 [9]. Such a decline need not mean the added spend was wasted, for two reasons. When output rises less than proportionally with spend, as it did with tokens within engineers in our data, output per unit of spend declines as spend grows even if the additional spend serves useful work; and output per dollar changes with token prices and models. In output per dollar, only merged work counts as output, so companies that use it should weigh benefits that commits do not capture. Respondents report several, which self-reports can overstate [42]: hours saved, tasks they would otherwise have skipped, and work that would otherwise have needed colleagues (Section IV-B2). The value of these benefits depends on how the work is used later, for example whether a prototype informs a decision, and need not grow with the tokens spent on it. Companies should weigh these benefits against costs that are not on the bill: 31% of technical agent users reported higher cognitive load from agents, and 55% of the 299 respondents who answered reported handling colleagues’ material they suspected was AI-generated, from any AI tool, at a mean cost of 1.6 hours a week. For setting budgets, spend is more useful summed over several weeks: five-week totals rank engineers consistently (projected rank reliability 0.87), whereas two single weeks rank-correlate at only 0.4 to 0.6. With ranks this stable, a team’s past spend shows which members will need the most budget; the budget’s level should be revised after a model release. Cutting spend is harder. A company may cap it per person [46], which limits mostly the heaviest users. Their share of spend not tied to output is the lowest (36%, vs. 51% and 52% for the other thirds), plausibly because the fixed cost of using an agent weighs less in their spend; but because they spend 79% of all tokens, they also account for most of the spend not tied to output (Section IV-B1). A company that caps therefore cuts spend tied to output along with spend that is not, and the token count does not show which. Lowering what each call costs may avoid that problem, since it leaves engineers’ use of agents unchanged. Most tokens are context sent to the agent, much of it re-sent on every turn, and in weeks with more spend than their output predicted, engineers used more of the newly released model and worked in longer sessions, in which that context accumulates. Companies that need to cut could therefore try managing or compressing context [31, 33, 35], caching repeated context, and routing routine calls to cheaper models before capping engineers. They should measure billed cost rather than tokens, since reducing context can raise cost when the agent re-reads what was removed [29]. What to measure instead. Organizations want to know what agent-assisted engineering is worth; Amazon now asks its teams to measure long-term outcomes [49]. Billing records supply the inference cost and the token count supplies the amount of agent use; the value needs other records. Two changes would begin to provide them, although some of that value, such as what engineers learn, may remain hard to measure. First, record at the gateway which issue or task each session served. With such a record, a company could join spend to each task’s outcome, such as a substantial product improvement or a decision that a prototype informed, rather than only to whether it produced code. Second, develop measures of the value of agent-assisted work. SPACE and DORA [22, 23] were designed for code that people wrote, and their metrics become noisier when the same number can come from different mixes of human and agent work [24]. We know of no validated measures of value across the outer loop of development, from what ships to how products and businesses improve; until there are, a company can record how often engineers report taking on tasks they would otherwise have skipped (58% of coding-agent evaluations here; SM A), as a sign of new work rather than of its value.
