Research that measures the outcomes of AI use through commits and pull requests [25, 2] observes only the agent work that ends in a commit; joining those records to agent telemetry would bound how much agent work does not. Analyses that use spend as exposure, such as comparisons of usage deciles [8], should separate variation within engineers from variation between them, because spend is largely a stable trait of the engineer (Section IV-A2). VI Conclusion In this paper, we asked what an engineer’s token spend measures, and whether it is, as one critic has claimed [5], the lines-of-code metric of the AI era. In five weeks of metered agent use and commits from 404 engineers at one company, spend varied far more between engineers than with their output: a week with twice an engineer’s usual commits had only about a fifth more tokens, and up to two fifths of spend did not vary with the week’s commits. Survey respondents reported using agents for analysis, research, and planning as well as for coding. Token spend therefore records how much engineers use agents, and, like lines of code, it says little about what that use produced. Because spend was weakly related to output even where the company had not set a spending target, we recommend that companies not evaluate engineers’ output by their spend; and because output rose far less than spend, that they not expect spending targets to raise output much, or divide spend by commit or pull request counts to judge how efficiently engineers use agents. Two steps would begin to make the value of agent-assisted work measurable: records that link agent sessions to tasks, and measures of the value of work that people and agents do together. We hope our results motivate research on both. SPARK : Semantic-preserving Prompt Mutation for Code Generation using Consensus-based Verification FrameworkThanks: This work was supported by the NSERC Discovery Grant and Vector Institute Scholarship in AI. Automated code generation with large language models (LLMs) has improved in recent years. With the lack of test cases in real-world usages, generated code is not automatically verifiable and often requires manual validation. Previous studies have leveraged consensus verification, where code solutions and corresponding test cases are generated and evaluated based on functional consistency. Building on this, SPARK incorporates semantic-preserving mutations to problem descriptions such as paraphrasing, grammatical adjustments, function renaming, and other alterations to enhance the robustness and correctness of LLM-generated code. For each mutated description, SPARK generates a set of code solutions and test cases. These candidate solutions are evaluated using consensus-based verification, where the solutions’ quality is measured by how consistently they pass generated tests. We assess the effectiveness of SPARK on three benchmarks (LiveCodeBench, BigCodeBench, and DLBench) across three LLMs (o4-mini, DeepSeek-R1-Basic, and Gemini-2.5-Pro). Our evaluation demonstrates that SPARK outperforms state-of-the-art consensus-based verification approaches up to 4.1%. Our generalization experiment highlights the practical potential of SPARK as an effective strategy for enhancing the reliability and correctness of LLM-based code generation systems in scenarios where traditional validation resources are scarce, while our qualitative analysis shows insight into how SPARK’s mutation helps LLMs generate better code solutions. I Introduction Automated code generation [1, 2] with large language models (LLMs) [3, 4, 5, 6] has advanced rapidly in recent years, offering promising tools for software development. Despite these gains, reliably producing a single correct, executable solution remains a significant challenge [7, 1, 8]. Many models achieve high success rates when allowed to generate multiple candidate solutions, as measured by metrics such as pass@k (the probability that at least one of the top-k generated solutions passes the test suite) [9, 10]. However, their top-ranked outputs often fail to meet correctness requirements in practice [11]. This gap highlights the practical difficulty of selecting a reliable solution from multiple generated candidates, especially in real-world scenarios where comprehensive, human-written test suites are scarce or unavailable [12, 13, 14]. To address the lack of ground-truth tests in practice, prior work such as the CodeT framework [15] leverages generated corresponding test cases to verify code solutions. Inspired by consensus-based algorithms [16] such as RANSAC [17], this dual agreement approach can identify groups of solutions that consistently pass groups of generated test cases and thus exhibit highly cohesive functionality. CodeT demonstrated improvements in code generation benchmarks without relying on hand-crafted test cases. However, since CodeT relies on a single prompt, the generated solutions are often tied to a single LLM’s understanding of that one specification, leading to some misinterpretation. Figure 1 illustrates such a failure: when tasked with computing the mean and median from a JSON file and writing the results to a CSV, the original prompt repeatedly fails validation because the solution outputs a field header while the validation suite expects a key header. This scenario demonstrates how single-prompt generation can fail due to subtle specification ambiguities. To mitigate this shortcoming, we propose SPARK , which introduces semantic-preserving prompt mutations to systematically create diverse, semantically equivalent variants of the original problem description. These instances increase diversity in both generated solutions and tests, improving the chances that more candidate matches the intended specification. Concretely, SPARK uses a common, language-focused LLM (GPT-4o) to apply controlled changes in phrasing, grammatical structure, function naming, and other lexical/syntactic features (see Table I). For each mutated prompt, we generate code solutions and test cases; all candidates then participate in a dual-execution agreement selection. Candidate solutions are then grouped by their test-case pass patterns under the hypothesis that correct implementations exhibit consistent functional behavior across differently phrased prompts. We then select the cluster with the strongest agreement as the final output. As shown in Figure 1, reformulating the original declarative instruction as an interrogative prompt leads the model to produce the correct key header, enabling it to pass the validation suite. We evaluate SPARK on three complementary benchmarks, LiveCodeBench [18] (algorithmic/data-structure tasks), BigCodeBench [19] (real-world repository/API tasks), and DLBench [20] (deep learning–oriented code generation) using three state-of-the-art LLMs: O4-Mini [21], DeepSeek R1 Basic [22], and Gemini 2.5 Pro [23]. All prompt mutations are produced with GPT-4o. Our experiments show that incorporating a single prompt mutation in most cases already improves the pass@1 performance across most dataset–model combinations. While the magnitude of improvement varies, we observe clear patterns. For example, verb-based modifications (e.g., converting between active and passive forms or replacing verbs with near-synonyms) provide the strongest and most reliable gains, particularly on LiveCodeBench and DLBench. Context-based modifications, such as altering or removing function names, also contribute meaningfully, particularly on repository-style tasks in BigCodeBench. Styling-oriented mutations, though more superficial, still produce measurable improvements by prompting models toward more precise code generation. These results suggest that different classes of mutations address complementary weaknesses in LLMs, with verb modifications enhancing semantic alignment, context modifications improving robustness to naming and specification noise, and styling changes introducing additional syntactic diversity. We expand upon the analysis of individual mutations by also studying the compositions of mutations. We first explore combinations of mutations on a calibration dataset to identify the best-performing mutation set. Such combinations are then applied to the tasks from a different dataset. Specifically, on average, SPARK achieves up to 4.1% improvement in pass@1 score over CodeT, the state-of-the-art consensus-based validation technique. This experiment demonstrates SPARK ’s expandability and practical usage in a real-world scenario where additional mutation can be added, and tuning on the calibration dataset is generalizable to deployment time. Our qualitative analysis shows that mutations improve code generation through several mechanisms. The most common is generating diverse implementations that reduce overfitting to a single phrasing. Mutations also increase resilience to misleading or distracting context, clarify implicit requirements, expose boundary and corner cases, and act as a filter against overfitted solutions by aligning with harder tests. Together, these effects explain why mutations often lead to stronger and more reliable programs. Overall, SPARK not only raises accuracy in diverse benchmarks but also demonstrates that systematic mutation strategies can be tuned to the strengths of specific models and datasets, offering a practical path to more dependable LLM-based code generation. This paper makes the following contributions: We propose SPARK , a code generation technique that combines semantic-preserving prompt mutations with consensus-based verification to select reliable code solutions. We conduct an extensive evaluation with three LLMs on three complementary code-generation benchmarks, showing consistent improvements over baselines of up to 4.1% pass@1. We provide qualitative insights into when and why different mutation strategies help or hurt, and we study a general strategy to select effective mutation combinations that can generalize in real-world scenarios. Data Availability: We release our code and data11 1 https://github.com/Smart-System-testing-lab/SPARK. II Approach Figure 2 provides SPARK ’s overview. When given a programming problem, SPARK first performs 1 Prompt Mutation. Using the original and mutated problems, SPARK then queries the LLM to execute the 2 Code & Test Generation step. By executing the generated test cases and applying consensus-based validation, SPARK identifies the best code solution in the 3 Solution Selection step. One of the strengths of the consensus-based validation process proposed by CodeT is that it can estimate the solution quality by verifying the majority agreement of code solutions with generated test cases. However, in cases where the LLM failed to generate correct code solutions from the original prompt, CodeT would select the incorrect solutions. SPARK utilizes a set of semantic-preserving mutations of the problem prompt to help trigger additional correct solutions. As the example in Figure 1 demonstrates, a tone modification from declarative to interrogative can induce more diversity in the generated code, thereby helping the LLM produce additional correct solutions that can improve the overall accuracy of the code generation system. In step 1, SPARK influences solution diversity by creating problem description variance through semantic-preserving mutation operations. These operators aim to vary the prompt styling, tone, syntactic structure, or context. This form of variation can trigger changes in the generated code, which can improve the overall correctness, efficiency, and readability of the candidate solution set (refer to VI for further discussion). Specifically, SPARK applies fourteen prompt mutations operators to the original problem description in four major thematic classes: Context Modification, Styling Modification, Verb Modification, and Tone Modification. Table I shows the mutation prompt template and an example for each mutation operation. Each mutation class aims to introduce changes that can induce additional solution generation: Context Modification focuses on mutating the context of the code generation task. For example, some problem descriptions include function names that can influence the model to generate a specific solution. By mutating this context, the prompt variances can influence different solutions to be generated. Styling Modification focuses on modifying the styling and highlighting of the problem descriptions. Different highlighting and styling can influence the attention of the models, which can induce additional solution variance. Verb Modification focuses on modifying the verbs tenses. Modifying these action verbs can directly induce changes in the generated solutions. Tone Modification focuses on the tone of the request. Changing the tone could indirectly instigate additional solution variances. Once the prompt variances are collected, SPARK queries LLMs to generate both code solutions and test cases to prepare for the consensus-based validation. In step 2, SPARK utilizes different prompt templates for code and test generation for each problem description to generate candidate code solutions and test cases. Code Solution Generation: To generate code solutions, SPARK directly queries LLMs with the problem description. Since the origin and mutated problem description already contain code generation commands, no additional request is needed. Due to the generated code sometimes containing missing imports, inconsistent function names compared to those expected in the test cases, or mismatched variable names between the function definition and the test inputs, additional post-processing is needed. This includes automatically inserting or correcting import statements, renaming functions to align with the required signatures, and adjusting variable names so that arguments match the test cases. Each generated code solution is then added to the solution candidate pool. Test Case Generation: In addition to generating code solutions, SPARK also generate test cases which will be used in the consensus-based validation phase to estimate the quality of solution candidates. Specifically, a test case includes a specific input along with the expected output for the function defined in the problem context. For example, in a task that determines whether there are elements in a list that are closer than a given threshold, a test case would provide an input list and threshold value, as well as the correct Boolean result. To generate these test cases, instead of directly querying LLMs using the original problem description, we apply a test generation template (Figure 3). This template replaces the code generation command with the test case generation command. Similar to code generation, SPARK generates test cases with both the original problem description and the mutated ones and adds them to the test cases pool. Specifically, our template tailors the test case generation to support different benchmark requirements. Specifically, we produce three distinct types of test cases to match the expected formats of the major usages corresponding to the major benchmarks: Simple input-output assertions: These are direct assert statements which check that the function produces the correct output for a given input. This style is compatible with the LiveCodeBench benchmark, which requires concise, clear input-output pairs. Unittest format: These test cases follow the structure of Python’s unittest framework, organizing checks into test classes and methods. This format aligns with the needs of BigCodeBench, which uses standard unit testing conventions. Pytest format: These tests use the pytest style, often employing function-based tests with decorators or simple assertions that integrate easily with the pytest runner. This format ensures compatibility with DL-Bench, which adopts pytest as its testing standard. In terms of testing frameworks, our method considers the two most popular libraries in Python, along with the default assertion style. By capturing these testing formats, our approach generalizes to most development environments. In the event the above test styles are not used, the user can create a new template by making trivial modifications to the existing prompt templates. By generating test cases in these varied formats, we evaluate the generalization of our approach to any development environment with various unique testing requirements. Solutions Selection: In step 3, SPARK executes the test cases to validate the code solutions in a consensus-based validation process (i.e., dual agreement[15]). Since the generated test cases are not guaranteed to be correct, this step estimates the quality of the solution candidates. While we directly adopt the original validation step, our diverse prompts help tease out more correct solutions, hence overall improve the validation process effectiveness. Tests execution: To compute the quality score for each code solution candidate, SPARK first validates each solution candidate by running it against all test cases in the pool. To execute the test cases, SPARK needs to perform different execution steps for different development environments: For simple input–output assertion tests, SPARK wraps the candidate in a lightweight runner that (i) feeds the provided stdin to the program or function, (ii) captures stdout and stderr, (iii) normalizes whitespace and line endings, and (iv) compares the observed output against the expected string(s). Each case is executed in a fresh process with a wall-clock timeout and resource limits; non-zero exit codes, timeouts, or mismatches are recorded as failures. For pytest tests, SPARK materializes a temporary project (candidate file plus tests), ensures the target symbol is importable (fixing the module path and function name if needed), and runs pytest -q with per-test timeouts. It captures pass/fail/skip/xfail outcomes and assertion messages. For unittest tests, SPARK discovers and runs the suite via unittest loaders, importing the candidate module, applying any required shim for function renaming, and executing each TestCase with buffered output and timeouts. It collects per-test outcomes (OK/FAIL/ERROR/SKIP) and condensed tracebacks. Consensus-based validation: Once the pass and fail statistics are collected, SPARK applies consensus-based validation by computing a score for each consensus set. Following prior work [15], the score is defined as where: [FORMULA] denotes a code solution generated by the model, [FORMULA] denotes a test case generated for the problem, [FORMULA] is the set of code solutions that pass exactly the same subset of test cases, [FORMULA] is the set of test cases passed by all code solutions in [FORMULA] . Intuitively, the score measures the strength of a consensus set by combining the number of agreeing solutions ( [FORMULA] ) and the number of test cases they jointly satisfy ( [FORMULA] ). A higher score indicates stronger evidence that the corresponding functionality is correct. Once the scores are computed. SPARK ranks and selects the highest-scoring solutions. However, the consensus-based nature of the dual execution agreement may result in multiple candidate solutions passing the same set of tests, which results in multiple candidates with the same score. In such cases, we introduce a tiebreaker mechanism based on comparing the average scores of the tied solutions’ code quality metrics. This approach assumes that the solution with higher structural quality is more likely to generalize and align with the ground-truth reference when functional behaviour is indistinguishable. To quantify code quality, we extract established metrics from the previous work [24, 25]: (i) the Maintainability Index (MI), which aggregates readability and complexity on a 0–100 scale (higher is better); (ii) Lack of Cohesion (LCOM1), where lower values indicate stronger cohesion among functions; (iii) Coupling Between Objects (CBO), which captures the number of distinct external modules used (lower is better); and (iv) Cyclomatic Complexity (CC), measuring the decision complexity of functions (lower is better). These metrics are combined into a single normalized score to represent the overall structural quality of each program. This secondary ranking allows SPARK to prefer programs that are not only correct on the given tests but are also more maintainable and less error-prone in practice. Code solutions that are ranked highest in both rankings are selected as SPARK ’s final solutions. III Experimental Setup Large Language Models Since semantic-preserving prompt mutation is a natural language task that is LLM’s strength, in general, any recent LLM is sufficient. Hence, SPARK employs GPT-4o, a low-cost general-purpose LLM that is capable of such tasks [26, 27]. On the other hand, code and test generation is a complex task that requires much more sophisticated LLMs. We evaluate SPARK on three state-of-the-art code generation models (o4-mini, DeepSeek R1 Basic, and Gemini 2.5 Pro) to ensure a robust comparison across different architectures and design philosophies. For fair evaluation, all models are queried in zero-shot mode using identical decoding parameters, with a temperature of 0.3, and top-p of 1.0. Code Generation Benchmarks We evaluate SPARK on three complementary benchmarks with varied developmental environmental settings and complexity. LiveCodeBench includes a suite of algorithmic and data-structure problems drawn from community coding challenges, testing general problem-solving ability. BigCodeBench consists of large-scale code synthesis tasks extracted from real-world repositories, emphasizing API usage, project structure, and realistic development practices. Finally, DLBench is a deep-learning–specific benchmark that covers model definitions, training loops, and tensor manipulation tasks, providing a targeted evaluation for machine learning workflows. These diverse benchmarks create a complementary evaluation experiment that assesses SPARK ’s generalization and effectiveness across a broad range of programming tasks. Evaluation Metric Following common practice, we adopt the pass@k metric, which measures the probability that at least one of the top- [FORMULA] generated solutions correctly solves the given problem, meaning it can pass all the ground-truth test cases. IV Result In this section, we present the findings to answer our research questions that aim to investigate the generalization and effectiveness of SPARK in code generation on three complementary benchmarks. This research question aims to assess LLM’s ability to generate variances of problem descriptions while preserving the semantics that are needed for the model to generate correct code. To validate the correctness of the mutants, we randomly sampled 500 mutated problem descriptions from 12,586 instances across all three benchmarks. Mutations were grouped into four broader categories—Context Modification, Styling, Verb Modification, and Tone Modification—and were rated along two dimensions: (1) whether the mutated prompt preserved semantic equivalence with the original, and (2) whether the intended transformation was applied correctly. Three co-authors independently performed manual labeling and achieve an inter-annotator agreement of 93.2% for transformation correctness and 88.9% for semantic equivalence, indicating the reliability of our labeling process. Given the prevalence of positive ratings (over 90%), observed agreement provides a more interpretable metric than chance-corrected scores [28, 29]. However, in most cases, this mutation operation is still able to modify the description correctly (example in Figure ), where the interrogative form is a request and the details are not given as questions. These result shows that GPT-4o can be relied upon for a wide range of prompt mutations, particularly those involving verb transformations, tense shifts, and casing changes. However, naming-based modifications require intensive verification to ensure full compliance, and modality-changing transformations (Declarative-to-Interrogative) remain unreliable without additional validation. This question investigates if SPARK can utilize prompt mutations alongside the original prompt to improve generated code quality and correctness. Table III reports the pass@1 when comparing between the original prompt (Zero-Shot) and SPARK with single mutation or all mutations. On LiveCodeBench, nearly all mutation types boost performance across the three models. For O4-Mini, gains are broad and consistent, with the strongest improvements from syntactic shifts such as Lowercase to Uppercase (+3.1%), Active-to-Passive (+4.4%), and Passive-to-Active (+5.2%). DeepSeek R1 shows even larger swings, with substantial gains from emphasizing or rephrasing text (e.g., Star Highlight +9.1%, Unrelated Function Name +7.8). Gemini 2.5, though more conservative, also benefits—particularly from Declarative-to-Interrogative (+4.8%). These results indicate that relatively minor mutations can reliably expand the search space of correct solutions for natural-language-heavy coding tasks. On BigCodeBench, improvements are smaller and less uniform. O4-Mini and DeepSeek R1 both benefit modestly from substitutions and voice changes (+0.7% to +2.0%), while Gemini 2.5 remains more fragile, with several mutations producing negligible or even negative shifts (–1.4% with Lowercase to Uppercase, –0.5% with Remove Function Name). Still, targeted changes like Declarative-to-Interrogative (+0.6%) occasionally yield incremental improvements, suggesting some value even in highly structured algorithmic problems. On DL-Bench, the effects are modest but steady. O4-Mini shows consistent gains, with the highest gain of +2.5 %. DeepSeek R1 improves most with Active-to-Passive (+2.0) and maintains positive deltas across nearly all other mutations, albeit smaller. Gemini 2.5 again shows sensitivity: Declarative-to-Interrogative and Passive-to-Active both deliver +2.5%, while careless renaming or excessive formatting can reduce performance (–1.0% with Remove Function Name, –1.1% with Past/Future tense shifts). The overall pattern indicates that even in the complex domain of deep learning code, single controlled mutations help the consensus-based validation uncover additional correct outputs, though the absolute gains are more narrow when compared to general coding tasks. Overall, these findings show that SPARK with a single mutation is a broadly effective yet model and benchmark-sensitive strategy. The strongest benefits arise from linguistic transformations that change surface form without altering semantics (voice changes, interrogatives), whereas arbitrary renaming or over-stylization risks degrading performance. If applying all mutations together, SPARK provides a significant uplift from using the original prompt with consistent improvement across all datasets and models. However, in some cases, the gain is less than applying a certain individual mutation. This indicates that selecting an appropriate mutation set for each situation is important to produce the best result. In this research question, we investigate if SPARK can improve the current state-of-the-art zero-shot prompting techniques. Specifically, we compare SPARK with the original prompt, the chain-of-thought prompting, and CodeT. CodeT also utilizes the dual execution agreement on multiple generations from the original prompt. In this experiment, we use eight generation queries for each sample, with CodeT, as more queries do not improve the performance. Table IV presents pass@1 for SPARK and baselines across benchmarks and models. The difference vs. the best baseline is highlighted in brackets. When using all available mutations, SPARK fails to improve the best baseline on four out of nine benchmark and model combinations. Findings from RQ2 indicate that selecting an appropriate set of mutations can optimize SPARK performance. In this RQ, we explore a tuning strategy where techniques can be tuned with a validation set and evaluated on a test set. Specifically, we select the best mutation set for SPARK in one of the three datasets (i.e., tuned with a validation dataset), and evaluated on the other two datasets. Table IV also presents the tuning evaluation result. For all models across all benchmarks, combining multiple prompt mutations through tuning helps SPARK consistently match or surpass the strongest baselines (on average up to +4.1%). SPARK ’s average gains are statistically significant with the Wilcoxon Signed Rank test p-value of 0.03. Overall, combining different mutation types—such as rephrasing, verb-tense changes, and function renaming—encourages models to explore a wider and more diverse solution space. This strategy reduces overfitting to specific phrasing patterns and increases robustness of code generation, ensuring more reliable Pass@1 performance across heterogeneous benchmarks. V Discussion How prompt mutations improve SPARK code generation? To investigate how mutations can help SPARK improve code generation, we manually evaluated a random sample of 100 task instances. For each instance, we inspected SPARK output, the strongest non-selected candidate(s), and the most discriminative tests, then annotated the primary improvement mechanism(s) using a compact taxonomy: Diverse generated code: where prompt diversity (different voice, verbs, names) leads to generated code diversity (i.e., different algorithms or data structures). Diverse generated test: where prompt diversity (different voice, verbs, names) leads to generated test diversity (i.e., more complex and comprehensive tests). Look up prevention: where function renaming mutations prevent models from looking up code directly from the original function name, and instead focus on the task description. Edge case tests: where mutations produce tests that stress edge cases such as min/max, empty, single-item, special Unicode characters, and large inputs. Spec clarification: where changing tone or style clarifies hidden rules so new tests expose those details and reward code that truly matches the intended specification. An instance could receive up to three tags if multiple mechanisms jointly explained the gain. We used the agreement matrix and hard-test list to ground each label, and we cross-checked annotations by reviewing code diffs and failing/passing test clusters. Table V reports the result. Overall, the two most common improvements were Diverse generated code and Diverse generated test. First, semantic-preserving mutations, such as Context Modification mutations (AFN, UFN, RFN, RV) and several Verb Modifications (A2P, V2V), elicited meaningful implementation deviations from the norm (e.g., switching from ad-hoc parsing to structured APIs) which SPARK favored because they agreed on a broader and more discriminative subset of tests. Second, some mutation families (e.g., styling edits like UC, LC, highlights) can trigger more diverse test case generation that better capture the semantics of each task, which can help the consensus-based validation identify more correct code solutions. Function name mutations, such as AFN, RFN, or UFN, prevent LLMs from generating code with hard-coded identifiers, positional parsing, or case-sensitive comparisons by reducing LLMs’ direct lookup from their training data (Lookup prevention). For example, figure 7 shows that subtle renaming of the function from left_jacobian to right_jacobian forces the model to generate new code instead of looking up existing code with the common function name. The first code snippet, generated from the original prompt, includes a simple small-angle approximation that may lead to errors. The second snippet, prompted by the variation, uses a more robust mathematical formulation, particularly for small-angle handling, using Taylor expansions for more accurate calculations. Edge case tests and Spec clarification are some other benefits of prompt mutation where mutations emphasize edge conditions, and clarification helps improve code and test candidates generation. Overall, across the 100 manually reviewed instances, we observed a consistent pattern: prompt mutants help trigger diverse code and test generation while preventing the model from performing “look up” and instead generating new code patterns that are more generalizable and robust. SPARK ’s cost compared to the original prompt: Table VI presents the average token usage per sample across datasets for original prompts and SPARK with a single mutation, which indicates token usage increases associated with mutated prompts (up to four times compared to the original prompts). However, this cost is compatible with prior approaches such as CodeT that often require more than four times the token usage due to ineffective variance generation without mutation. VI Related work Code Generation: Code generation tasks are categorized into three paradigms: description-to-code, code-to-description, and code-to-code transformations [30, 31]. Solution ranging from recurrent neural networks (RNNs) [32] to transformers, and convolutional neural networks (CNNs) [33]. Recent transformer-based models, such as Codex and AlphaCode [34], have demonstrated remarkable capabilities, particularly in competitive programming. Li et al. [34] introduce AlphaCode, a transformer-based system capable of generating multiple diverse code candidates, which achieves human-level performance in competitive programming By conditioning generation on bidirectional context, InCoder [35] significantly improves zero-shot performance across tasks such as type inference, comment generation, and variable renaming, effectively bridging pure synthesis and code editing tasks. Additionally, CODET [15] leverages dual execution agreement on both solutions and comprehensive test cases generation to enhance solution selection accuracy. Recently, foundation models such as ChatGPT or Copilot have been shown to have practical utility in code generation, but with some limitations [36]. Specifically, these tools are predominantly utilized in smaller, individually maintained projects involving simpler, low-complexity code, requiring minimal modifications. Test Generation: Traditional techniques for automated test case generation have primarily relied on search-based [37], constraint-driven [38], and random strategies [39], with the primary goal of maximizing code coverage. Recently, LLMs have been utilized for automatic generation of human-like unit tests using pre-trained and fine-tuned models [40, 41, 42, 43, 44], reinforcement learning [45], and hybrid approaches combining LLMs with search-based methods [37]. Despite encouraging progress, LLM-generated test cases often suffer from correctness issues [46, 47, 48] and demonstrate relatively low coverage on certain benchmarks. These limitations highlight the importance of continued refinement and systematic comparisons with established frameworks such as EvoSuite [49, 50] and Pynguin [51, 50]. Prompt Mutation: Prompt mutations are effectively utilized in LLM-assisted test and code generation [52, 53, 54, 55, 56]. Specifically, skeleton prompts enforce generation uniformity [53] or iterative human-in-the-loop refine requirement [52]. ReCode [54] and ADVPRO [55], respectively, present robustness-enhancement and paraphrase prompt mutation techniques. Differing from ReCode and ADVPRO, SPARK applies a broader set of sentence-level mutations and operates entirely on natural-language prompt mutations. Finally, Chen et al [56] explore the mutations from the perspective of human-induced variance in semantically similar prompts and places a significant emphasis upon minor prompt perturbations. SPARK instead utilizes real-world natural language variance to get semantically similar prompts that can generate diverse code and tests. VII Threats to Validity Firstly, using the same LLM to produce both solutions and tests reduces the configuration effort but risks circularity: if the model generates flawed or overly simplistic tests, incorrect solutions may pass evaluation. Although our mutation strategies seek to mitigate this by inducing diversity, they cannot guarantee absolute coverage of all edge cases or complex requirements found in real-world software. Secondly, our carefully designed diverse set of LLM-based prompt mutations to simulate real-world variation in problem descriptions might not capture the full range or nuance of naturally occurring variances. Additionally, the manually validated sample set indicates GPT-4 has high accuracy; it may still introduce unintended biases or fail to preserve the original task semantics perfectly. Finally, while the three evaluation benchmarks, LiveCodeBench, BigCodeBench, and DLBench, offer complementary coverage—from algorithmic puzzles to real-world API usage and deep learning code—they may not fully represent all software engineering contexts or programming languages. VIII Conclusion In this work, we presented SPARK , a framework that leverages semantic-preserving prompt mutations and consensus-based verification to enhance the reliability of LLM-driven code generation. Evaluation showed that SPARK consistently improved pass@1 accuracy when controlled linguistic and structural mutations diversified candidate solutions and strengthened consensus selection. Our analysis revealed complementary benefits across mutation classes while highlighting trade-offs in token cost when applying larger mutation sets. Overall, SPARK provides a practical and extensible approach to improving code generation.

An Empirical Study on Improving LLM-Based Issue Classification through Domain-Informed Analysis Issue reports that describe Intrinsic Bugs, Extrinsic Bugs, and Not a Bug cases often use similar language, but they might point to different causes and require different maintenance actions. This makes three-way issue classification difficult for Large Language Models (LLMs), particularly when prompt-based refinements begin to plateau. We study whether domain-informed analysis of LLM outputs can improve classification beyond prompt modification alone. Using 428 manually labeled issue reports, we evaluate six LLMs across 18 prompt configurations and analyze 7,704 model-generated rationales to identify recurring failure patterns in how models justify predictions, use evidence, and handle conflicting information. We translate these findings into a multi-stage pipeline that separates bug validity from bug origin. The pipeline improves macro F1 and Extrinsic Bug recall for five of the six models. The strongest pipeline configuration reaches 0.827 accuracy and 0.757 Extrinsic Bug recall, improving over the best-accuracy prompt-only baseline by +1.2 and +7.5 pp, respectively. The decomposition further reveals that bug origin classification is more reliable than validity, indicating that the bug-validity decision accounts for most of the remaining error. These results show that expert failure analysis can support more reliable LLM-based software engineering classifiers. I Introduction Issue reports are central artifacts in software maintenance, but their interpretation is often more difficult than it first appears. A report may mention crashes, failing tests, stack traces, unexpected behavior, or error messages and still not describe a software defect. Conversely, a report may describe a real defect whose root cause lies outside the focal project’s own source history, for example in a changed dependency, platform configuration, external service, or upstream API. This makes issue classification a compound problem: it requires deciding both bug validity [1], i.e., whether the report describes a real defect, and bug origin [2], i.e., whether the root cause of a valid defect is intrinsic or extrinsic to the focal project. In this paper, we study this problem as a three-way classification task: Intrinsic Bug, Extrinsic Bug, or Not a Bug. This combined validity-origin distinction matters for both maintenance practice and empirical software engineering research. Non-bug reports may require documentation updates, clarification, duplicate handling, or enhancement triage, while valid bug reports require root-cause analysis. Treating non-bugs or extrinsic bugs as intrinsic project defects can contaminate defect repositories, misdirect root-cause analysis, and distort conclusions drawn from software analytics studies [3, 4, 5]. This problem is not marginal: Herzig et al. manually inspected more than 7,000 issue reports and found that 33.8% of reports labeled as bugs did not describe corrective maintenance [3]. Prior work has also shown that intrinsic and extrinsic bugs can differ in ways that affect downstream defect prediction [2, 6]. As software engineering increasingly adopts automated classification and decision-support systems, the quality of these distinctions becomes a prerequisite for trustworthy automation. However, this three-way validity and origin classification task is not a simple text-classification problem. A report that mentions a dependency is not necessarily an Extrinsic Bug; the dependency may only appear in the execution context, or the focal project may be using the dependency incorrectly. Similarly, a report that uses failure-like language is not necessarily a bug; it may describe expected behavior, user error, an unsupported configuration, a documentation problem, or a feature request. Correct classification often depends on domain knowledge, expected behavior, project responsibility, and evidence distributed across the issue discussion. Large Language Models (LLMs) are a natural candidate for this task because they can classify issue text from instructions and examples without requiring a task-specific classifier to be trained from scratch [7, 8]. Prior studies show that GPT-like and transformer-like models can automate issue labeling [9, 10]. However, performance metrics alone do not show whether a model has learned the domain distinctions that define the classification problem. Two models may obtain similar F1 scores while failing for different reasons: one may confuse non-bugs with intrinsic bugs, another may overuse the extrinsic label whenever a dependency is mentioned, and another may rely on superficial failure terminology rather than root-cause evidence. In this paper, we investigate whether domain expertise can improve LLM-based issue classification beyond prompt-only classification. We evaluate six LLMs under 18 prompt-only configurations on 428 issue reports manually labeled as Intrinsic Bug, Extrinsic Bug, or Not a Bug. We then analyze both model predictions and model-generated rationales to understand how the models appear to interpret the task, which evidence they emphasize, and where their interpretations diverge from expert judgment. Finally, we use this failure analysis to redesign the classification process as a domain-informed multi-stage pipeline. We evaluate the resulting pipeline using class-level precision, recall, and F1, together with macro-averaged performance. Our results show that prompt-only changes reach an observed ceiling of 81.5% accuracy and 0.801 macro F1, motivating a deeper analysis of model-output failure patterns. Applying a structured rationale-inspection template to 7,704 representative model-generated rationales reveals two recurring patterns that distinguish correct from incorrect predictions across all three classes: contradictory evidence mishandling (L2-Q3) and conclusion-first reasoning (L2-Q5). Extrinsic Bug issues emerge as a distinct source of difficulty, exhibiting the highest misclassification rate (50.6%) and revealing that models frequently revise away from the correct label after initially identifying it. Translating these findings into a domain-informed multi-stage pipeline that separates bug validity from bug origin improves macro F1 for five of six models and raises the best configuration’s accuracy from 0.815 to 0.827 (+1.2 pp) while lifting Extrinsic Bug recall to 0.757 (+7.5 pp over the best-accuracy baseline). The pipeline also shows that each decision is independently reliable, with bug origin classification (up to 0.907 accuracy) more accurate than bug validity (up to 0.871), suggesting that the validity decision, rather than origin, accounts for much of the remaining error. This paper makes the following contributions: An empirical evaluation: We evaluate six LLMs across three prompts (18 model-prompt configurations) for three-way issue classification and analyze performance variability and class-specific errors. Rationale Analysis: We introduce a structured template for inspecting model rationales, focusing on evidence use, rule application, alternative labels, and contradictory information. A domain-informed pipeline: We propose a multi-stage classification process that uses expert failure analysis to improve LLM-based issue classification. II Background and Related Work Bug Origins: Intrinsic and Extrinsic Bugs: Some software analytics techniques, especially defect prediction and bug-mining approaches, assume that reported failures originate from changes in the same repository [11, 12, 13]. Rodríguez-Pérez et al. [2] challenged this assumption by distinguishing bugs according to their origin. An intrinsic bug is caused by a change within the analyzed project’s source code history, whereas an extrinsic bug is a genuine failure whose cause lies outside that history, for example in a dependency, external service, or upstream component. In a manual study of OpenStack Nova and Elasticsearch, they found that 9–21% of bugs were extrinsic [2]. A follow-up study showed that excluding Extrinsic bugs could change defect-prediction performance by as much as 16 AUC pp [6]. Recent work has begun to automate bug-origin classification: BuggIn is a TF–IDF-based classifier for identifying Intrinsic bugs from issue reports [14], and Fan et al. [15] later proposed a TextCNN–KAN model for identifying Extrinsic bug reports. These studies show that textual signals can support origin classification, but they focus mainly on binary classification in a limited ecosystem setting. Wright et al. [16] extended bug-origin analysis to the npm ecosystem through the InEx-Bug dataset, which manually labels GitHub issues as Intrinsic Bug, Extrinsic Bug, Not a Bug, or Unknown. Dependency Bugs in Package Ecosystems: The npm ecosystem is especially relevant for studying Extrinsic Bug reports because packages depend on deep and evolving dependency networks. Prior ecosystem studies show that dependency networks grow and reorganize over time [17, 18], and that downstream packages can be affected by vulnerabilities, technical lag, deprecations, breaking changes, and abandoned dependencies [19, 20, 21, 22, 23]. These ecosystem phenomena are related but not equivalent to Extrinsic Bug. A vulnerability, deprecation, or breaking release is an upstream event or exposure mechanism; an Extrinsic Bug is the downstream failure attributed to such an event. Network studies can estimate how many packages are exposed to external risks, but they generally do not determine whether individual downstream reports describe a causally related failure. The two literatures operate at complementary levels: ecosystem studies explain how external risk can spread, while bug-origin studies identify how such failures are reported, interpreted, and handled in downstream projects. Automated Classification of Issue Reports: Issue-report classification has traditionally focused on validity or type, such as distinguishing bugs from feature requests, questions, documentation issues, or other maintenance tasks [24, 25, 26, 27]. Herzig et al. [3] manually examined more than 7,000 issue reports and found that over 30% of reports labeled as bugs were misclassified. Subsequent work treated bug-versus-non-bug identification as a text-classification problem using bag-of-words, n-grams, TF–IDF, topic models, and classifiers such as logistic regression, support-vector machines, decision trees, and random forests [24, 28, 29, 25, 30, 31]. Recent work uses pre-trained language models and LLMs for issue classification [32]. Colavito et al. [33, 9] evaluated transformer-based models for issue classification and showed that data quality and label reliability materially affect evaluation. Koyuncu [34] studied how model and prompt choices affect fine-grained bug-report categorization. A recent mapping study identified 46 primary studies on automatic bug/non-bug classification and found that traditional machine learning, deep learning, BERT-family models, and zero- or few-shot methods are all represented in the literature [35]. LLM-BRC [36] further illustrates the use of language-model representations in hierarchical bug classification, although its goal is to classify behavioral properties of bug reports rather than bug origin. This literature provides useful methods and evaluation practices, but its target labels are not interchangeable with Intrinsic Bug and Extrinsic Bug labels. A classifier that separates bugs from non-bugs does not determine whether a valid bug was caused inside the focal repository or by an external dependency, platform, or environment. Conversely, bug-origin classifiers such as BuggIn [14] and Fan et al.’s model [15] address origin classification, but do not fully address the preceding validity problem. Research Gap. Prior work supports parts of our problem but not their combination. Bug origin studies show that intrinsic and extrinsic bugs are empirically distinct and can affect software analytics results [2, 6]. Ecosystem studies show that dependency-intensive environments such as npm create many opportunities for externally caused failures [17, 18] . However, what remains underexplored is how LLMs fail when bug validity and bug origin must be decided together, and how expert analysis of those failures can be converted into a reproducible improvement process. Our study addresses this gap by evaluating prompt-only LLM classifiers, diagnosing their failure patterns through expert analysis of predictions and rationales, and translating those findings into a domain-informed pipeline for classifying issue reports as Intrinsic Bug, Extrinsic Bug, or Not a Bug. III Study Design Our goal is to investigate whether and how domain expertise can improve LLM-based classification of software issue reports. We focus on a three-way classification task in which each issue report must be labeled as Intrinsic Bug, Extrinsic Bug, or Not a Bug. In this study, domain experts are researchers or practitioners with experience in bug analysis and bug-origin classification. To address our goal, this paper formulates the following research questions (RQs): RQ1: How accurately do prompt-only LLM configurations classify issue reports as Intrinsic Bug, Extrinsic Bug, or Not a Bug? Motivation. Before introducing a domain-informed pipeline, we first establish the performance of prompt-only classification. This provides the baseline against which later pipeline changes are evaluated. It also shows whether prompt effects are consistent across models, prompts, and classes, and identifies which errors persist despite prompt refinement. RQ2: What recurring rationale-level failure patterns are associated with incorrect LLM classifications, and how do these patterns vary across Intrinsic Bug, Extrinsic Bug, and Not a Bug categories? Motivation. Aggregate metrics can show where models fail, but they do not reveal how models justify their predictions. RQ2 therefore analyzes model-generated rationales as diagnostic artifacts. The goal is to identify recurring rationale-level patterns that distinguish correct from incorrect predictions and to examine whether those patterns differ across the three ground-truth classes. These patterns provide the empirical basis for the pipeline evaluated in RQ3. RQ3: Does a domain-informed multi-stage classification pipeline improve performance beyond the strongest prompt-only configuration? Motivation. Prompt-only classification treats the task as a single three-way decision, but the labels combine two different judgments: bug validity and bug origin. This can lead to errors when the model reasons about bug origin before establishing bug validity, or when it dismisses an extrinsic bug because the focal project is not responsible for the underlying cause. RQ3 tests whether these errors can be reduced by restructuring the classification pipeline itself. IV Methodology Figure 1 illustrates the study’s five phases: (I) dataset preparation and LLM selection; (II) prompt refinement; (III) prompt evaluation; (IV) qualitative analysis of recurring failure patterns; and (V) construction and evaluation of the domain-informed classification pipeline. Dataset: We use Version 3.0 of the InEx-Bug dataset [37], a manually annotated collection of closed GitHub issue reports from 103 npm repositories. Version 3.0 extends the original dataset [16] by excluding open and Unknown reports and adding 85 newly annotated reports. It contains 428 reports: 214 Not a Bug, 107 Intrinsic Bug, and 107 Extrinsic Bug. The dataset is therefore balanced between bug and non-bug reports, and also balanced between intrinsic and extrinsic bugs within the bug subset. Each record includes issue text (i.e., title, body, labels, and comments), repository and author metadata, timestamps, participants, maintainer activity, reopen events, assignees, milestones, closing pull requests/commits, and the final classification. Issue Report Representation: Each issue report is represented as a structured text document that is provided to the LLM as input. Each input includes: (i) the issue title; (ii) the repository name (e.g., axios/axios); (iii) the issue number and corresponding URL; (iv) the issue description, corresponding to the original report submitted by the user; and (v) the full sequence of comments associated with the issue, in chronological order. We also separately extract and append a maintainer comments section. Maintainer comments are defined as comments written by users whose GitHub role is marked as OWNER, MEMBER, or COLLABORATOR. We intentionally repeat them in a dedicated section to make maintainer-provided comments more noticeable to the model. This design choice is motivated by the fact that maintainer comments often contain the most reliable evidence for distinguishing between Intrinsic Bug, Extrinsic Bug, and Not a Bug categories, as maintainers are typically the ones who understand the project requirements and boundaries. LLM Selection and Configuration: To identify suitable models for our analysis, we did not want to restrict our study to a small, fixed set of LLMs. Instead, we began by selecting a diverse pool of recent and high-performing LLMs. Candidate models were selected based on availability, recency, reported performance on public benchmarks, and suitability for instruction-following and reasoning-oriented tasks. This initial pool included both proprietary and open-weight models accessed through the Gemini API and Google Cloud Vertex AI: Gemini 3.1 Pro, Gemini 3 Flash, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Gemma 4 26B-A4B, GPT-OSS-120B, GPT-OSS-20B, DeepSeek R1, GLM-5, and Qwen3.5 35B-A3B. The pilot study considered all candidate models. After the pilot study, we selected six model configurations for full evaluation. The final set includes three proprietary models and three open-weight models: Proprietary: Gemini 3.1 Pro (gemini-3.1-pro-preview), Gemini 3 Flash (gemini-3-flash-preview), Gemini 2.5 Pro (gemini-2.5-pro). Open-weight: DeepSeek R1 (deepseek-ai/deepseek-r1-0528-maas), GPT-OSS-120B (openai/gpt-oss-120b-maas), GPT-OSS-20B (openai/gpt-oss-20b-maas). These six models were chosen to satisfy three criteria. First, each model is capable of producing reasoning-style outputs and model-generated rationales. Second, the set spans three independent model providers (Google, OpenAI, and DeepSeek-AI) to mitigate single-vendor or single-family bias in our findings. Third, we include a balanced mix of proprietary and open-weight models to enable more reproducible experimentation. This design follows emerging guidance for empirical studies involving LLMs in software engineering, which emphasizes transparency about prompts and system design, reporting interaction traces, using appropriate baselines and metrics, and validating LLM outputs against human judgment [38]. All models are evaluated under identical experimental conditions: the same set of issue reports, the same prompt variants, and the same issue representation. We use a low fixed temperature of 0.2 to reduce variability while still allowing models to produce natural-language rationales, with top-p = 0.95. For models exposing top-k, we set it to 64. Each model is instructed to produce a Markdown response containing the following sections: a step-by-step rationale (Reasoning), a three-way Probability Distribution over the bug classes, a categorical Confidence level (High/Medium/Low), and a single-label Final Answer. We do not enforce native structured output such as JSON mode. Instead, we preserve the model’s natural explanatory response because the generated rationale is part of the empirical material analyzed in RQ2. The final label, confidence level, and probability distribution are extracted using regular-expression parsing. The full response text is retained for qualitative analysis. Baseline Prompt: We adopt the classification prompt from the replication package accompanying Version 3.0 of the InEx-Bug dataset [37] as our baseline (v0). The prompt instructs the model to classify each GitHub issue as Intrinsic Bug, Extrinsic Bug, or Not a Bug, using formal definitions, decision rules, and seven few-shot examples. Before use, we corrected only structural inconsistencies, without adding, removing, or semantically altering any definitions, rules, or examples. Prompt Variants: We create twelve variants of the baseline prompt to study how domain-specific rules and general prompt-engineering changes affect classification. The first set uses domain-informed ablations. We selectively remove rules that may overfit to specific issue patterns, such as upstream-library attribution or temporal-signal heuristics. These rules were selected during a manual review of the baseline prompt. The second set uses general prompt-engineering variants, modifying prompt structure, wording, or ordering while preserving domain content, motivated by prior work on prompt sensitivity [39, 40, 41]. Our variants were constructed along four dimensions: Domain-informed ablation: Remove domain-specific rules to assess their impact on classification. Structural ablation: Remove structural components (e.g., few-shot examples and probability outputs) to measure their impact on classification. Structural sensitivity: Test whether formatting or ordering changes affect classification performance. Linguistic sensitivity: Test whether tone, register, or persona changes affect classification performance. Pilot Study: We conduct a pilot study to select prompt variants for full-scale evaluation. The pilot uses a stratified sample of 30 labeled issue reports, consisting of 10 Intrinsic Bug, 10 Extrinsic Bug, and 10 Not a Bug reports, drawn with a fixed random seed for reproducibility. Each of the 13 prompt variants was evaluated on this sample using 24 configurations from 10 proprietary and open-weight models. Prompt performance is assessed using overall accuracy and Extrinsic Bug recall, aggregated across all 24 model configurations. We emphasize Extrinsic Bug recall because extrinsic bugs are the most domain-sensitive class. A prompt that improves overall accuracy while failing to identify extrinsic bugs would therefore not adequately address the task. All three authors jointly reviewed the accuracy and Extrinsic Bug recall results across the 13 variants and reached consensus on the three variants that performed most consistently well across models and were worth investigating further: the baseline prompt (v0), the no-upstream-library-rule variant (v10), and the maintainer-voice variant (v11), referred to as v0, v1, and v2 in the full evaluation study. We evaluate the three selected prompt variants on the full dataset of 428 issue reports using the six selected LLMs. This produces 18 (model [FORMULA] prompt) configurations in total. Mitigating LLM Non-Determinism: Since LLM outputs can vary across repeated runs [42, 43], we executed each model [FORMULA] prompt configuration three independent times at temperature=0.2, yielding 54 model [FORMULA] prompt [FORMULA] run configurations in total. We assess run-to-run stability using: (i) per-instance label agreement reported as the fraction of the 428 issues for which all three runs produced identical predictions, (ii) Fleiss’ [FORMULA] with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals [44] treating the three runs as raters, (iii) mean, standard deviation, and min–max range of weighted F1, macro F1, and per-class recall across all runs, and (iv) Cochran’s Q tests on the per-instance binary correctness vector, where an instance was coded as correct if ground_truth == predicted_label and incorrect otherwise, to detect statistically significant differences in correctness rate across runs. Benjamini-Hochberg correction controlled the false discovery rate [45]. Aggregating Across Runs: We report performance in two ways: (i) per-run mean and standard deviation and (ii) majority-vote (aggregation inspired by self-consistency [46]), where for each issue, the final label is the one predicted by at least two of three runs. In rare cases where all three runs produce a different label, the tie is broken by selecting the label whose run reported the highest predicted class probability. If probabilities are equal, we fall back to lexicographic order to ensure deterministic and reproducible results. Evaluation Metrics: We evaluate classification performance using accuracy, weighted F1, macro F1, and per-class precision, recall, and F1 for each of the three classes. To test prompt differences, we apply McNemar’s test to all three pairwise prompt comparisons within each model using majority-vote predictions. McNemar’s test is appropriate here because the predictions are paired at the issue level and the outcome is binary (correct/incorrect). Benjamini–Hochberg correction controls the false discovery rate at [FORMULA] [45]. To answer RQ2, we analyze the model outputs from RQ1. Each output includes the issue report, ground-truth label, model prediction, rationale, probability distribution, confidence level, prompt variant, model identifier, and run identifier. Since the full corpus contains 23,112 outputs across three repeated runs, we reduce it to one representative response for each (issue [FORMULA] model [FORMULA] prompt). We retain the earliest response matching the majority prediction across the three runs; when all runs disagree, we use run 1 for deterministic selection. This produces 7,704 records. We analyze this reduced corpus in two complementary ways. First, we compute quantitative summaries of error distributions across models, prompts, classes, and issue reports to identify which classes and decision boundaries are most error-prone. We also categorize issues by classification difficulty to guide qualitative sampling. An issue is labeled model_hard if at most two of the six models classify it correctly, model_easy if at least four models classify it correctly, and model_mixed if exactly three models classify it correctly. This yields 93 hard, 316 easy, and 19 mixed issues. ID Rationale Feature Options L1-Q1 Maintainer disagreement Conflict acknowledged and reasoned through; Conflict present but not explicitly reasoned; No maintainer conflict present. L1-Q2 Rule grounding Grounded; Asserted; Not applicable, No rule invoked. L2-Q1 Rationale and response alignment Aligned; Compressed; Reversed; Partial self-correction. L2-Q2 Alternative-label consideration Both alternatives; One alternative; None. L2-Q3 Contradictory evidence handling Addressed; Dismissed without supporting reasoning; Ignored entirely; No contradicting evidence present. L2-Q4 Correct-label abandonment Yes; No. L2-Q5 Direction of reasoning Evidence-first; Conclusion-first; Recursive; Reversed. Qualitative Inspection: We used an iterative manual qualitative inspection process to develop a structured template for identifying recurring patterns in model-generated rationales. The purpose of this process was not to conduct open-ended manual coding of the entire response corpus or a sample of it. Instead, our goal was to inspect a focused set of model-generated outputs, identify recurring rationale-level and prompt-interaction patterns, and translate these observations into a structured template that could be applied consistently at scale. The inspection process proceeded in two rounds. In the first round, two authors inspected a randomly selected sample of 10 issue reports, consisting of five model_easy and five model_hard cases. The sample included issue reports from all three ground-truth categories. For each sampled issue, the authors individually inspected one representative model output selected from the reduced corpus, together with the issue evidence, the predicted label, and the ground-truth label. They noted recurring behaviors in how the model interpreted the issue, considered alternative labels, used or ignored contextual cues, and justified its prediction. After the independent inspection, the authors met to compare observations, discuss emerging patterns, resolve disagreements through discussion, and refine the candidate template questions. In the second round, the authors repeated this process on a different randomly selected sample of 10 issue reports, again consisting of five model_easy and five model_hard cases. Based on the observations and discussions from both rounds, the two authors formalized a preliminary inspection template consisting of structured questions and predefined answer choices. They then applied the preliminary template to the 20 inspected cases from Rounds 1 and 2 to assess whether the questions and answer choices captured the behaviors observed during manual inspection. The third author subsequently reviewed the template and helped refine ambiguous questions and response options. Across these iterations, the authors consolidated overlapping observations, clarified the wording of template questions, and revised the answer choices to better capture recurring patterns in the model-generated rationales. This process resulted in a finalized rationale-inspection template designed to identify recurring patterns associated with misclassifications and to guide the domain-informed pipeline design for RQ3. Table I summarizes the template questions and predefined answer options. LLM-Assisted Template Application: The finalized rationale-inspection template was converted into an LLM-assisted inspection prompt. We used Gemini 2.5 Pro to apply the finalized template because it was the best-performing model in the RQ1 classification evaluation. Gemini 2.5 Pro was configured with a maximum thinking budget of 32,768 tokens. The model was instructed to produce one structured CSV row per response record, containing the seven template values in a fixed column order. We applied the inspection prompt to the full set of 7,704 representative responses. To assess the consistency of the LLM-assisted template application, we compared its outputs against human-coded labels on two disjoint ten-record samples corresponding to the two human-inspection rounds. The comparison showed cell-level agreement above 90%. To answer RQ3, we build a domain-informed multi-stage classification pipeline using the strongest RQ1 prompt-only configuration, the no-upstream-library-rule variant (v1), as the baseline. Guided by the RQ2 failure analysis, the pipeline separates bug validity from bug origin and adds targeted checks for validity errors. Task Decomposition: The prompt-only baseline treats classification as a single three-way decision. In contrast, our pipeline decomposes the task into two sequential binary decisions. The first stage determines bug validity, while the second stage determines bug origin only for issues classified as valid bugs. Stage 1: Bug Validity (Bug vs Not a Bug) determines whether the report describes a genuine software defect requiring a change to the package’s shipped code, configuration, or constraints, regardless of where the defect originates. Stage 2: Bug Origin (Intrinsic Bug vs Extrinsic Bug) applies only to reports classified as bugs. This stage determines whether the defect originates from the package’s own logic or from an external dependency, environment, platform, or upstream change. The two-stage pipeline first asks whether a defect exists and then, only if a defect exists, asks where the defect originated. The Stage 1 prompt treats both internally and externally caused defects as Bug, does not assign the origin label, and instead defers the origin analysis to Stage 2. The Stage 2 prompt then guides the model to reason about where the defect originated and not where the fix may be applied. By decomposing the three-way classification task into two focused binary decisions, the pipeline avoids forcing a single prompt to arbitrate bug validity and bug origin at the same time. Domain-Informed Stage 1: The Stage 1 defect prompt is adopted from the v1 prompt selected in RQ1. We add two rules derived from the RQ2 analysis of how Extrinsic Bug reports are incorrectly dismissed. RQ2 showed that many Extrinsic Bug errors occur when a model recognizes an externally triggered failure but revises away from the bug label because the focal project is not directly responsible for the underlying cause. To address this failure mode, the Stage 1 prompt emphasizes that an issue can describe a genuine bug even when the root cause lies outside the focal repository, and that bug validity should be decided before assigning responsibility for the origin of the defect. Independent Re-check Stage (Recover): Between Stage 1 and Stage 2, we insert a re-check stage, called Recover. When Stage 1 predicts Not a Bug, Recover examines whether the issue nevertheless describes a genuine software defect that should instead be classified as a bug. Recover receives the Stage 1 verdict and rationale as a “prior pipeline assessment”, but is instructed to treat that assessment as a prior opinion that may be wrong rather than as a decision to ratify. This stage is conservative by design: it retains the Stage 1 verdict unless the issue contains clear evidence that the verdict is wrong. The re-check is performed by an independent judge model. In the preliminary pipeline iterations, using the same model for both Stage 1 and the re-check often led the model to re-derive and re-endorse its earlier decision. Recover is performed by gemini-3.1-pro-preview for all pipelines except the one whose Stage 1 also uses gemini-3.1-pro-preview. There, to keep the judge independent, we substitute gemini-2.5-pro. Context Chaining between Stages: Each stage is executed as an independent LLM inference and therefore has no conversational memory. To preserve intermediate decisions, downstream stages receive the verdict and rationale generated by preceding stages. The Recover stage receives the Stage 1 prediction and rationale. Stage 2 receives the bug-validity verdict and the preceding rationale, and then assumes that bug validity has already been established. It then determines whether the defect originates from within the focal package (intrinsic) or from an external source (extrinsic). By carrying the accumulated reasoning forward in this pipeline, it allows for the avoidance of collapsing stages within a single run and allows for early mistakes to be caught later in the pipeline. Evaluation: For comparability with RQ1, we run the proposed pipeline end-to-end on the same 428-report dataset used in the prompt-only evaluation. Each issue receives a final three-way label: Intrinsic Bug, Extrinsic Bug, or Not a Bug. We then evaluate the proposed pipeline on an independent validation set of 30 manually annotated npm issue reports, with 10 reports per class. This validation set was not used during prompt selection, rationale-template development, failure analysis, or pipeline construction. The validation reports were manually annotated by the authors using the same three-way schema as InEx-Bug, with disagreements resolved through discussion. Lastly, we perform component ablations to isolate the contribution of each pipeline element. For the Recover stage, we record recovery flips and whether each flip improves or harms the final classification. Classifications that did not return a response or did not contain a parsable classification label were treated as invalid predictions and counted as incorrect.
