VI Discussion and Implications Prompt-only refinement plateaus, and added domain rules can negatively impact performance. It is worth noting that the strongest prompt variant was not the one that encoded the most domain guidance. In fact, v1 was a domain-informed ablation that removed the upstream-library-attribution rule. It achieved the highest macro F1 for five of six models and improved over the baseline v0 for all six models. Our results align with prior evidence that, for LLMs, more context is not necessarily better. Prompt sensitivity shows that small, semantically minor edits to a prompt can swing the classification outcomes [39, 40, 41]. Prior work shows that added context can distract LLMs and reduce performance, whether through irrelevant details, excessive examples, or agent “cursor rules” [48, 49, 50]. Our results show that even valid expert-authored domain rules can have this effect when encoded directly in prompts. Implication 1: For domain-sensitive tasks, prompt-only refinement can face a diminishing-returns ceiling, and adding more domain rules or context is not necessarily beneficial. Domain guidance should therefore be evaluated empirically rather than assumed to improve performance. Rationales are useful diagnostic artifacts, but not explanations of internal reasoning. Our RQ2 analysis used model-generated rationales to identify recurring patterns in incorrect predictions. Correct predictions were much more likely to be evidence-first, whereas incorrect predictions frequently anchored on a conclusion. Similarly, misclassified responses often ignored or dismissed evidence that conflicted with the final label. These findings should not be interpreted as proof of the model’s internal reasoning process. Prior work has shown that chain-of-thought and generated explanations can be unfaithful to the actual decision process [51]. We therefore treat rationales as observable artifacts: they show how the model presents and justifies its interpretation, not necessarily how the model internally arrived at the label. Even under this cautious interpretation, rationales are valuable. They expose recurring failure signatures that aggregate metrics cannot show. Implication 2: Researchers should avoid claiming that a model “reasoned correctly” merely because its explanation is plausible. Instead, generated rationales can be treated as diagnostic artifacts that can help identify failure patterns and guide the design of more reliable classification pipelines. Extrinsic Bugs are a distinct challenge, not just a lower-performing class. Prior bug origin research shows that extrinsic bugs are empirically important and can affect downstream software analytics [2, 6], while issue-report studies show that bug-labeled reports often contain non-bugs [3]. Our findings connect these concerns by showing that LLMs struggle when bug validity and bug origin must be judged together, even with explicit definitions, examples, and decision rules. The difficulty is not simply that Extrinsic Bug is a lower-performing class; it requires the model to recognize that a reported failure can be real even when the focal repository did not introduce the root cause. LLMs also revised away from the correct label more often for Extrinsic Bug reports. These results suggest that extrinsic bugs create a specific interpretive burden. This burden appears tied to how such reports are written and discussed, and it persisted despite explicit classification guidance in our evaluation. Implication 3: Extrinsic bug classification requires richer evidence than labels alone. Future datasets, issue templates, and reporting guidelines should capture dependency, environment, reproduction, maintainer, fix-location, and causal information needed to distinguish external causation from non-bug reports. For Extrinsic Bugs, the main bottleneck is bug validity, not bug origin. Our pipeline decomposes a complex task into smaller subtasks [52] and highlights where the difficulty lies when it comes to classifying Extrinsic Bugs. Extrinsic Bug was the hardest class to classify, and its dominant error direction is revealing: 32.5% of all misclassifications were extrinsic bugs mistaken for Not a Bug. Once an issue is established as a genuine bug, the origin decision is reliable: Stage 2 achieved up to 90.7% accuracy on Intrinsic Bug vs. Extrinsic Bug. The end-to-end performance is instead bounded by Stage 1, where extrinsic bugs are discarded as Not a Bug before the origin decision is ever reached. The persistence of this error even under domain-informed prompting suggests the boundary may be genuinely ambiguous, potentially difficult for human annotators as well. This motivates an in-depth study of these cases to identify what evidence distinguishes an externally-caused defect from a non-bug. Implication 4: Datasets, tools, and classification pipelines should treat bug validity and bug origin as separable judgments. Future work should aim to improve extrinsic bug detection by targeting the Bug vs. Not a Bug boundary. Comparison with non-LLM classifiers. Prior automated origin classifiers target a different task, dataset, and label schema. BuggIn [14] performs binary intrinsic-vs-rest classification with classical ML to identify intrinsic bugs (best F1 0.78), and Fan et al.’s TextCNN–KAN [15] performs binary intrinsic-vs-extrinsic classification (accuracy 0.75, F1 0.81 on 1,880 OpenStack samples). LLM-BRC [36] and Colavito et al. [33, 9, 53] classify behavioral or type-level properties rather than bug origin. The closest comparison to our work is at the binary-subtask level: our pipeline reaches 87.1% accuracy on the validity decision (Stage 1) and 90.7% on the origin decision (Stage 2), while jointly resolving both judgments that prior classifiers treat in isolation. VII Threats to Validity Internal Validity: LLM outputs may vary across identical runs, affecting classifications, rationales, and confidence estimates in both the prompt-only evaluation and the downstream analysis. We mitigated this by running each model [FORMULA] prompt configuration three times at temperature=0.2, aggregating predictions by majority vote, and measuring stability with agreement, Fleiss’ [FORMULA] , metric variation, and Cochran’s [FORMULA] tests. These results support using one representative response for RQ2 and single-run pipeline results for RQ3, though residual randomness remains. To code 7,704 rationales for RQ2, we applied the finalized template using Gemini 2.5 Pro, the strongest evaluated classifier. An automated coder may misread rationales, and using the model from the same family as some of the coded outputs may bias the coding. We mitigated this by developing the template through an iterative, human-driven inspection process and validating the automated coding against independent human coding on two disjoint ten-record samples, where cell-level agreement exceeded 90%. However, the validation set remains small. The template also encodes the authors’ judgments about which reasoning behaviors are salient, which may shape observed failures. To reduce this, two authors independently inspected samples across two rounds, reconciled disagreements, and a third author refined ambiguous questions and answer options. External Validity: All 428 primary issues come from npm because InEx-Bug is the only public dataset with the required three-way schema. While npm’s dependency structure makes extrinsic bugs especially relevant, results may not transfer directly to ecosystems such as Maven or PyPI, industrial codebases, or projects with different triage practices. Construct Validity: Our failure analysis uses model-generated rationales, which may not faithfully reflect internal reasoning [51]. We therefore do not interpret rationales as explanations of why a model decided as it did. Instead, we treat them as observable artifacts of how a model presents its interpretation of the issue. We acknowledge that an inferential gap between stated and actual reasoning remains. The three classes reflect judgments about bug validity and origin, which can be ambiguous when evidence is incomplete. We treat InEx-Bug annotations as ground truth. Any residual label noise or borderline cases would affect both the performance metrics and the failure analysis. Finally, because LLMs are pre-trained on large web corpora, some evaluated models may have encountered GitHub issues during pre-training, raising the possibility of training-data leakage. We consider this risk limited, as the threat is not exposure to the issue text, which is the intended model input, but to the ground-truth labels. The manually annotated InEx-Bug dataset was released in 2026 and postdates the pre-training data of most evaluated models. Moreover, if leakage had materially influenced the results, we would expect uniformly high accuracy across all three categories. Instead, we observe a class-dependent error profile. Nevertheless, model training cutoffs and data sources are not fully transparent. We therefore cannot rule out exposure to some issue text and labels during pre-training. VIII Conclusion Overall, our findings show that the value of LLMs for issue-report classification should not be assessed only by asking whether they can assign labels accurately. Prompt-only refinement plateaued at 0.815 accuracy and 0.801 macro F1, but a domain-informed pipeline derived from expert failure analysis improved macro F1 and Extrinsic Bug recall for five of the six evaluated models, with its strongest configuration reaching 0.827 accuracy and 0.757 Extrinsic Bug recall. Decomposing the task further showed that origin classification is more reliable than validity, indicating that the bug-validity decision may account for much of the remaining error. More importantly, these results show that model failures can reveal domain-specific sources of confusion that, when analyzed by experts, can be translated into a more reliable classification process. This paper therefore demonstrates how expert diagnosis can help identify and address failure modes in LLM-based bug classification.

Do They Do as They Are Told? Investigating Coding Agents’ Adherence to Explicit Instructions in Context Files Developers increasingly rely on agent context files (ACFs), persistent, project-scoped artifacts such as AGENTS.md, to steer the behavior of autonomous coding agents without renegotiating expectations at every interaction. Yet this governance mechanism rests on an untested assumption: that instructions written into an ACF are actually carried out, rather than ignored or loosely followed. Existing studies describe what ACFs contain, but not whether individual instructions are followed, leaving open which guidance can be trusted. We address this gap through an empirical study of real-world ACF snapshots and their linked agent-generated commits: characterizing the explicit, actionable instructions ACFs encode, operationalizing them into executable measurement scripts, and using these scripts to assess instruction-level compliance. We find that most observable instructions can be operationalized and that agents follow ACF guidance more often than not, but adherence splits sharply between instructions followed consistently and those never respected, with differences across instruction categories and coding agents. This split shows where ACF guidance works and where it does not, pointing to instruction types that may need rewriting and to agents that may need enforcement beyond the ACF. These findings lay the groundwork for systematic approaches to specifying, verifying, and enforcing project-specific instructions in autonomous software development. 1. Introduction The emergence of autonomous coding agents is progressively transforming how software engineering (SE) activities are organized and carried out (Hassan et al., 2025). When provided with appropriate instructions and contextual guidance, these agents can complete sophisticated development tasks with relatively limited human oversight (Li et al., 2025). Consequently, contemporary software development is increasingly moving toward a collaborative human–agent setting, where developers primarily specify goals, requirements, and constraints, while autonomous agents are responsible for translating them into executable development actions (Hou et al., 2024). In this context, a new class of software artifact has emerged: agent context files (ACFs). These artifacts (e.g., AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, or copilot-instructions.md) act as agent-oriented counterparts of traditional README files, explicitly defining how an AI agent should behave within a given software project (Chatlatanagulchai et al., 2025b; Chatlatanagulchai et al., 2025a). ACFs encode project-specific knowledge, including architectural overviews, build and test procedures, coding conventions, and operational rules governing tool usage and external service interaction (Chatlatanagulchai et al., 2025b). Modern AI-assisted development tools, including Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and GitHub Copilot, are designed to automatically load these files at the beginning of a session and use them as a stable reference when planning and executing code changes (Chatlatanagulchai et al., 2025a). Consequently, ACFs play a central role in shaping how agents interpret a codebase, adhere to development practices, and perform non-trivial software engineering tasks. Despite the growing adoption of ACFs, little empirical evidence exists on whether the instructions they encode are actually reflected in practice. The presence of guidance in a context file does not guarantee that an agent will follow it, and recent studies of agent-generated tests and of testing guidance in ACFs both name this question as future work (Hora and Robbes, 2026; Ardic et al., 2026). The question matters because ACFs are expected to act as persistent, project-specific sources of guidance (Mohsenimofidi et al., 2025) that let developers steer agent behavior in a controlled and predictable way. This expectation breaks down if instructions are systematically ignored, partially applied, or inconsistently interpreted, and recent evidence on agents’ compliance with documented repository rules suggests that such failures do occur (Yang et al., 2026). Answering it also matters beyond confirming that ACFs work, because an instruction-level account of compliance has implications for two related problems in agent governance. Knowing which instructions are consistently followed and which are essentially never respected shows how effective specific forms of guidance are, and points to instruction types that may need reformulation or reinforcement beyond the context file. Differences in compliance across coding agents show how agents differ in interpreting project-level constraints, and expose instruction classes for which particular agents are less reliable. This gives a basis for agent-specific guidance and for verification mechanisms that complement natural-language instructions. An empirical account of instruction-level compliance thus yields design and engineering implications, not only a check on whether ACFs work. A fundamental challenge in addressing this problem lies in the nature of the instructions themselves. Existing studies describe ACF contents through high-level categories (e.g., testing, implementation, or quality) that aggregate heterogeneous forms of guidance with different meanings and implications (Chatlatanagulchai et al., 2025a): a testing-related instruction, for instance, may mean running an existing test suite, adopting a specific framework, or generating new test cases. Such variation makes it difficult to reason about what it means for an agent to “follow” a given instruction type, or to identify observable evidence of such behavior in software artifacts. Hence, advancing our understanding of ACFs requires moving beyond high-level categorizations toward a more precise characterization of the instructions they encode—focusing on guidance that is explicit and actionable, directly stated in the ACF and prescribing concrete development behavior, and establishing whether each such instruction can be operationalized through measurable software artifacts. We address this gap by examining the relationship between explicit, actionable instructions in ACFs and the observable behavior of autonomous coding agents in real-world development. Rather than assuming the presence of guidance implies compliance, or treating compliance as a single aggregate figure, we structure the investigation as a three-phase empirical pipeline: characterizing the instructions ACFs encode, establishing whether they are concretely measurable through software artifacts, and assessing how closely agents follow them, at a granularity fine enough to attribute compliance variation to specific instruction types and agents rather than to ACFs overall. We conduct a three-phase empirical study grounded in a dataset of 621 unique ACF snapshots linked to 6,541 agent-generated commits across 268 repositories. First, we combine manual calibration with LLM-assisted classification to extract and characterize explicit, actionable instructions from real-world ACFs, validating the results on a statistically representative sample. In the second phase, we generate executable measurement scripts via test-driven code generation: a code LLM independently samples candidate scripts and test fixtures from the instruction’s behavioral descriptor, and a script is accepted only if it passes a minimum number of fixtures and is corroborated by at least one independently generated script. In the third phase, we apply the validated scripts to the reconstructed commit dataset and analyze the resulting compliance observations through descriptive statistics and comparative tests across instruction categories and agents. Throughout, compliance denotes artifact-level evidence, produced by a script that operationalizes the instruction’s own specified behavioral descriptor, that an applicable commit satisfies what the instruction prescribes. Applying this pipeline to the corpus, we find that most explicit, actionable, and observable instructions can be operationalized into executable measurement scripts and that, where compliance can be measured, agents follow ACF guidance more often than not—though adherence is far from uniform, splitting sharply between instructions followed consistently and those essentially never respected, with the gap shaped by both instruction category and coding agent. We use this split throughout the paper as evidence in its own right, indicating where current ACF content already functions reliably, where it does not, and which instruction classes and agents most warrant reinforcement beyond natural-language guidance alone. To sum up, this paper offers the following main contributions: A three-criteria characterization of the explicit, actionable, and observable instructions encoded in real-world ACFs, distinguishing genuinely verifiable guidance from high-level content categories used in prior work. An empirical evaluation of whether such instructions can be operationalized into executable measurement scripts and whether they are actually reflected in agent-generated commits, showing that compliance, while common, is neither guaranteed nor uniform across instruction types and agents. A discussion of the implications of these instruction-level compliance patterns for ACF authoring practices and for the engineering of agentic systems, identifying instruction types that may warrant reformulation and the classes of guidance for which verification beyond natural language appears most warranted. A publicly available replication package(Voria et al., ), including the extraction and classification pipeline, the generated measurement scripts, and the compliance dataset, to support future work on verifying and enforcing agent adherence to project-specific guidance. 2. Background and Related Work Software engineering practice is shifting from single-turn code completion toward autonomous coding agents that decompose high-level goals into multi-step plans and execute them with limited human intervention (Hassan et al., 2025). Wang et al. (Wang et al., 2025b) characterize such systems through a perception–memory–action framework, in which agent behavior is governed in part by an explicit form of procedural memory encoded in the agent’s configuration. This shift has broadened the range of activities agents are expected to perform, including automated program repair (Bouzenia et al., 2025), autonomous testing (Feldt et al., 2023), and agentic refactoring (Horikawa et al., 2025), moving agents progressively closer to end-to-end ownership of development tasks. Greater autonomy, however, introduces governance challenges. Empirical studies report integration defects and security risks specific to agentic settings (Shao et al., 2024), and consistently identify the absence of authoritative, project-specific knowledge as a primary failure mode (Wang et al., 2025b). This failure mode is not merely theoretical: agents contributing to real-world pull requests still require substantial human revision because they fail to follow project-specific conventions (Watanabe et al., ), indicating that capability alone does not guarantee conformance to project-level expectations. Maintaining human governance over autonomous agents has consequently emerged as a practical concern for professional developers. Huang et al. (Huang et al., 2025) find that experienced developers deliberately resist delegating full control to agents, relying instead on explicit strategies—detailed prompts, staged plans, and continuous supervision—to retain authority over design and implementation decisions. Their findings show that governance is not a theoretical abstraction: practitioners actively constrain agent autonomy because unconstrained agents produce outputs that violate quality, safety, and design requirements. This motivates the need for mechanisms through which developers can encode such constraints persistently and systematically, rather than re-asserting them at every interaction. In response to this need, developers have adopted persistent, project-scoped artifacts to communicate intent to agents (Le Hai et al., 2025; Shrivastava et al., 2023). Agent context files (ACFs)—named CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, .cursor/rules, or copilot-instructions.md depending on the tool—capture guidelines, constraints, and conventions that remain active across sessions (Chatlatanagulchai et al., 2025a; Chatlatanagulchai et al., 2025b). Modern agentic tools load these files automatically at the start of a session and treat them as a stable reference throughout planning and execution (Chatlatanagulchai et al., 2025a). Framed in terms of the perception–memory–action view introduced above, ACFs represent an explicit, developer-authored form of procedural memory: a mechanism through which project-specific knowledge is injected into the agent’s context rather than inferred from the codebase alone. Chatlatanagulchai et al. (Chatlatanagulchai et al., 2025a; Chatlatanagulchai et al., 2025b) conducted the first large-scale empirical study of ACFs, analyzing 2,300 files across 1,925 repositories. They find that ACF content skews heavily toward functional concerns—build and run commands (62.3%), implementation details (69.9%), and architecture (67.7%)—while non-functional requirements such as security (14.5%) and performance (14.5%) are rarely specified. Mohsenimofidi et al. (Mohsenimofidi et al., 2025) report substantial variation in how developers express instructions across projects, finding no established structural standard across the 466 projects examined. Galster et al. (Galster et al., 2026) identify eight distinct configuration mechanisms ranging from static context files to executable subagents. Ardic et al. (Ardic et al., 2026) study testing guidance in the ACFs of popular repositories with agent-authored pull requests. In a sample of 300 repositories, 249 include test commands, while guidance on test strategy, mocking, coverage, or naming is much less common. Beyond characterizing content, recent work has begun to quantify the operational impact of ACFs: Lulla et al. (Lulla et al., 2026) show that the presence of an AGENTS.md file is associated with a 28.6% reduction in agent runtime and a 16.6% reduction in token consumption. Together, these studies establish ACFs as a widespread and influential class of software artifacts and confirm that their content measurably shapes agent behavior. Existing characterizations, however, remain descriptive: they document what ACFs contain, typically through high-level content categories, rather than the extent to which the specific instructions they encode are actually followed. Whether the presence of an instruction in an ACF translates into compliant agent behavior remains largely unexamined. Adjacent evidence suggests it should not be assumed. Studies of AI-generated code quality show that functional correctness does not predict adherence to convention: code that passes all tests can still carry latent code smells and violate project-specific expectations (Sabra et al., 2025), and even where agentic refactoring yields measurable structural improvements (Horikawa et al., 2025), these gains are evaluated against generic quality metrics rather than against the developer-authored guidance the agent was given. Instruction following has also been studied as a general LLM capability, including for code. CodeIF-Bench (Wang et al., 2025a) measures whether generated code satisfies constraints stated in a single prompt, and AgentIF (Qi et al., 2025) extends this to long, multi-constraint system prompts in agentic settings. This work shows that instruction adherence is measurable and imperfect even for state-of-the-art LLMs. It evaluates instructions given within a single interaction, however, not a persistent, project-scoped artifact, and it does not look at the artifacts produced in real development. Studies of agents in real repositories come closer. Watanabe et al. (Watanabe et al., ) find that agent pull requests need substantial revision to meet project conventions, and Ehsani et al. (Ehsani et al., 2026) characterize at scale why agentic pull requests fail, without tying failures to the instructions an ACF documents. Hora and Robbes (Hora and Robbes, 2026) show that agents add mocks to tests more often than non-agents (36% versus 26% of test commits) and call for mocking guidance in agent configuration files, but they only check a few repositories anecdotally for whether such guidance is followed. Gloaguen et al. (Gloaguen et al., 2026) evaluate whether ACFs help agents resolve issues, and find slightly lower task success for LLM-generated context files, slightly higher for developer-written ones, and about 20% higher cost. Their trace analysis also shows that tools named in a context file are used far more often than tools that are not named. This measures tool usage in controlled issue-resolution tasks. We instead check, for individual instructions, whether their content shows up in the artifacts of real agent-generated commits. Closest to our setting, Yang et al. (Yang et al., 2026) directly measure coding agents’ compliance with documented rules. Their RepoComplianceBench covers repository-level AI-contribution policies (bans, disclosure requirements, verification gates) and uses a controlled set of 106 issues across four agents. It does not cover the broader development guidance that ACFs encode, nor compliance observed in real, mined commits. Existing work therefore establishes two main aspects. First, ACFs are widely adopted as behavioral governance artifacts. Second, agents do not reliably adhere to project conventions even without explicit, structured guidance. In this context, what remains missing is a systematic, artifact-grounded assessment of whether the specific instructions documented in an ACF are reflected in the commits an agent subsequently produces—and, more fundamentally, which of these instructions can be verified from produced artifacts at all. 3. Empirical Study The goal of this empirical study is to investigate the relationship between instructions encoded in agent context files and the observable behavior of autonomous coding agents in real-world software development, and to understand whether explicit guidance documented in these artifacts is reflected in the software modifications agents generate. The purpose is to characterize the types of instructions that can be empirically operationalized and to assess how far such instructions show up in downstream agent-generated commits. The study is conducted from the perspective of software engineering researchers and practitioners who want to understand how effective agent-oriented guidance is in practice. Rather than focusing on agent intent or internal reasoning, we take an artifact-centric view: we look at whether instructions are reflected in the observable software artifacts agents produce in real-world development. Despite the growing use of agent context files to guide autonomous coding agents, it remains unclear what types of instructions they actually encode in a way that can be measured. Existing categorizations are typically too high-level and group together very different forms of guidance that cannot be directly measured in development artifacts (Chatlatanagulchai et al., 2025a). To support a rigorous empirical investigation, we first need to identify which instructions are sufficiently explicit and actionable, meaning they are directly stated in the ACF and describe a concrete development behavior an agent can reasonably perform. Our first RQ builds a fine-grained dataset of explicit and actionable instructions from real-world ACFs, moving beyond high-level categories toward concrete guidance that supports downstream analysis. Characterizing explicit and actionable instructions is necessary, but not enough for empirical measurement. We also need to establish whether each instruction can be verified through observable development artifacts, meaning whether compliance can be checked by inspecting produced or modified files, without inferring agent intent or internal reasoning. Treating observability as a purely classificatory label is risky: an instruction judged observable in the abstract may still turn out impossible to measure in practice. Our second RQ investigates whether observable measurement proxies can actually be built for the instructions identified in RQ1. For each instruction, we generate a measurable indicator that can determine compliance from commit-level artifacts. Instructions for which no such indicator can be built are considered non-operationalizable and excluded from downstream analysis. This process produces a refined dataset of instructions paired with validated measurement proxies, which is the empirical foundation for RQ3. Given a validated dataset of instructions with matching measurement proxies, the central question is whether autonomous coding agents actually follow the guidance in their ACFs. It remains unclear whether these instructions show up in the software artifacts agents produce during real development, or whether they are systematically ignored, partially applied, or inconsistently interpreted. Our third RQ investigates how far observable instructions are reflected in downstream agent-generated commits. For each instruction-commit pair, we apply the matching measurement proxy to the code changes and check whether observable evidence of compliance is present. Figure 1 summarizes the research method we followed. We first mined and combined data on agent context files and agent-generated code from two complementary datasets (Chatlatanagulchai et al., 2025a; Li et al., 2025). We then built context file snapshots, unique versions of an agent context file defined by content and linked to the commits generated under that version, and classified their instructions using a mix of manual calibration and LLM-assisted qualitative analysis (RQ1). Next, we built a measurable proxy for each identified instruction, keeping only those for which a working indicator could be generated (RQ2). Finally, we applied the resulting measurement scripts to the reconstructed commit dataset and analyzed how far agent-generated code reflects the instructions in the associated ACF (RQ3). To investigate the relationship between agent context files and agent-generated development artifacts, we built a dataset by combining two complementary sources: (i) an existing dataset of ACFs mined from GitHub repositories (Chatlatanagulchai et al., 2025a), and (ii) a large-scale dataset of agent-authored commits (Li et al., 2025). Combining them required extra preprocessing and reconstruction steps to support fine-grained instruction-artifact analysis. We started from the ACF dataset introduced in prior work (Chatlatanagulchai et al., 2025a), which collects files from GitHub repositories based on the official naming conventions of widely used coding agents (e.g., CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, and copilot-instructions.md). We kept only repositories associated with three agents, Copilot, Claude Code, and OpenAI Codex, using the classification procedures from the original dataset for consistency. Agent context files change over time as developers update agent guidance. To capture the instructions available at the time of each commit, we built context snapshots: unique versions of an ACF, deduplicated by content, so identical file contents map to the same snapshot and any change in content produces a new one. Each snapshot was then linked to every commit generated while that version was active. This let us associate each commit with the exact instruction set available to the agent at generation time, giving 676 unique context snapshots reused across 10,763 commits and spanning 307 repositories. Context files varied a lot in size, with a median of 638 words (110 lines) and a maximum exceeding 16K words. To capture agent behavior in real-world development, we relied on the AIDev dataset (Li et al., 2025), which attributes pull requests and commits to autonomous coding agents using signals such as bot accounts, branch naming conventions, and co-authorship markers. These signals differ across agents, so we distinguished two confidence levels. Strict agent commits are those for which authorship can be inferred with high confidence from strong indicators, bot identities or unambiguous authorship metadata, following the same rules as AIDev. Non-human-suspected commits are those with no clear sign of human authorship but with less certain attribution. This distinction was needed because agents expose different authorship patterns: some appear as direct commit authors via dedicated bot accounts, others (e.g., Claude Code) appear as co-authors in commit messages, and tools such as GitHub Copilot may rely on indirect signals such as branch naming. All analyses reported in this paper use only the strict agent subset, favoring attribution precision over recall; non-human-suspected commits are not analyzed further. The two datasets were combined at the repository level, keeping only commits from repositories with at least one available ACF. Starting from 21,513 commits, 8,600 had context information, of which 6,580 also had file-level change data. After excluding 39 planning and merge commits (planning commits, 3,149 overall, mostly carry no file changes and had already been removed by this filter), the analysis-ready dataset is 6,541 commits across 268 repositories. For each selected commit, we rebuilt the full development context by cloning the corresponding Git repository and extracting commit metadata, diff patches, file-level change information, and the content of all modified files before and after the commit. The before version came from the parent commit; the after version is the current commit. All extracted artifacts were stored in a structured local format with automated completeness checks for missing commits, incomplete snapshots, and failed retrievals. All data and scripts are available in our replication package (Voria et al., ). Table 1 summarizes the final dataset. The corpus spans a wide range of development activity: 62.2% of commits modify source code, 21.1% involve test files, and 16.4% affect documentation, with smaller shares covering configuration and CI artifacts. It covers 26 programming languages, including C#, TypeScript, Python, and Rust. With a median of 1 modified file per commit and a mean of 3.95, most commits are small, focused changes, which makes instruction-level compliance assessment tractable at the commit level. To address RQ1, we used a three-phase approach combining manual qualitative analysis with LLM-assisted classification. The goal was to identify explicit and actionable instructions in agent context files, grounded in the high-level ACF categorization from prior work (Chatlatanagulchai et al., 2025a). We retain that work’s 19 categories as defined, including partially overlapping ones (e.g., Build and Build and Run, Management and Project Management), so that our results remain directly comparable to it rather than introducing a new taxonomy. The unit of analysis was the context snapshot: a distinct version of an agent context file, deduplicated by content and linked to the commits generated while that version was active. After removing empty and malformed snapshots, the final population was 621 unique context snapshots. We started with an iterative manual analysis of randomly selected context snapshots to set stable extraction procedures. Rather than fixing a sample size up front, we proceeded incrementally following qualitative saturation criteria (Treude, 2024): we continued until the extraction procedure, coding guidelines, and decision rules were stable enough to support prompt construction for automated classification. This phase covered 15 ACF snapshots, after which no substantially new decision patterns appeared, so we considered the procedure stable. During this phase, we extracted and labeled candidate instructions, grounding them in the existing high-level ACF categories from prior work rather than building a new taxonomy. Each candidate instruction was judged against three criteria. Explicitness: the instruction must be directly and clearly stated in the ACF, not inferred from examples or context. Actionability: the instruction must describe a concrete development behavior an agent can reasonably perform during software modification. Observability: compliance must be checkable through produced or modified development artifacts, such as source code, documentation, configuration files, or repository structure, without inferring agent intent or internal reasoning. The analysis focused only on behavioral guidance directed at agents; repository descriptions, architectural overviews, code examples, and other informational content were excluded. Disagreements and ambiguous cases were discussed among all authors and used to refine the coding guidelines. Once the coding procedure was stable, we used an LLM annotator to classify instructions across the full dataset (Tan et al., 2024; Ahmed et al., 2025). Manually coding all 621 snapshots would have taken substantial effort and introduced coder fatigue and inconsistency, so the LLM acted as a structured coding assistant rather than a source of ground truth. Annotation Pipeline. Each context snapshot was processed independently using a fixed few-shot prompt with three parts: (i) a system prompt defining the annotation task, the three coding criteria, and the output schema; (ii) a curated set of few-shot examples from the calibration phase, covering clear inclusion cases, clear exclusion cases, and borderline cases; and (iii) the target ACF content. Snapshots that exceeded the model’s context budget were split into paragraph-level chunks, annotated independently, and merged back at the snapshot level. For each extracted instruction, the model produced a JSON object recording the raw instruction text, high-level category, normalized label, coding decisions for each criterion, a candidate observable behavior field describing how compliance could be verified in produced artifacts, an inclusion decision, and a mandatory justification note. Prompt Engineering. The prompting strategy was developed iteratively through pilot runs on the calibration examples. Early versions systematically over-included vague or process-oriented statements as observable. The final version strengthened the observability criterion: an instruction now counts as observable only if a reasonably simple verification function could inspect the generated or modified files and determine compliance, with no access to agent reasoning, command execution, or internal workflow state. All prompt versions, model configurations, execution scripts, and few-shot examples are available in the replication package (Voria et al., ). Model Selection. We evaluated two candidate annotators, Ministral 3 14B Reasoning and Qwen 3.5 9B, both run locally via LMStudio with fixed inference parameters (32k-token context, temperature 0.1, top-p 0.85, GGUF Q4_K_M quantization). A cross-model comparison on a shared set of annotations gave an overall agreement rate of 74.8%, with 79.5% include-agreement and 76.1% observable-label agreement. Manual inspection of the disagreements showed that Ministral systematically over-extracted candidate instructions, accepting vague or process-oriented statements that Qwen correctly excluded. We therefore chose Qwen 3.5 9B as the primary annotator for the final extraction. We did not assume LLM-generated annotations were equivalent to human judgment. Following established practice for LLM-based annotation (Tan et al., 2024; Ahmed et al., 2025), we validated the automated classifications against the predefined coding criteria using a human annotator on a statistically representative sample. Sample Selection. The validation population was the 621 processed snapshots. Standard finite-population sampling at a 95% confidence level and 10% margin of error gave a validation sample of 84 context snapshots (13.5% of the population). We set the sampling unit at the snapshot level rather than the instruction level on purpose: validating a whole snapshot, rather than isolated instructions sampled across snapshots, lets the annotator check whether the extraction procedure correctly identifies all relevant instructions in a given ACF, including omissions that an instruction-level sample would miss. To ensure representativeness, we used proportional stratified random sampling based on (i) the agent associated with the snapshot (Copilot, Claude Code, OpenAI Codex) and (ii) instruction density (low: 1–10 instructions; medium: 11–30; high: [FORMULA] 30). The 84 sampled snapshots together contain 2,202 individual instructions for validation, both included and excluded by the LLM, corresponding to 14.8% of all 14,902 extracted instructions. This is the raw count of candidates the LLM extracted from these snapshots, before human review. The results (Section 4.1.2) also report a narrower count of 2,196 candidates that received a recorded validation decision, and a still-narrower count of 2,114 instructions confirmed as genuine. Each of these three counts excludes a different subset (undecided candidates, and false positives, respectively) and each is used where it fits that specific analysis. This instruction-level coverage is well above the minimum sample size needed for 95% confidence and 10% margin of error at the instruction level for a population this size (96 instructions), giving strong grounding for the instruction-level metrics we report. Validation Protocol. The validation was done by the first author, who had developed and applied the coding guide during calibration. Following Ortloff et al. (2023), we used a single annotator for this well-bounded classification task: their study shows that for tasks with a narrow interpretive range, one experienced coder can be enough, and may even give higher internal validity than multi-coder setups with reconciliation noise. This fits our setting because each of the three coding criteria is a binary decision grounded in explicit textual evidence, and because the coding guide had already been refined with all coauthors before validation began. Low-confidence decisions during validation were still discussed with all coauthors until we reached a shared interpretation. The resulting data were used to compute extraction-level precision, recall, and F1-score, and label-level accuracy for explicitness, actionability, observability, inclusion decisions, and category assignment. We also validated the candidate observable behavior field: high accuracy here shows that the LLM-generated behavioral descriptors are reliable enough to use as input for the measurement proxy generation step in RQ2. The output of RQ1 is a validated dataset of explicit and actionable instructions extracted from agent context files, grounded in the existing high-level ACF categorization. For each instruction, the dataset records its textual formulation, category, per-criterion coding decisions, and candidate observable behavior. This dataset gives a fine-grained picture of the concrete guidance documented in ACFs and how it is spread across repositories, agents, and instruction categories. Instructions validated as observable, together with their candidate behavioral descriptors, are the foundation for RQ2. To address RQ2, we investigated whether the explicit and actionable instructions from RQ1 can be turned into executable measurement scripts. Each instruction in our dataset is, by construction, explicit and describes a concrete development behavior verifiable through software artifacts. This makes each instruction suited to a functional specification: a well-defined procedure that takes commit-level artifacts as input and returns a binary compliance signal as output. Turning a natural language specification into such a procedure is a code generation task, and LLMs have shown strong, well-documented capability at this (Jiang et al., 2026). We treat an instruction as operationalizable only if a correct measurement script can be generated and validated for it; instructions for which this fails are excluded from the final RQ3 analysis. Each measurement script is generated independently for a single instruction. We first considered grouping instructions that share a topic (e.g., naming conventions, indentation style) under a shared canonical representative before generation, on the idea that behaviorally equivalent instructions should map to the same measurement procedure. A closer look at the RQ1 dataset showed that this equivalence rarely holds: instructions on the same high-level topic often prescribe different, mutually exclusive requirements. For example, one instruction may require camelCase for method identifiers, another PascalCase for type names, and a third snake_case for file names, all under “naming conventions.” Collapsing these into one canonical representative would either drop the specific requirement each instruction mandates, or require per-instance parametrization of a shared script, which carries the same overhead as generating a script per instruction directly while adding a new point of failure (an instruction wrongly assigned to a template family, or a parameter wrongly extracted). We therefore generate one measurement script per instruction. For each instruction retained by RQ1 (explicit, actionable, and observable), we use its candidate observable behavior field as the functional specification for script generation. This field, produced during RQ1 extraction and confirmed on the manually validated sample, describes in concrete terms how compliance can be verified by inspecting files modified or added in a commit. For an instruction prescribing camelCase naming for method identifiers, for example, the candidate observable behavior states that all method names added or modified in the commit must match a camelCase pattern. Script generation follows a test-driven approach, building on evidence that pairing a formal specification with independently generated test cases substantially improves the correctness of LLM-generated code (Mathews and Nagappan, 2024; Fakhoury et al., 2024). Rather than generating one script and repairing it against failures, we adopt the sampling-and-selection strategy from Chen et al.’s CodeT (Chen et al., 2022): for each instruction, the same code LLM independently generates [FORMULA] candidate measurement scripts and [FORMULA] candidate test fixtures, where each fixture is a pair of synthetic commits, one compliant and one non-compliant, synthesized from the candidate observable behavior specification. Each synthetic commit uses the same four-field commit object that scripts take as input, files_before, files_after, message, and branch, so a script is validated on exactly the input format it later receives for real commits. Fixtures carry an intended label since they are generated from an explicit compliant/non-compliant prompt, but we do not treat this label as ground truth without checking it, since the LLM can misread an ambiguous instruction when building a fixture, mirroring the test-case correctness issues reported for LLM-generated tests in general (Chen et al., 2022). Every candidate script is run against every candidate fixture. In CodeT’s original dual execution agreement procedure (Chen et al., 2022), scripts that give exactly the same verdicts across all fixtures form a consensus group, and the group scoring highest on the product of its size and the number of fixtures it passes is selected. We retain this principle, that a script is trusted only when independently generated scripts agree with it on independently generated tests, but replace exact-verdict grouping with the overlap-based acceptance criterion described in Section 3.4.3, because exact agreement proved too sparse at our sampling budget. [FORMULA] and [FORMULA] are small compared to the sampling budgets used in general-purpose code generation benchmarks, since the measurement scripts here target a narrower and more uniform class of checks than the algorithmic problems CodeT was originally evaluated on. We therefore use the exhaustive variant of the agreement procedure, comparing all script-fixture pairs directly rather than sampling from them. We use Qwen2.5-Coder-14B-Instruct as the generation model, matching the local execution setup used for instruction extraction in RQ1 (LMStudio, 32k context window, GGUF Q4_K_M quantization) to keep the infrastructure consistent and fully reproducible on the same hardware. We confirmed this configuration ran successfully on the available hardware before the full RQ2 run. Unlike the extraction stage, which favors deterministic, high-precision output (temperature 0.1), script and fixture generation needs diversity across independently sampled candidates for the dual execution agreement mechanism to work, so we set temperature to 0.8, the value Chen et al. (Chen et al., 2022) validated for this purpose, and kept top-p at 0.85. We fixed the sampling budget to [FORMULA] : ten candidate scripts and ten candidate fixture pairs per instruction, compared exhaustively (100 script-fixture pairs). This is deliberately smaller than the budgets in CodeT’s original evaluation (50–1,000, depending on benchmark difficulty), which targeted open-ended competitive programming problems with many structurally different correct solutions (Chen et al., 2022). In our setting, each instruction comes with an explicit candidate observable behavior specification that narrows the space of correct implementations considerably, so a smaller candidate pool is enough for the corroboration mechanism to reach a stable consensus. We did not tune [FORMULA] and [FORMULA] separately (the pilot described in Section 3.4.3 concerned the acceptance criterion, not the budget); the operationalization rate reported in RQ2 (the share of instructions for which a script is accepted) works as the direct empirical check on whether the fixed budget is adequate. A script is accepted only if it clears two bars: a minimum-correctness bar (it must pass a minimum number of fixtures outright) and a corroboration bar (at least one other independently generated script must agree with it on a large share of the fixtures it passes). Neither bar alone is enough. The first alone would accept a script that happens to satisfy one fixture by chance, and the second alone, agreement with no floor on correctness, would accept two scripts that are consistently wrong the same way. Requiring both keeps CodeT’s core principle, that an accepted solution must be corroborated and not just self-consistent, while staying feasible at the sampling budget used here ( [FORMULA] ). In a pilot run of the pipeline on a subset of instructions before the full RQ2 run, exact-match convergence across independently generated scripts and fixtures essentially never happened, leaving almost every instruction without an accepted script. We set the minimum-correctness bar to two fixtures passed and the corroboration bar to 60% overlap with the best-performing script’s passed-fixture set. Both values were fixed on that same pilot rather than through a separate calibration study: a lower correctness floor risks accepting a script that only happens to satisfy a single fixture, while a much higher overlap threshold brings back the sparsity problem that led us to abandon exact-match agreement in the first place. Instructions for which no script clears both bars are excluded from the RQ3 analysis. Rather than falling back to manually authored scripts, we treat exclusion as final, keeping one fully automated generation pipeline. Each exclusion is logged with the instruction’s high-level category, originating ACF, and coding agent, so we can check exclusions for patterns rather than treat them as missing at random. This pass/fail rule is our operational definition of operationalizability: an instruction resists operationalization if no script clears both bars within the sampling budget, regardless of whether it was classified as observable in RQ1. Relaxing exact-match agreement to overlap-based corroboration lowers the bar for what counts as agreement, which could in principle raise the risk of accepting a script that is subtly wrong. To check this, we manually inspect a sample of accepted scripts and verify that each one correctly implements its instruction’s candidate observable behavior, using the same single-annotator validation protocol as RQ1. We report the agreement rate between this manual check and the automated acceptance decision as a direct, empirical measure of how reliable the accepted scripts are, alongside the operationalization rate itself. We size the spot-check sample using the same finite-population-corrected Cochran formula, 95% confidence level, and 10% margin of error used for RQ1’s 84-snapshot validation sample (Section 3.3), applied here to the population of 4,123 accepted scripts instead of context snapshots. This gives a target sample size of 94. We stratify by category and allocate the 94-script target proportionally to each category’s share of accepted scripts, using the largest-remainder method to hit the target exactly and a floor of 1 script per category so none is left entirely unchecked. Within each category, scripts are drawn uniformly at random without replacement, using a fixed random seed for reproducibility. Each sampled script is reviewed by one author alongside its originating instruction’s raw text and candidate observable behavior specification, and judged agree (the script correctly implements the specified behavior) or disagree (it does not), with free-text notes for any judgment that is not immediately obvious from the two-way label alone. We refer to an accepted script together with the scripts that corroborate it as its consensus group. The output of RQ2 is a validated set of instructions paired with executable measurement scripts. For each instruction, the dataset records the candidate observable behavior descriptor, the generated script, the fixture set used for validation, and the operationalizability verdict. This dataset is the measurement infrastructure used in RQ3. Beyond the script artifacts themselves, we report the operationalization rate, the share of RQ1’s explicit, actionable, and observable instructions for which a validated script was obtained, both overall and broken down by high_level_category and by coding agent. This breakdown shows which classes of instructions are measurable at all, which directly bounds what RQ3 can say about adherence. If the operationalization rate were markedly lower for substantive categories (e.g., testing, security, architecture) than for surface-level categories (e.g., formatting, naming), that would mean RQ3’s adherence results, however precise, describe compliance for a subset of instructions skewed toward superficial conventions rather than the full space of explicit and actionable directives in ACFs. We report this breakdown as a required result of RQ2, independent of RQ3’s findings, and discuss what it means when interpreting the RQ3 results. To address RQ3, we applied the measurement scripts from RQ2 to the mined commit dataset and checked whether the instructions in each ACF are reflected in the matching agent-generated code changes. The analysis works at the level of individual (instruction, commit) pairs: for every commit generated while a given context snapshot was active, we consider each instruction from that snapshot for which RQ2 produced an accepted measurement script. Instructions without an accepted script are excluded from this analysis, by RQ2’s own definition of operationalizability. This is the coverage boundary discussed in Section 4.2.1 and revisited in Section 4.3. Design. Not every operationalized instruction is worth checking against every commit. A naming-convention instruction for Python method identifiers has nothing to say about a commit that only touches a YAML configuration file. Running its script against such a commit is not a neutral no-op: LLM-generated scripts tend to be permissive by default. They are written to look for evidence of a violation and report compliance when none is found, rather than requiring positive evidence that the check actually applied. So running a script against a commit it has nothing to check skews toward compliance with no real evidence behind it, rather than a neutral null result (Section 4.2.2 reports how common this default is among accepted scripts). Evaluating every instruction against every commit without filtering would inflate every adherence figure in this study with this kind of empty compliance, not genuine adherence. An applicability filter, run before script execution, is a methodological necessity, not an optional extra. We first considered setting applicability from hand-authored, category-level rules (e.g., “naming-convention instructions apply to commits touching source files,” “testing instructions apply to commits touching source or test files”). We reject this approach: it needs inventing and validating a new mapping from category to file type at a level of detail too high-level to be reliable. A category such as Testing covers instructions targeting Python test files, Go test files, JavaScript configuration files, and CI pipeline definitions alike, so no single category-level rule captures this. Implementation. We instead derive applicability directly from each instruction’s own accepted evidence, rather than from a newly written rule. Every accepted instruction in RQ2’s output carries the fixture set its script was validated against (fixtures_used), each fixture a realistic before/after commit example built specifically for that instruction. For each accepted instruction, we take the union of file paths in the files_before and files_after of all fixtures in its winning consensus group, and pull out from each path either its extension (e.g., .py, .json) or, for extensionless conventional filenames (e.g., Dockerfile, Makefile), its exact basename. This gives a small set of file patterns per instruction, grounded in the same artifacts RQ2 already validated the script against, rather than a newly introduced heuristic. A commit is applicable to an instruction if it touches at least one file matching one of these patterns. Instructions whose fixtures have empty files_before and files_after throughout, meaning their compliance criterion concerns only the commit message or branch name, are treated as universally applicable, since every commit has a message and a branch regardless of which files it touches. Instruction-commit pairs that fail the applicability check are excluded from evaluation entirely; they contribute no observation, compliant or otherwise. We report, per instruction, the number of applicable commits found, and separately flag any accepted instruction with zero applicable commits in the mined dataset. These cannot contribute an adherence observation despite being operationalizable, and are excluded from the statistical analysis in Section 3.5.3 on that basis. This is a further, separate loss beyond RQ2’s operationalization funnel, and we report it with the same transparency. We use compliance to mean the presence, in an applicable commit’s artifacts, of the behavioral evidence a script derives directly from the instruction’s own candidate observable behavior (Section 3.4). That field is written from the instruction’s own text during RQ1 extraction, and the script is generated and validated against fixtures grounded in it before ever being applied to a real commit, so a compliance verdict reflects what the instruction itself specifies as satisfying behavior. For every instruction-commit pair that passes the applicability filter, we run the instruction’s accepted script against that commit’s artifacts and record a binary compliance signal. The script’s input is exactly the four-field commit object defined in Section 3.4, files_before, files_after, message, branch, populated from the mined commit dataset rather than a synthetic fixture. Scripts do not additionally receive a line-level diff or patch; they were generated and validated only against full before/after file content, and extending the contract after the fact to include diff-level information would invalidate the already-generated and already-validated script population. This means instructions whose true compliance criterion depends on what was specifically added or removed, rather than the file’s final state, are evaluated on a weaker signal than they ideally would be. We treat this as a limitation of the current design, discussed further under construct validity in Section 6, rather than fix it by regenerating scripts. We do not compare instruction categories or coding agents directly on the raw (instruction, commit) observations, because these observations are not independent: commits from the same context snapshot share the same instruction set, and instructions evaluated within the same commit share the same agent and repository. Treating each pair as an independent sample would understate variance and risk finding significance that is not really there. We instead aggregate to one compliance rate per instruction, the share of its applicable commits in which it was followed, before making any cross-group comparison, so each instruction contributes exactly one observation regardless of how many commits it was evaluated against. We report descriptive statistics on this instruction-level compliance-rate dataset: the overall mean compliance rate, the rate by high_level_category, and the rate by coding agent (Copilot, Claude Code, OpenAI Codex), matching the reporting structure used for operationalization rate in RQ2. To test whether compliance rate differs across categories, we compare the distributions of per-instruction compliance rates using the Kruskal-Wallis test, a good fit given the expected non-normality of rate data bounded in [FORMULA] and the unequal group sizes across categories. Where this test is significant, we run post-hoc pairwise Mann-Whitney U tests between categories with Bonferroni correction for the number of comparisons, and report Cliff’s delta as the effect size for each significant pair, so the size of a difference is reported independently of the sample size behind it. We repeat the same procedure with coding agent as the grouping variable, to test whether adherence patterns differ by agent and not only by instruction category. Many instructions are evaluated against very few applicable commits: the median evaluated instruction has only 3, and 540 (26.3%) have exactly 1, which forces their individual compliance rate to 0% or 100% regardless of true adherence. To check whether this thin-evidence tail is driving the bimodal split and the two cross-group comparisons, we run a sensitivity analysis repeating the full statistical procedure above restricted to instructions with at least 3, and separately at least 5, applicable commits, and report whether the comparisons found significant in the full sample stay significant as this low-evidence tail is excluded. 4. Analysis of the Results We answer RQ1 by applying the classification pipeline from Section 3.3 to all 621 context snapshots. Section 4.1.1 reports how the extracted instructions split across the three coding criteria: explicitness, actionability, and observability. Section 4.1.2 then reports the manual validation we use to check how reliable this automated classification is. Table 2 shows how the 14,902 candidate instructions extracted from the 621 context snapshots (24.0 per snapshot on average) are classified by the three coding criteria. It also reports the same breakdown for the 84-snapshot validated sample, restricted to the instructions confirmed as genuine during manual validation (Section 4.1.2). Applied in sequence to the full corpus, the criteria narrow the candidates to 10,324 (69.3%) that are explicit, 8,726 (58.6% of all candidates) that are also actionable, and 6,552 (44.0% of all candidates) that are also observable. This final set, which satisfies all three criteria, forms the RQ1 dataset. It covers 592 of the 621 snapshots (95.3%), and 615 snapshots (99.0%) contain at least one explicit and actionable instruction. Explicitness is the first and, in absolute terms, the largest filter, discarding 30.7% of all candidates. Among the criteria applied to already explicit instructions, observability is the more selective: it removes about a quarter of the explicit-and-actionable instructions at the corpus level (24.9%) and close to half at the sample level (48.9%), whereas actionability removes 15.5% and 18.4% of the explicit ones, respectively. The much sharper observability cut on the validated sample than on the corpus is consistent with the per-criterion accuracies reported in Section 4.1.2, where observability is the hardest criterion for the LLM to judge correctly and its errors lean toward over-inclusion. Implementation Details is the largest category at every stage and grows further once observability is applied, from 42.8% of explicit-and-actionable instructions to 50.0% of the final dataset. Other categories shrink more once observability is applied: Build and Run drops from 8.8% of explicit-and-actionable instructions to 2.9% of the final dataset, and Build from 3.8% to 2.5%. This shows that process and execution guidance in these categories is often explicit and actionable, but rarely verifiable from the artifacts it leaves behind. For example, “run the linter” is a clear, concrete instruction, but nothing in the produced files shows whether the agent actually ran it. The agent distribution stays fairly stable across funnel stages: Copilot accounts for 55.4% of explicit-and-actionable instructions and 56.9% of the final dataset, Claude Code for 38.7% and 37.4%, and OpenAI Codex for 5.9% and 5.7%, roughly matching each agent’s share of ACF snapshots in the corpus. To check how reliable this classification is, we manually validated a stratified sample of 84 context snapshots (13.5% of the population), covering 2,196 individually scored instruction-level decisions. This is the 2,202 raw candidates the LLM extracted from these snapshots (Section 3.3), plus the 1 instruction it missed, minus 7 candidates for which no decision was recorded. Table 4 reports extraction precision, recall, and F1-score, overall and by agent. The LLM annotator correctly identified 2,113 genuine instructions (TP), incorrectly extracted 82 non-instructions (FP), and missed only 1 instruction that the human annotator later found during full-snapshot review (FN). This gives an overall precision of 96.3%, recall of 99.9%11 1 Recall is computed from a single recorded omission across the entire sample, so while the point estimate is high, it rests on very few observed misses., and F1-score of 98.1%. This covers explicitness, actionability, and observability, alongside inclusion, category, and the candidate observable behavior descriptor. Accuracy is high and consistent for explicitness (95.5%), actionability (97.3%), category assignment (96.6%), and the candidate observable behavior descriptor (97.5%). The last of these is the field reused as the specification input for measurement script generation in RQ2, so its high accuracy supports using it as a reliable input there. Observability (85.0%) and the resulting inclusion decision (85.2%) are noticeably less accurate. Over 90% of the disagreements on these two fields corrected an LLM yes/include decision to no/exclude, so the annotator’s errors lean toward over-inclusion rather than going in a random direction. Overall, the validation shows that the automated classification closely reproduces the explicitness and actionability criteria set during manual calibration (Section 3.3), and reproduces observability less accurately and with a systematic lean toward over-inclusion. This gives us enough confidence to treat the LLM-classified corpus as the basis for the RQ1 dataset, keeping in mind the upper-bound caveat on the observable/final stage noted above. Table 6 reports the outcome of the script generation pipeline from Section 3.4, applied to the 6,552 instructions RQ1 classified as explicit, actionable, and observable at the corpus level. This is the same final-stage population reported in Table 3. Of these, 4,123 (62.9%) reach an accepted measurement script under the sampling budget and corroboration criteria fixed in Section 3.4. The remaining 2,429 (37.1%) resist operationalization within that budget and are excluded from RQ3. Category-Level Variation. Operationalization rate is not the same across instruction categories, and the pattern only partly matches what a simple superficial-versus-substantive split would predict. Among the twelve categories with at least 50 instructions, Configuration and Environment operationalizes at the highest rate (269 out of 356, 75.6%), followed by Maintenance (48 out of 66, 72.7%), Architecture (95 out of 131, 72.5%), Build and Run (130 out of 189, 68.8%), and Testing (626 out of 927, 67.5%), all above the corpus-wide average. This runs counter to a concern raised when this pipeline was designed, that automated operationalization would systematically favor superficial formatting conventions over substantive engineering categories: Architecture and Testing instructions are, in practice, no harder to operationalize than average, and in this sample somewhat easier. At the opposite end, Management (31 out of 65, 47.7%) and Security (48 out of 99, 48.5%) operationalize at the lowest rates among these categories, more than 14 percentage points below the average. Implementation Details, the largest single category by volume (3,279 instructions, 50.0% of the final-stage corpus), operationalizes close to the overall average at 61.2% (2,008 out of 3,279). Because it is so large, it dominates the aggregate rate regardless of how other categories behave. Agent-Level Consistency. Operationalization rate varies little by coding agent: 2,367 out of 3,729 (63.5%) for Copilot, 1,520 out of 2,449 (62.1%) for Claude Code, and 236 out of 374 (63.1%) for OpenAI Codex, a spread of only 1.4 percentage points. Which agent’s context file an instruction came from has essentially no bearing on whether it can be operationalized. The category-level variation above is the main source of difference in coverage, not the originating agent. Table 7 breaks down the 2,429 excluded instructions by the bar they failed. Most of them (1,392, 57.3%) fail the minimum-correctness bar: for 1,006 (41.4%) no generated script passed even one fixture, and for 386 (15.9%) the best script passed only one. A further 997 (41.1%) clear the correctness bar, but no independently generated script agrees with the best one. Only 40 (1.6%) fail at candidate generation, with fewer than two syntactically valid scripts. This shows that generation-stage reliability is high, and exclusion is mostly a correctness or agreement problem, not a formatting or parsing one. Across all 6,552 instructions, the pipeline obtained the full requested budget of ten candidate scripts for 6,223 (95.0%) and the full ten candidate fixtures for 5,786 (88.3%). Truncated or malformed candidates are the exception, not the rule. Among the 4,123 accepted instructions, the winning consensus group has a mean size of 6.3 out of 10, and this splits into two clusters: 825 instructions (20.0% of accepted) reach full unanimous agreement across all ten sampled scripts, while 589 (14.3%) are accepted on the minimum admissible corroboration of exactly two agreeing scripts. The remaining 65.7% are spread fairly evenly in between. Operationalizability is therefore not a clean two-way split: many instructions have a candidate observable behavior specific and mechanical enough that independently sampled scripts converge on it readily, but the corroboration threshold is decisive for a substantial share of cases, both among accepted instructions (the 14.3% accepted on exactly two agreeing scripts) and among excluded ones (the 997 instructions whose correct-looking script found no corroborating peer). Consistent with the permissive-default tendency noted in Section 3.5 as the reason for the applicability filter, 2,569 of the 4,123 accepted scripts (62.3%) return True with no supporting evidence when checked against a commit that touches no relevant files. The applicability filter is built to exclude exactly these uninformative pairings from the RQ3 analysis, so this default does not by itself bias the compliance rates reported there. It does mean, though, that any instruction-commit pair that slips past the filter despite being irrelevant will count as compliant rather than as a neutral non-observation. The RQ3 compliance figures should therefore be read as an optimistic estimate: the reported non-compliance rate is a floor on true non-adherence, not a precise ceiling, since any leakage through the applicability filter can only push apparent compliance up, never down. The manual spot-check described in Section 3.4 finds that 67 of the 94 sampled accepted scripts (71.3%) correctly implement their instruction’s candidate observable behavior. Conversely, roughly three in ten accepted scripts do not faithfully implement their specification, so passing both acceptance bars is evidence of, not a guarantee of, a correct operationalization. The disagreements cluster around a small number of recurring patterns rather than spreading evenly. The most common is a script that hardcodes an example from the ACF itself, a specific filename, type name, or argument value used to illustrate a convention, as a literal requirement instead of generalizing the underlying rule. Genuine implementation bugs, such as a condition that can never be true, a missing import, or a regex typo that silently disables half a check, are comparatively rare in the sample. Because these errors are systematic rather than random, they cannot be assumed to cancel out: a hardcoded example typically makes a script stricter than the instruction it implements, which would bias the affected instructions’ RQ3 compliance downward. The RQ3 rates should therefore be read with this measurement error in mind, alongside the optimistic bias from permissive defaults discussed above. Table 8 reports how many of the 4,123 instructions operationalized in RQ2 could actually be checked against a real commit. An instruction contributes an adherence observation only if at least one commit generated under its originating context snapshot touches a file matching that instruction’s own applicability pattern, derived in Section 3.5 from the instruction’s accepted fixtures. Of the 4,123 operationalized instructions, 2,053 (49.8%) have at least one applicable commit. The remaining 2,070 (50.2%) are operationalizable in principle but never meet a commit that touches the relevant file type in the mined dataset, and are excluded from the compliance analysis on that basis. This is a further loss beyond RQ2’s own operationalization funnel: across the full pipeline, only 2,053 of the original 6,552 explicit, actionable, and observable instructions from RQ1 (31.3%) end up producing an adherence observation. The 2,053 evaluated instructions are checked against 18,594 instruction-commit pairs in total. Category-Level Coverage. Coverage is uneven across categories and does not track the operationalization rate from RQ2. Among the nine categories with at least 50 operationalized instructions, Documentation reaches the highest coverage (340 out of 505, 67.3%), while Configuration and Environment (99 out of 269, 36.8%) and Development Process (50 out of 130, 38.5%) fall well below the corpus-wide average of 49.8%; among smaller categories, Maintenance (15 out of 48, 31.2%) and Security (18 out of 48, 37.5%) are similarly low. This gap shows that being operationalizable and being evaluable are governed by different things: an instruction can be easy to write a correct measurement script for, and still rarely meet a matching commit in the mined dataset, because the file types it concerns are touched infrequently relative to how often the convention could in principle be checked. Agent-Level Coverage.
