Outlook for Low Precision Floating Point It appears that low precision formats and calculations are here to stay. For the purposes of deep learning, it is generally believed that bfloat16 is usually good enough to replace binary32 without any other changes such as the introduction of scale factors. Although use of formats like binary16 introduces range limits, this can be partially overcome with scale factors Brown et al., 2020. Mixed-precision training Micikevicius et al., 2018 with 8-bit floating point has been successfully demonstrated by many, with Microsoft using 39% less memory and running 75% faster than using bfloat16 Peng et al., 2023. Meta’s Llama 3 model Grattafiori et al., 2024 reportedly used 8-bit floating point inference only. However, both the DeepSeek v3 model DeepSeek-AI et al., 2024 and Meta’s Llama 4 model Inc., 2025 used 8-bit floating point for training and inference. In most cases, the weights and activations are quantized to 8 bits prior to MMA operations, but the MMA output and a master copy of the weights typically use bfloat16 or binary32 to accumulate tiny gradients which would otherwise be flushed to zero. Like binary16, 8-bit floating point also needs scale factors to overcome range limitations. Pushing even lower, NVIDIA has indicated success with training LLMs directly in its NVFP4 format NVIDIA et al., 2026. As hardware systems and AI/ML research evolve, fragmentation is still occurring. The best formats for training are not necessarily the best for inference. Even within inference, LLMs are showing two distinct phases of behavior: the first phase, prefill, is compute-bound and the second phase, decode, is memory-bound. How these systems will evolve to use low precision floating point formats, and how algorithms may adapt to better use them, are interesting open questions. Whether OCP or P3109 or some other format will be dominant in the future remains to be seen. Releasing the OCP specifications in 2023 gave hardware and software a head start. With its more consistent design and larger feature set, P3109 is a promising alternative. One thing is clear: P3109 or any other new format must offer compelling advantages to overcome the cost and effort of switching away from the base established by OCP. Beyond machine learning, the availability of low precision floating point hardware is already having a substantial impact on scientific computing. For example, emulation of binary64 matrix multiplication using low precision can be over 80 times faster than native computation Mazumder et al., 2026. Mixed precision arithmetic is also seeing widespread use, with many practical benefits Agullo et al., 2026. Computation and Language (cs.CL): Rethinking in Spikes: Mitigating Hallucinations in MDLMs with Step-Aware Decoding Recent advancements in multimodal diffusion language models (MDLMs) have exhibited strong global modeling capabilities through iterative refinement. We observe that mask uncertainty follows an overall downward trend during iterative denoising, while a few denoising steps exhibit localized entropy spikes closely associated with hallucinations. We argue that anomalous steps can be identified by measuring the entropy deviation of each denoising step from its neighboring temporal window. We hypothesize that discrete token commitment discards the distributional information at masked positions, limiting the continued interaction between candidate semantics and the context during entropy spikes. With this goal, we present StepRefine, a plug-and-play decoding strategy that leverages semantic context to achieve reliable denoising. The core of our method lies in a step-aware switch between discrete denoising and latent refinement. The model employs probability-weighted embeddings at entropy spike steps to preserve diverse reasoning hypotheses and performs multiple rounds of continuous refinement. Meanwhile, a refinement controller monitors distributional stability to reduce unnecessary loops and switch the model back to standard discrete denoising. Through extensive experiments, StepRefine demonstrates significant hallucination mitigation across different MDLMs on multimodal benchmarks. 1 Introduction Diffusion language models (Li et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2023; Han et al., 2023) replace autoregressive left-to-right generation with iterative denoising, forming an alternative paradigm for sequence generation. Current diffusion language models typically adopt a discrete masked diffusion mechanism (Nie et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2025b; Zhu et al., 2025a; Shi et al., 2024), in which multiple masked positions are predicted in parallel and progressively committed to discrete tokens. This paradigm has recently been extended to multimodal settings. Multimodal diffusion language models (MDLMs) (You et al., 2025; You et al., 2026; Li et al., 2025f; Ye et al., 2025a; Tian et al., 2025b) leverage bidirectional attention over visual and textual inputs to model global context, demonstrating strong potential in perception and reasoning tasks. Despite these advantages, MDLMs remain susceptible to hallucination. Existing inference-time methods for diffusion language models primarily focus on efficiency, such as cache reuse (Jiang et al., 2025; Wu et al., ; Zhu et al., 2026) and denoising scheduling (Lu et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026; Kim et al., 2025a), but these methods typically do not improve sequence reliability. Other decoding strategies attempt to improve quality by modifying token commitment policies, for example, by re-masking unreliable tokens (Hong et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025c) or introducing continuous token representations (Zhong et al., 2026a; Hersche et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026b). However, these methods typically treat uncertainty uniformly across denoising steps and do not explicitly account for temporal irregularities in the denoising trajectory. In this paper, we examine hallucination in MDLMs from the perspective of step-wise uncertainty dynamics across denoising steps. A natural expectation is that predictive uncertainty should steadily decrease as the sequence becomes progressively less masked and the context becomes more complete. Our analysis shows that the average entropy of the masked sequence indeed decreases. However, this decrease is not monotonic. A small number of steps show sharp entropy increases relative to their local temporal window. We refer to these steps as entropy spikes. Through statistical analysis, entropy spike steps are rare but highly correlated with hallucinated tokens in the final response. We observe that entropy spike steps exhibit a non-uniform distribution along the denoising trajectory, mainly occurring in the early-to-middle stages. At these stages, a large portion of the sequence remains masked, leaving the context information still limited. Moreover, we find that replacing standard confidence-based decoding with random decoding at entropy spike steps causes little performance change, whereas applying the same perturbation at ordinary steps results in clear degradation. At entropy spike steps, confidence signals may become less discriminative, making discrete decoding less reliably grounded in the current context. Therefore, our findings suggest that identifying entropy spike steps and applying contextual refinement before discrete commitment is crucial to mitigating hallucinations. In this work, we propose StepRefine, a plug-and-play decoding strategy that leverages dense contextual cues to improve denoising reliability. StepRefine adaptively switches between standard discrete denoising and latent probabilistic refinement based on the entropy dynamics of each step from its local temporal window. Specifically, StepRefine computes the average mask entropy at each denoising step and detects entropy spikes by comparing the current entropy change against trends within a local window. When such spikes are detected, the model switches to a probabilistic refinement mode, constructs probability-weighted token embeddings that implicitly preserve diverse hypotheses, and promotes sufficient interaction between candidate semantics and the context through iterative refinement. In addition, a refinement controller monitors distributional stability to reduce unnecessary iterations and switch the model back to standard discrete denoising when appropriate. Extensive experiments show that StepRefine significantly reduces hallucinations across multiple MDLM models on diverse reasoning benchmarks, demonstrating its effectiveness. Our main contributions are as follows: We analyze the relationship between entropy spike steps and hallucinations in multimodal diffusion models from the perspective of uncertainty dynamics across denoising steps. We propose StepRefine, a plug-and-play decoding approach that mitigates hallucinations through entropy spike detection and step-aware mode switching. Extensive evaluations across four MDLM backbones and diverse multimodal benchmarks show the superior performance of StepRefine, offering an effective solution for multimodal diffusion hallucinations. 2 Preliminary An MDLM takes an image and a textual prompt as input and generates text through iterative denoising. Entropy spike steps neither follow a uniform spacing nor occur at the same positions across samples, so a periodic schedule may fail to capture spikes in some inputs while spending refinement on already-stable steps in others. In contrast, our adaptive trigger conditions both the position and frequency of refinement on local entropy deviation, applying refinement only at steps with anomalous uncertainty. Effect of the Refinement Controller. We compare StepRefine’s adaptive termination criterion against fixed numbers of refinement rounds. Fig 5(b) shows that the adaptive scheme outperforms every fixed budget on both datasets, while no single fixed value performs consistently best across datasets. A single fixed budget allocates an equal number of refinement rounds to every spike step, regardless of whether the prediction has already converged. The adaptive criterion instead allocates refinement to each entropy spike step only while its predictive distribution continues to change, and terminates when it stabilizes. Robustness across Decoding Settings. StepRefine remains robust across diverse decoding settings. As shown in Table 3(a), StepRefine improves over the baseline under three remasking strategies with absolute MMHalu gains of +3.7% to +4.5%. Table 3(b) further shows consistent improvements across two generation lengths with three step budgets each, with MMHalu gains ranging from +1.8% to +4.8% across all six configurations. These results indicate that StepRefine generalizes across decoding configurations without per-setting tuning. The gain also holds at tight budgets, indicating that StepRefine remains effective even when total compute is constrained. 5 Related Work Multimodal diffusion LLM. Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) (Nie et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2025b; Zhu et al., 2025a; Jo and Hwang, 2025; AI et al., 2026) leverage their inherent bidirectional attention and iterative denoising process to exhibit strong global context modeling capability and flexible reasoning potential. In recent years, this paradigm has been further extended to multimodal settings. Multimodal diffusion models (He et al., 2026; Li et al., 2025e; Tian et al., 2025b; Chen et al., 2025a; Ji et al., 2025; Wen et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2025a; Li et al., 2026a; Cheng et al., 2025) are typically built upon pretrained dLLMs and incorporate visual representations to handle vision-language tasks. For example, methods such as LLaDA-V (You et al., 2025), LaViDa (Li et al., 2025f), and Dimple (Yu et al., 2025) align image features into the same embedding space as text tokens through visual instruction tuning, enabling joint modeling of visual and linguistic information. Another line of methods (Yang et al., 2025; Swerdlow et al., 2025; Shi et al., 2025), such as LLaDA-O (You et al., 2026), Lumina-dimoo (Xin et al., 2025b), and LaViDa-O (Li et al., 2025d), further combines fine-tuning and reinforcement learning to jointly model discretized visual and textual representations for unified multimodal generation and understanding. In addition, methods such as DiffusionVL (Zeng et al., 2025) and Fudoki (Wang et al., 2025a) transform autoregressive models into the discrete diffusion paradigm through diffusion fine-tuning, providing another path for multimodal diffusion modeling. Decoding strategy in dLLM. Despite the advantages of parallel generation and global modeling offered by discrete masked diffusion, the inference efficiency (Oba et al., 2026; Nguyen-Tri et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025a; Gao et al., 2025; Wu and Zhang, 2025; Wu et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025d; Ben-Hamu et al., 2025) and generation quality of diffusion large language models largely depend on the decoding strategy. One line of work leverages cache reuse (Li et al., 2025a; Jiang et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025d; Song et al., 2026; Ma et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025) and token pruning (Long et al., 2026; Xiao et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026c; Chen et al., 2025c; Chang et al., 2026) to alleviate the computational bottlenecks introduced by global attention. Another line of research focuses on optimizing sampling (Feng et al., 2026; Xiang et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026a; Li et al., 2026b; Dong et al., 2025; Kong et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025b; Qi et al., ; Wang et al., 2025c; Kim et al., 2025b), early stopping (Li et al., 2025c; Li et al., 2025b; Chen et al., 2025b), and step scheduling (Luo et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026b; Fu et al., 2025; Wei et al., 2025; Fu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026b; Bao et al., 2025; Luxembourg et al., 2025) to reduce redundant denoising iterations. Existing approaches for mitigating hallucinations in diffusion models include self-corrective decoding (Hong et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025c; Tian et al., 2025a; Chen et al., 2025e; Shu et al., 2026; Xin et al., 2025a; Zhong et al., 2026b) and prior constraints (Zuo et al., 2026; Cheng et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026; Seo et al., 2025; Xiong et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026a; Yang et al., 2026), which improve model reliability by reducing error accumulation. Prior work replaces the binary mask-to-token transition with continuous token representations at each decoding step (Ye et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2025b; Zhong et al., 2026a; Chen et al., 2026b; Hersche et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2025). We examine hallucination in MDLMs from the perspective of step-wise uncertainty dynamics during denoising. Based on this observation, we propose StepRefine, a plug-and-play decoding method that mitigates hallucinations by detecting entropy spike steps and selectively applying latent refinement. 6 Conclusion In this work, we extensively study hallucination in multimodal diffusion language models by looking at how predictive uncertainty evolves across denoising steps. We observe that during iterative denoising, MDLMs show sharp local increases in mean mask entropy at a small number of steps, which we call entropy spikes. These steps correlate with hallucinated tokens and mainly arise in the early-to-middle stages of denoising, where confidence-based decoding becomes less reliably grounded in the current context. Building on this observation, we introduce StepRefine, a training-free decoding strategy that detects entropy spikes via local trend deviation, switches to iterative latent refinement at those steps, and adaptively terminates once the predictive distribution stabilizes. Across four MDLM backbones and multiple benchmarks comprehensively covering general reasoning, hallucination, mathematical, and scientific reasoning, StepRefine obtains improved accuracy and can be combined with existing acceleration methods. In summary, our findings suggest that focusing refinement on a small number of high-uncertainty steps yields measurable improvements in MDLM decoding without additional training. Capacity Allocation at the Source: Sparse Target Optimization for LLM Knowledge Editing Knowledge editing has emerged as a promising approach for efficiently updating embedded knowledge in large language models (LLMs). It first computes an ideal target hidden state that steers the LLM toward the new output, and then edits the model parameters so that the original hidden state is mapped to this target. While most existing methods focus on the second stage of parameter editing in preserving other knowledge, we find that the upstream construction of the target hidden state also plays an important role in allocating the model’s limited capacity space. We first establish a theoretical connection between interference in the parameter space and interference between target hidden states, showing that the two are positively correlated. Building on this insight, we propose a simple yet effective [FORMULA] regularization method that prunes away unnecessary “tentacles” of each knowledge vector, retaining only the essential components. With fewer extraneous tentacles, each edit affects less other knowledge, enabling better coexistence. Extensive experiments across multiple LLMs and benchmark datasets verify the effectiveness of our method. Code: https://github.com/wintersdragon-c/STO. 1 Introduction Large language models (LLMs) encode a substantial amount of factual knowledge in their parameters, but that knowledge is inevitably incomplete, outdated, or erroneous. Updating such knowledge by continued pretraining or full fine-tuning is often computationally expensive and may undesirably perturb unrelated capabilities. This has motivated a growing line of work on model editing, whose goal is to modify a pretrained model so that it incorporates a small set of new facts while preserving unrelated behavior. One of the mainstream paradigms in this literature is locate-then-edit (LTE) (Meng et al., 2022; Meng et al., 2023): First, it precisely locates a decisive token in the input text and identifies the decisive layer in the model (usually the MLP). Then, if the hidden state of the decisive token at the decisive layer can be steered toward a target hidden state (e.g, [FORMULA] in Figure 1), the model will ultimately output the desired target knowledge. Figure 1 provides a toy example for quick intuition. More details will be introduced in [FORMULA] 3. Despite its strengths, current LTE methods still face a central challenge: because different knowledge items are stored through the same set of parameters, how to better allocate this parameter space and reduce mutual interference among different knowledge, thereby improving the coexistence of more knowledge, remains an under-explored problem. While existing methods account for allocating new knowledge and old non-target knowledge to distinct subspaces when editing parameters based on the residual (i.e., during the second stage of Figure 1), the allocation at the upstream target construction stage remains less-explored. In this work, we revisit model editing from the perspective of the residual representation (i.e., [FORMULA] in Figure 1) that induces the final parameter update and find that we need to consider not only the downstream mechanism of parameter update, but also upstream target construction. The capacity space of an LLM is limited. The more new knowledge items that occupy the same region, the higher the interference among them, and the greater the disruption to that region. This not only lowers the success rate of injecting new knowledge into the region but also damages the old knowledge originally stored there. To address this, we attack the problem upstream, at the target construction stage: by spreading new knowledge more thinly across the capacity space, we make space for both new and old knowledge to coexist. We first theoretically show that the interference between the parameter changes required for editing different pieces of knowledge is positively correlated with the inner product of their residuals. However, due to computational constraints, we cannot compute the residuals for all target knowledge simultaneously when solving via gradient descent, and thus cannot directly adopt inter-residual interference as an optimization regularizer. To address this issue, we try to reduce the expected interference by imposing a simple Lasso (Tibshirani, 1996) (i.e., [FORMULA] regularizer) on the residual vector [FORMULA] (which encourages sparsity in [FORMULA] ), which can induce a more localized update. Lasso encourages the support of the knowledge representation to be sparse, thereby reducing the expected overlap between the supports of different edits. As a result, the Frobenius interactions among the model parameter updates are also expected to be small. This practical approximation is also quite intuitive: if we limit the residual’s variation to only a few necessary dimensions during the residual computation stage, such that the modification of each piece of target knowledge occupies minimal capacity space, would reduce knowledge interference and relieve this allocation burden at its source. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: (1) We theoretically show that reducing the inner product between the residuals of different knowledge items decreases interference when editing target knowledge. (2) We propose a simple and practical method that reduces the expected inner product between knowledge residuals, thereby lowering editing difficulty from the data preparation stage. (3) Experiments across various LLMs and datasets validate the effectiveness of our method. 2 Related Work Locate-then-edit paradigm. Large language models (LLMs) encode a substantial amount of factual knowledge in their parameters, but that knowledge is inevitably incomplete, outdated, or erroneous, which motivates concerns on interpretability (Liu et al., 2025a; Liu et al., 2024), safety (Liu et al., 2025b), and reliability (Liu et al., 2026a). Recent work has increasingly focused on precise parameter editing, typically following a locate-then-edit (LTE) paradigm: identifying decisive tokens and layers and then modifying the corresponding hidden states or parameters to substitute target knowledge. Early methods such as ROME and MEMIT (Meng et al., 2022; Meng et al., 2023) introduced causal tracing to locate effective edit positions. Subsequent approaches, including RECT (Gu et al., 2024), EMMET (Gupta et al., 2024), PMET (Li et al., 2024), PRUNE (Ma et al., 2025), AdaEdit (Li and Chu, 2025), AlphaEdit (Fang et al., 2025), LTI (Zhang et al., 2025), AnyEdit (Jiang et al., 2025a), BLUE (Li et al., 2025a), NeuralEdit (Jiang et al., 2025b), and FE (Liu et al., 2026b), further extend this framework through improved localization, optimization, regularization, or sequential-editing strategies. With strong parameter efficiency and empirical performance, LTE methods have become a major paradigm for knowledge editing (Liu et al., 2026b). Target construction of LTE. The LTE paradigm consists of two stages: (1) preparing target hidden states, which play a role analogous to labels in supervised learning, (2) using these target states to guide parameter updates. Most prior work focuses on the second stage, namely how to solve or regularize the parameter update, while the upstream construction of target states remains much less explored. MEMIT (Meng et al., 2023) argues that the target hidden state should remain close to the original hidden state and introduces an [FORMULA] distance term to enforce this. EAMET (Dai et al., 2026) further argues that the KL divergence over residuals should match that over keys. Our work also studies target construction, but addresses a different aspect: we study how target residuals should be allocated within the model’s limited capacity space. By sparsifying target residuals, we reduce unnecessary overlap among edits, thereby mitigating interference with other edits and existing non-target knowledge. RAG-style inference-time knowledge editing. A parallel line of work maintains an external knowledge base queried at inference time to supply updated information (Hartvigsen et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2024). Because they leave model parameters unchanged, we regard them as retrieval-based augmentation rather than genuine parameter editing, and they fall outside the scope of this paper. Augmenting models with extra memory or hypernetworks. A second family equips LLMs with auxiliary memory modules or hypernetworks to absorb new knowledge. Methods such as MEND (Mitchell et al., 2022a), KE (De Cao et al., 2021), and RLEdit (Li et al., 2025b) exploit low-rank parameterizations for efficiency, yet typically exhibit poor generalization and require retraining for each new fact. Methods that offload knowledge to auxiliary parameters or networks—including T-Patcher (Huang et al., 2023), SERAC (Mitchell et al., 2022b), Grace (Hartvigsen et al., 2023), WISE (Wang et al., 2024a), and KDE (Xu et al., 2025)—face scalability issues as knowledge accumulates without retiring stale entries, and are generally more sensitive to hyperparameter choices than LTE-based approaches. 3 Preliminaries Notation. Question (1): Can the Lasso regularizer really lead to sparse residuals? We compare the residuals obtained by our method against those obtained without the Lasso constraint, measuring the proportion of dimensions whose values are close to zero. We use several different thresholds to determine whether a dimension is considered near-zero. The results are shown in Figure 3. Figure 3(a) shows that our method substantially increases sparsity. To further verify this, we sort the dimensions of residual vector [FORMULA] by magnitude and aggregate them in groups of 100, then examine the compression ratio across dimensions with and without Lasso. The results are shown in Figures 4(a) and 4(b). Figure 4(a) reports the compression ratio for the low, middle, and high regions, while Figure 4(b) shows the compression ratio across all dimensions continuously. This indicates that our method does not simply compress all dimensions; rather, it largely preserves the originally high-magnitude, important dimensions (retaining approximately [FORMULA] ) while more aggressively compressing the low-magnitude, unimportant ones. This aligns with the design principle of Lasso (Tibshirani, 1996) that it does feature selection rather than simple weight shrinkage. Question (2): How much does our method affect the original cross-entropy loss? Cross-entropy measures how accurately a given piece of knowledge is steered toward the target. Therefore, to ensure successful downstream editing, our method should not significantly affect the cross-entropy. We select 2,000 samples from MCF dataset and conduct experiments using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. We report the mean and median cross-entropy values, as well as the residual inner product corresponding to Eq. 12 (computed over 500K sampled pairs). As shown in Table 4, the inner product between residuals is significantly reduced, while the cross-entropy increases only marginally. Combined with the finding from Question (1)—that our method preserves high-magnitude dimensions and primarily compresses low-magnitude ones—this confirms that we retain the necessary dimensions while suppressing unimportant ones. Notably, although a higher cross-entropy would in principle suggest a disadvantage in editing success rate (Efficacy), our method instead achieves higher Efficacy, particularly on the harder ZsRE dataset. This indicates that reducing inter-knowledge interference indeed improves editing success. Question (3): Does the performance gain simply come from reducing the magnitude of each dimension in the residual [FORMULA] ? The comparison between our method and MEMIT directly addresses this concern. Our approach can be viewed as augmenting MEMIT with an additional Lasso constraint ( [FORMULA] ) on top of its existing [FORMULA] regularization on the residual. These two regularizers play complementary roles: [FORMULA] performs weight shrinkage by uniformly attenuating parameter magnitudes, while [FORMULA] induces sparsity and thereby acts as an implicit feature selector, retaining informative components while pruning redundant ones. The performance gain of our method over MEMIT therefore indicates that feature selection, beyond mere weight shrinkage, is essential in this setting. In practice, naively strengthening the [FORMULA] term in MEMIT does not resolve the issue and in fact hurts performance, since [FORMULA] penalizes all features indiscriminately and ends up suppressing the informative ones together with the redundant ones. 7 Conclusion, limitations, and future work This paper analyzes, from the perspective of target construction, how to better allocate target knowledge within the limited capacity space of LLMs during editing. We first establish a theoretical connection between interference in the parameter space and interference between target residuals, showing that the two are positively correlated. Building on this insight, we propose STO, a simple yet effective [FORMULA] regularization method that prunes away unnecessary [FORMULA] branches” of each knowledge vector, leaving only the essential components. With fewer extraneous branches, knowledge items are less likely to entangle, and the interference between residuals (and consequently in the LLM parameter space) is substantially reduced. Our results suggest that target construction is also a fruitful direction for improving the reliability of model editing. We hope this work encourages further investigation into how the structure of edit targets, not only the mechanism of parameter updates, shapes the success of LLM model editing. One limitation is that we do not have results for LLMs larger than 14B, mainly due to two practical reasons. One reason is that the hyperparameters for most baselines are often unavailable for larger LLMs. In addition, larger-scale experiments exceed our current computational resources. Nevertheless, the settings we use are commonly used in the literature, and we leave the study of larger LLMs to future work. Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition: Uncovering the Blind Spots of OKS-mAP: A Unified Protocol for Occlusion, Joint-Angle, and Temporal Evaluation of 2D Pose Estimators The dominant evaluation protocol for 2D human pose estimation—mean average precision based on Object Keypoint Similarity (OKS-mAP)—is insensitive to three properties that matter for downstream applications: it does not distinguish visible from occluded keypoints in the aggregate score; it does not measure joint-angle error; and it is silent on the temporal stability of outputs produced by tracking-free, frame-by-frame inference. We propose a unified supplementary evaluation protocol with three modules: (M1) OKS-mAP stratified by ground-truth visibility labels ( [FORMULA] ), together with [FORMULA] , which quantifies how much the aggregate metric masks occlusion-specific differences; (M2) joint-angle error (RMSE/MAE/P95) against angles derived from ground-truth keypoints, plus knee-valgus detection consistency (Cohen’s [FORMULA] ); and (M3) frame-to-frame displacement, median-filter residual jitter, and jump rate under tracking-free per-frame inference, before and after OneEuro smoothing. We executed the protocol on four public datasets (COCO val2017, CrowdPose, OCHuman, PoseTrack18) for four models spanning two architecture families—the official YOLO11s-pose, an occlusion-domain fine-tuned variant, and the transformer-based ViTPose-B/L—with all cross-family comparisons performed under a common detector-free GT-bbox oracle protocol and all metrics produced by an open-source harness in a single inference pass. I Introduction 2D human pose estimation is a fundamental computer vision task whose outputs feed action recognition, motion analysis, and real-time fitness-correction systems. For such applications, the gap between benchmark scores and real-world usability matters more than average precision alone: a model that ranks first on a benchmark can be markedly worse in scenes with occluded people, fast motion, or the need for precise joint-angle judgments—and this difference is invisible in the dominant metric. Whether such blind spots change model rankings or only mask magnitudes is itself an empirical question; we test it (RQ1) and find, for the model pairs studied, that the ranking is stable within each architecture family while the magnitudes differ substantially (Sections 5.4 and 5.5). The de facto standard evaluation protocol is OKS-mAP as defined by the COCO keypoints protocol [1]. It matches and scores predictions by Object Keypoint Similarity (OKS) and aggregates over the whole test set into a single scalar. This design has three blind spots. First, OKS aggregation ignores keypoint visibility: visible ( [FORMULA] ) and occluded ( [FORMULA] ) keypoints are averaged with equal weight into one score (missing, [FORMULA] , keypoints are excluded from OKS averaging), so occlusion-specific accuracy differences are diluted by averaging. Second, the protocol does not measure joint angles: OKS penalizes pixel-level keypoint position error, whereas downstream applications (e.g., exercise correction) care about whether the joint angles derived from those keypoints are accurate—and the two are not linearly related. Third, the protocol is blind to temporal behavior: most systems run frame-by-frame independent inference on video, and the jitter of the output between frames directly determines how the downstream consumer perceives it, yet a static-image protocol says nothing about it. Prior work responds to each problem in isolation—OCHuman organizes evaluation by occlusion level [2]; PoseTrack and SmoothNet extend the static protocol with tracking metrics (MOTA/MOTP) and a temporal-smoothness metric (per-joint acceleration magnitude, Accel), respectively [3, 15]; and the biomechanics community has validated joint angles from markerless pose estimation [4, 5, 6]. What is missing is a unified, reproducible, cross-dataset supplementary protocol, and any baseline numbers quantifying how large these three blind spots are on real models. This paper proposes a three-module unified supplementary evaluation protocol (Section 3) and open-sources its execution layer, an eval harness that produces official metrics and protocol metrics from a single inference pass, with three self-check gates. We executed the protocol on four public datasets with two representative models (Sections 4–5) to answer five research questions: RQ1 (occlusion): How much does full OKS-mAP mask occlusion-specific accuracy differences? Does model ranking change after visibility stratification? RQ2 (angle): Does joint-angle RMSE provide discriminative information beyond OKS-mAP? Is angle error amplified by occlusion? RQ3 (temporal): Under tracking-free per-frame inference, how much do models differ in temporal stability? Can smoothing buy stability at an acceptable accuracy cost? RQ4 (protocol economy): How do the metrics of the three modules correlate with each other and with full mAP? Is any of them redundant? RQ5 (architecture generality): Under a detector-free GT-bbox oracle protocol, do the three blind spots persist for transformer-based models, and does model ranking re-order within another architecture family? Our contributions are threefold: (1) to our knowledge, the first supplementary evaluation scheme that unifies occlusion stratification, angle error, and temporal jitter under one protocol, with explicit statistical conventions (bootstrap confidence intervals) and dataset-consistent stratification rules; (2) an open-source harness and all raw predictions, so that any new model can produce the full set of protocol metrics on the four datasets in one pass; (3) complete baseline numbers for four models from two architecture families—including a detector-free oracle protocol that isolates the pose head from the detector—that quantify, for the first time to our knowledge, the magnitude of OKS-mAP’s three blind spots (e.g., [FORMULA] as large as [FORMULA] on COCO under the oracle protocol). II Related Work Pose estimation evaluation protocols. The COCO keypoints protocol, with OKS at its core, has been the field’s de facto standard since 2014 [1]; its predecessor, percentage of correct keypoints (PCK) on MPII [16], shares the same structure our modules target: one aggregate over the whole test set. PoseTrack extends evaluation to multi-person pose tracking in video with a tracking convention centered on MOTA/MOTP [3]; SmoothNet goes further and proposes per-joint acceleration magnitude (Accel, in pixels/frame2) as a temporal-smoothness metric for video pose, and uses that convention in its filtering-vs-baseline comparisons [15]. Our M3 is complementary to Accel: Accel measures the size of the frame-to-frame second difference, whereas our frame-to-frame displacement and median-filter residual measure positional fluctuation and high-frequency noise separately, and we additionally report the accuracy (AP) cost of smoothing. On the data side, CrowdPose and OCHuman provide real visibility/occlusion labels ( [FORMULA] in CrowdPose; three occlusion levels in OCHuman) [2, 7]. The common boundary of this prior work is that each improves a single dataset in a single dimension; none of it forms a cross-dataset supplementary protocol with unified conventions. Occlusion-robustness evaluation. Prior work has attempted to quantify occlusion’s effect on pose estimation: Ghafoor and Mahmood build three experiments with synthetically removed joints to quantify occlusion’s impact on 3D pose error [8], and later work continues this line with robustness evaluation under synthetic occlusion [9] and a visibility-aware video occlusion benchmark [10]. The difference from our work: these studies use synthetic occlusions or non-real annotation-based stratification, and each focuses on a single dataset and a single metric. We stratify across datasets using real [FORMULA] labels from three datasets and report [FORMULA] against full mAP. Joint-angle validation. Biomechanics and sports science have a line of validity studies for markerless pose estimation: Turner et al. reconstruct joint-angle trajectories from BlazePose keypoints in 89 resistance-training videos and assess movement-technique quality by frame-wise RMSE against a reference movement [4]; Panconi et al. validate DeepLabCut joint angles in gait analysis [5]; Pemasiri et al. build a gait-analysis framework for biomechanical interpretation [6]. These studies answer the question “do estimated angles equal the clinical/marker-based gold standard?” (validity), and they require dedicated marker or expert annotations. We do not repeat validity validation; instead we use ground-truth-derived angles as a protocol metric for model-to-model comparison. The two lines are complementary rather than competing (Section 6 elaborates this boundary). The knee-valgus threshold takes its magnitude reference from the literature: frontal plane projection angle (FPPA) of 16.0–17.4∘ in a lateral step-down test [11]. Temporal consistency and smoothing. Temporal inconsistency of tracking-free per-frame inference has been discussed at a general level by Deep Video Prior and others [12]; in engineering practice, OneEuro causal filtering is widely used to smooth keypoint trajectories [13]. Our work turns “stability of tracking-free raw output” itself into a protocol metric, and compares two filtering domains (normalized-coordinate vs. pixel) in their joint effect on jitter metrics and AP—a comparison that reveals how the choice of filtering domain decides the benefit and cost of smoothing. The boundary between the angle protocol and validity studies. Our angle metrics use ground-truth-derived angles as the reference and answer “which model’s joint angles are closer to the annotated truth”—a model-comparison tool. They do not validate “do estimated angles equal a clinical gold standard”, which is the task of the markerless validity literature [4, 5, 6] and requires markers or expert annotations. The two are complementary: validity studies certify that a specific model is trustworthy in a specific scenario, while our protocol gives any new model comparable angle-dimension scores on standard datasets. Likewise, the knee-valgus detection consistency ( [FORMULA] up to 0.76 at the default threshold [FORMULA] ) asserts only “consistency with GT annotations”, not clinical meaning. Engineering implications of the temporal metrics. M3’s two findings directly guide system design: first, data-side interventions (occlusion training) do not change temporal stability, so temporal quality must be handled separately; second, the choice of smoothing domain decides the benefit—normalized-domain filtering looks theoretically correct but fails in practice due to the re-injection of GT-box scale noise; third, the oracle decomposition (Section 5.5) shows the residual jitter to persist after detector removal, so better detection is not the lever—post-processing or pose-head-level changes are; separating pose-head-intrinsic from preprocessing contributions requires a preprocessing-matched control experiment. The protocol fixes the pixel domain as the primary convention and recommends that any temporal smoothing method report the joint “jitter before/after + AP cost” table. Limitations. (1) The baseline covers two architecture families under two protocols: within-family comparisons are detection-based for the YOLO pair and oracle-based for the ViTPose pair, while all cross-family comparisons are made under the shared oracle protocol. The YOLO-oracle variant uses a GT-bbox crop with letterboxing rather than the transformers’ UDP preprocessing, and the two differ additionally in input resolution ( [FORMULA] vs. [FORMULA] ) and in the use of flip test (absent vs. present). The cross-family comparisons are therefore explicitly confounded: preprocessing, resolution, and flip-test differences are not separated from architecture differences, and any cross-family gap should be read as a joint effect rather than a pure architecture effect (Section 5.5 uses this phrasing). Extending the baseline to other architectures (e.g., RTMPose, DWPose) is left to future work; the protocol’s value is its conventions and tooling. (4) M3 covers a single dataset, and its retained-segment subpopulation covers only about 53% of annotated frames; the generality of the temporal conclusions awaits extension. (5) RQ4’s correlation analysis has small cell counts ( [FORMULA] cells over only 3 independent datasets) and is exploratory. VII Conclusion We proposed and executed a unified supplementary evaluation protocol for 2D human pose estimation, targeting occlusion, joint angle, and temporal stability, together with an open-source harness and a reproducibility contract. Baseline results on four models from two architecture families and four public datasets show that, in every model–dataset combination tested, full OKS-mAP masks occlusion-specific accuracy differences ( [FORMULA] up to [FORMULA] ), that the angle-error protocol captures partially independent information beyond OKS, that, on the matched retained-segment subpopulation of PoseTrack18 val, pixel-domain smoothing reduces temporal jitter at zero cost on the matched-scope AP, and that the detector-free oracle protocol shows the residual jitter to survive detector removal (it is not detector-intrinsic)—with the three blind spots persisting across architectures under a shared oracle protocol, and with cross-family ranking, training-data, and temporal-stability effects separable at significance level. The protocol is positioned as a complement to, not a replacement for, OKS-mAP: it does not change the underlying convention of mainstream rankings, but adds three previously invisible diagnostic dimensions for model selection and system design. The code and all raw predictions are open-sourced.

URL-Sim: Unified and Regulated LiDAR Simulation for High-Fidelity Reconstruction of Dynamic Driving Scenes Reconstructing high-fidelity LiDAR simulation scenes from real-world driving logs is essential for cost-effective safety validation of autonomous driving systems. While simulators based on Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) achieve realistic scene reconstruction, their large-scale adoption is limited by slow rendering speeds. Recent 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS) approaches have improved rendering efficiency through explicit primitive representation and differentiable rasterization. However, existing 3DGS-based methods remain largely restricted to rigid vehicles and produce redundant primitives through unconstrained densification. To address these limitations, we propose URL-Sim, a unified and regulated dynamic LiDAR simulation framework. URL-Sim constructs a dynamic Gaussian scene graph that decouples the modeling of traffic participants, including vehicles, pedestrians, and cyclists, enabling accurate reconstruction of heterogeneous dynamic objects within a single framework. It further introduces a regulated Gaussian densification strategy that ranks primitives with multi-dimensional importance scores and allocates Gaussians to the most critical regions while keeping the total primitive count bounded. Experiments on the Waymo and KITTI-360 datasets demonstrate that URL-Sim achieves higher quantitative accuracy and visual quality than existing baselines under comparable primitive budgets, and accurately recovers the geometry and poses of diverse dynamic traffic participants. I Introduction LiDAR sensors are integral to environmental perception in advanced autonomous driving systems [1], making the driving-scene data they provide critical for the testing and validation of perception and planning algorithms [2]. Since traditional on-road data collection is inefficient and offers limited scene coverage, there is an increasing need for efficient and realistic LiDAR simulation methods [3]. Traditional LiDAR simulation, whether physics-engine-based virtual worlds [4, 5, 6] or explicit geometric reconstruction [7, 8, 9, 10], suffers from substantial sim-to-real gaps, cumbersome pipelines, and limited support for dynamic scenes. Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) [11] narrow the sim-to-real gap for LiDAR simulation using continuous implicit representations and differentiable volume rendering [12, 13, 14, 15]. Some methods incorporate spatio-temporal constraints [16] and bounding box tracking [17] to handle dynamic scenes. However, the dense ray sampling inherent in volume rendering causes substantial computational overhead. The consequent slow training and rendering speeds cannot meet the requirements of large-scale modeling and real-time closed-loop simulation. Recent 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS) [18] has emerged as an effective alternative to NeRF, achieving order-of-magnitude improvements in rendering efficiency through its explicit Gaussian representation and hardware-accelerated rendering. While current mainstream methods [19, 20, 21, 22] primarily focus on camera data synthesis, seminal works such as GS-LiDAR [23] and LiDAR-GS [24] have successfully adapted 3DGS to the LiDAR imaging model by designing differentiable splatting pipelines tailored to LiDAR’s active perception mechanism. To handle dynamic scenes, LiDAR-RT [25] and SplatAD [26] employ a dynamic-static separation strategy to model rigid vehicles separately. Despite these advances, existing Gaussian-based LiDAR simulation methods face two primary challenges. First, current dynamic scene simulations primarily focus on rigid objects and provide limited support for non-rigid entities such as pedestrians and cyclists, who are vulnerable road users central to high-risk edge cases. Second, existing methods incur substantial computational overhead, driven by the inherent sparsity and non-uniform angular distribution of LiDAR point clouds, combined with the unrestricted densification of the Gaussian paradigm. These issues reduce training efficiency and simulation performance, potentially triggering training failures and constraining practical scalability and scene adaptability. To address these challenges, URL-Sim is proposed as a unified and regulated LiDAR simulation framework for the high-fidelity reconstruction and controllable editing of dynamic urban driving scenes. URL-Sim constructs a dynamic Gaussian scene graph that decouples individual dynamic entities from the static background for independent modeling. Rigid objects such as vehicles are simulated via standard rigid transformations. For non-rigid entities such as pedestrians, the Skinned Multi-Person Linear (SMPL) [27] model is introduced to serve as a deformation prior. Specifically, the Gaussian primitives of each pedestrian are bound to the SMPL mesh vertices, and the pose and shape parameters of the model are utilized to drive the skinning deformation of the Gaussians. For template-free non-rigid objects such as cyclists, a lightweight deformation network is employed to directly learn and optimize the local deformation parameters. Together, these three representations enable unified modeling and simulation of the principal traffic participants in autonomous driving. To curb the unconstrained expansion of primitives and the redundant accumulation of Gaussians inherent in the original Adaptive Density Control (ADC), a regulated Gaussian densification (RGD) strategy is proposed. RGD imposes a predefined global upper bound on the total Gaussian count and allocates a fixed budget for each densification step following a quadratic growth curve, establishing a deterministic training schedule. A Gaussian importance scoring system is constructed by integrating spatial gradients, image-domain features, and rendering accumulation attributes. Guided by these scores, targeted densification and adaptive pruning are executed within the allocated single-round budget. This controllable mechanism limits redundant proliferation and achieves higher rendering performance under a strictly bounded primitive count. In summary, our main contributions are as follows: URL-Sim is presented as a unified and regulated LiDAR simulation framework that models diverse dynamic non-rigid objects, addressing a relatively under-explored problem in LiDAR simulation. A regulated Gaussian densification strategy is proposed to balance simulation accuracy and computational overhead through quadratic budget allocation and multi-dimensional scoring. Extensive experiments on Waymo and KITTI-360 validate accurate recovery of non-rigid actor geometry and poses, as well as competitive 2D perceptual quality and 3D geometric accuracy. II Related work Classical LiDAR simulation relies on virtual platforms such as CARLA [4] and AirSim [5] for environmental control and closed-loop interaction [6], but inherently suffers from severe sim-to-real domain gaps. Efforts to bridge this gap through physical modeling [7] and real-world asset libraries [8, 9] are hindered by cumbersome procedures and high labor costs. Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) [11] have advanced LiDAR simulation through implicit spatial modeling and volume rendering, narrowing the sim-to-real gap. Early frameworks including NFL [12] and LiDAR-NeRF [13] integrate the LiDAR imaging process into NeRF to enable high-quality novel view synthesis. For complex dynamic scenes, UniSim [14] and NeuRAD [15] utilize feature grids and precise physical modeling to reconstruct and recompose traffic participants. DyNFL [17] and LiDAR4D [16] further isolate dynamic objects and capture temporal correlations to achieve editable digital twins and high-fidelity 4D spatio-temporal synthesis. Nevertheless, the reliance on high-frequency dense sampling induces considerable computational overhead and slow rendering speeds, precluding real-time closed-loop deployment. 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS) [18] offers a real-time alternative via its explicit primitive representation and highly parallelized rasterization. Early 3DGS-based methods such as GS-LiDAR [23] and LiDAR-GS [24] render substantially faster than NeRF-based counterparts with comparable reconstruction quality, but are limited to static scenes and lack editability. LiDAR-RT [25] separates dynamic and static components using bounding boxes and tracking IDs to enable customizable scene editing. SplatAD [26] and SIMULI [28] similarly rely on 3DGS for joint camera-LiDAR simulation. However, these approaches are predominantly restricted to rigid vehicles and overlook non-rigid objects such as pedestrians and cyclists. Moreover, current frameworks lack resource-efficient mechanisms for controlling redundant Gaussians resulting from unconstrained densification. Although 3DGS demonstrates promising sensor simulation capabilities, its heuristic cloning and splitting generate redundant Gaussian primitives, inflating VRAM consumption and storage [29, 30]. Various approaches have been proposed to optimize the computational efficiency of 3DGS for large-scale deployment. The first category targets post-processing of redundant models via compression and pruning. Compact 3DGS [31] and Compressed 3DGS [32] employ vector quantization and entropy coding to compress Gaussian parameters, reducing storage without altering underlying spatial geometry. Pruning strategies eliminate Gaussian primitives with marginal visual contributions, guided by metrics such as multi-view consistency, uncertainty scores, and global importance [33, 34, 35]. Although model volume is substantially reduced, excessive pruning at extreme compression ratios frequently leads to severe visual degradation and loss of foreground geometric details. The second category optimizes densification during training to prevent redundant generation at its source, replacing unconstrained growth with rigorous control. SteepGS [29] and Taming 3DGS [36] minimize redundant sub-Gaussians through analytical optimization and fixed-budget constructive pipelines. BUGS [37] employs a region-consistency-based bi-directional growing mechanism to adaptively regulate Gaussian density for compact scene reconstruction. For LiDAR geometry, GTLR-GS [38] and GeomGS [39] incorporate curvature-adaptive refinement and geometric confidence scores to govern densification. These works demonstrate that proactive densification is critical for compact, high-fidelity reconstruction. Nevertheless, these strategies are designed for visual modalities and rely on dense pixel-level observations. When applied directly to LiDAR simulation, they may misallocate Gaussian primitives by overlooking sparse ray-level geometry and intensity cues, thereby compromising range accuracy and foreground structural fidelity. High-fidelity sensor data is synthesized through a Gaussian rendering pipeline based on differentiable ray tracing. Alongside this rendering pipeline, a regulated Gaussian densification (RGD) strategy is introduced during the training phase to mitigate the resource redundancy caused by unconstrained primitive growth. IV Experiments URL-Sim is validated on the widely used Waymo Open Dataset [42] and KITTI-360 [43]. The Waymo data were collected at 10 Hz using a 64-beam LiDAR with a 20° vertical field of view (FOV), natively providing depth and intensity images at a resolution of 64×2560. KITTI-360 employs a 64-beam LiDAR operating at 10 Hz with a 26.4° vertical FOV. The raw KITTI-360 LiDAR data are spherically projected into 2D depth and intensity images at a 64×1030 resolution. Four dynamic scene sequences containing non-rigid dynamic instances were selected from each dataset. For each sequence, 50 consecutive frames were extracted, with every tenth frame allocated to the test set and the remainder used for training. Comprehensive model evaluation relies on a quantitative framework that targets two primary dimensions: 2D perceptual quality and 3D geometric accuracy. For 2D projections, pixel-level depth and intensity deviations are measured via Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) and Median Absolute Error (MedAE), with global fidelity assessed through SSIM [44], Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR), and LPIPS [45]. Rendering efficiency is evaluated via frame rate (FPS) and total Gaussian primitive count. Together, these operations enable the synthesis of diverse interactive scenarios, providing a potential source of simulated data for future closed-loop testing and safety validation. V conclusion This paper presents URL-Sim, a unified and regulated LiDAR simulation framework that builds a dynamic Gaussian scene graph for decoupled modeling and high-fidelity reconstruction of heterogeneous traffic participants. Integrating the SMPL prior with a lightweight deformation network bridges the gap in non-rigid LiDAR simulation, while the proposed RGD strategy employs multi-dimensional importance scoring and fixed budget allocation to direct resources toward critical regions under a fixed primitive budget. Extensive experiments on Waymo and KITTI-360 demonstrate significant improvements over existing baselines in both perceptual quality and geometric accuracy. Although URL-Sim delivers competitive dynamic LiDAR simulation, certain limitations remain. First, the dynamic decoupling relies on accurate bounding boxes and tracking, and reconstruction quality may degrade in crowded environments. Additionally, large viewpoint shifts during editing may distort unobserved regions. Integrating generative priors such as diffusion models represents a promising direction for overcoming these extrapolation challenges.

Attribute-Evidence Learning with Multimodal Prompt for Generalized Category Discovery Generalized category discovery (GCD) aims to discover novel categories from unlabeled data by leveraging limited labeled samples from old classes. Existing methods that rely solely on visual cues often neglect the multimodal nature of human perception, prompting recent approaches to incorporate textual information such as category tags and attributes. However, these approaches typically entangle global tags and local attributes within a shared global image representation, rendering attributes unreliable and potentially providing misleading cues that can drive the model toward incorrect predictions. To this end, we propose AptM-GCD, a novel multimodal framework that exploits apt textual guidance through attribute evidence learning and multimodal prompt reasoning. Specifically, we design an Attribute-Evidence Learning (AEL) mechanism that treats attributes as localized visual evidence rather than global category descriptors. By interacting attribute embeddings with patch-level visual tokens, AEL identifies reliable attribute-related regions and extracts discriminative local evidence, thereby reducing the impact of noisy or irrelevant attribute cues. Building upon the extracted evidence, we further develop a Multimodal Prompt Learning (MPL) mechanism to bridge local attribute semantics and global visual understanding. MPL converts fine-grained textual evidence into visual prompts and injects them into a multimodal prompt transformer, enabling attribute information to enhance category discrimination through contextual reasoning without enforcing direct global alignment between modalities. Extensive experiments on six datasets demonstrate that AptM-GCD consistently achieves SoTA performance across both fine-grained and generic benchmarks. Moreover, the proposed framework exhibits strong generalization ability, delivering consistent gains under unimodal and class-imbalanced GCD settings. I Introduction Humans possess a remarkable ability to recognize and organize novel concepts from limited prior experience, continuously expanding their knowledge of the world [1, 2]. Equipping deep learning models with a similar capability is crucial for open-world visual understanding, as real-world data distributions are constantly evolving and often contain categories that are absent from the labeled training set [3, 4, 5]. Generalized Category Discovery (GCD) has recently emerged as a promising framework for addressing this challenge. Given a small labeled dataset consisting of known categories and a large unlabeled dataset containing both known and unknown categories, GCD aims to simultaneously preserve recognition of known classes while discovering the underlying structure of novel categories [6, 7, 8]. This setting better reflects realistic learning scenarios, where labeled annotations are limited and new semantic concepts continuously appear. Compared with related paradigms, GCD poses a substantially more challenging problem. Novel Category Discovery (NCD) assumes that all unlabeled samples belong exclusively to unseen classes [9, 10, 11], while Open-Set Recognition (OSR) focuses primarily on identifying whether a sample is novel without further categorizing it [12, 13]. In contrast, GCD must not only distinguish known and unknown classes but also group unlabeled samples into semantically meaningful novel categories, requiring the model to balance representation transfer, class discrimination, and category discovery within a unified framework. Early GCD methods primarily rely on visual representations to discover novel categories. However, human perception naturally integrates visual observations with semantic descriptions and fine-grained attributes when recognizing unfamiliar concepts [14]. Inspired by this observation, recent studies have incorporated textual knowledge into GCD [15], leveraging category tags and attribute descriptions to provide complementary semantic supervision and enhance representation learning [16, 17]. A common strategy in these multimodal approaches is to construct a heterogeneous vocabulary that combines category-level concepts (e.g., sparrow) with attribute-level descriptions (e.g., gray crown), as illustrated in Fig. 1. Given a query image, the model retrieves semantically relevant textual items through global image-level matching and subsequently converts the retrieved tags and attributes into pseudo labels for cross-modal co-teaching with visual category predictions [16, 17]. Such a design implicitly treats category tags and attributes as equally informative global semantic descriptors, allowing textual information to directly influence category discovery. Although these methods introduce rich semantic guidance, they overlook a fundamental issue: attributes and category tags operate at different semantic granularities. Category tags describe holistic class identity and serve as image-level semantic anchors, whereas attributes correspond to localized visual evidence, such as color, texture, shape, or part-level patterns. Furthermore, the validity of an attribute often depends on the object category. For instance, the attribute blue may appear in many contexts, but it is not a reliable descriptor for a tomato in a natural scene. When performing global image-level retrieval, the attribute blue might still be selected if the background contains blue regions. As illustrated by the examples in Fig. 2(a), such retrieval can mistakenly associate local attributes with irrelevant background or contextual cues. Consequently, the retrieved attributes may provide misleading yet seemingly plausible semantic evidence, which can steer the model toward incorrect category predictions. This issue is particularly detrimental in the context of GCD, where novel classes lack labeled supervision and must be inferred solely from unlabeled data. As a result, the model heavily depends on the semantic structure provided by external textual guidance. When noisy or granularity-mismatched attributes are retrieved, they can bias the text guidance toward incorrect category-level predictions. These biased predictions are subsequently transformed into pseudo labels and propagated through cross-modal co-teaching. Consequently, erroneous attribute evidence contaminates the category discovery space, impairing the reliable separation of novel classes. To quantify this effect, Fig. 2(b) reports the attribute-induced prediction bias on fine-grained CUB [18] and Stanford Cars [19], using the attribute-based method [16]. Among misclassified novel-class samples, 64.92% on CUB and 54.23% on Stanford Cars involve retrieved attributes that provide misleading support for the predicted category, highlighting the substantial impact of noisy attributes on GCD performance. Beyond attribute-based GCD methods, this finding also raises an important question for tag-based approaches: can attributes simply be added as extra textual guidance? Fig. 2(c) shows that the answer is not straightforward. Naively incorporating attributes into a tag-based GCD baseline [20] does not consistently improve novel-class discovery and may even degrade performance. In contrast, when attributes are decoupled from category tags and integrated through our proposed strategy, they yield clear improvements over both the original baseline and naive attribute integration. These observations indicate that rich attribute semantics are beneficial only when their granularity is properly handled, rather than being treated as additional global category-level textual anchors. To this end, we propose AptM-GCD, a multimodal GCD framework that handles textual semantics by granularity: fine-grained attributes serve as localized visual evidence to refine image representations, while category tags act as global semantic anchors for final category discovery. Specifically, we introduce Attribute-Evidence Learning (AEL), an object-aware attribute grounding mechanism. Rather than retrieving attributes from a global image representation, AEL performs attribute mining over patch-level visual tokens conditioned on object regions. This allows attributes to be selected and grounded according to object-relevant visual evidence, suppressing noisy cues from background or irrelevant context. Building upon grounded evidence, we further propose Multimodal Prompt Learning (MPL). MPL transforms localized attribute evidence into soft visual prompts and injects them into a transformer-based visual backbone. This enables fine-grained attribute semantics to interact with global visual context, refining image representations without forcing attributes into global category-level alignment. Beyond AptM-GCD, MPL is architecture-agnostic and can be applied to both multimodal and unimodal GCD frameworks to improve category discovery without altering original learning objectives (Sec. VI-D1). To summarize, our contributions are four-fold: We identify a previously overlooked granularity mismatch in multimodal GCD, where local attributes are treated as global category-level semantics, potentially biasing novel-category discovery. To address this issue, we propose AptM-GCD, which leverages attributes as grounded visual evidence rather than category-level supervision. We propose Attribute-Evidence Learning (AEL), which performs object-conditioned attribute mining and attribute-to-patch grounding, replacing global image-level attribute alignment with localized evidence extraction. We design Multimodal Prompt Learning (MPL), which encodes localized attribute evidence as soft visual prompts and injects them into the visual transformer, facilitating interaction between fine-grained attribute cues and global image context. MPL is architecture-agnostic and can also be seamlessly integrated into existing multimodal GCD methods without altering their architectures. Extensive experiments demonstrate that AptM-GCD achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmarks. Beyond multimodal GCD, MPL also shows strong generalization to unimodal and unbalanced GCD settings, further validating its flexibility and effectiveness. II Related Work Generalized Category Discovery was first introduced by [6] as an extension of NCD, combining contrastive representation learning with semi-supervised clustering to discover both old and novel categories. Subsequent studies have mainly focused on improving representation learning and clustering strategies. For instance, DCCL [7] captures inter-class relations with a two-level contrastive objective, PromptCAL [21] mines reliable positives to alleviate false negatives, CiPR [22] enhances contrastive learning with hierarchical clustering. Moreover, recent multi-view clustering studies have shown that reliable cluster discovery can be further improved by exploiting complementary structures across different views, e.g., through selective cross-view topology learning [23] and cross-view graph matching[24]. Different from these clustering-based paradigms, SimGCD [8] replaces explicit clustering with a prototype classifier. Other works, such as LegoGCD [25], AllGCD [26], and ProtoGCD [27], further improve pseudo-label assignment, mitigate forgetting, or jointly model old and novel classes with shared prototypes. Multimodal Generalized Category Discovery. While early GCD methods rely on visual representations, recent studies have explored incorporating textual information to enhance category discovery. CLIP-GCD [15] is the first to leverage CLIP representations, combining image and text features to improve clustering quality. Building upon this direction, tag-based methods further exploit image-text supervision: GET [28] synthesizes pseudo textual embeddings from image features and jointly optimizes visual and textual branches with cross-modal consistency, while SpectralGCD [20] learns unified cross-modal representations by modeling images as semantic mixtures. More recently, TextGCD [16] and SSR2-GCD [17] introduce attribute-aware textual guidance. These methods typically adopt a global retrieval paradigm, retrieving tags and attributes from image-level representations and converting them into pseudo labels for novel-category discovery. However, by aligning local attributes with global category tags, they overlook the granularity mismatch between fine-grained attributes and image-level semantics, which may introduce noisy supervision and hinder the discovery of novel categories. Prompt Learning in Vision-Language Models. Prompt learning has emerged as an efficient strategy for adapting vision-language models (VLMs) to downstream recognition tasks without fully fine-tuning large-scale pretrained models. Existing approaches, such as CoOp [29], CoCoOp [30], VPT [31], MaPLe [32], and PromptSRC [33], mainly explore learnable prompts in either the textual, visual, or joint vision-language space to improve task adaptation. Recent works, such as ArGue [34] and ATPrompt [35], incorporate attribute descriptions into prompting to enrich fine-grained textual representations. However, these methods typically treat attributes as textual or visual prompts without explicit grounding in local visual regions, which may limit their effectiveness in modeling fine-grained visual evidence. It consists of two key components: Attribute-Evidence Learning (AEL) and Multimodal Prompt Learning (MPL). AEL first grounds attributes into local visual evidence through patch-grounded attribute reasoning, where patch-level visual tokens select reliable attributes and the selected attributes further guide localized discriminative evidence extraction. MPL then converts the localized attribute evidence into soft visual prompts and injects them into the visual transformer, enabling fine-grained textual cues to interact with global visual context and refine visual representations. The refined visual representations are finally fed into the standard GCD classification for discovering both old and novel categories. The fused representation is then processed by a residual prompt generator inspired by AttnRefine [45], as illustrated in Fig. 5. The generator incorporates a Gated Linear Unit (GLU) [47] and depthwise convolution [48] to selectively regulate channel-wise information flow and enhance local spatial details. Through this parallel prompt-attention design, the transformer preserves the global contextual modeling ability of standard QKV attention while biasing the refinement process toward object-specific and attribute-supported regions. By injecting attribute information into the visual transformer, the model can emphasize subtle object-specific evidence while still preserving the transformer’s ability to model global context [50]. For attribute-based multimodal GCD methods, we assess whether AptM-GCD mitigates spurious associations caused by aligning local attributes with global image representations, which can bias predictions toward incorrect classes. For tag-based methods, we examine whether grounding attributes as localized visual evidence enables effective use of rich attribute semantics, rather than treating them as additional global textual cues. These studies demonstrate that the value of attributes lies not in simply adding textual information, but in using it appropriately to guide category discovery. To ensure a fair comparison of textual resources, all attribute-related experiments in this section use the same tag and attribute dictionary provided by TextGCD [16].
