VII Conclusion In this paper, we presented AptM-GCD, a multimodal framework for harnessing fine-grained attributes as apt textual guidance in generalized category discovery. We first identified that directly treating attributes as global textual cues can introduce spurious semantic associations and mislead category discovery, especially harming novel-class discovery. To address this, AptM-GCD grounds attributes into object-aware local visual evidence via Attribute-Evidence Learning, and then injects this evidence into the visual transformer through Multimodal Prompt Learning for context-aware representation refinement. Extensive experiments on six benchmarks demonstrate that AptM-GCD achieves state-of-the-art performance. Moreover, MPL shows strong transferability to existing multimodal methods, unimodal GCD, and class-imbalanced settings. Our results highlight that the true value of attributes lies not in adding more textual cues, but in transforming them into apt guidance for category discovery. Nevertheless, challenging cases with insufficient visual evidence, such as background-camouflaged and heavily occluded objects, remain difficult for GCD due to unreliable visual-semantic correspondence. Future work will explore more robust object-centric representations and compositional visual-semantic reasoning to further advance open-world category discovery. VIII Biography Section

Partition, Refine, and Detect: Preserving Novel Category Capacity in Open-Vocabulary Object Detection Open-vocabulary object detection (OVD) expects the model trained on base classes to recognize both base and novel classes at inference. Typical methods rely on CLIP-style vision–language embeddings, yet the learned space is often biased toward base categories, with limited effective capacity preserved for novel concepts. Such a base-dominated representation can compress novel semantics, leading to semantic collapse and mis-calibrated confidence at inference. To address this issue, we present PR-OVD, a partition-and-refine framework that explicitly reserves capacity for novel categories and strengthens category separation, while being seamlessly integrated into different detector architectures. Specifically, PR-OVD first performs coarse partitioning to build global divisions for base, novel, and an explicit background partition in both visual and textual modalities, preventing object-irrelevant embeddings from leaking into category-specific representations. It then applies category-level refinement within each partition to sharpen decision boundaries and alleviate the lack of fine-grained region-level pretraining in CLIP. To further provide reliable visual anchors for novel categories, we design a cognitively inspired Structure Prompt (SP) that encodes both egocentric attributes and allocentric context, facilitating stable partition-and-refine learning. Extensive experiments on two OVD benchmarks show that PR-OVD delivers an average 6.5% proportional improvement on novel categories over the state-of-the-art methods. Notably, PR-OVD also benefits other open-vocabulary tasks, including segmentation and classification, further confirming its effectiveness and generality. I Introduction Traditional vision methods [1, 2] rely on a fixed set of predefined categories, limiting their applicability in real-world scenarios where new concepts frequently appear. Open-vocabulary understanding addresses this limitation by leveraging language information, such as category names or image captions. This paradigm has been applied to various tasks, including segmentation [3, 4], object detection [5], video understanding [6, 7], and autonomous driving [8]. In this work, we focus on Open-Vocabulary Object Detection (OVD) [9], which extends conventional paradigm to recognize objects whose categories are unseen during training. Unlike closed-vocabulary detection, where all categories are learned with instance-level annotations, OVD aims to recognize novel categories without corresponding visual supervision by leveraging semantic knowledge from language. Most existing OVD methods optimize detection loss using only base categories during training, while at inference time the model is required to recognize both base and novel categories [10, 5]. This misalignment between the training objective and the testing protocol introduces a fundamental optimization inconsistency. As training progresses, the embedding space is progressively reshaped to maximize separability among base classes only. Without inter-class constraints, nearby base categories tend to spread apart to occupy larger regions of the embedding space, implicitly compressing the representational capacity available to novel categories. At inference time, this imbalance manifests as a clear semantic collapsing phenomenon as shown in the left of Fig.1: novel category clusters are absorbed into semantically similar base clusters, lacking sufficient geometric margin. As a result, base predictions become over-confident, while novel categories consistently receive lower confidence scores, leading to severe calibration imbalance. To address this, we propose the Partition-and-Refine OVD (PR-OVD). Its core insight is to explicitly partition the embedding space to reserve dedicated regions for categories unseen in training but required at test time, preventing semantic absorption by dominant base classes. Within each partition, category-level refinement is then applied to further reinforce inter-category constraints. PR-OVD establishes clear decision boundaries between base and novel categories through an architecture-agnostic framework (as shown in Fig. 1, right), effectively mitigating semantic collapse and calibration imbalance. This design is inspired by human visual cognition [11, 12]. Humans perceive objects hierarchically: they first partition them into known and unknown, then perform fine-grained recognition within each group [11]. Importantly, unknown objects are maintained as structured representations rather than collapsed into known categories. Specifically, PR-OVD consists of two components: I. Coarse partition establishes a global spatial division in both visual and textual spaces by modeling base and novel prototypes, and additionally introduce a background prototype to account for the large number of background proposals inherent in object detection. Prototype-level contrastive learning is then applied to enforce clear global partitions. In the visual modality, two challenges emerge: (1) Prototype construction: novel classes lack real visual samples. Traditional pseudo-labeling methods leverage external captions [13, 14] or MLLMs to mine potential novel regions, yet such supervision is inherently noisy, yielding inaccurate region-word alignment [15]. We propose Structure Prompt (SP), a category-wise template that enables the LLM to generate multi-dimensional enhanced descriptions by combining intrinsic attributes with contextual cues. The descriptions then guide a generative model to synthesize a few representative novel images for visual prototype construction and subsequent category-level refinement. SP shifts from mining to generation, unlocking a controllable pathway for constructing reliable visual prototypes of novel categories. (2) Embedding learning: novel-background semantic overlap risks boundary confusion. We adopt asymmetric prototype learning in visual contrastive learning, where reliable relationships between base–novel and base–background partitions are established, while the novel–background relationship is not explicitly constrained due to unreliable supervision. II. Category-level Refinement, which performs bidirectional, region-level alignment within each partition, reinforcing inter-class constraints and compensating for the absence of region-level pretraining in CLIP [16, 17], which is crucial for detection tasks. Our main contributions are as follows: We identify and analyze a structural optimization bias in OVD, showing that the training–testing misalignment leads to semantic collapsing and calibration imbalance in embedding geometry. We propose PR-OVD, a partition-and-refine framework inspired by human visual cognition that simultaneously reserves dedicated regions for novel categories and performs fine-grained category alignment, establishing clear base–novel decision boundaries in an architecture-agnostic manner. We design a generative pseudo-labeling strategy, structure prompt (SP), to generate proxy visual features of novel categories. SP incorporates both egocentric (attributes) and allocentric (environment relations) perspectives, serving as visual prototype of novel category. Beyond advancing open-vocabulary detection, our work serves as a generalizable paradigm that transfers seamlessly to other ov-tasks such as segmentation and multi-label classification, consistently delivering significant gains. Extensive experiments validate the superiority and broad applicability of our framework, offering a fresh perspective for open vocabulary understanding. II Related Work Open-Vocabulary Object Detection. Existing OVD methods can be broadly categorized into CLIP-based and pseudo-label-based approaches. CLIP-based methods transfer CLIP’s open-vocabulary capabilities directly into detection frameworks [10, 18], or enhance CLIP with region-level perception through retraining [19, 20]. In contrast, pseudo-label-based methods aim to mine region-word pairs for novel categories, providing supervision signals for training. For example, RALF [21] assigns pseudo-labels by computing region-word similarity, further refining them through retrieval-based hard negative mining [22]. SAS-Det [18] decouples pseudo-label prediction for novel classes from base-class classification via a teacher-student framework. Moreover, ProxyDet [23] observes that novel categories often lie near the convex hull formed by base categories in the CLIP embedding space and synthesizes proxy novel classes through classwise mixup. However, pseudo-label-based strategies introduce noisy supervision by directly optimizing detectors with generated novel samples. Different from these approaches, PR-OVD does not recover missing supervision through pseudo labels. Instead, we propose the structure prompt which serves as a structured visual-anchor construction mechanism that generates category-relevant multi-scale visual anchors for novel categories, and constructs novel-category visual anchors to explicitly reserve representation space and performs partition-and-refine learning to improve base–novel separability. Vision-Language Alignment in Images and Regions. Vision-language pre-training has led to the development of models that learn well-aligned representations between images and text, especially under unsupervised or weakly supervised settings. Early methods such as MoCo [24] and SimCLR [25] perform instance-level discrimination on entire images, while CLIP extends it to cross-modal alignment using global image–text pairs. However, , such image-level paradigms lack the fine-grained, region-level semantics required for dense prediction, motivating recent advances in region-aware alignment. For example, DetCo [26] introduces self-supervised region-level objectives to capture structural relationships among image patches. DetCLIP [27] constructs proposal-text contrastive pairs atop CLIP to enhance region-level cross-modal alignment. Our PR-OVD implicitly learns region-word alignment through category-level refinement. By leveraging structure-prompt-guided novel features, it achieves fine-grained engagement with minimal additional cost. III Method Open-vocabulary object detection generalizes to novel classes by leveraging an open concept space and a class-agnostic region proposal network, reformulating the final classification stage as a region-to-text similarity task via CLIP’s cross-modal alignment. In general, base classes [FORMULA] refer to the categories with annotations available during training, while novel classes [FORMULA] that lack such supervision during training but required to be recognized at test time ( [FORMULA] ). Furthermore, we follow protocols of recent OVD methods [28, 18, 21, 15], the category names of novel classes [FORMULA] are available as semantic information, while their instance-level annotations are removed during training. At inference time, the model needs to detect objects from [FORMULA] . To mitigate the optimization misalignment between training and testing, the training process should reserve independent representational space for novel categories [29]. Therefore, our PR-OVD adopt a partition-and-refine framework, as illustrated in Fig.2. By enforcing structural separation among base, novel, and background partitions, the model prevents novel representations from being absorbed by dominant base clusters. It also refines category alignment within these constraints to sharpen inter-category boundaries. To build novel-class prototype, we further design a structure prompt to support representation learning for novel categories within PR-OVD. This module establishes a global spatial division in both language and visual embeddings, inspired by human cognition, which first distinguishes known from unknown [11] before fine-grained recognition. It explicitly carves out dedicated regions for base, novel, and background categories, preventing the embedding space from being monopolized by base classes and promoting separated high-level structures. Vision space partition. Similar to the textual modality, we construct base, novel, and background prototypes in the visual embedding space to establish partition-level geometry. However, unlike text embeddings, visual representations suffer from missing annotations for novel categories and semantic overlap with background regions, which makes direct prototype learning non-trivial. 1) Prototype construction. Base prototypes are computed by averaging region embeddings from ground-truth boxes and their matched positive proposals, while background prototypes are formed from negative proposals defined with respect to ground-truth annotations. The challenge arises for novel categories that lack bounding-box annotations and thus reliable proposals. Existing pseudo-labeling strategies, including mining novel-category samples with vision–language models or external caption datasets, often introduce noisy supervision and inaccurate region–word alignment [15]. To obtain cleaner visual anchors for the novel partition, we propose a generative pseudo-labeling strategy termed structure prompt (SP). SP leverages LLM-expanded (GPT-4o [31]) descriptions to guide a diffusion model (SD-3.5 [32]) in synthesizing representative novel images, incorporating both intrinsic object attributes (e.g., shape, color, material) and contextual cues (e.g., scene context and co-occurring objects) [33]. We extract multi-scale features of the generated images by interpolating activation maps from multiple layers of ViT-L/14 [5] and fuse them via a Feature Pyramid Network (FPN), relying solely on the inter-class semantic structure of generated images rather than their visual fidelity. 2) Asymmetric prototype learning. Another critical issue arises from the semantic overlap between novel objects and background regions. Since novel instances lack annotations, many of their regions are implicitly treated as background during training. As a result, enforcing negative contrast between novel and background prototypes may contaminate the novel partition and blur boundaries, as evidenced in Tab.IV. To mitigate this effect, we adopt an asymmetric prototype learning strategy in partition-level visual prototype learning [34], where contrastive optimization is performed only on reliable base–novel and base–background relationships, while the novel–background relationship is left unconstrained due to the lack of reliable novel-category annotations. We evaluate our method on two widely used benchmarks for OVD: OV-COCO and OV-LVIS. OV-COCO, introduced by OV-RCNN [9], divides the 65 object categories in COCO [45] into 48 base and 17 novel categories. The performance is primarily assessed using box Average Precision (AP) at an IoU threshold of 0.50. OV-LVIS, proposed by ViLD [44], contains 1,203 long-tailed categories from LVIS v1.0 [46], with 337 rare categories designated as novel classes and the rest as common or frequent. The evaluation focuses on the mean mask AP for the novel (rare) categories. We further evaluate our PR-OVD on other open-vocabulary tasks, including semantic segmentation and multi-label classification. For segmentation, following MaskAdapter [47], we train on COCO-Stuff [48] (118K images, 171 categories) and evaluate on ADE20K (A-150, A-847) [49] and Pascal-Context (PC-59, PC-459) [50] using mean Intersection-over-Union (mIoU). For classification, we adopt the RAM [51] protocol and validate on NUS-WIDE [52] (925 seen, 81 unseen categories), reporting top-3 precision (P@3), F1@3, and mean Average Precision (mAP). Implementation details. Following prior work [5, 40], we adopt Mask R-CNN [1] with a Feature Pyramid Network (FPN) [53] as the detection head and ViT-L/14 [19, 20] as the visual backbone. We freeze the CLIP encoder while training only the Mask R-CNN parameters. PR-OVD utilizes the 6th, 10th, 14th, and 23rd layers of ViT-L/14 to construct visual semantics, corresponding to relative image scales of 1/3.5, 1/7, 1/14, and 1/28, respectively [5]. These components follow the standard detector configuration for ViT-based object detection and are not introduced by PR-OVD. As a detector-agnostic framework, PR-OVD can be seamlessly integrated into different detector architectures without introducing additional structural modifications. The detector is trained on 8 NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 GPU with a batch size of 8 per GPU. We train for 3 epochs on OV-COCO and 48 epochs on OV-LVIS, using a fixed input resolution of 896×896. The AdamW optimizer is used with a learning rate of 1e-4 and a weight decay of 0.1. Quantitative comparison with SoTAs. These results validate the effectiveness of PR-OVD in reserving dedicated space for novel categories during training and reinforcing inter-class constraints to improve performance. Qualitative comparison with SoTAs. We compare our method with CLIPSelf [5] and RALF [21] by visualizing the top 90% of attention from each model’s final layer overlaid on the original images. In contrast, PR-OVD jointly constructs a global partitioned space, reserving regions for novel and background categories and enforcing inter-class constraints, thereby suppresses spurious, object-irrelevant attention while preserving fine-grained, object-centered signals. Specifically, the coarse partition establishes a global semantic structure that reserves dedicated space during training for categories unseen in training but required at test time, preventing them from being absorbed by dominant base classes. The category-level refinement then sharpens intra-partition structures by enforcing inter-class constraints and enhancing decision boundaries. To evaluate the cross-domain and cross-vocabulary generalization of our approach, we directly transfer the detector trained on OV-LVIS to COCO and Objects365 without fine-tuning, replacing only the test-time vocabulary. Visualization on OVD task. To qualitatively evaluate our method, we compare it with two leading baselines on OV-COCO: CLIPSelf [5] and RALF [21]. As shown in Fig.8, prior methods commonly suffer from: (1) missed detections of novel category due to occlusion, viewpoint variation (e.g., bus), or weak visual signals (e.g., skateboard), and (2) confused detections between novel and base classes due to high visual similarity(e.g., skis vs. snowboard). In contrast, our method alleviates these issues by explicitly reserving dedicated regions for novel categories and refining category-level geometry within the partitioned space. This leads to more robust detection, especially in visually ambiguous scenarios. Failure case analysis. We analyze two representative challenging scenarios commonly encountered in OVD, as shown in Fig. 9: tiny novel-category objects and novel objects in crowded scenes. Tiny objects provide limited visual evidence and are easily overwhelmed by background patterns, causing missed detections. Crowded scenes introduce severe instance interference and ambiguous object boundaries, leading to false positives or localization errors. These failures reflect inherent challenges of OVD, where novel categories lack direct region-level supervision. Despite these challenges, PR-OVD still achieves more robust predictions than CLIPSelf [5]. Future work will explore stronger multi-scale representations, object-centric generation, and instance-level reasoning to further improve challenging open-vocabulary scenarios. V Conclusions In this work, we propose a Partition-and-Refine framework for open-vocabulary object detection (PR-OVD), explicitly reserving dedicated capacity for novel categories to prevent semantic collapse and calibration imbalance. As its core, PR-OVD leverages a coarse partition and category-level refinement module to prevent novel representations from being absorbed by dominant base clusters and sharpen inter-class boundary. Additionally, we design a cognitively inspired structure prompt that generates visual cues to enhance novel category representation. Beyond detection, PR-OVD naturally transfers to other open-vocabulary tasks, achieving performance improvements while offering a fresh perspective for open vocabulary understanding.

Selective Surgical Action-Center Localization: Retaining Localization Gains through Supervised Scoring Surgical action-center localization requires both an accurate reference point and a decision about whether to report it. When frames with and without a reportable center are mixed, the benefit of improved localization depends on which correct candidates survive selection. We present a selective localization pipeline combining heatmap and coordinate supervision with a logistic-regression scorer. The scorer learns to identify predictions with a reportable center and a localization error within a specified tolerance. The internal evaluation uses 5,000 frames from 50 surgical sources, five source-grouped folds and two random seeds. Matched locator and scoring comparisons track correct candidates and their rejection. At an 80% acceptance quota per source and a tolerance of 0.10 times the image diagonal, our method retains 46.08 correct outputs per 100 inputs. The baseline locator with the same scoring approach retains 44.20. The gain is 1.88 (descriptive 95% source-paired bootstrap interval, 0.94 to 2.79). Under entropy-based selection, increased rejection of correct predictions offsets the higher supply of correct predictions on average. For the coordinate-supervised locator, supervised scoring reduces these rejections from 6.15 to 2.99 per 100 inputs. Evaluating retained correct outputs reveals whether a selection rule preserves or erodes an improvement in localization. 1 Introduction Surgical video analysis provides information about operative activity for computer-assisted surgery [1, 2]. Camera assistance adds a spatial requirement: the region of interest must be located within the field of view [3]. Surgical action-center localization estimates a task-related reference point whose displacement from the image center describes camera framing. The center of surgical action (COSA) dataset released by Ebrahimzadeh et al.11 1 A. Ebrahimzadeh, N. Esmaeili, P. Horvath, M. Ghadimi and J. Hagenah, CDS-COSA-Dataset-2026, Zenodo, 2026. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20627949 provides point annotations for studying this task. Within a surgical source, frames with an annotated center (POINT) occur alongside frames annotated as non-reportable (NA) (Fig. 1). A localization system must therefore decide whether to report each predicted point. An accepted point is correct when a reportable center exists and the predicted coordinate lies within a specified distance tolerance. Errors arise either from reporting a coordinate for a frame without a valid center or from placing it too far from an existing center. We therefore retain both annotation states and fix the acceptance budget, defined as the fraction of inputs retained. Counting correct outputs over all inputs evaluates reportability and localization accuracy together. Heatmap learning and coordinate supervision provide complementary ways to train a point locator. Heatmaps retain the spatial organization of the image, while coordinate losses directly penalize displacement of the predicted point. Integral regression connects these representations through a differentiable spatial expectation [4], and subsequent work examines bias in this coordinate readout [5]. Coordinate errors can thus guide learning through the heatmap. Related work on facial landmarks has also combined location estimation with uncertainty and visibility prediction, as in LUVLi [6]. Output selection requires a score that orders predictions by their suitability for acceptance. Selective prediction formalizes the trade-off between the fraction of predictions retained and their error [7, 8]. Medical image quality-control research likewise evaluates confidence scores through the predictions they retain or prioritize for correction [9, 10]. Comparisons must account for prediction quality as well as confidence ranking, with metrics aligned to the intended acceptance decision [9, 11]. For surgical action centers, we therefore ask whether a larger supply of correct coordinates translates into more correct reported points. At a common acceptance budget, the answer depends on both that supply and the correct candidates rejected by the scoring rule. We present a selective surgical action-center localization pipeline that combines coordinate-supervised localization with learned success scoring. The locator uses heatmap and coordinate supervision with an expectation-based readout to generate a candidate point. A separately fitted logistic-regression scorer then uses image features and prediction descriptors to rank these candidates. The training target marks a prediction as successful when its frame is reportable and its coordinate meets the distance tolerance. The scorer is trained on predictions from the frozen locator. At the prescribed acceptance quota, the highest-scoring candidates within each source are retained, and the remaining points are withheld. Our evaluation examines these two stages through controlled comparisons on 5,000 original frames from 50 surgical sources, with five source-grouped folds and two random seeds. We compare locators under the same scoring approach and compare scoring approaches with the locator fixed. This design relates output changes to correct candidate supply and selection losses. Entropy-based selection rejects enough additional correct predictions to offset the improved locator’s larger supply of correct points on average. Supervised scoring retains a positive output gain at the same acceptance quota. Source-paired analysis and alternative scoring comparisons characterize the gain, while fixed development thresholds reveal how acceptance varies across sources. Our contributions are twofold. We develop a selective localization pipeline for surgical action centers in mixed reportable and non-reportable frames. The pipeline combines coordinate supervision with a scorer trained on the joint reportability and accuracy criterion, aligning selection with the output being evaluated. We quantify how correct candidate supply and selection losses determine the output gain. Matched comparisons identify a mismatch between improved localization and entropy-based selection. Supervised scoring retains a positive output gain at the same acceptance budget. 2 Related work EndoNet jointly learns surgical phases and instrument presence from laparoscopic videos [12]. Rendezvous recognizes instrument–verb–target triplets, and CholecTriplet2021 benchmarks this fine-grained description of surgical actions [13, 14]. Camera assistance requires a spatial reference within the image [3]. The COSA dataset addresses this need through action-center coordinates and NA annotations. LUVLi jointly estimates facial landmark position, uncertainty and visibility through likelihood training [6]. Gu et al. account for instance size and visibility, then learn network-specific confidence adjustments with a post-hoc Calibrated ConfidenceNet (CCNet) [20]. In our surgical setting, reportability refers to the annotated presence of a valid action center. The success target combines that status with the predicted point meeting a distance tolerance. Uncertainty estimation offers several sources of reliability information, including data uncertainty and uncertainty in the fitted model [21, 22]. Calibration evaluates how confidence agrees with predictive accuracy [23], while dataset shift can change the quality of uncertainty estimates [24]. Output selection evaluates these scores through the errors remaining after low-scoring predictions are rejected. SelectiveNet learns prediction and selection jointly under a coverage constraint [8]. Studies of failure detection and pretrained classifiers also show that the predictor, training regime and evaluation protocol affect confidence comparisons [25, 26]. For action-center localization, we fit the scorer to a frozen locator and compare accepted coordinates at common quotas. Medical image quality control connects prediction uncertainty to the quality of a complete output. Mehrtash et al. study calibration and predictive uncertainty in medical image segmentation [27]. Geißler et al. show that structure size can confound correlations between uncertainty and segmentation quality [28]. Zenk et al. compare failure-detection methods with risk–coverage analysis and identify confidence aggregation as a major factor in performance [9]. SegQC predicts voxel-level errors and derives quality estimates that can prioritize corrections [10]. Uncertainty-aware quality prediction combines uncertainty maps with predicted segmentations and, in one formulation, the input image [29]. Wundram et al. use split conformal prediction to estimate ranges of segmentation performance [30]. Fournel et al. estimate image-specific segmentation difficulty from inter-observer agreement to inform quality thresholds [31]. Our target is a reported action center that satisfies both reportability and coordinate accuracy. Supervised confidence models estimate output quality directly from prediction features. Corbière et al. learn an estimate of true-class probability for failure prediction [32], and CCNet learns adjustments specific to a fitted pose estimator [20]. Our scorer combines image and heatmap features with the candidate coordinate and a reportability cue. Instance-preserving graded semantic reporting for surgical action triplets Complete-or-reject reporting of surgical action triplets can discard a correctly identified instrument and action when the target is uncertain. We introduce instance-preserving graded semantic reporting, which separates instance selection from the choice of semantic detail. Each selected instance retains its predicted mask and labels while hierarchical correctness scores guide instrument (I), instrument-verb (IV), or complete instrument-verb-target (IVT) reporting. The utility-increment rule DELTA weighs the expected gain from finer reporting against its error cost. We compare three decision rules on 5,641 test frames from eight surgical videos using fixed predictions and scores. At the 10% development calibration target, DELTA retains correct partial reports for 80.0% of candidates rejected by a matched complete-or-reject baseline (5,329/6,662). Adding IV increases source-normalized weighted correct-report yield by 19.13 to 23.13 per 100 frames across all three rules relative to separately recalibrated I/IVT controls. Weighted reporting risk changes by -0.77 to +1.01 percentage points, with complete correct-triplet counts unchanged or reduced. Graded reporting makes partial surgical predictions available as localized descriptions, with an explicit trade-off between report utility and completeness. 1 Introduction Surgical action triplets describe an interaction through the instrument, the action it performs and its anatomical target (Nwoye et al., 2022). Triplet detection adds spatial localization (Nwoye, Yu, et al., 2023), while triplet segmentation links each interaction to a pixel-level instrument mask, as formalized in CholecTriplet-Seg (Alabi et al., 2026). This association makes it possible to distinguish concurrent actions and relate semantic predictions to visible instruments. Yet the fields attached to an instance can differ in reliability. In Fig. 1(a), a hook and its dissecting action are correctly identified, whereas the predicted target is incorrect. The instrument-action pair still describes part of the observed interaction. In Fig. 1(b), the instrument alone is correctly recognized. These examples motivate a reporting problem: deciding how much semantic detail to attach to a selected spatial instance. Choosing a report determines which predicted fields the recipient sees. Reporting every complete triplet exposes all predicted fields, including uncertain verbs or targets. A complete-or-reject policy can withhold a prediction with low confidence in its full triplet, taking its usable components out of the report as well. Instrument-only output retains the selected instances but omits their actions even when those actions are reliable. An intermediate instrument-verb report offers a useful alternative when target identity is uncertain. Choosing among these outputs calls for separate decisions about which instances enter the report and how much detail each instance carries. Selective prediction provides an established foundation for choosing which outputs to report (Pugnana et al., 2024). Confidence-based rejection allows a trained classifier to trade coverage for accuracy (Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2017; Cattelan and Silva, 2024; Granese et al., 2021). Hierarchical recognition extends the available choices by allowing a prediction to move to a broader semantic category (Valmadre, 2022). Deng et al. (2012) formulated this accuracy-specificity trade-off and introduced Dual Accuracy Reward Trade-off Search (DARTS). Goren et al. (2024) developed hierarchical selective classification, including inference rules and hierarchical risk-coverage evaluation. These studies establish that uncertainty can be expressed through the specificity of an output (Anani et al., 2024). For surgical action reports, we consider an instrument (I), an instrument-verb pair (IV) and a complete instrument-verb-target triplet (IVT), each attached to the same predicted instrument mask. Spatially grounded reports bring an additional requirement: semantic correctness must remain tied to a particular instance (Oksuz et al., 2023). A report can fail through incorrect localization, competition for the same instrument, or an error in a displayed field. Its evaluation therefore depends on both the selected report set and the fields shown within each report. Changing the retained set can alter matching and correct-report yield before semantic granularity is considered. Holding that set fixed allows the contribution of semantic detail to be examined on the same spatial instances. We introduce instance-preserving graded semantic reporting to select the semantic detail attached to each admitted instrument instance. A base selection step establishes the candidate set and its ordering. A subsequent reporting step chooses I, IV or IVT for each selected candidate, retaining its mask and the predicted labels of its displayed fields. The framework uses hierarchical correctness scores to decide when additional semantic detail is worth reporting. We examine threshold-based selection (THR), an adaptation of DARTS, and the utility-increment rule DELTA under this shared interface. DELTA evaluates the expected gain from a finer report against its additional error cost, using I as the reference. The intermediate IV level lets the report retain an action description when confidence in the complete triplet is low. We compare three-level reporting against separately recalibrated I/IVT controls, sharing predictions, correctness scores and the same admitted instances (base support). At the 10% development calibration target, adding IV increases weighted correct-report yield by 19.13 to 23.13 per 100 frames on the test set. Yield is normalized by video source; each rule also shows a positive gain in all eight evaluated videos. Comparisons with complete-or-reject output establish how partial reports retain usable semantics among rejected candidates. Instance-level analyses identify the retained semantics and how these choices affect complete correct-triplet output and observed reporting risk. The study makes two contributions: An instance-preserving reporting framework for surgical action triplets that separates base instance selection from semantic granularity, supports I, IV and IVT outputs, and evaluates their joint spatial and semantic correctness. Evidence that partial reports retain usable semantics among rejected candidates and that the intermediate IV level increases correct-report yield across the evaluated rules. Recalibrated controls and instance-level analyses establish this contribution and explain its effects on complete records and reporting risk. Section 2 reviews surgical triplet prediction and selective reporting. Section 3 defines the framework, and Section 4 describes the evaluation protocol. Section 5 presents the results, followed by discussion and conclusions in Sections 6 and 7. 2 Related work Triplet recognition models use the dependencies among instruments, verbs and targets to identify interactions within an image (Chen et al., 2023; Gui and Wang, 2024; Zou et al., 2025; Jeon et al., 2026). Tripnet guides verb and target recognition with instrument activation maps and learns component associations through a trainable interaction space (Nwoye et al., 2020). Rendezvous develops attention mechanisms for component recognition and models their relationships through self- and cross-attention (Nwoye et al., 2022). These methods predict component labels and their combinations, providing structured descriptions of surgical activity. Spatial grounding assigns these interactions to individual instruments (Lin et al., 2022; Pei et al., 2025). CholecTriplet2022 benchmarks triplet detection through instrument bounding boxes and their associated action labels (Nwoye, Yu, et al., 2023). Sharma et al. (2023b) combine instrument-aware target embeddings with an interaction graph to associate localized instruments with verbs and targets. At the pixel level, Alabi et al. (2026) introduce CholecTriplet-Seg and TargetFusionNet, which combines instance queries with weak anatomy priors to improve target prediction. The segmentation formulation couples an instrument mask with its action and target. Our reporting framework starts from such instance predictions and chooses the semantic fields displayed for each retained mask. Selective prediction treats acceptance as part of the prediction problem (Wu et al., 2024). Confidence-based selection trades the fraction of accepted samples against their error rate (Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2017; Ding et al., 2023), while SelectiveNet jointly learns prediction and rejection (Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2019). Confidence calibration addresses a related requirement: how closely predicted probabilities reflect empirical correctness (Minderer et al., 2021). Guo et al. (2017) show that temperature scaling can improve this correspondence for neural classifiers. For structured reports, the event being scored must also be specified, since correctness depends on the combination of fields being displayed (Gupta and Ramdas, 2022; Kuzucu et al., 2025). Hierarchical prediction adds choices at different levels of semantic specificity (Valmadre, 2022). Deng et al. (2012) formulate recognition as maximizing specificity reward subject to an accuracy requirement and introduce DARTS to choose among hierarchy nodes. Goren et al. (2024) formalize hierarchical selective risk and coverage and develop inference rules for moving from specific predictions to broader ancestors. Their Climbing rule follows the path from the most likely leaf towards the root until the confidence threshold is met. The selected hierarchy level determines how specific an accepted prediction is (Cao et al., 2024). These approaches provide the basis for choosing I, IV or IVT on a fixed reporting path for each selected instrument instance. Under nested correctness scores and an instrument-level fallback, the threshold rule THR is equivalent to Climbing on this path. Our DARTS comparison adapts its decision rule to the same scores, report weights and development calibration procedure used by the other rules. The hierarchy here changes the fields displayed for an existing prediction, while its mask and labels remain fixed. The common reporting interface lets us compare semantic specificity while keeping spatial instance retention fixed. Triplet evaluation distinguishes individual components, combinations of fields and spatially grounded interactions. The ivtmetrics protocol reports average precision for individual components, instrument-verb and instrument-target pairs, and complete triplets (Nwoye, Alapatt, et al., 2023). Component-level scores describe recognition of each semantic category; pair and triplet scores assess increasingly specific combinations (Sharma et al., 2023a; Li et al., 2023). Triplet segmentation adds pixel-level grounding, requiring semantic correctness together with instrument localization (Alabi et al., 2026). These evaluations characterize predicted content at predefined semantic levels. Graded reporting introduces a further choice: the fields displayed for one instance can differ from those displayed for another. Selective risk-coverage evaluation measures error among accepted predictions as acceptance changes (Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2017; Traub et al., 2024; Franc et al., 2023), while hierarchical coverage accounts for the specificity of selected nodes (Goren et al., 2024). A grounded report is correct when its mask matches a ground-truth instance uniquely and every displayed field agrees with that instance. An IV report can therefore be correct even when its full triplet would contain an incorrect target. Joint report correctness complements component metrics by retaining the association among the displayed fields and their spatial instance. We measure weighted correct-report yield together with reporting risk and complete correct-triplet output. Comparisons account for the retained instance sets and use fixed predictions and scores to distinguish the effects of instance support, available report levels and decision rules. Once an instrument instance has been admitted, its identity can remain available while the report selects how much action and target detail to display. This separation gives partial predictions an explicit output form and a joint correctness criterion tied to their instrument masks. At the primary test configuration, DELTA retained correct partial descriptions for 80.0% of the candidates rejected by the matched complete-or-reject policy (Fig. 3). This connects selective and hierarchical prediction (Section 2) to reports whose semantic correctness remains tied to a specific spatial instance. The intermediate IV level provides a useful option when the evidence supports an instrument-action pair more strongly than its complete triplet. Joint correctness requires every displayed field to agree with the same matched instance, so adding a target introduces another condition. An IV report can retain a correct action description when that condition fails, as illustrated in Fig. 8(a). Utility increased for every tested rule-target pair and corresponding source comparison after the restricted controls were recalibrated (Table 3; Figs. 4 and 5). With masks, labels, scores and base support fixed, these gains arise from the reporting menu and its calibrated selection. The menu supplies an intermediate action description; the correctness scores and decision rule determine when that description is selected. The value of a partial report also depends on what its recipient needs to recover. Field-fraction weights give a correct IV description more credit than a correct I description, while reserving full credit for a correct triplet. The field analysis makes the associated completeness cost concrete. Relative to all-IVT output, DELTA withheld 3,078 incorrect fields and 4,444 correct fields at the primary configuration (Fig. 7b). Coarsening can therefore remove an erroneous statement or leave a correct detail unreported, as the examples in Fig. 8 show. A task that can use instrument-action descriptions may benefit from retaining them; a task requiring complete records must also account for omitted targets. The admitted candidates, complete labels, correctness scores and rule parameters specify each reporting decision. A recipient with these inputs and the base ordering can reproduce the selection. Choosing the available report levels and choosing a decision rule address different parts of the design. The IV option increased utility across THR, DELTA and the DARTS adaptation, while their operating points differed in observed risk and complete-triplet yield. At the three primary V-selected operating points, DELTA had the highest utility and risk. In the post-hoc finite-grid comparison under a 10% observed test-risk ceiling, DARTS achieved the greatest utility (Fig. 6). These comparisons make the intended operating conditions central to rule selection. Report utility, weighted reporting risk and complete correct-triplet output describe complementary consequences of the selection. Tracking instance support alongside them identifies how much of the change comes from retaining instances or changing their descriptions. Source transfer makes calibration part of the reuse decision (Ovadia et al., 2019). With the predictor, scorer and reporting parameters fixed, observed reporting risk exceeded the development target in all nine val configurations (Table 4). At the primary 10% target, observed risks ranged from 16.38% to 17.82%. The realized error level depends on the evaluated population, including the admitted instances and the correctness of their displayed fields. Applying the framework to another population therefore calls for target-source evaluation of both instance admission and semantic selection (Huseljic et al., 2025). The CholecTriplet-Seg evaluation provides this assessment for fixed Mask2Former predictions. The development analyses in Table 5 further identify matching and utility weighting as explicit choices to examine when adapting the reporting objective. Comparing correctness scores across additional predictors and prospectively reserved sources would clarify which score properties sustain the IV level’s contribution to report utility. Holding the reporting menu fixed would allow these comparisons to examine how source adaptation changes reporting outcomes. A complementary study could estimate report weights from a specified downstream task, including the costs of wrong displayed fields and omitted correct fields. Comparing these weights with the field-fraction objective would connect report selection to that task’s measured requirements. 7 Conclusion We introduced instance-preserving graded semantic reporting for surgical action triplets, separating instance admission from the semantic detail displayed for each retained mask. The framework selects I, IV or IVT using hierarchical correctness scores while preserving predicted masks, displayed label values and base ordering. On fixed CholecTriplet-Seg predictions, matched complete-or-reject comparisons showed that graded outputs retain correct partial descriptions among rejected candidates. Separately recalibrated two-level controls established the contribution of IV, with higher report utility across all tested rules and development targets. Instance-level analyses traced these gains to changes in displayed semantics and their trade-off with complete correct-triplet output. Choosing a reporting policy requires joint consideration of utility, observed risk and complete-record requirements on the intended source. Keeping partial descriptions attached to their instruments makes it possible to assess semantic yield and completeness on a common set of instances. Multimedia (cs.MM): Large-area Spatially Aligned Anchors Extended Reality (XR) technologies, including Virtual Reality (VR) and Augmented Reality (AR), offer immersive experiences merging digital content with the real world. Achieving precise spatial tracking over large areas is a critical challenge in XR development. This paper addresses the drift issue, caused by small errors accumulating over time leading to a discrepancy between the real and virtual worlds. Tackling this issue is crucial for co-located XR experiences where virtual and physical elements interact seamlessly. Building upon the locally accurate spatial anchors, we propose a solution that extends this accuracy to larger areas by exploiting an external, drift-corrected tracking method as a ground truth. During the preparation stage, anchors are placed inside the headset and inside the external tracking method simultaneously, yielding 3D-3D correspondences. Both anchor clouds, and thus tracking methods, are aligned using a suitable cloud registration method during the operational stage. Our method enhances user comfort and mobility by leveraging the headset’s built-in tracking capabilities during the operational stage, allowing standalone functionality. Additionally, this method can be used with any XR headset that supports spatial anchors and with any drift-free external tracking method. Empirical evaluation demonstrates the system’s effectiveness in aligning virtual content with the real world and expanding the accurate tracking area. In addition, the alignment is evaluated by comparing the camera poses of both tracking methods. This approach may benefit a wide range of industries and applications, including manufacturing and construction, education, and entertainment. 1 Introduction Extended Reality (XR) technologies, encompassing Virtual Reality (VR) and Augmented Reality (AR), are becoming increasingly popular for creating immersive experiences that blend the real world with digital content. From entertainment and gaming to education, healthcare, and manufacturing, VR and AR offer unique opportunities to immerse users in digital environments and augment their perception of the real world. However, as these technologies continue to evolve, the challenge of achieving precise and consistent spatial tracking over large areas remains a critical challenge. Accomplishing this in a practical manner adds further complexity. Using our suggested solution, Figure 1 presents two practical examples demonstrating how virtual scenes seamlessly integrate with reality. One showcases an artistic performance, while the other features utility infrastructure maintenance. Two tracking paradigms exist: outside-in tracking and inside-out tracking. With outside-in tracking, external devices/sensors such as cameras and optical base stations determine the pose of items of interest. Although outside-in tracking is very accurate, these technologies are often expensive and difficult to scale to large areas. On the other hand, inside-out tracking, which utilizes the cameras on the device itself, presents a more scalable solution that enhances user mobility without the need for additional sensors. However, the accuracy of these systems is limited by drift [12], caused by small errors accumulating over time. For larger areas, the drift will become too large to achieve co-location. Other techniques try to solve this by adding many markers and hardware sensors [17], which are both impractical. Preferably, this is solved within the standalone headset itself, by adding only a few to no markers at all. The objective of this paper is to address the issue of drift within the headset. Spatial anchors [21] mitigate this problem on a small scale by correcting drift on self-defined reference points within a limited area. The spatial anchors are most effective within an area of 3 m from the origin of the anchors. The aim of this paper is to extend this accuracy to larger areas. The proposed method achieves this by leveraging spatial anchors and an external, drift-corrected tracking method to establish anchors both externally and within the headset. These anchors serve as reference points to align the tracking methods with each other. Accurate tracking is crucial to integrate virtual and real-world elements in co-located XR experiences seamlessly. Virtual and physical elements coexist in co-located environments, allowing users to interact with both simultaneously. Ensuring a consistent mapping between the physical and virtual positions is necessary to prevent user collisions with the physical environment and accurately align AR content. Another benefit involves content authoring. Creating content becomes more challenging when using spatial anchors because each anchor has its own coordinate system. Also, spatial anchors are continuously being corrected for drift, which means the relation between spatial anchors changes, further complicating the matter. In contrast, our approach simplifies content authoring by providing one global system for building the scene. This paper was inspired by the system introduced by Michiels et al. [13], which also addresses the drift issue. However, a drawback of their approach is that the external tracking camera remains mounted to the headset the whole time, increasing the headset’s weight and thus, causing additional discomfort for users. Additionally, a backpack is required since the tracking method is executed on an external PC. Because tracking operates at a lower framerate, more complex sensor fusion is required. Our proposed method overcomes these problems by utilizing the headset’s tracking capabilities during the operational stage, enabling standalone functionality and enhancing user freedom. In addition, our proposed method introduces a decoupling of the external tracking method and the headset’s tracking capabilities, allowing for the integration of any accurate external tracking method with existing XR headsets that support spatial anchors. The method is empirically evaluated by overlaying a mesh of the environment on the passthrough layer of the headset. The accuracy of the alignment can be easily noticed. Additionally, the system is evaluated against the underlying external tracking method by comparing the corresponding camera poses. Our system is as practical as using default spatial anchors, but increases the range of the accurate tracking area from 3 meters. The code is publicly available on GitHub: https://github.com/EDM-Research/UE-LASAA. 2 Related work Numerous systems are designed with precise outside-in tracking capabilities. Outside-in tracking employs external measurement devices to track a user inside a room. These devices may be cameras [7], projective beacons [16] or even acoustic trackers [11]. Despite their accuracy, these systems are expensive and annoying to configure when scaling to large environments. Another approach for user tracking is inside-out tracking. With inside-out tracking, on-device sensors, such as cameras and IMU sensors, are used for tracking. The advancement of inside-out tracking techniques has made seamlessly integrating room-scale consumer devices like the Quest headsets, the HoloLens, and the Magic Leap affordable. Several IMU-based tracking methods have been researched, both completely relying on IMU sensor data [3] and combined with other sensors such as cameras using sensor fusion [1]. The most common visual technology within this category is SLAM [5], which tries to simultaneously find a user’s location while also constructing a map of the environment. Due to sensor noise and the limited precision of computing devices, small errors accumulate over time. This issue is called drift, limiting the accuracy of tracking. For example, whenever users revisit a place they already saw, there might be a gap between the real and virtual locations of users. Drift impacts most inside-out tracking methods, including IMU-based techniques. Solutions like loop-closing [15] have been proposed to reduce the impact of drift. Recent advancements employ Gaussian splatting for SLAM: SplaTAM [10] and Gaussian SLAM [24]. Also, visual-inertial SLAM solutions exist [4, 19] that combine the visual and inertial information for SLAM tracking. These SLAM approaches can be integrated into cheap and untethered portable devices. However, drift prevents these solutions from scaling properly to larger environments. McGill et al. [12] showed that the Oculus Quest is only accurate to [FORMULA] m in a small environment of 6 m², with increasing drift over time, especially when scaling to large areas. Although new-generation XR headsets improve tracking accuracy, they are not flawless. SLAM methods rely on natural image features for tracking. When possible, artificial image features consisting of ArUco codes [9] or other custom markers can be introduced, similar to the approach taken by Podkosova et al. [17]. These markers allow more accurate tracking since they can be used as real-world static reference points, thereby removing drift entirely. However, setting up an environment with a large number of markers is not always desired, mainly because it is impractical. Also, the markers should be visible at all times for tracking purposes. Small errors in pose estimation can still occur due to different factors such as inaccurate detection, markers not being completely flat, etc. Apart from loop-closing, other methods that reduce drift have been researched: Spatial Anchors [21] and World Locking tools (WLT) [22]. Spatial anchors are reference points in the physical world that are tracked and corrected for drift. Objects attached to a spatial anchor are continuously moving to adjust their pose to account for drift. Each spatial anchor does this independently of other anchors, which means they do not have a rigid relationship. This complicates content creation since the content must be placed per spatial anchor, and there is no fixed relation between the anchors. This approach to drift correction is only accurate within 3 m of the anchor [21]. Spatial anchors can be shared across multiple devices, easily achieving multi-user experiences. Microsoft’s World Locking Tools tries to scale this method to larger areas utilizing spatial anchors and space pins. Space pins are reference points in the physical world with a known pose, allowing us to align the real world’s coordinate system with the virtual world’s coordinate system. These points can be QR codes encoding additional information. This setup requires manually adjusting the virtual poses of the game engine’s space pins to match the markers’ physical layout. WLT adjusts the headset’s pose in relation to several anchors to correct drift for the whole environment. As shown by Teruggi and Fassi [20], WLT is accurate in the order of 15 cm in large environments of 40 [FORMULA] 85 m. We try to reduce drift inside the headset by using the headset’s tracking capabilities and spatial anchors combined with any external, drift-corrected tracking method. This approach reduces drift inside the headset while allowing standalone functionality. The proposed method works with any headset that supports spatial anchors. While our approach is similar to WLT, it is more flexible and easier to set up, and works with any headset that supports spatial anchors. Depending on the external tracking method that is used, artificial features are not necessary, contrary to WLT. Finally, this framework will be publicly available and can be easily used as a plugin in Unreal Engine 5. 3 Methodology overview The methodology consists of two stages: a preparation stage and an operational stage. In the preparation stage, the user walks around with an external tracking camera mounted on the headset, placing anchors (3D reference points) in the tracking environment. During this stage, two tracking methods are used simultaneously: the head-mounted display tracking and an external tracking method. The additional camera and external tracking method can be discarded during the operational stage, and the system works in standalone mode. A schematic overview is shown in Figure 2. There are two tracking methods: the head-mounted display’s (internal) tracking and the external, drift-corrected tracking method. For each technique, anchors will be saved. The spatial anchors inside the HMD will be called INT (internal) anchors, while the anchors in the external method will be called EXT (external) anchors. These anchors are in the same coordinate system as the content model. The proposed method works as follows: Set up the external tracking method and mount the camera to the headset. Place an INT anchor in the headset coordinate system where many features are inside the room. Simultaneously, save an EXT anchor of the same pose in the external coordinate system. This creates 3D correspondences between both tracking methods. Repeat steps 2-3 at least three times until a sufficient area of the scene is covered with anchors. Unmount the extra tracking camera and use the headset standalone. Align the EXT anchors with the INT anchors in every frame using a suitable cloud registration method. This is achieved by finding and applying transformation T, which is the transformation from the external to the internal tracking space. 4 Preparation stage During the preparation stage, all information is gathered to align the virtual content with the real world accurately. Correspondences between the tracking methods are obtained by simultaneously employing the internal and external tracking methods and placing anchor points in both tracking environments. In this paper two external tracking methods are demonstrated: marker-based tracking and an ORB-SLAM3 [4] implementation which aims to correct drift within the SLAM map. For this approach, the external tracking method is considered the ground truth. Our approach will never be more accurate than the external tracking method that is used. Essentially, any tracking method that corrects drift can be utilized. We are also not limited to vision-based external tracking methods. These methods are used to place the EXT anchors, which essentially consist of a 6DOF camera pose comprising both position and orientation. The pose is transmitted to the headset using a network protocol. The Open Sound Control (OSC) protocol [23] was employed in this case, thanks to its simplicity and support by most game engines and headsets. It is important to note that this is not a requirement for our system. Other scanning methods are improving and can also be employed. In environments where feasible, markers can be strategically positioned for tracking purposes. The markers that were used are from the aruco_mip_36h dictionary, as seen in Figure 5. Each location where we wish to place an anchor is marked. The markers are printed 16 cm in size. By obtaining a laser scan of the surroundings, the precise locations of these markers can be found. Then, employing marker detection techniques outlined by Garrido-Jurado et al. [9, 8] and Romero-Ramirez et al. [18], alongside the known 3D positions of the markers, the camera’s pose can be determined within the coordinate system of the laser scan. This approach inherently eliminates the introduction of drift, as the camera’s pose is only established in relation to the markers and thus in relation to the global world. However, errors can still occur due to inaccuracies in marker detection or deviations in the laser scan. This might be due to the marker not being completely flat, sudden movements, differing lighting conditions, etc. A second method is explored in situations where only a few markers are allowed, as studied by Michiels et al. [13]. The same markers were employed as in the marker-based tracking method. This approach is based on ORB-SLAM3 [4] and focuses on reducing drift by using a small number of markers and a laser scan as a ground truth. In this technique, a SLAM map is constructed utilizing an external camera. Subsequently, adjustments, such as deformations and optimizations, are made to this map to align it as closely as possible with the laser scan containing markers, thereby minimizing drift. Although this method still necessitates a few markers for alignment, the inclusion of ORB-SLAM3 enables tracking even when markers are not visible. Consequently, users are not limited to placing anchors around markers. The accuracy is approximately 10 cm, which is sufficient for many virtual reality applications where the user is completely separated from the real world, such as operator training VR simulations, gaming, etc. However, AR requires higher accuracy to integrate digital content seamlessly into the physical world. The additional keyframe alignment from Michiels et al. [13] can also be employed to improve accuracy further. Should a more precise tracking method emerge in the future, the system is ready to seamlessly integrate it without necessitating any adjustments. By simply incorporating the new approach, the performance of our current system can be enhanced. This means that our system’s accuracy relies on the external method’s precision. Another benefit is that the external tracking can operate at a slower frequency, as long as it maintains accuracy. However, if a few anchors are misplaced due to errors in tracking, the static cloud registration improves alignment by reducing the impact of the misplaced anchors. 7 Conclusion In conclusion, this paper has presented an approach to addressing the issue of drift within the headset for co-located XR spatial tracking systems. By leveraging spatial anchors and an external, drift-corrected tracking method, our proposed methodology offers a scalable solution to mitigate drift and improve accuracy over larger areas. Our approach builds upon existing research in this area, offering improvements over previous methods addressing practical challenges such as user comfort and additional equipment requirements. By enabling full standalone functionality of the headset during the operational stage, we enhance user freedom and usability. As the external tracking improves accuracy in the future, our method improves as well, without needing any adjustments. Future work could explore how to handle outliers and wrongly placed anchors. These outliers could be detected automatically using RANSAC [6], for example. Additionally, using different types of external tracking systems could be researched. The system’s compatibility with various XR devices can be expanded as well. Möbius Interaction Filtering: Order-Selective Spectral Regularization for Multimodal Humor Detection Multimodal humor detection requires interpreting language, vocal delivery, and visual behavior jointly. Expressive fusion must also regulate how interactions of different orders enter the final judgment. We propose Möbius Interaction Filtering (MoIF), which learns a modality-subset prediction function and imposes order-selective spectral regularization through its aggregation structure. Private temporal encoders and balanced reciprocal interaction construct supervised unimodal, bimodal, and trimodal predictors. Their uniform aggregate is exactly a Möbius-domain filter with a geometrically decreasing interaction-order response. This formulation retains higher-order representations while regulating their contribution to prediction. Controlled UR-FUNNY perturbations reveal a pronounced decline in label-aligned signal-to-noise ratio across interaction orders. The induced filter improves the final ratio by 1.62–2.79 times relative to the co-trained trimodal predictor while preserving its own clean class-aligned signal under perturbation. Five-seed experiments achieve 70.6% accuracy and weighted F1 on UR-FUNNY, exceeding thirteen reproduced methods on these detection metrics. CMU-MOSI and CMU-MOSEI evaluations establish applicability to sentiment prediction, and cross-seed analyses show more stable estimates on all three datasets. MoIF connects the organization of multimodal interactions to their statistical reliability through an executable spectral constraint. Code is available at https://github.com/D-ST-Sword/MoIF. 1 Introduction Humor is expressed through the interplay of words, vocal delivery, and visual behavior. A verbal statement may carry an apparent meaning that is reinforced, qualified, or overturned by its delivery. Multimodal humor detection therefore requires learning relationships between these streams while retaining evidence that is already informative within an individual modality Hasan et al. [2019], Poria et al. [2017], Baltrušaitis et al. [2019]. The challenge is not simply to construct increasingly comprehensive combinations. It is to determine how evidence from different interaction orders should contribute to a stable final judgment. Existing fusion methods offer increasingly expressive representations. Tensor fusion enumerates unimodal and cross-modal feature combinations, and low-rank factorization reduces their computational cost Zadeh et al. [2017], Liu et al. [2018]. Cross-modal attention relates unaligned temporal streams Tsai et al. [2019], while shared–private learning and unimodal supervision preserve modality-specific information Hazarika et al. [2020], Yu et al. [2021]. Dynamic Fusion Graph and Multimodal Routing explicitly organize information from different interaction orders Bagher Zadeh et al. [2018], Tsai et al. [2020]. Recent interaction-aware models further specialize representations or experts for complementary information Xin et al. [2025], Yang et al. [2026]. These approaches develop interaction representations and learned rules for their combination. We focus on the structure of the prediction operator: how its response across interaction orders relates expressiveness to estimation stability. Why not rely exclusively on the representation that combines all modalities? At the information level, complete inputs contain every subset. At the estimator level, however, a learned trimodal predictor is not guaranteed to dominate separately supervised subset predictors: finite data, shared parameters, and joint optimization determine which relationships are captured and how reliably they are estimated. Multimodal training studies document uneven learning across streams and insufficient exploitation of useful unimodal features Wang et al. [2020], Du et al. [2023], Peng et al. [2022]. Retaining unimodal and bimodal predictions gives the model access to several estimates of the same target, but a useful design must also explain what their combination does to the interaction structure. We address this question through Möbius Interaction Filtering (MoIF). The central design variable is not only which modalities are fused, but how the resulting interaction spectrum enters the decision. Predictions indexed by modality subsets define a set function whose Möbius representation resolves increments associated with individual modalities, pairs, and the complete triplet Grabisch et al. [2000]. Complete-input evaluation sums these increments with unit response at every order. MoIF instead induces a geometrically decreasing response through uniform subset aggregation. This connects the prediction rule to discrete-set signal processing Püschel and Wendler [2021]: the model retains expressive interactions while its aggregation structure regulates their contribution to the decision. MoIF realizes this principle as a learned lifting into the modality-subset function space, followed by a fixed prediction operator. Private temporal encoders, balanced reciprocal interaction, and trimodal composition jointly map an observation to supervised predictions across the subset lattice. Direct subset supervision retains task-relevant estimates at each input combination, while the primary objective trains their filtered decision. The learned function and the spectral constraint are thus coupled throughout optimization. Subset aggregation implements the operator exactly, without an explicit transform or a separate filtering network. The learned interaction spectrum has a measurable reliability structure. On UR-FUNNY, controlled feature perturbations reveal descending label-aligned signal-to-noise ratios from first- to third-order components across every tested seed–condition combination. MoIF’s geometric response attenuates the less favorable orders without discarding them, and the combined estimate achieves a higher signal-to-noise ratio while retaining its class-aligned response. Figure 2 connects the coordinate transformation, filter response, and these measured effects. Humor detection is the primary task; separately trained CMU-MOSI and CMU-MOSEI evaluations test the same interaction principle on sentiment prediction within the broader setting of multimodal affective computing. Cross-seed stability provides a complementary test of the resulting estimates. Our contributions are threefold. First, we formulate multimodal prediction as the design of an interaction-spectrum response and derive the exact subset-domain implementation of an order-selective Möbius filter. This separates the construction of expressive interactions from their weighting in the final estimate. Second, we develop a jointly supervised lifting with balanced reciprocal interaction, coupling private, pairwise, and trimodal predictors to the filtered task objective. Third, we connect the measured decline in interaction-order reliability to improved signal-to-noise balance under the induced response, supported by controlled perturbations and five-seed humor-detection and sentiment evaluations. Together, these contributions establish an executable spectral constraint linking multimodal expressiveness to estimation stability. 2 Related Work UR-FUNNY studies humor through language, acoustic cues, and visual behavior Hasan et al. MoIF retains the trimodal state and its supporting pairwise interactions, but does not require every interaction order to enter the estimate with unit response. Lower-order predictions provide the coordinates needed to resolve and regulate this spectrum. Their role extends beyond supplying additional votes: together with the complete-input prediction, they let the shared model implement the order-selective operator. The UR-FUNNY evidence connects this design to estimation reliability. The declining order-wise SNR shows why increasingly comprehensive interactions need not warrant increasingly strong decision responses. MoIF’s geometric response reduces the relative influence of the less reliable orders while retaining their signed contributions. Its benefit is determined jointly by label alignment and cross-order covariance, as verified by reconstructing the measured output SNR. Feature composition remains expressive, while the task loss optimizes the prediction under this response. The result is a learned subset function whose interaction structure supports both discrimination and stable estimation. The current model exhaustively represents the seven nonempty subsets of three modalities. Its filter response is fixed by this construction, and the Möbius coordinates describe learned predictors rather than orthogonal semantic factors. The controlled-noise analysis probes private-feature perturbations on UR-FUNNY; real recording artifacts and distribution changes provide complementary settings for future evaluation. The sentiment results already show that the same construction supports another prediction task, while the family comparisons reveal that the best composition can depend on the metric and dataset. Larger modality sets make exhaustive subset construction costly. Structured subset sampling and order-dependent responses learned from validation evidence offer routes to scaling the framework. Another direction is to combine quality estimates with the explicit dependency graph, allowing the model to regulate interaction contributions when inputs are unreliable. Both extensions should preserve the connection between an executable prediction rule and its interaction-domain action, so that added flexibility remains interpretable and testable. 6 Conclusion MoIF connects multimodal humor detection to order-selective spectral regularization on a learned subset function. Its central insight is that retaining expressive interactions and regulating their decision contributions are compatible objectives. The Möbius formulation exposes this distinction, and the measured interaction spectra, signal preservation, and cross-seed stability connect it to improved estimation. Future work will extend the framework to larger modality sets and quality-dependent responses, while preserving the explicit relationship between the prediction rule and its interaction-domain action.
