One Rater to Score Them All: Frozen Large Language Model Anchoring for Video Quality of Experience Quality of Experience results for video streaming cannot be compared across studies, because public databases share neither test material nor subjects. This work introduces a common reference rater: an open-weights large language models with a fixed rubric and greedy decoding that scores the delivery events of every session and supplies the shared items that score equating requires. The rater is used without training, and it reads only the playback event log of startup delay, stalls and quality switches, which most delivery databases retain even when they share nothing else. A monotonic curve then maps each study’s native scale onto the common scale. On 3,552 sessions from four studies covering four rating scales, the rater attains a Spearman correlation of 0.809 on VL04 of the ITU-T P.1203 collection, exceeding P.1203 mode 0 on the same sessions, with a Krippendorff alpha of 0.974 over repeated scoring and 0.951 across three serving providers. Sessions from three further laboratories give correlations from 0.756 to 0.787. After calibration, the four studies are placed on a single 0 to 100 scale with a held-out error between 7.8 and 13.3 points, and a mean VMAF of 60 corresponds to positions 17 points apart in two of the studies. I Introduction Quality of Experience (QoE) refers to how a viewer perceives a video stream, and it governs the design of video delivery systems. The field measures QoE through subjective experiments, in which viewers rate what they see, and through objective models that predict those ratings after being fitted to ratings collected in earlier experiments [1]. These measurements, however, do not accumulate, because each experiment defines its own conditions and reports on its own scale. Therefore, a mean opinion score (MOS) of 3.6 on the ITU-T P.910 scale, a z-scored rating, and a 0 to 100 panel mean describe different quantities that cannot be converted into one another. ITU-T P.1401 [1] aligns a model with subjective data in a pairwise fashion but discards the fitted mapping once the evaluation ends. Progress therefore cannot be measured across studies. The same limitation extends to QoE-based anomaly detection [2]. Network-based frameworks that estimate QoE from network measurements with machine learning face the same problem [3]. Prior work leaves this problem open. Alignment methods link separate experiments but require material that public databases do not provide [4, 5, 6, 7]. Raters built on large models read viewer comments or encoding metadata, not delivery events [8, 9]. ITU-T P.1401 fits its mapping per experiment rather than carrying it between them [1]. In this paper, the studies are bridged by a common reference rater rather than by shared material. Score equating requires common items, and QoE has none. The rater supplies those items by reading the playback event log of every session, the one record that all delivery databases retain, and scoring it under a fixed rubric (Fig. 1). Those scores become the shared items that score equating requires, and the anchor therefore exists even when the studies share nothing. This work makes three contributions. The first is a reference rater for delivery QoE that reads structured event logs as text and requires no access to the decoded video. The second is a calibration procedure that places subjective scores and objective metrics from independent studies on one common scale, with the residual error measured out of sample. The third is an evaluation on 3,552 sessions from four studies, including the alternative annotator test [10] and a reliability characterization over repeated scoring. The evaluation is extended by 74 sessions from three further laboratories and by 180 clips without delivery events, on which the rater is compared with LLMs that read encoding metadata. The common scale is also tested directly on sessions that two separate viewer groups rated, and ITU-T P.1203 is compared with the rater in the role of the anchor. The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work. Section III describes the proposed rater and its calibration. Section IV presents the databases and the evaluation protocol. Section V reports the results. Section VI concludes the paper. II Related Work Prior work on cross-study comparability in QoE falls into three groups. The first links separate experiments through shared material. The second predicts QoE from delivery events and picture quality. The third builds raters on large models. The standard ITU-T P.1401 prescribes a mapping fitted per experiment and then discarded, and is discussed with the first group. Table I compares representative approaches. Alignment methods link experiments through something they share. Iterated nested least squares uses an objective video quality metric as the shared variables, and offers a meta-test that shows selected clips from each dataset to one panel [4]. Unified scaling combines ratings with pairwise comparisons, and requires that no condition stay disconnected [5]. Mixed-dataset training puts a per-dataset scale and shift inside one quality model [6]. AlignNet fixes one dataset as the reference and maps the others to it [7]. Each method needs material that public delivery databases do not have. Iterated nested least squares needs an objective metric on the decoded video of every clip [4]. Unified scaling needs pairwise comparisons that cover the datasets [5]. Mixed-dataset training and AlignNet keep the link inside one trained network, which must be retrained whenever a database is added [6, 7]. None of the four puts two studies on a common scale without that material. ITU-T P.1401 prescribes a mapping between a model and subjective data [1]. The mapping is fitted pairwise, and the evaluation throws it away once the evaluation ends. A subjective experiment is a closed set that cannot be compared with other experiments, and the mapping is fitted per experiment, not carried between them. ITU-T P.1401 therefore does not give the link that cross-study comparison needs. Objective QoE models predict the opinion score of a session from its delivery events and a measure of picture quality, from the bitrate to a metric computed on the decoded frames [12]. ITU-T P.1203 standardizes a bitstream-based model with four levels of input detail, and it came with open databases and a reference implementation [11]. A comparison of 15 such models on four databases [12] reports that learning-based models do well on some test sets and worse on others, and the Spearman correlation of one model drops by 0.597 between two databases. Each model is judged by its correlation inside one database, which does not put the databases on a common scale. LLMs have also been used as raters. An LLM has assigned an opinion score from 1 to 5 to each viewer comment on live-streaming platforms, grouped per simulated service provider [8]. LLMs have also predicted the opinion score of encoded clips from their codec, bitrate and resolution [9]. Each rater reads a different input. The comment-based model reads viewer text [8], and the metadata-based models read encoding parameters [9]. None reads the delivery events of a session. III Proposed Reference Rater The proposed system converts every recorded streaming session into one fixed textual report, scores that report with a frozen LLM, and uses the resulting scores as the anchor items of a score equating procedure (Fig. 1). The left branch carries the raw material of a study through the report format to the rater, which produces an anchor score on a 0 to 100 scale; the right branch carries the scores the study itself reports into a monotonic calibration that maps them onto the same axis. The rater is the only element common to all studies, and therefore the only element that can carry a scale between them. The procedure has four steps. The first converts each session into a fixed report format (Section III-A). The second describes the rater and the rubric it follows (Section III-B). The third places each study’s native scale on the common axis (Section III-C). The fourth states the conditions under which a study can join the common scale (Section III-D). Delivery QoE depends mainly on startup delay, stalls, and switches of bitrate and resolution, and the report is restricted accordingly. Each session is rendered with a fixed field order: viewing device, screen resolution, video length, startup delay, a timeline of playback events in wall-clock seconds, and a summary of stall count, total stalled time and number of quality changes. A playback line is emitted only when the quality changes and only after a stall. Missing fields are written as not reported, which declares missing information rather than imputing it. The report carries no study name, identifier or score, which prevents the rater from recognizing the source of a session. An open-weights LLM serves as the rater, prompted with a rubric that defines six bands on a 0 to 100 scale, each band described by the delivery conditions that place a session within it. The rubric ranks the delivery conditions in a fixed order: stalls first, startup delay second, picture quality relative to the screen third, and the number of quality changes last. It also declares that a field marked as not reported is unknown, and states the bitrate a resolution requires in order to appear clean, because the model otherwise treats a picture that matches the screen resolution as top quality regardless of its bitrate. Decoding is greedy, with temperature and nucleus parameters fixed, and each session is submitted in its own request. The instrument consists of four archived components: 1) the model weights, 2) the report format, 3) the rubric text, and 4) the decoding parameters. Any change to one of them defines a new instrument and requires every session to be scored again. Each session has two numbers: the rater score and the value the study reports for it, which may be a subjective mean opinion score or an objective metric. For each study, a monotonic logistic curve maps the reported value onto the rater score. The curve is fitted by least squares, and the study is then represented on the common scale by the fitted values. The curve is fitted on one half of the sessions and evaluated on the other, and the halves are exchanged, so that no session is placed by a curve fitted to itself. One curve is fitted per study, per viewing context, and per reported metric, so the same metric can land at different points on the common scale in different studies. The logistic curve has four free parameters, and on a small study it can collapse into a step that assigns nearly every session one of two values. A study that provides fewer than 60 sessions to a fit is therefore mapped by a straight line, limited to the range from 0 to 100. From 60 sessions upward the logistic curve is used. A study joins the common scale under two conditions. It supplies the raw event logs or, where available, the stimuli of its sessions rather than its reported scores alone, because reported scores mix method quality with test difficulty and protocol. Absent fields are labeled. This labeling yields an explicit coverage label and prevents an incomplete report from being read as a favorable one. The rater version is then recorded with the resulting placement. IV Simulation The system is exercised on four independent subjective studies. They share neither test material nor viewers, and their reported scores lie on four different scales. The ITU-T P.1203 open dataset [11] provides 239 sessions rated 1 to 5 by a panel on scripted event lists. LIVE-NFLX-II [13] provides 420 sessions rated as z-scores under four adaptation algorithms. Waterloo-IV11 1 https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.08804 provides 1,350 sessions rated 0 to 100 by a panel of 32 under five adaptation algorithms. Poqemon22 2 https://github.com/Lamyne/Poqemon-QoE-Dataset provides 1,543 field sessions rated 1 to 5 by a single viewer, reported as totals without a timeline. The P.1203 dataset contributes five experiments: TR04 and TR06 are training databases, and VL04, VL13 and VL14 are validation databases; 14 sessions of VL14 carry a subjective score but no feature record and are excluded. Together the four studies provide 3,552 sessions. Fig. 2 summarizes the setup: the four studies and two external test sets are scored by the same instrument, and its scores feed four tests. PNATS-UHD-1-Long [14] serves as an external validation set and was scored only after the instrument had been frozen. It contains three tests from three laboratories. Rohde & Schwarz contributed 30 sessions viewed on a 5.5-inch phone, TU Ilmenau and Deutsche Telekom 30 sessions on a 35-inch 4K PC monitor, and Ericsson Research 14 sessions on a 5.5-inch phone. Sessions last 120 seconds in the first two tests and 300 seconds in the third, and panels of 27 to 32 viewers rate them from 1 to 5. Test 1 of AVT-VQDB-UHD-1 [15] serves as a second external set and is used for a comparison with LLMs that read encoding metadata [9]. It holds 180 clips of 10 seconds from six sources, encoded with H.264, H.265 and VP9 at 360p to 2160p and at 200 kbit/s to 40 Mbit/s, and rated by 26 viewers. The clips contain no stalls and no quality changes. Their metadata and opinion scores are taken from the public data of [9]. The report states the resolution, the bitrate and a screen of 3840 by 2160 pixels; codec and frame rate have no field in the report format. Every session is converted to the report of Section III-A and scored once by the reference rater, Qwen3-235B-A22B-2507, served through a commercial inference provider with temperature 0, a nucleus sampling threshold of 1, and one session per request. Instrument selection, namely the choice of model, the output scale and the rubric wording, was performed on TR04 and TR06 only; the validation databases were not consulted at any point. Three baselines are used. ITU-T P.1203 in modes 0 through 3 is available for the P.1203 study. Mean VMAF, PSNR and SSIM are available for LIVE-NFLX-II, and mean VMAF for Waterloo-IV. A second frozen rater, DeepSeek-V3.2-exp under the identical report format and rubric, is scored on all four studies to evaluate a panel of raters. In addition, the comparison of 15 objective QoE models on LIVE-NFLX-II and Waterloo-IV published in [12] is used. There, the models were optimized on two other Waterloo databases, except P.1203, whose training is not specified, and four continuous-time models, which were trained on LIVE-NFLX-I. The correlations of that work are computed on the same 420 and 1,350 sessions, and only the Spearman correlation is compared, because it does not depend on a mapping. Agreement with subjective scores follows ITU-T P.1401 [1]: a monotonic logistic curve is fitted between the predicted and the subjective values, and the Pearson correlation and the root mean square error are computed after that mapping, while the Spearman correlation is computed on the unmapped values. Reliability is characterized by five repeated scorings of the P.1203 study under a pinned provider, by scoring the same sessions through three different providers, and by a rubric perturbation. Replacement of a human viewer is tested with the alternative annotator test [10], which compares the rater against each of the 28 viewers of the P.1203 study in turn, corrects the resulting p-values with the Benjamini-Yekutieli procedure, and reports the winning rate, the share of viewers the rater outperforms at a given tolerance margin, together with the average advantage probability. The direct test of the common scale requires sessions that two separate groups of viewers rated. Waterloo-IV assigned each viewer at random to one of three devices, a phone, a Full-HD monitor and a UHD television, and each group rated the same 450 conditions. Since every group had its own playback run, a condition is retained only where the playback is identical in both groups, which leaves 283 to 308 shared sessions per pair of groups. Each group’s curve is fitted only on its sessions that are not shared, the shared sessions are placed by both curves, and the mean absolute gap between the two placements is reported. The same test is applied to TR04 and VL04, which contain three sessions with the same source and condition identifiers, and to the first two tests of PNATS-UHD-1-Long, which share four anchor conditions. In the P.1203 collection, the 82 conditions of TR04 and TR06 are also rated by a PC panel and by a phone panel. Every condition is shared there, so the half-split fit of Section III-C is used. The gap expected from the finite panels alone is obtained from the standard deviation of the individual ratings of each session and serves as a noise floor. To determine whether a standardized model could serve as the anchor instead, P.1203 mode 0 is computed for every session whose source data provide the inputs the model requires. The reference implementation [11] is used, and sessions encoded with H.265/HEVC or VP9 use a published codec extension33 3 https://github.com/Telecommunication-Telemedia-Assessment/itu-p1203-codecextension, which is not part of the standard. The output on the 1 to 5 scale is stretched linearly onto 0 to 100, and the shared-session test of Waterloo-IV is repeated with P.1203 as the anchor. Two further experiments concern the design of the instrument. The size below which the logistic curve becomes unreliable is determined by subsampling. For each sample size from 8 to 100 sessions, a sample is drawn from a large study 60 times, and the curve fitted on them is evaluated on the remaining sessions. A second rubric judges sharpness by the resolution of the picture and the type of device, rather than by the ratio between the picture and the screen resolution. Its decision rule was fixed before it was scored. The second rubric would replace the original one only if no study outside its design set lost more than 0.02 in Spearman correlation, and only if the device offsets of Waterloo-IV decreased. V Results The evaluation answers four questions: how closely the reference rater agrees with subjective scores (Section V-A), how it compares with the standardized model (Section V-B), how stable the instrument is under repetition and relocation (Section V-C), and whether the calibrated common scale renders independent studies comparable (Section V-D). Table II reports agreement, coverage and placement error for every study, and the four subsections take the questions in turn. Table II reports agreement for each study. The rater attains Pearson correlations between 0.533 and 0.710 and Spearman correlations between 0.397 and 0.728 across four scales and four protocols, without access to the decoded video and without training. Agreement is highest on LIVE-NFLX-II, whose sessions follow real traces, and lowest on Poqemon, whose reports carry no timeline and whose scores come from one viewer rather than a panel. The three external tests of PNATS-UHD-1-Long exceed every study of the main corpus in Spearman correlation. The tests are small, and the 95% bootstrap intervals are correspondingly wide: from 0.50 to 0.89, from 0.56 to 0.91 and from 0.39 to 0.95. AVT-VQDB-UHD-1, whose clips differ only in encoding, attains the highest Spearman correlation of the rater in Table II. A panel of two raters was also evaluated on the three panel-rated studies, by averaging the ranks of the reference rater and of DeepSeek-V3.2-exp under the identical report and rubric. Agreement improved on Waterloo-IV (0.586 to 0.599) and decreased on the other two, where the second rater attained only 0.598 and 0.486. Aggregation is therefore beneficial only among members of comparable strength. Among the 15 models evaluated in [12], the rater occupies a middle position, with Spearman correlations of 0.728 on LIVE-NFLX-II and 0.561 on Waterloo-IV against 0.906 and 0.699 for the best published models. On each of the two databases the rater exceeds nine of the models and is exceeded by six. SQI, BSQI, Bentaleb2016 and P.1203 exceed it on both, Xue2014 and Liu2012 only on LIVE-NFLX-II, and Video ATLAS and Spiteri2016 only on Waterloo-IV. The rater was neither trained nor tuned on either database, while most of the published models were optimized on other subjective databases. The published Spearman correlations [12], on LIVE-NFLX-II and on Waterloo-IV respectively, are 0.516 and 0.056 for Mok2011, 0.549 and 0.082 for FTW, 0.433 and 0.132 for NARX-QoE, 0.778 and 0.219 for Xue2014, 0.685 and 0.255 for Bi-LSTM, 0.710 and 0.299 for LSTM-QoE, 0.635 and 0.395 for TV-QoE, 0.732 and 0.468 for Liu2012, 0.686 and 0.541 for Yin2015, 0.673 and 0.670 for Video ATLAS, 0.711 and 0.662 for Spiteri2016, 0.883 and 0.692 for Bentaleb2016, 0.906 and 0.690 for SQI, and 0.893 and 0.699 for BSQI. That comparison reports 0.821 and 0.668 for P.1203 mode 0. Computed on the sessions of this work, mode 0 attains 0.833 and 0.648 (Table II). The LLMs of [9] were evaluated on the 180 clips of AVT-VQDB-UHD-1, and their released predictions permit a comparison on identical clips. Following that work, the correlations are computed on unmapped scores and the error on the 1 to 5 scale, to which the rater’s score is converted linearly. The rater attains a Pearson correlation of 0.823, and among the 17 single models of that work it would rank third. The best single model, DeepSeek-V3 used through its web interface, attains 0.870, a difference with a 95% paired bootstrap interval from 0.001 to 0.104. The best group of eight models attains 0.902, an interval from 0.041 to 0.126. In Pearson, Kendall and Spearman correlation and in error on the 1 to 5 scale, the rater attains 0.823, 0.657, 0.813 and 0.698. The corresponding values are 0.902, 0.720, 0.897 and 0.523 for the best group of eight models, 0.895, 0.706, 0.887 and 0.534 for the mean of 11 models, 0.870, 0.734, 0.877 and 0.569 for DeepSeek-V3 used through its web interface, 0.857, 0.710, 0.860 and 0.586 for Gemini-2.0-flash-light, and 0.810, 0.673, 0.826 and 0.681 for Gemini-2.0-flash [9]. The rater therefore exceeds Gemini-2.0-flash in Pearson correlation and trails it in the two rank correlations. The conditions of the two sides differ. The prompt of [9] was selected after other prompts had been tried on these clips, and the group of eight was chosen among all 131,072 subsets against the same opinion scores. The rater was frozen before the clips were seen and receives less information, as described in Section IV. Table II compares the rater with ITU-T P.1203 mode 0 on identical sessions. On the training databases the standardized model is clearly superior; on VL04 the ordering reverses, and on VL13 the two are within 0.05 of each other. What each database varies explains the difference: TR04 and TR06 contain many conditions that differ only in encoding quality at a fixed resolution, which a bitstream-level model observes directly and a textual event report cannot express, whereas VL04 varies resolution, bitrate and stalling jointly (Fig. 3). Replacement of a human viewer was tested with the alternative annotator test against each of the 28 viewers in turn. On VL04 under PC viewing the null hypothesis is rejected for 0.88 of the viewers at a tolerance margin of 0.1 and for 1.00 at a margin of 0.2, with an average advantage probability of 0.677; replacement requires a winning rate of at least 0.5. Over the PC sessions of the whole study the winning rate is 0.50 at a margin of 0.1 and 0.68 at a margin of 0.15. On the training databases the test is not passed, in agreement with Table II. Two candidates for the anchor are compared in Table II. Where P.1203 mode 0 can be computed, it agrees more closely with the viewers. The difference is largest on the P.1203 collection, which contains its training databases, and only on PNATS-UHD-1-Long, pooled over the 64 sessions that both score, does the rater agree more closely (0.818 against 0.768). However, P.1203 requires inputs that several databases do not report. It scores 2,009 of the 3,552 sessions of the four studies and none of Poqemon, whose records carry no per-segment information. A study without anchor scores cannot be placed on the common scale. Placement differs as well. Repeated with P.1203 as the anchor, the three Waterloo-IV pairs give gaps of 5.3, 11.6 and 17.8 points, against 5.7, 4.0 and 6.4 points with the rater. Divided by the spread of the respective anchor, which removes the difference in how the two anchors use the scale, the mean gap is 0.58 for P.1203 and 0.38 for the rater. The standardized model carries a larger device offset. On the UHD television it scores a stream 14.9 points below the Full-HD monitor and 18.3 points below the phone. The corresponding differences of the rater are 5.6 points (Section V-D) and 9.3 points, and the viewers rated the UHD group higher than both. Agreement within a study and consistency across studies are therefore separate properties, and an anchor requires the second. Five repeated scorings of the 239 sessions under a pinned provider give a Krippendorff alpha of 0.974 on the interval metric, with a mean standard deviation of 1.61 points per session against a between-session standard deviation of 17.1 points. Scoring through three different providers gives an alpha of 0.951, with mean absolute differences between 1.8 and 3.8 points. Exact numerical equality is stricter and is not attained: all five repetitions agree exactly on 53.6 percent of sessions and fall within 10 points on 92.5 percent. The residual variation originates in the serving stack, because providers batch requests and batching alters the arithmetic; the serving configuration therefore belongs to the instrument description. A single run on controlled hardware with batch size one remains to be performed in order to bound the variation attributable to batching alone. Rubric perturbation matters as well: adding the paragraph that states the bitrate each resolution requires altered scores by 4.95 points on average, approximately three times the repetition noise. The second rubric of Section IV addressed the device offset reported in Section V-D. It reduced the rater’s own gap between the Full-HD monitor and the UHD television versions of a stream from 5.6 to 1.8 points. The shared-session gap between these two groups fell from 4.0 to 2.4 points, against a panel noise of 2.6 points. It also lowered the Spearman correlation on LIVE-NFLX-II from 0.728 to 0.611 and on Poqemon from 0.397 to 0.323, while PNATS-UHD-1-Long rose from 0.787 to 0.807. Two studies thus lost more than 0.02, so by the rule of Section IV the original rubric remains the instrument, and the second rubric is reported as an ablation. Measured on held-out sessions, the placement error of the per-study calibration is 13.3 points for ITU-T P.1203, 7.8 for LIVE-NFLX-II, 11.3 for Waterloo-IV and 8.9 for Poqemon. Pooled over all 3,552 sessions the calibrated subjective scores attain a Pearson correlation of 0.846 with the anchor scores, against a root mean square error of 10.2 points. Objective metrics are placed on the same axis by the same procedure. Fig. 4 shows the curves fitted for mean VMAF in the two studies reporting it. A mean VMAF of 60 corresponds to position 49 on the common scale in LIVE-NFLX-II and to 66 in Waterloo-IV. That separation of 17 points quantifies the comparability gap between two studies reporting the same metric, and the two curves remove it. A worked example shows the same effect on subjective scores. In the P.1203 collection, session SRC14_HRC17 of TR06 plays at 1080p for 105 seconds, drops to 480p and 240p for 30 seconds, and contains one stall of 15 seconds; its viewers rated it 3.67 on the 1 to 5 scale. In Waterloo-IV, session 0710 of the Full-HD monitor group plays at 540p throughout, after a startup delay of 2.1 seconds and one stall of 0.2 seconds; its viewers rated it 39.9 on the 0 to 100 scale. A linear stretch of the two native scales places the first session at 67 and the second at 40. The calibration curves, fitted on all sessions of each study, place both at 55. The two ratings therefore describe the same position on the common scale, although their stretched native values differ by 27 points. The three pairs of Waterloo-IV viewer groups share 308, 288 and 283 sessions: phone and Full-HD monitor, Full-HD monitor and UHD television, and phone and UHD television. After calibration, the two placements of a session differ on average by 5.7, 4.0 and 6.4 points, against a panel noise of 2.7, 2.2 and 2.6 points. In every pair both groups rated on the same native scale, so their raw scores were already close; on Waterloo-IV the gaps before calibration are 5.0, 5.6 and 5.4 points for the three pairs. The test therefore measures the precision of the placement rather than an improvement over a scale the groups already shared. The calibration is intended for studies on different native scales, where no raw comparison exists. Its result does not depend on the native scale: when the phone panel of the P.1203 collection is converted to z-scores before calibration, the gap remains 3.5 points. Calibration reveals two effects of the anchor. When the rater judges both versions of a session alike, the calibration removes an offset between panels. The phone panel rated the 82 shared conditions 6.7 points higher than the PC panel; after calibration the mean difference is 0.4 points, and the mean absolute gap falls from 8.5 to 3.5 points, against a panel noise of 2.2 points. When the rater perceives a device difference that viewers do not, it introduces an offset of its own. It scores a stream 5.6 points lower on the UHD television than on the Full-HD monitor, whereas the UHD group rated the same sessions 5.2 points higher. A mean difference of 3.8 points remains after calibration. The two smallest pairs, TR04 with VL04 and the first two PNATS tests, share only three and four sessions and show gaps of 9.7 and 10.8 points, against 1.6 and 7.4 points before calibration and a panel noise of 1.5 and 1.1 points. TR04 is dominated by conditions the session report cannot express (Section V-B). The anchor conditions of the first two PNATS tests are not identical either: their quality ladders differ on two sessions, and the first test adds an initial stall of 1 second. On the 26 sessions that the first PNATS test provides to its fit, the logistic curve degenerated, which motivated the size rule of Section III-C. Subsampling of LIVE-NFLX-II, Poqemon and the three Waterloo-IV groups yields the rule. With 26 or fewer sessions, the logistic curve collapsed into a step in 18 to 55 percent of the draws. Its mean held-out error exceeded 15 points for every sample of 20 sessions or fewer, whereas a straight line stayed between 10.3 and 11.5 points. From 60 sessions upward the mean errors of the two forms differ by at most 0.2 points. A leave-one-out choice between the two forms performed worse than the straight line alone and was discarded. Under the rule, the gap of the PNATS pair falls from 10.8 to 5.9 points and that of the PC and phone panels from 3.5 to 3.2 points. The gap of TR04 and VL04 rises from 9.7 to 15.8 points, and the Waterloo-IV pairs, fitted on 142 to 167 sessions, are unchanged. The fits behind Section V-D use at least 119 sessions each, so the values reported there do not change. VI Conclusion This work addressed the absence of a common scale in video QoE measurement. Public delivery databases share neither content nor viewers, and the pairwise mapping of ITU-T P.1401 is discarded once an evaluation ends. The proposed solution is a common reference rater: a frozen open-weights LLM that scores the textual event report of a session under one fixed rubric. On VL04 of the ITU-T P.1203 collection, it agrees with subjective scores more closely than the standardized model on the same sessions, at a Krippendorff alpha of 0.974 over repeated scoring. As the anchor, it places four studies with no shared content, no shared viewers and four different scales on one common scale, with a held-out error between 7.8 and 13.3 points out of 100. Five limitations bound the result. The session report does not represent conditions that differ only in encoding quality at a fixed resolution. Exact numerical repetition is not attained on hosted inference. The rubric wording is part of the instrument. The rater carries a device offset on the UHD television. Studies with fewer than 60 sessions require a straight line instead of the logistic curve. Future work concerns longer sessions, modern codecs, and the harmonization of ground truths in QoE-based anomaly detection.

DASWeave: Weaving Evidence across Speaking Conditions for Multimodal Depression, Anxiety, and Stress Screening Multimodal screening for depression, anxiety, and stress in children and adolescents uses verbal and nonverbal behaviour. Most existing multimodal methods learn from a single recording or interview. Yet a participant’s behaviour changes with the speaking condition, and these changes hold evidence that is invisible in a single recording. We propose DASWeave to bring this evidence into a neural network that encodes each response and then combines all responses of a participant. We train supervised trees to find which behavioural statistics matter for screening, both within each response and in how they change across conditions. We feed the tree outputs into the network both before and after this combination. We fine-tune a large language model to relate what a participant says to how they say it across conditions, and feed its representation into the network after the combination. The language model reads behaviour as text descriptions. We therefore derive additional training targets for the network from a multimodal large language model that takes in the audio-visual features directly. On the official hidden test set of the ACM Multimedia 2026 AdoDAS Grand Challenge (Track 1), DASWeave ranks second among 95 eligible teams. Its mean F1 is 27.1% higher than that of the official audio-visual baseline. It also has the highest mean AUROC among the top five teams. Ablation studies on the validation set show that the supervised trees and the fine-tuned language model contribute most to mean F1. 1. Introduction Depression and anxiety can disrupt school attendance and schoolwork, and unaddressed mental health conditions in adolescence can have consequences in adulthood. However, many such conditions remain unrecognized and untreated (World Health Organization, 2025). Screening for depression, anxiety, and stress (D/A/S) in children and adolescents can help identify those who need support. Automatic screening can assist this process by analysing what participants say and how they sound and look while speaking. Research on automatic screening has mainly studied depression. Multimodal depression detection estimates a person’s depression status or severity from a recording of them speaking. It combines two or more modalities, such as the transcript, audio, and video. Existing methods follow two main directions. The first designs network architectures for the task. These networks can learn temporal patterns and cross-modal interactions related to depression within the recording, such as the question–answer sequence of an interview (Al Hanai et al., 2018; Gratch et al., 2014) and the interplay of audio and visual cues over time (Tao et al., 2024; Li et al., 2026). However, they learn these patterns only from labelled depression data, which are limited in size. The second transfers knowledge from speech and language models pretrained on large-scale data. Such models bring general knowledge of speech and language to the task (Gómez-Zaragozá et al., 2025), and a large language model (LLM) can further use psychological knowledge (Li et al., 2025). Yet the pretraining of these models serves general purposes rather than depression detection. A participant’s speech and facial behaviour change with the speaking condition, such as reading a fixed text or answering an open question. Such differences offer evidence that no single response contains. When reading a fixed text, all participants say the same words, so the reading reflects their habitual voice and expression. Differences between the open responses and the reading are therefore less affected by individual speaking habits. Comparing open responses with one another, such as answers about happy and sad memories, shows how strongly a participant’s behaviour reacts to emotional content. Existing methods model behaviour within each response and what participants say. Yet they have paid little attention to behavioural differences across speaking conditions. To address this gap, we propose DASWeave to bring behavioural differences across speaking conditions into multimodal D/A/S screening. Its neural networks and supervised trees learn patterns specific to D/A/S, while its language models add knowledge from large-scale pretraining and are fine-tuned for the task. Figure 1 shows its structure. We refer to each recorded response as a session. The Shared Session Encoder encodes each session from its audio-visual features. For open answers, it adds the question and the transcript as text input. The session representations are then aggregated into a participant representation. Two-Level Tree Fusion uses gradient-boosted trees (Ke et al., 2017) to learn from thousands of behavioural statistics. The tree outputs are added to each session representation and to the participant representation. The participant-level statistics include differences across speaking conditions. In Participant Language Fusion, a fine-tuned LLM reads all of a participant’s answers. Its input also describes how their speaking behaviour differs from the reading. The resulting language representation is added to the participant representation. During training, MLLM Auxiliary Supervision gives the main predictor additional targets derived from a multimodal LLM (MLLM), which encodes audio-visual features and transcripts together. We evaluate DASWeave on Track 1 of the ACM Multimedia 2026 AdoDAS Grand Challenge (Luo et al., 2026). It ranked second among 95 eligible teams on the official hidden test set, with mean F1 of 0.5853 against the official audio-visual baseline’s 0.4604, and its mean AUROC of 0.8019 was the highest among the top five teams. On the validation set, the full method outperforms the Shared Session Encoder alone. Each of the other three components improves F1 on all three targets, and Participant Language Fusion and Two-Level Tree Fusion contribute the most. Our contributions are as follows. We make behavioural differences across speaking conditions an explicit source of evidence for multimodal D/A/S screening. We propose DASWeave, which uses supervised trees on behavioural statistics and a fine-tuned LLM on text descriptions to bring these differences into a neural predictor that encodes each response. DASWeave ranks second among 95 teams in AdoDAS Track 1, with a mean F1 27.1% higher than the official baseline. 2. Method We study participant-level D/A/S screening from several speaking sessions. Each participant contributes one session per speaking condition. Conclusion DASWeave brings behavioural differences across speaking conditions into multimodal D/A/S screening. Two-Level Tree Fusion adds tree tokens of session statistics before session aggregation and of participant statistics after it. The participant statistics include differences between speaking conditions. Participant Language Fusion encodes all answers together with descriptions of how speaking behaviour differs from the reading. During training, MLLM Auxiliary Supervision brings joint audio-visual-text information into the main predictor through soft targets. In the matched validation ablations, each of the three components and the local text features improves F1 on all three targets. Participant Language Fusion and Two-Level Tree Fusion, which bring evidence across speaking conditions into the prediction path, contribute the most, and Stress has the largest gain over the backbone. DASWeave ranked second on AdoDAS Track 1 and achieved the highest mean AUROC among the top five teams. The gains for Stress motivate closer study of task-specific supervision and cross-session aggregation. Evaluating transfer to held-out schools and different recording conditions is another direction for future work.

Smiling Regulates Emotion During Traumatic Recollection We study when, where, and why 978 Holocaust survivors smile in video testimonies. We create an automatic smile detection model from facial features with an F1 of 85% and annotate detected smiles under two established taxonomies of smiling. We produce narrative features on 1,083,417 transcript sentences as well as emotional valence from three different modalities: audio, eye gaze, and text transcript. Smiling rates are associated with specific semantic topics, narrative structures, and temporal syntaxes across the corpus. Smiles often occur during periods of intense negative affect and we find negative-affect smiles are associated with more positive subsequent valence trajectories across all three modalities. Smiling reduces eye dynamics and blink rates, with both of these effects modulated by narrative valence. Taken together, we conclude that smiling plays a critical role in regulating emotion and social interaction during traumatic recollection. 1. Introduction Smiles are complex social behaviors. While we humans instinctually smile when we are happy (Freedman, 1964), we also smile during periods of great distress, as reactions to surprise, and to mask our underlying emotions. Smiling, therefore, is not simply a valence barometer; it is a carefully constructed display of social expression that balances internal affect and the emotions one wishes to display to the world. In this work, we investigate the social and narrative role that smiling plays during interviews of traumatic recollection with survivors of the Holocaust. We find this nonverbal behavior acts as a mediator of emotion, both in the emotions embedded into recalled narratives and into the social dynamics captured between survivor and interviewer. Existing smile taxonomies classify smiles directly via internal affect (Ekman and Friesen, 1982) and social role (Martin et al., 2017), but we find in our investigations that the emotional weight and complexity of survivor testimonies renders these existing taxonomies overly simplistic. We conducted a pilot smile annotation study under these two taxonomies with trained Holocaust historians and find smiling is associated with both underlying and projected emotional expressions and with changes in narrative emphasis. From these results, we performed a large-scale automatic annotation of narrative features and investigate the complex multimodal interaction that occurs during smiling between facial movements, eye gaze, audio, and semantic content. We identify associations between smiling and two types of survivor emotion: the “narrative valence” of the historical content being recollected and the “present-day valence” of the in-the-moment social dynamics when interfacing with interviewers. We find smiling typically occurs in emotionally congruent settings, such as during topics associated with pre-war and childhood events, but that almost a fifth of all smiles occur during moments of negative valence. Negative-valence smiles seem to be associated with emotional regulation, as the presence of such smiles improves the valence trajectories of surrounding sentences both in narratives and present-day, and across the three modalities of audio, eye gaze, and transcript. Smiling is also associated with differences in eye dynamics and blink rates that vary with narrative valence. Taken together, we assert that smiling plays a critical role in regulating emotion and social interaction during traumatic recollection. 2. Dataset The video data of this study were curated from the USC Shoah Foundation’s Visual History Archive (VHA)11 1 https://vha.usc.edu/home, which contains over 55,000 video testimonies of survivors and witnesses of the Holocaust and other genocides recorded between primarily 1994 and 1999 in over 50 countries and in over 30 languages. For the present study, we limit our analysis to 978 English-speaking subjects who survived internment at the various concentration camps. We selected a subset of 978 English-language interviews with each interview split into an average 4.1 tapes of about 30 minutes, totaling 1,965 hours of playtime. Each interview was conducted in a similar format, with the survivor seated and still in their home facing an interviewer behind the camera. Each survivor gave testimonies on pre-war life, Holocaust experiences, and post-liberation life, for an average interview duration of two hours. In these interviews, Holocaust survivors bear witness to a crime whose cruelty and scale defy human comprehension. In describing their experiences of deportation, camps, extreme hunger, medical experiments on human beings, arbitrary killings, and mass extermination, the interviewees repeatedly reach the limits of what can be said and described (Améry, 1980; Langer, 1995; Laub, 2016), owing to the Holocaust’s very nature as an irrational event that resists “adequate verbalization” (Quindeau and Kestenberg, 1995). The narratives often consist of deeply traumatizing memories, of which the processing shaped survivors’ entire lives and survival after liberation in 1945. Whether and how experiences of the past can be remembered and narrated in the interview situation depends fundamentally on the interview setting itself and on the social - and sometimes, therapeutic - relationship that interviewer and interviewee enter into (Laub, 2016). Dori Laub, a Holocaust survivor and psychologist, describes video interviews as a “testimonial intervention” (Laub, 2016). At the same time, the conditions under which the interview takes place shape the respective testimony itself (Bothe, 2019). Smiling plays a central role during communication and fulfills a variety of functions (Martin et al., 2017; Kraut and Johnston, 1979; Niedenthal et al., 2010), and during initial analysis, we often found incredibly complex emotional processing occurring simultaneously. We found smiles contained expressions of mixtures of pride, regret, and self-irony; unexpected smiles during extreme negative valence; and disassociation when smiling. While most subjects would smile during happy recollections, we found negative-valence smiling a very individually-variable behavior. In addition to the interview footage, the dataset also includes the following, derived from prior works: Original Video: 320 [FORMULA] 240 at 29.97 or 25 fps (H.264) (USC Shoah Foundation, 1994) Original Audio: 44.1 kHz stereo (AAC) (USC Shoah Foundation, 1994) Annotated Transcript: time-aligned human annotation and diarization (USC Shoah Foundation, 1994) Metadata keywords: minute-level annotations from a closed set of Holocaust-specific keywords (USC Shoah Foundation, 2022) Facial Action Units: 17 facial Action Units (AUs) (Ekman et al., 2002) from OpenFace (Baltrušaitis et al., 2018), captured at 30 fps Emotion from audio: Valence, Arousal, and Dominance (VAD) (Mehrabian, 1996) emotion values, temporally-aligned (Lertpetchpun et al., 2025; Feng et al., 2025) Emotion from eyegaze: temporally aligned values of VAD from five seconds of prior eye movement (Ma et al., 2026) Localized eye movement: subject eye movement that is normalized relative to inferred interviewer position (Ma et al., 2026) 3. Related Work and Pilot Study The modern scientific study of smiling began with the discovery of the “Duchenne smile” in 1862 (Duchenne de Boulogne, 1862), which contrasted smiles that engaged just the corners of the lip with those that also had raised cheeks and eyelid lowering. Duchenne smiles, which are associated with genuine signs of joy and positive valence (Ekman et al., 1990), have since been further formalized as specific Action Unit (AU) activations under Ekman and Friesen’s Facial Action Coding System (Ekman and Friesen, 1978). Ekman and Friesen proposed a three-class taxonomy of felt, false, and miserable smiles derived from affective state and physical markers (Ekman and Friesen, 1982); in recent years, building on evidence that smiling evolved chiefly as a social tool (Fridlund, 1994), Niedenthal et al.; Martin et al. established another taxonomy with smiles serving three social roles of reward, affiliation, and dominance (Martin et al., 2017). In dialogue interactions specifically, smiling has long been known to be a direct communication device, where humans subconsciously time the onset of smiles to maximize communicative impact and social signaling (Chovil, 1991; Bavelas et al., 2000). We begin our analysis with a pilot study where six annotators, including four trained Holocaust historians with graduate degrees, labeled smiles under the two taxonomies. Annotators met weekly over the course of two months to discuss disagreements, update instructions, and come to consensus on labels. Below, we describe the annotation process (§3.1), the agreement scores (§3.2), some analysis and results (§3.3), and a derived smile detector (§3.4). Annotators labeled each smile under two taxonomies summarized in Table 1: the Genuine/Polite/Masking scheme adapted from Martin et al. (2017) that captures social functions of the smile, and the Felt/False/Miserable scheme from Ekman and Friesen (1982) that characterizes the underlying emotional authenticity of the smile. In addition to assigning labels to smiles, annotators performed open coding (Strauss and Corbin, 1990) on randomly selected smiles by describing in plain text why they thought the smile was occurring without forcing a taxonomic label. While Martin et al.’s original taxonomy was Reward / Affiliative / Dominant, we used the terms Genuine / Polite / Masking as survivors rarely exhibited dominance. We replaced Dominant with Masking as we commonly observed a type of smile that did not map cleanly onto Martin et al.’s taxonomy, a kind of grimace meant to mask the horrible reality of what the interviewee was describing. This smile seemed to play both a social and emotionally regulatory role as it was associated with comforting the interviewer as well as personally processing emotion. We built a custom annotation interface that displays the time-aligned transcript alongside the interview video and audio (Figure 1). Each annotation task shows a video clip containing 3 s before the detected smile, the entire smile segment, and 2 s after, with the median smile lasting 1.37 s. Annotators could re-watch smiles as needed and relied on facial features, voice, transcript, and social context and met weekly over two months to discuss which elements of the interview motivated their labels. To gather smile candidates, for each video, we analyzed framewise AU12 (lip corner puller) intensity from OpenFace’s AU detector. Because of the low resolution of the archival footage, the OpenFace intensities are likely noisy estimates. We Gaussian-smoothed this time series with [FORMULA] , thresholded for AU values [FORMULA] 22 2 AU12’s intensity ranges from 0 to 5 with the median frame from our data being 0., removed occurrences of less than half a second, and merged segments occurring within half a second. This process yielded 287,991 smile candidates across 3,649 videos. In order to increase the likelihood of smiles during annotation, we applied additional filters during both taxonomy tasks: for the first we increased the AU12 threshold to [FORMULA] and for the second we trained a logistic regression model on 17 AUs (including AU12) that best fit the F1 of the first set labels and set the regression threshold at 75% specificity. Annotators had the ability to rate a stimulus as “not a smile” which we used later to train a smile detection model. We separately annotated a third set of 250 smiles whose ranges lay beyond the AU12 [FORMULA] filter but before either of the additional filters to have representative coverage of the entire candidate set. We report annotation numbers and agreement scores for both the 4-class setting (the three labels plus “not a smile”) and the binary smile vs. no smile setting in Table 2. Annotator agreement on both taxonomies was 0.244 and 0.455. We hypothesize since the first taxonomy emphasizes the social role of smiling while the second emphasizes the affective and physical role, annotators could more easily determine the latter as half the social dynamic between the subject and interviewer was hidden behind the camera. Agreement for the more objective task of smile vs. no smile detection was 0.575 and 0.714 across both taxonomies, and we attribute this improvement to the replacement of the AU12 [FORMULA] secondary filter with a 17 AU logistic regression model that best fit the first annotation set. We note the difficulty of the annotation task and the subjectivity required. During weekly discussion meetings, it was not uncommon for a single label to be discussed for many minutes without achieving consensus. Low annotator agreement is not just noise but a reflection of the inherent subjectivity and difficulty in the data (Chochlakis et al., 2025; Aroyo and Welty, 2015); additionally, annotators frequently noted that the three-class smiling labels applied were often too broad to apply perfectly onto the annotations. Survivors frequently reflected on incredibly emotionally charged topics as death, slavery, and unimaginable cruelty and these conditions presented situations with complex and ultimately subjective decision making. For example, in one case, a former doctor smiled during recollection of digging up corpses to learn anatomy because the hospital ran out of cadavers; even after explicit discussion attempting to form consensus, two annotators could not agree if the smile was genuine or masking. Survivors of the Holocaust, having survived by mere chance and confronted with the felt meaninglessness of their own existence, have been historically observed to process emotions in atypical ways known as survivor syndrome (Niederland, 1980). In the testimonies, annotators remarked one manifestation of this disposition is often concealing emotion behind a smile. The impact of the Holocaust has been described as a “rupture in civilization” (Diner, 2007) that has shaped subsequent generations around the world culturally, emotionally, and pervasively (Auerhahn and Laub, 1984; Quindeau and Kestenberg, 1995). Given the severity of this atrocity, even the notion of objective scholarship must be called into question. Interpretation of the open coding of 200 smiles reveals smiling often served both reflective and storytelling roles, with common patterns including fond memory recall, narrative emphasis, and irony. Consistent with existing literature on understanding how emotion shapes personal narrative, we found the most striking difference between the “Narrated I” (how the subject felt then) vs. the “Narrating I” (how the character feels now) (Lazarus, 1991; Bamberg, 1997). We observed associations between smiling and two kinds of emotion: the “narrative valence,” meaning the emotion the interviewee likely felt during the events of their stories, and the “present-day valence,” or what they felt speaking in the interview. We attempted to isolate which non-facial features (meaning not using the AU features) best predicted smile class across both taxonomies. We trained 108 lightweight classifiers to predict the three labels over a large sweep of features and models: three architectures (MLP, GRU, CNN), three modality combinations (include/exclude audio emotion, eyegaze emotion, LLM-derived semantic features), and six temporal windows surrounding the smile with leave-one-out cross validation. To derive these features, we prompted the open-source LLM GPT-OSS-120B (OpenAI et al., 2025) to assign 0 to 10 scores for ten prosodic features relating to affect and socialization: courtesy, nostalgia, humor, emotional weight, coping, direct interviewer response, topic shift, self-reference, positivity, negativity We find most models perform marginally better than chance, but that on the social roles taxonomy, inclusion of the LLM-derived features dramatically improves performance while no effect is recorded on the other taxonomy (Figure 2). We use this finding to motivate our large-scale collection of semantic narrative features in §4. Because 4-class agreement was low, we collapsed taxonomy labels into a binary “smile” vs. “not a smile” task for detector training. In addition to the initial AU features occurring during the smile, we calculated per-subject z-scores of AUs and AU values preceding and occurring after the smile itself and VAD affect scores from two new modalities for all timeframes, via audio and via eyegaze, for a total of 150 features. We hypothesize this asymmetry is a result of AU signal largely overlapping with eyegaze information while audio is mostly independent from observable physical features. Narrative Feature Processing In addition to pre-existing data on valence derived from audio (Lertpetchpun et al., 2025; Ma et al., 2026) and eye gaze (Ma et al., 2026), we run a large-scale automatic transcript labeling task via LLM inference to derive additional narrative features and another human annotation task to understand valence distribution. Horizontal bar chart of within-subject changes in smile presence across transcript topics relative to each speaker baseline. For every sentence in each video, we determine the following seven features from the interview transcript: Narrative era: whether the sentence occurred while discussing pre-war events, wartime or camp events, liberation, post-war life, present-day life, or other. Temporal syntax: the tense of narration, including the strict past (“this happened”), habitual past (“this was happening”), present-tense narration (“this is happening”), and present-tense reflection (“today, I realize”). Present-tense narration has strong ties to PTSD and trauma (Herman, 1997) and dramatic narrative emphasis (Romaine, 1984). Oral structural narrative: a simplified version of Labov and Waletsky’s oral narrative taxonomy (Labov and Waletsky, 1967), where narrative events fall into “orientation/scene-setting,” “complicating action,” “evaluation,” “resolution/coda,” and “other.” There has been substantial prior work demonstrating the effectiveness of automatic NLP methods for this task (Levi et al., 2022; Saldias and Roy, 2020) including on Holocaust testimonies (Shizgal et al., 2025). Topics: whether the sentence is related to any of the topics of “Parents,” “Captivity,” “Daily life (childhood),” “Daily life (imprisonment),” “Feelings and thoughts,” “Forced labor,” “Government,” “Health,” “Liberation,” “Post-conflict,” or “Refugee experiences.” Memory recall type: whether memory recall was semantic or episodic (Levine et al., 2002; Conway, 2005), using Levine et al.’s Autobiographical Interview terminology of “external” (describing places, things, habits) or “internal” (describing a specific event in time). Valence of the narrative: the inferred emotion of how the subject felt during the narrative based solely from described events, ignoring present-day commentary. Present-day valence: the inferred emotion of the subject as they are speaking, inferred based on how they interact with and describe the narrative content. We process transcripts via inference of the open-source LLM GPT-OSS-120B, providing sentences starting up to 20 seconds before and 15 seconds after the smile as context. The first five involve syntactic and semantic classification, tasks for which LLMs have demonstrated sensitivity to linguistic structure and grammatical constructions(Tenney et al., 2019; Hu et al., 2024), while the latter two are inferences on speakers’ emotions in the past and in the present. LLMs show promise in sentiment analysis tasks during oral narratives (Cherukuri et al., 2025) but also fail to capture nuances of human subjectivity (Ma et al., 2025; Santurkar et al., 2023). We recognize this limitation and use LLM annotations in this work as a logistical means to annotate narrative roles at scale. In preliminary checks, minor prompt and model changes had little effect on final label distributions with variability analogous to variation among human annotators. We annotated 1,083,417 sentences across the entire video corpus. We visualize how three features evolve over the course of the interview in Figure 4. Both narrative era and narrative structure follow predictable patterns; we observe smile rate peaks during interview beginnings, reaches its nadir in the middle of the interview, which coincides with the highest proportion of wartime content, and increases again as the interview shifts to post-war and present-day discussion. Smile rate is lowest when wartime content peaks and rises again in post-war and present-day segments. To validate the LLM valence labels, four annotators independently labeled the same 60 smiles as positive, neutral, or negative for both narrative valence and present-day valence in the same interface as Figure 1. We find the inter-annotator agreement similarly low to the pilot (§3.2): Fleiss’ [FORMULA] for narrative valence and [FORMULA] for present-day valence (Fleiss, 1971), with unanimous agreement on only 20% and 31% of tasks, respectively. Compared to human-human agreement, we find LLM-human agreement is actually slightly better for narrative valence [FORMULA] but much worse for present-day valence [FORMULA] , as a text-only transcript does not contain body language and speech patterns highly associated with emotional state (Zeng et al., 2009). We determine which of the three modalities (transcript, audio, eyegaze) best aligns with the two emotion types (narrative and present-day) to pick label modalities for corpus-scale smile analysis. We use transcript labels as-is and discretize audio and eye emotion into positive, neutral, and negative labels then compare against human majority-vote labels in Table 3. We find narrative valence is best predicted by LLM transcript outputs (53%) while present-day valence is best predicted by audio emotion (72%), and opt to use these two modalities as respective valence labels. 5. Smiling, Emotion, and Narrative Patterns In four analyses, we address how the presence and type of smile affects the emotions and narratives of the survivors. In §5.1, we see which semantic topics are most associated with smiling; in §5.2, we find which narrative structures and temporal syntaxes most occur with smiling; in §5.3 we observe how negative-affect smiles improve valence trajectories across all modalities and both emotion types; and in §5.4 we see how smiling changes eye dynamics and blink rates. We aim to understand which topics labeled from §4.1 occur most often with smiling. We define smile activation probability for each word as the chance a smile occurred within 0.5 seconds of word onset, then offset with a per-subject baseline smile rate to get probability deltas. We combine similar words such as “running” and “ran” into the same word lemma of “run,” then sum per-lemma deltas and average by topic. We plot smile frequencies in Figure 5. Intuitively, topics with typically positive valence (childhood, liberation) see significantly higher smile rates while negative topics (captivity, forced labor) see suppressed smile rates. We compare per-subject rates of each narrative-structure and temporal-syntax class in sentences with vs. without a nearby smile in Figure 6 via paired Wilcoxon tests. We observe two related patterns: first, smiling significantly reduces the rates of Orientation (-4.70%) narrative sentences and sentences set in the Strict Past (-6.15%), and significantly increases the rates of Evaluation narrative sentences (+5.62%) and sentences in the Present Reflection (+4.84%). We hypothesize both phenomena reflect shifts between two patterns of interviewee discourse; during matter-of-fact narration, tied with orientation and the strict past, the subject withholds emotional processing and interviewer socialization, and thus smiling, and during present-day reflection, the subject provides commentary and social interaction with the interviewer, which engages more emotional and social behaviors including smiling. This is consistent with literature finding that social function modulates smiling more so than pure emotional expression (Fridlund, 1994) and that nonverbal expressions of emotion such as smiling during narration are timed more for communicative function than narrative fidelity (Bavelas et al., 2000). Our findings contribute to the overall consensus that smiling itself serves a large role in social interaction and communication (Chovil, 1991; Fridlund, 1994; Ekman et al., 1990; Martin et al., 2017) beyond just individual emotional expression.
