We examine how eye gaze movements are influenced during smiling. While fine-grained eye movements such as fixation and saccades are well-studied and associated with cognitive processing (Rayner, 1998) and social interaction (Kleinke, 1986), the low video and temporal resolution (typically 320x240pp and 30 fps) and unknown interviewer location prevented us from directly modeling established behaviors such as direct eye contact, gaze aversion, and “staring off into space” (which itself is well known to be associated with dissociation and memory recall (Glenberg et al., 1998)). However, we find that two coarse eye movement features, total gaze dynamics and blink rate, have strong deviations from baseline during specific types of narrative-valence smiles. We find no significant effects running the same experiments stratified on present-day valence, highlighting the established role of eye gaze in memory and narrative recollection (Richardson and Spivey, 2000; Johansson and Johansson, 2014). We measure gaze dynamics as the total angular distance the eyes move over time, which we calculate as radian displacement per second (rad/s) averaged across both eyes. We again separate smiles by their associated narrative valence, and find that while neutral and negative smiles have gaze dynamics on par with the average non-smiling moment, positive smiles have significantly reduced eye movement ( [FORMULA] , [FORMULA] ); cf. Figure 9 (a). This is qualitatively consistent both with the open coding from §4, where happy smiles seemed to be associated with direct interviewer eye contact and/or fond memory recall with a fixed gaze during recollection; and with existing eye movement literature finding that eye dynamics decrease during sustained social interactions (Kleinke, 1986) and when averted during memory recall (Glenberg et al., 1998). We have direct frame-level binary blink labels from AU45 from the OpenFace features and calculate blink rate as blinks per second. We find blink rate is lower during all smiles, but observe that as narrative content becomes more negative, it drops more ( [FORMULA] , [FORMULA] for negative vs. [FORMULA] , [FORMULA] for positive); cf. Figure 9 (b). The relationship between blinking and cognitive engagement is well-studied, with dual evidence finding blink rate increases when the mind wanders (Smilek et al., 2010) and is suppressed during increased cognitive load (Holland and Tarlow, 1972; Stern et al., 1984). One interpretation of our findings is that smiling utilizes higher cognitive engagement, explaining the suppressed blinking, and that negative-affect smiling in particular is more effortful than positive smiling. Negative-valence smiling may function as a form of emotional regulation (Ekman and Friesen, 1982), which has long been linked to increased cognitive effort (Richards and Gross, 1999; Richards and Gross, 2000). 6. Cultural Differences and Limitations Smiling is both an instinctual and learned behavior (Freedman, 1964; Ekman and Friesen, 1969). It is important to consider the role that cultural influences play in interpersonal interaction and facial expressions. Our findings are limited by the cultural backgrounds of the subjects, and for example, we highlight one particular survivor from late Tsarist Russia and the Soviet Union who emigrated to the USA after the war. The survivor does not smile and describes her wartime experiences in a virtually emotionless manner. Taken in isolation and scrutinized via our analysis, this would imply a lack of felt emotion from the subject; however, in the context of the interview, it is revealed the survivor was socialized in a society where, due to the terror directed by the Soviet state, it could be a matter of survival to not show any emotions. While smiling typically demonstrates politeness and appreciation, this communication in Russian-speaking regions is often expressed through seriousness (Sheldon et al., 2017; Sternin, 2000). This cultural trait can still be observed today in Russian-speaking regions and differs significantly from cultural norms in Western societies (Arapova, 2016). The social and narrative role of smiling is heavily implicated by the personal context and smilers’ identities. 7. Safe and Responsible Innovation Statement In this work, we study Holocaust survivor video testimonies through facial, voice, and narrative processing. Analysis of this atrocity carries significant caution and ethical weight. All video was provided by the USC Shoah Foundation’s Visual History Archive (VHA) under institutional agreement, with no new data collection. We do not disclose any of the survivors’ names or personally identifiable information but we anonymously acknowledge their contribution and honor the memory of those who did not survive. This work is basic research understanding the role smiles play in traumatic narratives, and as a result, we report only corpus-level and anonymous statistics. We must consider the bias of cultural influence on smiling as well. We used generative AI to assist with coding, references, and building the annotation tool. 8. Conclusion We study the role smiling plays for regulating the emotional and social dynamics of narrative recollection and discover the multimodal interactions of smiling with valence, physical markers, and narrative content. These findings underpin how smiling is an incredibly complex and rich expression of human communication and hope this work inspires future research on human smile.
Social and Information Networks (cs.SI): EAGLE: Early Identification of Information Propagation Sources through Generalized Bayesian Inference in Large-scale Social Networks In the era of infodemics, rapidly pinpointing information propagation sources is essential for mitigating negative impacts and enhancing societal resilience. This study presents EAGLE (Early identificAtion of propagation sources through GeneraLized Bayesian infErence), a novel and effective framework for early source identification in large-scale social networks, which integrates evolutionary computation to strategically deploy sparse observers with generalized Bayesian inference to aggregate observational data of varying credibility. Unlike existing approaches, our method relies on limited input from human observers and explicitly incorporates the uncertainty and noise of the data. Comprehensive evaluations across diverse networks and propagation scenarios demonstrate that our approach consistently surpasses state-of-the-art models, without relying on assumptions about propagation characteristics or user attributes. Utilizing real-world datasets with empirical propagation paths from Twitter, our method is among the first capable of identifying potential sources in large-scale networks using limited observers, demonstrating its broad applicability. These findings highlight the effectiveness of generalized Bayesian inference in uncovering propagation dynamics and equip organizations and policymakers with critical tools to proactively address threats to digital trust and security. 1 Introduction As our society becomes more connected, both physically and electronically, the increased connectedness brings both immense benefits and tough challenges to humanity [1, 2]. Online social platforms, for instance, eliminate spatial-temporal constraints of traditional communication, fostering instantaneous global interactions [3, 4]. However, the same characteristics that allow for rapid information exchange also facilitate the uncontrolled spread of misinformation and disinformation, posing a major challenge for human societies [5, 6, 7]. Similarly, the interconnectedness of modern transportation networks, while pulling the whole world closer, has escalated the risk of disease outbreaks and pandemics, posing severe threats to both health and economic stability [8, 9]. The rapid and uncontrolled spread of misinformation highlights the critical need for effective monitoring and early intervention in complex networks, as effective management of these processes is vital for maintaining societal stability and trust [10]. Researchers have approached this challenge from multiple perspectives, including identifying influential spreaders [11, 12], analyzing network characteristics [13, 14], and facilitating group decision-making under uncertainty [15, 16, 17]. Among these efforts, localizing the propagation source is particularly crucial, as it forms the foundation for timely and targeted interventions [18, 19]. A wide range of methods have been proposed for source identification, including approaches based on maximum likelihood estimation, machine learning, and nonlinear dynamics. These approaches can broadly be grouped by their observation paradigm, including complete observation, snapshot observation, and sensor-based observation [20, 21, 22, 23]. Complete observation methods assume full access to the exact states of all nodes at a given time, allowing direct inference of the source. For example, rumor centrality [24] identifies sources in tree-like networks by considering the number of distinct propagation paths, while the local rumor center method [25] narrows the search space by limiting the set of potential sources. Under the Susceptible-Infective (SI) model, methods such as minimum description length [26] and dynamic age [27] leverage spectral properties of the Laplacian matrix. Despite their effectiveness, such methods are rarely feasible in practice, given the substantial data, computational, and knowledge requirements, particularly in large-scale and dynamic systems. Snapshot-based approaches relax these requirements by relying on partial observations of network states at a specific time. These methods typically require detailed knowledge of node attributes, such as influence intensity and susceptibility, and often assume diffusion models like SI or Susceptible–Infective–Recovered (SIR) [28, 29]. The Jordan center method [30], for instance, identifies the source by considering the optimal sample path that most likely results in the observed snapshot, while message passing [31] infers the most likely source via iterative probability updates. More recently, temporal-sequence based graph attention models [29] apply inductive learning to estimate the influence probability between users and distinguish the importance of sources without prior assumptions. Despite their sophistication, these methods often depend heavily on assumed diffusion models and tree-like structures, limiting their applicability to real social networks. To overcome the limitations of complete and snapshot observations, observer-based (or sensor-based) approaches provide a more feasible solution by collecting data from strategically placed or randomly deployed observers, which reduces the amount of required information [32, 18, 21]. Observers typically record the arrival time and direction of information from their neighbors. A seminal example is the Gaussian Estimator (GE) [33], which assumes Gaussian-distributed propagation delays in tree-like networks. To improve computational efficiency, the gradient maximum likelihood algorithm [34] limits the search to high-probability candidates. The Direction-Induced Search based Gaussian Estimator (DISGE) [35] further integrates directional information to refine source inference. In addition, Bayesian source estimators [36] employ iterative updates of belief propagation equations to infer the most probable source, though these too are primarily applicable to tree-like topologies. Beyond these, several heuristic or simulation-based techniques have been proposed [37, 38], such as label propagation [39], effective distance [40, 41], and Monte Carlo [42] methods, each with specific strengths and weaknesses. Despite substantial progress, existing methods face notable challenges when applied to real social media environments. First, many rely on strong assumptions about network topology (tree-like structures), propagation models (SI/SIR), or statistical properties such as propagation delays, which are rarely available in real-world social media [26, 27, 18, 30]. Second, most observer-based methods neglect optimal observer deployment, often placing sensors randomly or by degree centrality, which reduces localization accuracy despite similar resource costs [34, 39, 33]. Third, these methods generally assume post-propagation data collection, requiring all observers to be exposed before inference, which delays intervention and allows further spread [43, 40]. Fourth, they typically treat all observers equally, failing to account for heterogeneous reliability, noise, or structural positioning [33, 35]. Finally, traditional probability-based frameworks struggle to capture epistemic uncertainty: when multiple candidates are indistinguishable, they collapse belief into equal probabilities rather than explicitly representing uncertainty. This fundamentally limits inference accuracy under limited knowledge. Addressing this challenge is essential for developing robust and generalizable source localization frameworks that function reliably under the incomplete and uncertain conditions characteristic of real-world information ecosystems. Therefore, accurately inferring the propagation source in large-scale social networks remains challenging when the spread rate is low, the available observations are sparse, and no prior knowledge of the propagation dynamics and user attributes is available. To address these concerns, we propose EAGLE (Early identificAtion of propagation sources through GeneraLized Bayesian infErence), a novel and generalizable framework for early and robust source localization. EAGLE first minimizes observational blind spots through the strategic deployment of observers, identified via a discrete moth-flame optimization algorithm with a dedicated fitness function [44]. This optimization ensures a balanced trade-off between coverage and redundancy, enabling efficient information capture across large-scale networks. The framework requires only essential propagation data, including the timing and direction of observed propagation events, from a limited number of exposed observers. This design allows EAGLE to operate effectively even in early-stage propagation scenarios and when detailed knowledge of user attributes and diffusion parameters is unavailable. Crucially, EAGLE represents the likelihood of a candidate being the source using a belief function [45] rather than a conventional probability function. This enables the explicit representation of uncertainty and indistinguishability among candidate sources. The generalized Bayesian inference framework [46, 47] then integrates the likelihoods derived from various observer combinations in an explainable and theoretically grounded manner, offering a flexible, interpretable, and generalizable foundation for source localization. To further enhance reliability, EAGLE assigns distinct credibility levels to each combination of exposed observers, determined by their structural advantages within the network topology. This weighting mechanism mitigates the impact of noise and incomplete data, thereby improving inference robustness and accuracy. EAGLE’s performance has been validated across diverse real-world networks and varied propagation patterns, consistently outperforming state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods in both accuracy and efficiency. Importantly, EAGLE demonstrates robust performance in real Twitter networks with about 100,000 users, accurately identifying sources even when only 20 to 120 observers provide valid information. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first validation of source localization on the largest real social network with reconstructed propagation paths, where EAGLE achieves both a significantly reduced inferred source set and a marked improvement in F-score, outperforming all comparative SOTA models under the same conditions. The main contributions of this study are summarized as follows. A discrete moth–flame optimization algorithm is employed to strategically deploy a sparse set of observers via a dedicated fitness function, achieving a balanced trade-off between coverage and redundancy. The belief function is used instead of traditional probability measures to quantify the likelihood of each candidate being the source, enabling explicit modeling of uncertainty and indistinguishability among candidates. The method requires only the timing and direction of propagation arrivals at a limited number of exposed observers, allowing for early-stage identification with minimal human input. Sparse and noisy observational data are integrated through a generalized Bayesian inference model, where each observer combination is weighted according to its structural credibility. This mechanism enhances localization accuracy by systematically accounting for noise, uncertainty, and ignorance in the inference process. EAGLE reformulates source localization as a multi-criteria decision-making problem, providing a transparent, interpretable, and extensible framework that can incorporate additional information sources and reasoning mechanisms in future developments. To comprehensively benchmark EAGLE, we compare its performance against several SOTA observer-based source localization methods widely recognized in the literature. Specifically, Sequential Neighbor Filtering (SNF) [43] identifies the source by measuring the Pearson correlation coefficient between the minimum informed time vector and node radii once all observers have been exposed. Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) [40] assumes a linear relationship between infection times and effective distances to infer the source, requiring the knowledge of the diffusion start time, which is an often impractical assumption. Gaussian Estimator (GE) [33] utilizes maximum likelihood estimation under both observed and deterministic delays, which is ideally suited for tree-like structures under the heterogeneous diffusion process with known means and variances, with limited applicability to real-world networks. Direction-induced Search based Gaussian Estimator (DISGE) [35] is an extension of GE that integrates directional information, inheriting similar structural limitations. Evidential Source Localization (ESL) [41] aggregates observer data via a maximum likelihood-based evidential approach to consider the involved uncertainty and noise, though at the cost of substantial computational complexity. These methodologies represent the current methodological frontier for source localization and collectively provide robust benchmarks for assessing EAGLE’s performance across varying network topologies and propagation dynamics. These networks, consisting of 66,474 and 92,139 users respectively, represent the largest known real-world social networks with reconstructed propagation paths used for validating source localization methods. Users with extensive connections are selected as observers, and they are strategically placed across the entire network rather than being concentrated in a small range, ensuring a broad observational scope. It is evident from the distribution of observer counts within one-hop neighbors, where only approximately [FORMULA] of users have no observers among their one-hop neighbors, over [FORMULA] have one observer, and the remaining users have multiple observers facilitating cross-observation of behavior. These deployed observers are then utilized to infer the propagation source in these large-scale networks, each comprising over 60,000 users. To assess the efficacy of various localization strategies, three scenarios were constructed with an increasing number of exposed users and observers in the propagation, as depicted in Figure 8(b) and (h). Source localization is attempted at the early stages of propagation when only a limited number of observers are exposed to the propagated information. It can be found that there are only 20 to 120 exposed observers in these scenarios, which consumes very little deployment resources to observe a wide range of user behaviors in networks. Due to the exponentially increasing computational demands of the ESL approach in large networks [41], it was excluded from these tests. The performance of the remaining approaches was evaluated based on the error distance, F-score, and the size of the inferred potential source sets, with rankings displayed in Figure 8(c) and (i). EAGLE ranks first in almost all metrics and scenarios, and only ranks second in the size of potential sources in the third scenario (Figure 8(i)). In contrast, the other methods exhibited varying performance across different scenarios, highlighting their inconsistency. Hence, the stable and superior performance of the developed EAGLE in inferring the propagation source is demonstrated in the comparison. The performance of these approaches in two networks with real propagation paths is further discussed in three aspects. For the MoscowAthletics network, EAGLE reduced the error distance to half that of other methods in certain scenarios, consistently achieving smaller error distances across all scenarios as shown in Figure 8(d). Moreover, the error distances obtained by EAGLE are consistently below 2, indicating close proximity to the real source, in contrast to other methods, which always exceed an error distance of 3. The difference in the size of the inferred potential source sets is also notable, as illustrated in Figure 8(e). EAGLE can often pinpoint a unique potential source, thereby distinguishing the likelihood of users with close traits, while methods like SNF, GE, and DISGE identify over 1,000 possible candidates, which are inefficient for source localization. Despite some methods occasionally approaching the performance of EAGLE in terms of error distance or the size of potential sources, such as the size identified by OLS, their accuracy remains significantly lower (Figure 8(f)). This trend is consistent in the NYClimateMarch network, where EAGLE achieves the lowest error distances and sizes of potential sources (Figure 8(j) and (k)). While the OLS approach occasionally matches the size of EAGLE’s inferred source set, its F-score remains at 0, indicating inaccurate predictions, as illustrated in Figure 8(l). Across all experimental scenarios, existing SOTA approaches achieve near-zero accuracy, as measured by the F-score, indicating their inability to infer true sources when confronted with real propagation paths. In contrast, the proposed EAGLE method achieves F-scores ranging from 0.1 to 0.4, a substantial improvement over competing models that fail completely (F-score equals 0). Remarkably, in networks with nearly 100,000 users, EAGLE is the only method capable of accurately identifying the true source with only 100 exposed observers, whereas others generate inferred sets exceeding 1,000 potential sources without containing the actual one. These results demonstrate EAGLE’s robustness and scalability in large-scale and uncertain environments. The consistent performance across real propagation data validates its ability to capture the intrinsic dynamics of social diffusion. Beyond technical accuracy, this capacity has critical implications for mitigating the spread of misinformation and managing public health risks, as it enables early detection and targeted intervention in vast and complex information ecosystems. 5 Conclusion and Discussion This study introduces EAGLE, a comprehensive and generalizable framework for inferring information propagation sources in large-scale networks. This framework strategically integrates evolutionary optimization with generalized Bayesian inference, enabling accurate source identification with minimal observer input and no prior assumptions about propagation models or user attributes. Specifically, the discrete moth-flame optimization algorithm is utilized to optimally deploy observers across the network, maximizing the observation capability and enhancing situational awareness of limited observers. Unlike traditional probability functions, EAGLE employs belief functions to represent the likelihood of candidates being the source and incorporate uncertainty among indistinguishable candidates, allowing the model to reason effectively under incomplete or noisy observations. Using only the timing and direction of propagation from a small number of exposed observers, EAGLE performs early-stage source inference with minimal input, which is both practical and computationally efficient. Observational data are iteratively integrated through the generalized Bayesian inference model, where each observation is weighted by its credibility level. This approach mitigates the effects of noise and uncertainty, yielding accurate localization of potential sources. Comprehensive experiments across synthetic and real-world networks under diverse propagation scenarios demonstrate that EAGLE consistently outperforms existing SOTA methods, that is, identifying the smallest candidate set that reliably contains the true source, and often pinpointing it exactly. Notably, when applied to Twitter datasets with real propagation paths, EAGLE achieves accurate source inference even under diverse, unmodeled, and stochastic user interaction patterns – a feat not achieved by any comparative method. By modeling the diffusion of misinformation and other contagion-like processes, EAGLE enables early, reliable, and interpretable source identification, thereby enhancing both theoretical understanding and practical management of propagation dynamics in complex systems. This capability provides decision-makers, organizations, and researchers with actionable insights to design timely countermeasures, thereby protecting public health, economic stability, and digital trust. Moreover, the generalized Bayesian framework underlying EAGLE opens new directions for research on data-driven inference under uncertainty in large, interconnected systems, suggesting broad applicability to domains such as cybersecurity, epidemiology, and power-grid resilience. In the future, multi-source localization represents an important next step, as many misinformation campaigns originate simultaneously from multiple, loosely coordinated accounts. Developing techniques to identify these dispersed and dynamically evolving sources will be a key research direction. Moreover, adapting the framework to other domains, such as localizing faults in national power grids or identifying patient zero in spatially and temporally evolving epidemic networks, will require methodological advances in observer deployment, data integration, and spatiotemporal inference. These challenges offer clear directions for extending EAGLE’s theoretical foundation and practical impact across diverse networked systems. Programming Languages (cs.PL): Two-Sided Amortized Resource Analysis: Verifying Resource Lower Bounds via Ill-Typing This paper presents a two-sided type system with potential, a type-based technique for verifying resource lower bounds of functional programs. Automatic amortized resource analysis (AARA) verifies upper bounds: types carry potential, and a typing derivation certifies that the available resources are sufficient for evaluation. A lower bound, however, is a necessity statement—the program evaluates only if enough resources are available—and prior type-based approaches obtain it by switching the substructural discipline of potential, so that upper and lower bounds live in separate type systems. Yet the two kinds of bounds complement each other: a matching pair characterizes a program’s cost exactly, and the gap between them limits how much the cost can vary across inputs of the same size. Our type system combines AARA-style potential with the two-sided type systems of Ramsay and Walpole, whose central guarantee is that ill-typed programs do not evaluate. In a two-sided judgment, typing formulas may constrain arbitrary terms and may appear on both sides of the turnstile; the judgment [FORMULA] states that if [FORMULA] evaluates to a result of type [FORMULA] , then at least [FORMULA] units of resource must be available—that is, [FORMULA] is a lower bound. Because potential makes typing formulas non-replicable, our system follows an affine discipline instead of the replicable contexts of the original framework. We define the meaning of types by semantic typing over value states, pairs of a value and a remaining resource amount, and we prove soundness on a safety fragment; corollaries recover the classical two-sided guarantees and the soundness of both kinds of bounds in a single proof system. A prototype type checker in OCaml verifies, on a suite of 19 benchmarks, matching pairs of bounds that characterize costs exactly, as well as lower bounds for programs whose upper bounds are unavailable. Finally, as a parallel exploration, we study a two-sided linear type system in which every value is a non-replicable resource; there, closures that capture linear resources call for dual typing formulas, and the exact accounting explains the affine design of the main system. 1. Introduction Resource analysis reasons about how much resource—time, memory, energy—a program consumes. An upper bound is a (possibly symbolic) value that the actual cost never exceeds; a lower bound is a value that the actual cost never falls below. Figure 1 illustrates the two kinds of bounds. Upper-bound analyses are well studied; in particular, automatic amortized resource analysis (AARA) (Hofmann and Jost, 2003; Hoffmann and Jost, 2022) is a well-established type-based technique: types carry potential in the sense of amortized analysis. AARA has grown from linear potential functions to polynomial (Hoffmann and Hofmann, 2010), multivariate (Hoffmann et al., 2011), and exponential (Kahn and Hoffmann, 2020) ones, and has been adapted to higher-order, imperative, and probabilistic programs (Hoffmann and Jost, 2022). Lower bounds have received much less attention in type-based resource analysis. At first glance, a lower bound looks less useful, because it promises only that a program is at least so expensive. However, lower bounds complement upper bounds. A matching pair of bounds characterizes a program’s cost exactly and certifies that neither bound can be improved. Even a non-matching pair is informative: every cost lies between the two bounds, so the gap between them limits how much the cost can vary across inputs of the same size. This variation is what constant-time programming seeks to eliminate, because a cost that depends on secret data leaks information. A classical typing judgment is a sufficiency statement. The slogan “well-typed programs do not go wrong,” combined with potential, yields “well-typed programs are given sufficient resources”: the assumptions on the left of [FORMULA] are enough—possibly more than enough—for the conclusion on the right. The semantic soundness proof for recursive programs needs the semantic interpretation of types to behave like a safety property. Following Ramsay and Walpole (2024), we identify two key requirements. First, if a program satisfies a type, replacing one of its subterms by a less-defined term should not invalidate the type. A search state also carries a priority queue, represented as a list of left- or right-side formulas to decompose next. Related Work The two-sided type system of Ramsay and Walpole (2024) is one of the main foundations of this paper. It expresses typability and ill-typability in a single sequent-style judgment, where formulas may occur on both sides of [FORMULA] and an empty right-hand side represents refutation. We keep this position-sensitive reading, including the necessity arrow, but add potential annotations so that refuting typability can express that an under-resourced program cannot evaluate. This adaptation requires an affine context discipline, a value-state semantics, and a safety fragment. In the same line of work, Li et al. (2026) interpret types by sets of normal forms, making a complement operator sound and obtaining completeness. Our work stays closer to the value-based interpretation of Ramsay and Walpole (2024), because the main goal is to integrate two-sided typing with resource bounds rather than to obtain completeness for type refutation. Automatic Amortized Resource Analysis (AARA), pioneered by Hofmann and Jost (2003), infers symbolic resource bounds using amortized potential (Hoffmann and Jost, 2022): type annotations assign potential to data structures, and local typing constraints reduce bound inference to linear programming. AARA has been extended from linear to polynomial (Hoffmann and Hofmann, 2010; Hoffmann et al., 2011), exponential (Kahn and Hoffmann, 2020), and logarithmic (Hofmann et al., 2022) potentials, and adapted to higher-order (Jost et al., 2010), imperative and object-oriented (Carbonneaux et al., 2015), lazy (Vasconcelos et al., 2015), session-typed (Das et al., 2018), probabilistic (Ngo et al., 2018), and separation-logic (Atkey, 2011) settings. AARA is the other main foundation of this paper. Our system preserves its potential-based structure: types carry potential, resource consumption is local, and sufficiency-arrow judgments retain the usual upper-bound reading. The two-sided layer adds lower-bound and refutation reasoning while remaining compatible with standard AARA upper-bound analysis, so the system extends AARA along a two-sided dimension. Most AARA work focuses on upper bounds. The closest work to ours is that of Ngo et al. (2017), which verifies lower bounds and constant-resource behavior by varying the substructural discipline of potential: affine potential yields upper bounds, relevant potential yields lower bounds, and linear potential yields constant-resource guarantees. Our work addresses a similar problem and also relies on AARA potential, but obtains necessity from the two-sided position of formulas and the necessity arrow while keeping the main resource discipline affine. Beyond AARA, lower bounds have been studied with different methods. Žikelić et al. (2022) use anti-potentials to bound the cost difference between two programs. Frohn et al. (2020) infer worst-case lower bounds for integer programs with metering functions and recurrence solving. Wang et al. (2019) use martingales for expected-cost bounds in probabilistic programs. These approaches rely on recurrence reasoning, martingales, or anti-potentials rather than a two-sided type system. Incorrectness logic, introduced by O’Hearn (2019), provides a program-logic foundation for under-approximate reasoning: instead of proving that all executions avoid an error, it proves the presence of concrete behaviors. This idea has been developed for local heap reasoning (Raad et al., 2020), large-scale bug finding (Le et al., 2022), concurrency (Raad et al., 2022), outcome logics (Zilberstein et al., 2023; Zilberstein et al., 2024), non-termination (Raad et al., 2024), and backward under-approximate reasoning (Ascari et al., 2024). The closest connection to resources is the quantitative incorrectness logic of Jin and Wang (2026), which under-approximates worst-case resource usage using resource functions. Our lower-bound judgments have a similar flavor, but derive resource facts compositionally from AARA-style potential and two-sided typing rather than from program-logic triples. Linear logic (Girard, 1987) is a substructural logic in which contraction and weakening are not freely available. Linear and affine type systems (Wadler, 1990; Pierce, 2002) use these restrictions to control resources and support resource analysis (Hofmann, 2003). Linear logic also informs our rules, especially the exploratory two-sided linear type system (Section 5.2 and our technical report). Our systems are not presentations of linear logic with typing formulas as atoms: types carry ordered potential, the main system is affine, and the semantics is operational and resource-aware. Still, weakening, contraction, context splitting, and left–right symmetry follow the same broad structural intuition. 7. Conclusion This paper presented a two-sided type system with potential, in which a single proof system derives resource upper bounds, lower bounds, and refutations: sufficiency and necessity differ only in the position of formulas around [FORMULA] . We defined a semantic-typing model over value states and proved the soundness of the type system on a safety fragment that retains all the types used in our examples and benchmarks. A prototype checker verifies matching pairs of bounds that characterize costs exactly, as well as lower bounds for programs whose upper bounds are unavailable. Finally, a parallel exploration of two-sided linear typing showed that closures capturing linear resources call for dual typing formulas, which explains the affine design of the main system. Automating the search for annotations—type inference for two-sided judgments—is a natural next step.

Context Types: Bunched Modalities for Unifying Safety and Reachability Most type systems are designed to verify safety properties: the judgement [FORMULA] holds if [FORMULA] may evaluate to any value contained in the denotation of [FORMULA] , but nothing more. More recent type systems have considered the complementary class of reachability properties: in these systems, the typing judgment holds if [FORMULA] must be able to evaluate to every value denoted by [FORMULA] , and possibly more. This paper introduces a refinement type system for higher-order functional programs where types can capture both safety and reachability properties. Simultaneously supporting both is challenging because each imposes different constraints on how variable bindings in a typing context are interpreted. We address this challenge by treating typing contexts as a kind of resource that mediates which capabilities are available when typing a program. We formalize this notion by developing a resource algebra of contextual capabilities and a bunched modal context logic over this algebra. We then interpret our type system in this logic, establishing soundness with respect to a denotational semantics that unifies safety and reachability guarantees within a single typing judgement. 1. Introduction Static type systems are one of the most versatile and widely-used program reasoning techniques available today. While their particulars can vary wildly, common to all type systems are two key ingredients: the use of types to specify program behavior, and some deductive mechanism for compositionally verifying that the program is consistent with that specification. Type systems have traditionally targeted safety properties, a focus embodied by Milner’s famous slogan that “well-typed programs cannot ‘go wrong”’ (Milner+78). Here, the typing judgement [FORMULA] asserts that [FORMULA] may evaluate to many values (under any environment consistent with [FORMULA] ), but that set of values is entirely contained within the “safe” region specified by [FORMULA] . Dually, reachability properties seek to precisely capture a subset of the values that a program must reach. Rather than ruling out certain executions, reachability analyses seek to certify the existence of feasible executions. Reachability analyses are a well-established and practical technique for informing program optimizations and transformations (WS94; GM21; JTW+98). They have also been effectively used to find buggy behaviors (BMC+03); for example, several recent works (GOS19; ReverseHoareLogic; OHP19; ZDS23) have studied deductive “incorrectness” reasoning frameworks which can prove the existence of witnesses of safety violations, with a goal of avoiding the high false positive rate reported by typical bug detection tools. The question of how to develop type systems for reachability, however, has been largely unexplored. Recent works (RefinementTypeRefutations; CoverageType; Ill-types) that have studied type-based reachability reasoning have either focused on a particular property, e.g., checking completeness of test input generators (CoverageType), or a particular application, e.g., generating concrete counterexamples refuting refinement type specifications (RefinementTypeRefutations) or proving ill-typed programs do not evaluate (Ill-types), rather than providing a general type-based reachability framework. To unify these two views of types, this paper proposes a novel semantic model that can simultaneously capture both overapproximations (may-style) and underapproximations (must-style) of program behaviors, allowing safety and reachability specifications to be compositionally combined within a single type discipline. This model gives rise to a type system in which type qualifiers are equipped with a modality indicating whether they should be interpreted as an over- or under-approximate specification. The type system naturally supports both deterministic and nondeterministic higher-order programs, captures both may- and must-style function summaries (GN+10), and can be applied to a range of verification tasks, including incorrectness-style reasoning (OHP19) and proving completeness of test-input generators (CoverageType). Curriculum Proof Repair with Learned Counterexamples Language models (LMs) have substantially lowered the barrier to applying formal verification for building reliable and secure software. Existing approaches commonly follow the verifier-in-the-loop paradigm, but the verifier often provides only coarse, binary pass/fail feedback, which offers little actionable signal on how the proof should be repaired. Recent work shows that counterexamples provide more actionable feedback by grounding proof failures in concrete program states, but generating useful ones at inference time requires costly iterative refinement. We present TopoVerus, an LM-based framework for Verus proof repair that internalizes counterexample-guided diagnosis as a model capability, producing useful counterexamples in a single pass. Our key insight is to train counterexample generation not as a standalone validation task, but as a data-driven diagnostic objective: a counterexample is useful when conditioning on it helps the model produce a safe, verifier-passing proof. Given a failed Verus proof and verifier error, TopoVerus generates a structured source-level counterexample, repair rationale, and repaired proof in one trajectory, optimized with reinforcement learning from Verus feedback and a proof-code safety gate. To guide the order of invariant repairs and target counterexamples to specific invariants, TopoVerus introduces a curriculum with a topological graph reward based on invariant dependencies derived from inductiveness tests and encourages counterexample generation following the same topological order as these dependencies. Across seven Verus benchmarks with 471 problems, TopoVerus achieves 61.6%/72.2% weighted-average Safe-Pass@1/Safe-Pass@3, outperforming the strongest baseline, Claude Sonnet 4.5, by 5.7/6.3 points. We also show that TopoVerus’s learned counterexamples can directly augment the reasoning of existing LM-based proof repair approaches, improving their success rate by 64.3% compared to chain-of-thought diagnostics. We release the training and evaluation code at https://github.com/Etha-Sun/Topoverus and the TopoVerus-32B weights at https://huggingface.co/YuechunSun/TopoVerus-32B. 1 Introduction Formal verification provides machine-checked guarantees that software satisfies rich correctness specifications, enabling the construction of safety-critical, large-scale software systems (Lattuada et al., 2023; Leroy et al., 2016; Klein et al., 2009; Sun et al., 2024b; Zhou et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2023). However, these guarantees remain costly to obtain. Developers must write specifications, discover inductive invariants, and repair failed proof obligations. Recent work using language models (LMs) for verification automates parts of this proof-construction loop (Sun et al., 2026; Zhong et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2026a; Zhong & Si, 2025; Aggarwal et al., 2025; Mugnier et al., 2025; First et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2026b; Li et al., 2026b; Ye et al., 2026), lowering the expertise barrier for applying formal verification to real-world software. As LM-generated proof candidates are not sound by construction, existing LM-based approaches typically keep a verifier in the loop: the model proposes proof annotations, the verifier reports failures, and the model revises the proof based on the error messages (Yang et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2026; Zhong et al., 2025; Aggarwal et al., 2025). This loop resembles interactive verification, where developers debug failures by constructing concrete failing states and tracing where an invariant or postcondition breaks (Clarke et al., 2000; Clarke et al., 2003). However, verifier messages often expose only a failed proof obligation with limited diagnostic context, e.g., postcondition not satisfied, rather than the source-level state, execution path, or missing facts responsible for the failure. The LM must thus infer the root cause from ambiguous feedback, making repair brittle and token-inefficient. Existing LM-based proof repair approaches compensate for coarse verifier feedback in different ways. Some encode verifier-specific repair rules or syntax guidance in the prompt (Yang et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2026), supply in-context proof examples (Yang et al., 2025; Mugnier et al., 2025), or retrieve relevant proof fragments (Zhong et al., 2025). Others bypass explicit diagnosis and use verification outcomes, i.e., pass/fail signals, to guide search, data synthesis, self-improvement, or fine-tuning (Aggarwal et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025). While effective, these approaches leave a diagnostic gap: engineered prompt knowledge is costly to curate and does not generalize as verifier behavior and proof idioms evolve (Yang et al., 2026a; Yang et al., 2026b), whereas verifier-outcome objectives provide only sparse, indirect signals for repair. A more actionable feedback signal is a source-level counterexample: a concrete program state, optionally with a short execution trace, that falsifies a proof obligation. Unlike verifier-specific repair rules, counterexamples describe the concrete failing program state, making them largely independent of diagnostic formats and directly useful for localizing repairs. They are central to classic counterexample-guided verification (Clarke et al., 2000; Clarke et al., 2003; Bradley, 2011; Bradley, 2012), where failed states drive refinement or blocking of bad regions. Recent LM-based works also show that generated counterexamples can improve proof repair (Yang et al., 2026b; Li et al., 2026a; Huang et al., 2026). Unfortunately, a useful counterexample requires nontrivial, execution-level code reasoning: it must be feasible, expose the relevant corner case, and identify the missing proof fact, rather than merely state a plausible failure (Copet et al., 2025). This also explains why existing approaches often incur high inference costs, as they require iterative refinement to generate high-quality counterexamples (Yang et al., 2026b). Moreover, proof failures often conflate multiple missing or incorrect invariants, so which counterexample is most useful to address first is not well defined. Our approach. We present TopoVerus, an LM-based verification framework for Verus proof repair that internalizes counterexample-guided diagnosis as a model capability. Our idea is to formulate counterexample generation as a diagnostic learning problem where the counterexample is useful not merely when it is plausible (Yang et al., 2026b), but when conditioning on it helps the model produce a safe, verifier-passing proof. Given a failed Verus proof attempt and the corresponding verifier error, TopoVerus generates a structured source-level counterexample, a concise repair rationale, and a candidate repaired proof in this order within a single trajectory. We optimize the full trajectory using reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) from Verus, together with a proof-code safety gate that rejects repairs modifying the executable program or user-supplied specifications. As a result, counterexamples are not trained as standalone artifacts with hand-written validators (Yang et al., 2026b) or predefined verifier-specific repair taxonomies (Yang et al., 2025). Instead, they receive indirect credit through downstream repair success, biasing the model toward diagnostics that are actionable for safe proof repair. This formulation, however, creates a key technical challenge. The training signal for counterexample utility is sparse, delayed, and order-sensitive. A failed proof often contains multiple missing or incorrect invariants, so final verifier success alone does not reveal whether a generated counterexample was wrong, merely unhelpful, or aimed at a downstream proof obligation whose preconditions were not yet established (Section 2.1). To expose this latent structure during learning, TopoVerus approximates dependencies among invariants with a graph derived from inductiveness tests, and rewards repaired proofs whose invariants respect a topological order over the resulting graph. The resulting topological graph reward turns sparse outcome feedback into a dependency-aware curriculum, i.e., it establishes state-constraining facts first, then generates counterexamples and repairs for dependent obligations in the corresponding order, where the counterexample’s diagnostics become informative. Results. Our evaluation shows that TopoVerus improves Verus proof repair and provides actionable diagnostics for downstream repair tools. Across seven Verus benchmarks comprising 471 problems, TopoVerus achieves 61.6% and 72.2% in Safe-Pass@1 and Safe-Pass@3, outperforming the strongest baseline, i.e., Claude Sonnet 4.5, by 5.7 and 6.3 points, respectively. The gains are largest on structurally difficult settings such as VeriCogen and ObfsBench, where proof templates and syntactic hints are less reliable. Ablations show that counterexample-augmented reasoning in TopoVerus improves weighted Safe-Pass@1 by 11.2 points over the repair with natural-language diagnostics, while the topological graph reward further improves over binary verifier-only RL by 7.9 points. Importantly, TopoVerus’s generated counterexamples also transfer to other LMs used as proof repairers, improving their repair success by up to 64.3% (relative) over chain-of-thought diagnostics. We release the training and evaluation code at https://github.com/Etha-Sun/Topoverus and the TopoVerus-32B weights at https://huggingface.co/YuechunSun/TopoVerus-32B. 2 Overview We focus on Verus, a Rust-native verifier for verifying Rust programs. A Verus proof consists of executable Rust code together with specifications (e.g., preconditions and postconditions), and proof annotations (e.g., invariants, assertions). The verifier discharges the proof into Verification Conditions (VCs) and checks them with off-the-shelf SMT solvers (de Moura & Bjørner, 2008; Barbosa et al., 2022). Among the proof annotations, inferring invariants has been a key challenge of automating formal verification (Flanagan & Leino, 2001; Garg et al., 2014; Kamath et al., 2023). Loop invariants are properties that hold at the beginning of every loop iteration. Figure 1 shows the Verus code and proof that motivate our approach. The function implements binary-search insertion: it returns the position of target in a sorted array, or the index where target should be inserted. The requires (preconditions) assume the input to be a sorted array, and the ensures (postconditions) specify that target is inserted correctly. The loop invariants are the properties that are derived from the preconditions and execution code. They hold before entering the loop (base case) and remain true in each loop iteration (inductiveness). Note that invariants often depend on other invariants or are mutually dependent. We use this example to illustrate such dependencies and how fixing invariants following such dependencies benefits counterexample reasoning, diagnosis and repair of buggy proofs. Recent efforts have significantly lowered the barrier to formal verification using LMs, across both mathematical theorem proving (Polu & Sutskever, 2020; Yang et al., 2023; Lample et al., 2022) and program verification (First et al., 2023; Sun et al., 2024a; He et al., 2026; Zhong et al., 2025). In Verus proof generation, prior works primarily focused on encoding heuristics and repair strategies via either engineering prompts Yang et al. (2025); Sun et al. (2026), or constructing large-scale synthetic training sets Chen et al. (2025). However, a common limitation across these systems is their reliance on the traditional iterative-refinement paradigm, heavily depending on coarse, abstract feedback from the underlying SMT solvers. Such feedback often fails to isolate the root cause of verification failures, frequently causing LM-based repair to degenerate into inefficient trial-and-error generation. Our work advances this paradigm by moving beyond verifier feedback; we train the model to internalize diagnostic reasoning, integrating actionable, concrete counterexamples directly into the repair policy. Counterexample-guided feedback for proof repair. Traditional formal methods have long relied on counterexamples, i.e., concrete execution traces that witness proof failures, as the key actionable feedback to iteratively refine invariants and generate proofs (Clarke et al., 2000; Bradley, 2012). Recent works have begun to explore LM-driven counterexample generation to sidestep the challenge of reconstructing counterexamples from low-level SMT solver models (Yang et al., 2026b; Li et al., 2026a). Nonetheless, these existing methods often demand strict formal validation of the generated counterexamples, which is often intractable, especially for complex proofs where there are multiple counterexamples to different missing/wrong invariants. Following the philosophy of reasoning over counterexamples, TopoVerus aims to generate high-quality counterexamples, but in a principled way, i.e., internalizing the capability of generating high-quality counterexamples following the topological dependency graph. Rather than searching for arbitrary counterexamples for a proof, TopoVerus trains the model to produce counterexamples whose diagnostic content is useful for successful downstream repair. Reinforcement learning and curriculum learning. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards has shown strong results in theorem proving (AlphaProof & AlphaGeometry, 2024; Xin et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025) and code generation (Le et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2023), but optimizing complex verification tasks remains challenging due to reward sparsity and long proof trajectories. Curriculum learning (Bengio et al., 2009; Portelas et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021) mitigates such sparsity by structuring learning from easy to hard; traditionally this operates across episodes as a macro-curriculum over training data. More recently, work on long-horizon reasoning has begun exploring intra-episode micro-curricula that structure the generation process within a single rollout (Dou et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2026; Shen et al., 2025). These approaches define curricula through external heuristics (e.g., sequence length, task decomposition), whereas our Topological Graph Reward extracts an intrinsic micro-curriculum directly from the natural dependency DAG among Verus proof obligations, rewarding the model for establishing prerequisite invariants before more complex ones within each repair trajectory. 6 Discussion and Conclusion Limitations. First, the dependency-aware micro-curriculum is fundamentally targeting loop invariants. While invariants are often a key bottleneck of formal verification, this focus restricts the framework’s immediate generalization to other critical verification structures, e.g., assertions. Second, the validity of the generated counterexamples is not formally guaranteed. Because exact reachability checking is fundamentally challenging and often infeasible (Yang et al., 2026b), the model treats the counterexample [FORMULA] strictly as an intermediate reasoning step optimized for downstream repair success rather than absolute mathematical validity. Consequently, the model may occasionally hallucinate imprecise execution traces that provide ambiguous guidance. Conclusion. We presented TopoVerus, a 32B-parameter framework that transforms automated formal verification from a chaotic, unordered trial-and-error process into a dependency-aware generation pipeline. By training a response-level policy via GRPO, our model learns to synthesize structured, intermediate counterexamples in a principled way and incrementally repair the proofs. The Topological Graph Reward extracts a natural micro-curriculum directly from the DAG of proof obligations, explicitly incentivizing the model to establish foundational constraints before writing dependent invariants. Our extensive evaluations demonstrate that synergistically coupling counterexample-guided feedback with topological curriculum learning significantly mitigates the sparsity of verifier rewards and outperforms the baselines. Ethics Statement This work develops AI methods for automated formal verification, which aims to improve the reliability and correctness of software systems. We do not foresee direct negative societal impacts. All benchmarks used are publicly available or synthesized from open-source codebases. Our models are trained on code verification tasks and are not designed for generating harmful content. Retargetable Compilation for Tensor Kernels via a Unified Layout Abstraction Modern hardware accelerators achieve high performance through specialized instructions coupled with tightly managed memory hierarchies. These instructions impose strict layout requirements on their operands: where tensor fragments reside, how they are organized, and how parallel units access them. Such instruction-visible layout is critical to kernel performance, as it determines whether instructions execute correctly and how much data movement they incur. However, existing compilers either scatter layout requirements across handwritten programs and local scheduling rules, or provide layout representations and conversions specific to a single class of targets. Both approaches expose the same abstraction gap: the absence of a unified model for instruction layout requirements across backends. 1. Introduction High-performance machine learning systems increasingly rely on specialized hardware instructions such as tensor core MMA operations, AVX-512 VNNI, and Hexagon HMX matrix instructions (Weng et al., 2021; Feng et al., 2022; Zheng et al., 2022b). Extracting high throughput from such instructions requires coordinating specialized compute, local memories, explicit data movement, and hardware-specific parallel execution. This burden falls on both programmer and compiler. For the programmer, hand-tuning is costly. A layout mistake produces wrong results and manual optimization limits the design space (NVIDIA Corporation, 2026b; Hao et al., 2026), while porting across hardware with different architectures means starting the whole effort over from scratch. A retargetable compiler can relieve this burden from programmer. However, compilers face the same structural obstacle. Arithmetic semantics alone do not capture an instruction’s operand requirements. Correct execution also depends on where operands reside, how their dimensions are organized, and how their elements are distributed across parallel hardware units. Layout is therefore part of the usable interface of an instruction, and the challenge is to satisfy these instruction layout demands globally, so that the data path is free of unnecessary movement and ad-hoc conversion. A Hexagon kernel (Hao et al., 2026), for example, mixes DMA transfers, HVX vector operations, and HMX matrix operations across three memory spaces, each imposing a distinct operand layout. Stitching them into one data path requires explicit layout conversion at the boundaries. The ISA provides over a dozen dedicated primitives for this purpose alone, covering register transposition (vshuff, vdeal), element-width conversion (vpack, vunpack), and register reshaping (vcombine, vsplat, valign). We call instructions whose purpose is to convert between layouts repairs. A compiler that only checks arithmetic equivalence may select the correct instructions yet still produce an incorrect or repair-heavy data path. These layout challenges are not confined to Hexagon. They also arise on CPU and GPU, where matrix extensions and tensor instructions face the same underlying problem (Feng et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2025; Apache TVM Community, 2026). In a GEMM with epilogue, the tile matmul accumulates into MMA fragments, but the epilogue reduction needs a row-major view for axis-aligned access. The boundary between them requires explicit layout conversion. Hand-tuned kernels such as FlashAttention-2’s Ampere implementation (Dao, 2023) encode this conversion by hand. A global layout solver can search for compatible layouts systematically instead. Existing systems address different aspects of the cross-backend layout problem, but none provides a unified layout abstraction for retargetable compilation. Layout-guided tensor DSLs and scheduling systems (Feng et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2025; Apache TVM Community, 2026) make data placement part of the program or schedule, so porting a kernel can require re-deriving layouts for each target. The impact of a layout rejected by an instruction goes beyond performance to correctness. Synthesis-based systems (Kothari et al., 2024; Noor et al., 2025) move layout decision into the compiler, but resolve mismatches locally, potentially leaving conversions that a global layout choice could eliminate. Constructive layout algebras such as CuTe and Linear Layouts (NVIDIA Corporation, 2026b; Zhou et al., 2026) derive conversions between concrete layouts, but their conversions rely on GPU-specific ISA primitives for efficient lowering. On another ISA, the same construction may have no efficient lowering, or a suitable conversion algebra may have to be re-derived for the target. Generic fallbacks such as scalarization can be orders of magnitude more expensive. As a result, existing systems still struggle to combine consistent cross-backend programming with end-to-end performance. To close this gap, we present Arknife, a retargetable compiler for tensor kernels built around a layout algebra that treats layouts as unknowns to be solved. We model each target by its parallel hierarchy, memory spaces, and instructions, with parallel indices and local addresses forming a hardware coordinate space. A tensor layout is an injective mapping from logical axis factors into this space, while an instruction operand declares a partial mapping that constrains only the factors the instruction observes. All requirements of a tensor’s bound uses therefore conjoin into a single accumulated constraint, and binding legality reduces to its satisfiability rather than to layout construction. The constraint system is order-independent, monotone, and local to each instruction boundary, so the compiler can evaluate feasibility with a small integer program at any point of instruction search. An unsatisfiable constraint exposes the conflict, which a target-provided repair resolves. A satisfiable one yields globally chosen layouts, eliminating conversions by layout choice rather than post-hoc synthesis. Concretely, layout feasibility shapes every stage of Arknife compilation, which falls naturally into two phases. The first phase establishes layout feasibility. For each operator, Arknife enumerates the arithmetically equivalent target instructions and commits the cheapest candidate whose accumulated constraint remains satisfiable, with cost measured by the repairs that the candidate’s operand requirements would induce. Wherever requirements still conflict across a tensor’s uses, it inserts the corresponding target-provided repairs, so that every instruction boundary in the resulting graph is layout-feasible. The second phase optimizes within this feasible space. E-graph rewriting first removes redundant repairs, after which a single integer program assigns the remaining axis mappings, maximizing layout preferences while keeping every instruction boundary legal. The chosen layouts are then preserved through tiling, memory planning, and code generation, down to the emitted kernel. Together, the layout algebra and the compilation pipeline turn layout compatibility from a programmer decision into a compiler decision. Arknife reads operand requirements from target-side instruction descriptions and checks them at instruction boundaries. Retargeting requires defining the target’s instructions through the description interface, without changing the core layout algebra or solver. This paper makes the following contributions: We introduce a target-independent layout algebra that expresses what each instruction demands of its operand layouts. Porting it to a new ISA requires no new algebraic transformations. We provide a consistent programming interface across backends, delegating instruction-visible layouts to the compiler. We build a retargetable compiler that removes redundant repairs through e-graph rewriting and performs global layout solving, delivering high-performance operators on heterogeneous backends. We evaluate Arknife on x86 CPU, Qualcomm Hexagon NPU, and NVIDIA A100. It also achieves [FORMULA] over QNN (Qualcomm Technologies, Inc., 2026), the vendor Hexagon library. On A100, it reaches [FORMULA] over unfused PyTorch (Paszke et al., 2019) on FP16 MHA and 97% of cuBLAS (NVIDIA Corporation, 2026a) performance on TF32 GEMM. 2. Background and Motivation A tensor kernel depends on two classes of instructions: compute and conversion. Compute instructions perform arithmetic within one level of the memory hierarchy and assume their operands already lie in a placement they accept: _mm512_dpbusd_epi32, for instance, accumulates products of packed byte groups within a register. Conversion instructions change that placement, either by moving data between levels or by rearranging it within a level: _mm512_unpacklo_epi16 interleaves the 16-bit elements of its two operands, and vshuff interleaves bytes within a Hexagon vector register. A kernel is thus a chain of interleaved compute and conversion instructions, and either the programmer or the compiler must decide where the conversions fall in that chain. Four panels. That decision is hard, and the requirements differ from one backend to another. Figure 1(a)–(c) show three placements of the same logical GEMM [FORMULA] tile. On x86, adjacent elements are packed into one ZMM register; on Hexagon, rows are interleaved in pairs in VTCM; and on A100, ldmatrix distributes elements across lanes and registers. The consuming instruction imposes each layout and states it in its vocabulary. We call such a requirement an instruction-visible layout. Although absent from the instruction’s arithmetic, it determines whether the operand is legal. Such a requirement may be finer than whole-axis ordering. Because the order mixes factors of both axes, whole-axis permutations such as row-major or column-major cannot express it. The HMX tile-buffer fill follows this order, so any other arrangement is an invalid operand, not merely a slower one. This requirement reflects a broader difficulty: cross-backend layout handling is central to retargetable tensor-kernel generation. Instruction-visible layouts are imposed at different memory and parallel levels, in different vocabularies. A layout legal on one target may be invalid on another, and a conversion cheap on one may be prohibitively expensive on another. Four panels. Systems address this layout-handling difficulty differently. Figure 2 contrasts three current approaches (a)–(c) with the design of Arknife (d) along three dimensions: who states the layout, the scope of mismatch resolution, and the layout algebra. In layout-guided tensor DSLs and schedules, the layout starts as something the program states. TensorIR (Feng et al., 2022) fixes it in the schedule, and TIRx (Apache TVM Community, 2026) attaches it to the tensor type, where the user declares tile placement across lanes, warps, and registers. For a single target this is merely verbose, while across backends it becomes a heavy burden, as the user must re-derive the placement for each target’s hierarchy and instruction constraints. Worse, an unlucky or unchecked layout choice surfaces as incorrect results, not merely lost performance. Arknife aims to eliminate this burden (Figure 2(d)). The program drops the layout argument and the compiler derives the placement. Synthesis-based approaches take the layout decision into the compiler but keep mismatch resolution local (Figure 2(b)), with each rewrite patching mismatches in isolation and so potentially missing conversions that a global layout choice could eliminate. Hydride and MISAAL (Kothari et al., 2024; Noor et al., 2025), for instance, take a target-scheduled IR as input. Hydride synthesizes small windows of an expression separately, choosing each conversion from local information even when a layout choice one window away would have made it unnecessary. Solving globally across the graph, as in Figure 2(d), avoids this. In both, the layout must already be known before the algebra runs. This suffices where layout-change mechanisms are few, fixed in the ISA, and comparably priced. Within a GPU block, for instance, a shared-memory round trip converts any layout into any other at bounded cost. A retargetable compiler has none of these constants. In Figure 1(d), an HMX tile in VTCM has rows interleaved in pairs and its vector consumer expects row-major registers. The permutation between them crosses the VTCM--register boundary, where no comparably priced primitive exists. This motivates a constraint-based algebra that operates on requirements rather than layouts (Figure 2(d)). Each instruction contributes a partial operand requirement, and one layout is solved from all of them. The algebra itself would remain fixed across backends, and only its inputs would change, making the formulation retargetable. The two formulations answer different questions—given layouts, derive the transformation or given requirements, decide whether a layout exists and which to choose. Across all three approaches, what an instruction requires of its operands remains implicit, woven into program text, local rewrite rules, or target-dependent layout compositions. Retargeting re-encodes compatibility rules from scratch. Arknife therefore pursues two design goals. The first is representational: one layout algebra, tied to no vendor ISA, that decides whether an operand is legal on any target (Section 4). The second is algorithmic: remove redundant repairs and solve layouts globally across the compute graph (Section 5). 3. Overview Figure 3 shows the Arknife compilation workflow. The compiler takes a tensor program and a target description as input. The program specifies the logical computation, while the target description provides parallel levels, memory spaces, instruction templates, and their operand-layout requirements. The output is an executable kernel specialized to the target. Figure 6 instantiates the pipeline on a quantized-add excerpt for the Hexagon target. Compilation begins with instruction binding (Section 5.1), which considers candidate target instructions for each program operation. For each candidate, the compiler checks whether its operand-layout requirements can be satisfied directly or through target-provided repairs, such as reduce, data move, transpose, and broadcast. The layout algebra (Section 4) represents tensor layouts and operand requirements as mappings from logical axes to hardware axes. Repair insertion and feasibility checking (Section 5.2) then rejects combinations of candidate bindings and repairs whose axis-level constraints cannot be satisfied jointly. An e-graph rewriting pass (Section 5.3) simplifies the repair graph by eliminating redundant conversions. A global solver (Section 5.4) assigns concrete tensor layouts subject to the remaining constraints. Finally, layout-preserving lowering and code generation (Section 5.5) emit the executable kernel. 4. Implementation Arknife is implemented as a Python compiler framework. The frontend constructs an operation graph whose tensors, axes, instruction bindings, repairs, layout attributes, memory placements, and execution structure are updated by compiler passes. Targets are also described in Python through two descriptions. A hardware description declares parallel levels, memory spaces, capacities, and communication channels, while an instruction description declares operand semantics, layout attributes, resource effects, and code emission callbacks. The global layout and spatial tiling ILPs are solved through PySCIPOpt 6.0.0, backed by SCIP 10.0.0. The implementation includes x86, Qualcomm Hexagon, and NVIDIA GPU backends. Retargeting effort centers on per-target instruction descriptions. Across our current backends, hardware hierarchy descriptions take tens of lines, and each supported instruction fewer than ten. All kernels on a target share these descriptions, independently of kernel-specific scheduling decisions. 7. Evaluation Our evaluation addresses three questions: 1.
