Related Work Tensor DSLs and scheduling systems. Schedule-separation systems (Ragan-Kelley et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2018) decouple algorithms from optimization schedules, while automatic scheduling systems (Zheng et al., 2020a; Shao et al., 2022) search schedules over tensor IRs. Tiled programming systems (Tillet et al., 2019; Feng et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2025; Apache TVM Community, 2026) expose layout and memory placement in the program and support cross-backend code generation. Polyhedral and schedule-search techniques further extend this design space (Vasilache et al., 2018; Baghdadi et al., 2018; Zheng et al., 2020b; Zheng et al., 2022a; Ye et al., 2022; Sabne, 2020). TensorIR (Feng et al., 2022) checks intrinsic layout constraints during scheduling, TileLang (Wang et al., 2025) propagates layouts by operator priority, and TIRx (Apache TVM Community, 2026) dispatches primitives from explicit storage layouts. Arknife instead reconciles target-declared operand contracts across instruction boundaries. Retargetable instruction selection. Semantics-driven systems (Chen et al., 2021; VanHattum et al., 2021; Steuwer et al., 2017; Zheng et al., 2022b) use formal instruction descriptions to retarget computation across hardware. UNIT (Weng et al., 2021) detects tensorized-instruction opportunities and rewrites loop and data organizations to match instruction templates across architectures. Hydride and MISAAL (Kothari et al., 2024; Noor et al., 2025) apply semantics-driven retargeting across the full compilation pipeline. Equality saturation (Yang et al., 2021; Ahmad et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2021) and hardware-exposed scheduling (Ikarashi et al., 2022; Elliott et al., 2020; Thomas and Bornholt, 2024) push retargeting further but still leave instruction-level layout to the programmer or backend. These systems primarily establish or exploit computational equivalence for instruction selection and rewriting. Arknife adds explicit layout requirements for memory placement, axes organization, and parallel distribution, checks their agreement at shared tensor boundaries, and inserts target-provided repairs when the selected instructions disagree. Libraries, graph compilers, and layout optimization. Vendor libraries (Intel Corporation, 2026; NVIDIA Corporation, 2026a; NVIDIA Corporation, 2026b; Qualcomm Technologies, Inc., 2026) encode layouts in target-specific, hand-tuned implementations. Graph compilers (Rotem et al., 2018; Roesch et al., 2019; Jia et al., 2019) represent layout as an operator-level attribute rather than a per-instruction constraint. Layout-aware kernel systems (Zhu et al., 2022; Shi et al., 2023; Dao et al., 2022; Dao, 2023; Kwon et al., 2023) and mobile NPU work (Hao et al., 2026) demonstrate that explicit layout control is essential for performance. Operator fusion (Niu et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2022; Ma et al., 2020), memory-coordinated optimization (Jain et al., 2020; Unger et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2024; Park et al., 2026), infrastructure-level retargeting (Lattner et al., 2021; Guo et al., 2025) address complementary aspects. Linear Layouts (Zhou et al., 2026) unifies GPU layout representations and conversion code generation through algebra over [FORMULA] , with heuristic layout propagation in Triton. Tensor Seeks Layout (Eisenhofer et al., 2026) formulates global layout selection over an operator graph, minimizing operator and conversion costs before fusion and tiling. Mirage (Wu et al., 2025) searches layout-level rewrites through multi-level superoptimization for single-GPU inference. Arknife instead inserts and simplifies target-provided repairs on the bound instruction graph and then solves layout globally. 9. Conclusion We present Arknife, a retargetable compiler that treats instruction-visible layout requirements as first-class instruction semantics and globally coordinates layout assignments and repairs. It achieves [FORMULA] and [FORMULA] geometric mean speedups over MISAAL on x86 and Hexagon, respectively, while reaching 97% of cuBLAS performance on A100 TF32 GEMM. These results show that explicit layout requirements can combine retargetability with efficient data paths across diverse accelerators.

RECURSUM: Automated Code Generation for Recurrence Relations Exceeds Expert Optimization via LayeredCodegen Automated code generation can systematically exceed expert hand-optimization for recurrence relations–computational primitives ubiquitous in orthogonal polynomials, special functions, numerical integration, and molecular integral evaluation. We present RECURSUM, a Python DSL generating optimized C++ for arbitrary recurrence relations via three backends–template metaprogramming, a novel LayeredCodegen backend, and runtime loop-based evaluation–specifying recurrences in 10–30 lines of Python that generate 650+ lines of production C++. Program Summary Program Title: recurrence_codegen.py Licensing provisions: MIT License Programming language: Python 3.7+ (code generator), C++17 (generated code) Computer: Any system with Python 3.7+ and C++17 compiler Operating system: Linux, macOS, Windows RAM: Minimal for DSL ( [FORMULA] 100 MB), variable for C++ compilation (1–8 GB depending on L_MAX) Number of processors used: Single-threaded DSL, multi-threaded compilation supported Keywords: Template metaprogramming, SFINAE, recurrence relations, code generation, quantum chemistry Classification: 16.1 Computer Programs in Physics, 4.10 Quantum Chemistry External routines/libraries: None (DSL is standalone Python), generated code uses VCL (vectorclass.h) for SIMD Nature of problem: Recurrence relations in quantum chemistry require manual optimization (loop unrolling, constraint checking, SIMD) that is error-prone and tedious to maintain across multiple recurrence types. Different workload characteristics (cache-hot repeated evaluations vs. cache-cold frequent switching) benefit from different code generation strategies. Solution method: A Python DSL compiles declarative recurrence specifications into optimized C++ code via three backends: (1) template backend generating SFINAE-enabled templates with compile-time evaluation, (2) LayeredCodegen backend generating layer-by-layer evaluation with output parameters and forced inlining (achieving 9.8 [FORMULA] speedup over hand-written and 1.9 [FORMULA] over TMP), (3) runtime backend generating compact loop-based code. The same specification generates all three backends, enabling workload-dependent performance tuning. Restrictions: Template backend: users must set the maximum angular momentum L_MAX at compile time; high L_MAX increases compilation time (quadratic to cubic scaling) and binary size. LayeredCodegen backend: currently supports 3-index Hermite coefficients; 4-index tetrahedral Coulomb integrals under development. Runtime backend: no L_MAX restriction, but slower for cache-hot repeated evaluations. Running time: DSL code generation: [FORMULA] 1 second. Runtime evaluation: 1–50 microseconds per integral batch depending on backend and workload. 1 Introduction Recurrence relations are fundamental computational primitives across pure and applied mathematics. The canonical reference Handbook of Mathematical Functions [1] catalogs approximately 240 recurrence relations among its 2400+ mathematical formulas. Similarly, the NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions [2] provides recurrence formulas for essentially every classical special function: orthogonal polynomials (Legendre, Chebyshev, Hermite, Laguerre, Jacobi), Bessel functions, hypergeometric functions, and elliptic integrals. Mathematical Methods for Physicists [3] documents over 200 recurrence relations for applications in quantum mechanics, electrodynamics, and statistical mechanics. The ubiquity of recurrence relations across mathematical domains creates both a challenge and an opportunity for systematic optimization. Consider representative examples across the knowledge landscape: Pure Mathematics: Orthogonal polynomial evaluation via Bonnet’s three-term recursion, binomial coefficients through Pascal’s triangle, Fibonacci sequences, continued fraction expansions, hypergeometric function evaluation Numerical Analysis: Clenshaw’s algorithm for Chebyshev series summation, Golub-Welsch algorithm for Gaussian quadrature weights, Miller’s backward recurrence algorithm for numerically stable Bessel function evaluation, three-term recurrences in Lanczos and Arnoldi iterations for eigenvalue problems Computational Physics: Spherical harmonics via associated Legendre polynomial recurrences, multipole expansions using addition theorems, Green’s function recursions in scattering theory, Wigner 3-j and 6-j symbols, scattering amplitude computations Quantum Chemistry: Molecular integral evaluation via McMurchie-Davidson, Obara-Saika, and Rys quadrature recurrences; Boys function for Coulomb integrals; modified spherical Bessel functions for Slater-type orbitals; derivative recurrences for analytical gradients and Hessians Computational Statistics: Sequential Monte Carlo particle filters, recursive Bayesian estimation, Kalman filter update equations, autoregressive moving average (ARMA) models Signal Processing: Recursive digital filter implementations (IIR filters), wavelet transforms using orthogonal polynomial bases, fast Fourier transform butterfly operations, z-transform evaluations Despite this diversity, recurrence relations share common computational structure: multi-term linear recursions with validity constraints, base cases, and index-dependent coefficients. The mathematical form appears in contexts ranging from Legendre polynomial evaluation ( [FORMULA] ) to McMurchie-Davidson Hermite coefficients ( [FORMULA] ). Traditional implementations use runtime loops with conditional branches to handle different index cases and boundary conditions. This approach has several fundamental limitations: Branch mispredictions reduce instruction throughput on modern superscalar processors (15–20 cycle penalty on Intel architectures) Indirect function calls prevent inlining and disable interprocedural optimizations Validity constraints checked at runtime add overhead for every evaluation, despite indices often being compile-time constants in many applications Compilers often miss SIMD vectorization opportunities due to control flow complexity and dynamic indexing patterns Domain-specific implementations duplicate optimization effort–each mathematical domain (orthogonal polynomials, special functions, molecular integrals) typically implements recurrences independently despite shared computational structure Expert-written codes address these issues through aggressive manual optimization: loop unrolling, template specialization for specific index values, careful SIMD intrinsics, and hand-tuned cache blocking. However, this approach is labor-intensive (weeks to months of C++ development per recurrence type), error-prone (template metaprogramming has steep learning curve), and difficult to maintain when developers need to add new recurrence formulas. The expertise required–deep knowledge of both the mathematical domain and C++ template metaprogramming–limits who can contribute high-performance implementations. In this work, we present RECURSUM, a Python-based domain-specific language that automatically generates optimized C++ code for arbitrary recurrence relations across mathematical domains. The framework provides a declarative interface where users specify recurrence rules, validity constraints, and base cases in 10–30 lines of Python, and the system generates production-grade C++ implementations via three complementary backends: Template Metaprogramming (TMP) Backend: Generates SFINAE-constrained template specializations where: Template recursion evaluates recurrence relations entirely at compile time std::enable_if (SFINAE) eliminates invalid index combinations The compiler fully unrolls all loops, eliminating branching overhead The backend can average multiple equivalent branches for numerical stability LayeredCodegen Backend (Novel Contribution): Generates layer-by-layer evaluation code with output parameters, forced inlining, and exact-sized buffers, achieving 9.8 [FORMULA] speedup over hand-written implementations and 1.9 [FORMULA] speedup over traditional TMP through systematic application of architectural optimizations Runtime Backend: Generates compact loop-based code that fits in instruction cache, trading specialization overhead for reduced cache pressure when switching between different recurrence parameter combinations The same DSL specification generates all three backends. The choice of backend is a performance tuning decision based on workload characteristics (cache-hot repeated evaluations vs cache-cold frequent switching), not an algorithmic difference. While RECURSUM is a general-purpose framework applicable to any recurrence relation, we validate it extensively using quantum chemistry integral evaluation as the primary demonstration domain for three strategic reasons: Extreme performance demands: Electronic structure calculations must compute molecular integrals billions of times per self-consistent field (SCF) iteration. A single geometry optimization of a medium-sized molecule (50–100 atoms) requires [FORMULA] 1012–1014 integral evaluations. This represents one of the most performance-critical applications of recurrence relations in computational science, ensuring that we validate RECURSUM’s optimizations under the most demanding conditions. Algorithmic diversity: Quantum chemistry encompasses multiple recurrence families with fundamentally different mathematical structures: McMurchie-Davidson: Multi-index tensor recurrences with complex validity domains ( [FORMULA] ) Obara-Saika: Vertical and horizontal recurrence relations Rys quadrature: Coupled recurrences for quadrature weights and Hermite coefficients Boys function: Single-index special function recurrences with numerical stability challenges This diversity validates RECURSUM’s generality–if the framework succeeds for these varied structures, it will generalize to simpler recurrence types in other domains. Expert baselines for validation: Established libraries (Libint2 [4], SIMINT [5], Q-Chem, Psi4, GAMESS) provide expert hand-optimized baselines that performance-focused computational chemists have developed over decades. Matching or exceeding these implementations provides rigorous validation that RECURSUM-generated code achieves true production-grade performance, not merely academic benchmarks. The comprehensive benchmarks (Section 5) demonstrate that RECURSUM-generated code matches expert hand-coded validation baselines within 3.3% while requiring orders of magnitude less development effort (hours vs weeks). This validates the framework’s utility across mathematical domains where similar performance demands exist but expert-optimized implementations are unavailable or prohibitively expensive to develop. The key insight is that certain optimizations (output parameters, forced inlining, exact sizing) are tedious and error-prone to apply manually but trivial for a code generator to apply systematically across all recurrence types. This opens the possibility of DSL-based code generation serving as the performance ceiling for recurrence-based algorithms in scientific computing, rather than merely matching hand-coded performance. Having established LayeredCodegen’s architectural advantages, we situate RECURSUM within the broader landscape of performance-oriented code generation tools. Template metaprogramming in scientific computing. The Eigen library [6] pioneered expression templates for linear algebra, demonstrating that compile-time code generation can match hand-optimized BLAS performance. The Blaze library [7] extends this to advanced SIMD vectorization. Boost.Hana [8] provides metaprogramming utilities for compile-time computation. However, these frameworks target specific domains (linear algebra, expression evaluation) and require deep C++ template expertise. RECURSUM differs fundamentally: it provides a Python DSL accessible to non-C++-experts and targets the general class of recurrence relations across mathematics, not a specific application domain. Moreover, our LayeredCodegen backend demonstrates a novel approach distinct from traditional template metaprogramming, achieving superior performance through layer-by-layer evaluation with output parameters–an architectural pattern prior TMP frameworks have not explored. Domain-specific languages for performance. High-level DSLs for performance-critical domains include Halide [9] for image processing (production use at Google, Adobe), TACO [10] for sparse tensor algebra (100 [FORMULA] faster than NumPy for sparse workloads), Spiral [11] for DSP transforms (competitive with MKL, FFTW), and Tiramisu [12] for general polyhedral compilation. These systems separate algorithm specification from performance optimization through staged compilation or auto-tuning. RECURSUM follows this philosophy: users specify recurrence mathematics declaratively, while the code generator handles low-level optimization (SIMD, loop unrolling, branch elimination). Research gap: Existing DSLs target stencils (Halide), tensors (TACO), or transforms (Spiral), but no framework addresses the general class of recurrence relations across pure and applied mathematics. Furthermore, these DSLs generate runtime code; RECURSUM uniquely combines DSL-based specification with C++ template metaprogramming for compile-time evaluation, enabling zero-overhead recurrence evaluation when indices are compile-time constants. Layer-by-layer code generation. Our LayeredCodegen backend represents a novel approach distinct from both template metaprogramming and symbolic code generation. While template metaprogramming instantiates separate code for each index combination and symbolic approaches generate closed-form expressions, LayeredCodegen systematically generates code that computes all values at a given recurrence layer simultaneously. This approach achieves 9.8 [FORMULA] speedup over hand-written layered implementations and 1.9 [FORMULA] over traditional TMP by eliminating architectural overhead (return-by-value copies, missing inlining, cache pollution) that manual implementations suffer from. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration that automated code generation can systematically outperform expert hand-coded implementations by applying architectural optimizations that are tedious to implement manually but trivial to generate automatically. Symbolic code generation for quantum chemistry. The Libint2 library [4] pioneered symbolic code generation for Gaussian integrals using a custom C++ compiler that generates optimized integral kernels from symbolic expressions. Libint2 focuses on Obara-Saika and Head-Gordon-Pople recursions for electron repulsion integrals, with extensive compile-time specialization. Our DSL complements this approach: while Libint2 targets a specific family of integral recurrences with deeply optimized symbolic algebra, our framework provides a general-purpose tool for arbitrary recurrence relations across quantum chemistry and beyond. The DSL’s three-backend architecture (TMP, LayeredCodegen, runtime) offers flexibility for workload-dependent optimization that Libint2’s compile-time-only approach cannot provide. Moreover, RECURSUM’s Python DSL is significantly more accessible than Libint2’s complex C++-based specification language. Code generation for recurrence relations. Existing symbolic mathematics systems (SymPy [13], Mathematica) can generate code for recurrence relations by symbolically expanding formulas and applying common subexpression elimination. However, this approach does not exploit recurrence structure: our benchmarks show SymPy-generated code is 2–2.5 [FORMULA] slower than LayeredCodegen due to expression explosion at high indices (150+ terms after CSE at [FORMULA] ) causing instruction cache pressure. The techniques apply uniformly across all 17 recurrence types implemented in the codebase. The C++ template system provides a mechanism called SFINAE that enables compile-time selection among multiple function or class template specializations. The name derives from the principle: when the compiler attempts to instantiate a template with specific arguments, and that instantiation would be ill-formed (e.g., due to type mismatches or constraint violations), the compiler simply removes the instantiation from the candidate set rather than causing a compilation error. For recurrence relations, SFINAE allows us to write multiple template specializations, each valid for different index ranges, and let the compiler automatically select the correct one based on the indices provided. The libint2 library [4] uses a custom C++ code generator (the "libint compiler") to derive recurrence relations and generate optimized C++ code for integral evaluation. The TeraChem software [19, 20, 21] pioneered a related symbolic code generation approach for GPU-accelerated quantum chemistry integrals, employing a "meta-programming" strategy that leverages computer algebra systems for equation derivation and code generation [22]. Wang et al. [23] further developed and validated this approach for f-orbital integrals, demonstrating that automated code generation with common subexpression elimination can produce competitive GPU implementations for quantum chemistry integrals. Advantages: enables aggressive optimization, handles complex derivative recurrences, reduces manual coding errors. Disadvantages: requires specialized code generation infrastructure, produces code that can be difficult to debug, incurs long compile times for high angular momentum. Our DSL approach offers a middle ground: less aggressive symbolic optimization than libint2, but faster code generation and easier integration into existing codebases. The DSL does not require SymPy or Mathematica—only standard Python 3.7+. The DSL also generates runtime loop-based code (the “runtime backend” mentioned in Section 3.2). This is not hand-coded—the DSL automatically produces it from the same specification as the template backend. The runtime backend trades compile-time specialization overhead for a compact binary that fits in instruction cache. The choice is a performance tuning decision, not an algorithmic difference. Expert C++ programmers can manually write template metaprogramming code similar to what the DSL generates. This requires deep knowledge of template syntax, SFINAE, and instantiation rules. The DSL democratizes this approach: domain scientists specify mathematics, the generator handles C++ complexity. This section contextualizes these findings within the broader landscape of high-performance scientific computing. The 9.8 [FORMULA] speedup demonstrated in Figure 2 over expert hand-written code inverts the traditional performance hierarchy. Conventionally, hand-optimization by domain experts represents the performance ceiling, with code generators producing slower but more maintainable code. Our results demonstrate the opposite: LayeredCodegen’s systematic application of three architectural optimizations (output parameters, forced inlining, exact-sized buffers) eliminates pitfalls that even expert programmers miss. The microarchitectural model’s 1% prediction accuracy (Table 2) validates this understanding. We know exactly why LayeredCodegen is faster, which lets future generators apply these principles systematically. The performance scaling shown in Figure 3 reveals another critical advantage: LayeredCodegen maintains its relative advantage across all angular momenta [FORMULA] through [FORMULA] . This consistency demonstrates that the benefits arise from systematic architectural optimizations, not from fortuitous compiler choices on specific test cases. For production quantum chemistry codes requiring high angular momentum integrals (f- and g-type basis functions), this consistency is essential. The code the DSL generates, whether through the template metaprogramming, LayeredCodegen, or runtime backend, takes the form of ordinary C++ functions using the output-parameter convention, with no dependency on RECURSUM’s Python frontend at the call site. This makes the functions themselves ABI-stable, link-compatible C++ callables, which suggests a natural integration path: a thin binding layer rather than any modification to RECURSUM or to the target package’s integral core. For PySCF, whose extension model is Python-first, this would mean exposing the generated functions through pybind11; for Psi4, whose integral evaluation is implemented in C++, it would mean linking the generated translation units directly against Psi4’s core or plugin interface. Because PySCF already serves as this paper’s numerical reference, with all 24 recurrence types validated against it to better than [FORMULA] error (Section 5), the numerical-compatibility question such an integration would normally raise is already settled. What remains is the binding and build-system engineering, which we have not undertaken here and leave as future work. TeraChem [19, 20, 21] and libint2 [4] pioneered symbolic approaches to integral code generation for GPU-accelerated quantum chemistry, and Wang et al. [23] further developed them for f-orbital integrals; these approaches offer aggressive optimization through computer algebra systems like SymPy [13]. These pioneering works [19, 20, 21, 23] demonstrated that SymPy-generated closed-form expressions with common subexpression elimination (CSE) can achieve competitive performance for low to moderate angular momentum cases. However, as shown in Section 5.5, symbolic approaches face scalability challenges at high angular momentum due to exponential expression growth, instruction cache pressure, and register spilling. Our DSL-based approach offers complementary advantages: faster code generation without symbolic algebra dependencies, systematic application of architectural optimizations (output parameters, forced inlining), and explicit exploitation of recurrence layer structure that symbolic expansion cannot capture. The framework bridges the gap between mathematical recurrence formulas (as found in Abramowitz & Stegun’s Handbook of Mathematical Functions, the NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, and domain-specific literature) and production-grade optimized code, demonstrating that systematic code generation can serve as the performance ceiling for recurrence-based algorithms. RECURSUM demonstrates that diverse recurrence types–orthogonal polynomials, special functions, molecular integrals, quadrature weights, combinatorial sequences–share sufficient computational structure to enable unified code generation. The declarative Python DSL provides: Mathematical clarity: Specifications read like textbook recurrence formulas, requiring no C++ template metaprogramming expertise Automatic optimization: SFINAE constraints, common subexpression elimination, SIMD vectorization, and architectural optimizations applied systematically across all recurrence types Performance guarantees: Generated code matches or exceeds expert hand-coded implementations, with LayeredCodegen achieving 9.8 [FORMULA] speedup over manual optimization Rapid prototyping: Development time reduced from weeks to minutes–specify recurrence in 10–30 lines of Python, generate and validate production code in <5 minutes The framework provides three complementary code generation backends from a single specification: Template Metaprogramming (TMP): Compile-time evaluation with zero runtime overhead LayeredCodegen (novel contribution): Layer-by-layer evaluation achieving 1.9 [FORMULA] speedup over TMP through output parameters, forced inlining, and exact-sized buffers Runtime: Cache-friendly loops for workloads with frequent parameter switching This architectural flexibility enables workload-dependent performance tuning: users select backends based on application characteristics (cache-hot repeated evaluations vs cache-cold frequent switching) without modifying the mathematical specification. Fibered Separation Logic: Weakest Preconditions, Universal Constructions, and Local Independence This paper introduces a categorical framework for models of higher-order separation logic including the weakest precondition modality. Weakest preconditions are interpreted by strong monads on a category fibered over a model of Moggi’s computational lambda calculus. The fibered categories in question are termed bunched fibrations and shown to be equivalent to BI hyperdoctrines. 1. Introduction This paper introduces a systematic approach to the semantics of separation logic in terms of strong monads on models of bunched implications (BI). While BI, the logic of resources at rest, has been treated systematically by O’Hearn and Pym (O’Hearn and Pym, 1999), Biering (Biering, 2004) and many others, we find the dynamic aspects of separation logic have not yet received a comparable treatment. This is not for lack of material, as the literature on separation logic is extensive, well understood by experts and workers in verification, and organized, to some extent, into heuristics and rules. Separation logic extends ordinary Hoare logic with substructural logical connectives that permit compositional reasoning about resource-manipulating programs. The separating conjunction [FORMULA] holds on resources that can be separated into one part that satisfies [FORMULA] and another part that satisfies [FORMULA] . The frame rule says that a verified program [FORMULA] respects this notion of resource separation, in the sense that whatever [FORMULA] does to [FORMULA] is stable in the presence of additional resources described by a separate [FORMULA] . In the original incarnation of separation logic (Reynolds, 2002), the resources in question were fragments of the heap. Subsequent developments vastly generalized the notion of resource, leading to logics for higher-order mutable state (Svendsen and Birkedal, 2014; Jung et al., 2015), concurrency (Brookes, 2007), probability (Barthe et al., 2019; Li et al., 2023; Bao et al., 2025), entropy (Haselwarter et al., 2024), error (Aguirre et al., 2024), space (Madiot and Pottier, 2022; Charguéraud and Pottier, 2019), and time (Atkey, 2011; Haselwarter et al., 2024). As a result, the semantics of separation logic have become fragmented, which presents problems both for scientific communication and the design of new logics. The nascent theory of separation logic has improved the situation by identifying and classifying models of BI, the assertion language of separation logic (O’Hearn and Pym, 1999; Pym, 2002; Pym, 1999). Resources have been organized into resource algebras such as partial commutative monoids (Calcagno et al., 2007). Cao, Cuellar, and Appel (Cao et al., 2017) showed the soundness of common rules like dereliction depends entirely on the algebraic properties of the underlying resource algebra. Well-behaved classes of duplicable propositions [FORMULA] have been identified with persistence modalities [FORMULA] , which in turn are related to the lattice of idempotent elements of the underlying resource algebra (Bizjak and Birkedal, 2018; Gratzer et al., 2025). For higher-order BI, it has been shown that introducing rules for subset types [FORMULA] leads to the disappointing principle [FORMULA] (Biering et al., 2007, §2.2), establishing that desirable categorical models of higher-order BI are are not toposes but rather BI hyperdoctrines. Despite these insights into the logic of resources at rest, separation logics are still designed and verified by alternately following heuristics and proving soundness by exhaustive case analysis. This happens because the dynamic aspects of separation logic have so far eluded systematic analysis. In a modern logic, dynamic assertions, i.e., assertions about program behavior, are defined in terms of a weakest precondition modality: [FORMULA] The weakest precondition is meant to describe the resources and knowledge necessary for [FORMULA] to produce a result satisfying postcondition [FORMULA] . It is often defined by a logical formula involving the semantics of computations, the effects of [FORMULA] on resources, and the invariants the logic is meant to enforce. Presentations of these formulas in the literature either simply record the definition of weakest precondition without comment or show how to build it up by proof and counterexample (Lakatos, 1976) until all desired rules are true, as in Jung et al. (Jung et al., 2018, §§6.3, 7.3). This reflects the design process, in which a designer writes down a list of desired rules and then gradually adjusts the defining formula for [FORMULA] as they rotate between proposing candidate definitions, proving soundness of rules, and consulting the literature for ideas. In the end, one obtains a [FORMULA] that validates at the very least those rules shown in Figure 1, which permit decomposing monadic computations (WP-Return and WP-Bind), framing out unused resources (WP-Frame), and incorporating static reasoning from the assertion language (WP-Mono). This paper presents a systematic, categorical foundation for weakest preconditions satisfying the rules in Figure 1. First, we replace the BI hyperdoctrines of Biering (Biering, 2004) with an equivalent category of bunched fibrations. Then, following the analysis of weakest preconditions for Hoare logic by Aguirre et al. (Aguirre et al., 2022), we interpret [FORMULA] as a monad on a bunched fibration. We show that any such monad validates the laws WP-Mono, WP-Bind, and WP-Ret, and that WP-Frame amounts to the existence of a tensorial strength for the monad (Section 5). Our bunched fibrations provide a fibered account of first- and higher-order BI (Section 4.1). We prove that bunched fibrations correspond to existing models of BI, based on BI hyperdoctrines (Theorem 4.15), and give conditions under which bunched fibrations are stable under pullback (Propositions 4.21 and 4.22). We provide two demonstrations of the utility of our fibered framework for defining separation logics. First, Section 6 shows how it provides the language to precisely express the kinds of design patterns used to build complex separation logics. It considers three examples: a common pattern of “baking in” the frame rule, a pattern of adding credit-based cost reasoning to a program logic by upgrading the underlying resource algebra, and a pattern of defining a persistence modality in terms of universal quantification over all possible resources à la modal necessity. In two of these three cases we are able to find an accompanying universal property for the construction, giving it a canonical status with respect to other constructions for the same purpose. Our second demonstration showcases how our fibered framework can be used to build a new kind of separation logic. First, we leverage Simpson’s newly-introduced axiomatization of local independence structure (Simpson, 2024) to define a new monad that captures an abstract notion of allocation effect arising in the context of name generation, local store, probability, and nondeterminism. Then, we build a bunched fibration and a bunched lifting that generically construct a higher-order separation logic for this abstract notion of allocation. Finally, by using this abstract construction in combination with our pullback-stability theorems, we obtain a novel probabilistic separation logic for measure-theoretic probability that simplifies and clarifies the probabilistic separation logics put forward by prior work (Li et al., 2023; Bao et al., 2025; Ho et al., 2026). Our hope with this fibered framework is to lay the foundations of the following three-step recipe for making new separation logics in a systematic manner. First, one fixes a monad [FORMULA] on a category [FORMULA] that interprets the effectful operations of interest. This could be plucked from the functional programming literature, like the state monad or the reader monad, or constructed from an algebraic signature. It can be a sophisticated model, like the model of full ground store (Kammar et al., 2017), or an elementary one, like an ordinary state monad on [FORMULA] . Next, one builds a bunched fibration [FORMULA] , giving a separation logic for reasoning about the pure computations embodied by the objects and morphisms of [FORMULA] . This bunched fibration can be built in a number of ways. It could be one of the canonical kinds of bunched fibration, such as the versatile lax slice fibration described in Definition 4.24; it could come from a BI hyperdoctrine, via the correspondence to bunched fibrations; or it could come from the use of a change-of-base theorem. The resulting separation logic can be first- or higher-order depending on the structure of the fibration and of the category [FORMULA] . Finally, one lifts the monad [FORMULA] and its effectful operations to a monad and operations on the total category [FORMULA] of the bunched fibration. This too can be done in a number of ways, either by using a stock lifting — e.g., the frame-preserving state example — by the application of general constructions such as free frame, credits, or the independence lifting, or by change of base along a suitable functor. 2. Related Work Models of BI are typically based on a resource algebra. This umbrella term refers to algebraic structures including Kripke resource monoids (Galmiche et al., 2005), separation algebras (Dockins et al., 2009), partial commutative monoids (Jung et al., 2015), CMRAs (Jung et al., 2018), and maximal-idempotent resource algebras (Gratzer et al., 2025). Resource algebras provide an important class of models of separation logic, as any of them can be used to quickly build a model of higher-order BI. However, they are less helpful when it comes to designing [FORMULA] . Our bunched fibrations, via their equivalence to BI hyperdoctrines, are general enough to accommodate all models of BI that come from resource algebras, as well as models of BI that do not (Polzer and Goncharov, 2020); our fibered approach additionally permits a mathematical account of [FORMULA] s as bunched monad liftings. The higher-order separation logic Iris has developed a generic [FORMULA] that can be applied to a wide range of operational semantics; this combined with the ability to specify custom resource algebras makes Iris a powerful framework for building new program logics. In our view what distinguishes the present work from Iris is that Iris is focused on specific kinds of languages and logics; in particular, it is most suitable for step-indexed operational reasoning that makes use of features such as higher-order impredicative invariants and Löb induction. Machine Learning (cs.LG): An ensemble of graph generative models for assisted history matching of the Brugge field case Assisted history matching remains non-unique because many geological realisations can reproduce equivalent production responses with substantial differences between individual well matches. This ambiguity increases when a field comprises several depositional settings and modelling strategies. The paper applied a graph autoencoder approach to history matching of a benchmark Brugge field that comprises different depositional zones. Each stratigraphic zone is modelled with its dedicated generative model that comprises a joint latent space for optimisation history matching loops. Graph-based generators operate directly on the active cells of the corner-point grid, so its irregular geometry is handled without conversion to a regular lattice. The optimisation search in the 160-dimensional joint latent space is done with the Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy. The multi-component objective function includes static well data mismatch, dynamic production mismatch, and a geological realism penalty based on the Decoder induced latent metric. Latent space diagnostics with topological data analysis are applied prior to history matching to test whether one generator is sufficient or whether a multiple generator formulation is required. The results show that the zone-based formulation gives coherent latent spaces, preserves the main porosity and permeability relations that vary from one zone to another, and supports history matching while keeping the solutions within the learned geological manifold. The matched models reproduce field oil and water production within the prior uncertainty range and provide a comparable well-level match to previously published Brugge studies based on Ensemble Kalman Filter, Particle Swarm Optimisation with principal component analysis of parameterisation, and Multiple Kernel Learning with Particle Swarm Optimisation. 1 Introduction Assisted history matching (AHM) updates reservoir property fields so that simulated responses match observed field data. Because these observations constrain the reservoir indirectly and sparsely, different geological models can yield similar responses, and practical AHM must balance an acceptable data match, uncertainty representation, and geological consistency. The parameterisation must therefore permit dynamic calibration while remaining consistent with static data, geological structure, and petrophysical relationships, especially for field-scale corner-point grids [1, 2]. All AHM workflows depend on a prior defined by geological interpretations and conditioning data. For generative parameterisations, the learned model cannot recover geological features absent from the training ensemble [2]. Different parameterisation strategies address this trade-off in different ways, as illustrated by Brugge benchmark studies using EnKF, PSO with PCA parameterisation, kernel methods, and ensemble smoothers [3, 4, 5, 6]. Geostatistical workflows honour well data and prescribed geological rules but may lack freedom for dynamic calibration, whereas ensemble methods update property fields through sample covariances that may break facies boundaries, property relationships, and channel connections. Regularisation and covariance localisation reduce unstable updates but do not define the full set of admissible geological models, so neither approach can guarantee geological consistency by itself [1, 2, 7]. Deep generative models offer an alternative parameterisation: an Encoder maps each realisation to a compact latent vector, and a Decoder reconstructs the property fields, without replacing the geomodelling methods used to construct the prior [8, 7, 9]. For AHM, the optimiser then updates this compact vector instead of thousands of grid-cell values, reducing the search dimension and linking updates to patterns learned from the prior. Several generative architectures have been explored for subsurface parameterisation, including generative adversarial networks [10, 11, 12], variational autoencoders and ensemble-smoother extensions [13, 7, 2, 14], CNN-PCA [15], and latent diffusion models [9]. However, many such workflows assume regular lattice grids, whereas realistic reservoir models commonly use irregular corner-point grids with faults and non-uniform cell geometry [16]. Mapping these models to a lattice can introduce geometric artefacts and weaken the link to the simulator grid [17], motivating generative approaches that operate on the native grid. In an earlier study by the authors, we introduced a Graph-based Wasserstein Autoencoder workflow for history matching, referred to here as GWAE, in which the geological model on its native grid is represented as a graph and the latent variables of the generative model define the parameter space for optimisation [18]. In synthetic settings, GWAE showed that graph-based latent representations can support history matching while retaining geological structure. The present study extends this formulation to a field-scale Brugge benchmark case with a composite prior, where both the reservoir geometry and the prior structure are more complex than in synthetic demonstrations [3]. The study is focused on two aspects: (i) irregular corner-point unstructured grid that accounts for realistic geological structure and makes the graph modelling approach more relevant; (ii) a variety of depositional environments that represent a wide range of geological scenario variations. The second challenge concerns the composite structure of the Brugge prior: each realisation comprises four stratigraphic zones with distinct depositional settings and property distributions, and a separate diagnostic Schelde dataset combines Object Modelling (OM) and Sequential Indicator Simulation (SIS) realisations to test whether both strategies can share one latent representation. After training, the Encoder maps each realisation to a latent vector, and the resulting latent point cloud reveals how the Encoder organises these geological groups. If the latent point cloud contains separated components, the paths between them may cross regions of low model density, where the Decoder may be less reliable [18]. The representativeness of the latent space training samples is evaluated with topological analysis to understand how well the latent space represents multiple geomodelling concepts. Conventional geostatistical and ensemble-based AHM approaches, such as EnKF and ensemble smoothers, update reservoir models by regenerating and repopulating porosity and permeability fields at every iteration, either through direct geostatistical simulation or through covariance-based ensemble updates. The proposed workflow instead searches a lower-dimensional latent space learned from a prior ensemble of geological realisations. This reduces the dimensionality of the inverse problem and restricts the search mainly to geological variability represented in the prior. The latent space is learned by a Graph-based Wasserstein Autoencoder trained on porosity and permeability fields from the prior ensemble of realisations. After training, the Decoder maps a latent vector to full porosity and permeability realisations on the reservoir grid. Each decoded model is then passed to the flow simulator, and the optimisation algorithm updates the latent vector by minimising an objective function that combines production mismatch, static well-data mismatch, and a geological realism term. The methodology follows five steps: Graph construction: The native reservoir grid is converted into a graph representation used by the GWAE, preserving the active-cell topology and face-contact connectivity of the corner-point grid. Latent space construction: Graph representations are encoded by the GWAE into a continuous latent space, with each realisation of the prior mapped to a compact latent vector. Latent space diagnostics: The structure of the trained latent space is analysed using PCA, t-SNE, and topological data analysis to decide whether the prior should be represented by one generator or decomposed into several generators. Multi-generator and hybrid latent space construction: Where decomposition is warranted, separate generators are trained for coherent components of the prior, and their latent vectors are concatenated into a joint hybrid latent space. History matching: The hybrid latent parameterisation is optimised against a combined objective function integrating static mismatch, dynamic mismatch, and geological realism. A defining feature of the proposed workflow is that the generative model operates directly on the native reservoir grid rather than on a resampled rectangular array. As discussed in Section 1, field-scale reservoir models commonly use irregular corner-point grids, and resampling them to a regular lattice can distort cell geometry and weaken the link between the generated property fields and the simulator grid where flow physics is solved. To preserve this link, each reservoir realisation is first converted into an attributed graph by a fixed mapping: where [FORMULA] denotes the native corner-point reservoir model: the grid geometry, the active-cell mask, and the porosity and permeability values assigned to the cells. The graph [FORMULA] is the representation used by the neural network. The nodes [FORMULA] correspond to active reservoir cells, the edges [FORMULA] describe physical face contact between active cells, and the node feature map [FORMULA] stores the cell properties used in this study, namely porosity and permeability. The mapping [FORMULA] is applied to all prior realisations before training. After training, the Decoder generates porosity and permeability as node features on the same fixed active-cell graph, which are written back to the corresponding cells for flow simulation. Since grid geometry and the active-cell mask are fixed, the model parameterises only porosity and permeability, not the grid structure, and inactive cells are simply removed from the graph rather than retained as padding or masked nodes. Graph edges are created from geometric cell adjacency, not from index adjacency in the structured grid array. Two active cells are connected by an edge whenever their opposing faces share an intersection with positive polygonal area, regardless of whether the cells are adjacent in index space. This definition is suitable for corner-point grids, where faults, local distortions, non-uniform cell geometry, and partial face overlaps can make physical connectivity differ from regular lattice connectivity. This is the main practical difference from a lattice-based generator such as a convolutional autoencoder, which requires a rectangular array and must carry inactive cells as padding or masking (about 30% of the Brugge array), while still failing to represent the true face-contact topology of a faulted corner-point grid. The graph representation avoids these limitations by storing only active cells and convolving over their actual connectivity. The GWAE Encoder and Decoder are built from graph convolution operations defined on this active cell graph. The structure of a trained LS reflects how the prior ensemble is organised. Similar geological realisations are typically encoded close together, whereas distinct groups or scenarios may appear as separated regions of the latent point cloud. The connectedness of the encoded latent point cloud indicates whether the prior ensemble can be treated as a single coherent population or whether it comprises several distinct components. This diagnostic is applied before history matching to select the parameterisation: whether a reservoir with multiple depositional zones should be represented by a single generator trained on the combined prior or decomposed into zone-specific generators with independent latent spaces updated jointly, with decoded zone fields stacked before flow simulation. This matters because latent-space optimisation assumes continuous movement through training-supported regions. A single encoder spanning distinct populations risks producing a latent space with disconnected, poorly supported regions, which the diagnostics below are designed to detect. To determine whether the prior should be represented by a single generator or decomposed into separate generators, the encoded latent point cloud is analysed using complementary geometric and topological diagnostics. PCA [23] provides a linear projection of the latent vectors, and t-distributed stochastic neighbour embedding (t-SNE) [24] provides a nonlinear visualisation of local neighbourhood structure. Persistent homology is then used to quantify connectedness of the latent point cloud [25, 26]. The persistence diagram of the zeroth homology group, [FORMULA] , provides the primary diagnostic: it records the filtration scales at which initially separate connected components merge [18]. Although persistence is computed in different homological dimensions, only [FORMULA] features are used to select the generator parameterisation. For the latent point clouds considered here, higher homological dimensions have low persistence and are not used in the selection criterion. The generator parameterisation is selected from the connectedness of the encoded latent point cloud. If a GWAE trained on the relevant prior yields a single connected and sufficiently dense representation, the single-generator formulation is retained. Conversely, persistent separated [FORMULA] components indicate that the prior should not be treated as one coherent population but decomposed into more coherent components, each represented by a separate generator. For the Brugge case, a separate GWAE was trained for each stratigraphic zone of the prior ensemble. The latent dimensions in Table 3 were selected by progressively reducing them until validation reconstructions showed increased error and loss of spatial or petrophysical features [18]. The hybrid latent vector is formed by concatenating the four zone latent vectors: During history matching, the optimiser searches directly in this joint latent space. At each evaluation, the hybrid vector is divided into four parts, each part is passed through the Decoder trained for the corresponding zone, and the decoded zone property fields are stacked in stratigraphic order to form a complete Brugge reservoir model (Figure 1). This formulation assumes that the property distribution in one zone does not directly depend on the realisation in another zone. This is consistent with the construction of the Brugge prior, in which zones were generated separately without cross-zone coupling. If strong dependencies must be represented, the framework can be extended by coupling the zone generators. History matching in the hybrid latent space is performed using the Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (CMA-ES) [28]. CMA-ES is suitable because it is derivative-free, which is essential when the objective function includes a non-differentiable flow-simulation step. Its multivariate Gaussian search distribution is also consistent with the standard Gaussian latent prior [FORMULA] and the Wasserstein regularisation that encourages the aggregated encoder distribution [FORMULA] to match this prior (Section 3.1). The Gaussian distribution is used only to propose candidate latent vectors: CMA-ES adapts its covariance matrix from the ranked candidates at each iteration, allowing the search distribution to conform locally to a non-Gaussian or multimodal objective landscape. Together with the realism term, this adaptation reduces exploration of weakly supported latent regions. To reduce computational cost, history matching is performed in two stages. First, each zone-specific generator is optimised independently against the static mismatch and geological-realism terms, yielding latent vectors whose decoded fields approximately honour the well-log data while remaining in well-supported regions of the latent space. Unlike conventional geostatistical conditioning, this static match is approximate because the Decoder does not impose well data as hard constraints. Second, CMA-ES is initialised from the best first-stage solution and jointly minimises the full objective across all generators, including the dynamic mismatch term. Only the second stage requires flow simulation of the assembled reservoir model. Three independent optimisation runs produce three matched realisations. The static term is the mean squared error between the decoded property values and the well log values at the cells crossed by wells. This should not be interpreted as strict hard conditioning: a well log has a much smaller physical support volume than a simulation cell, so the exact match between a log measurement and a cell averaged property would be too strong [18]. The proposed formulation allows small deviations and treats them as small scale uncertainty. The dynamic term is the mean squared error between simulated and observed oil and water production rates, and is evaluated only in the second optimisation stage that implies reservoir simulation. The realism term penalises latent vectors located in less dense regions towards the edge of the latent space [18]. The Decoder induces a local scalar metric in latent space neighbourhood [FORMULA] through its Jacobian [29]: Ideally, the Jacobian-based metric should increase with distance from the training data, so that the realism penalty is larger in poorly supported regions. Because neural networks extrapolate poorly, the Jacobian term alone does not guarantee this. We therefore add a radial-basis-function precision network [30] that estimates the decoder uncertainty as the inverse of a precision centred on the encoded training data. This uncertainty is low near the data and grows with distance, so the realism penalty increases as the latent vector moves away from the training data. The static and dynamic terms guide the optimiser towards models that match the observations, while the realism term discourages geologically implausible solutions. 4 Application This section applies the GWAE AHM workflow to the Brugge benchmark, examining latent-space diagnostics, generator quality, and history matching in the hybrid latent space. A geological prior may contain realisations generated using alternative geostatistical algorithms that represent the same depositional setting through different spatial assumptions. In the Schelde diagnostic dataset, OM constructs explicit channel objects, whereas SIS simulates facies cell by cell using variogram-controlled spatial continuity. To test whether both modelling strategies can be represented within one coherent latent space, a single GWAE was trained on a balanced dataset of 2500 OM realisations and 2500 SIS realisations. A latent dimension of 100 was used, larger than that of the final Schelde generator, to reduce the likelihood that any observed separation resulted simply from insufficient latent capacity. Figure 2 summarises the latent-space diagnostics for the combined Schelde dataset. The PCA projection separates the encoded realisations into two distinct clusters corresponding to the two modelling algorithms. The t-SNE projection also shows two compact regions, with the separation becoming apparent when the points are coloured by the modelling algorithm. Topological data analysis, TDA, confirms the same structure: the [FORMULA] persistence diagram contains two long-lived connected components, shown as red dots, indicating that the latent point cloud is not represented as a single connected region. Taken together, these observations show that the combined Schelde prior is represented as two distinct latent subpopulations rather than one coherent region. For history matching, persistently separated components of the latent point cloud can make interpolation between the modelling groups unreliable: optimisation paths may cross regions with little training support, where the Decoder has not learned a well-constrained mapping to geological models. Hence, geological realism control in GWAE AHM is imposed on the optimisation by the shape of the latent space with a penalty for moving beyond its edges (see [FORMULA] in eq. 5). The shape and the density decay towards the edge of the latent space are defined during GWAE learning. When an OM Schelde realisation is encoded and reconstructed by the single GWAE, the reconstruction retains the overall property range but substantially smooths the sharp object-defined channel boundaries and the uniform low-property background of the original realisation (Figure 3). The reconstructed property fields are smoother and visually resemble the SIS realisations more closely. In the porosity-permeability cross-plot, the main trend is retained, whereas the overlapping OM points at a single low-property coordinate (blue) are replaced in the reconstruction by a continuous low-property tail (green). The single generator therefore fails on two levels: the latent point cloud splits into separated components, and the Decoder cannot reliably reconstruct the channel and shale structure of the OM subpopulation – a failure detected before any flow simulation. The zone-specific Schelde GWAE (Figure 4) retains the channelised pattern more faithfully. The four-zone Brugge formulation follows the prior construction and is assessed through the zone-wise diagnostics below. The generative quality was evaluated by comparing original prior realisations with their decoded reconstructions. The analysis used porosity fields, reconstruction error, porosity and permeability relations, and latent space diagnostics. Figure 4 shows that the decoded realisations reproduce the main spatial structure of the original models in all four stratigraphic zones. The reconstruction error is centred close to zero, which indicates that there is no strong systematic bias in the recovered porosity fields. The error is distributed evenly across the porosity field rather than localised in specific regions, so the remaining differences do not form large coherent artefacts. Reconstructed samples remain close to the original distributions for Schelde, Maas, and Schie, whereas for Waal the reconstruction preserves the central trend but shows a broader spread, particularly at lower permeability and intermediate porosity. A reference Brugge realisation was treated as unknown, except for static well data and production response. Figure 6 shows the matched solutions in the latent projections and in the property domain. In all four zones, the optimised latent codes remain within the projected support of the prior ensemble, but their proximity to the encoded reference differs between zones. The Maas solutions lie close to the reference in the PCA projection, whereas the Waal solutions form a compact group at a visibly different projected location. Nevertheless, the Waal reconstructions retain the main large-scale property trend and give a small pore-volume error. This illustrates the non-uniqueness of the inverse problem and shows that distance in a low-dimensional PCA projection should not be treated as a direct measure of geological or dynamic similarity. At the same time, the location of the optimised codes within the projected prior clouds is consistent with the intended role of the realism term: it discourages the search from moving towards poorly supported regions of the learned latent space without preventing improvement of the static and dynamic data match. Waal is recovered particularly well, which is important because it contributes the dominant share of total fluid production, and the matched Waal models preserve the smooth lateral property trend of the reference model. Schelde is more difficult to recover because its fluvial architecture contains abrupt property contrasts and uncertain channel connectivity. The well data provide only sparse local conditioning, so channel placement and the associated permeability connectivity between wells remain weakly constrained. Consequently, matched Schelde realisations can remain consistent with the available static and dynamic data while differing from the reference away from the wells. For Schie, the encoded reference lies near the edge of the projected prior cloud. Because Schie is thin and contributes less than 1% of total fluid production, both the static and dynamic terms carry little information about this zone, leaving the optimisation weakly constrained. With almost no data-driven signal to guide the search, the recovered Schie fields are noisier than the reference. 5 Results This section assesses the history-matching results in terms of data agreement and consistency with the geological prior. The analysis covers optimisation behaviour, bulk-property statistics, production response, and a qualitative comparison with published Brugge HM studies. The matched models reproduce the reference mean porosity reasonably well, while the porosity variability and pore-volume errors show zone-dependent departures. The absolute pore-volume error is up to 11 [FORMULA] for Schelde, about 4 [FORMULA] for Maas, 1–2 [FORMULA] for Waal, and 4–8 [FORMULA] for Schie (Figure 8(b)). These results indicate that the matched solutions remain broadly consistent with the reference in terms of bulk porosity and pore volume. Dynamic performance is assessed separately from the oil and water responses, which depend jointly on pore volume, permeability, connectivity, and phase-flow parameters. Figure 9 shows that prior coverage and matching quality differ between the field and well scales. At the field level, the reference oil and water responses are largely contained within the broad prior envelope, and the three matched solutions concentrate close to the observed profiles. At the well level, the coverage is less uniform because individual responses depend on local permeability and connectivity. In particular, the PR-P-18 history is not fully covered by the sampled prior ensemble, indicating a local bias in the prior dynamic response and making this well more difficult to match. The optimised responses nevertheless move towards the reference trend, although a larger residual mismatch remains where the history lies near or outside the prior envelope. Part of the remaining oil-water mismatch is also expected because only porosity and permeability are updated, while relative permeability and other phase-flow parameters remain fixed. Figure 10 places the GWAE results in the context of previously published Brugge history matching studies that report a well level good, fair, and poor classification: EnKF, Particle Swarm Optimisation with PCA parameterisation (PSO-PCA), and Multiple Kernel Learning with Particle Swarm Optimisation (MKL-PSO) [3, 4, 5]. More recent Brugge studies that combine production data with tracer or 4D seismic data are not included in the comparison because they do not report the same well-level classification [6, 31]. The published studies differ in their calibration variables, objective functions, data types, optimisation strategies, and reporting metrics, so the figure should be interpreted as a qualitative context rather than as a controlled benchmark. Within this limitation, as shown in Figure 10, the GWAE workflow achieves a competitive well-level match, with most wells falling into the good match category, and the number of poor matches is limited compared with the three reference methods considered. The more pivotal difference, however, is methodological. EnKF, PSO-PCA, and MKL-PSO update reservoir model parameters through different reduced or ensemble formulations, but they do not explicitly constrain every accepted model to remain inside a learned geological prior manifold. In the proposed GWAE workflow, the optimiser searches in the latent space of trained graph generative models, and the realism term penalises poorly supported latent regions. The comparison, therefore, indicates not only that GWAE can match production data, but that this match is obtained while maintaining an explicit link to the geological prior and while producing an ensemble of plausible matched realisations. These results show that the proposed workflow is effective for the Brugge benchmark. The graph generators operate on the native irregular grid, the multiple generator formulation gives a coherent hybrid latent space, and the optimiser finds matched models that reproduce both static and dynamic data while remaining connected to the geological prior. The remaining errors concentrate in zones with strong local heterogeneity (Schelde) or weak contribution to production (Schie), which suggests that further improvement is more likely to come from extending the dataset or the calibration variables than from changing the latent parameterisation itself. 6 Conclusion This study addressed assisted history matching of field-scale reservoir models with a heterogeneous, multi-zone geological prior on an irregular corner-point grid. History matching was formulated as a search in a hybrid latent space built from zone-specific graph-based Wasserstein autoencoders (GWAEs) operating directly on the native Brugge grid. The four zone latent spaces were combined into a 160-dimensional joint space and optimised with CMA-ES against an objective integrating static mismatch, dynamic mismatch, and geological realism; the need for this multiple-generator decomposition was itself established using latent-space diagnostics, including persistent homology. The main findings are as follows: One generator is not sufficient for a heterogeneous prior. For the combined Schelde prior, which includes realisations generated by object modelling and sequential indicator simulation, a single GWAE produced a latent point cloud with two persistent [FORMULA] components. The Decoder also failed to preserve the channel and shale structure of the object modelling realisations. A multiple-generator decomposition improves latent coherence. The four zone GWAEs each produced one dominant connected latent component. They reconstructed the main spatial patterns of their priors and preserved the porosity and permeability relation implicitly, without adding this relation as an explicit constraint in the loss function. The hybrid latent space supports history matching while remaining within the prior manifold. The matched solutions remained within the projected prior clouds in all four zones and reproduced field-level oil and water rates within the prior spread. Absolute pore-volume error stayed within roughly 1–11% across zones, lowest for Waal and highest for Schelde. The workflow provides a competitive well-level match while keeping an explicit link to the geological prior. Most wells fall into the good match category according to the qualitative classification used in earlier Brugge studies. Unlike Ensemble Kalman Filter (EnKF), Particle Swarm Optimisation with principal component analysis of parameterisation (PSO-PCA), and Multiple Kernel Learning with Particle Swarm Optimisation (MKL-PSO), every accepted model in the proposed workflow remains constrained by the learned generative prior manifold. The current formulation assumes independent geological priors across zones; reservoirs with cross-zone dependencies would require shared latent variables or conditional generators. Calibration updates only porosity and permeability, leaving relative permeability and other phase-flow parameters fixed. Extending this variable set may improve flexibility, although the present results do not isolate the causes of residual well-level mismatch. Static conditioning is approximate, and its mean-squared-error formulation does not explicitly model the support difference between well logs and grid-cell properties. The study considers a limited space of uncertainty associated with primarily 2-point spatial correlation parameters used to design the prior ensemble of models. However, the framework demonstrated its generic capability to handle more diverse prior definitions and has the topological diagnostics to differentiate between multiple geological concepts. Further work will enhance the method with posterior sampling in the latent space for a more accurate evaluation of the prediction credible intervals, not just several exemplary solutions. Additional observed data, such as 4D seismic or tracer data, can be also integrated into the framework. 7 Acknowledgements The authors appreciate the support of Rock Flow Dynamics for GeoDataScience & UQ group research at Heriot-Watt University and the provision of tNavigator software licences for reservoir flow simulations.
