Predictive Surprise as Self-Grounding Concept Bottleneck for Interpretable Time Series Time-series classifiers deployed in risk-sensitive domains must be (1) accurate, (2) interpretable, and (3) able to abstain when evidence is weak. Existing methods do not deliver all 3 at once, and the obstacle is structural, rather than logistical. Meaningful temporal patterns cannot be defined without knowing segment boundaries, yet meaningful boundaries cannot be placed without knowing which patterns to expect. Existing approaches break this circularity by using fixed windows or expert-annotated vocabularies, thereby sacrificing at least one of the 3 properties. We introduce ConceptTime, which closes the loop through a single self-supervised signal. A frozen probabilistic forecaster predicts a distribution over the next observation at every timestep of the sequence. We call the mismatch between its prediction and the realized signal the predictive surprise. This signal both locates segment boundaries and characterizes each resulting segment through the forecaster. Segments are thus grounded by how they behaved relative to expectation, not by what they look like. These summaries cluster into a vocabulary of dynamical regimes that we call concepts. A lightweight head classifies from the concept sequence, and the distance to the nearest concept yields reliability by design. Across 17 public benchmarks, ConceptTime is competitive with state-of-the-art black-box accuracy, beats every interpretable baseline, and retains near-98% accuracy on Epilepsy with 1% of labels. It further remains competitive with softmax, prototype-distance, and SHAP/TimeX/TimeX++ on OOD detection and deletion faithfulness, without human annotations, language model calls, or domain experts. Code is available at: https://github.com/Sachithx/ConceptTime.git 1 Introduction Time-series classifiers deployed in healthcare [24, 32], wearable sensing [22], environmental monitoring [41], and industrial telemetry [47, 61] face 3 simultaneous demands: (1) predictions must be accurate enough to compete with end-to-end deep models, (2) they must be interpretable so that users can inspect which temporal patterns drove a decision, and (3) they must support calibrated abstention, so that the system defers when its evidence is weak. However, existing methods cannot satisfy all 3 requirements simultaneously (Figure 1). Black-box classifiers target higher downstream accuracy; post hoc explainable methods describe a model’s output without constraining how it was produced, while interpretable-by-design methods come closest, but they fail to address the cost of concept annotation, which is rare for sequential data and expensive to obtain at scale. The deeper obstacle is structural and unique to sequential domains. Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs) for time series face a chicken-and-egg problem: meaningful temporal concepts cannot be defined without knowing where one segment ends and another begins, yet meaningful segment boundaries cannot be placed without knowing what concepts to look for. Every prior method sidesteps this circularity by decoupling the 2 stages. They first segment with fixed windows or threshold-based change detection, then learn concepts from the resulting chunks. Each gives up one of the 3 properties as a result. (a) Fixed-window CBMs [62, 57, 16] achieve interpretability but require predefined vocabularies and lose calibrated abstention. (b) Adaptive-patching methods [1, 46] segment well but feed patches into standard encoder-classifier pipelines, exposing no concepts at all. (c) Vector-quantized models [55, 60, 5] produce discrete tokens, but the tokens are latent codes without inherent semantic structure. The same self-supervised signal that locates segment boundaries can also describe what each resulting segment looks like. A frozen probabilistic forecaster predicts a distribution over the next observation at each time step. The mismatch between this prediction and the realized signal, which we call predictive surprise, is the natural place to draw a boundary, since high mismatch indicates a regime change. The same forecaster also produces predictive statistics that describe how each segment behaved relative to expectation. A single frozen model can therefore close the segmentation-concept loop, and no prior method exploits this dual use. We introduce ConceptTime, which operationalizes this opportunity. An Autoregressive Gaussian Density Model (ARGDM) is trained once on raw multivariate signals via next-step density estimation. At each time step, it predicts a Gaussian distribution over the next observation conditioned on the history. The negative log-likelihood of the realized signal under that prediction is our predictive surprise. This single quantity locates segment boundaries via length-constrained dynamic programming, placing exactly [FORMULA] patches at the moments when the signal most strongly violates prior expectations. The same model characterizes each resulting patch by its predictive statistics, yielding contextual fingerprints that describe how a segment behaves relative to expectations rather than what it looks like. Patches that violate prior expectations in similar ways receive similar fingerprints, even when their raw waveforms differ visibly. The path from raw signal to concept activation is fully deterministic. Signatures are statistics of the frozen model; prototypes are cluster centroids in signature space; and patch-to-concept assignment is a nearest-prototype lookup. A lightweight classifier is the only label-supervised component. The same prototype distances yield a built-in fidelity score that asks whether the input is even describable in the concept space rather than whether the classifier is confident. Across 17 benchmarks spanning UEA, human-activity, biomedical, and fault-diagnosis tasks, ConceptTime remains competitive with black-box accuracy, beats every interpretable baseline, and retains 98% accuracy on Epilepsy at 1% labels. Its fidelity score is also competitive with softmax and prototype methods on OOD detection and SHAP [39], TimeX [48], and TimeX++ [34] on deletion faithfulness, all without human annotations, language-model calls, or domain experts. Further, we demonstrate ConceptTime’s cross-domain transferability of the learned concept under a limited target label budget. Our main contributions can be summarized as follows: To our knowledge, we introduce the first concept-bottleneck framework that resolves the segmentation-concept circularity through a single self-supervised primitive, eliminating the need for fixed windows, expert annotations, and language-model supervision. We provide a fully non-parametric concept-grounding pipeline whose path from raw signal to concept activation is deterministic and inspectable, with all task-specific learning confined to a lightweight classifier on the concept tensor. We identify prototype distance as a built-in fidelity signal and propose a prototype-distance abstention mechanism for time-series concept bottlenecks. 2 Related Work Concept bottleneck models (CBMs) route predictions through intermediate concepts that users can inspect and intervene on [28]. The original formulation requires concept annotations. Later work reduces this burden through label-free concept discovery, including approaches that draw on vision-language models [45, 66, 53, 50]. Other work studies robustness, counterfactual explanations, and concept locality [42, 51, 11, 25]. Time-series CBMs use predefined statistical summaries [62], CKA-aligned concepts for forecasting [57], or Signal Temporal Logic predicates [16]. These approaches leave open how to discover both a temporal concept and its boundaries when its duration varies and its behavior is difficult to name in advance. The Byte Latent Transformer (BLT) places boundaries at peaks in next-token entropy [46]. EntroPE adapts this idea to time series by thresholding categorical entropy [1]. Related work learns boundaries through reinforcement learning [64] or uses content-aware compression [4]. A complementary line of work represents time series with discrete tokens, using learned codebooks in TOTEM and VQShape [55, 60] or value quantization in Chronos [5]. These methods address where to divide a sequence or how to encode it. A further question is whether the predictive signal that selects a boundary can also describe the behavior of the resulting segment. Prototype and shapelet classifiers explain predictions through representative subsequences and local shape patterns [67, 43, 21, 15, 59, 33]. Shape alone can miss a distinction that matters for time series. A flat segment may be expected after a quiet interval and surprising after a spike, even when the 2 segments look identical. Post-hoc explainers identify influential regions through saliency or perturbation [48, 34, 8, 23]. Their explanations describe an existing classifier’s behavior, while a concept bottleneck requires the classifier to base its prediction on the concepts it exposes. Common signals for selective prediction and shift detection include softmax confidence [18], ensemble disagreement [29], and distance-based OOD scores [30, 54, 36, 37]. In vision, concept-based models support abstention through uncertainty heads, calibration networks, or stochastic concept layers [26, 35, 58, 27, 52]. For time series, a complementary question is whether the learned vocabulary itself can indicate how well it covers a new input. ConceptTime uses one frozen Gaussian density model for both segmentation and concept discovery. Predictive surprise guides patch boundaries, and each patch is summarized by how its observations compare with the model’s predictions. Clustering these summaries yields concept prototypes without concept annotations or linguistic priors. Patches receive soft assignments based on prototype distance, which also supplies a fidelity score for abstention without an additional confidence model. The UCI-HAR ablation illustrates why the choice of features matters. With the same adaptive patches and vocabulary size, predictive moments achieve 87.7% accuracy versus 42.7% for raw-signal morphology, a 45.0-point difference (Section 4.4). 3 ConceptTime ConceptTime factors classification into stages with disjoint training signals: a self-supervised density model produces every representation, clustering induces a non-parametric concept vocabulary, and a lightweight transformer head consumes labels. Each intermediate step is human-inspectable, and prototype distances provide a built-in fidelity score for selective prediction at no additional cost. Further examples appear in Appendix F. 5 Conclusion We introduced ConceptTime, a concept-bottleneck framework that resolves the segmentation-concept circularity for time series through a single self-supervised primitive, predictive surprise. The same frozen model sets adaptive segment boundaries, grounds a non-parametric concept vocabulary, and provides prototype distances that also serve as a built-in fidelity score. Across diverse classification and cross-domain transfer benchmarks, ConceptTime maintains competitive accuracy with black-box methods, dominates all interpretable baselines, including in few-shot settings. The by-design fidelity score remains competitive with softmax, prototype-distance, and post-hoc explainers on OOD detection and deletion faithfulness. Interpretability, label efficiency, and reliable abstention emerge jointly when concept grounding is anchored in predictive surprise rather than human annotation. We fix the vocabulary size in advance, and the meaning of each learned prototype depends on human interpretation after training. Hierarchical vocabularies could capture patterns at multiple levels of detail, while online updates could help the vocabulary adapt as signal patterns change. Low-fidelity segments could also guide active relabeling by identifying examples for human review. Beyond classification, we plan to explore whether these concepts can help discover operating regimes, locate anomalies, and support decisions that users can inspect. Spike cameras encode dynamic scenes into high-temporal-resolution binary spike streams for efficient high-speed vision. Although spiking neural networks (SNNs) can process such signals with sparse and accumulate-only computation, existing SNN-based reconstruction methods are typically shallow and still lag behind ANN-based models in reconstruction fidelity. This paper proposes MADSNet, a Multi-scale Axial-attentive Dense Spiking Network for spike camera image reconstruction. MADSNet adopts a hierarchical spiking encoder–decoder, where a multi-scale spike stem extracts early features, axial spike attention captures long-range dependencies, a dense spiking bottleneck enhances feature reuse, and a spike-to-continuous decoder reconstructs continuous intensity images from spike-domain representations. Experiments on gray-scale and color spike reconstruction show that MADSNet outperforms SSIR by 4.3 dB PSNR and Spk2ImgNet by 1.94 dB on SREDS. Compared with Spk2ImgNet, it achieves about 15 [FORMULA] lower latency and uses only about 1/40 of the estimated energy, demonstrating that carefully designed SNN architectures can improve reconstruction quality while preserving computational efficiency. I Introduction Conventional frame-based cameras capture visual scenes by integrating photons within a fixed exposure interval. This imaging mechanism works well for ordinary scenes, but it inevitably suffers from motion blur, temporal discretization, and missing inter-frame information when recording high-speed dynamic processes. Spike cameras provide a neuromorphic alternative by representing visual signals as continuous binary spike streams [1, 2]. In a spike camera, each pixel independently accumulates incoming light intensity and asynchronously fires a binary spike once the accumulated signal reaches a predefined threshold, after which the accumulator is reset for the next integration cycle. This integrate-and-fire sensing mechanism enables ultra-high temporal resolution, e.g., up to tens of thousands of spike frames per second, while preserving dense temporal information for dynamic scene analysis [3, 1, 2]. The development of spike cameras has stimulated a broad range of visual applications, including high-speed image reconstruction [4, 5, 6, 7, 8], motion deblurring [9, 10], optical flow estimation [11, 12, 13, 14], tracking [15, 16], joint visual compression and perception [17], and color spike imaging [18, 19, 20, 21]. In parallel, the SpikeCV platform has been developed to support the spike vision ecosystem by providing spike datasets, hardware interfaces, data loaders, algorithm libraries, and unified processing pipelines for different spike-based visual tasks [2]. These efforts indicate that spike cameras are evolving from a specialized high-speed imaging sensor into a broader computational vision platform. Within this ecosystem, spike-to-image reconstruction occupies a foundational position: it converts raw spike streams into the intensity representations that human visualization and most downstream vision tasks still depend on. Yet recovering high-quality intensity remains challenging, as the task is inherently ill-posed: the network must infer continuous scene radiance from observations that are sparse, binary, temporally accumulated, and corrupted by photon-arrival noise and motion. Early reconstruction methods, such as TFP [3], TFI [3], TFSTP [22], and MAHTF [4], estimate image intensity from hand-crafted spike statistics or temporal filtering. Although these methods are computationally simple, they are limited in recovering high-fidelity textures and complex spatiotemporal structures. Learning-based methods, including Spk2ImgNet and recent self-supervised reconstruction frameworks, significantly improve reconstruction quality by exploiting data-driven feature learning and motion-aware supervision [5, 7, 9, 8, 23]. However, most of these methods are based on artificial neural networks (ANNs), whose dense multiply-accumulate operations lead to high latency and energy consumption. Spiking neural networks (SNNs) [24] provide a natural computational counterpart to spike cameras. By processing spike-domain activations with event-driven accumulate-only operations, SNNs have the potential to realize low-power and low-latency for spike cameras [25, 26, 6, 27]. SSIR [6] is a representative SNN-based reconstruction method that combines Spike-Element-Wise (SEW) residual blocks with a reparameterizable Progressive Filtering Module (PFM), reporting substantially lower energy consumption than ANN-based reconstruction. However, there remains a clear reconstruction-quality gap between existing SNN-based methods and high-capacity ANN models. We argue that this gap is not solely caused by the spiking neuron model, but also by insufficient architecture design. In particular, existing SNN reconstruction networks typically use single-scale early embeddings that overlook multi-scale spatial structure, rely on spike-domain encoders confined to local convolutions that cannot capture long-range dependencies, and adopt relatively direct decoding heads that handle the transition from discrete spike activations to continuous intensities only crudely. To address these limitations, we propose MADSNet, a multi-scale axial-attentive dense spiking network for spike camera image reconstruction. The core design principle of MADSNet is to improve representation capacity while preserving the accumulate-only, multiplication-free computation that underlies the energy efficiency of SNNs. Specifically, MADSNet introduces a Multi-Scale Spike Stem (MS3Stem) to jointly capture inter-channel temporal correlations and local-to-large spatial patterns from stacked spike frames. It further employs depthwise-separable SEW blocks and light spike blocks with axial spike attention to build an efficient spike-domain encoder. A dense spike bottleneck is introduced to enhance latent feature reuse and stabilize information propagation in deeper spiking architectures. Finally, spike pixel-shuffle upsampling and a spike-to-continuous fusion block are used to recover fine spatial details and convert discrete spike-domain features into continuous intensity predictions. MADSNet achieves a favorable balance between reconstruction accuracy and computational efficiency. On the SREDS benchmark, MADSNet reaches 37.232 dB PSNR, improving over the SNN baseline SSIR by +4.30 dB and surpassing the ANN-based Spk2ImgNet by +1.94 dB. At the same time, MADSNet remains much more efficient than Spk2ImgNet, achieving about 15 [FORMULA] lower inference latency, 3.4 [FORMULA] lower GPU memory usage, and only about 1/40 of the estimated energy consumption. These results suggest that SNN-based reconstruction does not have to trade substantial accuracy for efficiency; instead, with appropriate architecture design, SNNs can provide a strong accuracy–efficiency balance for spike camera reconstruction. The main contributions of this work are threefold: We propose MADSNet, a hierarchical spiking encoder-decoder built on the design principle of improving representation capacity while retaining the accumulate-only efficiency of spike-domain computation. We develop a coherent set of spike-oriented modules that progressively enrich the spike-domain representation along the entire pipeline, from multi-scale early embedding, through axial-attentive encoding and dense latent aggregation, to spike-to-continuous decoding. We conduct experiments on gray-scale and color spike reconstruction, demonstrating superior accuracy and efficiency trade-off over existing ANN and SNN baselines. II Related Work Early filtering-based methods estimate intensity directly from spike statistics without learning. TFP and TFI [3] infer pixel intensity from spike firing frequency and inter-spike intervals, respectively, while TFSTP [22] and MAHTF [4, 26] exploit short-term plasticity and motion-aligned temporal filtering for higher fidelity, albeit at high latency. Learning-based methods improve quality further: Spk2ImgNet [5] aligns multi-temporal spike features with deformable convolutions but is computationally heavy, whereas SSIR [6] proposes the first SNN-based reconstruction with SEW residual blocks and a reparameterizable PFM, reducing energy to about [FORMULA] of Spk2ImgNet but still trailing high-capacity ANNs in fidelity. The color spike camera (CSC) employs a Bayer-pattern Color Filter Array, introducing the additional challenges of spatially missing pixels per channel and inter-channel chromatic correlations. 3DRI [18] fills missing pixels via 3D residual interpolation using spatially and temporally neighboring samples, while subsequent work has developed deep demosaicing networks explicitly tailored for spike camera CFAs [20]. SJRE [9], a self-supervised gray-scale method, can be adapted to color streams by processing each Bayer channel independently, but lacks explicit inter-channel modeling. SSL-CSC [19] proposes a motion-guided pipeline that jointly estimates optical flow across color channels and trains a self-supervised network with a masked spike encoder to suppress quantization noise, establishing the current state-of-the-art among methods that do not require ground-truth supervision. Additionally, recent advances have demonstrated that aggregating long short-term temporal spike signals can further enhance continuous color reconstruction fidelity [21]. These methods, however, are purpose-built for color reconstruction rather than transferred from a general spike architecture. A closely related neuromorphic modality is the event camera, which records per-pixel asynchronous brightness changes as a stream of events, enabling high dynamic range and microsecond temporal resolution [28]. Because event and spike cameras both represent visual information as asynchronous data streams, their deep-learning reconstruction pipelines share methodological similarities, and event-to-video reconstruction has demonstrated significant progress. E2VID [29] is a seminal work for this purpose, employing a recurrent fully convolutional network to convert event streams into video frames. Following E2VID, numerous studies have augmented this paradigm from various angles, including FireNet [30], E2VID++ [31], and FireNet++ [31]. ETNet [32] further incorporates Transformer-based attention into event-to-video reconstruction, improving the modeling of long-range temporal dependencies. HyperE2VID [33] adopts a dynamic neural network architecture and uses hypernetworks to generate per-pixel adaptive filters, achieving state-of-the-art reconstruction quality. However, event cameras record only relative intensity changes and thus cannot recover absolute texture detail, making event-based reconstruction complementary to but distinct from the spike-based reconstruction discussed above. The Integrate-and-Fire (IF) neuron [24] fires a binary spike when its accumulated membrane potential exceeds a threshold, offering event-driven efficiency but limited temporal expressiveness. The Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) neuron [34] introduces membrane potential decay, enabling implicit short-term memory. To further improve adaptability, Parametric LIF (PLIF) [35] makes the time constant learnable, which is adopted in SSIR to improve training convergence. However, direct training via spatio-temporal backpropagation requires storing neuronal states across all timesteps, imposing significant GPU memory overhead, while the non-differentiable spike generation function necessitates surrogate gradient approximations that introduce inherent estimation errors and hinder stable convergence [36]. To address this, I-LIF [37] allows integer-valued spike emission during training while decomposing to binary spikes at inference, preserving accumulate-only (AC) computation on neuromorphic hardware. IBRA-LIF [38] further introduces a Range Alignment strategy that scales the effective dynamic range of integer spikes, alleviating quantization errors that accumulate across deep layers. These neuron-level developments improve the representational capacity and training stability of SNNs, but they are orthogonal to architecture-level designs for spike reconstruction. In this work, we adopt IBRA-LIF as the basic activation function for spiking layers and focus on designing an efficient encoder-decoder architecture for gray-scale spike reconstruction. Table I compares MADSNet with representative gray-scale spike reconstruction methods on SREDS. Conventional temporal filtering methods, including TFP, TFI, and TFSTP, achieve limited reconstruction fidelity, showing that simple temporal aggregation is insufficient for recovering high-quality intensity images from sparse spike streams. MAHTF improves the reconstruction quality by exploiting long-range temporal motion information, but still lags behind learning-based methods in reference metrics. Among ANN-based methods, the event-based models ETNet and HyperE2VID adapted for spike streams demonstrate strong capabilities, particularly HyperE2VID achieving 35.456 dB PSNR. Spk2ImgNet similarly achieves a competitive 35.293 dB PSNR. Compared with the SNN baseline SSIR, MADSNet improves PSNR from 32.930 dB to 37.232 dB and SSIM from 0.922 to 0.956, while reducing LPIPS from 0.050 to 0.028. This corresponds to a massive +4.30 dB PSNR gain within the SNN paradigm. Moreover, MADSNet surpasses both the dedicated spike reconstruction ANN (Spk2ImgNet by +1.94 dB) and the modern event-adapted ANN (HyperE2VID by +1.78 dB). These gains demonstrate that a carefully designed spiking architecture can achieve substantially stronger reconstruction fidelity than even advanced conventional ANN baselines. For no-reference perceptual metrics, MADSNet obtains competitive NIQE and BRISQUE scores. Although it does not achieve the best value on every no-reference metric, the overall results show that the proposed architecture substantially improves reference fidelity while maintaining excellent perceptual quality. Fig. 2 presents visual comparisons on real-captured gray-scale spike streams across three scenes, covering a bicycle, a car, and a decorative doll. The event-camera methods ET-Net and HyperE2VID produce visually plausible reconstructions but tend to introduce blurring or ghosting artifacts in regions with complex texture, reflecting the inherent limitation of event cameras in recovering absolute luminance detail. Spk2ImgNet recovers sharper edges than the event-based methods but still exhibits residual blur on high-frequency elements. SSIR reconstructs recognizable structure but loses fine detail, particularly on thin elements such as bicycle spokes. MADSNet produces the sharpest and most faithful reconstructions across all scenes: bicycle spokes are more precisely delineated, high-frequency fan textures are better preserved with higher local contrast, and fine ornamental details in the doll scene exhibit fewer boundary artifacts. These observations are consistent with the quantitative improvements reported in Table I. Although MADSNet is developed for gray-scale spike reconstruction, its design is not tied to a specific output modality. The multi-scale spiking encoder, axial-attentive feature extraction, and spike-to-continuous decoding are expected to remain useful when the input changes from gray-scale spike streams to Bayer-pattern color spike streams. Therefore, we further investigate whether MADSNet can be effectively transferred to color spike reconstruction, and whether it can serve as a strong SNN baseline for this more challenging task. Table II reports transfer results on the RBSS color reconstruction benchmark. Filtering-based methods TFP, TFI, and TFSTP remain below 24 dB PSNR, confirming their limited capacity to handle the spatial-chromatic coupling of Bayer-pattern spike streams. Among event-camera methods, ETNet achieves only 13.10 dB due to the fundamental modality mismatch between event streams and Bayer spike streams, while HyperE2VID reaches 27.34 dB, benefiting from its adaptive per-pixel filtering design. Spk2ImgNet achieves 29.13 dB, demonstrating the advantage of a spike-specific ANN architecture. SSL-CSC attains the highest PSNR (29.95 dB) and SSIM (0.8417) among all compared methods, benefiting from its motion-guided self-supervised design tailored for color spike reconstruction. Directly transferring SSIR to color spike reconstruction yields 24.31 dB PSNR and 0.6514 SSIM, showing that a spike-based SNN can generalize to the color domain to a reasonable degree, though with a substantial gap in fine chromatic detail compared with dedicated methods. In contrast, MADSNet achieves 29.36 dB PSNR, 0.8434 SSIM, and 0.1464 LPIPS, improving over SSIR by +5.05 dB in PSNR and outperforming all compared methods in both SSIM and LPIPS. Notably, MADSNet also surpasses the ANN-based Spk2ImgNet in all three metrics and closely approaches SSL-CSC in PSNR while outperforming it in SSIM and LPIPS, despite not being specifically designed for color reconstruction. These results demonstrate the strong transferability of the proposed architecture and confirm that MADSNet serves as a competitive SNN baseline for color spike reconstruction. Fig. 3 presents visual comparisons on real-world BSS color spike streams across three scenes. ETNet produces severely overexposed outputs, reflecting the severe modality gap between event cameras and Bayer spike cameras. HyperE2VID recovers plausible color but introduces noticeable chromatic noise and loses fine structural boundaries. Spk2ImgNet reconstructs coherent color images but still exhibits some color bleeding and texture blurring. SSIR recovers a coarse color approximation with recognizable scene structure, though with noticeably reduced chromatic fidelity and visible mosaic-pattern artifacts attributable to its limited Bayer-layout modeling. MADSNet reconstructs well-structured color images with the most faithful chromatic fidelity and sharpest object boundaries across all three scenes, consistent with its leading quantitative results in Table II. The quantitative and qualitative results together reveal a clear transferability hierarchy. SSIR transfers to color reconstruction with moderate success (24.31 dB), demonstrating that SNN architectures are not inherently incompatible with the color domain. However, its single-branch [FORMULA] spiking stem treats all stacked spike channels uniformly and provides limited receptive-field diversity, making it difficult to fully capture chromatic correlations across the Bayer mosaic. MADSNet transfers substantially better (+5.05 dB over SSIR) because its MS3Stem jointly captures inter-channel and multi-scale spatial patterns, while ASA contributes long-range horizontal and vertical context through its axial modeling. The spike-to-continuous fusion block further adapts discrete spike-domain features to the continuous RGB output space. These components jointly enable MADSNet to recover structured color images without task-specific architectural redesign, establishing it as a strong SNN baseline for color spike reconstruction. V Conclusion In this paper, we proposed MADSNet, a multi-scale axial-attentive dense spiking network for spike camera image reconstruction. MADSNet is designed to better exploit the complementary advantages of spike cameras and SNNs: spike cameras provide high-temporal-resolution binary visual streams, while SNNs enable efficient spike-domain computation. To improve reconstruction fidelity beyond existing shallow SNN designs, MADSNet enriches the spike-domain representation along the full encoder–decoder pipeline, from multi-scale early embedding, through axial-attentive encoding and dense latent aggregation, to spike-to-continuous decoding. Extensive experiments on gray-scale and color spike reconstruction demonstrate the effectiveness and generality of the proposed architecture. On SREDS, MADSNet significantly outperforms the SNN baseline SSIR and surpasses the ANN-based Spk2ImgNet in reconstruction accuracy, while maintaining much lower latency and estimated energy consumption than Spk2ImgNet. Color reconstruction experiments show that MADSNet transfers better than the direct SNN baseline. These results suggest that carefully designed SNN architectures can provide a favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-off for spike camera reconstruction. Nevertheless, MADSNet’s deeper architecture incurs higher latency and energy than lightweight shallow SNNs such as SSIR; reducing this overhead, e.g., through neuromorphic-hardware deployment or further architectural slimming, is a promising direction for future work.

Multimodal Graph Learning: A Survey of Models, Benchmarks, and Frontiers Multimodal attributed graphs (MAGs), in which nodes carry text, images, and other modalities while edges encode relations among entities, underlie e-commerce, social media, content platforms, and creative applications. Learning on MAGs has developed along two complemen- tary lines. Graph-centric methods redesign how modalities are fused, propagated, and connected within message passing, progressing from early multimodal graph neural networks to modality- aware propagation and multimodal graph structure learning. Foundation-model-centric methods instead pretrain transferable multimodal graph encoders or bring graph context into multimodal large language models for both prediction and generation. In parallel, several benchmarks have appeared with different datasets and evaluation protocols. This survey takes an algorithm-centric and evaluation-grounded view of the field and makes three contributions. Modeling: we introduce a unified message-passing formulation and organize methods into five levels at which multi- modal learning and graph structure are integrated, namely the feature, propagation, topology, learn- ing, and foundation-model levels, covering both discriminative models and graph-conditioned gen- erative models; within this formulation we derive representative methods as special cases, compare their assumptions, expressiveness, and cost, and identify cross-modal sensitivity as a property that separates architectures which otherwise appear similar. Datasets and evaluation: we review the benchmarks released in recent years, summarize their datasets with the metrics used for each task, define model-independent descriptors that characterize datasets by label homophily, average degree, clustering, and edge provenance, and map each evaluation protocol to the baselines it uses. Frontiers: we connect multimodal graph learning to AI agents, a currently active research direction, covering both the multimodal graphs that agents perceive and remember and graph engineering, the practice of organizing agent workflows as explicit graphs; we then discuss open problems, concrete efforts for the community, and research directions, including when graph structure helps in the presence of strong multimodal foundation models. Together, these parts are intended to help researchers choose model designs that match the properties of their data, compare methods under consistent protocols, and identify where multimodal graph learning can have the greatest impact. 1 Introduction Many real-world graphs are multimodal by construction. Products on e-commerce platforms are linked by co-purchase relations and described by titles, reviews, and images; posts on social platforms are organized into threads and carry both text and pictures; short videos are connected by co-viewing behavior and described by covers and captions; artworks are related through shared artists, schools, and styles. Such data are naturally modeled as multimodal attributed graphs (MAGs), in which every node carries attributes from several modalities and edges encode relations among entities (Zhu et al., 2025; Yan et al., 2025; Wan et al., 2026). Learning on MAGs, which we refer to as multimodal graph learning (MGL), has moved quickly from recommendation-oriented multimodal graph neural networks (GNNs) (Wei et al., 2019; Tao et al., 2020) to general-purpose MAG backbones (Zhang et al., 2026; Zuo et al., 2026b; Li et al., 2026d), multimodal graph structure learning (Zhu et al., 2026; Xue & Wu, 2026), multimodal graph foundation models (He et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2026b; Yang et al., 2026), and multimodal large language models (MLLMs) that consume graph structure (Yoon et al., 2023; Ning et al., 2025; Fan et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2026). Why multimodal graph learning? We see four reasons why learning on MAGs is more than the sum of multimodal learning and graph learning. Complementary semantics. Text and images describe the same entity from different perspectives. A product title states brand and function, while the image conveys style and appearance; neither is a sufficient description on its own. Benchmarks and recent methods show that jointly using textual and visual attributes can improve graph learning over either modality alone (Zhu et al., 2025; Yan et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026a; Xue & Wu, 2026). Relational context. The graph supplies information that does not exist in any single sample. Co-purchase edges reveal complementary usage and co-viewing edges reveal shared audiences; no amount of per-node encoding can recover such information from the node’s own attributes. This context also benefits generation: conditioning image synthesis on a node’s graph neighbors, rather than on its text alone, yields images more consistent with the ground truth (Jin et al., 2024). Cross-modal relational reasoning. The text of a neighbor can disambiguate the image of the target node, and vice versa. Recent analyses show that this cross-modal, cross-node interaction is not symmetric: when one modality is degraded, the useful direction of completion is from the stronger modality of the neighbors to the weaker modality of the target (Zuo et al., 2026b). Exploiting such interactions requires architectures that let information flow across modalities and across nodes at the same time. Noisy and incomplete modalities and topology. Real MAGs simultaneously exhibit feature noise, modality imbalance, missing modalities (e.g., cold-start items without images or isolated nodes without edges), and noisy or task-agnostic edges (Hu et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026). These imperfections interact: a reliable edge can compensate for a missing modality, and a reliable modality can reveal that an edge is spurious. Why neither side suffices alone. Multimodal foundation models such as CLIP (Radford et al., 2021) and LLaVA-style MLLMs (Liu et al., 2023) typically align modalities in a pairwise manner, one instance at a time, and overlook structural relations across data points (Liu et al., 2026a). Standard GNNs, conversely, treat node attributes as a single feature vector and perform one shared message passing over a single graph. This implicitly assumes that a neighbor is equally useful for all modalities, an assumption that does not hold empirically: text and image branches prefer different neighborhood organizations (Zuo et al., 2026b). Consequently, the default recipe of “encode each modality, concatenate, then run a GNN” leaves both cross-modal and structural signal unused (Xue & Wu, 2026), which motivates the designs surveyed in this paper. Three prior works review learning with multimodal graphs. Ektefaie et al. (2023) propose a blueprint for graph-centric multimodal learning with four components (identifying entities, uncovering topology, propagating information, and mixing representations), and apply it to image-intensive, language-intensive, and knowledge-intensive graphs. Peng et al. (2024) categorize multimodal graphs into feature-level, node-level, and graph-level types, and categorize methods into multimodal graph convolution (MGCN), multimodal graph attention (MGAT), and multimodal graph contrastive learning (MGCL). Wang et al. (2025) chart a roadmap toward multimodal graph large language models (MG-LLMs) and articulate five desired capabilities. These works established the vocabulary of the field. Since 2024, however, the field has changed in three ways that call for a new synthesis. Gap 1: Recent models have outgrown existing taxonomies. Early multimodal graph models, which exemplify the categories used by prior surveys, fuse modalities statically: they either concatenate modality features before propagation or, as in MMGCN and MGAT, propagate each modality separately and combine the results at the output. In neither case can the interaction between modalities adapt to the neighbors and the task during propagation. Recent methods instead fuse modalities dynamically, through cross-modal coupled propagation, role-aware neighbor routing, and the co-evolution of topology and modality representations (Zhang et al., 2026; Zuo et al., 2026b; Li et al., 2026d; Zhu et al., 2026; Xue & Wu, 2026). Neither backbone-based taxonomies (MGCN / MGAT / MGCL) nor fusion-stage taxonomies (early / intermediate / late) can distinguish these design choices. At the same time, MLLMs fine-tuned on a specific MAG can reach state-of-the-art results in many settings (Liu et al., 2026a), yet well-designed graph-centric models remain competitive and also achieve state-of-the-art performance (Xue & Wu, 2026; Zhang et al., 2026). Neither line subsumes the other, so we cover graph-centric and foundation-model-centric methods in one view, organized by where multimodal learning and graph structure are integrated within a single formulation (Sections 2 and 3). Gap 2: New benchmarks are not covered, and evaluation has fragmented. Earlier multimodal graph models were evaluated mainly on recommendation datasets with ranking metrics, or on domain-specific graphs such as multimodal knowledge graphs and biomedical networks with their own preprocessed features; prior surveys accordingly list domain resources rather than general MAG benchmarks (Peng et al., 2024). Three developments motivated a new generation of benchmarks: MAG backbones are now expected to serve general node- and edge-level tasks beyond recommendation; the choice of feature encoder, from CLIP to MLLMs, has become a variable that must be controlled; and modality-centric and generative tasks require datasets with raw text and images. Five benchmarks appeared within two years in response (Zhu et al., 2025; Yan et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026a; Wan et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026a). They differ in datasets, encoders, splits, tasks, and baseline sets, and recent method papers follow different ones, so a reported improvement is interpretable only relative to its protocol. Existing surveys predate most of these benchmarks and do not analyze their protocols. We review them, map each protocol to its baselines, and characterize the datasets (Section 10). Gap 3: Existing surveys do not connect the field to current research trends. The research agendas of prior surveys were set before the field’s recent shift. The challenges identified by Peng et al. (2024), such as modality imbalance, cross-modal alignment, temporal dynamics, and efficiency, remain relevant but are framed for GNN-based models, and the MG-LLM roadmap (Wang et al., 2025) centers on building a single multimodal graph LLM. Since then, AI agents have become one of the most active research directions. Agents increasingly rely on explicit graphs to organize planning, tool use, memory, and coordination (Bei et al., 2025); as they become multimodal, the graphs they perceive and remember increasingly carry multiple modalities, while the workflow graphs that organize their computation, a practice termed graph engineering (Feng et al., 2026), raise related questions about how information from different channels is combined. Existing surveys on multimodal graph learning predate these developments and do not connect the field to agents. At the same time, strong MLLMs make it necessary to ask when explicit structure is needed at all, a question that recent benchmarks now allow us to study empirically. We therefore connect multimodal graph learning to AI agents (Section 12) and discuss open problems, concrete efforts, and research directions (Section 13). Table 1 summarizes how this survey relates to prior work. Scope. We focus on MAGs whose nodes carry attributes from multiple modalities (primarily text and images), with a topology that is either observed or learned, and on both graph-centric tasks (node classification, link prediction, node clustering) and modality-centric tasks (modality matching, cross-modal retrieval, alignment, and graph-conditioned generation). Models that originated in multimodal recommendation are included when they have become standard MAG baselines. Multimodal knowledge graphs and biomedical multimodal graphs share some techniques but have distinct problem formulations and dedicated surveys; we mention them only briefly in Section 11. Contributions. Our contributions fall into three parts, which we expand into five specific contributions (C1–C5). Modeling and datasets are the main parts; the expansion places them in a broader context. Modeling. A unified formulation. We write multimodal graph learning as a single message-passing template in which each integration point is an explicit component, derive representative methods as special cases, and identify cross-modal sensitivity as a property that separates otherwise similar architectures (Section 2). An integration-level taxonomy. We organize methods into five levels (feature, propagation, topology, learning, and foundation-model level), including graph-conditioned text and image generation, and for each level we analyze differences, connections, strengths, limitations, and complexity (Sections 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8). Datasets and evaluation. A map of benchmarks, datasets, and baselines. We compare five recent benchmark platforms, summarize their datasets and task metrics, define model-independent dataset descriptors (label homophily, average degree, clustering, and edge provenance), and map each evaluation protocol to its baseline set (Section 10). Frontiers. Connections to AI agents (current research trend). AI agents increasingly rely on explicit graphs to organize planning, tool use, memory, and multi-agent coordination (Bei et al., 2025). We connect multimodal graph learning to two kinds of agent graphs: the environment and memory graphs that agents perceive and maintain, which can be modeled as MAGs when their nodes retain multiple modalities, and the workflow and communication graphs of graph engineering (Feng et al., 2026), which are not necessarily MAGs but share structural principles with multimodal graph learning. We close with directions at this intersection (Section 12). Open problems, concrete efforts, and research directions. Grounded in the evidence from current benchmarks, we identify open questions, including the expressiveness of cross-modal message passing and when graph structure helps in the presence of strong multimodal foundation models, and propose concrete efforts for the community and research directions suggested by recent methods (Section 13). Organization. Section 2 introduces notation, task families, and the unified formulation. Section 3 presents the taxonomy. Sections 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8 review the five integration levels. Section 9 discusses robustness, efficiency, and federated settings. Section 10 reviews benchmarks, datasets, dataset characteristics, and evaluation protocols. Section 11 covers applications, Section 12 connects multimodal graph learning to AI agents, including graph engineering, Section 13 discusses open problems and future directions, and Section 14 concludes. 2 Preliminaries We first define all symbols used throughout the paper. Applied to MAGs, they score pairs from concatenated features, so modality-specific evidence is collapsed before refinement and the modalities do not exchange information during propagation (Xue & Wu, 2026). Multimodal GSL must additionally decide which modalities induce the learned structure and how that structure feeds back into each modality. ReCoG (Xue & Wu, 2026) jointly optimizes the multimodal graph refiners introduced in Section 6.2 with coupled cross-modal propagation (Equation 9), allowing graph structure and multimodal representations to mutually reinforce each other. Topology refinement suppresses noisy edges and recovers semantically meaningful connections, providing a more reliable structure for cross-modal information exchange. Conversely, coupled propagation enables complementary information to flow across modalities and neighboring nodes, while its task gradients guide the refiner toward connections that benefit joint representation learning. Without refinement, cross-modal propagation remains constrained by noisy or incomplete topology; without coupling, the refined structure cannot fully exploit cross-modal neighbor interactions. Ablation results confirm their complementarity: removing either component degrades performance, while removing both yields the largest degradation, highlighting the importance of jointly learning graph structure and multimodal representations. TMTE (Zhu et al., 2026), a concurrent work, adopts a different co-evolution mechanism. It learns task-adaptive topology through multi-perspective similarity metrics over modality-specific and fused embeddings, using a node–anchor approximation for scalability. The evolved graph guides smoothness-regularized learning of fused representations, while cross-modal contrastive alignment preserves consistency across modalities. Updated representations then guide subsequent topology refinement. Unlike ReCoG’s explicit cross-modal neighbor exchange between separate modality streams, TMTE performs graph propagation on fused representations and learns non-negative similarity-based topology mixed with the observed graph. Several methods address modality-dependent neighborhood inconsistencies, where connected nodes may be similar in one modality but dissimilar in another. OptiMAG (Zuo et al., 2026a) addresses the same inconsistency without rewiring the graph, through a learning-level regularizer (Section 7.1). DMGC (Guo et al., 2025) explicitly disentangles homophilous and heterophilous relations by constructing a cross-modal consensus graph and modality-specific heterophily-aware graphs, applying low-pass and high-pass filters to preserve shared semantic consistency and modality-specific distinctions for clustering. NSG-MoE (Zhang & Kuruoglu, 2026) addresses the related problem of modality confusion, in which a general-purpose GNN mixes messages from different modalities indiscriminately. It splits each node into modality-specific components, rewires the graph into within- and cross-modality relations, and assigns relation-aware experts to the different message flows. Together with role-aware routing at the propagation level (Section 5.2) and modality-guided topology refinement (Section 6.2), these methods offer complementary strategies for handling inconsistent multimodal neighborhoods. Importantly, modality disagreement does not necessarily imply uninformative edges: such relations may contain useful complementary or heterophilous signals rather than noise. Learning-level integration is defined by the training objective [FORMULA] and the pretraining protocol, even when methods also introduce new feature fusion or message-passing operators. We organize existing methods into three directions: (i) graph-aware alignment and regularization objectives, (ii) self-supervised and imbalance-aware learning, and (iii) cross-graph pretraining for transferable multimodal representations. For foundation models, this section focuses on learning objectives and transfer protocols, while their architectural interfaces with large models are discussed in Section 8. Cross-modal alignment encourages consistent representations across modalities, but excessive alignment may suppress modality-specific information. Graph-aware objectives address this trade-off by incorporating structural context into alignment, regularizing consistency with the graph, or explicitly separating shared and private information. Cross-modal contrastive alignment. A common objective aligns different modalities of the same node while contrasting them against other nodes. Let [FORMULA] denote the representation of node [FORMULA] in modality [FORMULA] , [FORMULA] cosine similarity, [FORMULA] a temperature, and [FORMULA] a mini-batch. A standard objective is Applied to raw encoder features, this is CLIP-style alignment without graph context. Graph-aware methods instead align representations that incorporate structural information: LGMRec (Guo et al., 2024) contrasts the visual and textual global hypergraph embeddings of the same user or item, TMTE (Zhu et al., 2026) aligns each modality embedding with the other modalities and with a fused representation smoothed over the evolving topology, and CoMAG (Zhang et al., 2026) uses a matching objective on graph-contextualized modality representations to distinguish matched from mismatched pairs. Structural consistency regularization. Objectives can also encourage modality representations to respect relational structure rather than only matching one another. OptiMAG (Zuo et al., 2026a) introduces a plug-in unbalanced fused Gromov–Wasserstein regularizer that aligns modality-specific semantic geometry with graph distances derived from personalized PageRank. Its relaxed transport constraints reduce the influence of structurally inconsistent correspondences (see also Section 6.4). This approach injects structural consistency through the training loss and can complement existing propagation operators. Shared–private regularization. Forcing complete agreement may remove information unique to individual modalities. One approach decomposes each node representation into a shared consensus [FORMULA] and modality-private residuals [FORMULA] , then discourages their redundancy. CoMAG (Zhang et al., 2026), for example, employs squared cosine similarity: Graph-centric tasks can use the consensus, while modality-centric tasks also incorporate private components. A related role-separation objective appears in SMGFM’s frequency-aware pretraining (Section 7.3). Contrastive clustering. DGF (Zheng et al., 2026) targets node clustering on MAGs. It combines a node-domain graph filter with a feature-domain filter that denoises across feature dimensions, and trains with a tri-cross contrastive objective at the levels of modalities, neighborhoods, and communities. Beyond the task loss, training can exploit multimodal attributes and graph relations to generate self-supervision, or use branch reliability to moderate cross-modal guidance. The latter may still depend on supervised labels and should not be conflated with label-free self-supervised learning. Bootstrapped and graph-guided self-supervision. In multimodal recommendation, BM3 (Zhou et al., 2023) avoids negative samples and graph augmentation: it generates latent views by dropout, treats the dropped view as a stop-gradient target, and jointly optimizes interaction reconstruction with intra- and inter-modality alignment. On MAGs, MLaGA (Fan et al., 2026) pretrains a structure-aware multimodal aligner with a graph contrastive objective that pulls a node’s fused text–image representation toward its sampled neighbors, before the aligned representation is passed to an LLM (Section 8). Reliability-aware negative learning. A distinct challenge is node-level branch imbalance: structural, textual, and visual evidence may differ in reliability across nodes, and conventional cross-branch alignment can propagate incorrect supervision when the dominant branch is unreliable. GraphMNL (Wu et al., 2026a) scores the reliability of each branch per node from prediction confidence, neighborhood consistency, and uncertainty. Instead of requiring weaker branches to imitate the dominant prediction, it uses reliability-controlled negative learning that suppresses unlikely non-target classes while retaining ordinary target supervision. Multimodal graph foundation models (MGFMs) aim to learn representations or prediction mechanisms that are reusable across graph domains and tasks. From the learning-level perspective, they are defined by their cross-graph pretraining objectives and transfer protocols rather than by architectural scale alone. Reconstruction objectives. A common strategy learns transferable representations by reconstructing masked attributes or structural relationships. UniGraph2 (He et al., 2025) encodes nodes with frozen modality-specific encoders, aligns features across modalities and domains through a mixture-of-experts module, and reconstructs masked features with domain-specific decoders and graph structure with a shared shortest-path-distance decoder. PLANET (Liu et al., 2026b) reconstructs each masked modality from its own and from complementary modalities together with observed edges, whereas SMGFM (Wu et al., 2026b) combines masked feature and edge reconstruction with frequency-specific learning objectives. Alignment that preserves modality-specific evidence. Rather than aligning all modalities uniformly, recent MGFMs decide which components to align. PLANET (Liu et al., 2026b) separates local interaction from global alignment: embedding-wise domain gating incorporates complementary neighbor modalities, and node-wise discretization maps modality embeddings into a shared discretized semantic space with text-anchored alignment and quantization objectives. SMGFM (Wu et al., 2026b) decomposes modality-specific signals into graph-frequency bands with Chebyshev filters, aligns low-frequency consensus components, and preserves high-frequency modality-specific evidence with energy- and direction-preserving losses. Transfer protocols and settings. MGFMs also differ in how and where they transfer. CHARM (Yang et al., 2026) targets zero-shot transfer to unseen graphs without target-domain parameter updates, encoding retrieved contexts built from hierarchical semantic anchors and modality-complementary neighbors as graph tokens for a frozen LLM (Section 8.2). FedGAMMA (Li et al., 2026b) extends cross-graph learning to federated clients, combining shared–private semantic enhancement and optimal-transport-based alignment with topology-aware fusion and client-affinity aggregation, followed by prompt-based adaptation. Learning-level methods differ mainly in the supervision they add to the task loss. Alignment and regularization objectives constrain agreement between modalities and with the graph; self-supervised and imbalance-aware objectives construct signals from augmented views, structural relationships, or branch reliability; and pretraining objectives aim at representations that transfer across graphs. A question recurs across all three: which information should be aligned and which modality-specific differences should be preserved. Contrastive objectives push toward agreement, whereas shared–private decompositions, frequency-specific pretraining, and reliability-aware supervision deliberately keep parts of each modality apart, because cross-modal agreement is not always reliable supervision when modality features or graph context are noisy. Explicit learning objectives should be distinguished from architectural alignment through attention or coupled propagation (Section 5.2), even though both may be optimized jointly. Cross-graph pretraining additionally changes the training data and transfer protocol rather than merely adding a loss term. For pretrained models, evaluations should further separate in-domain performance, cross-domain adaptation, and genuine zero-shot transfer, and account for the scope and cost of pretraining. 8 Foundation-Model Level: Bringing Graphs into (M)LLMs Specialization of the unified formulation. Foundation-model-level integration connects multimodal graph structure to pretrained language, vision–language, or generative backbones. In Equation 5, an interface [FORMULA] converts an ego-subgraph [FORMULA] and its multimodal attributes into inputs to a foundation model [FORMULA] , or modifies its computation using graph structure. The principal choices concern (i) how structural information is represented, (ii) whether graph reasoning occurs in a graph-side encoder or within the foundation model, and (iii) how the pretrained backbone is adapted. The tasks also differ: some methods perform graph-centric prediction, mainly node classification and link prediction, whereas others generate the text (G2Text), the image (G2Image), or both for a target node. We first review serialization and graph-aware interfaces, then direct MLLM prediction, and finally graph-conditioned generation. The first three concern model interfaces and prediction; the last concerns a complementary output setting, so these categories are not mutually exclusive. The most direct interface represents graph context as a sequence of node attributes, structural descriptors, and prompts that a pretrained model can consume. Its appeal is compatibility with existing language and multimodal models, but serializing a graph does not by itself preserve all relations among the included nodes. MMGL (Yoon et al., 2023) targets G2Text, namely Wikipedia section summarization, and studies how pretrained language models can use multiple multimodal neighbors beyond one-to-one image–caption pairs. It compares ways to encode neighbors (raw text versus frozen embeddings, self- versus cross-attention), ways to encode the structure among them (sequential or Laplacian positional encodings, GNN embeddings), and parameter-efficient adaptation (prefix tuning, LoRA, Flamingo-style cross-attention). MMGL is thus not restricted to plain attribute concatenation: the central question is how much relational information the language-model interface can retain. GraphGPT-O (Fang et al., 2025) targets joint G2Text and G2Image, generating both the text and the image of a target node. It compares ways to linearize the multimodal neighborhood into an MLLM input, varying which modalities are included, their order, and the number of neighbors. Its results motivate a hierarchical aligner (Section 8.2), and it further compares sequential and parallel generation of interdependent text and images. Both works illustrate the trade-off between the flexibility of prompting and the difficulty of representing irregular neighborhoods in a finite token budget. Rather than serializing all neighbor content, graph-aware interfaces summarize structural context in continuous tokens or incorporate graph relations directly into a foundation model’s attention. Graph-to-token interfaces. MLaGA (Fan et al., 2026) first pretrains a structure-aware multimodal aligner that combines visual and textual attributes through a graph-guided objective. During instruction tuning, a lightweight projector maps the resulting representations into the token space of a frozen LLM, with task-specific demonstrations, for node classification and link prediction. CHARM (Yang et al., 2026) encodes retrieved structural, hierarchical, and modality-complementary context into continuous graph tokens for zero-shot node classification and link prediction on unseen graph domains (Section 7.3). GraphGPT-O (Fang et al., 2025) uses node-level and graph-level Q-Formers that first fuse each neighbor’s text and image tokens and then compress the neighborhood into a fixed set of subgraph tokens. InstructG2I (Jin et al., 2024) uses a Graph-QFormer to produce a compact set of graph prompts for image diffusion in G2Image (Section 8.4). Structure-aware attention. Graph4MM (Ning et al., 2025) follows a different route. Its Hop-Diffused Attention restricts self-attention to graph edges and diffuses it over multiple hops with decaying weights, while an MM-QFormer extracts text-conditioned visual features for the language model. Instead of treating topology as an independent modality appended to the input, this design lets graph structure shape intra- and inter-modal attention. Foundation models can also produce graph-level decisions directly, rather than serving only as feature extractors for a downstream GNN. This includes node classification and link prediction using multimodal node attributes, selected graph context, and task instructions. The model may be prompted, used with in-context examples, or fine-tuned for graph prediction. Roles of foundation models. The GraphVLM benchmark (Liu et al., 2026a) organizes the use of vision–language models on MAGs into three roles: VLM-as-Encoder, which supplies multimodal features to graph learners; VLM-as-Aligner, which bridges modalities in a latent or linguistic space for LLM-based graph reasoning; and VLM-as-Predictor, which uses a VLM as the decision-making backbone. The first two correspond to the feature and learning levels (Sections 4 and 7); the third places task prediction in the foundation model. The simplest predictors fine-tune an off-the-shelf VLM such as LLaVA or Qwen-VL with LoRA for node classification, optionally adding serialized neighbor context to the prompt (Liu et al., 2026a); MAGB additionally evaluates VLMs as zero-shot predictors (Yan et al., 2025). Modality-adaptive prediction. Mario (Sun et al., 2026) targets node classification and link prediction and adapts an LLM predictor to two properties of MAGs: the text and image of a node may be only weakly consistent, and different nodes benefit from different modalities. It first trains a graph-conditioned vision–language model in which a topology-aware mixer lets the summary tokens of sampled nodes attend to one another with shortest-path-distance biases under a text–image contrastive objective. It then instruction-tunes an LLM with a router that selects, for each node, a text-only, image-only, or multimodal prompt view. Most MAG benchmarks emphasize discriminative tasks. Graph-conditioned generation instead uses a node’s multimodal neighborhood to generate missing textual or visual content, including G2Text and G2Image (Section 2.2). We focus on using a given graph to condition content generation, rather than generating graph structures themselves. Problem formulation. OpenMAG standardizes both tasks as downstream probes (Wan et al., 2026); benchmark protocols are discussed in Section 10. When does structure help a foundation model? The GraphVLM benchmark shows that fine-tuned VLM predictors are strong even without structural input and that the benefit of structure depends on graph density and on how structure is supplied (Liu et al., 2026a). This does not make topology unnecessary: the relevant comparison is whether structured context improves predictions beyond the same foundation model given node attributes alone. Meaningful ablations should therefore hold the backbone, node attributes, and training protocol fixed while changing only the structural information supplied. Trade-offs among interfaces. Serializing neighbors keeps their content but lengthens the input: in MMGL, the variant that feeds raw neighbor text performs best but requires much longer inputs (Yoon et al., 2023). Compressing the neighborhood into a fixed number of tokens, as in the hierarchical aligner of GraphGPT-O (Fang et al., 2025), shortens the input, but the relations among neighbors must then be captured by the graph-side encoder. Structure-aware attention keeps these relations explicit by restricting attention to graph edges, at the cost of modifying the backbone’s attention (Ning et al., 2025). Connections across integration levels. Beyond serving directly as predictors and generators, foundation models also enter the other integration levels. At the feature level, MLLMs such as LLaVA and Qwen-VL supply node embeddings to GNNs and raise their performance (Yan et al., 2025) (Section 4). Graph-centric designs remain complementary on top of such embeddings: even with already aligned VLM features (Qwen2-VL, LLaMA-3.2-Vision), ReCoG still yields significant gains (Xue & Wu, 2026) (Section 5.2). At the learning level, multimodal graph foundation models pretrain on frozen foundation-model encoders, and their embeddings can in turn replace CLIP features in generation pipelines (He et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026b) (Section 7.3). 9 Cross-Cutting Issues: Robustness, Efficiency, and Federation The integration of multimodal attributes and graph structure introduces challenges that span all five levels of our taxonomy. We discuss three cross-cutting issues: robustness to incomplete or corrupted information, computational efficiency across different stages of the learning pipeline, and federated learning under distributed multimodal graph data. Missing modalities and cold-start nodes. In practical applications, new nodes may lack certain modalities, graph connections, or both. These cases are particularly challenging because they limit the semantic and structural evidence available for prediction. NTSFormer (Hu et al., 2026) addresses isolated cold-start node classification through a self-teaching Graph Transformer. A cold-start attention mask enables the same model to produce a student prediction using only the target node’s attributes and a teacher prediction using both self and neighborhood information. The teacher guides the student without requiring a separate MLP, while multimodal precomputation and mixture-of-experts input projections accommodate heterogeneous and missing features. In our formulation, missing modalities correspond to [FORMULA] , while isolated nodes satisfy [FORMULA] . Their combination tests whether a model can transfer knowledge from structurally contextualized training nodes to nodes with incomplete information; NTSFormer reports results separately for isolated nodes missing text, missing images, or neither. Noisy modalities and noisy edges. Multimodal graph models may encounter corrupted text, degraded images, unreliable edges, and noisy supervision, which methods at different levels address. At the topology level, the residual refiner of ReCoG weakens unreliable observed edges (Xue & Wu, 2026) (Section 6.2); at the propagation level, RoleMAG assigns neighbors different roles and completes a degraded modality of the target from the stronger modality of its neighbors (Zuo et al., 2026b) (Section 5.2); and at the learning level, GraphMNL avoids propagating supervision from unreliable branches (Wu et al., 2026a) (Section 7.2). These mechanisms can also fail: refinement based on feature similarity may introduce spurious edges when multimodal features are noisy or misaligned (Xue & Wu, 2026). OpenMAG evaluates robustness by injecting modality noise, label noise, and structural sparsity (Wan et al., 2026). Distribution shift. Beyond local corruption, the distribution of one or both modalities may differ between training and test data, for example when products come from different categories or images differ in color or background. OMG-NAS (Cai et al., 2024) addresses this setting through multimodal graph neural architecture search over GNN, fusion, and prediction operators. It learns sample weights that decorrelate unimodal and cross-modal features, reducing reliance on spurious correlations, and reuses the best weights across candidate architectures as a warm start for the search. Feature encoding versus graph learning. The computational cost of MAG learning depends strongly on whether textual and visual encoders are frozen or trained end-to-end. With frozen encoders, feature extraction is performed once and subsequent training operates on cached embeddings. In contrast, updating large text or vision encoders introduces repeated forward and backward passes that may dominate the overall cost. OpenMAG (Wan et al., 2026) supports both static and trainable encoders. Propagation-decoupled pipelines. Decoupled architectures move parameter-free graph propagation into a preprocessing stage and train downstream aggregation modules on precomputed multi-hop representations. This eliminates repeated edge-dependent propagation from the subsequent training epochs, although preprocessing and feature storage still incur costs. CAMPA (Su et al., 2026) systematically analyzes the efficiency of decoupled multimodal GNNs and introduces cross-modal alignment during precomputed propagation and trainable trajectory aggregation. LION (Li et al., 2026d) follows a similar paradigm, using Clifford-based geometric operations to support cross-modal interaction. These methods reduce repeated graph traversal, but their end-to-end efficiency also depends on preprocessing, cached representation size, and aggregation complexity (Table 3). Sparse structure learning. Learning semantic relations between all node pairs requires [FORMULA] affinity storage when the dense matrix is materialized. Scalable approaches restrict the candidate space through sparse KNN graphs (Zhang et al., 2021; Zhou & Shen, 2023), node–anchor approximations (Zhu et al., 2026), or, in ReCoG, target-centric candidates within sampled mini-batches followed by coarse-to-fine selection (Xue & Wu, 2026) (Section 6.2). These approximations reduce computation but may miss useful long-range relations. Foundation-model interfaces. Serializing graph context lengthens the input of an LLM or MLLM, whereas soft-token interfaces (Fan et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026) bound the number of tokens but still require graph sampling and encoding (Section 8.5). Multimodal attributed graphs are often distributed across organizations or platforms that cannot directly share raw text, images, or relational data. Federated multimodal graph learning enables collaborative training under these constraints, but clients may differ simultaneously in modality availability, feature distributions, graph structures, and label spaces. Benchmarking federated MAG learning. MM-OpenFGL (Li et al., 2026a) formalizes multimodal federated graph learning and provides a benchmark comprising 19 datasets across 7 application domains, 8 simulation strategies, 57 implemented methods, and 6 downstream tasks. Its simulated federated settings capture differences in modality availability, label distributions, and topological information, enabling systematic evaluation of multimodal learning under heterogeneous clients. Federated pretraining and alignment. FedGAMMA (Li et al., 2026b) extends multimodal graph foundation learning to federated settings (Section 7.3). It combines shared–private semantic enhancement with optimal-transport-based cross-modal alignment, topology-aware graph fusion, and affinity-aware aggregation across clients. The pretrained model is subsequently adapted through lightweight graph-aware prompts, reducing the need for full model fine-tuning at each client. 10 Benchmarks, Dataset Characteristics, and Evaluation Protocols This section reviews the benchmark platforms published in recent years, their datasets and the metrics used for each task, model-independent dataset descriptors, and the evaluation protocols together with their baselines. Because the platforms differ in datasets, encoders, splits, and baselines, we compare their designs rather than pooling accuracies from incompatible experiments. Table 5 summarizes five representative benchmark platforms. MM-GRAPH. MM-GRAPH (Zhu et al., 2025) provides seven text–image-attributed datasets of varying scale covering node classification (NC), link prediction (LP), and knowledge-graph completion (KGC). It evaluates standardized GNN, multimodal GNN, and multimodal KG baselines under aligned and unaligned feature encoders (CLIP, ImageBind, and T5 with ViT or DINOv2). KGC datasets are listed for completeness, although relational KG algorithms are outside the main scope of this survey. MAGB. MAGB (Yan et al., 2025) curates five graphs spanning Amazon product networks (Movies, Toys, Grocery) and social media (Reddit-S, Reddit-M). It studies GNN-as-Predictor and zero-shot VLM-as-Predictor paradigms, with an emphasis on modality preference and the choice of feature encoder, and finds that textual attributes are more informative in e-commerce graphs and visual attributes in social graphs.
