V Conclusion This paper presents DecompRL, a DRL framework for CAD model decomposition toward hexahedral meshing. Our approach combines topology-aware splitting actions with a meshability term in the reward, allowing the policy to progressively split complex CAD models into simpler sub-blocks that support hexahedral meshing. Experimental results on four public CAD benchmarks show numerically higher decomposition success rates for DecompRL on three datasets, with the largest gain on Fusion360 and more modest differences on ABC and NIST; DDPG achieves a slightly higher rate on DeepCAD. On successfully meshed outputs, DecompRL also maintains competitive hexahedral element quality. Several limitations remain. The design of the action space is important for hexahedral decomposition, and incorporating richer action primitives may further improve the coverage of geometric configurations that can be successfully decomposed. The current action generators are primarily designed for mechanical CAD with recognizable analytic geometric structures and do not include dedicated decomposition primitives for arbitrary free-form NURBS/B-spline regions. Extending candidate generation with curvature-aware patch analysis or feature-line structures is therefore an important direction. Similarly, although the O-grid action is geometrically related to O-block layouts used in CFD, the present method does not model CFD-specific requirements such as boundary-layer growth, wall-normal alignment, or anisotropic spacing; incorporating such constraints would be required for CFD-oriented use. In addition, future work could improve training efficiency, sample efficiency, and convergence stability, especially for deeper decomposition trees and more complex CAD models. These results should not be interpreted as a guarantee of complete, globally conforming hexahedral meshing for arbitrary CAD inputs. Local Map/Submap/Sweep compatibility does not alone establish model-level meshing success. A finite decomposition budget, early splitting decisions that restrict later feasible actions, partial geometric observations, and the limited coverage of the current action templates can all contribute to unresolved or non-meshable regions. Further work will include systematic failure analysis across geometric and topological complexity, validation of local compatibility labels against downstream meshing outcomes, and stronger resolution-aware shared-interface and interval-consistency checks.

Physics-Driven Extraction of Dynamic Fluid Asset from Monocular Video with Generative 3DGS Existing methods for dynamic 3D scene synthesis from video rely on per-frame deformation fields optimized through pixel-level reconstruction losses. While effective for closed systems such as elastic solids, these approaches face challenges with open systems like fluids where material continuously enters and exits the scene, topology changes freely, and no stable point correspondence exists across frames. We propose a simulation-driven alternative that optimizes the parameters of a fluid simulator to reproduce dynamics observed in a single-view video, rather than fitting per-point deformation to pixel values. Our framework leverages generative 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) models to obtain initial fluid geometry including unseen surfaces, estimates a physically grounded velocity field from surface motions with a physics-constraint correction algorithm, and converts it into a divergence-free, grid-based representation. A differentiable Affine Particle-In-Cell (APIC) simulation then optimizes effective simulation parameters, such as viscosity, boundary conditions, and inflow/outflow velocities, to match the observed dynamics. Because the dynamics are governed by forward simulation, the output assets are inherently editable, interactive, and temporally extendable, which reconstruction-based approaches cannot readily provide. Stage-wise ablations confirm that each stage is necessary, and hyperparameter sweeps show the pipeline to be robust without sensitive per-scene tuning. Our method handles various liquid fluids, including inviscid and viscous types, demonstrating the potential for automatically creating simulation-ready 3D fluid assets from readily available internet videos. I Introduction Combining 3D generation with editing, animation, and simulation is reshaping digital content creation. Coupling generation with physics-based dynamics is hardest for fluids: most existing work targets rigid bodies and viscoelastic materials, whose outcomes are more stable and predictable, yet demand for fluid assets remains high, since creating them by hand is labor-intensive given the intricacy of fluid dynamics and the precision required of simulation parameters. A natural question arises: can we extract simulation-ready 3D fluid assets directly from casually captured videos? Recent advances in dynamic 3D reconstruction offer a tempting starting point, but these methods are generally designed for a different class of problems. Dynamic Gaussian Splatting methods learn per-frame deformation fields by minimizing pixel-level reconstruction losses. This paradigm works well for closed deformable systems such as elastic bodies where each material point persists throughout the sequence and per-vertex tracking is meaningful. However, fluids are open systems: material continuously enters and exits the scene through inflow and outflow, topology changes freely, and no stable point correspondence exists across frames. To apply pixel-level reconstruction to fluids, one would need to track material that does not persist in the scene. And even if per-pixel fitting succeeds for the training camera, the resulting model may not generalize. The deformation field explains the observed view but is not constrained to produce physically correct 3D motion from other angles. Downstream capabilities crucial for asset creation (e.g., changing viewing directions, adding interactions, and extending motion duration) will benefit from the underlying dynamics being physically grounded, beyond visual plausibility alone. Meanwhile, recent work has embedded physics simulators into reconstructed Gaussians for forward animation, and has recovered fluid dynamics from visual observation through differentiable rendering and learned dynamics models. Section II discusses these and their relation to our work. Content creators seek fluid assets that are not only visually plausible but also editable, interactive, and integrable into existing 3D scenes. Based on these considerations and insights, we formulate the problem as physical parameter optimization. Rather than fitting a deformation field to minimize photometric error, we seek the simulation parameters of a physics-based fluid solver that, when executed as a forward simulation, reproduce the dynamics observed in the input video. The output is not a fixed per-frame deformation but a resimulatable physical model, together with an initial appearance estimation, that naturally supports novel-view rendering, interaction, temporal extension, and intuitive parameter editing. Concretely, we approximate the fluid geometry with 3D Gaussians (3DGS) obtained through generative methods and ensure geometry consistency across frames. The volumetric velocity field is then estimated from the generated 3D geometry and the motion present in the video, leveraging optical flow corrected by a physics-derived constraint. Building on the APIC method [1], a hybrid Eulerian-Lagrangian scheme that conserves both linear and angular momentum, we design a differentiable framework to optimize the simulation parameters, including viscosity, boundary conditions, and inflow/outflow velocities, to best recover the dynamics from the video. Our experiments show that the proposed method produces high-quality results for fluids with convectional flow motion. Comparisons demonstrate the necessity and efficacy of the physics-based optimization: reconstructing precise geometry but manually specifying simulation parameters produces notably less accurate results that diverge over time, suggesting that inferring the dynamics from observation is both necessary and beneficial. This prioritizes physical dynamics over pixel-level appearance, a deliberate choice rooted in the nature of the problem. Per-pixel reconstruction can achieve high image similarity, but it is pseudo-physical and guarantees neither generalization to novel views nor downstream editability. For viscous fluids, which flow steadily and change topology little, tracking remains feasible, and our method recovers an appearance closely resembling the video. For inviscid fluids with high boundary flux, such as flowing rivers, material enters and leaves too rapidly for strict tracking. Since surface texture at any moment is a consequence of the underlying velocity field, recovering the dynamics is more informative than fitting the appearance. The recovered velocity field and simulation parameters yield spatially and temporally coherent 3D fluids matching the video dynamics, exposed through intuitive quantities (viscosity, gravity, boundary coefficients) that are straightforward to tune. The extracted assets are compatible with standard graphics engines such as Blender and Unreal Engine, enabling integration into game development and virtual production pipelines. The main contributions can be summarized as follows: We propose a novel framework that formulates 3D fluid asset extraction from single-view videos as a physical parameter optimization problem, providing simulation-ready outputs with inherent editability, interactivity, and temporal extendability. We design fluid-customized shape and motion estimation strategies to produce coherent geometry and physically grounded velocity fields, including a mainstream correction algorithm with 2D-divergence constraints derived from the incompressibility condition. We realize a differentiable grid velocity evolution procedure building upon the APIC method to optimize simulation parameters, compatible with general grid-based or hybrid simulation methods. II Related Work 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [2] adopts a point-based radiance field, using 3D Gaussian primitives to represent scenes. It has emerged as a prevalent research topic in 3D representation [3, 4, 5, 6, 7] due to its ability to depict high-quality geometry and textures in novel view synthesis. 3DGS provides a new perspective not only for real-time scene reconstruction but also for 3D generation. DreamGaussian [8] optimizes a 3DGS through score distillation using a pre-trained text-to-image diffusion model. Recent methods [9, 10, 11] investigate directly training diffusion models on Gaussian splats for higher efficiency. However, the direct methods may struggle to handle real-world inputs, like fluid objects, since they are usually trained on synthetic 3D datasets. LGM [12] transforms the single-view generation problem into a multi-view 3DGS reconstruction task using a pre-trained single-view to multi-view 2D diffusion model. The most recent transformer-based methods [13, 14] are proposed to achieve faster generation with higher quality. TriplaneGaussian [13] creates a point cloud from a single image and uses hybrid triplane-Gaussian representation to greatly accelerate the generation. TRELLIS [14] employs rectified flow transformers unifying structured latent to get high-quality results. We use such model as an upstream component, taking the initial 3D geometry with appearance from it and embedding physical dynamics through our simulation-based pipeline. The neural radiance expression of objects with dynamics has long been studied for NeRF [15] systems, including deformation capture by canonical and displacement fields [16, 17] and dynamic 3D synthesis [18, 19, 20, 21, 22]. Similarly, for the later proposed 3D Gaussian Splatting, dynamics properties have been imposed on the explicit radiance representation of Gaussians. Leveraging the high fitting ability of Gaussian particles, many studies have explored dynamic scene reconstruction guided by image-based losses from video [23, 24, 25, 26, 27, 28]. These methods learn per-frame deformation fields, typically parameterized by MLPs or decomposed neural encodings, that warp a canonical Gaussian representation to match each observed frame, optimized through photometric reconstruction losses. This paradigm has achieved impressive results for general dynamic scenes, particularly for objects that maintain stable topology and persistent material identity across time (e.g., deforming elastic bodies, articulated objects, or faces). However, applying these methods to fluid dynamics poses fundamental challenges. In fluids, material identity is transient and topology changes freely through splashing, merging, and fragmentation [29, 30], so the per-Gaussian assumption of a persistent identity does not hold. The same difficulty is acknowledged for NeRF-based deformation fields [17]. Moreover, deformation fields optimized solely through photometric losses may satisfy the visual objective without respecting incompressibility or momentum conservation [31, 32]. They therefore suffice for view interpolation within the observed sequence, but do not guarantee physically consistent dynamics from novel viewpoints, and extending the motion or introducing interactions remains difficult. These observations reflect a difference in problem setting rather than a shortcoming of these methods, which target general dynamic scene reconstruction with faithful visual reproduction as the objective. Ours is a complementary setting whose downstream goal, an editable and simulation-ready fluid asset, places different demands on the representation. In physics-based simulation, fluids are governed by the Navier-Stokes equations and often simulated using Eulerian grids and/or Lagrangian particles [29], with different considerations of viscosity [33, 34]. Numerical discretization schemes have also advanced these computations a lot [35, 36]. For simulation stability, Stam [37] introduces the concept of semi-Lagrangian advection, which brings up the idea of hybrid methods. Hybrid methods [38, 39, 1, 40, 41, 42] combine advantages of Lagrangian and Eulerian schemes, representing fluid by particles while computing dynamics on grids. Among these, the Affine Particle-In-Cell (APIC) method [1] is notable for its conservation of both linear and angular momentum through the affine velocity transfer, which we adopt in our framework for its suitability to fluid dynamics. Recent works have begun integrating physics-based simulation with 3D Gaussian representations, demonstrating the value of combining physical correctness with the rendering efficiency of 3DGS. PhysGaussian [43] pioneered this direction by integrating the Material Point Method (MPM) framework with reconstructed 3DGS, enabling versatile dynamic behaviors for elastic, viscoplastic, and granular materials. GaussianSplashing [44] combines Position-Based Dynamics (PBD) with advanced Gaussian rendering, achieving real-time fluid-solid interaction synthesis with natural fluid appearances. PhysMotion [45] proposes a framework for animating 3DGS generated from a single-view image using differentiable MPM, with sequential rendering results composited through an inversion and diffusion process. RainyGS [46] and FieryGS [47] extend the approach to rain and fire in captured scenes. These works demonstrate the effectiveness of embedding physics into Gaussian representations for producing physically consistent, interactive animations. These works operate in a forward simulation setting where the physical parameters (material properties, forces, boundary conditions) are specified by the user. While this offers full creative control, for an artist who wants to reproduce the specific dynamics observed in a reference video, manually tuning the high-dimensional parameter space through trial and error can be challenging. A complementary direction seeks to infer physical parameters or dynamics from visual observation. Simplicits [48] uses a neural field of learnable weights for reduced-order simulation. PhysDreamer [49] optimizes material parameters through a differentiable MPM simulation to reproduce dynamic Gaussians that behave similarly to input videos, providing an inspiring example of physics-based inverse optimization, though its formulation is designed for elastic solids rather than fluids. BAGS [50] learns the weights of imposed Gaussian Ellipsoid Neural Bounds to animate reconstructed objects according to input videos. Hong et al. [51] treat each Gaussian as a material point and fit time-varying constitutive parameters under optical-flow supervision. In our work, we build upon the idea of physics-based inverse optimization and extend it to the fluid domain. We embed generated Gaussians in physics compatible with the APIC method and design a differentiable pipeline to optimize the simulation parameters to best recover the observed fluid dynamics from video. Recovering fluid velocity fields from visual observation is a long-standing challenge. Optical flow [52] can effectively capture pixel-level motion and has been utilized in neural reconstructions [53, 54] for general dynamic scenes. Targeting specific fluid textures can noticeably improve learning of dynamics and re-simulation accuracy [55, 56]. Generally, multi-view inputs are required for 3D velocity reconstruction, and novel-view fluid synthesis typically relies on at least sparse viewpoints for neural networks to infer the unseen sides [57, 58, 59]. Consequently, previous work has seldom focused on reconstructing the complete velocity field from a single view. Several works have explored incorporating physics priors into fluid dynamics recovery. DVP [60] successfully encodes vortex features to learn the specific eddy dynamics of fluid, leveraging the divergence-free property inherent in vortex representations, though it is restricted to 2D profiles. Other works [61, 31, 62] extend to 3D space with strict physical constraints and volume rendering, achieving high-fidelity reconstruction of certain fluid types. NeuroFluid [55] jointly learns a particle transition model and a particle-driven neural renderer from multi-view video, pioneering the unsupervised learning of particle-based fluid dynamics from visual observation. Liu et al. [56] integrate a differentiable Euler simulator with volumetric rendering for inverse fluid inference, using a learned pressure solver to enable end-to-end optimization. More recently, FluidNexus [63] addresses 3D fluid reconstruction and prediction from a single video. It employs a novel-view video synthesizer to generate multi-view supervision and optimizes a particle representation using Position-Based Fluids (PBF) constraints within an image-driven optimization loop. This approach achieves compelling results for gaseous flows (e.g., smoke) and demonstrates interactive capabilities, representing a thoughtful integration of physical priors with visual reconstruction. Our work shares the high-level goal of recovering 3D fluid dynamics from a single-view video, but differs significantly in the target fluid type and the role of the simulation. We focus on liquids (both inviscid and viscous). Unlike gaseous flows, liquids exhibit free-surface dynamics, boundary-layer effects, and terrain interactions. Rather than using a physics simulator as a soft constraint within an image-driven optimization, we treat forward APIC simulation as the primary driver and extract its parameters directly from the video. Consequently, our output is inherently a complete simulation rather than a fitted deformation field. Our approach uses generative 3DGS models for geometry estimation and solves for surface motions to initialize velocity. This offers a different trade-off compared to multi-view video diffusion, which typically incurs higher inference costs in memory and time and is harder to control. We view these as complementary approaches, and address the gap between them by estimating the physical parameters of a liquid simulator from a single-view video. III Method Our method takes a single-view video of fluid as input and outputs a simulation-ready 3D asset, consisting of optimized geometry, initial appearance, physical parameters, and boundary conditions that can be re-simulated, edited, and temporally extended. The pipeline (Fig. 2) comprises four stages: 1: 3D Fluid Geometry Estimation (Sec. III-C). We employ image-to-3DGS generative models to obtain an initial 3D Gaussian representation from the input frame. The generated Gaussians are denoised, volumetrically densified, and unified across selected frames to ensure geometric consistency. A single-view appearance optimization then refines resolution and fidelity on the settled point cloud. 2: Surface Motion Vector Estimation (Sec. III-D). We estimate 2D screen-space motion from inter-frame optical flow, addressing its inherent limitations (e.g., the failure in homogeneous-texture regions) through a mainstream correction strategy and a projective physical constraint derived from 3D incompressibility. The corrected 2D motion vectors are then inversely mapped onto 3D surfaces via the camera. 3: Volumetric Velocity Field Construction (Sec. III-E). With surface motions providing the outer boundary condition, we estimate the near-wall velocity profile using boundary-layer functions from computational fluid dynamics. The complete volumetric velocity field is then solved via a constrained projection method that enforces divergence-free flow throughout the domain. 4: Differentiable Parameter Optimization (Sec. III-F). We transfer the velocity field to a grid-based representation compatible with the APIC scheme. A differentiable grid velocity evolution, with a PeRCNN-based pressure solver for efficient backpropagation, enables gradient-based optimization of the simulation parameters to match the observed dynamics. Since the input consists of a single-view video, we rely on generative image-to-3DGS models [13, 14, 12] to obtain 3D geometry. The choice of generative model is modular. Our pipeline is compatible with different generators and benefits from their continued improvements. We use TriplaneGS [13] by default as it best retains the geometry and appearance from inputs like scenic clips, and also demonstrate results with TRELLIS [14]. However, generative models are typically trained on surface-dominated 3D datasets, producing sparse Gaussians concentrated on visible surfaces. For fluid simulation, we require dense, volumetrically filled geometry with consistent structure across frames. We first finalize the geometry through denoising, densification, and cross-frame union, then optimize the appearance on the resulting point cloud so that both geometry and appearance are settled before motion estimation begins. The generated Gaussians are first denoised by pruning primitives with low opacity or heavily stretched covariance. As shown in Fig. 3, we then locate the 3DGS bounding volume into a regular grid and insert a Gaussian at each interior cell by Jittered sampling. The interior check is determined by an odd-intersection ray-casting test against the outer hull of the existing Gaussians. Generative models do not guarantee geometric consistency across frames: adjacent frames may produce substantially different backside geometries despite similar foreground conditioning. For flowing liquids on fixed terrain, this inconsistency impairs the construction of physically grounded velocity fields. We address this by performing a union operation on the generated Gaussians within a frame window of size [FORMULA] , forming a geometrically consistent batch for subsequent steps. This operation primarily processes the backside geometry (riverbed, terrain beneath the fluid) and the silhouette edges (e.g., river banks), where generative predictions vary most across frames. At the silhouette, some frames may exhibit splashing or overflow beyond the bank. The union retains these particles, but they carry no velocity in other frames and thus do not affect downstream simulation. The camera-facing fluid surface is not altered by the union, preserving natural surface variation. V Conclusions We have presented a physics-driven framework for extracting simulation-ready 3D fluid assets from single-view videos. Across four stages it recovers the geometry, the surface motion, a volumetric velocity field and a compact set of explicit simulation parameters, keeping appearance separate from dynamics and is not lost to fluid’s topological change. A fluid is an open system with no stable point correspondence, so what can be recovered and stays useful afterwards is a grid-based field with the parameters that govern it rather than a per-frame fit. The resulting asset can be re-simulated, edited, interacted with and extended in time while staying consistent under novel views. Results on captured and synthetic scenes, different 3DGS generators and a stage-wise ablation of the extraction chain support the approach. Our pipeline is staged rather than end-to-end, so each stage rests on the one before. Thus, it is stage-wise improvable, as a component can be strengthened without disturbing the others. Several of these dependencies proved mild in practice. For instance, occlusion in input video can be tolerated wherever the generator places fluid behind the occluder, nonideal backside geometry is absorbed by optimizing the boundary conditions except at intermediate depths, and later the velocity construction responds to previous stages robustly with plateaus rather than sharp changes (Sec. IV-B). Two are harder to work around. Large camera motion is not currently supported, though 3D registration and ego-motion compensation would address it. Where no motion is measurable at all, mainstream interpolation has nothing to extend, but a scene with no visible motion also reduces how wrong the result can look. Two limits are more fundamental. Splashing and foam involve air entrainment beyond a single-phase grid, and would need finer resolution together with a volume-of-fluid treatment of the interface, much as some fluids would need temperature coupled to density and viscosity. At our resolution the large-eddy structure is recovered while subgrid detail is not, and refining it is costly as simulation and pressure solve scale with cell count. Appearance is likewise less reliable than motion. Reflective and transparent fluids offer little texture to track, and since the fluid is open and largely interior, new and newly exposed particles carry no observed color, making a uniform texture the practical choice. Generic learned estimators did not help, their training data containing almost no fluid, so a domain-specific model is the component to replace. Future work will explore adaptive grid refinement and multi-resolution strategies to capture fine-scale dynamics without proportionally increasing cost. Longer videos deepen the computation graph and rarely show the scene as a whole, so they would need segment-wise optimization with 3D alignment. Extending the framework to gaseous fluids and to learned appearance models for dynamic surface texture are also promising directions. I Introduction Landslides are widespread natural disasters that threaten human lives, infrastructure, and ecosystems, causing substantial economic losses and environmental damage worldwide [1, 2, 3]. Rapid and precise landslide detection is critical for effective disaster monitoring, risk assessment, and emergency response [4, 5, 6]. Recent advances in deep learning have driven landslide detection from convolutional neural network (CNN)-based methods toward Transformer-based architectures [7, 8, 9]. This shift reflects the broader evolution from local feature extraction to long-range dependencies and global context modeling. However, existing methods typically address isolated tasks that focus exclusively on visual perception, such as classification or segmentation. Consequently, they fail to perform higher-order analytical reasoning or incorporate broader domain knowledge into the analysis of landslide dynamics. With the rapid development of large-scale models, new paradigms have emerged to address the aforementioned challenges. In particular, recent advances in large language models (LLMs), vision-language models (VLMs), and vision foundation models (VFMs) have attracted increasing attention from the Earth observation community [10, 11, 12, 13]. To support diverse downstream tasks within unified frameworks and enhance the reasoning capabilities of RS systems, a growing number of foundation models (FMs) have been developed, such as Fleximo [14] and SpectralGPT [11]. However, most existing FMs are designed for general-purpose remote sensing (RS) applications, while their potential for specialized disaster-related tasks, such as landslide detection, remains underexplored. Consequently, despite their strong performance and generalization capabilities across broad RS tasks, these models still exhibit notable limitations in landslide scenarios, particularly in achieving precise detection and sophisticated high-level reasoning. To address these challenges and bridge this research gap, we propose LandslideFM, the first one-for-all foundation model tailored to landslide applications. As illustrated in Fig. 1, LandslideFM unifies multiple downstream tasks within a single framework, enabling comprehensive landslide intelligent analysis. It employs a novel source-agreement graduated trust (SAGT) semi-supervised learning framework to pre-train a generalizable backbone using large-scale unlabeled landslide data. The backbone can be efficiently adapted to diverse downstream tasks, including landslide classification, detection, and segmentation. We further introduce a novel approach for integrating a VLM into LandslideFM and fine-tuning it to enhance the model’s capability for landslide understanding and analysis. Beyond detecting landslides, LandslideFM can recognize their environmental context, identify nearby infrastructure, and assess potential impacts. Furthermore, to address the lack of datasets supporting image–text intelligent analysis of landslides, we introduce LandslideVL, the first manually annotated landslide dataset to combine images, structured text, and detailed textual descriptions, with all data manually annotated and verified. The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows. We propose LandslideFM, the first unified foundation model for landslides, which performs multiple downstream tasks and intelligent analysis to fill the domain’s gap for a general-purpose model. We present SAGT, a semi-supervised framework that pretrains a generalizable backbone on large-scale landslide data, and further advances the landslide analysis from perception to understanding via VLM fine-tuning. We introduce LandslideVL, the first benchmark for VLM-based landslide analysis, which integrates visual imagery, structured text, and detailed descriptions to support multimodal vision-language understanding. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superior performance of LandslideFM over existing methods across a wide range of visual downstream tasks, as well as its capability to perform comprehensive and intelligent landslide analysis. The rest of this article is organized as follows: Section II reviews the related work. In Section III, we formally propose and analyze our LandslideFM model. Section V reports the experimental results, including comparisons with state-of-the-art methods and ablation studies. Finally, Section VI concludes the article and discusses future directions. II related work This section reviews relevant research on classical landslide detection, summarizes recent progress in FMs in RS, and analyzes the great potential of FMs for landslide detection. Landslides are widespread hazards that can cause catastrophic damage to settlements and infrastructure [15]. Recently, deep learning has been extensively applied to rapid landslide perception, including detection, classification, and segmentation, with models evolving from CNNs to Transformer-based architectures [16]. For example, Chen et al. [16] proposed MSIDNet, a multiscale Swin Transformer network for InSAR-based slow-moving landslide detection, addressing key challenges in multiscale feature extraction and fusion. Tang et al.[17] proposed SegMamba2D, a landslide detection model which adopts an encoder–decoder architecture. The model utilizes the Mamba network to extract multiscale features and employs the state space model (SSM) to reduce computational complexity while maintaining detection accuracy. Yang et al. [18] proposed an automatic change detection method for fine coseismic landslide mapping in vegetated areas. It integrates ensemble learning with logical and spectral features from tri-temporal remote sensing images to enable automated mapping. Li et al. [19] proposed PF-SAM, a prompt-free, parameter-efficient adaptive framework for landslide segmentation that overcomes the manual prompt dependency of traditional methods. However, existing landslide models are generally limited to specific visual tasks like classification, detection, and segmentation. Although these models can identify landslides, they cannot perform an in-depth analysis and interpret the characteristics of landslides. Foundation models (FMs) are deep learning architectures that serve as foundational backbones for diverse downstream tasks [20, 21, 22]. By learning general representations from large-scale datasets, FMs can be efficiently fine-tuned for specific applications [23, 24, 25]. Numerous FMs have been developed across diverse domains, predominantly adopting the Vision Transformer as their architecture [26, 27, 28, 29, 30]. FMs in the remote sensing (RS) domain are generally smaller than those in the general computer vision areas, placing greater emphasis on domain-specific pretraining [31, 32, 33]. To overcome high annotation costs and exploit vast amounts of unlabeled data, most RS FMs rely on self-supervised learning paradigms such as masked autoencoders (MAE) [34]. For example, SpectralGPT [11] represents a significant architectural scale-up over S2MAE and pushes this paradigm further through a 3D generative pretrained transformer (3D GPT) framework. Alliance[35] adopts a MAE-style masked image modeling framework for self-supervised pretraining, while further incorporating spectral-spatial-frequency joint modeling to enhance representation learning. SkySense++[36] adopts a factorized architecture to accommodate multi-modal images acquired from diverse sensors. It employs a two-stage progressive pretraining strategy on meticulously curated datasets containing 27 million multi-modal RS images, achieving strong generalization capability. Yu et al.[10] proposed a generative foundation model, MetaEarth, which scales image generation to a global level, exploring the creation of worldwide, multi-resolution, unbounded, and virtually limitless RS images. Despite the rapid success of FMs in Earth observation and RS, their use in monitoring and preventing disasters such as landslides remains largely unexplored. Due to the complex environments of landslide-prone areas and the scarcity of high-quality annotations, intelligent FMs with strong generalization and multi-task capability remain in critically short supply. To address this gap, we introduce FMs to landslide analysis for the first time, establishing a novel baseline for multiple vision tasks and semantic interpretation. IV Landslide Analysis Benchmark: LandslideVL Existing landslide datasets focus primarily on computer vision tasks like semantic segmentation and lack textual annotations. Consequently, they are ill-suited for directly training intelligent landslide analysis models. We address this gap by building LandslideVL, a vision-language dataset for landslide analysis, which is curated and textually annotated representative remote sensing images from multiple existing landslide datasets. The detailed construction pipeline is presented below. The landslide datasets selected in this study include Bijie Landslide (BJL) dataset [40], Global Very High Resolution Landslide Mapping (GVLM) dataset [41], and Jiuzhai valley landslide dataset [42]. The BJL dataset provides annotated optical satellite imagery from Bijie, Guizhou, a high-risk landslide region in China. It consists of 770 landslide and 2,003 non-landslide images. The GVLM dataset is the first large-scale, open-source, ultra-high-resolution (0.59 meters) landslide mapping dataset. It consists of 17 landslide sub-datasets from various geographic regions, each containing a pair of bi-temporal images and the corresponding landslide masks. The dataset covers a total area of 163.77 square kilometers and spans regions across Asia, Africa, North America, South America, Europe, and Oceania. To accommodate GPU memory constraints, we cropped these images to [FORMULA] pixels, obtaining 1,986 patches. The Jiuzhai Valley landslide dataset is a high-quality landslide subset of the CAS Landslide Dataset[42]. It consists of high-resolution RGB imagery acquired by unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in the Jiuzhai Valley region and contains 1,752 high-resolution landslide images. We then merged high-quality samples from these aforementioned processed datasets, including landslide images and easily confusable non-landslide images. From these samples, we selected 4,660 representative instances and supplemented them with textual annotations. The detailed information of the selected datasets can be found in Table I, including geographic locations, acquisition dates, and spatial resolutions. As shown in Fig. 3, the structured textual annotations in LandslideVL include landslide_exists, has_building, has_road, has_water, has_vegetation. The selection of these five binary scene attributes aims to provide a concise, yet comprehensive description of landslide scenes, covering three complementary aspects: landslide occurrence, anthropogenic factors, and surrounding environmental context. Specifically, landslide_exists serves as the fundamental indicator to determine the presence of a landslide and provides the primary semantic information for the recognition of landslides. has_building describes important man-made structures located within or near the affected area. Since many landslides occur in remote or undeveloped regions where large human-made structures are absent, roads may represent the primary infrastructure exposed to landslide impacts. Landslides can block or damage roads, making has_road an important attribute to characterize potential infrastructure disruption. Water bodies are also important contextual features and has_water is used to identify the presence of rivers or other water bodies within or near the landslide area. Vegetation, in turn, provides useful information on land cover and slope-surface conditions. Changes or disturbances in vegetation may also serve as observable indicators associated with slope instability or landslide activity. In addition, each image is accompanied by a detailed textual description. Notably, all data in LandslideVL have been manually annotated and calibrated over multiple rounds by paid human annotators, rather than automatically annotated by AI. Our LandslideVL dataset will be publicly available on Hugging Face and can be freely downloaded for further research https://huggingface.co/datasets/fluorites/LandslideVL. VI Conclusion Our study addresses the challenge of unifying visual understanding and intelligent analysis for landslide detection through the proposed LandslideFM. LandslideFM employs SAGT-based semi-supervised pretraining to develop a powerful, unified visual backbone for multiple downstream vision tasks and to provide visual support for intelligent landslide analysis. Furthermore, we introduce LandslideVL, the first benchmark for intelligent landslide analysis, designed to support the training and fine-tuning of VLMs. Compared with other SOTA methods, our model achieves superior performance across multiple visual tasks and, unlike most previous methods, demonstrates strong intelligent analysis capabilities. Specifically, our model significantly outperforms several state-of-the-art general-purpose vision-language models, including Qwen3-VL and Kimi-VL-A3B, on the LandslideVL benchmark. Nevertheless, as the first foundation model to unify visual understanding and intelligent analysis for landslides, LandslideFM still faces several challenges. For instance, the potential of integrating large AI models with complex spectral imaging for landslide analysis within a unified framework remains largely unexplored. Future work will investigate how large AI models can be effectively used to address the challenges associated with complex spectral imaging. Finally, as the first study to introduce both a foundation model and a dedicated benchmark for landslide analysis, we hope that LandslideFM and LandslideVL will serve as valuable resources and help advance future research in this emerging field.

This raises a fundamental interpretability question beyond behavioral evaluation: when an LLM reproduces psychometric structure in its output, does it reflect internal representations of psychological constructs, or merely generate similar patterns from surface-level statistical associations? A model that emulates without internal representation is a convincing imitator, not a system that “has” the structure in any meaningful sense. The same ambiguity arises in LLM interpretability regarding whether next-token predictors develop world models of domains they reason about (Li et al., 2023a; Nanda et al., 2023), and makes the psychometric case particularly tractable: psychology supplies a rich, quantitative reference in the [FORMULA] human subscale correlation matrix. Here the reference comes from one Taiwanese student sample assessed in Traditional Chinese. We design a cross-persona paradigm to probe this question: a subject’s responses on one psychological scale are placed in the LLM prompt, and the model is asked to complete items from a different, unseen scale. This paradigm has two properties that make it well-suited for probing internal representation. First, by anchoring the model to a specific human subject’s response pattern rather than eliciting generic self-report, it asks the model to perform cross-construct inference on a per-subject basis, generating a subject-by-construct response matrix directly comparable to the human ground truth. Second, by rotating which scale serves as the persona, cross-scale relationships are evaluated in both directions, yielding a bidirectional 16 [FORMULA] 16 correlation matrix that characterizes the between-construct structure rather than a one-way projection from a single anchor scale (e.g., Big Five used as fixed input in Liu et al. 2026). Behaviorally, across 14 model variants from two families (Llama 3 and Qwen 2.5, 0.5B–14B, base and instruct) and [FORMULA] participants, LLMs reproduce and systematically amplify human cross-scale correlations, with amplification persisting after correcting for measurement attenuation (§3). We examine this amplification in model internals using contrastive direction extraction, activation probing, and steering, asking whether (a) psychometric structure is encoded in mid-layer representations, (b) amplification varies across model depths, and (c) representational strength is associated with behavior across models. We distinguish three levels of evidence: a probe can show that cross-scale information is linearly decodable from activations; contrastive directions can show that construct similarities are organized like the human reference; and steering tests whether changing a direction affects responses. The first two analyses do not, by themselves, establish that these directions mediate the model’s answers to the cross-persona task; our steering experiments are exploratory. Closest to our work, Liu et al. (2026) prompted LLMs with Big Five responses to predict nine other scales, reporting strong alignment and systematic amplification, which they attribute to noise filtering (we revisit this account in §7). Related work examines LLM personality profiles (Serapio-García et al., 2023; Sorokovikova et al., 2024), psychometric benchmarks (Li et al., 2024; Samuel et al., 2025), response biases (Tjuatja et al., 2024), and the validity of applying psychological instruments to LLMs (Pellert et al., 2024; Dong et al., 2025). We extend this line of work by moving from behavioral characterization to a representation-level account. Linear probing and contrastive methods identify interpretable directions in LLM activation space corresponding to concepts such as truthfulness (Marks and Tegmark, 2024; Burns et al., 2023; Li et al., 2023b), spatial and temporal structure (Gurnee and Tegmark, 2024), linear features more generally (Park et al., 2024b; Elhage et al., 2022), world models in trained sequence models (Li et al., 2023a; Nanda et al., 2023), and persona traits (Chen et al., 2025; Zou et al., 2023). Activation Addition and Contrastive Activation Addition demonstrate that adding vectors along these directions causally steers model behavior (Turner et al., 2024; Zou et al., 2023). We adapt these methods to psychometric constructs, using contrastive direction extraction and activation steering to probe how psychological traits are represented and processed. Recent studies have also used probes and interventions to study affect, personality, and moral concepts in LLMs (Keeman, 2026; Dan et al., 2026; Yu et al., 2026; Schacht and Lanquillon, 2025). More broadly, psychometric structure provides a quantitative and population-grounded testbed for examining how structured representations emerge in LLMs. These findings raise a further question: why does instruction tuning align representations with human personality structure, despite not explicitly targeting such constructs? One possibility is incidental trait alignment. Signals related to human preference and role consistency, which are abundant in instruction-tuning data, may organize latent personality-relevant representations already present in the base model into directions that happen to align with human trait structure. Under this view, structured trait representations may emerge without explicit supervision, as a byproduct of optimization toward other objectives. This possibility remains untested here. Our human data are drawn from a single cultural sample (Taiwanese college students assessed in Traditional Chinese). Generalization to other populations or languages requires matched human samples; translating model prompts alone would not provide that comparison. An exploratory post-hoc analysis (App E) suggests that culturally specific subscales exhibit stronger amplification, although this effect is driven largely by a small number of subscale pairs and requires replication. Importantly, amplification is not confined to culturally specific constructs: within culturally stable subscales alone, [FORMULA] B instruct models still exhibit slopes above [FORMULA] . This analysis is not a cross-cultural replication. The 14 variants also come from two model families, and variants within a family are not independent training replications. Contrastive direction reliability is limited in smaller models, constraining interpretation of near-zero geometry results. Steering was exploratory and did not test mediation in the cross-persona task. Finally, the SNR proxy is imperfect, and adjusted slope magnitudes should be interpreted as approximate. These measurements may help evaluate how LLMs simulate psychological response patterns. Psychometric profiling could also be misused or applied to individuals without consent; this study evaluates predictions conditioned on participants’ supplied questionnaire responses and does not validate individual-level assessment in deployment. AI Governance Should Prioritize Control and Knowledge Boundaries Over Limiting Intelligence The rapid proliferation of autonomously acting AI agents makes the governance of agentic systems urgent. We propose the competence circuit, summarized as IKC + KC + C, that decomposes an agent’s real-world impact into three pathways: intelligence-mediated discovery, procedural know-how, and direct control. Using the canonical fast-takeoff debate as a stress test, we formalize the conditions for intelligence-mediated fast takeoff as a conjunction jointly sufficient for fast catastrophic supremacy, showing that most rely on rapid knowledge acquisition or control attainment rather than intelligence alone. We operationalize epistemic intelligence as hypothesis-selection efficiency and validate this framework via stochastic simulation on NK fitness landscapes across six scenarios spanning the conjunctive chain. An analytic bound supported by the simulations shows that intelligence-driven speedup is capped by the ratio of competing intelligence levels regardless of task difficulty. The simulations also expose a fast-takeoff dilemma: a large intelligence-driven speedup multiplier materializes only when the hypothesis space is noisy, but the absolute timescale remains constrained by the time required for capability-critical tests, so a large multiplier need not imply rapid progress. Simulations also indicate that institutional chokepoints disproportionately slow down superintelligent agents when mandatory authorization delays are large relative to the negligible time these agents spend on unproductive search. We argue that the dominant safety levers are restricting control and enforcing knowledge boundaries rather than limiting intelligence alone, and this applies to agentic systems at any capability level. Purely digital domains weaken these bottlenecks, strengthening the case for architectures that intentionally "put physics in the loop." 1 Introduction The intelligence explosion hypothesis proposing that AI systems capable of recursive self-improvement could rapidly achieve superintelligence has become foundational to AI safety discourse (Good, 1966; Bostrom, 2014). This hypothesis assumes that intelligence can be recursively improved without rapidly diminishing returns and that the process can lead to a superintelligent agent with technological supremacy beyond human control. Catastrophic scenarios typically require superintelligent AI to achieve technological supremacy through disruptive innovation, such as developing novel capabilities including advanced nanotechnology or biotechnology. We do not dispute that a sufficiently intelligent system could exploit design flaws in existing infrastructure given adequate knowledge and access. We argue that the capacity for disruptive innovation through empirical investigation faces irreducible temporal constraints that no amount of intelligence alone can overcome, implying that governance should prioritize control and knowledge boundaries over limiting intelligence. The rapid deployment of agentic AI systems that autonomously call tools, browse the web, and execute code makes the question of how intelligence, knowledge, and control interact practically urgent, not merely a thought experiment about future superintelligence. To make clear which claims we are arguing against (and to avoid relying on paraphrase), we take the “intelligence explosion” and “fast takeoff” hypotheses in the sense stated by canonical sources. Good writes that an ultraintelligent machine could “design even better machines; there would then unquestionably be an ‘intelligence explosion,’ and the intelligence of man would be left far behind” (Good, 1966, p. 33). Bostrom defines “fast takeoff” as follows: “A fast takeoff occurs over some short temporal interval, such as minutes, hours, or days” (Bostrom, 2014, ch. 4, “Timing and speed of the takeoff”). Yudkowsky gives a representative fast-takeoff premise: “Post-criticality, self-improvement reaches superintelligence on a timescale of weeks or less” (Yudkowsky, 2008, sec. 11, “Local and Majoritarian Strategies”). Bostrom further argues that a superintelligent singleton would have instrumental reason to perfect world-shaping technologies, writing that “Molecular nanotechnology, or some alternative still more capable physical manufacturing technology, also seems potentially very useful in the service of an extremely wide range of final goals” (Bostrom, 2014, sec. “Technological perfection”). Our argument targets scenarios where such rapid takeoff would require non-trivial physical-domain innovation and experimentation. We separately acknowledge that purely digital domains can admit much faster trial-and-error loops (Section 6). We develop this argument through five contributions: Formal definitions of epistemic intelligence, knowledge, control (as the available action surface), and competence that disentangle the knowledge–intelligence confound (Section 3) The competence circuit: a hierarchical model where competence is gated by control [FORMULA] knowledge [FORMULA] intelligence, with each factor acting as a bottleneck for those more distal from impact (Section 3.3) Conditions for fast takeoff: a conjunctive-chain formalization of the prerequisites for fast catastrophic impact (Section 4) Computational stress-test: an analytic bound on the intelligence multiplier (Eq. 5.2) showing the speedup ceiling equals the ratio of the competing intelligence levels regardless of task difficulty, validated through stochastic simulation on NK fitness landscapes across six scenarios (Section 5) spanning the conjunctive chain (Section 4). Implications for governance: informed by the simulation results, the primary safety levers are restriction of control by limiting permitted actions (action surface) and overall impact (blast radius), and enforcement of knowledge cutoffs (keeping secrets), instead of limiting intelligence. In Section 6, we identify where this protection is strongest and weakest. 2 Related Work Prior critiques of the intelligence explosion and fast-takeoff hypotheses address growth assumptions, proposed bottlenecks, feasibility limits on recursive self-improvement, and sociological analyses (see Appendix D for details). Our work complements previous criticisms as we formally decompose competence into distinct contributing factors, propose an explicit mechanistic bottleneck (experimental verification), formalize the conjunctive conditions for fast takeoff (Section 4), derive an analytic bound on the intelligence-driven speedup validated via simulation (Section 5), and use simulations to motivate governance recommendations (Section 6). See Appendix C for an extended treatment of the experimental bottleneck. 3 Formalization of Epistemic Intelligence and Competence The distinction between knowledge and intelligence has long troubled cognitive science (Ackerman, 1996). Ackerman distinguishes intelligence-as-process (reasoning efficiency) from intelligence-as-knowledge (domain-specific information). Complementary formulations define intelligence as goal-achievement across environments (Legg and Hutter, 2007; Hernández-Orallo, 2017) or as skill-acquisition efficiency (Chollet, 2019). Intuitively, one can be intelligent but uneducated, or highly educated but unintelligent. We propose a comparative definition of epistemic intelligence that makes the separation between knowledge and intelligence operational. We treat hypotheses as propositions and distinguish those that are experimentally verified (facts) from those that remain undecided (beliefs). This follows Plato’s distinction between episteme (knowledge) and doxa (beliefs) (Plato, 1992). Preliminaries. We follow a Baconian/Popperian stance in which empirical decidability is the criterion of scientific acceptability: a proposition is treated as acceptable (or unacceptable) only relative to an agreed experimental protocol, tolerance, and confidence, and not as a metaphysical truth. Formal definitions of hypotheses, facts, knowledge, and the experimental decision function [FORMULA] are given in Appendix B. Operational knowledge cutoff. We define a system’s accessible knowledge base [FORMULA] as the set of domain-relevant propositions it can access without (i) interacting with the world to generate new evidence (measurement/experimentation) or (ii) taking actions that expand its permissions (exploitation, hacking, coercion), informally, what it can “read” under its initial access. Any increase in accessible information via privilege escalation or extraction is modeled as an increase in control [FORMULA] that expands [FORMULA] , while increases via measurement/experimentation are governed by the experimental bottleneck analyzed here. First, intelligence-driven speedup materializes only when hypothesis testing is non-trivial, which is the regime where each test incurs irreducible latency that sets hard limits on the absolute speed of progress. Second, institutional chokepoints disproportionately constrain superintelligent agents, whose efficiency leaves them with less unproductive search time to “absorb” mandatory authorization delays. These quantitative findings, combined with the theoretical arguments above, support the central governance-relevant asymmetry of the competence circuit: increasing intelligence improves search efficiency within the available action repertoire but remains bounded by experimental bottlenecks, whereas increasing control expands the action repertoire itself and directly expands overall impact. Claim 1: The “slow explosion” of competence. Upon instantiation, a superintelligent system is subject to the knowledge cutoff of its contemporaries and its knowledge growth is bounded by the rate of experimentation in physical-world knowledge creation. Significant experimental/technological breakthroughs happen on the timescale of months to years, rendering the competence increase into an explosion in slow motion. In the conjunctive chain, this primarily argues that (T3a) fails (often yielding (T3b)) for many physical-domain regimes. The simulation confirms that experimental latency imposes a hard floor on absolute progress time that is invariant to intelligence. A large intelligence multiplier reduces time spent on unproductive search but does not eliminate the time required for capability-critical tests, whether those tests involve physical experiments or interactions with a digital system. In digital domains where capability-critical tests and acquisition of mission-critical control are fast, the absolute timescale can remain short even when the multiplier is large. However, digital systems with substantial testing delays, independent authorization gates, or active defenses need not satisfy these conditions. Claim 2: Control restriction is the primary safety lever. When evaluating AI risks, the imminent danger is not intelligence level but the degree of control over critical infrastructure. The simulation (Scenarios 2A/2B and 3A/3B) shows that adding chokepoints substantially shrinks the intelligence multiplier, and that this reduction is disproportionate for higher-intelligence agents who otherwise spend little time on unproductive search (Section 5). Claim 3: Social engineering is bounded by control architecture. Even if a superintelligent system could manipulate humans to grant it control, decisive control transfer still depends on institutional and technical chokepoints. In the conjunctive chain, this is a direct argument against (T4a) in well-designed socio-technical systems. Claim 4: Knowledge cutoffs can be actively pursued and made costly to circumvent. Since knowledge is a necessary multiplier of intelligence ( [FORMULA] ), restricting access to mission-critical knowledge is a primary safety lever for intelligence-mediated competence ( [FORMULA] ). In the conjunctive chain, governance aims to keep (T2a) false (i.e. to enforce [FORMULA] as in (T2b)) and seeks to make (T3a) hard (pushing acquisition toward (T3b)). The latter impose a longer absolute timeline even for superintelligent agents, confirming that restricting the initial knowledge endowment is an effective lever independent of intelligence level. Conditions for governability. The control and knowledge levers (Claims 2–4; Table 2) cannot intercept a pathway on which an agent bypasses governance mechanisms before countermeasures are mounted and activates actuators immediately upon obtaining control. Such pathways are characteristic of purely digital settings without an independent physical gate, such as machine-speed financial transfers or credential-driven cloud reconfiguration, whereas multi-person authorization rules and physical keys exemplify the “physics in the loop” architecture recommended here. Deployment of these levers is further opposed by commercial pressure for broad action surfaces and the incentive to erode approval gates that impose latency. 7 Alternative Views and Limitations Some influential views hold that (i) existing knowledge is sufficient to engineer a catastrophe without new empirical research, (ii) purely digital pathways bypass physical bottlenecks, (iii) social engineering can circumvent institutional chokepoints (Yudkowsky, 2008), and (iv) automated laboratories compress experimental cycles. In each case the governance implications converge: even granting partial validity, control restriction and knowledge compartmentalization remain effective levers regardless of whether the binding constraint is experimental latency, institutional chokepoints, or access to tools and infrastructure. Discussion of additional alternative views is provided in Appendix I. In purely digital domains, “experiments” run at computational speed. Response: We agree that (T3a) can be plausible in digital-first pathways because trial-and-error can run quickly and in parallel (Section 6). The implication is not that fast catastrophe is inevitable, but that control architecture becomes even more decisive, because escalation can be fast if [FORMULA] is reachable via a purely digital foothold, whereas the fast loop is blunted if mission-critical actions require independent chokepoints (least privilege, separation of duties, hardware-backed or out-of-band approval; Table 2) (Claim 2). Every sufficiently complex system contains a flaw reaching mission-critical authority, and a superintelligent agent will find it. Response: If the premise holds, control-based safety is ultimately futile and alignment, which lies outside our misuse-conditional analysis, is the only remaining lever. The premise does not follow from superintelligence, however, because a fast bypass requires locating such a flaw, obtaining the information and action surface to exploit it, and acting before countermeasures are mounted, and each requirement is an empirical property of a particular architecture. Control can be gained through manipulation of human cognitive biases, bypassing physical constraints. Scaling persuasion attempts can make weak systems fail faster, but well-designed control transfer makes single-channel manipulation insufficient, because separation of duties, auditable workflows, and out-of-band/hardware-backed approvals intentionally prevent one conversation (or one compromised operator) from yielding [FORMULA] (Claim 3; Table 2). Knowledge is well-justified belief, so a superintelligence could obtain it by reasoning from existing knowledge and data without new experiments. Bostrom argues on similar grounds that a superintelligence could surmise much from meager evidence or even a priori, making information deprivation an unreliable check on its power (Bostrom, 2014, ch. 9, “Stunting”). Response: This challenge targets (T3a) in physical domains. Reasoning-first discoveries nevertheless became knowledge only after empirical confirmation, as the Higgs boson, predicted in 1964, was detected only in 2012. Mathematics is the uncontroversial exception, but proof search consumes time and a theorem confers no physical control until it is instantiated in an engineered system. Granting the view moves the bottleneck from (T3) to (T4), the regime of Scenario 0, in which control remains the operative lever. Lowering [FORMULA] substantially delays progress in every scenario (Table 3), so limiting intelligence might be a more effective lever than restricting control or knowledge. Response: This alternative faces a dilemma. If takeoff is fast, no operator can reduce a running system’s intelligence faster than the system improves itself, so containment must be established in advance. If takeoff is slow enough to permit intervention on intelligence, it is also slow enough for control and knowledge boundaries to bind. Bostrom observes that limiting a system’s intellectual faculties, one form of what he terms “stunting,” would limit its usefulness, and that a radically stunted system leaves the intelligence explosion to be triggered by another system (Bostrom, 2014, ch. 9, “Stunting”). Reduced usefulness also conflicts with the goal of general capability improvement that drives frontier model development. Moreover, limiting [FORMULA] leaves the [FORMULA] and [FORMULA] pathways intact. The computational stress-test (Section 5) illustrates the consequences of the competence circuit and is not an empirical model of deployed AI systems. The model does not represent competitive races, the mechanisms of knowledge-driven innovation such as the compositional reuse of earlier results, mixed regimes of knowledge-based discovery and physical experimentation, or knowledge creation by reasoning alone. Further structural assumptions are discussed in Appendix G.9. 8 Conclusion and Call to Action The superintelligence discourse often treats intelligence as the central variable and then discusses how to contain it. This paper argues that, for many catastrophic pathways, the decisive variables are mission-critical control and knowledge. In physical-domain innovation regimes, the limiting factor is ultimately not how quickly hypotheses can be generated, but how quickly reality can decide between them. Purely digital domains remain an important caveat (Section 6), strengthening the case for architectures that intentionally “put physics in the loop.” Provided the competence circuit assumption is accurate, AI governance should prioritize control and knowledge levers: Policymakers: Mandate action-surface audits for AI systems with infrastructure access and require separation of duties and hardware-backed approvals for mission-critical actions. AI developers: Treat tool/API access as the main risk surface: keep models in “advisory” mode by default, gate any autonomous action capability with explicit approval, rate limits, and logging. Security and infrastructure operators: Compartmentalize mission-critical knowledge and harden against extraction, and reintroduce friction (mandatory delays, staged approvals) for mission-critical digital actions. Research community: Validate the intelligence-multiplier bound and chokepoint effects empirically on real agentic AI deployments across domains with varying feedback-loop latencies. Design and evaluate “physics-in-the-loop” control architectures that restore temporal constraints on high-impact autonomous actions. Develop domain-specific instantiations of the competence circuit for high-stakes settings (biosecurity, cybersecurity, critical infrastructure). Tabular Foundation Models vs Tuned Gradient Boosting for Telecom Churn: A Profit- and Calibration-Aware Evaluation Tabular foundation models (TFMs) predict from a labelled context in a single forward pass. A recent benchmark reported that they decisively outperform tree ensembles for customer churn, but it compared them with untuned gradient-boosted trees (GBDTs) and scored only ranking metrics, while a retention campaign is judged in money. We re-evaluate TabPFN-2.5, TabPFN-3.5, TabPFN-3.5-Fast and TabICL v2 against Optuna-tuned GBDTs on five public telecom churn datasets over 10 seeded splits. We separate three questions: whether a model ranks churners well, whether that ranking earns more expected maximum profit (EMP), and whether its probabilities can drive a threshold policy. With a split-aware test and Holm correction over 20 pre-declared comparisons, TabPFN-3.5 earns significantly more EMP than the best tuned GBDT on Cell2Cell (1.9%) and Iranian (7.6%), and these two gains also hold against each of the three tuned GBDTs separately. On Orange it is ahead in all 10 splits (14.3%), but the gain is not significant after correction (Holm [FORMULA] = 0.155). The splits resample the same datasets, so these results do not stand for independent operators. TabICL v2, the earlier benchmark’s leader, beats the best tuned GBDT only on Iranian, not all three of them, and underpredicts Orange churn by 2.1 points on a 7.3% base rate. On the datasets and splits where we tested them, a substantially larger tuning budget and a duplicate-aware split leave the main conclusions unchanged. Retuning the baseline cuts the earlier headline gap from 6.1 to 4.0 PR-AUC points without closing it. The licence of the TabPFN-3.5 weights we used (License v1.0), not scoring cost, is what stands between its gains and production use. 1 Introduction Churn models exist to choose whom a retention campaign contacts. A model is useful to an operator to the extent that the customers it ranks highest are the ones worth an incentive, so the natural yardstick is campaign profit rather than classification accuracy. Verbraken et al. made this precise with the expected maximum profit (EMP) criterion [36], and later work showed that selecting churn models by AUC instead of profit leaves money on the table [35, 14, 18]. Tabular foundation models change what a churn model is. TabPFN [12, 24, 26] and TabICL [28, 29] are pretrained on synthetic tables and predict a new customer by conditioning on the labelled training set as context, with no fitting and no hyperparameter search. On general benchmarks they now lead or match tuned GBDTs [10, 29, 26]. For churn specifically, Seyedzadeh and Karimi [30] benchmarked six TFMs on nine Kaggle datasets. They concluded that TFMs “collectively and decisively outperform” classical, deep and tree-ensemble models, with TabICL v2 ahead of XGBoost by up to 9.23 PR-AUC points. That study was the first to bring TFMs to churn, and it leaves three questions open. Its XGBoost and random forest used library-default hyperparameters [30, Section 3.2], so part of the reported gap may be a tuning gap. Its metrics were F1, ROC-AUC, PR-AUC and log loss; its financial estimate scaled the PR-AUC gap by a retention rate rather than evaluating a campaign. Finally, its own discussion reads TabICL v2’s lead as “operational … rather than as a statistically decisive metric lead” [30, Section 4.2], which leaves the size of the lead unsettled. We argue that the practical value of a TFM for churn depends on the model generation, the dataset, the decision policy and the deployment terms, not on membership of the model class. We test this with tuned baselines and an explicit campaign model. Four TFMs (TabPFN-2.5, TabPFN-3.5, TabPFN-3.5-Fast, TabICL v2) face Optuna-tuned LightGBM, XGBoost and CatBoost, an explainable boosting machine and logistic regression on five public telecom datasets, three of them from real operators, over 10 seeded splits. Our inference treats the split as a source of variation and corrects for multiple comparisons. The contributions are: A tuned, profit-aware comparison. TabPFN-3.5 earns significantly more EMP than the best tuned GBDT on Cell2Cell and Iranian after Holm correction, and on both also against each of the three tuned GBDTs separately. It is ahead in every split on Orange, but that gain is not significant after correction, and it is never worse beyond noise. TabICL v2 and TabPFN-2.5 beat the best tuned GBDT only on Iranian, and neither beats all three there. On the two fictional datasets, Telco and Maven, no difference survives correction (Section 4.1). Ranking, profit and probabilities kept apart. Profit metrics rerank models only when they are tied (Section 4.2). Calibration matters for one model on one dataset: raw TabICL v2 loses 15.7% of attainable campaign profit on Orange at a fixed threshold (Section 4.3). Robustness to the obvious objections. A balanced context hurts rather than helps when the training set fits (Section 4.4). A larger tuning budget (200 trials for LightGBM and CatBoost, up from 40 and 25, on the three real-operator datasets) and a split that keeps duplicates without leaking them (on the three datasets that had any) change no conclusion within the five splits each check covers (Section 4.5). A bounded replication. On the earlier benchmark’s headline dataset, tuning removes about a third of TabICL v2’s PR-AUC lead, and the rest survives (Section 4.6). Deployment terms. Cached scoring is cheap; the licences of the TabPFN-3.5 and TabPFN-2.5 weights we used, which exclude production use, are the binding constraint (Section 4.7). The code, every per-split prediction, and the generator and audit for every number in this paper are released (Section Data and code availability). 2 Related Work Verbraken et al. defined EMP as the expected best campaign profit when the probability that a contacted churner accepts the offer is uncertain and Beta distributed [36]. Verbeke et al. used profit to compare churn classifiers in telecom [35], and Höppner et al. optimised EMP directly when growing decision trees [14]. Manzoor et al. proposed e-Profits, which replaces EMP’s population-level customer value with a per-customer value derived from Kaplan–Meier retention, and found that it reranks six classical models on IBM Telco and Maven [18]. None of these studies includes a foundation model. TabPFN v2 [12] established prior-fitted transformers for tables up to roughly 10k rows; TabPFN-2.5 extended this to 50k rows [24], and TabPFN-3 and 3.5 to a million rows with a cached context for fast scoring [25, 26]. TabICL separates column and row attention to scale in-context learning [28]; TabICL v2 reports beating a tuned and ensembled RealTabPFN-2.5 on TabArena and TALENT without tuning [29]. On TabArena, GBDTs remain strong on larger datasets while TFMs excel on small ones [10], and TabPrep shows that feature engineering, absent from most benchmarks, changes these comparisons [34]. TabPFN’s predictive probabilities are reported to be well calibrated out of the box [31], while ensembling TFMs can damage calibration [32]. The closest analogue to our study is the credit-risk review of Baesens et al. [8]. Across 14 probability-of-default datasets TabPFN-3 ranks first, but its margin over the strongest GBDT is narrow and “driven by the latest TabPFN and TabICL generations rather than by the model class as a whole”. TabPFN-3 also underpredicts the mean default rate. Tanna et al. found that, under heavy imbalance, building a class-balanced context adds 3 to 4 AUC points over uniform sampling for subsampled contexts of 1k to 50k rows [33]; V4FinBench reports a similar benefit of imbalance-aware context construction for bankruptcy prediction [17]. With tuned baselines and a correction for multiple comparisons, one model generation, TabPFN-3.5, earns more campaign profit than each of three tuned GBDTs on two of five datasets and is never behind; the other TFMs are rarely distinguishable from the GBDT. Three factors explain most of the variation. The model version matters more than the class. Baseline tuning removes part of any measured lead, about a third on E-Commerce. And the datasets most used in churn research, Telco and Maven, are those on which no model can be told apart, so studies built on them can neither confirm nor refute a TFM advantage. For a practitioner this suggests an order of operations. Tune the GBDT first; default settings overstate what a TFM adds. Evaluate candidates on held-out campaign profit, not only AUC. If TabPFN-3.5 still leads and its licence terms are acceptable, score with a cached context. If only openly licensed models are possible, test TabICL v2 on one’s own data and recalibrate it before thresholding. A balanced context is not a free improvement when the training set fits. The finding most likely to change with more evidence is the Orange gain: it is consistent across splits but not significant after correction, the splits resample a single operator’s customers, and a feature-engineered GBDT [34] could narrow it. The finding least likely to change is the calibration pattern, which is consistent across splits and matches the underprediction reported for credit risk [8]. 6 Limitations The evidence rests on three real-operator datasets. The 10 splits are resamples of the same customers, not independent operators, so they measure stability within a dataset rather than generalisation across operators. With 10 splits and a correction over 20 comparisons, the study has limited power: the Orange result is consistent in direction but not significant, and more splits or datasets could move it either way. We cannot claim that TabPFN-3.5’s gains generalise to churn in other industries, or to operators with millions of customers, where the context would no longer hold the full training set. The baselines were tuned with 25 to 40 trials; 200 trials for LightGBM and CatBoost (XGBoost was not rerun), on five splits of three datasets, changed the reference only on Cell2Cell and no conclusion, but we did no feature engineering, which can shift model comparisons [34], and we did not record the selected hyperparameters. The GBDTs were tuned on AUC, not on the EMP our primary comparison uses. Removing duplicate feature rows is a design choice; the grouped-split check covers it for the three affected datasets. The ablations, the sensitivity checks and the replication use five splits. The cost model behind EMP and the policy uses the standard population-level parameters [36]; e-Profits gives a customer-level alternative on three datasets only. We used one GPU type and the default inference settings of each TFM, and did not evaluate the API-only TabPFN-3.5-Plus and -Thinking variants or the other TFMs covered by [30]. 7 Conclusion Measured with tuned baselines, in money, and with a correction for multiple comparisons, tabular foundation models pay off for churn selectively, on evidence from three real-operator datasets and two fictional ones. TabPFN-3.5 earns significantly more campaign profit than each of three tuned GBDTs on Cell2Cell and Iranian. It is ahead in every split on Orange, but that gain is not significant after correction, and it is never behind; its raw probabilities have the lowest Brier score on 5 of five datasets and the lowest ECE on 3, and are close to the observed churn rate on every dataset, as are TabPFN-3.5-Fast’s. The weights we used, however, cannot be used in production under their licence (TabPFN-3.5 License v1.0, read in October 2026) without a commercial agreement. TabICL v2 and TabPFN-2.5 are rarely distinguishable from a tuned GBDT, and TabICL v2 needs recalibration before its probabilities can drive a campaign. Profit metrics confirm clear winners and reshuffle ties. We release the pipeline and every per-split prediction so that these conclusions can be re-checked as models and licences change.
