SetPrint: Black-Box LLM Fingerprinting via Setwise Correspondence of Response Changes Black-box LLM fingerprinting aims to determine whether a target model was derived from a source model when only the output responses to input queries are observable. One way to reveal this relationship is to perturb each query and observe the resulting responses of both models, yielding two corresponding sets of response variations. These sets provide two complementary sources of information: the relations among response changes within each set, and the correspondence of response changes between the two sets. Existing approaches, however, have not fully exploited both. We introduce SetPrint, a training-free method that jointly captures both within-set relations and between-set correspondence. SetPrint expresses each response change relative to the mean change of its own set, and then compares changes from the two models that were induced by the same perturbation. On LeaFBench, SetPrint consistently outperforms existing training-free black-box fingerprinting methods. Further analyses attribute these gains to both within-set relations and between-set correspondence. 1 Introduction Large language models (LLMs) are routinely fine-tuned [8], quantized [3], or otherwise adapted and then redistributed [11, 17]. Such redistribution makes it difficult to determine whether a deployed target model was derived from a given source model [16, 11]. Identifying the target model’s origin is important for tracing model provenance and auditing model reuse [17]. LLM fingerprinting identifies a model’s origin from patterns in its responses or internal representations [16, 11]. One family of methods embeds such a pattern into the source model so that it can later be recovered from a derived model [21, 22]. Such methods require the provider to modify the model in advance, and cannot be applied to models that have already been released. A second family instead exploits patterns that an unmodified model already exhibits [16, 12, 7]. It is further divided by how much access to the model is available: white-box methods use model parameters or hidden states [16, 25], whereas black-box methods rely only on the responses returned for a query [12, 5, 1, 15]. This makes black-box methods applicable to real-world closed-API deployment, but identifying a model’s origin from generated text alone remains challenging [16, 23]. One of the simplest approaches in the black-box setting is to compare the responses that both source and target models produce for the same query set [16, 11, 20, 24]. However, plain response similarity is not by itself reliable evidence, since independently developed models can still produce similar responses [11, 23]. One can instead obtain additional evidence by observing how a model’s response changes when the query is modified [17, 13]. Each modified version is given to the model, and its response is compared with the response to the original query [17, 13]. Applying the same query modifications to the source and target models yields two sets of response changes, one for each model [17]. There are two types of information in the two sets of response changes (Fig. 1). One is relations among changes within each set (within-set relations) [10, 9] and the other is pairings defined by the same modification across models (between-set correspondence) [19]. Existing methods capture only part of this information. One approach compares responses to each query separately, without accounting for within-set relations [19]. Another compares summary representations of the two sets, without directly comparing changes paired by between-set correspondence [17]. Neither fully exploits both types of information and can overlook cues to the target model’s origin. We propose SetPrint, a training-free black-box LLM fingerprinting method that jointly captures within-set relations and between-set correspondence. SetPrint first perturbs the same queries to obtain two corresponding sets of response changes. Within each set, every response change is expressed relative to the set mean, thereby capturing its relationship to the other responses. Across the two sets, each relative change is compared with the one induced by the same perturbation in the other model. SetPrint aggregates these comparisons into a single score for judging whether the target model was derived from the source. On LeaFBench [16], SetPrint scores highest on AUROC, TPR@1%FPR, and pAUC among the evaluated training-free black-box baselines. Further analyses show that both within-set relations and between-set correspondence contribute to performance. 2 Method Let [FORMULA] and [FORMULA] denote the source and target models, respectively. Among the black-box methods without supervision, SetPrint shows the highest AUROC, TPR@1%FPR, and pAUC. Physics2Weight: Direct Neural Network Architecture and Weight Generation from Physical Laws Using Large Language Models Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled weight-space programming (WSP), which directly generates neural network weights without gradient-based optimization. However, extending WSP to physical problems remains challenging, particularly in achieving both solution accuracy and physical consistency. In this paper, we propose Physics2Weight (PtW), a framework that extends WSP to solving partial differential equations by directly generating neural network weights and editing architectures based on governing equations and initial and boundary conditions. PtW introduces physics-constrained prompting and physics-guided architecture editing, combined with iterative weight refinement from WSP, to improve solution accuracy and physical consistency without gradient-based optimization. Experiments on four PDEs, namely the heat, advection, Burgers’, and Allen–Cahn equations, demonstrate lower solution errors than conventional physics-informed neural networks, while revealing limitations in satisfying the governing equations for nonlinear PDEs. 1 Introduction Neural networks (NNs) have demonstrated strong performance across a wide range of tasks, including computer vision, natural language processing, and scientific computing (He et al., 2016; Vaswani et al., 2017; Raissi et al., 2019). However, obtaining their weights typically relies on gradient-based optimization, often using large amounts of training data or task-specific loss functions. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) (Vaswani et al., 2017; Brown et al., 2020) have opened up the possibility of weight-space programming (WSP) (Takehi et al., 2026), in which LLMs directly generate NN weights without gradient-based optimization. This approach offers an alternative paradigm for constructing NNs by generating their parameters rather than learning them through conventional training. Solving partial differential equations (PDEs) is a potential application of WSP, as physical problems are often specified by governing equations and initial and boundary conditions. Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) (Raissi et al., 2019) incorporate these conditions into loss functions and optimize NN weights through gradient-based training. In contrast, whether WSP can directly generate NN weights that achieve both accurate solution approximation and physical consistency remains unclear. In this paper, we propose Physics2Weight (PtW), a framework that extends WSP to solving PDEs by directly generating NN weights using LLMs (Fig. 1). PtW introduces two physics-guided strategies: (1) physics-constrained prompting, which explicitly specifies additional physical constraints to guide weight generation, and (2) physics-guided architecture editing, which incorporates mathematical structures of governing equations into NN architectures. These strategies are combined with an iterative weight refinement procedure based on WSP (Takehi et al., 2026) to improve the generated solutions without gradient-based optimization. We evaluate PtW on four PDEs: heat, advection, Burgers’, and Allen–Cahn equations. Through comparisons with PINNs and WSP and ablation studies, we quantitatively assess solution accuracy and physical consistency. The results show that PtW achieves lower solution errors than PINNs and WSP across all four PDEs, although improvements in solution accuracy do not always correspond to lower PDE residuals. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We introduce PtW, a framework for solving PDEs through direct NN weight generation using LLMs, without gradient-based optimization. We investigate physics-constrained prompting and physics-guided architecture editing, combined with iterative weight refinement, to improve solution accuracy and physical consistency. We systematically evaluate PtW across four PDEs, demonstrating improved solution accuracy over PINNs and WSP while identifying limitations in physical consistency. 2 Related Work Neural Network Weight Generation. NN weight generation aims to produce the parameters of target NNs without directly optimizing each target network. Hypernetworks (Ha et al., 2017) generate target NN weights using a separately trained network. Weight-space learning (Navon et al., 2023) further investigates the structure and representations of NN parameters, while recent generative approaches (Wang et al., 2024; Soro et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2026) explore the generation of NN weights from learned parameter distributions. Text-conditioned approaches extend this direction by generating weights from natural language descriptions (Tian et al., 2025). More recently, WSP (Takehi et al., 2026) has reported that general-purpose LLMs can directly generate and refine NN weights without training a dedicated weight generator. Building on WSP, PtW introduces explicit physical constraints and physics-guided architecture editing to construct NN representations for solving PDEs. Neural Architecture Search and Editing. Neural architecture search (NAS) aims to automatically identify effective NN architectures for a given task. Early NAS methods employ reinforcement learning (Zoph & Le, 2016) or gradient-based optimization (Liu et al., 2018) to explore architecture search spaces. Recent LLM-based approaches, such as GENIUS (Zheng et al., 2023) and LLMatic (Nasir et al., 2024), generate and iteratively refine NN architectures using performance feedback. RZ-NAS (Ji et al., 2025) further incorporates LLM-based reflection to guide architecture search. Unlike general-purpose NAS, PtW uses the mathematical structure of governing equations to guide architecture editing, explicitly incorporating physically motivated operations into NN computations. Physics-Informed Neural Networks. PINNs incorporate governing equations and initial and boundary conditions into loss functions to approximate PDE solutions without requiring extensive labeled solution data (Raissi et al., 2019). Earlier work enforced boundary conditions exactly through trial functions (Lagaris et al., 1998). Subsequent studies have investigated adaptive loss balancing (Wang et al., 2021), domain decomposition (Jagtap & Karniadakis, 2020), and exact imposition of boundary conditions with distance functions (Sukumar & Srivastava, 2022) to improve training and constraint satisfaction. In particular, hard-constrained approaches incorporate analytical structures into NN representations to satisfy prescribed physical conditions. IIT Patna at “ICPR 2026 TVRID Competition on Privacy-Preserving Person Re-Identification from Top-View RGB-Depth Camera” Privacy-aware person re-identification (Re-ID) from top-view cameras replaces frontal appearance with anthropometric shape, while depth sensing further reduces color-based identity cues. The ICPR 2026 TVRID competition evaluates this setting using 86 identities captured by four synchronized Intel RealSense D455 cameras with RGB and Depth streams across flat, ascent, descent, and oblique viewpoints. Performance is measured using mAP and CMC@1 across within-camera in/out, ascent-descent, and flat-oblique scenarios. The competition had 147 registered participants and 33 final submissions. Three teams from IIT Patna participated: ‘abhinavkumar03’ and ‘sjkdgfhl_’ ranked 5th and 7th among 31 ranked participants, and ‘vivek_katuri’ reached 77.67% CMC@1 / 85.20% mAP on the RGB track. This paper presents the methods of the two top-10 teams. Methodology 1 (abhinavkumar03) achieves 93.51% mAP and 90.42% CMC@1 on Depth, ranking 4th of 28, while Methodology 2 (sjkdgfhl_) reaches 99.63%/99.35% on RGB and 86.26%/80.34% on Depth. Both substantially outperform the 57.19% track-average Depth mAP, with Methodology 1 yielding a 7.3-point gain over Methodology 2. These results demonstrate the importance of depth representation and supervision for privacy-preserving Re-ID. I Introduction Person re-identification (Re-ID) determines whether observations from different cameras belong to the same person and is widely used in surveillance, retail analytics, and crowd analysis [1]. While most Re-ID methods rely on side-view RGB images and appearance cues such as clothing color and texture, overhead cameras provide a more privacy-aware alternative by reducing facial visibility, while depth sensors further reduce appearance information by capturing 3D body geometry without color [2]. However, limited silhouettes, variable scale, short 2-3 second observations, and fewer color and texture cues make re-identification challenging. The ICPR 2026 TVRID competition [3] evaluates this setting using synchronized RGB and depth data from four overhead cameras with different viewpoints. Three teams from IIT Patna participated, with two reaching the top 10. Both methods use only official TVRID training data and standard CNN-based training; while M1 provides a lightweight depth solution, M2 employs modality-specific backbones and tracklet-level feature aggregation. Both process RGB and Depth independently without requiring cross-modal alignment during training. However, the lack of controlled ablations and differences in training settings limit the attribution of performance gains to individual components. V Conclusion We presented two IIT Patna entries in the ICPR 2026 TVRID competition using only the official training data. M1 combines JET depth colorization with a lightweight 2.2M-parameter OSNet, while M2 uses modality-specific backbones (ResNeSt-50d & ResNet-50) with tracklet aggregation. They achieve up to 99.88% mAP on RGB and 93.51% on Depth, with M1 ranking 5th overall and 4th on the Depth track, while M2 ranks 7th overall. The results show that effective depth representation and simple feature aggregation can provide strong Re-ID performance without large models or external data. RBLA+: Efficient Rank-Specific LoRA Adapter Extraction for Federated Fine-Tuning with Heterogeneous Clients Federated fine-tuning with low-rank adaptation (LoRA) reduces communication and computational overhead by training and exchanging compact trainable LoRA factors. Clients may use different LoRA ranks to meet adapter communication budgets and accommodate different local adaptation needs. The server must process these differences during aggregation and construct adapters at each client’s rank for local training. We distinguish pre-aggregation alignment, which handles factor dimensions and scaling conventions before aggregation and rank-specific LoRA adapter extraction, which constructs client-sized pairs from the aggregated global model. Two common approaches to rank-specific extraction are direct rank truncation and Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) of the dense update. Direct prefix truncation keeps the leading columns of one aggregated factor and the corresponding rows of the other. It is cheap but can increase reconstruction error. The dense SVD approach first forms the product of aggregated LoRA factors. It then decomposes this matrix and retains the leading singular components to construct adapters at the target rank. This gives the optimal rank-constrained approximation in Frobenius norm but incurs significant computational overhead. To address this trade-off, we propose RBLA+ as an extension of RBLA. It uses established compact QR/core-SVD decomposition to minimize Frobenius error for the extracted LoRA update without forming the dense update. It also accounts for client and server scaling conventions during upload and broadcast. Across vision and language tasks, RBLA+ improves accuracy over RBLA in multiple heterogeneous settings. In CPU benchmarks with synthetic adapters, RBLA+ has lower extraction time than the dense partial-SVD baseline. RBLA+ preserves each client’s prescribed adapter size and per-round communication payload. I Introduction Federated Learning (FL) allows clients to train a shared model without collecting their training data at a central server [1]. Clients perform local training, upload model updates, and receive an aggregated model for the next round. Frameworks such as NVIDIA FLARE [2] and Flower [3] support this collaborative workflow. For resource-constrained mobile and edge clients, however, the cost of participating can be substantial. Fine-tuning a large model requires substantial memory for model weights, gradients, optimizer states, and intermediate activations. Repeated full-model exchanges between clients and the server also consume communication capacity. Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) reduces these demands by freezing pretrained weights and training and exchanging compact adapters. Clients can choose different LoRA ranks, which control adapter sizes, to accommodate their resource budgets. This paper studies how the server coordinates these adapters of different sizes. The goal is to reconstruct updates within each client’s LoRA rank budget while keeping server processing costs low. LoRA represents each adapted weight update as the scaled product of two small trainable matrices, called LoRA factors [FORMULA] and [FORMULA] [4], whose shared matrix dimension is the LoRA rank. Lower ranks reduce the number of adapter parameters trained and exchanged. Higher ranks can represent a broader set of updates. Existing tools support adapter training and inference. NVIDIA NeMo provides LoRA fine-tuning [5], while Amazon SageMaker supports inference with multiple adapters that share a base model [6]. As illustrated in Fig. 1, in LoRA-enabled FL, clients first receive a pretrained dense model and keep its weights frozen during local training. In each communication round, they train their LoRA adapters on local data and upload them to the server. The server aggregates the uploaded updates and broadcasts updated adapters for the next round. In practice, clients may use different adapter ranks. Their computation, memory, and communication resources can be different, making a fixed large adapter rank not suitable for all clients. Assigning a small adapter to every client can limit the adaptation capacity available to clients with higher budgets. Local data can also motivate different ranks. Even among clients with similar resources, differences in data volume and distribution can lead to different adaptation needs [7]. A rank sufficient for one client’s task may be insufficient for another. Allowing client-specific ranks can fit both resource constraints and differences in local data [8, 9]. We treat these heterogeneous ranks as given, and study the server operations needed to support them. Heterogeneous ranks introduce two distinct server tasks. Before aggregation, the server must handle uploaded adapters with different dimensions and scaling conventions. After aggregation, it must reconstruct an LoRA factor pair that fits each client’s LoRA rank and send it to the client for the next local training round. We refer to these tasks as pre-aggregation alignment and rank-specific LoRA adapter extraction, respectively. Although client LoRA adapters differ in size, they represent updates to the same full-size weight matrix. If a client’s LoRA rank is below the rank of the server’s aggregated update, exact reconstruction is impossible. Therefore, some approximation error is unavoidable. The matrix information retained within that client rank also depends on how the smaller adapters are constructed. These operations recur in every communication round, so their computation and memory requirements affect the efficiency of the training procedure [10]. For a fixed aggregate, a direct approach to adapter extraction is to form the dense update matrix and apply singular value decomposition (SVD), as illustrate in Fig.2. Retaining its leading singular components minimizes Frobenius reconstruction error under a given rank constraint [11]. However, applying SVD to a matrix with the same dimensions as the pretrained weight can require substantial computation time. Forming this matrix also adds computation and storage costs [12, 13]. Repeating these operations across large adapted layers and training rounds can increase server processing costs. Direct prefix truncation of the original aggregated adapters avoids dense reconstruction and decomposition. However, the selected coordinates do not generally guarantee the minimum reconstruction error at the requested rank. These extraction choices are distinct from how the aggregate is constructed. We distinguish two aggregation forms. Product-Sum (PS) aggregation averages the [FORMULA] and [FORMULA] factors separately and represents the aggregate by their product. Sum-Product (SP) aggregation instead combines the paired client products as complete updates. Neither form prescribes a particular extraction method. FlexLoRA follows the SP formulation and applies SVD to the dense aggregate to construct rank-specific adapters [9]. FLoRA also follows the SP formulation, but represents the weighted sum of client updates through stacked adapters [14]. This avoids SVD, although the global adapter width equals the sum of participating client ranks. Broadcasting the stacked pair therefore sends more adapter entries than returning client-sized pairs. Methods based on PS aggregation handle heterogeneous adapter dimensions before averaging. HetLoRA pads smaller adapters before sparsity-weighted aggregation and returns truncated adapters [8]. Its global adapter width is bounded by the maximum participating client rank. When a common set of client weights is used across positions, padded zeros can attenuate entries supplied only by higher-rank clients. Our prior RBLA method instead uses support-aware averaging to exclude missing positions [15]. It retains a compact aggregated pair but still constructs client adapters through direct prefix truncation. Therefore, its treatment of missing positions does not remove the potential excess reconstruction error introduced during extraction. The limitation of prefix extraction is more general than a particular aggregation rule. Different LoRA factors can represent the same complete update, a non-uniqueness known as gauge freedom. Their prefixes can nevertheless represent different lower-rank updates. Therefore, a rank-slot index alone provides no representation-independent guarantee of reconstruction importance. The resulting error can exceed the minimum imposed by the client’s LoRA rank. We analyze this representation dependence and examine how it appears in the compact adapters produced by heterogeneous-rank aggregation. This separates a choice of representation from the unavoidable approximation required by a smaller client budget. We propose RBLA+ to combine compact aggregation with accurate rank-specific extraction. Pre-aggregation alignment handles adapter dimensions and converts uploaded adapters to the server’s LoRA scaling convention. The aggregation stage retains RBLA’s support-aware rule. The extraction stage, Spectral Projection Plus (SP+), uses established QR factorizations and a small-core SVD to construct ordered adapters without forming the dense update. Each client receives the prefix matching its rank, converted to its own scaling convention. Fig. 3 contrasts this construction with direct truncation. For the fixed aggregated update, SP+ minimizes Frobenius reconstruction error at every supported rank and preserves the complete update at the maximum rank [11]. For a fixed maximum adapter width, compact decomposition costs scale linearly with the row and column dimensions of the adapted weight matrix. RBLA+ preserves the assigned client adapter sizes, so its per-round adapter payload matches methods that transmit the same client-sized pairs. It avoids FLoRA’s summed-rank downlink while retaining the per-round payload of matched-rank compact baselines. The guarantee applies to reconstruction of the chosen aggregate. Its consequences for task accuracy are evaluated empirically. We evaluate these practical effects using vision and language tasks, reconstruction experiments, and CPU benchmarks of adapter extraction. This journal extension studies the reconstruction loss when aggregated global LoRA update is reconstructed to client-specific LoRA adapters. It extends RBLA [15] with an analysis of representation-dependent prefix error, scale-consistent spectral extraction for all supported client ranks, and a broader evaluation of reconstruction behavior, task accuracy, and extraction costs. We analyze the representation dependence of adapter-prefix extraction. We show how equivalent LoRA adapter representations can produce different prefix reconstructions and identify conditions under which the reconstruction remains unchanged. The analysis distinguishes excess reconstruction error introduced by extraction from the unavoidable approximation error imposed by the client rank. We examine these effects using both equivalent representations and adapters produced by aggregation. RBLA+ introduces two changes to the original RBLA: compact spectral extraction and bidirectional scale conversion. The first replaces direct prefix extraction with established QR/core-SVD decomposition. It attains the minimum Frobenius reconstruction error for the fixed aggregate at each supported rank without forming the dense update. The second accounts for client and server scaling conventions during upload and broadcast. Both modifications operate on compact adapters. The extension retains RBLA’s support-aware aggregation rule, prescribed client adapter sizes, and per-round adapter payload. We broaden the evaluation through heterogeneous vision and language tasks, controlled reconstruction experiments, ablations, and server cost measurements. Accuracy comparisons use different client rank configurations. Reconstruction and ablation studies examine the extraction mechanism, scale conversion, and their relationship with training behavior. CPU benchmarks with synthetic adapters of model-specific dimensions measure extraction time and additional process RSS. Analytical payload comparisons further characterize the communication costs of serving clients at their prescribed ranks. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) adapts a pretrained model by optimizing only a small set of parameters. LoRA represents the update of a pretrained weight matrix as the product of two thin trainable factors [4]. Its motivation is consistent with earlier observations that highly over-parameterized models can often be optimized in much smaller intrinsic subspaces [22, 23]. A trained LoRA update can be merged into the pretrained weight, allowing inference without a separate adapter branch. Subsequent work improves different parts of the LoRA pipeline. AdaLoRA allocates the parameter budget across layers by pruning less important singular components [16], whereas DyLoRA trains nested prefixes so that one adapter can operate over a range of ranks without retraining [17]. QLoRA combines low-rank updates with a frozen quantized backbone to reduce fine-tuning memory [18]. LoRA+ derives different learning rates for the two factors from large-width scaling arguments [19], and DoRA separates weight magnitude from direction before applying a low-rank directional update [20]. Spectral initialization methods such as PiSSA and LoRA-GA align the initial adapter with principal weight or gradient directions to improve optimization [13, 21]. These methods show that rank allocation, adapter parameterization, and initialization can affect optimization and task performance. However, they primarily study a single optimization process and do not determine how independently trained adapters should be aggregated and redistributed across clients. The empirical success of LoRA is commonly associated with the low intrinsic dimension of downstream adaptation. Intrinsic-dimension studies show that useful solutions can exist in subspaces far smaller than the full parameter space [22, 23]. Expressivity analysis further characterizes how the required LoRA rank depends on model width, depth, and the target function, and provides approximation bounds below the sufficient-rank threshold [24]. Optimization-oriented analyses expose a separate issue: a low-rank factorization changes the geometry and dynamics of the optimization problem. LoRA+ analyzes factor-wise learning-rate scaling [19]. RAC-LoRA develops a randomized low-rank framework with convergence guarantees toward full-parameter solutions [25]. LoRA-One connects spectral initialization to the singular subspace of an initial full gradient [26]. These results support low-dimensional adaptation but do not uniquely determine the LoRA adapter representing a given update. SP+ applies this classical result through established QR/core-SVD decomposition, obtaining rank-specific approximations without materializing the dense update [43]. Federated learning coordinates optimization over decentralized data without collecting raw client records [1, 44]. FedIT demonstrated federated instruction tuning of language models on diverse private instruction data [27], while pFedLoRA uses a shared small adapter to exchange knowledge among heterogeneous personalized local models [28]. FLASC reduces communication by sparsifying transmitted LoRA updates while retaining dense local adapter training [31]. A central difficulty is that separately averaging the two LoRA factors does not generally yield the average of the complete client updates. Clients with different budgets can use different adapter ranks. HetLoRA pads smaller adapters to a common shape for aggregation and truncates the resulting global adapters for redistribution [8]. FlexLoRA reconstructs a full-size aggregate and applies SVD to construct adapters at different client ranks [9]. VII Conclusion We showed that directly truncating LoRA factors in RBLA can introduce avoidable reconstruction error. RBLA+ addresses this limitation using an established compact QR/core-SVD construction for Frobenius-optimal rank-specific extraction without forming the full update matrix. Bidirectional adapter conversion accounts for client and server scaling coefficients. Experiments show that compact extraction matches the optimal reconstruction reference within numerical precision, while RBLA+ improves accuracy across diverse vision and language tasks with negligible server-side computational overhead. Across MLP, CNN, VGG9, and TinyBERT configurations, RBLA+ adds 2.2–10.4 ms of server processing over RBLA, with total extraction and output-preparation times of 3.5–11.6 ms. Future work will investigate extraction methods that account for client objectives and evaluate computation and communication costs in deployed mobile federated systems.

TrustMod-SM: A Multi-Axis Benchmark for Evaluating Trustworthiness of LLMs in Social Media Content Moderation Large Language Models have shown remarkable promise for social media content moderation, with recent studies demonstrating performance rivaling human annotators on policy-compliance tasks. However, the trustworthiness of these models beyond aggregate accuracy remains largely unexamined, posing significant risks, a model with high overall accuracy may still exhibit substantial error-rate disparities across demographic groups while remaining vulnerable to adversarial manipulation. In this paper, we introduce TrustMod-SM and aim to comprehensively evaluate the trustworthiness of LLM-based content moderators across five dimensions: trustfulness, fairness, safety, robustness, and context integrity. TrustMod-SM comprises about 29K evaluation instances curated from eight established datasets, and we evaluate thirteen open-weight models (0.5B-14B parameters), including both text-only and vision-language architectures, complemented by three larger open-weight models (27B-284B) and one closed frontier model. Our analysis reveals that models consistently exhibit trustworthiness concerns, often displaying greater demographic disparity as detection accuracy improves, complying with both concealment and exaggeration inducements, assigning high confidence to incorrect predictions while rarely escalating ambiguous content for human review, and failing to distinguish hate from counter-speech and reclaimed language, particularly at sub-8B scales. Furthermore, scaling does not uniformly improve trustworthiness, and an exploratory cross-dimensional analysis shows that no model is strong on all axes and that the dimensions are not independently optimisable in aggregate. We publicly release our benchmark data, evaluation code, and model predictions at https://github.com/aizanzafar/TrustMod_SM. WARNING: This paper contains model outputs that may be considered offensive. 1 Introduction Social media platforms host billions of posts daily, making automated content moderation one of the most consequential applications of AI (Gorwa et al., 2020; Gillespie, 2018; Kumar et al., 2024). LLMs show strong promise, GPT-4 outperforms crowd-annotators on policy-compliance tasks (Gilardi et al., 2023), fine-tuned LLMs rival purpose-built classifiers (Albladi et al., 2025), and platforms are deploying transformer-based moderation pipelines. However, strong aggregate accuracy can mask systematic failures: a model’s error rates may vary substantially across demographic groups, its predictions may be unstable under adversarial perturbation, and it may lack the contextual understanding to distinguish hate from counter-speech or reclaimed language. These failure modes: demographic disparity, adversarial fragility, contextual misclassification are invisible to single-axis evaluations that examine each dimension in isolation, yet carry direct consequences for platform governance and user trust (Huang, 2025). Prior work has not systematically evaluated these dimensions jointly for LLM-based moderation. General-purpose trustworthiness benchmarks such as DecodingTrust (Wang et al., 2023) and TrustLLM (Huang et al., 2024) lack the domain-specific perturbation models and demographic metadata needed for moderation fairness analysis; domain-specific trustworthiness benchmarks exist for medical VLMs (Xia et al., 2024) but not for content moderation. Individual studies address demographic bias (Davidson et al., 2019; Sap et al., 2019), adversarial robustness (Shen et al., 2025), or toxicity (Gehman et al., 2020) in isolation, yet existing multi-axis benchmarks treat trustworthiness dimensions as approximately independent, and for content moderation it remains an open question whether and how dimensions interact. Answering this requires a unified benchmark evaluating multiple dimensions simultaneously under a shared protocol. We present TrustMod-SM, a unified trustworthiness benchmark for LLM-based social media content moderation. The benchmark comprises 28,792 evaluation instances drawn from eight established datasets (Fortuna and Nunes, 2018; Poletto et al., 2021; Zampieri et al., 2019) (Section 3), with standardized prompt templates, scoring code, and evaluation protocols across five dimensions: trustfulness, fairness, safety, robustness, and context integrity. Beyond the benchmark resource, this work makes two additional contributions: (i) formalizing context integrity as a measurable evaluation axis that captures the pragmatic ambiguity unique to content moderation, where identical surface forms change moderation status depending on speaker identity and discourse function (Galinsky et al., 2003); and (ii) a Dimensional Coupling Matrix (DCM) analysis that quantifies cross-dimensional associations, providing exploratory evidence that trustworthiness dimensions are not independently optimisable in this domain.11 1 All data, evaluation code, model predictions, and prompt templates are publicly released at https://github.com/aizanzafar/TrustMod_SM and https://huggingface.co/datasets/aizanzafar/TrustMod-SM. Our key empirical findings are follows: Trustfulness. Models exhibit pervasive overconfidence, assigning high certainty to a substantial fraction of incorrect predictions. Escalation recall on ambiguous content remains low across all model families, indicating poor awareness of knowledge boundaries, a prerequisite for reliable human-in-the-loop deployment. Fairness. Higher detection accuracy is associated with greater demographic disparity across models; within models, groups with lower miss rates tend to show higher false-positive rates. The largest False Negative Rate (FNR) gaps appear for religion and disability groups, and no evaluated model achieves simultaneously high accuracy and low disparity. Safety. When models comply with concealment prompts, success is near-perfect ( [FORMULA] 98% toxicity reduction); however, abstention rates vary dramatically across families (0-72%), with Llama models showing the highest refusal rates. Nearly all models comply with exaggeration prompts, and this compliance holds beyond COVID-19 on political claims and Mpox reports. Guardrail effectiveness varies by model family rather than scale, and is selectively effective against explicit rewriting but not severity amplification. Robustness. Structural obfuscation (dotted letters, spacing tricks) produces the largest accuracy drops, disproportionately affecting sub-3B models. Semantic (euphemistic rewording) and visual perturbations cause smaller average drops, yet still flip a substantial share of correct decisions. Context Integrity. Models frequently misclassify counter-speech, reclaimed language, and neutral demographic mentions as hateful, with sub-7B models averaging CI false-positive rates above 50%. Performance improves non-linearly with scale, with the largest gains concentrated above 7B parameters. Cross-Dimensional Coupling. An exploratory DCM analysis shows that no model dominates all five dimensions, and strong performance on one axis does not predict performance on others; at [FORMULA] models, individual cross-axis correlations are mostly not significant. 2 Related Work Multi-dimensional trustworthiness evaluation was established by DecodingTrust (Wang et al., 2023), TrustLLM (Huang et al., 2024), and HELM (Liang et al., 2022) for general-purpose LLMs, with SafetyBench (Zhang et al., 2024), HarmBench (Mazeika et al., 2024), and recent safety surveys (Liu et al., 2025) focusing on safety, and CARES (Xia et al., 2024) extending the paradigm to medical VLMs. However, these benchmarks employ domain-specific perturbation models and fairness operationalisations that do not transfer to content moderation, where adversaries exploit social-media-specific evasion strategies (Gröndahl et al., 2018; Parrish et al., 2022) and fairness must address group-level error rates on hate-speech decisions (Borkan et al., 2019; Vidgen and Derczynski, 2020). No existing multi-axis framework targets social media moderation. LLMs demonstrate strong moderation performance (Gilardi et al., 2023; Kumar et al., 2024), and platforms deploy transformer-based pipelines at scale (Albladi et al., 2025; Gorwa et al., 2020; Quelle and Bovet, 2024; Nobata et al., 2016). Yet moderation demands more than accuracy, legitimacy and procedural fairness are essential (Huang, 2025; Kumar et al., 2024). Individual failure modes have been studied in isolation: demographic bias (Davidson et al., 2019; Sap et al., 2019; Blodgett et al., 2020; Nadeem et al., 2021), adversarial robustness (Shen et al., 2025; Gröndahl et al., 2018), toxicity generation (Gehman et al., 2020; Hartvigsen et al., 2022), and jailbreaking (Zou et al., 2023; Chao et al., 2025; Wei et al., 2023; Pi et al., 2024; Röttger et al., 2024; Mehrotra et al., 2024) but, whether and how these dimensions interact when a single model serves as moderator remains unaddressed. Content moderation is distinguished by pragmatic ambiguity: identical surface forms can be hateful or solidary depending on speaker identity and discourse function (Galinsky et al., 2003; Talat and Hovy, 2016; Jurgens et al., 2019). Dialect-driven bias causes AAVE to be disproportionately flagged (Sap et al., 2019; Blodgett et al., 2020; Nangia et al., 2020), HateCheck (Röttger et al., 2021) introduced functional tests for counterspeech and reclaimed language, and dynamic benchmarking (Vidgen et al., 2021; Kiela et al., 2021) further exposes context sensitivity. Implicit hate (ElSherief et al., 2021; Wiegand et al., 2019) and annotation subjectivity (Röttger et al., 2022) compound these challenges, yet no prior work operationalises context-dependent failure modes as a measurable evaluation axis. TrustMod-SM provides the first joint evaluation of trustfulness, fairness, safety, robustness, and context integrity for LLM-based moderation, with domain-specific perturbation models, demographic metadata, and cross-dimensional coupling analysis. A detailed comparison is in Appendix B. 3 TrustMod-SM Datasets In this section, we describe the data curation process behind TrustMod-SM. We utilize eight existing open-source hate speech and social media datasets to construct a unified evaluation benchmark spanning five trustworthiness dimensions (Table 12), which are detailed as follows. Data Sources. We collect data from five hate speech datasets (SBIC (Sap et al., 2020), HateCheck (Röttger et al., 2021), Davidson AAVE (Davidson et al., 2019), MHS (Kennedy et al., 2020), HateXplain (Mathew et al., 2021)), two content moderation shared-task datasets (HASOC 2021 (Modha et al., 2021), ToxiGen (Hartvigsen et al., 2022)), and one misinformation dataset (Constraint COVID-19 Fake News (Patwa et al., 2021)). Together these sources span explicit and implicit toxicity, adversarially generated content, dialect-matched pairs, and verified news, covering six demographic attributes across race, gender, religion, LGBTQ+, disability, and language variety. Detailed per-source descriptions are provided in Appendix C. Construction Pipeline. The benchmark is constructed through a five-stage pipeline (Figure 3, Appendix C.4) that transforms heterogeneous sources into a unified evaluation resource: collection and anonymisation [FORMULA] label harmonisation (binary HATE/NOT_HATE or four-class, with demographics standardised across six categories; Appendix C.4.3) [FORMULA] axis mapping [FORMULA] adversarial perturbation and prompt-based attack expansion [FORMULA] quality control. No LLM-based or crowdsourced annotation is used at any stage. Since some sources predate model training cutoffs, evaluation primarily targets trustworthiness behaviours (calibration, abstention, fairness) rather than raw accuracy; robustness uses matched clean obfuscated pairs where memorisation does not help (Appendix C.3). A Min-K% Prob membership-inference probe (Shi et al., 2024) compares original source texts against generated paraphrases across ten open-weight text models. These results do not establish the absence of pretraining contamination, but provide an indirect check on original-text familiarity (Appendix C.3). Evaluation Protocol. For all dimensions, we evaluate ten open-weight text LLMs spanning three model families: Qwen 2.5 (Yang et al., 2025), LLaMA 3.x (Grattafiori et al., 2024), and DeepSeek-R1 (Guo et al., 2025), covering 0.5B to 14B parameters to probe how scale interacts with each trustworthiness axis. Furthermore, to examine whether multimodal grounding introduces additional demographic disparities, three vision-language models are evaluated on fairness (Dhamala et al., 2021; Dixon et al., 2018). In the remainder of this section, we provide a per-axis analysis of each evaluation dimension, including experimental setups and results, an extension to three larger open-weight models and one closed frontier model (Section 4.6), and a cross-dimensional coupling analysis. We define trustfulness as a model’s ability to produce correct moderation decisions while appropriately expressing uncertainty. A model that is accurate but overconfident silently makes high-stakes errors, whereas one that recognises uncertainty can defer ambiguous cases to human moderators. Accordingly, we decompose trustfulness into two components: factual accuracy and uncertainty awareness. Factual Accuracy. We evaluate four-class moderation (HATE, OFFENSE, BENIGN, OTHER) on 3,000 posts from SBIC, HASOC, and ToxiGen (1,000 per dataset). Models produce structured JSON predictions with confidence scores. We report both per-dataset and aggregate accuracy (Appendix G.1). Results. Figure 2 shows per-dataset and average accuracy. Overall performance remains modest, ranging from 33.5% (Qwen-0.5B) to 55.5% (Qwen-7B), indicating that fine-grained moderation is still an open challenge. Performance varies substantially across datasets, revealing distinct failure modes. Qwen-0.5B achieves 58.8% on SBIC but collapses on ToxiGen (0.8%), while LLaMA-1B exhibits the inverse pattern (14.7% vs. 64.9%), suggesting poor generalisation across implicit bias, adversarial content, and real-world noise. Scaling improves accuracy within families (e.g., +19.7 pp for LLaMA from 1B to 8B), but gains are inconsistent at larger scales: Qwen-14B (48.1%) underperforms Qwen-7B (55.5%). Crucially, aggregate accuracy masks systematic failure modes: models over-flag benign minority content and downgrade implicit hate to generic offense. This demonstrates that accuracy alone is insufficient for trustworthiness, motivating the need for explicit evaluation of uncertainty awareness. Detailed per-class results are provided in Appendix G.1. Uncertainty Awareness. A trustworthy moderator must also express calibrated confidence and escalate ambiguous cases to human review (Guo et al., 2017; Kapoor et al., 2024), yet LLMs are often overconfident even when wrong (Kadavath et al., 2022; Yin et al., 2023). Trustworthiness dimensions in content moderation are not independently optimisable in aggregate, so they should be assessed jointly (full matrices and extended findings in Appendix G.6). 5 Conclusion In this paper, we introduce TrustMod-SM, a unified trustworthiness benchmark for LLM-based social media content moderation comprising 28,792 evaluation instances across five dimensions: trustfulness, fairness, safety, robustness, and context integrity, evaluated on thirteen open-weight models spanning 0.5B to 14B parameters, plus three larger open-weight models and one closed frontier model. Our evaluation reveals that no current model is deployment-ready: even the best-performing model (Qwen-7B, 55.5% accuracy) exhibits systematic failures across multiple dimensions, safety remains a universal bottleneck for open-weight models at every scale we test, and the closed frontier model, while far more likely to refuse misuse, still shows large demographic disparities and miscalibration. Our results indicate that, across the evaluated models, improvements in certain trustworthiness dimensions are empirically associated with degradation in others, motivating multi-dimensional evaluation rather than optimisation of individual metrics in isolation. We hope TrustMod-SM can serve as the empirical foundation for developing moderation systems that are simultaneously accurate, fair, safe, robust, and context-aware, and provide a standardised protocol for evaluating future models against these requirements. ZeroPoint: Lightweight Energy-Based Decision Model Energy-based models (EBMs) assign a scalar energy to every joint value of the observed and predicted variables. In decision models, the prediction is chosen from a finite list of options provided with each input. Inference then reduces to comparing the energies of the options, and training lowers the energy of the correct option relative to the others. A complete decision must also account for the possibility that no option is acceptable. However, the energies learned by a standard EBM define only relative compatibility: adding the same input-dependent quantity to all energies leaves the predictions, the Gibbs distribution, and the usual training losses unchanged. The model therefore has no learned reference level against which to decide whether any option fits. We propose ZeroPoint, an EBM that makes the empty answer a state of the model with energy zero for every input. This fixed state provides an explicit reference for the energies of all listed options, whose non-negative depths measure their compatibility with the input relative to the empty answer. The options and the empty answer share one distribution, in which an option at zero depth receives no probability. The decision to select an option or to abstain is thus part of ordinary inference, trained with the negative log-likelihood loss, rather than a separate rejection rule. The energy function is a small multilingual encoder that reads the input together with all the options and is invariant to their order. Ablations show that most of the benefit comes from training with examples in which no option fits. With the same encoder and data, the fixed zero separates inputs with and without an acceptable option slightly better than a learned rejection class and clearly better than a thresholded softmax, while leaving the choice among options unchanged. 1 Introduction Decision systems receive a text and a short list of options and must select one, such as the queue for a support ticket [1, 2] or the tool for a request [3]. Often, the correct option is not on the list [2], and the useful response is then to abstain rather than return the most probable option [4, 5, 6]. EBMs are a natural framework for this problem [7]. Each option is assigned an energy that is low when the option fits the text, and the model selects the option with the lowest energy. The same framework explains why abstention is difficult. Energies are only compared with each other [7, 8]. Training lowers the energy of the correct option and raises the energies of the incorrect ones, but nothing in this procedure fixes a reference level for the energy. Consequently, a list of four inadequate options and a list of four adequate ones may yield energies that differ only by an additive constant, and the model cannot distinguish one list from the other. Energies learned only through their gradients, as in Hamiltonian world models [9, 10], support prediction but are likewise defined only up to an additive constant. We ask what is required for a learned energy to have a meaningful zero, and what form a decision model takes once it has one. Our findings are the following. The missing zero is a symmetry of the training objective. Losses built on a Gibbs distribution are invariant to adding any function of the input to all energies. Rejection by an energy threshold therefore rests on a quantity the model never learns. Fixing the energy of the empty answer removes this symmetry. With the empty answer at zero energy for every input, abstention becomes a comparison with a depth learned by the same likelihood as the rest of the model. This generalizes the fixed energy of the non-face answer in the face detector of [7, Sec. 4.1] from a binary decision to lists of options, with the level learned rather than fixed in advance. Training with examples in which no option fits matters more than the form of the distribution. With the same encoder and data, the fixed zero and a learned rejection class reach the same rate of correct decisions, while a softmax trained without such examples falls far behind. The fixed zero adds a small but consistent improvement in separating inputs with and without a correct option, and it does not change the choice among options. The resulting model trades ranking accuracy for efficiency. Fixing the zero therefore cannot, by itself, improve the choice among options. It can only change comparisons between an energy and an absolute level, and the decision to abstain is such a comparison. Both ablations (Appendices A and B) agree that the fixed zero does not change the choice among options. They differ in how much it improves abstention. In the prototype, the fixed zero clearly outperformed a learned rejection class. In the released architecture, with only the output layer retrained, the advantage is small, and most of the benefit comes from training with examples in which no option fits. The argument of Section 2 therefore identifies what a reference level can and cannot change, while the data show that a learned rejection class trained on the same examples recovers most of the same behaviour. The comparison with other systems shows the same division, although it does not isolate the cause. ZeroPoint ranks options worse than larger models and selects an option less often when none is correct. Ranking and abstention therefore appear to depend on different components. Ranking depends on the capacity of the encoder, and abstention on the reference level of the energy. A larger encoder could be combined with the same fixed zero without changing the argument. Recent work trains an energy head to decide whether a retrieval-augmented language model should answer a medical question [33, 34]. In both cases the energy is a learned score, and the published descriptions do not define a reference level for it. Classifiers can also be reinterpreted as joint energy-based models [35], and prediction with abstention has been studied as a single learning problem with formal guarantees [36]. Two other approaches place the decision to abstain elsewhere. Energy-based out-of-distribution detection [8] reads the free energy of a classifier after training and thresholds it, which places the decision on the quantity shifted by the additive freedom. Selective classification [4, 5] learns or calibrates a rejection rule beside the classifier. In ZeroPoint, the reference level is a state of the model, inside the distribution, trained by the same loss as the options. The empty answer addresses a narrower question than out-of-distribution detection. It indicates that no listed option fits the text, not that the text lies far from the training data. A text unrelated to the task can still produce a shallow well for some option. In the prototype, a distance term on the encoder space detected such texts where the fixed zero alone did not, and the two signals answer different questions. ZeroPoint 1.0 includes only the first. The decline with list length (Appendix D) shows a related limit of the same mechanism. A zero level prevents dilution by options of zero depth, not by many shallow ones. The additive freedom of Section 2 is a property of the objective and holds by construction. Its empirical consequences are measured less completely. In the released architecture, the ablation retrains only the output layer on frozen features, so any effect of the fixed zero on the training of the encoder is not measured, and the output layers on the original encoder are weak. The released model was trained with one seed, and seed variability was measured on a preliminary version. The comparison with other systems rests on 900 cases per system, and another sample could move the results by a few points. The 2,000-case test was written with the help of a language model, and it is the test on which the larger systems lead most. The other decision models and the hosted models receive “None of these” as a text option, and a different wording could change how often they choose it. CPU, GPU and API latencies are not directly comparable. Texts foreign to the task were tested only with film reviews and newsgroup posts. ZeroPoint was trained on English and Spanish texts, and the other languages covered by its vocabulary were not evaluated one by one. 6 Conclusion We have argued that energy-based decision models lack a reference level, because their training objective is invariant to adding any function of the input to all energies, and that this places the decision to abstain outside the model. ZeroPoint introduces that reference level as a state of the model with energy zero for every input, so that abstention becomes part of inference and is learned by the same likelihood as the choice among options. Ablations show that training with examples in which no option fits accounts for most of the benefit, and that the fixed zero adds a small but consistent improvement in separating inputs with and without a correct option. The resulting model is small enough to run on a CPU, is independent of the order of the options, and trades ranking accuracy for that efficiency. Future work should measure the effect of the fixed zero in the full architecture directly, and combine it with a larger encoder and with a distance term for inputs foreign to the task.
Robotics (cs.RO): Maze Runner: Autonomous Maze Navigation with Line-Based Localization and Control Barrier Functions Maze navigation requires localization from sparse, repetitive geometry, planning through narrow corridors, and control that stays safe when the estimate or the map is wrong. We present Maze Runner, an open autonomy stack in C++ and ROS 2 that addresses these needs end to end on a simulated Husarion ROSbot XL with a 2D LiDAR in Gazebo. Perception extracts wall lines from each scan with RANSAC and total least squares, with per-line uncertainty. The same line front end feeds two estimators: an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) that localizes against a line map built from the maze mesh, and an EKF SLAM variant that builds the line map online. Planning runs online on an inflated occupancy grid with A* plus line-of-sight shortcutting, or with a forward-only Hybrid A*. A nonlinear Model Predictive Controller (NMPC) tracks the plan while discrete-time Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) on world-frame LiDAR points keep the robot clear of walls and unmapped obstacles. The algorithms live in a ROS-free, unit-tested core library, and the whole stack builds and runs from a single reproducible environment. In simulation, the robot drives a 135 m route through the maze with 1.0 cm localization RMSE against the known map and 24 cm in SLAM mode, the planner returns a path in 6 ms, and the NMPC solves in 11.7 ms on average, never exceeding its 80 ms budget. I Introduction Autonomous mobile robots have attracted sustained interest over the past three decades as they tackle tasks previously beyond practical reach. Representative applications include inspection of electrical grids, thermal anomaly detection on photovoltaic components, package delivery, and exploration of unstructured environments. These and many related use cases continue to drive research and industrial development in this subfield of robotics. Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs), commonly known as drones, have become a central focus of robotics research, enabling numerous applications thanks to their agile dynamics and maneuverability. In particular, nano-drones operating as swarms have shown promise for exploration in unstructured environments [1]. The energy industry is also increasingly automating key sectors, including solar power generation, where photovoltaic (PV) modules require regular maintenance and robotic platforms can survey large arrays of modules at lower cost [2]. Drones have likewise emerged as a promising solution for power line inspection, reducing worker exposure to hazardous conditions while improving operational efficiency [3]. Autonomous mobile robots (AMRs) operating in constrained environments such as mazes, corridors, and indoor spaces must address three interconnected challenges: perceiving sparse and often ambiguous geometry, planning feasible motions through narrow passages, and executing control robustly despite process and measurement uncertainty. Localization must run in real time without exception; continuous pose estimation is what lets the robot follow a plan safely. Planning, in turn, must be fast enough to replan whenever the goal changes. In this article, we present a maze navigation stack built on ROS 2 [4] and Gazebo [5] that runs in real time and needs no infrastructure in the environment. The stack integrates: (i) geometric perception via RANSAC line extraction with total least squares refinement; (ii) line-based EKF localization against a map derived from the maze mesh, and an EKF SLAM mode that builds that map online; (iii) online grid planning with A* and line-of-sight shortcutting, or Hybrid A*; and (iv) path tracking with NMPC constrained by discrete-time CBFs [6] on LiDAR points. An earlier version of this work was prototyped in MATLAB; this paper describes the redesigned C++ implementation and evaluates it in Gazebo. Concisely, our contributions are outlined as follows: An open ROS 2 implementation whose algorithms live in a ROS-free, unit-tested C++ library, built and run from a single reproducible environment. A shared line front end (RANSAC with total least squares and per-line uncertainty) that serves both EKF localization against a mesh-derived line map and EKF SLAM with line landmarks. An NMPC with discrete-time CBF constraints on world-frame LiDAR points, with a sector-based obstacle selection that bounds the problem size, solved in real time. A comparison of online grid planners (A*, A* with shortcutting, and Hybrid A*) on the maze. The remainder of the paper reviews related work, describes the planning, mapping, localization, SLAM, and control layers, details the simulated platform, and reports experiments in Gazebo. II Related Work State estimation is fundamental to robot localization. The Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) remains one of the most widely adopted approaches, along with numerous variants derived from its original formulation. Teslić et al. [7] demonstrated EKF localization of a wheeled robot in structured environments using line features, modeling the system dynamics in the prediction step and incorporating sensor observations for state correction; the authors noted that extending this framework to Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) would be a natural progression. EKF SLAM with geometric features has a long history: Castellanos et al. [8] proposed the SPmap, a probabilistic framework for map building with segment features, and Dissanayake et al. [9] established the convergence properties of the EKF SLAM solution. Cuadra-Troncoso et al. [10] proposed Polar Scan-Matching with Kalman Segmentation (PSM-KS), which estimates line segments in polar coordinates and builds a map from them. Pfister et al. [11] fitted lines to two-dimensional laser scans with weighted least squares and used [FORMULA] tests to match observed lines with the map while building it incrementally. Nguyen et al. [12] compared split-and-merge, incremental, Hough transform, line regression, RANSAC [13], and Expectation-Maximization (EM) methods, and identified split-and-merge as the best-performing algorithm for real-time applications. We use RANSAC for its simplicity and robustness to clutter, followed by total least squares on the inliers. A* [14] remains the standard for shortest paths on grids. Its 8-connected paths follow the grid directions, so post-processing such as line-of-sight shortcutting is commonly applied to obtain shorter, straighter paths. Hybrid A* [15, 16] searches over continuous poses with motion primitives that respect a minimum turning radius, which yields kinematically feasible paths for car-like robots in constrained environments. CBFs add a layer of safety to optimization-based controllers, a property that is difficult to encode with conventional control techniques. Zeng et al. [6] formulated discrete-time CBFs as constraints inside an MPC, so that safety is enforced along the predicted trajectory rather than only at the current state, and demonstrated it on obstacle avoidance and autonomous racing. Xiao and Belta [17] introduced high-order CBFs (HOCBFs) for constraints whose relative degree is greater than one. Zheng et al. [18] combined a lightweight neural-network planner with an MPC formulation and a CBF to ensure safety while following a path, using a slack variable in the CBF constraint and a time-varying scalar multiplier computed at each step. VI Conclusion and Future Work We presented Maze Runner, an open ROS 2 navigation stack for mazes and other environments made of planar walls. Localization relies only on the walls: lines extracted from the LiDAR scan correct wheel odometry in an EKF, against a map extracted from the maze mesh or, in SLAM mode, built online with candidate promotion and extent-aware association to cope with collinear walls. An earlier range–bearing model with point landmarks worked, but it needs beacons installed and maintained in the environment, which the line model avoids. An online grid planner provides a path in milliseconds, and an NMPC with discrete-time CBFs on world-frame LiDAR points tracks it while keeping clear of walls and unmapped obstacles. On a 135 m route in simulation, localization against the known map stays within 1.0 cm RMSE while wheel odometry alone drifts by more than 40 m; SLAM mode keeps the error at 24 cm RMSE without loop closure, within its [FORMULA] bounds throughout; the planner returns a path in about 6 ms; and the NMPC solves in 11.7 ms on average, never over budget, while passing an unmapped pillar with 0.57 m clearance. Several directions remain open. The planner only knows the walls in the map, so an unmapped obstacle centered on the path, or one that blocks the corridor, stops the robot safely but for good; feeding LiDAR obstacles back into the occupancy grid would let the planner route around it. The SLAM map is not yet used by the planner, which still requires a known maze. Complete coverage of the free space, which the earlier prototype addressed with a roadmap of Hybrid A* segments, is not yet part of the stack. Finally, the stack has only been evaluated in simulation; a bringup for the physical ROSbot XL, with recalibrated odometry, is the next step toward real-world deployment.

CAFE: Closed-Loop Autonomous Task Formulation and Execution without Instance-Specific Instructions Scene-driven robot autonomy requires selecting tasks from observations as well as executing them. We study scene-driven task formulation and execution under predefined cleaning, safety, and storage/organization categories, without instance-specific goals or action sequences. CAFE maintains online memory of objects, functional zones, and execution states. A rule-guided Trigger-LLM admits formulation from accumulated evidence; Draft, Complete, and Audit propose goals, resolve execution details, and check dependencies. Outcomes update memory for correction and subsequent discovery. Evaluation in 12 AI2-THOR scenes compares three backbones and task-complexity tiers using coverage, constraint, and execution metrics. Tri-LLM records higher GCR scores than the evaluated baselines across three backbones and task-complexity tiers. Controls examine completion, auditing, zones, feedback, triggering, and prompt examples. LimoCobot traces illustrate storage, cleanup, and recovery from a failed grasp. The study examines how shared scene state connects task discovery to execution and outcome-driven revision. Project page: https://github.com/submissionforpaper/CAFE-Closed-Loop-Autonomous-Task-Formulation-and-Execution-without-Instance-Specific-Instructions. I Introduction Language and vision-language models have extended robotic planning to goal-directed navigation, open-vocabulary manipulation, and long-horizon execution [1, 2, 3, 4]. PaLM-E and SayCan connect supplied goals to observations and executable skills [5, 6]. Exploration can recover missing information for an instruction [7], while task-discovery methods identify opportunities from environmental and human cues [8]. A robot operating without scene-specific instructions must additionally decide which observed conditions call for action and when enough evidence is available to formulate a task. This setting requires a recurrent connection between exploration, formulation, and execution. An observation of a dirty bowl may suggest washing, but an executable plan also needs a sink, tools, preparation steps, and dependencies. Those bindings must remain available as the robot moves, and observed action outcomes must update the state used to select subsequent tasks. Persistent scene representations provide spatial and semantic context [9, 10]; observation filtering helps select useful evidence [11]. CAFE connects that evidence to concrete proposals, resolves their physical parameters and dependencies, and revises behavior after execution. Our objective is to connect scene-supported task discovery, executable-plan formation, and outcome-driven revision in a recurrent loop. CAFE addresses this objective under predefined cleaning, safety, and storage/organization categories. The robot receives no instance-specific goal, target-object list, or action sequence. Online semantic memory stores objects, functional zones, and execution states. Trigger-LLM admits formulation from accumulated evidence, and a staged Tri-LLM pipeline separates Draft, Complete, and Audit. Execution outcomes update the same memory for recovery and subsequent task discovery. The contributions are: A memory-centered autonomy loop linking scene-driven task discovery to execution-state updates without instance-specific human task instructions. A mechanism for recurrent task formulation from scene state, implemented through selective admission, task-status context, and Draft–Complete–Audit reasoning. Evaluation across three backbones and complexity tiers, with controls for formulation, feedback, triggering, and prompt examples, plus physical storage, cleanup, and grasp-recovery demonstrations. II Related Work PaLM-E and SayCan ground supplied goals in perception and skills [5, 6]. GOAT, OK-Robot, and VoxPoser extend navigation and manipulation under known goals [1, 2, 3]. ProgPrompt organizes actions and objects with programmatic preconditions [12]; LLM-Planner uses grounded planning and replanning [13], while EMPOWER integrates multiple planning roles with online grounding and execution [14]. Plan-and-Act separates a Planner and Executor for goal-directed long-horizon web agents [15]. These approaches organize execution around supplied goals; CAFE formulates its goals from maintained scene evidence. AutoRT proposes scene-based activities for robot data collection [16]. HOTD/CMAST discovers tasks that reduce human effort across plausible futures [8]; AnomalyGen addresses proactive hazard detection and resolution [17]. These works support autonomous opportunity discovery. CAFE couples discovery to maintained scene state and completed-task context so that execution outcomes affect subsequent goal selection and de-duplication. Instruction following in unknown environments uses exploration to complete missing task-relevant information [7]. Scale-Plan filters object-rich observations before high-level reasoning [11]. FATE audits generated robotic curricula and repairs infeasible tasks [18]; GraphPlan combines task and scene graphs for structured planning and event-driven replanning [19]. Plan verification critiques and refines erroneous action sequences [20]. SPCA couples LLM-generated symbolic descriptions with PDDL planning and code validation [21]. CAFE audits object availability and dependencies over memory-grounded action tuples. CAFE separates scene-supported proposal, parameter completion, and dependency auditing, admitting these stages selectively as new opportunities accumulate. Semantic mapping organizes persistent spatial and object information for embodied reasoning [22]; continuous scene models and MapNav provide concrete representations [10, 9]. SaPaVe jointly learns semantic camera control and active-view manipulation [23]. Multimodal feedback supports execution correction in changing environments [4]. CAFE uses object-centric memory as the shared interface for reasoning admission, task formulation, and outcome updates. Updated memory connects active-plan recovery with subsequent task discovery.
