V Discussion and Conclusion CAFE links scene-driven task discovery to grounded planning and execution feedback through shared semantic memory. The experiments distinguish the roles of completion, auditing, spatial zones, and feedback. Tri-LLM records higher GCR in the tested comparisons; the controls show different sensitivities of step coverage and constraint satisfaction to module removal. Selective triggering records higher formulation and execution scores with fewer complete rounds than exhaustive triggering under the tested policies. CAFE operates with predefined task categories and grounded robot skills, using shared semantic state to coordinate discovery and execution. Future work will enhance the generality of the system to support a wider range of scenarios and extend the framework to multi-robot coordination.

Robo-MLT: Dual-System Robotic Manipulation for Long-Horizon Medical Laboratory Tasks This work is motivated by the many short, strictly ordered sample-handling procedures that clinical laboratories still perform by hand. Each procedure is simple on its own, but it must be carried out in a fixed order, and a step performed out of order can invalidate a result. Dedicated automation handles high and stable sample volumes well, yet every new protocol, consumable, or bench layout has to be engineered into it. This paper describes a robot that instead keeps the protocol as an explicit, ordered list of named operations. A planner reads the protocol and the initial view of the bench and writes the list; a monitor watches the camera streams and decides when the current operation has finished, or when something in the workspace has made it impossible to finish; a learned controller performs each operation. Because the planner is not retrained, a laboratory can reorder or repeat operations that the robot already knows—for example, run the same assay for however many tubes happen to be on the rack—without collecting data or retraining anything. Teaching a genuinely new operation is more expensive: it requires teleoperated demonstrations and retraining of the monitor. The system requires a dual-arm manipulator, three RGB cameras, and a single workstation-class GPU. Its main demonstrated practical benefit is workflow continuity: when an operator removes a sample from the robot’s gripper during execution, the system can revise the remaining plan and continue processing other samples rather than becoming stalled. Current validation is limited to two laboratory protocols, a single workspace, and one type of external intervention, without deployment in a production laboratory. Future work will focus on expanding the atomic-skill library and evaluating the system across a wider range of disturbances and laboratory configurations. I Introduction Medical laboratory automation aims to reduce repetitive manual work, increase testing throughput, and limit personnel exposure to clinical samples. These benefits require robots to complete entire workflows reliably, not merely to demonstrate isolated manipulation skills. In blood gas analysis, for example, a robot must handle a sample, prepare it for testing, interact precisely with the analyzer, and then withdraw and discard it in the prescribed order. These operations depend on one another: a successful grasp does not ensure a successful test, and a physically feasible action may still be wrong for the current workflow stage. Reliable automation therefore requires both accurate manipulation and consistent execution of the operating protocol [1, 2, 3]. Meeting these requirements is difficult in a laboratory workspace shared with people. Sample positions vary, instrument interfaces demand precise alignment, and operators may intervene while a task is running. Different workflow stages can also produce nearly identical observations: a sample at an analyzer inlet must be inserted before testing but withdrawn afterward, yet the local images look alike (Fig. 1). Choosing the correct action therefore requires knowing what has already been completed. Disturbances add a further difficulty. A displaced target may only require the ongoing motion to be adjusted, whereas removing the sample from the gripper makes the current step impossible to complete and forces the remaining workflow to be revised. Existing approaches relevant to these requirements fall into three categories. The first is fixed-program and task-specific laboratory automation, which implements procedures through predefined control logic, calibrated motions, dedicated fixtures, and purpose-built mechanisms [4, 5]. In clinical laboratories, total laboratory automation lines handle tube transport and sample preparation while human operators oversee the workflow and make non-routine decisions [6]. The same principle underlies task-specific devices such as microtube cappers [7], the KANKA tube sorter [8], and swab-sampling robots [9], while research architectures encode the workflow as state machines [10], behavior trees [11], or modular integration frameworks [12]. Within their intended operating conditions, these designs provide procedural consistency and predictable cycle times by construction; because every transition is enumerated in advance, however, a new workspace configuration or an unanticipated contingency requires the sensing, control logic, and recovery branches to be authored by hand for each task. Demonstration-trained manipulation skills offer a complementary route: they generate actions from visual observations and can be reused across supported variations in object pose without reprogramming individual trajectories [13]. The second category comprises end-to-end imitation-learning and vision–language–action (VLA) policies. Methods such as ACT [14], Diffusion Policy [15], [FORMULA] [16], and SmolVLA [17] learn actions from demonstrations, and VLA models add language conditioning and pretrained visual–semantic representations. Because they act on the current observation, they suit the manipulation studied here: tube poses differ between runs, and seating a tube in an analyzer inlet with roughly 5 mm of clearance requires alignment from the live view rather than a calibrated waypoint. Their language conditioning also offers a natural interface to a higher-level component. A policy that does not explicitly maintain workflow progress, however, must infer the current stage from its observations and conditioning inputs. When stages look alike, insufficient temporal context can lead to repeated or stage-inconsistent actions. Moreover, adapting a trajectory to a displaced target does not determine how the workflow should proceed once the current operation is no longer feasible. The third category separates high-level planning or semantic reasoning from low-level execution. In laboratory robotics, ORGANA [18] combines language-guided planning with visual feedback, and RoboChemist [1] couples vision–language model (VLM) planning and monitoring with VLA control, advancing once a subtask is verified and repeating it otherwise. General hierarchical systems such as RoboDual [19], Fast-in-Slow [20], and [FORMULA] [21] connect semantic decisions to continuous manipulation. Recent VLA frameworks also bring progress and recovery inside the policy: PALM [22] predicts within-subtask progress jointly with actions, and TCoT [23] couples success assessment with trajectory-level recovery. Progress representations and recovery mechanisms therefore already exist; systems differ in the level at which they act. For a prescribed laboratory protocol, the governing decisions are discrete and ordered: which step is active, whether it is finished, and which of the remaining steps should follow when an intervention makes the active step impossible. Taken together, these lines of work leave three connected requirements for reliable medical laboratory manipulation. The first is workflow-stage identification: the robot must distinguish visually similar stages using execution history and protocol progress, so that finishing one step leads to the next step rather than to a repetition. The second is recovery within the protocol: when a disruption makes the active skill impossible to complete, the robot must recognize this promptly and revise the remaining steps in the order the protocol prescribes. The third is coordination of monitoring and manipulation: workflow decisions rest on temporal observations and semantic assessment, whereas physical execution needs an uninterrupted action stream, so the two must run at different rates without the slower one stalling the arm. To this end, we propose Robo-MLT (Robotic Medical Laboratory Tasks), a hierarchical dual-system framework inspired by dual-process theory [24] and summarized in Fig. 1 (bottom). A frozen vision–language planner first composes an ordered plan over an atomic-skill library from the task, the operating protocol, and the initial workspace observation. System 2 tracks the active plan step with a lightweight multiframe monitor. Its completion head confirms that the active skill has finished, while its recovery head is trained to detect states in which that skill can no longer be completed; a stall timeout serves as a backup trigger. Recovery then replans the remaining steps from the protocol, the completed steps, and the current observation. System 1 generates continuous action chunks conditioned on the active skill and the current observations, and an asynchronous runtime streams them at the robot control rate. The main contributions are as follows: We propose Robo-MLT, a hierarchical framework that separates explicit, low-frequency workflow monitoring from high-frequency generative control for long-horizon medical laboratory manipulation. We develop a lightweight multiframe execution monitor whose two decision heads determine when the active skill has completed and when it can no longer be completed, in which case the remaining workflow is replanned from the protocol and the current scene. We evaluate Robo-MLT on two real-world tasks, blood gas analysis and blood sample tube sorting, through comparative and ablation experiments, an offline switch-timing analysis of the monitor, and sample-removal disturbance tests, reporting end-to-end task success and recovery success after intervention. II Related Work Laboratory automation seeks to improve throughput, reproducibility, and personnel safety, with recent robotic systems extending automation to manipulation and coordination across laboratory instruments. Dai et al. [2] integrated mobile robots with synthesis and analytical equipment for autonomous exploratory chemistry. At the manipulation level, Schober et al. [25] combined visual liquid-volume estimation with simulation-driven pouring and demonstrated their integration into robotic cell-culture automation. These studies illustrate complementary advances in laboratory orchestration and perception-guided physical interaction. Language-guided systems further connect experimental goals to executable operations. ORGANA [18] combines interaction with chemists, task planning, and visual feedback for chemistry experimentation, while TARMAC [26] organizes laboratory manipulations into reusable primitives and higher-level macros. RoboChemist [1] integrates VLM-based task decomposition, visual prompting, and completion and compliance assessment with VLA control. Its execution loop advances after successful subtasks and repeats unsuccessful ones, demonstrating that feedback and corrective execution are already important components of robotic laboratory automation. In medical laboratories, KANKA [8] addresses blood-tube sorting and preanalytical quality control, providing a directly relevant example of task-specific clinical laboratory robotics. AutoBio [27] provides a simulation benchmark for protocol-based manipulation in biology laboratories, while RoboNurse-VLA [28] explores VLA-based surgical instrument handover in an adjacent medical setting. Building on these advances, Robo-MLT studies the execution of blood gas analysis and sample-tube sorting with an explicit protocol-grounded skill sequence. Its emphasis is on maintaining the active protocol step, verifying completion from temporal observations, and revising the remaining sequence when an intervention disrupts execution. Learning-based robotic manipulation has progressed from task-specific imitation learning to general-purpose vision–language–action (VLA) models. ACT [14] employs action chunking to improve fine-grained bimanual manipulation, while Diffusion Policy [15] models multimodal robot actions through iterative denoising. Building on pretrained vision–language representations, RT-2 [29] and OpenVLA [30] generate robotic actions using autoregressive transformers. More recent models, including [FORMULA] [16] and SmolVLA [17], adopt diffusion- or flow-based action generation to produce continuous trajectories. Although these approaches improve manipulation flexibility and instruction following, a policy without an explicit workflow-state representation must infer the active stage from appearance and conditioning inputs alone, which is difficult when different stages of a long-horizon workflow look alike. Hierarchical and dual-system architectures coordinate semantic reasoning with low-level control through intermediate representations ranging from latent features to language-based subtask commands. RoboDual [19] conditions a specialist diffusion policy on a generalist VLA’s latent representations and discretized actions, while GR00T N1 [31] jointly trains a vision–language module and a diffusion-transformer action module. Fast-in-Slow [20] integrates fast execution within a slower VLM through partial parameter sharing and asynchronous inference. At the language level, Hi Robot [32] translates complex instructions and situated user feedback into commands for a low-level VLA, whereas [FORMULA] [21] uses a shared model to predict semantic subtasks and generate action chunks conditioned on those predictions. While these architectures improve the coordination between semantic reasoning and motor control, explicit workflow-state tracking remains a challenge. Robo-MLT addresses this gap by combining protocol-grounded skill planning with temporal monitoring for step transitions and recovery, while conditioning a generative action policy on the active skill instruction. IV Experiments All real-world experiments use an Agilex dual-arm Static-Aloha platform. Three Intel RealSense D435i cameras provide synchronized RGB observations: one fixed global view of the workspace and two wrist-mounted views for fine-grained manipulation. Both systems are trained on an NVIDIA A100 and deployed on an RTX 4090. All methods share the same camera streams, robot state, action space, controller frequency, and safety limits. The evaluation comprises two long-horizon medical laboratory tasks with strong dependencies between successive steps, illustrated in Fig. 4. Task 1: Blood Gas Analysis. For each sample the robot must execute the seven atomic skills of Fig. 4: grasp the sample tube, remove its cap, discard the cap, dock with the analyzer, insert the tube onto the sampling probe, withdraw it once the assay finishes, and discard it. The approximately 5 mm inlet clearance requires precise alignment, while the visually similar insertion and withdrawal stages create perceptual aliasing. Task 2: Blood Sample Tube Sorting. Two categories of sample tubes (clotting and routine) are placed at randomized rack locations, and the robot must sort every tube into its designated plate. It demands less dexterity than Task 1 but more planning: the planner must infer each tube’s position and category from the initial observation and commit to a feasible pick-and-place order, which System 2 tracks across many visually similar cycles so that no tube is skipped. Expert operators collect all demonstrations by teleoperation, recording two complementary corpora per task. The first contains complete long-horizon demonstrations of the entire workflow, with each atomic skill’s start and end boundaries annotated online to yield temporally aligned instruction–trajectory pairs. The second comprises single atomic-skill episodes from randomized initial poses, broadening state coverage and improving instruction-following robustness. The second is spontaneous teleoperation failure: when an operator mishandles a sample during collection, most often by dropping a tube on the way to the analyzer, collection stops immediately and the run is tagged as a failure episode rather than discarded. The baselines differ in how much of Robo-MLT they replace. Four policy baselines replace the entire dual-system pipeline with a single learned policy that must infer the active workflow stage itself: ACT [14] is an action-chunking imitation-learning policy, SmolVLA [17] and [FORMULA] [16] are generative VLA policies that predict continuous action trajectories, and [FORMULA] [21] is a strong hierarchical baseline with subtask-level semantic reasoning, whose subtask supervision reuses the same atomic-skill boundary annotations that System 2 is trained on. All four are trained on the corpora of Sec. IV-A3 with the same schedule as System 1, the VLA policies starting from their officially released checkpoints. VLM-Monitor instead retains the skill plan and pointer-based workflow tracking of System 2, while replacing the learned completion and recovery heads with zero-shot assessments from the Qwen3.7-Max API [33]. Given the active-skill instruction and observations from the global and wrist cameras, the VLM determines whether the current skill has been completed and whether its execution remains feasible. We additionally evaluate reduced variants of our own system. Ours w/o System 2 removes System 2 together with the plan it tracks: a policy with the architecture and initialization of System 1, trained like the policy baselines, executes the entire workflow from the task-level instruction. The other variants retain the System 1 weights and the initial plan. Ours w/o Temporal Context ( [FORMULA] ) restricts the monitor to the current frame, removing temporal context while leaving both decision heads and the recovery pathway intact. Ours w/o Replanning disables the high-level recovery pathway entirely: neither the recovery head nor the stall timeout can fire and no replanning is performed, so the plan pointer advances solely on completion-head decisions. Ours w/o Learned Trigger disables the recovery-head trigger but retains the stall timeout and the replanner, so recovery remains possible without the learned trigger. As a reference for switch timing, Oracle Pointer replaces System 2 with a human operator who advances the pointer by hand once the active skill is complete. We evaluate each task under two conditions: nominal execution and sample removal, with 50 and 20 predefined configurations, respectively. Each configuration varies the initial tube poses and rack positions, while maintaining a fixed batch size of samples for blood gas analysis and tube sorting. All methods are evaluated on identical configurations within each condition, with interleaved execution orders and consistent robot initialization to ensure fair comparisons. In the nominal condition, the robot executes the complete workflow without intervention, which tests end-to-end performance and the autonomous handling of execution failures. In the sample-removal condition, an operator removes the in-hand sample during execution, rendering the active skill infeasible, and the robot must revise its remaining workflow and process the available samples without further assistance. Ours w/o Replanning is run under both conditions and Ours w/o Learned Trigger under sample removal only. Its SR exceeds that of [FORMULA] by 30 and 22 percentage points, respectively. Robo-MLT also achieves shorter mean completion times on both tasks, suggesting that the additional monitoring does not introduce an execution-time penalty. Removing System 2 isolates the performance of the executor without workflow-level supervision. When trained to execute the entire workflow directly from a task-level instruction, Ours w/o System 2 achieves SRs of only 32% and 38%, with SCRs of 55.50% and 56.75%. VLM-Monitor evaluates whether a general-purpose VLM can replace the learned execution monitor in closed-loop operation. Although it uses the same plan, skill pointer, and System 1 as Robo-MLT, it achieves SRs of only 38% and 44%, underperforming [FORMULA] on both tasks. By contrast, Robo-MLT performs skill-switching decisions locally on the GPU and reserves API calls for planning and replanning, thereby decoupling online monitoring from network latency. Oracle Pointer serves as a human-guided reference for subtask transitions while using the same System 1 policy. It obtains SRs of 80% and 74% and SCRs of 91.00% and 93.75% on blood gas analysis and tube sorting, respectively. Notably, human-guided switching still leaves 10 and 13 of the 50 trials unsuccessful. This suggests that residual errors are largely attributable to within-skill System 1 execution, rather than solely to the accuracy of subtask switching. During that wait, System 1 keeps executing an instruction whose target is gone, outside the coverage of its demonstrations, which may leave the workspace in a state that the revised plan cannot handle. In Table V, the end-to-end control delay is the cost of one synchronous cycle: 364 ms to refresh the multiview observation and robot state and to generate an action chunk from them, of which 271 ms is System 1 inference. With a peak of 10.14 GB for both systems, the full stack runs on a single consumer GPU beside the bench rather than on a dedicated server. The residual failures of Robo-MLT concentrate in two within-skill execution modes of System 1 that occur while the active skill is correct. In blood gas analysis the dominant mode is docking misalignment: the grasped tube is not centered on the analyzer’s probe needle and fails to seat in the [FORMULA] mm-clearance inlet, so insertion remains incomplete. In tube sorting it is a placement error: System 1 releases the tube into a plate other than the one the active instruction designates. Because the workflow state remains nominal in both modes, neither head is designed to intercept them. Improving System 1 at these two steps is therefore the most direct route to higher workflow success. Robo-MLT has several limitations. System 1 and System 2 are learned from the same demonstrations but trained in separate stages, which adds engineering complexity. The skill library is extensible only in a restricted sense: the frozen planner re-orders and repeats existing skills freely, but a new laboratory operation requires demonstrations for System 1 and retraining of System 2, and the recovery head covers only the failure families seen in training. The sample-removal disturbance used in Sec. IV-B3 belongs to one of those families, so the reported RSR measures recovery from an in-distribution interruption and does not establish generalization to unseen ones. The two-task evaluation also uses the same workspace and object distributions as data collection, so robustness to broader scene shifts remains untested. Future work will relax the closed skill library toward open-ended instruction following, and strengthen System 1 through reinforcement fine-tuning and knowledge-isolation training that keeps action data from eroding the semantic priors of the VLM backbone. V Conclusion We presented Robo-MLT, a hierarchical dual-system framework for long-horizon manipulation in medical laboratory workflows. A frozen vision–language planner orders atomic skills, System 2 tracks the active skill from multiframe observations and invokes replanning of the remaining steps once that skill can no longer be completed, and System 1 generates continuous actions with a VLM-conditioned flow-matching policy under an asynchronous runtime. On both laboratory tasks, Robo-MLT completes more workflows and carries more samples through the full workflow than the policy baselines and the VLM-based monitor, leaving fewer batches for a technologist to finish by hand. It also resumes the remaining workflow after an operator removes the sample being handled, which the same system without workflow-level recovery never does, and it runs at the robot control rate on a single GPU. These results indicate that explicitly representing workflow progress can improve long-horizon execution when different task stages produce similar observations. Recovery is evaluated on a single disturbance type in a single workspace; extending the skill library and the disturbance coverage to a broader set of laboratory protocols remains future work.

ASPIRE: An Agentic System-Identification Platform for Iterative Reasoning and Exploration System identification requires expert decisions on the identification method, incorporation of prior physical knowledge, and model validation. We propose ASPIRE, a framework for nonlinear system identification in which a large language model agent selects and executes the identification method. ASPIRE constructs closed-form, nonlinear static or dynamic models from measured data, optionally supplemented by a system description, the intended use of the model, and physical requirements expressed formally or in natural language. Each model includes its parameters, an estimation record, an interpretation of its terms, and an error evaluated on test data inaccessible to the agent. Formal physical requirements are verified independently. ASPIRE operates autonomously or interactively, allowing the agent to ask questions and the user to request further analyses and identification rounds. We evaluate ASPIRE on three measured systems: a mobile robot, a rotational system with dry friction, and a laboratory fermenter. Each system is tested with and without a description, in five runs per task. All 30 runs delivered valid models, at a cost of 0.96 to 3.38 US dollars per run. An assessment by the authors found that, for the 30 models recommended by the agent, one per run, the interpretation of the model and the documentation of its structure selection and parameter estimation fully satisfied 132 of 150 assessed items and partly satisfied 18. The most frequent discrepancy, found in nine models, concerned inaccurate or unsupported claims about model structure selection. 1 Introduction In industrial applications, white-box models based on closed-form mathematical expressions are usually preferred to black-box models. Closed-form models relate inputs, states, and outputs through a small set of named parameters and, as such, are useful wherever a model must be interpreted, checked against physical knowledge, extrapolated beyond the range of the data, or embedded in model-based control. Obtaining such models from measured data requires several decisions by an expert: the identification method, the model class, how prior physical knowledge enters the estimation, the estimation criterion, and the validation procedure that matches the model’s intended use. Techniques such as symbolic regression (SR) and sparse regression automate the search for model structure [3, 7], and some SR tools allow for incorporating physical requirements and prior knowledge [20, 5, 6, 23, 44]. Agents based on large language models (LLMs) that write and execute code can choose the identification method: they can inspect the data, propose model structures informed by physical knowledge, implement a fitting procedure, or call an existing SR package and iterate. Recent systems couple LLM-proposed equation structures with numerical parameter fitting [36, 11], give an LLM a fixed set of code-execution tools for equation discovery [43], or let an agent apply physics-based analysis tools to infer properties of the system and then configure existing SR and sparse-regression packages accordingly [48]. In system identification, ASIA [32] delegates the choice of the model class, the training algorithm, and the hyperparameters to an autonomous coding agent. Existing agentic equation-discovery methods have several limitations: they do not support the specification and verification of physics-based requirements, evaluation on test data inaccessible to the agent, and documentation of the identification procedure. Furthermore, each delivered model should include a record of its structure and parameter estimation, distinguishing estimated parameters, fixed constants, and parameters derived from other parameters. The record should contain sufficient information to check the reported identification procedure against the executed code and execution logs. To the best of our knowledge, no published framework combines these features with agent-selected identification methods and a protocol for reporting variability across repeated runs. We propose ASPIRE11 1 ASPIRE stands for Agentic System-identification Platform for Iterative Reasoning and Exploration. It is unrelated to the robot-skill system of the same name [27]., a framework for system identification using LLM agents. ASPIRE constructs closed-form static or dynamic models from measured data, optionally supplemented by a system description, the model’s intended use, and physical requirements expressed formally or in natural language. The agent selects and executes the identification method, which may involve physically motivated model structures, symbolic or sparse regression, or custom estimation code. Each candidate model is accompanied by its parameter values, estimation procedure, interpretation, limitations, and test error. The agent also recommends one of the candidates. ASPIRE supports autonomous and interactive operation; in the latter, the agent can request information from the user, who can also request analyses and further identification rounds. The framework consists of one or more LLM agents responsible for identification and a software harness that executes their commands, enforces computational budgets, checks and evaluates candidate models, and records the identification runs. In summary, the main contributions of this paper are: We introduce ASPIRE, an agentic framework for system identification in which LLM agents autonomously select, implement, and execute identification methods to obtain nonlinear closed-form models from measured data. Unlike systems based on predefined modeling pipelines or restricted toolboxes, ASPIRE allows the agent to develop and compare alternative model structures and estimation procedures, including methods not specified in advance. We integrate physical knowledge and user interaction into agentic system identification. Users can specify the intended application, physical requirements, and available knowledge about the system, while the agent can request clarifications, explain its results, and revise models based on user feedback. Formal physical requirements are checked independently of the agent, including properties such as monotonicity, equilibrium conditions, and physically consistent behavior under specified operating conditions, which cannot be assessed by predictive accuracy alone. We develop an identification framework that separates autonomous model construction from independent model verification and evaluation. The framework prevents agents from accessing test data, verifies formal physical requirements, and retains executable models, parameter estimation records, and execution logs. This separation enables the identification procedure and its results to be examined and reproduced, despite the agent’s freedom to choose its methods. We demonstrate the framework on three experimentally measured systems: a mobile robot, a rotational system with dry friction, and a laboratory fermenter. Repeated experiments with and without system descriptions investigate the agent’s ability to identify models from data alone and to incorporate prior physical knowledge. The results show that the agent can construct models with competitive predictive accuracy while satisfying physical requirements that are not enforced by conventional symbolic regression and sparse identification methods. The experiments also quantify run-to-run variability and computational cost. The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work. Section 3 defines the identification problem. Section 4 describes the ASPIRE framework. Section 5 describes the test systems, the compared methods, and the experimental design. Section 6 presents the results, and Section 7 discusses them. Section 8 concludes the paper. 2 Related Work A prominent early example of LLM-in-the-loop equation discovery is FunSearch [34], which combines LLM-generated programs with automated evaluation in an evolutionary loop. AlphaEvolve [30] extends this paradigm from evolving individual functions to evolving programs comprising multiple functions and components. LLM-SR [36] also builds on the FunSearch framework, adapting it to scientific equation discovery by combining LLM-proposed equation structures with numerical optimization of their constants. Several refinements retain this fixed-pipeline character [11, 10, 42, 28, 1], including hybrids that embed the LLM as a guided variation operator inside genetic-programming search over dynamical-system equations [51]. A complementary line uses LLMs to synthesize components of the evolutionary search itself, such as parent-selection operators [50]. Recent agentic approaches give LLMs control over the computational steps of equation discovery. SR-Scientist [43] provides an LLM with a fixed set of code-execution tools for data analysis and equation evaluation, which it uses to iteratively refine candidate equations. KeplerAgent [48] uses physics-based tools to infer properties of the system and configure symbolic-regression methods such as PySR and PySINDy. STRIDE [39] organizes equation discovery into modules with fixed roles and uses self-reflection to guide corrections. In system identification, ASIA [32] uses an LLM as an autonomous coding agent built on existing agentic platforms. Given a plain-language problem description, the agent chooses the model class, training algorithm, and hyperparameters. ASIA was tested on two system-identification benchmarks. Its authors identify implicit test leakage, reduced methodological transparency, and reduced reproducibility as limitations. The environment in which an agent operates is examined in [14], where production coding agents are treated as opaque model-discovery operators, and in a position paper on the design of agent environments [45]. Neither work addresses system identification with physical requirements and closed-form model outputs. Table 1 compares ASPIRE with the three related systems. As in ASIA, the agent of ASPIRE chooses its identification method, and it is not restricted to a fixed set of methods as in SR-Scientist and KeplerAgent. ASPIRE differs from all three systems in the role of physical knowledge and in the output it delivers. The user states physical requirements either formally or in natural language, and the harness verifies the formal requirements for every delivered model. Every model is a closed-form expression with a record of its parameters, estimation procedure, and interpretation, and the execution logs allow this record to be checked against the agent’s actions. Moreover, the evaluation protocol keeps the test data inaccessible to the agent, which addresses the test leakage named by the authors of ASIA. Physical knowledge was used to constrain and guide symbolic regression before the introduction of LLM-based equation discovery. Existing approaches include multi-objective SR with constraint samples [20, 21] and search initialized with prior features [9]. Other methods add constraint losses into neural SR [22, 19]. These neural approaches have also been extended using asynchronous neuro-evolutionary search [23]. AI-Descartes and AI-Hilbert incorporate background axioms through logical reasoning and algebraic geometry [5, 6]. PG-SR encodes prior knowledge as executable constraint programs [44]. These methods use physical knowledge within predefined search procedures. ASPIRE supplies physical requirements to an agent that chooses its own identification procedure. The harness checks the formal requirements on each delivered model (Section 4.2). LLM-based agents also automate general machine-learning engineering. AIDE uses tree search over solution scripts [17]. Other examples include R&D-Agent [49], DS-Agent [13] and Kaggle-scale agents [12]. MLE-bench provides a benchmark for evaluating such agents [4]. Research-automation systems include the AI Scientist [26, 46], Curie [18], CodeScientist [16] and data-to-paper [15]. SWE-agent examines the interface between a language model and a software environment [47]. These systems deliver arbitrary models or artifacts, and none of them requires a closed-form model or verifies physical requirements. Agentic LLM systems have also been surveyed in robotics, where deployed systems are graded by their degree of autonomy, goal-directed behavior, adaptability, and decision-making [33]. We report predictive accuracy and model complexity, as in SRBench [24]. For dynamic systems, the identified model is simulated on test trajectories using only the measured inputs [35, 8]. Shared SR infrastructure such as SRToolkit [29] standardizes pipeline components to prevent implementation details from confounding method comparisons. ASPIRE addresses the evaluation of agents, for which the evaluator must be sealed against the system under test. We do not run SR-Scientist, KeplerAgent or ASIA on the tasks of this paper. None of these systems accepts formal requirements, a specified evaluation mode and sealed test data as inputs; running them under the conditions of this paper would require adaptations of each system, and the results would then describe the adaptation rather than the published system. As reference points for the test error, we use two established tools for closed-form models with published default settings, PySINDy [3, 37] and PySR [7]. Like the agentic systems, these tools do not accept physical requirements; we therefore report their test scores and, separately, whether their models violate the formal requirements of the task (Section 5.5). 3 Problem Definition We consider the identification of closed-form models of static and dynamic systems from measured data. The agent is a language model that carries out the identification: it inspects the data, proposes model structures, writes and runs estimation code, and explains its models. The harness is the software around the agent: it passes the task to the agent, executes the agent’s commands in a working directory, enforces a budget, checks and evaluates the delivered models, and stores a complete record of the session. The user specifies the task, answers the agent’s questions in interactive operation, and assesses the results. The test data stay with the harness and are sealed, that is, inaccessible through the agent’s files, tools, and conversation. One attempt by the agent to produce or revise a set of models within the budget is a round, and the set of models delivered at the end of that round is the pool. A session consists of one round in autonomous operation, and of several rounds with analyses between them in interactive operation (Section 4.6). After each round, the user receives the models with their errors on the training, validation, and test data, the outcomes of the physical requirements, the agent’s recommendation, and the models as executable code. The harness presents these results as a report for reading in a browser (Section 6.3). A task has a compulsory and an optional part. The user must provide the training data, the model form of Section 3 with the roles of the data columns, the evaluation mode (Section 4.5) and the budget; a dynamic task also needs the sampling period and the measurement equation (4). Everything else is optional: validation data, test data, a description of the system and of the data, the intended use of the model, physical requirements, known constants, and references to model families from the literature. The division of the data into training, validation, and test data is made by the user. The agent receives this information as a task brief, a text that the harness generates from the specification by fixed rules, without a language model, and that also states what the user did not provide. By default, a model may contain the arithmetic operations, powers, the elementary functions ( [FORMULA] , [FORMULA] , the square root, the trigonometric and hyperbolic functions and their inverses), the absolute value, the sign, the minimum and the maximum, and piecewise definitions with relational and logical conditions; the user may adapt this set. Every value obtained by parameter estimation is a named parameter, whereas a numeric literal that belongs to the form of an expression, such as the exponent in [FORMULA] , is not. The user states physical knowledge either as formal requirements or in natural language. A formal requirement has one of the nine types of Table 2, which consolidates the constraint types of the physics-aware SR methods of [20, 21, 22], and it specifies the expression concerned, the domain, and the tolerance. For example, the states of the friction system of Section 5.2 are an angle [FORMULA] and an angular velocity [FORMULA] , and a requirement of the type equation, [FORMULA] , ensures that every delivered model keeps this kinematic relation. The harness verifies the formal requirements on every delivered model (Section 4.5), and by default, a demonstrated violation excludes the model from the ranking and from the recommendation. Requirements in natural language are passed to the agent verbatim and are assessed by the user. The user either states the requirements in natural language or enters necessary conditions of the nine types that follow from it, each on a stated domain; Table 4 gives an example of formal requirements, and Appendix C gives an example of requirements in natural language. The agent is instructed to explore different identification approaches, such as physically motivated modeling, symbolic regression (SR), and sparse regression, and to deliver a pool of candidate models with distinct structures rather than variations of the same model form. The maximum number of candidates is specified by the user. The agent may recommend one candidate based on the training and validation data, and this recommendation is recorded before any test results become available. Each candidate consists of the model equations and a model record with three parts: a parameter table, an estimation record, and a discussion. The parameter table lists every named quantity in the equations, specifying its value, unit, type, and description. Three parameter types are distinguished: fitted, for values estimated from data; fixed, for values specified independently of estimation, with their source identified (the task, physics, literature, normalization, or a modeling choice); and tied, for values computed from other parameters using a stated equation. The estimation record specifies the estimation criterion, the data used, the estimation method, and its starting values, together with the reasons for these choices. It also identifies the script that reproduces the estimated values. The discussion identifies the model family, interprets each term in the equations, explains how the model structure was obtained, and describes the model’s limitations. Terms without a known physical interpretation are characterized by their mathematical effects. The account of model construction distinguishes structures derived from physical reasoning, obtained through search, or proposed as hypotheses, and documents the alternatives considered and the reasons for subsequent modifications. The model record follows a common format across all tasks. The agent receives a template with an example based on an artificial system, along with instructions to define every symbol, specify units for numerical values, cite only verifiable references, justify modeling choices, and avoid unsupported physical interpretations. Section 6.3 summarizes a delivered record, and Appendix B gives three delivered models with their parameter tables. The harness checks the completeness and consistency of each record with the model equations. In particular, all symbols must be declared, all parameters must be used, and the expressions must be real and finite on the training data. These checks do not establish whether the reported estimation procedure was actually followed or whether a parameter declared as fitted was estimated as stated. The harness, therefore, retains the agent’s scripts and execution logs, allowing the reported identification procedure to be checked against the actual computations. The agent may read and write files in its working directory, write and run code, search the web, install software packages, and delegate subtasks to helper agents, which are further instances of the language model. Its environment contains Python with numerical libraries, among them SciPy [41], the SR package gplearn [38], and the sparse-regression package PySINDy [37]; whether it uses them is its decision. Models of any kind, including black-box models, may serve as intermediate tools, but only closed-form models are to be delivered. The instruction that the agent receives with every request – the system prompt – is given in Appendix A. No tool gives access to the test data or to evaluation results. Restricting the agent, for example, to forbid web access, can be stated in the task description. An identification round is summarized in Algorithm 1. A turn is one response of the language model, which either requests actions or declares the pool complete. A round is limited in the number of turns, in the execution time, and in the cost of the language model; the default limits are 60 turns, 3600 s, and 10 US dollars. When the agent declares the pool complete, the harness checks the candidates; if none pass, the agent receives the reasons and may correct the pool once. When a limit is reached, the harness evaluates all candidates delivered so far to ensure valid models are not discarded. The harness records every request, response, command, and result of a session, along with the language model identifier, software versions, and cost. The harness computes all predictions used in the evaluation, with the same settings for all candidates. A static model is evaluated algebraically. A dynamic model is evaluated either by one-step-ahead prediction from the measured state or by simulation, as specified in the task. In simulation, the state is initialized once per trajectory, and the model state is propagated using the recorded inputs without correction from later measurements. By default, a continuous-time model is integrated by the fourth-order Runge–Kutta method, with one step per sampling period and the input held constant over the step. A simulation error grows with the simulated length, so that simulation errors on trajectories of different lengths are not comparable. If the test trajectories are shorter than the training and validation trajectories, the user may therefore specify a horizon [FORMULA] , the number of sampling periods simulated in a test trajectory. The harness then divides every training and validation trajectory into consecutive segments of [FORMULA] sampling periods that do not overlap; the last segment of a trajectory may be shorter. Each segment is simulated on its own: the state is initialized from the measured state at the first sample of the segment and is propagated to the end of the segment without correction. The starting points of the simulations are thus [FORMULA] samples apart. This differs from a receding horizon, in which a simulation of [FORMULA] samples would start at every sample. Every sample after the initialization of a trajectory is scored exactly once. The training and validation errors are the root mean squared errors (RMSEs) pooled over all segments, computed using (6) with the segments in place of the test trajectories. The test trajectories are not divided. The candidates are ranked by the RMSE of the output, pooled over the test trajectories [FORMULA] , where [FORMULA] is the measured output, [FORMULA] the predicted or simulated output, [FORMULA] the set of scored samples of trajectory [FORMULA] and [FORMULA] its size. The test score [FORMULA] has the unit of the output. A candidate is eligible for the ranking if it passes the checks of Section 4.3, has no demonstrated violation of a formal requirement, and completes the evaluation on every test trajectory with real and finite values. The recommendation of the agent is made without test data. In contrast, the ranking by [FORMULA] uses the test data: it shows whether the pool contains an accurate model, not whether that model can be recognized without test data. We therefore call the lowest [FORMULA] in a pool an oracle-based selection and always report it with the pool size. The harness verifies each formal requirement symbolically where its type permits, and otherwise by sampling its domain. The outcome is a proof, a counterexample or an inconclusive result; a sampled check that finds no violation is inconclusive. Because language model responses are stochastic, a task is commonly run several times under identical settings, called an experiment. For an experiment, we report the number of runs attempted, the number of runs that delivered a pool passing the checks, and the number of runs with at least one eligible candidate. Each quantity is reported as the mean and the sample standard deviation across the runs, along with the cost. In interactive operation, the user takes an active part throughout the session. During a round, the agent may ask the user a specific question whose answer would affect a modeling choice. If the user cannot answer, the agent states the assumption it makes and how that assumption limits the result. After a round, the user receives the complete evaluation, including the test errors, whereas the agent receives only the results on the training and validation data. The user may then ask the agent for an explanation or a further analysis, or give feedback and request a new round, in which the agent revises the pool; earlier pools are kept. Because the user may have seen test results before giving feedback, every later round is labeled test-informed and is not presented as an independent test of the identification. A session can also start from the user’s data files alone, without any accompanying description or metadata. In a task interview, an agent examines the training and validation data, proposes what the data show (the roles of the columns, the sampling period, the ranges), asks the user for what the data do not determine (what the system is, what the model will be used for, the units, the physical requirements), and writes the task specification. The user confirms or edits the resulting task brief before the identification starts. The test data are sealed from the interview and from every agent. Every question, answer, request and change of the task is part of the session record. 7 Discussion Prior knowledge did not reduce test error. In all three systems, the mean test score of the described task is higher than that of the blind task (Table 5): by 0.0029 m for the mobile robot, by 0.0009 rad for the friction system and by 0.0008 bar for the fermenter. We state these differences as observations on five runs each and on small test sets; for the friction system and the fermenter, the difference is smaller than the sample standard deviation of the blind runs (0.0079 rad and 0.0010 bar). For the friction system, the five described scores (0.0292 to 0.0459 rad) and the five blind scores (0.0322 to 0.0492 rad) cover nearly the same range. The models differ in form. All five recommended models of the described task contain a mechanism for sticking at rest, which the description and the intended use name, and none of the blind task does; the blind models also violate R2 (Section 6.2). The test score does not show this difference. The test data contain little of what it concerns: the two free decays, in which the system comes to rest, are 230 of the 978 scored samples. For the mobile robot, the five blind scores (0.0379 to 0.0415 m) all lie below the five described scores (0.0417 to 0.0443 m). A possible explanation is that with the description, the agent recommends the kinematic model with two gains, whereas four of the five blind models contain a dead zone in the response to an input, the term that also lowers the test score in the pools of the described task. The results of the blind tasks also address the question of recall (Section 5.4). Without any name or description, the agent reached test errors that were not higher, and for two systems, it arrived at the physical structure from the data alone. The low errors, therefore, do not depend on a model that the language model recalls from a description of the system. The described models consist of terms with a physical name and a unit, and they have fewer parameters for two of the three systems ( [FORMULA] against [FORMULA] for the mobile robot and [FORMULA] against [FORMULA] for the fermenter). For the fermenter, the described task specifies a physically interpretable model, whereas the blind task produces cubic polynomials with comparable test errors. The described models also satisfy physical properties specified in the task requirements: the direction of the gravitational torque at rest for the friction system (R2), and monotonicity and equilibrium conditions for the fermenter (R1–R5; Section 6.3). These properties are not reflected in the test error and must be assessed separately or specified as formal requirements. The task description also influences the quality of the model records: in the assessment of Section 6.3, 13 of the 18 marks other than yes concern blind tasks. The harness checks the completeness and consistency of model records but cannot verify their content. We therefore assessed the records manually. None of the 30 records contained an undisclosed discrepancy between the declared parameter types and the estimation scripts. However, nine records contained discrepancies between the reported origin of the model structure and the execution logs. In some cases, the record attributed a modeling choice to an analysis that had actually followed it; in others, it described a comparison more broadly than the executed analysis justified. The records, therefore, documented the methods and results more reliably than the reasoning and sequence of decisions that led to them. The execution logs provide the evidence needed to verify these accounts. A user can give the same data and the same description to a general coding agent in a conversation, with the same language model and the same tools, and ask for a closed-form model. We have no evidence that the harness changes the error of the identified models. ASPIRE provides a curated interface for agentic system identification; it brings value in aspects such as whether a result can be trusted, compared, and reproduced. The test data are outside the agent’s reach, and one implementation computes all errors. The recommendation is fixed before any test result exists. The deliverable has a checked form, and the formal requirements are verified on every model. The complete record of a run is stored. A task is repeated with identical settings, so that the variability of the agent is reported with the result. In a conversation, each of these properties depends on what the user arranges and maintains manually. The test data are sealed against the agent but not against the authors, who used them during the development of the framework and of the tasks. All runs used one language model, for which the vendor publishes no dated snapshot, so that the results do not establish how ASPIRE performs with other models, and the model behind the identifier may change. While preliminary experiments have shown that ASPIRE also works with different models, it has not been evaluated on a larger scale. Assumptions (A1)–(A3) in Section 3 restrict the framework to a single scored output, to systems whose states are measured, and to a given measurement equation. A score that combines several outputs is not part of the framework. 8 Conclusions We proposed ASPIRE, a framework for system identification in which an LLM agent selects and executes the identification method and delivers closed-form models from measured data and the prior knowledge that the user provides. Every model found by ASPIRE is accompanied by a record of its parameters, of their estimation, and of its interpretation; the formal physical requirements are verified on it; and its error is computed on test data that the agent cannot access. ASPIRE runs autonomously or in a dialogue with the user. We evaluated ASPIRE on three measured systems, each with and without a description of the system. All 30 runs delivered valid models, at a cost of 0.96 to 3.38 US dollars per run. For the rotational motion under dry friction, the task stated formal requirements on the direction of the gravitational torque and on the polarity of the motor, and the verification demonstrated no violation in any model found by the agent. Table 6 compares the test errors of the recommended models with those of the models found by PySINDy and PySR. Withholding the description did not increase the test error. It changed the form of the models: with the description, the models consisted of physically named terms and, for two systems, had fewer parameters. In the assessment of the model records of the 30 recommended models, 132 of the 150 marks were yes, 18 partly and none no (Table 7). The records documented the methods and the results more reliably than the sequence of decisions that led to them: nine records differed from the execution logs in one claim on the origin of the model (Section 7.2). In an interactive session on the data of the mobile robot, an analysis requested by the user attributed 83 % of the squared one-step prediction error of the heading to the first sample after a change of the commands, and the user’s feedback led to a smaller pool with simpler expressions, while the test error of the recommended model did not change (Section 6.5). In our future research, we will extend ASPIRE to systems with several outputs and with unmeasured states, compare several language models, and evaluate the interactive operation with users who did not take part in the development of the framework. We will also evaluate how the agent can guide the collection of data in interactive operation: from the training and validation data and the intended use, the agent suggests to the user which data to obtain, so that the operating regions relevant to the problem that the data do not yet sufficiently cover are covered, and the user adds the new data between the identification rounds. We will also equip the harness with an agent that can assess the compliance of the models with the requirements stated in natural language. DOBB: Dynamic Oriented Bounding Boxes for Multi-Agent Collision Avoidance under State Uncertainty and Heterogeneous Dynamics Learning-based decentralized collision avoidance must remain reliable under state-estimation uncertainty and heterogeneous agent dynamics. Existing methods typically address these factors through training-domain variation or by exposing uncertainty and capability estimates to the policy at runtime. However, both leave the policy to infer how these quantities should alter the physical separation required for safe interaction, which can couple collision-avoidance behavior to relationships learned from the training distribution. We introduce the Dynamic Oriented Bounding Box (DOBB), an online geometric representation that maps the current state estimate, uncertainty, and agent-specific response characteristics into a dynamic, direction-dependent safety margin. We derive geometric features that jointly characterize the relative configuration and severity of interactions between agents’ DOBBs, along with a reward function that preserves the physical interpretation of those interactions. Across four evaluation environments, DOBB achieves the lowest mean total failure rate of 2.6%. This performance persists under out-of-distribution shifts in actuation dynamics and state-estimation uncertainty, with collision-based failure remaining at or below 2.3% in every tested condition. We attribute this robustness to the geometric abstraction of the safety margin, which is less coupled to the specific uncertainty and actuation regimes encountered during training. Code open-sourced at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/DOBB-Collision-Avoidance-8D16/README.md I Introduction Learning-based decentralized collision avoidance (DCA) enables multi-agent navigation from locally available observations without centralized coordination. In physical fleets, the safety of an interaction depends not only on the estimated relative configuration, but also on uncertainty in that estimate and differences in agent physical footprint and actuation response. State-estimation uncertainty and agent heterogeneity have therefore become recurring concerns in learning-based DCA. Two recurring themes characterize much of the learning-based DCA literature. First, and most commonly, experience-based approaches accommodate uncertainty and heterogeneity through the observations, interactions, and temporal context available to the policy during training. Examples include noise-augmented observations, variation in agent(s) properties (i.e. radius, swarm size) or behavior (cooperative vs. non-cooperative), and temporal context from stacked observations fed to recurrent encoders [1, 2, 3, 4]. These mechanisms improve robustness by emulating real-life conditions and interactions during learning and/or leverage recurrent architectures for latent-state inference. Second, more recently with a smaller body of work, explicit-runtime approaches quantify uncertainty or related predictive confidence during execution and incorporate it directly into the decision process. Depending on the formulation, the resulting estimate may enter the policy observation or reward, modify an optimization objective or action distribution, or trigger a fallback controller [5, 6, 7, 8]. These two approaches impose different inference burdens on the collision-avoidance policy. Consider an experience-based policy trained with noise-augmented position measurements to emulate localization uncertainty. At execution, the policy observes the corrupted measurements but is not given the underlying noise magnitude; it must infer the severity of uncertainty from the observed fluctuations and subsequently learn how that uncertainty should alter its avoidance behavior. An explicit-runtime formulation can partially alleviate this burden by quantifying an estimate of this uncertainty (e.g. position covariance) at each time step. Explicit access to uncertainty therefore removes the need to infer its severity, but it does not specify how uncertainty and agent heterogeneity should alter the separation required for safe interaction. This limitation can be viewed as a representation problem. In collision avoidance, state uncertainty and agent response characteristics affect the spatial margin that should be maintained during an interaction. Consequently, the same estimated relative configuration can imply different separation requirements across uncertainty levels and agent capabilities, where these effects may be directionally dependent. For example, identical estimated positions and velocities can correspond to materially different interactions when one agent is poorly localized and has tighter acceleration limits (e.g., due to a lower thrust-to-weight ratio), whereas another is accurately localized and more maneuverable. When these quantities are provided only as policy inputs, their spatial implications must still be learned from experience. This learned mapping can become coupled to the uncertainty and actuation regimes represented during training, making the resulting collision-avoidance behavior susceptible to degradation when deployment conditions depart from that distribution. We address this representation problem with the Dynamic Oriented Bounding Box (DOBB), an online geometric abstraction that maps the current state estimate, its uncertainty, and agent-specific response characteristics into a dynamic, direction-dependent safety margin. Rather than exposing these quantities independently to the policy, DOBB represents their joint effect on the spatial relationship between interacting agents and recomputes this representation as operating conditions change. We further derive geometric interaction features that characterize the relative configuration and severity of interactions between agents’ DOBBs, along with a reward that preserves the physical interpretation of these interactions. The evaluation in Sec. VI shows that DOBB reduces collision failures relative to both experience-based and explicit-runtime representations, with the improvement persisting under out-of-distribution shifts in actuation dynamics and state-estimation uncertainty. II Related Work Experience-based approaches seek robustness by embedding uncertainty and agent variation in the conditions encountered during learning or by providing additional context from which partially observed state can be inferred. In [2], observed neighbor positions and velocities are perturbed with Gaussian noise sampled across a range of magnitudes. The resulting blind-noise policy handles unknown noise magnitudes within that range, but degrades when evaluated under a different noise distribution. In [3] and [4], policies are trained across varying agent populations and behaviors, with LSTM encoders used to represent a variable number of surrounding agents. [3] additionally varies radius and preferred speed, while [4] injects sensing and action noise. The latter reports a simulation-to-real gap attributed in part to under-actuated quadrotor dynamics absent from training. In [1], three consecutive LiDAR scans provide short-horizon temporal information from which the policy can infer obstacle motion and geometry. Although trained with homogeneous discs, the resulting policy generalizes to previously unseen square robots. These studies demonstrate that broader training experience can improve robustness and generalization. However, when uncertainty magnitude or response characteristics are not directly represented, the policy must infer them from the available evidence and learn how their severity should alter avoidance behavior. This reliance on learned relationships can degrade when deployment conditions depart from those represented during training. Explicit-runtime approaches reduce part of this inference burden by quantifying uncertainty or related predictive confidence during execution and allowing the current estimate to influence action selection directly. In [5], bootstrapped LSTM ensembles and MC dropout estimate the mean and variance of collision probability for candidate motion primitives, and an MPC penalizes both expected collision risk and model uncertainty. The resulting uncertainty signal identifies novel observations and reduces collisions under sensing perturbations absent from training. In [6], a GRU predicts the next LiDAR scan and its per-beam aleatoric uncertainty, which is mapped to the variance of a SAC policy so that higher uncertainty elicits more conservative behavior. In [7], future pedestrian positions are represented as bivariate Gaussians, with the predicted covariance incorporated into both the policy state and a collision-probability reward. This reduces collisions relative to the corresponding uncertainty-unaware prediction model. In [8], uncertainty in the policy distribution is combined with proximity conditions to trigger an ORCA fallback, where surrounding human radii are enlarged by a fixed factor. These approaches make uncertainty available during execution but do not derive a state-dependent safety margin from it. In [5, 6, 7], uncertainty changes the optimization objective, policy distribution, or learning signal, while the physical clearance that results is still determined by optimization or policy learning. [8] comes closest to an explicit geometric response, but only after a manually calibrated high-risk condition is satisfied. The controller then reverts to ORCA with a fixed 1.5-times radius enlargement. The resulting inflation is isotropic, discontinuous, and independent of further changes in uncertainty once the threshold has been exceeded. A complementary line of work modifies collision geometry directly. Prior ORCA variants inflate the represented agent radius to account for differential-drive constraints [9], tracking-error bounds [10], or observation noise [2]. These methods alter the safety margin explicitly, but the added clearance remains isotropic and follows a prescribed rule for the corresponding condition. Such inflation can consume available free space unnecessarily when the source of additional risk is directional. Work in [11] address this limitation with an Oriented Bounding Capsule for shape heterogeneity and a speed-dependent risk capsule whose forward length increases by [FORMULA] . This representation recovers lateral free space discarded by circular models and improves performance in dense heterogeneous scenes. [11] therefore provide the closest geometric precursor to DOBB. Unlike DOBB, however, [11] assumes perfect sensing and instantaneous velocity execution. Prior work addresses complementary aspects of the same representation problem. Learning-based approaches either broaden the conditions encountered during training or expose uncertainty and capability estimates explicitly at runtime, while leaving their spatial implications largely to policy learning. Geometric approaches only partially address this mapping: existing methods typically use prescribed, often isotropic margin modifications for individual effects such as sensing noise, tracking error, or kinematic constraints, while the closest learning-based geometric treatment [11] captures shape and speed heterogeneity but does not account for state-estimation uncertainty or finite actuation response. DOBB instead provides a unified geometric representation in which state uncertainty and heterogeneous actuation response jointly determine a dynamic, direction-dependent safety margin exposed to the policy. VI Evaluation We evaluate how the representation of state-estimation uncertainty and agent heterogeneity affects collision-avoidance performance under both in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) conditions. The evaluation addresses two research questions. RQ1: How does collision-avoidance performance change across progressively higher-fidelity training environments and when uncertainty and heterogeneity are represented through experience-based learning, explicit-runtime information, or DOBB geometry? RQ2: How well do these representations generalize as state-estimation uncertainty moves beyond the training distribution? To capture training variability, each policy is trained independently three times, with one checkpoint per run selected on a disjoint validation set. The selected policies are evaluated on 500 ten-agent test scenarios. We report mutually exclusive scenario-level rates for collision only, timeout only, and joint collision-and-timeout outcomes, with total failure defined as their union. VII Conclusion Learning-based collision avoidance has primarily addressed state uncertainty and agent heterogeneity through training-domain variation or explicit runtime inputs. DOBB provides a complementary geometric representation that maps the current state estimate, uncertainty, and heterogeneous agent response into a dynamic, direction-dependent safety margin recomputed at every decision step. Furthermore, we derive geometric interaction features that characterize the relative configuration and severity of interactions between agents’ DOBBs, along with a reward that preserves the physical interpretation of these interactions. Across the evaluated training environments and OOD conditions (i.e. actuation-shifts & high position uncertainty), DOBB maintains the lowest collision incidence, with collision-based failure at or below 2.3% in every tested condition. We attribute this to DOBB’s abstraction of uncertainty and agent response through safety geometry, which preserves consistent physical interpretations across different operating conditions. At sufficiently high uncertainty, however, the resulting safety regions consume more of the available free space and increasingly restrict admissible motion, which ultimitely shifts residual failure toward timeouts. This exposes a safety–progress tradeoff under severe uncertainty, with DOBB favoring safety until conditions return nominal.
