Ground Reaction Force-Aware Model Predictive Control [0.5ex]for Underactuated Upright Physical Assistance Many rehabilitation robots execute prescribed motions using reactive tracking controllers that do not explicitly incorporate the user’s instantaneous human–ground interaction. This paper presents Ground Reaction Force-Aware Model Predictive Control (GRF-MPC), a framework for upright physical assistance. By integrating live GRF and center of pressure (CoP) measurements directly into a human centroidal dynamics model, GRF-MPC formulates a real-time quadratic program (QP) that optimizes assistive forces and moments over a receding horizon. We deployed GRF-MPC on the Robotic Upright Stand Trainer (RobUST) in an underactuated 4-cable configuration and evaluated it against a fully actuated 8-cable Cartesian impedance baseline in nearly 300 trials across six healthy participants. Across tasks spanning impulsive perturbations, lunge trajectories, and voluntary limits of stability, GRF-MPC reduced peak planar center-of-mass (CoM) error by 19.6% during perturbations, lowered trajectory tracking error by 24.1%, required 28.7% less net mechanical work, and permitted a 45.9% greater normalized voluntary excursion area. The underlying QP solves in under 1 ms, comfortably enabling 100 Hz replanning and demonstrating that incorporating live human–ground interaction into predictive control yields stronger, more transparent physical assistance with half the actuators. I Introduction Individuals with mobility impairments resulting from spinal cord injury (SCI), cerebral palsy, and stroke are often wheelchair-bound or need significant assistance to stand. These conditions affect millions worldwide, with approximately 17,000 new SCI cases annually in the United States alone [1]. Prolonged sitting leads to further muscle deterioration, creating a vicious cycle where weakened muscles make it increasingly difficult to stand leading to further degeneration. To break this cycle, robot-assisted rehabilitation offers customized targeted interventions that enable precise motion control, quantitative assessment capabilities, and reduced physical burden on therapists [2]. However, many robots for human assistance or rehabilitation, including frame-mounted mechanisms or exosuits, primarily employ control strategies focused on kinematic outcomes or provide joint-level torque assistance. During healthy overground locomotion, humans generate stability and propulsion through ground-contact forces at the foot-ground interface. When an assistive controller injects forces based on trajectory deviations without accounting for these existing ground reaction forces (GRFs), the resulting net force can produce center of mass (CoM) accelerations that are misaligned with the intended movement direction. Such mismatch can lead to corrective assistance that opposes natural motion or requires compensatory action from the user or therapist. To address the lack of GRF consideration in real-time rehabilitative control, this paper adapts predictive techniques from legged locomotion to physical human-robot interaction. We propose a novel GRF-aware Model Predictive Control (GRF-MPC) framework that proactively optimizes assistance at every time step using real-time centroidal dynamics. Measured net GRF and center of pressure (CoP) are incorporated directly into the human centroidal dynamics, providing the external human-ground interaction needed to predict CoM evolution without estimating internal joint torques or forecasting a detailed multibody motion. Embedding this measurement-driven model in a constrained quadratic program (QP) inherently handles underactuation while explicitly enforcing cable tension limits. We experimentally validate this formulation on the Robotic Upright Stand Trainer (RobUST), a custom frame-mounted, cable-driven system (Fig. 1) that applies configurable forces to the user’s body with minimal added inertia [3, 4, 5]. Compared to an impedance control baseline, GRF-MPC demonstrates improved dynamic tracking and greater efficiency, despite allowing a larger permissible volitional workspace. The principal contributions are: The formulation of GRF-MPC, a centroidal dynamics controller for human physical assistance in which live GRF measurements serve as the enabling observation that completes the predictive model. A convex QP formulation with sub-millisecond solve times and 100 Hz replanning that natively accommodates underactuation and tension constraints. Human-subject validation on the RobUST platform across disturbance rejection, prescribed CoM tracking, net mechanical work, and voluntary workspace, comparing the underactuated 4-cable GRF-MPC against an 8-cable impedance-control baseline. II Background and Motivation Recent systematic reviews emphasize that effective robot-assisted gait rehabilitation relies heavily on intelligent control strategies that encompass assistive, resistive, and perturbative interventions [6]. From a clinical perspective, interventions that successfully combine trajectory-tracking with compliant or adaptive assistance demonstrate the highest efficacy for motor function recovery [7]. To deliver these clinically desired outcomes, many lower-limb rehabilitation or assistive robots predominantly employ a hierarchical control architecture. Systems ranging from treadmill-bound trainers [8] to more recent exoskeletons like WalkON [9] and Atalante [10, 11] typically operate by first synthesizing offline reference kinematic trajectories known to satisfy Zero-Moment Point (ZMP) stability criterion under quasi-static assumptions. During online operation, these controllers predominantly adopt a trajectory-tracking strategy that rigidly attenuates state deviations to enforce the reference motion [12, 13]. Because they act to minimize kinematic errors rather than regulating contact forces, they lack explicit, real-time modulation of the underlying ground reaction forces. Consequently, all natural gait variations are treated as tracking errors, resulting in corrective forces that fight human intent. While rehabilitation robotics still relies heavily on prescribed trajectory tracking, legged robotics has increasingly adopted dynamics-aware predictive control [14]. A key enabler of highly dynamic behaviors—including running, bounding, and acrobatic maneuvers—has been the explicit incorporation of ground reaction forces into the control formulation. This transition was largely enabled by utilizing a centroidal dynamics abstraction, which establishes a direct mapping between contact GRFs and the robot’s spatial CoM [15]. By formulating this relationship as an MPC problem, controllers can proactively optimize GRF profiles over a finite time horizon. Di Carlo et al. [16], for example, demonstrated that a convex approximation could be solved at high frequency on the MIT Cheetah 3 to support impressive real-time disturbance rejection and blind terrain traversal. Despite these parallel breakthroughs, contemporary reviews of lower-limb exoskeleton and rehabilitation control strategies confirm that the current state-of-the-art heavily relies on impedance, adaptive robust, or assist-as-needed architectures [17, 18]—techniques that remain fundamentally reactive. This lack of predictive foresight is largely due to a key distinction: in legged robotics, GRFs are control outputs—the robot generates them through known actuators at sensed contact points. For a human subject, GRFs are exogenous inputs generated from the user’s volitional muscle activity and can be neither commanded nor predicted by the assistive robot. Examining the centroidal dynamics (Sec. III-A), the CoM linear and angular acceleration depends on gravity, the robot’s exerted forces onto the user, and the user’s own GRF. Without measuring GRF, the net force on the CoM is unknown and no predictive model of the human’s spatial dynamics can be formulated. GRF measurement thus transforms an otherwise unobservable system into one amenable to predictive control. This is fundamentally distinct from approaches that add force feedback to an existing controller; the live measured GRF is what makes a meaningful predictive model possible. By closing the control loop around live GRF measurements, GRF-MPC bridges this divide thus advancing upright physical assistance from reactive kinematic tracking to proactive, dynamics-aware collaboration. VI Discussion The experimental data demonstrates a systematic superiority of GRF-MPC over the state-of-the-art baseline, despite underactuation. The transient perturbation data (Task 1) exposes a critical biomechanical limitation of many existing exoskeleton and rehabilitation robots. While it succeeds in quickly returning the user to a setpoint, it fails to meaningfully mitigate the initial peak excursion. In a purely reactive architecture, restorative forces are strictly proportional to state error; the user remains unassisted during the initial impact dynamics. Mitigating this initial displacement would require increasing stiffness gains, which inherently compromises dynamic comfort and compliance. GRF-MPC achieves a nearly 20% reduction in peak displacement compared to the impedance baseline. This reduction is achieved alongside lower energy metrics and higher compliance in subsequent tasks, demonstrating algorithmic superiority rather than mismatched or weak tuning. Lunging motion (Task 2) further confirms this performance advantage during voluntary motion. The lunge task establishes superior tracking performance by GRF-MPC. By actively predicting the required trajectory forces, GRF-MPC achieved 24.1% better tracking precision than the 8-cable impedance controller. Crucially, the concurrent 28.7% reduction in commanded mechanical work proves this precision is not the result of an under-tuned impedance baseline. The MPC intelligently coordinates the underactuated tensions to track the reference more efficiently, achieving tighter adherence while expending less robotic effort. Finally, the Permitted Workspace Mapping (Task 3) contextualizes the stiffness-compliance trade-off. Both active controllers constrain the operational envelope relative to the unassisted Transparent condition. However, GRF-MPC—which already established superior tracking and disturbance rejection—gracefully manages underactuation to expand the dynamically stable workspace, permitting 45.9% more volitional excursion area than the impedance condition. This was achieved while executed in a 4-cable configuration where standard pseudo-inverse Cartesian control is mathematically infeasible. Several limitations of the current implementation warrant consideration and motivate future improvements. First, the SRB approximation relies on a coarse estimated inertia matrix [FORMULA] and neglects configuration-dependent rotational dynamics. Second, treating the measured GRFs as constant over the prediction horizon enables a convex QP formulation, but compromises prediction accuracy when contact forces vary substantially. Extending the horizon indefinitely is therefore not necessarily advantageous, since longer predictions extrapolate stale contact-force measurements. Future iterations could address these linearizations by quantifying bounded deviations of [FORMULA] and [FORMULA] to implement Robust or Tube MPC techniques [31]. Third, the present validation was limited to healthy young adults; performance and safety in populations with neurological or musculoskeletal impairments remain to be established. Finally, the system currently relies on floor-mounted force plates to measure GRF and CoP directly. Because the control formulation requires measurement or estimates of human–ground interaction, deployment outside instrumented environments will require alternative wearable sensing paradigms or real-time GRF estimation techniques. Additionally, to provide an equivalent comparison to trajectory tracking in exoskeletons and rehabilitation robots, the current controller forces a time-based progression along [FORMULA] . However, clinical literature indicates that allowing rehabilitation patients to self-pace their progression through a path in space increases active participation and motor learning [32, 33]. A promising future extension is the adaptation of Model Predictive Contouring Control (MPCC) [34]. MPCC decouples path geometry from time by penalizing contour deviations while treating path progress as an optimization variable. By relaxing or removing the progress-maximizing term within the MPCC objective, the controller could provide dynamically safe, spatial-only boundaries, enabling fully patient-driven pacing during rehabilitation tasks. VII Conclusion Current robotic human motion assistance paradigms fundamentally rely on reactive kinematic controllers that neglect the dynamic influence of immediate ground reaction forces. To address this gap, this paper introduced GRF-MPC on the RobUST platform, translating centroidal predictive control methods from legged robotics to upright physical assistance. Experimental validation confirmed that explicitly modeling the relationship between GRFs and spatial center of mass dynamics enables proactive physical support. Implemented in an underactuated 4-cable configuration, GRF-MPC systematically outperformed a fully actuated 8-cable Cartesian impedance baseline. GRF-MPC safely arrested transient momentum with lower peak deviations during unexpected perturbations, achieved superior dynamic tracking precision while exerting significantly less mechanical work, and preserved a substantially larger kinematically transparent workspace during voluntary motion. Ultimately, this work demonstrates that shifting from rigid path-enforcement to dynamically consistent, GRF-aware control yields more fluid, efficient, and biomechanically accurate patient support.

Latent Barrier Steering: Hierarchical Safety for Generative Planning We introduce Latent Barrier Steering (LBS), a hierarchical semantic-to-path framework for safe flow-matching-based generative planning. Existing control-barrier-function (CBF) safety filters for diffusion and flow-matching planners act locally on generated samples, either during sampling or after prediction. Such repair is effective for small violations, but can struggle when a new constraint blocks the whole selected behavior mode rather than merely perturbing it locally. LBS decouples behavior selection from path certification through two coordinated interventions: it first steers the generator’s behavior latent toward rollouts with larger safety margin, then decodes the steered latent and applies a path-space CBF quadratic program (QP) only for residual violations. We show that latent steering increases the margin available to the path-space corrector, yielding finite-time recovery guarantees and reduced correction burden. Experiments across navigation and robot end-effector planning tasks show that LBS preserves safety while improving goal reaching and reducing correction burden compared with path-level safety filters. 1 Introduction Robotic path planning must combine expressive behavior generation with strong safety guarantees. Generative policies, including diffusion and flow-matching planners, are attractive because they model multimodal trajectory distributions and synthesize diverse high-dimensional behaviors from demonstrations [16, 10, 34, 23, 17, 5, 3, 2]. Yet deployment safety is not inherited from offline training: new obstacles, workspace limits, or feasibility constraints can shift the test-time problem away from the demonstrations used to train the generator. This has motivated safe generative planners that combine learned samplers with control barrier functions (CBFs), which encode safety through a barrier-defined set, and impose constraints through quadratic programs or related filtering steps [1, 13, 27, 39, 40, 8, 41]. Existing CBF-based generative planners instantiate this idea primarily as path-level repair: they inject barrier constraints into the denoising or flow-generation process, or apply a CBF correction phase after a trajectory has been generated [40, 8, 41]. In both cases, the intervention acts on sample or waypoint coordinates, pushing unsafe portions of the trajectory back toward the safe set while staying close to the generator’s original output. This is effective when the generated trajectory is already nearly safe, so that only a short segment must be moved away from an obstacle. Under larger constraint shifts, however, the new constraint may block a substantial portion of the selected behavior mode. The corrector is then no longer making a local geometric repair: it must reshape a long connected segment of the rollout, which can increase intervention energy and leave the final trajectory safe but far from the goal. When path-level repair has to reshape a long segment of a rollout, the desired solution may be another behavior that the generator already knows how to produce. A multimodal demonstration dataset can contain several valid ways to solve the same start-goal task, such as passing above, below, or between obstacles, and generative policies can represent these alternatives as diverse rollouts. In standard generative planners, however, this diversity is usually accessed through stochastic sampling: the initial noise or sampling seed determines which behavior appears, with no direct handle for a safety filter to choose a rollout that is easier to certify. Geometry-aligned behavior latents, as in parameterized diffusion policies (PDP), provide such a handle by learning a low-dimensional coordinate in which nearby latent values decode to similar trajectories and larger latent moves induce more substantial behavior changes [43]. This suggests a different division of labor for safe generative planning as shown in Figure 1: use the behavior latent to select or interpolate a safer rollout before asking a path-level CBF corrector to enforce the final constraints. In this paper, we propose Latent Barrier Steering (LBS), a two-stage framework for safe parameterized flow matching that separates behavior selection from path certification. LBS first applies a CBF quadratic program (CBF-QP) in the behavior latent space to steer the decoded rollout toward a larger robust safety margin. It then decodes the steered latent and applies a path-space CBF-QP only to the remaining waypoint-level violations. This semantic-to-path structure lets the planner change the selected behavior before invoking local path repair. Theoretically, we show that latent steering improves the safety margin handed to the path-space corrector, yielding finite-time latent recovery when a safe latent is reachable and tighter path-level correction-time and intervention-energy certificates. Empirically, LBS improves safety, goal reaching, and correction efficiency across constrained planning tasks. Our contributions are: Introduce semantic-to-path safety with parameterized flow matching. We build on a parameterized flow-matching planner whose geometry-aligned latent indexes different rollout behaviors. LBS uses this latent as the first point of safety intervention, steering the selected behavior before applying path-space CBF certification. Analyze when latent steering reduces path-space correction. We show that increasing the latent safety margin gives the path-space corrector a less-violating warm start. This yields finite-time latent recovery when a safe latent is reachable, and tighter correction-time and intervention-energy certificates for the downstream CBF-QP. Demonstrate safer and more goal-directed constrained planning. Across constrained planning tasks, LBS preserves safety while improving goal reaching and reducing correction energy compared with path-level safety filters. 2 Related Work Diffusion and flow-based generative models provide expressive trajectory priors for robot planning and control, with diffusion planners modeling flexible multimodal behavior through iterative denoising and flow-matching planners improving sampling efficiency through deterministic transport [16, 10, 34, 23, 24, 17, 5, 37, 29, 3, 2]. These models have been applied to offline RL, visuomotor imitation, navigation, manipulation, and diverse human-demonstration datasets [25, 33, 18]. Their strength is that a single learned sampler can represent many plausible trajectories for the same task context. However, the generated behavior is usually selected by conditioning variables or stochastic noise, so multimodal diversity does not by itself provide a controllable safety mechanism under new constraints. Control barrier functions (CBFs) and related invariance tools provide a standard way to enforce safety by maintaining the forward invariance of a superlevel set, often through a quadratic program that minimally modifies a nominal command [1, 13, 27, 39]. Recent safe generative planners attach this machinery to diffusion or flow sampling: SafeDiffuser embeds finite-time invariance into the diffusion process, SafeFlow introduces flow-matching barrier functions for safe trajectory generation, and SafeFlowMatcher decouples prediction from correction by applying a finite-time CBF certificate only to the final path-space correction phase [40, 8, 41]. These methods provide formal safety mechanisms at test time, but their interventions are still expressed in sample or waypoint coordinates. They therefore primarily address local path repair after the generator has already selected a behavior. Controllable multimodality has a long history in parameterized actions, options, and skills, where a policy selects both a discrete behavior and continuous parameters that adapt the behavior to a task instance [36, 20, 7, 15, 26, 32, 9, 11, 44, 14, 45]. Related work on skill discovery and latent-action imitation learns reusable behavior abstractions from demonstrations or interaction data [28, 33, 21, 31, 38]. PDP brings this idea to diffusion policies by learning a continuous behavior latent whose geometry is aligned with trajectory similarity, turning noise-driven diversity into an optimizable behavior handle [43]. These threads motivate our use of a behavior latent as the semantic coordinate for safety-aware steering before path-level certification. 3 Background Let [FORMULA] denote the waypoint space, and let [FORMULA] denote a planning trajectory over horizon [FORMULA] under context [FORMULA] . This is the warm-start role analyzed in Proposition 2 and Corollary 1. 6 Limitations and Conclusion We presented Latent Barrier Steering (LBS), a two-stage framework for safe flow-matching planning that steers a geometry-aligned behavior latent before path-space CBF certification. LBS gives the path-space corrector a safer, more goal-directed warm start, reducing the need to reshape an unsuitable rollout locally. Our analysis shows that latent margin improvement reduces the Stage II deficit, yielding finite-time recovery conditions and tighter correction-time and intervention-energy certificates. Empirically, LBS improves the safety–goal-reaching tradeoff over path-level safety filters across constrained planning tasks. The safety guarantee covers the planned path certified by Stage II. For Franka, this is the planned end-effector path, so tracking error and full-body collisions are outside its scope. The finite-time Stage I result depends on local regularity and non-vanishing pulled-back gradients of the learned latent-to-trajectory map, which the training objective encourages but does not certify. The current zeroth-order Stage I implementation also adds runtime overhead. Cheaper gradient estimators or learned margin critics are natural next steps. Curie’s Jarvis: Autonomous Robotic Chemistry Experiments from Printed Protocols A person running a bench experiment works from a printed instruction sheet, tells identical containers apart by the labels written on them, and looks at the bench again before each step. Lab automation usually works the other way around: the procedure is written as a script, and containers stand at fixed positions or carry fiducial markers. We present Curie’s Jarvis, a system that lets a robot arm carry out a chemistry experiment on a bench set up for people. It reads the steps from a photo of the printed sheet, finds containers on an ordinary bench with no fixed positions or markers, tells identical-looking containers apart by reading their labels in four camera views, locates its target again before every step, and sets how each step is carried out, including its speed, from what is being handled. On a Franka Panda arm, Curie’s Jarvis completed 5 of 5 runs of one protocol from a children’s chemistry kit and 4 of 5 runs of another, with no human intervention, and in 160 locates on printed and handwritten labels it identified every container correctly. This brings robots a step closer to doing bench chemistry the way people do. I Introduction A student running a bench protocol works from a printed instruction sheet. The reagents sit in containers that have been labelled by hand and set down wherever there was room, and identical cups are told apart only by their labels. The bench is shared, so a cup may not be where it was a minute ago; the student looks again before each step and finds it. The student also adjusts each step to what is being handled, carrying an empty cup quickly and a full one slowly. None of this is arranged for a robot: the instructions, the labels and the layout are all meant for people. Existing robots for automated experiments mostly adapt the experiment’s procedure, objects and layout to the system. The instructions have to be written as a script or in a chemical programming language [1, 2, 3]; every container and instrument needs a fixed or known position [4, 5]; and some systems identify containers by fiducial markers such as AprilTags rather than by the labels placed with them [6]. This makes automated experiments fast and accurate, but at the cost of flexibility: a new experiment requires substantial manual reprogramming instead of simply handing the system a printed instruction sheet, and if an object is moved during the experiment, the run may not be able to continue. This work aims to close this gap by letting a robotic system adapt to a lab arranged for people. We make this goal concrete as five properties. Our system, Curie’s Jarvis, (P1) starts from the printed instruction sheet, with no manual rewriting into a script; (P2) works on an ordinary bench, where containers need no fixed or preset positions and no visual markers; (P3) tells identical-looking containers apart by their hand-written or printed labels; (P4) looks at the bench again before every step, so it finds objects that have been moved; and (P5) adapts how each step is executed (how fast to move, how far to tip, how deep to dig) to what is handled and what the step asks for. Section II compares related work along these properties (Table I), and Section VII evaluates each of them. We implement Curie’s Jarvis with all five properties on a Franka Panda arm (Fig. 1). (P1) A vision-language model (VLM) extracts the steps from a photo of the sheet, and a planner turns them into parameterized calls to a fixed set of skills. (P2) SAM 3 [7] segments objects in four camera views, and positions come from multi-view geometry: the depth point cloud for opaque objects and silhouettes for transparent ones. The system only needs a list of the objects on the bench (with the size of each transparent container), not their positions. (P3) The VLM reads each container’s label in every view, and the cameras vote. (P4) Before each skill call, the target is located again if it has been handled or its image has changed. (P5) The VLM chooses each call’s pour angle from the wording of the step and its speed from what is held; a fixed rule sets the angles when the same container is poured from, or into, more than once, and the scoop depth comes from the measured powder surface. The contributions of Curie’s Jarvis are as follows: A system that carries out a chemistry experiment on a Franka Panda arm from a photo of the printed instruction sheet, on an ordinary bench with no fixed positions or markers for the containers. It completed 5 of 5 Magic Beaker runs and 4 of 5 jellyfish runs with no human intervention. A way to tell identical-looking containers apart by their hand-written or printed labels, which they stand on, read in each of four camera views and combined by a cross-camera vote. Because the position of each container comes from multi-view geometry, the label only needs to say what the container is and can be placed loosely. In 160 locates on printed labels and the handwriting of three people, every container was identified correctly. Re-locating and re-identifying the containers before every step, so the robot can find a container a person has moved between steps, even among identical-looking ones. II Related Work Robotic chemists and lab automation. Much of the reliability of automatic laboratories [8] comes from adapting the experiment to the robot system. Procedures are written as scripts or in a chemical programming language [1, 2, 3]; robots work between fixed stations, with fixed sample racks and taught paths [5, 9], and one localizes at each station by touching a calibration cube to within [FORMULA] 0.12 mm [4]; and containers or devices are identified or localized with fiducial markers such as AprilTags or QR codes [6, 10, 11]. More recently, large language models generate procedures from natural language and pass them to liquid handlers or cloud platforms [12, 13] or to robot arms at the bench [14, 15, 16, 17]. The closest to our system is ORGANA [15]: it also uses a Franka arm and perceives transparent glassware without markers, but the user assigns the role of each identical-looking vessel at start-up, and it does not replan online. As Table I shows, none of these systems starts from a printed instruction sheet, tells containers apart by reading their labels, or is evaluated with a person moving objects mid-run. Language models for robot planning. The role of language models in robotics has grown from turning instructions into skill sequences, programs or trajectories [18, 19, 20, 21] to setting execution parameters and closing the loop. For execution parameters, Code as Policies [20] and IROSA [22] adjust speed in response to a user’s natural-language corrections, and ELLMER [23] selects contact forces from object properties. For closed-loop operation, Inner Monologue [24] re-detects the scene after every step, and BioProVLA-Agent [25] uses a VLM to check conditions before and after each sub-task. Our system does not leave execution entirely to the model: the model chooses the pour angle from the wording of the step and the speed from what is held, a fixed rule assigns the angles when the same container is poured from, or into, more than once, and the scoop depth comes from the measured powder surface. Identifying objects in the lab. Fiducial markers such as AprilTags [26, 27] give both an exact identity and a pose, but every object needs its own tag, and the offset from each tag to its object must be calibrated, which is fragile and time-consuming to maintain [10]. Open-vocabulary models [28, 7] need no markers, but they find objects by category and cannot tell identical-looking containers apart. Robots have identified objects by reading the text printed on them with OCR [29, 30, 31]. We read the hand-written or printed label that each container stands on and combine the reads across four views; the label only says what the container is, while its position comes from multi-view geometry, so the same label can be read by both people and the robot. III System Overview Hardware. The system runs on a Franka Emika Panda arm with a Franka Hand parallel-jaw gripper. Four Intel RealSense D415 RGB-D cameras are mounted on a cage around the bench and view it from different sides; their extrinsics are calibrated to the robot base with a cube held by the gripper, which is used only for calibration. The bench holds ordinary lab equipment: shallow white dishes of powdered reagents, clear plastic cups, a plastic beaker, a plastic transfer pipette standing in a lidded paper cup, and a 3D-printed scoop, stirrer, and stirrer holder. Each container is stacked on a slip of paper with its contents written or printed on it. Software. The system runs as two processes: the segmentation model SAM 3 [7] runs as a separate GPU service, which the program controlling the arm calls over the local network. The agents follow the modular structure of PLATO [32] and consist of four parts. An instruction parser extracts the goal, steps, reagents and equipment from the photo of the sheet. A scene agent matches the objects seen by the four cameras to the names in the list of bench objects. A planner decomposes the goal into ordered sub-tasks and replans when a step fails. Before each sub-task, a skill-call agent produces one skill call from the measured state of the gripper; its output is constrained by a JSON schema to a fixed set of skills. All four use GPT-4.1. Each manipulation skill performs its own perception, grasp analysis and motion, and checks during execution that it has reached its target. Fig. 2 shows which parts run once per experiment and which run for every sub-task. Data flow. A run starts from one photo of the instruction sheet. The parser turns it into the goal and the steps, the scene agent turns two of the camera views into the names of the objects on the bench, and the planner turns both into an ordered list of sub-tasks. For each sub-task, the skill-call agent is given the sub-task, the state of the gripper read from the arm and the outcome of every earlier call, and returns one call, for example a pour with its target container and a speed. The skill fills any parameter left out with the value tested on this bench, locates its target with the label vote of Sec. IV-B and acts. If it fails, the planner is given the failed sub-task, the sub-tasks already done and the reason, and plans the rest again, up to three times before the run stops. IV Multi-View Perception The system needs only a list of the objects on the bench, not their positions. A tool is found by a SAM 3 text prompt, such as “white plastic tool” for the scoop. A labelled container is found by its category (“white bowl” or “clear plastic cup”) and its label (Sec. IV-B); a transparent one also has its radius and height listed. A locate captures a colour image and an aligned depth image from each of the four cameras, and SAM 3 returns every instance of the prompt in each image with its score. Opaque objects are placed from depth. Each camera’s highest-scoring mask, if its score is at least 0.5, is back-projected into the robot base frame. Only pixels whose depth is within the object’s apparent size of the mask’s median depth are kept, which removes the table seen past the object’s edges. The largest set of cameras whose centroids all lie within 50 mm of each other is merged. Two cameras that disagree are both refused, and the locate returns not found. Transparent containers cannot be placed from depth. Depth passes through the wall to the table, and the depth centroids of one cup from four cameras were up to 6 cm apart. Each camera instead casts a ray through the centroid of its mask. The largest set of at least two cameras whose rays pass within 25 mm of one point inside the container’s height is kept, so rays that only cross in mid-air are rejected. On four containers the rays passed 6 to 11 mm from the point. The skills receive a cylinder of the listed size at that point. When a category has several containers, every instance in every camera is placed this way, and instances from different cameras at the same spot are grouped as one container. The labels then tell these containers apart (Sec. IV-B). Labels are placed only on containers that look identical and cannot be told apart directly. Each such container stands on a slip of paper with its contents written or printed on it; each tool appears once and carries no label. Because a container’s position comes from multi-view geometry (Sec. IV-A), its label only has to say what the container holds. It needs no calibration and no fixed position or orientation, and people can read it. It does have to be visible next to its container: a container standing on or against its paper is read, and one with bare table between it and the paper is not (Sec. VII-C). Each instance in each camera is read on its own, from a crop of the container and the paper it stands on, with other containers greyed out. The VLM (GPT-4.1) chooses which of the labels on the bench is on that paper, or none; any other reply counts as unread. Sec. VII-C tests this on printed and handwritten labels (Table II) and with containers moved off their labels (Table III). Containers of one category form a vote group (the two white dishes, or the clear cups and the beaker). The labels of the group are given out, one container each, so that the most camera reads agree. A container can then be found by label or by elimination. It is found by label when every best assignment gives it the wanted label and at least one camera read that label on it. It is found by elimination when no camera read the wanted label, every other label of the group is settled on a container seen by two or more cameras, and exactly one such container is left. A tie goes to the container nearest where it was last seen, and any other case returns not found. A container the arm set down itself is taken to be the one within 50 mm of that spot, without reading labels, because its paper stays behind when the arm moves it. Fig. 3 shows the camera views, the label reads and the resulting position for one locate. V Manipulation Skills Every skill runs the same steps: (1) parameters a call leaves out take values validated on this bench; (2) the arm moves to its home pose, out of the cameras’ view, and the skill locates its target (Sec. IV), reusing a kept scan when one camera shows no change around the target; (3) the skill plans its motion from measured geometry, a container’s rim circle and, for a held object, its shape measured at the pick, and executes it; (4) it checks that its moves end near their targets, and checks the gripper width to detect a dropped object. The put-back skill is the exception: it goes straight to the remembered pick site without locating anything. The scans of everything a skill handles are dropped, so the next skill locates them again (P4). The skills and agents were first developed in a MuJoCo [33] model of the bench, where they ran end to end on random container layouts; the skills’ default parameters were then set on the real bench. Grasping. Every pick is a top grasp over the object’s centre, measured from its point cloud. A tool is closed on until the finger force reaches a set limit. A thin plastic cup gives no useful force reading, so the jaws close to its measured width less a small squeeze. A long tool lying at an angle, such as the scoop, is turned to: the wrist rotates to the tool’s long axis, so the tool sits in the jaws the same way wherever it lies. After closing, and again after lifting, the gripper width is compared with the measured width, which catches a grasp that closed on nothing, crushed the cup or lost the object in the lift. The pick also measures what it holds, such as how far the scoop’s head hangs below the jaws and the size of a held cup, and later skills use these measurements. Scoop and dump. The scoop digs along a straight line through the centre of the dish, as long as its head can travel without touching the wall of the cup. The powder level is read from the depth points where the head enters, and the head descends compliantly onto the surface and then to a fixed depth under it, keeping a fixed gap above the floor. The scoop then rolls from nose-down to level as it moves forward, and tilts back as it lifts so the powder stays in. A waypoint that ends far from its target counts as a jam, and the stroke is tried once more, higher. The dump carries the scoop over the target cup and tips it nose-down with the centre of its head held over the cup. The angle is capped by what the arm can reach at that spot, and the skill fails if the cap or the measured tip is below a minimum. Finally, it shakes the scoop and twists the wrist to release what is left. Pour. The pour takes the held cup’s size from the pick and locates the target’s rim. It places the lip of the held cup just inside the target’s rim and tips toward the arm’s base in steps up to the pour angle. At each step the wrist position is recomputed so the lip stays over the target and the cup’s body clears its rim. After each step the measured tilt is compared with the commanded one; a step that stops short is tried again more slowly, and if it still stops short the pour fails. The cup is held at the final angle, set upright in place and lifted clear. Stir and tool return. The stir holds the stirrer straight down, locates the target cup and measures its rim, then lowers the rod in small steps to its depth, stopping early if it touches anything. Each revolution is traced as one continuous motion on a circle sized to the measured opening, so the rod cannot scrape the wall, and the skill checks before, during and after that the stirrer is still held. A tool is put back where it was picked up, and the stirrer is lowered back into its holder. Pipette. pick_pipette takes the pipette out of its cup by the bulb, squeezed flat, dips the tip into the source and opens the jaws a little to draw liquid up; dispense releases it as drops. VI From Instruction Sheet to Skill Calls Instruction parsing. The parser sends the photo of the sheet to the VLM, which returns the goal, the ordered steps, the reagents with their quantities and the equipment as JSON. It is told to keep each step’s own wording for which container and how much. Without that line it read “the empty clear cup” as “the beaker” in 2 of 3 reads; with it, it read the step correctly in 3 of 3. Scene grounding. The list of bench objects is part of the bench setup: each object has a name, its label if it has one, and a short note, for example that a cup already holds its water. The scene agent looks at two of the four camera views and names the objects on the bench, choosing each name from this list, so every name it gives is one a skill can locate. It is told what the objects are called, not where they are. Planning and skill calls. The planner turns the goal, the steps and the named objects into an ordered list of sub-tasks. It is shown the fixed set of skills and the rules for combining them, for example that a scoop only fills the bowl and needs a dump to deliver anything, and that numbered steps on the sheet keep their order. For each sub-task, the skill-call agent returns one call under a strict JSON schema: a skill from the fixed set, its parameters, a speed and a short reason. A sub-task it cannot express as a skill is reported as infeasible, rather than mapped to a nearby skill, and goes back to the planner. The model is not asked for what it cannot know: the shape of the scoop’s head comes from its CAD model, and measurements taken at a pick, such as where the scoop sits in the jaws, are passed on to the calls that use the tool. Execution and recovery. Each call’s parameters, outcome, timing and the values the skill measured are written to a run record. A failed skill goes back to the planner, as described in Sec. III. An operator can step through a run, confirming each call before it runs, and a stopped run can be resumed from its record at a chosen sub-task without repeating the steps already done. VII Experiments We evaluate Curie’s Jarvis on two protocols, Magic Beaker and jellyfish, each given to the system only as a photo of its printed sheet. Both protocols scoop powders, pour liquids and stir; jellyfish also adds drops with the pipette. Both come from a National Geographic Kids chemistry kit: the sheets are pages of its booklet, and the reagents, cups, beaker, pipette and scoops are those of the kit. In Magic Beaker, citric acid and baking soda are each dissolved in a cup of water, giving an acid and a base, and red cabbage powder is dissolved in the beaker as a pH indicator. The indicator is poured into both cups, turning the acid red and the base blue, and the two are then poured into an empty cup, where the liquid fizzes and turns purple. The sheet pours the two at the same time; the robot has one arm and pours them one after the other. In jellyfish, baking soda is dissolved in a cup of water, vegetable oil is poured on top, and red cabbage indicator mixed in a second cup is dropped onto the oil with the pipette; the purple drops sink through the oil and turn blue in the base below. The planner decides the number of sub-tasks itself, so it varies from run to run: about 30 for Magic Beaker and about 20 for jellyfish. The bench is set up the way a chemistry lab would be. Every container of a liquid or a powder stands on a paper label naming its contents, as a lab labels its reagents. The tools (scoop, stirrer and pipette) carry no label, since a chemist knows them by sight, and the system has to as well. The reagents come already measured into their own containers, much like mise en place in a kitchen, so the robot transfers and mixes them but does not measure out amounts. Neither protocol depends on precise amounts; we return to this in Sec. VIII. Each protocol was run 5 times. A run counts as a success when every sub-task is carried out with no human intervention and the expected visible result appears. Between runs the containers and tools were shifted slightly by hand, but the arrangement stayed the same and no two objects swapped places. Magic Beaker succeeded in 5 of 5 runs and jellyfish in 4 of 5 (Table IV). A Magic Beaker run took about 30 minutes and a jellyfish run about 17. Every successful run ended with the result its sheet describes: in Magic Beaker the mixed liquid fizzed and turned purple, and in jellyfish the indicator drops sank through the oil and turned blue. The one failed run was a jellyfish run. Every sub-task went as planned until the final steps, where the pipette is picked up to drop the indicator onto the oil. There the system took the scoop for the pipette and grasped the scoop instead. Tools carry no label, so the label vote (Sec. IV-B) cannot catch this: the pipette is found only by the text prompt the system gives SAM 3 for it (Sec. IV-A). A pipette is something a chemist knows by sight, so it is left unlabelled on purpose, and the system has to recognise it the same way. We expect a stronger VLM to do better at identifying the pipette and choosing the prompt for it. Both label experiments use the same bench. Four containers stand in a square in front of the arm, each on its paper label: two identical white dishes (red cabbage powder and baking soda), a clear plastic cup (10 ml water) and a plastic beaker (vegetable oil). The VLM chooses among exactly these four label strings. Only the cameras are used; the arm does not move. Each locate is the same call a skill makes, and every memory is cleared before it (kept scans, last known position and tracked objects), so no locate is helped by the one before. Each locate is settled by label or by elimination, or returns not found (Sec. IV-B). The ground truth is each container’s position located with label reading switched off and named by its corner of the square; three repeats agreed within 0.4 mm. A locate with all four cameras took 14.1 s on average (13.2 to 18.1 s). Label legibility. The labels were swapped between four sets: printed, and handwritten by three different people. In each set every container was located 10 times (Table II). All 160 locates found the right container, with a mean offset of 0.2 mm from the ground truth and at most 1.1 mm. The vote across cameras is needed for this. In 21 of the 160 locates one camera read another label on the right container: camera 3 in 11, always on the red cabbage dish and on both printed and handwritten paper, probably because it sees that paper sideways at a low angle; camera 4 in 9, all on the beaker and 8 of them in one handwriting set; and camera 2 once. No locate had more than one camera misreading, so the other three outvoted it every time. Used alone, camera 3 would have found at most 149 of the 160 containers. Distance from the label. One container at a time (the baking soda dish, the water cup or the beaker) was moved away from its label to 5 or 6 spots between 2 and 44 cm, and located 3 times at each spot, 96 locates in all. The distance is how far its centre moved, measured by hand. Each container was tested twice: with the other three labels left on the bench, and with those labels removed while their containers stayed (Table III). None of the 96 locates returned the wrong container; every miss was not found. With the other labels present no locate failed, because whenever the moved container’s own label was not read, elimination found it (10 locates). With the other labels removed, 16 of 48 locates were not found. The distance of the centre does not predict whether the label is read. The water cup was read by all four cameras 18 cm from its spot, standing against the edge of its paper, and was not found at 16 cm with bare table between it and the paper. The baking soda dish was not read at 6 cm, where it stood on top of its own text. What decides the read is whether the label is still in view beside the container, that is, whether the container stands on or against its paper. We saw this in a few frames and did not measure the gap from the container to its paper or the direction of the move. Two results need care. First, with the other labels removed, elimination still settled 2 of the 48 locates, because the VLM named a container from what it holds: one camera read the red cabbage dish as “red cabbage powder” from its red powder, and another read the water cup as “10 ml water”. The rows without the other labels are therefore not a clean condition with no other labels. Second, two far reads counted as by label rest on a single camera and were not checked against the frames: the baking soda dish at 44 cm (2 of 3 locates) and at 18 cm without the other labels. They may come from the contents of the dish and not from its label. Elimination was not switched off in the code for the phase without the other labels. Removing those labels takes away the moved container’s only elimination partner without changing the system, so the test runs the same code as a real run. We have not yet evaluated this property with a person moving objects during a run. This section describes how the system is built to handle it. Every skill locates its target again from the home pose right before it acts (Sec. V), so a container a person has moved between two steps is found at its new spot. A kept scan is reused only if no skill has touched the object since and one camera’s current view of the object matches the view the scan came from; any visible change there, such as a hand moving the object, forces a full locate. Identity comes from the label vote and not from where a container stood before, so two identical cups that a person swaps, each with its label, are still told apart. A container the arm set down itself has no label under it; it is taken to be the one within 50 mm of where the arm left it, and if none is there, the labels are read instead. Tools carry no label and are found by their text prompt at every pick, so a moved tool is found the same way. If a person takes an object out of the gripper, the gripper width shows it, the skill fails, and the planner replans from the measured gripper state. Some cases are not covered. Each skill locates once before it moves, so an object moved while a skill is acting is not seen until the next skill. The put-back skill returns an object to where it was picked up without looking, so anything placed on that spot in the meantime is in the way. And because the label is the identity, a label moved to another container takes the identity with it, as it would for a person reading the bench. This property has not been evaluated on its own yet either; this section describes how it works. A person carries a full cup slowly and an empty one quickly, and so does Curie’s Jarvis. Every skill call carries a speed from 0 to 100 that scales the duration of every motion in the skill, from the pace each skill was tuned at (0, the slowest) down to 0.4 of that time at 100. Holds and waits keep their length. The whole call runs at one speed, so the skill-call agent chooses it for the call’s most delicate moment, following a short guide in its prompt: 0 for liquid in an open container, 20 for a scoop carrying powder, 30 for stirring, 60 for an empty tool and 80 with nothing held. One fixed pace would either spill liquid or waste time on every empty move. The other parameters are set the same way: the agent chooses the pour angle from the wording of the step, a fixed rule sets it when the same container is poured from or into more than once, and the scoop depth comes from the measured powder surface. All ten end-to-end runs of Sec. VII-B used the speeds the agent chose. Speed only shortens the motions, and much of a run is spent looking. Every skill locates its target again before it acts, which is what lets it find an object a person has moved (Sec. VII-D). A locate reads the four cameras one at a time. Opening all four RealSense streams at once overloaded the USB controller of the robot’s computer, and the GPU does not have the memory to run SAM 3 on all four views together, so each camera is started, read and stopped before the next, and SAM 3 and the label reads then run on each view in turn. A locate with all four cameras took 14.1 s on average in the label experiments (Sec. VII-C). Reusing a scan when nothing around the target has changed saves some of these, but with about 30 sub-tasks in a Magic Beaker plan the locates are a large part of why a run takes about 20 minutes (Table IV). A computer that can stream all four cameras and segment them at once would remove most of this wait. VIII Limitations The clearest limitation is amounts. The reagents come already measured (Sec. VII-A), both protocols work whatever the exact amounts, and the robot does not weigh or otherwise measure what it transfers. Our results therefore say nothing about how accurately Curie’s Jarvis could deliver a set amount, which most real protocols need. The evaluation is also narrow. It covers one bench, one arm and two protocols from a children’s kit, and the end-to-end runs kept one arrangement of the bench, shifting objects only slightly between runs. The arm’s joint limits restrict where on the bench some skills can be carried out; the dump, for instance, cannot tip as far over a cup near the edge of its reach. Properties P4 and P5 are built into the system, but neither has yet been tested on its own (Secs. VII-D and VII-E). Perception has its own gaps. Unlabelled tools are found by a text prompt alone, which is how the one failed run went wrong (Sec. VII-B). The cameras look down on the bench, so the underside of the scoop’s head is hidden and its measured depth below the grasp is only a lower bound. Every locate reads the four cameras one after another, which makes a run slow (Sec. VII-E). And the system depends on a hosted VLM, so it needs a network connection and is tied to the model’s behaviour. IX Conclusion We presented Curie’s Jarvis, a system that carries out a chemistry experiment on a robot arm from a photo of its printed instruction sheet, on a bench set up for people. Containers stand loosely on handwritten or printed labels, which the system reads in four camera views and combines by a vote, and it locates its target again before every step. It completed 9 of 10 runs of two protocols with no human intervention and identified every container in 160 label-reading locates. Next, we will test it with people moving objects during a run, compare the speeds it chooses against fixed ones, and move to protocols that need measured amounts.

I INTRODUCTION Cooperative object manipulation by multiple robots becomes necessary when a task exceeds the force, moment, or workspace capacity of any single agent [1, 2]. In marine settings, tugboats are deployed in groups to dock large vessels, reposition heavy floating barges, and move floating structures through narrow waterways, as illustrated in Fig. 1. Multiple agents, such as robots or vessels, can manipulate a shared floating object in several ways, including attaching, caging, towing, and pushing [2]. Among these, pushing requires the least mechanical setup: it needs no cables, attachments, or grasping mechanisms, and tugboats carry it out by pressing their bow or stern fenders against the hull of the target object. Cooperative pushing is nontrivial because object motion depends on both the control law and the contact locations. Under unilateral frictionless pushing, the contact normals and nonnegative contact force magnitudes define a wrench cone; if the commanded object wrench lies outside this cone, no nonnegative contact force can realize it [3]. Force closure provides the classical framework for this feasibility check. A contact configuration achieves force closure when contact forces can balance any external wrench on the object, or equivalently generate arbitrary planar wrenches [3]. Nguyen’s work established a constructive approach for synthesizing planar force closure grasps from the geometry of the object [4]. The method identifies independent contact regions and provides algorithms for constructing grasps from object shape information. These works provide a basis for contact-feasibility analysis, but rely on general geometric or algorithmic frameworks rather than a compact closed-form condition for the cooperative pushing geometry considered here. This contact feasibility issue is especially relevant in cooperative object manipulation, where multiple agents must jointly generate the forces and moments required for transport. Esposito [5] studied swarm-based cooperative pushing of floating objects in autonomous tugboat scenarios, highlighting how robot placement affects the manipulation capability of the team. Cooperative floating object transport has also been studied through layered control frameworks involving trajectory tracking, wrench allocation, and vessel formation control [6]. More generally, constrained control allocation has been widely studied for marine vehicles [7, 8]. Autonomous tugboat systems have addressed towing, waypoint following, heading regulation, and collision avoidance [9, 10]. Related pushing-based work with soft tactile sensing handled distributed force regulation and motion direction control for a rectangular object [11], where feasibility is assessed through moment arm signs relative to the object center of mass for a specific target direction. Recent work has also addressed collaborative planar pushing of polytopic objects using hybrid mode optimization and nonlinear MPC [12]. These approaches either assume that the selected contact geometry can produce the required object wrench or evaluate feasibility through numerical optimization. For one unilateral edge normal contact on each edge of a rectangular body, a closed-form condition that is independent of the object’s center of mass remains underexplored. This study tackles these gaps by deriving a necessary and sufficient closed-form condition for force closure with four frictionless, unilateral contacts on a rectangular floating object, stated purely in terms of the four edge contact positions. The condition is a single checkable algebraic inequality that requires no wrench-space computation and can be evaluated at the contact placement stage before applying a control technique. To demonstrate its use in control, we embed this result into a simple 3-DOF floating-body trajectory-tracking framework: the condition is checked once upfront to confirm that the contact geometry supports full-pose tracking, and if not, a pair-and-direction adjustment rule corrects the configuration before contact force allocation. In this framework, the pushing agents are modeled as ideal unilateral normal-force actuators at the contact points, allowing the study to isolate the effect of contact geometry on wrench generation. Simulation results demonstrate that contact configurations satisfying the proposed force-closure condition can produce the commanded planar forces and yaw moments required for full-pose tracking, while configurations that violate the condition lead to wrench errors and poorer tracking performance. The paper is organized as follows: Section II covers the problem formulation, Section III derives the force-closure condition, Section IV presents the tracking framework, Section V reports simulation results, and Section VI concludes. The condition depends only on the four edge contact positions and can be used as a geometric feasibility layer before contact force allocation. When the condition is not satisfied, the signs of its factors identify which opposing contact pair should be adjusted toward force closure. Static wrench tests and floating-body tracking simulations showed that force-closure configurations reproduce the commanded planar wrenches with smaller tracking errors, while configurations without force closure lead to wrench errors and poor tracking. RaMOD: Moving-Object Detection from Raw mmWave Radar Cubes under Ego Motion Millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar provides weather-robust sensing and direct Doppler measurements, yet automotive perception pipelines often reduce its output to sparse point clouds or two-dimensional projections, leaving raw range–azimuth–Doppler (RAD) cubes underutilized. Ego motion induces Doppler responses from world-static structures, while Doppler wrapping aliases radial velocities, complicating moving-object detection and velocity estimation. We present RaMOD (Radar-based Moving-Object Detection), a real-time framework for moving-object detection and velocity estimation from raw RAD cubes acquired by a vehicle-mounted single-chip radar. RaMOD explicitly estimates frame-wise ego motion and uses the estimated radar translational velocity to predict the Doppler region of world-static structures and suppress returns within it. It temporally encodes the suppressed cubes into multi-scale features to predict RAD-space boxes with class labels. For each detected object, it predicts radial and forward velocities under raw-Doppler and Doppler-unwrapped hypotheses, together with Doppler-wrapping probabilities. On our BRIDGE-Liv dataset, RaMOD outperforms all compared raw-radar methods across RAD-cube, RA, and RD detection settings, achieving [FORMULA] cube mAP at IoU [FORMULA] , [FORMULA] percentage points above the strongest RAD-cube baseline. I Introduction Moving object detection is a fundamental perception task for assisted and autonomous driving, where independently moving road users must be accurately localized, classified, and assigned reliable motion estimates. In current autonomous driving systems, optical sensors, especially cameras and LiDARs, play a decisive role in perception. In conventional modular pipelines, cameras provide rich semantic information for object detection and segmentation [1], while LiDAR provides accurate range and 3D geometric measurements for object detection [2]. Recent end-to-end driving frameworks further learn driving decisions from sensor observations [3], while emerging vision-language-action (VLA) systems incorporate language guidance into driving [4]. However, object motion in conventional camera- and LiDAR-based pipelines is typically inferred through temporal association, optical flow, scene flow, or frame-to-frame geometric changes, which can be sensitive to occlusion and unreliable correspondences [5, 6]. Moreover, cameras can degrade under poor illumination, glare, contamination, and motion blur, while LiDAR measurements can be affected by rain, fog, and snow [7], as well as smoke [8]. Millimeter-wave radar has therefore become an important complementary sensor in modern vehicles. Compared with optical sensors, mmWave radar uses longer-wavelength electromagnetic signals and is generally more robust under poor illumination and adverse weather conditions. More importantly, radar directly measures radial velocity through Doppler. Advances in semiconductor fabrication and antenna-in-package technologies have also enabled compact, low-power, and low-cost single-chip mmWave radars, making large-scale deployment practical in intelligent vehicles and autonomous systems [9]. Automotive radars have consequently been widely adopted in advanced driver-assistance systems (ADAS). However, automotive radar perception still commonly relies on processed point clouds and the clusters derived from them (Fig. 1(c)). Point clouds are typically generated through peak selection and sparsification, while clustering, data association, and tracking further produce object-level estimates. The resulting detections and tracks provide compact position and velocity information for conventional ADAS functions such as adaptive cruise control, blind-spot detection, collision warning, and automatic emergency braking (AEB) [10]. Nevertheless, peak-based sparsification may discard weak responses and only partially preserve the extended object support and reflection structures present in the full radar measurement tensor (Fig. 1(b)). For next-generation autonomous driving, mmWave radar has the potential to support high-level perception through its spatial measurements and directly measured Doppler information. Raw range–azimuth–Doppler (RAD) cubes preserve these measurement distributions before point-cloud sparsification, providing richer evidence for learning-based object detection, classification, and velocity estimation. Among these capabilities, identifying independently moving road users through spatial and Doppler evidence is particularly important for interaction, motion prediction, and collision-risk assessment. However, identifying independently moving road users becomes more challenging when the radar itself is moving. World-static structures, such as buildings and parked vehicles, also produce Doppler shifts under ego motion, so non-zero Doppler alone does not indicate independent object motion. Their responses may overlap with those of moving objects. Doppler wrapping introduces further ambiguity: when the relative radial velocity falls outside the unambiguous velocity interval, the return is mapped to an aliased Doppler bin, potentially increasing static–dynamic overlap. The extent of this overlap depends on radar Doppler coverage and the relative motions in the scene. The world-static Doppler field and the resulting ambiguity after wrapping are analyzed in Secs. III-C and III-D. Motivated by these observations, we propose RaMOD, a real-time framework for moving-object detection from raw RAD cubes acquired by a single-chip radar on a moving vehicle. It supports both single-frame and short-sequence inputs. Since world-static Doppler depends on radar motion and viewing direction, RaMOD estimates frame-wise ego motion as an explicit output and uses the estimated radar translational velocity to predict the static-consistent Doppler region. Suppressing returns within this region reduces ego-motion-induced background responses before detection. The suppressed radar representation is encoded into multi-scale features for RAD-space object localization and classification. RaMOD also predicts radial and object-level forward velocities under raw-Doppler and Doppler-unwrapped hypotheses, together with Doppler-wrapping probabilities. Experiments on BRIDGE-Liv, which contains moving-ego urban and highway sequences, show that RaMOD outperforms all compared raw-radar methods across RAD-cube, range–azimuth (RA), and range–Doppler (RD) detection settings. The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows: We propose RaMOD, a real-time moving-object detection and motion-estimation framework that directly processes raw RAD cubes from a single-chip radar under ego motion. It retains Doppler as an explicit detection dimension and combines multi-scale cube encoding, cross-scale feature refinement, and cross-view RA/RD auxiliary supervision for RAD-space object localization and classification. We develop an ego-motion-guided Doppler suppression mechanism. Frame-wise ego motion is estimated directly from unmasked RAD cubes as an explicit output. Its translational component is combined with the world-static Doppler model to construct an internal cube-level mask that suppresses returns within the predicted static-consistent Doppler region before detection. We design object-level velocity heads that predict radial and forward velocities under raw-Doppler and Doppler-unwrapped hypotheses, together with Doppler-wrapping probabilities. These probabilities guide selection between the two velocity pairs, associating each detected object with a velocity estimate that accounts for Doppler ambiguity. II Related Work Cameras and LiDARs are the dominant sensing modalities for high-level automotive perception. Camera-based methods have progressed from two-stage and real-time object detectors to transformer-based 3D detection, BEV representation, and occupancy prediction [11, 12, 13, 14, 1, 15]. LiDAR-based methods use accurate range and 3D geometry for multi-class bounding-box detection from point clouds [16, 2, 17, 18]. Motion perception with these sensors generally relies on temporal visual or geometric changes, including tracking-by-detection, optical flow, scene flow, temporal BEV fusion, and multi-scan association [19, 5, 6, 1]. LiDAR moving-object segmentation further distinguishes moving points from the static scene [20, 21]. This distinction is important because a road user may be movable without being currently in motion. In contrast, mmWave radar directly measures radial velocity through Doppler and remains robust under poor illumination and adverse weather, making it particularly suitable for motion-aware automotive perception. Radar point clouds are widely used because they provide compact target measurements after peak detection and thresholding. Early learning-based methods perform object classification and 2D or 3D detection from sparse radar points [22, 23, 24]. Subsequent methods introduce radar-specific feature aggregation to address sparsity and noise. RPFA-Net employs pillar feature attention, SMURF combines density features with multiple representations, and RadarPillars decomposes radial velocity before pillar-based detection [25, 26, 27]. Doppler is useful in these detectors but is generally treated as an auxiliary per-point feature. For example, the View-of-Delft study reports that removing Doppler reduces radar detection performance from [FORMULA] to [FORMULA] mAP [24]. Nevertheless, the resulting networks typically predict boxes, classes, and confidence scores rather than object-associated radial velocity, Doppler-wrapping states, or unwrapped velocity. Moreover, peak-based point-cloud generation may discard weak responses and only partially preserve extended object support, motivating lower-level representations that retain dense spatial and Doppler structure. Radar-based ego-motion estimation constitutes a related research direction. Classical automotive methods estimate instantaneous ego velocity from the azimuth-dependent Doppler measurements of world-static radar detections and infer yaw rate under a vehicle-motion model [28]. Subsequent approaches combine Doppler constraints with spatial registration [29], learn to identify static inliers for robust instantaneous estimation [30], or derive translational and rotational odometry from Doppler–azimuth and range–azimuth heatmaps in radar-only SLAM systems [31]. RaMOD incorporates frame-wise ego-motion estimation as an explicit network output and uses the predicted translational velocity to construct its internal static-consistent Doppler suppression region. Projection-based heatmap methods perform object detection or semantic segmentation in two-dimensional radar views. On the stationary-radar CARRADA benchmark [32], multi-view convolutional, attention, and state-space models learn radar-view semantics [33, 34, 35, 36], while RD detectors predict bounding boxes [37]. On vehicle-mounted datasets such as UWCR and CRUW, temporal models aggregate consecutive RA heatmaps or multiple radar views through spatiotemporal convolutions, recurrent memory, or attention [38, 39, 40, 41, 42]. Their outputs principally describe class-labeled object locations or semantic regions in radar views. A single-frame hybrid alternative combines extracted radar targets with local RAD crops for classification and subsequent object clustering [43]. RAD-space detectors instead predict boxes spanning range, azimuth, and Doppler. Existing designs include anchor-based convolutional detection [44], transformer-based encoding with anchor-free heads [45], and NMS-free set prediction [46]. These outputs retain Doppler localization, but the RADDet benchmark used in these studies was collected with a stationary radar and does not capture the ego-motion-induced static Doppler field encountered by a moving sensor. Another line of work learns spatial features directly from RD spectra or ADC signals. On DDM data in RADIal, learned signal transformations, transformer encoders, and sparse feature extraction support vehicle detection and free-space segmentation [47, 48, 49, 50]. The RADIal detection benchmark considers a single vehicle class. Complementary ADC–heatmap fusion enriches detection features on RADDet [51]. Radar representations also support detection in physical 3D space [52] and human pose estimation [53]. In automotive settings, volumetric radar features support 3D bounding-box detection [54, 55, 56] and tracking [57], while high-resolution RA heatmaps support oriented vehicle detection [58]. Temporal RAD tensors augmented with elevation-index information also enable binary 3D occupancy prediction [59]. A later RaDelft-based method predicts voxel-level semantic labels [60], while RadarOcc predicts foreground, background, and free-space occupancy on K-Radar [61]. These methods focus on spatial geometry, semantics, and tracking rather than object-level Doppler-wrapping decisions and unwrapped radial-velocity outputs. Object-level velocity estimation and signal-level Doppler unfolding have also been investigated. Major et al. combine projected radar representations with temporal modeling to estimate an ego-relative velocity vector for each detected vehicle [62]. For vehicle-mounted TDM-MIMO radar, Zheng et al.’s TDRadarNet pipeline combines learned Doppler unfolding with phase-migration compensation before temporal BEV vehicle detection [63]. Its unfolding stage resolves ambiguity for image formation rather than assigning a wrapping state to each detected object. In comparison, RaMOD combines ego-motion-guided cube suppression, RAD-space detection, and object-associated velocity estimation with explicit wrapping predictions.
