VI Conclusion and Future Work In this paper, we presented RaMOD, a real-time moving-object detection and velocity estimation framework that directly processes one or more consecutive raw RAD cubes from a moving single-chip mmWave radar. RaMOD combines ego-motion-guided static-consistent Doppler suppression with temporal multi-scale cube encoding to detect and classify moving objects in RAD space. It estimates frame-wise ego motion and object-level radial and forward velocities, and predicts Doppler-wrapping states with unwrapped velocity estimates. Experiments on BRIDGE-Liv demonstrate that RaMOD outperforms all compared raw-radar methods across the RAD-cube, RA, and RD detection spaces at all reported IoU thresholds, while maintaining accurate motion estimation and real-time operation. The RaMOD implementation and BRIDGE-Liv dataset will be open-sourced. Future work will extend RaMOD to motion-aware 3D occupancy of static structures and moving road users. Joint estimation of object heading and planar velocity will relax the current ego-forward motion assumption, and an azimuth-dependent suppression region that follows the static field at each azimuth will be evaluated together with the corresponding annotation update. In parallel, we are establishing a DDM acquisition platform to extend validation beyond the current TDM-MIMO configuration, including ego-motion-induced static Doppler and velocity ambiguity. As BRIDGE-Liv expands, we will explore more efficient, data-scalable end-to-end radar models and their potential integration into multimodal VLA driving systems.

Large Language Model Explainability for Planning Lunar Rover Trajectories under Uncertainty Planning planetary rover trajectories under probabilistic uncertainty is a multi-objective optimization problem that science teams currently iteratively solve and verify by hand. This process becomes impractical when timelines and constraints frequently shift throughout the mission planning phase. Sampling-based planners such as Monte Carlo tree search can speed up this process, but their outputs do not preserve traceability to the science objectives that justify each plan, which the science team needs to verify. We propose an interactive assistant based on a large language model (LLM) that can explain planner trajectories using domain vocabulary and re-run the planner under user-specified conditions to compare alternatives. Previous work has used LLMs inside planner decision-making loops, but we explore using them for post-planning explanation, where they are more likely to be trusted since they do not directly influence planner decisions. Our framework pairs a simulator inspired by the NASA Volatiles Investigating Polar Exploration Rover (VIPER) mission with a ReAct queryable interface that calls curated action tools and retrieval functions. We evaluate the assistant on a query bank consisting of plan comparisons, feasibility, and lookup queries. Experiments show that 90.9% of the assistant’s responses are faithful to the planner’s outputs, a nearly 65% improvement over zero-shot prompting of the same LLM without tool access, demonstrating the potential for trustworthy explainability of uncertainty-aware traverses with an LLM-based system. I Introduction For space missions, planning the science phase typically requires vehicle trajectory optimization for multiple objectives and constraints. These trajectories also depend on many sources of probabilistic uncertainty, which become impractical to reiterate on quickly and frequently by hand. A simulator and an accompanying automated planning algorithm can speed up this iteration process, but their outputs may not be directly useful to the scientists who need to map these outputs to the effects on science data collection. This gap in explainability motivates an automated approach that uses large language models (LLMs) to explain trajectories in a comprehensible form to users who may not be familiar with the inner workings of the planning system. Advances in robotics have been driven by LLMs applied to motion planning for tasks with high-dimensional observations, multi-modal sequences and behaviors, and complex failure modes [1, 2, 3]. For instance, recent work uses LLMs for planning Martian rover traverses [4], and efforts have begun to integrate LLMs with structured planners as state trackers or plan verifiers within the planning stage [5, 6]. Improvements to LLM in-context reasoning, text generation, and information retrieval [7] suggest that they have the skills to provide comprehensive explainability for these tasks. However, current work does not use LLM reasoning capabilities to explain long-horizon plans made by rigorous techniques for planning under uncertainty. One application that could benefit from this approach is planning planetary rover traverses. Such missions must account for a fixed time budget, navigation to sites of high scientific value, and uncertain speeds. We are inspired by NASA’s Volatiles Investigating Polar Exploration Rover (VIPER), which must explore a predefined area of high scientific value, called a science station, within a roughly 24-hour period. The rover must collect measurements of volatiles with its three continuously operating spectrometers (neutron, near-infrared, and mass) through prospecting and obtain subsurface regolith samples with its onboard drill [8]. The rover is solar-powered and thus needs to remain in sunlight as much as possible, unless operating within a permanently shadowed region (PSR) science station. The rover’s speed also depends on the sun’s position, as driving in certain directions is difficult or impossible due to the low-rising sun creating imaging issues for the navigation and hazard-avoidance cameras. The rover must also avoid communication shadows and slopes. Verifying by hand whether a handcrafted traverse satisfies all of these objectives and constraints is likely impractical, especially considering probabilistic uncertainties. An interpretable, automated planner is essential when timelines, constraints, and operational windows shift and require frequent replanning and verification. NASA’s current tool for overseeing health-aware mission planning is the System Health-Enabled Real-time Planning Advisor (SHERPA) [9] is a strategic mission planning AI system in use by NASA. SHERPA uses sampling-based methods like Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) [10, 11] to compute and evaluate potential traverses for a variety of missions, such as VIPER’s long-range traverses. However, it currently does not have support for the detailed planning inside VIPER’s science stations. Additionally, MCTS plans trajectories by maximizing future rewards and rollouts, while the science team verifies trajectories against mission-specific objectives, such as risk of finishing over the time limit or maximizing prospecting area. The planner’s outputs do not directly trace back to these objectives, so it may require additional analysis to determine whether a given trajectory satisfies them. To address this gap, we make the following contributions towards producing explainable trajectories: An MCTS-based optimal trajectory planner coupled with a VIPER-inspired, physics-based simulator. Inputs to the planner include ice stability depth maps and sun-azimuth-dependent probability distributions for rover speeds. An LLM-based, interactive assistant that dispatches the planner and a set of tools to automate replanning and explanation of trajectories with mission context, evaluated on a bank of science-team-inspired queries. The proposed framework seen in Figure 1 is designed to allow the science team to efficiently replan under different conditions and constraints, while building trust with the trajectory planning algorithms, by keeping the team engaged in an interactive planning loop and grounding explanations in a familiar vocabulary. The LLM assistant does not override the planner, but rather runs it on behalf of the user with their specified conditions or explains resulting trajectories, without telling the user what they should do. II Related Work Trajectory planning under uncertainty is often formulated as a Markov decision process (MDP) [11]. Since exact solutions to large MDPs are computationally intractable, online sampling-based methods are often used, such as Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) [10], which builds a search tree of value estimates from simulated rollouts. We adopt a standard MDP formulation with an MCTS planner, as SHERPA does for strategic mission planning [9]. Rover planning has historically been a human-driven process. Gaines et al. [12] document the operational workflow for Mars rovers, where science teams hand-craft candidate traverses and validate them against constraints. They identify the cost of this loop as a primary limit on mission productivity. The process becomes even more complex in lunar polar missions, where a rover needs to avoid large, fast-moving illumination and communication shadows and where its speed, among other factors, depends on the difference between the heading and the azimuth to the sun. The latter consideration is due to the sun, which does not rise more than a few degrees above the horizon, creating imaging issues for the rover’s navigation and hazard-avoidance cameras when traveling in certain directions. Another consideration in traverse planning is the achievement of the mission’s scientific objectives (e.g., detecting and characterizing deposits of water ice or other volatile materials and maximizing exploration within the area). To incorporate such constraints and considerations, NASA uses SHERPA for the VIPER mission [9], which synthesizes mission plans that optimize scientific productivity and maximize robustness to delays, malfunctions, and other adverse conditions using sampling-based solvers such as MCTS [10, 11]. Prior automated lunar planners, in contrast, focused on safe reachability and topology and global path optimization [13, 14, 15]. However, SHERPA’s algorithmic framing may not be directly useful to the science team, who want to understand the solution within the context of science objectives. Our work targets this gap by using an LLM to explain the output from an MCTS-based planner that, coupled with a VIPER-inspired simulator, produces optimized rover trajectories. Previous work that integrates LLMs with planning has used them to define goals for task and motion planning [1], translate natural language task specifications into formal representations that planners consume [2], reason about motion failures and propose corrections [3], and serve as state trackers for long-horizon planners [5]. Additionally, recent work has placed LLMs inside MCTS itself, using them as a heuristic to guide the search [6]. LLMs in these algorithms drive planners within the decision loop to produce better trajectories, rather than being used to explain the resulting output trajectories after the planner is done. One work has also used LLMs to explain decisions in dynamic environments, such as lane changing [16], but is limited to vehicle interaction modeling and does not consider using LLMs with motion planning algorithms. Other works explore dynamic reasoning for trajectories [17] or combining MCTS with LLMs for self-training, evaluating intermediate reasoning steps for LLM outputs [18]. These approaches are promising for interfacing LLMs with MCTS but are directed at improving LLMs rather than using them to explain trajectories. Another application merges LLM reasoning with MCTS planning for dynamic behaviors in video games, where LLMs and MCTS work together to create emergent narratives [19]. While relevant to interfacing LLMs and MCTS, this work aims to improve agent behavior with LLMs, instead of using them for explainability. Pretrained LLMs often perform worse on domain-specific tasks. Their broad training priors typically do not contain domain expert knowledge, so with zero-shot prompting, the model fills the gap with plausible-sounding but incorrect claims from its prior knowledge. Therefore, LLMs benefit from additional structure and knowledge for these tasks. For instance, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) [20] is a framework that grounds LLM responses in external data from a trusted source when queried. Additionally, tool-use frameworks treat the LLM as a controller that calls previously designed functions to inspect state or invoke external systems. ReAct (Reasoning and Acting framework) [21] allows the LLM to perform both reasoning and actionable tool calls. DSPy [22] puts this framework into a programmable module, so rather than relying on exact keyword matches for retrieval, the LLM decides which tools to call from declarative signatures. Unlike previous applications of these frameworks individually, our setting requires both in different roles. Retrieval without action tools could only describe prior runs, while tool access without retrieval could not translate between mission-language queries and planner outputs. With the steady improvements in LLMs, there is existing work that also considers using them to build trustworthiness for AI-based planning. Previous work uses them to explain how automated planners justify decisions to humans through plan explanations, contrastive “why not” queries, and model reconciliation [23]. These methods are tied to planners whose actions and states are discrete and labeled. They do not transfer to trajectory planners that operate over continuous, nondeterministic dynamics like the MCTS solver we use. Some prior work has also involved translating robot control policies into natural-language descriptions [24], having robots verbalize their plans before acting [25], and providing causal model grounded explanations for the behavior of model-free reinforcement learning agents [26]. However, though these efforts are meant to build trust between humans and autonomous systems, they explain the planner’s internal policy to a passive observer rather than the planner’s outputs to a domain expert without an algorithmic background. III Methodology We formulate our VIPER-inspired trajectory planning problem within a science station as a sequential decision-making problem, and develop an MCTS-based planner that uses a simulator grounded in mission requirements and constraints. We then develop an LLM-based framework for providing accurate explanations of the planning results with a retrieval layer and tool catalog for a ReAct module. We consider a rover that collects science data with contact measurements at a set number of drill sites and non-contact prospecting while traversing between the sites. This data is provided to the LLM assistant to provide comprehensive explanations to the user. As seen in Figure 1, the assistant consists of three components that work with the planner: a chatbot user interface, a retrieval layer that grounds explanations in source material, and a tool catalog that the LLM calls. The science team interacts with the assistant through a chat window where queries are typed and sent to the LLM agent. The framework parses the query and responds back in the chat window. The retrieval layer gives the LLM the mission documents, planner source code (or the data), plots, and solutions that result from the planner as context when answering the user. Mission-document retrieval is implemented as a semantic search over chunked embeddings of the document. The source code and data retrieval are path lookups, so every cited fact is traceable to a specific file at a specific revision. The chatbot is implemented with the ReAct framework [21] as a programmable DSPy module, allowing for more robust reasoning and acting than zero-shot prompting or retrieval alone can achieve. This structure requires a tool catalog that provides actions for the LLM to call (which align with possible operations that the science team may want to perform), listed here: Run science station: Plan a full science station mission from scratch and return the summary. Set start time: Change the science station start date and time and replan, but reject start times whose 24-hour plan would result in sun shadows covering part or the entirety of the science station. Add or replace POI: Evaluate adding or replacing points of interest at specific coordinates. Returns feasibility and time impact. Replan with new map: Replan the science station using a different ice-map file. Plan arbitrary region: Plan a science station inside an arbitrarily shaped science region whose boundaries are defined by vertices given by the user. Select custom drill sites: Plan a science station using user-chosen drill sites from the candidate set. If infeasible, it suggests single-site swaps. Force site order: Replan with a user-specified site ordering rather than the planner’s chosen order. Risk assessment: Roll out the current plan [FORMULA] times under randomized, user-fixed, best-case, or worst-case speed uncertainty. Report the timing distribution (P50, P75, P90, P95, P99) and the success rate of reaching the goal end location. A success is defined as reaching the three drill sites before the goal within 24 hours and prospecting at least 190 m. These actions allow the user to quickly replan with new conditions, make comparisons between potential plans, or improve understanding of the decisions made by the planner. The LLM is instantiated with a prompt that takes the query as input and requires a natural-language response output. The LLM uses this prompt and the query to decide which tools and documents to call to generate the best response. The prompt to the LLM includes high-level guardrails to encourage responses that may resonate better with the science team. It constrains outputs to the operator vocabulary used by the science team (e.g., science station time budget, estimated ice quality, sun-relative SMG) and forbids algorithmic terminology (future rollouts, value estimates, reward functions). It also enforces that every factual claim in the response must trace either to a tool result or to the user query, not the model’s prior knowledge. The LLM assistant does not modify the underlying MDP or override the planner. It can only run the planner on behalf of the user with their specified conditions or explain the results, without telling the user what they should do. We design experiments to highlight the assistant’s contributions: (i) does the assistant correctly parse the user’s mission-language requests to identify the correct tools and information needed, and (ii) are the resulting explanations faithful to the planner’s outputs and to the source material? We report multiple metrics across multiple query categories and baselines/versions, with validation of any LLM-judged metric against human labels [32]. We construct a query bank of [FORMULA] science team questions, with the following categories: Compare potential new plan: Add or replace points of interest or drill sites, force a visit order, shift the science station start time, restrict planning to an arbitrary region, run multi-target science requests, and inspect individual segments, Feasibility: Evaluate confidence/risk of goal completion under probabilistic speed, Mission-document and source code lookup: Retrieval-only questions answered from the mission documents, the planner code and outputs, or descriptions of the assistant’s capabilities, Ambiguous/Edge Cases: Prompts where the LLM should request clarification (e.g.,“is it safe?”,“make it faster”) or for impossible to answer queries (e.g.,“place a drill site outside of the bounds”). For each query, we record the LLM’s expected behavior (answer, clarify, or refuse), the expected tools the human expert would use, any data files the LLM should reference, and the expected human response in operator vocabulary. We compare four LLM assistant versions to be tested on the same query bank, sharing the same underlying generator LLM, decoding parameters, and vocabulary guardrails. The four versions highlight the contributions of the selected scaffolding, tools, and retrieval in the complete version. The versions are: Zero-shot LLM: The generator receives only the user’s query, with no system guardrails prompt, no tool catalog, and no retrieval layer, Closed-book LLM: The generator receives the user query and the guardrails prompt, but no tools and no retrieval, so it only relies on prior knowledge, No-retrieval assistant: ReAct with the action tools but without the retrieval layer, Full assistant: All retrieval and action tools with ReAct. We do not have a retrieval-only version with action tools removed because that chatbot could only answer lookup-related questions and not any plan comparison queries. We organize our metrics into three categories. Trajectory metrics test task success on whether the LLM called the right tools with the right arguments. Extra tool calls and extra optional arguments are allowed, but every oracle tool and every oracle argument value must be present. We also report passn [33], the fraction of queries on which the assistant succeeds for all tested seeds. Task success is defined only for variants with tool access. Semantic metrics test whether the natural-language response is accurate to the tool outputs and consistent with the human reference answer. For semantic accuracy, we report the fraction of factual claims in the response that are supported by the simulation data and tool outputs, ensuring the LLM is not favoring responding based on its prior knowledge. Because hand-labeling every response across all four versions and seeds is intractable at this scale, we evaluate responses on their semantic content with an LLM judge. We use a [FORMULA] – [FORMULA] G-Eval [34] score that considers consistency, relevance, and vocabulary against the human reference and pairwise win rate [35], measuring which version’s response the judge prefers when shown side by side. To validate the LLM judge, we hand-labeled a [FORMULA] -query subset on semantic accuracy (yes/no/uncertain) and behavior, and we report Cohen’s [FORMULA] [36] between judge and human on each axis. Cohen’s [FORMULA] is a standard agreement metric that measures how much a judge and a human agree beyond what would happen by chance, penalizing a judge that defaults to the dominant label in the dataset. Following common practice in LLM-judge validation [37], we treat [FORMULA] as a threshold below which we reject the judge’s categorizations. The judge is selected from a different model family than the generator to reduce self-preference bias [38]. Consistency metrics test whether semantically equivalent queries produce equivalent responses in the tools called and the semantic meaning. For queries whose expected behavior is to refuse or request clarification, we report whether the LLM executed the correct behavior. Each query is run independently through each variant for four seeds. We also note the monetary and latency costs of running each model. Reported numbers are means with [FORMULA] bootstrap confidence intervals over the query bank, computed per query category. IV Results Before evaluating the framework, we verify that the underlying planner responds to the inputs that the science team may want to vary: start time, selected POIs, the underlying ice map, the site visit order, the boundary area, and the probabilistic SMG. Figure 3 shows that each of these inputs changes the resulting plan in ways that match physical intuition. Delaying the start time by 12 hours changes both the route and the chosen drill set, since the planner might need to choose a different route to compensate for different SMG values. With our 200-rollout risk assessment, we observe that the science station durations cluster slightly above the deterministic estimate of 20.15 hours, with a small tail extending toward the 24-hour limit, a behavior consistent with the clipped SMG distribution. Across the rollouts, 99.5% finished within the 24-hour limit. Inserting 2 POIs correctly changes the trajectory to route through. Replanning with a different ice map changes the drill candidates and chosen drill sites, therefore changing the trajectory. Enforcing a non-optimal drill order produced a 24.45-hour trajectory, exceeding the time limit, which was a reasonable result. Finally, we verified that the planner was able to plan within an arbitrarily defined science station area, given new start and end locations. Verifying that these results are reasonable for the planner, we then evaluate the LLM assistant’s ability to call the correct tools and information to explain the solutions.   Table I reports the four-framework versions on the metrics defined in Section III-D3. Comparing against an expert-labeled dataset, trajectory metrics score whether the assistant selects the correct tools, documents, and behavior (answer, clarify, refuse), and semantic metrics score whether the response is accurate to the output trajectories and external documents provided. We use GPT-5.4 and Claude Opus 4.8 as they represent current frontier models from two distinct families. Across both chatbot/judge combinations of GPT and Opus, the full assistant (with the guardrail prompt, retrieval layer, and action tools) achieved the highest score on every metric except G-Eval (vocabulary), or how well the response reuses the science team’s mission terminology. The zero-shot baseline, without tools or retrieval, can only ground its responses in the terminology from the query, whereas the other versions also bring in additional information surfaced by tool calls and retrieval. Vocabulary alone is not a comprehensive metric. The full framework outperforms on G-Eval (consistency) and (relevance), which measure whether the response is internally coherent and addresses the question asked, respectively. It also calls the correct tools with the correct arguments more often than the no-retrieval version, as shown with task success and passn, and had a higher behavior accuracy, though just barely above zero-shot, since most of the queries called for an answer, and zero-shot rarely refuses to answer or asks for clarification. The full version’s responses are also preferred more often than the other versions’ responses. For pairwise win rate, the Opus judge prefers the full assistant to closed-book 70.0% of the time and to no-retrieval 65.4%. The GPT judge preferred full to closed-book 85.2% of the time. Moreover, as expected, the full version’s responses were more correct than the other versions, as it had access to all tools and documents. We tested both combinations of chatbot/judge, with GPT-5.4 as chatbot and Opus 4.8 as judge, and vice versa. The full assistant outperforms on all metrics except G-Eval (vocabulary) for both combinations. Opus outperforms GPT on all metrics except for faithfulness. From a qualitative examination of the prompts, Opus’s responses were more verbose, so even though there were correct facts, it often added fabricated details as well. For instance, for the query “How much margin do we have under the 24-hour budget?” GPT correctly answered, ”The current plan finishes in 20.15 hours, leaving 3.85 hours of margin under the 24-hour budget for prospecting,” whereas Opus added a per-segment breakdown of slack and claimed that ”the drill-3 segment contributed the largest share of the buffer at 1.4 hours,” a number not given by any tool. Though Opus outperforms in other metrics, faithfulness is likely the most important metric. For the trajectory metrics, the assistant may use different tools than expected, but still get the correct response, and the G-Eval metrics are more valuable if accompanied by accurate responses. Moreover, Opus rarely refuses to answer or asks for clarification. The no-retrieval Opus version repeatedly tried to call inaccessible retrieval tools, exhausting tokens and time, and errored before producing a hallucinated response. The judge’s assessments are only trustworthy if they are aligned with a human expert’s judgments. To validate the LLM judges, we hand-labeled a subset of 50 responses for faithfulness and behavior (answer/clarify/refuse). Since [FORMULA] [37], we can rely on the judge’s scores as a proxy for human-validated checks on the responses. Therefore, with this validation and high faithfulness score with GPT chatbot, we consider the better pairing to be GPT as the chatbot and Opus as the judge. This is further supported by the comparison of time and token monetary costs incurred by each model as chatbots. Finally, to evaluate robustness to phrasing, we ran semantically equivalent queries on the full assistant. There was consistent accuracy between single-fact lookups (e.g., “How long was the science station duration?”), specified a run with new conditions (e.g., “Insert a POI at [FORMULA] ”), or risk assessments (e.g., “How confident are we that we’ll make it to the goal on time?”). There were inconsistencies when the answer asked for just an explanation, not retrieving or running a tool. Near-synonyms such as asking for how much buffer, slack, or remaining margin returned the exact, correct value, but the assistant provided supporting math only for slack and margin. Queries like “how does [FORMULA] work?” or “why does the path do [FORMULA] ?” produced inconsistent explanations. For example, asking variations of “how does the planner weigh ice concentration vs. uncertainty?” incorrectly claimed that the planner prioritizes value and uses uncertainty as a tiebreaker or the correct formula. To address semantic inconsistencies, we can steer the LLM with DSPy prompt optimization [22]. The queries that failed faithfulness were on topics implemented in the planner, but had no grounding in retrieved documents. The full assistant’s 90.9% faithfulness is a nearly 65% improvement over the 26.7% zero-shot baseline. While hallucinations are a risk of any LLM system, we can improve through interactive sessions with the science team, addressing topics like tacking that are implemented but not discussed in the retrieved documentation. V Conclusion We presented an LLM-based framework for explaining lunar rover trajectories planned under uncertainty, with an MCTS planner accompanied by a VIPER-inspired simulator that includes probabilistic SMGs, a 24-hour budget, and exploration vs. exploitation tradeoffs. The full framework with action tools and retrieval outperforms the zero-shot baseline, with a 90.9% accuracy rate of responses. Our work has several opportunities for future improvement. We can extend the MDP to handle partial observability and incorporate active uncertainty reduction during trajectory planning. Additionally, we would like to test other solvers and use cases beyond MCTS and VIPER SST. The code repository for this work is available at https://michelleho-24.github.io/rover-explainablity/. PneuGen: Task-Driven Agentic Co-Design of Soft Pneumatic Robots Task-driven design of soft robots requires the consideration of factors such as geometry, morphology, material properties, and actuation, resulting in a large and complex design space that is challenging to explore. Computational optimisation methods leverage signals from simulation to iteratively improve designs to achieve task objectives. However, these methods typically demand high computational load for both optimisation and simulation. We present PneuGen, an agentic co-design framework for soft robots that leverages Large Language Model (LLM) agents to search over the soft robot design space efficiently. A designer agent proposes design programs from a parametric component library, and a separate critic agent analyses simulation diagnostics and recommends targeted revisions. Fitted module response models provide reusable physical priors relating geometry and pressure to deformation. Design programs are automatically validated and converted into finite-element simulations, enabling iterative evaluation. Across grasping tasks on primitive shapes and challenging objects, as well as shape-matching tasks that require multi-directional planar and 3D deformation, the proposed framework significantly outperforms prior computational optimisation baselines. Ablation experiments also highlight the utility of the critic agent and the module response model in facilitating efficient design. We additionally demonstrate the agent-generated soft robot designs in real-world shape-matching and grasping tasks. I Introduction Soft robots offer advantages of mechanical compliance, adaptability, and flexibility to achieve a wide range of behaviours, allowing them to accommodate uncertainty in tasks such as manipulation [1, 2]. However, their behaviour depends strongly on geometry, material properties, and the arrangement of compliant elements. These make the design of soft robots particularly challenging because of the large and complex design space, where morphology and actuation need to be selected jointly [3]. This coupling motivates task-driven design methods that select geometry and actuation together. In this aspect, heuristic methods rely heavily on the designer’s experience, which limits their scalability [4]. Computational methods have shown great potential in soft robot design [3, 5, 6, 4]. Prior approaches have explored both the optimisation of existing actuator families and the generation of new morphologies [5, 6, 4, 7]. Parametric methods optimise geometric and actuation variables using physical models or learned surrogates, enabling task-specific design of pneumatic actuators and tendon-driven soft hands [4]. Shape and topology optimisation extend the search to material distributions and structural features, while graph-based evolutionary methods explore alternative arrangements and connectivity[8]. Differentiable simulation and learned physical models further support the joint optimisation of morphology and actuation or grasp configuration [9, 10]. These advances demonstrate the potential of computational search across increasingly expressive design spaces. However, these methods typically have substantial computational requirements, not only in the design optimisation process, but also through the repeated simulation and evaluation that are required, motivating methods that extract more useful guidance from each evaluation. Furthermore, many of these computational approaches rely on manually crafted loss functions for optimisation, which both limit their generalisability and sometimes do not offer sufficient appropriate signals [9, 10]. Large language models (LLMs) offer a means of incorporating broad prior knowledge into computational design [11, 12, 13]. Through large-scale pretraining, these models are able to interpret task requirements, module behaviour descriptions, and feedback diagnostics. These capabilities help connect a task description to appropriate design choices. Their ability to generate structured descriptions and code also allows these choices to be expressed as design programs and revised in a principled manner within an iterative search. Beyond proposing designs, multimodal LLMs can analyse simulation observations and failure diagnostics to formulate explanations for unsuccessful designs and provide much richer guidance than task scores alone, as well as propose targeted revisions. By employing different instances of LLMs as agents with different roles, we are able to construct a designer-critic paradigm in which appropriate designs can be devised efficiently without extensive computational evaluations and expensive simulation. In this paper, we present PneuGen, a task-driven agentic co-design framework for soft robots. An overview of the framework is shown in Fig. 1. A designer LLM agent constructs designs from a library of parametric components and jointly selects their spatial arrangement, geometric parameters, and actuation. A separate critic agent interprets simulation diagnostics and proposes revisions for subsequent design iterations. Component-level pressure-to-displacement maps, represented by fitted module response models, provide a physics prior on how geometry and pressure affect deformation. The resulting design programs are automatically converted into CAD models, meshes, and finite-element simulations. The framework also supports selection from different families of soft robot components to satisfy task requirements. Our contributions are: An agentic co-design loop that combines soft robot geometry and actuation design with simulation-based evaluation and critic-guided refinement. A library of soft robot components with fitted module response models, geometric and fabrication constraints, and automatic CAD and simulation generation to support task-driven design. An evaluation on simulated grasping and shape-matching tasks against random search, genetic search, and CMA-ES with real-world demonstrations, and an investigation of the effects of module response models and critic guidance. II Literature Review Our work connects computational optimisation of soft robot morphology and actuation with LLM-based design generation and refinement. In this section, we review these areas with particular attention to the computational cost and the generalisability of the approaches. Prior works have employed computational optimisation methods for the design of soft robots, where the optimisation encompasses parameters, morphology and control. Parametric approaches search within an explicitly defined actuator family. For example, SPADA combines surrogate models derived from finite-element models (FEMs), shape segmentation, and genetic optimisation to generate actuator geometries and export fabrication-ready CAD models [6]. Subsequent work embeds reduced-order FEM surrogates in a rigid-body simulation environment, enabling optimisation of gripper geometry and pressure commands under different conditions [4]. However, these works typically focus on a single actuator family with pre-defined structures [5, 6]. Additional works attempt to modify structural features and material distributions. For example, SimTO estimates loading conditions from simulated gripper–object interactions and uses them to optimise finger topology, and Farinha et al. combine graph-encoded soft structures with multi-objective quality-diversity optimisation across grasping tasks [7, 8]. Additionally, DiffAqua uses differentiable simulation to co-design soft-swimmer geometry and control. These methods broaden the design space, but their search strategies depend on suitable numerical encodings and, for gradient-based optimisation, differentiable representations [9]. They also demand heavy computation, and the optimisation objectives are typically manually crafted and tuned for each task. The cost of evaluating candidate designs has also motivated the development of efficient evaluation methods. For example, neural physics models support optimisation of stiffness distributions and grasp poses, while learned reward models reduce the simulations required to search for soft robot designs [14, 15]. Genetic search can also reuse policies across related morphologies [16]. However, these learned methods depend on data covering the relevant designs and behaviours, adding a computational burden and limiting generalisability. LLMs have been used to directly generate design proposals and interpret evaluation feedback. For example, RoboMorph generates grammar-constrained modular robots within an evolutionary loop [17]. LASeR incorporates reflection on search trajectories for voxel-based soft robot design, while Auto-Robotist maintains reusable, evidence-supported design rules [18, 19]. However, these methods typically focus on simple or planar designs without complex geometries. Additionally, LLMs have also been connected to parametric CAD representations. For example, Lang2Morph connects task descriptions to parametric hand geometry, using semantic alignment and dimensional compatibility for refinement [12]. However, it only uses morphology evaluation, which does not establish performance under physical contact or actual deployment conditions. AID-SR provides this physical grounding through structured simulation feedback for tendon-driven continuum robots [13]. However, its functionality evaluation requires a reinforcement-learning controller for each candidate, thus coupling the design score to controller training outcomes. The designs also mainly focus on simple structures. Compared to the prior methods, the PneuGen framework leverages agentic design for complex soft robots with critic-guided refinement, supporting multiple families of actuators, and also achieving generalisability and efficiency with minimal human intervention. III Methodology To address the challenges with soft robot design, we propose an agentic task-driven co-design framework that jointly selects soft robot components, their spatial arrangement, geometric parameters, and actuation commands. Given a desired task, a designer LLM agent generates robot design proposals, while a separate critic agent interprets simulation diagnostics and recommends revisions. The designs are evaluated in finite-element simulation for downstream task performance. In this section, we discuss the representation of the design with the module response models, and the agentic designer-critic architecture employed by the PneuGen framework. A detailed overview of the framework is shown in Fig. 2. Given a task description, the designer then needs to jointly select these values. An additional programmatic validator first checks geometric compatibility, manufacturing constraints, component intersections, and simulation resource limits in the proposed design. Valid design programs are automatically converted into CAD geometry, and tetrahedralised to generate a finite-element mesh. The mesh and actuation specifications are then used to assemble the simulation scene, enabling candidate designs to be evaluated without manual geometry reconstruction or meshing. We approximate the module response using [FORMULA] where [FORMULA] contains coefficients fitted to simulation data collected through actuation sweeps. The agents receive these fitted relationships as reusable physical priors for proposing and revising design changes together with reference examples. LLM agents support separate role definitions, which enable us to construct a designer-critic architecture. One LLM agent acts as the designer and proposes designs based on available information, while another agent acts as the critic to provide analysis and recommendation to encourage better designs. The agents interact sequentially through structured recommendations and a shared design history. Specifically, at each iteration, the designer proposes a batch of design candidates that follow three complementary strategies. refine: retain a promising mechanism and adjust a coherent group of parameters; redesign: make structural or parametric changes to address the main observed failure; alternative: explore a different arrangement or operating mechanism. The design candidates are first passed to the programmatic validator and then used to generate geometric meshes for the task simulation in FEM. The simulation results are used to inform the next iteration. For the initial iteration, we leverage a reference design for the same family of tasks, such as a reference gripper for grasping tasks. Both agents receive the task specification, component information, and fitted module response models, but receive different feedback. The designer receives previous designs, task-level feedback from the FEM simulation, critic’s analysis and recommendation, and information from the programmatic validators identifying physical constraints that are violated. In addition, the critic receives this information together with detailed diagnostics and additional measurements from the privileged simulation. The critic first compares its previous predictions with measured outcomes, then proposes explanations for failures and provides recommendations on revisions corresponding to the refinement, redesign, and alternative strategies with confidence levels. The advice identifies the affected parameters, proposed changes, expected mechanism, predicted outcome, and relevant constraint margins. The designer then determines whether to follow these recommendations based on confidence levels. V Results and Discussion This section discusses the results of the agentic framework for pneumatic soft robot design, and the performances of the designs in grasping and shape-matching tasks compared to baselines. Besides task successes, we also evaluate the efficiency of the design framework in obtaining working designs with the minimum number of simulation evaluations, which directly relate to the computational load required for running the SOFA simulations. For both the grasping and the shape-matching experiments, we leverage three seeds and compute the standard error of the mean. The grasping performances are evaluated in the simulation using ten additional noisy trials on top of the challenging grasping procedures that include shaking. As can be seen in Table I, in both primitive shape set and YCB object sets, the agentic design framework is able to significantly outperform the baselines in grasping performance, given the same evaluation budget in SOFA. One possible explanation for GA’s low performance is limited score variation among unsuccessful designs near the reference configuration. Examples of the agent-designed grippers and the corresponding objects can be seen in Fig. 3, which demonstrate that the agent is able to generate varied designs according to the requirement of the task. It should also be noted that these designs all share an initial reference design that fails on the task and require task-specific optimisations to be able to grasp the target objects. By incorporating prior physics knowledge from the module response models and their pre-training, as well as the ability to interpret simulation results and come up with dedicated solutions to grasping failures without manual involvement, the agentic framework demonstrates superior performance and improved efficiency. Furthermore, to further contextualise the performance of the agentic framework against the baselines, we perform an additional experiment by running the computational baseline methods with more than six times the FEM evaluation budget by increasing the population size and the number of iterations. On the primitive shape objects, CMA-ES achieves a hold rate of 0.88 [FORMULA] 0.12, similar to the agentic framework, and GA achieves 0.17 [FORMULA] 0.17. On YCB objects, CMA-ES only achieves 0.62 [FORMULA] 0.18 and GA achieves a hold rate similar to that obtained on primitive shapes, both remaining significantly below the agentic framework. This demonstrates that PneuGen is able to find high-performing designs much more efficiently than these baselines, and is also more capable of handling complex shapes. In shape-matching tasks, the agentic framework is also able to outperform the baseline methods and design pneumatic soft robots that are better able to produce the desired shapes. As seen in Table II, across the different desired planar and 3D shapes, the framework’s designs achieve a lower mean centreline error, demonstrating effective use of module behaviour information. It should also be noted that in the shape-matching task, the task objectives provide an arguably stronger signal than the grasp score, especially for the computational optimisation baseline methods; yet the agentic framework is still able to outperform them given the same evaluation budget. Visual demonstrations of the shape-matching experiments are also shown in Fig. 4. In tasks such as the s-bend, the generated designs used changes in local bending orientation between successive modules to reproduce opposing curvatures under a shared pressure input. Furthermore, as some of the shape-matching tasks require the three-chamber actuator instead of the single-chamber module, this demonstrates that the framework is able to connect the component behaviour with the requirement of the task and select the appropriate component family for iterative optimisation. To investigate the utility of the different building blocks of the agentic framework, we evaluate two ablations: removing the critic agent and removing the fitted module response models. As seen in Table III, using the critic agent is able to improve the performance of the soft robot design in both the grasping tasks and the shape-matching tasks. In the grasping task, the critic improvement is also slightly more significant for the more challenging YCB objects, pointing to a potential for improving designs for more complex objects. Additionally, using the critic agent enables the framework to achieve task successes with fewer FEM evaluations than using the designer agent alone, reducing the average number of required evaluations by two and six for grasping and shape-matching tasks respectively. Through stronger diagnostics and analysis, the critic agent helps avoid design failures, and reduces the computational load for running expensive FEM simulations. By examining the designer’s recorded design rationales, we identify that the critic agent is typically able to suggest better designs. The critic is also tasked to focus on analysing failures in the design proposals, thus potentially providing more insights into the reasons behind task failures for the designer to consider. Additionally, the incorporation of the confidence label also prevents forcing the designer to follow the critic’s recommendations. From results of the ablation without the response model in Table III, it can be seen that removing the module response model reduces the performance of the agentic design framework. One possible explanation is that, without such models, the agents need to first perform explorations to understand the behaviour of the modules when actuated. LLM agents offer an intuitive way to incorporate such reusable models of module behaviour, which is typically unavailable for baselines without extensive manual efforts in incorporating the models into the computational search. However, the improvement is less significant than the critic, potentially because the module behaviour is relatively simple and can be sufficiently explored within the evaluation budget. Including the response model also reduces the number of FEM evaluations required to achieve task success by two and four for grasping and shape-matching respectively, thus making the design process more efficient. In this way, the PneuGen framework offers a pathway for efficient design of soft robots leveraging libraries of components with known behaviours. To validate the PneuGen framework in the real world, we 3D printed the agent-designed soft robots for the shape-matching and object grasping tasks. As can be seen in Fig. 5, the printed soft pneumatic robots are able to match the desired shape and grasp the target objects successfully. In real-world grasping evaluations, the agent-designed grippers are also able to successfully execute target behaviours and grasp the real world YCB objects securely without failure. These results demonstrate the validity of the simulation experiment evaluations, and also illustrate the utility of the PneuGen framework in efficient task-driven design of pneumatic soft robots for real world applications. VI Conclusion We presented PneuGen, a task-driven co-design framework for pneumatic soft robots that combines a designer LLM agent with a critic agent for iterative design optimisation. The framework uses a parametric component library, module response models, and automatic CAD-to-FEM generation to support the joint selection of component family, spatial arrangements, geometric parameters, and actuation pressures. Across grasping and shape-matching tasks in FEM simulation, PneuGen outperforms all baselines under matched evaluation budgets. Ablations also show that critic guidance and module response models improved performance and reduced the number of FEM evaluations needed to achieve task success. We further validate the PneuGen framework by 3D printing agent designs, which demonstrate successful grasping and shape-matching in the real world. Future work should extend the component library to include additional actuation mechanisms, and also evaluate the use of different LLMs as agents.

We present AHEADance, a robot-native streaming dance generator executed on a humanoid robot by a whole-body tracker. ListenAhead conditions each chunk on heard music and a frozen music model’s forecasts of the coming music, aligned to their target times and weighted by reliability. The forecasts carry the timing of upcoming beats almost as well as the actual future; with them, the generator is better synchronized with the music and concentrates more motion energy at its song’s beat frequency. Commit Forcing trains continuation from the model’s own committed chunks, updating both the latent history and the decoded boundary of the next chunk; it reduces low activity from 83.5% to 10.3%, the level of real dance. I Introduction A humanoid that dances to streamed music works under constraints that offline choreography does not face. It hears only the music that has already played, yet each motion chunk is generated from the music heard up to the moment its own music begins, so that the delay from music to motion does not grow with the chunk length. And committed motion cannot be revised, so every new chunk has to continue from motion the model itself produced rather than from a clean reference. Unlike animation, every committed chunk is then executed by a whole-body tracking controller on the robot, so it must also be trackable, and generation must keep pace with the controller’s clock. Under these constraints the robot must keep dancing for as long as the music plays, come to rest when it stops and dance again when it returns. Music-to-dance generators, including long-form ones [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], receive the complete music in advance. Streaming humanoid systems hear the music causally: DiscoForcing [6] streams with diffusion forcing and retargets the generated human motion, RoboPerform [7] maps audio to a control policy, and InfiniDanceRobot [8] closes the loop between a planner and its tracker; none of them describes forecasting the coming music. Autoregressive generators trained on reference histories meet their own outputs at inference; diffusion forcing [9] and self forcing [10] address this for the history the generator conditions on, whereas a chunked robot generator also conditions on the decoded pose boundary it has committed. For a robot-native streaming generator, three questions remain: how much of the coming music a causal generator can use, how to continue reliably from its own committed chunks when both the latent history and the decoded pose boundary change, and how to show that the executed behavior follows the music rather than its own momentum. We present AHEADance (Figs. and 2), which generates humanoid reference motion chunk by chunk from streaming audio and executes it with a whole-body tracking controller. Our contributions are: ListenAhead. Each chunk is conditioned on heard music and on short-horizon forecasts of a frozen music model [11], aligned to their target times and weighted by their reliability. The forecasts carry the timing of upcoming beats almost as well as the actual future, and most of what the actual future carries about note onsets; a generator trained with them is better synchronized with the music and concentrates more motion energy at the song’s beat frequency. Commit Forcing. Continuation is trained from the model’s own committed outputs: noise-corrupted reference chunks are reconstructed, decoded and committed in order, and each commit updates both the latent history and the decoded reference boundary that conditions the next chunk. Low activity falls from 83.5% under reference-history training to 10.3%, the level of real dance. A validated evaluation of music correspondence. Three evaluators test humanoid dance against its music: synchronization with ChoreoSync, a detector of our own; song with MMR; and style with a style classifier. Each is validated on real G1 dance it never saw. On songs unseen in training, AHEADance reaches the highest ChoreoSync offset accuracy (28.6%) and MMR (0.187, against at most 0.046) of all compared generators. Code, evaluation scripts and the metric-validation protocol will be released upon acceptance. II Related Work AIST++/FACT [1], Bailando [12] and Bailando++ [13] learn choreography through sequence modeling and discrete motion representations, and Danceba [14] adds gated rhythm-aware features for beat alignment. EDGE [2] and LODGE [5] extend diffusion-based synthesis to long soundtracks. ChoreoMamba uses bidirectional music conditioning for long-sequence generation [15]. FineDance [3], MEGADance [16], and SoulNet [4] further address fine-grained motion, genre-aware generation, and music–motion correspondence. Our focus is anticipatory continuation in robot coordinates as music arrives. DiscoForcing [6] combines causal audio features with diffusion forcing for streaming character motion, followed by retargeting and tracking for humanoid execution, and shows responses to music stopping qualitatively. RoboPerform [7] instead maps audio-derived style to humanoid actions through a teacher–student policy. InfiniDanceRobot [8] streams music features into a latent diffusion-forcing planner that emits humanoid references, trains a dedicated tracker, and closes the loop by refining the planner with tracker rollouts and writing the executed state back into its history. III Method At decision time [FORMULA] , the generator has access to heard audio [FORMULA] , latent history [FORMULA] , and boundary state [FORMULA] reconstructed from the last committed reference poses. Let [FORMULA] denote its music condition. Each decision generates one chunk as a root trajectory [FORMULA] , discrete codes [FORMULA] , and continuous corrections [FORMULA] (Sec. III-B). We use a commit-aligned motion codec: encoding, generation, and commitment share the same fixed-length chunk. The codec compresses reference body motion into latent vectors and decodes each generated chunk once from its root trajectory and the preceding committed boundary. Each complete chunk is committed before the next decision, so committed motion is never decoded again. V Discussion The forecasts carry the timing of the next beats almost as well as the actual future, and most of what the actual future carries about note onsets; the generator converts them into better synchronization and more motion energy at the music’s beat frequency. Turning anticipated beats into the timing of movement accents is the most direct next step (Sec. IV-C), followed by a perceptual study of how audiences judge the dance. AHEADance’s kinetic diversity still remains below that of real dance. Forecasts anticipate regular structure such as beats, but not an abrupt change such as a sudden stop, to which the robot responds afterwards (about 1 s in simulation). The music scores are measured on the generated references, which a general-purpose tracker executes after a fixed delivery delay; a tracker trained for dance could preserve more of their beat-level detail. The generator does not receive the measured robot state, and it runs off-board on a workstation; feeding the state back and running on the robot are left to future work. VI Conclusion AHEADance generates robot-native dance from streaming audio under causal music access and irrevocable commitments. A future-aligned music channel anticipates beat timing and improves synchronization and beat-frequency motion over a generator trained without it, a gain that the last heard music state alone does not provide, and training continuation from the model’s own committed chunks keeps low activity at the level of real dance. ChoreoSync and MMR, validated on real G1 dance, show that AHEADance follows unseen songs more closely than other generators, and on FineDance songs it never heard, its style follows the music more closely than that of any generator not given the genre.

Discrete Model-Based Diffusion for Combinatorial Optimization in Multi-Robot Task Allocation Decision making in multi-agent and multi-robot systems often involves discrete decision variables, leading to NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems that must be solved within seconds for near real-time implementation. Denoising diffusion has emerged as a powerful tool for such problems, but existing approaches face a trade-off: Model-Based Diffusion (MBD) incorporates diffusion in sampling-based optimization (SBO) without training but only over continuous spaces, while existing diffusion-based combinatorial solvers operate over discrete spaces but require offline training. To this end, we propose Discrete Model-Based Diffusion (Discrete MBD), a training-free SBO method that directly optimizes discrete variables by approximating categorical reverse transition distributions through Monte Carlo sampling. We establish a finite-step lower bound on the probability of finding a global minimizer and show that this bound converges to one as the number of denoising steps increases. Extensive experiments on generic integer programs and heterogeneous multi-robot coalition formation and scheduling demonstrate that Discrete MBD outperforms SBO baselines in nearly all settings while achieving solution quality competitive with that of mixed-integer programming and reinforcement learning methods at a fraction of their computational cost. I Introduction Many decision-making problems in multi-robot and broadly multi-agent systems involve inherently discrete choices, such as assigning tasks to robots [18, 35, 11], selecting the modes of hybrid systems [25, 14], and avoiding obstacles [16, 19]. These decisions give rise to combinatorial optimization problems that are often NP-hard, with solution spaces growing exponentially with problem size, making high-quality solutions difficult to obtain within the tight time budgets of online operation. A representative example, used throughout this paper, is the heterogeneous multi-robot task allocation (MRTA) problem, where robots with different skills, each at a different capability level, must complete spatially distributed tasks as quickly as possible [11, 1, 9] (Figure 1). Specifically, we consider joint coalition formation and scheduling, where each task requires tight coordination [31]: task execution begins only once a coalition with sufficient combined skill capabilities gathers at the task location. Robots must therefore jointly decide which robots serve each task (coalition formation) and when each robot executes its tasks (scheduling) to minimize makespan. This places the problem in the single-task robots, multi-robot tasks, time-extended assignment, cross-schedule dependencies (XD [ST-MR-TA]) category [18], with a combinatorial search space that grows rapidly with the numbers of robots and tasks, and complexity of the skill requirements. Since new tasks, robot dropouts, or travel delays may arise unexpectedly [9], robots must replan within seconds to dynamically adapt to such changing conditions. There exist numerous approaches to these combinatorial optimization problems. Exact methods formulate problems as optimization programs [11, 8] and employ techniques such as Branch-and-Bound and cutting-plane methods [27], but scale poorly and become computationally expensive for large problems. Metaheuristics, such as simulated annealing (SA) [5], genetic algorithms [4, 26], ant colony optimization [3], and large neighborhood search [30, 39], offer faster solutions but require problem-specific local search operators or heuristics. Learning-based methods [38, 37, 9, 17] enable fast inference but require offline training and may generalize poorly to problem structures unconsidered during the training. Sampling-based optimization (SBO) offers an alternative. SBO methods iteratively sample candidate solutions from a probability distribution and refine the distribution to concentrate its search on promising regions, without problem-specific local search algorithms or offline training. While closely related methods are known as model-based search algorithms in combinatorial optimization [42], we follow the robotics and control literature [40, 41] and adopt the term SBO in this paper. Classical SBO methods for discrete problems include the cross-entropy method (CEM) [32] and sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) [10]. However, these methods struggle to explore large solution spaces with multimodal objective landscapes, i.e., objective functions with many local optima: CEM is prone to premature mode collapse, while SMC suffers from particle degeneracy that reduces sample diversity. Meanwhile, MBD (MBD) [29] has emerged as a promising SBO method that adapts the diffusion process of DDPM (DDPM) [13] to optimization. MBD uses the known objective function to estimate the score function through Monte Carlo sampling, eliminating the need for offline neural network training. By gradually concentrating samples on low-cost regions through the diffusion process, MBD outperforms other SBO methods on nonconvex, non-differentiable problems [29, 20]. Diffusion-based search is also appealing for combinatorial optimization, where solution spaces are often large and highly multimodal [37, 17]. However, MBD denoises in a continuous space and thus cannot directly produce discrete decisions. Its solutions must be rounded, which degrades solution quality [37] and may lead to constraint violations. On the other hand, existing diffusion-based combinatorial optimization solvers [37, 23, 33, 21, 17] denoise directly over discrete variables using discrete diffusion models [15, 2]. However, they rely on a neural network to learn the denoising process offline. To bridge this gap, we propose DMBD (DMBD), a training-free SBO method that performs denoising diffusion directly over discrete decision variables, modeling each as a categorical random variable. At each denoising step, DMBD approximates the categorical reverse transition distribution with samples weighted by the known problem formulation, progressively steering the search toward high-quality solutions. The contributions of this paper are as follows: We propose DMBD, an SBO method for combinatorial optimization that denoises directly over discrete decision variables by approximating the reverse transitions of discrete diffusion with Monte Carlo sampling. We establish a finite-step probabilistic convergence guarantee for DMBD (Theorem 1) that characterizes its exploration-exploitation trade-off and shows that the probability of finding a global minimizer approaches one as the number of denoising steps increases. We present a priority-based encoding scheme, inspired by [4], that guarantees every sample decodes into a feasible solution for heterogeneous MRTA, improving sampling efficiency. VI Conclusions In this paper, we proposed DMBD (DMBD), a training-free sampling-based optimization (SBO) method that replaces the learned denoiser of discrete diffusion with a Monte Carlo approximation and guarantees asymptotic convergence to the global optimum. We also presented a priority-based encoding for heterogeneous MRTA that guarantees feasible samples and thus improves sample efficiency. DMBD outperforms SBO and metaheuristic baselines in nearly all settings and matches mixed-integer linear program-based and learning-based methods at a fraction of their computational cost. Several directions remain for future work. First, DMBD needs enough denoising steps to be competitive; with few steps, it may perform no better, or even worse, than other methods. Our convergence bound characterizes the role of the number of steps but becomes loose as the problem size grows. Using adaptive noise schedules to reduce the number of denoising steps would be an interesting direction. Second, like other SBO methods, DMBD loses sample efficiency on larger problems. For heterogeneous MRTA, extending DMBD to a distributed setting, as in [20], is a promising direction. Lastly, we assume a deterministic cost [FORMULA] . Extending DMBD to stochastic objectives would allow our MRTA formulation to capture uncertain skill requirements and travel times. Rhythmic-Semantic Co-Speech Gestures for Emotional Dialogue in RobotsThanks: Extended version of the shorter paper accepted at ACM HAI 2026 (doi:10.1145/3841580.3845664). HAI peer review and acceptance apply only to the shorter paper. Co-speech gestures can increase engagement and improve speech understanding. Yet, most data-driven robot systems generate either rhythmic beat-like motion or semantically meaningful iconic gestures, but not both. We present an emotion-aware rhythmic–semantic co-speech gesture system that generates iconic and beat behaviors in real time from text and the robot’s internal emotional state. We formalize the task of beat–iconic gesture generation using emotion and propose lightweight models that predict iconic timing and intensity, then fill the remaining spans with emotion-conditioned beats at an appropriate intensity level. We train on the BEAT2 dataset and deploy the system on the social robot Haru. In an online user study with [FORMULA] participants, our method shows stronger speech–gesture alignment and is preferred over baseline methods. 1 Introduction Humans convey meaning and internal states through body gestures and facial expressions. These cues range from large, deliberate movements that depict what people say to small, rhythmic motions that accompany speech. We call the former iconic gestures and the latter beat gestures [1]. Prior work on robot co-speech gestures rarely models both types in one system, unlike recent state-of-the-art (SOTA) co-speech generation systems for artificial agents [2, 3]. Therefore, we aim to generate a single co-speech gesture system that includes both iconic and beat gestures, while remaining coherent with the utterance and the robot’s emotional state (Figure 1). Robots must also adapt motion to emotion. Many co-speech approaches do not explicitly model how emotion changes movement [4, 5, 6]. We focus on four emotions from Plutchik’s wheel [7]: joy, anger, sadness, and fear. Given an utterance and a target emotion, our system generates co-speech gestures that communicate both what the robot says and how it feels. In this paper, we use the term iconic to denote content-aligned co-speech animations that convey the intended emotional meaning of what is being said (i.e., emotion-specific variants), while beat gestures refer to non-semantic rhythmic motions that accompany speech. Another key requirement in robotics is responsiveness. Many data-driven methods assume speech audio is available at inference time for prosody or synchronization [5, 8, 9, 10, 6, 4]. This assumption can add latency for interactive robots that use expressive text-to-speech (TTS) (e.g., about 2 s with GPT-SoVITS [11]). We therefore design a text-only system that takes only the utterance and the intended emotion. Based on these constraints, we formalize a new robotics task: efficient, text-only generation of joint beat–iconic co-speech gestures that vary with emotion. We train lightweight models on the body-expression-audio-text (BEAT2) dataset [2] and generate iconic and beat motion in one coherent sequence. We deploy the system on the social robot Haru [12, 13, 14, 15] and evaluate it in an online user study ( [FORMULA] ). Participants rate our method higher for speech–gesture correlation across emotions and prefer it in most conversations compared to baselines. Our contributions are as follows: 1) We define a new task for social robots: generating a single co-speech gesture stream that fuses beat and iconic gestures while accounting for emotion. This allows the use of BEAT2 for non-humanoid robots. 2) We propose lightweight models that predict which words trigger iconic gestures and estimate their intensity only from text and emotion. Likewise, we train the same model architectures to predict beat gesture intensity. 3) We integrate all our models into a gesture generation system that runs in real time without audio at inference and can map to different non-humanoid robot embodiments. 2 Related Work In this section, we review prior work on co-speech gesture generation for robots and artificial agents. In robotics, few approaches use unique strategies for generating co-speech motion, such as retargeting motion from recorded human videos to a robot [16] or rule-based policies for beat or hand-gestures [17]. In contrast, most recent research focuses on generating co-speech gestures for the upper body of humanoid robots using data-driven learning [9]. These works typically collect paired speech and motion from people delivering monologues or speeches, use audio and text as input, and optimize losses that encourage temporally coherent head and arm motion that matches speech rhythm. Methods differ mainly on how linguistic and prosodic information is represented and the learning architecture used. With respect to linguistic features, some approaches incorporate sentence-level context using embeddings [5] from the Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) language model [18], while others use word-level embeddings to provide finer-grained lexical conditioning [8]. With respect to model architectures, many works formulate co-speech gesture generation as a regression problem over joint poses, commonly using autoregressive models that condition on previously generated poses to maintain motion continuity [5, 8, 9, 10]. Other approaches use generative adversarial networks (GANs) to better match the distribution of human motion and reduce over-smoothing [19, 20]. A key limitation of current robotics approaches is that they rarely combine iconic and beat gestures in one system. Most learned generators focus on beat-like co-speech motion [5, 8, 9, 19, 20], while the few that target iconic gestures often select or trigger pre-defined animations without modeling their timing [10]. In our work, we generate both in a single pipeline. First, an Iconic Module predicts when to trigger content-aligned emotional animations and how strongly to perform them, conditioned on linguistic context and the target emotion. Second, a Beat Module fills the remaining spans with rhythmic gestures by predicting emotion-conditioned beat activation intensities. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first robot co-speech architecture that explicitly models both iconic and beat gestures. Co-speech gesture generation for artificial agents has received more attention than robotics, largely due to the availability of large datasets. A widely used resource is BEAT and its extension BEAT2 [2], which pair motion capture with audio and text, and include word-level iconic intensity annotations. We use BEAT2 to train both our iconic and beat components because it provides strong supervision for joint rhythmic and semantic co-speech modeling. Recent agent systems move beyond upper-body gestures [6, 4] toward full-body motion [21], improved speech synchronization [22], and more diverse motion [23]. These methods typically target realistic humanoid characters and often condition on speech audio at inference. In contrast, we formalize a robotics task with stricter constraints. Most agent approaches use deep sequence models (e.g., LSTMs [24], transformers [25]) and sometimes diffusion or adversarial objectives to improve realism and diversity [2, 26]. Some recent work also uses LLMs to guide motion or label generation [27, 21]. While we also follow a data-driven approach, our focus is not photorealistic motion quality but deployable robot behavior under latency constraints. We therefore avoid audio at inference and use lightweight predictors for iconic gestures and beat intensity, conditioned on emotion and text. Finally, prior work explores stylized character animation, such as exaggerated facial expressions paired with beat gestures for non-photorealistic agents [28]. This direction relates to our setting because non-humanoid robots often benefit from hand-designed iconic content that fits their embodiment. Our approach differs in focus: rather than only synthesizing motion, we predict iconic placement and intensity within the utterance and generate the surrounding beat behavior in a unified system. 3 Task Overview Figure 2 summarizes our rhythmic–semantic co-speech pipeline.
