G-BERT achieves the highest mean correlation, with significant gains over the LLM and Random baselines and a positive trend over the dataset-label baseline (Figure 3). We attribute this to (i) more accurate iconic timing from BERT, (ii) a beat-intensity distribution from RoBERTa that better matches BEAT2 labels, and (iii) the dataset labels come from human motion, and transferring them to a non-anthropomorphic robot can change how natural the gestures look. Our models adapt timing and intensity to Haru’s motion style, which may explain why they can match or exceed the dataset-label baseline in perceived correlation. In contrast, we find no significant differences in anthropomorphism or likeability. This may be because these constructs are driven largely by factors held constant across conditions (Haru’s embodiment, face, and voice), whereas our methods mainly vary when gestures occur and how strongly they move. Anthropomorphism remains low for all methods (a likely floor effect for a non-anthropomorphic robot). Likeability shows a non-significant trend in favor of our method, likely due to a ceiling effect and rating variance. Despite modest quantitative performance on the beat models, our data-driven approach still outperforms the Random and LLM baselines, which suggests it is sufficient for practical applications. The preference rankings mirror these trends. Participants most often select G-BERT as best (Figure 4), consistent with its higher speech–gesture correlation scores. We also find that our iconic intensity predictor shifts gestures from predominantly low-intensity in BEAT2 toward more medium- and high-intensity outputs. This may suggest that non-anthropomorphic robots benefit from more salient and frequent iconic gestures. 10 Limitations and Future Work Our paper has several limitations, which also point to clear next steps. First, our text-only inference improves responsiveness, but it ignores prosody. Future work can add a coarse prosody prediction from text, while keeping latency low. Second, our beat module uses a discretized intensity model. In future work, we will explore architectures that capture finer movement variations without sacrificing real-time performance. Third, our iconic gestures rely on a predefined library; while limiting coverage, curated animations are often needed for non-anthropomorphic robots, and could be augmented with procedural/generative motion. Fourth, we evaluated via online videos, a valid approach [36]. However, future work will test live interactions to assess latency effects. Fifth, we do not disentangle the effects of iconic and beat motion; future ablations should isolate each module. Sixth, the system can transfer by defining an embodiment-specific iconic library and specifying the available degrees of freedom and motion ranges for beats, but we evaluated only on Haru; future work should test other platforms. Finally, since this is the first approximation to a new task, we use separate models for iconic activation, placement/intensity, and beat intensity; future work will explore a unified model to reduce error propagation and improve overall performance. 11 Conclusions We presented an emotion-aware rhythmic–semantic co-speech gesture system that generates iconic and beat behaviors in real time from text. We formalized the task of efficient, emotion-conditioned joint beat–iconic generation and proposed lightweight models for iconic activation/placement/intensity and beat intensity. We integrated the models and deployed the system on the social robot Haru. In an online user study, participants reported stronger speech–gesture alignment and preferred our method over baselines. Overall, our work makes low-latency, emotion-consistent beat–iconic co-speech gesturing practical for social robots.

ExRL: Sample-Efficient Online Adaptation of Long-Chunk Policies via Execution Length Control Predicting long action chunks, often spanning dozens of timesteps, has become a key ingredient in increasingly capable robot policies. In this paper, we find that adapting these long-chunk policies with existing reinforcement learning (RL) methods can require many online samples due to the high dimensionality of the action chunks being optimized, making such adaptation impractical in real-world scenarios where interaction data are costly to collect. Our key insight is to shift adaptation from optimizing actions to optimizing how long to execute each predicted action chunk. This keeps the adaptation space low-dimensional while its expressivity grows with the chunk size. We thus introduce Execution at the Right Length (ExRL), a simple approach which augments the base policy with a lightweight adapter that predicts the execution length of each chunk and is trained using off-policy RL algorithms. Across simulation benchmarks and real-world robotic tasks, ExRL enables sample-efficient adaptation of a diverse range of long-chunk policies with minimal task-specific hyperparameter tuning. I Introduction Robot policies trained on demonstration datasets have enabled increasingly complex and generalizable behaviors across a wide range of robotic control tasks [57, 1]. A key technique shared by many of these policies is action chunking [70]. Rather than predicting a single action at each query, action-chunked policies predict a sequence of actions and execute them open-loop, which can help capture non-Markovian structure in demonstrations [32, 39] and reduce compounding errors [32, 68]. A common choice in recent robot policies is to predict long action chunks, often exceeding 20 steps and approaching 50, as in vision-language-action (VLA) models such as [FORMULA] [8] and [FORMULA] -FAST [48], and world action models such as DreamZero [65]. By producing many actions per model query, long chunks enable high-frequency control (e.g., 50 Hz) for dexterous tasks such as laundry folding [9], while reducing inference pauses for smoother, faster execution. These long-chunk robot policies, while performant, are rarely optimal when deployed in the real world due to limited demonstration coverage and imperfect generalization [55]. Reinforcement learning (RL) provides a direct way to adapt these policies from online experience. In other domains such as language modeling, online RL has been shown to be quite effective for adapting models pretrained on offline datasets [45, 24, 21]. For robotic control, however, online data collection in the real world is often slow, costly, and sometimes unsafe, making sample efficiency a central requirement. Yet we observe that long action chunks introduce a major bottleneck for sample-efficient adaptation (Figure , left). RL methods that optimize entire action chunks or their latent variables face an increasingly high-dimensional optimization space as the chunk length grows. This substantially increases the amount of online experience required for adaptation. This motivates us to seek an adaptation interface whose dimensionality does not grow with the chunk length. We observe that action-chunked policies naturally expose such an interface, namely, how long to execute a predicted chunk before querying the policy again. Although execution length is a simple scalar decision, adapting it to the current state and predicted action chunk can substantially alter policy behavior by controlling the trade-off between longer open-loop execution, which better exploits the benefits of action chunking, and shorter execution, which improves responsiveness to unexpected state changes or dynamics mismatch [39]. This makes execution length a meaningful variable for policy improvement, while being particularly attractive for long chunks: as the chunk size grows, the number of possible execution lengths—and hence the expressivity—increases, whereas the optimization itself remains a low-dimensional discrete problem. We instantiate this idea as Execution at the Right Length (ExRL), a sample-efficient online RL method for adapting long-chunk policies. It adds a lightweight execution-length policy that selects how many actions from each predicted chunk to execute before replanning, and trains it using standard off-policy RL algorithms. Because this adapter can be learned without modifying the base policy itself, ExRL provides a policy-agnostic interface that can be applied to virtually any class of action-chunked policies. Execution-length control is ultimately bounded by the capabilities of the underlying base policy. To go beyond this limitation, we can further optionally distill successful online trajectories back into the base policy during RL using simple imitation loss, allowing the base policy itself to improve alongside the adapter. Finally, ExRL can also leverage general offline data, such as human demonstrations, by reinterpreting arbitrary trajectory segments as off-policy experience under different execution lengths, further improving online sample efficiency. We empirically demonstrate the effectiveness of ExRL across simulated and real-world manipulation tasks, showing state-of-the-art online adaptation performance across a range of long-chunk policies, largely without task-specific hyperparameter tuning. These include standard action-chunked policies, different classes of pretrained VLA models such as [FORMULA] [8] and [FORMULA] -FAST [48], as well as a world action model, Cosmos Policy [27]. On real-world tasks spanning precise manipulation, long-horizon coordination, and clothing folding, ExRL efficiently adapts frozen [FORMULA] policies, approaching perfect success on cube stacking with about ten minutes of physical interaction. II Related Work Imitation learning in robotics. Imitation learning, particularly behavior cloning, has been widely used to train data-driven policies for robotic control [5, 51, 69, 18, 52]. Prior work has explored a wide range of action parameterizations and policy architectures for imitation learning. Earlier methods often represent actions with Gaussian or GMM policies [25, 41], while more recent approaches use expressive generative modeling techniques, including VAEs [70], diffusion or flow models [14, 44, 9, 7], and autoregressive next-token prediction models [72, 28, 48]. With the growing scale of human demonstration datasets and policy models [60, 26, 11, 46], imitation learning has further become a pretraining paradigm for generalist robot policies, absorbing broad prior knowledge into a single model that can be adapted for real-world deployment [44, 28, 9]. Our work provides an efficient method to adapt these diverse policy classes from online experience. Adaptive execution of action chunks. Action chunking, as used in ACT [70], has become a de facto design choice in robot policies learned with imitation learning. Recognizing that the execution length of action chunks strongly affects policy behavior [54, 68, 39], several concurrent works have explored adaptive execution strategies. Earlier RL methods such as Dynamic Action Repetition [31] and TempoRL [6] adapt how long a primitive action is repeated, rather than how much of a predicted action chunk is executed. AAC [36] selects the execution length of vision-language-action models using action entropy, while FFDC [61] selects the execution length for world action models using a learned verifier to check whether predicted future observations remain consistent with the real rollout. ExRL instead learns execution-length decisions directly from task rewards through online RL. TAS [63] uses online RL to select among actions cached from overlapping chunks at every timestep, rather than explicitly learning a chunk-level execution length. Two other recent works, ACSAC [13] and ACH [53], learn value-based adaptive chunk-size selection for offline-to-online RL. However, these methods train and evaluate specific chunked policies within offline and offline-to-online RL frameworks, and are not designed as plug-in adapters for arbitrary pretrained action-chunked policies. The closest work to ours is [71], a concurrent study that also adapts action-chunked policies through reinforcement learning over execution length. However, it relies on PPO for optimization; our comparison in Appendix B shows that off-policy learning can adapt execution lengths with substantially fewer online samples. Reinforcement learning for robot policy adaptation. On-policy methods such as PPO and GRPO have been used to fine-tune pretrained robot policies [34, 40, 12, 50], but often require many online rollouts, limiting their practicality on real robots. Off-policy RL algorithms such as SAC [22] and TD3 [20] can use data more efficiently, but their standard implementations typically use deterministic or Gaussian actors, making direct adaptation of more complex generative policies nontrivial. Policy-specific approaches address this challenge in different ways: DSRL [59] and ZPRL [66] optimize diffusion/flow policies in latent spaces. OGPO [47] uses off-policy critics to guide optimization of the diffusion or flow generation process, while RL-100 [33] applies PPO-style updates across diffusion denoising steps. These methods can improve sample efficiency, but remain tied to particular policy classes. Residual RL instead learns additive corrections to the base actions [67, 4, 3, 16, 56]. While policy-agnostic and lightweight, residual RL still requires continuous action optimization; correcting an entire chunk makes this space grow with chunk length. RL Token [64] learns a lightweight actor conditioned on VLA representations and reference chunks, with regularization toward the base actions. PA-RL [42] achieves policy-agnostic adaptation by casting RL as action optimization followed by supervised policy learning. RECAP [2] builds an offline-to-online pipeline for training advantage-conditioned policies, which can incorporate batch online RL [17] for efficient adaptation. In contrast to these action-modifying approaches, ExRL adapts the execution length of each predicted chunk, reducing online adaptation to a compact discrete decision space and enabling sample-efficient, policy-agnostic adaptation. Its prefixes of different lengths then provide real experience of executing the same action sequence for different lengths. Concretely, before online training, we enumerate trajectory segments of all lengths [FORMULA] from offline trajectories and add the corresponding execution-length transitions to the replay buffer. For each transition, the offline trajectory provides the accumulated rewards and resulting state for the executed prefix; from that state onward, the value target bootstraps with the current base policy and execution-length strategy. This anchors the value of each virtual chunk to the expected return under ExRL’s actual execution strategy, rather than to the behavior that generated the offline trajectory. When online behavior cloning is enabled, demonstration data can also be mixed with successful online trajectories to jointly update the base policy. Remark. One may ask why we do not simply use a short fixed execution length for previous RL methods to avoid high-dimensional optimization, or first select the optimal fixed execution length and then optimize on top of it. Always using a short execution length for RL, however, can be problematic for several reasons: it may yield very poor initial performance on some tasks, making RL optimization difficult; it requires more frequent policy queries, increasing training cost and inference overhead while potentially introducing inference–execution synchronization issues; and, on long-horizon tasks, it substantially increases the effective decision horizon, further complicating RL. Alternatively, preselecting an optimal fixed execution length instead requires extensive real-world evaluation, potentially hundreds of rollouts, which is already comparable to the interaction budget of a typical real-world online RL experiment. V Experiments The goal of our experiments is to answer the following core questions: Can ExRL enable sample-efficient adaptation across action-chunked policies, including generalist robot policies in both simulation and real-world tasks? Can updating the base policy with successful online trajectories and demonstrations further improve adaptation? What execution-length patterns does ExRL learn? To show the generality of our method, we conduct experiments on diverse classes of action-chunked policies. We consider both representative action-chunked policies trained with imitation learning and several pretrained generalist robot policies of different classes. Representative action-chunked policies: (1) Diffusion Policy (DP) [14]: an action-chunked policy that models multimodal continuous action chunks using denoising diffusion [23]; and (2) ACT [70]: a transformer-based policy that predicts action chunks using an encoder–decoder architecture. Generalist robot policies. (1) [FORMULA] [9] and [FORMULA] [8]: state-of-the-art VLA models that use flow matching [37] to model action chunks; (2) [FORMULA] -FAST [48]: an autoregressive VLA model that generates action chunks through efficient action tokenization; and (3) Cosmos Policy [27]: a world action model built on a large pretrained video generation model. We compare ExRL against execution-length baselines and several online adaptation baselines, with a focus on policy-agnostic methods for action-chunked policies. Our baselines include: Execution-length baselines. (1) Random- [FORMULA] : randomly samples an execution length from the feasible set at each policy query; (2) Optimal fixed- [FORMULA] : sweeps fixed execution lengths and reports the best-performing one. AAC [36]: A training-free adaptive execution method that selects the execution length using action entropy. Online BC: An ablation that directly distills successful online rollouts back into the base policy using behavior cloning without RL. Policy Decorator [67]: An off-policy residual RL method that freezes the base policy and learns additive corrections to its predicted actions, with bounded residuals and controlled exploration for stable online learning. DSRL [59]: A latent steering method for diffusion- and flow-based policies that keeps the base policy frozen and applies RL in its initial latent-noise space rather than directly modifying the generated actions. PA-RL [42]: A policy-agnostic RL finetuning method that uses a learned critic to improve action candidates through re-ranking and local optimization, and then distills the improved actions back into the base policy. OGPO [47]: An off-policy full-finetuning method for diffusion- and flow-based policies. It learns off-policy critics for data reuse and uses their values to optimize the full diffusion or flow generation process through a modified PPO objective. ResFiT [3]: A demo-augmented residual RL method that keeps the base policy frozen, constrains residual magnitude for stable exploration, and jointly trains on demonstration and online data; we adapt its original per-step residual formulation to operate over action chunks. DICE-RL [56]: Also a demo-augmented residual RL method that combines value-guided action selection with selective behavior regularization to reinforce high-value behaviors while remaining close to the pretrained policy. Simulation benchmarks and setup. Following prior work [59, 47], we use base-policy checkpoints that leave meaningful headroom for RL improvement. Our goal on these benchmarks is not to maximize base-policy performance, but to use them as a controlled testbed for evaluating long-chunk policy adaptation. For each variant of ExRL, we keep most hyperparameters fixed across tasks and make only a few task-level adjustments when necessary, such as the discount factor [FORMULA] and network width. ExRL improves a policy without changing its predicted actions, raising the question of how execution-length decisions reshape its behavior. Figure 9(a) reveals a consistent pattern: across Lift, Can, Square, and real-world insertion, ExRL selects shorter executions near the object or target than during free motion. The mean length roughly halves in simulation and falls to about a quarter on real-world insertion. ExRL therefore concentrates replanning near interaction, while allowing longer motions elsewhere. Short executions, however, need not serve the same purpose. Two Square rollouts illustrate how ExRL decides when to continue with a longer chunk. In Figure 9(b), it repeatedly truncates unsuitable predictions with little physical motion, then accepts a chunk that predicts a useful grasp-and-lift motion. Here, frequent replanning provides new candidate motions from nearly the same state. In Figure 9(c), short executions instead change the state through small corrections, bringing the nut closer to the peg before ExRL switches to longer execution. The distinction is between waiting for a useful prediction and moving into a state from which a longer prediction becomes useful. Both behaviors depend on the current state and the proposed chunk, rather than a fixed preference for short execution. Figure 17 in the appendix illustrates how this balance unfolds across four real-world tasks. Further analysis shows that shuffling the same execution lengths across states and chunks reduces success (Appendix D-B). It also suggests a complementary reason to preserve longer execution: under feature aliasing, locally similar policy features can repeatedly produce similar first actions, so frequent replanning may interrupt useful progression through a chunk (Appendix D-C). VI Conclusion We introduced ExRL, which shifts online adaptation of long-chunk policies from action generation to execution-length control. Conditioning this scalar decision on the state and predicted chunk provides substantial behavioral flexibility, while keeping optimization low-dimensional as chunk size grows. Across simulation and real-world tasks, ExRL enables sample-efficient improvement of diverse frozen policies, often surpassing their best fixed execution length. Online imitation learning and offline demonstrations further extend these gains and support continued base-policy improvement during RL. These findings show that learning how to execute a policy’s predictions can unlock capabilities already present in the policy, making execution length a practical interface for adapting long-chunk robot policies with limited online interaction. VII Limitations Our real-world experiments keep the base policy frozen and do not yet incorporate online BC. Performance therefore remains constrained by the actions the base policy can propose, and several tasks still fall short of [FORMULA] success. Extending online BC to these experiments may help address the remaining failures. We also adapt each task separately and have not evaluated joint multi-task adaptation or generalization to unseen tasks. Recent work demonstrates that sufficiently diverse multi-task experience and value-based RL can improve performance on unseen scenes and objects in simulation [29]; whether execution-length adaptation offers similar benefits remains open. Finally, we have not tested ExRL together with asynchronous inference methods such as real-time chunking (RTC) [10]. Understanding how adaptive replanning interacts with overlapping inference and execution is an important direction for extending ExRL to latency-sensitive deployments.
Information Theory (cs.IT): Reliability Analysis for Ground-Air Cooperative Wireless-Powered Internet-of-Things Battery-constrained Internet of Things (IoT) devices face significant challenges in maintaining long-term uplink data collection, especially in network-limited scenarios. This paper investigates a Ground-Air cooperative Wireless-Powered IoT network (GA-WPIoT), where ground power beacons (GPBs) provide radio-frequency energy supply and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) serve as flexible aerial access points for IoT data collection. Unlike conventional UAV-enabled wireless-powered solutions, GA-WPIoT decouples energy transfer and data collection, reducing the hardware and energy burden of UAVs. To capture the device-level performance variations among IoT devices, we develop a stochastic geometry-based analytical framework, where UAVs are modeled by a Matérn hard-core point process, IoT devices by a Poisson point process, and GPBs by a finite annular binomial point process. The conditional success probabilities of the GPB-device link (for energy transfer) and the device-UAV link (for data collection) are characterized, and device-level reliability distributions are obtained through the Meta-Distribution based analysis. Numerical results under suburban and urban environments reveal the impacts of UAV altitude and annular GPB deployment on reliability distributions, providing useful guidelines for GA-WPIoT. I Introduction Internet of Things (IoT) applications are proliferating by continuously collecting massive and heterogeneous data to support various data-driven services, e.g., smart cities, ocean monitoring, and intelligent agriculture[1]. For low-cost deployments, these applications are typically implemented using battery-constrained IoT devices under network-limited deployment scenarios, which leads to a critical sustainability challenge in maintaining long-term and stable data collection. Instead of establishing costly network infrastructures, the integration of ground power beacons (GPBs) and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) offers a low-cost and on-demand solution for wireless-powered IoT data collection. For brevity, we refer to this solution as a Ground-Air cooperative Wireless-Powered IoT network (GA-WPIoT). In GA-WPIoT, multiple GPBs are deployed to power distributed IoT devices via radio-frequency (RF) energy transfer[2], while UAVs act as aerial access points that provide flexible and on-demand coverage to collect uplink data from ground IoT devices [3, 4]. Unlike conventional UAV-enabled wireless-powered solutions, GA-WPIoT decouples energy transfer and data collection, reducing the hardware and energy burden of UAVs. Analyzing the reliability of GA-WPIoT overall IoT devices is crucial for its practical design and realization, yet it is challenging for two main reasons. On the one hand, conventional spatially averaged network metrics are not suitable to capture the reliability of data collection performance over different IoT devices in GA-WPIoT [5]. Given a specific IoT device, the spatial deployment of its nearby GPBs together with the serving UAV jointly determines the data collection performance, resulting in substantial device-level performance variations across different network realizations. On the other hand, successful data collection must satisfy a coupled energy-communication condition: each IoT device must first harvest sufficient energy from nearby GPBs and then reliably complete uplink transmission to its serving UAV. This coupled success condition complicates system performance analysis. Devices located far from GPBs may suffer from insufficient harvested energy, whereas devices situated near the edge of UAV service regions may experience severe device-UAV path loss and stronger uplink interference [6]. To sum up, in consideration of spatial deployments of GPBs, UAVs, and the IoT devices themselves, a device-level reliability analysis method is required to characterize the performance of GA-WPIoT. Prior studies on existing wireless-powered communication networks have analyzed the energy harvesting [7, 8] and uplink transmission performance, but typically under oversimplified spatial models, such as homogeneous user distributions or fixed GPB deployments [2]. UAV-assisted IoT networks have been investigated mainly by focusing on UAV trajectory design and communication performance, often assuming battery-powered devices or neglecting the spatial characteristics of energy provisioning [3, 4]. Overall, the joint spatial effects of GPB deployment, UAV spatial distribution, and random IoT-device locations in a ground-air cooperative wireless-powered IoT network, i.e., GA-WPIoT, have not been thoroughly characterized [9, 10]. To capture the device-level reliability, the meta distribution (MD) is a suitable tool to analyze data collection performance by characterizing the conditional success probability (CSP) of each IoT device, as well as its distribution across the spatial distribution of the served IoT device [11, 12]. Whereas [11, 12] studies clustered power-beacon deployment and meta distributions for energy and information transfer using a truncated Poisson cluster model, our model combines a fixed number of GPBs in each finite annulus with spatially separated aerial collectors modeled by a Type-II MHCPP. Relative to the UAV-assisted downlink SINR analysis in [11], we characterize the joint energy-qualification/uplink-decoding reliability of a ground–air architecture in which GPBs supply energy and UAVs collect data. To overcome this research gap, this paper has the following contributions. First, we develop a stochastic-geometry model for GA-WPIoT by jointly modeling UAVs’ deployment as a Matérn hard-core point process, random IoT-device locations by a Poisson point process, and finite annular GPBs’ placement by a binomial point process. Second, we derive the moments of the CSP for the GPB-device energy-transfer link and the device-UAV link, accounting for finite GPB deployment and spatially distributed uplink interference. These results enable the device-level reliability of both links to be characterized through meta distributions. Third, we obtain the meta distribution (MD) of the overall performance by jointly considering the harvested-power qualification and uplink-decoding requirements. Numerical results reveal the joint effects of the GPB inner radius, UAV altitude, and communication parameters, providing design guidelines for GA-WPIoT. V Conclusion We developed a stochastic-geometry framework for GA-WPIoT with spatially separated UAVs and annular GPB deployment. CSP moments and beta approximations characterize the reliability distributions of energy transfer, uplink transmission, and their joint success. Numerical results show that the GPB inner radius and UAV altitude jointly affect reliability, with the preferred deployment depending on the propagation environment. In particular, a moderate GPB inner radius balances energy provisioning between central and edge devices, while UAV altitude balances the LoS probability gain against increased propagation loss. These findings provide guidelines for joint UAV–GPB deployment to improve device-level reliability.

Closed-Form Gaussian Information Projection for Embedded Simplices and Simplicial Mixtures Thanks: Funded by the Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft (DFG) - Project number 471687386 We study Gaussian approximation of Dirichlet–Gaussian probability density functions on embedded simplices. We derive the unique information projection onto the family of nondegenerate ambient Gaussian probability density functions, obtaining closed-form expressions for the optimal Gaussian and the minimum divergence for arbitrary positive Dirichlet parameters. The minimum divergence depends only on the intrinsic simplex dimension and Dirichlet parameters, is invariant up to an affine isomorphism, independent of the ambient dimension, and independent of the normal covariance. Furthermore, by joint convexity of Kullback–Leibler divergence, we establish explicit intrinsic-dimension-dependent sharp upper bounds for finite Gaussian Mixture with shared component weights. For uniform probability density functions, these bounds reduce to dimension-dependent constants. The results provide closed-form Gaussian Mixture constructions and rigorous approximation guarantees for probability density functions associated with embedded simplicial complexes. A numerical example on a circular curve illustrates the theoretical results and their connections to geometric Gaussian Mixture representations. 1. Introduction Gaussian projection provides a canonical approximation of a Probability Density Function by a Gaussian Probability Density Function [1, 9], minimizing the Kullback–Leibler divergence. For Probability Density Function associated with geometric simplicial structures [5], this problem admits additional structure through barycentric coordinates and the geometry of the embedding [2, 10, 3]. We consider Probability Density Functions on embedded simplices generated by Dirichlet Probability Density Functions on the simplex tangent space and independent Gaussian Probability Density Functions on the simplex normal space. This formulation handles uniform Probability Density Function as well as non-uniform Probability Density Functions on simplices embedded in arbitrary finite ambient dimensions. We derive the unique information projection [9] onto the Gaussian family, which is characterized by moment matching [1, 9], and obtain a closed-form expression for the information projection divergence. Remarkably, this quantity depends only on the intrinsic simplex dimension and the Dirichlet Probability Density Function parameters, and is invariant under affine isomorphism (by construction), independently of the ambient dimension and normal Probability Density Function a result similar to [3]. Furthermore, we extend the componentwise result to finite Gaussian Mixtures of embedded simplicial Probability Density Functions. By joint convexity of the Kullback–Leibler divergence [9], we establish explicit intrinsic-dimension-dependent sharp upper bounds for the corresponding Gaussian Mixture. The uniform Probability Density Function follows as a special case. The main contributions are: Gaussian information projection: Characterization of the unique optimal Gaussian for embedded Dirichlet–Gaussian Probability Density Function. Closed-form divergence: Derivation of the information projection divergence and its invariance with respect to the affine isomorphism, ambient dimension, and normal Probability Density Function. Gaussian Mixture approximation: Establishment of explicit information projection sharp upper bounds for finite Gaussian Mixtures associated with embedded simplicial complex based Probability Density Functions. The remainder of the paper develops the geometric and measure theoretic probability framework, derives the componentwise information projection, and establishes the corresponding information projection Gaussian Mixture bounds. 2. Previous Work This work generalizes our previous results on a Gaussian Mixture representations of triangulated domains [3], which considered uniform Probability Density Function on full-dimensional simplices. We extend that framework in two directions: from uniform Probability Density Functions to arbitrary Dirichlet Probability Density Function with positive parameters, and from full-dimensional simplices to simplices embedded in arbitrary finite ambient dimensions with independent Gaussian Probability Density Function on their normal spaces. These extensions give a general closed-form characterization of the componentwise Gaussian information projection and corresponding Gaussian Mixture divergence bounds. The previous uniform model is recovered as a special case. 3. The resulting distribution retains the overall geometric structure of the target while replacing the individual segment distributions by nondegenerate Gaussian components. Although the present example focuses on a circular parametric curve, the underlying construction is by no means restricted to this particular geometry. It applies to general curves through their polygonal approximations, with each segment inducing a probabilistic geometric primitive and its corresponding Gaussian component. In particular, the framework accommodates smooth and closed curves, open curves, non-regular curves, as well as self-intersecting geometries and unions of curves. This generality has already been demonstrated from a computational perspective in the complementary work [2, 10], where a broad collection of canonical plane curves is employed as test cases to investigate the expressive capabilities of geometric Gaussian Mixture representations. These experiments demonstrate that the resulting Gaussian Mixture faithfully capture the local tangential and normal structure, as well as the global geometry of the underlying curves. The present work complements this computational investigation by providing the corresponding mathematical foundations and theoretical guarantees for the Gaussian approximation. In this sense, the circular example considered here serves as a representative instance of a substantially more general geometric probabilistic construction, rather than as a geometry-specific application. I Introduction DNA is a promising medium for data storage because of its high storage density and long-term stability. In a DNA storage system, digital information is encoded into nucleotide sequences, written into DNA molecules through synthesis, and retrieved through sequencing. The cost and speed of synthesis remain important obstacles to large-scale DNA storage [1]. Errors introduced during synthesis, storage, and sequencing also require suitable coding methods. Thus, efficient DNA storage calls for codes that reduce synthesis time while providing error correction. In the conventional synthesis model, multiple strands are grown in parallel according to a reference sequence. During each cycle, the machine processes the next symbol of the reference and appends the corresponding nucleotide to a selected subset of the strands. Each selected strand receives one nucleotide, while the other strands remain unchanged. A strand can therefore be synthesized if and only if it is a subsequence of the reference, and the synthesis time is the length of the reference prefix used. Under this mechanism, one question is how to maximize the code size within a prescribed number of synthesis cycles when the reference sequence is fixed. In 2020, Lenz et al. [2] showed that adding redundancy can reduce synthesis time and related the maximum information per cycle for a periodic reference to the capacity of a cost-constrained channel. Precise estimates for the number of sequences were developed in [3], while constructions and analyses of the tradeoff between redundancy and average or maximum synthesis time were studied in [4, 5]. A different question arises when the strands to be synthesized are given and the reference can be chosen. Makarychev et al. [6] studied how to partition a given pool of random strands into batches and obtained upper and lower bounds on the total reference length required for the batches. For random strands with a bound on homopolymer length, Elishco and Huleihel [7] proved the asymptotic optimality of an alternating reference under their Markov model. Error correction and sequence constraints have also been considered under the same synthesis mechanism. For deletion and insertion errors, Chrisnata et al. [8] constructed quaternary codes with bounded synthesis time under an alternating reference and provided polynomial-time encoders. Codes with a prescribed minimum Hamming distance were studied through Gilbert–Varshamov bounds in [9]. A different source of deletions is a synthesis defect: when a synthesis cycle fails, the strands scheduled to receive a nucleotide in that cycle lose the corresponding symbol. These deletions are therefore associated with the same failed cycle across the affected strands. Lu et al. [10] constructed codes correcting synthesis defects when the defective cycles are known and when they are unknown. For biological constraints, Nguyen et al. [11] combined a synthesis-time constraint with single-deletion or single-insertion correction and a runlength constraint. Wang et al. [12] studied the number of sequences satisfying synthesis-time, runlength, and GC-content constraints and the corresponding channel capacities. Liu and Duman [13] developed encoding and decoding methods under these combined constraints, including constructions that correct a single insertion or deletion. There are also related studies under different synthesis mechanisms. In shortmer synthesis, each cycle appends a specified short DNA strand, rather than a single nucleotide, to selected strands. Abu-Sini et al. [14] studied the choice of shortmers and reference sequences, developed an algorithm for minimizing the number of cycles needed to synthesize a given set of strands, and related information rates to the capacities of non-deterministic costly constrained graphs. Moav et al. [15] considered complex DNA synthesis, where each strand may receive one nucleotide chosen from a prescribed set in each cycle. They analyzed the maximum information per cycle and developed algorithms for finding optimal references for given strands. Unified Far-field and Near-field Codebook Design for XL-array Systems While extremely large-scale antenna arrays (XL-arrays) hold immense promise for next-generation wireless networks, the paradigm shift encompassing new near-field communications renders conventional discrete Fourier transform (DFT)-based Type-I codebooks inefficient. Meanwhile, existing near-field alternatives usually impose prohibitively high storage and/or feedback burdens. To tackle these challenges, we propose in this letter a unified codebook applicable to both far-field and near-field XL-array systems. Our key idea is to express the near-field channel steering vector in an equivalent form, which is a Hadamard product of an angular vector and a curvature-related vector. This new representation allows direct reuse of the legacy Type-I codebook for angle quantization, while only a lightweight auxiliary codebook is newly added for additional curvature quantization. Subsequently, we optimize the auxiliary curvature codebook by maximizing the average beamforming gain given the information of user distribution. By leveraging the local monotonicity of the beamforming gain with respect to curvature mismatch, the optimization problem is further reduced to a quantization-error minimization problem, for which suboptimal curvature codewords are obtained. Numerical results demonstrate that the proposed unified codebook achieves near-optimal beamforming performance that approaches its upper bound based on perfect channel state information (CSI), while significantly reducing the required feedback overhead as compared to various benchmark schemes. I Introduction To meet the escalating demands of next-generation wireless networks, extremely large-scale arrays (XL-arrays) have emerged as a pivotal technology for achieving unprecedentedly high spectral efficiency and spatial resolution [1]. By deploying thousands of antennas, the aperture of an XL-array expands significantly, rendering the users more likely to be located in the radiative near-field region of base stations (BSs). For this case, the traditional far-field planar-wavefront channel model is no longer accurate. Instead, the channels should be accurately characterized by the spherical-wavefront propagation model [2, 3]. Such new channel characteristics also unlock new spatial degrees-of-freedom, enabling advanced capabilities such as near-field beam focusing and enhanced spatial multiplexing [4, 5]. Although XL-arrays offer significant advantages, they also introduce new challenges for accurate channel state information (CSI) acquisition and beamforming design. In practical 3rd Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) New Radio (NR) systems, codebook-based precoding standardizes data transmission by allowing the user to select a preferred candidate precoder from reference-signal measurements and report the precoding matrix indicator, rank indicator, and channel quality indicator for precoder selection at the BS [6]. However, conventional 3GPP NR discrete Fourier transform (DFT)-based Type-I codebooks [7] rely solely on angular-domain sampling and thus suffer from considerable channel mismatch when applied to near-field spherical-wave channels. To address this issue, various near-field codebooks have been recently developed. For example, the polar-domain (PD) codebook was proposed in [8] that jointly samples the angular and range domains to capture the two-dimensional sparsity of near-field channels. However, its codebook size is the product of angular and range samples, resulting in demanding storage overhead. Moreover, although the wavenumber-domain (WD) codebook was developed in [9] to exploit the spatial sparsity of near-field channels, it generally incurs high feedback overhead. This is because the nonlinear mapping between the spatial and wavenumber domains requires finer codeword representations and a larger number of codewords to accurately capture channel characteristics. Alternatively, partition-based architectures proposed in [10] employ conventional far-field DFT codebooks over multiple subarrays to approximate near-field propagation. However, this approach generally incurs high feedback overhead because beam selection must be performed separately for each subarray, and the corresponding beam indices must be fed back individually. Moreover, the beamforming performance of subarray-based DFT codebooks usually is degraded due to the limited angular resolution in small-size arrays. Consequently, existing near-field codebooks face a fundamental trade-off among feedback overhead, storage overhead, and beamforming performance, making the realization of a unified design become a critical bottleneck for XL-array systems. Motivated by the above, we propose in this letter a unified codebook design for XL-array systems. To this end, we firstly show that the near-field steering vector admits a separable angle-curvature structure. Based on this observation, we develop a unified angle-curvature codebook that allows reuse of the legacy Type-I codebook for angular-domain representation and exploits an additional lightweight auxiliary codebook for curvature quantization, hence achieving backward compatibility with legacy far-field oriented codebook designs. Since the Type-I codebook is directly reused for angle quantization, we focus on optimizing the auxiliary curvature codebook to maximize the average beamforming gain under a uniform user distribution. By exploiting the local monotonicity of the beamforming gain with respect to (w.r.t.) curvature mismatch, we reformulate the codebook design problem as a quantization error minimization problem and obtain high-quality curvature codewords that are asymptotically optimal in the high-resolution regime. Numerical results show that the proposed codebook achieves superior beamforming performance which approaches its upper bound based on perfect CSI with only two curvature-sampling bits, hence significantly reducing feedback overhead while outperforming state-of-the-art benchmarks. By exploiting the separable angle-curvature structure of spherical-wave steering vectors, the proposed unified codebook extends the legacy Type-I codebook with a lightweight curvature codebook, reducing the storage overhead from multiplicative to additive scaling. Communication-Learning Co-Design for Pinching-Antenna-Assisted Federated Learning in Heterogeneous Wireless Networks Wireless federated learning (FL) suffers from two coupled bottlenecks: statistical heterogeneity across clients and communication-constrained model synchronization over unreliable wireless links. Instead of focusing on algorithmic design and/or wireless resource optimization, this paper provides a systematic study of pinching antenna (PA)-empowered FL for heterogeneous wireless networks and develops a unified communication-and-learning framework. Specifically, we integrate a segmented waveguide-enabled pinching antenna (SWAN) architecture with a heterogeneity-robust FL algorithm based on client variance reduction and dual quantization, so as to jointly mitigate communication bottlenecks and client drift. On this basis, we further develop a two-stage SWAN-assisted downlink protocol and formulate fairness-oriented uplink optimization problems for PA positioning, bandwidth allocation, and quantization design. Efficient solution frameworks are then derived for the resulting downlink and uplink optimization problems. Experimental results show the superiority of the proposed design in convergence speed and final accuracy under non-independent and identically distributed data and communication bottlenecks. I Introduction Federated learning (FL) has emerged as a promising paradigm for enabling distributed intelligence at the network edge, thereby supporting the increasing demand for network intelligence in sixth-generation (6G) wireless systems [1]. In FL, a central server coordinates a large number of mobile clients to collaboratively train a shared model through iterative local computation and global aggregation, without requiring the exchange of raw data [2]. Despite its promise, FL over wireless networks faces two fundamental challenges: 1) clients typically possess non-independent and identically distributed (non-i.i.d.) data, leading to significant statistical data heterogeneity; 2) client-server model synchronization relies on wireless links that are often resource-constrained, unreliable, and error-prone. These two issues jointly hinder training efficiency and lead to significant model performance degradation, substantially limiting the scalability and practical deployment of FL in wireless environments [3]. To address data heterogeneity, a wide range of FL algorithms have been developed, most of which build upon FedAvg by introducing mechanisms such as local regularization, adaptive aggregation, momentum-based updates, and variance reduction [4]. In essence, they correct local or global update directions so as to better align them with the global objective, thereby alleviating the adverse impact of non-i.i.d. data. However, most focus on algorithmic optimization and implicitly assume ideal or sufficiently reliable communication conditions. Such an assumption is often unrealistic in practical wireless networks, where limited communication resources, channel fading, transmission errors, and intermittent connectivity may severely impair client-server model exchange. Although several studies reduce communication overhead through model compression, device scheduling, and wireless resource optimization, the resulting performance gains remain fundamentally constrained by the intrinsic limitations of the wireless channel [5][6]. To fundamentally alleviate the communication bottleneck in wireless FL, it is necessary to move beyond conventional communication-efficient algorithm design and exploit physical-layer technologies that can actively reshape the propagation environment. In this context, pinching antennas (PAs), as a representative flexible-antenna technology, have recently emerged as a promising solution for wireless channel enhancement [7]. By leveraging dielectric waveguides together with dynamically activatable or movable pinching elements, PAs can establish flexible radiation points closer to users, thereby enabling effective link reconstruction and line-of-sight (LoS) restoration under blockage conditions [8]. Compared with conventional flexible-antenna schemes, such as fluid antennas and movable antennas, PAs support such reconfiguration over a much larger spatial range, making them particularly suitable for challenging propagation scenarios with severe path loss and LoS blockage. This capability, combined with low deployment cost, high flexibility, and strong scalability, makes PAs highly attractive for wireless FL, where reliable client-server communication is crucial for efficient and robust training. Despite the above potential, the integration of PAs into FL systems remains largely unexplored. A few studies have considered PAs alone but overlooked data heterogeneity across clients [9][10]. Different from conventional wireless optimization problems, FL performance couples communication quality with heterogeneous client dynamics. Thus, designing PA-assisted FL requires a unified framework jointly addressing link enhancement, communication resource allocation, and learning convergence. In this paper, we investigate PA-empowered FL in heterogeneous wireless networks. In particular, we aim to jointly address the two coupled bottlenecks in wireless FL under PA-enabled communication. To this end, we integrate a segmented waveguide-enabled pinching antenna (SWAN) architecture with a heterogeneity-robust FL framework, and develop the corresponding downlink and uplink transmission designs. The contributions can be elaborated from four aspects. We propose a SWAN-assisted heterogeneity-robust FL framework for wireless edge networks. Specifically, a SWAN architecture is deployed at the server side to enhance client-server communications, while a client-variance-reduced FL algorithm is developed to mitigate client drift under non-i.i.d. data. In addition, a dual-quantization mechanism is introduced to reduce downlink and uplink communication overhead, where common quantization is adopted for downlink delivery and client-adaptive quantization is used for uplink transmission. Thus, the proposed framework unifies communication enhancement and heterogeneity-robust FL design. We develop a two-stage downlink protocol for FL, consisting of a global-model multicast stage and a control-variable unicast stage. The design jointly optimizes beamforming, PA positioning, time allocation, and quantization bits under Rician statistical channel state information (CSI) and a common latency budget. To tackle the resulting mixed-integer non-convex problem, we establish a rate-oriented solution framework, under which the original design is reduced to multicast and unicast rate optimization, followed by closed-form recovery of the optimal time allocation and downlink quantization level. This yields an efficient and structured downlink design for supportable delivery. For uplink transmission, we develop a fairness-oriented SWAN-assisted design that optimizes uplink quantization, bandwidth allocation, and PA positions to maximize the minimum supportable quantization level across active clients. The novelty lies in uncovering the problem structure and deriving efficient solution frameworks for a hierarchy of uplink designs with increasing generality, including exact structural characterization of antenna-position optimization, and an equivalent inverse reformulation for the general joint design. These provide a systematic way to coordinate communication resources and SWAN geometry for robust uplink model delivery. We extensively evaluate the proposed design on the CIFAR-10 dataset under non-i.i.d. distributions and practical communication constraints. Experimental results show that the proposed method consistently and significantly outperforms representative baselines under various quantization settings and heterogeneity levels. Moreover, compared with a conventional base-station-based communication architecture, the proposed SWAN-assisted design achieves significant additional performance gains under communication bottlenecks, further validating the effectiveness of integrating PAs with heterogeneity-robust FL. Robust Joint Power Allocation and Antenna Placement for Pinching-Antenna Systems under Gaussian Location Uncertainty Pinching antenna systems (PASS) have attracted much attention recently owing to their capability to maintain reliable line-of-sight communication in high-frequency bands. By guiding signals through a waveguide and emitting them via a movable pinching antenna, PASS enable dynamic control of signal propagation and spatial adaptability. However, their performance heavily depends on effective resource allocation, including power allocation and antenna positioning, which becomes challenging under user localization uncertainty. Existing studies largely assume perfect user locations, while our prior work considered uniformly distributed localization errors. In this paper, we develop a robust resource allocation framework for multi-user downlink PASS under Gaussian-distributed localization uncertainty. An energy-efficiency (EE) maximization problem is formulated subject to probabilistic outage constraints, and the minimum transmit power is analytically characterized for any given antenna position. For the unbounded Gaussian model, we prove that the resulting one-dimensional antenna-placement objective is convex and derive a globally optimal derivative-bisection algorithm. We further consider a circularly truncated Gaussian model for bounded localization-error regions and develop a deterministic branch-and-bound method that returns an [FORMULA] -globally optimal antenna position. Finally, we discuss how position-dependent waveguide attenuation modifies the placement objective and may destroy its convexity. Simulation results verify that the proposed branch-and-bound solution closely matches the bounded grid-search benchmark, demonstrate substantial EE gains from optimized pinching-antenna placement over the bounded fixed-antenna architecture, and reveal an increasing distinction between the bounded and unbounded Gaussian models as the location uncertainty grows. I Introduction Pinching antenna systems have recently attracted considerable interest as a potential architecture for restoring line-of-sight (LoS) communication links in high-frequency regimes, including millimeter-wave (mmWave) and terahertz (THz) bands [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], and are therefore regarded as a key enabler for 6G and beyond networks. In such systems, user signals are first transmitted through a dielectric waveguide and subsequently radiated by a pinching antenna attached to it. By dynamically adjusting the antenna’s position along the waveguide, pinching antenna systems provide exceptional flexibility in controlling signal propagation, leading to improved spectral efficiency and adaptability [7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14]. A core challenge in pinching-antenna systems is resource allocation, which involves the joint optimization of transmission parameters such as power, bandwidth, and antenna position to maximize system performance [15]. Most existing studies assume perfect channel state information (CSI) or accurate user location knowledge. However, in realistic deployments, channel estimation errors and localization inaccuracies are inevitable due to noise, hardware impairments, environmental dynamics, and pilot overhead limitations [16]. Ignoring such uncertainties can lead to substantial performance degradation, underscoring the necessity of robust resource allocation designs. To the best of the authors’ knowledge, only two prior works have addressed robust resource allocation in pinching-antenna systems [17, 18]. In [17], a robust beamforming design is developed under imperfect CSI, where the actual channel is modeled as the superposition of an estimated component and an additive estimation error. However, the wireless channel component associated with the estimated CSI is assumed to be fixed and independent of the pinching-antenna position, which limits the practical applicability of the model, as the channel inherently depends on antenna placement. To overcome this limitation, [18] considers a joint robust power allocation and antenna position optimization framework under user location uncertainty. The uniform-error model in [18] provides a bounded uncertainty description with constant density. A complementary Gaussian model captures uncertainty concentrated around an available position estimate. Such models have been used in spatial wireless channel prediction [19], location-based rate selection and reliability analysis [20], and robust near-field beamfocusing [21]. In particular, [20] motivates a Gaussian localization-estimator model through asymptotic maximum-likelihood theory. This provides an estimation-based rationale for a local Gaussian approximation in a sufficiently accurate, approximately unbiased positioning regime. A potential vehicular application is infrastructure-to-vehicle downlink access in a parking facility or vehicle depot equipped with a fixed waveguide. Position-assisted transmission for vehicular links has been investigated, for example, in [22]. In the considered application, the access point (AP) uses estimates of vehicle-terminal positions to jointly select the pinching-antenna position and transmit powers while meeting prescribed rate and outage requirements. This connects the proposed framework to reliable, energy-efficient vehicular access under imperfect location information. Motivated by these observations, this paper investigates robust resource allocation for pinching-antenna systems under stochastic Gaussian user-location uncertainty, considering both unbounded and circularly truncated Gaussian models. Specifically, we formulate an EE maximization problem for a multi-user downlink pinching-antenna system subject to user-specific probabilistic outage constraints. We first derive the minimum transmit power required by each user for any fixed pinching-antenna position. For the unbounded Gaussian model, we then establish the convexity of the remaining one-dimensional placement problem and obtain its globally optimal solution through bisection on the analytical objective derivative. To account for physically bounded localization errors, we further formulate a circularly truncated Gaussian model and develop a deterministic branch-and-bound placement algorithm with an [FORMULA] -global optimality guarantee. Finally, we discuss how position-dependent waveguide attenuation changes the placement objective and the associated optimality properties. Numerical results validate the bounded branch-and-bound design against grid search, quantify the EE gain provided by antenna-position optimization, and illustrate the impact of truncating the Gaussian location-error distribution. VI Conclusion This paper investigated robust joint power allocation and antenna placement for pinching-antenna systems under Gaussian location uncertainty. Using the Marcum-Q function, we characterized the outage probability and derived the minimum required transmit power. For the unbounded Gaussian model, we established the convexity of the antenna-placement objective and developed a globally optimal derivative-bisection algorithm. For the circularly truncated Gaussian model, we proposed a deterministic branch-and-bound algorithm with an [FORMULA] -global optimality guarantee. We further showed that position-dependent waveguide attenuation may destroy convexity. Numerical results demonstrated that the proposed branch-and-bound solution closely matches the grid-search benchmark and that optimized antenna placement substantially improves energy efficiency over fixed-antenna deployment. Moreover, the bounded and unbounded Gaussian models exhibit increasing performance differences as localization uncertainty grows. Future work will investigate multi-waveguide and multi-antenna architectures under location uncertainty.

This encourages a similar approach for lattices of higher dimension and modulus, where an exhaustive search cannot be derived. Avenues for future work include measuring the effect of improved bit-labeling on soft information estimation, an alternative bit-labeling strategy for set-partition coded modulations. Like their classical counterparts, QLRCs are developed as a step toward achieving quantum distributed storage. In such a model, an erroneous qubit (node) can be recovered by connecting to a small set of local qubits rather than requiring the device to have an all-to-all connectivity, thus minimizing the possibility of long-range connections. Erasure models assume that the positions of lost symbols or qubits are known in advance, reducing decoding to a reconstruction problem rather than error identification. This makes erasures fundamentally easier to handle than general errors in both classical and quantum settings [12, 21, 23]. Recent experimental results further support this approach, showing that in platforms such as neutral-atom and superconducting systems, detectable faults can be mapped to erasures [44, 45]. Thus, although QLRCs are motivated by erasure recovery, they support quantum error correction more broadly by enabling low-overhead local repair of detectable faults. More broadly, QLRCs are expected to be relevant to future quantum memory architectures. Many leading quantum error-correcting code families are Calderbank–Shor–Steane (CSS) codes, including surface codes [7, 13, 34] and numerous quantum low-density parity-check (QLDPC) constructions [8], which require dual containment of the underlying classical codes. Entanglement-assisted quantum error-correcting codes (EAQECCs) were introduced in [9] to relax this dual-containment constraint required in CSS code constructions [11, 42]. EAQECCs not only allow more flexible constructions, but can also improve the achievable dimension–distance tradeoff by leveraging pre-shared entanglement [9, 31]. These codes directly inherit the structure of classical linear codes, allowing them to integrate with well-established classical coding theory. Moreover, pre-shared entanglement can improve quantum coding performance: entanglement-assisted quantum error-correcting codes may achieve better parameters than comparable unassisted schemes by relaxing orthogonality constraints and enabling constructions from arbitrary classical linear codes [22]. In both the classical and quantum settings, erasure recovery is often easier than general error correction because the error locations are known. Furthermore, on hardware platforms such as superconducting as well as neutral-atom devices, various types of errors can be converted to erasures (errors whose locations are known). Entanglement-assisted codes were developed as a way to relax the orthogonality requirements for quantum CSS codes. These codes are known to improve tradeoffs involving the number of encoded logical qubits as well as the number of recoverable erasures. In this work, we presented EAQLRCs with availability. Classically, if an erasure can be recovered by more than one set of coordinates that are pairwise disjoint, the code is said to be locally recoverable with availability. While it has been demonstrated in [18] that disjoint recovery sets and hence the notion of availability cannot be defined for quantum CSS codes, we define availability in the entanglement-assisted setting. Here, we show that given two classical LRCs, we can construct an EAQLRC. We compute code parameters – including dimension and distance – which require determining the hull of the classical LRC. We also determine a Singleton-like tradeoff among length, dimension, distance, locality, availability, and entanglement consumption for EAQLRCs. With respect to code constructions, we present both random and explicit constructions. Our explicit constructions rely on variants of algebraic-geometry codes such as Tamo–Barg codes, folded Tamo–Barg codes, Hermitian codes, Suzuki codes, and fiber product codes. It remains to determine whether the explicit codes presented here are optimal with respect to the Singleton bound presented. This depends on computing the dimensions of the relevant hulls and the minimum weights of the complements appearing in the entanglement-assisted distance formula. Determining these parameters will also allow a more precise comparison with the parameters of quantum CSS LRCs. Another interesting question is the nature of quantum hierarchical local recovery in the entanglement-assisted setting, which is a work in progress.

Prior-Aided Masked Vector Quantization CSI Feedback for FDD Massive MIMO Systems Downlink channel state information (CSI) feedback is a key bottleneck in frequency-division duplex (FDD) massive MIMO systems, as the user equipment (UE) must convey its estimated channel to the base station (BS) over a limited uplink (UL) budget. To improve CSI reconstruction accuracy under tight feedback constraints, we propose prior-aided masked vector quantization (PM-VQ), a learning-based separate source–channel coding (SSCC) feedback scheme conditioned on the average angle–delay power map—a compact representation of the channel second-order statistics available at both the UE and the BS. In PM-VQ, a prior-aided encoder maps the CSI to latent tokens, and a spatially-adaptive masking module (SAMM) scores and selects the most informative tokens within the feedback budget. The selected tokens are vector-quantized and fed back together with their positions, while an adaptive de-masking module (ADM) completes the latent representation at the BS before prior-conditioned decoding. To support variable-rate compression, a single model is trained over a range of selected-token counts, enabling operation across multiple feedback dimensions without retraining. We evaluate PM-VQ against three representative baselines on a Sionna-generated 3GPP TR 38.901 UMa dataset, focusing on the most challenging diffuse regime where channel energy is spread across many angle–delay coefficients. Simulation results show that PM-VQ achieves the lowest NMSE across all tested SNR levels and feedback dimensions in this regime. Moreover, the angle–delay power-map prior remains beneficial even when estimated from only a few channel realizations. I Introduction Accurate downlink (DL) channel state information (CSI) is the cornerstone of next-generation wireless systems, since it directly determines the quality of DL precoding and the achievable spectral efficiency. Acquiring such CSI with low complexity, low latency, and limited overhead becomes increasingly critical as systems scale toward more users, larger antenna arrays, and wider bandwidths. How CSI is acquired depends on the duplexing mode. In time-division duplex (TDD) systems, channel reciprocity allows the base station (BS) to infer the DL channel directly from uplink (UL) pilots through an open loop, at the cost of tighter transceiver synchronization and hardware calibration. Frequency-division duplex (FDD) systems avoid this calibration burden but lack channel reciprocity, which makes DL CSI acquisition intrinsically harder. In this case, a closed feedback loop is required: the BS transmits common pilots, each user equipment (UE) estimates the DL channel and feeds a compressed description back over the UL, and the BS reconstructs the CSI from this feedback. This loop exposes a fundamental tradeoff between pilot/feedback overhead and CSI reconstruction accuracy. Designing feedback schemes that can accurately reconstruct high-dimensional DL CSI under a limited UL feedback budget is the central problem addressed in this paper. The CSI feedback sent from the UE to the BS over the UL can be designed in two main ways, following the classical source–channel coding dichotomy [1]. In separate source–channel coding (SSCC), the UE first compresses the DL CSI into a bitstream using a source encoder and then protects these bits against UL noise using a channel code. The BS decodes the received bits and reconstructs the CSI. In joint source–channel coding (JSCC), the UE instead maps the CSI estimate directly onto UL channel symbols, and the BS reconstructs the CSI from the noisy received symbols. The two strategies are attractive for complementary reasons. SSCC is modular and well understood: in the infinite-blocklength limit, a rate–distortion-optimal source code followed by a capacity-achieving channel code is optimal according to Shannon’s source–channel separation theorem. In practical finite-blocklength systems, however, this ideal behavior may not be fully realized. For a given modulation and coding configuration, the decoding-error probability can increase rapidly when the instantaneous UL channel quality falls below its supported operating region, leading to the familiar cliff effect. Moreover, the bit-level source-coding, channel-coding, and decoding pipeline introduces additional latency. JSCC gives up this modularity, but by mapping source representations directly to channel inputs, it avoids an explicit bit interface and often degrades more gracefully with the UL SNR in practical noisy-feedback regimes. Its main difficulty lies in code design: information-theoretically optimal source–channel mappings exist in principle, but are generally not available in closed form, and simple linear mappings can be far from optimal in feedback-limited regimes. Given these complementary tradeoffs, we adopt the SSCC framework for two reasons. First, it is directly deployable: CSI reporting in FDD standards such as 5G NR is digital, with the UE conveying bits over standardized, channel-coded uplink control channels. An SSCC bitstream is compatible with this pipeline, whereas JSCC transmits CSI as analog channel symbols that current digital feedback links do not support. Second, and more fundamentally, the SSCC framework lets us treat source coding and channel coding separately. By combining a rate–distortion-optimal source code with a state-of-the-art, near-capacity channel code, the CSI feedback problem reduces to a source-coding problem, so the design can concentrate on the source encoder. This encoder can then be built around well-understood rate–distortion principles. In a practical digital UL such as 5G NR, the rate at which information bits can be reliably delivered to the BS over a given resource allocation depends on the UL SNR. For a given UL SNR, this reliably supportable rate depends on the employed modulation and coding scheme (MCS), the decoder implementation, and the target block error rate. Through link adaptation, a higher UL SNR generally permits a higher-order modulation and a higher code rate while maintaining the prescribed reliability, whereas a lower UL SNR requires a more robust configuration and therefore supports a lower information rate.
