The CSI feedback problem can be modeled as a remote source-coding problem, where the UE must encode the DL CSI from the noisy DL channel observation under a rate constraint relating to the UL feedback channel capacity. To study the information-theoretic limit, Khalilsarai et al. [2, 3] derived, for a Gaussian channel model, a lower bound on the CSI normalized mean-squared error (NMSE) under a given rate constraint using remote rate–distortion theory. The corresponding high-SNR scaling law characterizes how the error scales with the DL pilot dimension, the UL feedback dimension, and the channel rank. This result provides two useful design guidelines for CSI feedback. First, linear JSCC achieves the optimal high-SNR scaling in all regimes except one: the regime in which the DL pilot dimension exceeds the channel rank, while the UL feedback dimension remains smaller than the rank. In this feedback-limited regime, nonlinear encoding can in principle improve the scaling behavior. Second, for a Gaussian source, rate allocation of the rate–distortion-optimal solution follows reverse water-filling over the eigenmodes of the source covariance, allocating more rate to high-variance modes and no rate to modes below the water level. This suggests that an efficient feedback encoder should exploit channel second-order statistics and allocate the available feedback budget non-uniformly across channel components. Motivated by this observation, Song et al. [4, 5] exploited the low-rank eigenspace of spatially correlated channels [6] and proposed a low-complexity JSCC scheme that encodes the dominant Karhunen–Loève coefficients with optimized power allocation. This demonstrates that exploiting the channel covariance structure can substantially simplify CSI feedback and guide the allocation of limited feedback resources. However, an important gap remains between these asymptotic information-theoretic characterizations and practical CSI feedback. Rate–distortion achievability is inherently asymptotic: when each CSI matrix is viewed as one realization of the source, the rate–distortion function [FORMULA] is approached by jointly encoding blocks of source realizations, with the asymptotic limit attained as the source-coding blocklength tends to infinity. CSI feedback, in contrast, is naturally a one-shot source-coding problem: within each channel coherence interval, the UE must compress the current CSI realization and convey it to the BS under a stringent latency budget. The UE therefore cannot, in general, accumulate an arbitrarily long sequence of CSI realizations and jointly encode them using an asymptotically optimal rate–distortion code. Consequently, although remote rate–distortion theory provides a fundamental performance benchmark and reveals structural principles, such as reverse water-filling in the Gaussian case, it does not directly specify how to realize these principles with a practical finite-rate encoder operating on a single CSI realization. For the reasons explained before, we pursue these theoretical guidelines within an SSCC framework. The open question we address is therefore how to design a trainable, variable-rate source encoder that operates effectively in this one-shot regime, exploits channel second-order statistics, and allocates the available feedback budget selectively across channel components on realistic channel data. The stringent latency and complexity requirements of CSI feedback in multi-user massive MIMO systems have motivated a broad class of learning-based feedback schemes. Learning-based JSCC maps the CSI representation directly to channel inputs, and the BS reconstructs the CSI from the noisy received symbols. Early work adopted CNN-based encoder–decoder architectures for CSI feedback [7]. Subsequent studies improved robustness by introducing SNR-adaptive transmission strategies [8] and feedback-aided variants that exploit channel-output feedback [9]. A comprehensive overview of recent JSCC developments can be found in [10]. In parallel, a large body of work has studied learning-based SSCC CSI compression. A representative example is CsiNet [11], which employs a CNN autoencoder to compress and reconstruct angle–delay CSI. Later extensions improved the reconstruction quality by enlarging the receptive field [12], introducing multi-resolution feature extraction [13], and incorporating generative priors [14]. An overview of learning-based SSCC feedback schemes is provided in [15]. More recently, attention-based architectures, such as TransNet [16], have been introduced to capture long-range dependencies in CSI and are therefore adopted in this paper as the backbone of the neural network baselines. Despite these advances, existing learning-based CSI feedback schemes still have several limitations that motivate our design. First, since latent representations are often learned purely from data, different latent components may carry different amounts of information about the CSI. As a result, the feedback budget should concentrate on the most informative components. However, most existing schemes do not explicitly identify or prioritize the most informative components under the feedback budget. Second, although rate–distortion theory highlights the importance of channel second-order statistics, most learning-based schemes do not explicitly exploit it in the compression and reconstruction process. Zhuang et al. [17] exploited the channel second-order statistics but only at the decoder for reconstruction. Together, these two limitations suggest that the encoder should not only learn a compact CSI representation, but also identify and prioritize statistically important latent components. Third, most learning-based CSI feedback schemes support only a fixed compression ratio, requiring a separate model for each feedback budget. Existing variable-rate methods typically construct nested latent representations and transmit the first [FORMULA] features according to the available resources [18, 19, 20]. However, their feature ordering is generally fixed across channel realizations. Fourth, most existing evaluations rely on datasets generated from a single fixed channel profile, such as the standardized CDL-C or CDL-D models [21], with limited variation in delay profile, angular spread, array geometry, and user layout, which limits conclusions about generalization when the deployment environment differs from the training distribution. Motivated by the above limitations, we propose a learning-based SSCC feedback scheme, called prior-aided masked vector quantization (PM-VQ), for DL CSI feedback. Inspired by the reverse water-filling structure of the rate–distortion-optimal solution, PM-VQ uses the average angle–delay power map as prior side information to guide non-uniform latent-token selection under a given feedback budget. It combines vector-quantized latent compression with prior-aware token masking and mask-based latent completion, so that the encoder transmits only the most informative latent tokens and the BS reconstructs the full channel from the received tokens, with the channel statistical prior injected at the encoder, token-scoring module, and decoder. The main contributions are summarized as follows. Multi-level prior conditioning. We exploit the average angle–delay power map as prior side information and inject it at multiple semantic levels: gated fusion in the encoder, SPADE-style modulation for token scoring and decoding, and BS-side prior skip connections. This conditions both compression and reconstruction on the channel second-order statistics. Selective latent-token transmission. We introduce a spatially-adaptive masking module (SAMM) that scores latent tokens using both the instantaneous CSI and the long-term prior and retains only the most informative ones under the available feedback budget. At the BS, an adaptive de-masking module (ADM) reconstructs the masked tokens from the received quantized tokens. Content-adaptive variable-rate feedback. Because SAMM selects a variable number of tokens per channel realization, a single trained model operates across multiple feedback dimensions [FORMULA] without retraining, and the selection adapts to each individual CSI sample. Geometrically diverse dataset. We generate a DL CSI dataset with the Sionna simulator under the 3GPP TR 38.901 UMa model, sampling diverse UE locations around a fixed BS to introduce geometric diversity beyond single-profile training. Unified benchmarking. We compare PM-VQ and all baselines under a common UL feedback dimension [FORMULA] measured in channel uses. On a UMa dataset spanning channel-rank conditions from diffuse to sparse, we focus the evaluation on the most challenging diffuse regime, where the channel energy spreads across many angle–delay coefficients. Extensive simulations show that PM-VQ achieves the best NMSE across SNR levels and feedback dimensions [FORMULA] in this regime, and its advantage over the baselines is especially pronounced. III Proposed Prior-Aided Masked Vector Quantization CSI Feedback Scheme In this section, we present the proposed CSI feedback scheme, a learnable SSCC-based design conditioned on prior side information. As shown in Fig. 1, the scheme builds on the encoder–decoder framework with vector quantization (VQ): the encoder at the UE compresses the DL CSI into a latent representation, the latent vectors are quantized to indices of a learned codebook and fed back, and the decoder at the BS reconstructs the DL CSI from the received indices. This framework is standard in learning-based CSI feedback [15], but it suffers from three limitations: The network must be retrained for every target compression ratio, since the latent dimension is fixed by the architecture. The compression mapping is purely data-driven: it exploits the redundancy of the high-dimensional CSI, but provides no measure of which latent dimensions are more informative and should be prioritized under a limited feedback budget. There is no principled mechanism for integrating side information into the compression and reconstruction designs. The proposed prior-aided masked vector quantization (PM-VQ) feedback scheme addresses these limitations one by one: it supports a range of feedback dimensions with a single trained model by varying the number of transmitted latent tokens; it scores the latent tokens so that only the most informative ones are fed back; and it incorporates prior side information, i.e., the average angle–delay power map introduced in Section II-B, which is assumed to be available at both the UE and the BS, at multiple points in the encoder, SAMM, and decoder. VII Conclusion We proposed PM-VQ, a variable-rate SSCC scheme for FDD CSI feedback that uses the average angle–delay power map as side information. SAMM selects the latent tokens to be vector-quantized and transmitted, while the prior-free ADM completes the missing latent positions at the BS. Budget-randomized training allows the same model to operate over multiple feedback dimensions without retraining. PM-VQ outperforms the baselines across all tested UL SNRs and feedback dimensions in the challenging diffuse regime. The ablations show that the prior gain comes mainly from the decoder-skip pathway; encoder and decoder-pyramid conditioning provide secondary gains, whereas direct prior input to SAMM adds little. A coarse power-map estimate is sufficient for most of the benefit, but removing the prior entirely causes a performance loss. In contrast, SAMM’s learned selection rule remains important and outperforms both latent-energy selection and random masking, especially at intermediate feedback dimensions. These findings suggest a clear design principle: use the prior primarily to guide reconstruction at the BS and use learned content-adaptive selection to allocate the instantaneous feedback budget.

Computing the entropy rate of a quantized stationary Gaussian process The entropy rate of a uniformly quantized stationary Gaussian process is the limit on how far the quantized signal can be compressed without loss. It has no closed form, and the classical high-resolution formula fails when the spectral density is small on part of the band, as it is after routine smoothing or filtering. Here we present two ways to compute it. The first is an analytical approximation in which the quantization noise acts as a floor on the spectral density. The second is a particle-filter estimate of the exact rate. For quantization steps up to the signal standard deviation, the two agree to within a few millibits per sample in most cases, including processes on which the classical formula fails. At a step of a quarter of the standard deviation, linear predictive coding comes within 2 to 4 percent of the rate, while general-purpose compressors remain 12 to 89 percent above it. 1 Introduction A basic question about any digitized noisy signal is how far it can be compressed without loss. When a continuous-valued signal is digitized by uniform quantization, the resulting integer sequence is what is stored, and its entropy rate is the fundamental limit on lossless compression [1, Chs. 2 and 4–7]: the number of bits per sample the signal actually carries. We take the underlying signal to be a stationary Gaussian process, so the entropy rate is determined by the spectral density and the quantization step. Modeling the signal as pure noise is less restrictive than it may appear: in a noisy measurement the incompressible content is largely the noise rather than the structured underlying signal, so the noise entropy rate accounts for most of the compression cost. The application that motivates this work is extracellular electrophysiology, where multichannel recordings sampled at tens of kilohertz are dominated by filtered noise and the storage cost is a practical concern. The background of such recordings, the summed activity of many distant neurons together with thermal and amplifier noise, is commonly treated as Gaussian [2]; spikes are non-Gaussian but occupy a small fraction of the samples, and stationarity holds approximately over windows short enough for the spectrum to be roughly constant. Moreover, the Gaussian has the largest entropy rate for a given spectrum [3], so at fine quantization the computed rate is approximately an upper bound for a non-Gaussian signal with the same spectrum. The approximation replaces the spectrum [FORMULA] in the classical high-resolution formula with [FORMULA] , the exact spectral density of the dithered process, and thereby remains finite and accurate for the bandlimited and strongly filtered processes on which the classical formula fails. The estimator follows the route established for the information rates of channels with memory [11, 12], which reduces the rate to the log-likelihood of a filter evaluated on a single long typical sequence; its components (minimum-phase spectral factorization, the hidden Markov structure it induces, and the fully adapted particle filter that the model admits in closed form) are standard, and the contribution is the manner in which they are combined into a practical method that works at all quantization scales. The method has several limitations, each a candidate for future work. The lattice error in the Riemann-sum step is expressed exactly as a Poisson sum but not quantified; bounding it would turn the approximation into a controlled estimate in the fine-to-moderate regime. The slack in the Gaussian entropy upper bound, namely the per-sample non-Gaussianity of [FORMULA] , is likewise not quantified. Note that the second error pushes the formula upward, whereas the sign of the lattice error is not established. In the extreme coarse regime the constant floor is an artifact of the additive-noise model, and the formula should not be used there. The estimator, for its part, needs [FORMULA] : when [FORMULA] vanishes on a band the moving-average representation of Section 4.2 does not exist and the filter cannot run, so the strictly bandlimited case is served only by the approximation. Its leading behavior there is correct [9], but we have not tested its accuracy at finite [FORMULA] , since the spectra of Section 5 are positive almost everywhere. Finally, the development assumes an exactly Gaussian, stationary process. Measured signals are neither, so the rate computed here is best read as the rate of a Gaussian model fitted to the signal’s spectrum, a reference against which a real recording can be compared, rather than the exact rate of that recording. Extending the methods to non-Gaussian sources would narrow this gap. Both methods also take [FORMULA] as given; on measured data [FORMULA] is itself estimated, and that error propagates into the rate, so the reference is only as good as the spectral estimate behind it. Both methods appear to lie above the rate. The estimator converges from above, as discussed in Section 4.4, and the approximation presumably overestimates as well: its Gaussian error acts upward by the argument of Section 3.4, and the measured errors of Section 5 are consistent with an overestimate wherever the filter is converged. The true rate is thus constrained on one side only, and a complementary lower bound would be needed to certify it. However, that the two estimates, which share no machinery, agree to within a few millibits over most of the range of Section 5 is reassuring. The two methods are complementary. When [FORMULA] the approximation is accurate to a few millibits and runs in milliseconds, so it is the natural choice. The estimator is needed in the remaining cases: when the quantization is coarse, when the exact rate is wanted rather than a close approximation, and for checking the approximation on a new process, as we have done here. The estimator also does more than measure the rate. At each step the filter reports the predictive distribution [FORMULA] , and an arithmetic coder driven by it would compress at close to [FORMULA] , reaching the limit that the practical coders of Section 5.3 fall short of. This comes at a much higher cost than the linear predictor of that section, so its value is as a bound on what is achievable rather than as a codec for routine use. Together the two methods make the entropy rate computable at any quantization scale, including the strongly filtered regime the classical formula cannot reach. The rate then serves as a reference: for a measured noise process, how many bits per sample it carries, and how close a given lossless coder comes to that limit. Stabilizing Vector Approximate Message Passing with Circuit-Designed Lag-Lead Damping Vector approximate message passing (VAMP) often fails to converge on ill-conditioned matrices, and its damping factor is tuned either manually or adaptively. Using the fact that VAMP iterations are the discretization of an electric circuit, we show that the denoiser and the likelihood act as nonlinear resistors, the Onsager correction is a mirror resistor and damping is a lag filter. This circuit gives a closed-form loop gain whose spectrum can predict when VAMP fails. Because a lag filter cannot isolate the oscillating modes, we add a lead capacitor whose design often results in a negative capacitance. Across a wide range of condition numbers, our proposed damping strategy achieves a higher convergence rate than adaptive damping and Anderson acceleration at a lower mean iteration cost. On ill-conditioned multipath channels, across ranks and sparsity levels, it also converges more reliably than existing damping baselines. I Introduction Vector approximate message passing (VAMP) is among the most effective iterative estimators for the linear inverse problem [FORMULA] [1]. Its state evolution is exact for rotationally invariant [FORMULA] in the large-system limit [1, 2]. On a fixed ill-conditioned matrix, however, it often oscillates. The usual heuristic solution is damping with a factor chosen by trial and error [1, 3]. Adaptive damping adjusts this factor over iterations based on a free-energy cost [4], while Anderson acceleration serves as the generic fixed-point accelerator [5]. Long-memory variants of approximate message passing (AMP) change the state evolution rather than the loop [6, 7, 8, 9]. None of these works, however, explains why VAMP oscillates. First-order optimization algorithms are discretizations of circuits of resistors, inductors and capacitors, in which the subdifferential of the objective is a nonlinear resistor [10]. From this perspective, algorithmic design becomes network design. This view builds on continuous-time models of optimization [11, 12, 13, 14] and on certificates obtained by semidefinite programming [15, 16, 17, 18]. We apply this framework to VAMP and present the following three contributions: We describe the circuit associated with VAMP. Its extrinsic update is a mirror resistor, and damping is a lag filter. We show that the loop gain of this circuit explains the oscillation. Its closed-form spectrum can predict when VAMP fails and shows why damping is a heuristic solution. We propose circuit-adaptive damping strategy based on a lag-lead filter designed from the loop gain, often with negative momentum. It outperforms existing damping strategies on ill-conditioned channels. Notation. Bold letters denote vectors and matrices, and [FORMULA] . Information Retrieval (cs.IR): Exploiting Feature-invariant Scaling Laws for Efficient A/B Experimentation in Recommendation Systems Researchers and engineers improve recommendation systems by performing A/B experiments with new model architectures, optimization methods, and data features. However, running full-scale experiments (e.g., full-model training with online data) for every feature change is prohibitively computationally intensive, while the result from a single small-scale experiment is often misleading. To address this challenge, we show that modern recommendation models exhibit feature-invariant scaling: the change of a model’s performance follows a predictable scaling-law even when different feature changes are applied to the baseline model. We introduce an efficient method that exploits scaling-laws and uses statistical inference to predict (with confidence intervals) the full-scale effect of an A/B experiment in recommendation systems. This enables practitioners to efficiently filter out neutral or regressive feature changes with only small-scale experimentation. We validate our method on three distinct recommendation model families—Wukong, HSTU, and LLM-based recommendation models—across more than 40 architectural, optimization, and data changes. Our method accurately distinguishes beneficial feature changes from neutral and regressive ones while using only a fraction of the compute required for full-scale evaluation. It also identifies several changes that improve HSTU’s state-of-the-art performance on MovieLens-20M. Our results demonstrate that scaling laws can be practically exploited to make compute-efficient decisions for improving recommendation systems. 1. Introduction Researchers and engineers often develop new feature changes (e.g., architecture changes, new optimization techniques, new data features) to improve the prediction accuracy of a recommendation model, which serves as a major driver for many large-scale online platforms. An important part of this process is to perform A/B experimentation to ensure that a new feature actually improves the model performance. This often requires a large amount of compute resources and time. For example, to know whether an architecture change improves a recommendation model, we need to retrain the full model on the full training data and compare it against the baseline model performance. A popular approach is to run small-scale experiments (i.e., a small-sized model trained on a subset of the data) to assess the effectiveness of a new feature change before committing to a full-scale run (Zhang et al., 2024b; Athey et al., 2026; Brennan et al., 2024). While these experiments offer some useful early signals, a single small-scale experiment is often an unreliable predictor of full-scale performance. An illustrative example is shown in Fig. 2, where new item information given to an LLM-based recommendation model degrades performance at a small scale but improves performance at full scale (see Sec. 3 for in-depth analysis). Hence, relying on small-scale results alone can lead us to reject a beneficial feature change (or vice versa). In this paper, we propose an efficient method that exploits scaling laws to improve the reliability of A/B experimentation in recommendation systems. Our approach exploits an important insight that we introduce in this paper: the change in performance of modern recommendation models with increasing data and model scale is governed by predictable scaling laws. More importantly, the functional form of these scaling laws remains consistent across a wide range of feature changes. As such, we can fit a scaling curve to a handful of small-scale experiments to predict the outcome of a full-scale A/B experiment. Specifically, our contributions are: We show that modern recommendation models enjoy feature-invariant scaling laws, where their performance varies predictably with increasing data and model scales. In addition, the functional form of these scaling curves remains consistent across different new features (e.g., architecture changes, new optimization techniques, new data features). We introduce an efficient method that leverages a series of small-scale experiments and feature-invariant scaling laws to improve the reliability of small-scale experimentation. Our method uses statistical inference to infer the effectiveness of a new feature at the full-scale. This allows us to predict the effect of new feature changes without performing intensive full-scale experimentation. We also show that, in general, the cumulative resource use of these small-scale experiments is smaller than that of a full-scale experiment. We show that feature-invariant scaling laws hold true for different classes of recommendation models, including Wukong (Zhang et al., 2024a), HSTU (Zhai et al., 2024), and GR2 (an LLM-based recommendation model) (Liang et al., 2026). Then, we show that our method makes reliable predictions for a large range of new feature changes on these models (in determining if they improve or degrade performance). In this process, we also found several new features that improve the state-of-the-art performance of recommendation models on existing open-source datasets. 2. Related Work Extensive research has been devoted to developing new feature changes for recommendation models (and ML models in general). Examples include architectural changes (Zhai et al., 2024; Naumov et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2024a), interaction modeling techniques (Wang et al., 2021), optimization methods (Xie et al., 2021; Tang et al., 2020; Gupta et al., 2018), and more. To determine if a new feature change is “good”, a common practice in an industry setting is to add it to the baseline model and retrain the model from scratch with the entire set of (offline or online) training data. This is also colloquially known as full-scale A/B experimentation (Gilotte et al., 2018; Quin et al., 2023). The major drawback of full-scale A/B experimentation is that it is computationally costly, especially when full-scale retraining is required. In addition, it must be repeated for every candidate feature change (which can be in the hundreds in an industrial setting). One naive approach is to make use of small-scale experiments, which aim to build faithful surrogate small-scale models (Chen et al., 2026b; Kadra et al., 2023) that allow for fast iterations and reject ineffective feature changes if they do not show performance improvement at small scale (Zhang et al., 2024b; Athey et al., 2026; Brennan et al., 2024). However, a single small-scale experiment often produces misleading signals (see Sec. 3). As such, one could draw a wrong conclusion about the effectiveness of a new feature change, forgoing potential performance improvement (and revenue) in recommendation systems. Our work aims to circumvent such pitfalls associated with conventional small-scale experimentation. Scaling laws (Kaplan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2024a) describe how the performance of recommendation models or LLMs changes with increasing model and training data scale. Most existing literature merely describes the existence of these scaling laws. As far as we know, our paper is the first to show that a recommendation model with a new feature change applied still follows a scaling law with the same functional form but different coefficients. In this paper, we refer to this phenomenon as feature-invariant scaling. This property makes scaling laws useful for large-scale A/B experimentation. Because the functional form is known in advance, we can perform a few small-scale experiments and extrapolate the full-scale effect of every candidate feature change, allowing us to filter out ineffective changes cheaply. 3. A Motivating Case Study We begin with a case study on an LLM-based recommendation model (Fig. 2). We call the original model the baseline model, and the model with a new feature added the experimental model. In this case study, the new feature change is movie genre information added to the training prompt. We want to know if this feature improves the model after full-scale training. If the performance gain is neutral, we do not want to add the feature, because it increases inference latency. In this particular example, we vary the training scale by changing the amount of training data from MovieLens-20M (Harper and Konstan, 2015). Misleading signals from small-scale experiments. We first ask ourselves: How informative is a single small-scale experiment? Fig. 2 shows that the HR@10 of the experimental model is lower than that of the baseline model at a small training scale. However, this small-scale result is misleading because genre information actually produces a significant performance improvement at the full training scale. Therefore, relying on the result of a single small-scale experiment here would have led us to mistakenly reject a new feature change that is, in fact, useful for a recommendation model. At first glance, we might be tempted to move the small-scale experiment to the 0.5 scale to produce a more conclusive result than at 0.1 scale. However, we cannot do this in an ex-ante (before-the-fact) manner because our experiments (Fig. 5) show that different categories of features produce different signals across small scales. Feature-invariant scaling Before we can use scaling laws to predict the performance of an experimental model, we need to make sure that the scaling behavior holds across different feature changes. In this section, we show that recommendation models enjoy feature-invariant scaling. We ran a small experiment: we applied three different feature changes (adding dropout layer, changing optimizer to SGD, and adding attention layer) to the Wukong recommendation model (Zhang et al., 2024a) and observed the scaling law of the three experimental models (See Fig. 3). Our results show that the performance of a recommendation model with different features added is governed by the same scaling law function family with different fitted coefficients. The scaling law fit generally enjoys high [FORMULA] (see Table 1) regardless of whether a feature is detrimental (e.g., using SGD) or beneficial (e.g., adding dropout) to the model. Specifically, this suggests that when we apply different features to the baseline model, the change in model performance with training scale should still follow a scaling law in the same functional family. We demonstrate that feature-invariant scaling holds true across a large variety of different features and recommendation model families later in Sec. 8.2. 5. Resource savings from small-scale experiments A natural question is whether a sequence of small-scale experiments is actually less resource-intensive than a single full-scale training run. If we co-scale both training and model scale, a half-scale run uses approximately one quarter of the cost of a full-scale run. Consequently, a sweep of small-scale experiments at [FORMULA] incurs about [FORMULA] of the resource needed to run a single full-scale training run. In addition, co-scaling data and model size offers another practical and important benefit. In many industrial settings, experimentation is often GPU-bound. That is, the compute available for experimentation may simply be insufficient to hold the full-scale model in memory. In such settings, a full-scale run to validate a new feature change on the full-sized baseline model is simply impossible. In this case, down-scaling model size in small-scale experiments is the only way for us to perform A/B experiments. 7. This strongly suggests that our method and the Bayesian decision rule are effective in determining, at a small-scale, whether a new feature is effective, without actually performing full-scale experimentation, hence saving computational resources. Last but not least, the right of Fig. 6 shows that our method produces a small prediction error for the out-of-sample full-scale experimental model performance based on small-scale experiments. In addition, this prediction error decreases with more small-scale observations. 9. LLM-based Recommendation Models The popularity of LLM-based recommendation models (Liang et al., 2026; Xue et al., 2026; Xie et al., 2026) has risen in recent years. In this section, we demonstrate that scaling laws can also be exploited in LLM-based recommendation models to predict the effectiveness of a new feature. We consider a text-based recommendation setup where an LLM (or agent) receives information related to historical interaction events of a user with past items. The LLM is then prompted to recommend a single item from a large pool of candidate items. We probe the probability logit output of the LLM to compute the top [FORMULA] recommended items, which allows us to compute popular evaluation metrics such as HR@K. We perform full-parameter finetuning on pretrained LLMs. Before finetuning, we preprocess the MovieLens-20M dataset so that in each data point, the LLM is given a historical context of the movies that the user has previously watched and rated. A list of 100 candidate movies with the correct next-watched movie inserted randomly is given to the LLM and the LLM is prompted to produce the next movie watched. Fig. 8 shows an example of one such preprocessed data point. The numerical score of each recommended movie corresponds to the probability logits produced by the finetuned LLM. Similar to the HSTU case, we treat the last movie watched by all users as a held-out validation set. Because our candidate set in the prompt is a list of 100 movies, we expect the HR@10 for this setup to be higher than that of HSTU (which considers all movies as candidates). xxx We performed our experiments across two open-source LLM families—Qwen3-Instruct (Yang et al., 2025) and Llama-3.1-Instruct (Touvron et al., 2023). Because we finetune the model from pretrained checkpoints, we only adjust the training data scale in our experiments. However, we expect our results to hold true even if we co-scale both data and model sizes for LLMs. We finetune the LLMs with 8 A100 GPUs, with an AdamW optimizer and a peak learning rate of [FORMULA] with a cosine decay schedule and a 3% linear warmup, and global gradient-norm clipping at 1.0. We use a batch size of 8 sequences, a maximum sequence length of 4096 tokens, and train for a single epoch. We apply four different features during the fine-tuning of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. The first two are addition of genre and rating information to each movie in the prompt, while dropout and extra layer are model-specific feature changes to the LLM itself. Detailed descriptions of these features are provided in App. B. As shown in Fig. 9, LLM-based recommendation models also exhibit feature-invariant scaling, just like traditional recommendation models shown earlier. This suggests that our method is equally effective in predicting the effectiveness of new features for LLM-based recommendation systems (as shown in Fig. 6). The [FORMULA] values reported in each panel are also consistently close to 1, indicating a strong fit to the scaling-law predictions regardless of which feature is applied to the baseline model. Interestingly, these scaling relationships hold not only for validation loss (top row), but also for downstream performance metrics such as HR@10 (bottom row). These results suggest that scaling laws can even be used to predict other performance metrics (e.g., NDCG (Järvelin and Kekäläinen, 2017), Normalized Entropy (He et al., 2014)). We also found that LLMs across different model families (Qwen and Llama) and sizes (from 0.5B to 8B) consistently (apart from an edge case, which we discuss in Sec. 10.2) enjoy feature-invariant scaling. For instance, Fig. 9 shows that both Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct enjoy feature-invariant scaling laws. In addition, the same scaling behavior holds true for LLMs with varying sizes (Fig. 12). 10. Interesting case studies In this section, we present some interesting case studies we found in our experiments. The first case study highlights the prevalence of “crossover” effects during the training of recommendation models. The second case study presents some edge examples that we encountered in which scaling laws fail. When applying new features to baseline recommendation models, we often observe “crossover points” in scaling curves. This is shown in the top row of Fig. 10, where the baseline model outperforms (or underperforms) the experimental model at a small-scale but the trend reverses at a larger scale. However, as seen from the bottom row, our method is still effective in predicting the full-scale performance correctly. In addition, the top row of Fig. 10 shows that a new feature that is effective for one LLM might not be effective for another LLM family. While adding genre information improves recommendation models powered by Llama, it regresses performance for Qwen. Nonetheless, in both cases, the scaling law still holds true and hence our method can still effectively predict the effectiveness of these features. We occasionally observe that the scaling law in some settings does not follow a power-law fit. One extreme example is shown in Fig. 11 below, where the scaling law of Qwen-0.5B does not follow a power-law fit after we included movie genre information into the training data (orange curve). In addition, this also regresses the LLM performance significantly as compared to the baseline. We hypothesize that this happens because adding movie genre information increases the context size by around 30%. As a result, a small LLM does not have sufficient capacity to capture the added information within context, causing the scaling behavior to break down. In general, we concede that such unusual settings would hinder the application of our method (since we are performing predictions by assuming a power-law function for the scaling curves). However, we do not expect them to appear often. 11. Conclusion In this paper, we presented a method that exploits the feature-invariant scaling behavior of recommendation models to more efficiently determine the effectiveness of new feature changes. We show that different recommendation model families enjoy feature-invariant scaling laws. Then, we show that our method accurately predicts (with confidence intervals) the effectiveness of new feature changes on recommendation models, revealing numerous feature changes that improve HSTU’s SOTA performance on MovieLens-20M. Our method can be used as an efficient way for practitioners to evaluate large volumes of new recommendation algorithms and features at industry-scale.

Auditing LLM Pseudo-Label Distillation for Review Informativeness at E-Commerce Scale We study hard-label distillation from Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite to compact encoders on 5.34 million Turkish marketplace reviews. A strict new-SKU temporal test measures teacher fidelity; a separate, teacher-label-blind audit by one company annotator measures editorial agreement. An H3 category prefix slightly improves teacher fidelity on the full new-SKU test. On the 16,000-review chronological audit subset, it instead reduces agreement with both Gemini and the annotator, with a clearer paired difference for CORN than for cross entropy. Thus the context effect depends on the evaluation population, and teacher fidelity alone does not establish editorial alignment. Under the measured offline configurations, a single-L4 student pipeline processes reviews 50.2 times faster than the teacher pipeline. I Introduction An informative review offers product-specific evidence useful to a purchase decision. A delivery-only comment gives little evidence about the product, whereas a concrete fit, durability, or compatibility observation may be informative regardless of sentiment. This construct is narrower than general helpfulness [1]. At marketplace scale, language models can label millions of reviews for smaller models, but a student’s agreement with its teacher and its agreement with an editorial reference answer different questions. We examine these questions using Turkish reviews, frozen Gemini pseudo-labels, a SKU-disjoint temporal test, and a separate single-annotator audit. The contribution is an evaluation of what survives entity and time shift, how input context affects the result, and the throughput of the resulting offline scoring path. A combined market/language shift and a teacher-relative ranking benchmark provide further operational checks. The audit lets us test whether a gain on the full test population holds on annotated reviews. II Related Work Weak supervision creates training data from imperfect signals [2]; hard-label LLM-to-encoder training is a practical form of distillation [3]. We compare BERTurk [4], multilingual XLM-R [5], and Turkish encoders with cross entropy (CE) and conditional ordinal regression (CORN) [6]. Our emphasis is evaluation against distinct targets rather than a new model architecture. III Data and Protocol The source contains 5,344,302 reviews dated June 2025–June 2026. A cutoff of May 7, 2026 was fixed before training. Historical SKUs were assigned exclusively to train (3,844,147 reviews), validation (486,000), or IID test (479,724); all six pairwise SKU intersections were checked to be empty. The strict out-of-time (OOT) set retains 159,570 reviews from SKUs first seen after the cutoff. Excluding 374,861 future reviews of previously seen SKUs leaves 4,969,441 reviews in this protocol. The 37-day strict OOT window contains 139,258 SKUs, only 1.15 reviews per SKU on average; it primarily tests classification for newly appearing products. Variants with distinct catalog SKUs remain distinct entities. The frozen Vertex AI gemini-3.1-flash-lite teacher received review text, product name, and product type, but not rating, media, votes, freshness, or the production score. The prompt defines three ordinal classes: 0, no concrete product evidence; 1, a limited relevant attribute; and 2, specific actionable evidence. Temperature and thinking budget were both set to zero. Structured output requires informativeness_score, reason, and signals; the nine allowed signal types cover use, measurement, attributes, comparison, pros/cons, product terms, emotion only, shipping only, and short text. Only hard scores train the students. Model ID, prompt revision, and generated labels were frozen before training; reasons and signals were never student inputs or targets. One native-Turkish company annotator, selected for domain expertise, labeled 40,000 reviews spanning 1,189 product types without seeing Gemini’s labels. No calibrated pilot preceded the audit. The annotator saw the same text and product metadata as Gemini; there was no second annotator or adjudication. The audit contains 4,000, 12,000, 8,000, and 16,000 reviews from the original train, validation, IID, and chronological OOT pools. The 16,000 future reviews were not used for training or checkpoint selection. They are temporally held out, but only 4,748 belong to the strict new-SKU set; 11,252 concern previously observed SKUs. BERTurk students use review text alone (T) or an H3 category prefix plus text (C). CE and CORN are crossed with both inputs over seeds 17, 42, and 73. XLM-R, COSMOS Turkish BERT, and Turkish ModernBERT use CORN+C, giving 21 runs (see Tables I and III). All use 64-token truncation, AdamW at [FORMULA] , batch size 64, and at most three epochs; validation QWK against Gemini selects checkpoints. We report accuracy, macro-F1, mean absolute ordinal error (MAE), and quadratic weighted kappa (QWK). For audit contrasts, we resample SKUs 1,000 times, keeping the same draws for paired models and averaging differences across the three fixed seeds. The resulting percentile intervals reflect audit-sample uncertainty conditional on those seeds. CORN estimates [FORMULA] and [FORMULA] ; ranking uses the expected class, rescaled to 0–100. Run records retain model revisions, seeds, split assignments, checkpoints, hardware, and per-review class probabilities. Table I measures reproduction of Gemini labels, not human accuracy. The breadth-oriented Amazon sample covers eight domains and 5,377 leaf product types; two failed teacher labels leave 29,998 reviews [7]. This benchmark includes previously seen SKUs and is separate from the strict new-SKU test. BERT-Join is a separate BERTurk model with a CORN head that combines the review-text representation with 16 engineered numeric features, including length, measurement, and product-related signals. It ranks reviews by the expected ordinal score; its inputs and training setup differ from the 21 text/H3 runs reported above. The semantic scores order Gemini labels better than the deployed production composite on this artifact. Students were trained on Gemini-derived labels, the production score also includes a separate Gemini richness feature, and the systems use different inputs. Thus the high NDCG values show teacher-relative ordering, not independent ranking quality; low within-SKU label diversity can also inflate them. At [FORMULA] , Class-2 precision is 19.73% for BERTurk CORN/C versus 17.57% for the production composite, a smaller gain than the graded NDCG difference. Of 324,795 SKUs in this artifact, 76.01% have a single review and cannot enter these NDCG groups. The production composite uses media, votes, freshness, length, and a separate Gemini richness signal. V Operational Scope and Limitations The teacher measurement covers 858,904 reviews newly scored in a resumable labeling run: rows with existing score or attempt outputs were skipped. With up to 64 concurrent API calls, the run took 5.3986 hours (44.19 newly scored reviews/s, including resume-scan overhead). A BERTurk student processed 100,000 reviews at 2,218 reviews/s on one L4 GPU, including tokenization and data transfer but excluding one-time loading. The observed pipeline-rate ratio is 50.2 [FORMULA] under these configurations; it is neither hardware normalized nor an online latency or production A/B result. Recorded single-L4 training lasted 7.0–11.1 hours per run across the compared encoders. At batch size 128, the student’s 10K-review rate was 2,247 reviews/s, only 1.3% above its 100K rate; peak allocated GPU memory was 795 MB. Editorial agreement is with one teacher-label-blind annotator, not an estimate of inter-annotator reliability. The annotator and teacher saw product name and type, whereas students saw only text or text with an H3 prefix. Given this input mismatch, our finding is a partial-context comparison; divergence may partly stem from information asymmetry. The 16K audit is chronologically held out, while the full strict OOT is SKU-disjoint; neither comparison should silently stand in for the other. The external Amazon test combines several shifts and cannot isolate a language effect. VI Conclusion Compact encoders reproduce frozen LLM labels on new SKUs, with measured offline throughput 50.2 times that of the teacher. The H3 category prefix gives small teacher-fidelity gains on the full strict new-SKU test, while it lowers both teacher and annotator agreement on the chronological audit. Because those populations differ, the results do not establish a same-population trade-off between teacher fidelity and editorial alignment. The Amazon and ranking checks are also teacher-relative. Broader editorial claims require multiple annotators and matched teacher/student inputs, alongside explicit reporting of the evaluation population and reference target. Artifact availability. Due to proprietary company constraints, the full teacher prompt, output schema, and experiment configurations are archived in an internal GitLab repository and are not publicly released.

SHARP: Semantic Hierarchical Agentic Reasoning for Next POI Prediction with Dynamic Memory Next point-of-interest (POI) prediction supports personalized location services by anticipating users’ next destinations. Recent methods leverage large language models (LLMs) for semantic reasoning and graphs for collective mobility modeling, improving POI prediction. However, three challenges still remain. Bridging LLMs’ semantic reasoning and specific POI prediction remains challenging. User mobility also evolves over time, making it necessary to retain and update historical knowledge within limited LLM contexts. Meanwhile, global transition graphs smooth out time-specific category transition patterns. To address these challenges, we propose Semantic Hierarchical Agentic Reasoning for Next POI Prediction with Dynamic Memory (SHARP), an agentic hierarchical framework in which category-level reasoning guides specific POI prediction. A trajectory memory agent maintains a dynamic trajectory memory bank that preserves earlier mobility patterns and tracks behavioral changes with limited context growth. We construct multi-granularity time-aware category transition graphs with global and time-conditioned views to preserve temporal regularities obscured by global aggregation. A category predict agent combines these graphs with trajectory memory to predict likely next categories. SHARP learns semantic IDs (SIDs) through a residual-quantized variational autoencoder (RQ-VAE) to construct semantic POI representations, which are jointly optimized with a category-guided POI predictor end-to-end. On three real-world datasets, SHARP improves Acc@5 and Acc@10 by an average of 5.29 and 4.52 percentage points, respectively, over the strongest baseline. 1. Introduction (a) Challenge 1: Connecting Semantic Reasoning with Specific POI Prediction. (b) Challenge 2: Capturing Evolving Mobility within Limited Contexts. (c) Challenge 3: Preserving Time-Conditioned Transition Patterns. The widespread use of location-based social networks and mobile location services has generated extensive data about points of interest (POIs) and users’ visits to them (Yang et al., 2022; Feng et al., 2018). Platforms such as Foursquare provide user check-ins (Yang et al., 2015), while mobile applications collect location records (Feng et al., 2018). POI attributes and user reviews further describe the places users visit (Gao et al., 2015). This wealth of data enables the study of individual preferences and collective mobility, making next POI prediction an important task for anticipating where people will go. Such predictions support applications such as personalized location recommendation (Gao et al., 2015), intelligent transportation (Feng et al., 2018), and urban planning (Feng et al., 2018). Next POI prediction aims to predict the POI a user is most likely to visit next given their past check-ins and available context, accounting for individual preferences, sequential dependencies, and spatiotemporal factors. Recent methods advance next POI prediction through sequential modeling, graph learning, and semantic reasoning. DeepMove (Feng et al., 2018) and STAN (Luo et al., 2021) capture historical regularities and spatiotemporal relations, while GETNext (Yang et al., 2022) and STHGCN (Yan et al., 2023) model shared transitions through graphs, enabling prediction to incorporate population-level mobility patterns. Beyond these behavioral signals, LLM-Mob (Wang et al., 2023) and LLM4POI (Li et al., 2024) bring the prior knowledge and semantic reasoning of large language models (LLMs) into prediction. AgentMove (Feng et al., 2025) and CoMaPOI (Zhong et al., 2025) use agentic reasoning and collaboration to integrate complementary mobility information, while GNPR-SID (Wang et al., 2025) and SPAR (Wang et al., 2026) encode POI relations through semantic IDs for generative prediction, allowing related POIs to share semantic information through their identifiers. Despite these advances, three challenges remain. (1) Connecting LLMs’ semantic reasoning with specific POI prediction remains challenging. (2) A user’s mobility patterns evolve over time, requiring earlier routines and preferences to be considered alongside recent behavioral changes within limited LLM contexts. (3) Global POI transition graphs smooth out local regularities under different temporal conditions, obscuring patterns relevant to prediction. Challenge 1: Connecting Semantic Reasoning with Specific POI Prediction. Directly predicting specific POIs with LLMs (Wang et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024; Zhong et al., 2025) places the entire prediction task on the LLM, requiring it to turn semantic reasoning about mobility into a specific POI prediction. This mapping is difficult, especially when the outputs are raw identifiers whose meanings are not accessible from the identifiers themselves. Figure 1(a) contrasts this direct prediction with predicting a POI category. Category names such as Restaurant and Shopping Mall have recognizable meanings that align with LLMs’ prior knowledge and semantic reasoning, making category prediction a substantially easier task for LLMs than directly predicting specific POIs. This motivates separating category prediction from specific POI prediction within a hierarchical framework, where LLMs predict categories to guide subsequent POI prediction. Semantic POI representations connect the LLM’s semantic guidance with the POI predictor, rather than requiring the LLM to produce the final POI itself. Challenge 2: Capturing Evolving Mobility within Limited Contexts. A user’s mobility patterns evolve over time, but earlier trajectories remain informative about recurring routines and preferences (Feng et al., 2018; Zhong et al., 2025). These long-term patterns may be absent from recent check-ins, so considering only recent trajectories provides an incomplete view of the user’s mobility. Retaining the complete history in LLM inputs, however, makes input token consumption grow linearly with accumulated check-ins and eventually exceed the context window (Feng et al., 2025; Zhong et al., 2025). Figure 1(b) illustrates this tension between retaining historical information and keeping the input within the available context. This motivates a dynamic trajectory memory bank that preserves earlier mobility patterns and incorporates changes revealed by new trajectories. By carrying this memory forward, the agents can interpret recent behavior in light of long-term patterns without repeatedly processing the full history, limiting context growth and token consumption. Challenge 3: Preserving Time-Conditioned Transition Patterns. Graph-based methods such as GETNext and STHGCN capture collective mobility by graph representations (Yang et al., 2022; Yan et al., 2023). POI-GDE further incorporates time through time-serial graphs and interval-aware updates (Yang et al., 2024). Global aggregation, however, can smooth out regularities prominent under specific time conditions, as illustrated by the weekend-night transitions in Figure 1(c). Even when temporal information is encoded, latent graph embeddings do not explicitly convey transition semantics that LLMs can directly interpret. Preserving temporal regularities and making them accessible to LLM reasoning therefore requires explicit semantic descriptions of these transitions. We construct multi-granularity time-aware category transition graphs, preserving global and time-conditioned patterns in a semantically interpretable form for LLM reasoning. Building on these insights, we propose Semantic Hierarchical Agentic Reasoning for Next POI Prediction with Dynamic Memory (SHARP), an agentic hierarchical framework that connects category-level reasoning with semantic POI prediction. A trajectory memory agent maintains a dynamic trajectory memory bank that preserves long-term mobility patterns and captures recent behavioral changes without repeatedly processing the complete history. Multi-granularity time-aware category transition graphs complement this memory with global and time-conditioned population-level patterns in a form accessible to LLM reasoning. Unlike CoMaPOI’s direct POI prediction (Zhong et al., 2025), our category predict agent combines memory and graph information to predict categories that guide POI scoring without restricting eligibility. For specific POI prediction, we learn semantic IDs (SIDs) through a residual-quantized variational autoencoder (RQ-VAE) (Lee et al., 2022). Unlike GNPR-SID’s autoregressive SID generation (Wang et al., 2025), we use the selected codebook vectors to construct semantic POI representations. A category-guided POI predictor integrates these representations with agent predictions, trajectory information, graph information, and individual mobility patterns to predict the next POI. The semantic POI representations and the POI predictor are optimized jointly end-to-end. Experiments on NYC, TKY, and CA show that SHARP outperforms twelve baselines, improving Acc@5 and Acc@10 over the strongest baseline by an average of 5.29 and 4.52 percentage points, respectively. Dynamic trajectory memory reduces input token consumption by 86.14%–91.86% compared with Full History in our token analysis, while improving category Acc@5 by 10.11–12.70 percentage points over analyzing only the current trajectory. Our contributions of this work are summarized as follows: We propose SHARP, an agentic hierarchical framework that connects category-level reasoning with semantic POI representations. Jointly learning these representations and a category-guided POI predictor enables fine-grained prediction by agent reasoning. We develop a dynamic trajectory memory bank that preserves earlier mobility knowledge and tracks behavioral changes, supporting category prediction with substantially reduced token consumption. We construct multi-granularity time-aware category transition graphs that capture global and time-conditioned mobility patterns, providing temporally differentiated collective information for agentic category prediction. 2. Related Work Non-LLM-Based Methods. Methods without LLMs primarily model mobility through sequential dependencies and collaborative relations. PRME (Feng et al., 2015) learns personalized transition metrics, while recurrent models (Liu et al., 2016; Feng et al., 2018) capture spatiotemporal dependencies. LSTPM (Sun et al., 2020) models long-/short-term preferences, while STAN (Luo et al., 2021) and MTNet (Huang et al., 2024) capture spatiotemporal relations. GETNext (Yang et al., 2022) combines graph information with a Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017), STHGCN (Yan et al., 2023) models higher-order relations, and LoTNext (Xu et al., 2024) addresses long-tailed visitation. These approaches learn representations from behavioral and item information, but do not exploit the broader semantic knowledge and reasoning capabilities of pretrained LLMs. LLM-Based Methods. LLM-based methods use pretrained knowledge to reason about mobility. LLM-Mob (Wang et al., 2023) uses prompting, while LLM4POI (Li et al., 2024) and Refine-POI (Li et al., 2025) employ supervised and reinforcement fine-tuning of LLMs, respectively. AgentMove (Feng et al., 2025) and CoMaPOI (Zhong et al., 2025) extend this direction through agentic reasoning and collaboration. Semantic indexing also supports LLM-based generation. LC-Rec (Zheng et al., 2024) aligns item identifiers with language and collaborative semantics, and GNPR-SID (Wang et al., 2025) uses semantic IDs for generative POI prediction. ROS (Lv et al., 2026) and SPAR (Wang et al., 2026) further incorporate spatial knowledge into generative prediction. Despite these advances, preserving evolving mobility patterns within limited LLM contexts and integrating time-conditioned collective transitions remain challenges. 3. Preliminary Next POI Prediction. Let [FORMULA] , [FORMULA] , and [FORMULA] denote the sets of users, POIs, and POI categories, respectively. Each POI [FORMULA] is represented as a tuple [FORMULA] , where [FORMULA] is its unique identifier, [FORMULA] and [FORMULA] are its longitude and latitude, and [FORMULA] is its category. For a user [FORMULA] , an observed check-in trajectory is a time-ordered sequence [FORMULA] , where each pair [FORMULA] records a check-in by user [FORMULA] at POI [FORMULA] and timestamp [FORMULA] . Given a split position [FORMULA] , we divide [FORMULA] into the historical trajectory [FORMULA] and the context trajectory [FORMULA] , where [FORMULA] contains earlier check-ins that characterize long-term mobility patterns, and [FORMULA] contains the most recent check-ins that reflect current mobility tendencies. Given these two trajectories and a target time [FORMULA] , the next POI prediction task aims to predict the POI [FORMULA] that user [FORMULA] will visit next. Semantic IDs. Conventional POI identifiers distinguish POIs but carry no information about their relationships. A semantic ID (SID) instead represents an item as a tuple of discrete codes learned from its representation, so related POIs can share part of their SIDs (Rajput et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2025). For example, two similar POIs may be assigned [FORMULA] and [FORMULA] , sharing the first two codes while remaining distinguishable. Common SID construction methods include Residual-Quantized Variational Autoencoder (RQ-VAE) (Lee et al., 2022), Residual Quantization K-Means (RQ-KMeans) (Wang et al., 2026), and hierarchical K-means (Wang et al., 2022). These methods map continuous item representations into discrete code tuples. 4. Method As illustrated in Figure 2, SHARP follows a hierarchical process that first predicts likely POI categories and then uses them to guide specific POI prediction. Given historical and context trajectories, the trajectory memory agent maintains a dynamic trajectory memory bank that captures long-term mobility patterns and recent behavioral tendencies. This memory is updated as new trajectories arrive. The category predict agent combines the memory with the context trajectory, target time, and information retrieved from multi-granularity time-aware category transition graphs to predict likely next categories. For specific POI prediction, SHARP uses semantic POI representations constructed from SIDs learned through RQ-VAE. A category-guided POI predictor encodes the trajectory using these representations and combines it with the target time, agent category predictions, graph information, and personalized mobility statistics to predict the next POI. This connects category-level reasoning with distinctions among individual POIs. The semantic POI representations and the prediction network are optimized jointly end-to-end. A user’s mobility patterns evolve over time. Relying only on recent trajectories overlooks recurring preferences and routines reflected in earlier activities beyond those trajectories. Ignoring this longer-term historical information leaves an incomplete account of the user’s mobility patterns and limits the historical context available for interpreting current behavior. Effective user modeling therefore requires considering longer-term mobility patterns alongside recent behavior. Repeatedly feeding all preceding trajectories to an LLM, however, makes the number of input tokens per prediction grow linearly with the number of accumulated check-ins, eventually exceeding the model’s context window. We therefore use a trajectory memory agent to maintain dynamic trajectory memory and a category predict agent to predict the next category using this memory, the target time, and multi-granularity time-aware graph information. Trajectory Memory Agent. Conclusion We presented SHARP, an agentic hierarchical framework that connects category-level reasoning with semantic POI representations for next POI prediction. The representations and category-guided POI predictor are jointly optimized end-to-end. Dynamic trajectory memory preserves earlier mobility patterns and tracks behavioral changes, while multi-granularity time-aware category transition graphs provide global and time-conditioned patterns for both prediction stages. Experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate SHARP’s predictive advantages and substantial token savings through dynamic trajectory memory.

DotRAG: Retrieval-Time Reasoning Along Relational Paths Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GraphRAG) faces significant challenges in complex relational retrieval tasks, particularly in densely connected knowledge graphs where the number of possible paths grows rapidly with reasoning depth. Existing GraphRAG retrieval algorithms either rely on rigid, predefined heuristics to identify relevant graph context or employ costly LLM-based reasoning to guide graph traversal. To address these limitations, we propose DotRAG, a lightweight, training-free GraphRAG retrieval algorithm that uses large language model (LLM) reasoning to narrow the search space and recover task-relevant relational paths. During indexing, DotRAG constructs an entity-relation knowledge graph, generates a graph-wide overview summarizing its contents, and leverages graph reachability indexing to avoid expensive online graph traversals. At query time, the LLM uses this overview to identify promising graph regions and hypothesizes relationship sequences connecting graph information to the query. The LLM then performs targeted relational searches, using graph constraints to restrict the candidate pool progressively. On MetaQA 2-hop queries, DotRAG achieves 97.78% retrieval recall and 51.27% F1, compared to the best baseline scores of 34.74% and 6.33%, respectively. On STaRK-MAG, DotRAG achieves 85.07% recall on 2-hop queries while demonstrating greater computational efficiency than reasoning-based GraphRAG baselines, with 12.2 [FORMULA] lower retrieval latency than HopRAG. 1. Introduction Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) grounds large language models (LLMs) to external knowledge (Lewis et al., 2020; Karpukhin et al., 2020). Recent work has leveraged graphs (GraphRAG) to enhance the retrieval process (Han et al., 2024; Peng et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2024). However, most existing GraphRAG retrieval methods rely on predefined heuristics, typically based on semantic similarity, graph-topological properties such as node degree, or combinations of these signals (He et al., 2024; Edge et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025b; Chen et al., 2026). These heuristics struggle with complex relational queries that require retrieving specific sequences of relations connecting entities (Yu et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2025; Lau et al., 2026; Guo et al., 2026). This challenge becomes more pronounced in densely connected knowledge graphs, where the number of possible relational paths grows combinatorially with reasoning depth, making it increasingly difficult to identify the paths needed to retrieve the correct evidence for a query (Peng et al., 2025; Liang and Gu, 2025; Du et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2019). Consequently, heuristic-driven retrieval can introduce two key failure modes in complex relational tasks: (i) retrieving irrelevant entities and relationships, which introduces noise into the model’s context and complicates downstream reasoning (Chen et al., 2026; Guo et al., 2025a; Huang et al., 2026), or (ii) failing to retrieve necessary evidence, leaving the model without the information required to answer a query, even when that information exists in the graph (Zhan et al., 2026; Guo et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2025). To move away from predefined traversal rules, some GraphRAG retrieval algorithms incorporate LLM reasoning directly into retrieval decisions, allowing the model to determine which graph regions to explore, which relationships to follow, and what context to retrieve. However, these approaches face two key limitations (i) as graph size and connectivity increase, the number of retrieval decisions can grow substantially, limiting scalability to large knowledge graphs; and (ii) the high latency of LLM reasoning makes repeated retrieval decisions computationally expensive and often impractical. To address these challenges, we introduce DotRAG, a lightweight, training-free GraphRAG retrieval algorithm designed to recover task-relevant relational paths from knowledge graphs. During offline indexing, DotRAG builds an entity-relation knowledge graph and generates two complementary information sources to support retrieval. First, it generates a global overview that summarizes the graph’s contents, informing the LLM at inference time what information the graph contains. Second, it constructs a graph reachability index that records the shortest-hop distances between entities, telling the LLM which types of entities are reachable and at what distances. At query time, the LLM uses this information to decide which graph regions to explore and how to constrain the search to find task-relevant relational paths progressively. Thus, DotRAG keeps the search task-focused, reduces the number of LLM calls needed for graph exploration by grounding retrieval decisions in the knowledge base, and avoids costly online graph traversals by precomputing structural information in the reachability index. We evaluate DotRAG on STaRK(Wu et al., 2024) and MetaQA(Zhang et al., 2018), two challenging relational retrieval benchmarks. A common limitation explicitly acknowledged in prior GraphRAG evaluations is the lack of reliable ground truth for directly assessing retrieval effectiveness, leading many studies to rely on downstream answer quality and LLM-as-a-Judge, which can introduce subjective judgments and model-dependent biases (Guo et al., 2025b; Chen et al., 2026; Edge et al., 2024). We use these two benchmarks to ensure that all methods are evaluated on the same knowledge graphs, including any existing graph-construction errors, natural-language queries, and ground-truth answer entities. Both contain graphs derived from automatic extraction pipelines from unstructured data and include realistic GraphRAG noise, such as duplicate entities, mislabeled entities, and other extraction errors. This enables reproducible and fair comparisons that isolate retrieval algorithm performance from differences in graph construction and downstream answer generation. Our results show that DotRAG substantially improves multi-hop retrieval effectiveness, achieving 97.78% recall and 51.27% F1 on MetaQA 2-hop queries and 85.07% recall on STaRK-MAG 2-hop queries. These retrieval gains translate into stronger downstream answer quality, with DotRAG achieving the highest answer recall and F1 across all evaluated settings, demonstrating its effectiveness in recovering task-relevant relational evidence that LLMs can successfully utilize. In summary, our contributions are: Our key contribution is we introduce a novel LLM-guided relational retrieval algorithm that performs localized semantic searches directly over graph relationships, progressively constraining the search space rather than allowing irrelevant candidates from the global graph to compete. We introduce two complementary graph indexing mechanisms: a compressed global graph overview that provides prior knowledge of the graph’s contents and relational structure, and a precomputed reachability map that enables targeted retrieval without exhaustive graph exploration or beam search. We provide interpretable relational retrieval through structured, logically connected traversal paths that expose how retrieved evidence relates to the query, making retrieval decisions traceable and explainable. We establish a large-scale relational retrieval evaluation on STaRK and MetaQA. Our largest evaluation graph contains 88,815 entities and 486,616 relationships, exceeding the largest graph evaluated in HopRAG by approximately 119% in nodes and 183% in edges. We demonstrate that DotRAG substantially improves multi-hop retrieval effectiveness and downstream answer quality across MetaQA and STaRK, achieving the highest 2-hop retrieval F1 across all evaluated datasets and the highest answer recall and F1 across all evaluated settings. 2. Related Works As illustrated in Figure 1, we distinguish LLM reasoning used during retrieval from reasoning used for final answer generation. Based on the degree of LLM control over retrieval decisions, existing RAG methods can be categorized into three paradigms: Retrieve-Then-Generate, Reason-Retrieve-Generate, and Reason-In-Retrieval-Then-Generate. These paradigms correspond to three levels of LLM control over retrieval, namely no retrieval control, input-level control, and algorithm-level control, respectively. In this paradigm, retrieval operates without explicit LLM reasoning guiding its decisions. As depicted, the user’s original query is passed directly to the retrieval algorithm without invoking an LLM before or during retrieval. The algorithm identifies relevant context from the knowledge source, which is then provided to an LLM for final answer generation. Classic RAG approaches fall under this paradigm (Lewis et al., 2020), commonly employing lexical or semantic retrieval methods such as BM25 (Robertson and Zaragoza, 2009) and dense vector search (Karpukhin et al., 2020). While these methods enable efficient and scalable retrieval, a known limitation is that their effectiveness tends to decline as reasoning complexity increases, particularly for multi-hop queries (Trivedi et al., 2023; Shen et al., 2025; Melo et al., 2025; Shi et al., 2024). To address Retrieve-Then-Generate’s limitations, prior work uses LLM reasoning to refine the inputs provided to retrieval algorithms. In these approaches, the LLM does not make graph traversal decisions; instead, it reformulates the query and passes it to an existing retrieval algorithm. This may occur in a single step (Ye et al., 2023; Ma et al., 2023) or iteratively, where the LLM submits a query, examines the retrieved results, and formulates follow-up queries to retrieve additional information (Jiang et al., 2023; Yu et al., 2026; Trivedi et al., 2023). However, the LLM does not control the retrieval algorithm’s internal decisions about which evidence is relevant or which graph regions and relationships should be explored. For example, LightRAG (Guo et al., 2025b) and PathRAG (Chen et al., 2026) use an LLM to transform the original query into keywords, which they then provide as input to their graph retrieval algorithms, while the algorithms independently determine which evidence to retrieve. Reason-In-Retrieval approaches incorporate LLM reasoning directly into the graph retrieval process, allowing the LLM to decide which graph regions to explore, which relationships to follow, and which evidence to retrieve (Sun et al., 2024; Han et al., 2026; Hu et al., 2025). For example, HopRAG (Liu et al., 2025) iteratively uses LLM reasoning during graph traversal to evaluate candidate relationships, select which edges to follow, and progressively retrieve relevant passages across multiple hops through a retrieve-reason-prune mechanism. A key limitation of these approaches is that they often incur substantial computational overhead due to repeated LLM calls during retrieval, increasing latency and cost (Liu et al., 2025; Liang and Gu, 2025; Lee et al., 2025). In contrast, DotRAG is a training-free Reason-In-Retrieval-Then-Generate approach that combines LLM-guided retrieval decisions with graph-structural constraints to enable targeted relational path retrieval. By leveraging offline graph indexing, DotRAG provides the LLM with prior knowledge of the graph’s contents and structure, while progressively restricting semantic search to structurally relevant candidates. This enables informed decisions about which relational paths to explore and when to stop, reducing unnecessary exploration and computational overhead. 3. Problem Formulation Following Guo et al. DotRAG’s retrieval algorithm proceeds in four key stages: trajectory discovery, trajectory ranking, relational path search, and relational path ranking. The discovery phase deterministically identifies query-relevant seed entities and constructs graph-supported retrieval options. The LLM then ranks these options from most to least promising. Relational path search extends the highest-ranked options through coordinated semantic searches. Finally, relational path ranking orders the recovered evidence and selects the paths that fit within the final token budget. A key design principle of DotRAG is to restrict LLM reasoning to selecting among graph-supported options and coordinating search. This avoids the computational and latency overhead of requiring excessive LLM calls to explore the graph.
