Experiments We evaluate DotRAG on relational retrieval benchmarks spanning varying graph scales and query complexities, addressing four research questions: (RQ1) How effectively does DotRAG retrieve relevant evidence across different reasoning depths and graph scales? (RQ2) How do retrieval improvements translate into downstream answer quality? (RQ3) How do DotRAG’s components and backbone LLM affect retrieval performance? (RQ4) What are DotRAG’s computational costs and scalability trade-offs? Our evaluation uses MetaQA, STaRK-MAG, and STaRK-Prime, which provide natural-language queries, densely connected knowledge graphs, and ground-truth answer entities. MetaQA is a movie knowledge graph connecting movies, actors, directors, years, ratings, and tags through relationships such as acting, directing, and release information. STaRK-MAG is an academic knowledge graph connecting research papers, authors, institutions, and fields of study through authorship, citation, and affiliation relationships. STaRK-Prime is a biomedical knowledge graph connecting diseases, drugs, genes, proteins, and biological pathways through biomedical relationships. We adapt MetaQA’s complete knowledge graph to our GraphRAG setting, while evaluating STaRK-MAG and STaRK-Prime using subgraphs of their respective knowledge graphs. We provide dataset statistics, preprocessing details, and graph statistics in appendix B, appendix C, and Table 9, respectively. We evaluate retrieval across four dimensions: retrieval accuracy, structural relevance, computational efficiency, and downstream answer quality. To measure retrieval accuracy, we use Recall, Precision, and F1 to assess how well retrieved entities match ground-truth answers. The MetaQA and STaRK benchmarks provide anchor entities, ground-truth answer entities, and annotated hop distances for each question, but do not annotate ground-truth relational paths. To avoid penalizing path-based retrieval algorithms for potentially relevant intermediate entities, we exclude non-answer entities lying on anchor-to-answer paths within each question’s specified hop distance from retrieval precision calculations. To assess structural relevance, we introduce Golden Proximity (GP), which measures the proportion of structurally relevant intermediate entities recovered during retrieval. This metric proxies the retrieval algorithm’s effectiveness at exploring structurally relevant graph regions by measuring its coverage of intermediate entities along anchor-to-answer paths. To assess computational efficiency, we also track the number of LLM calls made during retrieval for each query. Finally, we evaluate downstream answer quality using Answer Recall and F1, comparing the LLM’s generated answers against the complete ground-truth answer set. We provide formal definitions in Appendix D.1. Following Guo et al. (2025b); Chen et al. (2026), we use GPT-4o-mini as the backbone LLM for all methods, with a uniform retrieval budget of 10,000 tokens. We select representative baselines from each retrieval paradigm: BM25 and vector similarity search (VSS) for Retrieve-Then-Generate, LightRAG and PathRAG for Reason-Retrieve-Generate, and HopRAG for Reason-In-Retrieval-Then-Generate. Baseline configurations are provided in Appendix D. As shown in Table 1 and our expanded Table 3 in our appendix, DotRAG achieves the highest F1 across MetaQA hop settings and substantially improves Recall on multi-hop queries. On single-hop queries, most methods achieve high Recall, while reasoning-in-retrieval methods attain higher F1, suggesting greater selectivity in retrieved evidence. However, on two-hop queries, all baselines experience substantial declines in Recall, whereas DotRAG maintains its performance. Our Golden Proximity (GP) evaluation dimension reveals that although BM25, VSS, and LightRAG successfully retrieve entities within the intended anchor–answer boundary, they struggle to recover the actual answers. In contrast, DotRAG effectively translates focused graph exploration into higher Recall and F1. Additionally, on three-hop queries, identifying relevant graph regions becomes increasingly difficult, yet DotRAG achieves the highest golden proximity scores, Recall, and F1. Moreover, DotRAG consistently outperforms HopRAG across all hop settings while requiring substantially fewer LLM calls, demonstrating more effective and efficient retrieval-time reasoning. Additionally, we evaluate DotRAG and the baselines on STaRK-MAG and STaRK-Prime, which provide more realistic and heterogeneous graph settings. Similar to MetaQA, reasoning-in-retrieval methods achieve the strongest F1 scores, with differences becoming more pronounced on two-hop queries. On STaRK-MAG, DotRAG achieves the highest two-hop Recall and F1. Although BM25 achieves a higher golden proximity score, DotRAG is more effective at translating relevant graph exploration into answer retrieval. STaRK-Prime presents a greater challenge across all methods. Unlike STaRK-MAG, which focuses on academic publications, STaRK-Prime contains biomedical knowledge with specialized terminology, diverse entity types, and complex relational queries. Retrieval performance declines substantially, with VSS achieving the highest Recall and DotRAG achieving the highest two-hop F1. These results suggest that accurately interpreting domain-specific relational requirements may limit retrieval effectiveness, a dependency we investigate further in our backbone analysis. Notably, PathRAG encounters prohibitive computational expense on both STaRK datasets, exceeding 20 minutes per query. This behavior stems from its enumeration of candidate relational paths, whose number can grow combinatorially in densely connected graphs. This limitation is one of the motivating examples for DotRAG’s use of precomputed reachability information to constrain graph exploration without expensive online path enumeration. Although a retrieval algorithm may retrieve more correct answer entities, we argue the LLM may not necessarily recognize or include them in its generated response. We therefore measure downstream performance to quantify how effectively the LLM utilizes retrieved information to produce correct answers. For this experiment, we select the best-performing retrieval algorithm from each paradigm: VSS, LightRAG, and DotRAG. We then provide our backbone LLM with the retrieved context and ask it to return a list of answer entities, which we use to compute answer-level recall, precision, and F1. We compare these scores with the retrieval algorithm’s raw recall, precision, and F1 to assess how much the LLM recognized the retrieved answers. Across all settings, we find that DotRAG consistently preserves more of its retrieval advantage in downstream answer generation compared to the baselines. On MetaQA 1-hop, STaRK-MAG 1-hop, and STaRK-Prime 1-hop, VSS achieves the highest retrieval recall, yet its answer-level recall drops to 67.08%, 63.92%, and 37.35%, respectively. This suggests that retrieving more correct entities does not necessarily translate into better answer generation, as irrelevant or distracting surrounding context may hinder the LLM’s ability to identify correct answers. Thus, high retrieval recall does not guarantee high answer recall. Another notable finding is that answer-level F1 substantially exceeds retrieval F1 across all settings, suggesting that the LLM effectively filters out irrelevant retrieved entities when generating its answers, albeit at the cost of reduced recall. We conduct five ablation experiments to assess the contributions of DotRAG’s key design components in Table 7. First, we replace all LLM-guided retrieval decisions with random decisions, eliminating LLM calls during retrieval and effectively transforming DotRAG into a retrieve-then-reason approach. Second, we remove the graph-wide description to evaluate its role in grounding the LLM’s retrieval decisions in the graph’s knowledge. Third, we remove the entity and relationship samples provided before traversal decisions to examine their influence on the LLM’s ability to select relevant routes. Fourth, we remove the graph-reachability constraints from semantic search to investigate whether constrained search reduces noise introduced by globally prominent but irrelevant entities. Finally, we evaluate DotRAG using different backbone LLMs to examine whether its retrieval effectiveness generalizes across models. We replace all LLM-guided retrieval decisions with random choices, reuse the initial query instead of generating new search queries, and randomly determine when to terminate retrieval. Despite removing LLM reasoning entirely, DotRAG achieves competitive recall on MetaQA 1-hop and outperforms all baselines on MetaQA 2-hop in both recall and F1. Notably, it achieves 47.81% recall and 21.05% F1 on MetaQA 2-hop without making any LLM calls. These results suggest that DotRAG’s underlying retrieval design is effective even without LLM guidance, as its graph traversal mechanisms can narrow the search space and expose relevant answer entities despite random decision-making. However, this effectiveness diminishes as retrieval complexity increases. On MetaQA 3-hop, recall and F1 drop sharply to 13.90% and 3.09%, respectively. Similarly, on STaRK-Prime, performance deteriorates from 1-hop to 2-hop queries. These results suggest that while DotRAG’s underlying retrieval design can identify relevant graph regions without LLM guidance, reasoning becomes increasingly important for navigating longer, more complex retrieval paths. During initial graph indexing, a graph-wide description is generated to provide a general overview of the graph and a comprehensive summary of each entity type, grounding the LLM in the graph’s knowledge to support informed retrieval decisions. We find that removing the graph-wide context has a small and inconsistent impact on retrieval performance. Notably, its removal results in a nearly 7-percentage-point drop in recall on STaRK-Prime 2-hop, while producing only modest changes across the remaining settings. Although the graph-wide description provides the LLM with a broader understanding of the graph’s structure and contents, these results suggest that local graph information plays a more substantial role in guiding retrieval decisions than the global graph description. Before the LLM ranks anchor–trajectory pairs or generates follow-up search queries, each branch provides samples of relationship descriptions semantically similar to the current or previous query to support informed graph exploration. In this experiment, we replace all previews with the text "No Preview" to examine their influence on local retrieval decisions. Our results suggest that the effectiveness of previews is dataset-dependent. On STaRK-Prime, removing previews reduces recall by approximately 8–9 percentage points across both hop settings, with F1 also declining. This suggests that entity types and biomedical terminology alone may provide insufficient context for the LLM to make informed traversal decisions. On MetaQA and STaRK-MAG, removing previews reduces 1-hop recall by 3.39 and 8.57 percentage points, respectively. However, 2-hop recall improves substantially on STaRK-MAG, while MetaQA exhibits a slight improvement at 3 hops. These findings suggest that previews can help guide local retrieval decisions, but their effectiveness depends on the characteristics of the underlying knowledge graph and the retrieval depth. In this experiment, we remove the constrained semantic search component from DotRAG. In our standard design, constrained search restricts retrieval candidates to entities of a specified type and hop distance, preventing semantically similar but structurally irrelevant entities from being retrieved. Without these constraints, semantic search operates over the global embedding space, where relevant candidates compete with entities across the entire graph. We also remove the requirement that newly retrieved entities must be reachable from the preceding retrieval trajectory. Our results show that removing constrained search substantially degrades retrieval performance across all datasets and hop settings. Notably, on MetaQA 2-hop, recall drops from 97.78% to 36.18%, while F1 decreases from 51.27% to 3.45%. These findings highlight constrained semantic search as a critical component of DotRAG, demonstrating the importance of incorporating graph structure into semantic retrieval to prevent irrelevant entities from dominating search results. We further evaluate DotRAG using GPT-4.1 and Mistral 3.2 24B-Instruct as alternative backbone LLMs to investigate how retrieval performance varies across models and whether DotRAG’s effectiveness depends on the reasoning capabilities of the underlying LLM in Table 6. We find that GPT-4.1 generally achieves the highest recall and F1, suggesting that DotRAG benefits from stronger backbone models. Interestingly, Mistral also performs competitively in most evaluated settings, but its performance can deteriorate sharply as reasoning complexity increases, approaching that of random retrieval decisions. These findings suggest that while DotRAG generalizes across backbone models, its effectiveness on more complex retrieval tasks remains sensitive to the reasoning capabilities of the underlying LLM. To evaluate the computational efficiency and scalability of DotRAG, we compare its retrieval cost against the baselines, including the number of LLM calls, latency, and associated token expenses in Table 5 and 8. We also examine DotRAG’s performance across knowledge graphs of varying sizes and structural complexity. Our results show that DotRAG is substantially more computationally efficient than HopRAG, with both methods following the reason-in-retrieval-then-generate paradigm. For instance, on STaRK-MAG, DotRAG costs $3.99 per 1,000 queries compared to $11.21 for HopRAG, representing approximately a 64% reduction in cost. Similar trends are observed across the remaining datasets, demonstrating that DotRAG achieves lower computational costs while incorporating LLM reasoning during retrieval. Furthermore, we evaluate DotRAG across knowledge graphs containing approximately 40K–89K entities and 110K–487K relationships. Despite the size and structural complexity of these graphs, DotRAG maintains strong retrieval effectiveness while requiring relatively few LLM calls per query. These results demonstrate DotRAG’s ability to operate efficiently on large, densely connected knowledge graphs without incurring excessive computational overhead. We also observe that DotRAG achieves relatively low retrieval latency for a reason-in-retrieval-then-generate method. On STaRK-MAG, HopRAG requires an average of 156.87 seconds per query, compared to just 12.91 seconds for DotRAG. Despite incorporating LLM reasoning during retrieval, DotRAG maintains latency within the same order of magnitude as LightRAG and PathRAG on MetaQA. Furthermore, DotRAG remains practical on denser knowledge graphs, where PathRAG exceeds 20 minutes per query on both STaRK datasets. This suggests that DotRAG’s retrieval design avoids the computational explosion associated with extensive online graph traversal, allowing it to incorporate retrieval-time reasoning while maintaining manageable computational costs. 6. Conclusion In this work, we introduced DotRAG, a training-free GraphRAG retrieval algorithm that incorporates LLM reasoning directly into graph retrieval. DotRAG combines a global graph overview with precomputed reachability information to guide the exploration of task-relevant relational paths while constraining semantic search to structurally relevant candidates. Experiments on MetaQA and STaRK demonstrate substantial improvements in multi-hop retrieval effectiveness and downstream answer quality compared to existing retrieval paradigms. Our results further show that DotRAG achieves these gains with significantly lower computational overhead than HopRAG. Overall, these findings highlight the importance of combining LLM-guided retrieval decisions with graph-structural constraints for effective and efficient relational retrieval.

SAM-D2Q: Aligning Multimodal Doc2Query with Search Demand and Conversion for E-commerce E-commerce search often suffers from vocabulary mismatch between user queries and merchant-authored product titles, since short titles cannot fully cover diverse user expressions or visual product attributes. Although Doc2Query alleviates this issue by generating pseudo-queries for document expansion, traditional methods are text-only and not optimized for e-commerce business objectives. As a result, they may produce semantically plausible but commercially ineffective expansions and miss key attributes present in product images. To this end, we propose E-commerce Search-Aligned Multimodal Doc2Query (SAM-D2Q), a business-aligned multimodal document expansion framework for e-commerce search under Boolean retrieval constraints. SAM-D2Q consists of three stages: (1) task-adapted multimodal supervised fine-tuning to enhance vision-language understanding of product titles, images, and user queries; (2) multimodal data augmentation to improve perception of key visual attributes and expansion coverage; and (3) reinforcement-learning-based preference alignment toward search business objectives, encouraging the model to generate pseudo-queries that better match user intent and commercial value. Offline experiments show that SAM-D2Q substantially improves retrieval performance over traditional Doc2Query methods. Deployed in the AliExpress production search system, SAM-D2Q improves online business metrics, increasing GMV by +3.38% and Pay Count by +2.27%. 1. Introduction With the rapid growth of e-commerce, online shopping has become an integral part of daily life for billions of users worldwide. In this digital ecosystem, search engines serve as the key gateway connecting user intent with massive product inventories. A typical e-commerce search pipeline consists of query understanding, retrieval/recall, and ranking. Although neural retrieval methods such as dense retrieval and generative retrieval have made significant progress, keyword-based retrieval built on inverted indexes remains the backbone of large-scale e-commerce search systems due to its low latency, high interpretability, robustness for cold-start products, and reliability in exact matching scenarios such as brands and models. However, keyword-based retrieval still suffers from the vocabulary mismatch problem, where user queries and product descriptions may express the same intent using different terms. To alleviate this issue, document expansion methods have been widely studied. In particular, Doc2Query (Gospodinov et al., 2023; Nogueira et al., 2019a; Nogueira et al., 2019b), which enriches document representations by generating potential user queries, has achieved strong performance in general web search. Nevertheless, directly applying traditional Doc2Query methods to e-commerce search faces two major challenges. First, existing Doc2Query methods mainly optimize semantic relevance based on textual data, while overlooking critical business signals such as search Page Views (PV) and Conversion Rate (CVR). As a result, the generated queries may be semantically related but have limited commercial value. For example, in the “dress” category, high-performing queries often contain concrete style attributes such as “sexy dress” or “casual dress”, which typically correspond to higher search demand or conversion potential. In contrast, a generic Doc2Query model may generate low-value variants such as “chic dress” or simply reorganize existing title words, introducing index redundancy without clear business gain. Second, e-commerce products are inherently multimodal, while product titles are often short and incomplete due to length constraints. Many key attributes, such as color, style, pattern, and material, are mainly expressed in product images rather than text. For long-tail products with sparse titles, such as “man shirt 2025”, text-only expansion methods may fail to capture visual details such as sleeve length or specific colors, causing relevant products to be missed during retrieval. To address these challenges, we propose SAM-D2Q, a Search-Aligned Multimodal Doc2Query framework for e-commerce search. Instead of focusing only on semantic enrichment, SAM-D2Q aligns query generation with search business objectives while incorporating multimodal product information. By integrating visual signals, multimodal data synthesis, and business-aligned optimization, SAM-D2Q generates expanded queries that are both grounded in product content and valuable for downstream commercial performance. SAM-D2Q consists of three stages: (1) information-gain constrained multimodal SFT for coarse semantic alignment; (2) hybrid multimodal SFT with CPV-guided counterfactual augmentation for visual grounding; and (3) GRPO-based preference alignment toward search business objectives. The novelty of SAM-D2Q lies in the industrial formulation and deployment of multimodal Doc2Query under Boolean retrieval constraints, where expansion terms must provide recall gain, visual grounding, and business utility. Deployed in AliExpress Search, SAM-D2Q brings a 3.38% GMV lift and a 2.27% Pay Count increase in online A/B testing. The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows: Industrial multimodal Doc2Query formulation. We reformulate Doc2Query for Boolean e-commerce retrieval, where expansion terms must provide information gain rather than TF re-weighting, and align generation with recall, visual grounding, and business utility. Counterfactual visual grounding. We convert text-covered logs into multimodal counterfactual samples by masking visual attribute terms from product text while preserving product images, forcing the model to recover visually grounded expansion targets. Large-scale deployment. We deploy SAM-D2Q in AliExpress Search via offline indexing without online model inference, and validate it through offline experiments and online A/B testing. 2. Related Work Document expansion aims to alleviate vocabulary mismatch by enriching documents with additional terms before indexing. Given a document [FORMULA] , Doc2Query-style methods generate synthetic queries [FORMULA] and append them to the original document for retrieval. Early Doc2Query (Nogueira et al., 2019b) uses a Seq2Seq Transformer to generate queries, while DocT5Query (Nogueira et al., 2019a) further improves effectiveness with a larger T5 model. Recent studies also explore LLM-based query generation, but their advantages over strong T5-based baselines remain mixed (Weller et al., 2024). Since generative expansion may introduce irrelevant or hallucinated terms, Doc2Query– (Gospodinov et al., 2023) filters generated queries with a relevance model to reduce noise. However, e-commerce search differs substantially from general web retrieval. Industrial systems typically follow a recall-ranking cascade, where the sparse retrieval stage prioritizes high recall under strict latency constraints. Moreover, product titles are short and incomplete, while many key attributes are expressed visually in product images. Finally, e-commerce expansion should not only be semantically correct but also commercially valuable, since query traffic and conversion rates vary significantly across terms. These differences motivate our business-aligned multimodal Doc2Query framework. Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), such as LLaVA (Liu et al., 2023) and Qwen-VL (Bai et al., 2023; Bai et al., 2025), have shown strong vision-language understanding capabilities. However, studies in Visual Question Answering (VQA) show multimodal models may over-rely on language priors and ignore visual evidence (Agrawal et al., 2018; Goyal et al., 2017; Niu et al., 2021). For example, if most answers to “What color are the bananas?” are “yellow”, models may learn dataset shortcuts instead of grounding the answer in the image. To mitigate such biases, prior work constructs counterfactual or augmented samples by modifying images, questions, or their associations. MUTANT (Gokhale et al., 2020) creates semantically distinct samples through input perturbation, CSS (Chen et al., 2020) masks critical objects or words, and SimpleAug (Kil et al., 2021) leverages semantic annotations for question pairing. Inspired by these ideas, we construct CPV-guided counterfactual samples for e-commerce products, masking visual attributes from text while preserving images, so that the model must recover visually grounded attributes from product images. Supervised fine-tuning provides basic instruction-following ability, but it does not necessarily align generation with downstream objectives. RLHF, commonly implemented with PPO (Schulman et al., 2017; Ouyang et al., 2022), is widely used to align LLMs with human preferences, but it is often costly and unstable. Offline alternatives such as DPO (Rafailov et al., 2023) and IPO (Azar et al., 2024; Ethayarajh et al., 2024) avoid explicit reward modeling, but are limited by static preference data and weaker online exploration. Recent online RL methods such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) (Shao et al., 2024) reduce training overhead by removing the value network while retaining group-based exploration. Unlike standard safety- or helpfulness-oriented alignment, we adapt GRPO to optimize e-commerce query generation with semantic, commercial, and visual rewards. This aligns document expansion with both retrieval effectiveness and business utility. 3. Preliminaries E-commerce retrieval operates under distinct paradigms compared to general web search. The nature of product data and the reliance on Boolean matching necessitate a specialized approach to document expansion. Unlike general web search, where probabilistic models like BM25 are standard, industrial e-commerce search relies heavily on Boolean Matching for its inverted index. This choice is mandated by three operational requirements: Deterministic Matching: To handle queries with strict intent slots (e.g., brand or model constraints), Boolean logic ensures precision by prohibiting the "fuzzy" retrieval typical of probabilistic models. Data Conciseness: Product titles act as structured keyword sets rather than natural language, rendering TF-based relevance weighting largely ineffective. Latency Constraints: Boolean retrieval offers superior computational efficiency at the scale of hundreds of millions of items, which is critical for maintaining real-time system performance. These factors imply that document expansion in this domain must not just "add keywords" as in Doc2Query, but must produce high-precision, business-aligned terms that strictly comply with the Boolean retrieval logic—a challenge that motivates our proposed SAM-D2Q framework. This paradigm shift fundamentally alters the objective of Doc2Query. In standard literature (Lin et al., 2022), generated queries serve two purposes: (1) Expansion (adding new terms) and (2) Re-weighting (repeating existing terms to boost TF). However, under the Boolean Matching constraint, re-weighting is functionally redundant—a term’s presence is binary (0 or 1). Repeating a token that already exists in the title provides zero marginal utility for recall. Consequently, in our system context, the value of a generative expander is strictly defined by its ability to generate new terms—latent keywords that are semantically relevant but lexically absent from the seller’s description. This insight directly motivates our Information-Gain Constraint design in Stage 1 (Section 4.1), where we use non-covered query-item pairs for lexical expansion and reserve text-covered pairs for counterfactual visual augmentation. This Boolean-aware formulation distinguishes SAM-D2Q from standard Doc2Query methods that are primarily designed for probabilistic ranking-oriented retrieval. 4. Methodology Formally, we define the e-commerce document expansion task as learning a conditional generation policy [FORMULA] , parameterized by a Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM). Here, [FORMULA] represents the multimodal product context, consisting of textual metadata [FORMULA] and visual content [FORMULA] , while [FORMULA] denotes a sequence of tokens representing a potential user search query. Unlike traditional retrieval methods that rely on exact matching, our LLM-based Doc2Query approach leverages the extensive world knowledge and reasoning capabilities of the pre-trained MLLM to infer latent user intents that are semantically implied but lexically absent in the source document. Standard approaches typically maximize the likelihood [FORMULA] over raw Query-Item click logs. However, we argue that naive optimization of MLLMs on noisy industrial logs leads to objective misalignment, where the model learns spurious correlations rather than true semantic expansion. To address this, SAM-D2Q adopts a Three-Stage Curriculum Learning pipeline (as illustrated in Figure 1), which progressively evolves the MLLM from learning basic semantic associations (Stage 1) to mastering cross-modal reasoning (Stage 2), and finally aligning with complex business utilities (Stage 3). The primary objective of the first stage is to instill the capability of Lexical Expansion. A significant challenge in training generative models on raw e-commerce logs is the "summarization shortcut": models tend to converge to a local optimum where they merely extract subsets of tokens from [FORMULA] to form [FORMULA] , achieving low training loss but zero retrieval gain. To bridge this mismatch, we split query-item click logs according to whether the query provides information gain over the product text. For Stage-1 pre-SFT, we retain only samples where the query contains new terms that are not fully covered by the product text: where [FORMULA] and [FORMULA] denote the set of unique tokens in the query and product text, respectively. The remaining text-covered pairs, where [FORMULA] , are not used for Stage-1 pre-SFT. Instead, they are reserved as candidates for Stage-2 counterfactual visual augmentation. By training Stage 1 on [FORMULA] , the policy [FORMULA] is discouraged from mere extraction and is encouraged to learn latent semantic mappings from product context to informative expansion queries. The first stage enforces lexical expansion by excluding query-in-text samples from pre-SFT. However, many text-covered pairs still contain strong relevance signals, especially when they involve visually expressed attributes. To further improve cross-modal grounding while preserving the information-gain property learned in Stage 1, we construct the Stage-2 training corpus from two complementary sources: CPV-guided multimodal augmentation data and high-quality human-labeled data. We leverage the platform’s accumulated Category-Property-Value (CPV) knowledge base to identify visual attributes of products. In the CPV schema, attributes such as color, material, pattern, and sleeve style are defined as visual attributes because their values can be directly perceived from product images. Unlike Stage 1, which uses log pairs where the query already provides information gain over the product text, counterfactual augmentation starts from text-covered log pairs satisfying [FORMULA] . These samples usually contain strong relevance signals, but the target query can be generated by simply copying terms from the product text. To remove such textual shortcuts, if the query contains visual attribute values defined in the item’s CPV schema, we mask these values from the product text while keeping the product image unchanged. Formally, for a text-covered query-item pair [FORMULA] , we construct a counterfactual textual input: where [FORMULA] denotes the set of query tokens, and [FORMULA] denotes the set of visual attribute values derived from the CPV schema. We then retain only the augmented samples that satisfy the information-gain constraint after masking: The model is trained to generate the original query from the masked textual input and the image: In this way, the original query is fully supported by the product text before masking, but becomes lexically absent after removing visual attributes. The model must therefore rely on the product image to recover the missing visual information. Conclusion We present SAM-D2Q, a multimodal document-to-query framework for industrial e-commerce search. SAM-D2Q bridges vocabulary mismatch in sparse retrieval by generating semantically relevant, visually grounded, and commercially valuable expansion queries. It combines multimodal SFT, counterfactual data synthesis, and business-aware GRPO alignment with semantic, commercial, and visual rewards. Extensive offline experiments show consistent improvements in generation quality and retrieval effectiveness, while online A/B testing on AliExpress Search further demonstrates significant gains in core business metrics, including GMV and Pay Count. These results validate the effectiveness and deployment feasibility of SAM-D2Q in large-scale industrial search systems. Recommendation unlearning aims to remove the influence of specific historical interactions that should no longer affect future recommendations, such as noisy clicks or outdated user preferences. However, performing recommendation unlearning becomes much harder in modern Machine-Learning-as-a-Service (MLaaS) architectures, where the recommendation model is remotely hosted by a model provider (MP) and accessed by service operators (SO) only through APIs. In this setting, a service operator serves end users but cannot access or modify internal model parameters. As a result, existing unlearning methods are difficult to apply because they require access to model internals for retraining, fine-tuning, or other parameter updates. To address these challenges, we propose Causal Explanation-based Unlearning (CEU), a novel unlearning framework tailored for MLaaS environments. Instead of modifying internal model weights, CEU operates through a two-step output-level score intervention. First, it estimates how the forgotten interaction causally contributes to the current recommendation. Second, guided by this causal signal, the system removes the influence of the forgotten interaction by adjusting the final ranking scores of affected items. Because CEU leaves model parameters untouched, it naturally supports continuous unlearning requests while avoiding the error accumulation that can result from repeated parameter updates. Extensive experiments on three public datasets show that CEU achieves unlearning effectiveness comparable to full retraining while preserving recommendation utility and significantly reducing computational cost. The source code is available at: https://github.com/zhang-haichao/Explain-and-Forget. I Introduction Driven by growing model complexity and the high cost of training and maintenance, modern recommender systems increasingly adopt the Machine Learning as a Service (MLaaS) architecture [20, 7, 17]. In this setting, the model provider (MP) trains and hosts the recommendation model, while the service operator (SO) serves end users by querying the model through APIs [15]. This separation means that the SO can use the model but cannot access or modify its internal parameters. As the direct interface with users, the SO is responsible for maintaining the quality of recommendation results. However, user preferences change over time. Users may lose interest in previously preferred items or accidentally click irrelevant ones. Such noisy or outdated interactions can cause the system to repeatedly recommend unwanted content [23, 4, 8]. To maintain user engagement, the SO should allow users to revoke specific historical interactions and remove their influence on future recommendations. This practical need motivates the task of recommendation unlearning [13], which aims to remove the influence of selected historical interactions from a trained recommendation model. Achieving recommendation unlearning in the MLaaS setting introduces two critical. First, a strict asymmetric access constraint: the SO has no access to the recommendation model’s internal parameters or gradients. Since the model is controlled by the MP and exposed only through APIs, the SO cannot directly modify model weights to remove the effect of specific training data. Second, unlearning requests may arrive continuously as users interact with the system [14, 21]. Repeated approximate updates across sequential requests may accumulate errors, gradually degrading overall recommendation quality [10]. These two constraints make existing unlearning methods difficult to apply, because most of them require access to model internals or control over the training process. Existing methods can be broadly grouped into three categories: retraining-based methods (e.g., GraphEraser [5], RecEraser [2]) that retrain affected model partitions; fine-tuning-based methods (e.g., GNNDelete [6], UnlearnRec [3]) that apply lightweight representation updates; and influence-based methods (e.g., SCIF [12], IFRU [31]) that adjust weights based on estimated data influence. Despite their different techniques, these approaches share a common limitation: they require access to model internals, training procedures, or updatable model components. As a result, they are difficult to apply in MLaaS systems where the model can only be accessed through APIs. Given the strict constraints of the MLaaS paradigm, recommendation unlearning should shift away from parameter updates, as the Service Operator (SO) can only observe outputs via APIs. This suggests a different unlearning strategy: instead of updating model parameters, the system should revise recommendation outputs to remove the effect of forgotten interactions. However, executing output-level unlearning is non-trivial and presents two major challenges: (1)Which items to adjust? To revise outputs correctly, the system must first identify which candidate items in the recommendation list were actually influenced by the forgotten interaction. (2)How much to adjust? Once the affected items are identified, the system must carefully penalize their scores to erase the forgotten data’s influence. This adjustment must be highly precise. If the score reduction is too aggressive, it will distort the user’s normal preferences; if it is too weak, the model will fail to truly forget the revoked interaction, leaving unwanted data traces behind. To address these challenges, we propose Causal Explanation-based Unlearning (CEU), a novel framework (illustrated in Fig. 1) for recommendation unlearning through output-level score intervention in MLaaS environments, without modifying internal model parameters. To address the first challenge, our framework employs a Causal Contribution Identifier (CCI). This module identifies the historical interactions that causally support a recommendation and estimates their contribution strengths. Instead of exposing internal model parameters, the MP only needs to provide these attribution scores to the SO through the API interface. This design remains compatible with the MLaaS access setting without exposing model internals. To address the second challenge, we introduce the Unlearning-driven Rank Adjuster (URA). Guided by the causal contributions provided by the CCI, the SO uses this module to adjust the scores of affected items and remove the influence of the forgotten interaction. Because CEU does not modify model parameters, it is naturally suited to continuous unlearning requests and avoids the error accumulation caused by repeated parameter updates. Appendix results under increasing forgetting ratios further support this property. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: We propose CEU, a novel recommendation unlearning framework designed for MLaaS environments. CEU removes the influence of forgotten interactions through output-level score intervention without modifying internal model parameters. We design the Causal Contribution Identifier (CCI) to identify the causal drivers of recommendations, thereby solving the attribution challenge in complex models. We introduce the Unlearning-driven Rank Adjuster (URA), which removes the influence of forgotten interactions by applying localized score adjustments guided by the causal contributions identified by CCI. Extensive experiments on three public datasets show that CEU achieves unlearning effectiveness comparable to full retraining while preserving recommendation utility and significantly reducing computational cost. II Related Work Recommendation unlearning seeks to eliminate the influence of selected interactions from trained recommender models, e.g., removing outdated or noisy behaviors. Existing approaches can be broadly grouped into three categories. First, retraining-based methods (e.g., GraphEraser [5], RecEraser [2]) aim for complete removal by partitioning data and retraining affected sub-models (SISA [1]). While exact, this paradigm severely limits efficiency and scalability. Second, fine-tuning-based methods (e.g., GNNDelete [6], UnlearnRec [3]) avoid full retraining by applying lightweight representation updates to correct the influence of the forgotten data. Third, influence-based methods (e.g., SCIF [12], IFRU [31]) efficiently approximate the gradient or loss impact of deleted data to adjust model weights. Furthermore, prompt-tuning-based recommendation unlearning has also been explored, where lightweight prompts and a teacher–student objective are used to forget target interactions while preserving useful retained knowledge (e.g., Prompt-Tuning for Recommendation Unlearning [30]). Despite their efficiency, both fine-tuning and influence-based approximate methods often suffer from incomplete forgetting, unintended performance drift, and accumulated errors during continuous sequential requests. Crucially, because all three paradigms require accessing model internals to update parameters, they are incompatible with the strict asymmetric access constraints of MLaaS. This motivates our parameter-free framework. Recent studies use causal and counterfactual perspectives to identify what truly drives a recommendation, generally falling into two directions. The first builds causality-aware models incorporating explicit reasoning structures. For example, using reinforcement learning on knowledge graphs [28] or neural symbolic reasoning (CAFE [29]) to trace underlying user intents. The second focuses on post-hoc counterfactual explanations, analyzing trained black-box recommenders by asking “what-if” questions. CountER [26] searches for minimal input changes reversing a decision, while CF2 [25] combines factual and counterfactual reasoning to capture necessity and sufficiency. While these methods quantify causal influence for interpretation and transparency, they do not leverage these attributions to execute recommendation unlearning, especially under the strict constraints of MLaaS architectures. VI Conclusion In this paper, we addressed recommendation unlearning under the strict asymmetric access constraints of MLaaS architectures, where parameter updates are prohibitive. To tackle the lack of interpretability and side-effect propagation in existing methods, we proposed CEU, a novel parameter-free “Explain, then Forget” framework. CEU first identifies minimal causal support sets via CCI and then performs localized score adjustment via URA to remove the influence of forgotten interactions without modifying model parameters. Extensive experiments across three benchmarks verify that CEU preserves recommendation utility close to that of the original model while significantly outperforming existing unlearning baselines in both forgetting quality and efficiency. The ablation study further confirms that causal guidance is essential for avoiding destructive side effects and maintaining model fidelity. Overall, CEU offers a practical solution for efficient and reliable recommendation unlearning in API-only MLaaS environments.
Hardware Architecture (cs.AR): Priority-Aware Deficit Round Robin for AXI4 Bandwidth Fairness in ASAP-7nm Process Modern systems-on-chip place real-time clients, processor cores and bulk data engines on the same AXI4 interconnect, where they contend for shared slaves. AXI4 fixes the ordering rules and carries a 4-bit quality of service (QoS) field, but leaves the service policy to the implementer, and that policy determines how long each master waits and how much bandwidth it receives once a slave saturates. We propose a QoS-aware deficit round robin (DRR) architecture that charges each grant in beats, and benchmark it against two architectures built behind the same port list: round robin, and QoS priority with anti-starvation aging. Charging in beats recovers bandwidth fairness while leaving every burst whole, so the address phase is issued once and locality for memory access is preserved. All three are driven by the same deterministic traffic generator and taken from RTL to GDSII on the ASAP7 7-nm predictive PDK. Under a 1:16 burst-length mismatch, the round robin and QoS architectures both hold the beat ratio between the two competing masters at 1:16, while our design brings it to 1:1 at full load. Mean read latency for the priority master falls from 95 cycles under round robin to 67 with QoS and 37 with QoS-aware DRR. At 500 MHz this serves the priority master in 74 ns against 190 ns. The measurements give a per-policy price and a traffic-based guide for choosing among the three. I Introduction Heterogeneous systems-on-chip (SoCs) connect processor cores, direct-memory-access (DMA) engines, and domain-specific accelerators to shared memories and peripherals through burst-based on-chip interconnects, and AMBA AXI4 is the prevailing protocol for these fabrics [1, 2]. The AXI4 specification defines the channels, handshakes, and ordering rules of a transaction. However, it leaves the arbitration among contending masters to the implementer [3]. Once a shared slave saturates, that arbitration policy decides how long each master waits and how much bandwidth each master receives. Two traffic situations make this choice consequential. In the first, a latency-critical master [4, 5] with little data shares a slave with masters that move bulk data. A processor stalled on a cache miss depends directly on transaction latency, while DMA controllers and graphics processors issue traffic to the same memory controller [4]. Mixed-criticality automotive SoCs show the same pattern, with short cache-line-sized transactions from cores competing against long bursts from accelerators [5]. AXI4 attaches a 4-bit QoS identifier to each address request for use as a priority indicator [1], and this can be used as an arbitration priority [4]. A priority arbiter admits the critical request first. It cannot interrupt a long burst already in service, and it needs an aging mechanism to keep low-priority masters from starving [6]. In the second situation, masters of equal priority issue bursts of very different lengths. Round-robin arbitration, the common default in AXI interconnects, is fair in the number of grants, so a master receives bandwidth in proportion to its burst length. On FPGA SoCs, seven interferers issuing 256-beat bursts reduce a victim accelerator to under 1% of the bus bandwidth [3], and the same effect appears in bus arbitration for real-time multicore processors [7]. A router in a packet-switched network faces the same contention where multiplexing variable-length packets from many flows onto one shared link. Fair queueing solved it by serving each flow in proportion to its data rather than its packet count [8], and deficit round-robin (DRR) is the low-cost approximation where each flow holds a per-round quantum and a running deficit [9]. An AXI4 burst is the on-chip counterpart of a packet, holding the slave for as many beats as its length. DRR alone meters bandwidth but carries no notion of urgency. So we combine this with QoS, so that priority and bandwidth share are set by separate controls. In our interconnect design, a per-transaction QoS value orders who is served first, and a per-master weight sets each master’s beat quantum. Existing AXI4 work attacks these problems in multiple ways. Some reshape the traffic before it reaches the arbiter such as the burst equalizer splits long bursts so a grant-counting arbiter divides bandwidth evenly [3]. AXI-REALM fragments bursts at the ingress under a per-manager budget [10, 5]. Some throttle the source using credit and reservation schemes to cap each master’s share over a time window [7, 11]. Some leave transaction admission untouched and reorder them once buffered [12]. Splitting a burst into [FORMULA] sub-requests multiplies address-channel occupancy by [FORMULA] and requires the returning read data to be reassembled [3]. Addtionally it presents the downstream memory controller with [FORMULA] short accesses in place of one, where row-buffer locality sets the achievable efficiency. So, we design the arbiter to meter bandwidth by beats while still granting by priority, without reshaping any transaction or an extra regulator upstream. The read queue then serves buffered bursts by that same priority. We build three service scheduling architectures for a [FORMULA] AXI4 crossbar and take each through RTL-to-GDSII on ASAP7 7-nm predictive PDK [13]. Our contributions are: A QoS-aware DRR arbiter for AXI4 that keeps priority and bandwidth share as separate controls. Priority travels per transaction in AxQOS, and share is a per-master weight held in configuration. A master can therefore be high-priority and low-bandwidth, and equal-priority masters can receive weighted shares. The arbiter charges each grant in beats and needs no aging counters. A head-to-head physical implementation of RR, QoS with aging, and QoS+DRR from one RTL base under identical constraints, reporting cell area, power, critical-path delay, and wire length for each policy at an advanced nod. A traffic-based decision guideline, backed by RTL simulation under identical stimulus, that assigns each policy to the traffic class it serves best. II Crossbar Architecture AXI4 splits a transaction across five channels; addresses (AW, AR), write data (W), and responses (B, R). Address and response channels carry an ID; W does not, so write data is bound to its address only by order [1]. Fig. 1 shows the interconnect architecture as designed. It has a per-master interface, a common fabric for shared bookkeeping, and a per-slave interface, with the three policies of Section III differing inside the arbiters and the AR queue. Each of the five channels is buffered by a skid buffer. The address decoder uses buffered AW/AR address to issue a target-slave select, or an error code when the address is unmapped or the burst would cross a slave boundary. The fabric widens every ID with a tag identifying the originating master. This tag is later used for the return path. The B and R arbiters allow the beats to be claimed by the master whose index matches its tag. So, different masters may accept responses from different slaves in the same cycle. AXI4 requires a master to issue W data in AW order, so a W-destination FIFO is filled in AW-grant order and drained per W burst. When a master’s AW is granted to a slave, that slave’s index is pushed; the head names where this master’s next W burst is steered. The ID extension block extends the ID with a tag and drives a scoreboard that permits one outstanding transaction per ID. AXI4 allows responses out of order across different IDs but requires same-ID ordering. One transaction per ID guarantees no two in-flight requests share an ID, so any reordering the fabric performs is protocol-legal. The valid-transaction request array is the masters [FORMULA] slaves eligibility grid presented to the arbiters. A master is a candidate at a slave when its decoded target matches, its tagged ID is free, and, for writes, its W-destination FIFO has room. Requests blocked upstream are withheld from arbitration, so the anti-starvation guard of Section III do not mistake a scoreboard stall for starvation. Two things fix the W routing: the master’s W-destination FIFO says which slave its data goes to, and the slave’s AW queue head says which master that slave is currently accepting. The W interlock matches these to forward one master’s W beats at a time, till the end of the burst. Each address channel has a per-slave arbiter that selects one master from the request array and drives the slave port. Accepted addresses wait in a queue until the corresponding engine can service them. The read and write channels are independent, so a master reading back a value it just wrote must wait for the B response before issuing the read. The AW queue is a strict FIFO in all three. Reordering it would make the interlock’s source tag name a different burst than the one whose data is arriving, and since W beats carry no ID the mismatch would commit the wrong master’s data with nothing to catch it. The AR queue is a FIFO in the round-robin architecture and reorderable in the other two, where an entry is selected by policy rather than by arrival order. The write engine consumes W beats from the interlock, commits them to the register array, and emits one B response at the end of the burst. The read engine services one AR entry at a time, streaming its beats to the R channel until the final beat staying locked to a burst. Service scheduling policies therefore act at burst boundaries, choosing which transaction is served next, and never preempts one in flight. Each slave backs a [FORMULA] -bit register array, kept small to focus on measuring interconnect fabric cost rather than memory-macro area. An address that the decoder marks as unmapped or boundary-crossing is routed to an error slave, which drains the burst inputs and returns a DECERR response. III Traffic Service Policy In the fabric of Section II, several masters can address the same slave and one master can receive responses from multiple slaves at the same time. A policy therefore acts at two points. At admission, the per-slave arbiter chooses which contending master enters the slave’s queue. At service, the read engine chooses which queued request to run next. That choice sets the latency each master observes and how the interconnect’s bandwidth is divided. It takes effect only under contention: below saturation knee requests rarely queue and every policy behaves alike. A latency-sensitive master must be served promptly but consumes little bandwidth, while a bandwidth-heavy master issues long bursts and tolerates delay. We implement three scheduling architectures and compare them under identical traffic. Each makes the admission and read-reorder decisions differently in three hooks: Eligible, which decides who may compete; Pick, which chooses the winner among them; and OnGrant, the state update after a grant is accepted (Algorithm 2). On the read path the slave’s reorder pool applies the same Pick rule to choose the next queued burst, while the write path stays strictly in address issue order in all three. Round-Robin (RR): Every requester is eligible, and Pick takes the first requester encountered scanning from the round-robin pointer, which advances past the winner on each accepted grant. OnGrant keeps no state, and the read queue is served in arrival order. Grants are fair per request count, so a master issuing longer bursts receives more beats. Quality of Service (QoS) Priority: Every requester is eligible. Pick takes the highest priority, which equals a request’s arqos/awqos value unless the master has waited starve_limit rounds, then starved master’s priority is raised to the maximum. OnGrant clears the winner’s age and increments the age of every master still waiting. The read pool selects the next burst by the same effective-priority rule. The aging term bounds a low-priority master’s wait, which higher-priority requests would otherwise extend indefinitely [6]. Deficit Round-Robin with QoS (QoS+DRR). Under RR a master issuing long bursts wins the same number of grants as one issuing single-beat requests, so the former takes a larger share of bandwidth. To make it fair per beat, each master holds a deficit counter and a per-round credit as its quantum [FORMULA] , where [FORMULA] is a per-master constant that sets its share of bandwidth. A grant costs [FORMULA] beats, and a master is eligible only while its deficit covers that cost. Among eligible masters Pick takes the highest priority, a round-robin pointer breaks ties, and OnGrant subtracts the granted cost from the winner’s deficit. When masters are requesting but none is eligible, the round ends and every requester is credited its quantum. Charging in beats ties each master’s bandwidth share to its quantum, and so to its predefined weight. The quantum floor is a correctness condition. Every master’s quantum must cover its largest possible burst, otherwise a master whose burst exceeds its quantum can never accumulate enough deficit to become eligible because the deficit is not carried beyond the round in which credit is granted. Each requester is credited its full quantum at every round end, which bounds the worst-case wait to one round. The QoS+DRR architecture therefore carries no age counters. IV Methodology The three architectures are separate RTL trees with identical top-level ports. Every functional and physical run uses the same stimulus, constraints, and technology. Performance is measured on the read path under sustained contention. All three masters read from Slave 0 so they compete at a single arbiter, which is where the scheduling policy acts. Master m0 is the latency-sensitive client: short bursts (arlen=3), high priority (arqos=15), and low bandwidth. Masters m1 and m2 are the bulk pair, with equal weight and no priority (arqos=0). They differ only in burst length: m1 issues single-beat reads (arlen=0) and m2 issues 16-beat reads (arlen=15). At equal weight this [FORMULA] burst disparity is the condition that separates per-request from per-beat fairness. The QoS+DRR architecture uses weights [FORMULA] in both profiles, which gives m1 and m2 equal quanta. Two profiles are swept. In the latency profile, m0 is held at a fixed low offer rate while the bulk pair sweeps, and the reported quantity is each master’s average total latency versus offered load. In the fairness profile, m0 is silent and only m1 and m2 compete, giving the m1:m2 beat ratio on its own. Offered load is swept from 1% to 100% per cycle per master. Offered load is generated by a per-master Bresenham credit accumulator [14]. Each master accrues credit proportional to its load setting every cycle and issues a read once its credit reaches one transaction and a free ID is available; the credit is clamped to bound backpressure banking. Because injection is deterministic, the offered load is bit-identical across the three architectures whatever the fabric does downstream. Each RTL tree is taken through an RTL-to-GDSII flow on the ASAP7 7-nm predictive PDK. The behavioral RTL is synthesized against the technology .lib with a 2 ns clock period. This target period was chosen since 500 MHz clock is within the range of high-end microcontroller core [15]. The netlist is floorplanned to 60% core utilization with master ports on the left side and slave ports on the right, and a power mesh is defined. Timing, Connectivity and DRC are rechecked after each stage. The implementation setup and constraints are listed in Table I and are held identical across all three physical runs, so any difference in area, power, timing, or wire length in section V reflects the scheduling logic. The bulk masters m1 and m2 issue reads at equal weight, and their load is swept from 1% to 100%. m0 models a latency-critical client such as a sensor interface: it issues rarely but needs each request served quickly. Below this knee, latency just follows burst length and the three architectures stay within a few cycles of each other. Above it, the read path is full and the policy decides only how the beats and the waiting are shared. QoS lowers the latency of all three masters above the knee. m0, the only master carrying a priority value, falls from 95 cycles under RR to 67. However, m1 and m2 also fall from 105 to 79 and from 110 to 87. This gain comes from faster admission rather than at service. QoS+DRR charges each grant in beats, so a single 16-beat burst empties m2’s deficit and locks m2 out until the round ends. For the rest of that round, m0 faces no long-burst rival.
