Whether that cost is worth paying depends on the traffic. It is returned only above the saturation knee and when a latency-critical master shares the slave with bulk bursts. Below the knee and without that mix, the three behave alike and the cheaper one is the right choice. VI Conclusion We implemented three service architectures for a 3×3 AXI4 crossbar in ASAP7 and measured both their transaction behavior under contention and their physical cost. Round-robin arbitrates per request, so a burst-heavy master takes bandwidth in proportion to its burst length and a latency-critical master waits its turn regardless of priority. QoS with aging serves the priority master first but cannot stop a long burst already in service, and leaves bandwidth share untouched. QoS-aware DRR charges each grant in beats, so a latency-critical master meets no long-burst rival, and it brings two equal-weight bulk masters to beat parity at full contention. It reaches that parity without modifying the transactions so each burst is admitted or held as a whole and reaches the slave as issued. Priority and bandwidth share stay separate, one carried per transaction on the bus and one held per master in configuration, so a master can be given low latency without a large share, or a large share without priority. QoS-aware DRR has the longest critical path and the most wire length of the three, yet it delivers the lowest service latency to the latency-critical master at the same clock, because the reduction in cycles a request waits outweighs the added delay per cycle. The added area and power buy a scheduling behavior that the faster, smaller architectures cannot reach at any clock. RR is the cheapest and suffices when contention is light or masters are symmetric and QoS with aging buys latency ordering at moderate cost. In an interconnect where a real-time client shares a slave with DMA or accelerator traffic, whose contention peaks above the saturation knee, QoS-aware DRR is the one of the three that serves both classes of traffic in that regime, and the measured cost figures give the price of choosing it.

An Open Implementation Flow for the Xilinx Spartan-3E and Spartan-6 that Runs in the Browser, Checked Byte for Byte Against ISE The author describes an open implementation flow, from HDL to a programmable bitstream, for the Xilinx Spartan-3E (XC3S100E to XC3S1200E) and Spartan-6 (XC6SLX16, XC6SLX45), devices that only the discontinued ISE 14.7 supports. The flow runs unchanged in a web browser or in Node.js: Yosys and nextpnr compiled to WebAssembly, with nextpnr’s Himbaechel framework given Spartan-3E and Spartan-6 architectures generated from Silinx’s own device descriptions, bit database and timing model, and Silinx’s own bitstream writer. The bit database was built by black-box observation of ISE’s documented XDL and bitgen tools, using codeword-batched experiments; the router is given only switches whose bits were measured, and the writer refuses a feature it has not measured. ISE is the oracle: for the same placed and routed design, the bitstream is byte-identical to the one bitgen writes and ISE’s DRC is clean. Placement and routing were first done by an in-house annealer and PathFinder router, which nextpnr replaced once it matched them. On 67 open-source designs for the XC3S1200E, compared with ISE at the same optimisation goal (45 designs built by both), the flow uses 15% fewer slices and has 14% shorter critical paths at goal Area, 21% fewer slices and 8% shorter paths at Speed, and 20% fewer slices but 12% longer paths at Fast (geometric means). XST cannot read 15 of the designs. The flow is published as the npm package silinx-fpga (Apache-2.0). I Introduction Open FPGA flows exist for the Lattice iCE40 (IceStorm) [1], the ECP5 (Trellis) [2] and the Xilinx 7-series (X-Ray) [3], among others, built on Yosys [4] and nextpnr [5] or VPR [7]. Older Xilinx families have been left out, although many of their boards are still in use. The Spartan-3E is a case in point: it is the device of the Digilent Basys2 and Nexys2 teaching boards, it is supported only by ISE 14.7, unchanged since 2013, and Vivado does not support it; the same holds for the Spartan-6 of the Nexys3 and Atlys. This paper describes the implementation flow of Silinx, an open (AGPL-3.0) design environment for teaching digital systems that runs in the browser. Its contributions are: a bit database for four Spartan-3E and two Spartan-6 devices, obtained by black-box observation of ISE’s documented tools with codeword-batched experiments, and a writer that refuses any feature it has not measured (Section II); compact device descriptions, small enough to ship to a browser (Section III); nextpnr Himbaechel architectures for the Spartan-3E and Spartan-6, generated from that data and run in WebAssembly (Section V), after an in-house placer and router that they replaced (Section VI); a validation method with ISE as an oracle (Section VII); and a comparison with ISE at three optimisation goals on 67 open-source designs (Section VIII). II Bitstream and Bit Database The Spartan-3E packet structure follows Xilinx’s UG332: a sync word, register writes (frame length, options, IDCODE), one Type 2 FDRI write of all frames, and a CRC. A frame holds [FORMULA] bits for [FORMULA] CLB rows (frame counts in Table I). The CRC is a CRC-16 (polynomial 0x8005, bit-reversed) over the 32 data bits followed by the 5 register-address bits of every register write, reset by RCRC and by each check word; with the CRC disabled both check words are the constant DEFC. As in the projects above, the database records which bits each feature sets: a LUT memory bit, a slice setting (e.g. CYSELF:F), a pad’s direction and standard, a routing switch (PIP). Test designs are written in XDL, ISE’s documented text format, converted by xdl -xdl2ncd, written by bitgen, and compared. No ISE executable or internal data file is examined; the legal basis (Art. 5(3) of Directive 2009/24/EC) is documented in the repository. Features combine by bitwise OR, with a few documented exceptions that clear bits; this makes batching possible. Each PIP of a routed design is assigned a binary codeword of length [FORMULA] and weight [FORMULA] ; variant [FORMULA] of the design keeps the PIPs whose codeword has bit [FORMULA] set. Each bit of the bitstream then follows the OR of the codewords of the PIPs that set it, and a PIP’s bits are those whose pattern across the [FORMULA] variants matches its codeword. Twenty variants measured all 4 072 PIPs of a course design. The Spartan-3E database was built in stages, each validated before the next: one design that numbers all 2 448 slices of the XC3S250E in their LUTs; slice settings on a harness routed once by ISE; routing switches and pads (about 185 ISE runs); block RAM contents, multipliers, distributed RAM, DCMs and the clock tree (about 1 780 runs); the XC3S100E, XC3S500E and XC3S1200E, whose tiles share the XC3S250E’s tile-type bits (about 2 250 runs); and the remaining DCM settings, side global buffers and IOB registers (about 2 000 runs; 112 held-out designs byte-identical). Under x86 emulation on an Apple Silicon machine an ISE run takes about one minute. After the routing stage, 59 177 of the 64 329 PIPs of one tile of each of the XC3S250E’s 85 tile types had measured bits (92%). Unmeasured PIPs are left out of the routing graph given to the router, and the writer returns the list of unmeasured features it would need instead of a bitstream. Settings first measured as unreliable were refused until measured properly: random IOB input delays were identical in only about 60% of held-out designs until each pad’s delay was measured on its own (970 designs). III Device Descriptions Placement and routing need the tiles, sites, wires and PIPs. They are computed from ISE’s documented xdl -report -pips -all_conns output (204 MB of text for the XC3S250E, 595 MB for the XC3S1200E). Most tiles of a type are identical, so each distinct tile content is stored once as a template (wires, PIPs and site pins by local index), each tile names its template, and wires joined across tiles are stored as varint-coded nodes. For the XC3S250E, 576 CLB tiles share one template, and the file loads in about 90 ms. Descriptions are shipped only for the devices of the supported boards (Table I, and the XC6SLX16 and XC6SLX45). The four Spartan-3E dies have also been described purely by observation, using ISE as an oracle of existence and its DRC to decide whether wires join; the examples routed on each measured description pass ISE’s DRC with byte-identical bitstreams. The shipped files are still the computed ones. IV Synthesis and Optimisation Goals Silinx’s own VHDL/Verilog front end writes the elaborated design as one flat Verilog module for Yosys (synth_xilinx -family xc3se). The stock mapping gave 886 LUTs and 522 slices on a course design, against XST’s 309 and 180. Mapping with ABC [8] onto LUT4s at their cost, narrow arithmetic as tables, SRL16 inference and a second, depth-oriented mapping (SOP balancing) brought it to 278 LUTs and 165 slices. Further candidates were added later: ABC9 onto LUT4s, adder chains written as gates rewritten onto MUXCY/XORCY, trees of 2:1 multiplexers mapped onto MUXF5–F7, state machines tried one-hot, and wide decodes on the critical path collapsed to BDDs and mapped again. Optimisation is chosen, as in ISE, by a goal: Fast: the usual mapping alone and one placement. Since release 15.23.0 a design deeper than 16 levels of logic (at most 1 500 LUTs) also gets Speed’s synthesis, kept when it is 10% faster by the estimate. Area (the default of a new project): the smaller (by slices, then LUTs) of the usual mapping’s netlist and Speed’s, and one placement. Speed: every mapping for speed, and several placements, each routed, the fastest kept by Silinx’s timing analysis (32 for designs of up to 100 slices, 8 above; since 15.23.0, 4 above 500 slices). V Placement and Routing with nextpnr nextpnr’s Himbaechel framework takes an architecture as a generated chip database plus a C++ micro-architecture for packing and placement rules. Silinx’s architectures for the Spartan-3E and Spartan-6 live in a fork of nextpnr [6]; each is compiled to WebAssembly and published as an npm package (at versions 1.4.1 and 0.1.3). A generator reads Silinx’s device description: one tile type per template, the wires, PIPs and nodes, and the BELs inside the sites, written by hand because the description has no site internals. PIPs whose bits the database does not know are left out (28 030 of 2 108 744 on the XC3S250E in the first build), so that nextpnr cannot route on them. nextpnr counts a PIP’s delay rather than a wire’s, so each PIP carries Silinx’s delay for the class of the node it drives (double, hex, long, OMUX, IMUX, global clock, and so on). A LUT’s inputs are wires of their own, each reached from every site pin by a PIP carrying that pin’s delay, so the router puts critical signals on fast pins; the conversion back rewrites each LUT’s equation for the pins chosen. The Spartan-3E micro-architecture takes every cell Silinx’s own packer took: LUT–flip-flop pairs sharing a slice’s control set, carry chains, wide multiplexers in the CLB’s fixed F5–F8 pattern, SLICEM memories and shift registers, multiplier cascades, DCMs, IOB registers and DDR, latches, falling-edge flip-flops, clock switches, and the global clock lines (a clock pad’s buffer placed where its dedicated path reaches). Constants that need no LUT are routed after placement from ISE-style dummy sources or a VCC site, and inverters on a flip-flop’s enable or set/reset become the slice’s CEINV/SRINV. On the Spartan-6, Silinx’s own packer forms the slices first, and its rules place the pads, global buffers, block RAMs and DSPs, which nextpnr is given as fixed. Two changes to nextpnr’s placer mattered for speed: the refinement after HeAP [9] runs as an anneal from a warm temperature (it had been a greedy pass), and the placer’s delay prediction follows the driver (a LUT, through an OMUX from a flip-flop) and the net’s fanout, through a new architecture hook. Router 1’s effort is bounded, after which router 2 continues with alternative weights. nextpnr’s routed design is converted to XDL: one instance per used site with its settings, each net’s pins and PIPs. Silinx’s static timing and bitstream writer read that XDL, so the oracle of Section VII is unchanged. A research check simulates the converted XDL against nextpnr’s netlist cycle by cycle, comparing every flip-flop, because ISE’s DRC cannot detect a wrong LUT equation. Wire delays were fitted by non-negative least squares to 10 486 connections timed by trce (rms 0.099 ns); cell arcs come from trce reports, including block RAMs and multipliers. Over 21 clocks the estimate was within 1.4% of trce on average (worst 4.0%). The report also gives pad-to-setup, clock-to-pad and pad-to-pad times, checks OFFSET constraints and derives DCM output periods. The chip databases are not shipped with the release: the first Place and Route of a device fetches them (about 5 MB for a Spartan-6 device) and the browser keeps them in its cache. The same back-end interface also carries a third family without new reverse engineering: Lattice iCE40 designs build with the existing tools, YoWASP’s nextpnr-ice40 and icepack, downloaded on first use. VI Build, then Replace From 10 October 2026 the flow used its own placer and router. Placement was simulated annealing over slices and rigid groups (carry chains, F6–F8 patterns) with VPR’s schedule and a cost mixing half-perimeter wirelength and criticality-weighted connection delays; routing was PathFinder [10], with A* from the whole net tree, two passes of critical rerouting and register replication. It placed a course design of 777 LUTs in about 1.5 s and routed it in under a second. Table II gives its comparisons with ISE (ISE at XST’s default; Silinx at two synthesis efforts, Normal and High). On 29 October a first Spartan-3E architecture for nextpnr placed and routed a counter (37 LUTs, 24 flip-flops) with a clean DRC and a byte-identical bitstream; its period was 8.43 ns by trce, 7.15 ns once LUT pins could be permuted, against 6.72 ns with Silinx’s engine on the same netlist. The changes of Section V closed most of the gap: with the new placer refinement the best of four placements was 5.4% slower than Silinx’s engine on the examples (7.4% before), and a later version shortened periods by a further 1.4% on average; the remaining gap was accepted. Routing constants and folding inverters as Silinx’s packer did brought the slice counts to Silinx’s (traffic 66 against 66, vga 143 against 144). nextpnr became the default with the old engine as a fallback in release 15.21.0, and the only engine in 15.22.0, on both families; register replication was removed with the old engine. On the Spartan-6, nextpnr’s speed gap to the old router was also accepted. The quality measured with nextpnr is reported next. VII Validation check-open-flow writes the placed and routed design as XDL and has ISE convert it, run its DRC (drc -z) and write a bitstream. Silinx’s bitstream must be byte-identical to ISE’s, with the CRC on and off, and the DRC must report 0 errors and 0 warnings. This holds for the course examples on all six devices, for feature fixtures (block RAM, multipliers, SRL16, DCMs, IOB registers, wide multiplexers, constants, start-up options) and for the corpus designs checked; it runs in the nightly ISE tests. The oracle proves the bitstream and the legality of the routing; it says nothing about the quality of the placement, which Section VIII measures. A design with all PIPs removed gives 372 DRC errors; a single dangling PIP gives an “antenna” error and no bitstream; without the per-tile PIP exceptions, ISE refuses 51 PIPs in 11 of 12 designs. Bitstreams synthesised, placed, routed and written with no Xilinx tool run on a Basys2 (XC3S250E), among them a nextpnr-routed counter whose blink rate matches the one built by Silinx’s earlier engine. VIII Quality of Results The corpus holds 67 open-source designs: CPUs (T80, light8080, PicoRV32, NEORV32, SERV, FemtoRV32), peripherals (UART, SPI, I2C, FIFOs, IWLS’05 cores), cryptographic cores (AES, SHA-1, SHA-256, SipHash), floating-point units and benchmarks (EPFL [11], ITC’99, VTR [7]). Each is built by both flows for the XC3S1200E-FG320 with the same top; a design with more ports than pins goes through the same I/O wrapper in both. Silinx 15.22.1 (nextpnr architecture 1.4.0) builds each design at each goal; ISE 14.7 at the matching XST setting: Area against -opt_mode Area -opt_level 2, Speed against Speed, level 2, and Fast against Speed, level 1, XST’s default. ISE’s map and par get their best chance at every goal: map -c 1 (the tightest packing) and a 5 ns clock constraint, so that par works for speed. Both critical paths are measured by trce on the routed designs (8 November 2026). Run times are each flow’s whole build, the Silinx flow in WebAssembly, and are only indicative. Of the 67 designs, 45 are built by both flows at every goal. XST cannot read 15 of them ($clog2, VHDL-2008 constructs such as reading an output port, libraries other than work, port type mismatches, some loop and sensitivity-list forms), among them PicoRV32, NEORV32, SERV and the AES and SHA cores; 7 more fail in ISE’s constraint step on the I/O wrapper’s pins. Silinx reads and implements all of them, except epfl-multiplier at Area and Fast, where nextpnr 1.4.0 stopped on an error; version 1.4.1, released the same day, builds it (3 418 slices, 141.8 ns), after the measurement. Designs without a clocked path are not timed, which leaves 39 or 40 timed by both. At every goal Silinx uses 15–21% fewer slices than ISE (Table III), with as few LUTs or fewer on 26 to 33 of the 45 designs. The advantage comes largely from ABC’s mapping, SRL16 inference and the inverters folded into the slices. vtr-mkPktMerge is extreme (0.12 of ISE’s slices) because ISE implements its FIFOs as 153 SRL16s plus logic where Yosys infers far less. The opposite extreme is itc99-b05, a small control circuit, at twice ISE’s slices at every goal. At Area, Silinx’s critical paths are 14% shorter than ISE’s at its Area setting, and as short or shorter on 29 of 39 designs. This is partly because XST’s area mode leaves deep logic deep: the EPFL adder (a 128-bit adder written as gates) takes 113.3 ns with ISE, whose critical path crosses 127 LUTs, and 15.0 ns with Silinx, which maps it onto the carry chain. Silinx’s Area keeps the smaller netlist even when it is slower: epfl-priority is 1.82 times ISE’s path at Area and 0.41 at Speed. At Speed, against ISE’s Timing Performance setting, the paths are 8% shorter (28 of 40 as short or shorter). At Fast, Silinx’s critical paths are 12% longer than ISE’s, and only 10 of 39 designs are as fast or faster. Fast maps with the usual area-oriented mapping and makes one placement, and deep logic stays deep: epfl-max takes 68.2 ns over 57 levels of logic against ISE’s 25.7 ns over 17, epfl-priority 43.1 against 20.8 ns. Fast is not the old engine’s Normal of Table II ( [FORMULA] ): Normal kept a depth-oriented mapping for deep designs, made several placements and replicated registers. Release 15.23.0 gave Fast the depth rule back (Section IV); it is not included in this measurement. The comparison splits each critical path, as trce reports it, into logic (LUTs, carry, clock-to-out and setup) and routing. On the designs slower than ISE, at Area (10 designs) and Fast (29) both parts are longer, logic more than routing; at Speed (12 designs) the logic is as ISE’s ( [FORMULA] ns) and the difference is in the routing ( [FORMULA] ns). At this goal the gap therefore comes from nextpnr’s placement and routing on this architecture. At Area and Fast a whole build takes 80–84% less time than ISE’s, in geometric mean; at Speed, with up to 32 placements, 11% less. The largest designs remain slow in WebAssembly (secworks-aes and itc99-b17, about 9 and 11 minutes at Area). Mapped onto 6-input LUTs, the EPFL combinational benchmarks give 1.82 times the size records and 1.95 times the depth records of the EPFL competition (geometric means over the 17 of 20 the flow maps). Those records came from SAT-based resynthesis and long optimisation runs; the flow synthesises in seconds. IX Spartan-6 The same method covers the XC6SLX16 and XC6SLX45 of the Nexys3 and Atlys boards. The bitstream reader and writer follow UG380 and bitgen’s packet sequence (16-bit configuration words, frames of 65 words, a 22-bit CRC). The LUT, slice (SLICEX, SLICEL, SLICEM), routing, clock management (DCM, PLL), block RAM, DSP48A1 and pad bits were measured with ISE, and the static timing model is fitted to trce, each constraint within 5% of its slack or 2.5% of its period. Silinx packs the slices and nextpnr’s Spartan-6 architecture places and routes them, in the local server and in the browser. The examples on both boards, including a small processor running from block RAM, give byte for byte the bitstream bitgen writes for the same routing, with no DRC error. DCM and PLL configurations beyond those measured are not covered yet, and the quality of the Spartan-6 flow has not been compared with ISE on the corpus. X Discussion The Spartan-3E database took about 7 000 ISE runs, each about a minute under emulation. Codeword batching was decisive: measuring routing switches one per design would have needed hundreds of thousands of runs. Two properties made it tractable: features combine by OR with few exceptions, and tile types repeat, so that bits measured on one tile hold for every tile of the type and, across the family, for the other devices. Because the router sees only measured switches and the writer refuses unmeasured features, a gap in the database shows up as an error before a bitstream of unknown effect can reach a board. Writing a placer and router first gave a reference to measure nextpnr against, and the delay and packing knowledge (pin delays, fanout loads, constants, inverters) that the architecture then needed. Moving to nextpnr cost a few per cent of speed on the examples and register replication, and moved place and route onto a widely used open engine that also supports other families. Keeping the flow in JavaScript and WebAssembly costs speed compared with native code, but removes installation: the same flow runs on locked-down school computers, students’ laptops and tablets. The shipped device descriptions are still derived from ISE’s report. ISE’s oracle checks bitstreams and routing legality, not placement quality. The iCE40 flow has no such oracle yet. The Fast goal is slower than ISE at its matching setting. The quality comparison covers one device (XC3S1200E) and one ISE version. XI Conclusion The flow produces vendor-identical bitstreams for two discontinued FPGA families and runs entirely in a browser; with nextpnr placing and routing on architectures generated from observed data, it builds smaller circuits than ISE at every goal and faster ones at Area and Speed. The database, the experiments that measure it and the flow are open at https://github.com/pmnmalo/Silinx, and the environment runs at https://pmnmalo.github.io/Silinx/. The toolchain is also a package of its own, silinx-fpga 0.3.0 on npm (Apache-2.0, code and data), with a public API for Node.js and the browser, taking a flat Verilog netlist or Yosys JSON as input. Tri-Stack-PIM: A Heterogeneous Multi-Die 3D-Integrated Processing-in-Memory Architecture for Efficient LLM Inference Large language model (LLM) inference during autoregressive decoding is fundamentally memory-bandwidth-bound. Existing three-dimensional (3D) stacked processing-in-memory (PIM) architectures alleviate the off-chip bandwidth wall, yet remain constrained by several limitations: physical layer (PHY), controllers, and direct memory access (DMA) engines compete with arithmetic units for advanced-node base-die area; hybrid-bonding keep-out zones fragment the base-die floorplan and impede physical design; compute tiles built in a dynamic random access memory (DRAM) process are restricted to low logic density, capping achievable throughput; and nonlinear operations offloaded to the host reintroduce a communication bottleneck. 1. Introduction LLMs are now deployed across a wide range of applications, such as conversational assistants, code generation, document summarization, retrieval-augmented question answering, and agentic workflows. During autoregressive decoding, generating each token requires fetching the full set of model weights along with a key-value (KV) cache that grows with sequence length; as a result, model throughput is mainly bound by memory bandwidth. 3D-stacked PIM is one promising solution to this bottleneck, and two complementary hardware trends make it practical. First, near-memory and in-memory computing move bandwidth-sensitive computation adjacent to—or directly inside—the DRAM banks, eliminating off-chip traffic and exploiting the abundant internal bandwidth of the memory array (Kim et al., 2023; Park et al., 2024; Heo et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025; Kwon et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2021; Gómez-Luna et al., 2022). Second, hybrid bonding (HB) provides dense, low-parasitic die-to-die interconnects that deliver far higher inter-die bandwidth and lower transfer energy than conventional microbump-based stacking, allowing logic and memory dies to be integrated at fine pitch (Wuu et al., 2022; Lu, 2024; Wang et al., 2023; Bai et al., 2020). Together, these two advances enable practical 3D-stacked architectures for LLM decoding. Prior LLM-oriented PIM systems have explored this direction along several paradigms. First, DRAM-process PIM (Park et al., 2024; Kwon et al., 2022) places compute logic directly inside the DRAM array. This maximizes proximity to the data, but is fundamentally constrained by the low logic density achievable in a DRAM process, which limits the arithmetic capability that can be integrated. Second, microbump-based 3D-stacked designs (Heo et al., 2024) typically retain operations other than general matrix multiplication (GEMM) on the host processor. This reintroduces host-device data movement, so performance is again bottlenecked by the bandwidth-limited host-device link that PIM is meant to eliminate. Third, HB has recently matured into a practical die-to-die integration technology (He, 2026; Kagawa et al., 2016; Chew et al., 2024), enabling a more flexible partitioning. HB-based 3D-stacked systems (Wuu et al., 2022; Li et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026) stack a dedicated compute die—fabricated in a high-performance logic process—directly beneath the DRAM die, and connect the two through dense HB interconnects that offer high inter-die bandwidth. Decoupling the compute die from the DRAM process removes the logic-density limitation of the first paradigm, while the HB link avoids the host-device bottleneck of the second. This flexibility, however, comes at a cost: the HB bonding pads impose keep-out zones on the base die, fragment the logic die into many small regions, increasing placement and routing complexity for compute logic (Li et al., 2026). As Table 1 shows, no prior design closes all four gaps at once. DRAM-process PIM is capped by the low logic density of the DRAM process; host-side handling of nonlinear (non-GEMM) operations reintroduces the bandwidth-limited host-device bottleneck that PIM should remove; interface logic and control remain interleaved with arithmetic on the same compute-dedicated die; and none supports dynamic, cross-die scheduling at runtime. This last coupling is the most costly. When wide HB interfaces, host-facing PHYs, and control share one logic die with dense compute engines, they compete for the advanced-node silicon and routing meant for arithmetic. The cost is twofold: the consumed silicon, and the keep-out zones that HB bonding pads impose on the base die—fragmenting routable area and tightening place-and-route. This pressure only intensifies as interface width and operator complexity scale. Closing these gaps is not a matter of incremental refinement—a better neural processing unit (NPU) microarchitecture or a faster host link leaves the underlying coupling intact. What the industry needs is a fundamentally new, forward-looking 3D architecture. We present Tri-Stack-PIM, a heterogeneous three-die 3D-stacked PIM architecture that resolves the above bottlenecks by physically disaggregating storage, interfacing, and computation across three specialized dies. A top DRAM die provides high-capacity storage; a middle Buffer Die on a mature node handles interfacing, control, and nonlinear computation; and a bottom Base Die on an advanced node is reserved exclusively for dense matrix computation. The Buffer Die is the key enabler, and it pays off in two distinct ways. First, it restores a clean floorplan for the Base Die. To sustain full bandwidth, HB partitions the DRAM die into hundreds of independently-accessed banks; bonding their input/output (I/O) pads directly to the compute die below would scatter bond points across its entire area, shattering the floorplan into small, disjoint regions and sharply inflating placement-and-routing complexity for the compute logic (Li et al., 2026). Inserted between the two, the Buffer Die aggregates the per-bank I/Os and re-exposes them through a regularized interface, leaving the Base Die a contiguous canvas for arithmetic—at negligible cost to delivered bandwidth. Second, it turns the freed mature-node area into an active execution layer. Aggregation consumes only a fraction of the Buffer Die—so what should fill the rest? We use it to pull every fixed-function block off the critical compute die: the host-facing PHYs, the HB controller, the DMA engines, the softmax and reduction engines (SREs) that execute nonlinear operators, and the channel-local dynamic scheduler. This is a deliberate technology-function match. High-speed I/O, control, and datapath glue scale poorly with process node, so hosting them on a mature die costs almost nothing in performance while reclaiming scarce advanced-node silicon for the one thing that truly rewards a leading-edge process: compute density. Better still, co-locating the nonlinear operators here keeps all non-GEMM work inside the stack, eliminating the host round-trips that throttle prior designs. The main contributions of this work are: We show that coupling interface, control, and compute on a single logic die throttles compute provisioning as HB width scales—both by consuming advanced-node silicon and by fragmenting the base die’s floorplan—and propose a heterogeneous three-die partition that separates DRAM storage, mature-node interface/control, and advanced-node dense compute. We design a UBAR-based scheduler on the Buffer Die that tracks dependency readiness, DRAM timing, and backend occupancy to issue micro-operations out of order, reclaiming cross-die idle cycles that static scheduling cannot. We develop a coupled search over dataflow choices and hardware parameters that finds markedly better-balanced operating points than tuning either in isolation. Across the evaluated workloads, Tri-Stack-PIM achieves geometric-mean speedups of [FORMULA] over GPU-only, [FORMULA] over AttAcc, and [FORMULA] over H2-LLM. 2. Motivation As planar scaling yields diminishing returns (He, 2026), 3D integration has become the primary architectural path for sustaining performance growth. Within this paradigm, HB constitutes the most aggressive realization: by transcending the pitch constraints of conventional microbumps (Zhou et al., 2024; Lu, 2024), HB achieves sub-micron interconnect density that unlocks vertical memory bandwidth at a granularity fundamentally unattainable through prior 3D stacking approaches—transforming the economics of memory-bound computation. However, state-of-the-art hybrid-bonded 3D PIM architectures remain subject to several practical constraints. First, because each DRAM bank bonds vertically to the base die through a dedicated HB interface, the proliferation of banks induces a commensurate proliferation of keep-out zones on the logic tier, progressively fragmenting the floorplan and penalizing placement-and-routing closure. Second, the co-integration of host-facing high-speed I/O, and control infrastructure consumes non-trivial silicon area on the base die, eroding the budget available for compute logic. From an algorithmic standpoint, the arithmetic demand imposed on the logic die during decoding is intensifying. The widespread adoption of GQA/MQA (Ainslie et al., 2023; Shazeer, 2019) means that a single KV-cache fetch is mathematically broadcast across [FORMULA] query heads (e.g., [FORMULA] in LLaMA-2-70B), while batched inference further amplifies effective arithmetic intensity in proportion to [FORMULA] , where [FORMULA] denotes batch size. Exploiting this reuse, however, demands a dedicated on-die buffer to stage KV heads across the broadcast and batching dimensions. Consequently, surrendering an excessive fraction of the already-constrained logic-die silicon to non-compute structures directly strangles the compute-engine budget and forfeits the very arithmetic density that modern attention mechanisms could otherwise sustain. Consequently, existing HB-enabled PIM systems encounter a fundamental tension: the logic die is squeezed simultaneously from both the physical and algorithmic directions—per-bank keep-out zones and host-facing I/O infrastructure fragment and consume its already finite silicon, while GQA/MQA broadcast reuse ( [FORMULA] arithmetic intensity) demands precisely the dense compute fabric that such overheads displace. These limitations motivate our heterogeneous three-die stacking strategy. The maturation of multi-layer hybrid bonding and fine-pitch through-silicon-via (TSV) interconnects in industrial packaging (Li et al., 2026; He, 2026; Wang et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2025) now renders such multi-tier 3D integration manufacturable. We leverage these advances to interpose a mature-node buffer die between the compute and DRAM tiers. The benefits are twofold. First, redistributing all DRAM-facing hybrid-bond I/Os onto the buffer tier—rather than the logic die—eliminates the per-bank keep-out zones that would otherwise fragment the compute floorplan and inflate placement-and-routing complexity. Second, what should occupy the residual buffer-die area? We make the decision to co-locate the high-speed I/O PHYs, the nonlinear-acceleration unit, and controllers on this die. The rationale is economic: analog/mixed-signal circuits gain little from dimensional scaling, and advanced FinFET nodes actively worsen noise, variability, and voltage-headroom margins for PHY designs (Razavi, 2002). A mature planar node (e.g., 40/45 nm) thus provides a superior substrate—lower cost, simpler process, well-characterized models—while liberated advanced-node silicon is reclaimed exclusively for computation-heavy engines. We therefore propose Tri-Stack-PIM (as shown in Figure 1), a heterogeneous three-die stacked architecture: the top DRAM dies furnish storage capacity; the sandwiched mature-node buffer die hosts high-speed I/O PHYs and memory-proximal low-arithmetic operators; and the bottom advanced-node base die dedicates its silicon exclusively to dense arithmetic. However, this architecture introduces a critical scheduling challenge. Because the Base Die embodies the costliest advanced-node silicon in the stack, its utilization is the first-order determinant of attention throughput. Yet strict data dependencies between Base-Die GEMMs and Buffer-Die Softmax inherently expose the pipeline to Base-Die stalls absent effective scheduling (Figure 1). A static software schedule is the first step: a compiler constructs a macro-operation directed acyclic graph (DAG), determines operator placement, and overlaps independent operators across dies (Dennis and Misunas, 1974; Fisher, 1983; Arvind and Nikhil, 1990). This macro-instruction granularity marks the exact boundary of compile-time schedulability. Yet each macro-instruction decodes into numerous micro-operations whose readiness depends on runtime state-DRAM timing, die-to-die link congestion, heterogeneous-unit availability-none statically predictable. A static schedule is therefore brittle, and streaming compiler-generated µop sequences over the host link would trigger a control-traffic explosion. Inspired by the CDC 6600 scoreboard (Thornton, 1964), we adopt a hardware-dynamic out-of-order µop scheduler that resolves these hazards at runtime. Moreover, µops contend simultaneously for heterogeneous resources; mere hazard detection for correctness alone is insufficient without scheduling quality. The scheduler must perform prioritized multi-resource arbitration that maximizes utilization. We therefore introduce UBAR, a micro-scheduler that couples out-of-order issue with quality-driven multi-resource arbitration to dynamically orchestrate µop execution. In summary, we propose Tri-Stack-PIM—a heterogeneous three-die architecture interposing a mature-node buffer die between DRAM and an advanced-node compute die to consolidate I/O and mixed-signal functions off-chip while reclaiming compute silicon exclusively for dense arithmetic—and UBAR, a hardware-dynamic out-of-order micro-scheduler coupling hazard resolution with quality-driven multi-resource arbitration to orchestrate µop execution where static scheduling cannot. 3. Tri-Stack-PIM Architecture Tri-Stack-PIM is a command-driven dataflow near-memory platform. It contains no program counter, no instruction cache, and no branch predictor; execution advances by dependency readiness within an offline-compiled DAG. This maximizes arithmetic silicon on the base die. Three principles underlie the design. (1) Data Proximity. Rather than incrementally optimizing GPU/NPU architecture, Tri-Stack-PIM attacks the memory wall at its root: each DRAM bank connects via hybrid bonding directly to a dedicated compute tile, delivering ultra-high bandwidth at ultra-low latency. (2) Separation of Compute and Control. In 2 die stacked designs, host-facing I/O, controllers, and scheduling logic compete for area and routing resources with the compute fabric. Tri-Stack-PIM resolves this by concentrating all non-compute functions onto the buffer die (Figure 2), leaving the base die’s entire area budget for arithmetic. This yields two advantages. First, the buffer die is fabricated on a mature node well suited to mixed-signal PHYs and control datapaths, while the base die targets an advanced node that maximizes MAC density per unit area. Second, it eliminates routing congestion on base die. (3) Hybrid Static/Dynamic Scheduling. Programming this near-memory platform presents a fundamental tension: a multiple-instruction multiple-data (MIMD) model demands per-tile firmware of prohibitive complexity; a single-instruction multiple-thread (SIMT) model requires a full compiler backend mapping attention kernels onto lockstep lanes. Tri-Stack-PIM sidesteps both extremes with a clear division of scheduling responsibility. The host compiler owns macro-level decisions—emitting a statically scheduled DAG of macro-instructions that encodes operator type, operand placement, and inter-operator dependencies—while UBAR resolves all µop-level ordering at runtime, exploiting dynamic state invisible to any compile-time analysis. Figure 2 illustrates the overall architecture. The top DRAM die provides storage; the bottom base die contains one compute tile per bank—each equipped with SIMD lanes—mapped one-to-one to the DRAM banks above via hybrid bonds. The middle buffer die integrates the host-facing PHY, UBAR scheduler, DMA engine, and SRE units for near-memory softmax and reduction. The host compiler emits macro-instructions, each encoding a coarse-grained operation together with its data-dependency constraints. Four macro types suffice to express the complete attention dataflow: (1) LAUNCH_GEMM—a tiled matrix–vector multiply distributed across DRAM banks and base-die compute tiles, carrying a repeat_count field that encodes the GQA query-head fan-out over the fetched KV tile; (2) SRE_SOFTMAX—softmax accumulation and partial-sum reduction executed in the buffer-die SRE; (3) DMA_H2D—host-to-device tile transfer; (4) MODE_SWITCH—a global barrier that serializes execution phases. Every macro carries a compiler-assigned tag together with a predecessor list (pre_tag), collectively forming a static inter-macro dependency DAG; a successor may issue only after all of its predecessors have retired. Because macros belonging to independent GQA groups carry no cross-group dependencies, they may be dispatched concurrently across channels. Upon arrival at the per-channel controller, each macro-instruction is decoded into micro-operations (µops) and posted to a hardware scoreboard. The controller maintains no program counter: issue eligibility is purely predicate-driven—a µop becomes ready when its outstanding dependency count reaches zero and the requisite execution resources are available. A naïve in-order policy enforces strict head-of-line ordering: whenever the oldest ready µop is denied issue due to a timing or resource constraint, all younger µops stall irrespective of their individual eligibility, squandering a substantial fraction of available issue slots under high concurrency. Exploiting What NVIDIA Profilers Hide: Fast and Accurate Analytical GPU Performance Modeling GPUs have become essential to many fields, including AI and scientific computing. As GPUs grow more complex, the design space of their hardware configurations becomes increasingly large, yet cycle-level simulators remain too slow to explore it. Analytical models make this exploration much faster. However, existing GPU analytical models fall short of accurately predicting performance across hardware configurations, because they re-estimate or scale every stall of a warp on the target configuration. We observe that fixed-latency stalls stay the same across configurations, whereas queueing stalls vary with the pressure on each hardware unit. Based on this observation, we propose ForeSight, a queueing analytical model that reuses the fixed-latency stalls measured on GPU hardware and recomputes the queueing stalls of each hardware unit from its pressure. To provide ForeSight with the counter values of each hardware unit, we build UnitSight, a profiler that recovers these values, which NVIDIA’s official profilers hide by aggregating across units. Our evaluation on hardware configurations of nine NVIDIA GPUs shows that ForeSight predicts kernel execution time with a mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 8.3%, compared with 14.1% for the best baseline. ForeSight also predicts the end-to-end execution time of LLM inference on vLLM with a MAPE of 2.0%. It runs 49 [FORMULA] faster than the cycle-level simulator Accel-Sim and faster than interval-based models such as GCoM. With the aid of ForeSight, we explore configurations derived from the H20 GPU for LLM inference and find one with 1.78 [FORMULA] its performance/cost. 1. Introduction GPUs have become the workhorse of AI and scientific computing, powering tasks from training large models to serving inference for massive user bases. These workloads place different demands on hardware resources. For example, training and prefill are compute-bound, whereas decode is memory-bandwidth-bound. To meet these diverse demands, vendors derive several GPUs from the same microarchitecture. These GPUs share the same streaming multiprocessor (SM) design but differ in their hardware configurations: the number of SMs, the capacity and bandwidth of the L2 cache and DRAM, and the clock frequency. Architects must therefore predict the performance of workloads across many candidate hardware configurations to select the configuration of each GPU, a process known as design space exploration (DSE). Cycle-level simulators (Khairy et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2023) are the most widely used prediction tools in DSE. They model each hardware unit of a GPU in microarchitectural detail and simulate the behavior and interactions of these units cycle by cycle. Simulators can evaluate arbitrary hardware configurations, but they are extremely slow. For faster prediction, researchers have proposed performance models, including data-driven methods (Lee et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026) and analytical models (Huang et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2022; Cao et al., 2025; Wang and Chu, 2018). Rather than simulating hardware behavior cycle by cycle, they directly estimate workload execution time. Data-driven methods train machine learning models on execution times measured across multiple GPUs to learn how workload features and hardware configurations relate to execution time, but these models generalize poorly to workloads and GPUs outside their training distribution. Analytical models capture the first-order factors of GPU execution in mathematical equations. Among them, interval-based analytical models (Huang et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2022; Cao et al., 2025; Cha et al., 2025) compute the execution time of a representative warp as the sum of its issue and stall cycles on the target configuration, and then estimate how concurrent warps hide stalls and contend for hardware units. Scaling-based analytical models (Yu et al., 2021; Nath and Tullsen, 2015) first measure workload execution time on GPU hardware and then scale it to the target hardware configuration by the ratios of parameters such as bandwidth and frequency. However, we observe that not all stalls of a warp change when the hardware configuration changes. Fixed-latency stalls, in which an instruction waits a fixed number of cycles for a pipeline result, stay the same. Queueing stalls, in which warps or memory requests wait at a busy hardware unit, vary because the configuration changes the pressure on that unit. Interval-based analytical models re-estimate all stalls on the target configuration from formulas, and derive memory queueing stalls from the bandwidth of the whole GPU rather than from the pressure on each unit. Scaling-based analytical models instead scale both types of stalls by the same parameter ratios, so they change fixed-latency stalls and derive queueing stalls from these ratios rather than from pressure. Based on this observation, we propose ForeSight, a queueing analytical model. To predict the execution time of a workload on a target configuration, ForeSight reuses the fixed-latency stalls measured on GPU hardware and recomputes the queueing stalls. Because the pressure can differ across hardware units, ForeSight computes queueing stalls for each unit individually. However, existing profilers (NCU (NVIDIA Corporation, 2026c) and CUPTI (NVIDIA Corporation, 2026b)) cannot provide the pressure on each unit because they report only aggregated values across units. We find that these profilers actually collect the counter values of every hardware unit but aggregate these values before reporting them, which hides this pressure. Based on this finding, we build UnitSight, which recovers these values before the profilers aggregate them and provides them to ForeSight. With these per-unit values, ForeSight replays the dispatch of CTAs to the SMs of the target configuration and, at each moment of the replay, solves the queueing at the pipelines of each SM and at each L2 slice and DRAM channel. Beyond providing per-unit values to ForeSight, UnitSight, as a profiler, can also help developers analyze the performance bottlenecks of their kernels. Its per-unit values reveal what aggregated metrics hide, such as load imbalance across SMs. It also allows a kernel to read performance counters with PTX or SASS instructions, so developers can profile any code region of the kernel rather than only the whole kernel. To evaluate the accuracy of ForeSight in DSE, we construct diverse hardware configurations across nine NVIDIA GPUs by varying the SM count, the SM frequency, and memory resources, and compare its predictions with the real execution times on these GPUs. ForeSight predicts execution time with a mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 8.3%, compared with 14.1% for the best baseline. Background and Motivation GPU compute resources are organized hierarchically into Graphics Processing Clusters (GPCs), Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs), and SM sub-partitions (SMSPs). A kernel is divided into cooperative thread arrays (CTAs) dispatched to SMs, while warps serve as the basic scheduling units within each SMSP. Each SMSP contains a warp scheduler and multiple execution pipelines, such as the ALU, FMA, and tensor pipelines. Every cycle, the warp scheduler selects a ready warp and issues an instruction to a pipeline. When the warp scheduler cannot issue an instruction from a warp, the warp stalls, for instance when waiting for an operand from a prior instruction or for data from memory. A memory request first accesses the per-SM L1 cache, which serves as both data cache and shared memory. Requests missing in the L1 cache traverse an on-chip crossbar to reach the L2 cache, which consists of multiple L2 slices. Requests missing in the L2 cache proceed to off-chip DRAM, which consists of multiple DRAM channels. Each request goes to the L2 slice and DRAM channel that its address maps to. We refer to warp schedulers, pipelines, L1 caches, L2 slices, and DRAM channels as hardware units. Each hardware unit has performance monitoring (PM) counters, which record events such as instruction counts, request counts, and stall cycles. NVIDIA’s profilers, Nsight Compute (NCU) (NVIDIA Corporation, 2026c) and CUPTI (NVIDIA Corporation, 2026b), configure these counters and compute the metrics that the user specifies. Each metric aggregates the counts of all units of the same type, such as their sum or average. Existing analytical models lose accuracy when the hardware configuration changes. We restrict 50 kernels from LLM inference and microbenchmarks to fewer SMs of an H100 PCIe GPU with green contexts (NVIDIA Corporation, 2026a). With all 114 SMs, Habitat (Yu et al., 2021), a scaling-based model, predicts their execution times with a MAPE of 1.1%, but with 16 SMs its MAPE reaches 42%. The MAPE of GCoM (Lee et al., 2022), an interval-based model, grows from 43% to 82%. To understand why, we examine how the stalls of these kernels change with the configuration. These stalls arise from two sources: pipeline fixed latencies and queueing at hardware units. A fixed-latency stall occurs when a dependent instruction waits a fixed number of cycles for an earlier instruction to finish in a pipeline, so it does not change with the configuration. A queueing stall occurs when more warps or memory requests reach a hardware unit than it can serve at once: warps queue at the pipelines inside an SM, and memory requests queue at L2 slices and DRAM channels. When the configuration changes, the number of warps and requests using each hardware unit changes, so queueing stalls change as well. We verify this distinction on the SiLU kernel by measuring its stall cycles per instruction with 114 and 16 SMs. Fixed-latency stalls remain nearly unchanged (3.5 to 3.7 cycles per instruction), whereas memory queueing stalls drop from 11.8 to 3.8 cycles per instruction (Figure 1a). Interval-based models derive both types of stalls on the target configuration from formulas and latency tables, so the errors of these estimates enter the prediction. For example, in the experiment above, GCoM predicts 0.89 ms for the SiLU kernel with 16 SMs, whereas the kernel actually takes 0.41 ms. Scaling-based models multiply the measured time by a single factor built from hardware ratios, so the fixed-latency stalls are scaled together with the queueing stalls instead of staying constant, and the queueing stalls are not recomputed from the new pressure. In the same experiment, Habitat predicts 0.27 ms for the SiLU kernel with 16 SMs, 34% below the measured 0.41 ms. Moreover, the queueing at each hardware unit grows with the pressure on that unit, and this pressure can differ across units and change with the configuration. Across SMs, the pressure differs when the CTAs of a kernel cannot be dispatched evenly to the SMs, and some SMs then receive more CTAs and more work than others. This load imbalance across SMs changes with the number of SMs. Across L2 slices and DRAM channels, the pressure differs when the address hash maps the requests of a workload unevenly to these units. This happens when the requests fall in a small address range. In addition, on some GPUs, the L2 slices and DRAM channels are divided into two partitions, and each SM sends its requests only to the slices of its own partition (Liu et al., 2026). When the two partitions hold different numbers of active SMs, their slices receive different pressure, and so can their DRAM channels. We verify this by varying the SMs assigned to two kernels with green contexts on the H100 PCIe GPU. The FP8 GEMM kernel of the QKV projection in Llama-3.1-8B always launches 114 CTAs. With 64 SMs, these CTAs cannot be dispatched evenly, and 50 SMs stay busy 1.8 [FORMULA] as long as the other 14 (Figure 1b). Similarly, for the SiLU kernel with 40 SMs, 8 in one partition and 32 in the other, 40 L2 slices receive 3.98 [FORMULA] as many requests as the other 40 (Figure 1c). Therefore, the same workload can put very different pressure on individual hardware units under different configurations, and queueing stalls must be recomputed for each unit rather than from GPU-wide totals. Observation: When the hardware configuration changes, fixed-latency stalls remain unchanged and can be reused, whereas queueing stalls change and must be recomputed from the pressure on each hardware unit. ForeSight (Section 4) builds on this observation and recomputes the queueing stalls of each hardware unit from its pressure. However, NVIDIA’s profilers, NCU and CUPTI, report only metrics aggregated across units, which hide this pressure. We therefore build UnitSight (Section 3), which profiles each hardware unit individually and thus reveals this pressure. 3. UnitSight This section presents UnitSight. Section 3.1 analyzes CUPTI’s profiling flow and the layout of CounterData, Section 3.2 presents the design of UnitSight and its in-kernel PM reading mode, Section 3.3 validates its per-unit values, and Section 3.4 uses a case study to show how it diagnoses a real LLM kernel. At the hardware level, an NVIDIA GPU tracks performance per unit: each SM, each L2 slice, and each DRAM channel has its own PM counters connected to the GPU’s PM system (Figure 2, middle). At the profiler level, on Volta and earlier GPUs, NVIDIA’s previous profiler nvprof and CUPTI’s previous Event API reported the values of each unit’s PM counters (NVIDIA Corporation, 2026e; NVIDIA Corporation, 2026b). Starting with Turing, however, they no longer support counter collection and are replaced by the new profiler NCU and CUPTI’s new Profiling API. NCU and the Profiling API report only aggregates of these per-unit values: the sum, average, maximum, or minimum across all SMs, all L2 slices, or all DRAM channels. To understand this gap, we study CUPTI’s profiling flow (Figure 2, left). First, the user specifies the metrics to profile, and NVPerf, a closed-source library, resolves them into raw counters, the hardware events counted by the PM counters (Resolve). From these raw counters, NVPerf builds the config image (Config), a configuration assigning each PM counter a raw counter, and passes it to CUPTI (1). CUPTI then writes this config image through the CUDA driver into the GPU’s PM system (2), and the PM system sets each PM counter of every unit to its assigned raw counter. With the counters configured, the application launches the kernel through the CUDA driver onto the SMs (3), and every unit’s PM counters record events during execution. After the kernel finishes, the PM system reads the resulting counter values back into CounterData, a buffer in CPU memory (4). Finally, NVPerf’s Evaluator computes the requested metrics from CounterData and returns them to the user (5). We find that after the read-back, CounterData does contain the counter value of every unit, but NVPerf’s Evaluator aggregates these values into the metrics it returns, which hides the value of each unit. NCU uses the same NVPerf library to compute metrics, and therefore also reports only aggregates. We analyze the layout of CounterData (Figure 2, right): it consists of a header followed by one segment per profiled kernel, each containing one block per raw counter. The header holds the format version of CounterData (version), the number of raw counters resolved by NVPerf (#raw counters), the counter table, and the offset of each segment (segment offsets). Each row of the counter table describes a raw counter by the 64-bit hash NVPerf computes to identify it (counter hash), the offset of its block within a segment (offset), and the number of per-unit records reserved in the block (max records). A block starts with a block header holding the number of records with data (count) and the sum of their values (sum), followed by the reserved records. Each record has a flag telling whether it holds data (valid) and the counter value of one unit (value). The value field, however, does not store the counter value directly. We find that the counter value of a unit is the XOR of the content of its value field after CUPTI initializes CounterData before profiling and after the read-back, and the count, sum, and valid fields are also computed by XOR. With this layout, we can read the counter value of every unit for each raw counter in each kernel. To read raw counter B on unit [FORMULA] in kernel [FORMULA] , we locate the segment of kernel [FORMULA] from the segment offsets in the header, find B’s row in the counter table by its counter hash, follow its offset (577) to B’s block in that segment, and XOR the value field of unit [FORMULA] ’s record after initialization and after the read-back. Based on these findings, we build UnitSight, the first hardware-counter-based profiler for NVIDIA GPUs since Turing that can profile each hardware unit individually. As shown in red in Figure 2, UnitSight keeps CUPTI’s counter collection (2–4), but replaces NVPerf’s Resolve with a catalog that maps metrics to raw counters (Catalog, 1) and NVPerf’s Evaluator with a decoder reading the per-unit values directly from CounterData (Decoder, 5). Beyond the flow in Figure 2, UnitSight can also read an SM’s PM counters inside the kernel to obtain the counter values of a code region, a capability that CUPTI and NCU do not support. In CUPTI, the user can only specify metrics, and NVPerf’s Resolve decides which raw counters to configure. To allow the user to configure raw counters directly, UnitSight builds the Catalog. The Catalog is a table listing all raw counters of a GPU chip and the raw counters used by each metric, and we build one for every chip UnitSight supports. For example, the Catalog for the H100 GPU covers 2,785 raw counters and about 236,000 metrics. The user selects raw counters from the Catalog, and the Catalog passes them to NVPerf’s Config to build the config image. The user can also specify metrics as in CUPTI, and the Catalog converts each metric into its raw counters before passing them to Config. UnitSight then profiles the kernel with CUPTI as usual: CUPTI writes this config image into the GPU’s PM system, the application launches the kernel, and the PM system reads the counter values back into CounterData. Instead of NVPerf’s Evaluator, UnitSight passes CounterData to the Decoder, which extracts the value of each raw counter on each unit in each kernel, using the method described in Section 3.1. To turn these values into the metrics the user specifies, the Decoder needs the expression computing each metric from its raw counters, which we call the metric’s formula. Like CUPTI and NCU, UnitSight provides two profiling modes: range profiling and PM sampling. Range profiling accumulates the counter values over a range and gives one value per range. By default, each kernel is a range, and the user can also mark an interval containing several kernels as one range. PM sampling reads the PM counters at a fixed time interval during execution, giving a time series of values, so changes within a kernel become visible. With the Catalog and the Decoder, UnitSight gives one value per unit for each range and one value per unit for each sample. Beyond these two modes, UnitSight also allows a kernel to read the PM counters of its own SM during execution, which we call in-kernel PM reading. It is a combination of instrumentation-based and hardware-counter-based profiling. We find that PTX and SASS, the virtual and native assembly languages of NVIDIA GPUs, both provide special registers for PM counters (%pm0–%pm7 in PTX, SR_PM0–SR_PM7 in SASS), and that these registers count the raw counters configured through Config. Because UnitSight allows the user to configure raw counters directly, the user can decide which raw counter each register counts. We further observe that PM0–PM3 accept only SMSP-level raw counters, and a warp reading PM0–PM3 gets the counter value of its own SMSP. PM4–PM7 accept only SM-level raw counters, and a warp reading PM4–PM7 gets the counter value of the whole SM. Figure 3 shows an example of profiling a code region of a kernel by reading a PM register in SASS: the kernel reads SR_PM4 with the instruction CS2R before and after the code region, and the difference is the value of PM4’s raw counter on the SM during the code region. With in-kernel PM reading, UnitSight can locate a kernel’s bottleneck to a specific code region and explain it with the hardware counters of that region, which neither the other profiling modes nor instrumentation can do. For example, Section 3.4 locates the bottleneck of FlashAttention-3 decode using this mode. To validate the correctness of UnitSight’s per-unit values, we compute their sum, average, maximum, and minimum and compare them with CUPTI’s results on the same CounterData. On H20, we check about 44,000 SM and SMSP metrics, about 29,000 L1 cache metrics, and the metrics of L2 slices, DRAM channels, and other units. All are exactly equal. Next, we check whether each value belongs to the right unit. We construct test kernels to set the activity of each unit, and compare UnitSight’s per-unit values with this activity. For SMs, a test kernel gives different SMs different numbers of active cycles. Each CTA records its SM with %smid and its cycles with clock64. Compared with these records, UnitSight’s per-SM active cycles have a median error of 0.0% and a maximum error of 0.2%. The small deviation is expected because the in-kernel clock reads and the PM counter cover slightly different cycles. For L2 slices, a test kernel uses the L2 address hash of H20 to read only the cache lines of one slice, and we repeat it for every slice. In every run, UnitSight counts at least 99.99% of the L2 sectors on the targeted slice and nearly none on the other slices. To show how UnitSight diagnoses a real LLM kernel, we profile vLLM’s FlashAttention-3 (FA3) decode kernel. FA3 is a persistent kernel: each SM runs one CTA, with a producer warpgroup loading K and V and a consumer warpgroup running the MMAs. For a Llama-3.1-8B shape with batch size 16 and context length 8,192, the kernel takes 359 [FORMULA] s on H20. First, the per-SM values from range profiling show that 50 SMs execute about twice as many instructions as the other 28 SMs. This is because the kernel has 128 tiles for 78 SMs, so 50 SMs process two tiles and the other 28 SMs process only one. Therefore, we split each sequence’s KV into three parts to balance the tiles across the SMs. This makes the kernel 11% faster, reducing runtime from 359 [FORMULA] s to 319 [FORMULA] s. Second, we apply in-kernel PM reading. For each KV block, the producer and the consumer read the PM registers and the clock at the start and end of each of their steps. The consumer waits for data only 6% of its time, whereas the producer spends more than half its time waiting for the consumer to free buffer slots. The bottleneck is therefore the consumer’s computation. The PM registers further show that the tensor cores reach about 88% of H20’s BF16 peak during the consumer’s compute steps, so they limit the consumer. Since the tensor cores limit the kernel, we run the attention in FP8 instead of BF16, which the tensor cores compute twice as fast. This reduces the runtime from 359 [FORMULA] s to 223 [FORMULA] s, by 38%. For comparison, we also profile the kernel with NCU. NCU averages the stalls of all warps on all SMs, mixing the producer and the consumer. Its performance diagnosis ranks memory latency and occupancy as the top optimization opportunities, while the actual bottleneck is the tensor cores. Following this diagnosis, we optimize the memory side by enlarging the KV page size, but the runtime does not improve (362–364 [FORMULA] s). UnitSight finds the actual bottleneck because in-kernel PM reading measures each step of the producer and the consumer separately. 4. Warp-specialized kernels. Recent GPUs such as Hopper provide a TMA engine and asynchronous MMA instructions on the Tensor Core, which allow a kernel to use warp specialization: the warps of a CTA execute different instructions and synchronize through barriers in shared memory (Figure 5). To support such kernels, ForeSight uses NVBit on [FORMULA] to record the instructions each warp executes and the synchronization relations between warps, neither of which changes with the configuration (Section 4.1). ForeSight then simulates the warps within a CTA on [FORMULA] in time order, computing the execution time of each warp between two synchronizations and the time of each synchronization. Warp-specialized kernels use two classes of instructions, which differ in how their dependences are enforced. Dependences on ordinary instructions are enforced automatically by stalling the issue of any instruction that uses a pending result. Explicit synchronization enforces dependences on asynchronous instructions (TMA copy instructions on the TMA engine and asynchronous MMA instructions on the Tensor Core), so a warp stalls for an asynchronous instruction only at a synchronization. The execution time of a warp between two synchronizations therefore depends only on its ordinary instructions. For those instructions, ForeSight keeps their execution time measured on [FORMULA] and recomputes only their memory queueing stall with the memory latency [FORMULA] on [FORMULA] . We find that ordinary instructions in warp-specialized kernels barely queue inside the SM (0.9% of warp execution time on the H20), so ForeSight does not recompute their SM queueing stall with MVA. The time of a synchronization is the moment when all participating warps have reached their synchronization instructions and all asynchronous instructions it depends on have completed. ForeSight obtains when the warps reach their synchronization instructions from the execution times of their ordinary instructions. It obtains when the asynchronous instructions complete from their execution times, computed as the number of operations divided by the Tensor Core throughput for an MMA instruction and as the size divided by the TMA engine bandwidth plus the memory latency [FORMULA] for a TMA copy instruction. From these two times, ForeSight computes the time of each synchronization in time order until all warps of the CTA finish. The completion time of the last warp gives the CTA execution time, by which the CTA progresses in the replay (Figure 4, 2) instead of the IPC from the SM model. Figure 5 shows this simulation on an example CTA: a producer warp loads data into shared memory with TMA copy instructions, consumer warps compute on these data on the Tensor Core, and the producer loads the next data into the same location only after they are consumed. In time order, ForeSight first computes the time of the producer’s ordinary instructions (yellow). The producer issues copy 0 (orange) during them. Copy 0 completes after the memory latency [FORMULA] (hatched) and triggers the consumers’ first synchronization (data 0 ready), which ends the consumer stall (pink). Next, ForeSight computes the time of the consumers’ ordinary instructions, during which they issue MMA 0 (green). The second synchronization depends on both these ordinary instructions and MMA 0. The ordinary instructions finish later, so the synchronization happens when they finish (data 0 consumed). The producer then resumes and issues copy 1. In the second round, MMA 1 finishes after the ordinary instructions and triggers the synchronization (MMA 1 done). Evaluation This section evaluates how accurately and how fast ForeSight predicts the performance of kernels and of end-to-end LLM inference on target configurations. To check these predictions, we construct the target configurations on real GPUs and measure the execution time of each kernel (Section 5.1). We compare the accuracy of ForeSight and existing methods by the mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of their predictions against the measured times (Section 5.2). Finally, we compare their prediction speed (Section 5.3). Platforms and workloads. We evaluate ForeSight on nine GPUs of four architectures (Table 1). On these GPUs, ForeSight predicts the execution time of 50 workloads on each target configuration. Forty-seven of these workloads are operators executed by vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023) during LLM inference, including GEMM, attention, MoE, normalization, activation, rotary embedding, and quantization. Their input shapes follow the Llama-3.1 (8B, 70B) (Llama Team, AI @ Meta, 2024) and Qwen3 (8B, 32B, 30B-A3B) (Qwen Team, 2025) models. On Hopper and Blackwell, vLLM selects warp-specialized kernels (Section 4.3) for part of the attention and GEMM operators. On Hopper, for example, 24 of the vLLM kernels are warp-specialized. The other three workloads are microbenchmarks testing whether ForeSight accurately predicts kernels dominated by DRAM reads and writes or by FP32 FMA computation. Target configurations. To evaluate ForeSight when the number of SMs and their distribution across GPCs change, we construct target configurations with green contexts (NVIDIA Corporation, 2026a), which restrict the SMs available to a kernel. For clock changes, the target configurations are the original GPU with a locked SM frequency. For memory-side changes together with the SMs, we use MIG instances (NVIDIA Corporation, 2026d) as target configurations, each with fewer SMs, L2 slices, and DRAM channels and a smaller L2. Finally, to evaluate predictions across GPUs, we collect the profile on one Ada, one Hopper, and one Blackwell GPU and use the other GPUs of the same architecture as target configurations. These GPUs differ from the GPU of [FORMULA] in the number of SMs, the L2 capacity, and the DRAM bandwidth (Table 1). The original GPU without any of these changes is also a target configuration. On some MIG instances and on another GPU, vLLM selects a different kernel or grid for a workload, and we evaluate only the workloads whose kernel and grid stay the same. We run each kernel 30 times on each target configuration and take the median as the measured execution time. Together, these configurations cover SM, clock, and memory-side changes within a GPU and changes across GPUs, all on real GPUs. Prior evaluations on real GPUs typically test one type of change: prediction across GPUs (Yu et al., 2021; Lee et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026), changes of the SM count only (Lin et al., 2026), or changes of the frequency only (Wang and Chu, 2018). Other studies evaluate several types of parameter changes, but take simulator results as the ground truth (Lee et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2020; Cha et al., 2025). Baselines. We select three classes of existing methods as baselines and run each as described in its paper: (i) the simulator Accel-Sim (Khairy et al., 2020), (ii) the analytical models DuetServe (Gao et al., 2025), Bullet (Lin et al., 2026), LLMCompass (Zhang et al., 2024), Habitat (Yu et al., 2021), Wang and Chu (Wang and Chu, 2018), GCoM (Lee et al., 2022), AMALI (Cao et al., 2025), and a roofline model computed from datasheet peaks (Williams et al., 2009), and (iii) the data-driven models NeuSight (Lee et al., 2025) and PipeWeave (Zhang et al., 2026). Because Habitat’s MLPs support only FP32 matrix multiplications and ours are BF16 or FP8, we use only its wave scaling. Some baselines do not support all workloads or target configurations: NeuSight, PipeWeave, and LLMCompass support only a subset of operators, Accel-Sim, GCoM, and AMALI do not support Blackwell GPUs, and Wang and Chu supports only frequency changes. We compare each baseline with ForeSight only on the workloads and target configurations supported by that baseline. Overall accuracy.
