Case Study To show how ForeSight helps architects with DSE, we present a case study: we change the configuration of H20 to find the one with the highest performance/cost for 8B-model inference on a single GPU. H20 has 78 SMs, a 60 MB L2, and 6 HBM stacks, each providing 16 GB of memory and about 0.67 TB/s of bandwidth. Each configuration keeps the SM design and clock frequency of H20 and changes only the number of SMs, the L2 capacity, and the number of HBM stacks. The inference workload is the same as in the end-to-end evaluation of Section 5.2: Llama-3.1-8B (Llama Team, AI @ Meta, 2024) in BF16 serving 64 requests, each with 2048 input tokens and 2048 output tokens, so each configuration needs at least 50 GB of memory for the model weights and the KV cache. From the profile of this workload on H20, ForeSight predicts the throughput of each configuration in output tokens per second, which we take as its performance. We compute the cost of each configuration with the cost model of LLMCompass (Zhang et al., 2024). The cost is the sum of the on-chip die cost, which depends on the total area of the units, and the off-chip HBM cost, which depends on the number of HBM stacks. We search 180 configurations, with 32 to 128 SMs, 10 to 60 MB of L2, and 4 to 6 HBM stacks, to find the configuration with the highest performance/cost. Figure 7 shows the predicted throughput and the cost of the 180 configurations, both normalized to H20. Each gray line connects the configurations with the same number of SMs, and each colored line connects the configurations with the same number of HBM stacks and a 10 MB L2. More SMs give higher throughput, but the gain from added SMs is uneven: going from 64 to 72 SMs or from 86 to 94 SMs raises throughput by only 1% to 2%, going from 102 to 104 SMs raises it by 12%, going further to 126 SMs adds only 5%, and going from 126 to 128 SMs raises it by 20%. L2 capacity barely affects throughput: across all configurations, reducing the L2 from 60 MB to 10 MB changes throughput by at most 0.1% and lowers cost by 8% to 14%. HBM stacks also have little effect on throughput: with at most 102 SMs, reducing the HBM stacks from 6 to 4 lowers throughput by less than 2% and cost by 24% to 31%. With 104 or more SMs, however, the bandwidth of 4 HBM stacks starts to limit throughput, which becomes 2.7% to 14% lower than with 6 HBM stacks. The performance/cost of a configuration equals the slope of the line from the origin to it, and the dashed line in Figure 7 is the steepest of these lines and thus marks the highest performance/cost. Therefore, the configuration we search for has 4 HBM stacks, a 10 MB L2, and 104 SMs, and reaches 1.78 [FORMULA] the performance/cost of H20, with 1.33 [FORMULA] the throughput at 0.747 [FORMULA] the cost. 7. Related Work Simulation. Cycle-level simulators such as Accel-Sim (Khairy et al., 2020) simulate each unit of a GPU cycle by cycle and can predict performance under any configuration. However, they are slow. To speed up simulation, sampling methods simulate only representative kernels (Baddouh et al., 2021; Chung et al., 2025), warps and basic blocks (Liu et al., 2023), or thread block sets (Yang et al., 2024), and scale-model simulation extrapolates from a GPU with fewer SMs (SeyyedAghaei et al., 2024). Unlike these works, ForeSight does not simulate the execution and takes tens of seconds per target configuration. Analytical models. Interval-based models compute the execution time from the issue and stall cycles of a representative warp on the target configuration. GPUMech (Huang et al., 2014) and GCoM (Lee et al., 2022) count the stalls of each type, GCScaler (Cha et al., 2025) scales the stall cycles of a simulated GPU, MDM (Wang et al., 2020) models the NoC and DRAM queueing caused by memory divergence, and AMALI (Cao et al., 2025) adds tensor core and instruction cache models for LLM inference. LLMCompass (Zhang et al., 2024) and TileSight (Mo et al., 2026) estimate the execution time tile by tile. Scaling-based models, closest to ForeSight, start from the execution time on the original GPU and scale it to the target configuration. CRISP (Nath and Tullsen, 2015) scales it to other frequencies, Habitat (Yu et al., 2021) to other GPUs with wave scaling, and Van Lanker et al. (Van Lanker et al., 2024) to a new GPU with a hierarchical roofline model. Unlike them, ForeSight reuses the fixed-latency stalls measured on the original GPU and recomputes the queueing at each hardware unit on the target configuration. Earlier GPU queueing models use a single DRAM queue (Wang and Chu, 2018) or explain latency hiding (Volkov, 2016) and shared-memory atomic bottlenecks (Dong and Pai, 2025). Data-driven models. Wu et al. (Wu et al., 2015) pick a measured scaling curve with a neural network, NeuSight (Lee et al., 2025) predicts each tile with MLPs, and PipeWeave (Zhang et al., 2026) feeds per-pipeline demands from an analytical model to a machine learning model. They describe a GPU only by its specifications, so they cannot capture how a workload loads each hardware unit. Unlike these models, ForeSight needs no training and profiles each kernel on one GPU. GPU profilers. Profilers based on hardware counters, such as NCU (NVIDIA Corporation, 2026c) and CUPTI (NVIDIA Corporation, 2026b), compute metrics from the PM counters but report only values aggregated across units. Instrumentation tools such as Neutrino (Huang and Wu, 2025) and KPerfIR (Guan et al., 2025) record timestamps and program values but do not read the hardware PM counters. Unlike these tools, UnitSight recovers the counter values of each unit and lets a kernel read performance counters during execution. 8. Conclusion This paper presents ForeSight, a queueing analytical model that predicts GPU performance across hardware configurations. It builds on our observation that fixed-latency stalls stay the same across configurations, whereas queueing stalls vary with the pressure on each hardware unit. ForeSight therefore reuses the fixed-latency stalls measured on GPU hardware and recomputes the queueing stalls of each unit from its pressure. UnitSight provides ForeSight with the per-unit counter values that NVIDIA’s profilers hide. On configurations of nine NVIDIA GPUs, ForeSight predicts kernel execution time with a MAPE of 8.3%, compared with 14.1% for the best baseline. It also predicts the end-to-end execution time of LLM inference on vLLM with a MAPE of 2.0%. It runs faster than cycle-level simulators and interval-based models. In a DSE case study, ForeSight finds an H20-derived configuration with 1.78 [FORMULA] its performance/cost.

Uncovering the Memory Hierarchy of Modern NVIDIA GPUs for Accurate Simulation Emerging artificial intelligence workloads, particularly Large Language Models (LLMs), place unprecedented demands on GPU memory systems. Consequently, architectural innovations increasingly target the memory system to alleviate these bottlenecks. However, existing works still rely on outdated memory hierarchy models that fail to capture the complexities of modern hardware. This fidelity gap leads to inaccurate characterization and could misguide optimization strategies. I Introduction In recent years, GPUs have evolved from graphics accelerators into general-purpose computing platforms and are now widely used for throughput-oriented workloads, including bioinformatics [7, 38], molecular dynamics [34, 31], reacting-flow simulation [44], and deep learning [8, 37, 42]. As GPU computing capabilities continue to advance, improvements in the memory system have not kept pace, making memory performance an increasingly important bottleneck[15]. More recently, LLM training and inference have become the primary workloads on modern GPUs. As model sizes and context lengths increase, the memory footprint of model parameters and the KV cache imposes high bandwidth and capacity demands on the memory subsystem [9, 29]. Consequently, overall performance of GPU system has become increasingly sensitive to memory hierarchy behavior and data path efficiency. However, the memory hierarchy of modern commercial GPUs remains largely opaque at the microarchitectural level. Existing reverse-engineering studies on modern GPUs have focused on SM-core internals, providing detailed analyses of scheduling and execution behavior [18]. In contrast, reverse engineering of the memory hierarchy remains fragmented and coarse-grained [1, 35, 54, 28, 24, 51], making it difficult to explain memory-dependent performance behavior on real hardware and perform fine-grained performance optimization. To address this gap, we present GemAtlas, a unified reverse-engineering and modeling framework dedicated to the memory hierarchy of modern GPUs. GemAtlas characterizes key memory-hierarchy behaviors at cache-set granularity across the L1, L2 data cache, and constant-memory hierarchies (L0, L1, and L1.5). Table I summarizes our specific reverse-engineering contributions across these levels, detailing newly exposed set associativity, topologies, mapping policies, and replacement mechanisms. To validate our findings and evaluate their impact, we incorporate them into AccelSim, a widely used GPU simulator [26, 18]. Evaluation on a benchmark suite spanning traditional GPU benchmarks and real-world LLM operators shows substantially improved fidelity, reducing the average MAPE over four GPUs from 31.69% to 22.24%, and from 34.04% to 23.98% for the LLM operators, with particularly large gains for memory-sensitive workloads, whose MAPE decreases from 36.33% to 20.61%. In summary, GemAtlas makes the following contributions: We reverse-engineer the L1 data cache/shared memory microarchitecture on H20, H100, A800, and RTX 4090 and disclose its sliced organization, slice routing and cache set indexing, tag–data asymmetry, and replacement policy. We reconstruct the complete topology of the distributed Hopper L2 cache across partition, Frame Buffer Partitions (FBP) and slice levels; derive the memory-interleave hash; expose coherence/replacement behavior; and introduce an efficient hash-guided eviction-set construction method for modern GPUs. We systematically dissect the constant memory hierarchy across L0, L1, and GPC-level L1.5 cache, recovering hierarchy organization, cache-set hash indexing rules, and replacement policy. We develop a benchmark suite, GemAtlas-Bench, that extends GPU simulation beyond traditional workloads to include real-world LLM operators drawn from vLLM [27] and PyTorch [43]. We integrate the recovered mechanisms into AccelSim [26], a widely used GPU simulator, and validate the model against four GPUs (H20, H100, A800, and RTX 4090) using GemAtlas-Bench, substantially improving accuracy for LLM operators and memory-sensitive workloads. II Background and Motivation GPU Architecture and Memory Hierarchy. Modern NVIDIA GPUs are organized hierarchically into Graphics Processing Clusters (GPCs), Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs), and SM-subpartitions (SMSPs) [32, 40]. In the CUDA programming model, a kernel is decomposed into thread blocks, blocks are scheduled onto SMs, and warps are the basic scheduling unit within an SMSP. The on-chip memory hierarchy consists of three parts. Each SM has a unified L1 cache that integrates data caching, shared memory (SMEM), and texture functionality [40]. A dedicated constant-memory hierarchy provides access paths for read-only data through the Indexed Constant Cache (IDC), Data Constant Cache (DCC), Immediate Constant Cache (IMC), and GPC Constant Cache (GCC) [41]. All SMs access a shared L2 cache through the on-chip network (NoC). This L2 is distributed across partitions, each connected to a subset of GPCs [24, 33]. Each partition contains multiple Frame Buffer Partitions (FBPs) that interface with the memory controllers directly, and each FBP groups multiple independently addressed L2 slices. Undocumented Memory Hierarchy Details. Modern GPU workloads, particularly LLMs, are increasingly bottlenecked by memory hierarchy behavior [15], and architecture-specific optimizations that explicitly exploit it have delivered substantial performance gains [12, 11]. Newer GPU features, such as thread block clusters with multicast, L2 cache residency control, and the Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA), also build on this hierarchy. Understanding the memory hierarchy is therefore a prerequisite both for optimizing these workloads and for studying and modeling these features. Yet the memory hierarchy remains opaque. Official documentation describes only coarse-grained properties, such as cache capacities [40]. Prior reverse-engineering studies go further and measure finer-grained properties, such as line sizes, latencies, and the associativity of some caches [54, 22, 21, 23, 1, 24, 35, 51]. However, for the large, sliced caches of recent GPUs, set-level mechanisms, such as address mapping and replacement policies, remain unknown. As a result, developers cannot reliably predict the performance impact of high-level optimizations, making performance tuning inherently empirical. In addition, the lack of microarchitectural understanding limits architecture research. Existing GPU simulators [5, 26, 18] rely on simplified or outdated memory-hierarchy models and have been evaluated primarily on traditional benchmark suites. Although some evaluations include GEMM kernels, modern LLM workloads comprise a much broader range of operators with diverse memory behavior, leaving their performance simulation unexplored. Our evaluation shows that existing simulators are inaccurate on these operators: Consequently, the fidelity of existing simulators on modern GPU workloads remains uncertain, undermining the reliability of architecture exploration. Together, these limitations motivate systematic reverse engineering of the modern GPU memory hierarchy and its accurate modeling in GPU simulators. By exposing the underlying mechanisms, we aim to bridge this knowledge gap and establish a high-fidelity foundation for systematic performance optimization and architectural analysis. III Reverse Engineering Methodology GemAtlas is a fully automated framework that performs reverse engineering end to end and feeds the recovered parameters directly into simulation. It consists of three components: (1) a SASS microbenchmark suite that implements every probe in Sections IV–VI as a parameterized template and assembles it for the target GPU; (2) an analysis pipeline that runs the suite and applies the inference steps of Sections IV–VI to produce a parameter table for each cache level; and (3) an extended AccelSim whose memory hierarchy is configured directly from this table (Section VII). For a previously unseen GPU, the user only specifies the target architecture, and probing, inference, and simulator configuration then run without manual intervention. Test Platform. We evaluate GemAtlas on NVIDIA H20 and H100 GPUs, both based on the Hopper microarchitecture, as well as A800 (Ampere) and RTX 4090 (Ada), using CUDA 12.8 and cuAssembler [10]. We use H20 as the primary platform for presenting results and report the results on the other GPUs in Section VI-C. GemAtlas is hardware-agnostic and can be readily extended to Blackwell and future architectures with support for their corresponding SASS ISAs. CUDA provides a high-level programming abstraction for NVIDIA GPUs, where applications are written in a C-like language and compiled into PTX, a virtual ISA, before being translated into SASS, the native ISA executed by the hardware [18]. However, neither CUDA nor PTX offers sufficient control for microarchitectural characterization. Compiler optimizations in both the offline backend (ptxas) and the Just-In-Time (JIT) compiler can reorder instructions and alter register allocation, obscuring true latency and invalidating carefully constructed access patterns [16]. As a result, deterministic analysis requires direct manipulation of SASS. Modern NVIDIA GPUs also rely on a compiler-driven scoreboard mechanism rather than dynamic hardware scheduling to manage memory dependencies. SASS instructions carry explicit control codes that manage dependency barriers and dictate when subsequent instructions may issue [18, 10]. Direct SASS programming enables two key capabilities for microarchitectural characterization. First, explicit control of scoreboarding allows us to serialize dependent operations and measure memory latency with cycle-level precision. Second, fixed instruction streams ensure deterministic code footprints, which are critical for isolating cache behaviors. For example, in the GCC study (Section VI-B), we place instruction lines into a chosen GCC set with a chain of branches to induce instruction-driven cache evictions. Because NVIDIA does not provide an official SASS assembler, we build our microbenchmarks upon the open-source cuAssembler [10]. We extend its Ampere (SM86) support to Hopper (SM90) by updating the ELF parser and packer for the newer cubin format [39], thereby enabling direct SASS execution and microbenchmark construction on Hopper GPUs. An eviction set is a group of addresses that map to the same cache set, forming the basis for recovering cache indexing and replacement behavior. As a case study to validate the effectiveness of our SASS-level microbenchmarking framework, we construct L1 eviction sets using the Group Elimination algorithm [53], but implemented entirely at the SASS level. The algorithm iteratively prunes a candidate pool while preserving its ability to evict a target line. Each iteration dynamically generates a SASS sequence that accesses the target address [FORMULA] followed by the candidate pool. Using this workflow, we recover stable L1 eviction sets. For example, the eviction set for target address 0x0 is {0x13880, 0x20d80, 0x33500, 0x4bb00}. Figure 1 shows the latency of re-accessing 0x0 as these lines are accessed one by one: 0x0 remains an L1 hit (31 cycles) after three of them and becomes a miss after the fourth, whereas lines from another set never evict it. The minimal cardinality of four indicates 4-way associativity and provides the basis for the L1 analyses in the next section. IV L1 Data Cache Modern NVIDIA GPUs use a unified memory structure that dynamically partitions capacity among the L1 data cache, shared memory (SMEM), and texture cache. In this section, we use SASS microbenchmarks to recover the organization of the L1 data cache within this structure. We find that the L1 consists of four slices of 128 4-way sets each, indexed by an XOR hash of the virtual address. It keeps a fixed tag array while its data array shrinks with larger SMEM allocations, and it uses a Segmented LRU (SLRU) replacement policy. We begin by characterizing three baseline L1 properties using our SASS-level methodology: line size, associativity, and hit latency. We observe a 128 B cache line grouped into four 32 B sectors, 4-way associativity (confirmed by a minimal eviction-set cardinality of four in Section III-C), and a 31-cycle hit latency measured with the SASS probe in Listing 1. Accurate Capacity Measurement. Prior studies typically estimate L1 capacity using CUDA-level pointer-chasing microbenchmarks [36, 51]. In contrast, we measure L1 capacity at cache-line granularity using the SASS-level eviction sets derived in Section III-C. For each of the nine SMEM configurations, we fill each cache set until the first capacity-driven eviction and determine the data-array capacity from the number of resident lines. As shown in Table II, the combined L1 data cache and SMEM capacity is 249 KiB in every configuration, 7 KiB below the 256 KiB unified capacity reported in official documentation [40]. Notably, under the default configuration, where the kernel requests no SMEM, the effective L1 data cache capacity is only 217 KiB, revealing an implicit 32 KiB reservation for SMEM. We discuss a possible cause of the 7 KiB gap in Section VIII. The 4-Slice Topology. During per-set cache filling, evictions occur before the aggregate L1 capacity is reached. Moreover, the evicted lines always come from the same one-quarter of the filled sets, for example, 108 of 432 under the default configuration. This indicates that the L1 is divided into four slices, each holding one-quarter of the sets with its own tag and data arrays (Fig. 2(a)). Once the data array of one slice is full, a new line in that slice evicts a line from another set of the same slice, while the other slices still have free space. We call this a cross-set eviction and explain it with the tag–data asymmetry (Fig. 2(b)) later in this subsection. Across all SMEM configurations, the four slices have equal capacity, reported in Table II in KiB and as the number of 128 B cache lines per slice. Address Indexing and XOR Hash. We then recover the L1 indexing logic that maps each virtual address to a slice and an in-slice cache set. Using eviction-set probes at a 128 B cache-line stride, we find that the 512 cache lines within a 64 KiB address span map one-to-one onto 512 distinct slice/set pairs, that is, 128 sets in each of the four slices. Each address is therefore mapped by a 9-bit logical index, consisting of a 2-bit slice index and a 7-bit in-slice set index. Using bit-flipping analysis [14], we determine how virtual-address bits generate this 9-bit logical index. Bits [FORMULA] – [FORMULA] do not participate because they encode the 128 B cache-line offset, and we do not consider bits above [FORMULA] , which lie outside the 96 GiB address range of H20. For example, the mapping for cache set index bit [FORMULA] is To validate this mapping, we apply it to the measured eviction sets of all 512 sets (15,873 addresses): every address maps to the slice and set of its target. For example, 0x0 and its eviction set in Figure 1 all map to slice 0 and set 0. Hardware Asymmetry: Tag Array vs. Data Array. The tag array follows this fixed logical index: its 512 4-way sets with 128 B lines cover 256 KiB (Fig. 2(b)). We recover identical XOR mappings under all SMEM configurations, so changing the SMEM allocation does not alter this organization. The data array, however, is smaller. Even in the configuration with the largest L1, each slice holds only 482 lines (60.25 KiB; Table II), fewer than the 512 lines needed to fill its 128 4-way sets, and it shrinks further as more of the unified capacity is allocated to SMEM. We refer to this mismatch between a fixed tag array and a smaller data array as the L1 tag–data asymmetry and discuss it further in Section VIII. This asymmetry leads to three allocation cases. (1) When the target set is full (regardless of whether the data array of the slice is full), the incoming line replaces a line in the same set under the in-set replacement policy (Section IV-B). (2) When the target set has a free tag entry and the slice still has free data capacity, the line is allocated normally. (3) The key case arises when the target set has a free tag entry but the data array of the slice is full, a situation that cannot occur in a conventional cache. In this case, the hardware performs a cross-set eviction within the slice: it first selects a victim set from the sets in the slice, then evicts a line from that set using the local replacement policy, and finally allocates the new line to the target set. To determine how the victim set is selected, we repeat the per-set filling experiment 13,500 times under the default configuration and record the victim sets in each run. The victim set changes from run to run, and its selection probability depends on the fill order: among the 108 sets in the slice, the first 27 filled are selected about 2.5 times as often as the last 27. All nine SMEM configurations show the same trend. We leave the exact selection rule to future work. Our measurements show that the L1 data cache employs a Segmented LRU (SLRU) policy [13] rather than conventional unified LRU. Each set contains Probationary and Protected segments: new lines enter the Probationary Segment, while re-accesses promote them to the Protected Segment. V Distributed L2 Cache Modern NVIDIA GPUs (e.g., A100, H100, and B200) organize the L2 cache into two partitions, each connected to a subset of GPCs through the on-chip interconnect [24, 33]. In this section, we use SASS microbenchmarks to recover this distributed L2 on H20. We find that its 96 slices are grouped into 12 FBPs across the two partitions and are selected by an XOR hash with a 128-to-96 remapping. Using slice-constrained eviction sets built with this hash, we further characterize replacement and set-level cross-partition coherence. Mapping SMs to GPCs and Partitions. We read both mappings directly from special registers with the SASS S2R instruction. For the SM-to-GPC mapping, SR_AFFINITY returns the GPC ID of the executing SM. Alternatively, SMs can be grouped by SR_CLOCK, which, unlike the GPU-wide SR_GLOBALTIMER, is shared only by the SMs of one GPC (e.g., two GPCs differ by 2,315,338 cycles). Both methods yield the same grouping. For the GPC-to-partition mapping, SR_SW_SCRATCH returns the same value for all SMs of a partition: 0xA0000000 for 42 SMs and 0x80000000 for the other 36. The resulting topology is asymmetric: Partition0 connects GPC0, GPC1, GPC2, and GPC4, whereas Partition1 connects GPC3, GPC5, and GPC6 (Figure 5, which also shows the SMs of GPC4). Prior L2 eviction-set (ES) construction techniques [53, 57] fail on modern, distributed L2 architectures such as H20. The large capacity of these caches (e.g., 60 MiB) forces traditional group elimination algorithms to filter very large candidate pools, accumulating noise that discards true ES members. Furthermore, undocumented cross-partition coherence traffic introduces interference into the measurements. To overcome these challenges, we introduce a slice-constrained group-elimination method. Because only addresses mapping to the same set in the same slice contend, we use our recovered slice hash (Section V-C) to restrict the candidate pool to the target slice. We also perform profiling from an SM in the same partition, avoiding cross-partition coherence interference. Within this reduced pool, group elimination iteratively discards candidate groups that are unnecessary to evict the target, leaving an ES for the target set. This slice constraint aggressively prunes the search space by [FORMULA] : in our 120 MiB candidate pool, only 10,542 of 983,040 lines fall in the target slice. Successful construction of ESs also provides validation of the recovered slice hash, since stable ESs require a correct slice mapping. From the resulting ESs, we infer that each H20 L2 cache set is 16-way associative and follows a standard LRU replacement policy. Specifically, exactly 16 conflicting accesses evict a line, even if it was accessed ten times before, ruling out SLRU. Moreover, when the 16 lines of a set are re-accessed in random orders (900 trials), a new line always evicts the least recently used one, ruling out pseudo-LRU. Using the slice-constrained ESs constructed in Section V-D, we first access all lines in an ES from an SM in the home partition, placing them in that partition and verifying that they contend for a single cache set. We then access the same lines from an SM connected to the remote partition to create coherent copies. These copies continue to contend for a single cache set, showing that coherence preserves this cache set indexing rather than distributing the lines across multiple sets. Moreover, all 16 ES lines can be coherently replicated into the remote partition and simultaneously occupy this set. Thus, each cache set can hold any mixture of lines mapped to that partition and coherent copies from the peer partition, with no additional per-set capacity limit beyond the standard 16-way associativity. Our measurements further indicate that corresponding cache sets in the two partitions maintain independent LRU states. Evicting a line from one set does not change the LRU order or trigger an eviction in the corresponding set of the other partition. During a cross-partition coherence event, the event behaves as a normal cache hit in the home partition and promotes the target line to the most recently used (MRU) position. In the remote partition, the same event behaves as the insertion of a new cache line: the coherent copy is inserted at the MRU position, and if the set is full, its current LRU line is evicted. VI Constant Memory Hierarchy In modern GPU workloads, constant memory is widely used to store network weights, scaling factors, and kernel parameters. Official documentation [41] names several constant-cache components (GCC, IDC, DCC, and IMC) but does not describe their organization. In this section, we use SASS microbenchmarks to reconstruct this hierarchy. We find three levels: L0 and L1 constant caches in each SM, both with 2 KiB, 4-way sets and Tree-PLRU replacement, and a 128 KiB GCC that is shared by the SMs of each GPC and also holds instructions. At the SM level, official documentation distinguishes three constant-data access paths, each associated with a different class of SASS instruction [41]. Immediate operands encoded in instructions (e.g., MOV) use the Immediate Constant Cache (IMC) path, ULDC uses the Data Constant Cache (DCC) path, and standard LDC uses the Indexed Constant Cache (IDC) path. We measure their cache hit latencies as 2, 15, and 25 cycles, respectively. DCC and IMC Share a Single Physical Cache. Cross-instruction probing shows that MOV and ULDC share a single cache: warming a constant address with MOV makes a subsequent ULDC access hit, and capacity evictions through MOV also evict data brought in by ULDC, whereas cross-probing between LDC and either MOV or ULDC misses in both directions. Thus, the IMC and DCC are physically unified, while the IDC is separate. We attribute the latency difference between MOV and ULDC to their distinct data paths: ULDC routes data through the uniform-register path, whereas MOV uses direct operand fetch. Cache Placement and Structural Parameters. We identify the physical placement of the IDC through SASS-level cross-warp probing: when one warp warms a cache line using LDC, other warps on different sub-partitions within the same SM still observe a hit, indicating that the IDC is shared at the SM level. We therefore classify it as the L1 Constant Cache. In contrast, the physical placement of the IMC/DCC cache cannot be directly determined due to limitations in the current SASS assembler tool. The documentation is also inconsistent: it places the IMC at the SM-subpartition level and the DCC at the SM level, even though our measurements show that the two are physically unified. Given the 2-cycle hit latency of the IMC, we conjecture that this shared cache resides at the SM-subpartition level and treat it as the L0 Constant Cache. Using SASS-level microbenchmarks, we characterize the structural parameters of the two intra-SM constant caches. The L0 and L1 constant caches exhibit identical structural parameters: each has a 2 KiB capacity, a 64 B line size, 4-way associativity, and 8 sets. In both caches, set indexing follows the same linear function, [FORMULA] . To solve this limitation, we follow prior work [54, 22, 21] and leverage the unified nature of the GCC by using instructions to force data evictions. A timed probe then checks whether each constant line is still in the GCC. With up to eight lines in the set, no constant line is evicted, even when all eight are constant lines. With nine lines, for example eight constant lines and one instruction line, one constant line is evicted in every run. Because this bound does not depend on which line the replacement policy evicts, the GCC is 8-way set-associative, with a capacity of [FORMULA] , much larger than the SM-level constant caches. Non-Standard Replacement Policy. In mixed instruction and data microbenchmarks, the GCC replacement behavior deviates from standard LRU, FIFO, or Tree-PLRU policies: after eight constant lines fill a set, the next insertion does not evict the first filled line, and re-accessing any line other than this victim does not change the victim. We leave a detailed characterization of the GCC replacement policy to future work. Sections IV–VI recover the memory hierarchy of H20. To show that GemAtlas is hardware-agnostic, we apply the same microbenchmarks to H100 (Hopper), A800 (Ampere), and RTX 4090 (Ada). As Table III shows, all four GPUs share the organization we recover on H20 at every cache level and differ only in parameters, such as the L1 associativity and the number of L2 slices. The only structural difference is that RTX 4090 has a single L2 partition. Its hash still folds eight logical FBPs onto six physical FBPs, but the folding target rotates every 32 KiB instead of every 128 KiB. VII Modeling and Evaluation To evaluate the architectural impact of our reverse-engineered memory hierarchy, we integrate the recovered mechanisms into AccelSim and validate the simulation results against real hardware. Specifically, we use AccelSim v1.3.0 [26] as extended by the open-source release of Huerta et al. [18]. Prior cycle-level GPU simulators have been evaluated primarily on traditional benchmark suites and CUTLASS GEMM workloads [5, 26, 18]. However, modern LLM workloads extend far beyond GEMM, and performance simulation of their diverse operators has received little attention. To broaden this coverage, we construct GemAtlas-Bench with 25 traditional GPU workloads widely used in prior work [5, 26, 18] and 28 LLM operators. These operators span attention [52], normalization and activation [4, 55, 17, 49], KV-cache management, token processing, quantization, and MoE. We take their implementations from vLLM [27], PyTorch [43], and FlashAttention-3 [48], with tensor dimensions configured based on the Qwen3-30B-A3B model [46]. The complete benchmark suite is listed in Table VII-C. Hardware measurement. We measure the execution cycles of each workload with Nsight Compute. Nsight Compute locks the GPU clocks and flushes all caches before each kernel, and the simulator likewise starts each kernel with cold caches. We repeat each measurement five times and use the average. Baselines. The simulator released with [18] does not cover the GPUs we evaluate. We therefore define a baseline (BL) with their RTX A6000 model, the closest of these models to our GPUs, and set its SM count, clock frequency, and shared-memory size to those of each target GPU (e.g., 78 SMs for H20). All other parameters keep their RTX A6000 values, such as the 6 MiB L2 cache (Table IV). We then improve it (denoted as BL-Impv) by further aligning its memory parameters with those documented by NVIDIA for each GPU, such as the 60 MiB L2 cache and the 4 TB/s memory bandwidth of H20. BL-Impv includes none of our reverse-engineered mechanisms, so any accuracy gain over BL-Impv comes from our findings. Configurations. To isolate the contribution of each recovered cache level, we incrementally extend BL-Impv with three configurations. The L1D configuration replaces the L1 data cache of BL-Impv with our recovered model, L1D+L2D further replaces the L2, and GemAtlas further adds the recovered constant-cache hierarchy, so it includes all the mechanisms we recover. Table IV lists the parameters of each configuration. We simulate all 53 workloads under BL, BL-Impv, and the three configurations L1D, L1D+L2D, and GemAtlas. Table VII-C reports hardware cycles and per-workload cycle errors. Overall MAPE is 36.83% with BL. Applying the documented memory parameters reduces it to 27.58% with BL-Impv, and our recovered models further reduce it to 27.36% with L1D, 20.62% with L1D+L2D, and 20.04% with GemAtlas. Each incremental model improves aggregate accuracy, with distributed L2 modeling providing the largest reduction. Compared with BL-Impv, GemAtlas reduces MAPE for both traditional benchmarks, from 28.69% to 19.31%, and LLM operators, from 26.59% to 20.69% (Figure 7). This contrast indicates that the simplified memory hierarchy in BL-Impv is a major source of error for sensitive workloads, while the recovered model corrects much of this error. Beyond improving simulation accuracy, the mechanisms we recover provide architectural insights for both software optimization and hardware design. L2-aware data placement. Eq. (1) gives the partition of every address, so software can place the data that each SM reads in the SM’s local partition. This avoids both the extra latency of cross-partition accesses (Section V-A) and the L2 capacity taken by their coherent copies (Section V-E). We apply this placement to the vLLM paged-attention decode kernel on H20. It removes 99% of the cross-partition requests, lets more KV data fit in the L2, and speeds up the kernel by 1.10–1.12 [FORMULA] over the same kernel without this placement. The hash also suggests placement at the FBP level: because of the rotating remap in Eq. (2), the FBP load is balanced only over three consecutive 128 KiB ranges, so a hot region of about 128 KiB could be spread over 384 KiB to use all FBPs evenly. Decoupled L1 tags and data. The recovered L1 decouples its tag and data arrays, which appears to let it switch capacity between the L1 and SMEM. The tag array is fixed, so the L1 keeps the same XOR index under every SMEM configuration, while the data array shrinks as the SMEM allocation grows (Section IV-A). The data array can therefore fill up before the tags do, and the L1 needs cross-set eviction to make room, similar to the global data replacement of the V-Way cache [45]. Cross-set eviction starts when the L1 data and SMEM together hold 249 KiB, 7 KiB below the 256 KiB unified capacity (Table II). We conjecture that this 7 KiB is a buffer that holds incoming lines when cross-set eviction cannot keep up with heavy fill traffic. Because data entries are allocated independently of the tags, we suggest a possible design that may improve performance: one tag owns several 128 B data entries as a larger line, and all of these entries are released when the tag is evicted. Data with spatial locality could then use larger lines while other data keeps 128 B lines, without adding tags. We leave the evaluation of this design to future work. Prior work has studied GPU caches and TLBs from GT200 to A100 [54, 36, 30, 25, 22, 21, 23, 56] and GPU NoCs [2, 24], and, more recently, Hopper-era features, automated topology discovery, and the L2/DRAM NUMA topology [35, 51, 33]. These studies provide component-level visibility but do not reconstruct a unified, cache-set-level hierarchy. We next compare our methods and architectural findings with these studies. Our probes build on group elimination [53], bit-flip analysis [14], and GCC eviction with instruction fetches [54, 22, 21]. Our SASS probes measure latency more accurately than the CUDA/PTX benchmarks of prior work [35, 24, 51, 33]: our probes time only the load, whereas these benchmarks also time cold misses or dependent instructions. We also introduce five new methods: (1) SASS-level eviction sets for the L1 and constant caches, (2) L1 capacity measurement at cache-line granularity instead of CUDA pointer chasing [36, 51], (3) reading the SM-to-GPC and GPC-to-partition mappings from special registers instead of inferring them from latencies and thread-block clusters [23, 24, 33], (4) grouping L2 slices into FBPs by latency correlation, and (5) slice-constrained group elimination, to our knowledge the first method to reliably and efficiently construct eviction sets on partitioned GPU L2 caches, where prior techniques fail [53, 57]. Several of our architectural findings refine or extend prior measurements, and Table I marks them as improved (I). For the L1, we improve three prior results. First, Jia et al. find the L1 capacity of Volta and Turing 7 KiB below the nominal size and conjecture that a new replacement policy causes this gap [22, 21], whereas our line-by-line probe finds the same gap on H20 before any set holds more than four lines, which rules out replacement within a set (Section VIII). Second, prior work reports the L1 associativity only for Fermi [36], and to our knowledge we are the first to measure it on a modern GPU (4-way on H20). Third, the benchmarks of Luo et al. and MT4G yield L1 hit latencies of 41 and 38 cycles on H20 [35, 51], whereas our SASS probe measures a more accurate 31 cycles. For the L2, we improve two prior results. First, Jia et al. report a 16-way L2 on Volta and Turing [22, 21], and to our knowledge we are the first to measure the associativity of a partitioned L2 (16-way on H20). Second, Mei and Chu conclude from aperiodic miss patterns that the Fermi L2 does not use LRU, and note that its address mapping is irregular [36]. Our eviction sets access a single set, which separates the replacement policy from the address mapping, and show that H20 uses LRU. For the constant caches, we improve three prior results. First, prior work reports a 2 KiB, 4-way L1 constant cache with 64 B lines and 8 sets on GT200, Volta, and Turing [54, 22, 21], but only its capacity and line size on H100 [51], whereas we find the same geometry on H20 together with its linear set index. Second, prior work measures a single hit latency per constant-cache level [54, 22, 21, 23, 51], whereas we find that the latency also depends on the instruction: MOV and ULDC both hit in the L0 but take 2 and 15 cycles. Third, Jia et al. measure the GCC capacity on Volta, Turing, and A100 [22, 21, 23], and MT4G cannot measure it beyond 64 KiB on H100 because CUDA limits constant memory to 64 KiB [51]. Evicting GCC lines with instruction fetches [54, 22, 21], we fill a single set with both constant and instruction lines and find 64 sets of 8 ways (128 KiB). The remaining findings, marked as new (N) in Table I, have not been reported before to our knowledge. For the L1, they are the four slices, the XOR set index, the tag–data asymmetry that causes cross-set evictions, and the SLRU policy. These findings also explain two observations of Jia et al. on Volta and Turing [22, 21]: the four L1 sets they report appear to be the four slices, and the random evictions they observe appear to be cross-set evictions. For the L2, they are the partition/FBP/slice hash with its 128-to-96 remap and the set-level coherence, whereas prior work observes the address interleaving between the two partitions and characterizes coherence at cache-line granularity [23, 33]. For the constant caches, they are the L0 shared by MOV and ULDC with its geometry and index, the GCC index, and the Tree-PLRU policy of the L0 and L1, whereas prior work identifies the L0 [18] and finds only that the L1 does not use LRU [22, 21]. These memory-system gaps also affect GPU simulators such as GPGPU-Sim [5], Accel-Sim [26, 25], gem5 and its GPU models [6, 20, 47], and MGPUSim [50], and recent work revisits their hardware assumptions [19, 18]. However, existing simulators lack hardware-faithful slice routing, set indexing, replacement, and cross-partition coherence. In this paper, we present GemAtlas, a systematic reverse engineering study of the memory hierarchy of modern NVIDIA GPUs. We develop a SASS-level microbenchmarking suite to recover undocumented microarchitectural behavior. We characterize the L1 data cache in depth (including sliced organization, XOR-based routing, tag/data asymmetry, and segmented replacement), reconstruct the L2 partition/slice/FBP hierarchy, recover address hash and remap logic, expose cache-set granularity cross-partition coherence and replacement behavior, and introduce an efficient hash-guided slice-constrained, eviction-set construction method for modern GPUs. We further characterize the constant-memory hierarchy, covering its fine-grained geometry and replacement policy. Finally, incorporating these findings into a cycle-level GPU simulator reduces the average MAPE over four GPUs from 34.04% to 23.98% for real-world LLM operators, from 36.33% to 20.61% for memory-sensitive workloads, and from 31.69% to 22.24% overall.
